## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library**, containing all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, compared carefully with one another and with several manuscript codices, most diligently corrected; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume and each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject treated below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority and weight in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately apparent to the reader which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in which passages of their works they have done so.

An exceptionally accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others if the following are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection—unique, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time brings together in our library six hundred fragments and short works previously scattered here and there, gathered from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.

**FIRST SERIES.** In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of complete courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# Pope Felix IV

[Col. 0009]

## Notice

*(From the Book of the Pontiffs.)*

[Col. 0009A]

[**Note: [Col. 0009A] Felix.**] Theodoric, the murderer of John, having rashly usurped for himself the right of choosing and nominating the bishop of the Apostolic See, after the matter had been debated during an interregnum of fifty-eight days, nominated Felix, a man highly esteemed in the Roman clergy, so that no opportunity might exist for resistance to his will. This nomination, and the approval of the nominee made by the entire clergy, took place on 24 July in the year of the Lord 526, in the ninth year of the Emperor Justin’s reign and the thirty-fourth year of King Theodoric’s reign in Italy.

But without delay God struck down Theodoric, the author of so great a crime, that savage, barbarous, and harsh tyrant, by a sudden vengeance sent from heaven, and after his swift and dreadful death consigned him forever to hell. Procopius says in Book I of *The Gothic War* that, when servants had set before him as he dined the cooked head of a fish of extraordinary size, it seemed to him to be the head of the recently murdered Symmachus, with its teeth fixed and protruding from the lower lip and its eyes staring grimly, furiously and bitterly threatening him. Terrified by this vision, he fell ill and died not long afterward.

Saint Gregory reports in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 30, that a certain solitary saw him, stripped of his belt and barefoot, between Pope John and the patrician Symmachus, whom he had killed, led away with his hands bound and thrown into Vulcan’s cauldron.

Athalaric, his grandson through his daughter, succeeded him in the kingdom of Italy. After exacting from the Romans an oath of loyalty, he requested by letter that his kingdom be secured through the prayers of the bishops. During his reign Saint Ephrem became bishop of the Church of Antioch.

Justin, weighed down by illness and old age, had administered the empire with the greatest equity and piety up to the ninth year. Concerned for the future welfare of the state, and with the agreement of the entire Senate, he appointed Justinian, his nephew through his sister, as successor to the empire. At the beginning of his reign Agapetus, a deacon of the Holy Roman Church, admonished him in writing how he ought to conduct himself in the administration of the empire.

After making peace and concord with Athalaric and the other nations, he confirmed the Catholic faith by edicts and enactments.

[Col. 0010A] As for ecclesiastical affairs, the laws he promulgated were published, at least in his name, by the bishop of Constantinople, so that they might receive greater observance; or, if he himself enacted any of them, he did so not because he was assuming the office of bishop, but rather so that he might restrain heretics who despised the canons by imperial authority.

[Col. 0010B] When, as a result of this treaty, the Goths became more arrogant, invaded the rights of the Churches, and dragged clergy everywhere before secular tribunals, Pope Felix, together with the Roman clergy, vehemently protested about these matters to the king himself. When he had heard them kindly and treated them humanely, he issued, at their request, an enactment by which he completely prohibited such wicked, unauthorized, and rashly presumed actions. The constitution itself is found in Cassiodorus, Book VIII, chapter 24.

Dionysius Exiguus, who was the first to begin counting the years from the birth of Christ and who gave the badly translated Greek canons a more elegant Latin form, began a paschal cycle in the second year of Felix, which is the year of Christ 527, and extended it through a cycle of ninety-five years. Marianus Scotus quotes a fragment of that cycle in his chronicles, under the consulship of Mavortius, in the fourth year of Felix’s pontificate [Binius is mistaken], which is the year of Christ 529.

The Emperor Justinian completed, confirmed, and published the code called *Justinian* after his name. In this matter he made particular use of the services of Tribonian, a pagan and extremely greedy man, with whom justice was for sale. Do not therefore be surprised if you find the impious emperors Zeno and Anastasius—erased from the catalogue of emperors and utterly condemned by the judgment of the pope, the Council of Constantinople, and Justin—mentioned in the code under the distinguished title of piety.

**Severus Binius.**

Felix was of Samnite nationality, the son of Castorius.

[**Note: [Col. 0010C] He occupied the see for four years.**] It is inferred from the beginning and end of his pontificate that he sat for four years, two months, and eighteen days.

He sat for four years, two months, and thirteen days (three years, two months, and thirteen days, from 24 July 527).

He lived during the times of King Theodoric and the Emperor Justinian, from the consulship of Maburtius [Mavortius] to the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, from the fourth day before the Ides of July to the fourth day before the Ides of October.

[**Note: [Col. 0010C] Justin. Manuscript Luc. 490.**]

He built the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian in the city of Rome, in the place called the Sacred Way, beside the temple of the city of Rome. During his time the basilica of the holy martyr Saturninus on the Salarian Way was consumed by fire; he rebuilt it from its foundations.

He was ordained peacefully and lived until the time of Athalaric. He held two ordinations in the city of Rome, during the months of February and March: fifty-five priests, four deacons, and twenty-nine bishops for various places.

He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on the fourth day before the Ides of October.

[**Note: [Col. 0010C]**] He died during the reign of King Athalaric, on 3 October, and was buried at the blessed Peter’s.

[**Note: [Col. 0010C] The episcopate ceased for three days.**] Three days intervened between Felix’s death and the election of Boniface II. In some places it is read that the see was vacant for one month and fifteen days; this should be understood of the period when, after the schism had been removed, Boniface was recognized by everyone as the legitimate pontiff.

**Severus Binius.**

The episcopate was vacant for three days.

[Col. 0011]

# Epistles and decrees of Pope Felix IV *(C, S)*

## First epistle, formerly III

### Pope Felix IV to Caesarius of Arles

**On not promoting laymen to the priesthood before testing them.**

[Col. 0011A]

Felix to his most beloved brother Caesarius.

I have read what has been established among your fraternity: that no one may be rashly promoted from a lay manner of life to the priestly office before being tested. A report has also reached us that some, after ordination, have returned to the ways of secular life. Although such presumption is wicked, neglect is even more dangerous. For whoever can resist an approaching evil but, concealing the matter, allows it to happen is himself judged the more responsible author of the evil deed.

Let no one therefore hope to escape by appealing to an ancient custom; for things begun unlawfully, if they are condemned afterward, cannot produce their proper fruits. For one who is trained through the degrees, if he reaches his appointed position without completing his instruction, fails under examination because he has not acquired firmness. Nor can anyone preserve an honor through fear if he has once attained its glory by labor. Empty praise, when bestowed on someone, harms him, nourishing him toward arrogance rather than urging him to the work of true virtue.

The chosen vessel writes to his own spiritual son Timothy, saying: “Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others” (1 Tim. 5). What does “do not lay hands too hastily” mean? It means that the dignity bestowed is bestowed so that it may endure unmoved. Before it is granted, it must be considered under prolonged deliberation.

Where is the teacher who does not know the beginnings of the elements? Where is the helmsman who has not demonstrated his service among sailors? He does not know what conduct is owed by teachers who have not bent their hearts to obedience; nor does he know how he ought to conduct himself in the house of God so as to become an example to those who come after.

The words of the apostolic admonition should be present in all clergy, and especially in those who are to be chosen for the priesthood: “He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside” (1 Tim. 3).

Therefore, with common agreement and under observance of the venerable canons, choose a priest for ordination, so that we may be concerned both for our own salvation and for the welfare of those who have been carefully admitted to this order.

May God keep you safe, dearest brother.

Given on the third day before the Nones of February,

[**Note: [Col. 0011D] After the consulship of Mavortius.**] in the year after the consulship of Mavortius, a most illustrious man (in the year of Christ 528). [Note: The published subscription reads “after the consulship of Mavortius, or of Boethius, a most illustrious man.”]

This false subscription long kept learned men in perplexity. They understood that, during the time of Felix III, to whom this letter was attributed because of the consulship of Boethius, the name of Caesarius could not fit, since he was not yet a bishop; while, conversely, during the time of Felix IV, to whom Caesarius’s episcopate would fit, the consulship of Boethius did not fit at all.

Now, however, with the true reading restored from the Arles manuscript, the difficulties have been resolved and the letter restored to its proper author, namely Felix IV. His second year fell in the year after the consulship of Mavortius, that is, in the year of Christ 528, when Caesarius was in the twenty-fifth year of his episcopate—or rather the twenty-ninth, since Pope Symmachus had already written to him from the year 502.

**Jacques Sirmond.**

Agnellus of Ravenna, a ninth-century writer, preserved in his *Pontifical of the Bishops of Ravenna*, published by the illustrious Bacchini and reprinted and collated with a manuscript by Muratori in *Italian Affairs*, volume II, part 1, under the life of Saint Ecclesius, bishop of Ravenna, a certain constitution of Pope Felix, issued on the occasion of a disagreement concerning the Church and the clergy under his jurisdiction. Here it is:

# Constitution of Felix IV concerning the Church of Ravenna

Felix [IV, Muratori], bishop of the city of Rome.

The concern of our predecessors for ecclesiastical peace and tranquility [Muratori: “constitution”] is worthy of praise, because the shepherd who watches over his flock and must restrain disputes either condemns or corrects them. As we walk along this same path, we ought to be seen as like them, since those whose place we hold by God’s mercy are the ones whose examples we ought to follow.

Through envy, such things have occurred among the priests of the Church of Ravenna as are known to have saddened the hearts of all Catholics [Muratori: “which”]: disputes, seditions, and corruptions that sought to break apart the whole of ecclesiastical discipline. These matters we again [lacuna], having the true fear of God before our eyes, so that we neither give license to unlawful transgressions nor cast aside [lacuna] the ordering by our constitution of what is just. This is according to Solomon’s saying: “Do not give a passage to water” [printed reading *dures*; Muratori: *dares*, “give”].

Therefore, having reviewed the articles submitted to us by our brother [omitted in Muratori] Ecclesius, by the priests, deacons, and clergy [Muratori: “clergy”], and by the notaries of the Church of Ravenna, in the presence of our brother and fellow priest Ecclesius and of the clergy listed below, we decree what we have seen to be consistent with reason: those whose life and conduct cannot be challenged by the authority of the sacred canons ought to undertake the office of the clergy.

As for clerics, only those willing and announced are to be admitted according to the rules of the holy Fathers. With regard to priests and deacons, we order that they be solemnly promoted at the appointed times.

Concerning the Church of Ravenna and of Classis, let the ancient custom be preserved.

Let clergy or monks not seek the patronage of powerful persons in order to obtain an order or position to which they are not entitled; otherwise the bishop may appear either ungrateful when he does not comply or unjust when he does.

The fourth part of the patrimony of the Church of Ravenna—that is, three thousand solidi—shall be completed through the customary distributions to all the clergy, or to those to whom it is customary to distribute them. If, however, by the will of our Lord, anything should increase from rents or inheritances, then, with the same Lord’s help, it shall also be added to the fourth part [variant: shall be beneficial to it], provided that, when written statements have been arranged, what is distributed to each person cannot remain hidden. [Lacuna]

According to merits and according to positions, since God establishes all things according to justice and measure, so that each person, except in the necessity of illness or for a legitimate reason concerning the altar, may vigilantly observe everything belonging to his office.

We decree that the revenues of estates [printed reading *redditus*; Muratori: *excepta*, “excepted”] and their increases ought to benefit the bishop, for household expenses, gifts offered by various persons, and banquets which it is necessary to provide for them, whether on account of his position, merit, or the reception of visitors.

Let no one from the clergy attempt to form any conspiracy or secret gathering—something that cannot remain unpunished even among lay people in the Church of God.

For just as we wish that heavenly mercy would not permit such a thing to be admitted, so, if anyone attempts it, let him experience the authority of the canons and ecclesiastical discipline, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Correct those who offend in the presence of all, so that the rest may have fear.”

Let the good deserve praise, those who keep watch in God’s works. Let those who seem by their obedience to adorn their purpose experience the affection of their own priest. Let those who do not cease from works pleasing to God, together with their service, glory in the love of their pontiff, as the divine utterances say: “The laborer is worthy of his wages.”

As for the Church’s patrimony, according to the judgment of their bishop [lacuna], let persons chosen from the clergy be sent, with the assistance which the bishop has assigned for information, under suitable surety, once their fidelity and diligence have been proven. Thus the nourishment of the poor will not suffer fraud, the amount of the Church’s patrimony cannot remain hidden, and every cleric, under fear of God and of his own priest, will faithfully render an account of what has been entrusted to him.

There is one matter that must be utterly condemned with a devout resolve; we ought neither to have mentioned it nor to have set it out in words. It has come to our attention that some of the clergy attend spectacles. This is so cruel a matter that it disturbs the souls of Catholics through its very abhorrence, so that it sees gathering contrary to the commandments at spectacles those whom it has heard reciting the divine utterances in the house of God. In these things discipline is brought to shame and divine precepts are trampled underfoot.

Therefore the bishop ought also to be concerned about this matter, so that, if they do not attend, they may not attend in the future; and, if they do attend, they may be corrected according to ecclesiastical discipline.

If anyone from the clergy occupies urban or rural estates belonging to the Church, we decree that these be assigned to them by written instruments drawn up according to a fair assessment of the rent. The reason is that they themselves may retain what they are accustomed to receive by their own customary methods, and contribute what remains toward ecclesiastical benefits.

With regard to urban or rural estates and other movable property left by the faithful by name to various basilicas for the sake of their souls, let the ancient custom be preserved.

The notaries, according to the order of the register—*primicerius*, *secundicerius*, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh—shall, at their own risk, receive ecclesiastical documents in the presence of priests and deacons, under an inventory of trustworthy briefs, so that whenever the matter requires it they may faithfully produce, hand over, and receive them.

We order them to carry out everything under the command and arrangement of their bishop. All ecclesiastical documents must be recorded for this reason: so that, in no way, documents once received may perish, or, when they are needed, be unable to be produced for ecclesiastical uses.

The notaries who are observant and energetic in their office shall receive, without diminution, the benefits assigned to them or to their predecessors from ancient times.

They too, as reason and antiquity require, shall hand over the documents and safeguards of the entire ecclesiastical patrimony, subscribed by the bishop’s own hand, to those concerned.

But where ecclesiastical estates, urban or rural, have been given to people living a secular life who have no need connected with household property, the bishop, through such clerics as he commands, shall restore them to the ownership of the Church; and thereafter no one shall presume to give them away except for the reason stated above.

Mastalo, archdeacon of the Church of Ravenna, shall receive without diminution the benefits assigned to him [Muratori: “to that position”] according to ancient custom, just as it is clear that those who held it before him obtained them.

The monasteries of men and of women devoted to God shall be organized by the bishop, so that order, justice, peace, and discipline may be preserved for all.

The responsibility of our office requires us not to keep these matters silent [Muratori: “to be kept silent”]; it imposes upon our brother Ecclesius the duty of guarding them, because peace is generated when justice is preserved together with the canons.

From justice proceeds charity, through which we see God and by whose grace we are able to keep these commands.

Therefore it is fitting that we be negligent in nothing, but watchful in all things, so that we may return to him, the giver of all good, the talent entrusted to us with an increase [Muratori: *augmento*] of good works.

We have reviewed this.

**Coelius.**

I, Felix, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, have subscribed this constitution between the parties.

# Admonition concerning the following epistle

As I was examining that ancient epitome of the canons which I found in the very old Lucerne manuscript, nine hundred years old, I encountered a synopsis of a certain epistle of Felix to the Sicilian bishops, under which heading eight canons are placed.

Since I recognized in these canons some matters relating to the reception into the Church of Arians who were coming to repentance, others that cut down the heresy of the Pelagians or Semipelagians, and finally certain matters introduced against the Manichaean doctrine that evil was produced by God, I judged that all these could agree only with Felix IV.

First, the Pelagian heresy cannot in any way be associated with Felix II, since it began to become known and to be condemned long after Felix II’s death. Once that pontiff is excluded, Felix III and Felix IV remain.

The reason for removing this epitome from the time of Felix III is that nowhere do we read that the Manichaeans disturbed the Church during his time. On the other hand, everything agrees with Felix IV. We learn from canon 5 of the Council of Vaison, held in the year 529—that is, under Felix IV—that Arians were troubling Africa and Italy.

The matter of the Manichaeans is clear from the anathemas of Prosper, converted from Manichaeism around this time, which are to be read in Labbe, volume V, page 800 of the Venetian edition.

Finally, the doctrine of the Semipelagians was attacked by the Second Council of Orange, held in that same year, 529.

With these observations made in advance, the epitome is now to be brought forward. I present it as it stands in the manuscript, with numerical marks attached to each canon. These marks, since they preserve not a continuous series of numbers but an interrupted order, plainly show that the items given here were excerpted from some larger collection.

# From Felix’s epistle to the Sicilian bishops

## XVII

[**Note: [Col. 0016B] “The Arians,” etc.**] Thus Pope Siricius says to Himericus, chapter 1.

Let Arians who come to the Catholic faith be received by the laying on of hands.

## XVIII

[**Note: [Col. 0016B] “Every Sunday,” etc.**] Concerning communion on feast days, which had become customary to receive on those days, see the Council of Mérida, held in 666, canon 14.

It is good to receive communion every Sunday, if one abstains from sin.

## XXIV

[**Note: [Col. 0016B] “Without God’s invitation.”**] See the Second Council of Orange, canon 19.

No one comes to salvation without God’s invitation.

## XXVII

[**Note: [Col. 0016C] “That evil was not made by God.”**] See the anathemas signed by Prosper the Manichaean, chapters 1 and 2.

Evil was not made by God.

## XXX

[**Note: [Col. 0016C] “Marriages are good; continence is better.”**] See Augustine’s entire book *On the Good of Marriage*.

[**Note: [Col. 0015C]**] The Ballerini brothers, having found this same excerpt from Felix’s epistle to the Sicilians in the Verona manuscript 59, observe that they compared the statements placed under this heading with the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, published in the appendix to volume VIII of Saint Augustine. From the numbers and the subject matter itself they discovered that these statements designate nothing other than that same book on dogmas. They judge that Felix’s name was prefixed because, in the manuscript from which this abridger made his excerpt, Felix III’s epistle to the Sicilian bishop was immediately followed by it. See Ballerini, *Works of Saint Leo*, volume III, page 261; Mansi.]

Marriages are good.

## XXXI

Continence is better.

# Appendix to the epistles of Felix IV

## Epistle II

### Pope Felix IV to all bishops

*(This epistle and the following one suffer from the defect of νόθεια, that is, spuriousness.)*

[Col. 0015D]

1. That the celebration of Mass ought not to take place anywhere except in places dedicated to God, unless grave necessity compels it.

2. What ought to be done concerning the doubtfulness of the consecration of churches.

To our most beloved brothers, all the bishops established throughout the various provinces: Bishop Felix sends greeting in the Lord.

[Col. 0016D] By the great gift of God’s mercy, the joys of the whole Catholic Church have been multiplied, since the condition of the Churches flourishes in the order established by the successors of the apostles. But when we recognize that this order is being disturbed by the cunning of the ancient enemy, we are saddened by no small grief.

For this reason, brothers, we exhort, admonish, and earnestly urge you never to depart from the path of apostolic instruction, nor to dissent from the head, but to hold without any hesitation the faith and order established by the apostles and apostolic men.

For if the pillars of some great house should collapse, the house itself afterward could not stand. So also you, who are the pillars of the Church: if you begin to be shaken, the holy Church governed through you wastes away and falls.

These things that I say are greatly to be feared, to be weighed with the utmost moderation, and guarded against lest they occur. For Truth itself says: “You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be salted?” (Matt. 5).

Therefore, beloved, I admonish you because I am your debtor and love you very much. When I hear good things about you, I am exceedingly glad; conversely, when I hear evil things, I am exceedingly troubled.

Although I am separated from you by long distances of land and sea, I am nevertheless entirely joined to you in heart.

[Col. 0017B] I trust in every way that the same is true of your blessedness toward me, because, when you in turn love me, you are not far from me.

Therefore we give thanks to that mustard seed (Luke 14; Matt. 13), which, from the form of a small and despised seed, rises and spreads its branches from the same root, extending everywhere, so that the birds of heaven [variant: all of them] may nest in them.

Let thanks also be given to that leaven which mixed the whole mass of the human race into unity through three measures of flour.

And thanks to the small stone cut from the mountain without hands, which occupied the entire face of the earth and extended itself everywhere for this purpose: that, once the whole human race had been brought into unity, the entire body of the Church might be perfected, and that this partial distinction of members might contribute to the welfare of the whole structure.

[Col. 0017C] Thus we too are not far from you, because in the One who is everywhere we are one (John 20).

Let us therefore give thanks to him, because, having abolished enmities in his flesh, he made one flock and one sheepfold throughout the whole world under one shepherd. Let us always remember what the eminent preacher admonishes us, saying: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4).

I have gratefully received the writings of your holiness which you sent to the Apostolic See concerning certain questions, as to the head, so that you might receive answers from the place from which the whole Church received the beginning of its religion; and I have taken care to reply to you briefly.

## I. On the Consecration of Churches and the Celebration of Masses

It is clear to all who know the precepts of the New and Old Testament that the consecration of churches and the celebration of Mass ought not to take place anywhere except in places consecrated to the Lord, unless there is great necessity. We read that Moses made and consecrated the tabernacle at the Lord’s command, together with its table, altar, and the other vessels and utensils required for divine worship (Num. VII). We know that he consecrated these not only by divine commands and prayers, but also, at the Lord’s command, by anointing them with holy oil.

How these things were done, and how the sacred objects themselves were handled, carried, erected, and taken down only by priests anointed with sacred unction and consecrated to the Lord with holy vestments, and by Levites, is found in the very institutions written through Moses, at the Lord’s command, in the law of the Lord.

How, then, David, the most devout of kings, enlarged the worship of God and wished to build the temple of the Lord, but was prevented on account of the great quantity of blood which he had shed; how he himself collected the funds, and how Solomon his son completed, with God’s command and assistance, what David had wished to do, and consecrated the temple, together with the altar and the other things needed to provide for divine worship, is read among other things in the Book of Kings as follows:

> “Building,” says Solomon to the Lord, “I have built a dwelling for you, your most strong [most firm; so also chapter Just.] seat forever” (III Kings VIII).  
> 
> Then the king turned his face and blessed the whole assembly of Israel. For the whole assembly of Israel was standing, and he said:
> 
> “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who spoke with his mouth to David my father, and with his hands has brought it to completion, saying: ‘From the day when I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I did not choose a city from all the tribes of Israel in which a house should be built and my name should be there; but I chose David to be over my people Israel.’  
> 
> “David my father wished to build a house for the name of the Lord, the God of Israel, and the Lord said to David my father: ‘Because you considered in your heart building a house for my name, you have done well in having this very thing in mind. Nevertheless, you shall not build the house; rather, your son, who shall come forth from your loins, shall build the house for my name.’  
> 
> “The Lord confirmed the word which he had spoken. I took David my father’s place and sat upon the throne of Israel, as the Lord had spoken, and I built a house for the name of the Lord, the God of Israel. I appointed there a place for the ark, in which is the covenant of the Lord that he made with our fathers when they came out of the land of Egypt.”
> 
> Solomon then stood before the altar of the Lord in the sight of the assembly of Israel, spread out his hands toward heaven, and said:
> 
> “Lord God of Israel, there is none like you in heaven above or on earth below, who keeps covenant and mercy with your servants who walk before you with all their heart. You have kept for your servant David my father what you spoke to him. You spoke with your mouth and fulfilled it with your hands, as this day proves.  
> 
> “Now therefore, Lord God of Israel, preserve for your servant David my father what you spoke to him, saying: ‘There shall not fail you a man before me to sit upon the throne of Israel, provided only that your sons guard their way, so that they walk before me as you have walked in my sight.’  
> 
> “And now, God of Israel, let your words be confirmed which you spoke to David your servant, my father. Is it truly to be thought that God dwells upon earth? If heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house which I have built! But look upon the prayer of your servant and upon his supplication, Lord my God. Hear, Lord, the hymn and the prayer which your servant prays before you today: that your eyes may be open over this house night and day, over the house of which you said, ‘My name shall be there,’ so that you may hear the prayer which your servant prays to you in this place; that you may hear the supplication of your servant and of your people Israel, whatever they pray for in this place, and that you may hear in the place of your dwelling, in heaven; and when you have heard, you will be merciful.
> 
> “If a man sins against his neighbor, and some oath is imposed upon him by which he is bound, and he comes on account of the oath before your altar in your house, you will hear in heaven, act, and judge your servants, condemning the wicked and bringing his conduct back upon his own head, while justifying the just and repaying him according to his righteousness.
> 
> “If your people Israel flee from their enemies (for they will sin against you), and, repenting and confessing your name, come and pray and supplicate you in this house, hear in heaven, forgive the sin of your people Israel, and bring them back to the land which you gave to their fathers.
> 
> “If heaven is closed and there is no rain because of their sin, and they pray in this place, repent before your name, and turn from their sins because of their affliction, hear them in heaven, forgive the sins of your servants and of your people Israel, show them the good way in which they should walk, and give rain upon the land which you gave to your people as a possession.
> 
> “If famine arises in the land, or pestilence, or corrupt air, or blight, or locust, or mildew, and their enemy afflicts them by besieging their gates—whatever plague, whatever sickness, and every vow and imprecation that befalls any person among your people Israel—when anyone recognizes the plague of his heart and spreads out his hands in this house, then you will hear in heaven, in the place of your dwelling, and be reconciled; and you will act, giving to each according to all his ways, as you see his heart—for you alone know the hearts of all the children of men—so that they may fear you all the days that they live upon the face of the land which you gave to our fathers.
> 
> “Moreover, when a foreigner who is not of your people Israel comes from a distant land for the sake of your name—for your great name, your strong hand, and your outstretched arm will be heard of everywhere—and when he comes and prays in this place, you will hear in heaven, in the firmament of your dwelling, and do everything for which the foreigner calls upon you, so that all the peoples of the earth may learn to fear your name, as does your people Israel, and may know that your name has been invoked over this house which I have built.
> 
> “If your people go out to war against their enemies, by whatever way you send them, and they pray to you toward the way of the city which you have chosen and toward the house which I have built for your name, you will hear their prayer and supplication in heaven and execute their judgment.
> 
> “But if they sin against you—for there is no one who does not sin—and, being angry, you deliver them to their enemies, and they are led captive to the land of their enemies, whether far or near, and in the land of their captivity they repent in their heart and, having turned, supplicate you in their captivity, saying, ‘We have sinned, we have acted wickedly, we have behaved impiously,’ and they return to you with all their heart and all their soul in the land of their enemies to which they were led captive, and pray to you toward the direction of their land which you gave to their fathers, and of the city which you chose, and of the temple which I built for your name: hear their prayer and supplication in heaven, in the firmament of your throne, execute their judgment, and be merciful to your people who have sinned against you and all their iniquities by which they have transgressed against you. Grant them mercy before those who have taken them captive, so that they may have compassion on them.
> 
> “For they are your people and your inheritance, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, from the midst of an iron furnace, so that your eyes may be open to the supplication of your servant and of your people Israel, and so that you may hear them in everything for which they call upon you. For you separated them as an inheritance from all the peoples of the earth, as you spoke through Moses your servant when you brought our fathers out of the land of Egypt [Egypt—variant], Lord God.”
> 
> When Solomon had finished praying to the Lord this entire prayer and supplication, he rose from before the altar of the Lord. For he had fixed both knees upon the ground and had spread out his hands toward heaven. Then he stood and blessed the whole assembly of Israel, saying in a loud voice:
> 
> “Blessed is the Lord, who has given rest to his people Israel according to all that he spoke; not one word has failed of all [of all the good things] that he spoke through Moses his servant. May the Lord our God be with us as he was with our fathers, neither abandoning nor casting us away. May he incline our hearts to himself, so that we may walk in all his ways and keep his commandments, ceremonies, and judgments, whatever he commanded our fathers. May these words of mine, with which I have supplicated before the Lord, draw near to the Lord our God day and night, so that he may execute judgment for his servant and for his people Israel day by day, and so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord himself is God, and that there is no other besides him.  
> 
> “May our heart also be perfect with the Lord our God, so that we may walk in his statutes and keep his commandments, as also at this day.”
> 
> Then the king and all Israel with him sacrificed victims before the Lord. Solomon slaughtered as peace offerings the sacrifices which he offered to the Lord: twenty-two thousand oxen and one hundred twenty thousand sheep. Thus the king and the sons of Israel dedicated the temple of the Lord.
> 
> On that day the king sanctified the middle of the court which was before the house of the Lord. For he made there a burnt offering, a sacrifice, and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar which stood before the Lord was too small and could not contain the burnt offering, the sacrifice, and the fat of the peace offerings.
> 
> At that time Solomon held a solemn festival, and all Israel with him—a very great multitude—from the entrance of Hamath to the Brook of Egypt before the Lord our God, for seven days and seven days, that is, fourteen days; and on the eighth day he dismissed the people.

The Jews, therefore, had the places in which they sacrificed to the Lord consecrated by divine supplications [variant: they consecrated them by supplications], and they offered gifts to the Lord nowhere except in places dedicated to God. If the Jews, who served the shadow of the law, did these things, how much more ought we, to whom the truth has been revealed [Burchard adds: “and grace and truth were given through Jesus”; Mansi], build temples to the Lord and adorn them as best we can, and devoutly and solemnly consecrate them, together with their altars, vessels, vestments, and the other utensils needed to complete divine worship, by divine prayers and holy anointings. We ought to celebrate Masses and offer sacrifices to the Lord nowhere except in places consecrated to the Lord by bishops, not by chorepiscopi, who have often been forbidden to do so, unless, as stated above, the greatest necessity demands it.

If the greatest necessity compels this, it must not be done in houses, since the sacred canons forbid sacrifices to be offered in houses, but in tents appointed by bishops through divine prayers, upon tables consecrated to the Lord and anointed with sacred unction by bishops. It must be done for the greatest necessity, as stipulated above, and not according to anyone’s preference or laziness.

**[Statute.]** It is therefore better not to sing Mass [Council of Paris, book I, chapter 47; and Capitularies VII, 334], or not to hear it [St. Gregory, letter 18, book III], than to do so in places where it ought not to be done—unless, as has often been said, the greatest necessity happens to arise, since necessity has no law.

Hence it is written:

> “See that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see, but in the place which the Lord your God has chosen” (Deut. X).

And in Exodus we read:

> “You have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven. You shall not make gods of silver, nor shall you make gods of gold for yourselves. You shall make an altar of earth for me, and upon it you shall offer your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen, in every place in which the memory of my name shall be” (Exod. XX).

And just as no priests except those consecrated to the Lord ought to sing Masses or offer sacrifices upon the altar, so it is not permitted to sing Masses or offer sacrifices anywhere except in the aforesaid places consecrated to the Lord.

But if, as is read in chapter 26 of the Council of Laodicea [according to the version of Dionysius Exiguus], those who have not been ordained by bishops cannot perform exorcisms either in churches or in houses [Burchard inserts “if”], then, much more, ministries of a higher grade may not be performed, nor sacrifices offered, except by those who have been consecrated to the grades whose offices they are to exercise.

That offerings ought not to be made in houses, as was briefly stated above, is also found prohibited in chapter 58 of the same council [chapter 59 in the variant], as follows:

> “It is not fitting for offerings to be celebrated in houses by bishops and presbyters.”

The solemn celebrations of the dedications of churches and of priests ought, however, to be solemnly celebrated every year, since the Lord himself has given an example. To provide a model for all in celebrating the feast of the dedication of the temple, he came with the other people to celebrate that same festival, as it is written:

> “The feast of the Dedication took place in Jerusalem, and it was winter; and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s portico” (John X).

That the Dedication is to be celebrated for eight days, you will find in the Book of Kings (III Kings VIII), after the dedication of the temple had been completed [variant: “you (plural) will find”].

## II. On the Consecration of Churches

Whenever there is doubt concerning the consecration of churches, and there is neither a certain document nor reliable witnesses by whom their consecration is known, know without any doubt that they are to be consecrated, lest such hesitation cause deterioration; for what is not known to have been done is not shown to have been repeated (St. Leo, letter 92, chapter 15).

Brothers, these testimonies of Scripture, confirmed by apostolic authority, should suffice as a brief answer to your inquiries. Nevertheless, you must take care, and preach to everyone, that unlawful things not be done, that the Lord’s commands be preserved, and that they be faithfully carried out.

We ask you, brothers—so that we may repeat the words of the Apostle:

> “Correct the restless, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient toward all. See that no one repays evil for evil to anyone; but always pursue what is good toward one another and toward all. Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things. For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for all of you. Do not extinguish the Spirit; do not despise prophecies. Test everything; hold fast to what is good. Abstain from every form of evil. May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, so that your spirit, soul, and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (II Thess. 5).

Given on the Kalends of March, during the consulship of the most illustrious men Lampadius and Orestes (in the year of Christ 530).

## EPISTLE III (FORMERLY II). TO SABINA

### [Col. 0022B]

He praises in her the zeal and devotion she shows toward the Church, and that she places the honors of her lineage and vain pomp below religion.

The greatness of your devotion, as a singular member of the Church, and the reverence with which we esteem it, are sufficiently manifest to everyone. For, although you stand at the very summit of nobility, you devote yourself to the Church’s much nobler calling; with an even more joyful recognition of Christ you obey his commands; and you take greater delight in faith than you boast of the splendor of so great a lineage.

It is the highest virtue [a virtue of the highest order] to have conquered the glory of the flesh, and it is a great grace [a grace of great magnitude] to have surpassed nobility by your character, my deservedly illustrious daughter. Therefore, dearest daughter, being certain that whatever spans this life contains, strive to illumine them with eternal and divine duties, so that he who made you distinguished may render you more glorious to himself throughout the ages.

Therefore we urge your affection not to delay in always completing the good which you have begun, for it is not the beginning but the end that is praised. We urge you to love and examine wisdom, so that you may arrange and judge rationally and wisely the things entrusted to you, as the Lord says through the prophet: “Be instructed, you who judge the earth.”

Therefore fear the Lord, keep his commandments, and love him with all your inward being, and your neighbor as yourself. The Most High God created wisdom in the Holy Spirit, saw it, numbered it, measured it, and poured it out over all his works; and according to his gift he bestowed it upon all flesh that loves him.

The fear of the Lord is glory, boasting, and a crown of exultation. The fear of the Lord will delight the heart and give gladness and joy for length of days. It will go well with the one who fears the Lord at the end, and he will be blessed on the day of his death.

The love of God is honorable wisdom; and those to whom it appears in vision love it when they behold it and recognize its great works. The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; it was conceived together with the faithful in the womb, it walks with chosen women, and it is recognized among the just and faithful.

The fear of the Lord is religious devotion to knowledge. Religious devotion will guard and justify the heart; it will give delight and joy. It will go well with the one who fears the Lord, and he will be blessed in the days of his completion.

The fullness of wisdom is to fear the Lord, and the fullness of wisdom comes from its fruits. It will fill his entire house through the generations and his storehouses with its treasures. The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, filling one with peace and the fruit of salvation; and he saw it and numbered it, though both are gifts of God.

Wisdom will distribute knowledge and understanding of prudence, and it exalts the glory of those who possess it. The root of wisdom is to fear the Lord, and its branches endure for a long time. In the treasures of wisdom are understanding and religious devotion to knowledge; but wisdom is an abomination to sinners.

The fear of the Lord drives out sin, for the one without fear cannot be justified. The anger of his indignation is his overthrow. The patient person will endure until the appointed time, and afterward there will be a return of joy.

Good sense will conceal his words for a time, and the lips of many will recount his understanding. In the treasures of wisdom is the indication of discipline; but for the sinner, the worship of God is an abomination.

My son, if you desire wisdom, preserve righteousness, and God will give it to you. For wisdom and discipline are the fear of the Lord; and what is pleasing to him is faith and gentleness, and it will fill his treasures.

Do not be obstinate or incredulous toward the fear of the Lord, and do not approach him with a divided heart. Do not be a hypocrite before men, and do not stumble by your lips. Pay attention to these matters, lest you fall, place a stumbling block before your soul, bring dishonor upon yourself, and God reveal your secrets.

Fight always for faith, justice, and the salvation of your soul; and act courageously for the help of your brothers, so that you may receive your reward from the Lord.

For it is written (Ecclus. IV):

> “My son, preserve the time, and avoid evil. For the sake of your soul, do not be ashamed to speak the truth.”

There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings grace and glory. Do not show partiality against your own person, nor speak falsehood against your own soul. Do not show deference to your neighbor when you stumble, nor hold back your word at a time of salvation. Do not hide your wisdom in its beauty.

For wisdom is recognized in the tongue, and sense, knowledge, and instruction are recognized in words of truth [variant: “in the word of the sensible person”], while strength is recognized in works of righteousness. Do not in any way contradict the truth, and be ashamed of the falsehood of your ignorance.

Do not be ashamed to confess your sins, and do not subject yourself to every person because of sin. Do not resist the face of the powerful, nor strive against the force of a river. Fight for justice for your soul, and contend for justice even unto death, and God will conquer your enemies on your behalf.

Do not be hasty with your tongue, nor useless and slack in your actions. Do not be like a lion in your house, overturning your household and oppressing those subject to you. Let your hand not be stretched out to receive while being closed for giving.

Supported by these authorities of Scripture, stand upright always and do not turn away from the way of truth, so that you may acquire God’s grace and enjoy the friendship of good people. Then your will [variant: mind] will more easily escape the love of this world, the more it is driven onward as it is called.

For we desire to see you while you are present, and in your absence we wish at least to converse with you by letter. Therefore we also desire that blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, may happily bring you to his threshold, so that by the grace of almighty God we may be deemed worthy to enjoy your presence.

[Note: Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November.]

This monthly chronology is erroneous (indeed, the entire epistle is fictitious). For by this month Boniface had already been made pontiff, as is clear above. [Severus Binius.]

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November [at the end of October in the year 530 Boniface, not Felix, was seated at Rome], during the consulship of the most illustrious men Lampadius and Orestes.

## AT THE SAME TIME

[Note: That is, 526–530.]

### PROSPER, CONVERTED FROM MANICHAEISM

### PROSPER’S ANATHEMAS AND PROFESSION OF THE CATHOLIC FAITH

(C, S)*

## CHAPTERS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE WHICH THOSE SUSPECTED OF BEING MANICHAEANS ARE TO READ ALOUD PUBLICLY AND SIGN WITH THEIR OWN HAND

### I

If anyone believes that there are two uncreated natures existing from different principles, one good, which is God, and the other evil, which God did not create, opposed to one another, let him be anathema.

[The Gervasian manuscript reads: “having its own princes and its own evils, which God did not create”; let him be anathema.]

### II

If anyone believes that the two natures waged war against each other, and concludes that a part of God’s nature was mixed in that war with the princes of darkness and with all peoples belonging to the evil nature, and was held bound, entangled, oppressed, and defiled by them—thereby also making it a belief that God’s nature is changeable and capable of defilement—let him be anathema.

### III

If anyone believes that a part of God, held bound and defiled, is kept in demons, in all animals, and in every kind of fruit (fructuum) [variant: shrub, fruticum], and is released and purified through the food of the Manichaean Elect, so that it is believed that God’s polluted part is held in cucumbers, melons, radishes, leeks, and every kind of most worthless little herb [variant: herbs], and that it is aided when these are eaten by the Manichaean Elect, let him be anathema.

### IV

If anyone believes that the first human being, who was called Adam, was not made by God but begotten by the princes of darkness, so that the part of God held captive in their members might be held in him more abundantly and plentifully, let him be anathema.

### V

If anyone believes that the human being was created in this manner: that male and female princes of darkness had intercourse, gave their offspring to the greater prince of darkness, and that he ate them all and had intercourse with his consort, and thus begot from her the one whom they blasphemously call Atlas, the father of Adam, binding in him the great part of God which had been bound in all the offspring of the princes of darkness whom they had given him to eat, let him be anathema.

### VI

If anyone believes that the princes of darkness are bound in heaven like a sphere, containing within themselves, bound in confinement and anguish, the vital substance—that is, the part of God—and that it is now released from their members when the blessed Father, who possesses luminous ships, dwellings and habitations, namely the sun and the moon, transforms his powers into beautiful women whom he sets before the male princes of darkness as objects of desire, and into beautiful men whom he sets before the female princes of darkness as objects of desire, so that through that desire the vital substance—that is, the part of God—may be released from them and, freed from their members, purified, let him be anathema.

### VII

If anyone believes that the part of God which could not be freed and purified from its mixture [variant: commixture] with the race of darkness is condemned and eternally fixed [variant: afflicted] in a horrible globe, in which globe the race of darkness is enclosed, let him be anathema.

### VIII

If anyone believes that the law given through Moses was not given by the good and true God, and [variant: nor] that the prophets who were among the people of Israel and are found in the canon of the divine Scriptures received by the Catholic Church spoke by the Spirit of the good and true God, let him be anathema.

### IX

If anyone believes that the Son of God, Jesus Christ, did not possess true flesh, was not born from the seed of David of the virgin Mary, did not possess a true body, did not truly suffer death in the flesh, and did not rise from the dead, but was only spirit [without flesh], and that he therefore wished to appear in the flesh in such a way that flesh which did not exist would be thought to exist—and by this contradicts the Gospel, where the Lord himself says, “See my hands and my feet; touch and see, for a spirit does not have bones and flesh, as you see me have” (Luke XXIV). Therefore, whoever thus confesses Christ as true God yet denies that he is also complete man, let him be anathema.

### X

Whoever does not immediately believe that the coming of the Spirit Paraclete, whom the Lord promises in the Gospel would come upon the apostles after the Lord’s ascension, on the day of Pentecost, was fulfilled, but believes that he came many years later in Manes or in his disciple Adimantus, let him be anathema.

### XI

[Note: The following articles are not found in the Gervasian manuscript, except articles 18 and 19; nor are they found in the penultimate appendix to volume X of the complete works of Saint Augustine.]

Whoever denies that this flesh which we carry, that is, human bodies, will rise again, let him be anathema.

### XII

If anyone believes that human souls are transferred again into other bodies or animals, let him be anathema.

### XIII

Whoever says that the sun and moon are heavenly ships for transferring souls or the substance of God, and attributes to them, or to this visible light, some element of divinity, rather than believing that they were created like the rest of creation for human service by the Lord of heaven and earth, let him be anathema.

### XIV

If anyone believes that all the flesh of quadrupeds, serpents, flying creatures, and aquatic creatures, or of everything that exists in the world, was not created by the true God but by the princes of darkness, let him be anathema.

### XV

If anyone, instead of detesting the Manichaean creed or prayer, wishes to venerate it, remember it, or utter it with his mouth, let him be anathema.

### XVI

If anyone believes that human souls are from the substance of God, while human bodies were either made or are being made by the prince of darkness, let him be anathema.

### XVII

If anyone believes that the devil was not made by God as a good angel and, having fallen through pride by his own will, became the devil, and asserts that he was not created by God among the other angels but was always coeternal with God, let him be anathema.

### XVIII

If anyone believes that Manes, or Manichaeus, who preached all the things written above that are worthy of anathema and condemnation, possessed the Holy Spirit Paraclete, although the Spirit of truth could not have taught all those things, but rather the spirit of falsehood, let him be anathema.

### XIX

Anathema also to Manes himself, or Manichaeus, who taught and wrote all the impieties mentioned above, along with other sacrilegious and condemnable fables, and attempted to persuade wretched people to believe them, paying heed to seducing spirits, doctrines of demons, and lying speakers.

### XX

Anathema to Adimantus and to all his disciples and followers; and, as has already been said, whoever believes that the Spirit Paraclete came upon him, let him be anathema.

### XXI

Anathema also to all the authors of the aforesaid perversity, to their doctrine or law, to all their secrets, to their prayers and sacrileges contrary to the Catholic faith, and to all their writings which are held outside the canon of the Church and which the right faith does not accept.

## ABJURATION AND PROFESSION OF PROSPER

In the name of Christ, I, Prosper, have reread this document of the anathema of the Manichaeans; and, pronouncing anathema upon all the errors written above, I have signed it with my own hand. Having rejected all their impieties, I have pronounced, and do pronounce, anathema upon their doctrines and traditions with the fullest faith. I promise and undertake, under divine witness, that I believe and follow in all things whatever the Catholic Church confesses.

Recorded on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, during the consulship of Olybrius the Younger, a most illustrious man (in the year of Christ 526).

## NOTE OF JACQUES SIRMOND, S.J.

In the manuscript of the Church of Lyons, which supplied these chapters to us, they are appended to the Council of Carpentoractum; but the order of the consuls requires that they precede it. For Olybrius held the consulship in the year of Christ 526, and Mavortius in the following year.

These materials are, moreover, very similar to the following, except that they contain fewer items, which are found in Saint Augustine, volume X, in the appendix under this title: “The Memorandum of Blessed Augustine addressed to the Church,” [intended for the whole Church], concerning the precautions under which Manichaeans are to be received if they are converted.

## OBSERVATION OF PHILIPPE LABBE, S.J.

In an old manuscript kept in the library of the Gervasian College in Paris, said to have been the book of the priory of Saint Salvius, bishop and martyr, at Valentiana in the march of France, written in the time of Prior Hugh, the following items immediately follow Saint Augustine’s book *On Heresies to Quodvultdeus the Bishop*. They contribute clarification to the preceding work.

## ALSO, AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF THE CATHOLIC CHURCH

I have already anathematized Manichaeus, his doctrine, and the spirit which through him spoke such execrable blasphemies, because it was a seducing spirit, not of truth but of wicked error. And now I anathematize the aforesaid Manichaeus and the spirit of his error.

I, Felix, who had believed Manichaeus, now anathematize him, his doctrine, and the seducing spirit which was in him. That spirit said that God the Father had mixed his nature with the race of darkness, and that he would disgracefully free it by transforming his powers into women against male demons, so that afterward he might fix the remnants of his own part forever in the defilement of darkness. I anathematize all these and the other blasphemies of Manichaeus.

I, one of the converts from the Manichaeans, have written this, because if I depart before the proceedings are signed, I am to be regarded as though I had not anathematized Manichaeus.

Felix, converted from the Manichaeans, declared under God’s witness that he confessed everything truthfully. I know that there are Manichaean men and women in the Caesarean districts: Maria and Lampadia, the wife of Mercury the silversmith, with whom we also prayed together at the house of the Elect Eucharis; Caesaria and her daughter Lucilla; Candidus, who lives at Thipasa; Victorina; Hispana; Simplicianus, the father of Antoninus; and Paul and his sister, who were at Hippo. Through Maria and Lampadia I also learned that these women were Manichaeans. This alone I know. If anything else should be discovered which I know beyond what I have said, I myself confess that I am guilty.

## MEMORANDUM OF SAINT AUGUSTINE, BISHOP, TO A MANICHAEAN PRESBYTER

You are evading without cause, although it is plainly evident what sort of person you are. The brothers who spoke with you have informed me.

It is good that you do not fear death; but you ought to fear the death which you bring upon yourself by blaspheming such things about God. You understand that this visible death, which all people know, is the separation of the mind from the body; understanding that is not difficult. But when you add that, according to your doctrine, there is a separation of good from evil—if the mind is good and the body evil—then the one who mixed them is not good. You say that the good God mixed these things. Therefore he is either evil or he feared evil.

Why do you boast that you do not fear a human being, when you imagine for yourself a god of such a kind that he feared darkness and therefore mixed good and evil? Do not be lifted up in spirit, as you wrote, because we make you great by trying to prevent your poisons from spreading like a pestilence among human beings. The Apostle does not make those whom he calls dogs great when he says, “Beware of dogs”; nor did he make great those whose speech he said spread like cancer.

Therefore I warn you in the name of Christ: if you are ready to solve the question at which your predecessor Fortunatus failed, and for which he departed from here intending not to return until, after comparing arguments with his own people, he had found what he could answer against us, then debate with the brothers.

But if you are not prepared for this, leave here, and do not pervert or entangle the ways of the Lord, or infect weak souls with poisons, lest, with the help of the right hand of our Lord, you be put to shame in a manner you did not expect.

## MEMORANDUM OF SAINT AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF THE CATHOLIC CHURCH, ON HOW ONE SHOULD DEAL WITH MANICHAEANS WHO ARE CONVERTED AND REPENT OF THIS WICKED ERROR
When they have anathematized that same heresy of the Manichaeans according to the form written below, and each of them has presented a written statement of his confession and repentance, requesting a place among the catechumens or penitents in the church, then, if his statement [Note: [Col. 0027D] This word, entirely necessary, is absent from the printed editions.] pleases the bishop and he receives him, the bishop shall give him a letter bearing the date and the consul’s name, so that he may suffer no harassment on account of the preceding period, whether from the public laws or from ecclesiastical discipline. If after that date he should appear by any evidence to be a Manichaean, he shall experience the severity of justice that must be applied in such matters—that is, Christians shall abstain from his company, friendship, and every form of association with him, in accordance with apostolic discipline (authority). [Note: [Col. 0027D] The printed appendices to volume X of the works of Saint Augustine falsely read *potens* (“powerful”) for *petens* (“requesting”).]

Those who have received letters from the bishop shall be commended to devout Catholics living nearby or with them, whether clergy or laity, through whose care they may regularly attend the hearing of God’s word and by whose testimony they may become known. If they are catechumens, they should not readily be admitted to baptism; nor, if they have been admitted to the place of penitents, should they readily be admitted to reconciliation, unless the danger of death is pressing, or unless the bishops learn through the testimony of those to whom they have been commended that they have been tested for some considerable time.

[Col. 0028D] The form, therefore, according to which those who are corrected must anathematize this heresy, is as follows.

I. He who believes that there are two natures, etc.—these words were printed shortly before with certain omissions, as we briefly noted in the note to Article XI.

## FORM OF THE LETTER [Note: [Col. 0027D] The appendix to volume X, as published, erroneously reads [Col. 0028D] “concerning a certain bishop of that sect.” We have also removed from it the most serious errors, as you will gather from comparison.] THAT THE BISHOP GIVES TO CONVERTS

Since you repent of having been a hearer of the Manichaeans, as you yourself have confessed by pronouncing an anathema against their blasphemies and their most impious and filthy heresy, [Col. 0029A] and since only the Catholic faith has saved you from it, you shall have this letter as protection against those who may think that the error of your past period, insofar as it concerns this wicked sect, ought to be held against you. It was written on such-and-such a day, in the consulship of such-and-such a person.

Letters should not readily be given to the Elect of the Manichaeans who say that they are converting to the Catholic faith, even if they too have anathematized that same heresy according to the preceding form. Rather, they must remain with servants of God, whether clergy or laity, in [Col. 0030A] a monastery or a hospice, until it becomes evident that they have completely abandoned that superstition. Then they should either be baptized, if they have not been baptized, or reconciled, if they have been admitted to the place of penitents, lest, after quickly receiving letters, they abandon the places to which they had been commended.

The commonitory of blessed Augustine, bishop, concerning the Manichaean heresy under the curse of anathema, ends here.

## YEARS 530–531 [Note: [Col. 0029B] See note * at column 9.]

## POPE BONIFACE II

[Col. 0029]

### NOTICE

*(From the Book of the Pontiffs.)*

[Col. 0029B] **Boniface.** After a three-day interregnum, in the Basilica of Julius, in the year of the Lord 530 (529 is more likely), which was the fourth year of Justinian and the second of Athalaric, king of Italy, Boniface II, a Goth by birth, was made pope on 15 [Col. 0029C] October. Dioscorus was elected against him in schism in the Constantinian Basilica—the same Dioscorus whom Pope Hormisdas had sent to the emperor Justinian at Constantinople together with the bishops Germanus and John and other priests and deacons, and who, having been branded with the stain of simony, was condemned by an unjust judgment. King Athalaric appears to have furnished the cause of the schism: while perhaps designating and presenting the pope on the example of his predecessor, he found some among the clergy supporting him and others opposing him. It happened, however, by God’s singular favor, that when the schismatic was overtaken by a speedy death, the schism was extinguished.

At the beginning of Boniface’s pontificate, Belisarius, commander of the imperial troops, was placed in danger by the Persians together with his army, after having fought successfully against them for four years. He converted the coastal peoples, whose assistance he had requested against the Persians, from idolaters into Christians. Procopius, *Persian War*, book I. Theodobert, son of Theodoric and grandson of Clovis, succeeded Theodoric, king of the Franks. From Procopius and Gregory of Tours. Baronius, year 530, no. 49. Ado writes of Boniface in his martyrology that he dedicated a church built in the name of Saint Michael the Archangel on the summit of the circus. **SEV. BINIUS.**

Boniface, a Roman by nation, son of Sigisbulbus, [Note: [Col. 0029D] He held office for two years and twenty-six days.] more accurately for one year and two days (Binius is wrong here). For since he admits that Boniface died on 17 October in the year after the consulship of Lampadius, which is the year of Christ 531, and since it is established from what I said above at the beginning of these notes that he was made pope on 15 October in the year of the Lord 530, he could have been pope for no more than one year and two days. **SEV. BINIUS.** He held office for two years and twenty-six days. He lived in the time of Athalaric, the heretical king, and [Note: [Col. 0030D] The Lucerne manuscript, no. 490, reads “Justin.”] Justinian Augustus.

He was ordained together with Dioscorus amid a dispute. Dioscorus was ordained in the Constantinian Basilica, while Boniface was ordained in the Basilica of Julius. There was dissension among the clergy and the senate for twenty-nine days. [Note: [Col. 0030D] The same manuscript reads “twenty-eight.”] At that time Dioscorus died on the day before the Ides of October. [Note: [Col. 0030B] “In those same days Boniface,” etc.]

After Dioscorus’s death, Boniface, moved by excessive zeal, condemned the same Dioscorus by a sentence of anathema, as though polluted by the crime of simony. To avoid the danger of a future schism, he convened a synod and designated the deacon Vigilius as his successor. When the synod recognized that this was contrary to the sacred canons after his passions had been set aside, he convened a second council and completely annulled what he had wrongly done, expiating the erroneous act by performing penance. Boniface’s successors, Agapetus and Silverius, confirmed the acts carried out in this synod. **SEV. BINIUS.**

In those same days Boniface, led by zeal and deceit, reconciled the clergy under the bond of anathema and a written undertaking, with great bitterness; he sealed the written undertaking in the church archive, as though [Note: [Col. 0030C] “Condemning Dioscorus.”] condemning Dioscorus. That Boniface condemned Dioscorus as a simoniac on a financial charge is expressly written in a letter of the emperor Justinian to Pope John, delivered to Vigilius, in which he says:

“Although Dioscorus had committed no offense against the faith, nevertheless, solely on account of ecclesiastical order, he was anathematized after death by that same Roman Church. If, therefore, bishops who have committed no offense against the faith are subjected to anathema and to condemnation after death solely on account of ecclesiastical order and a financial charge, how much more so Theodorus,” etc.

Agapetus absolved Dioscorus, who had been condemned by an unjust sentence, as is clear from Anastasius in his life of Agapetus. **SEV. BINIUS.**

Boniface assembled the clergy, but no one among them subscribed to him in the episcopate, although a very large multitude had been with Dioscorus. He offered the priests, deacons, subdeacons, and notaries plates from inherited property and assisted the clergy, who were in danger of hunger, with many provisions. [Note: [Col. 0030D] “Here he convened a synod.”]

When the Gothic kings had wickedly usurped for themselves the election of the Roman pontiff, Boniface judged it beneficial to the Church to wrest from Gothic hands such a presumptuous and forcibly usurped license, by having his successor elected while leaving no interval during which the see was vacant. Although this seemed to bear a certain appearance of justice, it was afterward rejected by everyone. **SEV. BINIUS.**

He convened a synod in the Basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle and enacted a decree [Note: [Col. 0030D] The same manuscript reads: “He enacted a decree with the written undertakings of the priests and, by an oath, appointed the deacon Vigilius before the confession of the Apostle Peter, at that same time.”] that he should appoint his own successor. In accordance with this decree, with the written undertakings of the priests and an oath, he appointed the deacon Vigilius before the confession of blessed Peter the Apostle.

At the same time, [Col. 0031A] [Note: [Col. 0031A] “At the same time a second synod was held.”] after a second synod had again been held—he means the second Roman synod, by which he rescinded and annulled the acts of the earlier council—this was decreed by all the priests out of reverence for the holy see. Since the act had been contrary to the canons, and since the fault rested with him for appointing his own successor, Pope Boniface himself confessed that he was guilty of treason because he had appointed the deacon Vigilius before the confession of blessed Peter the Apostle by his subscription to the written undertaking. He burned that decree in the presence of all the priests, clergy, and senate. [Note: [Col. 0031B] “At the same time a report arrived.”]

At that time Bishop Reparatus presided over the Church of Carthage. [Col. 0032A] **SEV. BINIUS.**

At the same time a report arrived from the African bishops concerning the decree, instructing the bishop of Carthage to conduct everything with the advice of the apostolic see.

Boniface was buried in the Basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle on 17 October, [Note: [Col. 0032B] The same manuscript reads “in the consulship.”] after the consulship of Lampadius. And [Note: [Col. 0032A] The episcopate was vacant for two months and fifteen days.] the episcopate remained vacant for two months and fifteen days.

From this number of months and days one would have to say that John, the successor of Boniface, was made pope on the Kalends of January in the second year after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes. Yet Anastasius not only admits that he himself contradicts this by saying that John was substituted for Boniface in the first year after that consulship, but the inscription on the title of Eudoxia, in the church of Saint Peter ad Vincula, also clearly indicates the same thing. See Baronius, year 531, no. 8. **SEV. BINIUS.**

[Col. 0031B]

# LETTERS AND DECREES OF POPE BONIFACE II

*(C, S)*

## FIRST LETTER  
### FORMERLY THE ELEVENTH

**Pope Boniface II to Caesarius of Arles.** At his request he confirms what had been defined in the Synod of Orange.

[Col. 0031B]

**Boniface to his most beloved brother Caesarius.** [Note: [Col. 0031D] “Caesarius to Boniface.” We saw a third copy of this letter in the Tolian manuscript at Angoulême; the deacon Cyprian also mentions it in the life of Saint Caesarius, book I, near the end. JAC. SIRMOND.]

Through our son Armenius, priest and abbot, we received a letter from your brotherhood [Col. 0031C] [Note: [Col. 0031D] “Which, as it appears, you sent to me, still unaware of the priesthood entrusted to me, at the beginning of that priesthood,” etc. Certain things at this point had been corrupted in the ancient copies; from their traces these words seemed recoverable: “which, as it appears, you sent to me, still unaware of the priesthood entrusted to me, at the beginning of that priesthood,” etc. JAC. SIRMOND.] which, as it appears, you sent to me, still unaware of the priesthood entrusted to me, in the charity by which we are bound in God. In it you had requested that what you had sought from our predecessor, Pope Felix of blessed memory, for the security of the Catholic faith should be explained by the force of my insistence.

But since the heavenly will decreed that what you had hoped to obtain from him through us you should instead obtain from us, we did not delay giving a Catholic answer to your request, which you conceived with such commendable concern.

For you indicate that certain bishops of Gaul, although they have already agreed by God’s grace that the other good things come to be, wish faith alone—the faith by which we believe in Christ—to be of nature, not of grace; and that they say that it remained in human beings descended from Adam, which is unspeakable, by free choice, and is not even now [this preposition *ac* is absent in the Palatine manuscript and others] bestowed individually through the generosity of divine mercy.

You ask us, in order to remove this ambiguity, to confirm by the authority of the apostolic see your confession, by which you, in opposition to them, define according to Catholic truth that right faith in Christ, and the beginning of every good will, are inspired in the minds of individuals through God’s prevenient grace.

And therefore, since many Fathers, and above all Augustine, bishop of blessed memory, as well as our predecessors, the bishops of the apostolic see, are demonstrably shown to have discussed this matter at such length that no one ought any longer to remain in doubt that faith itself also comes to us from grace, we judged that an extended response could be dispensed with. This is especially so since, according to the passages from the Apostle that you sent, in which he says, “I obtained mercy in order to be faithful” (1 Cor. 7), and elsewhere, “It has been granted to you for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1), it clearly appears that the faith by which we believe in Christ, like all good things, comes to individual human beings from the gift of heavenly grace, not from the power of human nature.

We rejoice that your brotherhood also, after conferring with certain priests of Gaul, has understood this according to the Catholic faith—namely, that they unanimously defined that the faith by which we believe in Christ is bestowed with the prevenient grace of the Divinity. They also rejected the claim that there is any good according to God which anyone can will, begin, perform, or complete without God’s grace, in accordance with the saying of our Savior himself: “Without me you can do nothing.”

For it is certain and Catholic that, in all good things, whose head is faith, divine mercy goes before us when we do not yet will, is present in us when we do will, and then follows us so that we may persevere in faith, as the prophet David says: “My God, his mercy shall go before me” (Ps. 58); and again: “My mercy is with him” (Ps. 88); and elsewhere: “His mercy shall follow me” (Ps. 22).
