Likewise blessed Paul says: “Or who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid him? For from him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. 11).

Therefore we are greatly astonished that those who think otherwise are still so weighed down by the remnants of their ancient error that they say that people come to believe in Christ not through God’s gift but through nature; and that they claim that the good of that very nature—which is known to have been corrupted by Adam’s sin—is the author of our faith more than Christ is. They do not understand that they are opposing the Lord’s statement: “No one comes to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6).

They also oppose blessed Paul, who cries out to the Hebrews: “Let us run with perseverance the race set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Heb. 12).

Since these things are so, we cannot discover what they assign to the human will as the cause of believing in Christ without God’s grace, when Christ is the author and perfecter of faith.

Therefore, greeting you with fitting affection, we approve the confession written above as agreeing with the Catholic rules of the Fathers.

But those who, as you indicate, wish to attribute the other things to grace while placing faith first [the Palatine manuscript reads: “with faith in second place, the other good things, as you indicate”], we bind by their own profession, so that they may be compelled all the more to ascribe faith also to the gift of grace. Apart from faith, no one can perform any good thing according to God, as the blessed Apostle says: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14).

Since this is so, either they will attribute no good thing to grace if they attempt to remove faith from it, or, if they say that some good thing comes from grace, faith itself must necessarily be attributed to grace. For if there is no good without faith, but faith itself is denied to come from grace, then no good thing—God forbid—will be attributable to grace. [Note: [Col. 0033D] The Palatine manuscript adds: “For every good gift is acknowledged to be divine, as it is written: ‘Every…’”]

The Apostle James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1).

They themselves also admit, as you say, that the other gifts are bestowed through grace, while they do not doubt that all those good things subsist through faith. Faith itself, therefore, must necessarily be attributed to the grace from which they cannot separate the good that they attribute to grace.

Having briefly established these points, we did not think it necessary to respond to the remaining absurdities of the Pelagian error that the letter seems to contain—the letter that you said had been sent to you by a certain priest—because we hope from the mercy of God that, through the ministry and teaching of your brotherhood, he will deign to work in the hearts of all those whom you have said disagree, so that they may come to believe that every good will proceeds not from themselves but from divine grace, when they find themselves already willing to defend what they had stubbornly tried to oppose.

For it is written: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 19, according to the Septuagint), and elsewhere: “I knew that I could not be continent unless God gave it, and this itself was wisdom, to know whose gift it was” (Wis. 8).

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brother.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, [Note: [Col. 0033D] “In the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes.” Boniface could not have written in the month of January during this consulship, since, according to Anastasius, he was made pope only in October of that same year. Therefore an error has entered the consular notation, and perhaps it should read “after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes,” which was the year of Christ 531. JAC. SIRMOND.]

### OBSERVATION OF FATHER ANTONIO PAGI ON THE YEAR OF CHRIST 529, NO. 11

This letter is said, both in Sirmond’s edition and in that of Holstenius, to have been given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, men of illustrious rank, in the year 530. But since Felix IV ended his mortal life on 18 September of that year, Sirmond suspected that an error had entered the consular notation and that it should read “after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes,” by which the year 531 was indicated.

Yet Boniface II, saying in this letter, “we did not delay giving a Catholic answer,” overturns that emendation and indicates by those words that the added clause is spurious and should be regarded as worthless.

**In the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, men of illustrious rank (in the year of Christ 530).**

# THREE PETITIONS OF STEPHANUS TO BONIFACE  
*(C, S)*

## FIRST PETITION

To my holy and wholly most blessed lord, and truly venerable father of fathers, universal patriarch Boniface: Stephanus, an insignificant bishop.

I do not approach with unreasonable confidence, nor am I unaware of my insignificance. Rather, with a contrite soul and humble spirit, and with many tears, I offer this petition of mine to you. I therefore consider it acceptable [Col. 0034B] before you, most blessed father, because formerly also those who entreated God with tears prayed with confidence, not as with whole burnt offerings, rams, and bulls, but with ten thousand fat lambs: “A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50).

Therefore you yourself, most holy father, will not despise me, surrounded by many evils and looking only to God and, by paternal custom, to your fatherly compassion. For no ecclesiastical order can surpass that power of yours which was conferred upon you by the Savior of all and the first shepherd. Whatever is insignificant or humble is not beneath the concern with which you look upon it.

The more you surpass everyone before God, the more you must consider that this is the test of those who love God: after God, the father and teacher of the holy Church, Peter, bears witness to you and to the whole world. For when the Lord said three times, “Do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21), he first entrusted these commands to you and afterward, through you, granted them to all the holy Churches throughout the world.

Finally, because those venerable men who came before you, and all those who deserved to possess that holy see, became renowned—living bodily in the glorious city of Rome but adorning in spirit all things that were rightly done—and because many members of the Church were freed by God and by the venerable apostolic see from the violence of hostile accusers, I beg you: judge me, the humble and poor man, and, as it is written (Ps. 81), justify me.

In secular life I had previously held the provincial rank of soldier; I passed my life humbly, as one of modest condition. But when Proclus of blessed memory, who had become bishop of the Church of Larissa, died, it was necessary that a bishop be ordained for that Church. A decree was jointly drawn up by the clergy and people, by the metropolitan, [Col. 0035A] and by those whose assent was necessary for the action. In accordance with ancient custom, three men were selected: Alexander, priest of Sciathus, [lacuna], a priest, and myself, an insignificant man. Having obtained the better testimony, I won the palm of the election.

But, conscious of myself, I judged that I was unworthy of so great a responsibility. Nevertheless, I willingly consented, attributing everything to God’s grace and mercy. I looked to the examples of the thief, the publican, and many others of this kind. These examples encouraged me, for God suddenly rescued such men from the greatest evils—or, as one must say, from the very depths of evil—and a certain hope of a good purpose was given to me.

Accordingly, they all transferred their election to me and subscribed to the decree together. Since, according to ancient custom, the ordination had to take place not elsewhere but in that same city, the holy synod of the province, the landowners of the entire city, and the whole body of the Church assembled. With the common testimony of all, without diminishing the custom, I was ordained bishop in the Church.

The lover of God Probianus, bishop of the city of Demetrias, showed such enthusiasm for this matter and embraced the act so warmly that he even urged the Church of God to praise the person of my humility. And, without my saying anything about myself, it is clear from those who desired and elected me that this ordination came about according to God’s will.

Therefore I beg you, most blessed father, to deign to hear these matters gently. I do not present them, as Scripture says, because I love praise from my lips; for one who glorifies himself cannot be approved by God. Rather, I present them so that, once you know these facts, the calumny that has been raised against me may clearly appear.

I have considered it unnecessary to recount to you what the provincial bishops and the clergy of the holy Church subsequently said, showing that they rejoiced in my election. When the enemy of all good was at rest, and God did not regard my sins, the Church suffered no disturbance, and the charity of all concealed the fault, as it is written.

But I do not know from where they were stirred up: Antonius, a God-fearing priest and steward, and Probianus, the slanderer, bishop of the city of Demetrias—I mean that Probianus, most blessed father, who drove away others when they hastened to speak my praises, but himself proclaimed titles of praise for me in the Church of God, together with Demetrius, the lover of God and bishop of the city of Sciathus. He also persuaded others to share in his portion, without being ashamed of the subscriptions contained in the decree.

Neither Probianus nor anyone else took into account his own praise and the testimony of the whole Church, nor what they themselves had said or done: how they had embraced my ordination, how they had previously found my person pleasing, and how they had willingly accepted the ordination once it had been celebrated. Instead, they suddenly departed for the imperial city and, fabricating an accusation, lodged complaints against me with Epiphanius, the most holy archbishop of that city. They said that my ordination was wholly contrary to the sacred canons, hoping that another bishop would be substituted in my place.

As I begin to speak of these things, anguish naturally holds me. If I relate what they have done to me, the storm that now threatens my life, or the things they threaten—which are more savage still—let no one judge me insolent or reckless for saying anything about so great and eminent a bishop of the Church.

But if I keep silent, as I must [read: “woe is me,” HARD.], where shall I find help? Entrusting myself to the judgment of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, to your blessedness, and to the piety of the most serene emperor, I could not remain silent.

When my accusation had reached the most holy archbishop Epiphanius—and again and repeatedly I ask pardon for what I am about to say; let the most holy fathers judge that these things proceed not from insolence or boldness but from necessity—he prepared a *commonitory*, as they call it, in the name of Andreas, a most devout man, and sent it to the province of Thessaly through the deacons and notaries of his holy Church.

He ordered me to withdraw from the sacred ministry, on the grounds that I had not been ordained according to the canons. Without using any proof of the accusations or any canonical summons, he suspended the other bishops of that province and the clergy of our holy Church from communion with me. Finally, he did not even permit me to receive food or the necessities of life from ecclesiastical property. Thus he is known to have inflicted upon me, before any judicial examination had taken place, the treatment ordinarily inflicted upon convicted persons.

Indeed, the Churches have established abundant mercy even for those who truly commit offenses. This, then, was what Andreas, the devout man whom I mentioned above, was ordered to inflict upon me.

So that I might present myself before the judgment of the man who had suspended me from communion and answer him, he was also ordered to bring with him Eustathius, bishop of the city of Gomphi, Elpidius of Thebes, and Stephanus of Laminum, as though they were equally responsible for my unlawful ordination.

But the man who was compelling me to appear in court kept with him Demetrius and Probianus, devout men who had previously formed a large part of my election and ordination, and encouraged them wholly toward my destruction.

The aforementioned devout man Andreas did not find me there, because shortly before I had departed for the great city of Thessalonica. He gathered the clergy and as many others as he could find, read the commonitory to them, and read the letter addressed to them.

The same most holy man had written such a letter to the clergy. He drew up an official record before the city’s defender, copies of which I have not failed to append to my little petitions.

A summary was also made concerning the sacred vessels and ecclesiastical property. Some people were removed from responsibility for ecclesiastical affairs by Antonius, a devout man who everywhere winked at the actions of the devout Andreas.

When the aforementioned Andreas came to the great city of Thessalonica, he showed me and the bishops Elpidius and Stephanus, the lovers of God mentioned above, what had been ordered and threatened.

I, however, fearing neither the efforts of the accusers nor those of anyone else, but looking only to God, to the laws of the holy Church, and to the primacy of the holy Churches entrusted to you, immediately declared in the official proceedings that, if it pleased anyone to require me to answer an accuser or to judge anything concerning my ordination, I had to state my case—but elsewhere, before one with whom the law of the sacred canons is observed and the custom hitherto preserved.

I invoked the memory of your holy person and of the apostolic see. I said that you were the lords of this examination and begged that nothing new should be done against me, or anything that could disturb what had been properly arranged.

For what place of remedy would have remained for me with you, most blessed lords of judgment, if I had not said these things? Nor did I say only this; I also produced certain documents useful to the case.

The official records that were made indicate these things. I have attached to my little petitions both the decree made against me and the titles of praise.

I thought that this testimony could have supported my petition if, once you had been named as those to whom God had granted judgment, the person who was incompetent to hear the case had withdrawn himself. “For God is not a God of confusion but of peace” (1 Cor. 14:33).

But neither these things nor others were sufficient to secure my peace. Against my will I was brought to the imperial city.

Had certain God-fearing men, mindful of and awaiting the promise laid up through the visitation of prisoners, not promised that my presence would be forthcoming, I would certainly have been bound—a man who, as I believe, had harmed no one, except that I consented to those who elected me and, entrusting myself to God’s hope, deserved to be ordained; and because I had boldly said that, if any examination were required, it ought to be conducted by the one appointed lord of that examination.

I do not doubt that other things were also done and inflicted upon me.

I am being compelled, and I have no time even to breathe. Nor can I find anyone who will consider my case amid such disasters. I confess that I am awaiting worse things from those who threaten me: condemnation, exile, and every sort of criminal penalty, though I do not deserve them.

Therefore, trusting in you and in your apostolic see, I now ask you for the one remedy. For, as the divine word says, “Hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5).

If there were someone presiding whom the sacred canons appointed as judge in this matter, he ought, as I think, first to judge and investigate the lives of the accusers, because they cannot be accusers of one who, although humble, has obtained the honor of the episcopate.

But because, as I have said, I offended through my confidence in you, these things have been brought forward on my behalf, and I have been placed in the evils named above. Therefore I beg you—if there is any mercy of God, any compassion, any love—come across and, in the Holy Spirit, according to the blessed Apostle, bring me help here. Remember yourselves and your predecessors of that blessed see, since they never allowed anyone to be unjustly harmed by another.

If you quickly come to the aid of the oppressed, I trust that I shall be saved from my evils with equal speed. But if, God forbid, my sins have delayed your compassion, at least, if anything is quickly done by those lying in wait, it is fitting that you should be present according to the sacred canons and carry out what has been neglected.

For this is your task, most blessed father: by day and by night to preserve in every Church, and especially in your province of Illyricum, the laws and decrees of the holy Fathers and of your venerable and apostolic see.

[Col. 0038A] **In another hand:** I, Stephanus, an insignificant bishop of the holy Church of Larissa, have subscribed this petition, made by my own hand, and have sent it to my most holy and wholly blessed lord, the most venerable father of fathers and universal patriarch Boniface.

Abundantius, bishop of the city of Demetrias, rising from his seat, said:

“I could not pass over the name of Probianus when I heard it. This Probianus, the very man under discussion, invaded my Church. When I came to your blessedness with a bishop’s letters, he took advantage of my absence, usurped my place through his recklessness, and, according to the sacred canons, ought not to be called a bishop. Against him I ask your blessedness that the discipline of the apostolic see come to my aid.”

Bishop Boniface said:

“Let both the reading of the petition that has been presented and the statement of our brother and fellow bishop Abundantius be entered into the proceedings; and if there are any other matters, we wish to learn them.”

Theodosius, bishop of the city of Echinos in the province of Thessaly, said through an interpreter:

“The same most holy Stephanus, metropolitan bishop, has also sent another petition to your blessedness through my service. I ask that you order it to be read before your judgment.”

Bishop Boniface said:

“Let the petition that he presents, once received by the notaries, be read.”

When it had been received, the notary Menas read it.

## SECOND PETITION

A petition from Stephanus, an insignificant man, to my holy and blessed lord, truly venerable father of fathers, archbishop, and patriarch Boniface.

What previously existed in hope, and made me fear and tremble and invoke your holy apostolic see—when these things seized and constricted my wretched life, they compel me all the more to appeal to your Beatitude. Behold the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (1 Cor. 6). Deliver me from my enemies, and rescue me from those who persecute me; for the waters have encompassed me even to my soul, venerable father, and the deepest abyss has surrounded me: let my life rise from corruption, as it is written. For if God’s mercies do not go before me, I have indeed become what my enemies themselves wished me to be. But I weep and mourn, because [Col. 0038D] the ecclesiastical order too is then endangered.

Since, therefore, according to the great mercy of God, who by no means reckons sins against human beings, I was elected and ordained bishop in the city of Larissa, which belongs to the province of Thessaly, some of those who elected me—and who had often confirmed their election in writing, judging me worthy of the priesthood—observing that I intended to restore the ancient custom in our holy Churches, brought accusations against me before the most blessed prelate of the Church of the holy imperial city. But he accepted the accusation and, without first examining anything concerning what ought to be investigated in the case of an accused bishop, immediately removed me from every ecclesiastical ministry, sending one of the religious clergy of his holy [Col. 0039A] Church to the province of Thessaly with letters which they call a *commonitorium*.

Although these actions accord neither with civility nor with secular laws, and although the order of the canons plainly does not permit punishment to precede judicial examination—while divine Scripture has long proclaimed most emphatically, “Do not admit an empty report”—nevertheless, when a most religious man came to Thessalonica bearing the command and wishing to contend with me over certain matters, I immediately said to him: “It is proper that the apostolic see, that is, your Beatitude, should both hear and conclude the cases of our province.”

But the most holy archbishop of the imperial city, refusing to desist, also ordered that I be brought before him contrary to the canons. When I came and convened a meeting of the bishops residing there, I did not delay repeating this argument, imploring the apostolic see of your holy and blessed head, and insisting that the custom which until now had prevailed in our province ought not to be overturned. I begged that the authority of the apostolic see—which, just as it was given by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the sacred canons, has likewise been preserved by ancient custom—not be violated in any respect.

But he was unwilling to withdraw from his purpose. Rather, having assumed jurisdiction, he had only one aim: to appear to be lord and judge in the holy Churches of the province of Thessaly. Therefore, seeing the storm in which I was tossed, I fled to your holy and safest harbor, and, submitting a petition and laying these matters before your Beatitude, I sent it to you, begging that you show toward me the mercy of God and of the holy Church, which always comes to the aid of those in danger.

But when those plotting against my life perceived, as I suppose, that you do not despise what has been done, but carry it through—as is the custom of your holiness—and vindicate the order of the holy Churches, they used every effort to accomplish their will before any decision of yours could arrive. Although nothing had been established against me and no fault deserving canonical punishment had been found, they pronounced sentence and, condemning me, suspended me from priestly office. Yet it is clear that I had not been allowed fully to present my case; nor had I been permitted, when I asked, to produce certain things that might benefit my cause.

Therefore I begged that sentence not be pronounced before the proceedings had been reported to your Beatitudes, so that your examination of the case might thereby be preserved. This statement provoked them still further against me, since they thought that something was being taken away from the jurisdiction of the sacred Churches of the imperial city because I had appeared to mention your apostolic see. For I said that the authority of the apostolic see, which was given by God and by our supreme Savior to the chief of the apostles, surpasses all the privileges of the holy Churches, and that in its confession all the Churches of the world find rest.

After the sentence had therefore been read, I again implored a just hearing before you, whose justice no one’s dispute can disturb; for the fear of God which dwells in you itself causes each person’s rights to be restored through you. But I think, venerable fathers, that, disregarding what they formerly did against me, they will again do the same on a second occasion [Col. 0040A]; and I suspect that they will not be satisfied even with this, but will extend their hostility also to my wretched body, so that when I die no accuser may remain.

For after the sentence had been issued, I was immediately handed over to the custody of certain God-loving defenders of the holy Church. But some who feared God and pitied my misery, seeing that I had been abandoned on every side, received me under their protection, promising a large sum of money on my behalf, on condition that I would not depart but would remain under guard in the imperial city. All who contrived these things against me had this matter especially arranged, so that I might not be able to hasten to the feet of your Beatitude and receive from you, in accordance with God’s command, some mercy.

I therefore beseech you: have pity on a humble man [Col. 0040B] and one cast down in spirit; help me by the grace which has been bestowed on you by the Lord. For if by the word of God you have received authority to forgive other sins, since divine Scripture says that whatever you loose on earth shall also be loosed in heaven (Matt. 16), how much more authority will you have over the things that have been done and decreed against me? “To you the poor man is left; you are the helper of the orphan” (Ps. 9), because I am known to have been abandoned by every human hope.

**And in another hand:** I, Stephen the humble, have subscribed to this petition of mine.

Bishop Boniface said: “Let what has been read be entered in the ecclesiastical annals.” And he added: “Since the greater part of the day has passed, at the next session, if you believe that anything else remains, do not delay making it known.”

## SECOND SESSION

[Col. 0040C]

After the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, most illustrious men, on the fifth day before the Ides of December, in the meeting hall of the blessed apostle Andrew, with the venerable man Pope Boniface presiding, together with Sabinus, bishop of Canusium; Abundantius, bishop of Demetrias; Carosus, bishop of Centumcellae; and Felix, bishop of Nomentum; and with Sanctulus, Mercurius, Vivulus, Peter, Eventius, Albinus, Ursus, Peter, Epiphanius, Benedict, Servant of God, Gaudiosus, Peter, Valentinus, Renatus, Florentius, Hilary, Paul, Bacauda, Innocent, Andrew, Gaudiosus, Philip, Crescentio, Libertinus, Januarius, Sebastian, Cyriacus, Vivulus, Dulcitius, John, Pullio, Andrew, Bonus, Laurentius, Seleucus, Rusticus, Caelestine, Barbarus, Laurentius, and Redemptus, presbyters, also seated; and with Tribunus, Agapitus, Donatus, and Probus, deacons, standing by [Col. 0040D], the archdeacon Tribunus said:

“Theodosius, bishop of the city of Echinos in the province of Thessaly, is waiting, as you determined in the previous session. What do you command?”

Bishop Boniface of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome said: “Let him enter.”

When he had entered, Bishop Boniface said: “Let him state what he wishes to present.”

Theodosius, bishop of the city of Echinos in the province of Thessaly, speaking through an interpreter, said:

“Elpidius, Stephen, and Timothy, my venerable fellow bishops of the province of Thessaly, are known to have sent through me petitions to be presented to your sacred Beatitude. Since I am presenting them, command that they too be read to you.”

Bishop Boniface said: “Let this document also be disclosed by the notary’s reading.”

When it had been received, the notary Menas read:

“To our holy and most blessed Lord, and truly venerable father of fathers and archbishop, Boniface the patriarch, Elpidius, Stephen, and Timothy, humble bishops.

Your Beatitude formerly knew the necessities that constrained us. Therefore, most holy father, composing a brief petition, we recently declared and reported the evils we have suffered and the harsher ones we expect. Those who serve the will and threats of the men plotting these things against us have one purpose: that Stephen, a God-loving man, be deprived of the episcopal office.

But while he was still speaking, another messenger arrived, reporting even worse things. For, after the earlier proceedings, the most holy prelate of the Church of the imperial city and the holy synod that had been with him, persisting in their former intention, took from us Stephen, the God-loving shepherd of our—more precisely, of the holy Church of Larissa, which is the metropolitan city of the province of Thessaly [Col. 0041B]. They drew up a sentence of condemnation as they pleased and added that he was not permitted to depart for the province of Thessaly.

But the aforementioned God-loving man repeatedly protested during the proceedings to the most holy prelate of the imperial city and to the synod assembled with him that they were not permitted to assume this jurisdiction or, above all, to issue any decision, since this belongs to the Beatitude of the apostolic see. But they disregarded his protest and, becoming all the more inflamed by it, pronounced a merciless sentence.

They thought thereby to remove him from our holy Church, while preparing to establish jurisdiction over our province, so that by this example no one would dare say anything concerning the rights of our holy Churches, or mention their antiquity or the rights they have maintained until now. For their purpose is to make us wretched subjects of the authority and jurisdiction of the Church of the holy imperial city.

For all these things we weep day and night and pour out tears to our God and Savior of all, Jesus Christ, and we display our wretched gray hairs, beseeching you not to allow us to be handed over into their hands.

For these matters we appeal both to your Beatitude and to the apostolic see; and through it we believe that we hear and adore the thrice-blessed Peter [Col. 0041D] and Christ, the first shepherd of the holy Church, our Lord [Col. 0042A]. We hope that you will not despise the petition of wretched men, which we have presented with souls full of anguish and pain; but that, correcting these matters with an appropriate remedy and coming to their aid, you will deign to provide relief, because ‘our spirit has failed’ (Ps. 142), as is said in the Psalms by him who pleaded in anguish of soul.

Thus may the God-loving man, who, striving to protect the right of the apostolic see, appears to have endured such great dangers, be restored to his office by apostolic authority. In the future, take care that the custom of the holy Churches of our province be in no way overturned.

For if God’s mercy and your assistance do not come before us, a third or fourth messenger bringing similar news will arrive [Col. 0042B], because their intention does not cease with Stephen, the God-loving man; they will do the same to many others, and they will not rest until they have brought their desires to fulfillment.

**And in another hand:** I, Elpidius, humble bishop of the holy Church of Thebes, petitioning through John, my presbyter, because I was unable to subscribe with my own hand through grief, had him subscribe at my command.

I, Timothy, humble bishop of the holy Church of Dicaesarea, petitioning, have subscribed.

I, Patricius, humble presbyter of the holy Church of God at Lamia, having come to the imperial city on behalf of Stephen, my holy bishop, petitioning at his command, have subscribed.”

Bishop Boniface said: “Let what has been read be transcribed.” And he added: “If there is anything else, let it be presented.”

Theodosius, bishop of the city of Echinos in the province of Thessaly [Col. 0042C], speaking through an interpreter, said:

“From the rereading of the petitions your Beatitude has learned what was done against the holy canons and against the ordinances of your predecessors. For it is established that the venerable pontiffs of your see, although throughout the world the apostolic see rightly claims primacy over the Churches and although it is necessary to appeal to it alone in ecclesiastical cases everywhere, nevertheless specifically claimed the Churches of Illyricum for their own governance.

You know the writings of all the preceding pontiffs. Nevertheless, I am producing copies of certain letters, and I now ask that their authenticity be established from your archive.”

Bishop Boniface said: “Let the letters produced be read, and let the authenticity of the documents be sought in the archive of the apostolic see.”

When the copies of the letters had been received [Col. 0042D], the notary Menas read:

## APPENDIX TO THE WRITINGS OF POPE BONIFACE II

[Col. 0041]

### [LETTER II]

[Col. 0041D]

### OBSERVATION OF PHILIPPE LABBE, S.J., ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

Baronius, Bellarmine, and other learned men declare this letter false and spurious; Binius himself does not deny it, both here and in his notes on the Sixth Council of Carthage, where he calls Isidore Mercator—or whoever else lies hidden under his mask—an impostor, forger, and contriver of lies. Indeed, this is proved more clearly than daylight by many things, especially the words of the Roman pontiffs [Col. 0042D], Saint Leo, Hormisdas, and Gregory the Great.

“Gregory could not have taken those words from Boniface,” says Bellarmine, *On the Roman Pontiff*, book XI, chapter 25, “since the style is entirely Gregorian.” By this argument all the wares of Pseudo-Isidore are blown away. “Let these things be dismissed,” says Baronius under 16 October; “the Church of God, which is the pillar and foundation of truth, neither rests nor is supported on straws; rather, let us expose the trick and uncover the imposture,” and so forth. See the same author under the years 419, no. 92 and following, and 530, no. 5.

**[Note: [Col. 0043B] Letter]** This letter says that, from the times of the pontiffs Boniface and Celestine, the African Church, because of the displeasing manner in which an appeal had been made to the apostolic see, was divided from the Roman Church in schism through the agency of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, and no longer maintained communion with it until the time of Pope Boniface II. It says that when Eulalius, bishop of Carthage, had presented a supplicatory petition to the aforementioned Boniface in order to establish concord and recover communion with the Roman Church, he returned to communion. All of this is fabricated and notoriously false.

For it is evident that the communion of the African Church with Boniface I, Celestine, and their many successors, down to Boniface II, was never interrupted even for the space of a single day or the moment of a single hour. Aurelius and those who lived with him maintained communion with Celestine, as is clear from the conclusion of the synodal letter which they sent to him from the African council, where they write: “May our Lord preserve your holiness, who prays for us through a long age, lord brother.” They would certainly not have written these customary signs of mutual peace, concord, and Catholic communion, used in formal letters, to a pontiff as though he were a schismatic, if they had cut themselves off from union with the Roman Church—especially since, as Augustine testifies in letters 162 and 163, the words quoted above were customarily written only to Catholics, not to schismatics.

Concerning Augustine, the colleague of Aurelius, Celestine writes in his letter to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 2: “We have always held Augustine, a man of holy memory, in our communion on account of the merits of his life,” and so forth. Capreolus, Augustine’s successor, maintained communion with the sacred ecumenical Council of Ephesus, and consequently with the whole Church, through letters and legates honorably received there, as may be seen from the notes on that council above.

Leo the pontiff instructed the successors of the bishops of the African Church when they sought solutions to various questions by letter. Hilary admitted those same men to the decisions of the Roman council. Pope Symmachus fed and clothed those exiled to Sardinia by the Arian king Thrasamund. When, during the persecution, bishops and priests were lacking because of the king’s edict forbidding the appointment of other bishops in place of the deceased, the Roman Church supplied them with ministers for baptism and the other sacraments, as Victor establishes in book I of *The Vandal Persecution*.

Saint Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, when he was to dispute publicly with the Arians, openly professed the Roman Church to be the head of all Churches, as the same Victor records in book II of *The Vandal Persecution* [Col. 0044B]. What is more, pagans and Arians—as may be seen in the same Victor, book I of *The Vandal Persecution*, and in Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 25—called the African Catholics “Romans,” for no other reason than that they maintained communion with the Roman Church in faith and religion, and that in all their letters they alike honored and respected its pastor, the vicar of Christ.

Since it is therefore clear from these facts that the African Church not only never departed from the unity and communion of the Roman Church, but rather recognized it, even during the persecution, as the mother of its own Church and of the other Churches, who would not accuse this letter of falsehood, in which some Eulalius, bishop of Carthage, is said to have offered a petition for restoring unity, at a time when all the Catholic bishops were in exile under the Arian king Gelimer?

Who would not charge with falsehood the letter that is alleged to have been sent to Eulalius of Alexandria—a bishop of Alexandria by that name never lived, as is clear from Nicephorus and others—while Timothy, the third bishop of Alexandria bearing that name, an heretic, was occupying the see?

Who, finally, would not say that the letter is full of imposture and fraud, when it states that the African Church was schismatic for more than a hundred years, although it never severed itself from the unity of the Roman Church even for a single hour?

Such a fiction had to be devised so that they could expunge Augustine, Eugenius, Fulgentius, and men renowned for holiness, together with Aurelius—whom they themselves call the author of the schism, while Prosper of Aquitaine calls him “a father and a bishop worthy of remembrance,” a citizen of the heavenly homeland—and together with the ranks of certain holy martyrs and confessors who died for the Catholic faith during the Vandal persecution, from the register and sacred roll of the saints.

For if the African Church remained in schism for a full century before this time, namely from Boniface until the present, then no one during that period could have received the legitimate crown of martyrdom or been rewarded with the prize of confession, since by the unanimous agreement of all the Fathers it is certain that schismatics can have no crown, inasmuch as it is granted only to those who contend legitimately in the arena of the Catholic Church. See Baronius in the notes on the martyrs under 16 October, section b. Also see what we noted above in the Sixth Council of Carthage, under the word “Council.” **Severus Binius.**

## LETTER II (FORMERLY I) OF POPE BONIFACE II TO EULALIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA  
### On the Reconciliation of the Church of Carthage

[Col. 0043A]

**Boniface, bishop, to Eulalius, his fellow bishop, greetings.**

From the beginning we received such great confidence from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that—with the Lord’s help—we possess authority to assist the universal Church and to correct and amend by apostolic authority whatever is harmful.

For this reason divine providence or dispensation established different ranks and distinct orders, so that, while those of lesser rank showed reverence to their superiors and superiors extended love to their inferiors, one structure of concord might arise from diversity, and the administration of each person’s duties might be rightly conducted [Col. 0043B]. Indeed, the whole cannot subsist in any other way unless an order of this kind, with its great distinctions, preserves it.

Since no creature can be governed or live in one and the same equality, the examples of the heavenly armies instruct us [variant: “the example instructs us”]. For while there are angels and archangels, it is clear that they are not equal, but that one differs from another in power and rank, as you know. If, therefore, this distinction is acknowledged among those who are without sin, what human being would refuse willingly to submit to their ordering?

From this, peace and mutual charity embrace one another in turn; firm concord remains, together with sincerity in reciprocal love pleasing to God.

Since every office is then healthfully fulfilled when there is one superior to whom recourse may be had, we do not wish your Charity to be unaware of our desires, lest one who shared the burden of concern be excluded from the fruit of joy. Therefore we inform you through our letters that the Church of Carthage [variant: “the Church of Constantinople,” as you read in Hormisdas] has returned to our communion, with the Lord’s favor, and that the sequence of the commands which we gave to our legates has been completed in every respect.

So that joy concerning this matter might reach your affection more fully and perfectly, we have thought it right to send copies of the petitions of our brother and fellow priest Eulalius, bishop of Carthage, and of the sacred documents of Justinian, the most merciful emperor of the East [Col. 0044B], indicating also that many bishops throughout the eastern regions have acted in the same way.

It remains for divinity, entreated by our persistent prayers, to grant that we may rejoice also in the restoration of the other Churches. You should take care to convey what we have wished to report to those priests who are near your Fraternity, so that they too may not cease to give thanks with us for the favor of heavenly mercy arising from so great a matter.

For Aurelius, formerly bishop of the aforementioned Church of Carthage, began—these things are entirely false—to grow proud with his colleagues, at the prompting of the devil, against the Roman Church during the times of our predecessors Boniface and Celestine. But when Eulalius saw that he had been separated from the communion of the Roman Church through the manner of Aurelius’s sin [variant: “the sinning Aurelius”], he humbled himself, acknowledged that he had sinned, and, seeking the peace and communion of the Roman Church, subscribed together with his colleagues and, by apostolic authority, condemned all writings that had been produced by any means against the privileges of the Roman Church.

[Col. 0045B]

## COPY OF HIS PETITIONS AND OF THE AFOREMENTIONED EMPEROR JUSTINIAN  
**[Note: [Col. 0046D] These too were fabricated by a crafty forger.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0045D] “The first salvation.”]** This profession of faith cannot belong to Justin, since he died four years before the time when this profession was issued and delivered. Nor can it belong to Justinian, both because it is mixed together from the letter of Pope Hormisdas to the bishops of Spain, from the letter of John, bishop of Constantinople, and from several others, so that it appears to be a badly sewn-together patchwork; and also because it is dated under the third consulship of Justinian, when no longer Boniface but John presided over the Roman Church. This prudent collector of the pontifical letters, considering the matter carefully, rejected the suspicious formula of faith as an interpolation. Baronius, year 530, no. 5. **Severus Binius.**

The first condition of salvation is to preserve the rule of right faith and in no respect to deviate from the decrees of the Fathers. Since the declaration of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be set aside—“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16)—the truth of these words is also demonstrated by events, because in the apostolic see Catholic religion has always been preserved without stain.

Desiring in no way to be separated from this hope and faith, and following the decrees of the Fathers, we anathematize all who, in their pride, raise their necks against the holy Roman and apostolic Church. We follow the apostolic see in all things and proclaim all its decrees. In every respect I hope that I may deserve to be in communion with you, the communion which the apostolic see proclaims, in which there is the complete and true perfection and solidity of the Christian religion.

I promise that those separated from communion with the Catholic Church—that is, those who do not consent to the apostolic see—are not to have their names recited among the sacred mysteries. If I should ever attempt to deviate in any respect from my profession, I declare by my own sentence that I am an accomplice of those whom I have condemned.

I have subscribed this profession of mine with my own hand and sent it to Boniface [Hormisdas has “to Hormisdas”], the holy and venerable pope of the city of Rome, condemning both my predecessors and successors and all who strive to cancel the privileges of the holy Roman and apostolic Church.

From this the evidence of heavenly mercy is fully displayed [Hormisdas, Letter 80, act 5 of the Council of Constantinople under Menas], when secular rulers join matters of faith with the ordering of the state, and the prelates of the Churches, mindful of their office, carry out what belongs to their administration.

After the storms of discord, the Christian religion needed such rulers—men who, by prudent administration, would restrain the whirlwinds and restore the peace that had long wandered abroad once the storm had been driven away. Thus, in future ages, those who strive toward the examples of their purpose might unquestionably show that whatever they did, pleasing to the Lord and offered to posterity for imitation, should be attributed to them.

Let us bless the Lord, dearest brothers, that this has been granted in our days, and let us strive with all the strength of our prayers and concerns so that what has begun well through God’s aid may, with his help, be completed in every respect.

For we must hope that the remaining members, which are still divided, will hasten to the joining of the body, and that the lesser will not be separated from the greater. When your affection urges me to this through the zeal of Christian charity, it ought to follow what it invites and embrace what it advises us to love.

Since we are already sharing a similar concern for the faith, through religious patience we hope for an equal reward from our devotion to the good work. We must not yield to difficulties. Faith is not wearied by hardships; no one reaches the heights of heaven along an easy path, nor does anyone merit a reward without the exercise of labor.

Therefore, lest we grow weary in doing good, we are specially admonished, as the Psalmist also testifies: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice justice at all times” (Ps. 105). For it is not the beginning of labor that customarily finds the reward of the prize, but its completion.

Therefore, taking up the zeal of vigilance, since those who share one communion also share one belief, just as we rejoice together in the Lord over the unity of the apostolic see and the Church of Constantinople, so let us rejoice also—according to the affection with which you exhort us—in the restoration of the others [Col. 0046C]. Let us take care of the reward [perhaps: “the first reward”; thus it is read in the *Justinian* chapter], so that we preserve our faith and integrity unstained by every contamination.

For you know, dearest and most holy brother, that the bonds of the Church preserve concord and protect us from the snares of heretics; through them also the integrity [variant: “authority”] of the canons is preserved. When these things are guarded with the utmost vigilance in their strength, remedies may be hoped for.

The order of ecclesiastical rules, and the very form of justice, require that rational medicine not be denied to those who hope in kindness and fidelity, nor is anyone so estranged from humanity that cautious simplicity cannot bend him away from the rigor of strictness.

But so that you may carefully resolve this and the other complaints or errors of any age [variant: “of any matter”], dearest brother, you ought in this matter to put on my person, knowing what must be avoided in such cases, as has been stated. You must foresee everything in such a way that you do not doubt that you will have to render an account to God of this administration.

Nevertheless, ensure that those who are joined to you in communion, or who through you declare in writing their adherence to the apostolic see, also specify which petitions they have offered and what their contents were [variant: “the contents of the petitions which they have offered”] [Col. 0047A].

We must likewise keep humility in mind, while nevertheless preserving the dignity of our rank in honor, so that in us there may be neither timid humility nor proud reasoning.

May almighty God, dearest brother, guard you by his protection and bring you to the reward of the heavenly homeland with abundant fruit of souls [Col. 0048A]. May God keep you safe, most reverend brother. Amen.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [this consular date is false], in the third consulship of Justinian and that of Orestes [or: “under the consulship of Valentinus II and Orestes, most illustrious men,” in the year of Christ 530 or 533].

# In the Year of the Lord 527: Montanus, Bishop of Toledo

*(From the Collection of the Holy Fathers of Toledo.)*

[Col. 0047]

## INTRODUCTION

[Col. 0047B]

### NOTICE TO THE READER

We begin, excellent reader, with the edition of Montanus among the holy Fathers of Toledo, because throughout all earlier antiquity he is the first—not the first to publish literary monuments, but the first whose writings have survived to us. For who would doubt that learned prelates preceded Montanus in the see of Toledo, men distinguished by their excellence in writing?

Concerning Audentius, whom no one doubts to have been bishop of Toledo, the testimony of Gennadius, chapter 14, is known in these words:

“Audentius, a Spanish bishop, wrote against the Manichaeans and Sabellians, and against the Arians, who are now called Bonosiacs, a book which he entitled *On the Faith against All Heretics*. In it he showed that the antiquity of the Son of God was coeternal with the Father, and that he did not then receive the beginning of his divinity from God the Father when, with God as maker, he was conceived and born as man from the blessed Virgin Mary.”

Trithemius calls this same man learned in the Scriptures and endowed with talent. But this work of Audentius, like those of others, has perished.

Montanus is therefore the first to appear whose letters, written in the sixth century and praised by Saint Ildefonsus, have survived the ravages of time and have been found in various manuscripts. They were first published by D. Garcia Loaysa, then by the eminent Aguirre in his *Collection of the Councils of Spain*, and finally by Father Flórez, collated, as he himself states, with a great many Gothic manuscript codices. They were presented much more accurately than in the earlier editions in the appendix to volume V of *Sacred Spain* [Col. 0048B].

We have followed his edition, without recording any variant readings from our own sources, since we possessed no manuscript against which to collate the letters. The variants, therefore, have been transcribed from Flórez’s own edition. The notes placed at the foot of the page we took from the eminent Cardinal Aguirre, although we have supplemented them with our own observations at the end, in order to shed whatever light we can on the most obscure passage of the second letter, which has caused difficulty for every editor up to the present.

We did not think it pointless to place a life of Montanus before his letters, so that we might first give an account of the author before presenting his writings. We have followed the same method in publishing the other Fathers.

In the case of Montanus, however, because the eulogy written by Saint Ildefonsus is shorter, we have woven together a somewhat longer account of his life, collecting what we found written by other historians.

Farewell.

[Col. 0047C]

## LIFE OF MONTANUS

Montanus, the successor of Celsus as bishop of the Church of Toledo [Col. 0047D], flourished during the reign of Amalaric, king of the Goths, and presided over that Church from the year 522 until 531, according to the succession of the bishops of Toledo recorded by D. Juan Bautista Pérez, canon of Toledo, and by the illustrious Loaysa and Aguirre. We shall provide a fuller and corrected version of this succession at the end of volume II.

From Saint Ildefonsus we understand how brightly he shone with many and great virtues. He was endowed with the highest courage of spirit, most eloquent in speech, most prudent in governance, worthy of every highest honor, and especially commended and blessed for the innocence of his life.

Indeed, the eminence of his holiness is amply confirmed by an ancient and trustworthy tradition, which in the time of Saint [Col. 0048C] Ildefonsus was almost universally reported: that the most holy prelate, attacked by a vile accusation from envious men, vindicated his innocence by a remarkable miracle, holding burning coals in his own garments for as long as he himself performed the sacred mysteries, without the garments meanwhile suffering even the slightest damage or the fire losing any of its force.

We read that in later centuries Saint Anselm and other most holy men, inspired by the Holy Spirit, used a similar purification.

The eloquence of Montanus and the splendor of his learning are sufficiently evident from the two letters that have survived to us. The first was written to the dearest brothers and sons of the territory of Palencia, the second to the distinguished Lord Thuribius. They are also evident from the Second Council of Toledo, over which he presided [Col. 0049A]. Anyone who carefully reads its canons will unquestionably notice in them a certain purity of speech redolent of the golden ages and exceedingly rare in the times of the Goths.

There is no doubt that the name of Montanus was illustrious throughout all Spain. The fame of his wisdom spread so widely that the Second Synod of Toledo, held in the year 527, is entitled in this manner: “Synod held in the city of Toledo in the presence of Montanus, bishop.” Moreover, the Fathers repeatedly mention him in the final chapter, asserting that the following council was to be summoned by Montanus and held in his presence.

Eighty-three years after the aforesaid synod had passed, at the Council of Carthage held under King Gundemar in the year 610, the Fathers refer to the acts of the Second Council of Toledo in these words: “at Saint Montanus.” These words, added to what was said above, clearly demonstrate that not only Montanus’s wisdom but also his holiness was exceptionally renowned in Spain.

Although he is not entered in the calendar of the saints of Toledo, he cannot be deprived of the encomium of Saint Ildephonsus, who calls him “the most blessed priest,” nor of the acclamation of the Carthaginian Fathers, who designate him “Saint Montanus.”

Although he flourished in praise of every virtue, he appeared especially to burn with zeal for the house of the Lord. He continually fought for the preservation of the orthodox faith in its entirety and for the restoration of the discipline of the sacred canons, against the monsters of error and the depraved practices spreading through Spain. [Col. 0049C] This is attested by the already mentioned letter, which breathes zeal throughout: whether he sharply rebukes the Palentine priests who prepared chrism and summoned bishops of another jurisdiction to consecrate basilicas; or reproves the frivolity and folly of those who, while rejecting the abominable heresy of Priscillian, continued to honor his name; or when he entrusts his authority to the most reputable priest Thuribius in order to suppress these evils. Finally, the reverence with which he regarded the admonitions of the Roman pontiffs, and the zeal with which he ensured that the canons of the holy councils were observed, may be inferred, not implausibly, from the second letter; we shall explain this more fully in the notes to that letter. For when a certain bishop, unlawfully elected and ordained without the knowledge of Celsus, the metropolitan who preceded Montanus, or of the bishops of the province, had seized the Church of Palencia, Montanus, after being raised to the see of Toledo, did not permit the guilty man to remain unpunished for long, nor could he be persuaded by the pleas of many to relax anything of the severity of the decrees of the holy Council of Nicaea.

All these things commend Montanus’s virtue all the more, since it is still more remarkable that so wholly upright a shepherd, and one so firmly attached to the sound teaching of his Fathers, flourished at a time when the Arian heresy had occupied almost the whole of Spain, sitting boastfully upon the throne together with the Gothic kings. Yet he did not hide in some remote corner; rather, in the very heart of Spain, before the heretical ruler and the entire crowd of Arian courtiers, [Col. 0050A] he offered such conspicuous testimonies of piety and tireless devotion to the defense of orthodox religion. From this, everyone can see that the greatest glory redounds to this holy metropolitan Church of Toledo; and from it all will understand how deservedly Eufemius, the fourth bishop of this see after Montanus, called it Catholic in his subscription to the Third Council of Toledo: namely, because it had always had pastors who, like Montanus, never departed from the right and orthodox Catholic faith, even amid the deepest darkness of error and the greatest storms of persecution.

Montanus died in the last year of King Amalaric, in the ninth year of his episcopate, in the year 531 of the Lord’s Incarnation. To this year, therefore, should be assigned what many historians, both Spanish and foreign, report concerning the plundering of [Col. 0050B] Toledo by the Gauls, after their victory over the impious and cruel Amalaric, the persecutor of the Catholic Clotilda. For this reason, we do not rashly suppose that the most holy bishop was worn down less by old age than by grief: when he saw the city crushed by so great a calamity, and his spouse, the Church—dearer to him than all his life—stripped of her possessions; when as many as sixty sacred vessels were carried away, together with fifteen patens and twenty Gospel-book covers, all fashioned from the purest gold and adorned with the most precious gems; then, exhausted by so great a catastrophe, he closed his eyes, and that most grievous event hastened his death. As a final crown, we give the words of Saint Ildephonsus, in which he expressed the encomium of so great a man, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 3.

[Col. 0050C] “After Celsus, Montanus held the chair of the city of Toledo, the first see of the province of Carthage. A man distinguished both by the virtue of the Spirit and by the appropriateness of his eloquence, he retained and arranged the governance of his office according to a fitting and heavenly law, as well as in due order. He wrote two letters filled with the discipline of ecclesiastical utility. In one of them, addressed to the inhabitants of Palencia, he is said to prohibit with great authority that priests should prepare chrism and that bishops should consecrate churches of another diocese in another territory, affirming through testimonies of the sacred Scriptures that this must not be done at all. He also rejects and reproaches those who loved the sect of Priscillian, although they did not practice the same things, because they nevertheless retained his memory with affection; he recalls that, in the books of the most blessed Thuribius sent to Pope Leo, the same heresy of the Priscillianists had been exposed, convicted, and properly rejected. In another letter, addressed to the devout Thuribius, he praises him because he had destroyed the worship of idols, and entrusts to him the authority of priestly vigor, by which he might restrain with vigorous rebuke priests who prepared chrism and bishops who consecrated churches of another jurisdiction in another diocese. This man, according to a very ancient and trustworthy account, is said to have held burning coals in his garment for so long, to refute the accusation brought against him, until he himself had completed the entire celebration of Mass before the sacred altar of his see. When the solemn rites had been completed, neither had the coals lost their fire nor had the garment lost its appearance. Then, when thanks had been rendered to God, the simple nature of fire exposed both the detestable falsehood of the accuser and the innocence of the most blessed priest. He was illustrious during the reign of King Amalaric. He held the dignity of the pontificate for nine years.”

[Col. 0051A]

## THE LETTERS OF MONTANUS (C, S)

### FIRST LETTER

[Note: In this letter Montanus, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Toledo, severely rebukes the fact that certain priests of the territory of Palencia, whether ignorant or rash, prepared sacred chrism, although this belongs only to bishops; furthermore, that foreign bishops were admitted for the consecration of basilicas; and finally, that some held in honor the infamous and repeatedly thunder-struck sect of the Priscillianists. He also advises them to read the books of Bishop Theoribius written against that sect. We have said enough about all these matters above, in the notes to the Council of Zaragoza, the First Council of Toledo, and the general Spanish council, as well as in the famous letter of Saint Leo the pope to Thuribius, bishop of Astorga. [Col. 0051D] Cardinal Aguirre, from volume III of the *Greatest Collection of All the Councils of Spain*.]

To the most beloved lords, brothers and sons of the territory of Palencia, Montanus the bishop: eternal salvation in the Lord.

#### I

The most eminent [Note: Another manuscript: “the most experienced.” Loays.: “the most devout bishops of the Lord.”] shepherds of all the Churches of the Lord are shaken by that terrifying admonition spoken through the prophet Ezekiel (chapter 33), under the name of the watchman. It says: “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. Therefore, hearing the word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me. When I say to the wicked man, ‘Wicked one, you shall surely die,’ and you do not announce it to him, nor speak so that he may turn from his wicked way and live, he himself indeed shall die in his iniquity, but I shall require his blood from your hand,” and so forth. The order of this passage shows what must be sought from the minds of the one who admonishes and the one who is admonished. [Note: The Gerundensis and Urgellensis manuscripts read *anima*, “soul,” rather than *animis*, “minds.”]

#### II

Moved, therefore, by this saying, and knowing that I have undertaken the necessity of this office, I have taken care to ensure that Christ does not seek from my hand the soul of anyone who has been lost. This is especially so because ancient custom has granted the city of Toledo the privilege of a metropolitan see, and because the priest of this city is concerned not only with the care of parishes but also with that of cities. Therefore, as the Apostle says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in charity and a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Cor. 4:21).

For a novel presumption on the part of the priests presiding over you has struck our ears—if it can be called novel at all, rather than detestable, since it is proved to have crept in at no time from the beginning of the Catholic faith until now: namely, that an ignorant priest should presume to prepare for himself the chrism which the invocation of the Triune Divinity, through the hands of the highest pontiff, has been accustomed to sanctify. If this is due to negligence, such a priest ought not to have been so foolish; if it is due to presumption, who does not know that the man who introduces, at the world’s old age, an unheard-of practice contrary to religion is a schismatic? [Col. 0052B] [Note: Loays. reads “judges” rather than “introduces.”]

#### III

Let the most sacred Book of Numbers be turned over in your hands, O priests (11:16), in which the honor of your office was inaugurated in the persons of the seventy elders; and you will discover what matters have been granted to you by prerogative. God wished you to be helpers of our labor, in the second degree of dignity; he did not permit you to be violators of certain sacred things. [Note: Loays. reads: “The Lord wished you to be his helpers.”] Thus Nadab and Abihu, when they offered strange fire (Lev. 10:1–2)—that is, fire not assigned to their office—were consumed by divine fire. Thus Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, envying Moses, who by the grace of God enjoyed the divine utterances, and saying:

[Note: “The Lord has spoken not only to you, for the entire congregation is holy.” Montanus cites these words from Numbers 16 according to the Old Latin translation, which the Church used until the Vulgate later began to prevail almost everywhere in the time of Saint Gregory the Great. The earlier words, however, are not found in the Septuagint, where one reads only: “Let it be enough for you, because the whole congregation, all are holy, and the Lord is among them” (*Εσχέτω ἐν ὑμῖν, ὅτι πᾶσα ἡ συναγωγὴ πάντες ἁγίοι καὶ ἐν αὐτοῖς Κύριος*). Nor do they occur in the Hebrew text according to Pagninus’s translation, or in the Chaldean Paraphrase. I therefore have no doubt that the earlier words, “The Lord has spoken not only to you,” were cited from the Old Translation, which Flaminius Nobilius began to restore in the preceding century with Herculean courage and incredible labor—if only he had also completed it. See what we prefixed in volume I, dissertation IV, no. 20 and following.]

Saint Ildephonsus also mentions this very letter of Montanus and offers several further praises of him in Book IV of *On Illustrious Men*, saying:

“After Celsus, Montanus held the chair of the city of Toledo, the first see of the province of Carthage. A man distinguished both by the virtue of the Spirit and by the appropriateness of his eloquence, he tempered and arranged the governance of his office according to a fitting and heavenly law, as well as in due order. He wrote two letters filled with the discipline of ecclesiastical utility. In one, addressed to the inhabitants of Palencia, he is said to prohibit with great authority that priests prepare chrism and that bishops consecrate churches of another diocese in another territory, affirming through testimonies of the sacred Scriptures that this must not be done at all. He also rejects and reproaches those who loved the sect of Priscillian, although they did not practice the same things, because they nevertheless retained his memory with affection; he recalls that, in the books of the most blessed Theoribius sent to Pope Leo, the same heresy of the Priscillianists had been exposed, convicted, and properly rejected.”

Thus far Ildephonsus concerning the letter mentioned above. Immediately afterward he mentions another letter of the same Montanus, which we now present. [Col. 0052D] Thus far Cardinal Aguirre.

“Not only to you has the Lord spoken, for the entire congregation is holy” (Num. 16:3). A new death of new destruction [Note: Loays. reads “preaching” rather than “destruction.”] came upon the new schismatics, so that the earth, with hungry mouth, swallowed without satisfaction those whom divine indignation had condemned. [Col. 0052C] Why should I mention Uzziah (2 Chron. 26:16 and following), who, not content with royal insignia and unwilling to refrain from exercising the priestly office, was lifted up against right and law by the arrogance of power [Note: The Gerundensis and Urgellensis manuscripts read this way; others have “clad in power.”] and prepared to offer the expiatory sacrifice, which was due to priests alone? He was so covered with leprosy by heavenly vengeance that from then until his death he remained deprived of the office of priest and kingdom. [Note: P. Flórez printed the text from a manuscript. We think it should read: “that he remained deprived of the office of priest and kingdom until his death,” a reading confirmed by Aguirre’s edition: “so that he lacked the office of priest and kingdom, and, hated,” etc.]

Likewise, when Uzzah, insofar as it depended on him, sought to support the Ark of God in devout service, as the oxen kicked and the Ark might otherwise fall, he was struck and destroyed by a divine blow (2 Kings 6:7). God thereby wished to show that, for no reason whatsoever—not even under the pretext of humility—should those who presume to do so touch the divine offices and heavenly sacraments when the office does not belong to them.

#### IV

Let those who think that something is lawful for themselves which they do not fail to recognize as unlawful for others take care—yes, let them take care—lest a punishment like that of those whom we have mentioned strike them. [Note: Loays. reads “do not know”; Flórez, “do not know.”] Or do you perhaps not know the regulations of the holy Fathers and the synodal constitutions, by which parish priests are ordered [Note: Flórez inserts *ut*, “that,” from the same manuscripts; we do not approve this unless *praecipiuntur* is changed to *praecipitur*, “it is ordered,” though no manuscript has that reading] to request chrism annually from the bishop presiding over them, not through inferior persons but either personally or through the wardens of the shrines? I believe that those who ordered it to be requested entirely removed the power of consecrating it.

Your charity will therefore take care that, after this prohibition issued in our humility, until the Lord provides you with your customary bishop, no one presume to repeat what is forbidden and begin to endure the more severe censure of ecclesiastical discipline. Let each person use the privilege granted to his own rank, which he knows to belong to the order of priesthood; let no wicked minister assume what belongs to the highest pontificate. Whoever, after this admonition, is found in any way to have done such things must know that he is condemned under the unbreakable bond of anathema. In this matter, however, no small measure of humanity is being granted him, since for now we allow him to pass unpunished.

#### V

Certainly, if the Lord wills, when the time of the Paschal festival arrives, if it is impossible for you to come to request it, you ought to inform us by sending your letters [Note: Other codices read “you will be obliged to inform us”], and we shall be able voluntarily to transmit to you the grace of this sacred liquid, provided that nothing unlawful is presumed. [Note: The Gerundensis and Urgellensis manuscripts read “provided that unlawful things are not presumed”; Loays.’s edition omits *praesumatur*.]

#### VI

We have likewise learned that bishops of another jurisdiction are invited by you for the consecration of basilicas. Although they are joined to us in Christ by the bond of the one faith, they are nevertheless not recognized as fitting either the privileges of the province or the interests of the Lord’s affairs, since a report of this kind has already reached the person concerned. [Note: Loays. reads “has already been brought forward.”] We have therefore determined, as a salutary regulation, that whenever such a necessity arises, you must inform us by letter, and that either through us or through whichever of our brothers and fellow bishops seems appropriate to us, the consecration of the churches may, with God’s favor, be celebrated.

#### VII

Furthermore, we know that the utterly depraved sect of the Priscillianists is honored among you, both in its deeds and in its name. I ask: what sort of madness is it to drift needlessly into love for one whom you do not wish to imitate in practice? For, to bring a few of his impurities to your attention—apart from the things in which he burst forth profanely against the Divinity and blasphemed with sacrilegious mouth—a whole mass of every vice flowed together in him as into a cesspool of filth, so that, shamelessly adulterous, he might rob his female followers of their chastity. [Note: Loays. has this reading; Flórez, from the Gerundensis manuscript, printed “the unrestrained adulterer might break out.”] And, to reach the effect of his unspeakable crime more easily, the accounts also attribute to him the practice of magic.

What, finally, does any faithful soul venerate in this man that is consistent with religion? He was not only rejected by holy priests; even worldly rulers condemned him by the justice of their laws, in accordance with the nature of the crime mentioned above. [Note: The reading is Loays.’s. Flórez, from his manuscripts, printed: “What, nevertheless, does anyone venerate in this man?”—not without error.]

#### VIII

Anyone who reads the books of the most blessed and most devout man, Bishop Thoribius [Note: Flórez, from the manuscripts; Loays. has “Theoribius”], sent to the holy Pope Leo of the city of Rome, will learn more fully what kind of man he was. In them he explained and exposed this filthy heresy, and brought into the open what had been hidden in darkness and covered by a cloud of perfidy. [Col. 0054C] From those books, the pious reader will discover how he may guard against the sacrilegious and what answer he may make to them. [Note: This is the reading of the Urgellensis manuscript; Loays.’s edition has “is found.”]

Therefore, I ask you, condemn and anathematize the perfidy together with its author, hold fast to the rule of the true faith, and take care to make yourselves more cautious concerning all the matters written above. In this way, condemnation may not come upon me for my silence, and so that you may provide yourselves with the greatest fruit of obedience before Christ our Savior and God. The peace of the Lord be with you all. Amen.

### SECOND LETTER

[Note: Saint Ildephonsus mentions this letter in the cited book *On Illustrious Men*, while discussing Montanus, bishop of the Church of Toledo. After speaking of his preceding letter, as we saw in the notes to it, he adds: “He also wrote another letter to the devout Thuribius, in which, praising him because he had destroyed the worship of idols, he entrusts to him the authority of priestly vigor, by which he might restrain with vigorous rebuke priests who prepared chrism and bishops who consecrated churches of another jurisdiction in another diocese.” Immediately afterward he adds his notable praise in these words: “This man, according to a very ancient and trustworthy account, is said to have held burning coals in his garments for so long, to refute the charge of infamy, until he himself had completed the entire celebration of Mass before the sacred altar of his see. When the solemn rites had been completed, neither had the coals lost their fire nor had the garment lost its appearance. Then, when thanks had been rendered to God, the simple nature of fire exposed both the detestable falsehood of the accuser and the innocence of the most blessed priest. He was illustrious during the reign of King Amalaric. He held the dignity for nine years.” Aguirre.]

To the distinguished lord and foremost worshiper of Christ, my lord [Col. 0055A] and son Thuribius:

[Note: Who this Thuribius was, to whom Montanus writes, is a sufficiently complicated question. Some maintain that there was only one Theoribius, or Thuribius, to whom everything read in this letter applies: both the books written against the Priscillianists in the time of Saint Pope Leo and the deeds and preaching against the admirers of that sect, undertaken at the urging of Montanus, bishop of Toledo. But Saint Ildephonsus himself easily proves this opinion false, for in the same place, *On Illustrious Men*, he openly distinguishes between the two Thuribii. Speaking of the letters of Montanus mentioned above, he says: “He recalls that in the books of the most blessed Thuribius sent to Pope Leo, the same heresy of the Priscillianists had been exposed, convicted, and properly rejected. He also wrote another letter to the devout Thuribius, in which, praising him because he had destroyed the worship of idols, he entrusts to him the authority of priestly vigor,” and so forth, as we wrote shortly above.

Here Ildephonsus plainly distinguishes two Thuribii: one a bishop and contemporary of Saint Pope Leo, to whom he sent books written against the Priscillianists; the other later, not a bishop but a devout man and preacher against idolatry, to whom the later Montanus, bishop of Toledo, wrote this letter while he was alive. It is therefore clear that there were two Thuribii, not one.

The same is clearly demonstrated by the *Chronography*, according to which the bishop Thuribius who wrote books against the Priscillianists and sent them to Pope Leo flourished in Leo’s own time and therefore around the middle of the fifth century, since Leo presided over the apostolic see from the year 440 [Col. 0055D] to 441. I omit the fact that the same Thuribius, at Pope Leo’s command, held a council in Spain in the year 447, as is well known to everyone.

Thuribius—or rather Theoribius—to whom this letter was written was much later and flourished at the beginning of the following century. Since Montanus wrote to him while he was alive and participated in and subscribed to the Second Council of Toledo in the Spanish era 565, that is, in the year 527, the fifth year of King Amalaric, and since Saint Ildephonsus says that he was illustrious during the reign of King Amalaric, it plainly follows that this Theoribius was approximately eighty years later and therefore entirely different from the earlier Thuribius.

From this it is clear that Loaysa, although extremely learned, was mistaken in the notes to this very letter when he wrote: “Whether this Thuribius was that monk whom Ildephonsus mentions in *On Illustrious Men*, in the Life of Montanus; or another notary of the apostolic see sent by Blessed Pope Leo into the regions of Spain to eradicate the Priscillian heresy, as is clear from the opening of the First Council of Braga—for such men were called regional notaries; or whether he was the bishop of Palencia and Astorga, is not sufficiently certain.” I accept the last opinion, since it is evident from the first letter that he both wrote very learned books against the Priscillianists and is called by Montanus in the second letter a priest, that is, a bishop: “so that you may use,” he says, “the authority of the most severe priest.”

Loaysa was mistaken, I say, since Saint Ildephonsus’s testimony sufficiently establishes that this Theoribius was the man whom he mentions in the Life of Montanus: Montanus writes to him as a contemporary approximately eighty years after the other Thuribius, whether notary or even bishop, had flourished in the time of Saint Leo and had written the books mentioned above.

Montanus himself also supports the same truth of the matter in both of the letters mentioned above.
