In the first, addressed to the brothers and sons of the territory of Palencia, when speaking of the errors and vices of Priscillian, he says: “Anyone who reads the published books of the most blessed and devout man Thuribius—not Theoribius—bishop, sent to the holy Pope Leo of the city of Rome, will learn more fully what kind of man he was; in them he explained and exposed this filthy heresy and brought into the open what had been hidden in darkness and covered by a cloud of perfidy.” Here Montanus speaks of those books as having been written long ago by the bishop Thuribius in the time of Saint Pope Leo.

In this later letter, however, he gives the heading: “To the distinguished lord, foremost worshiper of Christ, my lord and son Thuribius, Montanus the bishop.” Here he calls him “son,” not “brother,” as he should have done if he were a bishop; and he addresses him as a living man at a time approximately eighty years after the Thuribius who had been a writer [Col. 0056D] and bishop of Astorga had flourished. Nor does Loaysa’s argument help him, namely, that Montanus says in this passage: “so that you may use the authority of the most severe priest.” From this it follows that Theoribius was already counted among the priests, or presbyters, and that Montanus, as metropolitan, further delegates to him his own authority for restraining such offenses.

Moreover, whenever this letter speaks of bishops, it calls them not sons but brothers: “Our brothers,” it says, “bishops of another jurisdiction.” In the preceding letter, likewise, it does not call bishops priests, but “highest pontiffs,” and calls their dignity “the highest pontificate.” I pass over many other points by which the same conclusion could be confirmed. But whether this Theoribius was at that time a bishop or not, his distinction from the writer and bishop Thuribius of Astorga is manifest. Thus far Aguirre.]

Montanus the bishop.

#### I

We have both known and approved you as a pupil of the Catholic faith and a friend of holy religion, while you were still active in worldly affairs. For while you yet flourished in the world, your life shone forth with such distinction that, according to the Lord’s command, you did not refuse to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and with devoted mind you rendered to God the things that are his. Rightly, therefore, especially in this province, I shall call you an author of divine worship.

Do you imagine how great a reward remains for you with God, through whose diligence, or persistence [Note: Loaysa reads “and persistence”], both the error of idolatry has departed and the detestable and shameful sect of the Priscillianists has withered? If only they would finally cease to honor even his name [Note: The Gerundensis and Urgellensis manuscripts read “his name still”], whose works they know to have collapsed through your admonition.

For what should I say about the faith of earthly lords? You devoted your labor to them in such a way that you brought the fierce spirits of those dwelling with you [Col. 0056A] to a salutary rule and the norm of regular discipline. [Note: The Gerundensis and Urgellensis manuscripts preserve this reading.] I have therefore taken care to indicate to your Eminence what has reached us from the Palentine assembly, so that through your rebuke this wicked presumption may more easily be quieted in the future.

#### II

As has been reported to us, certain priests, with rash audacity, presume not so much to consecrate sacred things as to violate them. They unhesitatingly assume, by I know not what device—or shall I call it madness?—the right of consecrating chrism, which has been unheard of among men of their order throughout all the centuries from the beginning of the Catholic faith and belongs only to the highest pontiffs. I do not believe that the most devout conscience of your Eminence is unaware how sacrilegious this is. I therefore hope that, to weaken this very excess, you will use the authority of the most severe priest and restrain with stricter rebuke those who presume to commit so great an offense. If, after receiving an admonition, they presume to repeat their crime, their obstinacy shall be condemned by an appropriate sentence. [Col. 0057A]

#### III

We have likewise learned that, because of the need to consecrate basilicas, our brothers, bishops of another jurisdiction, are invited and assemble in these places. Although throughout the whole world there is one bridal chamber of Christ, and its bishops are joined together in one clasp by the union of charity and faith, nevertheless, this privilege—

[Note: Cardinal Aguirre has offered absolutely no comment on the meaning of this sentence. Yet its extreme difficulty, surrounded as it is by the densest darkness, has greatly troubled almost all the editors of these letters. The context is most corrupt at this point. How it should be remedied is indeed the task, the labor.

Padilla thought that a fragment from another letter had been read after these words and appended here through the incompetence of the copyists. But no plausible reason persuades us of this.

The learned Father Flórez thinks that the preceding sentence can easily be restored if, after the words “joined together in the union of faith,” these further words are added from the preceding letter, in which Montanus concludes a similar sentence as follows: “nevertheless, they are not recognized as fitting either the privileges of the province or the interests of the Lord’s affairs.” We approve this conjecture. But we cannot equally approve what he adds to explain the convenient meaning of the word “privilege” at this point.

He supposes that Celsus and the other bishops of Carpetania and Celtiberia had perhaps been appointed by the bishop of Palencia as executors of his will, in order to carry out some pious intention of his—I do not know what—and that they had asked something of Montanus, the bishop of Palencia, contrary to this, and had therefore been rejected by him. “For,” he says, “it is not apparent in what other way an inferior bishop and suffragan could be said to have granted a privilege to his metropolitan and fellow-provincial bishops.”

The explanation is attractive in wording, but its force is plainly weakened by what follows. Montanus continues: “And certainly we granted to the same man the municipalities—that is, Segovia, Britablo, and Cauca—not indeed reasonably, but on account of the dignity of his name.” This manner of speaking clearly indicates that what precedes must refer to the same matter. He would not write “we granted to the same man” unless he had previously spoken of the same fellow bishop.

After carefully considering all these points, we have taken another path toward explaining the passage.]

We therefore think that *privilege* should not be understood in its common meaning, but rather as an unjust action undertaken against another person’s right, so that *privilege* has the same force as an injury or harm inflicted upon another. We know from Dufresne’s *Glossary of Medieval and Low Latin Writers*, under the word *PRIVILEGIUM*, that this word was used more than once in that sense in those times. He writes:

“*Privilegium*, the same as the foregoing *pravilegium*—that is, a word used in a bad sense, meaning something contrary to law—… *Life of Saint Dunstan*, volume IV of May, p. 356: ‘Through the spiritual womb of sacred baptism the Church regenerated him from the privilege of the first parent.’”

Carpentier, in the new glossary or supplement to Dufresne, likewise has: “*Privilegium*, the same as tyranny.” Saint Eulogius, Book II of the *Memorial of the Saints*, chapter 1, says: “Abd al-Rahman occupied almost the whole of Iberia by a dreadful privilege.” In this sense, when someone arrogantly assumes another person’s proper right and violates it, he may be said to have inflicted a *privilege* upon that person.

Having set this out, we advance our conjecture as all the more probable because it agrees remarkably with everything written at length about this whole matter by the same distinguished author in the second edition of volume VIII of *Sacred Spain*, p. 18. As far as we can conjecture, the matter occurred as follows.

When the see of Palencia was vacant, a certain man had been elected and ordained bishop of that Church contrary to the discipline of the sacred canons. Pope Innocent I, wishing to restore that discipline, which had collapsed in Spain, had admonished the Fathers of the Second Council of Toledo by letter [Note: See volume III of Cardinal Aguirre’s *Collection of the Councils*] to watch carefully that no one should be elected or ordained bishop by anyone other than the bishops of the same province, with the authority of the metropolitan, as had already been decreed by canon 4 of the Council of Nicaea.

This man, then, unlawfully elected and ordained and an invader of the Church of Palencia, had inflicted a great “privilege” upon Celsus, the metropolitan, and the other bishops of the province. Montanus himself, an outstanding zealot for the sacred canons, expelled him from the see he had unjustly occupied, in accordance with canon 6 of the same Council of Nicaea, which provided that one who had been made bishop contrary to the judgment of the metropolitan ought not to be a bishop.

Nevertheless, he did not punish him so harshly that he failed to take account of his episcopal ordination and dignity. Instead, he designated for him three municipalities in the same diocese, whose care he should undertake and from which he might at the same time receive a suitable means of support.

When these things had happened, the Palentines who supported that man—for he would not have undertaken so great a crime without the support of many—brought their pleas to Montanus. They begged him to restore the aforesaid fellow bishop to the see of Palencia. We think that this was the petition which Montanus calls wicked in this letter, since it was contrary to the severity of the sacred canons. Without doubt he had clearly explained this very point to them in the copies which he says he sent them.

At the same time, so that they might understand how mercifully he had dealt with the man, Montanus adds that he had assigned those municipalities to him not reasonably—that is, moved by some merit of his—but solely because of his episcopal dignity. Moreover, lest the Palentines should suppose that those municipalities would henceforth remain permanently separated from the Church of Palencia, or lest the beneficiary, elevated by indulgence, should think himself a proper shepherd rather than merely a delegate, he adds that this had been granted to him only while he lived.

Nor does the fact that we read that Segovia already had its own bishop in the year 589, who subscribed to the Third Council of Toledo, cause us to abandon this conjecture. Although it may have been Montanus’s intention that those three municipalities should in no way be separated from the Church of Palencia, it could nevertheless have happened that the people of Segovia, finding a favorable opportunity after that first bishop had died, requested a pastor of their own to succeed him, and obtained one without much difficulty—especially since the diocese of Palencia was enclosed within such extensive boundaries that it could not conveniently be governed by one shepherd.

We read that many divisions of dioceses of this sort were made in that century for a similar reason in the province of Galicia, so that, with the episcopal boundaries made narrower, the needs of each flock might be better provided for. Let this suffice, then, for shedding some light, insofar as possible, upon a most obscure passage. Meanwhile, we arrogate nothing to ourselves, but hope that others may devise better explanations.]
to our predecessor, and likewise to our lords and brothers, the bishops of Carpetania or Celtiberia, [Col. 0058A] your fellow bishop [Note: [Col. 0057D] Thus Loays. Flórez, from Ger. and Urg., printed *your bishop also*.] sent in copies to your Charity, so that you might know what outcome an improper petition could have had [Note: [Col. 0058D] Loays: *effect*].

IV. And indeed we granted to him the municipalities—namely Segovia, Brittablo, and Cauca—not, to be sure, reasonably, but out of regard for the dignity of his name, lest the blessing bestowed should be cheapened by the person’s wandering away. Know that this was granted to him only for as long as he lived. We therefore wish you to take care that you do not in any way neglect the ancient custom. But if this admonition of ours has achieved nothing among you, it will be necessary for us thereafter to report the matter to the ears of our Lord, and likewise to bring it to the attention of our son Ergani; and the commands or judicial severity of his high authority will punish such an attempt with the utmost rigor, not without harm to you. [Col. 0059A] For, by the Lord’s granting, his piety is so great that he will permit nothing to be changed in what he is shown to have preserved as the ancient right. May the divine Trinity guard you. Amen.

[ELEUTHERIUS OF TOURNAI.]

[Col. 0059]

THE LIFE OF SAINT ELEUTHERIUS, ARRANGED BY GUIBERT OF THE ORDER OF MINORS.

(From the Library of the Fathers and a manuscript.) (G, S)

[Col. 0059A] PROLOGUE.—1. To the reverend father and lord John, venerable bishop of Tournai by the grace of God, Guibert, by origin a Tournai man, by profession a Minorite, in merit the least of men, [Note: [Col. 0059C] The following words are lacking in the printed edition; in their place appears *sal*.] that he may be armed with the spirit of counsel as wisely [Col. 0059B] as he may be animated with courage.

Reverend lord, you have asked me either to arrange the deeds and praises of Christ’s glorious confessor Eleutherius, or to explain them for the present and future generations with a more careful polish or a better style. It is a pious request, by which a later age may perpetuate the holiness of so great a shepherd through its celebration of him, and the present generation, by following in his footsteps, may be inflamed more greatly to love God and neighbor. These are the foods which Sacred Scripture declares to be found in the fallow fields of the Fathers (Prov. 13:23), while posterity is instructed by the examples of the saints.

I know that the origin of this request derives from the glory of Christ, who is glorified in his saints; from the special grace by which you love in Christ, with particular sincerity, the bishop and patron of your city; from the pastoral foresight by which you care for your clergy; and from the singular goodwill which one so great and eminent shows toward me, such a tiny little man, almost nothing. Thus you virtually compel me either to chatter in trifles or, rather, to write foolishly.

While I therefore measure myself inwardly in my own mind, I am pulled and led in different directions by uncertain feelings. For amid the continual anxieties of reading and the impenetrable labyrinths of questions, the models of discourse and the axioms of counsel into which I am constantly plunged and transformed, it is hard for me to write, and harder still to resist the command of so great a dignity. Why should I not call your requests a command?

[Col. 0060B] Not because a powerful man supplicates with a bared sword, but because the long-standing intimacy between us, our common citizenship, our homeland, kinship, closeness of blood and affinity, and all the other things of this kind which either win reverence or preserve it once won, demand and require that, desiring the favor of your will, I should judge the inclination of your affection to be a command and an order.

Yet you would more usefully have sought the fulfillment of this from several persons advanced in age, distinguished in faith, renowned for their works, ready in speech, retentive in memory, and, in short, superior in every endowment of lofty merit—men whom you have at hand both among the number of your canons and in the various communities of monks throughout your diocese. For the mediocrity of my eloquence produces only very meager crops, and in expressing the glory of so great a confessor it grows heavy with no fruit from a second harvest.

Thus, deprived of time and occupied in mind—one whose inclination is more toward humility than toward the pleasure of polished words, and more toward historical narrative than toward literary convention—I do what you command. I offer you the sequence of the holy pontiff’s life and, as I had been asked on your behalf, send you the office with its appendices. To make the tenor of the page clearer, let it be divided under certain headings, if you please. [Note: [Col. 0059C] We add these here and afterward write the bare headings in the margin. [Col. 0059D] [We, in the heading of the notes, use the preceding numerals. EDIT.] For the rest, we distinguish them according to our custom. The author had divided the work into these headings:

Chapter I. On the origin of the city of Tournai.  
Chapter II. On the arrival and preaching of Blessed Piatus at Tournai.  
Chapter III. On the relics and seed of Blessed Piatus and the birth of Blessed Eleutherius.  
Chapter IV. On the good character of Blessed Eleutherius.  
Chapter V. On the proscription of the faithful and of Blessed Eleutherius from Tournai.  
Chapter VI. On the advancement of Blessed Eleutherius to the bishopric of Tournai.  
Chapter VII. On Blanda, who tempted the bishop, and on her death and restoration to life.  
Chapter VIII. On the manner in which the people of Tournai were converted to the faith through Blessed Eleutherius.  
Chapter IX. On the miracles performed by Blessed Eleutherius at that time.  
Chapter X. On the miracles performed at the exposition of the holy relics when the Saint had returned from Rome.  
Chapter XI. On the conflict he had with heretics.  
Chapter XII. On the plots and wounds inflicted on the Saint by heretics.  
Chapter XIII. On his final words and exhortations. [Col. 0060D]  
Chapter XIV. On Satan, whom he saw standing beside him when he lay dying.  
Chapter XV. On the blind and mute woman whom he illuminated and healed.  
Chapter XVI. On the restoration of the episcopal see.  
Chapter XVII. On the revelation of Blessed Eleutherius and the death of Thecla.  
Chapter XVIII. On the raising of the widow’s son.  
Chapter XIX. On the death of a woman and the raising of a young man at the same solemnity.  
Chapter XX. On other miracles performed on the same day.  
Chapter XXI. On the binding of Saint Feriolus when he visited the Saint’s tomb.  
Chapter XXII. On his release by Blessed Eleutherius and the death of the tribune.  
Chapter XXIII. On the raising of the tribune.  
Chapter XXIV. On the transfer of the body from Blandinium to Tournai.]

CHAPTER ONE. The Fabled Origin of the City of Tournai. The Faith of Christ Brought by Saint Piatus.

[Col. 0061A]

[Note: [Col. 0061C] Elsewhere, Chapter I.] 2. On carefully reviewing cosmographies and chronicles of the ages, histories of peoples, and annals, we read that Tournai of Belgian Gaul is a very ancient and famous city, claiming for itself a singular dignity above the other neighboring cities in power, nobility, and glory. It borders the sea [Note: [Col. 0061D] The boundaries of the diocese formerly extended beyond Bruges as far as the sea.], is watered by sweet streams [Note: [Col. 0061D] Especially by the river Scheldt, which cuts through the city.], is rich in crops, and is filled with wealth and delights. Its countryside spreads through forests, is painted with meadows, is rich in herdsmen, and abounds in flocks. Its river, called the Scheldt, flowing alongside and through it, divides Gaul and Germany—that is, imperial and royal power. [Note: [Col. 0061D] Here begins the fable concerning the origin of Tournai. It was once a favorite story among the people of Tournai themselves, but is now rejected both by them and by outsiders. We have said that these fables were attached to the revelation of Henry the Canon so that they might present some appearance of truth.]

This city, then, Priscus Tarquinius, the fifth Roman king after Romulus [Note: [Col. 0061D] Was so extensive an empire assigned to him, and later to Julius Caesar, who first among the Romans brought arms into Belgium? Under Tarquinius the Roman kingdom was still confined within narrow boundaries.], is said to have built in the tenth year of his reign through the Romans; and, rising in costly buildings, it was considered under the name of a second Rome. In the 143rd year from the founding of the City [Note: [Col. 0061D] Tarquinius began to reign in the 140th year from the founding of the City, and reigned until 177; it was during his reign that the Jews were carried into captivity.], the foundations of this same city were laid, around the time when the most holy temple of the Lord was burned by the Chaldeans and the holy city Jerusalem was overthrown by Nebuchadnezzar. In those days Ezekiel was carried into exile, and King Jehoiachin is recorded as having been taken captive, while Tarquinius, king of the Romans, was killed. Servius succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0061D] Servius reigned from A.U.C. 177 to 221, but within the chronological limits assigned to Tarquinius’s reign.], and raised the lesser Rome, now called Tournai, above 125 cities or towns, so that he might collect from them taxes and tributes to be sent afterward to the Romans.

But when, through the multitude of its resources, it became insolent, in the 24th year [Col. 0061C] of King Servius it ceased paying tribute; thus, for forty years from its foundation, the city in question rested in peace. But the Romans, sending their legions against the rebels, provoked a battle; and after many engagements on both sides, in the thirty-fourth year of Servius, the people reconciled and restored peace with the Romans by resuming the burden of their former tribute. It was no longer called a second Rome, but was named the Hostile City.

As time passed, while Artaxerxes was reigning [Note: [Col. 0061D] Artaxerxes began war against Egypt in the second year [Col. 0062C] of the 101st Olympiad, A.U.C. 379.], the Hostile City was destroyed. In the twenty-sixth year of King Ptolemy, while Eleazar was ruling the Jews, it was rebuilt and named Nervius [Note: [Col. 0062D] During the reign of Ptolemy Philometor, Eleazar and the seven Maccabean brothers were killed by Antiochus Epiphanes, king of Syria, around A.U.C. 586 and 168 before the birth of Christ.]. First it was called another Rome, because of the dignity of its glory; second, the Hostile City, because of its strength; third, Nervius, after Servius, king of the Romans—though the first letter was changed, lest it should perhaps be marked by an appellation of servitude. [Note: [Col. 0062D] But this was 360 years, and more, after the death of Servius.]

3. As time progressed, when Julius Caesar was sent to acquire Gaul and remained occupied in the exercises of war for a decade,

> He held Gaul in war for two lustrums, and at last triumphed over Gaul;  
> he exalted barbarian and untamed nations. For he

> subdued the fierce Cappadocians, Cilicians, and Taurians;  
> the subdued Arab acknowledged him, and Judea,  
> surrendered to the rites of an unknown God.

And as that distinguished historian says: After much bloodshed, Gaul submitted to his dominion:

> and the excessively rebellious Nervius,  
> polluted with the blood of the slain Cotta. (Lucan)

This is read more clearly in the second book of Julius Caesar, entitled *The Gallic War Waged by Himself*. At the same time, Turnus was king over the people of the Nervii [Note: [Col. 0062D] This too is an old wives’ tale of the people of Tournai, with no trace of it in Julius Caesar.]; from him the city of Tournai received its name. For just as Turnus fought bravely against Aeneas, so this man fought bravely against Julius.

[Note: [Col. 0061D] Elsewhere, Chapter II.] After the death of Julius Caesar, while Augustus Caesar was reigning, in the forty-second year of his rule, in the year 5,199 from the creation of the world, in the 752nd year from the founding of the City, and approximately the 593rd year from the first foundation of Tournai [Note: [Col. 0062D] We do not wish to refute this sequence of years, although not even one of them is correctly ordered, since many learned men have done so.], the Lord Jesus Christ was born of the Virgin in Bethlehem. In the second year of Nero [Note: [Col. 0062D] In the consulship of Quintus Asinius Marcellus and Marcus Acilius Aviola, or in the year 54 of the Christian era, Nero succeeded the emperor Claudius after the latter’s death.], that is, around the fiftieth year from the Lord’s incarnation, the city of Tournai was restored by the Romans [Note: [Col. 0062D] The Acts of Saint Piatus state that the city of Tournai was then first founded.].

4. The apostles ran throughout the foreign nations, lavish alike of life and labor; everywhere throughout the world they scattered Christ. What was scattered sprouted into Catholic and faithful men. While, according to the Prophet (Isa. 27:6), they filled the face of the world with seed, the weeds of vice were cleansed, and the fruits of morals and the disciplines of faith flourished.

After the apostles came martyrs and confessors, illuminating the world’s darkness at the appointed times with shining rays of truth. Thus, to brighten the night of the present life, the stars come forth across the face of heaven, each according to its strength, until at dawn people see the Morning Star shining. For while the span of night is illuminated by the courses of the stars that descend and succeed one another, it passes with great adornment of the heavens; so, until the true Morning Star of glory appears, the night of the Church militant glows and flashes, instructed by teachers succeeding one another.

Thus sons were born for the fathers—apostolic men, namely—who, filled with the light of wisdom and kindled by the fervor of faith, received different regions of the world as their lot. For just as Thomas received the Parthians, Matthew the Ethiopians, Bartholomew Nearer India, Andrew Scythia, John Asia, Peter Pontus and Galatia, and the others illuminated the remaining provinces, so afterward Dionysius went to the people of Paris with his companions, Lucian sought the people of Beauvais, Quintinus the people of Amiens, Crispin and Crispinianus the people of Soissons, and Piatus the people of Tournai. [Note: [Col. 0063D] These apostles of Gaul are commemorated: Dionysius on 9 October; Lucian on 8 January; Quintinus on 31 October; Crispin and Crispinianus on 25 October.] Though noble by birth, he was nobler by faith; by origin a Beneventan, by office a preacher, sweet in speech, a martyr in desire but an apostle in zeal. After long and persistent preaching he converted untamed and uncultivated peoples to the discipline of the faith.

While Diocletian and Maximian were reigning, after many kinds of torture, he finally earned the long-desired prize and crown by the cutting off of his head in the territory of Tournai itself. After his martyrdom he left sons and grandsons, whom, having begotten through the Gospel in Christ, he made sharers in his glory and confessors of the Catholic faith.

CHAPTER TWO. The Birth, Education, Exile, and Episcopate of Saint Eleutherius.

[Col. 0063C]

[Note: [Col. 0063D] Elsewhere, Chapter III.] 5. After the passing of this venerable blessed father, as time advanced but vice succeeded him, the people multiplied but did not increase in joy. A large part of the people of Tournai returned like a dog to its vomit, and, as instruction in the truth failed, unbelief and sin grew fierce again.

For since offenses do not in any way die with old age, crimes are not buried by the passage of time, and wrongdoing is not entombed by forgetfulness, the excellent condition was changed. The faith of many perished in Tournai, and, as it is written (Hos. 5:11), the people began to go after filth.

For every tree that is not planted by the heavenly Father—who alone grants growth to mystical plants—will be uprooted. Thus, its branches cut off, its leaves shaken loose, and its fruits scattered, Daniel’s typical tree (Dan. 4) was cut down, to such an extent that the birds dwelling in the tops of its branches fled. It was cut down, not simply uprooted, because its root-shoot continued and sprouted in the earth.

When the city had been prostituted to the mockery of idolatry and covered with the thorns of vice, a wise man was found in it, conspicuous in faith and an outstanding follower of Piatus’s teaching, named Irenaeus. While he instructed his descendants in the faith, by his wisdom he freed the city from guilt. This is the Irenaeus who publicly confessed Christ and, having accepted martyrdom, departed happily to triumph. [Note: [Col. 0063D] The Acts transmitted thus far are silent about his martyrdom. It is hinted at in the *Life of Eleutherius* from a manuscript breviary of Tournai.]

6. He fathered a son, in reality and in name Serenus [Note: [Col. 0064D] The same Life calls him his great-grandson.], who was filled with the glory of riches, the power of his ancestors, the wisdom of truth, and an abundance of piety. His wife was called Blanda, both truly and by her proper name, so that you might think that serenity of heart and sweetness of speech were enriching them through a kind of spiritual marriage.

And because a good tree produces good fruit from itself, and a son does what he has seen his father doing, when they had advanced somewhat toward the evening of old age and, for the propagation of the worship of faith, abstained from the duty of marital union, by divine gift they received an heir, successor both to their goods [Col. 0064B] and to their piety and faith.

They call their son, already reborn in Christ and received from the sacred font, Eleutherius; and, as though by the interpretation of his name, they foreshadow and designate that he would be an ornament of the world. [Note: [Col. 0064D] Ἐλευθέριος (*Eleutherios*): freeborn, noble, liberal.]

Could that joy foretold by the angel as future (Luke 1) not already seem renewed, when John was born of the just and advanced-in-age parents Elizabeth and Zechariah? [Note: [Col. 0064D] Valentinian died in 451, Marcian in 457. The names of the emperors are not supplied in the manuscript or in the other Acts, just as the ancient Franks were not accustomed to add them. Saint Eleutherius was born in 456.] Thus, while the emperors Valentinian and Marcian were reigning, the boy Eleutherius was born at Tournai, in what was then merely a town.

[Note: [Col. 0063D] Elsewhere, Chapter IV.] 7. When the boy was entrusted to teachers to be instructed in letters, he grew in grace and increased in wisdom. He diligently displayed to the Creator the ardor of charity, to himself the beauty of chastity, and to his neighbors the honor of humility. He appeared pious in heart, sober in speech, energetic in action, modest in face, mature in bearing, devoted in affection, kindly in conversation, moderate in dress, and gracious in all things.

He displayed such an appearance of propriety in himself that, from the outward arrangement of the man, one could read the inward disposition of grace and virtue. For just as, in the vestibule of an external house, one easily infers the inner goodness hidden within the house, so here. Hence Medardus, later to become bishop of Noyon, forewarned by the spirit of prophecy, predicted that this same Eleutherius would become bishop of Tournai, while Eleutherius was still a boy of school age.

8. This also greatly advances his praise: that he was a boy of good character among the wicked. For just as it is a more serious fault not to be good among the good, so it is a greater distinction to be good even among the wicked.

Hence Job is exalted with great praises (Job 30:29), because he was a brother to dragons and a companion to ostriches. And it is said of Lot (2 Pet. 2:8) that he was righteous in sight and hearing, dwelling among those who day after day tortured the soul of the righteous with their wicked deeds.

Thus this saint, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, shone like a luminary in the world, as it is written in the Song of Songs (Song 2:2): “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters.” He was a thorn among thorns, restless among the restless; a lily among lilies, peaceful among the disciplined; a thorn among lilies, Saul among the prophets. Yet with those who hated peace he was peaceful, and thus a lily among thorns.

[Note: [Col. 0065D] Elsewhere, Chapter V.] 9. It happened in those days that the tribune of the Scandinenses [Note: [Col. 0065D] The printed edition has *Scandiensis*; elsewhere, *Scaudiniensis* and *Scaldiniensis*, referring to the river Scheldt.], who also presided over the city of Tournai, assembled the elders of the people. With the unbridled multitude of paganism, he decreed publicly that all worshipers of the Christian faith, without distinction of condition or sex, should indiscriminately be expelled from the city of Tournai with disgrace and be entirely deprived of their possessions.

Thus Serenus, Blanda, and their only son Eleutherius were driven out of Tournai to their injury, stripped of their possessions and deprived of estates and temporal glory. But the exercise of virtue, which had been hidden in prosperity, became increasingly known in adversity.

For ointments do not spread their fragrance more widely unless they are shaken; spices do not extend their perfume unless they have been kindled by fire [Note: [Col. 0065D] The printed edition has: “do not extend their fragrances.”]; and the power of a mustard seed is not recognized unless its capsule is vigorously crushed. What is uncrushed is light; once crushed, it burns more intensely and forcefully reveals the energy hidden within its sharpness.

So in persecution the strength of the soul is revealed; so what had been hidden in the parents and the son is disclosed more brilliantly. Hence another reading says (Ps. 41:9): “By day the Lord commanded his mercy,” [Note: [Col. 0065D] The Vulgate edition has: “and by night his song.”] “and by night he declared it.” For God’s gratuitous gift, poured out in a time of serenity, is revealed in tribulations. But what has straw to do with wheat? says the Lord (Jer. 23:28).

10. In order, therefore, that those who had been separated in their actions might also be separated in place, persecution was stirred up like a wind. And just as, when a whirlwind grows strong, the chaff, adulterated grains, and empty husks are winnowed and finally rejected, while after many turnings the solid grains gather together, forming an inseparable portion of a single mass [Note: [Col. 0065D] In the printed edition the preceding words are repeated: “In order, therefore, that those who had been separated in their actions might also be separated in place, persecution was stirred up against the Christians.” They are lacking in the manuscript.], so the Christ-worshipers and faithful expelled from the royal city, not divided but united, not crushed but stirred up, gathered more vigorously around Eleutherius and his parents. At the place called Blandinium they constructed and built a basilica in honor of Blessed Peter.

There, many pagans came to Serenus out of their old familiarity with him and also because of his outstanding merits. Abandoning the error of paganism, reborn in the baptismal font, they cast away the filth of idolatry, accepted the worship of the Catholic faith, and changed their way of life.

[Note: [Col. 0065D] Elsewhere, Chapter VI.] 11. When the sun that had previously been hidden in clouds shone forth again, serenity dawned, with the assembly of the faithful gathered in the church. The assembly of orthodox believers rejoiced. It seemed that the times of the prophets had returned (1 Esd. 3), when the temple was rebuilt under Zerubbabel.

Indeed, joyful imagination carries us farther, to contemplate the times of the Maccabees, when the Maccabees recalled their scattered brothers, raised up the fallen laws, renewed the ceremonies, cleansed the sacred things, and redeemed the losses of a long desolation through an extraordinary saving of strength.

Let us recall the infancy of the newly born Church and the condition of Christ’s poor; we shall see a similar measure of humility, from which the Church of Tournai took its beginning and development. No fat hung from its walls when no one claimed anything as his own.

But lest the humble people, like a headless body, should wander through the fields of license, or, [Note: [Col. 0066D] The printed edition has *of the earth*.] in a filthy and disorderly manner, expose themselves to dangers through heresies, Theodore was confirmed as the first bishop of Tournai by the few faithful.

But after a few days had passed, he died, struck by a divine arrow. [Note: [Col. 0066D] They commonly maintain that he was struck by lightning and, because of pride, perished. Some commend him; Catullius says that he is also reported to have died a martyr.] Thus the first angel fell through the fault of apostasy; thus Saul, the first king of the Hebrews, was rejected because of the sin of disobedience (1 Sam. 15); thus the first bishop of Tournai was struck down by divine vengeance, so that, according to the saying of the Wise Man, when the pestilent man is punished, the little one may become wiser (Prov. 19:25). For when mercy is granted to the insignificant, the powerful will suffer powerful punishments.

But he who overthrows the seats of the proud and establishes the humble in their place brought it about that Eleutherius was elected bishop. After his election had been confirmed by the supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. 0066D] In the other Acts he is said to have gone to Rome.], he was freely consecrated bishop of Tournai after Theodore [Note: [Col. 0066D] In the year 487.].

CHAPTER THREE. A Dead Woman Raised by Saint Eleutherius; the Blind, Lame, and Leper Healed; the People of Tournai Converted to the Faith; the Sin Revealed to King Clovis.

[Col. 0066C]

[Note: [Col. 0065D] Elsewhere, Chapter VII.] 12. Raised to the pastoral mitre, Eleutherius filled the office of pontiff with good works. He had striven more to merit the office than to purchase it. He lived in an orderly manner toward himself, sociably toward his neighbor, and humbly in the presence of the Creator: disciplined in conduct, fervent in love, gentle in company, steadfast in his promises, strong in patience, inclined to concord, and firm in correction.

He was upright in judgments, discerning in commands, diligent in administration, energetic in action, attentive in giving assistance, trustworthy in counsel, and cautious in his replies.

While he was once refreshing his spirit through prayer [Note: [Col. 0066D] The printed edition has: “light.”], behold, a certain deranged daughter of the tribune Scandinensis, who had secretly loved him, was harassed by an ancient spirit of lust. Finding an opportunity in his solitude and casting aside the seal of modesty, she rushed into the secluded place and interrupted that divine conversation.

Shame on it! She confessed her desire, sought intercourse, and disturbed the Sabbath-rest of the pontiff’s heart. But behold another Joseph, who left his cloak and fled outside, leaving the woman’s garment behind lest he leave his chastity. But she, covered by the cloak, after the holy pontiff had soundly admonished and rebuked her, breathed out her spirit.

13. Hearing of his daughter’s pitiful death, the tribune was astonished. But if he wished to profess the faith of Christ with a true heart, Blessed Eleutherius, trusting in divine mercy, promised that his daughter would be raised.

The father agreed. After the solemn rites of Mass had been celebrated according to custom, the holy shepherd struck the earth with his pastoral staff. As he tried to give the father confidence in the promise, a terrible earthquake occurred.

What more is needed? The father’s unbelief was disclosed by clear signs. The Saint therefore spent the night in prayer and began the work in the morning. But when the earthquake occurred again, the father’s unbelief was confirmed.

Struck with remorse, he returned a third time, threw himself at the bishop’s feet, disclosed his guilt, revealed his deceit, and received his daughter, raised by Blessed Eleutherius in the name of Christ.

After she had been instructed in the rudiments of the faith and purified by a six-day fast, she was regenerated in Christ. Blanda, the venerable mother of the bishop, received her from the sacred font and gave her the name Blanda. This daughter of the tribune afterward gave her name to Blandinium.

When her father returned to unbelief, he inflicted many hardships upon her because she was faithful. But the virgin, gaining Christ, considered insignificant the patrimony taken from her by her father’s repudiation [Note: [Col. 0067D] The manuscript has “the renunciation and the patrimony taken away.”]; persevering in the faith, she rested in peace [Note: [Col. 0067D] After her father’s full conversion, she was buried by him, as others relate.]. She was buried in the village of Blandinium, on the day before the Kalends of June [Note: [Col. 0067D] The manuscript has “the day before the Ides of June,”], before the shrine and altar of Blessed Peter.

[Note: [Col. 0067D] Elsewhere, Chapter VIII.] 14. Wishing to produce for himself a substantial people, the Lord chastised the people of Tournai with a plague of sudden death, by which he struck some of the pagans there. The signs of the wounds remained hidden; the cause of the effects was unknown. The punishment of the deaths was felt, while an ineffective remedy was sought.

For at a certain twilight hour of the night they went with weapons to Blandinium. They found the Saint praying, bound him with chains, brought him before the tribune Censorinus Caesar, beat him three times with rods, imprisoned him, and shut him in again.

But that same night an angel visited him, stood beside him, opened the prison doors, showed him the road by which he should go to Blandinium, broke his chains, and led the bound man out.

15. Once released, he gave thanks and afterward devoted the day to the solemn rites of Mass. Falling into ecstasy and placed in a state of mental rapture, he prayed for the tribune and entreated God in prayer for the salvation of the people of Tournai.

He remained in that state of mind and, having experienced for a short time the sweetness of prayer—which utterly transcends human understanding, which no sound of the voice, movement of the tongue, or expression of words can distinguish, but which the devout mind, illuminated by the infusion of heavenly light, expresses in angelic rather than human speech—he poured it forth abundantly from a certain exceedingly rich fountain, with the senses gathered into one and the affections mortified.

While the holy pontiff offered this in the ministry of a holocaust, he immediately received a *xenium* as a sign of the favor obtained. [Note: [Col. 0068D] The manuscript has *exenium*, a hospitality-gift, as *xenium*, for which, according to French usage, *e* is prefixed. On this, Rosweyde should be read in the *Onomasticon*.] For he was at once assured by an angelic promise that his prayer had been heard.

16. Therefore, because Jerusalem is instructed through every scourge, and through affliction the sharpness of understanding is opened, the hand of the Lord soon intensified the plague against the pagans and made it heavier. They could not go out in public; they were forced to deny the demons an answer; and finally the pagans decided to kill the tribune if he would not agree with Eleutherius in all things.

They came to the Saint, shed tears, and threw themselves at the feet of the holy pontiff. The prophecy of Isaiah was fulfilled: “The bent sons of those who humbled you shall come to you, and those who spoke against you shall adore the traces of your feet” (Isa. 60:14).

After this, a solemn seven-day fast was proclaimed. On the eighth day, the tribune and the people, clothed in sackcloth, went out from Tournai. The Saint enrolled them among the number of the sealed and chosen through the mark of baptism and the sacrament of faith.

For those who wish to come forth from darkness into light and embrace Christ’s most gentle law must first consecrate the beginnings of their conversion through the bath of baptism, so that, with the oldness of sin laid aside, they may be reborn in the waters of regeneration into a new innocence of soul and infancy of life.

That solemn day was therefore celebrated with joy on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, when through Eleutherius the people of Tournai were converted from the error of paganism to the Catholic faith. This is the day which no forgetfulness ought to erase, but on which the voice of praise and thanksgiving should overflow. For so great a multitude of people was converted in a marvelous and astonishing manner through both indignation and mercy, as it is written (Isa. 60:10): “In my indignation I struck you, and in my reconciliation I had mercy on you.”

After this, the holy pontiff entered the city in glory, and the entire people received him with due reverence as the defender of their homeland.

[Note: [Col. 0067D] Elsewhere, Chapter IX.] 17. The lamp had long been hidden beneath a bushel; now, placed upon a lampstand, it began to illuminate the household more brightly.

While the people rejoiced at the presence of the pious shepherd, the cause of their exultation increased, because a blind man brought to the pontiff was given sight. [Note: [Col. 0068D] The printed edition has “assembly.” Other versions also relate the giving of sight to a blind man.] The light of faith infused into him also cleansed his inner blindness. [Note: [Col. 0068D] The printed edition has *raritas*.]

He also gave sight on the day of the Lord’s Nativity to another blind man, named Mantilius. Deprived of his temporal livelihood and abandoned by the assistance of a guide, he begged alms in the church.

Passersby rebuked him and told him to be silent. The Saint, moved by compassion for the unfortunate blind man, set before him the example of that evangelical blind man who, when asked to be silent, cried out all the more (Luke 18). After impressing the sign of the cross upon his eyes, he restored his sight.

On the day when the true Light came into the world to enlighten every human being, the Saint who bore witness to the Light opened the blind man’s eyes, so that outwardly he might lose his blindness and inwardly recognize the truth.

The Saint also restored a man lame from birth to the power of walking. [Note: [Col. 0069D] The same source has *progressui*, “for walking.”]

18. A certain man named Peritius, struck by leprosy, was despised by everyone as though he were an abomination. He lay at the door of the church, which at that time was called Mantilia, awaiting the chosen bishop of God, so that he might receive from him the sacrament of regeneration. He had waited for him for approximately forty days.

When the Saint saw him and felt compassion, he regenerated him through the water of baptism and granted his flesh the benefit of complete health. Shining with the grace of holiness, he was afterward appointed by Blessed Medardus as the city’s first abbot.

Thus the fragrance of his good name spread more and more for the life of the nations, and the light of his radiance filled the hemisphere of the Church.

19. His fame compelled King Louis to enter the bishop’s city. This was that Louis, the first king of the Franks baptized by Blessed Remigius. He took extraordinary pleasure in hearing Eleutherius preach and committed to memory his discourse seasoned with the salt of wisdom. This king had committed a sin after the washing of baptism, but shame prevented him from confessing it. When the saint perceived this in the spirit, he disclosed it to the king. The king, overwhelmed with shame and tears, immediately acknowledged his guilt; and when he begged that, during the solemn celebration of Mass, the saint act as his advocate, he obtained pardon for him, as the outcome itself confirmed. For in the morning, as he consecrated the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, a radiance of light shone in the church for the space of an hour. Through angelic ministry the saint received knowledge of the nature of the guilt and, concerning pardon, a sign of certainty. Thus the king, certified by a writing revealed by an angel both of his guilt and of his pardon, gave thanks to God and, returning home, freely bestowed many gifts upon the holy man of God. Thus the lamp placed upon its lampstand shone through miracles: he who later spread his teaching even more widely among secular people.

## CHAPTER IV. Saint Eleutherius’ Roman journeys, the synod held, the heretics attacked, and the wounds inflicted upon him by them

[Note: Elsewhere chapter X.]

20. Since, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 11:19), “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved by the Lord may become manifest even to human beings,” heresies arose in those days. They were destroying the unity of the divine essence, the mystery of the Son’s incarnation, and the procession of the Holy Spirit. After quarrels in words, blows to bodies followed, so that many Catholics were killed by heretical violence and ambushes in the River Scheldt. In the tenth year of his ordination, with Pope Anastasius presiding—Gelas[ius] having already died—

[Note: Anastasius succeeded Gelasius, who died on 19 November 498. Under Anastasius he converted the people of Tournai, and afterward heresy arose, as another Life relates.]

he brought the disorderly back to the faith and the unbelieving back to Catholic unity. And because what is hidden is often brought forth into public view when it has been more secretly nurtured, in the fourteenth year of his episcopate, seeing the viperous offspring dividing the womb of Mother Church and barking with increasing shamelessness, with poisoned tongues, against the divinity of the only-begotten Son of God—

[Note: The manuscript has “with deadly tongues.”]

he approached Symmachus, who was then presiding at Rome. He presented him with Catholic discourses, and, honorably received by him, returned to his homeland, confounded the heretics, and converted them.

21. In those days the heresy of the Acephali gained strength.

[Note: It arose after the Council of Chalcedon, against which they favored Eutyches, refusing to admit the distinction of two natures in Christ. The emperor Anastasius joined himself to the Acephali; during his reign Gelasius, Anastasius, Symmachus, and Hormisdas held the papal office.]

The pontiff of Christ returned to Rome, and in the twenty-fifth year of his episcopate, Symmachus having already died, he found Hormisdas presiding.

[Note: These matters are referred in the earlier Acts to Symmachus; either “thirtieth” or another year should be read in place of “twenty-fifth,” or else he certainly made another journey in the twenty-fifth year of his ordination.]

[Note: Thus Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, is said to have held certain possessions in his own possession during the episcopates of his predecessors, in the Life of Gundulf, bishop of Rochester, in Selden, notes on Eadmer, p. 197, line 7. Hence the word *episcopate*, used by Eucherius, Bede, and others, is derived from the Latin *praesul*, who was the first of the Salii. The printed edition has *presiding*.]

With him he courteously discussed the affairs of his Church. From the pope, the pious shepherd obtained relics—namely, those of Mary the Egyptian, together with the shoulder of Blessed Stephen the Protomartyr—and carried them back to his homeland. On his return, when the clergy and people of Tournai met him with due veneration, he is said to have ascended the Mount of Saint Andrew, which at that time was called the Mount of the Hidden Treasure. When he reverently displayed the relics to all the people who were present, an immeasurable radiance surrounded them. Two women and four men in the crowd were suffering from the disease commonly called the “sacred fire.” Before the men he placed the shoulder of the Protomartyr, and before the women the glorious head of the Egyptian woman.

They all fell prostrate and kept their faces fixed upon the relics. The saint roused the multitude to prayer and begged the saints to come to their aid, declaring with confidence that the crowd would not cease praying until those who were suffering had been healed. O wondrous steadfastness of the man, proceeding from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith! Truly, all things are possible to one who believes. Thus, through the efficacy of such a mighty voice, all were healed together. Behold, such power was granted to his voice that the flesh which disease had corroded and erysipelas had consumed was also—wondrous to say—restored at once.

[Note: Elsewhere chapter XI.]

22. The time had now come; the dignity of his merits demanded that, after many victories in battle, the veteran soldier should be summoned to his crown. For in accordance with the justice of civil law, soldiers enrolled under oath and serving the commonwealth faithfully were formerly released, once they had completed their military exercises and lawful terms of service; estates from which they might live were assigned to them, and at last they were sent back to their own homes. Yet God gave him a fierce contest, so that he might conquer and the end might appear more glorious. He had now labored for nearly forty years in the office of pastoral government. For nine years he had ruled the Church of Blandinium and for thirty-one the Church of Tournai.

The Lord raised up against him obstinate heretical adversaries, enemies of Catholic doctrine and the name of Christ. But because they were raging toward the destruction of souls, the good shepherd, unable to tolerate their disturbance, expelled from the enclosures and walls of the city, by decree of the supreme pontiff, those alone who refused to return to the bosom of ecclesiastical unity. Yet, lest they attribute the punishment of their own wickedness to the harshness of authority, and lest the authority of Scripture crush their shameless foreheads, they appointed a day for disputing the Catholic faith. The bishop convened a synod so that he might overcome and confound the heretics, and, once they were confounded, prescribe silence and impose it upon them. When both parties had therefore been summoned, the good shepherd rose in their midst, imposed silence with his hand, confessed the Catholic faith, and publicly expounded it.

23. He explained with what veneration God is called Father; by what mystery Jesus Christ our Lord is regarded as his Son; with what perfection his Holy Spirit is named; how the blessed Trinity is one in substance yet personally distinct; what the Virgin’s childbirth was; what the Word’s birth in the flesh was; what the mystery of the cross was; what benefit came from the divine descent into hell; what the glory of the resurrection was and the return of souls from captivity in hell; what his ascent into heaven was and the expectation of the Judge who is to come; what the Church is; what the vain assemblies opposed to it are; what the remission of sins is; what the resurrection of the flesh is; what eternal life is; and what everlasting destruction is. His discourse treated all these matters at greater length.

What more is there to say? The Catholics unanimously confessed the faith; the heretics were confounded; once confounded, they fled and turned to arguments of wickedness. Thus the one who had given him the courage to fight and confidence to conquer gave the combatant victory. In this way the shepherd David felled with a single stone the mighty Goliath, fortified with terrible weapons and immense stature; he threw the foreign camp into confusion and put the Philistines to flight. He was already in his seventy-first year when he achieved this triumph.

[Note: Elsewhere chapter XII.]

24. Although Samson’s foxes are said to have different faces, they nevertheless have their tails tied to one another (Judg. 15:4). When the sons of eternal damnation saw how, as time passed, the Church of Tournai flourished through the merits and virtue of Eleutherius, and how prosperity smiled upon it more each day, they assembled a council against Eleutherius, asking how they might seize and kill him, so that he would perish. For they said: “What shall we do? This man performs many signs. If we let him continue in this way, we shall be disgraced, despised, and driven away. Come, let us kill him, and when he is dead our name will grow.”

Thus what was spoken in those days came to pass—something that whoever hears it will have his ears ringing. Men of blood and deceit went forth in treachery and unanimously attacked the minister of the altar, the holy pontiff, Christ’s servant, a citizen of heaven. Who could recount the rest with dry eyes? In their hands were instruments of death; men of hidden minds were concealed in the hiding places beyond the corners.

But Father Eleutherius, soon to become a victim of Christ, already advanced in years and distinguished by the title of his merits—he was seventy-six years old—

[Note: The printed edition has “Anastasius.”]

was leaving the church of Blessed Mary the Virgin with the deacon Athanasius and Andoenus, his faithful disciple.

And behold, that crooked and perverse generation, the seed of Canaan and not of Judah, the offspring of vipers, the agents of a criminal faction, did not fear to plow, furrow, and rake with deep wounds that head worthy of the sight of angels, nor to disfigure with shameful marks that face fashioned in the image of heavenly beauty.

[Note: The manuscript has “to injure.”]

Why, you wicked murderers, why, treacherous assassins, do you remove from the flock of Catholics this excellent man, who only a little earlier had fervently entreated God in the temple on your behalf, pleading earnestly through ardent prayer? But they struck him repeatedly, blow after blow, and, leaving the cultivator in the vineyard, the pontiff before the church, the patron in his domain, the shepherd in the sheepfolds, and the master of the household on his own estate, half-dead, they went away. And, to be conformed to the Lord’s Passion, the disciples, abandoning the shepherd, fled.

25. When Censorinus heard what had happened, he grew exceedingly angry with the criminals and proposed to remove them from the midst of the people by the most savage torment of the cross. For it is the concern of public justice that those who neither fear God, nor show respect to the Church, nor love the saints, nor revere the discipline of the canons should be destroyed by cruel punishment.

But O wondrous and deeply rooted compassion of the father! Imitating the Son of God, he begged the judge for the salvation of the criminals, and at last the judge was restrained by his prayers and reverence.

O how great was the grief of the faithful! How much greater especially the lamentation and groaning of the poor! Men and women of every condition mourned, lamenting the common danger of all, indeed the danger proper to each individual.

## CHAPTER V. Saint Eleutherius’ final illness, death, and miracles

[Note: Elsewhere chapter XIII.]

26. Thus Rachel wept for the son of her womb, and could not be comforted.

> For who, unless bereft of reason, would forbid her  
> to weep at the funeral of her child?

Especially at those bloody obsequies, when the heart ought to show compassion, the eye to shed tears, and the judicial hand to exact vengeance.

The pontiff was carried in his own blood by bearers to his own house, to the urban place mentioned above. He ordered a bed of sackcloth to be prepared for him, and, surviving for five weeks, caused his sanctity to shine forth magnificently. During that interval he gave sight to a blind man and healed many afflicted and distressed by various illnesses.

Already foreseeing his death in the spirit, as he awaited the approaching dissolution of his body, he told those standing by that his departure was near and that in that same week he would migrate from the prison of the body, from the confinement of the flesh, as experience made clear through an evident sign.

27. Seeing, therefore, that he was passing from this world to the Father, having loved his own, he loved them to the end. At the moment of death he uttered words sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. He admonished them to pursue unity, to practice repentance, to cherish chastity, to acquire patience, and to despise the vanity of the world. After exhorting them concerning their conduct, he added, in a more extended discourse, a useful instruction concerning faith in the divinity and humanity.

Then, placed as though in a kind of middle point between bodily pains and mental sorrows, he poured forth groans and tears. Suffering in his own body but grieving in his heart with the Church, he turned to the Lord and recited his faith in burning words. He entreated God for friends and enemies alike; he commended to the Lord the Church of Tournai and those who would hold him especially and devoutly in their memory.

“You have seen my struggle, Lord,” he said, “you know my desire. For I am already being poured out, and I am entering upon the way of all flesh. It is time, Lord, for you to entrust my body to the earth. As the deer longs for the water of the spring, the traveler for the end of his journey, and the servant for the reward of his labor, so the saint longs to enjoy the sight of the Savior.

“Does he not seem to have said this to us when his long agony was extended: ‘I am borne onward by desire, but held back by the weight of the body’? For a long time I have carried this burden; for a long time I have watched over the people entrusted to me. I would wish to be freed from this obedience, stripped of the exceedingly heavy garment that I wear, and clothed in one more subtle. In you, Lord, I trust; I desire to see you; I seek you. While placed on earth, I have always worshiped you, to whom I have devoted myself with all my love. Free me, Lord my God, who are blessed forever and ever.”

28. And behold, soon there was a sure sign that his prayer had been heard, through sight and hearing. A great radiance appeared, and a voice from heaven sounded like the wings of an eagle:

“Eleutherius, your prayer has been heard. For the laborer is worthy of his food. You have praised the Trinity as a Catholic; you have fought manfully and diligently. Now at last you have obtained the efficacy of being heard. Complete what you have begun, my servant, lest a good ending be rendered void afterward. The good book will be emptied, but it will be restored; it will be cast into the burning of fire, but it is the Lord’s will that after these things it be revealed to the Church.”

After these words, the voice that had been heard and the radiance that had been seen disappeared. The saint immediately burst forth wonderfully into thanksgiving. Whoever wishes to see these should read carefully his discourses, which, to avoid excessive length, we have omitted in their proper places.

[Note: Elsewhere chapter XIV.]

29. We always read that the saints were never sluggish in their diligence. Since the speech of heretics spreads like cancer, they constructed many books and discourses, lest the rampart of faith be breached either openly and stubbornly or secretly. Therefore, through the teachings of the saints, the foundation of faith stands firm.

For this reason, when the blessed pontiff Eleutherius was at the point of death, he summoned Andoenus and ordered that, after the departure of this father, his beloved son hasten to Rome and present to the supreme pontiff Boniface the defenses of the faith that the saint had composed.

Then, turning again to the sweetness of prayer, he saw Satan standing at his left. Satan wished either to interrupt the discourse of the one praying or to disturb the spirit of the departing man by the terror of his presence. But that dreadful fork-bearer appeared to him only in vain, since he would find nothing belonging to him, nothing dreadful. The saint rebuked him in words and drove him away, displaying the sign of the holy cross.

From this, brothers, we are warned that when the final hour of our appointed end draws near, we ought to practice continual prayer. If, when we plan in this world to travel to unknown or distant places, we commend ourselves to the prayers of those near us and pour over ourselves, at the very moment of departure, a continual flood of tears, beseeching God that we may hasten through peaceful journeys, how much more diligently ought we to do such things at the end? 

30. Hence the blessed bishop prayed continually to the Lord, commending his spirit into his hands. Having received the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, crowned with an unfading laurel, and amid immense light seen and rejoiced in by all who were present, he passed over, invited to the banquets of paradise.

Thus the precious pearl once trampled underfoot by human beings is now treasured in heaven, honored by angels, and enjoys the presence of the Trinity—worthy of a royal treasury, worthy of a palace, worthy of heaven. It is no longer shut up in a prison, oppressed by poverty, or banished into exile; it gazes freely.

For this is Blessed Eleutherius: by the ministry of the Gospel, the proper apostle of Tournai; a martyr by his own blood. Cause and punishment make a martyr: the cause of his martyrdom was the freedom of Catholic faith within him; the punishment was the bitterness of the suffering inflicted upon him. The severity of abstinence and the vigor of repentance likewise made him a confessor. Purity of mind and integrity of flesh made him a virgin; through these he shone graciously, and now he flourishes gloriously in his homeland.

31. The glorious pontiff and confessor of Christ, Medardus of Noyon, who was soon to succeed him in governing the people of Tournai, committed his body to burial. After arranging the solemn funeral rites—which are rather consolations for the living than aids for the dead—the venerable instrument of the Holy Spirit was buried by common agreement in the church of Blessed Peter of Blandinium. He who, as a child, had kept the faith among unbelievers; as a young man, had taught that same faith; and for it had fallen as a veteran was buried in the church whose faith would remain undefiled forever.

[Note: Elsewhere chapter XV.]

32. [Note: This miracle is said in the Life of Eleutherius, from the manuscripts of Cornelius Duynius and of Tournai, to have been reported to the writer of Tournai by Bishop Heidilo; it is narrated, and more suitably, after the elevation of the body and the miracles then performed. For Saints Eligius and Amandus flourished in the seventh century and died, the former in 665 and the latter in 684, as we demonstrated on 6 February in connection with this Life. In the chapter headings placed after the preface, the heading of chapter XVI was inserted here: “On the translation of the body of Saint Eleutherius to the city of Tournai.” That chapter is placed last, perhaps by someone correcting Guibert’s error.]

“Truly precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints,” as was made manifest on the day of the deposition of the confessor of Christ. For a certain woman, blind and mute, while being led before the altar, was released after being led there; once released, she fell asleep; once asleep, she was healed. While sleeping briefly, she saw a vision that opened her outer ear, while inwardly revealing understanding.

What more is there to say? The woman recovered both the use of speech and her sight. The glorious pontiff Eleutherius appeared to her with the martyrs of Christ, Nicasius and Piatus, and the holy confessors Eligius and Amandus. He impressed the sign of the cross upon the woman’s eyes and, as though inserting a fiery staff into her mouth, healed the illnesses from which she suffered.

O confessor and martyr of Christ, Eleutherius, venerable with good reason: you have illumined the militant Church with the twofold privilege of grace. Look upon the weaknesses of our frailty with the eye of mercy. Through the protection of your patronage, Father, lay our groans before the presence of the divine majesty, so that, stripped of the burden of the mortal tunic and freed from the disturbance of carnal desire, we may share in your prize and crown, through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong all honor and glory without end. Amen.

[Note: Elsewhere chapter XVI.]

33. The venerable confessor and pontiff of Christ, Eleutherius, is said to have presided over the government of the Church of Tournai for forty-five years. When he had paid nature’s debt and returned his spirit to heaven, he deserved to have a faithful successor, namely Blessed Medardus, bishop of Noyon. While Eleutherius was still alive but weakened by infirmity and old age, he had employed Medardus as his assistant for consecrating churches and celebrating ordinations.

[Note: Buzelinus reports this same account from a manuscript chronicle of Tournai; older writers are silent. The printed edition reads “for preserving” instead of “for consecrating.”]

Thus, as a longer period of time subsequently passed, a single pontiff presided over both Noyon and Tournai. For the city of Tournai is said to have been deprived of its own shepherd for more than six hundred years. But the blessed Son of God, who has compassion on the losses of souls, gathers the scattered and raises up the fallen according to the appropriate measure and order.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1146, with Pope Eugenius presiding and Blessed Bernard lending his support, a proper bishop was restored to Tournai. At that time Anselm, formerly a monk of the church of Blessed Medardus of Soissons, distinguished for the excellence of his reputation and life, had already held the office of abbot for several years in the church of Blessed Vincent of Laon. At Rome he was consecrated bishop by Eugenius.

[Note: On the Sunday in the middle of Lent. The bull separating the bishoprics of Noyon and Tournai is found in Cognatus, book IV, chapter 46. It is dated at Viterbo, on the ninth day before the Kalends of August, in indiction 9, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1146, but in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius.]

After the restoration of cathedral government at Tournai, he was the first to hold the dignity with the mitre. Thus we believe that this was accomplished by divine Providence: the dignity of the cathedral of Tournai, lost in Blessed Medardus, was restored to the people of Tournai through the son of Blessed Medardus.

## CHAPTER VI. The elevation of the body of Saint Eleutherius; a dead man restored to life; the sick healed

[Note: Elsewhere chapter XVII.]

34. During that intervening period of time in which the two aforesaid dioceses are said to have been united, Heidilo presided. He was a man endowed with much renown and the twenty-sixth successor after Blessed Eleutherius.

[Note: Consult the *Gallia Christiana* of Claudius Robert, who also places Hedilo twenty-sixth.]

During his time the fury of the Normans is said to have raged through Tournai.

[Note: The chronicle of the deeds of the Northmen, carried down to the year 896 and printed in volume II of Chesne, p. 527, reports under the year 880: “The Northmen devastated the city of Tournai and all the monasteries above the River Scheldt with iron and fire, killing the inhabitants of the land and taking them captive,” and so forth. Cognatus discusses the calamity inflicted upon the people of Tournai at greater length in book II, chapter 70.]

In the time of this pontiff, the Lord further glorified his saint. He revealed the confessor Eleutherius to the faithful of Christ, no longer permitting the lump of so venerable a body to remain hidden.

[Note: The printed edition has “hidden.”]

, so precious a treasure, and so noble a pearl to remain hidden. His spirit already shone crowned with glory in heaven, while his body, committed to burial and adorned with singular grace, now breathed upon earth.

It happened, therefore, that a certain noblewoman of Tournai named Thecla, noble by birth and nobler still in the dignity of her character, while her heart’s senses were cleansed and her mind rested, and while the eyes of her body were asleep, was carried away in spirit and fell into ecstasy. She seemed to see, as if in a dream, a man dressed in white, gentle, gracious, cheerful, and modest. He secretly instructed her to go to Blandinium, where she would find the relics of Blessed Eleutherius among the buried bodies of the saints. He likewise instructed her to go to Bishop Heidilo and report to him the vision that had been granted her.

When she delayed carrying out what she had been commanded, the same vision appeared to her on three successive nights:

> “Sister Thecla, what dreams terrify you as you lie awake?  
> What you have seen is neither a waking illusion nor a fantastic dream,  
> but something better described as an oracle,  
> or, more truly, as a most lucid vision.”

> The features and words remain fixed within her breast,  
> nor does anxious care grant peaceful rest to her limbs.

35. What she had seen repeated for the third time became for her a sign of certainty. At daybreak Thecla arose and set out; she fulfilled the vision and revealed it to Bishop Heidilo. The bishops of the neighboring cities were summoned, votive Masses were celebrated, and fervent prayer was poured forth. All—men and women alike, of differing conditions—came with reverent fear to the appointed place.

The bishops, carrying suitable mattocks in their hands as though digging up a treasure, rejoiced greatly when they found the tomb. When the body was lifted from the sarcophagus, joy was doubled among both people and clergy.

36. Thecla, having received the reward of her revelation, prayed and at that very hour departed to the Lord, after receiving from the bishop the sacrament of the Lord’s body. O happy passage of the noblewoman—not a destruction—which first of all delights the army of the saints crowned with laurel. She was gathered and taken away from the face of evil, lest evil perhaps alter her understanding.

[Note: Elsewhere chapter XVIII.]

37. While the continuous solemn celebration was proceeding in this way, behold, the occasion for joy was renewed. A widowed woman entered, desolated by the death of her son. She had sent him into the field to guard the livestock, when a demon attacked the boy. Its likeness and appearance were that of a lion. Coming out of the thicket, roaring, attacking, and killing, it immediately fled and withdrew into the hidden woods.

When the wretched mother learned the sequence of this sad event, casting off feminine softness, she gave herself over to groans and tears, and wasted away with repeated sighs, so that, even if you did not know she was a mother, you would recognize her as one. Her grief revealed both the affection of her sorrow and the excess of her tears in the manner of her mourning. Like Jacob, believing that her son had been devoured by a beast, she continued her lamentation without cease.

The only boy was nowhere to be seen, and therefore the woman had no consolation. The solemn celebration was changed into mourning, and joy into compassion. The clergy and people inwardly bewailed their grief with tears. After indulging their sighs for a little while and recovering confidence in hope,

[Note: The printed edition has “confidence in faith.”]

they entreated Blessed Eleutherius that her son might be restored to life. The clergy and people, moved by compassion, asked the same through vows and prayers. Truly, according to the Lord’s saying (Matt. 21:22), “It is impossible that the prayers of many should not be heard.”

Blessed indeed is the Lord, who makes tranquility after the storm and brings consolation after mourning. When the cloud of sadness had been driven away, he immediately introduced the clear sky of joy. The ground where the boy lay lifeless was shaken, and suddenly an immense radiance from heaven surrounded him. The boy was restored to life; the woman was made joyful; and the glorious pontiff and minister of Christ was magnified among the people.

After his resurrection, the one who had been dead began to reveal the compassion of the blessed pontiff and the power granted to him by the Lord from heaven. For what can be set against the power of one who has the Almighty in harmony with his will in all things? What wonder is it if the saints, already conformed to Christ in soul, perform wonders concerning bodily matters according to the present dispensation, with the assistance of him whose grace has already made them participants in his divinity?

[Note: Elsewhere chapter XIX.]

38. Truly, on the day of his manifestation, a great prophet arose and appeared, since he so solemnly restored the widow’s son to life. Was not the spirit of Elisha already fulfilled in the saint, when it is written that the son was restored alive to the Shunammite woman? As it is written (4 Kings 4:34):

> “The dead boy lay upon his bed, and Elisha lay upon the boy, placed his mouth upon his mouth, his eyes upon his eyes, and his hands upon his hands. He bent over him, and the boy’s flesh grew warm.”

He applied the mouth of gentle propitiation and supplication to God, the eyes of compassionate mercy, and the hands of effective action; thus the dead man rose again.

In this way, too, the insignia of his leader were renewed in the soldier who restored the dead only son to his mother.

[Note: In the same work these words are inserted: “in the city of Nain, the widow’s son.”]

Thus the woman received her son back from the resurrection. Common joy revived; the saint’s patronage was commended; and his holiness, compassion, and power were confirmed by evidence made manifest in many ways.

O wondrous and astonishing goodness, when at the same solemn celebration a young man is raised and a noblewoman dies! For it is written of the Lord (Deut. 32:39): “I kill, and I make alive; I strike, and I heal.” Yet compassion was present in both events: the young man was recalled to grace, while the noblewoman, now ready to be wedded to Christ her bridegroom, was called to glory.

39. What do you perceive in these events, brothers, except that the case of the dead provided clear evidence that the saint had passed into the fellowship of him who holds dominion over life and death? Or, since faith in the resurrection is proper to the Catholic religion, it was fitting that the faith which the saint had taught in words should be confirmed at his elevation by an example. For if a dead man was raised, then we too shall rise in like manner.

The raising of the dead is, in some way, a trace of the resurrection, because in both cases that which had been deprived of life is recalled to life. Nevertheless, there is a difference between a raising and a resurrection: one who has been raised is recalled for a time, only to depart from life again; in the resurrection, however, human life will continue forever, either in glory or in punishment.

Whether someone says this or something else, we are certain that the young man was raised to the glory of God and to confirm the efficacy of the holy pontiff.
