Hence it is also written concerning the raising of Lazarus (John 11:4): “This illness is not unto death, but for the glory of the Son of God.” And if one of the saints asks for something that the Lord has not determined to do, the Lord in no way permits it to happen. From this it is plainly concluded that if something is obtained from the Lord through the prayers of the saints, their efficacy in heaven is thereby declared.

[Note: Elsewhere chapter XX.]

40. But behold, while we were occupied with the miracles brought about on the holy day of the elevation,

we have suffered a slight digression. For when a river flows through its channel, if it encounters hollow valleys at the side, it immediately diverts the course of its current into them and afterward pours itself back into its channel. Hunters, too, may abandon the beast they are pursuing if they happen unexpectedly to see another emerge at once.

Let the river therefore return to the accustomed path of its channel, the hunter to the beast he was pursuing, and the pen to the subject it began. We would also be planting a grove contrary to the law in the Lord’s temple if we attended only to the leaves of words. For it is certain that whenever the stalks of a grain crop advance through their leaves, the grains swell with a lesser fullness of ears.

On that solemn day, therefore, which we have thus far been recounting, the Lord restored sight to the eyes of two blind men, in order to manifest the holy pontiff. Joys were joined to joys as signs followed one another. On that same day three paralytics were healed: the spirit was restored to the instruments of the senses, and thus full sensation and movement were restored to limbs that had been numb and insensible.

A lame man, too, whose progressive power had failed, immediately leapt up and walked, after the soles and bases of his feet had been strengthened. A woman who had long suffered from a flow of blood is also said to have been freed that very day from her former illness through the prayers of the holy confessor.

These and similar events, so difficult and so extraordinary, beyond the hope and capacity of those who marveled, plainly show that the reverence paid to the holy pontiff was pleasing to the Lord. He so declared his saint that those in need found a harbor of consolation and fled to his patronage as to timely assistance.

## CHAPTER VII. Through the aid of Saint Eleutherius, Feriolus is released from bondage and Libertinus is restored from death
[Note: [Col. 0079D] Elsewhere chapter XXI.]

### 41

Christ’s mighty works increased from day to day; miracles shone more brilliantly than light through the merits of the Saint, and crowds of people flocked in throngs to Blandinium. The good fragrance could not be concealed, but, passing from nation to nation, it spread from one kingdom to another people. For foreign pilgrims visited the territory of Tournai because of the fragrance of the Saint’s ointments.

In the second year after his elevation, therefore, a certain priest named Feriolus came as a pilgrim from Vienne to Tournai. Anointed with the oil of compassion and outwardly devoted to works of charity, he acted mercifully toward the wretched, and the blessing of the one who was perishing came upon him.

In those days there was a certain Libertinus, tribune of the people of Tournai. He was miserably dragging to execution a man condemned to death, accompanied by a multitude of people. Feriolus looked upon him and, sympathizing with the suffering man, earnestly begged the tribune to show mercy to the condemned man.

But the tribune became harsher at the admonitions and more insolent at the prayers, and without cause or justification he gave expression to his anger: his face was irrationally inflamed. His clouded mouth, trembling body, savage eyes, whitening foam, burning face, monstrous shouting, and refusal to spare insults clearly revealed the passion of his enraged heart. Turning to his attendants, he said:

“Go, seize this sacrilegious priest, bind him in chains, and lead him to the torment of the gallows.”

Truly, the people and its minister were according to their judge. Thus, while the impious man was swelling with pride, the poor man was unjustly fettered in heavy chains.

Virtue is always opposed to vice: holiness is hateful to the sacrilegious, integrity to the corrupt, frugality to the dissolute, and harsh mercy to the cruel; but piety is likewise unbearable to the impious. Thus do the impious judge while sitting in the place of judgment; thus is innocence destroyed where tyrannical savagery rages.

[Note: [Col. 0079D] Elsewhere chapter XXII.]

### 42

God does not forget to show mercy, but delivers the righteous in tribulation when his virtue is tested through patience. Whatever may happen to him does not disturb the righteous man; rather, when the moment of temptation approaches, he turns to the Lord in prayer.

Accordingly, Feriolus, awaiting the sentence of death, was passing before the church of Blandinium, where clergy and people had assembled to celebrate the memory of the holy confessor Eleutherius. He turned to prayer and, calling upon Christ’s confessor with the whole devotion of his heart, prayed most earnestly. Recalling the prize of martyrdom, the title of confessor, and the undefiled glory of virginity, he asked for timely assistance.

“O holy bishop Eleutherius,” he said, “if what I have heard about your merits is true, help the oppressed; release the one bound through the mystery of your mercy.”

After these words he escaped from the hands of the attendants and hastened to the church. As he stood before the tomb of the blessed confessor, the chains with which he was bound were suddenly loosened, and the chain was broken.

### 43

Then the plagues of Erebus, the contagions of crime, the monsters

of Hell, Pluto’s citizens, the fosterlings of death,

having emerged from Tartarus’ chaos, poured throughout the world;

they formed a hideous council and gathered into one.

They showed neither glory to God, nor reverence to the place, nor mercy to the wretched, nor justice to the innocent. Those who had been filthy became still filthier. Shameful indeed! They again fastened a chain around his neck and bound his hands, so that he might leave the precincts of the church; they drove and pushed him away with whips and threats.

What such things are ever reported to have been done by those savage men—

by Sinon with his Punic pine, or Scyron from his deep crag,

or Phalaris with his bull, or Sulla with his prison?

All thirst for innocent blood; all, with one accord and a common resolve, seek to fasten the holy priest of the Lord to the cross of execution.

“What madness, citizens! What such license of the sword?”

Standing before the tomb of the blessed confessor, Feriolus, poised between fear and confidence, repeated the Saint’s praises; repeating, he pleaded; pleading, he obtained his request; obtaining it, he rejoiced in freedom, and from the depths of his heart celebrated the Lord’s Sabbath.

Placed among the enemy’s ranks, fearful and trembling, he raised his eyes to heaven and implored the Lord’s confessor not to reject his humble prayer.

“O glorious bishop of Christ, Eleutherius,” he said, “you deservedly raised Blanda, the tribune’s daughter, by divine favor. You subjected the virgin’s father and the people of Tournai to the yoke of the Catholic faith. Through you the son of a widow is reported to have been wonderfully raised. The blind glorify you, the mute glorify you, and your miraculous works praise God. Father, I invoke your mercy, that I may once again feel your hand helping me.”

A wondrous sight: suddenly the chain was loosened; once loosened, it broke; once broken, it leapt forth; leaping forth, it struck the tribune in the very middle of his face and killed him.

Meanwhile, the walls were filled with grief of a different kind.

[Note: [Col. 0080D] Elsewhere chapter XXIII.]

### 44

But the tribune’s wife was especially tormented by the unexpected event. Through her efforts, the dead man’s body was carried to Blandinium; it was placed before the tomb of the most blessed confessor—a mournful expiation for his own people, a shameful spectacle to strangers.

They humbly implored Saint Eleutherius and, through devout prayers, summoned and invited him to raise the dead man. But the Saint’s charity never failed. Although he was already joined to God, he had not cast away the compassion of charity, despite the symptoms of human frailty [Note: In the printed edition, *syntheomata*]. For, transformed into a certain divine affection, what could he perceive or grant to the wretched except what was merciful? If God is love, then the closer anyone is joined to God, the fuller of love he is shown to be.

As they all wept and implored the confessor’s mercy for the tribune, an immense brightness shone from above, and a voice was heard from heaven:

“Ask the priest to pray to the Lord Jesus Christ for Libertinus.”

Those standing nearby saw no one, but nevertheless heard the voice. They persisted in prayer, and Feriolus repeatedly placed the confessor’s relics upon the dead man’s body. After the eleventh hour, the man who had died rose again.

### 45

All fell silent and held their mouths closed as they heard what the dead man had seen. He recounted the encounters with demons and the variety of punishments, which surpassed human understanding not only according to the word of the prophet but also according to the sense of poetic verse. Hence that distinguished Mantuan poet says (*Aeneid* VI):

> Not if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths,  
> an iron voice, could I comprehend every form of crime  
> or pass through all the names of punishments.

The same tribune frequently related the sad and dreadful departure of his soul and the host of demons waiting most attentively. When they hurried to meet his terrified soul, they were prevented both by the archangel Michael and by the confessor Eleutherius. Thus the demons were thwarted, because the soul was sent back to revisit its own body and return.

### 46

The same tribune Libertinus also used to recount, among other things, that the memory of the glorious confessor had become, as it were, blotted out and erased over the passage of many ages; but that in the final times, when the world was declining into old age, his memory would flourish again into a new youth.

We now see and lament that this has been fulfilled in part in our own times. Indeed, if it is proper for one who receives a benefit to acknowledge that he is bound to offer some return, then, even though we can repay Christ’s confessor nothing worthy of him—he who strengthened the city of Tournai and its borders in the faith—we nevertheless ought, through abundant acts of thanksgiving, to seal his memory in the innermost chambers of our hearts.

If we do not do so, I fear that we may worship either an image of irreligion or an idol of ingratitude. These ill-starred offspring of monstrosity—the first shapeless, the second infamous—are both without praise, and neither is without defilement. The darkness of irreligion and the obscenity of ingratitude bury past benefits, corrupt present ones, and repel future ones. Through their negligence it came about that the Saint was not held in the honor due to him in his own homeland for a long time.

### 47

At last, after Libertinus the tribune had paid the debt owed to nature, he commended his spirit into the hand of the Lord in holy confession, Catholic faith, common hope, and sincere charity. He rests with Censorinus Caesar, tribune of Scandia, in the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

And so that every fiction may cease and human invention vanish, the chain mentioned above was carried to Vienne as an effective proof of a wondrous and memorable event.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### The Translation of the Body of Saint Eleutherius to the City of Tournai

[Note: [Col. 0081D] Elsewhere chapter XXIV.]

### 48

In those days a miracle occurred, one that no antiquity of time can erase. The merits of the confessor became ever more renowned, and the mighty works of the Creator were praised in him.

The citizens of Tournai, no longer able to endure the absence of the holy body, hurried to Blandinium. They entered the church, found the holy relics, took what they had found, and carried them away so that they might display and deposit them with greater magnificence in the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

For we believe that divine Justice so ordained it: he who had lain hidden at Blandinium while persecution raged there would receive there, as it were, a hidden place of burial. And he who had afterward administered the responsibilities of the episcopate openly would, as his merits grew radiant, be placed more gloriously in T[— lacuna].

The aforesaid citizens, carrying the relics of the holy body with them, returned joyfully to the city, as victors are accustomed to exult when carrying off captured spoils.

### 49

But when the inhabitants of that territory saw the citizens of Tournai carrying away the relics by force,

they themselves entered into the contests of battle

and sent their souls into open danger.

They bent their fierce bows and whirled their thongs.

Behold, the ground was strewn with missiles; harsh battle arose.

Then an arrow flew, the herald of death, and

with violent force sought the enemy. But, driven back by a reversed motion,

it returned upon the man who had shot it and struck him with a wound.

The countrymen were thrown into confusion, pierced by their own weapons.

The blade, fixed in its sheath, grew sluggish and did not easily

emerge, resting in prolonged torpor;

bewildered, it refused its service in the various blows.

A wondrous thing: some of the pursuers were wounded, some were even struck blind, and some were left half-dead along the road. Since none of the citizens received a wound, they offered acts of thanksgiving to God and thus returned to their own homes.

[Col. 0082D]

> And they roared with joy and raised their spirits to the stars.

### 50

And so, amid the joy of the entire city, the body of the most glorious confessor was placed in the church of Mary, the Mother of God.

Those suffering from paralysis came to meet the Saint’s relics. Those sitting in the streets cried out; twenty-five of them received complete healing through contact with the relics.

Miracles continued to be extended from day to day through the Saint’s merits. In those days, moreover, seven blind people received the gift of sight, through the favor of the Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0083A]

# Sermons of Saint Eleutherius (C, G)*

## Sermon, or Confession, on the Holy Trinity

[Col. 0083A]

Beloved, confessing Christ Jesus, Lord of all, and venerating the Holy Trinity in unity, be subject to him alone. Fear the immortal God, to whom honor belongs forever and ever.

The Holy Trinity is God, one God indeed: the Father of the living Word, the perfect begetter of the Perfect One. He received a beginning from no one and will contain an end in no one. For how could the unbegotten Father of the only-begotten Son have his being from another—he who was, and is, Alpha and Omega?

The only Son of God willed to be born from the one God the Father. He is the wisdom of the Father, through whom all things have been created: all that exists, all that flourishes, all that has flourished, all that will be born, and all that will perish.

The true Son is from the true Father; eternal from the eternal, immortal from the immortal, incorruptible from the incorruptible, invisible from the invisible. And there is one Holy Spirit, in whom the perfect life of believers abides; in whom holiness itself and the fountain of holiness and the minister of true edification are found. Through him God is in all believers and above all, and the Son is through all.

Although the Father derives his existence from no one, the Son has his origin from him, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, nevertheless these three are not gods, but one true God. His Trinity is to be venerated in the persons, and his unity is to be adored in substance.

The Trinity is perfect glory, an everlasting kingdom, a perpetual and indivisible reign. For the Son was never absent from the Father, nor the Spirit from the Son. The Holy Father is equal to the only-begotten Son; the Son is equal to the unbegotten Father according to the power of divinity, but lesser in the assumption of our humanity.

The Holy Spirit likewise is not lesser than the Father and the Son, but is their coeternal comforter of the sorrowful, strength of the weak, sevenfold, everlasting, and most subtle giver of grace.

The true Son is the true image of the Father’s light and the true splendor of inward brightness. Wishing all people to attain knowledge of his name, for their salvation and the washing away of sins he descended from heaven to earth. He was incarnate, became man, suffered, and then became obedient unto death.

The apostle Paul bears witness to this obedience, saying:

> Although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from the things he suffered; and, having been made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him, having been called by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

This same Christ rose from the dead on the third day. Then he ascended into the heavens from which he had descended, and by his wondrous power he led our captivity captive.

Therefore let all who serve the Catholic faith believe that he will come from there and judge the living and the dead. The holy and Catholic Church must anathematize those who assert that Christ is changeable or capable of alteration.

Accordingly, although he became man—that is, although he assumed flesh from the holy Virgin Mary—and although he became man in the assumption of flesh and blood, he nevertheless remained what he was: God by nature and in truth.

Do not say that the flesh was changed into the nature of the Godhead, nor that the inseparable essence of the Word of God was changed into the substance of flesh. For he is inseparable, immutable, and unchangeable; according to the Scriptures, the almighty Lord remains the same, blessed forever and ever.

He cannot be greater or lesser; he cannot be bounded by magnitude or contained by time. Whatever is celestial or divine is known to be without quantity and without mass; it is contained by no limits.

Confess the Word of God according to his subsistence. Worship one Son and our Lord Jesus Christ. Do not define or separate God and man as though they were joined to one another only by a unity of dignity and authority. Do not name one Christ especially as God the Word who is from God, and another Christ especially as the one born of a woman.

Recognize, venerate, and adore only one Christ, the Word of God the Father, together with his own flesh. For Christ is one, Son and God—not as though there were merely some conjunction in a unity of the dignity and authority of man and God.

Can nature be united merely by an equality of dignity? Certainly not. Peter, shepherd of the Lord’s flock, and John the evangelist and apostle, the chosen virgin, are equal to one another in dignity; for that reason they are called disciples of Christ and suitable witnesses of the truth. Yet neither of these two is one and the same person as the other.

Therefore, my dearest little sons, do not assert the Word of God the Father to be a separate God or Lord, lest you once more divide the one Christ and Lord more openly into two and fall into the crime of sacrilege, making him God and Lord of himself.

God the Word was united to the flesh, as we have said, according to subsistence. He is God, ruler of all, creator of the entire universe, and redeemer of humanity through his most precious blood.

He plainly denies unity who divides the one Christ into two. Such a person is an apostate, truly wretched, and truly destined to be subjected to everlasting torment. For him the devil and his angels rise up as plunderers; for him evil spirits come to receive his soul. Countless torments are prepared for him, and the evil deeds he committed in life are set before his eyes.

Therefore, lest you come to these terrible places, confess that Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, is understood to be one, and that he is to be venerated with one service together with his own flesh.

Confess with a pure mind, praise with a perfect heart, and glorify with a gracious mouth the only-begotten Son, God, who was born from God the Father.

Although according to his nature he was without suffering, nevertheless for our sake he endured suffering in the flesh according to the Scriptures. In the crucified body of his own flesh, he impassibly appropriated the suffering to himself.

By the grace of God he tasted death for all people, also giving up his own body, although he is by nature life itself and the resurrection of the dead. In order to overcome death by his ineffable power, wondrous strength, and immeasurable majesty; in order to become, in his flesh, the firstborn from the dead and the first fruits of those who sleep; and in order to make a way for human nature to return to incorruption, he tasted death for all by the grace of God, as has been said. Rising on the third day, he stripped the fiercest jaws of Hell.

Therefore, although it is said that the resurrection of the dead came through a man, you must understand “man” to mean the Word who is from God, and that through him the dominion of death was destroyed.

As Scripture bears witness:

> In the last times one Son and Lord will come in the glory of the Father to judge the world in righteousness.

It is also necessary for you to believe in the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, his birth, circumcision, manifestation, Gospels, passion, death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. For this is the right faith.

But because the Virgin conceived God united to flesh according to subsistence, and the Virgin gave birth, confess her as the Mother of Christ—not because the nature of the Word received from flesh the beginning of its existence. For:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

He himself is the creator of the ages, the Father of the universe.

There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; these three are one.

Therefore confess one Creator of all in substance and the Trinity in persons, so that you may deserve to attain the joys of heaven, where the merits of the saints flourish and whose joy and exultation will never cease, forever and ever, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns with the coeternal Father, through the cooperation of the grace of the Holy Spirit. To him be praise and dominion throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# The Passing of Saint Eleutherius, Bishop

In those times, while the blessed Eleutherius was the second bishop presiding over the Church of Tournai, a great dispute arose among the clergy of Tournai.

Certain heretics were introducing innovations of their own heresy and attempting to destroy the preaching of the truth. They dared to corrupt the mystery of the divine dispensation and denied that the heavenly paranymph had announced the Virgin’s childbirth.

Other heretics, introducing confusion and wrongly combining the nature of flesh and divinity as one, spread the claim that, through such confusion, the divine nature of the only-begotten was capable of suffering. They shamelessly asserted that the one born from the most blessed Virgin Mary was a mere man.

Others opposed the Holy Spirit. Still others, devoted to and serving God, believed the truth and did not obey falsehood.

The dispute among them was so great that the heretics even attacked the Catholic sons of the Church of Tournai and drowned many of them after cutting them down in the river called the Scheldt.

At that time the blessed bishop of the Church of Tournai had gone to Rome, and he had carried away with him the head of Mary of Egypt. He had secretly received it from the Roman Church of the blessed apostle Peter and brought it to the Church of Mary, the Mother of Christ.

Thus the man of God returned from Rome and was received with great rejoicing by the entire people. The clergy rejoiced and, dressed in dalmatics, went out to meet their blessed shepherd. But suddenly everyone’s joy was doubled, for the bishop himself was bringing the relics of blessed Mary, who had endured so many and such great evils.

When he entered through the Nervian Gate, a great miracle was manifested by God in that place. As joyful crowds and likewise ranks of clergy came to meet him, the blessed bishop, wearing a cloak, climbed the mountain called the Mountain of the Hidden Treasure, now called Mount Saint Andrew. He displayed to all the people the relics of Saint Mary of Egypt and the shoulder of the blessed Stephen, the protomartyr.

Suddenly a certain brightness descending from heaven appeared around the relic of Saint Mary’s head. It was seen by everyone until the relic entered the church of Mary, the Mother of Christ. Over the shoulder of the blessed Stephen an even brighter radiance appeared in the form of a circle, like silver.

When he entered the church surrounded by the entire crowd of people, four men and two women were suffering from a serious illness called the fire of Gehenna.

Moved by compassion, the man of God placed the head before the women and the shoulder before the men, saying:

“Let us all pray.”

When they had fallen down and were praying, he said:

“Saint Stephen, protomartyr, help these men. Saint Mary, have mercy on this female sex. We will certainly not rise from prayer until they have been made well.”

At this word they were all delivered. The flesh that they had lost during the illness was restored in that very hour.

A mute man who was standing nearby also spoke, saying:

“Behold the relics of blessed Stephen and Saint Mary.”

Then everyone was astonished and amazed. In those times the relics of the saints were not placed in gold or silver.

These things took place on the Nones of October.

The blessed Eleutherius had by then governed the Church of Tournai for thirty-one years and the church of Blandinium for nine. When he heard that the sons of the Church were disturbed, he was grieved. Then, by the authority of the Roman pope, he decreed that all heretics should be expelled from the city, so that they might unanimously confess Christ, the Son of God the Father.

Accordingly, compelled by the bishop, they chose a suitable day on which the bishop of Christ, Eleutherius, would convene his synod. The day on which the synod had been convened arrived. The Catholic sons also came, confounding the sect of the heretics, and some of the heretics who opposed them were present as well.

The holy man of God Eleutherius rose, made silence with his hand, and said:

“Listen, all of you who confess the Lord the Father and his Son together with the Holy Spirit.”

## Sermon on the Trinity

Believe in one God, the almighty Father, and in his one Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who was born from God the Father: the only-begotten Son, boundless from the boundless, immortal from the immortal, invisible from the invisible, everlasting from the everlasting, through whom and with whom the Father made all things contained in heaven, on earth, or in the sea.

Therefore, my beloved, I urge you: believe that our Lord Jesus Christ descended from heaven for the salvation of humanity and the liberation of the world, was incarnate, and suffered as a man under the governor Pontius Pilate. Furthermore, believe that on the third day he rose from the dead and again ascended into heaven, from which he had descended.

My dearest sons, you must hold and observe these decrees. You must devoutly obey them if you wish to earn the joys of heaven.

Obey the doctrines and decrees of the ancient Fathers, carefully and most clearly considering what it means for the Word of God to be incarnate and to become man.

You must not assert that the nature of God was changed, but rather that he joined to himself flesh animated by a rational soul, and that Christ the Son of God became man irreproachably, ineffably, and substantially, and was also called the Son of Man.

Therefore Christ Jesus, who was born before all ages from the eternal Father, was also carnally brought forth from a woman, that is, from the blessed Virgin Mary. This does not mean that his heavenly nature received its beginning from the holy Virgin, nor that he needed to be born a second time for his own sake, after that glorious birth which he had from the Father.

For it is neither fitting nor anything but foolish to affirm that Jesus Christ our Lord, who is coeternal with the Father before all ages, needed another generation after the Father’s generation in order to begin to exist through what he assumed from the Virgin.

But let the holy Catholic universal Church affirm and believe that, for the salvation of humanity and the washing away of sins, he joined a human nature to himself and came forth from a virginal womb—a womb undefiled and most worthily guarded by heavenly angels.

For this reason the Catholic Fathers assert, and we on the authority of our predecessors affirm, that he was born carnally. In his kindness and mercy, wishing to turn all people toward the path of divinity, he joined flesh to himself from that virginal and undefiled womb, as has been said, and underwent a carnal birth, making the birth of his own flesh his own birth.

Then believe that he was crucified and rose from the dead on the third day—not because God the Word in his own nature was struck with blows under the governor Pontius Pilate, then fastened to the cross, or because he endured for us the piercings of spear and nails and such great wounds—for God is incorporeal and beyond suffering—but because that body which became his own endured these things for us.

For this reason it is said that he suffered for all people for the redemption of sins. In the body that suffered, God was present, although he could in no way suffer.

You must understand his death in the same way. The life-giving Word of God is naturally incorruptible and immortal. But because, by the grace of God, his own body tasted death, according to the teaching of the apostle to the Gentiles, Paul, God is therefore said to have suffered death for us—not because he himself experienced death insofar as his nature is concerned, for it would be improper, indeed foolish, to assert this, but because, as we said above, his true flesh tasted death.

Thus, when his flesh rose again, affirm the resurrection—not because it fell into corruption, but because that same body rose.

Therefore, beloved, I beseech your brotherhood to venerate the true God and his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, devoutly; adore him with a kindly heart, praise him with a pure mind, and confess him with tearful sighs. Do not glorify him in word as though he were merely a man, lest you introduce a kind of division. Honor one and the same Christ, for his body, with which he also sits beside the Father, is not alien to the Word.

Nor should you testify as though there were two sons sitting beside the Father, but one Son with flesh through unity.

Furthermore, your faith must believe that Christ our Lord became the mediator between God and humanity and the reconciler who restores us to peace with God the Father, offering himself for us as a fragrant offering.

For this reason he said through the prophet:

> Sacrifice and offering you did not desire; burnt offerings for sin did not please you; but you prepared a body for me. In the heading of the book it is written of me: “I have come to do your will, O God.”

He offered his own body not for himself, but for us, as a fragrant offering.

My brothers, who among you would any longer doubt that the true and spotless Lamb was sacrificed for the salvation of the human race and crucified by the impious Jews?

He is the one who redeemed us through the wondrous virtue and ineffable power of his divinity, conquered the rebellious and proud Jews, and stripped the bars of Gehenna, leading captives out of bondage and releasing prisoners from places of darkness, who cried out and said:

> O good conqueror of the world, O merciful destroyer of diabolical deceit, most gracious Jesus, in these torments and punishments our lamentations awaited you. Merciful Christ, the sighs of the sorrowful cried out for you in the dark places. Behold, you have come, whom we awaited from ancient times. Deliver us, whom we once worshiped devoutly while placed on earth.

He is the one who, after the destruction of the devil and the liberation from darkness of the saints who cried out, rose on the third day. Ascending into the heavenly kingdom, he sits at the right hand of God the Father.

He is the Son of Mary, who conceived as a virgin from the Holy Spirit and, remaining undefiled in virginity, gave birth to God and man. She also remained both Virgin and Mother of the Savior after giving birth.

He offered himself, as has been said above, as an immaculate offering, an offering pleasing to God the Father.

But if anyone says that he offered himself as a sacrifice to God both for himself and for us, he will not escape the final punishment; rather, he will suffer eternal penalties in destruction with the impious.

When he said to his disciples concerning the Holy Spirit, “He will glorify me,” understand this, my sons, as referring to one Christ and Son. Do not confess that he received glory from the Holy Spirit as though he needed another’s glory, because the Spirit is superior to him and better than he is.

Although the Spirit is his according to substance and a personal distinction is understood according to the fact that he is his Spirit and Son, nevertheless he is not alien to him. For he was called the Spirit of truth, and Christ is truth.

Therefore the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son just as from the Father.

For the Holy Spirit, performing miracles through the hands of the holy apostles, glorified God Jesus Christ after he had ascended into heaven through his glorious resurrection—from which he had descended for the liberation of our souls.

Therefore Christ is believed by us and by certain Catholic men to be God by nature, displaying through his Spirit mighty works and glorious miracles to the nations scattered throughout the whole world.

For this reason our Lord Jesus Christ said, “He will take from what is mine and announce it to you.”

But the Holy Spirit is by no means said to be powerful or wise through participation in another, because he is perfect in every respect and in all things and is entirely in need of no good thing.

The Holy Spirit is believed to be the Spirit of the Father’s heavenly virtue and wisdom, that is, of the Son. Therefore, because virtue and wisdom subsist in reality and power itself, he is shown to be virtue and wisdom.

Dearest brothers, this is the right faith, and it must be held by all Catholic men. Unless each person firmly and rightly believes it, he cannot be delivered from fellowship with the devil.

Confess one God in substance and three in persons, so that you may deserve to reach the heavenly kingdom and rejoice perpetually in eternal blessings, where the angels rejoice, the apostles are glad, the glorious throng of martyrs exults, and the company of confessors and virgins applauds.

The Redeemer of the world crowns them with an everlasting wreath. He is God, who lives and reigns, almighty, invisible, eternal, and incorruptible. To him belong honor, praise, beauty, and dominion; unfailing power, unfading majesty, perpetual glory, and ineffable strength, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

If anyone should contradict these decrees concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, let him be anathema.

After these words, blessed Pontiff Eleutherius sat down. The Catholic men who had been summoned to the holy synod raised their voices with joy and glorified God, saying:

“We venerate and worship the Trinity in unity; we profess unity in substance and devoutly adore it. On the other hand, let the heretics be confounded.”

Then they withdrew from the holy synod in confusion. When the synod had returned to its own places, the holy Eleutherius likewise returned to his own residence, which was situated in a country settlement, together with the Catholic men; he was then seventy-one years old. For five years thereafter, while the invincible priest still lived, [Col. 0090D] the Church of Tournai was exalted by Catholic men. Meanwhile, the party of the heretics was thrown into confusion. What were they to do? They took counsel and sought to determine what should be done with him. They said:

“If he continues to prevail among us in this way, our way of life will be despised; but if we prevail, we shall have gained the victory and its praise.”

As they were conversing together one day, behold, the blessed pontiff was coming out from the church of blessed Mary of Tournai with Athanasius the deacon and Audoenus, his faithful disciple. When the heretics saw him, having concealed themselves behind a corner—for they were plotting against him in many ways—they said:

“Behold the destroyer of our law. Come, let us kill him.”

Then, raising their clubs, they beat him savagely. After inflicting wounds upon him, they left him half alive before the church and secretly went away. His disciples likewise abandoned their shepherd [Col. 0091A] and fled.

When Caesar Censorinus heard this, he would have affixed them all to the cross on the gallows, had not the prayer of the man of God prevailed. A tumult arose throughout the city: the young men cried out, matrons mourned, and virgins sprinkled themselves with ashes. The old men competed to see the half-living bishop. He himself lay lifeless, and from the holy man’s head—as well as from both sides—blood was flowing [the wording is uncertain].

Then, after the citizens of the city had prepared, as he had requested, a bed covered with haircloth, he was carried into his own house. He lived for another five weeks and, during that illness, restored sight to a blind man and healed several sick people.

At length the end of the days of the most blessed Eleutherius drew near. He summoned his brothers and the worshipers of true religion, and openly received the body and blood of Christ. He foretold that during that same week he would depart from the prison of the body.

[Col. 0091B]

What were they to do? They saw that their father desired heavenly things, and they mourned because he was already about to leave the Christians. He addressed them gently, saying:

“As I am about to enter upon the end of all flesh and to receive from the Lord the eternal joys promised to me, I exhort you, dearest ones: flee hatred, sow concord, destroy schisms, pursue virtue, and endure temporal evils for the sake of your Judge, so that you may be found worthy to offer Christ the fitting fruit of repentance.

“For every human being is grass, and his flesh is like the stubble of the field. In the morning it is green and blossoms; in the evening it becomes dry, falls, and is made worthless. Be patient, remain chaste, fear the Lord, and persevere in every good thing. For you have heard David say: ‘Man has been made like vanity.’

“Therefore we are dust; at the judgment we shall rise again before the tribunal of Christ. As Scripture bears witness, [Col. 0091C] we shall all stand there.”

After these words, such a great brightness shone upon the settlement where he had been born that all who had come to the funeral of so great a father, as though in a trance, saw his spirit being lifted by an angel in a cloud. They saw it penetrate the heavens with the brightness of the cloud, and then saw neither it nor the brightness flying with it any longer.

Thus, having been drenched in a flood of sacred blood, the true martyr and confessor departed in peace.

The day before the Kalends of July.

These things were done by the heretics on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, and in that same year blessed Eleutherius fell asleep in peace, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigned, to whom be honor and power throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON ON THE INCARNATION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0091D]

Paternal authority urges brotherly charity to believe and mercifully entreats it to cease from evils. We cry out, but no mortal heeds. We invoke Christ, and heavenly Christ hears. Nevertheless, let the faithless hear faithfully, and let the foolish understand wisely.

We believe in God the Father almighty, creator of visible and invisible things. We adore Christ, the perfect Son of the perfect One. We venerate the Paraclete, the Spirit proceeding from both.

Just as the Father is without beginning, so also the Son—whose Father is God—remains without beginning. The Only-Begotten, descending from the Unbegotten, was always God; he who was always the Son remained so, and we confess that his Father is God. Before the world existed, the Father possessed the Word; [Col. 0092A] he possessed Wisdom and did not lose Power.

The Catholic Fathers call the Word the strength of God and the wisdom of God, which we do not doubt has always existed. But so that we may believe more certainly that Wisdom herself existed from the beginning, let us hear what she plainly says:

“I came forth from the mouth of the Most High.”

For when the Most High established the firmament, strengthened the earth, and caused a spring of water to burst forth from the depth of the abyss, “I was in the highest places with the Father, arranging all things with him.”

And again it is said:

“All wisdom is from the Lord God; it has always been with him and exists before the age.”

Moreover, to show more openly that the Word existed from the beginning, the Father himself declares, saying:

“My heart has uttered a good Word” (Psalm 44:1).

We believe that he is God in such a way that the Father always remains so, because the Word, Wisdom, and Strength [Col. 0092B] of the Father is his Son.

Indeed, the prophets proclaimed beforehand the birth from Mary the Virgin. Concerning the birth of Christ, the prophet Isaiah bears witness, saying:

“Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and he shall be called Counselor, Mighty God; his power and dominion shall remain forever” (Isaiah 9:7).

Therefore Christ, the Only-Begotten of the Unbegotten Father, was born according to the flesh from the seed of David. He became visible as a human being, while his Father is the invisible God. It was indeed necessary for the human race that the one whom the Father had begotten invisible from the beginning should be conceived by a virgin, that a virgin should bring him forth visibly for us, and that she should remain a virgin after giving birth. Christ, begotten in God—perhaps, “by God”—before all ages, without intercourse with a woman, was from the heavenly Father; and the perfect human being was born from a virginal womb, without a human father.

[Col. 0092C]

For the Holy Spirit entered the virginal chamber of chastity and caused Christ, made human from her, to come forth: he would restore what had been lost and forgive the sins of all. Though innocent, he would pour out his innocent blood for the redemption of human weakness, and through the visible human being, the invisible God would present his visible Only-Begotten to humanity.

Therefore Jesus Christ was born according to the flesh and was circumcised on the eighth day. In the circumcision of his flesh, just as circumcision brought an end, so through Christ’s baptism the consecration of baptism received its beginning. The water of the Jordan did not sanctify him by washing him; rather, the Son of God purified those same waters by entering them.

Thus, just as the Father had foretold through his prophets, a virgin conceived, and creation brought forth its Creator upon the earth.

[Col. 0092D]

He is said to have risen on the third day after his passion and to have ascended into heaven in the sight of the apostles. Concerning his glorious passion, the apostle Paul, writing to the Philippians, says:

“Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Philippians 1).

Therefore, holding this understanding concerning God, we do not say that he who was born of the Virgin Mary was merely a human being. Nor do we proclaim separately one son of man and another Son of God, lest we make one person of the flesh and another of the Godhead. Rather, in the Word of God and in the flesh we profess and believe in one Christ, and we testify and worship him as the Only-Begotten [Col. 0093A] Son according to nature.

We also make this openly clear: the Word of God had a beginning in flesh and blood, and he specially made our body his own. A perfect human being proceeded from the virgin, yet without casting aside the heavenly Godhead and thereby losing the generation which he possessed from the eternal Father. This is indeed what the reasoning of the Catholic faith bears witness to.

In this religion we have learned that the holy Fathers, God’s chosen soldiers and true combatants, truly believed that the mother of our Lord Jesus Christ was a virgin—not because the Godhead and nature of the Word received its beginning in her, but because a rational soul, coming from that same undefiled virgin womb, gave life to the most sacred body of Christ, to which we know that the Word of God was substantially united and was born according to the flesh.

Concerning him the apostle Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, says:

“For they themselves report concerning us what sort of entrance we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God, and to await his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus, who rescued us from the coming wrath.”

[Col. 0093B]

Therefore, as worshipers of this holy faith and followers of Christian law, we profess that the Word of God is united in substance to flesh, and that the one Christ, God and at the same time human being, is to be worshiped together with his own flesh.

With our heart we bear witness, with a pure mind we affirm, and with a restrained mouth we confess that the Son of God was crucified in the flesh, suffered death in the flesh, and became the firstborn from the dead. In him remains the perfect life of believers, since as God he is the giver of life to all the faithful.

[Col. 0093C]

I write these things, dearest ones, so that peace and concord may be preserved among the Churches, that the indissoluble bond of charity may remain, and that the gifts of divine generosity may not be diminished.

We venerate and believe in the Trinity in unity. We confess that the Father and the Son existed in the beginning, just as we confess and worship the Paraclete proceeding from both—not three gods, but one God alone. Let us faithfully render to him what is owed, so that the Lord and our Redeemer may not disdain to forgive us our offenses. He wondrously works such great miracles in his servants, and we shall see greater things than these, with the help of him whose majesty and beauty, unfading glory, power, and immeasurable honor remain throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0093D]

“Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” Behold, in these days we see fulfilled what is said through the voice of the prophet Isaiah:

“Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel.”

Behold, a virgin conceived without male seed; a virgin gave birth without any violation of the flesh. Through the birth of this same Son, the joy of the human race is increased, while by his coming the enemy of our nature is confounded in grief.

For that adversary of ours, who at dawn arose like Lucifer, who delighted in the foods of pleasure in the paradise of God, fell from heaven and deserved to hear:

“Though you be exalted like an eagle, from there you shall be shamefully dragged down by the Lord.”

That enemy of the human race, who [Col. 0094A] had said that he was like the Most High, having slipped through pride, roars like a lion and seeks someone to devour. He does not seek an unbelieving person, nor an angry one, nor those who are outside; rather, he seeks to cast down the humble, the restrained, and the rational person, or anyone belonging to the Church of Christ.

This envious one drove the human being, expelled from the paradise of God, into this misery and valley of tears. He wanted to drive blessed Job far from God, but he could not. For concerning that spotless and simple man it is said:

“His strength is in his loins, and his power is in his navel.”

Thus, through the disobedience of the first human being, death and misery entered the world; but through the nativity of the second human being, salvation and joy entered. The star gave the sun; the Virgin gave birth to God as human being without a human father; the staff brought forth a flower.

If Mary had not remained a virgin, she would certainly not have given birth to the Son of God. O virginity worthy of all praise!

[Col. 0094B]

The most blessed Isaiah says:

“A virgin came forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isaiah 11:1).

The Virgin is the mother of Christ, simple, humble, and undefiled, with no external seed joined to her, and fruitful through a union made in the image of God.

It was truly necessary for human beings that a virgin should conceive the Son of God: this was troublesome to Satan but fruitful for us. Concerning that flower which the staff of Jesse brought forth, it is written:

“I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.”

If virginity had not benefited the Virgin, the prophet would not have indicated that the Virgin would be born from the Virgin.

Widowed continence is nevertheless excellent; virginal chastity is better. The law of Moses, however, had been given differently. For it is written:

“Blessed is he who has seed in Zion.”

And:

“Cursed is the barren woman who does not give birth.”

And elsewhere:

“There was not one feeble person in their tribes.”

[Col. 0094C]

But in the law of our Lord Jesus Christ it is said:

“Rejoice, barren woman; do not consider yourself a dry tree. You shall have a place in eternity in place of sons and daughters.”

Now even the one who is weak is made stronger, as the Apostle bears witness, saying:

“I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.”

Therefore, because Christ was begotten from the eternal Father before all ages, this was the ineffable mystery of divine power. But insofar as he appeared visibly to us from a virgin as a human being, he became the grace of human salvation.

Death entered the world through Eve; but the life that had been lost is restored through Mary. After the Virgin conceived him in her womb, the Virgin gave birth to the light that enlightens every human being coming into this world:

“His dominion shall be upon his shoulder; he is the Mighty God, the Father of the age to come” (Isaiah 9:7).

The curse pronounced against the entire human race was dissolved.

[Col. 0094D]

Who, however, could comprehend the secret of this divine plan: that a virgin should receive him in her womb, that a virgin should give birth to God, begotten before all things by the Father without a mother; that the invisible God should appear through a visible human being; that, assuming death under the condition of human mortality, he should come forth from an original human womb under no law of bodily generation; and that his own mother should remain an incorrupt virgin?

Therefore Christ, born before the ages without a mother from the invisible Father—not for himself, but because it was necessary for the human race—was born a second time without a human father from a visible mother.

And because we were endangered through the disobedience of the first woman, it was necessary that we should be saved through a woman.

[Col. 0095A]

Let the human race rejoice, for Christ is born and, wrapped in humble swaddling clothes, is placed in the manger of animals. The lowliness of the swaddling clothes is a great and ineffable mystery. For that lowliness of the swaddling clothes is worshiped by the Magi, and gold, frankincense, and myrrh are offered to the child lying in the manger and reigning over the angelic creation.

Gold is fitting for a king; the offering of frankincense for the great priest; myrrh for the burial of the dead. Gold signifies that the Son of God, born from the Virgin, already reigns upon the earth. Frankincense signifies that he offers himself for us as a sacrifice to the heavenly Father, the high priest. Myrrh signifies that this same Son of the Virgin is buried and rises again for the salvation of the human race.

Therefore the swaddling clothes with which the Virgin mother binds the infant are, as we know, our sins, as the prophet says:

“Truly he bore our weaknesses, and he himself carried our sins.”

[Col. 0095B]

Through these humble swaddling clothes it is made evident that he took upon himself our offenses.

But the fact that he is placed in the midst of two animals is an immeasurable mystery of God. Behold, what is said through the voice of the prophet Habakkuk has been fulfilled:

“Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works and was terrified: in the midst of two animals.”

It is fitting that the Son of Man should be placed among humble animals. For he is the life of human beings, the food of angels, and the nourishment of beasts. Therefore it was necessary that he who was the living bread should be placed in a manger between two animals, crying as an infant.

For he is the one who says:

“I am the living bread that came down from heaven.”

He is the spotless Lamb, whose undefiled body, after it has been touched by the priest and eaten by the entire faithful people, [Col. 0095C] remains unharmed and undiminished.

After what the prophets had foretold concerning the Virgin’s childbirth, and what the patriarchs had proclaimed beforehand, had been fulfilled, and after everything that had to be done concerning Christ through the angel Gabriel had been completed, it was fitting that a new, pure human being, proceeding from a human being—“a virgin stripped from a virgin” [reading uncertain]—should acquire for himself a new family: so that he who was worshiped by angels in heaven might also establish angels for himself on earth.

Then he wished to be baptized by John: the king by a soldier, the Lord by a servant. This was not because he had committed any crimes, but so that our sins might be erased through his baptism. The water did not cleanse him; rather, by entering it he blessed it—he who baptized in Spirit and truth.

Then, announcing to the people the word of life and truth, he appointed some to be disciples [Col. 0095D] and others evangelists.

For the twin brothers, namely James and John, left their father Zebedee and the boat. Following the Savior, they unanimously set aside and abandoned the care of their household and the affection of blood relations.

After this came many other disciples, to whom the Lord Jesus said:

“If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”

For divine Scripture contains this:

“No soldier goes into battle with his wife.”

If anyone wishes to follow the footsteps of the Redeemer, let him leave everything and not look back, as Lot’s wife did. For:

“No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

But if anyone has the means by which he can redeem his soul from the enemy’s fraud, [Col. 0096A] let him feed the poor, practice hospitality, and cover the naked person with a garment, even if it is a poor one.

When Christ wished to ascend from the earth to heaven and pass from the underworld to the heights, as he had foretold to his disciples long beforehand, he suffered death so that he might free the dead from sin. He preached so that he might show us the way of salvation. He rose so that those who had been given life might live.

Therefore, dearest ones, following his footsteps, let us not please ourselves, but God and our neighbor. For when Jesus was announcing peace to the people, he said to his disciples:

“I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.”

When the Son of Man was fulfilling the will of God, the Jews said that he was sinning against God. Rather, by refusing to receive the Son whom the Father had sent, they reproached the Father; and therefore, without cause, they affixed the Son of God, who had committed no offense, [Col. 0096B] to the gallows of the cross.

Thus the sins of sinners fell upon Christ, who, though found innocent, was killed as though he were a blasphemer.

Then the victorious Lord Jesus, stripping the places of darkness, rose on the third day and happily ascended into the heavens from which he had descended.

But how did humanity ascend, unless the Godhead had first descended into the lower parts of the earth in order to be united to human nature? The heavenly Godhead descended so that the humanity of the Redeemer might ascend. He is one and the same person.

For he was always in the Father, always with the Father, and always was with the Father. After the ascension of his humanity, he also sent the Holy Spirit, appearing in tongues of fire, to his disciples.

The Spirit is indeed the power of the Son, which went forth from him and healed everyone. Yet he is said to proceed from the Father, and is customarily referred back to him: from him he is, and what he is belongs to him.

For Christ himself bears witness, saying:

“My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.”

The Son has from the Father that he should be God. For he is from God, God. From him he has that the Holy Spirit should proceed from him.

[Col. 0096C]

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us celebrate with due veneration the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let us flee pride, lest we be overwhelmed in hell like the evil angels. Through pride a human being is puffed up, by greed he is shaken, and by ambition he is delighted.

Do not boast of worldly riches. Do not place yourselves above others, lest an evil thought creep in. And you who now desire golden garments, may it please you henceforth to sit in squalor, so that you too may please Christ, to whom be honor with the invisible Father throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF THE ANNUNCIATION

[Col. 0096D]

Concerning the threefold solemnity of the most blessed Virgin Mary, dearest brothers—on which the angel announces, the Virgin conceives, and the Only-Begotten Son of the Unbegotten is clothed in flesh—some things must be said, although the one who announces is worthy of manifold praise, the one who conceives through the ear is worthier, and the one who announces is worthiest; the one who conceives through the ear is worthier; but the one who is conceived is worthiest.

This is the saving day, to be celebrated by us with due veneration, on which earthly things are reconciled with heavenly things; on which the divinity of the Redeemer descended to us so that our humanity might ascend to heaven.

This is that solemn day which takes its beginning from the angel: how he announced [one] to be born of a Virgin from a Virgin [as printed]; [Col. 0097A] how the power of the Most High overshadowed the Virgin; how the untouchable God deigned to be touched—he who is the eternal light that enlightens every human being coming into this world.

This is the solemn day that raises and lifts us from earth to heavenly things and honorably exalts us above the heavens of heavens, as the present sermon will make clear.

For after the first human being had been expelled through the tree of knowledge, which had been forbidden by the Lord and tasted inappropriately, the deception of demons deceived human beings wandering through the allurements of vices, enslaved them by deceiving them, and plunged them into the outer darkness. There, as the Lord bears witness, we hear weeping and the gnashing of teeth.

For when the glory of the devil had aroused ambition, and ambition had provoked envy, he grieved that the human race was being transferred from earth to heaven. Because he had fallen miserably, he thereby brought himself consolation in his misery.

[Col. 0097B]

Therefore, when the Father considered the destruction of the human race through the serpent’s deception, he deigned to free the world through the incarnation of his Only-Begotten Son. Since a woman had been expelled from the seats of paradise through the serpent’s exhortation, she would, through an angel’s salutation, deserve to receive the glory of immortality.

The exhortation of the enemy deceived Eve; the salutation of Gabriel strengthened Mary. The angel announces so that the devil’s deception may be destroyed. The Virgin is overshadowed by the power of the Most High, the angel announcing, so that the woman who had long before been deceived by Satan’s message might be restored.

The incorruptible God is clothed in flesh and descends so that through him the old human being, who had come into this misery and valley of tears by tasting the fruit inappropriately, might ascend as the human being Jesus.

[Col. 0097C]

For it is written that when the woman had deceived her husband, the Lord said to her:

“In pain you shall bear children, and your desire shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.”

All who do not imitate Mary’s virginity suffer these three disadvantages, as though the Lord were saying to her:

“When your desire is toward your husband, you will be subjected to his service; and when you give birth, you will suffer the losses of pain and sorrow.”

These three things, however, are excluded from the blessedness of the Virgin Mary—not only from the Virgin herself, but from all who devote their virginity to Christ.

Come, therefore, virgins who vow virginity to the Virgin. Vow to the Virgin bodily integrity, for she displayed undefiled chastity to the Lord.

Hear, then, how great the merit of this same Virgin was. She not only deserved to be visited through an angelic address, but also to contain within the enclosure of her virginal womb [Col. 0097D] him who could in no way be contained.

Our mother Eve was burdened by three evils, but blessed Mary was excluded from them and rejoiced in a threefold happiness. For she was strengthened by the angelic salutation, strengthened and blessed, and announced to be fruitful through the fullness of grace.

For thus it is written:

“An angel was sent to a virgin.”

We confess that this is the virgin concerning whom it is read in Isaiah:

“A staff shall come forth from the root of Jesse”—that is, the Virgin Mary—“and a flower shall rise from his root”—that is, Christ.

For he himself bears witness in the Song of Songs, saying:

“I am the flower of the field.”

And entering to her, he said:

“Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you. Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.”

[Col. 0098A]

O angelic voice, full of sweetness and joy! When he said, “Hail, Mary,” he offered a heavenly salutation to the Virgin. When he said, “Full of grace,” he showed that the sentence by which the first parents were made far from God had been excluded, and that the grace of heavenly blessing had been restored, by which they were freed from servitude and brought into paradise.

When he uttered, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb,” he expressed not only that the fruit of her womb was blessed, but also that all those who followed Mary the Virgin and remained in virginity were blessed.

O blessed Virgin, O Virgin especially chosen by the Creator of the world! You shall conceive him who was begotten before all ages, without a mother, by the eternal Father; you shall become a mother without the union of any man.

[Col. 0098B]

For there the little ear was the wife, while the angelic word became the husband. You shall conceive as a virgin, and after giving birth you shall remain a virgin. The Son of God shall descend into you so that he who was about to ascend with the power of sublimity and the glory of his radiance toward the East might turn the grace of his majesty toward the West.

Let hearing not confound you; let conception not disturb you. For this conception is not necessity but the immeasurable power of God. He shall be clothed in flesh and conceal himself in your virginal womb, and the Son of God shall begin to be the son of man, while always remaining what he was.

For we believe him to be unchangeable, yet in mercy he assumed what he was not, so that he who could not be carried by the whole world might be contained in you.

Through this conception virginal chastity will not be diminished, but the integrity of chastity [Col. 0098C] will be increased in you. You became the mother of the Creator while he was with the Father; and when he was born from you, the Mother, he remained with the Father.

For he was always with the Father, because, being without beginning, he has no temporal beginning. He was always with the Father, who remains without beginning and without end.

You became a heavenly ladder by which heavenly glory descended to what is below, so that humility might be carried upward to the heights of heaven. You flourished as Aaron’s staff above the others—that is, you shone as more worthy than the others in virginity.

O new and unheard-of union! O ineffable and wondrous mingling! He who had created all things from nothing is created; he who could not be contained is contained; he who makes all things abound in riches becomes poor; Christ, who is perfect, deigns to be emptied.

For he is said to have emptied himself in time of the form of Godhead, so that we might be enriched by that same heavenly perfection.

[Col. 0098D]

(Therefore, dearest brothers, let us entreat the Virgin, so that she may reconcile God to human beings and harmonize earthly things with heavenly things. Let her intercede for past things, entreating the Son concerning future things.

O Virgin, grant not only bodily food, but the bread of angels descending within the enclosure of your womb. Make us fear the Son of God. For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.)

If anyone fears the Lord, he will keep his commandments. Then bodily purification will follow, so that we may be able to contemplate the rays of divine light. After bodily purification has been given to us, illumination of our heart will follow.

(Hear, then, and incline your ear to our prayers. O Virgin, who are rightly praised by us, who, [Col. 0099A] remaining a virgin after childbirth, are venerated by us, pray to God for us, so that he may grant constancy and bestow patience; so that concord may be strengthened and endurance increased; so that, when the pain of sorrow and misery, calamity and grief comes, you may deign to present us to your Only-Begotten Son, who is one God.

We confess him to be one in substance and three in persons; he is in all, and above all, and in us all; he is sought in part and known in part; he does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn from his evil way.

Pray that we may be made perfect light, so that we may praise you together in the glory of your Son; to whom be honor and power throughout all ages of ages. Amen.)

## PRAYER OF BLESSED ELEUTHERIUS, AS HE WAS DYING, TO GOD FOR THE FAITH AND THE CHURCH OF TOURNAI

[Col. 0099B]

The Catholic faith believes, confesses, adores, and venerates not three gods, but one God. Unity remains in the Trinity; the perfect Trinity consists in unity.

The true God, the same our Lord Jesus Christ, was born from the true Father according to divinity; according to humanity, he was begotten from an undefiled virgin. From both proceeds the Holy Spirit, who causes the hearts of unbelievers to be turned toward recognition of the truth.

The Son is equal to the Unbegotten Father; the Holy Spirit is equal to his Only-Begotten Son. The Son, eternal light from eternal light, proceeded; the unfailing lamp shone forth from that invisible brightness when the Virgin Mary, foretold as the Mother of the eternal Judge, conceived from the Holy Spirit.

The Virgin, remaining in chastity, brought forth the Son of God upon the earth, and [Col. 0099C] after her wondrous childbirth, remaining in virginity, nourished Christ Jesus with divine milk.

O that holy angelic proclamation! The angel Gabriel is sent to the Virgin, who is unaware of the mystery. The mother of the Redeemer is likened to a servant when she answers the angel; for she says:

“Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

Therefore the Son of God, made flesh so that the angel’s word might be fulfilled, is born from the glorious Virgin by divine inspiration. He is laid in a manger and then announced to the shepherds by an angel.

He reigns in heaven and governs all things, while the little Son of God lies in the manger. He is nourished by his virgin mother and worshiped by the Magi with their gifts.

To show us the humility of his power and the magnificence of his divinity, he deigned to possess all things as a human being without sin. He had no sin; he endured death; and through his death he displayed to us the life of the immortal One.

[Col. 0099D]

O wondrous birth of God’s Only-Begotten! O marvelous proclamation of the Son of Man! O unheard-of wisdom of so great a youth!

The Son of God had appeared in the synagogues and through the Holy Spirit convicted all the scribes and teachers of the law. Yet, insofar as he is the Son of God, he did not receive power from that same Spirit, as though the Spirit were supplying it. For the Son, coeternal with the eternal Father, never needed the assistance of another, because he is perfect and blessed throughout the ages of ages.

The wise marvel at a wisdom unheard of by the world. For this reason the Jews scourged the Son of Man, delivered by Judas, the impious and most wicked betrayer, and pursued him with insults.

Thus Christ Jesus, [Col. 0100A] who for the salvation of human weakness voluntarily inclined himself to humiliation, offered his own body—not for himself, but for our redemption—as a true sacrifice to the eternal Father, a sacrifice pleasing to God as a sweet fragrance.

What sacrifice or offering would he have needed, since he existed as God, free from every sin? But if all have sinned and lack the grace of God—for human nature has been made sick by sins and evil deeds—he himself was not so, although he assumed the likeness of a servant and willingly accepted death.

The prophet David understood the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ in this way when he said:

“Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit” (Psalm 50).

For the Father is the beginning of all things, with whom the Son made all things: King of kings, Father of the universe, [Col. 0100B] and reformer of the passing age.

During these words, the holy man’s pain from his wounds and the anguish of his spirit were constricting him severely. What was he to do? He saw the day of his death approaching, and he knew that the churches he had built within the walls would fall.

Therefore, turning with tears, he prayed, saying:

Almighty, most merciful God, who willed that your glorious name be invoked with a threefold invocation in your three holy patriarchs—namely Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—so that through your only-begotten Son Jesus the outstanding worshipers of the Catholic faith might recognize and firmly believe that in the perfect Trinity you are God: the unbegotten Father, equal to the only-begotten Son and coequal with the Holy Spirit; the true Father who begot the true Son before the foundation of the world and before the establishment of all things; who sent from heaven the Holy Spirit proceeding from you, so that he might strengthen the hearts of your disciples and make the name of Christ renowned among human beings. His true Trinity consists in unity; one Godhead abides in the Trinity, equal to the Son and coequal with the Holy Spirit. For nothing is greater in you, nothing lesser in the other.

You are the same God everywhere; everywhere are your majesty, your dominion, and your power. You formed all things from nothing through your only-begotten Son. Descending into the womb of the undefiled Virgin, you deigned to assume the form of our servitude and, perfect God, to put on a perfect human being, so that, having become flesh, you might aid humanity, and, having become incarnate as a human being, might turn unbelievers toward the way of truth. After the Virgin’s childbirth, placed as a child in a cradle, he displayed the humility of his condition. To shepherds keeping watch, and to the Magi with the star of Ethiopia going before them, he was revealed by rejoicing angels. He endured the devil’s temptations, reproaches on our behalf, and other torments, so that he might free us from the snares of visible and invisible enemies and cleanse the stains of our crimes. He endured the gallows of the cross so that he might restore us to the glory of the heavenly court, which we lost through Adam. The Son of Man became incarnate so that he might make the sons of human beings sons of God and participants in heavenly blessings.

I beseech you, who became the author of our resurrection, to open the heavenly entrance for us, to take the devil’s dominion captive, and, ascending into heaven by your wondrous power, to lead our captivity captive. By your death you restored life to the dead and healing to the captives.

I call upon you mercifully; I appeal to you compassionately: preserve and defend from every disturbance of demons, raise up and exalt, the churches of Tournai, which I have elevated as far as my smallness permitted, and all the dwellings of the saints. Guard my few sheep, those now present and those who will follow, until the final generation, so that they may know that you are gentle, Father of mercy and compassion, giver of knowledge and truth.

But to those who pursued me, your unworthy servant, even unto death with swords and clubs, graciously grant pardon; and deign to gather me with your saints into your granary. To those also who have reverently honored my memory, grant faith and bestow friendship, most merciful God, in whatever way your clemency knows how to make them rejoice on behalf of the Catholic faith and the Christian religion. For all things are naked and open to your eyes.

Behold, now the time of my departure is drawing near. Eternal God, what shall I do? Send me forth so that I may follow David, who says: “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.” And again he says: “My soul thirsted for the living God: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” If it can be done, permit me to be made like blessed Job, who says: “I have been compared to mud and made like dust and ashes.” In you I trust, my God; I seek you; I desire to see you, whom, while placed on earth, I have always worshiped; to whom I have devoted myself with complete love. Deliver me, you who are blessed for ever and ever.

And immediately, breaking out again into the praises of God, he said:

The Catholic faith declares that he is the Son to whom the Father cries out through the prophet and says: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” And again: “With you is dominion on the day of your power, amid the splendors of the saints; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.”

He is Jesus Christ our Lord, equal to the invisible Father, proceeding from the invisible, another from the eternal, immortal from the immortal. Uniting the nature of our humanity to himself according to subsistence, he endured birth from that corporeal and virginal womb—not because he had need of that glorious birth, but in order to sanctify the first beginnings of our substance itself. Thus, when Christ, united to flesh, proceeded from the blessed Virgin Mary, that wretched curse which had been pronounced against the whole human race ceased, and no longer consigned souls and mortal bodies to death. He thereby also showed the truth of what he had foretold through the prophet’s voice: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” And elsewhere: “God has wiped away every tear from every face.”

He is Christ, the Son of the Virgin Mary, who restored hearing to the deaf and sight to the blind; who walked across the sea on dry feet; who drove out demons; who calmed winds and seas; who cleansed lepers; who healed paralytics; who raised the dead; and who said to the unbelieving Jews: “If you do not believe my words, you ought at least to believe my powers and miracles.”

There is one Son of God in Christ: just as in truth he is the invisible Son of God, so in truth Christ is visible. For perfect God put on a perfect human being, so that he might offer perfect salvation to human beings.

And concerning the Holy Spirit, let us hear the prophet praying and saying: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me.” It is a great act of presumption to separate the Son from the Father, the Father from the Son, and the Holy Spirit as though he did not proceed from both. For God is inseparable, unchangeable, and impassible.

The Son, as was said above, is equal to the Father. The Holy Spirit is neither superior nor better than the Son, but equal to the Father, coequal with the Son, proceeding from both. The unbegotten Almighty God sent the Holy Spirit into the world so that he might glorify his only-begotten Son.

Because Christ, the Son of God, performed human miracles, healed lepers, raised the dead, and did other things unheard of in the world, and because, in order to demonstrate his Godhead, he used the power of his own Spirit, he was said to be glorified by that Spirit. Nevertheless, it is not proper to affirm that our Lord Jesus Christ was glorified by the Holy Spirit, as though he had used an alien power through him and had taken power through that same Spirit against unclean spirits. Rather, we must confess that the Spirit was his own, through whom he performed such splendid miracles.

It is also fitting for every believer to affirm that he offered an oblation or sacrifice to the Father, not for himself but for the redemption of the human race, since he who was undefiled by sin had no need of any offering. Therefore the Catholic faith should believe and affirm that the flesh of the Word himself was made life-giving and proper to him. For, since he naturally possesses life as God, and since he was personally united to the flesh, he confessed that flesh to be life-giving.

Yet when he says, “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have eternal life,” we must not regard it as the flesh of one human being. For according to its nature, how could the flesh of one human being be life-giving?

Let the wretched Jew flee; let the heretic who denies Christ’s birth be destroyed. The faithful praise God as three in persons but one God in subsistence. The wretched await him in wrath, consigned to infernal punishments, and evil angels rejoice in their fellowship.
