The just, however, await him as the reward for their labors, and the angels of God rejoice in their company. May he assist us whose benefits are bestowed upon the weak and through whom joy is given to the afflicted. To him be honor, dominion, and power, with the unbegotten Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout endless ages of ages. Amen.

## In the Year of Our Lord 533. Saint Fulgentius, Bishop of Ruspe

## Dedication

To the most illustrious prince of the Church, the Lord Charles Maurice Le Tellier, Archbishop and Duke of Reims, born legate of the Apostolic See, primate of Belgica Secunda, first peer of France, prefect of the royal chapel, etc.

To put an end to the reckoning of benefits for which I am indebted to your most noble family, there are qualities in you, most illustrious archbishop, that made it appropriate for this new edition of the works of Saint Fulgentius to be dedicated to you.

For while you have always shown yourself an outstanding patron of the entire teaching of the holy Fathers, you have seemed especially devoted to and protective of those of their writings in which the monuments of ancient discipline survive. You do not pursue this merely to seek amusement or to hunt after empty glory; rather, the greatest benefits have flowed from it to the Christian commonwealth.

By your example you have encouraged lovers of Sacred Scripture to investigate more attentively the memory of ecclesiastical antiquity, and you have led pastors of souls to observe more carefully the customs of the Church in former centuries. Nor have you considered that you had sufficiently fulfilled your episcopal office, either by repeatedly traversing all the villages, rural districts, cities, and places of your province, urging pastors and sheep to perform properly the duties of Christian devotion—sometimes by gentle admonition, sometimes by vehement exhortation; or by establishing at Reims a seminary of clerics, most of whom you supported at your own expense and took care to train through suitable men for sacred ministry; or by adorning, repairing, and constructing sacred buildings; or by relieving everywhere the distress of needy families; or by overthrowing the schools of the Sedanese heretics and converting the royal stipend of the teachers in them, by the king’s own grant, to the support of Catholic scholars; or, finally, by fully carrying out all the duties of archiepiscopal care.

You considered none of this sufficient unless you made your concern for the flock entrusted to you in some way perpetual and transmitted it to your successors for imitation, having described and gathered into one body what you judged necessary for governing the diocese of Reims according to an eminently Christian plan.

As for the other matters that you undertake daily in the sight of the whole kingdom—before the Most Christian King, through the influence that you possess everywhere; before assemblies of learned men, whom you frequently convene; and at the meetings of the Gallican clergy, for preserving the majesty of divine things, asserting the rights of the Gallican Church, and defending purer doctrine—why should they be mentioned, since they are before everyone’s eyes?

Thus, while your father, the most illustrious chancellor of France, demonstrates his fidelity to prince and citizens in administering justice throughout the kingdom, a fidelity exercised through various and most important public offices throughout his life and still retained, full of strength of mind and vigor, in the extreme of old age; and while your brother, the most illustrious marquis, emulates your father’s devotion to the prince in managing affairs of war and peace, you watch over the ordering of sacred matters, especially by restoring the institutions of the Church to the examples of ancient piety.

You were recently doing this when, appointed one of the two presidents of the assembly of French bishops, you directed and adjusted the rights of political authority to the weight of ecclesiastical power with such balance that, once the precautions you advanced with the greatest gravity of speech had been applied, neither could harm the other, and both could mutually provide the greatest assistance. In this you displayed both the reverence of a son toward the Apostolic See and the obedience of a subject toward the king.

Therefore, most illustrious archbishop, favor our labor, and protect these works of Saint Fulgentius, now newly corrected and once more brought to the light, under the patronage of your name—that is, assert them by the support of your judgment: the teaching of a bishop whose apostolic zeal for increasing, strengthening, and cultivating religion you strive to imitate in action and thought.

Your most devoted and obedient servant,  
**GUILLELMUS DESPREZ**

## Prolegomena

### Preface

All writings of the Fathers possess this particular gift: they not only strike minds with the radiance of truth, but at the same time implant in the hearts of their readers an intimate sense of piety. I am not sure, however, whether this praise has belonged more properly to anyone than to Fulgentius. From his writings breathes such ardor of charity, and such abundance of spirit pours forth from them, that one not only understands but actually feels that his breast is filled with God.

Know that he was a disciple of Augustine, not merely through agreement in doctrine, but through similarity of virtues and through the various gifts of intellect and character by which he reproduced the whole of Augustine.

Augustine’s style is indeed somewhat more polished and less affected by the faults of his age, since Fulgentius never took care to wipe away the mark of his own age. Yet the vigor of mind is the same in both, the same acuteness, the same weight of thought, the same felicity of intellect, the same diligence, skill, and abundance in handling Scripture, the same fairness, gentleness, and meekness of character, the same ardor of charity shining from their writings, and the same zeal for truth.

Nor were their opponents different. Augustine frequently struggled with the Arians, and this heresy exercised Fulgentius throughout his life. Augustine fought with the emerging Semipelagians, and Fulgentius with the same men once they had grown stronger, with equal success in both cases. Neither of them entirely crushed this error, but both defeated and subdued it so thoroughly that the whole company of Latin theologians has always joined itself to both of them.

Since Fulgentius therefore rightly holds a place among the writers of the Church, many lovers of ecclesiastical literature were distressed that his works had until now been treated so carelessly, so that they had served rather as additions to the writings of other authors than stood in their own right as a collected volume. When a most distinguished man, who has deserved well of all Gaul and especially of letters, wished this corrected, he ordered a new edition of Fulgentius to be prepared as soon as possible, by virtue of the authority he possessed.

This is the edition now coming to light. As I was about to write this preface at the request of those who supervised the edition, nothing seemed more useful to me than to draw up a brief catalogue of the surviving works of Fulgentius and to explain briefly their occasions and subjects.

Fulgentius was first a monk from the office of a royal procurator, then superior of a monastery, afterward a presbyter, and soon a bishop. He was immediately exiled with other African bishops to Sardinia; from there he was recalled to Africa by Thrasamund, who, I know not whether genuinely or merely in appearance, professed a love of learning, because of Fulgentius’s outstanding reputation for intellect and education. After that first return from Sardinia, he wrote various works both in defense and for the instruction of the Church.

His first work appears to be the one whose title in this edition is: *One Book of Saint Fulgentius Against the Arians, Containing Ten Objections and Ten Responses*. The objections are remarkable both for their barbarity and for their obscurity; the responses, nevertheless, are lucid and carefully aligned with the teaching of the earlier Fathers.

Thus he teaches that the Scriptural passage, “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways,” is to be understood not of Christ’s eternal but of his temporal generation. Later writers, however, refer it not unreasonably to the eternal generation of the Word, undeterred by the word “created,” since the Hebrew more nearly expresses what the Vulgate edition has: “The Lord possessed me as the beginning of his ways.”

Three books addressed to Thrasamund should be appended to this work. Fulgentius himself explains their occasion at the beginning. A certain Felix, a royal official, had brought Fulgentius some writing from the king, to be read rapidly and hastily—or rather merely sampled—and had immediately demanded a response. Nevertheless, the king insisted that Fulgentius answer as soon as possible.

Certainly no contest was ever arranged more unfairly. Who was ever ordered to answer a book whose reading was forbidden to him? Fulgentius nevertheless accepted the conditions of the contest, lest, as he himself says, he be thought either swollen with disdain or bound by the fault of silence. Whatever had remained in his memory from that hurried reading, he refuted with great force in three books.

A certain Arian bishop named Pinta undertook to refute these works, but Fulgentius in turn splendidly confuted him. Nevertheless, I am led by many considerations to doubt that the work bearing the title on page 535 of this edition—*For the Catholic Faith Against Pinta the Arian*—was written by Fulgentius.

First, there is no mention in it of Pinta, of the books addressed to Thrasamund, or of this entire controversy. Further, the interpretation of *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιος, “of the same substance”) that it offers is not sufficiently compatible with Fulgentius, who was by no means lightly educated in Greek. Accordingly, both Sirmond and others much more plausibly deny this work to Fulgentius, although it is clear that it was written in Africa during the Vandal persecution.

Not long afterward, driven once more into Sardinia by Arian hostility, he undertook the books addressed to Monimus. Monimus was one of his principal friends and distinguished also for virtue and learning. But because he was less well versed in the teaching of Saint Augustine, he had fallen into the opinion that human beings are predestined by God to evil just as they are to good, and he twisted certain passages of Augustine in support of this view. Yet, trusting Fulgentius more than himself, he submitted the whole matter to Fulgentius’s judgment, earnestly asking him not to hesitate to prescribe what should be thought about it.

Fulgentius treats this matter lucidly in the first book. He denies that Augustine teaches that human beings are predestined to evil, since God predestines only what he himself will do. It follows that, just as doing evil is foreign to God, so also is predestining anyone to evil. But because the punishment of evil is not itself evil, but rather medicine for the evil person, he teaches that human beings may rightly be said to be predestined to punishment, although God predestines no one to guilt.

This is the subject of the first book, which Florus calls *The Book on Predestination*. In the second book, among other matters, he teaches that sacrifice is offered to the whole Trinity, and that the Arians’ claim—that sacrifice is offered to the Father alone—is not true. In the third he refutes various sophisms of the same Arians.

The two books *On the Remission of Sins* should be appended to these books addressed to Monimus. From Fulgentius’s Life it is clear that they were written in exile. In them Fulgentius teaches that forgiveness of sins is granted by God neither outside the Church nor outside this life, since God has appointed only the span of life for repentance to be undertaken fruitfully.

It is evident that Fulgentius is speaking of that forgiveness by which someone is made just from unjust and pious from impious. As for whether some temporary punishments remain for the just after this life, from which they may be freed through prayers and good works, Fulgentius does not address the matter in either direction.

Various letters should be assigned to the same period of his second exile, and they seem to have been written in the following order.

First place should be given to the letter he sent to Proba, a Roman virgin distinguished both by birth and by virtues. She belonged to the family of the Anicii, in which the name Proba and the consulship were both frequent. Rejecting the luxuries in which she had been raised, she had consecrated her virginity to God. Among Roman girls she shone not only by the praise of chastity but also by the example of humility. Desiring to cultivate these virtues, she had often approached Fulgentius through a certain servant of God, asking him to write something for her both about virginity and about humility.

Fulgentius complied, being accustomed to serve Christ in his brothers, and composed a treatise on this subject for Proba. It was counted among his letters, although he himself calls it a little book.

At her same urging he also wrote two books *On Fasting and Prayer*. Some think that these are nothing other than the fourth letter, entitled *On Prayer and Compunction of Heart*, addressed to Proba. But since that letter is entirely concerned with explaining the grace of Christ, humility, and compunction of heart, and contains nothing separately about prayer, its title—*On Fasting and Prayer*—does not fit these books very well.

Baronius reasonably believes that Galla, whose name was no less illustrious, was addressed in writing by Fulgentius and praised by Saint Gregory. She was the daughter of the consul Symmachus and married to a consul. Soon widowed within a year, she had had enough of experiencing the allurements of the world. Although physicians advised against it and warned, not without reason, that if she pursued continence excessive heat would cause her to grow a beard, she immediately after her husband’s death withdrew into a monastery.

When Fulgentius learned of this, he consoled her in a letter over her husband’s death and instructed her concerning the state and duties of widowhood.

With a similar ardor of charity, he strengthened Theodore, a Roman senator and consul who had placed Christ before worldly grandeur, in his holy resolve through many exhortations. Baronius rightly commends the following passage:

“I rejoice greatly that you are no longer held by the bonds of worldly affection, and that, by despising the world, you trample upon the very thing by which, when you loved it, you were trampled upon. For although Christ died equally for all the faithful and bestowed an equal benefit of redemption upon all—since the Apostle says, ‘All of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ; there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus’—nevertheless, the conversion of the powerful of this world greatly advances the acquisitions of Christ.

“For just as many brothers, friends, clients, and subjects, both known and unknown, are stirred by the authority of such people to the ardor of worldly affection, and are kindled all the more by the fire of secular desire when they see the great willingly held captive by worldly love, so whenever he who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble, who touches the mountains and they smoke, mercifully regards hearts intent upon earthly matters and compels them to tremble at the consideration of his judgment, in the trembling of such people very many tremble together, and in the conversion of such people many flee for the aid of divine mercy.

“Thus it comes about that those who are established at the summit either destroy very many with themselves or acquire many with themselves on the way of salvation. A great punishment awaits such people if they provide many with a snare of evil imitation, or great glory if they display to many an example of holy conduct.

“It should no less be noted that he says the following concerning two kinds of pride: ‘The pride of the human heart is damnable when a person does what God condemns in human beings; but more detestable is the pride by which a person attributes to himself what God gives to human beings. Damnable is the person who uses the substance of the world badly; more damnable is the person who is arrogantly lifted up by spiritual gifts.’”

The date of Fulgentius’s remaining letters is uncertain, especially that of the letter generally regarded as the first. Its subject is sufficiently perplexing.

“A woman,” says Fulgentius, “having been married to a certain man, received the laying on of hands during a serious illness and performed penance according to the custom of the Christian religion. Attached to this penance was a vow of continence, suspended, however, upon her husband’s consent.”

This had caused the still-young husband scruples, and he referred the matter to Fulgentius. Fulgentius therefore resolved the difficulty by a general doctrine: neither husband nor wife can properly vow continence without mutual consent. But if one party consents to the vow, that person has no right to change the decision, and each must fulfill fully what he or she has promised to God, even if compelled by some necessity. At such a time the only remedy against the temptations of the flesh is prayer and vigorous struggle against desire. Divine help will not be lacking where the will to continence is complete and true humility does not cease from prayer and good works.

The letter to Eugyppius, or Egyppius, an abbot and presbyter distinguished by several works, seems to belong here. Fulgentius repays a blessing received from him—that is, as I interpret it, a small gift—with many expressions of grateful affection, and, inflamed by a strong ardor of charity, devotes himself entirely to commending charity.

The letter to Venantius, a woman foreign and unknown to Fulgentius, was granted at the request of a certain Junilius, his friend. In it he teaches that sins committed after baptism can be wiped away through penance, and he exhorts her to hope for forgiveness, joined to repentance. He explains that we are called and drawn to repentance in various ways, among which bodily illnesses hold no minor place, so that we who, by abusing health, have brought illness upon ourselves may through illness restore the benefits of health.

A treatise *On Faith*, addressed to Donatus, is also counted among the letters. Its occasion was an argument proposed to him by the Arians, by which they sought to make the Father greater and the Son lesser. Fulgentius first praises and approves this in Donatus: although he had not been able to respond, firm belief in the truth had nevertheless remained in his heart. He then lucidly sets forth the Catholic faith concerning one nature in three persons, followed by the doctrine of the Incarnation, after rejecting the errors.

Nothing can more suitably follow these letters than the treatises composed by Fulgentius in the case of Maxentius. They were not written at one time or continuously, but because their subject matter is connected they should by no means be separated. Their subject must be sought in the history of this controversy, from which we shall here draw only a little.

Who this Maxentius was and to what people he belonged is not sufficiently agreed among the learned. Nor should Ussher be followed, since he wants him to be the same as John of Antioch, whom Gennadius mentions in his *Catalogue*, although neither their dates nor their opinions agree.

He was certainly the leader or defender of the Scythian monks, entangled in the same opinions as they, but he was not a Scythian; he himself strove to remove that belief about him. He assumed for himself the name and title of abbot, but he did not persuade his adversaries, who maliciously cast at him the unspoken name of his monastery and that of the abbot under whom he had made his profession.

His style proves that he was born or educated in the West: it is not entirely unpolished and reflects the genuine Latin of that age.

Those Scythian monks and their supporter Maxentius had convinced themselves that the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies could not be sufficiently excluded unless it were asserted that one of the Trinity had suffered. Many people, however, were offended by the novelty of this expression, which rested on the authority neither of councils, nor of Leo the Great, nor of ecclesiastical usage. Soon the whole East was divided into parties, with some approving and others condemning the formula.

The Scythian monks, nevertheless, urged on by Maxentius—a man of exceedingly fiery temperament, in whom some, whether justly or unjustly I do not determine, found moderation lacking—did not slacken at all in their vehemence.

The case was first brought before the legates sent to Constantinople at that time by Hormisdas, the Roman pontiff. Soon afterward, when the monks found those legates less favorable to their cause than they wished, the case was transferred to Hormisdas himself at Rome, and the monks sent legates to Rome concerning it; one of them was the deacon Peter.

It is not the place here to recount what outcome the monks’ embassy had at Rome, or by what process their doctrine and formula, at first vigorously attacked by Hormisdas and almost condemned as heresy, were later approved under Pope John II, with John himself and the emperor consenting and the whole Church in agreement.

We need only observe, in keeping with our purpose, that the Scythian monks, finding everything hostile to them at Rome, sought to win the support of the African bishops exiled in Sardinia.

Accordingly, in the year 520 or 521, an exposition of faith was delivered in the name of the deacon Peter and his companions to Datianus, Fulgentius, and the other confessors exiled in Sardinia. It was composed in the form of a letter, with prayers added, asking the African Fathers to write back what they thought about the whole controversy.

So that they might know more fully what was at issue, the monks carefully explained their own position concerning both the person and the grace of Christ, defended the formula “one of the Trinity suffered” against its detractors, and finally struck Pelagius, Caelestius, and Julian, together with the books of Faustus, with an anathema.

When questioned about the faith, the African Fathers did not refuse to respond concerning the faith or to express their view on the proposed questions. They disputed splendidly and subtly concerning the Incarnation, but less acutely concerning the formula “one of the Trinity suffered,” since in its place they used, as though equivalent in meaning, the expression “one person of the Trinity was crucified.”

Those who were less favorable to the formula “one of the Trinity suffered,” however, considered the two expressions so different in meaning that, while admitting the former, they utterly rejected the latter.

Just as the monks’ writing was occupied for the most part with explaining the mystery of grace and predestination, so the response of the African Fathers contains much devoted to confirming and fortifying those same doctrines.

Both groups considered this timely and necessary because, when Faustus’s books were brought to Constantinople, great disputes had arisen among many people. Some rejected Augustine’s teaching as new and unheard-of, while others—including the Scythian monks—vigorously defended it and fiercely attacked Faustus.

The importance they assigned to these doctrines is shown by the conclusion of the entire response, where the bishops speak as follows:

“If anyone refuses to receive with heartfelt faith or to profess with his mouth the truth of this predestination, by which the Apostle testifies that we were predestined in Christ before the foundation of the world; if, before the final day of this present life, he does not cast away the stubbornness of his impiety by which he rebels against the living and true God, it is clear that he does not belong to the number of those whom God, before the foundation of the world, freely chose and predestined in Christ for the kingdom.”

Nor was it enough for the Scythian monks to have elicited this writing from the African bishops. Since the disputes at Constantinople nevertheless continued to boil, they arranged for Faustus’s own books to be sent to the bishops. Fulgentius opposed them with an outstanding response contained in seven books. In them he exposed the man’s profound cunning and crushed the doctrines hostile to the Catholic faith beneath the weight of Scripture and the Fathers.

The lovers of ecclesiastical learning will grieve the loss of this most excellent work, by far the foremost among Fulgentius’s books, for as long as they are deprived by the injustice of time of so great and desirable a treasure.

Fulgentius had scarcely completed this labor when, after the death of Thrasamund in the year 523, the situation of the African bishops changed. Hilderic, more favorably disposed toward the Catholic faith, recalled them from exile and restored them to their sees. He also granted them the authority to appoint new bishops in place of those who had died.

This return brought Fulgentius a new life and occasions for different labors.

First among them are three books *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, sent, I believe, to John, Maxentius, and Venerius in Constantinople. Chiffletius the Jesuit, a man who deserved well of letters and especially of Fulgentius, was the first to publish the third of these.

The bishops, formerly exiles and now restored to their homeland, added an excellent letter to the same John and Venerius. In it they carefully explain, according to Augustine’s mind and positions, the principal doctrines of Christian grace. You will find these books praised in the Council of Paris of the year 823 and the Council of Aachen of the year 836.

From the extensive work comprising twelve books against Fabianus, Chiffletius eventually published several extracts, though they are lengthy. Fabianus was an Arian of no ordinary reputation who had met Fulgentius somewhere and, after spreading false rumors about the conversation, forced Fulgentius to refute them.

The book written to Victor *Against Fastidiosus* should be assigned to the same period. Fastidiosus had once been a Catholic, indeed a monk, and had attained the dignity of the presbyterate in a monastery. But after being shamefully overcome by the allurements of the flesh, he first abandoned his profession and soon afterward his faith as well, and defected to the Arians.

Refuting the speech sent to him by Victor, Fulgentius shows that it by no means follows from the essential union of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit that the Father and the Holy Spirit were joined to human nature together with the Son.

The final labor of Fulgentius was the work he undertook at the request of Count Reginus to explain two matters. First, what should be thought about the controversy recently arising among the Alexandrian Eutychians: whether Christ’s body had been free from corruption immediately from the Incarnation, or had become so only after the resurrection. Second, what a military man should observe in order to retain and cultivate piety in that way of life.

But before the first part of this work had been completed, he was called to the heavenly kingdom.

After his death, at Reginus’s earnest request, the deacon Ferrandus completed the work he had begun, although he first declared himself unworthy in many respects to be regarded as Fulgentius’s successor:

“Have I been filled with wisdom as he was? Have I the same power of eloquence? Has a similar authority of dignity been granted to me? Or is even the innocence of my conduct at least equal to his?”

We have assigned the foregoing works of Fulgentius to definite periods as far as we could. There are others for which this could not be done. First among them is the excellent treatise *On the Faith to Peter*. Peter was not a deacon, as he has until now been incorrectly called in the title; nor was he a monk, as Blondel first believed (*On the Primacy*, p. 412), and Noricius later accepted incautiously. Rather, he was a military man who, preparing to depart for Jerusalem and fearing that some heretical perversity might insinuate itself into him, requested from Fulgentius a rule of faith.

Thus, wishing to accommodate Peter’s pious concern, but constrained by lack of time, Fulgentius first gave a fuller discussion of the Trinity, the Incarnation, the creation and fall of angels and human beings, and various other topics; finally he condensed the doctrines of the faith into forty articles, declaring that whoever dared to oppose any of them was to be regarded as a heretic. This, I think, is the rule of faith that Ferrandus requested Fulgentius to send him, and which Isidore designates by the same name. Nevertheless, that treatise was long mixed among Augustine’s works; later, by various arguments, and especially by the character of its style, it was restored to Fulgentius by the consensus of the learned. Indeed, Bertram had already cited it long ago under Fulgentius’s name.

Noricius thinks it was written in Sardinia, on account of the mention of persecutions found at the end of the work; but the conjecture is not sufficiently secure. Fulgentius could have recalled persecutions already past, or anticipated future ones in his mind.

[Col. 0112C] The following works must be counted among the treatises of uncertain date: the little book *On the Trinity to Felix the Notary*, and *On the Incarnation of the Son of God to Scarila*.

Felix’s request provided the occasion for the former. Exposed to the company and arguments of heretics, and insufficiently equipped to refute them, he wished Fulgentius to teach him how they could be resisted. Fulgentius complied with this deeply religious desire and not only ably defended the Catholic faith concerning the Trinity against the arguments of the Arians, but also discussed other articles of the faith with distinction. In this work one finds passages from some Father quoted without naming him; most of them, at least, are Augustine’s.

Fulgentius himself recounts the subject of the second work in Scarila’s own words:

> While at the table of Eventus, a Christian son of the Catholic Church, he says, a discussion arose concerning God’s Incarnation. One of the guests maintained concerning the Incarnation that it was not God the Father who put on flesh, but only the Son of God. Another said: “The very God who is one in three persons deigned to assume flesh, so that he might lead us into freedom from the slavery in which we were held bound through the transgression of our father Adam.” It seemed appropriate to choose as arbiter of this dispute Fulgentius, whom they knew to have been endowed with abundant illumination. Another question was added, concerning the creation of lowly and harmful animals, such as flies and scorpions, which some of the guests denied to God while others affirmed it of him.

[Col. 0113A] Fulgentius therefore discusses both matters brilliantly in this treatise, entitled *On the Incarnation and the Author of Lowly Animals, to Scarila*.

Two letters or books to the deacon Ferrandus remain. In the first, Fulgentius answers questions proposed by Ferrandus concerning the baptism of a dying Ethiopian slave. The man had admirably fulfilled all the duties of a catechumen; then, having been seized by a fatal illness, he was carried to the place of baptism almost at his final breath. There, without voice or movement, with the ministers answering in his place as though for an infant, and with his mind entirely absent, he received baptism; immediately afterward he died without participating in the Eucharist.

From this Ferrandus was troubled by two questions. First, whether another person’s confession could suffice for the salvation of an adult; second, whether those who, after receiving the sacrament of baptism, were prevented by the speed of death from eating the Lord’s flesh could attain salvation, since the Savior’s words were well known to the faithful: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.” Ferrandus therefore sought instruction on this point: whether it harms, how much it harms, or whether it does not harm at all if someone baptized in the name of the Trinity is deprived of the sacred food and drink.

Fulgentius examines these two questions separately. To the first he replies that a sincere desire for baptism, previously possessed, is sufficient, provided that baptism is conferred while the person is still alive, even though he perceives nothing. To the second he replies that no baptized person is deprived of salvation because, overtaken by death, he could not partake of the Eucharist, since through baptism itself he has received, if not the sacrament, at least the reality signified by the sacrament. For baptism has the power to insert us into the body whose head is Christ and to make us a true member of it; this incorporation is signified by the sacrament of the Eucharist.

In the second writing to Ferrandus, Fulgentius answers four questions proposed by him concerning the Trinity, together with one concerning the two cups given at the supper. For this reason it is entitled *On Five Questions*.

These, then, are Fulgentius’s writings that are counted under the names of books or letters. Something must also be added concerning the sermons that, in considerable number, must have been either written by him or dictated by him for delivery, whether by himself or by others.

[Col. 0113D] Among these are those bearing the following titles:

*On the Stewards of the Lord*, p. 546.  
*On the Twofold Birth of Christ the Lord*, p. 551.  
*On Saint Stephen the Protomartyr*, p. 555.  
*On the Epiphany and the Massacre of the Innocents*, p. 558.  
*On the Love of God and Neighbor*, p. 563.  
*On Saint Cyprian*, p. 566.

These are entirely worthy of Saint Fulgentius.

The sermon *On Saint Vincent*, p. 570, abounds so extravagantly in *ὁμοιοπτώτοις*—similar case-endings or homoeoteleutic phrasing—that, although this figure was sufficiently familiar to Fulgentius, I would nevertheless more readily attribute it to another than to Fulgentius.

The conclusion of the sermon on the passage from Micah, found on p. 572 of this edition, expressed in the words “turned toward the Lord,” strongly recalls Augustine. It is not unworthy of Fulgentius; nor are the sermon *On the Robber*, p. 567, and the one entitled *On Pentecost*, p. 569.

Concerning the two sermons added at the end, p. 664, the editors responsible for this edition have informed the reader in a special note what should be thought of them.

Various sermons have been thrown into the appendix. Some belong to Augustine, some to Chrysologus, and others to an ancient African author; but all have been wrongly attributed to Fulgentius.

Theophylus Raynaudus, moreover, engages in remarkable controversy in order to assert that the book *On Predestination and Grace*, formerly placed in the appendix, belongs to Fulgentius, as though it had been written in Sardinia. Much stronger, however, is the authority of Bellarmine, Possevinus, and the scholars of Louvain, who deny this work to Fulgentius and even maintain that it is by a suspect author. It is certainly scarcely probable that, after writing a book under this title, he would have given three other works almost the same title.

From these considerations it may be gathered that Fulgentius’s works can be divided threefold according to three periods.

The first period is that extending from his first return to Africa from exile until his second exile. To it should be assigned the following works mentioned above:

*Against the Arians*, one book containing ten replies to ten objections, p. 51.

*To Thrasamund*, three books, p. 69.

The second period encompasses the entire time of his second exile. To it belong the following works:

*To Monimus*, three books, p. 3.

*On the Remission of Sins, to Euthymius*, two books, p. 360.

*To Proba*, two letters: the first *On Virginity and Humility*, p. 163; the second *On Prayer and Compunction of Heart*, p. 177.

*To Galla*, one consolatory letter *On the Death of Her Husband and the State of Widowhood*, p. 151.

*To Theodore*, one letter *On Conversion from the World*, p. 186.

*On Conjugal Debt and the Vow of Continence*, one letter, p. 144.

*To Eugyppius the Abbot, On Charity*, one letter, p. 182.

[Col. 0114D] *To Venantius, On True Penance*, one letter, p. 190.

*Treatise on the Faith, to Donatus*, p. 197.

*Fulgentius and Certain Other African Bishops, to Peter the Deacon and Others Sent from the East to Rome in the Matter of the Faith, On the Incarnation and Grace of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, book or letter 17, p. 286.

The third period extends from Fulgentius’s second return to Africa after the death of Thrasamund until the end of his life. To it belong the following:

*On the Truth of Predestination and Grace, to John and Venerius*, three books, p. 434.

*Letter of the African Bishops on the Grace of God and Human Free Will, to John and Venerius*, p. 269.

*Against Fabianus*, twelve books, of which fragments remain, p. 577.

*Against the Sermon of Fastidiosus the Arian, to Victor*, one book, p. 340.

*Letter to Reginus*, p. 323.

The following works are of uncertain date:

*On the Faith, or On the Rule of True Faith, to Peter*, p. 500.

*On the Trinity, to Felix the Notary*, p. 328.

*On the Incarnation of the Son of God, to Scarila*, p. 406.

*To Ferrandus, a Letter on Questions Concerning the Salvation of the Dying Ethiopian*, p. 216.

*The Same Author’s Letter to Ferrandus, On Five Questions*, p. 229.

These, then, are the remains of Fulgentius’s labors that still survive. Yet it is established not merely by conjectures but by certain indications that he wrote much more. For, apart from that outstanding work *Against Faustus*, which perhaps lies hidden somewhere in the corners of libraries, there are other works for which there is scarcely any hope of discovery.

The true reply against Pinta exists nowhere, although it is established that Fulgentius himself wrote it.

The book *Debate*, in which he discussed the faith with King Thrasamund and which Saint Isidore mentions, exists nowhere.

The book *On the Holy Spirit, to Abragila*, in which he proved from many passages of Scripture that the Holy Spirit is one God with the Father and the Son, exists nowhere.

The distinguished letter to the Carthaginians exists nowhere. Its exhortation, as the author of his *Life* says, was lofty and clear; in it he set out, with the gravest lament, nearly all the deceits and seductive false blandishments by which wretched souls were enticed to death.

The two books *On Fasting and Prayer*, which he is known to have written to Proba, exist nowhere.

The two letters written in Sardinia to Stephania, a noblewoman, in his own name and that of the bishops, exist nowhere. An Arian had transferred a passage from one of them into his own sermon.

The letter written by Fulgentius to a certain bishop John exists nowhere. In it he clearly proved that a person guilty of crimes ought not to be handed over to a secular judge.

The ten books to Fabianus exist nowhere; only fragments of them survive.

[Col. 0115D] This is what I thought should be prefaced concerning Fulgentius’s works. What the ancients thought of them can be learned from Isidore, who says that Fulgentius was abundantly learned in the divine Scriptures, sweet in speech, and subtle in argument. Certainly the learned men of the ninth century took no small pains to excerpt substantial passages from him. The entire Church of Lyon honors him with this same eulogy:

> Blessed bishop and glorious confessor, who, on account of his admirable and venerable writings, has always been faithfully received by the Church and deservedly numbered among ecclesiastical writers.

There is certainly a singular power of intellect in him, seasoned with no ordinary sweetness. Some, however, would prefer him to be more concise and less repetitive in turning over and repeating the same thoughts. Yet it is precisely through this that he impresses his ideas more deeply and clearly upon the mind.

With these preliminary remarks, I must now briefly indicate what commends this latest edition.

First, it seemed important that all the writings of this eminent man should now be available separately, rather than, as formerly, being found scattered among various volumes or lying hidden, submerged in the vast ocean of the latest *Bibliotheca Patrum*.

Second, and of even greater importance, whereas in other editions the later editors followed the errors of the earlier ones without due care, so that the number of mistakes was increased rather than reduced, much labor has certainly been expended in this edition on correcting and purging them. Many passages that were completely without meaning have been restored to their integrity. The notes placed at the foot of the pages attest to the care devoted to this task. Would that it had been possible to advance further in this work and that a greater supply of manuscripts had been available, by which very many passages that remained obscure could have been illuminated! It is nevertheless something to have surpassed the others in this diligence of correction and to have encouraged them to undertake the work with greater assistance.

The reader will sometimes encounter divisions of chapters that have been altered, but he will easily discover the reason for the alteration. Those sections had formerly been made with such carelessness that not infrequently the same period was split into two parts, with the first becoming the conclusion of the preceding chapter and the second the beginning of the following one; thus the entire sentence was deprived of all clarity and meaning.

Where the titles of works have been somewhat altered or enlarged, the reason has either been added at the same time, so that the change may not appear arbitrary—as can be observed in the treatise *On the Faith to Peter*, where the name “deacon” has correctly been removed and the new title justified in a note from Fulgentius himself—or, if this has occasionally been omitted, the reason will reveal itself to readers and almost leap into their eyes. Thus, in the title of the book *On the Incarnation of the Son of God*, the words “and the Author of Lowly Animals” have been added: first, because nearly half of the work deals with this subject; and second, because this addition more clearly distinguishes the treatise from another bearing the title *On the Incarnation and Grace*.

Some may perhaps be surprised that so many works have been relegated from the main volume to the appendix. But this was not done without just and evident reasons, which have been displayed at the beginning of each work. Nor was it attempted on private judgment, but after the opinions of learned men had been carefully weighed.

Regarding the two sermons that were added, both what seemed appropriate has been explained and the entire matter has been left to the judgment of the readers.

An index of the manuscripts and printed books from which this edition was corrected has been added at the end of the volume.

Nor should we omit here the gratitude owed to Chifflet, the Jesuit and a man of outstanding learning, as a testimony of our thankful disposition, on account of his singular service to Fulgentius and especially to this edition. The variant readings that he had formerly copied from various manuscripts of the Carthusian library at Portes, extending across nearly all of Fulgentius’s works, he most generously communicated to those who were laboring to correct this latest edition. From these materials they corrected the writings of Fulgentius that still remained to be printed and carefully entered those received later into the register of variant readings.

[Col. 0118A] These are the things undertaken or accomplished to promote the public good. If they are not approved because of the intrinsic value of the results, we seem nevertheless entitled to hope that fair-minded judges will approve them for the merit of our intention and diligence.

# Life of Saint Fulgentius, Bishop of Ruspe, Written by a Certain Disciple of His and Dedicated to Felicianus, Bishop and Successor of Saint Fulgentius

[Note: Father Chifflet and others think that this work was written by Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, on account of the reasons he himself gives in the preface to the works of Fulgentius published by Ferrandus at Dijon in 1649. Others, however, are not persuaded by these arguments, since the author of the *Life* appears not to have left Fulgentius’s side, whereas this cannot be affirmed of Ferrandus. See the Bollandists, 1 January, p. 32, § 3.]

(C, G, S)

## Prologue

Two things are necessary for teachers of the Catholic Church: a good life and sound doctrine. Blessed Fulgentius, Felicianus’s predecessor as bishop.

### 1

Every most faithful steward of the New Testament, in whom Christ speaks, holy Father Felicianus, takes the greatest care over good works, so that by his example he may easily persuade others that he should be believed; and whatever he tells others to do, he himself does first. For he strives in vain to teach wisely unless he has lived innocently.

Two things, therefore, are judged necessary for teachers of the Catholic Church: a good life and sound doctrine. A good life commends the person who teaches wisely; sound doctrine adorns the person who lives well. A good life makes one lovable; sound doctrine makes one praiseworthy. A good life is continually believed worthy of imitation; sound doctrine is never judged fit to be rejected. A good life removes opportunities for detractors; sound doctrine resists those who contradict.

For this reason, while I had long been thinking about the name and grace of blessed Fulgentius the bishop—for he was your predecessor, and we were nourished together under him—and while that distinguished teacher frequently occupied the eyes of my heart, I grieved that the African peoples had been deprived of the consolation of so great a man. Although he had departed for better things, destined to rejoice in heavenly joys, I sighed among us because a similar teacher was now lacking, being well aware of his wisdom.

### 2

A certain relief was granted to my sorrowful remembrance whenever I myself read his most delightful books, letters, or sermons that he delivered in the presence of the people, or whenever I heard others reading them. Nevertheless, I silently considered that in those distinguished little works one could recognize the man’s intelligence and wisdom. But what his justice, integrity, and mercy had been, and how commendably he had lived his life with his associates—as you know well—I did not doubt that many knew, yet I felt that very many were unaware of it. I was always more greatly afraid that, in the future, the goodness of his way of life might become unknown through the long passage of time.

After long reflection I said: “Behold, the sound doctrine of blessed Fulgentius shines forth, since his books are read by everyone. He speaks, as it were, when his book, bearing his name, is read. But how will it happen that his good life may likewise become known to everyone? As long as those who knew him, or heard something about his virtues from the most reliable witnesses, are still alive, living memory can bear true testimony concerning him. What will the generations to come do? What will the multitude of the faithful living far away in the regions across the sea do? When they come to know the book in which that most blessed bishop speaks though absent and, though dead, lives, they will certainly admire his wisdom. But from where will they learn his innocence? Therefore, just as his doctrine is renowned, so let his life also become more renowned. Let us speak and tell our brothers how so great a bishop lived.”

### 3

Nor must I fear that, through my inferior eloquence, I will make insignificant a priest who acquired a great name throughout all the churches of the world. Whatever merit my speech may possess, it can neither increase nor diminish the merits of so great a man; it can contribute only to the testimony of my love, in which I have always desired to remain attached to him. In response to his saving admonitions, I turned toward undertaking the profession of the monks and lived day and night before him in that very small monastery that, while exiled in Sardinia for Christ’s sake, he had established for himself, where you now reside as a priest.

There, the streams of his heavenly eloquence, sweeter to me than honey and the honeycomb, frequently watered me.

[Note: The manuscript adds: “and, like a river of paradise, flowed more abundantly from his mouth and watered his eyes in the manner of tears.”]

Had not the barrenness of my dry intellect hindered it, the soil of my heart would have produced a hundredfold harvest. But unworthy as I was, I could scarcely take in a tiny portion of such abundance. Nevertheless, relying on the prayers of your fatherhood, I resolved to undertake the labor of this little book. In it I shall briefly explain everything that he himself used to recount from memory in our hearing, as well as what we saw with our own eyes or, having been placed under his instruction, know how it occurred. I have no fear whatever of incurring the charge of falsehood, since nothing is hidden from your venerable fatherhood.

[Col. 0118D] I am not now telling you anything as though you were unaware of it; rather, these matters are simply arranged so that they may be confirmed by your testimony.

[Note: In later editions: “are directed.”]

## Chapter One

The family of Fulgentius. His mother Mariana. Fulgentius’s education. He administers his paternal household. He is appointed a procurator.

### 4

Blessed, and truly blessed, Fulgentius was born of noble lineage according to the flesh. His parents belonged to the number of the senators of Carthage. His grandfather, named Gordianus, when King Gaiseric invaded the aforesaid Carthage in triumph and compelled very many senators—or rather all of them—to sail to Italy after losing all their possessions, willingly undertook the exile imposed upon him along with the others. He wished at least, though deprived of his property, not to lose his freedom.

(See Book I of Blessed Victor’s *On the Persecution of the Vandals*.)

After his death, two of his sons returned to the African province in hope of recovering their inheritance. They were nevertheless quite unable to remain within Carthage, since their own house had been given to Arian priests. After recovering part of their possessions through royal authority, they proceeded to Byzacium.

[Note: Thus the manuscript; the other copies read “finally.”]

[Note: The manuscript reads “Honeric.” The Antwerp edition has “Huneric and Genseric,” and the margin has “Geiseric.”]

[Note: The manuscript and Chifflet have “they remained already.”]

[Note: The manuscript and the Antwerp edition read “to Byzantium.” Chifflet has “to Byzacium.” The same reading appears in the margin of the Antwerp edition, with “Bithynia” added.]

There, in the city of Telepte, one of them, named Claudius, happily fathered by a wife named Mariana this man to whom such great glory was destined. She was a Christian and honorable woman.

[Note: The Antwerp edition reads “Marriana.”] He immediately named him Fulgentius, as though he already knew what he would become.

[Note: The manuscript and the Antwerp edition read *praescia*, “foreknowing”; Chifflet has *praescius*, “foreknowing” in the masculine.]

After his father died, his devout mother promptly entrusted him to be instructed in Greek letters. She permitted him no instruction in Latin letters until he had recited the whole of Homer from memory and had read through much of Menander. She wished him, while still in tender years, to acquire knowledge of a foreign language, so that, destined to live among Africans, he might more easily speak Greek with its aspirates preserved, as though he had been raised there.

### 5

The prudent provision of his devout mother did not deceive her. Whenever he wished to speak Greek, even after a long disuse of speaking and reading it, he uttered his words in such well-formed sounds that he might have been thought to live among Greeks every day.

[Note: The manuscript reads “after a long disuse.” Chifflet and the Antwerp edition add in the margin “of his habit.”]

After acquiring knowledge of Greek letters, he was taught Latin letters at home—the letters that schoolmasters customarily teach—and was also sent to the lecture hall of grammar. By the greatness of his intellect, he retained accurately and by memory everything taught to him.

He was soon withdrawn from these studies, however, by the pressing necessity of domestic affairs. As a young man he assumed the administration of his father’s household, submitting himself so completely to his mother’s commands that in this also he became an imitator of Christ, concerning whom the sacred Gospels testify: “And he was subject to them” (Luke 2:51), that is, to his parents.

His venerable mother rejoiced and consoled the sorrow caused by the loss of her husband through the excellent character of her wise son. In that household there had begun to be a man who returned service to his friends with goodwill, repelled enemies reasonably, governed and corrected slaves with both gentleness and firmness, carefully cultivated his patrimony, and became most dear to those in higher authority.

For this reason, as his reputation increased day by day, he was suddenly appointed procurator, thereby making a beginning in commanding, advising, and governing very many people.

## Chapter Two

The blessedness of monks.

### 6

While he exercised this authority with clemency, desired by his inborn compassion—or goodness—not to harm anyone, and was ordered to practice cruelty in collecting rents, the burden of secular affairs began to appear oppressive to him, and empty prosperity began to displease him. As praiseworthy patience gradually took its place, love for the spiritual life began to arise; his desire for reading also grew, as did his unwearied zeal for prayer.

Accordingly, he visited the most delightful flocks of monasteries more frequently and learned the conduct and way of life of the servants of God. Among those who practiced abstinence, he perceived that there were no joys of the world, but also no wearinesses. Living in complete abstinence, he saw that no one feared an accuser, but that they loved one another. He also observed many young men devoted to perpetual continence and able to abstain entirely from sexual intercourse.

With such thoughts he wavered within himself, and, breaking out into these words, he said:

> “Why, I ask, do we labor in the world without hope of future blessings? What can the world ever provide for us? If we desire to rejoice—and although it is better to weep well than to rejoice badly—how much more do those rejoice whose conscience is thus tranquil before God, whom the violence of a wicked tax collector scarcely frightens, who fear nothing except sins and do nothing except what enables them to fulfill God’s commands!
>
> “They are not worn out by public journeys, nor are they forced either to weep miserably or to fear shamefully over the loss of their property. Working with their hands, they do not oppose the interests of others. They live among themselves peacefully, soberly, gently, humbly, and harmoniously. They have no concern for lust; rather, they have great solicitude and constant guardianship of chastity.
>
> “Let us imitate such praiseworthy men; let us seize this steadfastness in living well. Let what we have deserved to learn through grace’s revelation be useful to us. Let us cast aside our former ways and change our labors. Formerly we strove to appear more noble among noble friends; now let us strive to become poorer among the poor servants of God. If we have been compelled to exact payment from debtors, let us now attempt to convert sinners.
>
> “Christ our Lord often makes teachers of the Church out of public tax collectors. Matthew was called from the tax office to become an apostle. Nor do we think that our person is suited to this honor. But if he, having laid aside the office of collection, received the office of preaching, will I not be permitted, after laying aside my procuratorship, to take up the lamentation of a penitent?
>
> “God is our refuge. Let there be no excuse arising from the weakness of age. God is powerful: he gives continence to so many young men whom we see living in monasteries, and he can grant a similar grace to me, a sinner.”

[Note: The manuscript, with Chifflet, reads: “Nor do we believe our person suited to this tax collector’s honor.”]

[Note: The manuscript reads “living in the monastery.”]

## Chapter Three

He contemplates the monastic life. Reading Blessed Augustine, he is converted.

### 7

After he had long revolved these words in his heart, he resolved—through the revelation of the Holy Spirit—to renounce worldly pleasures altogether and become a companion of the life he praised.

First, however, he considered that a sudden change, disturbing both mind and body, might at the very beginning of his conversion create a serious obstacle or cause of scandal for him. He therefore secretly began to practice occasional fasts; then, advancing little by little, he tried to avoid the company of his former companions.

Frequently separated from the crowds, he would sit sadly on his own estate, unknown to his parents and dependents, as though troubled by the demands of his duties. There he prayed, read, fasted, reduced the excessive abundance of his meals, and never went to the baths. Even while still professing the lay state, he already lived as a complete monk.

Everyone who knew him was astonished at the remarkable frugality of a man accustomed to luxury, and they interpreted the cause of this change as arising from the narrowness of a fainthearted spirit.

[Note: Thus the manuscript. The other copies read: “and they interpreted the change in so delicate a man, etc.”]

But in him, day by day, his love of the holy profession and of mortification grew into a more earnest concern.

### 8

Once he had experienced everything that seemed hard to him and had perceived, with the help of spiritual grace, that he possessed the capacity to carry out his will, he was admonished and moved by Blessed Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 36. He resolved to make his vow public, eager to change his clothing lest he be compelled to endure even those who came to him in friendship—people with whom he had long lived in the world.

[Note: The manuscript reads: “with whom he had long lived wickedly.”]

That most prudent man considered that the conversion of his heart would benefit only himself if it could remain hidden, but that once made public it would provide many others with a good example of abandoning their former sins. For who of moderate means or poverty would be ashamed to become a monk when he saw Fulgentius, with the arrogance of his innate pride withdrawn, walking the hard paths of abstinence with steps of patience?

## Chapter Four

He goes to Bishop Faustus. He becomes a monk. [Lacuna] Others imitate his example.

### 9

At that time there was a bishop named Faustus, worthy of high praise, who had been ordered to go into exile not far from his see on account of the Catholic faith. The crafty wickedness of Huneric, the persecuting tyrant, had arranged this for many priests, so that, suffering the hardship of exile near their own homeland, they might be more easily bent toward denying God.

In the very place where he was held in exile, Faustus had built a monastery for himself. Living spiritually there, he was held in honor by all Christians.

Saint Fulgentius—who was very well known to him—came eagerly to him and faithfully disclosed the vow of his heart.

[Note: The manuscript reads: “But he, knowing that Fulgentius had lived entirely in the world.”]

But Faustus, knowing that the young man had lived entirely in the world, was reluctant to believe such promises. He said to him:

> “Why do you lie, my son, and take pleasure in deceiving God’s servants? Will you really become a monk? Will you suddenly change your former habit of luxury so that the poor preparation of cheap food and the humiliation of dirty clothing will not offend your mind? First become at least a less luxurious layman; then perhaps I shall consider it believable that you either wish or are able to renounce the world.”

At these words the young man was inflamed more and more. He humbly kissed the hand that repelled him and, lowering his eyes to the ground, prayed:

> “The Lord Father is powerful enough to give ability to one who wills, just as he grants willingness to one who does not will. Only permit me to cling to your footsteps. Open to me the monastery door; provide the assistance of holy instruction; make me one of your disciples. God knows how he will free me from my iniquities.”

When the most blessed old man heard this, he considered it a grave matter to reject the petitioner any longer. At last, moved to consent, he said:

> “Remain with us, my son, as you wish. Let us test for a few days whether your deeds agree with your words. Would that my fear prove needless and your profession be found steadfast!”

### 10

After Saint Faustus the bishop had granted the petitioner’s request, word immediately spread among relatives and acquaintances that Fulgentius had become a monk. The good rejoiced; the wicked were confounded.

His former life of luxury caused some to despair, while his renowned knowledge and singular intelligence led others to expect great progress from him quickly. Some of his close companions, for whom he had been a beloved and most faithful friend from childhood, wished to imitate him. They too despised the world and joined themselves, with wills mortified, to the flocks of the monasteries.

## Chapter Five

His mother is tortured by his decision. He is denied the opportunity to see his mother. Fulgentius’s constancy.

### 11

His mother hears from many informants that Fulgentius has fled to the company of monks, entirely abandoned the care of managing and administering the household, and can no longer be recalled from such a resolution.

She is disturbed and terrified. Driven by the longing of excessive love, as though Fulgentius were already dying—although he was dying well, since he was dying in this way—she strikes heaven with excessive lamentations and, as mothers commonly do at the funerals of their children, knows no limit to her tears.

She rushes in a frenzy to the monastery by reckless paths and does not hesitate to attack Saint Faustus with insults and abuse.

> “Give the son back to his mother,” she says; “give the master back to his servants. Priests always confer many benefits upon widows. Why, then, is a widow’s household now being ruined through you?”

The bishop answered her patiently—or wisely:

> “If you had taken my son from me, woman, I ought to rebuke you as much as grief required. But now you rightly insult me, because I have taken your son from you. Since it displeases you that he is going to serve Christ, you do well to heap insults upon Faustus.”

While patiently enduring such words and smiling pleasantly at her,

[Note: The manuscript reads “mocking her kindly.”]

he gave her absolutely no opportunity even to see her son.

Knowing how deeply her son loved her, she wailed with great cries before the monastery door. Calling out Fulgentius’s name again and again, she pitifully pleaded her desolation.

12. This first temptation drove blessed Fulgentius with great force, when he heard with his own ears his mother, whom he had always loved and served with the greatest devotion, weeping. Yet, with his heart set on higher things, he heard and did not hear; nor did he think it right to heed her entreaties, because by religious cruelty he was overcoming his customary compassion. There he already offered, amid many labors, a most faithful example of the patience that was to come, [Col. 0123B] and, made as it were like a drunkard through spiritual grace, he somehow failed to recognize that she was his mother.

Here blessed Bishop Faustus first approved that he had been wholly converted in heart, and said joyfully to the other brothers: “This young man will easily be able to endure whatever labor we impose, since he can already disregard a mother’s grief.”

When that mother realized that she had often lamented without her son coming out to her, she believed that he was no longer in that place; for, since she was still unaware of his strength, she thought that, had he been there, he could not have endured his mother’s grief. Thus, going and returning repeatedly, she caused both the bishop annoyance and her son many difficulties, until, overcome by weariness, she returned to her own home.

*Note:* The manuscript reads *sanctissimam* (“most holy”) instead of *suam* (“his own”).

*Note:* The manuscript reads *non dolere* (“not to grieve”) in place of *non ferre posse dolorem matris* (“not to be able to endure his mother’s grief”).

## CHAPTER VI. His Incredible Abstinence. His Desire for Progress.

13. Blessed Fulgentius therefore tormented himself with the labors of abstinence beyond what could be believed, eating and drinking without wine or oil, and so sparingly and meagerly that the severity of his fasting forced the dried skin of his body to split into various ulcers, while the beauty of his delicate body was disfigured by the scurf they call *impetigo*.

At that time many thought that blessed Fulgentius, under cover of this illness, would either abandon his purpose of holiness altogether or thereafter become lukewarm, so that he would not even observe the frugality of the common rule. But, contrary to everyone’s expectation, governed by the aid of God’s prevenient mercy, he drew greater strength of spirit from the weakness of his body; and the weaker he became, the more abstinent he was. He continually thought about eternal salvation, while committing the health of his body to the Lord’s will. He said this to many:

“We all know that life is ordinarily sustained by food, but that health cannot thereby be conferred. For if, in order that illness may be cured, the appetite of the stomach must be satisfied, why do those who are daily stuffed with more sumptuous banquets also become ill?”

Thus he endured his illness patiently and practiced abstinence with sufficient humility. For he considered everything he did to be little and longed to become better from day to day. The merciful and compassionate God, supporting this purpose of his heart with the help of heavenly assistance, quickly restored his bodily health.

## CHAPTER VII. He Gives a Portion of His Property to His Mother.

14. Then the mind of the wise man, moved by a higher piety, crucified the world to itself with its whole heart and, itself crucified to the world, walked from its youth along the straight path, as it is written (Eccli. 51:20). Although he had a younger brother named Claudius, he transferred a portion of his own property by gift solely to his mother, so that afterward she might give it to his brother, if he served her well.

By this salutary plan he wished to tame the pride of his younger brother: the one who did not wish to be humble out of filial devotion might learn to be humble for the sake of his inheritance. His most holy mother also, after the departure of her beloved son, whose service could no longer gladden her, would deserve to be consoled by this benefit of his.

How many praises and thanksgivings did everyone there then offer to the Lord, when they saw blessed Fulgentius, having trampled down worldly desire, utterly renounce possessions that he could neither sell nor give to the poor, lest he offend his good mother, so that he might deserve to find Christ as his teacher!

## CHAPTER VIII. He Leaves His First Monastery Because of Persecution. He Is Chosen Co-Abbot.

15. Everything that had seemed to afflict him at the beginning of his conversion had now come to an end. But because this life can never pass without its own temptations, another persecution of the faith arose, one that forced Bishop Faustus, of holy memory, to move from one hiding place to another and did not allow him to remain continually at the monastery itself.

At that time blessed Fulgentius, fearing either to remain alone in that place or to move too frequently from place to place, first consulted Bishop Faustus and then sought a neighboring monastery. There Felix, an abbot presiding over a few but simple brothers, lived; he had been his friend since adolescence, and even while still a layman had always lived with him in close familiarity.

Felix the abbot therefore received him joyfully, and, knowing himself unequal to Fulgentius’s virtues, handed over to him both the title and authority of abbot. Full of zeal for humility, Fulgentius excused himself from exercising this authority; and after many struggles of mutual affection, overcome by the force of charity and with the consent of the whole community, he scarcely agreed to be the colleague of his good companion.

Thus the two most holy men, loving God and neighbor equally, alike in character, both superior in purpose, equal in manner of life, though one surpassed the other in knowledge, undertook the good yoke of governing the community.

*Note:* The Antiochene text reads *recusabat* (“he refused”). Chiffl. agrees with the manuscript and has *excusat* (“he excuses himself”); the Antiochene text also gives this reading in the margin.

16. O how happy was the number of God’s servants over whom Fulgentius had begun to preside! O how brightly that monastery shone, whose steward Felix remained!

They themselves even gave one another an auspicious sign of no lesser praise through their names. Fulgentius, running along the way of the Lord, was called Felix; and as Fulgentius’s reputation grew, Felix received the fruit of his own eminence.

One of them—namely blessed Fulgentius—devoted himself especially to teaching the brothers; the other labored more diligently in the daily service. When brothers arrived, one preached the word of God privately, while the other carefully prepared hospitality and offered it cheerfully.

Neither did anything without the other’s consent, but both commanded the others in such a way that they believed themselves placed under a single rule. Thus, while Felix feared offending Fulgentius and Fulgentius feared offending Felix, each lived with his own will mortified. They were praiseworthy in the benefit they provided for the brothers and exalted in the mutual submission they rendered to one another.

Who could express in words the virtue of this affection? A peaceful harmony had united them, and not even deadly conflicts were able to separate them.

*Note:* The Antiochene text reads *crebrescente* (“increasing”) instead of *crescente* (“growing”).

## CHAPTER IX. He Is Forced to Flee with Felix.

17. But when the province was suddenly disturbed by an incursion of a barbarian people, they saw that temporal safety had to be secured by flight. At once they undertook the hardships of a journey into exile and, after careful deliberation, withdrew far away, to a place where no expectation of the emerging war would prevent them from fully establishing a monastery.

Thus the illustrious leaders of the heavenly army advanced the spiritual camp, and, accompanied together by their band of monks, traveled through unknown regions of Africa, everywhere bringing joy to the good and provoking the envy of the wicked.

Finally, while they were considering establishing fixed dwellings in the territory of Sicca, delighted by the fertility of the region and welcomed by the devotion of faithful men, a certain presbyter of the Arian sect preached his perfidy on the estate of Gabardilla. His name among men was Felix, but his will toward God was always unhappy. A barbarian by birth, savage in character, powerful in resources, and a fierce persecutor of Catholics, he perceived that blessed Fulgentius’s name was becoming well known in those regions and suspected that many whom he had secretly deceived would be reconciled.

Nor did he believe that a man worthy of the priesthood was still truly a monk; rather, he thought that, under a monk’s habit, Fulgentius was performing the office of a priest. And in fact he was even then fulfilling the office of a priest commendably—not by reconciling only some, but by inviting all whom he could reach to reconciliation through salutary admonitions.

His speech was gentle and upright, and because it softened even hard hearts, it rightly compelled that presbyter to fear him on account of his own perfidy.

*Note:* The manuscript, together with several witnesses examined by Chiffl., reads *favore* (“with favor”); the Antiochene edition prefers this reading in the margin to *devotione* (“devotion”).

*Note:* The manuscript punctuates the passage as “a fierce persecutor. This man….” The other witnesses punctuate it “a fierce persecutor who….”

*Note:* The manuscript reads, apparently more correctly than the others, “and indeed he was then fulfilling the office of a priest, not by reconciling some…,” rather than “not only by reconciling some….”

18. The presbyter, therefore, stirred by the goads of frenzied rage, began to persecute the servants of God cruelly. Having stationed guards along every road, he beset the routes of those traveling innocently.

It had been necessary for these strongest athletes, prepared for every endurance by the voluntary labors of abstinence, to be delivered for a while into the hands of their persecutors, so that, made participants in the martyr’s contest, they might learn to endure the punishments inflicted upon them, and might prove what progress they had made if, while their limbs were torn apart by lashes, they did not in the least depart from the true faith.

Knowing nothing, therefore, of the wicked serpent’s designs and trusting in the testimony of their conscience, they feared nothing and walked together, speaking with one another.

*Note:* The Antiochene text reads “a barbarian multitude”; the manuscript reads “of the Moors.”

*Note:* The manuscript and the codices cited by Chiffl. read *custodibus distributis* (“with guards distributed [along the roads]”). The printed editions read *deputatis* (“assigned”); the margin has *distributis*.

## CHAPTER X. They Are Brought before the Arian Presbyter. The Arian’s Astonishing Cruelty. The Abbot Felix’s Vehement Charity. Felix Is Beaten.

And behold, suddenly, as though by the violence of a most savage storm, the attack fell upon the unsuspecting men: it separated those who were joined, bound those who had been separated, and brought them, loaded with savage chains, bound before the presbyter. Suddenly they became accused without a crime and captives without the fortune of war. The Arians inflicted punishments upon those whom the Moors had been unable to harm as they fled.

Before they were seized, Felix the abbot had simply thrown aside a few solidi, with which the brothers’ poverty was supported, wherever fear had advised—or overtaken—him; and he entrusted them to God himself to keep for the servants of God.

O the singular power of a divine miracle! No one was able to see those solidi that had been thrown down; no one was permitted to take the poor people’s sustenance from the poor. Only those who were thus to be tested were seized, bound, and brought before the presbyter.

In a terrible voice the violent presbyter thundered at them: “Why have you secretly come from your regions to overthrow Christian kings?” He rightly called them “Christian kings,” for in them he had pitifully spit upon Christ, the King of kings, and, like another Antichrist, had taught them to deny that the Son was equal to the Father.

*Note:* The manuscript reads *adhuc* (“still”) in this passage.

As they were preparing to answer with words of the truest response, he first ordered them to be beaten.

19. Then Felix the abbot, moved by vehement charity, said: “Spare brother Fulgentius, who cannot endure the tortures. Do not beat this man, who may perhaps die in your hands. Turn your cruelty upon me; I know what I confess, and the whole cause is mine.”

Struck with wonder at such love, the presbyter ordered blessed Fulgentius to be removed for a while and commanded his savage attendants to beat Felix more severely.

Then Felix the abbot submitted to the blows with a cheerful spirit. He endured the pain with joy, because he saw that blessed Fulgentius was still suffering nothing.

Behold what blessed Fulgentius was like toward his friends: he deserved to be loved even unto death. This charity of blessed Felix provides a great testimony to the holiness of his life. For he would not have disregarded his own safety for Fulgentius’s sake unless he had first perceived that it was useful and pleasing both to himself and to many others.

Let both men be imitated by those who desire to please God. Let blessed Fulgentius teach others to live among their brothers in such a way that they are loved and cherished, and that, in the greatest necessities, they are considered bound to give aid even when danger is present. Let others take the example of the abbot Felix’s good deed and extend every favor of good will to better brothers and to those making greater progress in the fear of God.

For whenever such charity exists among brothers as existed between these most holy men, the force of every temptation is easily overcome, while the obstinacy of enemies is immediately broken.

Although even then the most savage presbyter was not at all satisfied by the injury done to the abbot Felix, and did not think that blessed Fulgentius should be spared.

## CHAPTER XI. Fulgentius Also Is Beaten. After the Beating He Is Dismissed Disgracefully with the Others.

20. Blessed Fulgentius, however, a man of exceedingly delicate body, being born, as he was, of an illustrious family, scarcely endured the violent blows of the clubs as the bitterness of the sudden pain increased. As he later recounted to us, he thought about either softening the madness of the raging presbyter, if he could, or at least distracting him for a little while until his rage should break out afresh, so that during the delay he might find some opportunity to breathe and the continuous punishment might not become wholly intolerable.

“I will say something,” he cried while he was being beaten, “if I am granted the power to speak.”

Then the presbyter, thinking that he wished to confess something, ordered the beaters to stop and, with Fulgentius still suspended for the lashes, commanded him to say what he wished.

Blessed Fulgentius then began, in his customary eloquent speech and gentle words, to relate the story of his journey. He astonished the presbyter, and, after long soothing him with the extraordinary sweetness of his words, almost made him forget all his cruelty.
