The presbyter marveled at blessed Fulgentius’s eloquence, approved his wisdom, and, judging him to be some great man, blushed to inflict violence upon him. But, lest he reveal to his men that his savagery had been overcome, he said: “Beat him again vigorously and tear the talkative man apart with multiplied lashes. I think he is also planning to deceive me; I do not know what he is trying to accomplish by the long circuit of this empty tale.”

Again the mad hand of the torturer grew fierce, and blessed Fulgentius was scored with countless lashes.

*Note:* The manuscript reads *nequitiam* (“wickedness”) instead of *saevitiam* (“savagery”).

*Note:* Other witnesses read *manus saeva* (“the savage hand”).

21. At last the presbyter, ashamed of the beating he had inflicted, recognized the merits of the praiseworthy men. He did not dare keep them with him any longer, but, having disgracefully shaved their heads and removed all their clothing, he cast them naked and destitute out of his house.

Yet neither did the shaving of their heads bring disgrace upon these most holy men, nor did nakedness bring them shame. For the injury they had endured on account of their love of religion had already adorned them with the ornament of their first confession, and heavenly grace was to support them.

They therefore went out from the presbyter’s house as from a place of glorious combat, crowned with the laurels of a distinguished victory.

When they returned across the field where they had been captured, they found the solidi that, as we said, Abbot Felix had thrown down, preserved there in their full number. They received them cheerfully, as though restored by the hand of God, and, giving ineffable thanks to God, who consoles the humble in all their tribulation, returned to the nearby brothers.

The detestable report of this most cruel deed grieved the entire region at once; the story was also reported at Carthage.

*Note:* The manuscript, Bollandus, and the Antiochene text in the margin read *propter odium* (“because of hatred”). Both readings are sound: although the injury was inflicted because of hatred of religion, it was endured because of love for that same religion.

22. Among the others, an Arian bishop also grieved that blessed Fulgentius had been struck down by a severe beating. Since this bishop knew his parents and had especially loved blessed Fulgentius while he was still a layman, he was greatly angered against the presbyter of his own religion and diocese who had been responsible for the beating. He prepared to avenge blessed Fulgentius, if Fulgentius had been willing to lodge a complaint against the presbyter in question.

But blessed Fulgentius, although many urged him to do so, said: “It is not lawful for a Christian to seek vengeance in this world. The Lord knows how to defend the injuries done to his servants. If, through my agency, this presbyter receives punishment among men for a very grave crime, we shall have lost the reward of patience with God—especially since he might scandalize many little ones if I, a Catholic and a monk, were to seek the judgment of an Arian bishop, even though I am whatever sort of sinner.”

Therefore, unwilling to repay evil for evil and knowing that his life was necessary for the good, they left that province once again, lest they perhaps suffer another act of violence from the heretics, and quickly returned to the neighboring regions of their own province, choosing rather to have the Moors as neighbors than to endure the most troublesome Arians.

## CHAPTER XII. Fulgentius Considers Traveling to Egypt. He Lands at Syracuse. Saint Eulalius, Bishop of Syracuse. Saint Eulalius’s Monastery. He Is Called Back from the Journey He Has Begun Because of the Schism of the Egyptian Monks. A Guest Practices Hospitality.

23. Near the city called Ididi—for some witnesses have *Ydidi*, others *Indidi*—they began to establish a monastery. There they devoted themselves for a short time to works of charity in the service of the Lord, until blessed Fulgentius suddenly began reading about the admirable lives of the Egyptian monks. Enkindled by spiritual meditation on both their institutions and their conferences, he decided to travel by ship to those regions, for two reasons: either to lay aside the title of abbot there and live in humility under a rule, or to submit himself to stricter laws of abstinence.

Because his desire might be hindered if it became known, he first sought an opportunity to travel to Carthage. Then, having come to the walls of that city, he boarded a ship bound for Alexandria with only one brother, named Redemptus, chosen as his companion on the journey. He carried with him perhaps none of the expenses necessary for so great a voyage, but firmly placed his hope in God, who is rich, and sang sweetly with David: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing” (Ps. 22:1).

As favorable winds followed them, they happily reached the Syracusan harbor. Guided by the providence of the supreme God, he was brought to that city, where blessed Pope Eulalius then governed the Catholic Church. He was a man of exceptional holiness, admirable hospitality, and perfect charity. In his heart lay hidden a treasure of spiritual wisdom, by the commerce of the Lord’s talents enriching many.

Adorned above all by the virtue of discernment, he especially loved the monastic profession. He himself also had his own monastery, to which he always remained attached whenever he was free from ecclesiastical duties.

*Note:* Some manuscripts read *Ydidi*; others, *Indidi*. See Chiffl.’s note on this passage in Ferrandus.

24. When blessed Fulgentius came to him, he was willingly received, among the other travelers, in the exercise of hospitality. Yet he was not allowed to remain hidden for long. For, as is customary at a priests’ banquet, when conversation about divine matters arose, his speech immediately revealed the man of singular learning.

From the refinement of his speech and the moderation of his replies, the bishop understood that a great teacher lay hidden beneath the monastic habit. Nevertheless, while the guests were present at the meal, he postponed asking who he was and why he had come.

After the meal, while he was walking in his house during the midday hours before evening, the bishop looked through a window and saw blessed Fulgentius passing before him like the others. He immediately called him aside and said: “You began speaking about the institutions and conferences while we were dining. If you are carrying a book, please bring it to me.”

Without delay, Fulgentius obeyed the command and brought the book. Ordered to explain in his own words what it contained, he did so. Saint Eulalius marveled at the young man’s learning and, delighted by such a guest, carefully asked why he had come from Africa.

Fearing that he would incur a reputation for arrogance if he confessed his desire, Fulgentius replied: “I am seeking my parents, whom I have heard are living as exiles in those regions.” In truth, he was seeking his parents, whose most gracious ways he wished to imitate.

The bishop understood that the answer was not explicit and investigated the reasons for his entire journey through the other brother.

*Note:* The manuscript reads somewhat differently: “through the other brother, for he was simple-minded….”

There blessed Fulgentius was beneficially exposed, confessed the truth simply, and said that he was going to the remotest desert of the Thebaid so that there, as the reading had urged, he might live dead to the world, where the greater number of those practicing abstinence would create no obstacle to his undertaking, but might rather perhaps provide an example.

“You are right,” replied the bishop, “to desire to pursue better things. But you know that without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6). The lands to which you desire to go have been separated from the communion of blessed Peter by a faithless dissension. All those monks whose marvelous abstinence is praised will not share with you the sacraments of the altar.

What, then, will it profit you to afflict the body with fasts where the soul, which is far better than the body, will lack spiritual consolations? Return, my son, lest, while seeking a better life, you suffer danger to the true faith.

“Behold, when I too was once young, before the dignity of pontifical honor, which found me unworthy, came upon me, I long considered fulfilling the purpose of this most holy profession in the monasteries of that province. But this reason prevented me from carrying out what I had undertaken.”

*Note:* Chiffl. reads, “Behold, I too….” The manuscript reads, “For I….”

25. Blessed Fulgentius therefore yielded to the salutary counsel of the father who advised him. Laying aside the ardor of his intention, he was persuaded to spend several months there near Syracuse, with Saint Eulalius providing him with suitable food and lodging.

But because a good mind never lies idle and is always practicing works of charity, in the very small lodging he had received he began to show hospitality to many travelers who arrived, and, himself needing the comfort of another, to receive travelers who needed consolation.

Saint Eulalius marveled at the generous freedom of the holy man’s spirit and was nourished with great joy when he saw that, through the hand of blessed Fulgentius, to whom he supplied daily food despite his having nothing, food was being supplied to those who had none.

And, if it is permissible to say so, just as the greater often grow through comparison with the lesser, although Saint Eulalius was entirely perfect in caring for the poor, when he observed the works of blessed Fulgentius he became more merciful and generous from day to day—

*Note:* Chiffl. reads *bonae indolis mens* (“a mind of good character”) instead of *bonae mentis indoles* (“the disposition of a good mind”).

## CHAPTER XIII. He Visits Bishop Rufinianus. He Travels to Rome for Religious Reasons. He Visits the Monuments of the Martyrs.

26. When the winter then present had ended, an intense concern moved blessed Fulgentius to see a certain bishop named Rufinianus. Fleeing the violence of persecution, Rufinianus had sailed from the Council of Byzacena and was staying on a very small island near the province of Sicily, living a monk’s life commendably. Fulgentius wished to see him without hesitation, so that, strengthened a second time by his advice, he might learn what he ought to do.

He did this not because he trusted Bishop Eulalius less, but because he believed that, in doubtful matters, the counsel of many is always most useful.

After many hardships of a journey on foot, he came to that place in Sicily which lay closest to the island where Saint Rufinianus the bishop lived. He was carried across in a small boat and quickly presented himself to the venerable priest.

Rufinianus likewise warned him not to persist in traveling to Egypt. Fulgentius immediately decided to return to his own monastery, but not to omit visiting the apostles’ memorials.

27. When a more favorable opportunity for sailing was found, he came to Rome and entered the city in haste. Secular authors had always praised it with unanimous voice and truly called it the head of the world.

At that time there was great joy in the City, for the presence of King Theoderic brought happiness to the assembly of the Roman Senate and people.

Thus it happened that blessed Fulgentius—whose world had once been crucified to him—after reverently visiting the holy places of the martyrs and humbly greeting all the servants of God whose acquaintance he could briefly make, observed at the place called the Golden Palm the nobility, dignity, and order of the Roman court arranged in distinct ranks, while King Theoderic delivered an address. Hearing with chaste ears the acclamations of the free people, he came to understand what the glorious pomp of this world was like.

Yet he took no pleasure in gazing at anything in that spectacle, nor was he captivated by those worldly trifles and carried away by a superfluous delight into consenting to them. Rather, from that sight he burned intensely with a desire for the happiness of the Jerusalem of the heavenly city, and admonished those present with this salutary reflection:

“Brothers, HOW BEAUTIFUL can the heavenly Jerusalem be, if earthly Rome shines in this way! And if in this world such dignity of honor is granted to those who love vanity, what honor, glory, and peace will be granted to the saints who contemplate truth?”

*Note:* The Antiochene text has *Theodorici* (“of Theoderic”). We correct the text on the basis of the manuscript and Chiffl.’s explanation in his notes.

*Note:* The manuscript refers *decoratam* (“adorned”) to *nobilitatem* (“nobility”); the other witnesses have *decoratum* (“adorned”) in agreement with a different construction.

*Note:* Chiffl., agreeing with the manuscript, reads “from there to desire happily the Jerusalem of that heavenly city,” omitting *civitatis*. The Antiochene text reads “from there to desire happily the Jerusalem of the heavenly city.”

*Note:* Chiffl. reads *intuitus, nugis illis saecularibus* (“having gazed at them, [he did not consent] to those worldly trifles”).

## CHAPTER XIV. He Returns to Africa. He Builds a Monastery. Secretly He Seeks Another Monastery, Having Laid Aside the Title of Abbot. The Practices of Saint Fulgentius.

28. Blessed Fulgentius discussed many similar matters profitably on that day. Now longing with his whole heart to revisit his monastery, he sailed quickly to Africa by way of Sardinia. His monks scarcely believed, in their excessive joy, that blessed Fulgentius had returned.

The holy brotherhood plainly did not know what to do first: whether to complain about the father’s absence or rather rejoice over his presence. No one, however, dared blame him for having departed; all instead strove to give thanks to God for his return.

Laymen too joined in the joy of God’s servants. All honorable and noble men rejoiced that blessed Fulgentius, predestined to be a teacher of the African Church, had not remained long absent, occupied in lands across the sea. Finally, one after another, they hastened to offer greater comforts of devotion—or charity—with which the mind of the returning man might be refreshed.

At last, a certain Sylvester, a good Christian and a leading man of the province of Byzacena, offered a place suitable for constructing a monastery. Its soil was rich and fertile, favorably suited to the establishment of gardens, and—what seemed more worthy of choice—it was still far from the fury of war and offered the fullest security of peaceful quiet.

Many honorable men lived on neighboring estates, and their frequent offerings promised the monks the easiest means of exchange, so that those seeking the kingdom of God would not be hindered by any worldly concern for transactions.

*Note:* The manuscript, together with several witnesses cited by Chiffl., reads *Sylvestrio* (“Sylvester”), rather than *Sylvestro*.

*Note:* The manuscript and the Antiochene text read *Byzantinae* (“Byzantine”); the margin has *Byzacenae* (“Byzacenian”), in agreement with Chiffl.

*Note:* The manuscript, with some witnesses cited by Chiffl., reads *caritatis* (“charity”) instead of *pietatis* (“devotion”).

29. Blessed Fulgentius gladly accepted the devout offering of the religious man. Without delay he founded a monastery in the place granted to him, invited many to conversion through pious admonitions, multiplied the number of monks, and became the father of a great community.

Although he constantly desired to meditate on spiritual things, he was compelled to be drawn out by still greater concern: seeking holy leisure out of love for truth, while undertaking many affairs out of the necessity of charity.

Thus, at times overcome by the contemplation of better things and desiring to devote himself solely to reading and prayer, he considered for a long time how he might cast off the burden of his present office. Placed under the governance of others, he would himself live under a rule rather than give a rule for living to others, judging it more useful, according to the Lord’s command, for those who command to obey than for those who obey to command.

As he continued pondering these matters, the following thought suddenly arose: In the midst of the shallow sea there is a monastery close to the shore of Vivecensis—or *Vivecensi*—and contiguous for the most part with Bennefensis. There, a narrow strip of tiny rocks permits neither the cultivation of gardens nor even the provision of a little comfort in the form of wood or drinkable water; rather, enough of both necessities is prepared daily by very small boats.

In this monastery an ancient discipline of strict purpose is preserved. From childhood to extreme old age, many live there in the greatest holiness and commendably perform works suited to their holy profession.

At that time two particular presbyters, admirable in merit and venerable in the honor of their stainless old age, served in the office of abbot. They never left the monastery, but nourished many suitable men for ecclesiastical dignity.

*Note:* The manuscripts vary. The Antiochene text in the margin reads *Vincensi*; the manuscript has *Juncensi*; Chiffl., *Vicensi*. Some manuscripts cited by Chiffl. have *Vivecensi*, while most have *Vincensi*.

*Note:* The manuscript and other witnesses cited by Chiffl. read *Bennefensi*. The Antiochene text has *Vennefensi*, agreeing with certain manuscripts seen by Chiffl.; Chiffl. himself reads *Benefensi*.

*Note:* Chiffl. reads *distendi* (“to be drawn out” or “to be burdened”), which we adopt instead of *discendi* (“of learning”), on the basis of the manuscript, which reads somewhat differently: “he became a father; although he… he was compelled to be drawn out by greater concern.” The Antiochene text reads, “Although indeed….”

30. Blessed Fulgentius secretly went to this monastery and there laid aside the title of abbot amid so large a community. Joined to the multitude of monks, he shone above the others by his remarkable learning and distinctive eloquence, but subjected himself to everyone through praiseworthy humility and singular obedience.

Mindful of that evangelical saying in which our Lord says, “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38), he mortified all his own desires. He devoted himself also to fasts, prayers, vigils, and abstinence, crucifying himself wholly, together with his vices and worldly desires, and he also cheerfully worked with his own hands.

He practiced the art of writing commendably and very often wove fans from palm leaves. He also engaged in this work when he had been abbot, in his own monastery. In his cell he frequently devoted himself to reading before the brothers, beloved, respected, and cheerful among them all.

## CHAPTER XV. He Is Forced to Return to the Office of Abbot. He Is Ordained a Priest.

31. But just as great joy arose in that monastery, so sudden sadness arose in his own. Those who had received him rejoiced; those who had lost him grieved. A new struggle of charity arose between them.

These men embraced their new companion tenaciously; those men humbly begged that their former father be restored to them. These confessed that his presence adorned them; those that his absence weakened them.

Blessed Fulgentius, however, preferring to learn rather than to teach, agreed to remain where he had been inferior and trembled at returning to the place where he could be superior to all.

Then the grief of Abbot Felix and all the brothers whom he had left took counsel from necessity and appealed to Saint Bishop Faustus. Faustus immediately claimed, by episcopal authority, that Fulgentius was his monk and affirmed that he ought to be returned to him and live wherever Faustus commanded.

He threatened excommunication against those who resisted and declared that Fulgentius himself, unless he consented, should be judged like the disobedient.

Why say more? Blessed Fulgentius was brought back once again to his own monastery and ordered to undertake the office of abbot. And, lest he should again become changeable in his spiritual desire, the priest suddenly ordained him presbyter, so that, adorned with the office of abbot and priest, he could neither leave the monastery nor be ordained in another church.

*Note:* Chiffl. and the Antiochene text read *in illius discessu* (“at his departure”); the manuscript lacks both words.

32. Thus overcome and bound by the fetters of honor, blessed Fulgentius began to govern his monastery with equanimity. As his praiseworthy reputation grew, he became known throughout all the provinces of Africa. In the territory of the Nuntorians—called *Vintorum* in the Antiochene margin—he was honored as though he were their own bishop.

Whenever the opportunity to ordain a bishop was granted, everyone stood ready to seek blessed Fulgentius first, both in word and in mind, and would permit no one but blessed Fulgentius to be consecrated for them.

*Note:* The Antiochene text reads, “to seek blessed Fulgentius as their first priest.”

God saw the desire of the people, and it was not hidden from blessed Fulgentius himself.

## CHAPTER XVI. A Royal Prohibition Is Issued against Ordaining Bishops. He Flees the Episcopate. After the Ordination of the Bishops Has Taken Place, He Returns.

[Col. 0133C]

But because royal authority had then prohibited the ordination of bishops, and it was not permitted to provide shepherds for widowed congregations, he passed the period of this prohibition securely, judging it superfluous to refuse an honor by means of flight when it was neither lawful for anyone to confer it nor for anyone to receive it.

33. But after the sacred company of the remaining bishops, having taken counsel together, resolved to celebrate episcopal ordinations everywhere in defiance of the king’s command—thinking either that the king’s anger, if it should arise, might thereby be softened, so that those ordained could more easily live in their own places or among their own congregations; or that, if the violence of persecution arose, those whom they found worthy of promotion might be crowned through their confession of the faith, and that they would more easily fulfill their ministry and provide consolation to their own congregations amid the very tribulations themselves—a common undertaking suddenly began. They hastened, each to his own place, eagerly to seize, bless, and consecrate presbyters, deacons, and anyone whom the election might find, lest anyone should be found tardy or last in such an endeavor. [Col. 0133D] [Note: The *Antiphonary* reads “in the places”; the manuscript, together with Chifflet, lacks the particle *in*.]

Then blessed Fulgentius, forestalling the electors’ wishes by a swifter flight, hid himself in unknown retreats and could not be found, however much he was sought. The people of the place where the monastery had been established were thinking of postponing their election altogether [Col. 0134A] until they found blessed Fulgentius. Nevertheless, fearing that, while blessed Fulgentius was being sought for a long time, this report might reach Carthage and a renewed royal prohibition might arise from there, they were persuaded—necessity compelling them to hurry—to seek another from among their clergy. Thus, in the many places where blessed Fulgentius had been elected either first or alone, after he could not be found at all, he gave others permission to assume the highest honor. [Col. 0134D] [Note: Chifflet reads “permission to assume the highest honor.”]

34. The province of Byzacena had already been filled with new priests, and scarcely any chairs of the few remaining congregations were left vacant. The king’s fury had also been stirred up, and he had now decreed that all should be handed over to exile. The sentence proceeded first against the original ordainer, namely the primate Victor, who had already been seized by the king’s departing servants [Col. 0134B] and was being led to Carthage. As still greater sorrow followed, the joy of the ordination that had been undertaken was turned into public mourning. Then, when secret messengers informed him that the time for carrying out the ordination had passed, blessed Fulgentius, thinking that the sees closest at hand now had bishops of their own, returned once more to govern the congregation of his monastery. He neither doubted nor feared anything, but rejoiced altogether that he had escaped the burden of pontifical dignity.

## CHAPTER XVII. The deacon Felix seeks the see of Ruspe. Fulgentius is compelled to accept the episcopate of Ruspe. The rejected deacon Felix prepares an ambush for Fulgentius.

35. Nevertheless, our God, fulfilling by a higher plan what he had predestined, now wished to give authority to the salutary teaching for which he had granted him the ability to teach beneficially [Col. 0134C], so that the Catholic faith should not lack a most faithful preacher against the Arians. Therefore, in a time of tribulation, he did not wish to conceal the vessel of election through whom he had determined to fulfill the ministry of preaching. [Alternative reading: “he wished.”]

Ruspe was still a noble town, altogether distinguished by its most illustrious inhabitants. No bishop had been ordained for it, because a certain deacon named Felix, who had sought the honor of the bishopric, had been rejected; and in that place he neither deserved the office himself nor allowed another to receive it. For his own brother, a close associate of the procurator, supplied the forces of ambition through the power of secular influence.

A vehement grief tormented the minds of the honorable citizens: why had they alone remained without a spiritual father, when they seemed to surpass the others in noble birth according to the flesh? [Col. 0134D] [Note: The *Antiphonary* reads “deeply distressed them.”] [Note: Thus the manuscript; the other witnesses read, “Then suddenly.”] Suddenly, however, truthful report announced to the grieving people that blessed Fulgentius—whom so many places had judged worthy of the first priestly office, but who had not been found at all at the time of the ordinations—had remained a presbyter, clothed in even greater glory because he had thus trampled underfoot his desire for the higher honor. The one who had rejected the proud seeker of office pleased them as a praiseworthy man who had declined it. All agreed that he had been preserved for them precisely for this reason: that he had not been ordained when so many congregations were seeking office-holders.

Without blessed Fulgentius’ knowledge, the primate Victor was sought on the road by the people of Ruspe [Col. 0135A], so that he might grant the neighboring bishops permission to ordain Fulgentius. [Note: In the *Antiphonary*: “and to the neighboring [bishops] … permission is granted”; these words are absent from the manuscript, with Chifflet.] When Victor gave his consent, a violent crowd was assembled. Suddenly blessed Fulgentius was found in his own cell, suffering from sore eyes; he was attacked, seized, and led away. He was not asked to become bishop but compelled to do so. From there he was brought to the bishop who had been instructed to celebrate the ordination, and was made father of a people whom he did not know, so that the prophetic oracle seemed to be fulfilled in him: “A people whom I did not know served me” (Psalm XVII, 45).

36. The appearance of the exceedingly gracious wise man, together with the favor of the supporting people, increased their enthusiasm. Though at that time he was unknown to everyone who saw him, he was regarded as pleasing because of the humility of his clothing and venerable because of his modest bearing. Whenever reason occasionally compelled him to wish to say something [Col. 0135B], the whole crowd hung upon his lips, perceiving from his familiar speech what the future teaching of a spiritual master would be like.

For this reason, from every estate wherever he passed, the people flocked together to show their support, confessing that the longer it had taken for the Church of Ruspe to receive a bishop, the better its bishop had proved to be. But when the deacon saw that the efforts of his ambition had utterly failed, he raged—this was the only course left to him in his disappointment—and, gathering countless traitors, placed a stumbling-block beside the path of the coming son of peace, as the sacred psalm says (Psalm CXXXIX, 6). [Col. 0135D] [Note: The manuscript reads, “he rages, and [with] the tardy …”; it continues: “when countless [men] had been gathered from the roads for the coming son of peace.” The *Antiphonary* reads: “when countless [men] had been gathered from the roads.”]

The hostile aspirant therefore blockaded the road by which the chosen servant of God was coming. But Christ everywhere assists the simple, and a man cannot obstruct the election of a priest when ambition has not preceded it. By some command of the Holy Spirit who was admonishing them [Col. 0135C], the people who were leading the way went along another road, and, while the enemy was still sitting in the road, placed blessed Fulgentius upon his own episcopal chair.

On that same day the divine mysteries were solemnly celebrated, and the whole people, receiving Communion from the hands of blessed Fulgentius, departed joyfully. When the deacon later heard this, he yielded to the divine will, although belatedly. Blessed Fulgentius immediately received him when he returned, kindly, courteously, and mercifully, so that afterward he ordained him presbyter.

But divine justice very swiftly displayed the deserved punishment. The deacon himself, by then a presbyter, died within a year, while the procurator who had agreed with him was reduced to poverty. They paid the penalty for their temporal boldness—though God is able to prepare for them in the future the grace of heavenly forgiveness. [Col. 0135D] We thought this should at least be mentioned in order to show that, from this point onward, blessed Fulgentius’ authority over individuals increased, when they recognized that divine severity had kept watch in these events.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Honors do not change Fulgentius’ conduct. His clothing. He abstains from meat permanently.

37. Meanwhile blessed Fulgentius accepted the episcopate without any ambition and with the greatest devotion, while divine vengeance remained against those who had opposed him. He did not become a bishop in such a way as to cease being a monk; rather, after receiving the dignity of a bishop, he preserved the integrity of his former profession [Col. 0136A]. The integrity of his profession, once preserved, adorned the episcopal dignity all the more. [Note: The manuscript reads “the integrity.”]

He never sought costly clothing, nor neglected his daily fasts, nor ate delicately seasoned foods even among guests, nor wished, by reclining at table, even to take rest and relax his rigorous discipline. Instead, he patiently wore one extremely poor tunic, both in summer and winter. He never used a stole, though all bishops did; as a monk he used a leather belt—or perhaps was girded with one. [Col. 0136D]

Thus, through his devotion to humility, he shunned vanity in clothing: he did not even accept the shoes worn by clerics, nor did he use worn-out boots in winter or light sandals in summer. [Note: This is the reading of our manuscripts; certain others cited by Chifflet read *vilissimis* (“the poorest”) for *ultimis* (“the last/worn-out”).] Inside the monastery he sometimes wore slippers, but often walked barefoot. He neither possessed nor allowed his monks to possess a costly chasuble or one of proud color. Beneath the chasuble he walked wrapped in a blackish or milky-pale cloak. [Col. 0136B] [Note: The manuscript reads “a pale woolen cloak”; perhaps not incorrectly.]

When the weather was mild, he was covered inside the monastery only by his cloak. We never saw his shoulders bare, nor did he seek sleep after removing even his belt. Trusting, with God as his witness, in the purity of his continence, he slept in the tunic in which he celebrated the sacrifice; and at the time of the sacrifice he used to say that hearts, rather than garments, ought to be changed. [Col. 0136D] [Note: The *Antiphonary* reads “of his conscience.”]

38. No one ever forced this most blessed priest to take meat of any kind. As long as he was young, he ate only simple vegetables, porridge, and eggs, without oil; when he grew old, he ate them with oil poured over them. [Col. 0136C] [Note: Chifflet reads: “therefore he was more readily persuaded to take oil.”] He was persuaded to take oil so that the prevailing dimness of his eyes would not obstruct his reading.

While in good health he always abstained from wine. If, however, the necessity of illness ever compelled him to use a little wine, he poured a small amount of unmixed wine into cups filled with water, and did not enjoy either its taste or its pleasant smell. [Col. 0136D]

Before the brothers announced the hour of the vigils, he was always watchful in heart and body, either praying, reading, dictating, or devoting himself alone to some spiritual meditation, because he knew that during the day he was continually occupied with the needs of the children of the Church. Sometimes he went down to keep vigils with the servants of God; but he practiced private vigils by himself, with the studies I have mentioned, much more laudably.

## CHAPTER XIX. He never lives anywhere without monks.

[Col. 0136D] 39. He was never seen to live in any place without monks. For this reason, when he had been ordained bishop, he first asked the citizens of Ruspe to grant him a suitable place for building a monastery. Then, as several citizens hastened to obey, a certain man named Posthumianus—most Christian and the noblest citizen among his people—faithfully offered his own small estate to the excellent priest. It was situated not far from the church, where the beauty of a charming grove flourished, with pines rising high into the sky.

Blessed Fulgentius gladly accepted the place, whose timber he also saw would be suitable for the future building [Col. 0137A]. He immediately persuaded blessed Felix the abbot to come more quickly, with almost the entire congregation, except that he left a very few brothers in that monastery and appointed one of the brothers, named Vitalis, over them. He instructed both monasteries to live under this law of charity: although separated by location, they were to be united in harmony as though they had not been divided. [Col. 0137D] [Note: The *Antiphonary* reads: “He instructed them to be united in this way”; in the margin: “he ordered them to be united.”]

If Christ acquired any new monks in either monastery, they were to preserve among themselves the order of their conversion and their rank. Whenever they came to see one another, and only when their superiors ordered them to do so, they were to be received not as guests but as members of one congregation. Governed jointly by the provisions of blessed Fulgentius the bishop, they were to venerate their spiritual father with sincere affection [Col. 0137B].

Blessed Fulgentius arranged everything in such a way that, after undertaking the burden of governing the clergy, he would not lose the consolation of the monks. [Note: Chifflet reads: “so that he would not postpone the care or consolation of the monks.”]

## CHAPTER XX. He is thrust into exile. How highly the bishops valued his judgment. He replies by letter in the name of all the bishops. The effectiveness of Fulgentius’ writings. Monks and clerics live together.

40. Meanwhile, servants of royal fury were suddenly sent out, so that this distinguished confessor of Christ himself, once detained with the others, might be thrust into exile in Sardinia. He was therefore led away quickly. Although he grieved that his Church, not yet instructed by any admonitions from his writings, would immediately remain abandoned, he wisely overcame his sadness with a greater joy: he was beginning to share in so glorious a confession.

Accompanied by monks and clerics alike, the excellent teacher of both forms of religious life departed from the chair of honor for the place of blessed struggle, while all the laypeople wept. [Col. 0137C] He was ready to confess the Catholic faith with a free mind and a strong voice before kings and authorities.

Carthage welcomed him when he arrived. Faithfully tasting the fruit of knowing him during the few days he remained there, the people offered many gifts, which blessed Fulgentius instructed them to devote to the monastery he had commissioned to be built. [Col. 0137D] [Note: Chifflet, together with the manuscript, reads “in his few days.”] He himself boarded the ship with a crucified heart and naked in body, carrying with him immense riches of unique knowledge, by which he nourished everyone wherever he went with unfailing generosity.

41. Among the other bishops with whom he shared exile, he was lower in rank at the time of ordination [Col. 0137D], but not inferior in the virtue of patience and charity. In matters of doubt, when advice was especially sought, if the most blessed confessors ever discussed their common welfare among themselves, he indeed sat last. Nevertheless, the primate, or all those who followed the primate, wished to hear and follow his judgment, although he claimed nothing for himself through empty glory and paid fitting honor to his superiors. [Note: The manuscript reads: “For if … he was always ready to obey those who commanded, so that he would not presume …”; the *Antiphonary* reads: “For if … he was ready … and did not presume.”]

Thus he was compelled to answer those who consulted him, always ready to obey those who commanded, but never presuming to force anything upon those who did not wish it. [Col. 0138A]

After the very long delays of deliberation, whatever the common decision had found was left to blessed Fulgentius to express eloquently and commend to the understanding of the others. Whenever the bishops were questioned by letters from overseas about the faith or various questions, all imposed upon him the task of replying on behalf of everyone.

Thus, just as Aurelius, the bishop of the Church of Carthage, of blessed memory, had earned among his privileges the right to write alone the letters to be issued by the African council, so this man had earned the right to dictate alone the letters to be sent from that council. At that time more than sixty bishops were bound together by the chain of exile; blessed Fulgentius the bishop was their tongue and intellect. Therefore, whenever they wrote back to those who consulted them, [Col. 0138B] the names of all the bishops were given in the heading, but only blessed Fulgentius’ words were held in the text.

42. Besides these public letters of doctrinal discussion, if any of the bishops wished to correct or admonish his absent congregation, he would approach blessed Fulgentius humbly and, through the ministry of his tongue, fulfill the duty of his own administration. O wondrous man, born not for himself alone but for everyone! The Church of Ruspe alone had deserved to have him as its teacher, yet the greater part of the council of Byzacena lived by his speech.

Whoever in any congregation of the exiled priests attempted to cause unrest or to disregard the commands of his own bishop was so rebuked in his absence by blessed Fulgentius’ dictation that, seeking the remedy of satisfaction, he would immediately cross the sea, present himself, and through that same blessed Fulgentius—whose eloquence he had experienced while excommunicated—humbly obtain forgiveness. [Col. 0138C]

For blessed Fulgentius himself was both avenger and intercessor: an avenger for a colleague, an intercessor for a minister. From him proceeded the sword with which the hard neck of the proud was struck; and through him, in turn, the medicine of benevolence was supplied until the faintheartedness of the suppliant brothers was healed.

43. In the very first beginnings of his glorious exile, he could not gather a monastery by bringing even a few monks with him. Yet, not knowing how to live without a fraternal congregation, he persuaded his fellow bishops—namely Illustrius and Januarius—to live with him, since they were willing. Serving them with a single affection of charity, he wisely created the likeness of a great monastery in which monks and clerics were joined together. [Col. 0138D]

They had a common table, a common storeroom, common prayer, and common reading. No one insolently exalted himself over another, nor did anyone care for his own brothers more or more particularly, except that the monks who followed blessed Fulgentius, observing a stricter rule of abstinence, possessed absolutely nothing of their own and did not live among the other clerics according to clerical custom. [Note: The following words are not found in the manuscript or in Chifflet.]

Such was blessed Fulgentius’ instruction that, through spiritual admonitions, it transferred the hearts of those subject to him from earthly pleasures to spiritual and heavenly delights. Thus, while the discipline of their good purpose remained firm, they were not led astray by the laziness of weaker brothers who were unwilling to imitate the examples enacted daily before their eyes. [Col. 0139A]

Who could adequately describe the praises of that dwelling? That house was then the oracle of the city of Caralis. The afflicted came there to receive the remedy of consolation; there faithful covenants of peace and harmony were made among those who were at odds; there the Lord offered an edifying exposition in its fullness to those who desired to hear the divine lesson more attentively.

Noblemen delighted, if possible, to see blessed Fulgentius disputing every day. Those enduring want gladly begged bodily alms from the place where they also received spiritual instruction. [Col. 0139B] Frequently blessed Fulgentius freed from temporal hunger those to whom he gave generously, and, by wisely admonishing them, led them to renounce the world. Although he urged those who possessed nothing to despise the desire for possessions, he was always eager to acquire brothers for the monastery, so that, although he knew that all things belonged to everyone, he nevertheless both desired and wished to associate all people with the profession of the monks.

As this fame grew day by day, it also stirred the people of the Church of Carthage to still greater joy, and, through the most reliable witnesses coming from that province, commended blessed Fulgentius to those who were absent.

## CHAPTER XXI. King Trasamund’s persecution. Trasamund summons Fulgentius. The fruit of Saint Fulgentius’ teaching.

[Col. 0139C] 44. Meanwhile, King Trasamund’s implacable mind and terrible anger toward the Catholic religion—amid harsh persecutions and deceitful factions by which he now compelled Catholics through threats, and now invited them by promises, to deny that Christ was equal to God the Father—began, under the pretense of wishing chiefly to deceive the multitude, to feign that he was simply seeking an understanding of the Catholic religion. He thought that no one could be found by whose argument he might be convicted in his errors.

He proposed many snares of foolish questions [Col. 0139D], and, if anyone wished to answer him, he neither despised nor rejected him; indeed, pretending to listen patiently, he boasted that no adequate answer could be given him. [Note: The manuscript reads “many”; the *Antiphonary* reads “bold.”] And truly, what human being could have shown the light of truth to so hardened a heart?

Nevertheless, by the boldness of his faith, he caused many religious men to convict the king’s blasphemies on occasions prepared by the Lord. It is said that, when he had long been asking who could most fully defend the truth of Catholic doctrine with clear testimonies, he was told that blessed Fulgentius was among the exiled bishops: nothing was lacking in his knowledge, grace overflowed in him, and he would satisfy the king’s questions wisely and eloquently. [Note: The manuscript reads approximately: “It is said that at last he asked … It is said that among …”; the precise wording is uncertain.]

45. Immediately, wishing to test the priest to whom the entire Church of our religion generally bore good testimony, the king sent a capable servant swiftly [Col. 0140A]. The servant led Fulgentius away and brought him without delay to Carthage, where he arrived joyfully.

There, finding an opportunity to distribute the talents entrusted to him, like a most faithful steward, he began carefully to teach the orthodox Catholics who came to him in his little lodging. He explained how the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are proclaimed by the faithful as one God, while the distinction of the three persons remains.

Such was the sweetness of blessed Fulgentius’ eloquent speech, and such joy shone in his face, that holy charity drew all the faithful eagerly either to question the most learned man or to hear him whenever he answered their questions. He shared the word of God without grudging envy, responded to everyone’s questions, despised no one, and judged no one wicked. [Col. 0140B] He was even ready, if God had perhaps revealed something better to someone through the Holy Spirit, to hear it, learn it, retain it, follow it, and approve it, kindly and gently practicing the humility of a disciple while serving as a teacher.

As a result, he became much more learned and better than he had been, seeking greater gains for Christ. He taught some who had already been rebaptized to lament their error, and he reconciled them. He warned others not to lose their souls for the sake of earthly advantages. Those whom he sensed were already close to destruction he softened with such gentle words that, out of regard for his kindness, they were ashamed to carry out the evil they had conceived and quickly returned to repentance.

Others, strengthened by his words and seasoned with the salt of his teaching, rebuked the Arian heretics with complete confidence. Thus, by a marvelous grace, it came about that through one priest—whose wisdom the king had wished to test—the number of the wise increased at Carthage, and through the ministry of persecution the Catholic faith received growth rather than decline. [Col. 0140C]

## CHAPTER XXII. Blessed Fulgentius’ reply to ten objections of the Arians.

46. Learning all this through secret messengers, the king approved the excellent priest’s intelligence, wisdom, teaching, faith, piety, gentleness, and continence; and, in accordance with the praises of his reputation, he recognized that Fulgentius was as he had been proclaimed to be.

He therefore quickly sent him certain statements filled with the poison of unbelief, demanding that a reply be returned to him. The most learned bishop received them and divided the absurdities of the very long discussion into sections of objections [Col. 0140D]. He added brief, convincing, and necessary answers, weighty with the authority of testimonies and radiant with the light of complete reasoning.

After these answers had been discussed for a long time and at length with many learned men, and had been brought to the knowledge of the faithful people, he delivered them to the king, who had been kept waiting for a long time. That barbarian king read them with the greatest attention. Because he had never been predestined for salvation, he praised the wisdom, admired the eloquence, and proclaimed the humility, but nevertheless did not deserve to understand the truth.

The people of Carthage, interpreters of the spiritual triumph, joyfully acknowledged with murmurs that the king’s propositions had been refuted [Col. 0141A]. Together with their praises of blessed Fulgentius, they gloried that the Catholic faith had always been victorious.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Three little books addressed to King Trasamund. Blessed Fulgentius’ book against the Arian bishop Pinta.

47. Still wishing to test the most learned man, the king questioned him again about other matters and ordered his question to be read to blessed Fulgentius only once, granting him no opportunity either to meditate or to write it down. He feared that, as before, the words he had set forth for refutation might be incorporated into Fulgentius’ replies, and that he would once again be shown to have been defeated by the judgment of the entire city.

Blessed Fulgentius, scarcely able to recall what had been read to him once, delayed answering. But the king increasingly ordered him to answer, criticizing the delay in his reply and judging the holy man’s caution to be distrust. Therefore that bishop, supported by the virtue of prudence, lest falsehoods perhaps be spread among the people—by which it might be alleged either that blessed Fulgentius had been unable or unwilling to meet the king’s questions—composed three remarkable little books. [Col. 0141B]

In them, addressing the king simply, he extensively revisited the whole sequence of the question as he had perceived it through his imperfect hearing, teaching that the rational soul was by no means absent from Christ the Lord in his assumption of flesh. [Note: The manuscript reads: “he discussed at length the sides of the whole question, which he had perceived through imperfect hearing.”]

Then, filled with the greatest wonder, the king dared to ask nothing further [Note: The manuscript reads *nisus*, “having endeavored” or “having attempted”], except that one of his bishops, named Pinta, made a kind of attempt to answer. He preferred not to remain silent, although he was unable to offer any answer. Blessed Fulgentius immediately opposed him with a truthful disputation in another work, which he entitled *Against Pinta* [Col. 0141C], and showed that, in his first defense, the defeated opponents had rashly attempted to renew the contest.

## CHAPTER XXIV. A book, or memorandum, on the Holy Spirit addressed to the presbyter Abragila.

48. In a very brief memorandum addressed to the presbyter Abragila, who had questioned him about the Holy Spirit, he produced many testimonies, teaching him that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit must simply be confessed as one God.

He also arranged the statements of this memorandum between the two works of that period, so that they ought to be copied. All the faithful Catholics read them and marveled; the Arians blushed and murmured in grief against him [Col. 0141D]. [Note: The manuscript reads “in the very [work/place].”]

This continued until, on the occasion of a malicious suggestion, wicked and evil men said to the king, who wished to retain Fulgentius longer in Carthage:

“King, you are laboring in vain. Your diligence accomplishes nothing. The teaching of Bishop Fulgentius has already prevailed to such an extent that he is reconciling some of your priests. Therefore, unless you come to our aid quickly, our religion will fail. [Note: The manuscript reads “our religion will fail”; the context may imply “our religion.”] Anyone baptized by us will, once reconciled, publicly preach the *homoousion* again. Nor, even if you wish to stir up persecution, will royal fury be capable of inspiring fear. The presence of Fulgentius greatly strengthens and makes steadfast all the bishops.” [Col. 0141D]

## CHAPTER XXV. Fulgentius is exiled again. He foretells his speedy return.

[Col. 0142A] 49. With such things being suggested to him, the king, as though constrained by some great necessity, agreed and compelled blessed Fulgentius to return to exile in Sardinia. In the dead of night—for the king had ordered that it be done in this way—blessed Fulgentius was brought to the ship without the people’s knowledge.

But because contrary winds resisted, he was delayed on the shore for so long that nearly the whole city gathered there for many days, bidding him farewell and receiving Communion from his hand. There, filled with prophetic grace through the Holy Spirit, he said to Juliateus, a deeply religious man who was greatly afflicted and lamented the departure of the blessed bishop: [Note: Other manuscripts cited by Chifflet read *Juliteus*, others *Viliateus*, and another *Villeus*.]

“Do not weep any longer; soon we shall return to you. You will see us when the freedom of the Catholic Church has been restored [Col. 0142B]. But, I beg you, let this remain a secret with you, for excessive charity has compelled me to reveal it.”

Thus blessed Fulgentius always carefully fled from boasting and never sought human glory in spiritual gifts. He was content with the testimony of his conscience and relied solely upon the mercy of God. Therefore he was never pleased to perform miracles, nor did he in any way desire that this grace be given him.

If he was ever asked to pray for the sick and suffering, or for those enduring the necessities of temporal tribulations, he poured out his prayers with this devotion:

“YOU KNOW, LORD, what is suitable for the salvation of our souls. Therefore, when we ask for what necessity urges, may your mercy grant that by which spiritual usefulness is not hindered. If it is expedient, then let the prayer of our humility be heard by you in such a way that your will may chiefly be fulfilled.” [Col. 0142C] [Note: The *Antiphonary* reads “may it prosperably [or happily] be fulfilled.”]

God Almighty frequently granted many things to his praying priest. But Fulgentius attributed nothing to his own merits; rather, he assigned everything to the faith of those for whom he was heard, saying that the gift had been granted not to him but to them.

## CHAPTER XXVI. He returns to Sardinia amid universal rejoicing.

50. But, so that we do not delay too long, let us insert one of his statements concerning the performance of miracles. “Miracles,” he used to say, “do not confer righteousness upon a person, but knowledge of that person. Whoever becomes known to human beings, unless he is righteous, will reach eternal punishments in condemnation. But the person who, justified by the works of heavenly mercy, lives righteously in the sight of God alone—even if he is little known to human beings [Col. 0142D]—will, crowned, receive the blessed joys of the saints.”

This remarkable man therefore feared receiving praise for miracles, although each day, through the greater miracle of his most holy exhortation, he led many unbelievers to believe, reconciled many heretics, and caused many devoted to the worst conduct to accept the laws of continence. [Note: Thus the manuscript. The *Antiphonary* reads: “although each day he performed greater miracles through exhortation.”] Through his most salutary admonitions, drunkards learned sobriety, adulterers followed chastity, and the avaricious and rapacious were taught to distribute everything to the poor. With their purpose changed, humility became sweet to the proud, peace to the quarrelsome [Col. 0143A], and obedience to the disobedient.

Blessed Fulgentius always devoted himself diligently to such miracles. Accompanied by these deeds, he was glorious in every place and at every time. When favorable calm weather eventually enabled him to be carried back to Sardinia, he restored joy to the hearts of his fellow bishops in exile. He also made the province itself splendid by the light of his presence, since the presence of so many priests gave it distinction.

Christians came from every direction with joy to see the strongest athlete of Christ return to the divine camp, adorned with the insignia of victory, having broken the attack of the raging king in single combat and rejoined his former comrades-in-arms. He displayed humility all the more laudably toward each of them, the more he knew that his own virtue had shone forth, remembering undoubtedly the warning of Scripture: “Son, the greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Ecclesiasticus III, 20). [Col. 0143B]

## CHAPTER XXVII. He builds a new monastery there. Who the true monks are.

51. Blessed Fulgentius no longer wished to live for long in the former house accompanied by many brothers. Instead, he found a vacant place beside the basilica of the holy martyr Saturninus, far from the noise of the city. After first asking the venerable Brumasius, bishop of the city of Caralis, as was fitting, he built a new monastery at his own expense. [Note: Some report the name as Brumasius from Chifflet; others read Viliateus; another reads Villeus. Chifflet reads “of Caralis.”]

Gathering more than forty brothers there, he preserved the order of coenobitic discipline inviolate. He gave no one permission to transgress the rule of the holy profession, but chiefly taught the monks this principle to be observed: none of them should claim anything as his own, but all things should be common to everyone. [Col. 0143C]

For he frequently said that a monk ought not—and could not rightly—be judged a monk if his will persuaded him to possess a private fund. Bodily illness may sometimes compel a monk to use somewhat richer foods; but to desire to claim ownership, under private right, of even the smallest things is clear evidence of proud will and avaricious desire.

He himself distributed the necessities of life to the servants of God with the greatest discretion, considering each person’s strength and weakness. Nevertheless, whenever he provided more for certain men than for the others, he admonished them all the more to preserve humility, saying to them:

“WHOEVER RECEIVES SOMETHING MORE FROM THE COMMON SUBSTANCE BECOMES THE DEBTOR OF ALL THOSE TO WHOM THAT SUBSTANCE BELONGS; AND HUMILITY ALONE HELPS THE DEBTOR.” [Col. 0143D]

In this way he ensured that no one would be scandalized when one person seemed to be given more because of illness.

### 52 [Cols. 0144A–B]

He was also exceedingly concerned to anticipate the requests of all the monks, granting beforehand whatever either necessity or manifest reason showed ought to be granted to each one. But if anyone presumed to ask before receiving, he immediately refused him, even if he deserved to receive it, saying that monks ought to be content with what they had been given. Moreover, those who ask for themselves what they need—or more than they need—before receiving it are still serving carnal desires. [Note: Ant.: *qui sibi plus quam indigeant*, “who ask for themselves more than they need.”] and are not thinking perfectly of heavenly things, since, so long as they hasten to provide for themselves whatever they consider necessary, at least by asking when they cannot obtain it by bargaining.

He also said that those were true monks who, having mortified their own wills [Note: MS: *voluntatibus suis*, “their own wills”], were ready to want or reject nothing, but only to observe the abbot’s counsels or commands. For this reason he did not allow even the brother who held the office of superior to do anything without his counsel.

He loved less those brothers who labored and exercised themselves tirelessly in manual work but had no devotion to reading, and he did not consider them worthy of the highest honor. But anyone in whom there was a love of spiritual knowledge—even if deprived of bodily strength and entirely unable to work with his hands—was especially loved and esteemed by him.

### 53 [Cols. 0144B–C]

When he disputed in the presence of the brothers, he loved it if someone proposed difficult questions in which his outstanding intellect would have to labor. He allowed all the brothers, even those naturally simple or of limited understanding, to ask whatever they wished; nor would he cease from giving an answer because of weariness or labor before they acknowledged that they were satisfied.

He possessed a great and marvelous grace in correcting the restless with a tranquil heart. Thus, precisely when others thought that he was becoming violently angry, the greatest calm prevailed and reigned in him; and, without himself being disturbed, he disturbed many who were doing wrong, like one disturbed, but with a salutary force. Hating vices but loving people, he appeared severe only for as long as the benefit of spiritual discipline required.

At other times he was so gentle, approachable, and affable toward individuals that he never addressed any of the brothers by name alone, nor did he command anyone, however insignificant, with the arrogance of secular domination.

### CHAPTER XXVIII  
### What Fulgentius wrote. King Hilderic, a Catholic, recalls the bishops from exile.

### 54 [Cols. 0144C–0145A]

At the same time he wrote the Carthaginians a letter distinguished by lofty exhortation, in which he set out, in a most serious complaint [Note: MS: *cum quaestione*, “with a question”], almost all the deceits and deceptive flatteries by which unhappy souls were being seduced to death. [Note: In the margin of the Ant. edition, concerning this work, it is written: “I think this is the one which we have addressed to Donatus.”]

At that time also he promptly replied, in two little books, to the religious man Euthymius, who had consulted him about the forgiveness of sins. He also, in a salutary discussion, instructed the man who wished to know the testimonies concerning predestination and grace and their distinctions. [Note: MS: *differentia*, singular, “distinction,” rather than *differentias*.]

He frequently sent familiar letters—though containing spiritual edification—to those living in Sardinia, to those dwelling in Africa, and to Romans, especially senators, widows, and virgins whose reputation was praiseworthy. To Proba, a virgin of Christ, he composed two little books, *On Fasting and Prayer*.

[Note: Thus Chiffl. But Ant.: “Thus he was so well known to almost all nations that the two books which Bishop Faustus of Gaul composed against grace in deceitful language, secretly favoring the Pelagians while nevertheless wishing to appear Catholic, were sent from Constantinople, where many brothers had taken offense at them, to blessed Fulgentius for examination.”]

For he was so well known to almost all nations that even the two books which Faustus, bishop of Gaul, composed against grace in deceitful language, secretly favoring the Pelagians while nevertheless wishing to appear Catholic, were sent from Constantinople—where many brothers had taken offense at them—to blessed Fulgentius for examination. To prevent the hidden poison from spreading, he himself answered them in seven books, laboring more to explain than to refute; for to explain Faustus’s obscure arguments was itself to refute the arguments of a madman.

### 55 [Cols. 0145A–B]

The great labor of this work quickly received its fitting reward. For as soon as his dictation had been completed, the chain of the very long captivity was immediately broken. The death of King Thrasamund, and the extraordinary goodness of Hilderic, who was beginning to reign, restored liberty to the Catholic Church established throughout Africa, granted the people of Carthage their own bishop, and commanded, with the most merciful authority, that episcopal ordinations be carried out everywhere.

### CHAPTER XXIX  
### Fulgentius is received and escorted with the highest honor. He departs from Carthage. The glory offered to him makes Fulgentius more humble. He employs monks in ecclesiastical ministries. His remarkable humility. He wrote many homilies and delivered sermons to the people. Ten books against Fabianus. Three books on the truth of predestination and grace. Near death he devotes himself especially to repentance. Fulgentius’s prayer amid the greatest and sharpest pains. Fulgentius distributes everything to the poor as he is dying. The holy bishop dies. His honorable monument. The Moors ravage the territory of Ruspa.

[Cols. 0145B–C]

Thus blessed Fulgentius, after wisely defeating the Pelagians, was granted the joy of seeing the Catholics rejoice. Then, just as the Holy Spirit had foretold through him, he returned to Carthage with all his fellow bishops, although he had departed from there alone.

He found joyful those whom he had left sorrowful. He found burning with extraordinary exultation those whom he had left enduring the violence of persecution. He found possessing a spiritual father those whom he had left grieving that the Church, their mother, was widowed. He found awaiting him with joy those whom he had left groaning in weariness.

### 56 [Cols. 0145C–0146B]

Such was the devotion of the citizens of Carthage, who longed to see blessed Fulgentius again, and so ardently did the whole people await him whom they had seen fight manfully in their presence, that, when the other bishops had disembarked before him, the silent multitude stood along the shore, searching with eyes and minds among all the bishops for blessed Fulgentius, whom they knew familiarly, and looking for him from every ship.

When his face appeared, an immense shout arose. Everyone disputed who should first greet and recognize him [Note: MS: *agnoscendo, quis caput supponeret ad benedicendum*, “recognizing him, who should place his head for blessing”], who should place his head beneath the bishop’s hand for a blessing, who might deserve to touch him as he walked, even if only at the tips of his fingers, and who might deserve to see him, even from a distance. Divine praise resounded from every tongue.

The people, following and preceding him to the basilica of Saint Agileus, celebrated the noble triumph of the blessed confessor. An enormous multitude, hastening together, pressed around blessed Fulgentius, whom it honored above all others, until the holy foresight of certain Christians, making a circular passage around him, provided a free route through the crowd for him as he passed in the middle.

Still wishing to test the love of the faithful, the Lord miraculously drenched the people as they walked with abundant rain. And who could recount works of piety—or, alternatively, charity—without sacrificing truth? The immense rain frightened no one and prevented no one from offering service to the religious priest. [Note: MS: *sacerdotibus gloriosis*, “to the glorious priests.”]

Indeed, as though a heavenly blessing were descending from above, the faith of the nobles grew so greatly that, gladly spreading their cloaks over blessed Fulgentius, they repelled the rain and fashioned, through ingenious charity, a new kind of tabernacle. They became imitators of those who in earlier times spread their garments on the road before the Savior seated upon a donkey’s colt and coming to Jerusalem, as the Gospel relates: “They spread their garments on the road” (Matthew 21:8).

These people were doing something similar: with their own clothing they unanimously protected the uncovered head of blessed Fulgentius. As evening was scarcely approaching, they were brought before Boniface, the bishop of holy memory; and all blessed and praised God together.

Then, throughout every street of the city of Carthage wherever he passed, blessed Fulgentius was pointed out with hands and eyes and proclaimed with countless praises.

### 57 [Cols. 0146C–0147A]

After he had hastened [Note: Thus MS; the other witnesses read *petitus*, “having been sought/requested”] to visit and bless the homes of all who loved him, and had deigned to rejoice with those who rejoiced—he who had previously wept with those who wept—he satisfied the desires of all. Then, bidding farewell to the brothers, he departed from Carthage.

Along all the roads of his long journey he found still greater joy, as peoples from every direction came out to meet him with lamps, torches, and branches of trees, giving ineffable thanks to God [Note: Chiffl.: *agentibus Deo gratias ineffabiles*, “rendering ineffable thanks to God”], who had wonderfully made blessed Fulgentius gracious in the sight of everyone.

In every church he was received as though he were its own bishop, and thus the entire province of Byzacena rejoiced at his return as though it were a single people. Who, I ask, would not be lifted up by the greatness of such glory? Yet blessed Fulgentius was moved by it to pursue greater humility.

For he arrived amid popular glory, and his episcopal dignity was enhanced by the privilege of special veneration; nevertheless, after he had taken his seat, he desired to continue living among the monks. And so that his arrival might not seem to diminish the authority of Abbot Felix, he voluntarily deprived himself of every power to command the monks, wishing himself to follow not his own will but that of another.

Though, while still a monk, he had received responsibility for administering the brothers, now as a bishop he did not wish to rule in his own monastery. He was so careful not to distress Felix the abbot that, when providing hospitality for visitors, if necessity required either that more bread be produced or that something additional be supplied, he first sought the advice of Abbot Felix.

In every council of Byzacena he was the first to be consulted about important matters; in his own monastery he humbly consulted Abbot Felix about the smallest matters.

### 58 [Cols. 0147A–B]

It was not enough for blessed Fulgentius to follow and preserve this humility in words and actions unless he also confirmed in writing that he claimed nothing as his own in that monastery and lived among the monks not by authority but by charity.

This prudent man, considering that the simple servants of God might later suffer some disadvantage, placed in this document an obstacle to contradiction for his successors, since he put nothing before the welfare of the monks serving God.

Nevertheless, he purchased a house beside the church and devoted the greatest care to its construction, so that his future successor would not lack lodging. Restoring whatever services of the clergy were deficient, he transferred many monks from among the brothers whom he had found trustworthy into ecclesiastical service.

There also he cared for charity, so that, while ordaining nearly all the clergy from that monastery, the familiarity born of their former association would prevent any quarrel from arising at some time between the monks and the clergy.

### 59 [Cols. 0147B–D]

He also took the greatest care that no cleric should be adorned in ostentatious clothing or, occupied with secular business, wander for too long from ecclesiastical service. He ordered them all to have houses not far from the church, to cultivate a garden with their own hands, and to devote the greatest care to singing psalms sweetly or to reading aloud.

Each week he established that all the clergy and widows, and any of the laity who were able, should fast on the fourth and sixth days—that is, Wednesday and Friday. He instructed everyone to attend the daily vigils, fasts, and morning and evening prayers.

He restrained some restless people with words and others with blows, those whom manifest guilt had compelled to be scourged. Thus he attacked everyone’s vices with salutary discussion that, without inserting anyone’s name, compelled all to fear and to abandon even hidden sins through a salutary dread.

Yet how could he exercise less caution among his own clergy, when he also settled the prolonged quarrels and contentious disputes of neighboring congregations? Finally, he calmed the hostility of the people of Maximiana, who refused to receive the bishop appointed for them, by a salutary admonition; and, establishing a fitting end to a very serious scandal, he arranged and reconciled everything among them with moderation and good judgment.

### 60 [Cols. 0147D–0148A]

At the council of Vincensis [Note: The manuscript reads “Juncensis”; Ant. reads “Vivecensis”], he was placed before and preferred to a certain bishop named Quodvultdeus by the judgment of all the priests who had assembled, although Quodvultdeus maintained that he was the earlier in precedence.

On that very day and at that very time Fulgentius remained silent, nor did he wish to diminish the authority of the council by making excuses. But when, after the council, he perceived that the bishop was grieving, he feared that his own honor might generate scandal for his brother. Judging it better to become lesser through charity than greater without charity, he later looked toward the distinguished assembly of the council of Suphetana and, in the presence of all, offered a humble prayer that, since he himself wished it again, Bishop Quodvultdeus should be preferred, so that, once his name had been recited afterward, he might henceforth live happily with the mind of his fellow bishop reconciled.

The bishops marveled at the humility of one making such a request, and they did not wish to distress a man who was offering God the sacrifice of humility in order to preserve fellowship of spirit in the bond of charity.

Where are now those whose desire to rise above others dominates them, who even place themselves before their own predecessors and claim privileges not owed to them? Behold blessed Fulgentius: he did not wish to defend even the primacy he had deserved, because he had no desire to be first before anyone without charity.

### 61 [Cols. 0148B–C]

Although, amid various responsibilities, the singular teacher and doctor of the Catholic Church had little free time here in Africa, he nevertheless dictated many ecclesiastical sermons to be written down and delivered to the people. Wherever he preached, he charmed everyone’s hearts, producing not empty and utterly vain applause but compunction of heart.

Boniface, the bishop of the Church of Carthage, of holy memory, awaited him at Burnos—or Furnos—to dedicate a church. For two days, while Fulgentius was present, he preached; Boniface was so delighted to hear the word of the Lord from his mouth that, until Fulgentius finished his sermon, he himself irrigated the ground with tears [Note: Chiffl.: *ipse lacrymis genas rigaret*, “he himself wet his cheeks with tears”], giving thanks to God, whose grace continually raises up outstanding and illustrious teachers in the Catholic Church.

After his return from exile, he composed many new works, including ten books refuting the false narratives fabricated by the lying Fabianus. He also produced three little books on the truth of predestination and grace, as well as many other works. Whoever wishes to know them will find them faithfully written in his monastery.

### 62 [Cols. 0148C–D]

It is now time for us to say how, after all his good works, he came to rest, having been transferred to the kingdom of heaven.

Approximately one year before he was taken from this world, moved by profound compunction of heart, he suddenly withdrew from ecclesiastical responsibilities. Secretly leaving even his own monastery, he sailed with a few accompanying brothers to the island of Circina. There, on a small rocky island called Chilmi, where he had already ordered a monastery to be built, he devoted himself to reading, prayer, and fasting.

As though he knew that his final day was approaching, he practiced repentance with his whole heart. Although his entire life, from the time when he was converted and wholeheartedly embraced the profession of a monk, had been a time of repentance, on this island he mortified his members much more extensively and diligently, like one who was just beginning, and wept in the sight of God alone.

When many people began to murmur about the priest’s absence, he was compelled by the necessity of charity to return once more to his monastery, to offer the customary consolations to religious people and patiently to endure the most difficult labors for the benefit of his neighbors.

### 63 [Cols. 0149A–B]

Not many days had passed when, behold, the good Lord sought his faithful servant. He suddenly fell into the sharpest pains of bodily illness. Weakened by sickness for nearly seventy days, he frequently said only this:

“Lord, grant me patience here now; afterward, pardon.”

He never ceased repeating these words, whether pain afflicted him, fever inflamed him, or exhaustion weakened him.

When the physicians urged him to use the baths, he said:

“Will baths be able to prevent a mortal human being from dying when the time of life has been completed? If the remedies of warm waters cannot repel approaching death, why, I ask, do you persuade me to relax at the end the strictness of a profession long preserved?”

[Note: The manuscript reads: “But if death approaches …” and so forth.]

Thus, faithfully entrusting his salvation to the will above, when he realized without any doubt that he was about to die, he summoned all his clergy in the presence of the monks and addressed them, saying:

“Brothers, in looking after the salvation of your souls I have perhaps been troublesome and difficult for you; and therefore I ask you to forgive me, whoever is grieving over anything. And if our severity has perhaps exceeded the proper measure, pray that the Lord may not count this against me as sin.”

As blessed Fulgentius expressed these words with tearful sobs, all fell together at his knees, crying out that he had always watched over the salvation of everyone, as was fitting, always good and always affable. Then he said:

“May my Lord God provide you with a shepherd worthy of himself.”

### 64 [Cols. 0149C–D]

Then, having ordered silence, he rested for a little while. Afterward, caring for the poor, he asked for the total amount of money from which the most faithful steward daily supplied the needy, and ordered all of it to be spent.

He himself recalled by name the widows, orphans, foreigners, and all the needy who were there, and by his own decision determined what should be given to each individually. Since he had no heirs in this world, he left the poor the inheritance of this benevolent care.

Nor did he defraud his own clergy of the blessing due to them; he mercifully provided for their poverty as well. Arranging everything secretly in advance, praying continually, and blessing each person who entered, he remained sound in mind until his final hour.

Finally, on the last day of the Kalends of January, after evening prayer had been completed, he happily handed over his blessed spirit into the hands of the Lord. He was then in the twenty-fifth year of his episcopate and the sixty-fifth year of his entire life, as he had indicated to many brothers when he was near death.

### 65 [Cols. 0149D–0150B]

On that very day his holy body could not be buried. It was placed in the monastery’s oratory, and throughout that night it invited both the monks and the clergy to keep vigil in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.

In the morning, after a very large multitude of people from the neighboring regions had come to the funeral, he was carried by the hands of the priests to the city church called the Second Church, where he had also established relics of the apostles, and there received an honorable monument.

He deserved to be the first bishop placed in that basilica, where ancient custom allowed no dead person—neither priest nor layman—to be buried. But the great force of affection removed the obstacle of custom, as all the citizens pressed for this and sought with the greatest devotion that, where the holy man beloved by God had been consecrated, he might also always be locally present in the prayers of each person.

They had often experienced how many benefits the prayer of blessed Fulgentius had brought them and how many evils it had driven away.
