This later became unmistakably clear from evident signs, when, not many days after his summons—or, alternatively, his death—the hostile people of the Moors suddenly ravaged the territory of Ruspa, devastating much through plunder, killings, and fires, and slaughtering everyone they could find even within the very walls of the church.

Who would not marvel at the grace of blessed Fulgentius? As long as he lived, the city entrusted to him did not experience the fury of war. And while almost the entire province endured a terrible captivity, Ruspa remained unharmed because of its venerable priest, whose life was a wall for his fellow citizens.

### 66 [Cols. 0150B–D]

Nor did I judge that this should meanwhile be passed over in silence: while a suitable successor was being sought for him, disagreement arose between the laity and the clergy, and the prolonged dispute lasted almost a full year. On the very day on which he himself died, your holiness took your seat upon his chair.

The first solemnity of his deposition deserved to be adorned with this privilege, so that it might become much more venerable through the joy of your ordination.

But do you wish to know how these things did not occur through accidental movements but are shown to have been granted through his prayers? Recall the most trustworthy vision of blessed Pontianus, bishop of Thenis, which he himself related as follows:

“As I was going, at the command of the primate Datianus, so that a bishop might be chosen for the Church of Ruspa, that same most blessed Fulgentius appeared to me during a period of rest. Greeting me familiarly with the gracious expression he ordinarily wore, he said: ‘Where is your holiness now hastening so quickly?’

“I replied: ‘So that a bishop may be chosen for the Church of Ruspa.’

“But he, smiling slightly, said: ‘He has already been ordained.’”

Is it not evident that what he had foretold was accomplished through his prayers? He who knew the confirmation of one not yet elected or ordained had also deserved, by praying, to know the day on which the man who could sit upon the episcopal chair would already be ordained.

Therefore, with continual prayers and faithful devotion, we always desire that, having become a sharer forever in his glory, you may live happily, not unworthy of so great a predecessor; that together with us you may give thanks to the Lord for the completion of this work; and that, for whatever may perhaps have been expressed inadequately, you may eloquently ask pardon from all learned readers.

---

## THE THREE BOOKS OF SAINT FULGENTIUS TO MONIMUS (C) [Col. 0151]

### PROLOGUE OF SAINT FULGENTIUS, BISHOP OF RUSPA, TO THE THREE BOOKS TO MONIMUS

### 1 [Cols. 0151A–0152D]

I give thanks to the Lord that you do not cease to bring forth good things from the good treasure of your heart (Matthew 12:35). And your *lingua Eucharis*—“grateful tongue,” which abounds in a good man—reveals the purity of your heart.

Although it overflows with the divinely granted streams of eloquence, I do not believe that your words express as much as I know is contained in the inner chambers of your heart. For, kindled by divine fire, you continually sympathize with us in such a way that even those tribulations which befell us but were overcome with the Lord’s help you almost always endure on our behalf. Whenever you recall them in your heart, you are in a certain sense compelled to suffer them again.

Behold how much good charity possesses; behold how great a praise it holds before God and human beings: when it grieves over what has happened to the one it loves, by recalling it frequently it itself endures the suffering more intensely.

The only thing remaining, therefore, is that you should continually do for us what charity itself is accustomed to do. And what else is this except that you should always pray for us to the one in whom you love us purely?

For charity always asks on behalf of those whom it loves, even when it fears for things that are secure. Yet it fears not with the fear which charity itself casts out—for “perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18)—but with the fear which it is accustomed to possess not for fear’s sake but for love’s sake.

It fears, therefore, not with a timid fear [Note: The manuscript of Thuan reads “with fear”; alternatively, “with love”], but with a chaste one. For it does not fear through dread of crime, but through the strength of purity and the firmness of virtue.

Moreover, you demand from me a debt which, with the Lord’s help, I promise to repay quickly. I do not acknowledge this debt in the manner in which your Maro recalls that a certain person acknowledged his own debt but confessed that he could not repay it. Rather, I confess that I owe that debt in which I do not deny that I can repay, but promise to do so.

For he himself gives me the means by which I may repay, who gave me the obligation to owe. Unless we received from him, we could not only repay but could not even owe the debt itself.

What else do we owe one another except charity? Blessed Paul clearly demonstrates this when speaking to the faithful:

“Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Romans 13:8).

But who would acknowledge a debt if he denied that he had received it? Therefore, in saying that we owe, we plainly show that we have received. For the blessed Apostle says:

“What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (Romans 5:5 [as cited in the source]).

Elsewhere also he testifies:

“Because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

Therefore, he who gave us what we ought to repay will himself grant us the ability by which we can repay what we owe. He is therefore the author of the debt who is the author of the gift.

Indeed, in his generosity he deigned to make himself a debtor—not because, being needy, he received anything from someone, but because, being abundant, he generously bestowed it. When he placed the half-dead man upon his own beast and entrusted him to the innkeeper’s care, giving two denarii, he declared himself a debtor by saying:

“If you spend anything more, when I return I will repay you” (Luke 10:35). [Note: The words “when I return, I will repay you” are absent from the Thuan manuscript.]

What does “if you spend anything more” mean except “if you receive anything more from me”? For the one who spent more—doing what he had not received as a command but giving counsel from charity—also confessed that he had received mercy. He says:

“Now concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give advice, as one who has received mercy from the Lord, so that I may be faithful” (1 Corinthians 7:25).

He therefore received mercy not only to accept what he was to distribute, but also to distribute more abundantly.

Behold what our Lord is like: by giving, he becomes a debtor, and the more he gives, the less he is ashamed to be a debtor. To the extent that he gives freely, to that extent he is found to be a debtor. Nor can anyone have him as a debtor except in what he himself has deigned to confer by free generosity.

Therefore, ask him continually on my behalf to grant me the ability to repay the debt, since he gave me the gift of owing you, in him, the free service of charity.

To confess everything frankly to your heart, which is my own heart—for just as I can conceal nothing from my own heart, so I cannot conceal anything from yours—the reason for my delay in repaying the debt was this:

I was compelled to respond to the empty words of a certain heretic who did not hesitate to attack even my name under the charge of the Photinian—or alternatively, Fotinian—error. He also wished to turn against me the words of the holy Augustine and Jerome, as though they were contrary to my confession.

I have postponed putting his name into writing for now, but you can doubtless remember it yourself. For, while you were there with us at Carthage, his statements were brought to me, and, if I remember correctly, they also came to your attention. Indeed, while you were there, I could not read anything that I could not offer to you for consideration.

Therefore, if the Lord wills, I shall quickly send those same little books to your charity. I do not doubt that you will patiently tolerate my delay in repaying what I owe you, since I know how much you delight in—or rather, how much you continually urge us—to respond to heretics without reluctance, with the Lord’s help.

## BOOK ONE: ON GOD’S DOUBLE PREDESTINATION—ONE OF THE GOOD TO GLORY, THE OTHER OF THE EVIL TO PUNISHMENT

### CHAPTER ONE  
### God inspires us to seek him and is found by those who seek him

### 3 [Cols. 0153A–D]

Your letter, dearest son Monimus, demonstrates the delightful sincerity of your mind and the praiseworthy ardor of your spiritual zeal; at the same time, with complaining kindness, it seems to accuse the delay of my reply. It appears that I love you less than I ought because I have not taken care to answer your inquiries quickly.

But believe me: just as your person has by no means been despised in my heart through the charity of Christ, so my response has been delayed not by my will but by the variety of my responsibilities.

Nevertheless, amid the very responsibilities which I am compelled to endure unwillingly, I rejoice in your zeal as much as I delight in your affection. I embrace your holy purpose of eagerness all the more because, like a truly spiritual merchant pursuing the profits of the inner person and desiring increasingly to enlarge the gain of heavenly merchandise, you first demand from me the debt I owe and then continually increase it through the interest of further questions. Thus the very necessity of my delay serves to increase your advantages.

Accordingly, I trust in the mercy of our God that, if something is not granted to me on the basis of my own merit through the work of this inquiry and discussion, it will be granted to me for the sake of your desire. For God will in no way allow your inquiry to be defrauded of the result of discovery, since he spiritually inflamed you to inquire, and no circumstance can invalidate his faithful promise when he says:

“Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Luke 11:9).

The inner Teacher, therefore, from whom we receive the assistance of heavenly instruction, not only opens to us who inquire the secrets of his words, but also freely inspires the desire that we should seek.

For we cannot hunger for that bread which came down from heaven (John 6:33) unless hunger is given by him to those who are fastidious, since he deigns to give himself to satisfy the hungry. It is also from him that we run thirsty to the fountain, for he gives himself to us so that we may drink.

He, therefore, is to be praised for the grace of both gifts [Note: Thuan manuscript: *munere gratiae*, “gift of grace”]: whether when he awakens us, sleeping, to seek him, or when he grants himself to us who seek him so that we may find him. For he is in no way found unless he himself awakens us to seek him.

### CHAPTER II  
### On the same subject

[Cols. 0153D–0154B]

Turning over your writings, as though they were my own accounts, so that I might learn how many questions, and of what kinds, I owed you, I was able at present to find two letters.

One contained words of Saint Augustine, which he is known to have included in his book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness* concerning those predestined to destruction, among other matters. Immediately following it I seemed to find another question, namely, concerning the sacrifice which some think is offered to the Father alone.

In the other letter I found the following inquiry: What is meant by the Apostle’s having been able to spend more than the two denarii he received?

When, therefore, I found only these two letters, I immediately remembered a third, which had not been given to me by the notary. I remember that it contained a question concerning the Holy Spirit: namely, why the Holy Spirit, who is to be sent by the Father to consecrate the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood, is asked to come.

For the present, these are the four questions: three of them I recalled from your two letters, and one was supplied by memory.

[Note: The manuscript of Thuan reads “perhaps.” Alternatively: “if there are other questions that you sent us to solve and you do not find them either placed or solved in this work…”]

If there are perhaps other questions which you sent us to solve, and you do not find them either included or answered in this work, I ask you not to attribute this to contempt or weariness, but patiently to forgive forgetfulness—especially since I could not pass over in silence the question concerning the Holy Spirit, which I recalled even though the letter itself had not been found.

But since you undoubtedly remember all the questions, if there are any others, do not hesitate, when you write back, to remind me of them. I hope that, insofar as the Lord assists, my answer will follow, if it is supported by the help of your preceding prayer.

### CHAPTER III  
### The first question concerning predestination. Monimus’s words about double predestination
[Col. 0154C] In seeking, therefore, to understand the first question—in the name of him of whom it is written, “The Lord gives wisdom, and from his face come knowledge and understanding” (Prov. II, 6)—I have thought it more suitable and advantageous to reread both your words and those of blessed Augustine, which you included in your letter, so that, after rereading them, both the intention and the solution of the question might more easily be recognized.

“You say that, while reading the book On the Perfection of Human Righteousness, I reread in sequence the prophet’s testimony, and, listening cautiously, reflected upon it little by little, where he says: ‘There is none who does good, not even one’ (Ps. XIII, 3). And the interpreter himself, most truly and without any obscurity or hesitation, expressed that the human race is of such a kind that it does not do good—that is, the race predestined to destruction.”

[Col. 0154D] And so that your argument might be supported by the eloquence of that holy man mentioned above, you append the same words spoken by blessed Augustine (*On the Perfection of Righteousness*, chapter 13):

“For,” you say, “the same most glorious Augustine says: ‘Here we must understand him to have spoken of that good which he says there: “God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there were any who understood or sought God” (Ps. XIII, 2). This good, then, which consists in seeking God, no one did; there was not even one—but among that race of human beings which was predestined to destruction.’”

[Col. 0155A] Having concluded this statement of blessed Augustine and directing the intention of your letter toward me, you say that you understand why I repeat these matters again: namely, because, although you were often resisting me, I maintained that predestination is spoken of not only with respect to good but also with respect to evil. When you said that you had read of predestination with respect to evil, I myself, in teaching you, said that another predestination could be spoken of with respect to the punishment deserved, not with respect to the doing of evil.

[Col. 0155B] You also confirm this, as you have written. Nevertheless, you assert that you know what I answer here in defense of my position: namely, that “destruction” means nothing other than death. You add that, meanwhile, you have read and even affirmed that a people was predestined to destruction. Then you urge me to consider the wording of the passage itself and, as a teacher of my disciples rather than as an advocate of my own propositions, to make you understand what ought to be followed.

## CHAPTER IV. A modest and theological invocation of the author

[Col. 0155C] My dearest friend, insofar as I am able, with the Lord graciously granting me grace, to recognize the measure of my own littleness, I am placed under that one Lord and Teacher, in his school. I do not desire to be called the master or teacher of my brethren, whose fellow student in the truth I always desire to remain.

Therefore I never cease asking that true Lord and our Teacher to deem me worthy to learn from him those things which I may set forth and affirm in such a way that, in my propositions and assertions, I may always cling to the truth—which neither deceives nor is deceived—and may always be found obedient and consenting to it. For, so that I may obey and consent to the truth, the truth itself enlightens, the truth itself helps, and the truth itself strengthens. From it I ask to be taught much more than I do not know, since from it I have received the little that I do know.

[Col. 0155D] I ask it, by a mercy that both precedes and follows, to teach me whatever I do not know but ought to know for salvation; to preserve me in the things I know to be true; to correct me in those matters in which, as a human being, I am mistaken; to strengthen me in those truths about which I waver; and to rescue me from false and harmful things. Thus, in my thoughts and words, may it find what it graciously grants for salvation, and may it cause to proceed from my mouth those things which are above all pleasing to it and which may therefore become acceptable to all the faithful.

## CHAPTER V. Answer to the first question: how some are predestined to destruction. The death of sinners is not predestined by God

[Col. 0156A] Insofar, therefore, as the truth itself—which is the true light—has enlightened my darkness (Ps. XVII, 29), and insofar as I have thus far been granted the ability to understand in investigating this question, I think that nothing else should be understood in that statement of blessed Augustine, in which he firmly declares that some are predestined to destruction, except destruction by punishment, not destruction by wrongdoing; not the evil which they unjustly commit, but the torment which they will most justly suffer; not the sin by which they either do not receive or lose the benefit of the first resurrection, but the torment [Col. 0156B] which their own iniquity wrongly produces for them and divine justice rightly repays; not the first death of the soul, in which infants are born or into which criminals fall when, as blessed James says, they are drawn away and enticed by their own desire (James I, 14), but the second death, which they must suffer when the most just Judge repays them—whether they depart from this world before receiving the grace of baptism, or, having received the grace of God in vain (II Cor. VI, 1) after baptism, prefer to remain slaves of sin until the end of this present life and refuse, while the time is acceptable and the day of salvation, to turn from their evil way and live.

They do not know that God’s kindness leads them to repentance; instead, in accordance with their hardness and impenitent heart, they store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment (Rom. II, 4–5).

It is of that death, then, which sinners summoned upon themselves by their hands and words, and which they flowed toward while imagining it to be their friend, that Scripture says: “Do not zealously pursue death in the error of your life, nor acquire destruction for your souls, because God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living” (Wis. I, 2).

[Col. 0156C] And elsewhere it says of this death: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world; and those who belong to his side imitate him” (Wis. II, 24).

To make us understand that this death is alien to God’s work and predestination, God himself speaks through the prophet in this way: “Turn back, and turn yourselves away from all your ungodliness, and they will not be a punishment to you for iniquity. Cast away from yourselves all your iniquities which you have committed wickedly against me, and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. And why do you die, house of Israel? For I do not desire the death of the one who dies, but [variant: how] that he should turn from his evil way and his soul should live” (Ezek. XVIII, 30).

This is the death of ungodliness, which God did not make, and which entered the world through the devil. Those who belong to his side imitate him in this.

## CHAPTER VI. God repays this death with a double death. The death of the soul in Gehenna

[Col. 0156D] To this one death—which the sinner unjustly summoned upon himself by desiring it in contempt of the divine command—God, in just judgment, has assigned a double death: the first, in the separation of soul and body; the second, in the eternal torment of soul and body.

Accordingly, the first occurs when the soul departs and the flesh alone dies; the second occurs when the soul returns to the flesh and is tormented in that same flesh, and with that flesh, in which it sinned. Thus, with the flesh with which it shared the death of sin—which God’s goodness forbade human beings—it shares the death of punishment, which divine justice prepared for the sinner.

Our Savior speaks of this death: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. X, 28).

[Col. 0157A] Therefore, that the wicked perish before Gehenna is not God’s work but the human being’s. That they will perish in Gehenna is the work of God’s justice, which takes no pleasure in the iniquity of the one who sins. “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X, 6).

John says: “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity; and sin is iniquity” (I John III, 4). And God says through the prophet: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. XVIII, 4).

But concerning the Son of God John says: “We know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and there is no sin in him” (I John III, 5). Therefore, just as sin is not in him, so sin does not come from him. What does not come from him is certainly not his work. And what is never in his work was never in his predestination.

## CHAPTER VII. How the wicked are predestined by God, not to guilt but to punishment. God precedes those who are to be saved and finds those who are to be condemned

The wicked, then, are not predestined by God to that by which they act wickedly, being drawn away and enticed by their own desire, but to that which they unwillingly suffer justly.

For the name “predestination” does not express some coercive necessity imposed upon the human will [Note: [Col. 0157D] Thuanus manuscript codex: “coactive”]; rather, it proclaims the merciful and just eternal disposition of God’s future work.

The Church sings to God of mercy and judgment (Ps. C, 1). His work in the human being is that, by the hidden counsel of his will—which nevertheless is not unjust—he either bestows gratuitous mercy upon the wretched or repays the unjust with the justice that is due.

Indeed, he either mercifully forgives a debtor what he could justly demand if he wished, or justly demands with interest what is his own (Matt. XXV, 27), and repays the wicked debtor what is owed for his iniquities. Thus he either wholly precedes one who is unworthy of mercy, or finds another worthy of wrath.

For he freely grants grace to the unworthy, by which the ungodly person, having been justified, is enlightened with the gift of good will and the capacity for good action. Thus, through mercy that precedes, he begins to will what is good; and through mercy that follows, he is able to do the good that he wills.

God prepared both things through predestination in that immutable will in which he disposed the future renewal of the human being in such a way that the person’s will could not fail to become new in the new work.

## CHAPTER VIII. The grace of God both initiates human merit toward righteousness and brings it to completion in glory. How the will is prepared by the Lord

[Col. 0157D] He also grants grace to one who is worthy in the repayment of eternal reward. Thus, whether the merciful and just one justifies the ungodly, because the Apostle says of him, “so that he himself may be righteous and may justify the one who is of the faith of Jesus” (Rom. II, 26), or whether the pious one justly glorifies the righteous, because “those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII, 3), it is the same operation of grace that both initiates good human merit toward righteousness and brings it to completion in glory.

First it begins a good will in the human being; then it assists that will once begun, so that the same will may be good through divine gift, may be able to overcome evil desire through divine assistance, and, when God brings it to perfection, may eventually become such that it cannot possess evil desire.

Thus in the present life, through the help of grace, it does not yield to weakness; in the future, through the gift of grace, it will not have weakness. Now it is continually restored by the assistance of healing; then it will enjoy the eternal fullness of health.

As God always possessed these things in predestination, so through grace he brings them about as he had predestined them.

The recognition of this predestination is indicated when Scripture says: “And the will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. VIII, 35, according to the Septuagint). It is called “prepared” for no other reason than that it is foretold as something to be given. The one who prepares it through eternal goodness is the one who gives it through unmerited grace.

[Col. 0158A] The Lord himself testifies to this through the prophecy of Ezekiel, saying: “I will give you a new heart, and I will give a new spirit within you; and the heart of stone will be taken away from your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh; and I will give my spirit within you. And I will cause you to walk in my statutes, to observe and perform my judgments” (Ezek. XXXVI, 26).

God therefore gives a new heart so that we may walk in his statutes; this pertains to the beginning of good will. He also gives us the ability to observe and perform his judgments; this pertains to the effect of good action.

## CHAPTER IX. Both the will and the capacity for good action come from God. “In God we shall perform virtue,” that is, the work of virtue. “The one who does the truth comes to the light.” God himself performs every good work in us

From this we know that it is God’s gift both that we wish to do good and that we are able to do good.

David entirely agrees with this understanding, showing that the grace of willing well is given through the direction of divine generosity: “The steps of a person shall be directed by the Lord, and he shall will his way” (Ps. XXXVI, 23).

He also declares that good work is performed in us only by God and by us in God, saying: “Strengthen, O God, what you have worked in us” (Ps. LXVII, 29).

And elsewhere: “In God we shall perform virtue” (Ps. LIX, 14)—that is, the work of virtue.

Here he says that virtue is performed in place of the work of virtue, just as John said that righteousness is performed in place of the work of righteousness. For he says: “The one who does righteousness is righteous, just as he is righteous” (I John III, 7).

Paul likewise desires that we perform the will of God, saying: “The God of peace, who brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, our Lord Jesus, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you with every good thing to do his will” (Heb. XIII, 20).

What is it to do his will except to do the works which his will inspires in us and performs in us?

We find something similar in the words of our Redeemer himself, when he says that the truth is performed, meaning the work of truth. For he speaks as follows: “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his works may not be exposed. But the one who does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, because they have been done in God” (John III, 20).

What we do in God is what God, acting in us, grants us to do. This is clearly shown in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where, after it has been said of God, “May he equip you with every good thing to do his will,” it immediately follows: “Doing in you what is pleasing in his sight” (Heb. XIII, 21).

[Col. 0159A] Every work, therefore, which is done by us in God, God performs in us. “From him and through him and in him are all things” (Rom. XI, 36). Therefore both good will and good action come from him.

The Doctor of the Gentiles affirms this in these words: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good will” (Phil. II, 13).

Therefore, just as Solomon says that “the will is prepared by the Lord,” so Paul also asserts that our good works are prepared by the Lord—that is, disposed in predestination. He says:

“By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God. It is not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them” (Eph. II, 8).

Therefore, just as the will by which we desire good has been prepared by the Lord through predestination, so God has also prepared good works so that we might walk in them.

## CHAPTER X. Through predestination God prepares not only the will but also the good work and eternal life

Let us also consider eternal life and the kingdom of heaven, prepared by God for the faithful through faith [Note: [Col. 0159] In printed codices, “faith for the faithful,” but the Thuanus manuscript lacks “faith”].

Christ himself shows that he will say to those on his right: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34).

This too is the work of grace. For by grace not only a good life is given to those who have been justified, but eternal life also is given to those who have been glorified.

We know this from Paul’s preaching, where he says: “The wages of sin is death. But the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. VI, 23).

Why is death called a wage, but eternal life grace, except because the former is repaid while the latter is given?

But when God repays death, he punishes the sinner’s evil work, which the human being would never have committed had he not departed from God. When God gives eternal life, however, he completes his own work: he began it by justifying the ungodly and completes it by glorifying the righteous.

Both these graces—that is, both good life and eternal life—are in Christ Jesus our Lord. “From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace” (John I, 16): namely, the grace of eternal glorification in exchange for the grace of unmerited justification.

Thus the grace of justification, through an unmerited benefit, removes every evil merit and continually confirms good merit through constant assistance, so that the grace of glorification may be justly repaid to it as a reward.

[Col. 0159D] Grace itself is not unjustly called grace because God repays his gifts with his gifts, but because even there the grace of divine recompense so abounds that it incomparably and ineffably surpasses every merit, however good, of the human will and action—although that will and action are themselves given by God.

For the blessed Apostle Paul shows that not only the light of believing in Christ but also the strength to suffer for him are given to us by God, saying: “To you it has been granted for Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. I, 29). Both belong to the grace of the present good life.

Nevertheless, he places the grace of the future life above all the sufferings of the present time, saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

And elsewhere: “This momentary and light burden of our tribulation is producing for us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory in sublimity” (II Cor. IV, 17).

## CHAPTER XI. Grace begins the good work by preceding it and preserves it by following it. All grace of calling, justification, and glorification is contained in predestination

He says that this grace remains not only in the justification of the present life but also in the recompense of the future age, and that it abounds above us—that is, above all the merits of every human being—in God’s goodness. He says: “So that in the ages to come he might show the abundant riches of his grace, in goodness toward us in Christ Jesus” (Eph. II, 7).

Grace, then, is the pious recompense by which God in the present time repays evil people with good: namely, those whom he justifies as ungodly, so that faith may be reckoned as righteousness. David speaks of this recompense: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?” (Ps. CXV, 12).

There is also that just recompense by which God, repaying his good people with better things, will glorify the righteous. This too will be the work of grace. For, so that they may merit this, grace itself mercifully begins by preceding them and preserves them by following them.

This grace is also called “mercy” in Scripture. David says of it: “My God, his mercy will precede me” (Ps. LVIII, 11). And elsewhere: “Your mercy follows me through all the days of my life” (Ps. XXII, 6).

It therefore precedes the ungodly so that he may become righteous; it follows the righteous so that he may not become ungodly. It precedes the blind so that it may give him the light he does not find; it follows the seeing so that it may preserve the light it has bestowed. It precedes the fallen so that he may rise; it follows the one who has been raised so that he may not fall.

It precedes by giving a person good will; it follows the one who wills well by working in him the capacity for good action. Thus God’s mercy follows in a human being what it itself gives by preceding him.

Therefore it not only calls back the one who has gone astray to the way by justifying him, but also guards and helps the one who walks well, so that it may lead him to the gift of eternal glorification.

[Col. 0160D] God has always possessed all these things in predestination: both the beginnings of our calling, the growth of justification, and the rewards of glorification. For in the calling, justification, and glorification of the saints, he foreknew the future works of his grace.

For this reason the Apostle ascribes everything to God, saying: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII, 29).

Nevertheless, when we hear that those who have been justified have also been glorified, we must not assign the work of justification and glorification alike to the present time. The grace of justification is given in the present; the grace of glorification is reserved for the future.

The one belongs to faith, the other to hope [variant: sight]. Paul says: “For now we walk by faith, not by sight” (II Cor. V, 7). What the saints now believe, they will then see.

For this reason it is said to the Church: “Hear, daughter, and see.” Faith comes from hearing; hence the righteous person, living by faith, confidently says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI, 13).

This, then, is the order of divine redemption and recompense in the human being: the one who is justified now believes what he will receive when glorified.

For this reason Paul says: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect” (Phil. III, 12).

## CHAPTER XII. God is said to have done what he predestined to be done. God’s promises are certain because of his omnipotence

In this justification, therefore, the saints go on their way weeping as they go and sowing their seed; in that glorification, those who come will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves.

In this life the workers of the master of the household labor in the vineyard; in that life they will undoubtedly possess the denarius as their reward.

God now grants the former, so that the unworthy may freely receive the beginning of good merit; but he keeps the latter reserved for the future, so that the one who received the beginning of good merit while unworthy may become worthy to receive the reward of good merit.

When Paul says, “Those whom God justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII, 30), he does not assign both to the present life. Rather, by the faith through which what is future is established as though it were already accomplished, he confirms it in the same way in which the prophet speaks of God: “He who made the things that are to be.”

For in the immutability of his counsel, according to his good pleasure [variant: benevolent purpose], which he set forth in him, “in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, both those in heaven and those on earth” (Eph. I, 9–10), he has already accomplished in the eternity of his disposition, in predestination, whatever he determined to accomplish at the appropriate time through the effect of his work.

Just as every work of the Creator could not and cannot be made without a beginning, so his eternal will is never subject to change, because it has no beginning of existence. Whatever always is, without having begun to be, is certainly such that what is cannot become nothing.

True immutability is therefore rightly called true eternity. In that eternity, the Creator is said already to have done, in the immutability of his will, what he has duly disposed to do in mutable creation at the time he has fittingly appointed.

Therefore we say that whatever he has promised is already accomplished, because we must not doubt what is to be done.

For Abraham our father, as the Apostle says, did not waver in distrust of God’s promise, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, fully convinced that whatever he had promised, he was also able to do (Rom. IV, 20).

There is therefore no falsehood in God’s promises, because for the Almighty there is no difficulty in doing what he is to do. For this reason the effect of his will is never absent, because his will itself is found to be power.

Whatever he wills, he can do; as much as he wills, so much he can do. Therefore it is rightly said of him alone: “He has done whatever he willed” (Ps. CXIII, 11). And again: “Power is yours whenever you will” (Wis. XII, 18).

For this reason we said that the power of the will is as great there as the will itself is powerful: because, since the ability to act is always at his disposal whenever he wills, in him willing and being able are one and the same.

## CHAPTER XIII. God’s just predestination to punishment for sins. God gives grace to the saints and justice to the ungodly. God’s future wrath is condemnation to punishment

[Col. 0162A] Since God is compelled by no necessity to promise anything unwillingly, he is certainly hindered by no obstacle of adversity from doing what he has promised either less fully or more slowly than he wills.

Accordingly, he could, as he wished, predestine some to glory and others to punishment. But those whom he predestined to glory, he predestined to righteousness. Those whom he predestined to punishment, he did not predestine to guilt.

Sin could arise from God’s predestination if any human being could justly sin. No human being, however, sins justly, although God justly permits him to sin.

The one who abandons God is justly abandoned by God. And because the human being sins by abandoning God, God, while abandoning the sinner, preserves justice.

What could be more just than that the one who already sins through the desire to sin, and who by desiring to sin makes himself harmful, should be permitted to injure himself through his own sin?

God therefore crowns in the saints the righteousness which he himself freely grants, freely preserves, and freely perfects. But he will condemn the wicked for the ungodliness or injustice which he himself did not produce in them.

In the former he glorifies his own works; in the latter he condemns works that are not his own.

God therefore predestined what he himself was going to do or grant. He did not in any way predestine what he himself was not going to do, whether through grace or through justice.

Accordingly, it seems necessary to inquire most carefully what God works in those whom he freely justifies and what he works in those whom he justly condemns.

The distinguished Doctor of the Gentiles says: “But if our iniquity commends the justice of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust when he inflicts wrath? I speak according to human understanding: certainly not” (Rom. III, 5).

Here he uses “wrath” for condemnation, just as John the Baptist says elsewhere: “The one who does not believe in the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John III, 36).

He announces this wrath with rebuke to the Pharisees and Sadducees, saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. III, 7; Luke III, 7).

The Lord Christ has rescued us from this wrath. Paul confirmed this in truthful preaching when he said to the Thessalonians: “You turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God and to await his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead—Jesus, who rescued us from the coming wrath” (I Thess. I, 9).

Elsewhere he calls this wrath—that is, the punishment prepared for the wicked—“destruction,” saying: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, like labor upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape” (I Thess. V, 3).

## CHAPTER XIV. Whether the works of those who are to be condemned are predestined as the works of the righteous are. The beginning of good will is predestined by God. God causes us to do good

Let us therefore ask whether God should be believed to have predestined the works of the wicked, for which he condemns them, just as he is said to have predestined in the saints what he crowns.

When we seek the cause of the condemnation of the wicked and the glorification of the saints, we do not deny that either group has been predestined—some to punishment, others to glory. But should we believe that, just as the good works for which the righteous will be glorified were divinely predestined, so the evil works for which the unrighteous will be punished eternally were also divinely predestined?

For it is said in the Book of Psalms: “The unrighteous will be punished, and the offspring of the ungodly will perish; but the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord” (Ps. XXXVI, 28).

Our Savior says of both groups: “Then they will go into eternal burning, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. XXV, 46).

In both groups, therefore—that is, in the righteous and the unrighteous—I think that three things must be considered: the beginning of the will, the progress of the work, and the end of recompense.

In these matters, whatever we see to be just and good, let us attribute to the just and good God; but let us recognize as unworthy of God those things in which we find neither goodness nor justice.

Considering the quality of the works, let us believe those works to have been predestined by God which are found worthy and suitable to divine mercy or equity. For “the Lord is merciful and compassionate and just” (Ps. CXI, 4).

First, then, we confess that the beginning of every good will comes from that eternal Trinity, which is the one and only true God, and that it is both predestined and given.

Through gratuitous justification, God grants to the human being the prepared gift which he had prepared to grant in eternal predestination.

I demonstrated this preparation of the will above from the testimony of Holy Scripture, where it is said: “The will is prepared by the Lord.”

The will is therefore prepared by him who mercifully works in us both to will and to accomplish. For the Apostle says: “It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good will” (Phil. II, 13).

God also speaks through the prophet and confirms that he himself does what he grants the faithful to do, according to the oracle already cited above: “I will cause you to walk in my statutes and to observe and perform my judgments” (Ezek. XXXVI, 27).

What is “I will cause you to do” except “every good thing that you do will be my work”?

He therefore causes us to do what we do; when he works in us, every good thing that we do comes to be.

Of him it is said in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “May he equip you with every good thing, doing in you what is pleasing in his sight” (Heb. XIII, 21).

Since God’s grace in the human will and action has thus been demonstrated, who would deny that the glory of future recompense, which will be given to the saints, is also from divine grace?

Whether we believe or act, although faith is ours and the works are ours, the Lord himself says: “Let it be done for you according to your faith.”

Blessed John also proclaims: “This is the victory that conquers the world, our faith” (I John V, 4).

Paul likewise writes: “I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Eph. I, 4).

The Lord himself also testifies to our works, saying: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

Yet, because we do not possess these things as things born from ourselves but as gifts from God, as the Apostle says, “We have not received the spirit of the world but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God” (I Cor. II, 12), and because we cannot possess any of the things he grants us to do unless he himself bestows them upon us, [Col. 0164A] so we cannot do them unless he himself works in us the things he has granted,

## CHAPTER XV. We must not claim any good work as our own. In this life no one is perfect except in hope of future glory. Paul was both perfect and imperfect

For this reason we are in no way permitted—indeed, we are salutarily forbidden—to claim anything as our own, either in our faith or in our work.

The Vessel of Election says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7).

And in the holy Gospel the voice of the Lord’s precursor says: “A human being cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven” (John III, 27).

The Apostle James also declares: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James I, 17).

What gift is more perfect than the future glorification of the saints?

For now the perfection of divine gifts, so to speak, is not yet perfect, since every person who is perfect is still in need of perfection.

The one who said, “Let us all who are perfect have this mind” [variant: “all who are perfected”] (Phil. III, 15), also says: “Not that I have already received it or am already perfect” (ibid., 12).

He was therefore perfect in hope of future glorification, but imperfect under the burden of corruption and mortality. “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX, 15).

He was perfect in expectation of the gift, but imperfect in the weariness of the struggle.

He was perfect because in his mind he served the law of God, but imperfect because in his flesh he served the law of sin.

He was perfect in desiring “to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. I, 23), but imperfect because, as long as he was in the body, he was away from the Lord.

He was perfect because he knew with complete certainty that God is able to do whatever he has promised (Rom. IV, 21), but imperfect because God had not yet done in his saints certain things among all that he had promised.

For this reason all the ancient righteous, “approved by the testimony of faith,” did not receive the promise, since God had provided something better for us, so that they might not be made perfect without us (Heb. XI, 39).

Therefore, just as the earlier saints, approved by the testimony of faith, were not made perfect without the perfection of those who follow them, so the later saints cannot be made perfect without those who came before them.

The perfect gift will therefore be given to all when eternal glorification is bestowed upon the saints.

Then, as the Truth says, “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII, 43).

This perfect gift also comes from the one from whom the beginning of the whole gift comes. It would not be called a gift if this too were not given by grace.

## CHAPTER XVI. God freely accomplishes our salvation. True glory comes from God alone
But there is one God, who freely calls the predestined, justifies those whom he has called, and glorifies those whom he has justified. And just as to justify is nothing other than to make just, so to glorify is nothing other than to make glorious. Therefore, because God both justifies and glorifies his own, just as it is his grace at work when he makes them just, so it will be his grace at work when he makes them glorious. For just as no one can possess true righteousness unless he has been justified, so no one can possess true glory unless he has been glorified.

But from where true glory comes, our Savior showed when he rebuked the Jews, saying: “How can you believe, who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?” (John 5:44). Paul had this same understanding and spoke truly when he said: “But we have the mind of Christ” (1 Cor. 2:16). Just as he knew that true glory comes from God, so he affirmed that true righteousness comes from God, saying: “That I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is from the faith of Christ, the righteousness that is from God through faith” (Phil. 3:9). And although there are exceedingly many proofs showing clearly that not only the grace of good will and good action, but also the glorification itself of the saints, is wholly begun and completed by God, I nevertheless think that even these things which we have set forth are in some measure sufficient.

## CHAPTER XVII. The beginning of every sin is pride. The fall and punishment of Lucifer. The fall of the first human being.

And therefore, so that the sequence of this little book may be properly balanced, we must also consider the will, action, and recompense of the wicked. We must determine whether God, being just, predestined the wicked to do what he will punish as having been done by them; or whether he predestined the unrighteous to punishment justly for this reason: although he knew beforehand that their evil works would occur, he did not himself predestine that they should occur, because he himself did not cause them to occur.

Thus, if the beginning of sin is sought, nothing other than pride is found. For Scripture says: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Sir. 10:15). It then took its beginning when the angel, lifted up against God and cast down by that very exaltation, through desire—which is the root of all evils—wished to usurp what had not been given to him by God. He departed from God and fell; had he remained steadfast, he would not have fallen. But through evil desire, because he desired more outside himself, he became less within himself. Although he was unable to fulfill this desire in action, he nevertheless retained it in his will. Thus he himself became his own punishment, so that evil will would always be a torment to the wicked, like blindness itself to a blind person. The desire to sin would become a torture to the sinner; and he who was rebellious and fugitive, having fled from that undisturbed rest, would henceforth serve disturbance and would justly be abandoned by the good Lord whom he himself had unjustly abandoned.

Thus it happened that, while remaining disordered through himself, he was ordered within himself; and in him who had lost order within himself, the principle of the divine order did not perish. The same thing happened in the human being, whom the devil himself cast down through his serpentine cunning. For by dissenting from the good Lord and consenting to the evil servant, he could not attain the full effect of an evil will, because the evil itself of the will did not come from God. For if he had not departed from God, he would not have possessed it.

## CHAPTER XVIII. A rational creature cannot be blessed unless it loves the Creator more than itself. If a rational will submits itself to God, it is exalted; if it exalts itself, it is brought low. God makes the humble; he does not find them already humble.

[Col. 0166A]

God, then, is the creator of good natures. For “God saw,” as it is written, “everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. 1:31). Among all the things he made, he made the rational creature better than the rest. Yet he willed that a greater good should exist in the more excellent creature, so that no substantial evil should exist even in the lowest creature. Accordingly, the good that was created above the lowest good would be better, and the highest good—which was not created, and from which every mutable created good came—would justly rule over it. By participation in that highest good, the rational creature would be blessed if it served the highest good with humble love.

For the rational creature could not, cannot, and will not be able to have any other blessedness than this: recognizing the one by whom it was not only made but also made rational, it should show greater love to the good Creator than to itself. Nor could reason exist in it in any way unless love of the Creator could exist in it; for there is no other true wisdom or understanding of a rational creature than love of the Creator. In this love, the love of self is greater or lesser according as the creature shows greater or lesser love toward its Creator.

The will of a rational creature cannot exist without some kind of love; nor can it love in such a way that it does not wish to bind its love to something. Set midway, as it were, between the highest good, by which it was created, and the lowest good, over which it was placed, it must either lie miserably in the lowest good or rest truly and happily in the highest good. For it is seized by a certain love: either it is raised through obedience and rightly subjected to the good Creator, or it is brought low through pride, so that it wrongly rules over a good creature. For just as one becomes humble through exaltation, so one becomes exalted through humility.

Our Lord and Teacher says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). For this reason it is likewise written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6; 1 Pet. 5:5). Nor does God find the humble to whom he gives grace humble before grace has been given; rather, by giving grace he makes them humble. For God himself grants this through grace:

[Note: [Col. 0165D] The words “through grace” are absent from the manuscript codices.]

whoever receives it becomes humble. Therefore the Only-Begotten himself, the teacher and giver of holy humility, says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:29). Those who rejected humility and swelled up against their own life through pride lost this rest and fell into death. Of such people it was said: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. 72:18).

God therefore resists such people because he himself did not create pride in them. Through it they unjustly prefer to fall into sin, and through it they justly deserve to remain in sin.

[Note: [Col. 0166D] Another reading is *remain*; this is found in the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XIX. Destruction does not come from God but from pride. God is the avenger, not the author, of sin.

Therefore, since the beginning of the evil will is pride, which does not come from God, it is plainly evident that the destruction resulting from evil action does not come from God to human beings, but that destruction as vengeance is repaid to the wicked by the just Judge. An evil will does not belong to the supremely good Creator; but the just condemnation of the unjust angel and human being belongs to the supremely equitable Judge.

[Note: [Col. 0167] The words “of the unjust angel and human being” are absent from the Codex Thuaneus and from Victorinus; they are read in the Codex Corbeiensis.]

God therefore did not predestine the human being to an evil will, because he himself was not going to give it to the human being. For how could God predestine to an evil will the human being whom he made in his own image, when he himself did not create that evil will? Thus the human being began to sin at the point where he departed from God. For it is written: “The beginning of pride is apostasy from God” (Sir. 10:14). And elsewhere: “Behold, all who distance themselves from you will perish; you have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you” (Ps. 72:27).

Those, then, who distance themselves from God and commit fornication away from him perish through sinning, by their own evil will, which does not come from God. God, however, will destroy them by judging justly; this is fitting for God. For God would not destroy them by judgment unless they themselves had perished through their iniquities. For it is written: “They failed and perished because of their iniquity” (ibid.).

The falling away from the highest good to the lowest good is therefore the sinner’s own voluntary evil, by which the unrighteous person destroys himself. And because God is not the author of this evil, but the perverse human being is, eternal destruction is rightly repaid in torments to the human being who destroyed himself through sin: he should indeed perish because he wished to perish, but he should not perish in the manner he wished.

For one who perished in this way, enticed by the pleasure of sins, so that, if it could be, he might remain perpetually in the practice of sin, was rightly abandoned to the destruction of sin, into which he fell by his own will. Yet he was not to be abandoned there with impunity, lest God, who is faithful and in whom there is no iniquity, who is just and holy, should seem to approve sin if he always left the sinner unpunished.

God rebukes this opinion in certain people through the prophet Malachi, who say: “Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and he is pleased with such a person; and where is the God of justice?” (Mal. 2:17). The severity of the Judge therefore rightly followed where the sinner’s iniquity had gone before, because God is the avenger of that whose author he is not—namely, iniquity, which God can punish but cannot create.

For it is written: “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity; and sin is iniquity. And you know that he appeared to take away sins, and sin is not in him. Everyone who remains in him does not sin” (1 John 3:4–6). And again: “God is faithful, in whom there is no iniquity; the Lord is just and holy” (Deut. 32:4). Since iniquity is not in God, it certainly does not come from God.

## CHAPTER XX. Iniquity comes from disordered love of the world. The beginning of sin is disordered affection.

What, then, is iniquity except evil desire? The Apostle John makes clear that it does not come from God, saying: “If anyone loves the world, the charity of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world” (1 John 2:15–16).

Here, however, by the name “world” he means human beings who love this world. They are not to be punished for loving the world because they love some evil substance—for no substance is naturally evil—but because, failing to preserve the order of love, they love the world more than is right and love God less than they ought to love him.

God did not make anything disordered, nor did he predestine anything disordered to come into being; through his Apostle he commands that everything be done honorably and according to order (1 Cor. 14:40). For this reason, in the sacred writings, charity is commanded to be ordered so that sin may be avoided. For it is written: “He ordered charity within me” (Song 2:4). The Apostle rejoices in this order when he says: “For although I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order” (Col. 2:5).

If the beginning of sin is considered, I think that it is nothing other than the rational creature’s disordered love of things ordered by God. By voluntarily destroying the order of love, it also destroyed salvation. The rational creature was not predestined to this. For its predestination is nothing other than the eternal preparation of its future works, and in this no cause of evil can be found, because the origin of sin never proceeded from God’s will.

## CHAPTER XXI. God does not predestine the human being to sin. The predestination of the good comes from God’s gratuitous mercy.

17 For the Lord is merciful and just, of whom it is written elsewhere: “The Lord God loves mercy and truth” (Ps. 83:12). In all his works, therefore, either just truth is preserved or merciful compassion is granted.

Now, we cannot deny that the good human being was made by the good God. If we were to say that he was predestined by God to some evil work, we would be attributing to the merciful and just God such a work—which God forbid—in which neither mercy nor justice could be found. For if, when the human being was being made by God, he was good in God’s present work but evil in God’s predestination, then without doubt he would be destined to become evil through the work of God, by whom he was predestined to sin.

At once there would follow the absurdity that God—of whom the prophet says, “He made the things that will be” (Isa. 9)—would have possessed within himself, God forbid, the origin of iniquity, if he himself had predestined the human being made by him to be a sinner. For his predestination is the preparation of his works. And just as it is fitting for the good God to be the cause of every good work, so it is unfitting to attribute to him the cause of any evil work.

Let us further observe that no reason is given by which it may be believed that the human being was predestined by God to sin. For if, among those whom God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ blessed with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ—just as he chose them in him before the foundation of the world, that they should be holy and blameless before him in love, having predestined them for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ in him (Eph. 1:4–5)—if, then, the cause of predestination is sought in these people, no other cause is found except God’s gratuitous mercy.

He is the one of whom the psalm says: “The Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy. He will not always be angry, nor will he be indignant forever. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities. For as high as heaven is above the earth, so far has he removed our iniquities from us. As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him” (Ps. 102:8–13).

In all these and so many other good things that the Lord grants to the wicked, what else is sung but undeserved mercy? What else is proclaimed but gratuitous kindness? For in the fact that “he has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities,” the gratuitous justification of the ungodly is made manifest. And in the fact that “as a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him,” adoption as sons through the same justification by faith is clearly gratuitous. For the Father would not have compassion on us as on children unless, having become our Father by grace, he deigned to make us his children. “As many as received him, he gave them power to become the sons of God” (John 1:12).

## CHAPTER XXII. No one is predestined to commit sins.

This, then, is the cause of divine predestination in the saints: namely, the preparation of undeserved justification and adoption. Since the evil will of the human being did not deserve this, it has no cause except God’s good will.

But in those who are thought to have been predestined not to suffer punishments but to commit sins, when the cause of predestination is sought, I do not find what anyone who considers asserting this could answer. For just as we rightly say that the saints were predestined for this purpose: that, with God mercifully working in them, they should become good from evil and just from ungodly, so—when we say this to the glory of God—could we rightly say that the unrighteous were predestined for this purpose: that, with God working in them, if not mercifully, at least justly, they should become evil from good or ungodly from just?

Far be this from us and from all Christians: that anyone should dare to assign the cause of any sin to divine equity, since the cause of any malice or ungodliness can exist nowhere except in the one who is evil and ungodly. Therefore, for human beings to become good from evil and just from ungodly, God’s mercy is to be praised. But if human beings are said to become evil from good or unrighteous from just because of divine predestination, then justice would have to be blamed—which God forbid.

Indeed, justice would not even be called just if it were said that it had not found the guilty person to punish but had made him guilty. The injustice would be greater still if God were said to repay the fallen with punishment after having predestined him to fall while standing.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The evil will of the human being is not God’s planting. The gracious and good Lord did not create the bitterness and malice of a perverse will. God foreknew that human beings would sin, but did not predestine them to sin.

I ask, then, how God could have predestined the first human being, whom—as it is written—the Lord made upright (Eccles. 7:30), to sin, that is, to the evil will which is the origin of all sin. This evil will God must either be believed to have given to the human being before he sinned, or to have repaid to him after he sinned.

If he gave it to the human being before he sinned, then he himself, God forbid, became the author of iniquity, giving an evil will to a good human being, through which the sinner deserved to be punished with eternal punishment. And where then is the statement that “God did not make death” (Wis. 1:13)? And that “there is no iniquity with God”? And that “the just Lord loved justice; his countenance saw equity” (Ps. 10:8)?

But if God did not give the beginning of the evil will to the sinful human being, but repaid it to him, so that sin is believed to have begun from the human being while the beginning of the evil will is said to have been returned by God, what sin could the human being have committed in whom there was no evil will? For no fruit of iniquity can arise except that which the root of an evil will has produced.

“For from the heart,” as the Truth says, “come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies. These are the things that defile a human being” (Matt. 15:19). For this reason God himself rebukes the evil of the human will through Jeremiah in such a way as to show decisively that it is alien to him. He says: “I planted you as a fruitful vine; how have you been turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jer. 2:21).

He calls the vine foreign to himself, not because of any defect in the divine creation, but because of the turning away of its own will. That will is rightly blamed because it produced the bitterness which God himself did not create in it. For it possessed that bitterness neither from God’s predestination nor from God’s work, but from the malice of its own will.

For this bitterness God again rebukes it through the prophet mentioned above: “Know how evil and bitter it is for you to have abandoned the Lord your God and not to have my fear within you” (ibid., 19). Since it is evil and bitter for the human being to abandon the Lord and not to have the fear of God within him, who could be so opposed to the truth as to think that a human being was predestined by the good and gracious God to the malice of the will by which he would abandon the good God, or to the bitterness of defiance by which he would not fear the gracious Lord?

Of this good and gracious God it is written: “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart” (Ps. 72:1). And: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:18). The Apostle says of him: “That in the ages to come he might show the abundant riches of his grace in goodness toward us” (Eph. 2:7). Of his graciousness it is sung: “Taste and see how gracious the Lord is” (Ps. 33:9). And of his words it is again proclaimed: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 118:103). Again: “The judgments of God are true, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and a precious stone in great abundance, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. 18:11).

Who, then, could think that the good and gracious God predestined the human being either to the malice of the will by which he would abandon the good God, or to the bitterness of defiance by which he would not fear the gracious Lord?

It therefore befits the faithful to believe and confess that the good and just God indeed foreknew that human beings would sin, because nothing future could be hidden from him—for things would not even be future if they had not been present to his foreknowledge—but that he did not predestine any human being to sin. For if God predestined a human being to some sin, he would not punish the human being for sins.

By God’s predestination, either the merciful remission of sins or the just punishment of sins has been prepared. God therefore could never predestine the human being to do what he himself had determined both to prohibit by commandment, to wash away by mercy, and to punish by justice.

Thus God, who foresaw that the unrighteous would end this life in sin, predestined them to be punished with unending punishment. Just as the foreknowledge of human iniquity is not to be blamed, so the predestination of the most just vengeance is to be praised, so that it may be recognized that the human being was not predestined by God to any sin whatsoever, while he was predestined to be punished on account of the merit of sin.

## CHAPTER XXIV. God mercifully predestined the good to glory and justly predestined the wicked to punishment. God did not promise everything he foretold, nor predestine everything he foreknew.

[Col. 0171B]

God therefore foreknew all human works, whether good or evil, because nothing could be hidden from him. But he predestined only the good works which he foreknew he would accomplish in the children of grace. As for the evil works that would belong to those whom he did not predestine to the kingdom but foreknew would be destined to destruction, he ordered them through his almighty divinity and provident goodness.

Since he foreknew that these same evil works would not only not be done by him, but also would not be done by human beings insofar as they adhered humbly to him, he showed us even more clearly the unconquerable power of his foreknowledge, because he did not permit the predestination of his justice to be absent even in the case of evil.

Therefore, intending to show what he foreknew would be repaid and what would be given, God predestined to punishment those whom he foreknew would depart from him through the fault of an evil will. And he predestined to the kingdom those whom he foreknew would return to him through the help of prevenient mercy and would remain in him through the help of subsequent mercy.

In the latter he preserves mercy; in the former he maintains justice. To the latter he piously gives what he promised; to the former he justly repays what he nevertheless foretold.

God therefore did not promise everything he foretold, although he foretold everything he promised. Likewise, he did not predestine everything he foreknew, although he foreknew everything that was predestined. For he foreknew the good and evil wills of human beings, but he did not predestine the evil wills, only the good.

And although it was not part of his predestination that he should give malice to the human will, it was part of his predestination what he would repay to the malice of the human will. Therefore, because—as the Psalmist testifies—“the Lord is merciful and just” (Ps. 114:5), he predestined the just to glory and the unrighteous to punishment.

He both foretold and promised the work of his mercy predestined for those who would be justified and glorified. To the unrighteous, however, he merely foretold the work of his justice predestined for them; he did not promise it.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the same subject.

If someone asks why God foretold everything that was predestined, but did not promise everything that was predestined, we answer that something cannot be called a promise unless something is foretold as going to be done for the purpose that, once accomplished, it may benefit the one to whom it is promised.

A promise always concerns a gift, but does not always concern judgment, since the generosity of a promise always brings joy, whereas the severity of judgment sometimes brings sorrow. Fearing this, the prophet pours out this prayer to God: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2).

For he knew that all would be held under the same bond of punishment unless God, in those on whom he wished to bestow mercy, made judgment triumph through mercy (James 2:13). Justification [another reading: “judgment”] and glorification, therefore, which do not come to the human being from the human being but from God, were foretold and promised because they would greatly benefit the saints. Punishment, however, which would harm the ungodly eternally, was merely foretold, not promised.

This is also more easily shown by divine testimonies. In that passage of the prophet both matters are expressed together, where through Isaiah God rebukes those who do not serve him in these words: “Behold, those who serve me shall eat, but you shall hunger. Behold, those who serve me shall drink, but you shall thirst. Behold, those who serve me shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame. Behold, those who serve me shall exult in gladness, but you shall cry out because of the sorrow [another reading: “from the sorrow”] of your heart, and howl because of the contrition of your spirit” (Isa. 65:13–14).

In all these statements, whatever pertains to the persons of the unrighteous was merely foretold, not promised. For it cannot be said to have been promised through the generosity of goodness when severity threatens to inflict something because of the merit of iniquity. Whatever pertains to the persons of those serving God was both foretold and promised.

Something similar is found in that saying of our Savior in which he says: “Then they will go into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46). He foretold and promised the reward in which the righteous will rejoice; but he did not promise the punishment by which the unrighteous will be punished—he merely foretold it.

Nor, just as he predestined the saints to receive righteousness, did he predestine the unrighteous to lose that same righteousness. For the merciful and just Lord could freely liberate from depravity whomever he wished; but he was never the author of depravity, because no one was ever depraved except insofar as he departed from God. Nor did God predestine him to depart, although divine knowledge foreknew that he would depart.

## CHAPTER XXVI. God works good from the evil deeds of the ungodly. God predestined the good differently from the wicked. The wicked are called vessels of wrath; the good, vessels of mercy. Why the Apostle calls the good vessels of mercy rather than vessels of justice.

[Col. 0172D]

Therefore, although God is not the author of evil thoughts, he is nevertheless the disposer of evil wills, and from the evil deed of every evil person he never ceases himself to work good. Nor does he abandon the just order of his works even in the deeds of an unjust will, since this too belongs to that order: that he justly abandons an evil will. Yet he abandons it, as it departs from him in its evil deeds, in such a way that the good activity of God who permits it is not absent there: while he himself fulfills justice even in the unjust will of the sinner, and from the evil by which he judges the sinner confers a benefit on those whom he wills.

In the saints, therefore, the Lord will bring to completion what he freely gave in order that they might be good. What he foreknew that he would give, he predestined in the eternal disposition of his goodness. [Col. 0173A] For the predestination of God is precisely the everlasting disposition of God’s future work. But in the unrighteous he will punish what he did not give in order that they might be evil; nor did he predestine them to any iniquity, because he himself was not going to give them that they should will wickedly. And because the persistent iniquity of an evil will ought not to remain unpunished, he predestined such persons to destruction, because he prepared for such persons the punishment of just chastisement.

The Lord himself plainly taught this in saying that there was prepared by him not only a kingdom in which the good may rejoice, but also eternal fire in which the wicked may be tormented. For to the good he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34); but to the wicked he will say: “Go, accursed, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 46).

Behold to what the Lord predestined the unrighteous and ungodly: namely, to just punishment, not to any unjust work; to penalty, not to guilt; to punishment, not to transgression; to the destruction which the wrath of the just Judge repaid to sinners, not to the destruction by which the iniquity of sinners provoked God’s wrath against itself. This is made clear by the preaching of the blessed Apostle, who calls the wicked whom God will condemn eternally vessels of wrath, not of guilt. For he says: “But if God, wishing to show wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order that he might show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory” (Rom. 9:22).

I ask you, dearest Monimus, to consider this passage of the Apostle carefully. For it is evident that God’s wrath cannot be spoken of except where it is believed that human iniquity has preceded it.
