God could neither be ignorant nor unjust, so as either not to recognize the guilt of the sinful human being or to inflict a punitive judgment upon one who had not sinned. For the blessed Paul himself proclaims that God’s justice is commended in human iniquity, in order to show that the wrath of the Almighty is not inflicted unjustly. For he says: “But if our iniquity commends the justice of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust who inflicts wrath? (I speak according to man.) Far be it; otherwise, how will God judge the world?” (Rom. 3:5).

Therefore it was not without reason that he made such a distinction between those to be punished and those to be glorified, calling the former vessels of wrath and the latter vessels of mercy, in order to show that, both in vessels of wrath and in vessels of mercy, their own iniquity had preceded. For such is the true Lord, whose mercy is gratuitous and whose wrath is not unjust. Accordingly, he anticipates with goodness those whom he justifies, though unworthy, and finds worthy of punishment those whom he condemns; and thus it appears both that in vessels of mercy it is not from themselves but from God that they are good, and that in vessels of wrath it is not from God but from themselves that they are evil.

[Col. 0173D] The Apostle could have called those whom he called vessels of mercy instead vessels of justice; but if they were called vessels of justice, perhaps they would be thought to possess justice from themselves. But now, when he calls them vessels of mercy, he undoubtedly does not leave unspoken what they themselves had been, since he clearly shows what was bestowed upon them by God. For if they had been just through themselves, the Lord would render them a reward for their works rather than grant mercy to them; as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “To the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace, but according to debt” (Rom. 4:4).

Therefore vessels of mercy have been prepared for undeserved glory because they have obtained mercy freely. The blessed Apostle himself testifies that he is among them, saying: “I who was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man, nevertheless obtained mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Tim. 1:13). This is God’s work in vessels of mercy: that to blasphemers, persecutors, and insolent persons, the destruction that was due was not repaid, but the free gift of mercy was granted.

But God would never repay destruction to vessels of wrath unless a human being were found to have sin voluntarily, for God would not justly inflict wrath upon a sinful human being if that human being had fallen into guilt through God’s predestination. But because a human being derived the cause of his iniquity from his own will, blessed Paul therefore declares that God endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction. Thus this wrath repaid destruction to such vessels because it found in them the desert of voluntary iniquity. When, indeed, would the just Lord have inflicted wrath upon a sinful servant, if the servant had sinned through the Lord’s predestination?

Therefore God fitted these vessels for that to which he predestined them, namely destruction: that destruction, of course, which Paul announces will suddenly come upon the wicked, saying: “For when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thess. 5:3). If God predestined such persons to sin, the Apostle would not have preferred to call them vessels of wrath but vessels of guilt, nor would such vessels be said to have been fitted for destruction but for sin. But now they are called vessels of wrath in order to show that, in such persons, what they committed wickedly is not from God’s predestination, but what is rightly repaid to such persons is.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How justly God abandons the wicked and repays them destruction. The unrighteous are predestined to the lake of fire and sulphur. The first death of the soul is in sin; the second is in the lake of fire. The Lord does not know the ways of the ungodly because he did not make them. The first death of the soul comes from the human being; the second is inflicted by God. God predestined sins not to be committed, but to be justly punished.

For to the wicked, destruction is rightly imposed by God, although it is a wicked destruction for those who are now justly abandoned and will afterward be justly tormented. For in such people God begins his judgment with abandonment and completes it with punishment. Indeed, even at the present time, when God abandons the wicked as they depart from him, he does not work in them what displeases him; rather, through them he works what pleases him, intending afterward to repay them what they deserve from his justice. For they will receive recompense not because God made good use of their evil deeds, but because they themselves made evil use of God’s good works.

Thus God fitted such people for the destruction of punishment, which the just Judge, by a just predestination, decreed for the sinner. He did not fit them for the sin that a human being began—not by divine predestination, but by his own will—through evil desire, and completed through evil action: “For desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it has been completed, gives birth to death” (James 1:15). Therefore the wicked were not predestined to the soul’s first death; they were predestined to the second, that is, to the lake of fire and sulfur.

Concerning this the blessed John says: “And the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur” (Revelation 20:9). And elsewhere: “And death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death. And whoever was not found written in the book of life was thrown into the lake of fire” (ibid., 14). Again he says: “But the cowardly, the unbelieving, the polluted, murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars—their portion is in the lake burning with fire and sulfur, which is the second death” (Revelation 21:8).

He calls that death “the second” which follows from the sentence of the just Judge, not the death that preceded it in the sinner’s evil desire. Of that death the Savior declared certain people dead, saying: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matthew 8:22). And concerning the widow the Apostle says: “But she who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Timothy 5:6). He also says to the Ephesians:

“And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the power of the air, the spirit that now works in the sons of unbelief, among whom we all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of our thoughts. And we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest. But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ” (Ephesians 2:1).

Of this death, by which a human being is dead in sins, God says: “I do not desire the death of the one who dies, but that he turn back from his evil way and that his soul may live” (Ezekiel 18:32). How, then, can God be believed to have predestined a human being to the death of sin, when he himself declares that he does not desire it?

This death, therefore, is the evil way of the one who dies; and because it is evil, it is unknown to God. For it is written: “The ways that are on the right the Lord knows, but the crooked ways are those on the left” (Proverbs 4:27). Therefore he knows the ways that God made; those he did not make he causes to perish, because he does not know them. Hence it is written: “The Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish” (Psalm 1:6).

He, then, who knows all things before they happen, whose eyes observe the good and the wicked in every place, and whose face is against those who do evil, “to destroy their memory from the earth” (Psalm 33:17)—he does not know the evil way, not because anything in human actions escapes his knowledge, but because he did not make the death of the one who dies. Yet he justly repays the dead person with death.

The soul’s first death, then, which the human being inflicted upon himself, is the cause of the second death; and the second death, which God repaid to the human being, is the punishment of the first death. And because the unjust person unjustly inflicted the first upon himself, he justly received the second from the just Judge: so that, because in the first death the heedless sinner willingly sows the seed of iniquity, in the second he unwillingly reaps the fruit of punishment.

“For whoever sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but whoever sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Galatians 6:8). But whoever sows in the Spirit and reaps eternal life from the Spirit has from God the gift both of the harvest and of the seed. We know this from Paul’s testimony, for he says:

“He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will also supply and multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness” (2 Corinthians 9:10).

But whoever sows in the flesh and reaps corruption from the flesh will not rejoice in the harvest, because in the seed he had himself, not God, as its author.

God, therefore, certainly foresaw in sinners all the sins of human beings as future; and because he himself did not predestine them to be committed, he justly predestined them to be punished in judgment. If you consider this also in the very words of Saint Augustine that you inserted into your letter, you will surely recognize it. After he had said:

“This good, then, which is to seek God, there was no one who did it, there was not even one” (Psalm 52:4),

he immediately continued, speaking of that class which has been predestined to destruction:

“Over this, therefore, the foreknowledge of God looked and pronounced sentence.”

By these words he plainly and sufficiently showed that God saw, through his foreknowledge, the sins of human beings, and by predestination decreed sentence against them. For what else should we understand by this pronouncement of God’s sentence than punishment prepared for the sinner?

He who is a sinner, having been foreknown by divine knowledge, is justly predestined to punishment by divine equity—for he was going to commit by his own will the iniquity to which he was not predestined by God. Thus, where God’s foreknowledge saw that an unjust deed would occur, there, by the sentence of predestination, it prepared a just punishment.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. It Is Confirmed from Saint Augustine That the Cause of No Human Sin Is to Be Referred to God

Although you yourself, and others like you, through your eagerness to read or your quickness of understanding, can very easily recognize from this passage of Saint Augustine’s statements, which you placed in your letter, what the Catholic understanding is concerning those whom we hear to have been predestined to destruction, nevertheless, lest those who are slower should think that this single passage is insufficient for them in this question, I have also inserted certain passages from other books of Saint Augustine. In them he taught that the sole cause of human iniquity is pride, and that human beings were predestined by God not to sin but to condemnation; and that the reason they are not helped by God lies in themselves, not in God.

Thus, in the second book of *On the Baptism of Infants*, writing to Marcellinus, he says among other things (chapter 17):

“Ignorance and weakness, then, are vices that impede the will, so that it is not moved to do a good work or to abstain from an evil work. But for what was hidden to become known, and for what did not please to become pleasing, this is the work of God’s grace, which helps human wills; and the reason why they are not helped likewise lies in themselves, not in God—whether they have been predestined to be condemned because of the iniquity of pride, or whether they are to be judged and instructed against that very pride, if they are children of mercy.”

Immediately afterward Saint Augustine added the prophet’s testimony, saying:

“Hence Jeremiah, after he had said, ‘I know, Lord, that a human being’s way is not his own, nor does it belong to a man to walk and direct his steps’ (Jeremiah 10:23), immediately added: ‘Correct me, Lord, nevertheless in judgment, and not in your anger.’ It is as though he were saying: ‘I know that it pertains to my correction that I am helped less by you, so that my steps may be perfectly directed. Nevertheless, for this very reason do not deal with me as though in the anger by which you have determined to condemn the wicked, but as in the judgment by which you teach your own not to be proud.’ Hence elsewhere it is said: ‘Your judgments will help me’ (Psalm 118:175).”

Thus, while instructing the aforementioned Marcellinus with this teaching, Saint Augustine continues and says:

“Therefore do not refer the cause of any human guilt to God; for pride is the cause of all human vices.”

In these words of Saint Augustine, my dearest, observe, I ask you, the following. First, the reason why human beings are not helped by God is said to lie in themselves, not in God. Next, they are said to be predestined to be condemned because of the iniquity of pride; this belongs to judgment, not to being made depraved, which belongs to sin. Third, consider also that he warns us not to refer the cause of any human guilt to God; for if any iniquity of a sinner is believed to have been predestined by God, the cause of that iniquity will be placed—or, alternatively, established—in divine predestination. I think no Christian can fail to see how impious this is and how contrary to the Christian faith.

In another passage of the same book (chapter 19), the aforementioned Saint Augustine says:

“To be lifted up in the pride of one’s own will is the work of human beings, not of God. For God neither compels nor helps them to this.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. Predestination Cannot Exist without God’s Foreknowledge, Although Foreknowledge Can Exist without Predestination. In Sins There Is Not God’s Work but Judgment

And so that our assertion may be supported by a clearer indication from his statements, we must set down something from the book he wrote *On the Predestination of the Saints*. There he shows more clearly that God’s foreknowledge can exist without predestination, but predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge; and that God foresaw even what he himself does not do, namely, sins.

In the aforementioned book, this is the judgment of the same blessed Augustine (Book I, chapter 10):

“Predestination is something that cannot exist without foreknowledge; foreknowledge, however, can exist without predestination. For by predestination God foresaw what he himself was going to do, whence it is said: ‘He made the things that were to be.’ But he can also foresee what he himself does not do, such as all sins. For even if there are certain things that are sins in such a way that they are also punishments of sinners, whence it is said, ‘God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting’ (Romans 1:24), it is not God’s sin in that case, but judgment.”

I think these words of the blessed Augustine plainly show that God foresaw and predestined his good works—that is, both those pertaining to mercy and those pertaining to justice. But evil works, that is, sins, he merely foresaw and did not also predestine, because in that case it is said that there is not God’s work but judgment.

There is not God’s work in sin because he did not predestine sin to occur. It is judgment, however, because what the evil person does without God’s activity is not left unpunished.

## CHAPTER XXX. Prosper’s Response to the Fourteenth Objection; Response to the Fifteenth; Conclusion Concerning Predestination

You are also aware that, in an earlier period, certain Gauls objected to that illustrious work of Saint Augustine which he wrote *On the Predestination of the Saints*: namely, that in asserting divine predestination the blessed Augustine said that sinners were predestined not only to judgment but also to sin. Because Augustine himself was overtaken by a premature death, the learned and holy man Prosper rightly defended his statements with faithful and copious discourse.

Of these chapters of the Gauls, to avoid setting down many at present—for the necessity of disputation already compels this little book to be long, and it would seem excessive for our will to make it still longer—we have decided to insert passages from two responses.

The fourteenth objection of the Gauls runs as follows:

“That those who do not believe the Gospel preaching do not believe by God’s predestination; and that God so determined it that whoever does not believe does not believe by his own decree.”

To this perversity, which was brought against the statements of the blessed Augustine not from truth but from malice, Prosper replied in these words:

“The unbelief of those who do not believe the Gospel is in no way generated by God’s predestination. For God is the author of good things, not of evil things. God’s predestination, therefore, is always directed toward good, whether it pertains to the recompense of justice or to the granting of grace. ‘All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth’ (Psalm 24:10). Therefore the unbelief of those who do not believe must be referred not to God’s decree but to his foreknowledge. This foreknowledge did not thereby impose the necessity of not believing, because it could not be deceived concerning the unbelief that was going to occur.”

The fifteenth objection was also inserted in these words: that foreknowledge and predestination are the same thing. To this Prosper replied:

“He who distinguishes God’s foreknowledge in no respect from his predestination tries to attribute to God concerning evil what must be attributed to him concerning good. But since good things are to be referred to God as their giver and co-worker, while evil things are to be referred to the voluntary wickedness of rational creation, there is no doubt that, without any temporal difference, God both foresaw and predestined those things that were to be done with him as their author, or that were to be repaid to evil merits by a just judgment; but he foresaw alone, and did not also predestine, those things that were not going to have in him the cause of their activity.”

Therefore, my dearest, we preferred to insert these few passages for the time being from the books of Saint Augustine and from Prosper’s responses, so that everyone might know what they ought to think concerning the predestination of the saints and of the wicked, and also so that it might be evident that the tenor of our view agrees with the statements of the same blessed Augustine.

Since, then, as I believe, we have sufficiently shown that the wicked were predestined not to sin but to punishment, we ought now to bring this volume to an end, so that the reader’s zeal may be renewed for a more attentive review of the discussion of the remaining questions by the measured divisions of the books.

# BOOK TWO. CONTAINING THREE QUESTIONS: ONE CONCERNING THE OFFERING OF SACRIFICE, ANOTHER CONCERNING THE MISSION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT, AND A THIRD CONCERNING THE SUPEREROGATION OF THE BLESSED PAUL

[Col. 0179]

## CHAPTER I. A Brief Epilogue Concerning the Predestination of the Righteous and the Wicked

[Col. 0179A]

27 My dearest Monimus, the preceding discussion, insofar as the Lord has deigned to assist our weakness, has, as I believe, both treated and resolved the question concerning the difference between the predestination of the righteous and that of the wicked—that is, between those whom God’s gratuitous mercy, coming beforehand, converts by justifying them and will glorify once converted, and those whom God’s just severity abandons in their sins and will punish once condemned.

Thus most people, although they are accustomed to be seriously disturbed by this question, can readily be instructed by the testimonies of the divine books, and can be taught by the books of Saint Augustine and by the responses of Prosper, that most learned man. From these they may recognize that God’s predestination is nothing other than the preparation of his works: in his eternal disposition, he foresaw that he would carry them out either mercifully or justly.

And because neither mercy nor justice is found in sins, all the wicked will of the wicked, by which they sin, was foreseen but was not therefore predestined by God. They would not have possessed that evil will in any other way than by departing from the Lord. Nor did God predestine the human being’s departure from him, since the sole cause of that departure was the sinner’s voluntary turning away. Because this turning away was not hidden from God as something future, it found prepared for itself in his eternal foreknowledge the punishment of a just recompense.

## CHAPTER II. Monimus’s Second Question Concerning the Sacrifice of Christ’s Body and Blood. Heretics, Blinded by Their Malice, Destroy the Trinity Both in Substance and in the Veneration Due to the Father. The Question Concerning Abraham’s Faith Must Be Set Forth First

[Col. 0179C]

Now, with the Lord as our guide, let the aim of our discussion be directed toward investigating the remaining questions. You say that some people have asked you about the sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood, which most of them think is offered to the Father alone. You also assert that this is, as it were, the principal question of the heretics.

But it is not surprising that heretics, deprived of the light of truth, should think that they can overcome the truth by propositions through which they are very easily overcome: “For their glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things” (Philippians 3:19). Following this course, the heretics regard as apparently decisive and invincible those propositions from which they do not see that shame is impending for them. But when they are overcome by the truth, what is fulfilled in them is that they are confounded by the very things in which they glory.

It is therefore not surprising if those whom their own malice has blinded—as it is written—and whom truth itself, which is the true light, has abandoned, whose foul gaze of a perverse heart has been surrounded by the darkness of hideous error, strive accordingly to impiously shatter the inseparable Trinity by an unequal service of honor, although they do not hesitate to proclaim it unequal in substantial distinction.

And since they are convicted of sinning against Wisdom itself, the word of that Wisdom is fulfilled in them, so that, while they sin against her, they admit the sin of impiety into their own souls. For Wisdom herself says: “Those who sin against me act impiously against their own souls, and those who hate me love death” (Proverbs 8:36).

How could they not hate the Son of God, whom they cannot deny in words to be the Only-Begotten, but whom in their thoughtless perversity they distinguish from the nature of the Father? Or how could they not act impiously against their own souls, since they neither agree to glorify the Only-Begotten Son of God, the true God, together with the Father, nor permit him to be honored equally with the same sacrifice?

With God’s help, insofar as the structure of the present work permits, we shall answer them briefly. We first put this question to them: Let them say whether God gave his Church the faith by which our father Abraham pleased God through believing in him, and in which he received the promise that all the nations of the earth would be blessed in his seed—or whether they profess that another religious standard was divinely handed down to them, so that they consider the faith of the patriarchs and prophets to be rejected.

Although, as the truth will demonstrate, they are entirely alien to this faith, they nevertheless say that it was given to the Church and insist that it remains inviolate among them.

## CHAPTER III. The Question of Sacrifice Is Determined from the Faith of the Fathers. The Promises Made to Abraham and His Seed. Abraham Built an Altar to Offer Sacrifice Not to the Father Alone but Also to the Son. To Invoke in the Name of the Lord Is the Same as to Invoke the Name of the Lord. Abraham Built an Altar to the God Who Appeared to Him. An Irrefutable Argument against the Heretics from Abraham’s Sacrifice and Faith

[Col. 0180C]

Since the question of sacrifice is therefore being disputed between us and them, we must return to those fathers whom God, like lights in the world, made radiant as an example for our instruction in the true faith. He so displayed their faith as inspired by himself that he is found most plainly to name himself their God, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; this is my eternal name and memorial from generation to generation” (Exodus 3:15).

When we say that the sacrifice is offered not to the Father alone but as one sacrifice jointly to the Father and the Son, while they think that it is offered to the Father alone, let us seek in the sacrifice of the patriarchs evidence of a true immolation pleasing to God.

We must begin the series of proofs with the one in whose seed the future blessing of all the nations is found to have been promised, as Paul says:

“Promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, ‘and to seeds,’ as of many, but as of one: ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Galatians 3:16).

And again:

“So that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations in Christ Jesus, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith” (ibid., 14).

Let it therefore be entirely clear that those who are found to follow Abraham’s faith in sacrifice are participants in divine blessing and sharers in spiritual grace.

In the Book of Genesis we read:

“The Lord God appeared to Abraham and said to him: ‘To your seed I will give this land.’ And Abraham built there an altar to the Lord who had appeared to him, and departed from there to the mountain east of Bethel; and he built there an altar to the Lord God, and invoked in the name of the Lord God who had appeared to him” (Genesis 12:7).

Let the heretics now choose what they wish: either let them confess that the Father appeared to Abraham, or let them agree that Abraham built an altar to the Son. The reading of the Old Testament frequently makes clear that an altar is built for no other reason than to offer sacrifice to God.

For Moses speaks in this way about righteous Noah:

“Noah built an altar to God.”

And as though he were being asked for what purpose the just man had built that altar, he immediately added:

“And he took from all the clean cattle and from all the clean birds, and offered a sacrifice upon the altar to God” (Genesis 8:20).

It is therefore clear that the holy Abraham too, the faithful friend of God and father of faithful nations, built an altar to the God who had appeared to him for this reason: so that he might offer him a sacrifice of fitting immolation.

But lest anyone think, when it is said that he invoked “in the name of the Lord God,” that one God was invoked in the name of another God, since “to invoke in the name of the Lord God” means nothing other than “to invoke the name of the Lord God,” divine Scripture took care to demonstrate this also with a subsequent clear statement. A little later it says:

“Now Abraham was heavily laden with cattle, silver, and gold, and he went to that place—or, alternatively, ‘there’—from which he had come, into the desert as far as Bethel, to the place where his tent had previously been, between Bethel and Ai, to the place where he had first made an altar and where Abraham had invoked the name of God” (Genesis 13:4).

Thus it is recognized that “to invoke in the name of the Lord God” is the same as “to invoke the name of the Lord God.”

Therefore let the heretics say whether they think Abraham built the altar to the Father or to the Son. For the one to whom he built the altar is certainly the one whose name he invoked. But he built an altar only to the God who had appeared to him, whom the heretics are accustomed to call the Son.

For, striving to teach that the substance of the Father and the Son is different, they think that all visible forms of bodily things are to be attributed only to the Son. The almighty God, Lord of the whole creation, adapted these forms, as he willed, to temporal places and persons in order to reveal himself to human beings. On this basis they assert that the Son is unequal and inferior to the Father, because his nature was capable of mutable forms; and, as though his divinity had naturally been visible in the very fact that he did not disdain to display himself through visible things for the instruction—or, alternatively, “formation”—of human minds.

We need not discuss this matter in the present work, since the purpose of the present question demands only this: because holy Abraham is known to have sacrificed to the God whom divine Scripture testifies to have appeared to him, let them say either that the Father appeared to Abraham or let them agree that Abraham sacrificed to the Son.

By either alternative, as by a double-edged sword, their impious claim of diversity is cut down. For if they say that God the Father appeared to Abraham, so as to assert that sacrifice was offered to him alone, then, insofar as he is said to have appeared, the invisible Father cannot be set before the invisible Son as though he were superior. But if the Son appeared and the holy patriarch offered sacrifice to him, the Son is not to be set before the Father in any respect; for Abraham would not have offered sacrifice to him if he had believed anyone else to be superior to him.

And so these people, who think that our faith is shaken by the force of this question, must in either case acknowledge the falsehood of their belief—or, alternatively, “of their unbelief.” Would that, once recognizing it, they might cast it away and return humbly and peacefully to the true faith, which they vainly and rebelliously oppose!

Abraham, who built an altar not to another God but to the one who had appeared to him, necessarily either saw the Father or sacrificed to the Son, according to the very principles by which the heretics argue.

## CHAPTER IV. Isaac Also Built an Altar to the God Who Appeared to Him. Jacob Likewise Was Commanded to Build an Altar to the Same God. The Sacrifices of the Patriarchs Correspond to Ours, Which Are Offered to the Whole Trinity

Abraham built an altar to this God who appeared to him, certainly for no other purpose than to offer sacrifice. Isaac too saw him and, holding fast to his father’s faith, built an altar to him. For it is written concerning Isaac—as the Book of Genesis contains the passage:

“He went up from there to the Well of the Oath, and the Lord appeared to him that night and said: ‘I am the God of Abraham your father. Do not be afraid, for I am with you; I will bless you and multiply your seed because of Abraham your father.’ And Isaac built an altar there and invoked the name of the Lord” (Genesis 26:23).

Without doubt, he invoked the Lord who appeared to him and promised the assistance of his presence, the gift of blessing, and the increase of his multiplying seed.

Jacob too is known to have made an altar not to another God but to the one who had appeared to him. And what is more, he did not undertake this of his own accord, but fulfilled it in obedience to divine commands. Holy Scripture testifies to this in these words:

“God said to Jacob: ‘Rise, go up to Bethel, dwell there, and make there an altar to the God who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esau your brother’” (Genesis 35:1).

And it continues:

“Jacob came to Luz, which is in the land of Canaan, that is, Bethel, he and all the people who were with him, and built an altar there, and called that place ‘House of God,’ for there God had appeared to him when he fled from the face of his brother Esau” (ibid., 6).

Behold, the word of our faith stands on the testimony of two and three witnesses. Behold, the offering of the Catholic Church agrees completely with the sacrifice of God’s friends: she sacrifices to the Father in such a way that she sacrifices at the same time to the whole Trinity.

For the holy patriarchs too knew that, when they were commanded to offer sacrifice to the Son, they were rendering to the Father and the Son together an offering of acceptable worship. They were divinely commanded to build an altar to the Son not because sacrifice was not to be offered to the Father, but so that what was sacrificed by the saints might be sacrificed jointly to the Son and the Father—not so that the Son would be set before the Father, but so that the one begotten might not be thought inferior in any respect to the one who begot him.

Therefore, although no one should doubt that the testimony of the patriarchal sacrifice supports the correctness of our faith, and although whoever thinks that it must be opposed with an obstinate heart strays alienated from the fellowship of faith and from the saints, we could also add testimonies of equal firmness and strength from the prophets, if, mindful of the full debt that must be paid, we did not prefer to hasten to the resolution of the remaining questions.

## CHAPTER V. Another Testimony from the Prophets, Showing That Sacrifice Is Also to Be Offered to the Son. The Heretics’ Obstinacy in Refusing to Sacrifice to the Son. Catholics Offer Sacrifice to the Whole Trinity Even When They Express the Name of the Father Alone

Nevertheless, lest anyone think that under the appearance of abundance we have concealed—or, alternatively, “veiled”—a lack of defense, we shall produce one testimony from the prophets by which it can clearly be shown that the holy prophets, inspired by God, foretold with certain and wholly faithful prophecy that in the time of the New Testament spiritual sacrifices would be offered by the faithful not to the Father alone but also to the Son.

[Note: [Col. 0183D] The following words had intruded from the margin: “A prophet’s testimony concerning the sacrifice that is now performed in the Church.” We erased them because they are found in none of the manuscripts and contribute nothing to the sense.]

For Zephaniah says:

“Wait for me, says the Lord, for the day of my resurrection as a testimony; for my judgment will be upon the gathering of the nations, so that I may receive kings and pour out upon them the anger of my wrath. For the whole earth will be consumed in the fire of my jealousy. For then I will change the language of the peoples for their generations, so that all may invoke the name of the Lord and serve him under one yoke. From beyond the rivers of Ethiopia I will receive those who observe me; those who have been scattered will bring sacrifices to me on that day” (Zephaniah 3:8).

What, I ask, is clearer than this prophecy? Or what hiding place of dark obstinacy can heretical unbelief find here, by which it might escape the light of so great a manifestation? For “the Lord has placed his tent in the sun” (Psalm 18:6), so that there is no one who can hide himself from its heat.

For—perhaps, “From which point onward”—if anyone, stunned by the icy cold of unbelief, hides himself, he may withdraw from himself the help of reconciliation, but he cannot hide himself from vengeance.

Behold, the one who commands that he be awaited on the day of his resurrection himself shows that sacrifices are to be offered to him by all the nations, so that it might be recognized that the sacrifice acceptable to God is that which the pure devotion of the faithful offers jointly to the Father and the Son.

When the heretics are admonished by these and similar testimonies, would that they might not hear with deaf ears, but recognize the truth of the faith through the illumination divinely granted to them, so that, once they have received the light of salvation, they may cease henceforth to wander in the darkness of deadly unbelief.

By refusing to offer sacrifice to the Son, and by miserably withdrawing in their obstinacy from the faith of the patriarchs and prophets, they sin impiously and show themselves condemned by themselves. For the Apostle is known to have condemned every heretic by this pronouncement: that a heretic is to be avoided entirely after the first and second admonition (Titus 3:10), because such a person is not only subverted but also condemned by his own judgment.

But if any Catholic believers have until now seemed unaware of this mystery, they must henceforth know that every act of honor and every salutary sacrificial service is offered equally by the Catholic Church to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, to the holy Trinity.

It is certainly evident that holy baptism too is celebrated in the one name of the Trinity. Nor is any prejudice created against the Son or the Holy Spirit when the prayer of the one offering is directed toward the person of the Father. The conclusion of that prayer, when it embraces the name of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, shows that there is no distinction within the Trinity.

For when the language of honor is directed toward the person of the Father alone, the whole Trinity is honored by the faith of the one who rightly believes; and when the intention of the one making the offering is directed toward the Father, the sacrificial gift is offered to the whole Trinity by the one and the same service of the offerer.

Therefore, when we offer one sacrifice to the Trinity, who is the one and true God, let us not be disturbed by the empty objections of the heretics. For in following and firmly retaining this teaching we are instructed both by divinely proclaimed oracles and strengthened by the examples of the saints who preceded us.

## CHAPTER VI. Monimus’s Third Question: Why, in Sacrifices, Is Only the Mission of the Holy Spirit Requested? The Holy Spirit Is Not Inferior Because He Was Sent by the Father and the Son, since the Son Also Was Sent. The Mission of the Son and of the Holy Spirit Did Not Take Place Locally. Scripture Teaches the Immensity Not Only of the Father but Also of the Son and of the Holy Spirit
32 We must now also take up the question concerning the sending of the Holy Spirit: namely, why, if the sacrifice is offered to the whole Trinity, only the sending of the Holy Spirit is requested for sanctifying (or: sacrificing) the offering of our oblation [Col. 0184C]—as though, so to speak, God the Father himself, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds, could not sanctify the sacrifice offered to him; or as though the Son himself could not sanctify the sacrifice of his body, which we offer, although he himself sanctified the body that he offered in order to redeem us; or as though the Holy Spirit must be sent to consecrate the Church’s sacrifice as if the Father or the Son were absent from those who sacrifice.

First, therefore, we must remember that in the designation of this sending the Holy Spirit must not be understood as inferior or lesser; for if he is lesser, he is certainly inferior, and if inferior, certainly lesser. We have prefaced this because we know that the heretics frequently press this point against our faith above all: that the Holy Spirit must be believed lesser than the Father and the Son because he was sent both by the Father and by the Son. But if the one who sends is to be considered superior to the one sent, let them recognize that their unbelief is refuted by this fact: just as the Holy Spirit is read to have been sent by the Father and the Son, so the Son is found to have been sent by the Father and the Spirit. The Son himself said this through the prophet long before he was sent, and after he was sent confirmed it by his own testimony.

For when he came to Nazareth and entered the synagogue, and, with the book of the prophet Isaiah handed to him for reading, he unrolled the passage where it is written, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor” (Luke 4:18), after returning the scroll [Col. 0185A] he testified by the present accomplishment that the truth of that prophecy had been fulfilled, saying, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21). In another passage of the same prophet he likewise shows in these words that he was sent by the Lord and by his Spirit: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isa. 48:16).

Before his passion he declares in this way that he himself sends the Holy Spirit to the disciples: “But when the Paraclete has come, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me” (John 15:26). Earlier he had also taught that the same Spirit is sent by the Father: “But the Paraclete,” he says, “the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything” (John 14:26).

Thus the Son was sent by the Father and by the Spirit, and the Spirit was sent by the Father [Col. 0185B] and by the Son. Nevertheless, no Christian ought to understand the sending of the Son or of the Holy Spirit as having taken place locally; rather, by the name of “sending” we should understand the work of an imparted manifestation. For the Son was not sent locally, nor is the Holy Spirit sent locally, just as the Father himself has no local coming anywhere (quoquam; alternatively quoque, “also”). Yet the Son promises his beloved not only his own coming but also that of the Father, saying: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (ibid., 23).

Therefore, just as the Father and the Son are nowhere absent and yet come to whomever they will—for they come by grace, although by their power they are nowhere absent—so also, in the sending or coming of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0185C], no local movement of his should be understood; rather, the effect of our sanctification should be believed. For if the Son was sent locally according to his divinity, or if the Holy Spirit is thought to be sent locally, then God the Father too would be believed—God forbid—to be confined to a place.

And where then is what God himself thus reveals to us concerning his immensity, saying, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24)? The prophetic word also commends to us the immensity of the Son. Concerning him holy Jeremiah speaks thus: “He is great and has no end; he is exalted and immeasurable” (Baruch 3:25). And because he himself is the power and wisdom of God, this is said of him: “He reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things gently” (Wis. 8:1).

We also know from apostolic preaching that “in Christ all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him” (Col. 1:16). What, then, is there that he cannot fill with his presence, in whom the Apostle declares that all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, hold together?

Scripture speaks of the immensity of the Holy Spirit in this way: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the inhabited world” (Wis. 1:7). For this reason David, believing in his heart for righteousness and confessing with his mouth for salvation the one substantial immensity of the holy Trinity, sang as follows:

“Where shall I go from your Spirit,  
and where shall I flee from your presence?  
If I ascend into heaven, you are there;  
and if I descend into the underworld, you are present.  
And if I take my wings before the dawn  
and dwell at the farthest end of the sea,  
even there your hand will lead me,  
and your right hand will hold me” (Ps. 138:7).

## CHAPTER VII. The whole Trinity is everywhere. By the name “Spirit,” spiritual gifts of grace are sometimes signified.

Since, therefore, as we have said, the whole Trinity remains naturally immeasurable and infinite in the unity of its divinity, and thus is nowhere locally while nevertheless being absent nowhere, and is wholly everywhere, so that it can neither be divided into parts throughout the whole creation nor enclosed by the totality of creation, whenever the Holy Spirit is requested for the consecration of the sacrifice, the first principle of faith and the first salutary precaution to be firmly maintained by all Christians is that the coming of the Holy Spirit must in no way be conceived or considered local [Col. 0186B].

For the Apostle says to the faithful: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). And elsewhere: “Praying at all times in the Spirit, and keeping watch in him” (Eph. 6:18). The Savior himself also says to his disciples: “If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it does not see him or know him; but you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you” (John 14:15).

For this reason Paul also proclaims that we have received the same Spirit of adoption: “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again for fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:15).

To the faithful, then, who are God’s temple and in whom God’s Spirit dwells—indeed, who are the temple of the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says, “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God?” (1 Cor. 3:16)—to those whom the same Apostle commands to pray and keep watch in him, how can the Holy Spirit be believed to be sent as though previously absent? No one can pray or keep watch worthily unless the Holy Spirit has poured himself into him.

Accordingly, as the Apostle says, “comparing spiritual things with spiritual” (1 Cor. 2:13), and thinking of nothing bodily, temporal, local, or mutable in the Spirit, who is naturally God, we must consider that the name “Holy Spirit” sometimes designates the gifts of spiritual grace.

For we read in the Book of Kings that when Elijah was to be taken away by divine favor, and before he was taken up had given his disciple the confidence to ask for whatever he wished, the disciple requested that a double portion of the spirit received by Elijah be granted to him. Here, clearly, by the name “spirit” the gift of spiritual grace is signified. For the substance of the Holy Spirit cannot be increased or diminished: just as he is eternal, without beginning and without end, so he is perfect, without increase or loss.

## CHAPTER VIII. The gifts of the Holy Spirit can increase or diminish in us, but not the Spirit himself. Just as the same sun illuminates different things more or less, so the same Spirit is received differently by different people.

Yet concerning his gifts, according to his inscrutable and irreproachable will, just as we believe that they can increase in human beings, so we do not deny that they can diminish in them [Col. 0187A]. For since the gifts of the Holy Spirit are “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control” (Gal. 5:22), and since “to one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, and to another faith in the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:8), all these things can both increase and diminish in human beings.

Hence the Apostles’ request that the Lord grant them an increase of faith, when they say, “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke 17:5). The blessed Apostle himself also shows that we grow in love when he says: “But speaking the truth in love, let us grow in every respect into him” (Eph. 4:15). How do we grow in love unless we receive an increase of love together with the gift of spiritual grace? “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

The same is understood concerning the other spiritual gifts, which are said to increase or diminish in us according to each person’s capacity. For the increases and decreases of such charismatic gifts are spoken of with reference to the fact that they are present in some people more and in others less—not because they can themselves be increased or diminished.

The sun, too, is as great when seen by healthy eyes as when seen by injured eyes. It is not diminished when it is perceived less by troubled eyes, nor increased when it pours more fully into healthy eyes. That difference in vision arises not from a difference in the sun but from a difference in health and weakness. And although it illuminates one person less and another more, it nevertheless has in itself one and the same light, which one sees less and another more.

So also, while the Holy Spirit remains in himself immutable, without increase or loss, Eliseus requested a double spirit insofar as he requested an increase of spiritual grace.

## CHAPTER IX. Those who are said to have spoken in the tongues of angels. Those who teach the law but do not do it. Where love is, there is the Holy Spirit.

When, therefore, the coming of the Holy Spirit is requested for the sanctification of the sacrifice of the whole Church, it seems to me that nothing else is being requested except that, through spiritual grace, the unity of love may continually remain unbroken in the body of Christ, which is the Church.

For this is the principal gift of the Holy Spirit. Without it, whoever speaks in the tongues of human beings and angels can produce a sound like ringing bronze or a clanging cymbal, but cannot possess life. Even if he has all prophecy, knows all mysteries and all knowledge, and has all faith so as to move mountains, if he does not have love, he is nothing. Even if he distributes all his possessions as food for the poor and gives his body to be burned, if he does not have love, it profits him nothing (1 Cor. 13:1–3).

Since the Apostle says that the law was “ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator” (Gal. 3:19), those who taught orally what belongs to the law (alternatively, legebant, “read”)—and opposed the law by their wicked deeds—spoke in the tongues of angels. Of them the Savior himself says: “Whatever they tell you, do and observe; but do not do what they do, for they say and do not do” (Matt. 23:3).

[Col. 0188A] Saul also had prophecy, and Simon Magus believed and received the sacrament of baptism. Even demons, when they believe and tremble, seem to have faith; but it profits them nothing because they do not have love.

Many also distribute their possessions to the poor, but because they have not taken care to devote themselves to acquiring love, they have indeed given away their property. This profited them nothing because they lost themselves by failing to acquire the love they ought to have acquired.

These examples therefore show that the Holy Spirit is present where the end of the commandment is found—namely, “love from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unhypocritical faith” (1 Tim. 1:5). Where love is not present together with faith, there may be various gifts of the Holy Spirit, but the Holy Spirit himself cannot be present. Consequently, the abundance of those gifts profits nothing where someone possesses a gift of the Spirit in such a way that he does not possess the Spirit himself.

Therefore, although such people may seem to share in whatever paternal gifts, they are not partners in the paternal inheritance, because “the Holy Spirit is the pledge of our inheritance” (Eph. 1:14). And in him God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, “just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love.”

## CHAPTER X. The Church therefore rightly requests the coming of the Holy Spirit in the sacrifice. Through Christ’s incarnation we have peace and unity with God. Through the Holy Spirit both Christ was born and the Church was reborn. Christ and the Church. Through the Holy Spirit there is unity between Christ and the Church. Through the Holy Spirit we are built into a holy temple in the Lord.

[Col. 0188C]

When, therefore, the Church asks that the Holy Spirit be sent to her from heaven, she asks God to grant her the gift of love and unanimity. When could holy Church, which is the body of Christ, more appropriately request the coming of the Holy Spirit than when the sacrifice of Christ’s body is consecrated? She knows that her very head, according to the flesh, was born from the Holy Spirit.

For the angelic message thus instructs Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). The evangelist Matthew, filled with the same Holy Spirit, also affirms that when his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit (Matt. 1:18). And he records that the angel said to Joseph in a dream: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife; for what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.”

What else was accomplished through the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation except that divided things might be united and things at variance might be reconciled? Paul is witness concerning Christ: “For he himself is our peace, who made both one and broke down the middle wall of separation, abolishing enmity in his flesh, annulling the law of commandments expressed in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself (alternatively, semetipsum, “himself”) as one new human being, making peace, and might reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, putting the enmity to death in himself. And coming, he preached peace to those who were far away and peace to those who were near, because through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Eph. 2:14).

This, then, was accomplished by divine love: that the body of that head should be reborn from the same Spirit from whom the head itself was born. Therefore it is necessary for us that, just as Christ was born from the Holy Spirit—when the only-begotten God, united to a human being, came forth from the Virgin’s womb as a bridegroom from his bridal chamber—so the Church, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, should cleave to Christ as a woman to her husband and as a body to its head.

For the Apostle says, “Christ is the head of the Church, he himself the savior of the body.” And again: “We are members of his body, from his flesh and from his bones. Therefore a man will leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two will be one flesh” (carne una; alternatively carnem unam, likewise “one flesh”) (Eph. 5:29). Explaining this, he added: “This mystery is great; but I am speaking with reference to Christ and the Church.”

When the Lord brought forward this testimony of the Old Testament against the Pharisees’ testing, he followed it by adding: “Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh. What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6).

Thus, so that in that holy marriage, which took place in the bridal chamber of the Virgin’s womb, there would no longer be two but one flesh, it was accomplished by spiritual grace. Spiritual grace also works so that this may remain perpetually unbroken: so that this unity may cleave to its head, and, knowing that all who distance themselves from him will perish and that he will destroy all who commit fornication away from him, it may itself say chastely and sweetly, “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. 72:27). And again, “My soul has clung to you” (Ps. 62:9).

That love of God accomplishes this, which “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

Through this Holy Spirit the unity of Christ and the Church is so great that, although the Chosen Vessel says, “Christ is the head of the body, the Church” (Col. 1:18), he nevertheless does not hesitate to call the very body of Christ truly “Christ.” Thus he writes to the Corinthians: “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ” (1 Cor. 12:12).

And to show that this body, which is Christ’s in such a way that it is Christ, remains and subsists as one despite having many members only through the grace of the Holy Spirit, he immediately continues: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, whether slaves or free; and we were all given to drink of one Spirit” (ibid., 13).

That spiritual grace, therefore, does not cease each day to build up the body of Christ through the unity of peace and love. It fashioned in the Virgin Mary’s womb the gift of wisdom, which is the head of this body. Hence the blessed Apostle shows in these words that we too are built up in him: “Therefore you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but you are fellow citizens with the holy ones and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone. In him the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in him you also are built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit” (Eph. 2:19).

Elsewhere the Apostle testifies that this building, by which we are built in the Spirit, takes place for no other purpose than “the completion of the saints for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ.” Indicating the unity of this same spiritual building, which consists in love, he says: “Until we all attain to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect human being, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be infants, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine, by human wickedness and cunning for the deceitful scheming of error. But speaking the truth in love, let us grow in every respect into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and knit together through every supporting joint according to the working in due measure of each individual member, makes the growth of the body for the building up of itself in love” (Eph. 4:13).

## CHAPTER XI. This spiritual building is most rightly requested when the bread and cup are consecrated. Nevertheless, our sanctification is accomplished by the whole Trinity. Those who withdraw from the unity of the Church lose the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0190B]

This spiritual building of the body of Christ, which takes place in love—when, according to the words of blessed Peter, living stones are built into a spiritual house, into a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (1 Pet. 2:5)—this spiritual building, I say, is never requested more appropriately than when, by the body of Christ itself, which is the Church, the very body and blood of Christ are offered in the sacrament of bread and the cup.

“For the cup that we drink is participation in the blood of Christ, and the bread that we break is participation in the body of the Lord; because we, though many, are one bread and one body, for we all share in the one bread” (1 Cor. 10:16).

Therefore we ask that, by the same grace through which it came about that the Church became Christ’s body, all the members may likewise, with the bond remaining intact, persevere in the unity of the body through love.

We rightly ask that this be accomplished in us by the gift of that Spirit who is the one Spirit of the Father and the Son. For the holy natural unity, equality, and love of the Trinity, which is the one and only true God, sanctifies by unanimity those whom it adopts.

In that one substance of the Trinity there is unity in origin, equality in offspring, and in love the communion of unity and equality. There is no division of that unity, no difference of that equality, no weariness of that love. Nothing there is discordant, because equality remains naturally and unchangeably loving and one, unity equal and loving, and love equal and one.

Because, therefore, from that communion, if it may be so called, of the Holy Spirit, the one love of the Father and the Son is made manifest—a communion which the blessed Apostle commends in these words, “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with all of you” (2 Cor. 13:13)—and elsewhere, “If there is any consolation in love, if there is any communion of the Spirit” (Phil. 2:1)—for this reason it is said: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

The Holy Spirit, who is one Spirit of the Father and the Son, works in those to whom he grants the grace of divine adoption what he also worked in those who are found in the Book of the Acts of the Apostles to have received the same Spirit. Of them it is said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and soul” (Acts 4:32). For the one Spirit of the Father and the Son, who is one God with the Father and the Son, had made the multitude of believers in God one in heart and soul.

Therefore the Apostle carefully says that this spiritual unity must be preserved in the bond of peace, thus exhorting the Ephesians: “I therefore, a prisoner in the Lord, urge you to walk worthily of the calling to which you were called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit” (Eph. 4:1).

By departing, those lose this Spirit who, corrupted by unbelief [or: faithlessness] or puffed up by pride, separate themselves from the unity of the Church’s body [Col. 0191B]. The apostle Jude clearly shows that such people are without this Spirit, saying: “These are the ones who separate themselves, merely natural people, not having the Spirit” (Jude 19). Because they are merely natural, they do not have the Spirit.

For this reason the Apostle Paul says: “The merely natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14). Such people are therefore readily disposed to division because they do not have the Spirit, in whom the members of Christ preserve their spiritual unity as one.

It is therefore clear that among all heretics there is no grace of the Holy Spirit, and that their sacrifices, so long as they are heretics, cannot please God. Nor can the sanctification of spiritual grace be attributed to the sacrifices of those who offer them while separated from the unity of the ecclesiastical body. For God is pleased only by the sacrifices of the Church; spiritual unity makes these sacrifices (alternatively, “this sacrifice”) for God. Thus faith’s truth believes no distance within the Trinity, and steadfastness in peace preserves fraternal harmony in love.

## CHAPTER XII. The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. Those who return to the unity of the Church present themselves as a living sacrifice pleasing to God.

But lest anyone think that, when the Church requests the coming of the Holy Spirit in the prayer of the sacrifice, we understand love—inappropriately—by the name “Holy Spirit,” love which has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, we have thought it useful to fortify our position beforehand with the judgments of the Fathers.

For holy Augustine, in his books On Baptism (Book 3, chapter 16), while treating the question of receiving heretics without repeating baptism, says among other things in the third book of that work:

> “But by the Holy Spirit, who is said to be given in the Catholic Church alone through the laying on of hands, our predecessors evidently wanted this to be understood: what the Apostle says, ‘The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us’ (Rom. 5:5). For this is the love which those who have been cut off from communion with the Catholic Church do not have.”

Consider, I ask, how blessed Augustine, divinely instructed in the holy Scriptures, marvelously disclosed in one passage the meaning not only of the holy apostle Paul but also of the holy apostle Jude under the name of the Holy Spirit.

Earlier he says:

> “But by the Holy Spirit, who is said to be given in the Catholic Church alone through the laying on of hands, our predecessors evidently wanted this to be understood: what the Apostle says, ‘The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.’”

Then, without leaving room for doubtful ambiguity, holy Augustine also explained what the apostle Jude set down in his Epistle. For the apostle Jude says: “These are the ones who separate themselves, worldly people, not having the Spirit.” And blessed Augustine, speaking of the love of God that has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, says:

> “For this is the love which those who have been cut off from communion with the Catholic Church do not have.”

Would anyone say that the Holy Spirit is given to heretics returning through the laying on of hands in a way different from that in which he is divinely granted through the spiritual sacrifice?

Whoever thinks or says this plainly does not yet understand how, when some schismatics and heretics abandon their deadly error and return to the unity of Catholic truth, they present themselves as a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to God. There, while offering to God a contrite spirit, they themselves are a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to God [Col. 0192B].

For through the contrition of a humbled heart they return to the unity of the members of that priest who loved us, as the Apostle says: “He gave himself for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling fragrance” (Eph. 5:2).

For them to return and become a spiritual sacrifice, the love of God accomplishes this—love which has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

God therefore willingly accepts only the sacrifice of Catholic truth and communion. For while the Church preserves within herself his love, poured out through the Holy Spirit, he makes the Church herself a sacrifice pleasing to him. She continually asks to receive the grace of spiritual love, through which she continually asks to present herself as a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to God.

## CHAPTER XIII. Monimus’s fourth question concerning the Apostle’s supererogation. Blessed Ambrose’s exposition in Book VII on Luke 4. Blessed Optatus’s exposition before the middle of Book VI.

Furthermore, you write about that passage of the Apostle where he says: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give advice.” In the letter I recently wrote to you, I mentioned that this advice pertains to what the faithful innkeeper, having received two denarii from the Lord, spent in addition (Luke 10:35).

Although you assert that holy Augustine did not establish the meaning of this passage in precisely that way, you nevertheless affirm that other distinguished men understood it in this manner. This is indeed true: holy Augustine said that what was supererogated by the Apostle was that, although according to the command he could, if he wished, live from the Gospel, he nevertheless preferred to work with his own hands not only for himself but also for those who were with him, as he truthfully said to the Ephesians:

> “You yourselves know that (alternatively, quomodo, ‘how’) these hands ministered to my needs and to those who were with me. In everything I showed you that by laboring in this way we ought to support the weak” (Acts 20:34).

Writing also to the Thessalonians, he says: “For you remember, brothers, our labor (alternatively, laborem, ‘toil,’ etc.) and fatigue, working night and day so that we might not burden any of you” (1 Thess. 3:8).

To the Corinthians, too, he says that this is his reward: that, while preaching the Gospel, he should offer the Gospel without cost, so as not to abuse his authority in the Gospel (1 Cor. 9:18).

Although holy Augustine presented this fittingly and appropriately, it should nevertheless not seem unfitting or inappropriate that holy Ambrose located the supererogation of blessed Paul either in his sermons and letters or in the excessive labor of his mind and body.

Holy Optatus of Milevis, in the sixth book Against Parmenianus, testifies that Paul supererogated the advice concerning virgins in these words:

> “For virginity is a matter of the will, not of necessity. Finally, that apostolic innkeeper, Paul, to whom the people wounded by the injuries of sins were entrusted, had received the two denarii that he had spent (or: was to spend)—namely, the two Testaments. These he expended through teaching, as though they were provisions. He taught how married Christians ought to live; and when he was asked concerning him (de quo; alternatively a quo, ‘of him’) what he commanded concerning virgins, he replied that he had no command from the Lord concerning virgins (1 Cor. 7:25). He confessed that he had expended the two Testaments, that is, the two denarii. The provisions had, in a sense, been exhausted, but he who had entrusted the wounded man had promised that he would repay whatever more he might spend on his care after the two denarii had been expended. Paul spends not a command but advice concerning virginity. It neither hinders those who wish it nor drives or compels those who do not wish it.”

## CHAPTER XIV. Behold, one passage of the Apostle has been expounded in three different ways by three holy men. Moreover, the same passage is found expounded in different ways by one teacher. Augustine’s various exposition of Noah’s ark. It is useful to cite different interpretations concerning one matter, but not a different faith.

[Col. 0193C]

40 Since, then, this passage of the blessed Apostle has been expounded in three different ways by the three holy men whom we named, whoever sets forth one of these three interpretations certainly does not depart from the truth. For it is not necessary that what is understood in multiple ways be inserted in multiple ways in every written work. Indeed, those holy men themselves, through whose ministry God has deigned to disclose the secrets of his Scriptures, have said that many things may be understood—not merely in one way, but in several—without impropriety, provided that the true faith is not offended thereby.

This is known to be what the blessed Augustine himself did concerning the mystery of Noah’s ark in his work Against Faustus. For when the Manichaean asserted that the books of the Old Testament contained no prophetic reference to Christ’s future coming in true flesh, the most blessed Augustine showed that our ancient Scripture is filled with prophetic signs concerning Christ and therefore divinely inspired. Among other things, he explains the passage in which God commands the ark mentioned above to be constructed with two and three stories. In the fifteenth book of *The City of God*, he explained the mystical meaning of this same passage in two other ways—not in the words of human wisdom, but truly, as the Apostle says, “in the teaching of the Spirit”—no less sweetly than wonderfully. To make this more readily understood, I shall append the words of both works as he wrote them.

Thus, in *Against Faustus*, he wrote:

> “That the lower parts of the ark are constructed with two and three compartments means that the Church gathers from all nations either a twofold multitude, on account of circumcision and uncircumcision, or a threefold one, on account of Noah’s three sons, whose descendants filled the world.”

But in the fifteenth book of *The City of God*, when he undertook to explain the mystery of the ark in accordance with the suitability of the passage, after some intervening material, when discussing the statement that Noah’s ark was to be constructed with two and three compartments, he introduced a reference to the interpretation contained in the books *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, adding the following:

> “It may indeed happen that one person explains these things in one way, and another in another, more suitably. Provided, however, that all the things said are referred to this city of God of which we are speaking, journeying in this wicked age as though in a flood, so long as the person who explains them does not wish to depart far from the sense of the one who wrote them. For example, if someone should wish to understand what is written here—‘You shall make its lower parts two-compartmented and three-compartmented’ [*bicameratam et tricameratam*; alternatively, *bicamerata et tricamerata*]—not as I explained it in that other work, namely, that the Church is gathered from all nations and is called two-compartmented on account of the two classes of human beings, circumcision and uncircumcision, whom the Apostle also calls Jews and Greeks (Gal. III), and three-compartmented because all the nations were restored after the flood from Noah’s three sons, but should give it another interpretation that is not alien to the rule of faith.

> “For since he wished the ark to have dwellings not only in its lower parts but also in its upper parts, and called these two-compartmented, and in the uppermost parts above the upper parts, and called these three-compartmented, so that the third dwelling rose from the bottom upward, the three things commended by the Apostle—faith, hope, and love (I Cor. XIII, 13)—may here be understood. The three fruitful measures of the Gospel may also be understood much more suitably: thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold; so that conjugal chastity dwells in the lowest part, widowhood above it, and virginity above that. And anything else that may be understood and said according to the faith of this city may likewise be proposed.

> “I would say the same about the other things that are to be explained here, because although they are discussed in more than one way, they must nevertheless be brought back to the one concord of the Catholic faith.”

Again, the blessed Augustine, in the first book of *On the Trinity* (chapter 3), asserts that it is useful for several books to be produced by several authors, in different styles but not in different faiths, even concerning the same questions, so that the matter itself may reach many people—some in one way, others in another.

If, therefore, the blessed Augustine placed in one passage two interpretations of the matter concerning Noah’s ark, and two men each take one of them and set it forth in different passages, will not both rightly be declared steadfast defenders of the truth—provided that each appears to support the interpretation inserted into his own words in such a way that he approves the other interpretation, which he likewise sets forth as agreeing with the truth, more peaceably than he attacks it contentiously?

## CHAPTER XV. Response to Monimus’s Question Concerning Paul’s Supererogation

Therefore, dearest brother, although the interpretation that I have set forth may perhaps not be found in the writings of Saint Augustine, it is nevertheless found most plainly in the books of Saint Optatus, as you yourself know together with me. Nor is your prudence unaware that, whatever we set forth concerning those things found in the writings or defenses of the holy Fathers—who, in the teaching of the Holy Spirit, defended the sound rule of the Catholic faith in various ways—we ought to establish an interpretation agreeing with the truth of that passage without denying assent to the other statements of the Fathers that likewise agree with the truth.

For one does not depart from the truth if, in this matter of the Apostle’s supererogation, we too, while preserving the truth of the faith, hold what Saint Ambrose, Saint Augustine, or Saint Optatus held. For if it is rightly believed that, after receiving the two denarii, Paul supererogated something by preaching the Gospel at the expense of his own labor and not demanding from the faithful the support due to him, then it is also rightly believed that he supererogated something in that, having no command from the Lord concerning virgins, he gave counsel instead. Without doubt, he had both from the one who bestowed them; unless he had received them, he could not have supererogated.

# BOOK THREE. ON THE TRUE EXPOSITION OF THE EVANGELICAL STATEMENT: “AND THE WORD WAS WITH GOD”

[Col. 0195]

## CHAPTER I. Praise of Love. The Argument of the Third Book Against the Arians Concerning the Statement: “And the Word Was with God.” The Arians Think That “With God” Means Something Other Than “In God”

42 Whenever, dearest Monimus, [Note: [Col. 0195D] “And servant of Christ.” Thus the Thuanus and Victorius manuscripts; but the Corbie manuscript reads “from servants of Christ.”] the virtue of love is considered and weighed by the servants of Christ, it is found to be no less marvelous than delightful. For who would not marvel at it, or who would not be greatly pleased by it, since, when its burden is carried, it does not weaken the soul through weariness but strengthens it through gladness? For when it burdens, it lifts up; and in a wondrous manner it does not allow the one whom it burdens to be crushed, nor the one whom it lifts to become exalted.

It is love itself that, as I discharge with the Lord’s help the debt I previously owed you, once again makes me your debtor. For I had already completed two books on the four questions that you had sent me to treat, wishing to repay what I owed you, with the help of him who grants wisdom to the little ones. Suddenly, however, an opinion concerning a certain Arian assertion struck my ears—an opinion born of an invention all the more useless because it is found to be remote not only from every understanding of the divine Scriptures but also from the common understanding of humanity itself.

For I have discovered that they are now sowing [or inserting; or seeking] an unfamiliar question concerning the beginning of the Gospel according to John. They think that the statement, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John I, 1), ought to be understood and explained in such a way that the very Word’s being with the Father is to be taken as its being not in the Father but outside the Father.

Indeed, as I have learned by hearsay, when a dispute one day arose among some of them concerning the two prepositions—that is, *in* and *with*—one of them took a certain *birrus* [a cloak or outer garment], held it in his hands, and asked whether, since the cloak was with him, it was also in him. He then concluded his argument with this definition, as though thereby confirming his opinion: when something is said to be “in us,” it is to be understood as within us; but when it is said to be “with us,” it is to be understood as outside us.
