And because that cloak which he was holding was with him in such a way that it was not in him, and therefore, by being with him, was nevertheless not in him, it was outside him and not within him, so likewise, they say, the Word of God—which is God—is to be believed to be with the Father but not in the Father, and therefore not of one substance with the Father. For whatever is with someone in such a way that it is not in him is plainly with him in such a way that it cannot be of one substance with him.

This is their reasoning, contrary to reason. This legalistic argument is intolerably hostile to the law of God.

## CHAPTER II. It Is Absurd to Argue About God in Terms of Bodies. An Example Concerning the Breath of the Nostrils Would Have Been More Appropriate Than One Concerning a Cloak Held in the Hands

For this reason, with Christ granting it, my mind was stirred to write something, lest the hearing of the little ones be disturbed by poisonous words. It belongs to the duty of our service to prepare the salutary remedies of the divine utterances against the rising pestilence of any deadly opinion.

Thus, when the holy Apostle carefully warns the faithful, saying, “See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ; for in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. II, 8), these men, by contrast, not only previously followed the error of worldly philosophy according to the elements of the world and thought that one should argue about God in those terms, but they have so completely forgotten the whole of religion that, when they argue about God, they do not even attend to the elements of this bodily world. And thus, while they stubbornly close the eyes of their understanding even against the things that are visible, they never perceive the invisible things of God through the things that have been made.

For what could be said more absurdly than that, when someone argues about God, he should draw the evidence of his argument only from the coarser bodies? That man thought he had discovered something significant when, taking a cloak and holding it in his hands, he asked whether, just as it was with him, it was also in him. From this he wished to teach that the Son is with the Father in the same way that the cloak is with a man: since the cloak can be with a man but cannot be in the man, so the Son is indeed with the Father but is not in the Father.

I ask: if, in arguing by way of example from these tangible bodies, he took pleasure in choosing something—even though the elements made by the truth could in no way support him in his argument against the truth—then, to make his statement at least tolerable, why, leaving other things aside, did he display the cloak that he was holding in his hands, and not at least attend to the breath that he was drawing through his nostrils?

For if that cloak could be said to be with him and not in him, this breath, which we draw from the surrounding air when we inhale it, is nevertheless both with us and in us when we receive it by breathing. Whatever of it we give back through exhalation, once we have returned it, we have neither with us nor in us.

Or perhaps he will say that this element of air, when we receive it by breathing, is only in us and is not also with us? Let him then say when it can be with us—perhaps when we return it and no longer have it in us? But I think he would not dare say this even about that cloak, if he returned it to the one from whom he had received it. For he sees that he had it with him when he received it; but after he returned it, he ceased to have it with him. Just as receiving caused him to have with him what he had not previously had, so returning caused him not to have what he had had with him.

Therefore, if he said that the cloak is not in him but is with him, I think he will not say that this breath, which we alternately take in from the surrounding air and give back, is not with a person when it is in the person. For a person has it both with him and in him when he receives it by inhaling. But when he returns it by exhaling, he has it with him no more than he has it in him.

## CHAPTER III. It Is Therefore False That the Word Which Is with God Is Outside God and Not in God. It Is Utterly Absurd That We Should Be Interior to God but the Word Exterior. Another Absurdity Would Result If the Creature Were Set Before Its Maker. An Even Greater Absurdity Follows: That the Creature Should Be of One Nature with the Creator

It was therefore useless for him, in that argument concerning the statement “The Word was with God,” to assert that whatever is in someone is always interior, while whatever is with someone is always exterior, when breath received into the body is in a person in such a way that it is also with the person. And again, when it is returned from the body, it is not with the person in the same way that it is not in the person.

He paid less attention to the fact that he was trying to establish this absurdity by an example than to the still graver absurdity in which he would subsequently find himself entangled. For when it is said, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word,” if everything that is with God is exterior and everything that is in God is interior, what remains for that most skilled disputant except to contend that we are superior to the Son of God?

For the Apostle says concerning God: “For in him we live and move and are” (Acts XVII, 28). And elsewhere: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him” (I Cor. VIII, 6). Now, whoever he may be who, under the Christian name, is not afraid to argue so rashly against Christ, when he hears that the Word is with God and that we are in God, let him say, if he dares, that the Word is exterior and we are interior.

If he thinks this should be said, let him pass judgment on his own statements. For in such a speech no other judge need be sought, since the very person who says this is plainly to be condemned by himself.

Again, what will he answer to that statement of the same blessed Paul in which he says concerning God: “For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory forever. Amen” (Rom. XI, 13)? Paul testifies that all things are from God, through God, and in God, whereas the evangelist John’s preaching makes known that the Word is with God.

But if, according to the Arian sense, everything that is in God is interior and everything that is with God is exterior, since the Arian believes that the Word, which is with God, is not in God but exterior, then the remaining conclusion is that what is with God is to be declared inferior to everything that is in God.

Once this has been accepted—for it is written of the Word, “All things were made through him”—the correct Arian rule of faith will be that the creature must be placed before the maker. Who would not now see into what precipice those heedless men fall who, resisting the true faith, strive to defend faithlessness?

For what else is accomplished by such words except that, in defending this opinion, the creature, forgetful of its condition and redemption, dares not only to make itself equal to the Son of God but even to place itself above him?

I am astonished that those who assert this do not consider how much worse a fruit of abominable blasphemy arises from it. For they say:

> “What is in God is to be believed to be interior; but what is with God is to be regarded as exterior. Therefore, if what is with God, and is exterior, is not to be believed to be of one nature with God, it follows that what is in God, and is interior, is to be believed to be of one substance with God.”

This reasoning is therefore brought to the conclusion that, just as the Word is separated from God’s nature on the ground that it is with God, so the creature, on the ground that it is in God, is believed to be of one nature with God.

Thus they are convicted of holding opinions by which they dare to place us before the Son and strive to make us equal to the Father. Those who dissent from the truth confuse everything in this way. Behold by what arguments unbelieving error is asserted; behold by what inventions the truth of the faith is attacked.

## CHAPTER IV. “They Said to Themselves, Thinking Wrongly.” To Speak to Oneself Is the Same as to Speak within Oneself. Likewise, to Speak within Oneself and to Think to Oneself Are the Same. Finally, to Think to Oneself and to Think in One’s Heart Are the Same

However violently heretics may strive to batter the holy Church with their rams, we are certain concerning the Lord our God that they will not be able to overthrow the city established upon a mountain. Rather, they completely overthrow and destroy themselves, those who provoke the true God, the only Son of God, with insulting assertions. Nor do they refrain from injuring the Father, while they repay the grace of the Savior with ingratitude.

Therefore it seems appropriate to seek the meaning of this word in other passages of Scripture, so that it may become clear whether, according to their opinion, we should always regard whatever is said to be with someone as exterior to that person.

In the Book of Wisdom we read the following concerning certain people: “They said to themselves, thinking wrongly” (Wis. II, 1). We demand from the Arians an explanation of this passage: does one who thinks “to himself” think inside himself or outside himself? For human thought is not only outside the human body; it is not even an action of the body.

Indeed, since that very thing called thought is found not only outside the human being but not even in the human body itself, who does not see that thought belongs solely to the soul, to which the power of thinking has been divinely given through the faculty of reason? In a human being, the mind rules by thinking, while the body provides service by acting.

Thought has been given to the human being where the distinction between good and evil has been implanted. The inner person, therefore, performs the office of thought; he also received the power of understanding because he was created in the image of God.

When a person thinks to himself, then, he thinks not outside himself but within himself—even if thought belonged to the external person, he would not think outside himself. How much more, therefore, does he think within himself, since it is not the external person but the inner person who thinks?

Yet, according to the testimony of Scripture, he is said to think “to himself,” and this is plainly found not in the activity of the external person but of the inner person. For Scripture says, as was already cited above: “They said to themselves, thinking wrongly.”

What is it to speak to oneself except to speak in one’s heart? Hence elsewhere it is said: “What you say in your hearts, and be moved to compunction on your beds” (Ps. IV, 5).

To speak to oneself, therefore, is the same as to speak within oneself. Accordingly, that Pharisee who had invited the Lord to dine, when a sinful woman entered, drenched the Savior’s feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair, was thinking within himself; he was certainly saying within himself what he was saying by thinking.

For the evangelist says: “But when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said within himself” (Luke VII, 39). What does “he said within himself” mean except “he thought within himself”?

Nevertheless, by the teaching of Scripture we know that one who thinks within himself thinks to himself. That is why it is said: “They said to themselves, thinking wrongly.”

But lest the Arians wish to join the expression “within themselves” not to the preceding words but to the following words—so that the sentence would not mean “they said to themselves,” but rather “they said,” followed afterward by “thinking to themselves”—let them hear further testimonies from the divine Scriptures and recognize that the activity of human thought belongs not to the external but to the inner person.

The evangelist says that when a paralytic was brought to the Lord, and the Lord saw the faith of those who had lowered him through the roof tiles, he said, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.” And behold, certain scribes said within themselves, “This man blasphemes.” When Jesus saw their thoughts, he said, “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. IX, 2–3; Mark II, 4–5; Luke V, 18–19).

The people whom the evangelist said had spoken within themselves, the Lord says had thought evil in their hearts. What is it to think evil in one’s heart except to think wrongly within oneself?

However the Arians distinguish the meaning of this passage, they must find there the confusion of their own perversity. Would that they were so confounded by their error that they might be converted to the truth!

For if they say that this verse of Scripture must be divided as follows—“They said within themselves, thinking wrongly”—and, joining “within themselves” to the preceding words, distinguish it in this way: “They said within themselves,” adding afterward, “thinking wrongly,” they are immediately refuted by David’s utterance, which shows that to speak within oneself is nothing other than to speak in one’s heart. For he says: “What you say in your hearts” (Ps. IV, 5).

But if they wish to distinguish it otherwise, joining “within themselves” not to the preceding words but to what follows, so that they first say “they said,” pause, and then add, “thinking wrongly within themselves” (Wis. II, 1), let them also hear the Savior’s rebuke and recognize that thoughts belong to the heart. For he says: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Luke V, 22).

Elsewhere the same Lord also teaches: “For evil thoughts proceed from the heart” (Matt. XV, 19). And again he says: “The good person brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil person brings forth evil things from the evil treasure” (Matt. XII, 35).

Do they now recognize the great error in which they are entangled, those who strive to assert that the Word is with God not interiorly but exteriorly?

## CHAPTER V. Her Memory Is Known to God and to Human Beings. “I Will Enter to Him,” and “We Will Come to Him and Make Our Dwelling with Him.” Thus the Word Is Both with God and in God. Likewise, What Is in God Is the Same as What Is with God; There Is No Iniquity with God. One and the Same Spirit in Moses, David, and Paul

Again, in the same book we read this written concerning Wisdom: “For her memory is immortal, because it is known to God and to human beings” (Wis. IV, 1).

But how is she known among human beings if she is not within human beings but outside them? Unless she enters the human soul, she cannot be known to a human being. For Scripture says of her: “Although she remains in herself, she renews all things, and through the nations she passes into holy souls” (Wis. VII, 27).

And so that it may be understood that “to pass into souls” means nothing other than “to enter souls,” the text of Holy Scripture again speaks of her in this way:

> “She delivered the righteous people and blameless offspring from the nations that oppressed them. She entered the soul of the servant of the Lord and stood against dreadful kings with wonders and signs” (Wis. X, 15).

She also indicates this entrance by which she enters souls in the Apocalypse of John, saying:

> “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. III, 20).

By this entrance the Father and the Son come to the one who loves them and make their dwelling with him, as the Son himself says:

> “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23).

But if, when the Father and the Son come to the one with whom they make their dwelling, they are not interior but exterior, let them tell us where they come to him and make their dwelling with him.

Meanwhile, we know through Paul’s preaching that Christ dwells interiorly in his faithful, for he says: “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, in the inner person” (Eph. III, 17).

Or perhaps they will say that Christ dwells in our inner person through faith in one way, but that, when he comes with the Father, he makes his dwelling with the one who loves him in another way—so that Christ meanwhile can dwell alone in our inner person, while the Father, remaining exterior, not only cannot himself remain interiorly with the one with whom he makes his dwelling, but also prevents the Son, through the fellowship of his coming, from being able to dwell in the inner person.

The Son of God also promised the Holy Spirit to his faithful in such a way that he would remain with them and be in them. For he says:

> “If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive because it does not see him or know him. But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you” (John XIV, 15–17).

Behold: with whom he remains, in them the Holy Spirit is. Let them say, then, what difference there can be here between his remaining with them and his being in them. For in one passage both prepositions are used, and the possibility of both conditions is assigned to the Holy Spirit: he remains with those in whom he is.

Is it really the case that the Holy Spirit remains with the faithful in such a way that he can be in those faithful, while the Word, who is God, is with God in such a way that he cannot be in God?

What shall I say to those who wish to argue from the Scriptures in such a way that they seek no path to spiritual understanding, and who, turning their eyes away from the true light, continually delight in wandering in darkness?

Holy Scripture itself shows in other passages that being with God is the same as being in God. For Moses says: “A faithful God, in whom there is no iniquity, the Lord is just and holy” (Deut. XXXII, 4). David also sings: “For the Lord our God is just, and there is no iniquity in him” (Ps. XCI, 16). But the Apostle Paul says that there is no iniquity with God. For he says: “Is there iniquity with God? By no means!” (Rom. IX, 14).

Let the Arians choose here whatever they wish and, to display their wisdom clearly, pass judgment on the legal, prophetic, and apostolic statements.

Moses says: “A faithful God, in whom there is no iniquity.” David also says: “The Lord our God is just, and there is no iniquity in him.” But Paul says: “Is there iniquity with God? By no means!”

Either, then, let them admit that the apostolic sense agrees with the legal and prophetic sense, or let them say that the Apostle Paul differs from the legal and prophetic understanding.

The Apostle Paul says that he has the same spirit of faith that blessed David had and that holy Moses received, as he himself testifies, saying:

> “But having the same spirit of faith, as it is written: ‘I believed, therefore I spoke’; we too believe, and therefore we speak” (II Cor. IV, 13).

But how did they have one spirit of faith if they had different opinions concerning the faithful God? There is a great difference in meaning if what Paul says—“There is no iniquity with God”—is different from what Moses and David say—“There is no iniquity in God.”

And if, when Paul says that he has the same spirit of faith as the prophets had, there is a different meaning in their faith, then—God forbid—the Apostle must be declared a liar, since he testifies that Christ speaks in him. For he says: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (II Cor. XIII, 3).

But because Christ truly spoke in Paul, Paul is certainly not a liar. And because he does not lie when he says that he has the same spirit of faith, the two senses are found to agree: what Moses and David said—there is no iniquity in God—is the same as what Paul says—there is no iniquity with God.

If this does not please them, and they think that the two statements say opposite things, then the only thing left for them is to contradict either the prophets or the Apostle.

## CHAPTER VI. “With Whom There Is No Change.” Many Examples in Which *With* Is Used for *In*

Although the heretics’ opinion is shown by so many and such great testimonies to be unsupported by any truth, let them nevertheless answer what they think about that passage of the Apostle James, where he says:

> “Every good giving and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (James I, 17).

With whom there is no change, there is certainly no mutability; and with whom there is no mutability, there is immutability. Let them say, then, whether this immutability, which is with God, is exterior or interior. For if it is interior, then this is precisely what it means to be in God and to be with God.

Let them cease, therefore, from thinking perversely and hasten to agree with Catholic rectitude. But if this immutability, which is with God, is believed to be not interior but exterior, then it is certainly not believed to be in God. And if immutability is not believed to be in God, God himself is consequently declared mutable.

And lest they dare [or wish] to assign this to the Son, let them hear that the Father of lights is named in the same passage.

Therefore, when we hear that there is no change with God, let us understand this according to the truth of the Catholic faith: there is no change in God. And when it is said, “The Word was with God,” let us understand nothing other than, “The Word was in God.”

When Wisdom says in Proverbs, “I was with him, arranging” (Prov. VIII, 30), let us understand nothing other than, “I was in him, arranging.”

When it is said to God, “With you is the fountain of life” (Ps. III, 5), let us understand nothing other than, “In you is the fountain of life.”

And when John says, “We announce to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was manifested to us” (I John I, 2), let us understand nothing other than, “the eternal life that was in the Father.”

For truly God the Word is with God, because God the Word is in God. Truly wisdom is with the wise God, because wisdom is in the wise God. Truly life is with the living God, because God is life in the living God. Truly God the truth is with the true God, because God is truth in the true God. Truly God the power is with the strong God, because God is power in the strong God.

But why should it be surprising that the Son’s being with the Father is the same as his being in the Father—since, naturally born from the Father, he remains always in the Father—when we also read concerning human beings, insofar as substance is concerned, by which human beings naturally exist, that when something is said to be with them, it means nothing other than that it is in them?

Accordingly, we shall produce very clear testimonies. In the Book of Isaiah there is contained the prayer of King Hezekiah, which he poured out to God after fifteen years had been added to his life. Among other things, he says:

> “My spirit was made to be with me, like a weaver approaching to cut off the web” (Isa. XXXVIII, 12).

What else is understood here by “my spirit with me” except “my spirit in me”? Or will it also be said here that a human spirit is with a human being but is not in the human being, when the Apostle clearly says:

> “For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him?” (I Cor. II, 11).

And what of the statement quoted above, “They said within themselves, thinking wrongly” (Wis. II, 1)? What else is it than “they said inside themselves”?

Again, in the Book of Wisdom it is said: “Thinking this within myself and remembering it in my heart, that immortality is in the consideration of wisdom” (Wis. VIII, 17). By saying that he thinks this within himself and remembers it in his heart, he showed that both the thought and the remembrance were present not externally but internally.

It is also said in Proverbs:

> “My son, let not evil thought seize you, which abandons the teaching of youth and forgets the divine covenant; for it has set its house in death, and its paths in the underworld with earth-dwellers” (Prov. II, 16).

If, then, the evil thought that placed its house with death is outside death and not in death, it plainly lives. And if, placed with the underworld, it is not in the underworld, it remains that this thought, which is neither in death nor in the underworld, must be said to have life in heaven.

That is why it is said to God, “For you have rescued my soul from death” (Ps. CXIV, 8), because by faith he gave life to the soul, saying, “But my righteous one lives by faith” (Rom. I, 17).

And again, for this reason it is said to him, “You have rescued my soul from the lower underworld” (Ps. LXXXV, 13), because souls are rescued from the underworld by God’s grace so that they may dwell in heaven. Hence the Apostle says: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20).

Now, how was the soul that was with death through evil thought freed from death if it was not in death? And how was it snatched from the underworld if, being situated in the underworld, it was not in the underworld?

For plainly, if it had not been in death, it would not have been dead. Who does not know that through an evil will—that is, through sin—the soul dies, when God says: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. XVIII, 20)?

It is certain, therefore, that when the soul is thinking wrongly and is with death, it is in death; and when it is with those below, it is in the underworld.

What of the fact that the Savior also says: “The things that are impossible with human beings are possible with God” (Matt. XIX, 26; Luke XVIII, 27)? Shall we therefore say that all things are possible for God in such a way that this very possibility is with God but is not in God? What power does God have with himself if he does not have the very power in himself?

## CHAPTER VII. “Do You Not Believe That I Am in the Father, and the Father Is in Me?” The Word Is with God as a Word Is in the Mind
By these and similar testimonies it is clear that when it is said, “The Word was with God,” nothing other than “The Word was in God” should be understood. For the Son himself, who is the Word God, testifies not only that the Father is in him but also that he is in the Father, saying: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John 14:10).

Now, the Son’s being with the Father and being in the Father should not be understood as though one human being might be with another, whether by the right of hospitality [alternative: hospitalitatis, “hospitality”] or by the affection of love. The apostle Paul says that he stayed with the apostle Peter for fifteen days (Gal. 1:18), evidently by the right of hospitality and in the purity of affection. Although, through the unity of faith and love, their souls were one and their hearts one, Paul nevertheless did not remain with Peter as the Word remains with God. For a human being cannot be with another human being in the way that the Word God is with God the Father. A human being is with another in such a way that he can not only fail to be with him but, even when he is with him, cannot be substantially within him.

Indeed, whoever is with another in this way is outside him, because, even when he is with him in the sincerity of affection, he is distinguished from him by place, however great the mutual love that unites them may be. But the Word is with God as a word is in the mind, as a plan is in the heart. For when the mind has a word within itself, it has it by thinking, since to speak within oneself is nothing other than to think within oneself.

When, therefore, the mind thinks and, by thinking, generates a word within itself, it generates the word from its own substance. It generates it from itself in such a way that, once generated, it has it with itself. Nor does the word that arises from the mind possess anything less than the mind from which it arises; for as great as the mind is that generates the word, so great also is the word itself. Just as the word is born from the whole mind, so, once born, it remains within the whole mind.

And because, when the mind is thinking, there is no part of it in which the word is not present, the word is therefore as great as the mind itself from which it proceeds. When it is with that mind, it is in that mind; and whatever the mind itself is, that is what the word is which is from it and in it. As great as the mind is, so great also is the word, because it is from the whole mind and in the whole mind. Thus the word itself is as great as the mind together with the word; for the word does not arise from the mind in such a way that it is separated from it by place.

That birth, indeed, which shows what something is and from what it is, itself shows that what has been born cannot exist outside that from which it was born, nor be less in any respect. Rather, it is from that source in such a way that it is with and in that source; it is as great from it as it is in it, and as great in it as it is with it.

## Chapter VIII. We are not in God as the Word God is in God. God generated us in one way, the Word in another. The heretics’ blasphemies against the Son of God.

Scripture does, in a certain sense, say that we too are in God and with God, but not in the manner in which the Word God is with God and in God—the only-begotten Son. For it is said of us that “in him we live and move and have our being.” And it is said to God himself: “If we have not sinned, we know that we are counted as being with you.”

Nevertheless, when this is said of us, our natural unity with God is not being revealed; rather, either the power of the Creator or the mercy of the Redeemer is being understood. For we who believe are in God and with God in the same way that, being begotten from God, we are sons of God. For it is written: “Beloved, now we are sons of God” (1 John 3:2). And again: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth” (James 1:18).

God therefore begot us by the word of truth, whereas that Word begot truth. He gave us the power to become sons of God; but he was not made the Son of God by power—he was naturally born from God as the Son of God. God begot us by his will, because the will preceded our generation. In the generation of the Only-begotten, however, no will of the one generating preceded it; there eternal birth remains without beginning—naturalis (“natural”) [alternative: naturali, “natural”].

Thus, we have been begotten, but not as the only-begotten God; we are sons of God, but not as the one and true Son; and we are gods, but not as the Word, who is true God. So too we are in God and with God, but not as the Word God is with God and in God—the Word who was naturally born from God.

Although he is called Son and we are called sons, he is called God and we are called gods, he is begotten and we are begotten, there is nevertheless a great difference in reality between what appears to sound alike in name. He is naturally what he is—God, Son, and Only-begotten—because he was born from the Father’s nature. We, however, are gods, sons, and begotten ones not by nature but by grace, because, although we did not possess by nature the ability to be this, it was freely given to us that we should become so.

If the heretics, through God’s merciful gift, perceive this distinction, they will see the true light and will cease from their insults against the Only-begotten Son. They disparage him not only in respect of his being with God, but also strive to deny that he possessed a human soul. The Son of God himself identified them in a verse of the psalm, saying: “This is the work of those who slander me before God and speak evil against my soul” (Ps. 108:20).

For who slanders Christ more grievously before God than one who, hearing that the Word God is with God, says that the same Word is not in God? Or who speaks more evil against Christ’s soul than one who denies that Christ possessed a human soul? The Word who is God is with God, from whom he is, in such a way that through the unity of nature he is in God and, through that same unity of nature, is one God with him. That soul, together with the flesh assumed, was received by the Only-begotten God, so that in Christ our soul and our flesh might together be saved.

Without doubt, the one who recognizes in him the full truth of both the divine and human nature will obtain everlasting salvation from him.

[Col. 0205B]

**A Single Book of Saint Fulgentius Against the Arians, Containing Ten Replies to Ten Objections. (C)**

It was said that the Father ineffably begot the Son from himself—that is, from what he himself is. It was added that he was born not from outside but from God. These points require no reply, because they agree with our faith.

### First Objection

What is to be said about this? If he was born from God, he is from within God; but if he is not from within, neither is he from him. If different terms are used, what benefit is there if the truth itself is not confessed?

### Reply

Certainly, when the Father and the Son are named, a difference of words is recognized in these two names. Indeed, through these two different names the one nature of both is signified. The difference between these names does not divide their natures; it reveals the truth of the generation, so that from one true Father we may recognize one true Son to have come forth.

Thus, while the true generation of the Father and the true birth of the Son are proclaimed, in one begetter and one begotten not only the unity of substance but also the distinct property of person in each may be recognized. Otherwise one might think that the one who begot was himself born, or that the one who was born was something other than the one who begot him.

For the Father is not himself the Son, since the distinct property of the persons is preserved in both. But what the Father is, the Son also is: from God, God; from the perfect, perfect; from the immense, immense; from the omnipotent, omnipotent. The Son was born from the eternal Father, coeternal with him, as the same truth says: “All that the Father has is mine” (John 17:10).

“Father” and “Son,” therefore, are relational names. They do not separate the nature of the begetter and the begotten; rather, they signify one nature without doubt. We call something relational when we refer it to the recognition of another, so that by naming one we indicate another. Thus, among human beings, these relational terms are frequently used: father and son, son and father, father-in-law and son-in-law, son-in-law and father-in-law. A man is called a father so that he may be understood to have begotten a son; a man is called a son so that he may be shown to have been begotten by a father.

Nor is a diversity of natures found in this diversity of names, since both are called human beings in the same way, although one is called father and the other son. The one nature of father and son could not be recognized if these were not different names. For if both were called fathers, they would plainly be unlike in nature: each would exist from himself and would not possess a common substance with the other. Nor would there be one deity if they did not have one nature. It would then follow that two fathers would beget two sons, because unless true offspring existed from each of them, the truth of the name “father” would appear in neither.

Now, in the case of two sons born from different fathers, even if there could be no difference in their relational name, let us consider whether they could have a common nature. Who does not see that the name “son” is one in both, while their nature is not one? Each son has a nature in common not with the other son, with whom he shares one relational name, but with the father from whom he came forth.

But why continue arguing about two fathers and two sons, when the truth of this assertion does not require a diversity of persons and can more readily be supported by considering one human being? From this example it may be recognized that the difference of relational names does not chiefly indicate a difference of natures, but pertains above all to the signification of persons: when one is indicated, the person of the other is also recognized.

There is, however, one name that is always common to father and son—not one that displays personal relation, but one that demonstrates substantial property. Consider Seth, born from Adam his father, and begotten from one who was not himself begotten. Was Adam called the son of his father? Seth could not be called a father until he had reached mature manhood and begotten a son. Before he begot one, he was only a son; but when he begot one, he also began to be a father.

When the additional name “father” was therefore applied, no natural difference occurred in him. Although one man had begun to bear these two names, his nature was not changed, divided, or duplicated. He was a son because he had come forth from a father; he was a father because he had begotten a son. Yet he did not possess the nature of the son in which he had been born in such a way that, remaining in it, he could not be a father. Nor did he acquire another essence together with the name “father,” so that he lost the substance of the son in which he had been born.

Rather, what is true is this: just as he was a human being when he became a son by being born, so he remained a human being when he became a father by begetting. He was none other than a human being—what Adam was, from whom he himself was born, and what Enos was, who was begotten from him.

Therefore, in God the Father and God the Son, while the distinct property of the persons is preserved, let it not be called impossible that this should be established by the example of any human being. Let us distinguish what is understood to pertain to relation from what pertains to substance.

“Father” and “Son” are names of relation; “God” is the one name of substance. The individual names of relation are therefore retained, while they commonly possess one name of substance. Although one is called Father and the other Son, the Son is nevertheless God in the same way that the Father is God. Through those two names the true generation is recognized; through the one common name, substantial unity is demonstrated.

### Second Objection

We do not recall ever having read what was proposed above, because it is written of him: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). And did Scripture not say, “No one,” who could declare it? These men must be admonished to say that they can know that his generation is indescribable, but not unknowable.

### Reply

It is written: “I believed, and therefore I spoke; we also believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4:13). We confidently profess that the generation of the Son is indescribable but not unknowable. For it does not follow that what cannot be described cannot be known, since no one can describe God himself, yet no one is thereby permitted to remain ignorant of him.

God is so far knowable, although indescribable, that the blessed Apostle declares certain people inexcusable for this very reason: although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks (Rom. 1:21). For if the Lord had not wished us to know him, he would not have said: “If you had known me, you would certainly have known my Father also” (John 14:17).

Nor would he have rebuked Philip, who said, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us,” with these words: “Have I been with you for so long, and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” By this saying the Lord wished to show that everything being sought was found in him. For it cannot be that the Son possesses anything less than the eternal and immense Father, in whom “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:9).

God, therefore, is not unknowable although he is indescribable. He is known by believers so that he may be loved, although he cannot be described either by human tongues or by angelic ones. The apostle Paul shows that ignorance of God is nothing other than slavery to demons, saying: “But at that time, when you did not know God, you served those who by nature are not gods” (Gal. 4:9).

Therefore, just as we ought not to be ignorant of Christ’s divinity, although we cannot describe it, so, although no one is able to provide an account of his birth, knowledge of it has not been taken away from believers. For who would proclaim one as born whose birth he did not know? Who would call him Son and not know that he was begotten? Who could believe in the Father without considering that he had begotten?

The Father truly begot, and the Son truly was born. We have therefore been granted recognition of the Son’s true birth, although we have not been granted the ability to explain how he was born. For the prophet did not say, “Who has known his generation?” but “Who has declared it?” (Isa. 53:8).

Accordingly, we rightly recognize the divine generation, insofar as it is permitted to human beings, when we both call it a true generation and proclaim that this true generation is indescribable. The Son is therefore recognized as truly born from the Father’s substance, since his birth, which is from the indescribable God, is proclaimed indescribable. The true birth of the Son is unquestionably indescribable because he shares one substance with the indescribable begetter.

### Third Objection

It is correct to profess his generation in the manner in which the Lord himself speaks through the Scriptures: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways; before the ages he founded me” (Prov. 8:22). And it continues: “And before all the hills he begot me.” Again: “I came forth from the Father and came into this world” (John 16:29). Again: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Ps. 2:7).

After he became known in the flesh, the evangelist professes concerning him: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). And the Apostle says: “He is the Firstborn of all creation” (Col. 1:15).

There it is: we profess him created, founded, and begotten, without any unreasonable ambiguity.

### Reply

In both births of Christ, the one who professes in Christ, the Son of God and of man, both full divinity from the Father and a complete human being from his mother is not deceived. He recognizes both substances as true in him, distinguishing with faithful devotion what belongs to eternity and what belongs to time.

We must not be ignorant that he who, in the world and according to the flesh, was created from a human being, was, according to his divinity, generated from the Father as Creator without beginning. In that birth which has no beginning, the majesty of eternal divinity is recognized; in this birth, the mercy of eternal divinity is found. For he who was not created but was the Creator, begotten from the Creator, had in his goodness created the human being; afterward, in his mercy, he himself was created from a human being.

He did not disdain to become his own work, so that through him the condition of his work might be restored. Wishing, therefore, to foretell the mystery of this creation and to reveal the future sacrament of his Incarnation, Wisdom said in the prophetic manner by which future events are customarily narrated under the expression of past time: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his work” (Prov. 8:22).

He reveals the reason for the creation when he does not conceal that he was created as the beginning of God’s ways, for God’s work. To show that what is called created does not belong to that eternal birth but to this temporal one, in which the Son of God is found to have assumed flesh, consider what he said beforehand: “If I announce to you the things that happen daily, I shall recall to declare the things that are from the age” (ibid. 21).

Since these things were happening daily, he announces beforehand that things done from the age are to be declared. He shows that what he is about to tell us belongs not to eternity but to time. For this reason he immediately added: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his work.”

That Wisdom was created was not before the ages but from the age; and that the Son was created as the beginning of the Lord’s ways means nothing other than that he himself became the way for us, so that, with him as guide and ruler, the entrance to advancement in virtue might be opened to us by the divine gift of the adoption we have received.

To make this clearer, we must attend to the fact that the Son was made the beginning of creation not to establish a new creation once again, but to renew what had long before perished through decay (vetustate; alternatives: vetustatem, vetustam). The apostles too are found to have made the beginning of this creation, since through their ministry they restored what had previously collapsed. Blessed James says of God the Father: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth, that we might be a kind of beginning of his creation” (James 1:18).

The clearest indications therefore demonstrate that in this passage “creation” refers not to the making of all creatures but to the restoration of human beings. Thus holy David prayed when he had been terrified by the recollection of a double crime—not only the violation of a marriage but also the killing of an innocent husband. As he considered washing away the stain of so great a crime in a flood of tears, he poured forth amid the groans that bore witness to his grief: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Ps. 50:12).

By this he signified that a clean heart was created in him when the right spirit within his inward parts was renewed. Christ therefore willed to be created for this purpose, and he willed his apostles to become the beginning of this creation, so that through him the human being who had perished through old age might be renewed.

Wisdom said that she had been founded before the age in order to demonstrate that her birth, by which she was born from the Father, was unchangeable. For what is said to be founded cannot be overthrown by any reasoning; and what cannot be overthrown does not change.

But so that the birth of his divinity may be understood to be without beginning, attention should be given to what follows: “Before he made the earth, before he established the abysses, before the springs of waters came forth, before the mountains were set in place—before all the hills he begot me” (Prov. 8:23–26).

Whenever this word “before” is used, every beginning whatsoever is preceded. This must be considered because wherever the divine and eternal birth of the Son is demonstrated, the time of his birth is not stated; rather, “before” is always placed there. Thus, whatever a human being wishes to conceive of infinity and eternity, the birth of the Son must always be conceived as preceding everything conceived by thought. In this way the birth of the Son of God is recognized as without beginning, since nothing is continually found there except what is placed before all else.

We would like our opponents to answer whether “begotten” is the same as “created.” If the two are considered one and the same, let them say that the world was begotten by God, by whom it could not be begotten, and created. Let them also call unbelieving human beings sons of God, although they have not been freed from the power of darkness; let them call heirs of future blessedness those who do not receive faith in the Savior.

But if, as is true, to be created is one thing and to be begotten another, let it be distinguished in which substance Christ is said to have been created by God and in which he is proclaimed to have been begotten from the Father. For the very passage of Scripture readily shows those who inquire in what nature Christ should be called created.

It is, namely, in the nature in which it calls him “Lord,” so that he may show in himself the truth of the form of a servant, just as he also speaks in the psalm, saying: “O Lord, I am your servant; I am your servant and the son of your handmaid” (Ps. 116:16).

He who was born from the handmaid is therefore the servant; he who was generated from the Father is the Lord. It was because of the form of a servant that he said, “The Lord created me.” He does not say that he was created by the Father, but by the Lord.

Where he is said to have been begotten according to his divinity, the Father is immediately named, as he truly said: “I came forth from the Father and came” (John 8:42). And the blessed evangelist says of him: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father” (John 1:14).

You see that he did not say here “from the Lord,” but “from the Father.” When the Apostle calls him “the Firstborn of all creation” (Col. 1:15), “creation” is understood to mean the creation that was restored, not the creation that was made. It is the creation of the sons of God, through which those who had been his servants became his brothers—he who is not ashamed, according to the Apostle’s statement, to call us brothers, saying:

“I will proclaim your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will praise you.” And again: “I will put my trust in him.” And again: “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me.”

Therefore, since the children shared in blood and flesh, he himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death he might destroy the one who held the power of death—that is, the devil—and free those who throughout their lives were held in slavery through fear of death. For he did not take hold of angels anywhere, but he took hold of the offspring of Abraham. Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make atonement for the sins of the people.

For because he himself suffered and was tested, he is able to help those who are tested (Heb. 2:11–18). We hear that Christ has brothers; we hear of the offspring of Abraham; we hear that through death he destroyed the one who held the power of death; we hear that he was tested; we hear that he suffered—and do we hesitate to profess that Christ is the Firstborn of all creation according to the mystery of the Incarnation?

Again, the blessed Apostle shows by the testimony of his preaching in what sense we must understand him as Firstborn: “We know,” he says, “that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose, who are saints. For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the Firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. 8:28–29).

He who, according to his divinity, had always been the Only-begotten without brothers became, according to his humanity, the Firstborn among many brothers.

This is taught still more clearly by another testimony of the Apostle, where he is called “the Firstborn from the dead” (Col. 1:18). For what is “the Firstborn from the dead” except Christ Jesus, the first human being from among sinful human beings, exalted as the Son of God?

He was born not as a sinner from sinners, as a human being from human beings, but as a human being, received by God without any sin, so that he might reconcile sinful human beings to God after freeing them from every sin. Such a human being had to be received by God, through whom human beings could be joined to God by gratuitous justification.

He is therefore “the Firstborn of all creation” (Col. 1:15)—the creation of which we heard the blessed apostle James speak shortly before: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth, that we might be a kind of beginning of his creation” (James 1:18).

The apostle Paul also speaks of this creation: “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation” (2 Cor. 5:17). David had also foretold it: “Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 104:30).

Otherwise, if Christ is understood as the Firstborn of all creation according to his divine birth, by what testimonies is he shown to be the Firstborn from the dead before all creation, when those who had not yet been created could not be called dead?

We therefore recognize Christ as the Only-begotten from the Father and profess him as the Firstborn from the virgin [alternative: profess him]. In the former birth he is truly the Only-begotten, in which he was born without beginning, God alone from God alone. In this birth he is the Firstborn of all creation (Col. 1:16), that is, of those whom he graciously adopted as his brothers through faith.

“As many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12).

This generation is also recognized as proclaimed in the second psalm, where Christ, speaking in the person of the human nature he assumed, says: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Ps. 2:7).

To show that this had been said according to the future mystery of the Incarnation, he added: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession.”

For how could he ask to possess the ends of the earth according to the form of God, when he promises and grants his faithful the kingdom of heaven, which is greater? He therefore who, remaining in the form of God, became a servant for the salvation of servants, asked, according to the form of a servant, to receive the nations as his inheritance and the ends of the earth as his possession.

According to his divine nature, just as he made all things with the Father—whatever is in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible—so with the Father he always possessed all things.

That the generation indicated by the second psalm pertains to the mystery of the Incarnation is attested by the book of the Acts of the Apostles, when Paul was speaking in the synagogue. His words to the Jews are found to be as follows:

“And we announce to you the promise made to our fathers, that God has fulfilled this for our children by raising Jesus, as it is also written in the second psalm: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Acts 13:32).

The Apostle therefore shows that what the psalm said was spoken of the Son in the sense in which he declares that he was raised from the dead. Let us therefore consider what nature in Christ rose from the dead, and it will be understood in what respect Christ, begotten today, received the ends of the earth as his possession.

Let the property of both natures in Christ be recognized, so that without error he may be understood as created, founded, and begotten. He was begotten and founded according to the fact that, as Lord, he was ineffably born from the Lord; he was created according to the human birth by which, as a servant, he was born from the handmaid. Thus, for our salvation, the Father might beget by grace him whom he alone had begotten by nature before all things.

Accordingly, we must recognize both natures in Christ the Lord, so that we may neither appear arrogant toward the Creator nor be ungrateful for the benefit of our Savior [alternative: be judged ungrateful]. Otherwise, before the Savior, the one who denies the true deity of the Creator, God the Father, denies for himself the salvation he seeks.

### Fourth Objection

But those who irrationally presume to say that the Son was born from the Father’s substance should nevertheless demonstrate from the Scriptures how it is not a false profession arising from error when someone, while saying that his generation is indescribable, asserts that he was born from the substance of the Father.

### Response

[Col. 0212C] The deficiency of an assertion is recognized when someone tries to destroy another’s rule of faith while unwilling to state clearly the firm conviction of his own belief. For this reason we believe and confess that the Son of God was born from the substance of the Father—that is, from that which the Father is. For whatever is not the substance of God we cannot worship or honor as God, carefully observing the commandment of the Law, which says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one.” And: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deut. 6:4, 13). We believe that this God is not the Father alone, but the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

For our faith, by which we worship and fear one God, is neither contracted by personal union nor divided by substantial diversity: otherwise, by worshiping different substances, we would worship gods in the pagan manner; or, with Sabellius, we would deny the Son and the Spirit by failing to preserve the persons in the Trinity [Col. 0212D]. The correctness of this faith is taught to us not only by prophetic but also by apostolic truth. For when Isaiah [Latin: *Isaiae*; alternate form: *Isaias*] is deemed worthy of the vision of God, the conviction of this faith is conveyed when two seraphim cry out: “Holy, holy, holy” (Isa. 6:3), and proclaim once: “The Lord God of Sabaoth.” What does it mean that “Holy” is said three times, unless there are three persons in the Godhead? Why is “the Lord God” said once, unless there is one substance in the Godhead?

The Lord also, wishing to bless the people through Moses, commanded that the blessing be given in this form: “Thus,” he said, “you shall bless my people, and I shall bless them. May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord illuminate his face upon you and have mercy on you. May the Lord lift up his face upon you [Col. 0213A] and give you peace” (Num. 6:23–26). The Lord is named three times, yet one Lord is always named, so that in the Trinity, which is the true God, neither the distinctiveness of the persons is confused nor the unity of substance denied.

David too, wholly pleasing to God, prays under this conviction that the grace of divine blessing be poured out upon the faithful people in these words: “May God bless us, God our God; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him” (Ps. 66:8).

The blessed Apostle agrees with this statement. After saying in one place, “There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we for him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him” (1 Cor. 8:6), he also says of the Holy Spirit: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4:30). [Col. 0213B] Remembering that he had said “from the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit,” in order to show that this Trinity is one God, he says elsewhere: “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things. To him be glory forever and ever” (Rom. 11:36). He expressed the conclusion in the singular: “To him be glory.”

That the Son was born from the substance of the Father is rightly proclaimed by Christian faith and recalled by Holy Scripture. The Apostle Paul says of the Son of God: “Who, being the radiance of his glory and the likeness of his substance” (Heb. 1:3). The Lord again says to Jeremiah: “Upon the mountains take up lamentation, and people did not hear the voice of my substance, from the birds of heaven to the cattle” (Jer. 9:10). [Note: [Col. 0213D] The Corbie manuscript adds: “And mourning over the paths of the wilderness, because they have failed from [Col. 0214D] the fact that they are not.”]

That the Son is the substance of the Father the Book of Wisdom clearly demonstrates, saying: “You fed your people with the food of angels; you supplied [Col. 0213C] them bread from heaven, prepared without labor, possessing every delight in itself and every taste of sweetness. For you were displaying your substance and your sweetness, which you have toward your children” (Wis. 16:20–21). Scripture testifies that the bread given from heaven is the substance and sweetness of God; and that the bread given from heaven is the Son of God is shown by the words of the Son himself, who says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41). Of this bread David says: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25).

Behold, we believe reasonably that the Son came forth from the substance of the Father, and we also confirm it by testimonies, Scripture saying: “Whoever loves the one who begets loves him who has been born from him” (1 John 5:1). True faith knows what it believes, even if it cannot yet see what it hopes for and believes.

Those who deny that the Son was born from the substance of the Father ought certainly to say [Col. 0213D] from what they think the Son of God came into being: from nothing, or from something? If he came into being from nothing, he must be called a creature, not the Creator. But if he is said to have come from something, then God also made that very thing from which he begot the Son. Or perhaps they say that he had something coeternal from which he could beget the Son? If something coeternal is thought to have existed from which the begotten Son is believed to have come, the error of the Manichaeans is confirmed by this assertion. But if there was nothing from which the Son could be begotten, and yet he is not said to have been born from the substance of the Father, then the only remaining possibility is that they openly confess that the Son of God came into being from nothing, while striving to proclaim him lesser in divinity.

[Col. 0214A] But perhaps it is said that the Son was born by the will of the Father. Let them say, then, whether the Father begot the Son from himself or from elsewhere. If he begot him from himself, the will could not have preceded the generation, because it is impious to believe that something which had not always existed newly occurred in God. Hence it is understood that God created every creature from nothing by his will, but begot the Son from his substance, or nature.

If the Son is said to have been born from elsewhere, either his origin is asserted to be from nothing, or—as was said above—it is proclaimed contrary to the rule of true faith that something besides God always existed. For the blessed Apostle, knowing that the Son was begotten as true God from the Father’s essence, and therefore, with the Father, one Lord and God, and not forgetting [Col. 0214B] the Lord’s command by which we are forbidden to serve two masters, commanded that the Lord Christ be served as true God. He knew that Christ was to be honored equally with the Father, since the Lord himself says: “That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John 5:23).

John the Apostle testifies that he is true God, with the Lord himself speaking in him, saying: “That we may be in his true Son Jesus Christ; this is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). Therefore the rule of true faith must be held: the Son of God is believed to have been ineffably born without beginning from the substance of the Father—that is, from that which the Father himself is—and is worshiped and held [or: feared] as true God with the Father. [Note: [Col. 0213D] The Corbie manuscript lacks *per* (“through”).]

For it is not permitted to Christians to serve as true God one who is not God by nature; nor is it lawful for anyone not to serve Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, as true God. [Col. 0214C] The blessed Paul clearly shows that the one who serves Christ pleases God—Paul who had forbidden serving “gods” (alternative reading: “those”) that are not gods by nature—saying: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. For whoever serves Christ in this is pleasing to God” (Rom. 14:17).

Therefore, recognizing that Christ is true God, let us not dare to separate him from the equality of the Father’s substance. For he is true God who is God by nature; and God by nature is he who possessed divinity through the eternity of true birth, not one who acquired it by a gift of grace. [Note: [Col. 0214D] The Corbie manuscript has “by the gift of grace.”] For what is born is joined by origin; but what is adopted is advanced by generosity alone.

### Objection 5

[Col. 0214D] Disturbances of minds which are spoken without reason, when they urge attention, do not seem to have truth grasped or professed by them, because it is absurd to say or believe that the Father and the Son are unbegotten. Whoever persuades himself to devise these things wishes to deceive himself by a fraud which indeed requires this to be said by those who maintain that the Father and the Son are equal.

### Response

Those who wish to call the Father and the Son unbegotten certainly disturb minds that are either sluggish or ignorant; but those who are known to proclaim the Father and the Son equal do not do this. For in two unbegotten beings there is found a different divinity. But in one begotten—or only-begotten—being, from one unbegotten being, natural unity is demonstrated.

Two unbegotten beings cannot have one nature, since neither does one in one find a true generation from himself, nor does one truly recognize in himself the substance of birth [Col. 0215A] from one. We, however, neither call the Father and the Son two unbegotten beings nor name them two begotten beings; neither do we confuse them personally nor separate them substantially.

And therefore we call them equal without ambiguity, because we find them in no way different from each other: one begot one, and one was born from one. Since an unchangeable Son came forth from an unchangeable Father, and the eternal and perfect Father begot a coeternal and perfect Son, the Son therefore could possess neither a lesser nor a different substance from the true Father.

It is an insult to the divine nature if the Father, in begetting the Son, could not be in the Son as great as he remains in himself. Natural power is impiously taken away from the Begetter if equality with the Father’s substance is denied to the Son, since [Col. 0215B] apostolic teaching does not conceal this. The evangelist John says: “For this reason the Jews were seeking to kill him, because he not only was breaking the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18).

This equality was not maliciously charged by the hostile Jews, as some think; rather, it was plainly declared by the truthful authority of the evangelist. Just as he truly said that Jesus broke the Sabbath, and truly said that he called God his own Father, so he truly said that, by confessing the name of the Father, he made himself equal to the divinity and omnipotence of the Begetter.

The true Son himself proclaims and demonstrates this equality when he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Elsewhere: “Whatever the Father does, the same things [Col. 0215C] the Son likewise does” (John 5:19). He also says: “Father, glorify your Son, so that the Son may glorify you” (John 17:1). And elsewhere: “That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John 5:23). We have omitted many other passages to avoid excessive length.

To make oneself equal to God by confessing the Father’s name; to be one with the Father; to do in the same way everything the Father does; to be glorified and himself glorify; to demand for himself equality of the Father’s honor—these things, just as they do not belong to one who is lesser, so they demonstrate, beyond any doubt, that he is equal.

### Objection 6

Meanwhile, when the subject is light, they do not understand what is written: that the Father of light is one, while another is the one called light, who shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend him. Therefore attention must be paid to what the Law commands or teaches human minds. Between that author of light and this light shining in the darkness, which illuminates every person coming into this world, through which the Son was made life and was shown to be the light of human beings, the one who was made what is shown is not the Father and cannot be equal to him [Col. 0215D].

### Response

The equality of the Father and the Son always demonstrates that whatever is a matter of diminution or honor is common to both alike. Thus, when the Son is distinguished from the equality of the Father contrary to the rule of faith, the Father is detracted from more than the Son. The assertion made in this passage demonstrates this more clearly: when the Son alone is believed to be called light, the name “light” is denied to the Father himself, who begot the light [Col. 0216A].

Whoever does not possess the name “light” substantially cannot possess the title of divinity substantially. For the blessed Apostle John says: “God is light” (1 John 1:5). If, then, the one who is God is light, the one who is not light is not God. Therefore the Son must be believed to be light from light, because God was born from God, lest, while the Son is called light, God the Father be intolerably blasphemed.

And lest we think that we call the Father light by conjecture rather than by truth, we must also confirm this by testimonies. In the sacred writings it is said of Wisdom: “Wisdom is more mobile than all that moves;” [Note: “More mobile than all that moves” is the manuscript reading; other forms are “more mobile than all movable things” or “more mobile than all things moved.”] “she reaches everywhere because of her [Col. 0216B] purity. For she is a vapor of the power of God and a pure emanation of the glory of the almighty God” [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “of love” instead of “of glory.”] “Therefore nothing defiled enters into her. For she is the brightness of eternal light, the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness” (Wis. 7:22–26).

Wisdom is called the brightness of eternal light, and the whole Christian community confesses that the eternal light is the Father. If some should perhaps think that this eternal light, whose brightness is Wisdom, should not be understood as the Father, then, while denying that God the Father is eternal light, they must seek another eternal light whose brightness they can clearly show Wisdom to be.

Let them determine for themselves how they can find either a light that is not God or another light, besides Wisdom, that is coeternal with God. Let the Father therefore be acknowledged as light, so that at least in this way the Son may not be doubted or denied to be equal to the Father [Col. 0216C].

We have already taught by one testimony that God the Father is light; it is better to demonstrate the same thing also by apostolic preaching. The blessed Paul testifies that we are children of God, saying: “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. For you did not receive a spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’ The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. 8:14–16).

The evangelist John also says: “But to all who [Col. 0216D] believed in him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12). Thus, to show that the God whose children we are is light, Paul also called these same children children of light, saying: “But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day may overtake you like a thief; for you are all children of light and children of the day” (1 Thess. 5:4–5). And the Son said to the disciples: “So that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:45).

No one can deny that the Son himself is light. Of him the evangelist says: “He was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9). And again: “The life was the light of human beings, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:4–5). The Son himself also testifies in his own words that he is light: “I am,” he says, “the light of the world” (John 8:12).

That the Father is recognized in the Son, light in light, is taught by John’s testimony, which says: “God is light, and there is no darkness in him [Col. 0217A] at all.” Then he adds: “If we walk in the light, as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another” (1 John 1:5, 7). To show that he was speaking of the Father, he added: “And the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from every sin” (ibid., 7). He asserted that the Father whom he called light is in the light.

What, then, is this light if not the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1:9)? It has therefore been shown that the Father is light, just as the Son is light. It is also demonstrated that the Son is day, just as the Father is day, when the prophet says: “Proclaim his salvation from day to day” (Ps. 95:2).

Therefore let the Father be recognized as being in the Son as light, and the Son in the Father as light, since the Light himself testifies concerning himself: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:12)—as though he were saying: “I am in the light, and the light is in me.”

[Col. 0217B] Where no difference of light is found, the equality of divinity must not be denied. Otherwise, while apostolic preaching says that God is light, the one who is not said to be light would also, impiously, be denied to be God.

### Objection 7

We have omitted [Note: Other readings are “we have admitted” or “we have lost.”] superfluous arguments that would not weary the hearers, and the matter has been brought to the point for which the statement sought an explanation. Since there is a distinction between the Father and the Son, and since what is said is not so because there is no difference between them, the Savior himself, who must be believed, says: “There is another who bears witness about me” (John 5:32).

Likewise, the Son himself says of the Holy Spirit: “I will send you another Paraclete” (John 14:16). He called the Father “another,” and said that the Paraclete is “another.” When divine rights and mysteries are not observed, people become advocates of paganism by asserting that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God [Col. 0217C].

### Response

True faith has never had superfluous arguments, but always sound ones; nor does weariness arise from them, provided that truth is heard without contentiousness. The Father was called “another” for the purpose of distinguishing the persons, not to demonstrate a substantial difference.

For when he said “another,” he showed that he had his own distinct person; but by naming the Father, he demonstrated that he had one substance with him, as follows: if the Father who bears witness to the Son is truly “another,” so that the person of each may be distinguished, then he is also truly Father, so that [Col. 0217D] substantial unity may be demonstrated.

If the Father’s fatherhood is true, the offspring’s birth is also true; and if the Son’s birth is true, there cannot be substantial diversity between the Father and the Son. For the true and eternal substance from which true birth came forth could no more be diminished or divided by begetting than, remaining wholly in itself, it could fail to give its entirety to the whole truth of the coeternal birth. Thus the Begetter and the Begotten would possess not only equality without diversity, but also natural unity without confusion or loss.

The name and reality of divine birth, just as they show the distinct person of the Begetter and the Begotten, do not permit their substance to be considered different [Col. 0218A]. The Father was therefore called “another” so that the truth of the generation might be demonstrated, not so that he might be thought prior or superior.

For if we must regard as superior the one whom we hear called “another,” we are compelled also to confess the Spirit, the Paraclete, superior to the Son because he is called “another.” Just as the Son called the Father “another,” so he named the Paraclete “another.”

If it pleases you—and if the truth of faith demands—that the one called “another” be considered better, then, since the Father is called “another” and the Paraclete is also called “another,” the Son must now be subjected to both, so that at least in this way the Paraclete may be made equal to the Father. Because he is called “another,” he is said to be placed before the Son; and through the common use of this pronoun, a communion of divinity is demonstrated in the Father and the Paraclete.

But if the Paraclete, although called “another,” is nevertheless not placed before the Son, then neither should the Father be placed before the Son because he is called “another.” For this pronoun indicates a distinction of persons, not of nature [Col. 0218B].

Finally, lest we abandon the rule of truth through uncertainty about the faith and be carried around through wandering errors, the Lord himself showed us both that he retains one substance with the Father and that he has another person, saying in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

Those who strive to weaken the meaning of divine unity in the Father and the Son endeavor to refer this saying not to substantial unity but to harmony of will. If the Lord had wished it to be understood in this way, he could have said: “I and the Father will one thing,” not “I and the Father are one.”

[Col. 0218C] But now let each person choose what he wishes: whether in God he thinks willing is one thing and being another, or whether he believes that in God being is the same as willing, so that the truth of this saying of the Lord may become clearer to him.

For if he says that there is one will in God, which is called willing, and another essence, which is understood as being, then what was said according to essence cannot be referred to will: “I and the Father are one.” For “being” is derived from essence. But if it is believed—as is certain—that in God being is the same as willing, then, while the unity of will is asserted, substantial unity must not be denied. Thus, in the word “one,” it may be recognized that the Son is not other than what the Father is; and in the word “are,” it may be recognized that the Son is not himself the Father.

Following this teaching of Christ in every respect, our Fathers said that the Father and the Son are of one substance [Col. 0218D]. In Greek this was called *Homousion* (“of the same substance”), for the following reason: at that time a new heresy had arisen in Greece which attempted to separate the only-begotten Son from the substance of the Begetter. Its purpose was that whoever accepted this teaching would appear not to be a worshiper of the Creator but rather of a creature.

It is remarkable that some attend only to the sound of this word and do not investigate its meaning, since many expressions were not spoken in ancient times but were inserted into the confession of faith as the circumstances and needs of the times required.

For example, “unbegotten Father” is found nowhere in the canonical Scriptures, yet, according to the truth of the faith, the Father is proclaimed unbegotten—namely, against Sabellius, who understands the Father and the Son as one not through communion of substance but through personal singularity and therefore confuses them [Col. 0219A].
