If sound rather than sense is considered in words, then the Church should not be called “catholic,” since that name is found in neither the Old nor the New Testament. But if all these expressions, although found in no canonical book, are nevertheless rightly held in the faith, why should we be forbidden in *Homousion* to consider not the sound of the word but its sense, and not to attend to the novelty of the word but to understand the force of the mystery?

It is remarkable that those who, on account of their belief in one substance, want us to be called *homousians* do not want themselves to be called *Triusians* on account of their belief in three different substances. Even if they avoid being classified by such a name, the character of their belief nevertheless shows that this is what they are.

Therefore we rightly worship the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as one God, while preserving the distinctiveness of the persons, because true faith neither accepts three gods, as the polytheistic pagans do, nor asserts that its God was created, as worshipers of a creature proclaim [Col. 0219B].

### Objection 8

Let people who desire to follow saving commands recognize that it is a crime and very great blasphemy. For the falsity of a profession can never benefit those who seek to worship or venerate God by injuring him through blasphemy. [Note: [Col. 0219] The Corbie manuscript reads “to injure God.”] If injury is not tolerated by human beings, how can it be tolerated by the Lord himself, the Author? He shows his rebuke of unbelievers when he says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

### Response

[Col. 0219C] The apostolic faith does not insult God but honors him. It asserts that the divine substance could neither be diminished nor changed; and therefore it proclaims the Son equal to the Father, because the one substance of both preserves the fullness of its perfection in each.

An injury is then inflicted upon God when, through a difference in divinity, a creature is worshiped together with the Creator. The term “creation” is to be applied to the Son only in the sense that, for the redemption of human beings, he became a human being from human beings.

If the Lord wished the Holy Spirit also to be understood as a creature, he would never have commanded that the Spirit be joined to himself and the Father in the sacrament of baptism, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them [or: baptize them] in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

### Objection 9

[Col. 0219D] As for his generation, who could doubt that the statement “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3) was spoken of a bodily birth? For the preceding inscription itself shows you that, in order to understand what the prophet says, he was begotten before the morning star “in the splendors of the holy ones.” And the “splendor of the holy ones” (ibid.) is shown to be the proclamation of the prophets, and their prophecy concerning him is shown to have been fulfilled, so that it might show “that it is” (*ipsam esse*, referent uncertain), with the prophet saying: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” A splendid thing occurred: he was born through a virgin, as the prophetic mouth had previously said. Who could doubt that this birth took place as Scripture records?

### Response

[Col. 0220A] The one who does not believe that this passage of Scripture applies to the divine birth is greatly mistaken. Hearing God say, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you,” and thinking that a bodily womb cannot be believed to exist in God, he supposes that the meaning of this passage must be fitted only to the generation according to the flesh. Yet the preceding verse more strongly suggests the meaning of divine generation, in which the Father says to the Son: “With you is the beginning” (ibid.), so that the Father and the Son may be recognized as one beginning.

The term “womb” is used metaphorically to signify the divine nature itself. In the same way, the incorporeal substance of God is customarily named with bodily terms, so that the minds of human beings may be led to an understanding of divinity through terms familiar to their own nature. [Note: [Col. 0219] The Corbie manuscript reads *consuetudinis* (“of custom/use”) in place of the printed *consuetis* (“familiar/customary”).] For God’s eyes are said to see everything, as it is written: “In every place the eyes of God observe the good and the wicked” (Prov. 15:3).

Who could doubt that God sees everything wholly through his nature [Col. 0220B], just as we confess that through the infinity of his nature he fills all things? We also find various terms for bodily members applied to God, as was said, so that through the operations of these things the incorporeal character of his substance may be understood.

Thus here too he said that he had begotten the Son from the womb, so that, when we hear that he was begotten from the womb, no one might consider him alien to the Father’s nature.

When he said “before the morning star,” he showed that the Son’s perpetual birth is not subject to a temporal beginning. For “morning star” is the name of a star; and at the beginning of the world, when God had made the luminaries and the stars, he commanded them to serve for days, months, seasons, and years (Gen. 1:14). Through these cycles of names all time revolves.

The phrase “in the splendors of the holy ones” has not been correctly understood as referring to the prophecies of the prophets. For the splendor of the holy ones consists not in the office of proclamation but in the glory of the resurrection. Concerning this splendor the Lord says: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43).

The prophet Daniel also recalls the splendor of the future resurrection in these words: “And many of those sleeping in the furrow of the earth, in the covering [reading uncertain: *in opertione*], will rise: these to eternal life, and those to everlasting reproach and confusion; and those who understand will shine like the splendor of the firmament, and many from among the righteous, like the stars forever” (Dan. 12:2).

This splendor will then be granted by the Lord to the holy ones, when, according to the Apostle’s saying, he “will reform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:21) [Col. 0220C].

[Col. 0220D] In this splendor the holy ones will then fully understand that the Father and the Son are one beginning and that they differ from one another neither in substance nor in majesty.

Although we confess that the Son was brought forth according to the flesh from the womb of the Virgin, we nevertheless do not doubt that he was begotten from the womb of the Father—that is, from the substance of the Father. Rather, we confess that the Son was born as true God from the womb of God [Note: [Col. 0220] The Corbie manuscript reads “from the true God”], just as we do not doubt that a true human being came forth from the womb of the Virgin.

Otherwise, God forbid, if a true human being is believed to have been born from the substance of his mother while a true God is denied to have been born from the substance of the Father, human nature would be considered superior: it was able to bring forth what it is, whereas divine substance was unable to generate true God.

### Objection 10

[Col. 0221A] It is no small [or: excessive] disgrace for a mind that understands badly to be deceived by its own artifices, so that at one time two are said to be one, and at another three are said to be one. Does the gift of benefit not come to mind, when one is not designated with two?

It is a mockery to believe that God consists of three parts, while, what is worse, it is said of them that one God must be believed in this way, even though the Father is not himself the Son, nor the Son himself the Holy Spirit. They profess that these have distinctions among themselves, yet claim that each cannot possess his own honor unless a malicious mind is found to unite them in one God.

[The supplied source ends here.]

### Response

No one is deceived by any fraud, whether his own or another’s, who worships the one God in such a way that, in the Trinity, he understands neither to confuse the persons nor to separate the substance. He understands that one nature to be the one God in whom he recognizes the eternity of true divinity; for it is said to us: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deut. 6:4). Again: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (ibid., 13).

But if we must understand “the Lord God” as the Father alone, then we should neither serve the Son as God nor worship him. For whatever does not pertain to the nature of the Lord God alone, as God, ought not to be worshiped by us. What, then, shall we say about the Son, whom all the angels and all the powers in heaven continually worship and praise—so much so that, even when he had taken the form of a servant and, because of the suffering of death, had been made a little lower than the angels, the angels are commanded to worship him? Moses says:

> “Rejoice, heavens, together with him, and let all the angels of God worship him” (Ps. 96:8).

[Note: The manuscript reads this way. The editions have: “Let human beings also worship him.”]

David, divinely inspired, adds human beings to this worship and says:

> “All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations serve him” (Ps. 72:11).

How, then, is he worshiped by both human beings and angels if he is separated from the substance of the one God? How do we dare to offer him the service owed to God alone if he does not share one nature with the Father?

Since there is one God, the prophet says to us:

> “I am God, and there is no other besides me; righteous and saving, and there is no other besides me. Turn to me, and you shall be saved, for I am God from the farthest end of the earth, and there is no other. By myself I swear: righteousness shall go forth from my mouth, and my words shall not turn back; for every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall swear by God” (Isa. 45:21–23).

Behold the God who, in this passage, saying that he alone is God, testifies that there is no other besides him. If anyone refuses to understand the whole Trinity here, he will be compelled to assign this utterance to the Son alone. For who is the God besides whom there is no other except the one to whom Isaiah says:

> “Egypt’s labor, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians and of the Sabeans—men of stature—shall pass over to you; they shall be your servants. They shall follow you, bound in chains; they shall worship you and pray to you, for God is in you, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it, God of Israel, Savior. They shall be ashamed and disgraced, all who oppose him, and they shall go away in confusion” (ibid., 14–16).

Behold: in him is God, and besides him there is no God; and he is the God of Israel, the Savior.

Earlier, the one who said, “I am God, and there is no other besides me,” added: “Righteous and saving, there is no other besides me.” But who is righteous except the one to whom David says:

> “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity” (Ps. 45:8)?

And who is saving except the one about whom the angel spoke to Joseph in a dream, saying:

> “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he himself will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:20–21).

[Note: The manuscript of Corbie reads: “Receive.”]

To whom does it belong to say, “Turn to me, and you shall be saved, for I am God from the farthest end of the earth, and there is no other” (Isa. 45:22), except the Son? Of him David says:

> “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him” (Ps. 22:27).

As for what follows—“By myself I swear”—who should be believed to say this except the one who is found to have sworn in this manner earlier to Abraham? Yet those who insist on proclaiming the Son inferior to the Father according to divine nature assert that this one is not the Father but the Son.

This God, who swears by himself, and whether he has anyone greater than himself, is shown to us by the blessed Paul. Writing to the Hebrews, he says:

> “For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom he could swear, he swore by himself, saying: ‘Surely, blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you’” (Heb. 6:13–14).

Let us see, then, what follows concerning this God who swears by himself because he has no one greater by whom he might swear:

> “For righteousness shall go forth,” he says, “from my mouth, and my words shall not turn back; for every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall swear by God” (Isa. 45:23).

From whose mouth did righteousness go forth except from the one of whom Isaiah said:

> “A shoot shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isa. 11:1)?

And shortly afterward:

> “He shall judge the poor with righteousness and shall reprove the earth [or: the lands] for the meek with equity” (ibid., 4).

Then follows: “This is the God besides whom there is no other,” and he says: “My words shall not turn back.” Whose voice is this except that of the one who says in the Gospel:

> “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. 24:35)?

Again, this God besides whom there is no other adds and says:

> “For every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall swear by God.”

The apostle Paul, instructed by Christ’s teaching, shows us how this is to be understood. Writing to the Romans, he says:

> “None of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself. For whether we live, we live for the Lord; and whether we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s” (Rom. 14:7–8).

And, to demonstrate that he had spoken of Christ, he added:

> “For to this end Christ died and rose again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living. But you—why do you judge your brother? Or you—why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the tribunal of God” (Rom. 14:9–10).

Immediately he adds this prophetic testimony, saying:

> “For it is written: ‘As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God’” (Isa. 45:24).

He himself again testifies that we shall stand before the tribunal of Christ, saying:

> “For we must all be revealed before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to the body according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10).

The same apostle teaches that every knee must bow to him, saying:

> “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:10–11).

Let us now reconsider everything said above. God says: “I am God, and there is no other besides me.” And Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Son, says:

> “For God is in you, and there is no God besides you; for you are God, and we did not know it, God of Israel, Savior” (Isa. 45:15).

The God of Israel is one God. What follows, however, we have shown by the testimonies cited above to pertain to the Son: he swears by himself, having no one greater; he saves his people; he judges justly; every knee bows to him—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; every tongue confesses to him, from whom recompense for deeds is to be rendered.

Therefore the one of whom all these things are said declares through the prophet: “I am God, and there is no other besides me.” Do we understand this God besides whom there is no other to be the Son alone, in such a way that we separate the Father and the Holy Spirit from him? God forbid; this is impossible. For there is no God the Son apart from God the Father, because he is from the Father and is in the Father. There is no Holy Spirit apart from the Father and the Son, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, and is in the Father and in the Son.

Thus it is known that this Trinity is one Lord God, of whom it is said:

> “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord [or: God] is one” (Deut. 6:4).

And:

> “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve.”

To this Lord the prophet Isaiah also says:

> “Lord, besides you we have known no other; we name your name.”

Our Savior reveals this name when he says to his disciples:

> “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

This is the name of the Lord besides whom we know no other. When this name has been invoked, we are freed from death and rescued from the power of darkness, so that we may be transferred into the kingdom of the Son.

In the Father, therefore, and in the Son and in the Holy Spirit, we recognize unity of substance, but we do not dare to confuse the persons. For the blessed apostle John testifies, saying:

> “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit; and these three are one” (1 John 5:7).

The most blessed martyr Cyprian also confesses this in his letter *On the Unity of the Church*, saying:

> “Whoever breaks the peace of Christ and the harmony acts against Christ; whoever gathers elsewhere, outside the Church, scatters Christ’s Church.”

To demonstrate that the one Church belongs to the one God, he immediately inserted these testimonies from Scripture. The Lord says:

> “I and the Father are one.”

And again:

> “Of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit it is written: ‘And these three are one.’”

In his book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, moreover, wishing to show that the Trinity belongs to one divinity and possesses no diversity among its members, he recalled that Daniel and the three young men were accustomed to pour forth prayer as the cycles of three hours revolved. There, both in the course of the three hours and in the service of one prayer, he clearly showed that the Trinity is one God.

We do not, therefore, worship one God composed of three parts. Rather, retaining the rule of apostolic faith, we confess the Son to be perfect and coeternal, begotten without beginning from the perfect and eternal Father, not unequal in power, and equal in nature.

We also confess that the Holy Spirit is nothing other than God: neither different from the Son or from the Father, nor confused with the Son or the Father. For he is one and the same Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeding wholly from the Father, existing wholly in both; he is not divided among the individual persons, because inseparably he is common to both.

[Col. 0223C]

## The Three Books of St Fulgentius to Trasamund, King of the Vandals. (C)

# Book One: On the Mystery of Christ the Mediator, Who Retains Two Natures in One Person

## Chapter I. A book sent by the king to Fulgentius. Fulgentius’ reply at the king’s command. To refuse to affirm the faith is to deny the faith. The necessity of answering arises from a divine command.

[Col. 0223D]

I could never believe, most devout king, that it has escaped your triumphant mind through forgetfulness [or: been consigned to forgetfulness] that recently you commanded a certain book to be sent to me by the bearer Felix, ordering me to reply at once. Since it was so lengthy that it required somewhat longer examination, and the end of the day’s course was at hand, with night approaching, I had scarcely, in the rapid course of a hurried reading, sampled the beginnings of that same book, when I requested that the space of one night be granted us in order to read through everything in the orderly completeness of an examination. But your gracious will determined that this should altogether be refused, so that you did not command even time to be assigned to us for reading the remaining part of the writing.

Yet while I awaited for some days an instruction from your Highness, and thereafter, the tenor of that question having been withheld, a reply alone was demanded of me, I sent to your graciousness for examination a few observations on that same question which I had imperfectly learned from the beginning—such as the smallness of my intellect suffices for, with the Lord’s help—lest perhaps I should be thought puffed up through disdain, or judged liable to blame for silence, since your Excellency might suspect that I had either refused to give an answer through pride or kept silence through distrust of the true faith.

For I do not doubt, most merciful king, that it is known to your zeal that, among those redeemed through participation in Christian grace, to be unwilling to affirm the faith is almost the same as to deny it. For the only-begotten God himself, creator and redeemer of the human race, declares with entirely definite pronouncement that, just as he will confess the one who confesses him, so he will deny the one who denies him, saying: “Everyone who confesses me before human beings, I also shall confess before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before human beings, I also shall deny before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:32–33).

Likewise, when he comes in his majesty, he himself will be ashamed of the person who is ashamed of him and of his words. Luke is known to have set forth the rule of this saying in this sentence, where he so establishes the silence of one who keeps silent as destructive through this shame that he does not fail to say that the ashamed person is consigned to perdition, recording among other things that the Lord said: “What does it profit a human being [variant: man], if he gains the whole world but loses himself and suffers the loss of himself?” (Luke 9:25). Then, indicating the cause of this destruction, he added: “For whoever is ashamed [variant: is ashamed] of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his own majesty and that of his Father and of the holy angels.”

Nor without reason is such a servant both rejected and punished, because by one and the same silence he confirms error: possessed by fear or lethargy [variant: warmth], he does not, by speaking, establish the truth. Whoever does not uphold the Lord’s glory empties it, and whoever does not refute divine insult increases it. Often a cowardly soldier, oppressed by sleepy lethargy, hands over the royal camp to attackers because he does not defend it with the requisite watches.

I have taken particular care to state these things beforehand, lest your piety should in any way wish to charge me with a proud reply, when the very necessity of replying imposes upon me the duty of a free answer. For when the matter concerns God, it is no light guilt if that which pertains to salvation is kept silent. Thus we ought to believe with the heart unto righteousness, so that confession of the mouth may likewise be unto salvation (Rom. 10:10), since the word of God is not bound (2 Tim. 2:9).

Added to this is that oracle of the divine command which binds the person of every ecclesiastical preacher in a certain common obligation not only of faith but also of service [variant: reaches], when the Lord says: “Cry aloud, do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1). What is said to Isaiah in one person is commanded to many, the only-begotten God himself saying to his disciples: “What I say to one of you, I say to all” (Mark 13:37). Therefore blessed Peter also, by the prompting of fatherly love, commands us to be ready to answer: “Always,” he says, “be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the faith and hope that are in you” (1 Pet. 3:15). When we are commanded to render an account of our faith and hope to everyone who asks, every exception, whether of rank or person, entirely ceases. For to whom should the communication of truth be thought to be denied, when the prophet testifies that he spoke without shame before kings, saying: “I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not ashamed” (Ps. 119:46)?

## Chapter II. Regard for royal dignity must be observed in answering. God is to be feared and honored more than a temporal king. Praise of a barbarian king for his zeal for wisdom.

Therefore, when we answer freely for our faith, insofar as we have received ability from God, we ought not to be marked by any suspicion of obstinacy or insult. For we are mindful neither of our own lowliness nor of royal dignity, and we know that fear is to be offered to God and honor to kings, as apostolic teaching thus forewarns us: “Render to all their due”; and shortly afterward: “To whom fear, fear; to whom honor, honor” (Rom. 13:7). Blessed Peter opened to us the knowledge of the manifest distinction between this fear and honor, saying: “As servants of God, honor all; love the brotherhood; fear God; but honor the king” (1 Pet. 2:17).

Nor does anyone render little affection and honor to your clemency who gives you, when you ask, an answer belonging to the truth of faith. We therefore offer to your graciousness the fitting service of honor, since we see that the summit of royal eminence has been bestowed on you by divine generosity. Yet no wise person fails to know how greatly that eternal King of kings and Lord of lords ought to be regarded with fear, he who commands temporal kings also to be honored. Whoever fears him too little greatly despises him; whoever diminishes [variant: does not mention] his honor increases the injury done to him. Nor does one escape the guilt of ingratitude if one judges the boundlessness of the Creator’s perpetuity and the boundlessness of his eternity by the qualities of creatures [variant: of the creature].

Your graciousness undoubtedly perceives this; the acuteness of your intellect and zeal recognizes it. Whoever knows how to consider it pronounces it truly admirable—not because it is unusual for a human being to apply himself to the study of the Scriptures, but because until now it has been regarded as rare for the mind of a barbarian king, continually occupied with the many cares of a kingdom, to blaze with so ardent a delight in knowing wisdom, when efforts of this sort, always tireless, are customarily possessed only by someone at leisure or by a Roman.

Through you, most merciful king—through you, I say—the pursuits of learning endeavor to invade the laws of a barbarian people, which used to claim ignorance for itself as though by an inborn right. You have been found to be greater than yourself, since you preside over the government of Africa in such a way that you desire more to enlarge the capacities of your soul than those of your kingdom. You know, venerable king, and, as I do not doubt, hold firmly established by judgment, how much better are the advantages embraced by one who desires to know the truth than by one who, having subdued nations, desires to extend more widely the boundaries of a temporal kingdom.

## Chapter III. The king’s erroneous zeal in Arian faithlessness.

The inquiry into truth confers a great good; yet it is not then disappointed of its desired result unless the mind rests upon straight lines leading to knowledge of the truth. Even a swift course of intellect will then be advantageous, if the steps of one tending toward truth are held by no error of perversity [variant: are held]. But how can a belief be judged wholesome which thinks the worship of divine religion consists in this: either that divinity must be deprived of natural truth, while that is denied in it [variant: in the matter] which is not denied in a human being [variant: in the name]; or that, when the mystery of our redemption is perverted [variant: forestalled] by uncertain confusion, someone dares to deny that the Lord Christ, Son of God and of man, is either truly God by nature from the Father or perfect man? Or if divinity is thought to have been subject to the sufferings of humanity, or the whole human being is not believed to have existed in the powers of deity?

Thus truth is emptied by no dissimilar error if either, in the one person of Christ, true God and true man, what is evidently substantially different is confused, or if, in the divinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, once a substantial diversity is believed, what belongs to the Trinity as one and indivisible is separated. For neither does divine simplicity permit a partial diversity to be attributed to itself, whereby it would deservedly be subject to composition; nor does rational intelligence need in any way the worship of diversity, since it knows that faith in one simple and eternal nature alone is sufficient for the fullness of its salvation. It does not fail to know that God himself thunders to it in heavenly oracles: “Hear, Israel, the Lord your God, the Lord [variant: God] is one” (Deut. 6:4); “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve”; and “You shall have no gods besides me.”

Nor should human minds be ignorant how great a loss of eternal salvation anyone incurs [variant: is changed] who does not fear to inflict, in impious and deadly thoughts or words, the insult of local motion or any mutability whatever upon the immeasurable and eternal substance of the true God’s proper and only-begotten Son, so far as his divinity is concerned. Such a person deservedly stands condemned by that utterance of David’s song: “The fool has said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 14:1). [Note: The manuscript of Corbie reads thus; the editions have: “that utterance condemns them thus.”] For in truth, if he is local, he is not immeasurable; if mutable, he is not God.

## Chapter IV. The errors of heretics arise from a bad understanding of the mystery of the Incarnation; hence also the blindness of the Jews.

It is certain that nearly all [variant: every] errors of heretical perversity have crept in from this source in various ways: some do not believe, as it is, the great sacrament of piety, which “was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the nations, believed in this world, and taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:16), or do not believe it at all. [Note: The manuscript of Corbie reads: “either believe as it is, or, etc.”] And that stone which was rejected by the builders and made the head of the corner becomes, to some possessed by the blindness of perverse belief, “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (1 Pet. 2:8).

Thus, not without reason, when Simeon, rejoicing, had deserved to carry in his aged arms the infant Christ, Lord of the temple, brought to his temple by the command of his law [variant: brought in], and, bearing the figure of the present age, already worn out by bodily old age, the old man received the new human being—namely, him who alone could not only remove ingrained old age from sinners, as one who had said in old age, “You are God my Savior, and I have waited for you all [variant: the whole] day” (Ps. 25:5), but even renew youth like the eagle’s; for of him the apostolic trumpet would truly sing: “As the truth is in Jesus, put off, according to [variant: as] your former manner of life, the old human being, who is corrupted according to the desires of error; but be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new human being, him [variant: the new one] created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. 4:22–24)—that Simeon, seeing the effect of the salvation and renewal of the world at hand (for “God did not send his Son to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” [John 3:17]), when he first prayed to be released from the distresses of this present life, saying: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared [Note: The words “before the face” are absent from the manuscript of Corbie.] before the face of all peoples, a light for the unveiling of the nations and the glory of your people Israel” (Luke 2:29–32)—shortly afterward testified concerning him: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many” (ibid., 34).

There, then, faithlessness produces ruin for those who believe wrongly, where right belief exalts the faithful. In one and the same Christ, the true Son of God and true man, the dim sight of those with deficient perception is still darkened, in whom the manifest knowledge of the true light shines brightly for the enlightened. Hence the Jew saw Christ the man blindly and fell, although Isaiah had long before not ceased to proclaim to him: “With hearing you shall hear and not understand; and seeing you shall see and not see” (Isa. 9:6). What they would not see despite seeing, he next showed when he testified in clear prophecy that God would be born of a Virgin: “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14), which the Evangelist interprets, saying: “God with us” (Matt. 1:25). Hearing, then, the Jew remained deaf; seeing, he became more blind. He neither believes the eternal and only-begotten Son of the true Father nor acknowledges the fruitfulness of incorrupt virginity.

## Chapter V. The Manichaean error concerning Christ’s flesh. Refuted from the Book of Wisdom. Convicted from John’s epistle.

Hence also the Manichaean fears to believe true flesh in the true God. Believing human flesh to be polluted not by the vice of fault but by a natural property, he blindly attributes such power to the evil nature which he falsely invents for himself [Note: The manuscript of Corbie reads thus; the manuscript of Victor has “any nature for himself,” etc.; the Cologne and Antwerp editions, “the evil of nature”; the Basle edition, “an evil nature falsely invents for himself, and to it.”] that, if he believed that the true God had assumed the true nature of flesh, he would not believe divinity—which he calls, in a deceitful profession, incapable of defilement [Note: The manuscripts of Corbie and Victor read thus; the editions have “defilable.”]—to be free from flesh’s pollution. Therefore he preferred to believe a phantom of flesh in Christ rather than its nature; and, because he did not see human weakness assumed by him [variant: it] with healing power, he, wretched man, excluded himself from the remedy of salvation.

But this madness of impure falsehood was extinguished by the foreknowledge of the Holy Spirit before it was born. The sequence of the Old Instrument commends wisdom’s incapacity for defilement in these words: “Wisdom is more mobile than all moving things; and because of her purity she reaches everywhere. For she is a vapor of God’s power and a pure emanation of the glory of almighty God; therefore nothing defiled falls upon her. For she is the splendor of eternal light, the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness. Though she is one, she can do all things; abiding in herself, she renews all things” (Wis. 7:24–27).

Concerning this incapacity of wisdom for defilement and the truth of the Incarnation, the one who was illumined and deserved to draw understanding of heavenly mysteries from the breast of Wisdom himself says with confidence: “Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. Every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not from God, and this is Antichrist” (1 John 4:2–3). For he did not experience the defilements of foul flesh, who came to assume the true substance of flesh and to cleanse that same foulness of flesh. Since he deigned to take immaculate flesh in order that, by saving flesh, he might remove every stain of flesh, John again testifies: “We know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and there is no sin in him” (1 John 3:5). Again: “In this the Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil” (ibid., 8). For because God’s work was held bound by the chain of the devil’s work, the Son of God appeared in order to destroy the latter and save the former.

## Chapter VI. The heresy of Photinus. Many errors refuted from the beginning of John. The Word was God naturally, not merely by title.

Photinus too is ignorant of the great sacrament of piety mentioned by the Apostle (1 Tim. 3:16), for he affirms Christ’s beginning from the Virgin. He is ignorant that in the one Christ the truth of flesh from time must be believed in such a way that the natural truth of eternal divinity from the Father is not denied. Therefore he does not believe that God was born substantially from God the Father without beginning, even though he confesses the truth of flesh from the Virgin. He does not understand that the Word which was substantially born from God the Father, and which, made flesh in the fullness of time, dwells [variant: dwelt] among us, was in the beginning, was with God, and was God according to the divine substance which it has from the Father (John 1:1).

In these three sentences of the Evangelist are shown the eternal birth of the Word, the unconfused personal distinctness, and the inseparable substantial unity of Father and Son. Thus, in the Word made flesh [variant: in flesh] and dwelling among us, the statement that it “was in the beginning” removes the suspicion of a birth that began; the statement that it “was with God” excludes the union of Sabellian error through the unconfused distinctness of each person; and the statement that “the Word was God” shows, through the truth of this essential name, the unity of substance of begetter and begotten.

For John did not say, “The Word was called God,” but “The Word was God,” so that, when the natural truth of divine essence is recognized in God the Word, it may consequently be proved that the truth of the name is not titular but natural. For the truth of a nature is never without the truth of its name. Thus the true incarnation of that Word—not an uttered word but a substantial one [variant: most true]—is believed savingly only if we believe that the eternal Word, which assumed flesh [variant: our flesh] in time, is not subject to a beginning of existence, is not confused in person with the Father, and is not other than God in nature [variant: other than God].

## Chapter VII. Another error of those who deny both true deity and true humanity in Christ. Another error of those who refer the acts of humanity to deity.

There are also some people exceedingly ungrateful for the Savior’s grace in this respect: in Christ—true God and perfect man [Note: The word “true” is absent from the Antwerp and Basle editions; it is found in the manuscript of Corbie and the Cologne edition.]—they claim to receive the nature of God and man in such a way that they do not hesitate to proclaim in the Son of God one substance false and the other half-complete. For they refuse to believe in Christ’s true deity, whose true birth from God the Father they deny to have existed substantially, wishing to take from God the Son the nature of the true name, though they cannot take from him the name of natural truth.

For they say that in the name of the only-begotten God there is not a natural substance from the Father’s generation, but a designation consisting only in the bestowal of a word. They also believe human nature in Christ in such a way that they remove what is better in humanity and retain what is lower. And, giving insufficient consideration to the great sacrament of piety mentioned by the Apostle, they endeavor to separate a rational soul from that marvelous assumption of the Mediator; they assert that it was wholly absent in the Mediator of God and human beings.

Another offense is also added to this error, by which they admit the most shameful trafficking in confusion. In the unity of the person—in which God and man are the one Christ, demonstrating the unconfused and inseparable truth of each nature, showing himself true God by divine works and true man by human sufferings, possessing as impassible that by which the human being was created sound, and assuming as passible that by which the sick human being might be healed—these people are so deceived by I know not what delusion that they do not fear to attribute to the dishonor of divinity everything that the Lord humbly did or said in showing the true assumption of the form of a servant. They subject divinity to the suffering of mutability [variant: and to mutability], because they make no distinction, despite the most brilliant manifestation in sayings and deeds of the truth of both natures. They do not observe where weakness is shown as assumed by invincible and impassible power, or where through weakness the marks of invincible power shine forth. Thus they endeavor to frustrate the effect of the divine mystery, because truly humanity could not be saved if either the one who assumed humanity had not naturally been true God, or something of humanity had been absent in the assumption by the true God.

## Chapter VIII. The Mediator’s twofold nature must be demonstrated from the Scriptures. From Isaiah’s words three things in Christ are proved: flesh, soul, and divinity.

[Col. 0231B]

And so, to remove every uncertainty of doubt, the perfection of the divine and human substance in the one person of the Mediator, Christ Jesus, must be demonstrated by prophetic and apostolic testimonies. Isaiah, as we mentioned above, says:

“Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb, and shall bear a son, and his name shall be called” (or: “you shall call,” or “you shall call his name”) “Emmanuel. He shall eat butter and honey, before he knows or can declare what is evil; he shall choose the good. For before the child knows good or evil, he does not believe in evil, so that he may choose what is good; and the land shall be left desolate. For before the child knows how to call his father or mother, he shall receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria” (Isaiah 7:14–16).

In this testimony the entire fullness of the mystery of salvation is contained. For the reality of the flesh is recognized in the virginal conception; the intellectual soul is revealed in the choice of what is good; and the true nature of the deity is shown in the name Emmanuel. Thus, in the true God there was neither a false nor an incomplete assumption of humanity. For it was fitting that, in the mystery of human redemption, neither reality should be absent from perfection nor perfection from reality.

For if there was no true flesh in Christ, what did the Virgin conceive in her womb? And if it is believed that the soul, or the intellectual nature of humanity, was absent from Christ, what is it that is said to have been ignorant of good and evil in the infant? Are we to subject that divine nature of the Son of God to ignorance of good and evil, so as to deny that Christ had a human soul? Is one to believe that the humanity assumed by God could in some measure know the things that belong to God, when the very Wisdom is said to have lacked knowledge of good and evil?

Therefore the human soul, naturally made capable of reason, is said not to have known good and evil in the infant Christ; and according to the evangelical truth it is narrated that, in the boy Jesus, it advanced in wisdom and grace. Thus Luke records and says:

“But the child grew and was strengthened, full of wisdom, and the grace of God was in him” (Luke 2:40).

And shortly afterward:

“Jesus advanced in wisdom, age, and grace before God and human beings” (ibid., 2:52).

For just as it belongs to the flesh to advance in age, so it belongs to the soul to advance in wisdom and grace. Yet it could in no way advance in wisdom if it did not possess natural understanding—the understanding granted to human beings on account of reason—not because God, the one who assumed humanity, needed this, but because the remedy of our salvation required this effect of his merciful assumption: that, while both flesh and rational soul were assumed by God, both might likewise be saved.

For the flesh itself would not have been assumed by the Son of God unless it were to be saved through the divine assumption. And if God had no need of flesh but accepted it in order to save it, so likewise God had no need of a rational soul, but assumed it together with the flesh in order to save it. The holy David prophetically discloses this assumption of the human soul, saying:

“For behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the one who assumes my soul” (Psalm 53:6).

He certainly helped what he assumed; and beyond doubt, unless he had assumed it, he would not have helped it.

## CHAPTER IX. The wandering sheep is the sinner who strays from God. The way of the Lord is faith, justice, mercy, and truth.

I consider it necessary that Christ’s complete assumption of humanity also be demonstrated by the evangelical parable of the wandering sheep—namely, the sheep whom the Lord carried back home upon his own shoulders. Long before, David had demanded help in finding it with tearful supplication, saying:

“I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost; seek your servant” (Psalm 118:176).

When the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (Luke 15:2), the evangelist reports that the Lord spoke this parable to them:

“Which of you is the man who has a hundred sheep, and if he loses one of them, does he not leave the ninety-nine in the desert and go after the one that was lost until he finds it? And when he has found it, he places it on his shoulders, rejoicing; and when he comes home, he calls together his friends and neighbors, saying to them: Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost” (ibid., 15:4–6).

Since this sheep signifies the nature of sinful humanity, in what sort of error shall we say that it went astray? In an error of the heart or of the body? Through the error of its feet or through the error of its conduct? I do not think anyone is so deprived of human understanding as to suppose that a human being strays from God through the distance of his dwelling rather than through the perversity of his thought.

On God’s way one walks not with bodily steps but with the movement of the mind. The way of God is right faith, which is shown to be truly a way insofar as the Apostle testifies that we walk upon it: “For we walk by faith,” he says, “not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7). The way of the Lord is justice, by which blessed David recalls that he was led, saying:

“He led me beside the waters of refreshment; he restored my soul; he led me along the paths of justice for his name’s sake” (Psalm 22:2).

The ways of the Lord are also mercy and truth (Psalm 24:10), and upon these one walks not with bodily steps but rather with the inclination of the soul. Blessed John makes this teaching concerning our manner of walking known to us, saying:

“Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought to walk just as he walked” [Note: The manuscript adds “thus”] “and himself also to walk” (1 John 2:6).

Christ himself commands us to follow him along this way, saying:

“If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have, and give to the poor; and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:21).

No one, therefore, follows Christ or strays from Christ merely by bodily movement. [Note: The Corbie manuscript adds: “And indeed.”] Indeed, the Lord himself, our Savior, showed the character of this error when he rebuked the Sadducees, saying:

“You are in error, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God” (Matthew 22:29).

They were therefore wandering miserably because they did not know him who is the power of God. Just as knowledge of God’s power is the firm foundation of the heavenly journey, so ignorance is the mother of error. Blessed David also shows this, speaking of certain people:

“They have not known, nor have they understood; they walk in darkness” (Psalm 83:1).

By these and similar testimonies it is demonstrated most clearly that the error of that sheep must be attributed not only to the body but also to the soul. For although some sin may appear to be committed bodily by a human being, it takes its beginning from the heart; and nothing is completed outwardly unless it is first presented inwardly by the judgment of thought. Truth itself showed us the truth of this matter when it spoke to the disciples as follows:

“For from the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies. These are the things that defile a person” (Matthew 15:19).

Each person, therefore, goes astray in that by which he stains himself through the assent of an evil thought.

## CHAPTER X. From the parable of the restored sheep it is proved that the whole human being was assumed by Christ. Through his soul Christ received the Church in marriage. Christ is rightly called the head, and the Church his body.

Therefore, since this error is understood to belong simultaneously to soul and body, if the Son of God accepted only human flesh, without a rational soul, he brought home the lower part of that sheep upon his shoulders, but left the better part—God forbid—in perpetual error. For it is evident that he recalled what he carried back upon his own shoulders.

But if he himself professes to have carried back the entire sheep after placing it upon his own shoulders, [Note: The word “placing” is absent from the Corbie manuscript.] then let the whole human being be recognized in Christ. Human redemption must be believed in that case, if in the Son of God’s assumption of humanity—that is, in the restored sheep—the fullness of the assumption was not lacking.

For God saved in us what he accepted for us; and the Son of God made that nature a participant in eternal salvation which he joined to himself in the unity of his person. He introduced it into the heavenly palace, together with which the bridegroom came forth from the chamber of the virginal womb:

“For he, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Psalm 18:6–7).

Who, then, would dare to say that the bride of the Word of God was flesh and not soul? To this soul it had long before been said by the Lord himself through the prophet:

“And I will betroth you to myself forever; and I will betroth you to myself in justice” (or: “in righteousness”), “and in judgment, and in mercy, and in compassion” (Hosea 2:19).

Isaiah also proved a faithful witness to this mystery. Speaking in the person of Christ, he says:

“Rejoicing, I will rejoice in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in God” (or: “my God”), “who has clothed me with the garment of salvation and wrapped me in the robe of justice, like a bridegroom adorned with a crown and like a bride adorned with her jewels” (Isaiah 61:10).

Behold, there is one bridegroom and there is one bride, and he testifies that he also possesses a soul. To show that it was assumed not without understanding, he demonstrated that the heart—which is proper to the human soul—exulted together with the flesh in God, speaking in the person of the assumed human being:

“My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God” (Psalm 83:2).

And because, in assuming the firstfruits of nature, the Lord accepted in his body the body of all the faithful, and in his soul the souls of all the faithful, through the unity of nature and the grace of justification, through this he took the whole Church to himself in the marriage of perpetual incorruptibility. The faithful servant of the bridegroom commends the wondrous mystery of this betrothal to the bride herself in such a way that it is understood to belong more to the mind than to the body, saying:

“For I betrothed you to one man, to present a pure virgin to Christ. But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2–3).

Thus the spiritual adulterer seeks to corrupt the chastity of the virginal marriage precisely where he sees that fidelity in marriage must be preserved for the heavenly bridegroom. But the Apostle would command the soul’s chastity to be guarded in vain if the human being assumed by God did not possess in himself the firstfruits of this union—especially since the same teacher of the nations never ceases to proclaim Christ and the Church as head and body, saying:

“According to the operation of the power of his might, which he worked in Christ Jesus, raising him from the dead and setting him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come; and he subjected all things beneath his feet, and gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all things in all” [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “because all things are fulfilled in all.”] (Ephesians 1:20–22).

Elsewhere it is said (or: “he says”):

“A man is the head of a woman, just as Christ is the head of the Church, he himself the Savior of the body” (Ephesians 5:23).

How, then, can the soul of the Church be saved if the Savior lacked a soul? Or what kind of effect of liberation will be believed to follow in the body if it did not first occur in the head? For just as he says to his faithful:

“If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36),

so also he declares concerning himself:

“For he was made like a man without help, free among the dead” (Psalm 87:5).

Therefore, what the free head made free in itself, it also liberated in the body, because, entering the house of the strong man and binding the strong man (Matthew 12:29), he freed from servitude there what he first assumed in himself as a servant. And nothing else will reign in the body except what in the head went before (or: “proceeded”) into heaven.

Faithfully and confidently holding this belief, Paul exults and says:

“But our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

There, therefore, he does not doubt that his soul dwells, where he trusts that the human soul reigns in Christ. For this reason he also exhorts the Colossians with words of this kind of preaching, saying:

“If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God.”

## CHAPTER XI. Another argument from Peter.

Nor should that which Peter commends in Christ with a great marvel of preaching be omitted: that he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. For he says:

“Christ died for us” (or: “for you”), “leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps; he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22).

For if the Son of God did not have a human soul in his assumption of flesh, and if blessed Peter is believed to have said this concerning his divinity, what is there that is said as a great praise of Christ—that his divinity could be free from the stain of sin—when it belongs properly to God not only not to sin but also to save from sin? He alone can grant pardon because he alone cannot commit guilt; he alone is the physician of the wounded because the divine nature never receives a wound in itself.

But if this is believed to refer to Christ’s flesh, how will justice be preserved in our souls, for which Christ’s assumption did not provide the apostolic example mentioned? Yet to show that justice, which he commands us to imitate, went before in both Christ’s soul and flesh, blessed Peter continued:

“When he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (or: “he did not curse in return”).

This pertains properly to the soul’s patience. For this reason he also says elsewhere:

“Not returning evil for evil or insult for insult, but on the contrary blessing, because you were called to this, so that you might possess the inheritance of blessing” (1 Peter 3:9).

Our Savior commends the origin of this blessing as proceeding from the heart, saying:

“A good person brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart” (or: “will bring forth”) (Matthew 12:35).

It is therefore established that benevolence exists in the soul, from which we can return blessing to those who curse us. But to demonstrate to us the example of both soul and flesh in Christ, blessed Peter, after saying, “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (or: “he did not curse in return”), continued:

“When he suffered, he did not threaten; but he entrusted himself to the one who judges” [Note: So the printed editions read. But the Corbie and Victor manuscripts have: “he entrusted himself to the one who judges him unjustly.” In the Corbie manuscript, the particle “himself” and the first syllable of “unjustly” were added, perhaps by the same hand. The Port manuscript reads: “but he entrusted himself to one who judges unjustly.”] “justly; he himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree, so that, separated from our sins, we might live in justice; by whose bruise you have been healed” (or: “we have been healed”). “For you were wandering like sheep, but now you have returned to the shepherd and guardian of your souls” (1 Peter 2:23–25).

## CHAPTER XII. Christ is rightly called both shepherd and sheep and lamb. Another argument from Leviticus: because Christ, although he was high priest, was bound by the Law to be complete as a human being.

The Son of God, therefore, is the guardian and shepherd of our souls, because he deigned to become the one who assumed a human soul. To him, in the person of the future assumption of humanity, it is said in the psalm:

“Receive me according to your word, and I shall live” (Psalm 118:116).

Christ, therefore, is our shepherd, and apostolic authority testifies that we are his sheep. Yet, in order to show fully that he deigned to be the one who assumed our nature, he did not disdain to call himself not only shepherd but also sheep (or: “to be called a sheep”); for concerning him, the prophet, moved by the Holy Spirit (or: “touched by the Holy Spirit”), testifies:

“He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7).

And again, through Jeremiah:

“I was led like an innocent lamb to be sacrificed, and I did not know it. They devised an evil plan against me, saying: Come, let us put wood in his bread” (Jeremiah 11:19).

John the Baptist also proclaims concerning him:

“Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sins” (or: “the sin”) “of the world” (John 1:29).

The Apostle Peter likewise says something similar concerning Christ (or: “concerning him”):

“Knowing that you were not redeemed with perishable silver or gold from your empty manner of life handed down by your fathers, but with the precious blood, as of an unblemished and spotless lamb, Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19).

One and the same Mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, is himself shepherd and sheep, himself bridegroom and bride, himself priest and victim. One and the same person became both the offerer of the gift and the gift offered, so that neither the offerer would depart from the character of the gift nor the gift differ from the merit of the offerer.

If he possessed less than human nature, he could neither assume the person of a high priest nor be offered for sins. For no one could exercise the priesthood under the Law if he possessed anything lacking in himself as a human being (or: “if anyone among human beings possessed anything lacking in himself”); nor was anyone permitted to offer a blemished or imperfect animal as a sacrifice. Who, then, would doubt that Jesus Christ is our high priest, whom Paul commends expressly under this title?

“We have,” he says, “a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God; let us hold firmly to our confession. For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who was tempted in every respect according to likeness, without sin. Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of grace, so that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help” (Hebrews 4:14–16).

To demonstrate that this priestly office belongs to human nature, he added:

“For every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. He is able to have compassion on those who are ignorant and wandering, since he himself is also surrounded by weakness. And for this reason he ought to offer for sins on behalf of the people, and likewise for himself. Nor does anyone take the honor upon himself, but the one who is called by God, as Aaron was. So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but the one who said to him: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Hebrews 5:1–5).

Yet he says that this priest was tempted in every respect according to likeness, without sin. He clearly showed above in what respects he was tempted, saying:

“For he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the offspring of Abraham. Hence he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make atonement for the sins of the people. For because he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted” (Hebrews 2:16–18).

## CHAPTER XIII. Another argument from Paul: Christ was tempted both in flesh and in soul.

Therefore, if he gives help to those who are tempted in that in which he himself was tempted, he certainly does not give help to those who are tempted in that in which he was not tempted. It follows that those who assign to Christ only human flesh and deny him a soul seek Christ’s help only in the flesh, while remaining destitute in the soul. For the Son of God helps in a human being that which he assumed for the human being.

But if they take delight in obtaining Christ’s help both in soul and in flesh, they must necessarily confess—as the truth requires—that he was tempted both in soul and in flesh. The human soul, therefore, and the flesh were simultaneously tempted in Christ. And if both soul and flesh were simultaneously tempted in Christ, both were simultaneously assumed by him. If he deigned to assume both, he undoubtedly deigned to save both.

For it was fitting and suited to our salvation that the true God, substantially born alone from the true Father, should assume the true soul and flesh of the human being whom he himself had made; that in both he should struggle with the tempter, conquer in both, and thereafter supply help in both to those who are tempted, while in both providing an example of victory to the weak and dying.

That saying also plainly demonstrates the mystery of the Mediator, which Truth itself uttered, saying:

“For the Son of Man came to save and seek what had perished” (Luke 19:10).

Let us therefore consider what perished through the fall of the earthly human being, and recognize what was sought through the coming of the heavenly human being. Let us consider what the servant sold by sinning (or: “in sin”), and it will become clear what the Lord redeemed by assuming. Let us consider what the robber wounded in the deception of the human being, so that it may be clear what the physician healed in assuming the human being.

Did not the first human being, composed equally of flesh and soul, receive God’s command? And if it is recognized that he received God’s command in both, he ought to have kept obedience to the command in both. But if obedience to the command was required in both, transgression was committed by both, since, just as sin began with the soul’s desire, so it was completed by the fleshly eating. Therefore, because the whole human being incurred the guilt of transgression, the devil took the whole human being captive.

And if the whole human being was held by the bond of captivity, the whole human being needed the help of a liberator. But if mercy had to liberate the whole, divine majesty had to assume the whole. Therefore the whole nature of the human being had to be assumed by God, since captivity itself had to be taken captive in the whole human being, so that victory over captive captivity might be won wholly and at once. Thus, according to the Apostle’s teaching, “leading captivity captive” (Ephesians 4:8), he might confidently lead principalities and powers in triumph, openly triumphing over them in himself (Colossians 2:15).

## CHAPTER XIV. Another argument from division into four parts.

Finally, let it be said why the nature of the soul was not assumed together with the flesh by that ineffable divinity. Was it not made by God? Or was it not corrupted by sin? Or did the universal medicine despise it as being of less value than the flesh? Or was the omnipotent one unable to heal it after it had been wounded by sin?

Those who hold the first and last of these views are rebels both against the Creator’s power and against the Savior’s might, if they suppose that some creature was not made by God or say that the Almighty lacked the power to bring salvation to the soul.

As for the two alternatives in the middle, they consider neither the sin nor the merit of the rational creature. They do not understand that she who gives life to the flesh cannot be inferior to her own flesh, nor that the one which, through understanding, was more able to resist the tempter was more gravely wounded.

That omnipotent power and merciful wisdom, therefore, neither despised as foreign what it knew to have been made by itself, nor rejected as needing healing what it knew to have been more gravely wounded, nor excluded from the remedy of salvation the one it had made superior to the flesh. Rather, just as the devil struck the whole human being by deception, so God saved the whole by assuming it, so that he might be recognized as both the Creator and Redeemer of the entire creature: the one who was able both to make what did not exist and to restore what had fallen away.

## CHAPTER XV. Another argument from the name “Mediator,” showing that he possesses the whole nature.

Moreover, all who desire to be participants in eternal salvation must equally acknowledge and hold that Jesus Christ is not without reason called the Mediator of God and human beings, except because the same God assumed in himself the whole nature of humanity, and the same human being possesses in himself the whole substance of deity (or: “divinity”).

For because humanity was separated from God through sin, a person of such a Mediator had to intervene between the angry God and sinful humanity [Note: The Basil edition has: “it was necessary that he intervene”; the others have: “there ought to intervene.”]—one who, in order to reconcile God to humanity, would possess in himself the whole and true God, born from God; and who, in order to reconcile humanity to God, would contain in himself the whole and true human being, born from humanity. Thus one Christ would exist from both and in both, so that the fullness of deity would not consume the humanity it assumed but elevate it, and the fullness of humanity would neither diminish the immeasurable deity [Note: The printed editions have “immeasurable” in the masculine form; the Corbie manuscript has the feminine form.] nor change its impassibility.

In this way the nature of humanity, which had been changed for the worse, would be wholly restored through him, than whom nothing is better. For this reason he deigned to demonstrate himself as the Mediator of God and human beings, fully God and fully human.

## CHAPTER XVI. Further arguments from various passages of Scripture.

But if anyone doubts or altogether refuses to believe this, let him choose whether he wants what we assert to be demonstrated by name or by deed. For holy Scripture did not omit, in one and the same Christ, either the title of God or that of human being, as the evangelist says:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–2).

And shortly afterward:

“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 1:14).

He asserts that the Word who became flesh is the one whom he earlier recalled to be God, so that he might show that the same one is true God from the Father and true human being from humanity.

He further shows in what respect we should believe him to be eternal by nature from God the Father, and in what respect we must accept him as temporally made human from humanity, presenting one thing at the beginning and another in what follows. The eternity of the Son of God is therefore asserted when the Word is proclaimed to be God in the beginning. There he does not say that the Word was made, since he knew it to have been begotten from the Father; there is no mention of time where there is eternity, which can have neither beginning nor end.

But when he comes to the designation of flesh, then he says that the Word was made flesh, so that we may recognize that he who had not been made, but had always existed as one born from the Father, then willed to be made, when, having been made, he deigned to restore the work he had made.

In this act blessed Paul likewise took care to profess the reality of humanity as well as the reality of time, saying:

“When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law, so that he might redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:4–5).

The apostolic authority preserves this same teaching, everywhere agreeing with the prophets (or: “with the prophetic [testimonies]”), so that, when it proclaims Christ to have been made, it clearly shows both what he was made and from what he was made. Thus it may be recognized that the Lord of all things assumed the form of a servant in such a way that he received true flesh not from elsewhere but from humanity.

David therefore says:

“Mother Zion will say: ‘A human being, and a human being was made in her’; and the Most High himself founded her” (Psalm 86:5).

Behold: just as one person is asserted beyond doubt in the one Christ, so the reality of God and of humanity is shown without confusion. For the one who was made a human being in her is himself the Most High who founded her.

The apostolic statement must plainly be compared with this saying:

“Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9:5).

What David says, “A human being was made in her,” Paul confirms when he says, “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh.” But what David asserts, “The Most High himself founded her,” Paul follows when he says, “Who is God over all, blessed forever.”

The Old Testament harmonizes with the New; David agrees with John and Paul. The one whom David calls a true human being when he says, “Mother Zion will say: ‘A human being, and a human being was made in her,’” he believes and proclaims to be the same true God, because “the Most High himself founded her.”

John recognizes as a true human being the one whom he hears saying:

“You are seeking to kill me, a human being who has spoken the truth to you” (John 8:40).

He shows him to be the same true God when he says:

“This is the true God and eternal life.”

He acknowledges Christ as a true human being because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”; and he shows him to be the same true God [Note: The printed editions read “Word”; the Corbie manuscript, “true”] because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

Paul knew him to be a true human being because, through voluntary mercy, the Lord of humanity was made from a woman, and the Lord of the Law was made under the Law (Galatians 4:4), as he himself testifies:

“God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law,”

and because he was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, and because “whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh.” Yet he does not cease to confess him as the true God, saying:

“Who is God over all, blessed forever.”

## CHAPTER XVII. The objection that, since Christ became flesh, he lacked a soul. “Flesh” used for the whole human being. “Soul” used for the whole human being.

Nor are we unaware of the opposing objection: when it is said, “The Word became flesh,” and, “He was made from the seed of David according to the flesh,” and, “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh,” some people’s carnal understanding clings so tightly to the word “flesh” in these passages that, although flesh is assumed, they do not believe that Christ also assumed a rational soul.

But those who think this way pay insufficient attention to the fact that this is a feature of human speech, in which the whole is sometimes signified by a part. Let them therefore learn that in the holy Scriptures the whole human being is sometimes shown merely by the name “flesh,” and sometimes by the designation of the soul alone. I shall easily prove the truth of this not only from the Old Testament but also from the New.

David signifies the whole human being by the name “flesh,” saying:

“Hear, O God, my prayer; all flesh will come to you” (Psalm 64:5).

What is “all flesh” except “every human being”? Likewise the same author says in another psalm:

“In God I will hope; I will not fear what flesh can do to me” (Psalm 55:5).

And to show that by the name “flesh” he designated the whole human being, he says again shortly afterward:

“In God I will praise the word; in God” (or: “in the Lord”) “I will praise the speech; in God I will hope; I will not fear what a human being can do to me” (ibid., 11).

Isaiah’s words also agree with these statements when, announcing our Savior’s coming in the flesh, he says:

“The crooked things shall become straight, and the rough ways into smooth paths, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isaiah 40:4–5).

What is “all flesh” except “every human being”? Or shall we perhaps exalt flesh as though it were lifeless, so that we do not hesitate to attribute to it a divine vision?

In the New Testament also, the Creator and Lord of the human race is found to have named the whole human being by the term “flesh,” when, foretelling the character of the final tribulation, he says to the disciples:

“For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor shall be. And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened” (Matthew 24:21–22).

The sequence of the Old Testament likewise demonstrates that the whole human being is signified by the term “soul,” when it says:

“And all the souls of Jacob were seventy-five” (Genesis 46:27). [Note: Thus the printed editions read; but the Corbie manuscript has “is demonstrated by the sequence.”]

Again, in the same Testament:

“Any soul that sins unintentionally before the Lord, in any of the Lord’s commandments that ought not to be done, and does one of them—if it is the anointed high priest who has sinned, so that the people also commit sin—let him offer for his sin, in which he sinned, an unblemished calf from the herd to the Lord” (Leviticus 4:2–3).

Behold, the term “soul” is used, and afterward the anointed priest is named, so that when we hear “soul,” we may understand the whole human being at once.

Nor could this usage be absent from the New Testament. When the disciples, strengthened by the coming of the Holy Spirit, cast off their fear and began the office of public preaching, after Peter had completed his sermon, the book of the Acts of the Apostles, as Luke narrates, contains this account:

“Those who received his word were baptized, and about three thousand souls were added on that day” (Acts 2:41).

Anyone who attempts to deny that human beings are signified here by the name “souls” must necessarily show how the apostles are believed to have administered the sacrament of baptism to souls without bodies.

Blessed Peter also sets something similar in his Epistle:

“In the days of Noah,” he says, “while the ark was being built, in which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water” (1 Peter 3:20).

Since it is therefore evident that, according to the usage of Scripture, the whole human being is sometimes designated by the term “flesh” and sometimes by the term “soul” alone, it is plainly shown that, when the evangelist says, “The Word became flesh,” nothing else should be understood except that the Word became human. [Note: These words, through the end of the chapter, were absent from the printed editions but have been restored from the Corbie manuscript.]

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Mediator Christ therefore assumed the whole human being. On account of the two natures in Christ, he is called both the human Son of God and God the Son of Man. In Christ there are true flesh and a true soul.

85

Therefore the Apostle rightly proclaims the Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus; for since the Word was God, in that God assumed the whole human being for our sake, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. The Word certainly became flesh inasmuch as in Christ there is one person of God and human being. And he dwelt in us because in Christ the whole divine and human substance remains. For the Word dwelling in a human being was not changed into a human being. Where, moreover, could the Word dwell more suitably than in that substance which he made in his own image—that is, in the soul of the human being whom he assumed?

We perceive this prophetically intimated through Solomon by spiritual grace, when it is said: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wisdom 7:27).

[Note: Antwerp and Cologne read “is the seat”; Basel reads “is a seat”; the Corbie manuscript reads “the seat of wisdom.”]

Now, to show that Christ dwells especially in the substance of the soul, Paul offers us the support of his testimony in truth. He says: “For this reason I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named: that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner human being, that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Ephesians 3:14–15).

[Note: Basel reads “and that Christ may dwell.”]

Behold, he names the soul and calls it the heart, affirming that Christ dwells there. Thus it is clearly recognized that God the Word assumed the whole human being, since the dwelling of the Son of God is shown more in the soul than in the flesh.

This inseparable truth of the mystery—by which God deigned to assume the whole human being, and the whole human being is shown to remain assumed in God—caused that which is naturally from the human being to be called the Son of God, and that which is naturally from God the Father to be called the Son of Man. The angel said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).
