Mark’s assertion also agrees with this, for he begins his Gospel as follows: “The Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (Mark 1:1).

Nathaniel likewise—the one of whom he had said, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” (John 1:46)—does not hesitate to call him the Son of God: “Rabbi,” he says, “you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel” (ibid., 49).

There Jesus, to reveal the full mystery of his graciousness, gladly heard not only what he eternally is by nature from the Father, but also most clearly proclaimed what he mercifully became from a woman, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (ibid., 51).

Because of this unity of person in Christ and the unconfused truth of his divine and human substance, one and the same Christ is called by Isaiah both a Child and is likewise proclaimed Son and God, as he says: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us; sovereignty is upon his shoulder, and his name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God” (Isaiah 9:6).

[Note: Antwerp and the Corbie manuscript read “God, Mighty”; Cologne and Basel read “Mighty God.”]

In the one Christ there are not two persons, so that one was called a child and another God; rather, in one person there is complete God and perfect human being. Substantially, the child is one thing and God another, yet personally the child is not one and God another. For there is one Son, both child and God: the child who was born to us is the same son who was given to us, and his name is called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God.

This child, however, just as he had true flesh, so also had a true soul, so that the true divinity might both assume the whole human nature in order to renew it and, having assumed it, might renew it, as was shown above through Luke’s testimony: “The child, that is, Jesus, increased in age and wisdom and grace before God and human beings” (Luke 2:51).

For this reason the Lord himself did not fail to show in himself either the name of flesh or that of soul. He demonstrated that he possessed flesh most truly when he said: “What is born from flesh is flesh” (John 3:6). The full truth of this also shone forth through the manifestation of his deeds: when he was born as an infant, he was not only wrapped in swaddling clothes and enclosed in a narrow manger, but, receiving circumcision, he also showed that he had true flesh. Moreover, after the resurrection he instructed his hesitant disciples, saying: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24:39).

He did not cease to indicate, either by name or by deed, that he had assumed a soul together with flesh, when he said: “I lay down my soul for my sheep” (John 10:15), and “My soul is troubled” (John 12:27), along with the other passages that will be presented below.

Through Isaiah, the divine oracle shows that Christ assumed this soul not without rational understanding: “Behold, my Servant will understand, and he will be exalted and greatly glorified.”

## CHAPTER XIX. The final proof from the Acts of the Apostles concerning the true flesh and soul of Christ

[Col. 0243B]

Although many things remain by which our assertion may be confirmed, nevertheless, since the sequence of our discourse is hastening toward the end of the book, we shall also set forth from the Acts of the Apostles the clearest indication of this mystery: the sermon of the blessed apostle Peter, which he poured forth concerning that wondrous drunkenness with spiritual new wine.

For when, instructing the Jews on divine authority, he had introduced David’s words—words which David, taught by God, had sung concerning Christ—he said:

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “although he had introduced David’s words.”]

“I foresaw the Lord always before me, because he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken. Therefore my heart rejoiced, and my tongue exulted; moreover, my flesh also will rest [or: rests] in hope. For you will not abandon my soul in Hades, nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption. You have made known to me the paths of life; you will fill me with joy in your presence” (Psalm 15:8–10).

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “I foresaw.”]

When the blessed Peter recalled this testimony from the psalm, in order to show that it had plainly been spoken about Christ, he continued:

“Men, brothers, let me speak boldly to you concerning the patriarch David: he both died and was buried, and his tomb is among us to this day. Therefore, since he was a prophet and knew that God had sworn to him with an oath that he would set one from the fruit of his loins upon his throne, foreseeing this, he spoke concerning the resurrection of Christ: that neither was his soul abandoned in Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption” (Acts 2:29–31).

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “foreseeing.”]

We have inserted this testimony at the present point so that the evident distinction between the names and the realities might teach that both flesh and soul are present in Christ. It will be given a more suitable place of its own when we discuss the mystery of the Lord’s passion (below, Book III, chapters 22, 23, and 24). There, too, we hope—God assisting us—to treat in such a way that it will be evident that the true substance of flesh and soul in Christ is demonstrated not only by names but also by the manifest indications of their natural functions, including these statements:

“My soul is sorrowful even unto death”; “Now my soul is troubled”; and “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his soul for his friends.”

## CHAPTER XX. Epilogue of the first book, concerning the divine and human nature of the Mediator in one person; and the subject of the following two books

Therefore, if the truth of our salvation is believed to be in the Savior, then it must consequently be affirmed that in the one and same Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, there is the undivided and unconfused perfection of the divine and human substance. For the Son of God, begotten from the substance of the Father, neither lost the eternity of the divine nature when he assumed what was temporal for the eternal salvation of temporal beings; nor was he deprived of the dominion of true and natural divinity, since he exalted the truth of the servant’s form, which he had accepted, with an interminable and inalienable dominion; nor could true power be weakened when it assumed our weakness, since it removed the defect of weakness from the weak; nor could he be imperfect who granted perfection to the imperfect; nor did the divinity of Christ descend locally into Hades, since, without bulk or extension, it exists wholly everywhere in such a way that, although no place can be without it, no place can contain it locally.

For that true and infinite substance of God exists ineffably, wholly in each creature and wholly in all creatures. It is not diminished in the smallest, nor increased in the greatest; it is not enclosed by time, nor bounded by quantity; it did not begin with a beginning, nor will it be brought to an end. From it the whole human being was both created for righteousness and, after the Fall, assumed without sin.

Now, since the truth of our discussion concerning the mystery of the Mediator—so far as he who is the Father’s Word granted by the gift of his grace—has left nothing ambiguous by which it might be shown that one and the same Christ naturally possesses the whole deity from the Father and the whole human nature in the human being, we must next address the fact that some people, thinking carnally about divine matters, are all the more gravely clouded by the error of their conceived falsehood because they assert that the divinity of Christ either came locally from heaven or descended locally into Hades. Some of them also do not hesitate to maintain that Christ suffered in the flesh and that his divinity suffered along with him.

I have therefore assigned separate little books to treating the truth of these matters as far as will be sufficient: the second to display the immeasurable divinity of the Son of God; the third to contain, with the clearest exposition of the facts, the mystery of the Lord’s passion.

[Note: Perhaps one should read *curavi deputare*, or rather *deputavi curare libellos* (“I took care to assign the little books”).]

Let this first little book, with due moderation in argument, now come to its close, so that in what follows God may open for us the door of discourse.

# BOOK TWO. ON THE IMMENSITY OF THE DIVINITY OF THE SON OF GOD

[Col. 0245]

## CHAPTER I. The incomprehensibility of the divine Trinity; infinite essence; since human beings do not fully know what is within themselves, they can know God above them even less

[Col. 0245A]

Whenever the weakness of the human condition, immediately seeking to know itself, attempts to extend its limits somewhat beyond the bounds of its smallness, and, pregnant with the conception of heavenly illumination, begins to bring forth an inquiry into its Creator and Redeemer, it will find, as I think, only that unchangeable eternity of the Trinity whose incomprehensibility is worthy of wonder. It surpasses everything we can think or understand just as it surpasses everything that we are.

The truthful sequence of the divine books testifies to this for us, Isaiah saying:

“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are my ways your ways, says the Lord. For just as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so my ways are exalted above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts” (Isaiah 55:8–9).

What expertise in human learning, then; what liveliness of spirit; what discernment of heart could reach the secret of that essence—that is, of the Trinity, which is the one true and only God? It neither began to exist nor ceases to exist. In its substance there is nothing that was not; nothing that was can fail to be. Nothing of it is confined by place, because it is wholly immeasurable; nothing precedes it by origin, because it is wholly eternal. It showed itself especially by this sign to be eternal, uncreated, and unchangeable: from nothing—that is, from what did not exist—it was able to create what would exist.

It also exalted the rational part of its creation above all else by this privilege of grace: having been granted the gifts of eternity and reason, that part would clearly recognize the essence of its Creator and Restorer as entirely without beginning, while it would understand that although it itself had not been made without a beginning, it would nevertheless never afterward be consumed by total annihilation.

It would thereby immediately be warned how greatly the creative power and wisdom of all things surpassed the measure of intellectual creation in the heights of infinity and incomprehensibility. For the rational creature itself, whose complete self-knowledge is comprehensible and finite to its creator but incomprehensible and infinite to itself, would be wearied by this very knowledge.

When it saw that the investigation of its own nature—which is not outside it—was both intimate and hidden to it, so that, although it is not above itself but within itself, it could not investigate itself wholly as it is, then, growing all the more fearful and amazed at the greatness of the supreme infinity, which exceeds all the boundaries of understanding, it would look upon itself as advancing toward knowledge of the Most High by the sole ascent of humility. His peace, as Paul says, surpasses all understanding (Philippians 4:7), and his judgments are a great abyss (Psalm 35:7). By the fall of proud thought, the creature had once deserved to be separated from him.

## CHAPTER II. Angelic nature could not restore the human being, because it too fell

But it could never have undertaken this at all if it had lacked either an example or assistance. One therefore had to be sought whose gift would restore it, whose light would shape it, and whose power would strengthen it, so that eternal equality might justify the impious, truth might instruct the ignorant, and power might strengthen the weak.

But could a human being accomplish this through a human being alone, or find it in any merely human being? In no way. For what human being could exist as a physician for the human wound, when all were surrounded at the root by the fellowship of natural corruption in a corrupted nature? Or how could one bring healing by oneself to the wounded when one’s own origin was held within the wound? Or how could one exist as the universal giver of beneficence when nature showed one to be in need of another’s aid?

The human being, drained of the riches of true salvation and deprived of the perpetual possession of good things, perhaps had to be raised up by angelic assistance. The one who, polluted in the prison-house of a house of clay, could not in any way aspire to the capacity for a purer life might be helped by the grace of angelic aid. Through it he might cast off the filth of his former offense and resume the dignity of the purity he had long ago lost.

Nevertheless, this gift of restoration could not be obtained even through angelic assistance. Angelic nature would have been in some measure suitable for restoring the human being if it had never naturally been bound by the instability of falling. But since it bears witness, by the evidence of a ruin it shares in common, that it itself is in need of help, it is clearly understood that it is much less able to contribute effectively to the restoration of the human being, since it cannot suffice even for its own stability.

[Note: The Victor manuscript reads “its own steadfastness.”]

It could reasonably be believed sufficient for its own preservation if no part of it were to fall into a worse condition. For the natural unity embracing the totality of angelic nature would undoubtedly remain supported by the fortress of impassibility if it could not be subject to suffering, nor ever suffer in what remained something it could not suffer in the whole.

But since a part of it is seen to have fallen from the summit of heavenly blessedness into the lowest and everlasting misery, as the blessed Peter says—“God did not spare the angels who sinned, but handed them over to gloomy prisons of Hades, keeping them for punishment in the judgment” (2 Peter 2:4)—it is plainly understood that all could have been crushed by participation in a uniform ruin, had not that power defended from the fall of wickedness those whom it willed to defend. It alone could not naturally be changed or corrupted.

## CHAPTER III. Divine power alone restored the human being and preserved the angel; Christ is the power and wisdom of the Father; Christ is naturally God, immeasurable, most high, eternal; the Father is in the Son as the Son is in the Father

That same power was therefore necessary for the restoration of the human being, because nothing other than that which could restore fallen humanity after its fall could preserve the standing angel from ruin. One grace operated in both: in one, so that he might rise; in the other, so that he might not fall; in the one, so that he might not be wounded; in the other, so that he might be healed. From the one it drove away weakness; the other it did not allow to become weak. It is the food of the former and the medicine of the latter.

Whoever rightly judges this one to be sound does not doubt that he is the Son of God, who is the power and wisdom of the Father: wisdom, because it ordered all things; power, because it created all things; wisdom, because it enlightens; power, because it provides assistance; wisdom, because it is unchangeable; power, because it cannot be overcome.

He is always naturally present to every creature by infinite power, and, being immeasurable, is never absent. He naturally possesses in himself what the Father is, and therefore was able both to establish the angel in the heights and to descend to the lower regions for the restoration of fallen humanity, as he himself testifies, saying:

“I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 6:38).

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “the Father.”]

When some hear that he descended, they attempt to assert that his descent was local, because they do not know how to consider God’s power as they ought. Nor can they recognize that God became human for the sake of humanity in such a way that, having accepted human form, he remained an unchangeable divine substance. Nor do they understand his temporal birth in such a way as to maintain that he has always existed eternally.

These are the people who also refuse to consider how he descended while remaining immeasurable, or how he was humbled while remaining most high.

If his nature is sought, he is essentially God, because “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” He is also eternal, because the power and divinity of God are eternal (Romans 1:20). He is immeasurable, because Jeremiah says of him:

“He is great and has no end, exalted and immeasurable” (Baruch 3:25).

A little later, to show that he had said these things about the Son, he added:

“This is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him. He discovered every way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (ibid., 36–38).

[Note: The printed editions of Cologne and Antwerp read “Thereafter” (*posthac*).]

Who would dare deny that the Son of God is most high? David says of him:

“The mother of Zion will say: ‘A human being, and a human being, was born in her, and he himself, the Most High, founded her’” (Psalm 86:5).

[Note: Cologne and Basel read “says.”]

Zachariah likewise proclaims of him at the birth of John:

“And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (Luke 1:76).

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “to prepare.”]

If, then, he is taught to be naturally God, immeasurable, most high, and eternal, let it be said: what is better than God, what greater than the immeasurable, what higher than the Most High, what earlier than the eternal?

God, therefore, does not differ from the Father; the immeasurable does not lack the Father’s equality; the Most High is not deprived of exaltation; and the eternal is not later in origin.

For since nothing changeable can exist in God the Father, God was born from God; since nothing local exists in him, the immeasurable proceeded from the immeasurable; since nothing lowly exists in God, the Most High generated the Most High; and since nothing initiated can be found in God, the eternal brought forth the eternal.

That generation did not display any separation of the Father and Son; rather, it excluded the error of confusion, lest we fail to believe him born whom we heard to be one with the Father. God could be born from God, but the immeasurable could not be separated from the immeasurable. He was born into existence, not departed; for that divine and ineffable birth is such that the one whom the Father begot from himself, he had within himself.

Isaiah shows us this rule of faith concerning the unity of his true divinity. The prophet says:

“For in you is God, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it, God of Israel, Savior. All who oppose him will be ashamed and confounded, and they will go away in confusion” (Isaiah 45:16–17).

But who opposes the Son of God except those who deny that the Father is in him and he in the Father through natural unity, and who dare to separate the Father and the Son through the natural diversity of a wicked unbelief?

For the Father is in the Son as the Son is in the Father. Natural unity shows both to be equal in such a way that the immeasurable generated the immeasurable, and the immeasurable begotten from the immeasurable possessed nothing less of the Father’s immensity.

## CHAPTER IV. The Father made all things through the Son

I ask you, illustrious ruler, not to suppose that the things we say about God are to be conceived corporeally. The one who made all things surpasses everything he made. As it belongs substantially to him alone to exist without beginning, so it belongs to him alone substantially to beget without beginning. As it belongs to him, through ineffable immensity, to fill entirely what he made, so through the unity of nature it belongs to him to be wholly in the Son and always to have the Son wholly in himself—the Son whom he begot.

If the Son did not order all things with the Father, he is not the wisdom that says:

“When he prepared the heavens, I was there with him; and when he set apart his throne above the winds; when he made the clouds strong above, and when he established the springs beneath heaven” (Proverbs 8:28–29).

And below:

“When he made firm the foundations of the earth, I was with him, arranging all things.”

If wisdom is not believed to be co-eternal with the Father, then God too must be proclaimed changeable in the ordering of what he began. If the Son did not make all things, he should neither be called power nor hand.

And where is what is said through the prophet?

“Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet. What house will you build for me, says the Lord? Or what is the place of my rest? Did not my hand make all these things?” (Isaiah 66:1–2).

The evangelist also says:

“All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

[Note: The printed editions read “anything.”]

If the Son is absent anywhere, he is not immeasurable. If the Father did not utter him from his heart, he ought not to be called the Word. If he was not begotten from the Father’s womb—that is, from the Father’s substance—then, falsely (which God forbid), he is called the true God, concerning whom John testifies: “This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20).

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Here eternity is shown; here immensity is found; here essential nature is revealed.

For what was in the beginning never was not, because it always was. What was with God was not local but immeasurable, because since God is not local, the Word who was with God was not in a place. And because the Word was God in the unity of nature and the truth of the name, he was precisely what that God was with whom the Word, God, was.

## CHAPTER V. Objection concerning the statement “In the beginning,” and not “Before the beginning,” was the Word; Christ is the beginning and the end; Christ is eternal life; how catholic truth understands Christ as beginning and end

Or perhaps, because we have heard it said that he was “in the beginning,” we dare to assign to the Son some beginning of existence, and therefore do not believe that he was born without beginning because John testifies that he was not before the beginning but in the beginning?

Far be it that such foolish thinking should touch the mind of any wise person! Far be it that such a contagion of deadly unbelief should infect the purity of the Christian religion in anyone!

Who would not understand that “beginning” is rightly said of that which no beginning could precede? For whatever you wish to think of as existing before any beginning, you must necessarily confess to be the true beginning. And because no one, by thinking, ever finds an end to the beginning, that must truly be called the beginning which is essentially eternal.

This is plainly why the Son himself, wishing to show the Jews the immensity of his eternal existence by an entirely certain manifestation, answered those asking who he was:

“The Beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8:25).

But perhaps, because he is called “the beginning,” he will rather be thought subject to a beginning of existence. If someone attempts from this word to construct a prejudice against the truth—so that, because he knows him to be called by the name “beginning,” he supposes that he had some beginning of birth—he will certainly also assign to the Father, which is impious, some beginning of existence, since we know the Father to have been named “beginning” together with the Son, as he himself says:

“With you is the beginning on the day of your power, amid the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.”

What will the person who asserts from the name “beginning” that the Son has a beginning of birth answer?

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “from the name of the beginning.”]

If someone believes that, because he is called “the beginning,” the Son’s birth had a beginning, it follows that, because he is called “the end,” he must also have an end. For the Lord himself affirmed to the Jews who questioned him that he was the beginning, saying:

“The Beginning, who also speak to you.”

Paul, however, calls Christ the end, saying:

“For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4).

The Lord himself also says of himself:

“I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end” (Revelation 1:8).

If, because he is called “the beginning,” he is asserted to have begun, then, because he is called “the end,” he may also be thought destined to end. And where would be that outpouring of John, which he drank from the breast of the living fountain?

[Note: Basel reads “had drunk.”]

“We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the True One and be in his true Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:21).

Whoever asserts that this life will cease must deny that it is eternal.

Yet he who is the true God and eternal life says that the righteous will go into eternal life. How, then, will the life of the righteous be eternal if eternal life itself will one day cease? Or why is this labor of holy conduct and continual struggle against temptations endured if the reward will one day be taken from the victors?

Is this the praiseworthy aim of the saints’ entire course? Is this why they discipline their bodies and subject them to service? Is this why they run not as though uncertainly and fight knowing that they do not beat the air (1 Corinthians 9:26)? Is this why they know that their struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers and authorities, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Ephesians 6:12)?

For this reason they resist firmly in faith the roaring lion that prowls tirelessly, seeking someone to devour (1 Peter 5:8), so that after living patiently here amid tribulation, once the deceptive rather than true recompense of the divine promise has at last been exhausted, they may live miserably—or not live at all?

Christ is called life, as he says:

“I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Christ is called the beginning and the end, because he likewise said:

“I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end” (Revelation 1:8).

But if this life, because it is called “the beginning,” is thought subject to a beginning of birth, it follows that, because it is called “the end,” it may eventually be thought destined for final destruction. How will those to whom eternal life is given live without end if the eternity of life itself comes to an end?

Since these conclusions are altogether absurd, the truth of the catholic and apostolic faith must consequently be retained. It calls Christ “the end” because it believes him to be perpetually without end not only in the substance in which he was born, naturally eternal from the Father, but also in that which he took from his mother in time. It likewise rightly and truly proclaims him “the beginning” because in the divine substance that he possesses he is always asserted to be co-eternal with his Begetter.

There is no doubt that nothing is earlier than the true beginning and nothing later than the true end. Christ is therefore the beginning because, being eternal, he precedes all things; Christ is the end because, being perpetual, he encompasses all things. Christ is the beginning because he himself began what was to be completed; Christ is the end because he himself completes what was begun. Christ is the beginning because through him things that did not exist receive existence; Christ is the end because through him certain things that began to exist receive everlasting existence.

## CHAPTER VI. Objection concerning Melchizedek, who is said to be without father and without mother; Christ is the king of righteousness and peace; Christ is without mother as God and without father as human being; the twofold birth in Christ’s one person

What grounds for doubt are thought to remain here, when the Apostle demonstrates that in Melchizedek—who bore the type of Christ, the future high priest—the person of the one and same God and human being, Christ, was signified? He shows that Christ is, according to his divine substance, eternal without beginning, and, according to the servant’s form which he accepted in time, perpetual without end.

[Note: The Corbie and Victor manuscripts read: “showing him to be eternal according to the divine substance, and perpetual according to the servant’s form.”]

Thus the same teacher of the nations speaks to the Hebrews:

“For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, to whom Abraham apportioned a tenth of everything—first, as his name is interpreted, king of righteousness, and then also king of Salem, which is king of peace—without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, remains a priest forever” (Hebrews 7:1–3).

Perhaps someone resisting the light of truth could bring some objection in this testimony against the person of Melchizedek if it were to be believed that any creature naturally existed without beginning. But since it is clear that every creature, having been made entirely from nothing, does not lack a beginning—and since its origin is understood to have been brought forth from nothing solely by the will and power of the Creator, when he judged that it should be made, although the ordering of mutable works was always held immutably by him—it cannot at all be accepted that Melchizedek either was not begotten from a father and mother, which belongs to the first human being, or naturally lacked a beginning of existence, which belongs to God alone.

The one who naturally retains the truth of this figure, then, is he who in both births was wondrous, never lacking the truth of a natural origin, and who was singularly born in both.

For who is the king of righteousness except our king, Christ, who was made sin for us so that we might become the righteousness of God in him?

Who also is the king of peace except the one who says:

“My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27)?

For he is our peace, who made both one (Ephesians 2:14). The prophet cries out to him:

“Lord our God, grant us your peace. For you have given us all things, Lord our God; possess us. Lord, apart from you we have known no other; we invoke your name” (Isaiah 26:12).

Christ the Son of God did not have a mother in the substance of God, which he always has from the Father. Again, he did not have a father in the nature of a human being, which he assumed from his mother alone.

In truth he preserved the singularity of both births, both of parent and of offspring: although he was first born from the Father alone and afterward from the Virgin alone, it was nevertheless one and the same person who was first from the Father and afterward born from the Virgin.

Thus, in the wondrous and ineffable mystery of one true God and true human being, Christ, the one begotten did not lack the natural substance from the begetter, nor was the person doubled in begetter and begotten. Although in one Christ the unconfused truth of the divine and human natures’ origin is preserved, the undivided truth of both natures presents one person in Christ.

[Note: The printed editions read “the truth of the natures” rather than “the truth of the natures’ origin.”] Thus neither does the twofold birth appear to double the person of the one Christ, nor can the unity of the person abolish the true substance either of God in the human being or of the human being in God.

Although each true substance in the one Christ bears witness within itself both to the natural birth of its origin and to the origin of its birth, the wondrous enduring mystery of piety has nevertheless provided for us in this human birth a clear line of understanding concerning that divine and ineffable generation which has no beginning.

[Note: Cologne and Antwerp read “in this.”]

For the one who is always God from God is, in time, God and human being from a human being. In the one whose eternal birth possessed the fullness of the Father’s substance naturally, natural truth displayed the fullness of human nature.

The Son of God, in order to raise our understanding from visible things to invisible things, demonstrated in himself the truth of human nature, so that we might consequently believe that from the nature of the true God there naturally existed the true God whom it is evident was naturally born as a true human being from a human being.

# CHAPTER VII. Christ’s temporal birth leads to knowledge of the eternal one. Christ’s immeasurable majesty, because his birth is everlasting. There was no place before the Son of God in which he might be born. Nor was any place coeval with the Word.

Christ also had the beginning of his birth in the nature of man, in which she who gave birth could not be a mother without a beginning. Thus, once the truth of nature had been recognized, it might be acknowledged that the divine birth had no beginning [Note: [Col. 0251D] The word “beginning” was absent from the printed editions and has been restored from the Corbie and Victor manuscripts.], just as the eternal Father had no beginning of existence, and no birth of an initiated generation was added to him.

Thus Jesus Christ demonstrated in himself the truth of both substances: just as in the substance of the man Christ, without prejudice to the prerogative of that unique dignity, there is substantially what is naturally established in man, so in the same Christ God it must be believed that there is substantially what naturally subsists in the Father. Thus, when the truth of man is seen in the man Christ, the truth of the Father’s deity is recognized in the same Christ God; and when this birth is found to be subject to a beginning—the birth which temporally came substantially from a temporal man—that birth too must be believed to be without beginning, which substantially and eternally subsists from the eternal God [Note: [Col. 0252D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “substantial and eternal.”].

He himself, therefore, is without a mother in his divine substance [Note: [Col. 0252D] The Victor manuscript reads: “by which” (*qua*).], naturally begotten from the Father alone; he himself is without a father, the fruit of the inviolate Virgin, whom no marital embrace touched; he himself is without genealogy, of whom it is written: “Who will declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8) [Note: [Col. 0252D] The Cologne and Basel editions read: “Who has declared it?”]. Thus, while faith grants us knowledge in the true generation of the Son of God, eternity surpasses speech; and while the firmness of belief is nourished by the support of faith (or rests upon it) [Note: [Col. 0252D] Basel reads: “foundation”], the boldness of speech is restrained by faithful fear, so that the true and natural eternity of the divine generation may be recognized.

For since the divine is certainly true by nature—because there is nothing false in the true God—and since it neither began nor was created, just as it surpasses the reach of thought concerning every nature that has begun and been created, so it exceeds every power of speech. Or perhaps, when we have learned from the truth of apostolic authority about the peace of God, do we hesitate to accept the same thing altogether concerning his generation? For the most blessed Paul says to us: “The peace of God, which surpasses every understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7).

If, then, his peace, although it surpasses all understanding, is nevertheless believed to be true, eternal, and natural, why should the natural truth and boundless eternity of his generation—which utterly surpasses all speech—be denied? Therefore, where there is eternal peace, let eternal birth also be believed; and of him whose birth is to be believed eternal, let immeasurable majesty not be denied. For what is not held within the beginning of a birth is not enclosed by any natural limit; and therefore that substance is recognized as altogether immeasurable whose birth did not begin but is true.

For whatever is circumscribed by some limit must necessarily be held by place or by time. But how can it be believed that he made time and place if he himself is subjected to place or time? “Through him every place was made,” because “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). Time too is recognized as having been made through him, concerning whom Paul says: “In many and various ways God spoke of old to the fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages” (Hebrews 1:1–2) [Note: [Col. 0253D] Basel reads: “and through the prophets.”].

Therefore, he through whom place was made is not local, nor is he temporal through whom time was made. For if he himself, being local, made place—and it is certain that everything local is in a place—it follows that he was previously in a place and was thus able to create place [Note: [Col. 0253D] Basel reads: “was not able”]. But this place in which the Son of God is said to have been: I ask whether it is believed to be earlier than the Son or coeval with him. [Note: [Col. 0253D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “What if?”]

If some think that the place was earlier than the Son, let them see into what abyss of impious assertion they fall, when they place the material for any work before the maker of all things. And since John recalled that all things were made through him [Note: [Col. 0254D] The Corbie and Victor manuscripts read: “mentions”], he could not be said to have possessed any truth in himself—God forbid—if any work preceded its maker. For how could he have made a place before which he could not exist, or without which he could not exist, if he himself could not have been made in that way?

Next, let them carefully consider that they appear to assign the infinity of eternity to the place which they attempt to take away from the Son of God. For if they assert that the Son of God was not born without a beginning because the evangelist says, “In the beginning was the Word,” and does not say, “Before the beginning was the Word,” then those who assert that the place existed before the Word must also confess that it existed before the beginning, since they think that what existed before the Word had no beginning.

But if the place had no beginning, it is undoubtedly coeternal with the eternal Father. And since one eternal thing cannot be distant from another eternal thing, this impiety necessarily produces the absurdity that either God is thought to be local, or the place is believed to be what God is, or they suppose that place itself is some principle existing without God, which naturally persists uncreated by virtue of its own eternity. [Note: [Col. 0254D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “this absurdity will follow.”]

But since these things cannot be believed without impiety, the place must be said to be not only earlier than the Son, but not even coeval with him. For nothing made can be placed before or compared with him through whom all things were made (Psalm 148:5). Since he arranged all things in number, weight, and measure, he could no more be numbered by time than measured by place.

Accordingly, the psalm truly sings: “Great is the Lord our God, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number.” And to show the boundless immensity of this wondrous eternity, it is said elsewhere: “Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, and of his greatness there is no end” (Psalm 144:3).

For what is naturally eternal must necessarily be declared naturally immeasurable, because what always exists is not contained by number, and what is wholly everywhere is not enclosed by place. Therefore, in another testimony of Scripture, Wisdom is said to “reach everywhere because of her purity” (Wisdom 7:24). And shortly afterward: “She reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (ibid., 8:1).

When we hear that Wisdom reaches from end to end, it must certainly be understood that, in reaching from end to end, she surpasses both ends by the immensity of her infinity. For he can reach every creature whom no creature can contain. Just as he remains immeasurable while filling heaven, so, reaching from end to end, he remains infinite.

For “she reaches mightily from end to end” is like what is said through Jeremiah: “I am God who draws near, and not God from afar. If a man is hidden in secret, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?” (Jeremiah 23:23–24). He who fills all things sees all things.

And he showed what “I shall see him” means when he added: “I fill heaven and earth.” God must not be thought to see in a bodily manner, as though he himself were in one place when he sees and what he sees were in another. For whatever he sees, he sees not outside himself, because he himself fills everything that he sees.

For it is written: “In every place the eyes of the Lord observe the good and the wicked” (Proverbs 15:3). And elsewhere: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Psalm 33:16).

# CHAPTER VIII. How the omnipresence of the divine nature is to be understood

[Col. 0254D]

Here an occasion arises for a question that must not be passed over, in the words of Solomon: “In every place the eyes of God observe the good and the wicked.” And again the prophet says to the Lord: “Your eye is pure; you cannot look upon evil” (Habakkuk 1:13).

For it must be feared that he who is said to see what he is said to fill may be thought to be absent somewhere when he is said not to see something, since he would not be substantially everywhere if he were not even among the wicked. But if humility of heart is maintained in the divine utterances, no contradiction of the truth will be found.

In one sense, therefore, God sees everything, and in another sense God does not see certain things; just as in one sense he is wholly everywhere, and in another sense he is not somewhere—not because he is substantially absent anywhere [for it is written: “All things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him” (Colossians 1:16); and, according to the prophetic saying, “He measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and heaven with his span, and enclosed the whole earth in his closed hand” (Isaiah 40:12)], but because he is not equally present to all.

For he is everywhere present by power, but not everywhere by grace: by the power through which God fills and contains all things, and through which he sees all things; but by grace he is said to see that which he himself bestows and works in his faithful ones: “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31).

Accordingly, even where he does not see certain things in order to bestow, he sees them in order to repay. Thus he sees evil and does not see evil: what he does not see in order to approve, he sees in order to judge; and what he does not see as something granted through his grace, he sees as something to be demanded from the sinner by justice. For where the generosity of justification is absent, the severity of judgment is not absent, as blessed Paul says: “See, then, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you continue in goodness” (Romans 11:22).

Since these things are so, how can he be substantially absent anywhere, when even “the light shines in the darkness, although the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5)? Or how can he substantially fail to see anything concerning whom blessed Paul most clearly testifies, saying: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. And no creature is invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Hebrews 4:12)? [Note: [Col. 0255D] These words are found here in only one printed codex; they are absent from the Corbie and Victor manuscripts and from the Cologne, Antwerp, and Basel editions.]

Nor here, as we said above, should any suspicion of bodily vision intrude, as though the Son of God were in heaven and from there saw everything while not being elsewhere. For to God, seeing is being; and he wishes his substance to be believed as extensive as the vision he reveals, so that when we hear [Note: [Col. 0255D] Basel reads: “hear”] that all things are naked and open to his eyes, we should think that no limit bounds his substance.

# CHAPTER IX. That infinity belongs equally to the Son and to the Father

To show that the Son shares one infinity with the Father, Holy Scripture took care to say concerning Wisdom: “For she is the radiance of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness” (Wisdom 7:26).

In this testimony the natural unity, the distinction of persons, and the immeasurable equality of the Father and the Son are all shown. No one doubts that in this passage the Father is called light and the Son radiance. Concerning him apostolic authority also says: “He is the radiance of glory and the exact representation of his substance, and he upholds all things by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3).

Behold: the Son is said to be radiance, and to uphold all things. If anyone therefore thinks the Father immeasurable but believes the Son to be bounded by some quantity, let him show us how light and radiance can be different substances, since they are neither confused in name nor separated in kind, and neither differs from the other in quantity.

Again, radiance is so indivisibly united to light that it cannot in any way be separated from it. Light contains in itself as much radiance as radiance contains light; nor can light be deprived of radiance in order to shine, nor radiance of light in order to radiate. Rather, whatever light fills, radiance, remaining equal within it, also fills; and radiance, existing equally within the light, fills the same things.

Therefore, if that eternal light could neither exist without its radiance nor be deprived of it, then either one limit of quality and quantity must be assigned to the Father and the Son, or both must necessarily be proclaimed equally immeasurable. For you must confess that the radiance of that light is as great as the light of that radiance, since its radiance equals the light in every respect, so that neither can be greater or lesser there [Note: [Col. 0255D] This is the reading of the Corbie and Victor manuscripts and of the older Cologne, Antwerp, and Basel editions; the two more recent editions read: “so that nothing there can in any way be greater, nor can anything be called lesser.”].

# CHAPTER X. The Son did not descend locally from heaven. The Father too is said in Scripture to descend and come, but not locally.

We are greatly astonished at those who conspire against the Son of God, thinking that, according to the substance of his deity, he either passes from one place to another by local movement, or cannot simultaneously fill all things by the immensity of his deity. They go so far as to believe that, when they hear that he descended to earth, he was not in heaven or among the dead, and to affirm that he descended to the underworld according to the substance of his deity in such a way that they suppose he was then absent both from heaven and from earth.

Why do they not consider that, according to the manner of Scripture, by which heavenly utterances are commonly adapted to the understanding of little ones, similar expressions are sometimes also found concerning the person of the Father? To pass over those passages in the legal books in which it is said, “The Lord descended to see the city and the tower” (Genesis 11:5), as though he would not have seen them if he had not descended—although above we demonstrated that Scripture says, “In every place the eyes of God observe the good and the wicked”—the Lord himself says to the prophet: “I am the Lord God of all flesh; is anything hidden from me?”

There is also the passage that follows shortly afterward: “Come, let us descend and confuse their languages there” (ibid., 7). Let these passages, then, for the moment be left unmentioned, since some are accustomed to assign them not to the whole Trinity but to the person of the Son alone. [Note: [Col. 0256D] Basel reads: “some.”] [Note: [Col. 0256D] Perhaps the better reading is: “not to the whole Trinity, but …”]

What will they say about that passage of the Gospel in which the Son himself, instructing his disciples before his passion, says: “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, that is the one who loves me; and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and I will manifest myself to him” (John 14:21)?

When Judas the disciple—not the betrayer—had answered, saying, “Lord, what has happened, that you are going to manifest yourself to us and not to the world?” Jesus answered and said to him: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him [Note: alternative reading: “loves him”], and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (ibid., 23).

They love together, they come together, and together make one dwelling with the one who loves them; together they manifest themselves, because by the one light of their coming they illumine the heart of the one who loves them. And because they manifest themselves by revealing themselves, they do not reveal themselves without the Holy Spirit, since they do not manifest themselves without the Holy Spirit.

For they cannot be known without his [Note: alternative reading: “the Holy”] Spirit, just as they cannot exist without their [Note: alternative reading: “the Holy”] Spirit. Therefore, just as there is one manifestation, so there is one revelation of the Trinity; and where the gift of divine revelation is one, there the coming of the undivided Trinity is one.

For just as the Father is shown to reveal, when the Son himself says, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17), so the Son is shown by his own word to reveal the Father. For he says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matthew 11:27).

The revelation of the Holy Spirit must not be judged dissimilar, in whom there is the natural recognition of God, as the Apostle says: “For who among human beings knows what belongs to a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also no one has known what belongs to God except the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:11).

The same Teacher of the Gentiles says concerning him: “For God has revealed it to us through his Spirit” (ibid.). Again he writes to the Ephesians: “May the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation” (Ephesians 1:17). And to show that the Spirit works the revelation of the knowledge of God in us, after saying, “May he give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation,” he added: “in the knowledge of him.”

The Trinity alone, however, can reveal itself, because the Trinity alone can fully know itself. To the extent that it gives itself to be known, to that extent it grants itself to be revealed. And there is full knowledge of itself where there is no natural distinction. For the immeasurable is fully known by the immeasurable; and the infinity of knowledge remains where the substance has no end, nor is the limit of knowledge touched by any creature, where what is immeasurable is in no way bounded.

# CHAPTER XI. God comes to human beings not by movement but by loving-kindness

There is therefore one Trinity alone which, when it manifests itself, comes ineffably, and when it conceals itself from the unworthy, departs altogether ineffably. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit come and go in their own incomprehensible manner; yet neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Spirit moves locally. They know how to come and go in such a way that they neither come locally to a place nor depart locally from a place.

This coming of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit shows not the mobility but the loving-kindness of God who comes. For the one deity of the Trinity [Note: [Col. 0258D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “and the Trinity, which fills and contains all things, …”], which fills and contains all things, is said to come to the one to whom it deigns to manifest itself; and it departs from the one from whom it conceals the light of its love. Yet it does not become locally absent when it justly abandons one who is unworthy, nor does it become locally present when it mercifully visits one whom it has made worthy.

Therefore, although God says, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24), it is nevertheless said of someone: “God is not in his sight” (Psalm 9:5). And although the Father fills everything, it is nevertheless said in the Book of Wisdom: “For perverse thoughts separate from God” [Note: [Col. 0258D] This is the reading of the Corbie manuscript and the Antwerp edition; Basel reads: “For those who think perversely separate themselves from God.”] (Wisdom 1:3).

And although it is said of the Son—that is, of the Wisdom of God—“She reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1), the same Wisdom nevertheless says of herself: “The wicked seek me and will not find me.” Again it is said: “Wisdom will not enter a deceitful soul, nor dwell [Note: alternative reading: “dwell continually”] in a body enslaved to sins.”

The Holy Spirit too, although he is proclaimed in every respect immeasurable, since “the Spirit of the Lord has filled the inhabited world,” is nevertheless said to be such that “the Holy Spirit will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts that lack understanding.”

Therefore, as regards his substance and power, the Trinity, the one God, is everywhere: wholly filling everything by power, not by mass; wholly present in each creature and wholly present simultaneously in all creatures.

But as regards our thoughts, God is said to descend to us when he so divinely adapts his word to us that, speaking with us in human fashion, he deigns to make his knowledge and love known to us. He ascends in us when we ascend through love and knowledge of the deity, so that we may learn neither to conceive anything local within the immeasurable, nor to judge anything lowly concerning the Most High, nor to believe anything changeable in God, nor to think anything temporal in the eternal.

# CHAPTER XII. God rested and worked by will, not by labor

Such must be believed to be the coming of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For just as, after the world’s original work had been completed, God is said to have rested—although he did not labor in the work, since he accomplished all things by will alone—so it is said to him: “For it is present with you to exercise power whenever you will” (Wisdom 12:18). We hear likewise in the psalm: “Whatever he willed, he made, in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths” (Psalm 134:6).

The leper in the Gospel, recognizing through divine illumination the omnipotence of this will, testifies that it is sufficient for the effect of his cleansing, saying: “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean” (Matthew 8:2). By saying, “If you will, you can,” he shows that the divine will itself is the fullest power.

Finally, the Lord also mercifully demonstrated by the effect of healing what the man who asked had faithfully believed. For he said: “I will; be cleansed,” and immediately his leprosy was cleansed.

Therefore, just as, when he made the world, he experienced no inconvenience of labor, as though his strength, exhausted by the work, needed to be restored by the success of rest—but when he says that he rested, he shows that we shall rest after good works—so, when he is said to have come or descended, the grace of divine revelation toward us is commended; and when he is said not to descend but to ascend, the progress of our illumination and knowledge is shown.

# CHAPTER XIII. The meaning of the saying, “Do not touch me,” and the dissolution of the apparent contradiction among the Gospels

The Lord Jesus signified such an ascent when he prohibited Mary Magdalene from touching him. After the resurrection, when he mercifully appeared to her as she wept, John records that he said: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17).

This touch of which the Lord speaks is proved to concern belief, not the body. Otherwise the evangelists’ testimony would appear contradictory. For John testifies that the Lord himself, by his command, prevented Mary from touching him, saying: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (Acts 1:3). Scripture confirms that the Lord ascended into heaven, according to his humanity, on the fortieth day after the resurrection—a truth retained not only by the unimpaired faith of the holy Catholic Church, but also proclaimed with complete agreement by the diverse and multifaceted belief of the various heresies, at least those that do not deny the mystery of true flesh in the Son of God.

If, before the Lord had ascended to the Father, he did not wish Mary to touch him bodily, how does Matthew, on the very day of the resurrection, say that Mary Magdalene and another Mary held Jesus’ feet? To make this clearer, we have thought it right to insert into this work the whole passage as Matthew presented it.

He says:

“Now, late on the sabbath, as it was dawning toward the first day of the sabbath, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake. For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and came and rolled back the stone, and sat upon it. His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow. From fear of him the guards were terrified and became like dead men.

“But the angel answered and said to the women: ‘Do not be afraid. For I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord was laid. And go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen; and behold, he goes before you [Note: alternative reading: “will go before you”] into Galilee. There you will see him. Behold, I have told you.’

“And they went out quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, running to announce it to his disciples. And behold, Jesus met them, saying: ‘Greetings.’ They came up and held his feet and worshiped him” (Matthew 28:1–9).

How, then, did he forbid Mary Magdalene to touch him because he had not yet ascended to the Father, while on that same day he allowed her to hold his feet? Is anyone so carried away by perverse reasoning that he thinks Christ’s statements were altered by momentary changes—as though, after reconsidering the matter more wisely, he later granted Mary what he had earlier denied her?

But the Chosen Vessel immediately opposes such a thought. Concerning the Son of God, according to the unchangeableness of eternal divinity, he does not permit us to fall into any suspicion of change. He writes to the Corinthians:

“For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you through us—through me and Silvanus and Timothy—was not ‘yes’ and ‘no’; but in him there was ‘yes.’ For all the promises of God are ‘yes’ in him” [Note: [Col. 0259D] This is the reading of the printed editions; the Corbie manuscript has “there was not ‘yes’ and ‘no,’” in accordance with the Greek text οὐκ ἐγένετο ναὶ καὶ οὔ, “it did not become yes and no.”] “Therefore, through him also we say ‘Amen’ to God for his glory and for ours” (2 Corinthians 1:19–20) [Note: [Col. 0259D] Basel reads: “in him there is ‘yes’”; the Corbie manuscript, as well as the Cologne and Antwerp editions, read: “in him there is.”] [Note: [Col. 0260D] This is the reading of the printed editions; the Corbie manuscript and the Greek text read: “therefore, through him also, Amen, to the glory of God for us.”]

The understanding of the evangelists does not therefore differ here. Christ neither pointlessly forbade himself to be touched because he had not yet ascended to the Father, nor pointlessly allowed his feet to be held. In one case he demonstrated the truth of his flesh; in the other he intimated the glory of his deity. There he permitted the hand; here he removed understanding [Note: [Col. 0260D] The Victor manuscript reads: “he admonished.”], so that in the man Christ the truth of resurrected flesh might be touched, while in the same Christ God the equality of the Father’s divinity might be believed.

He therefore says, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father,” because Mary Magdalene did not yet believe him equal to the Father; she mourned him with feminine devotion as though he had been extinguished.

For what is “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” except: “Do not believe in me only what you think; do not establish in your heart only what you suppose? For as long as you attend in me only to the things of the flesh, you do not perceive my equality with the Father”?

And truly, Christ has not yet ascended to the Father for those who do not confess the Son equal to the Father. Therefore, each person must hasten, believing in the perfection and truth of the human nature in the Son of God, to hold Christ’s feet, as it were, and to confess that the substance of the same Son was born from the Father, so that Christ may ascend to the Father for him through the equality of natural divinity.

For what is “I have not yet ascended to my Father” except: “You consider him lower than the Father, whom you mourn as dead”? And what is “Do not touch me” except: “Do not fix the movement of your faith upon this”?

Whenever we wish to touch something with any bodily member, we do not speak of touching unless we have brought the movement of that member to an end. We must move the member until we come to the thing we wish to touch; beyond that, once we have reached complete contact, we do not extend the movement of the member further [Note: [Col. 0260D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “of the other.”]

So too we fix the movement of our mind upon what we establish in our heart through belief. Therefore, if we believe about Christ what is worthy and fitting, then we touch Christ.

But whoever does not believe the Son of God equal to the Father according to the divine nature has not yet had Christ ascend to the Father for him. And the one for whom the Son has not ascended to the Father does not receive the ability to touch Christ. But the Son has truly ascended to the Father for the one who does not doubt that the Son is equal to the Father in the likeness of eternity and immensity, so that he does not consider the Son, God naturally begotten from God the Father, to be either later or lesser.

For if he is lesser than the immeasurable, he is not equal; and if he is later than the eternal, he is not coeternal. Each of these beliefs separates a person from the touch of Christ, because it does not make the Son equal to the Father but diminishes him.

Such a person rightly hears from Christ: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.” For whoever is not permitted to touch Christ is certainly separated from his body. And what is the body of Christ except the Church of Christ?

Hence it is understood that, until someone believes the Son of God equal to the Father according to the divine substance, he cannot be joined by the touch of faith to the members of Christ. But the one whose Son has ascended to the Father surely holds together the structure of the Lord’s body; and the Son has ascended to the Father for the one who confesses the Son’s deity equal to God the Father.

It is therefore plainly evident that through the Son’s ascent to the Father the progress of our faith is rather demonstrated. For we raise him up, in a certain sense, in our hearts when we grow in our understanding of him, so that we think of him, as the true God, what is worthy of the divine majesty [Note: alternative reading: “worthy by the divine majesty”].

# CHAPTER XIV. What it means to exalt God; what it means to sanctify him

The holy David urges us toward this exaltation of God, saying: “Exalt the Lord our God, and worship at the footstool of his feet, for he is holy” (Psalm 98:5). And shortly afterward: “Exalt the Lord our God, and worship on his holy mountain, for the Lord our God is holy” (ibid., 9).

What, then, does it mean to exalt the Lord except to believe of the Most High what is most exalted? This is certainly what it means to worship on the mountain: when we think about God, to conceive nothing lowly about him. He is exalted in us when we exalt him, although he himself is always Most High; just as he is sanctified in us when we sanctify him, although he himself always remains holy.

For blessed Peter admonishes us, saying: “Sanctify the Lord Christ in your hearts” (1 Peter 3:15). What does it mean to sanctify Christ except to think about Christ what is holy? Such thought does not sanctify him but us; and by sanctifying us it preserves us, as Solomon says: “Holy thought will preserve you.”

The Lord himself also commands us to say in prayer: “Hallowed be your name.” Yet the blessed Cyprian is known to have understood this passage of the prayer in such a way that, in this sanctification of the divine name, he said that it is not God who is sanctified, but that the gift of divine sanctification is conferred upon us.

For in his letter on the Lord’s Prayer, after making some preliminary remarks, he speaks as follows:

“After this we say: ‘Hallowed be your name,’ not because we wish God to be sanctified by our prayers, but because we ask him that his name may be sanctified in us. For by whom is God sanctified, since he himself sanctifies? But because he said, ‘Be holy, for I also am holy’ (Leviticus 11:44), we ask and pray that we who have been sanctified in baptism may persevere in what we have begun to be, and we pray daily for this. For we need daily sanctification, so that we who sin daily may cleanse our offenses through continual sanctification [Note: [Col. 0261D] The Victor manuscript reads: “cleanse” (*purgemus*)]” [Note: [Col. 0261D] The Corbie manuscript and the printed editions have this reading; the Victor manuscript reads: “not that God is sanctified,” and so forth.].

If, therefore, by sanctifying Christ we are sanctified, and by asking that God’s name be sanctified we receive the gift of sanctification, why should we not believe that, when we exalt God, we ourselves are exalted through progress in understanding? [Note: [Col. 0261D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “we should be believed to be exalted.”]

And if, when we exalt God, we are rather exalted ourselves [Note: alternative reading: “we rather exalt him”], then similarly, when he is said to come to us, we ought to believe that our progress is being indicated, in that the divine majesty deigns to reveal itself to our hearts.

# CHAPTER XV. How power went out from Christ when the woman touched his fringe; how Christ is said to come to us, and in what sense. The Holy Spirit too is immeasurable. The whole Trinity is immeasurable.

For if the Son of God descended to us by a local movement, then power went out from him locally. For when a certain woman, afflicted with an issue of blood (Luke 8:43 ff.), having exhausted her resources and strength and spent everything she possessed because of her illness, yet being unable to bring to an end the one thing she did not wish to have—her illness—and desiring to be freely cured by the heavenly physician, secretly touched his fringe and, by a believing act of seizure, stole for herself the effect of healing, he, conscious of her faith and salvation, said: “Someone touched me; for I know that power has gone out from me.”

[Note: These words—“and desiring to be freely cured by the heavenly physician”—are absent from the manuscript codex Victorinus; they are found in the other codices, editions, and the manuscript Corbeiensis.]

What, then, is this power that went out from the Lord? Did he depart by going out? Or, when it came to heal her, could it reach her in such a way that it could not go out locally from the Savior? But if power went out locally from him who is called Power, let it be said how Power departed from Power. If, however, such a belief seems inconsistent with Christian faith, let us understand this departure of power from Christ not as something else, but as the effect of divine healing: for the Savior’s power went out to the woman when she recognized in herself the power of divine healing.

Thus the Son of God, who is the Power and Wisdom of God, the creator of places and times, just as he, being eternal, precedes all time, so, being boundless, transcends every place. He is said to come to us when he deigns to illumine us. For the evangelist says of him: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him [or: through it], and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him.” How, then, is he both said to have been in the world and affirmed to have come into the world? Is the former to be attributed to his power and the latter to his grace?

Certainly. According to his divinity, he was never absent from heaven, hell, or the world: “For all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him” (Colossians 1:16–17). According to his grace, however, he came into the world when, in wondrous compassion, he came to the aid of the perishing world. He himself also testifies to this, saying: “For God did not send his Son to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17).

The Son of God is therefore boundless, like the Father and the Spirit, since it was said of him: “Great is he, and he has no end, exalted and immeasurable” (Baruch 3:25). Shortly afterward it is said of him: “After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (ibid., 38).

The Holy Spirit also is immeasurable. Knowing this, the prophet said to God: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?” (Psalm 138:7). To show that this Spirit of God is the Holy Spirit himself, the aforementioned prophet says to God: “Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 50:13). The Apostle likewise indicates, by this testimony, that the Spirit of God is the Holy Spirit himself: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4:30).

[Note: Basil reads “for the day,” following the Greek εἰς ἡμέραν, “into the day.”]

And elsewhere: “But whoever rejects these things does not reject a human being, but God, who also gave his Holy Spirit in us” (1 Thessalonians 4:8).

David declares this Holy Spirit of God to be so immeasurable that he says to God, as we mentioned above: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into hell, you are present. And if I take up my wings toward the east, or, as another translation has it, before dawn, and dwell at the farthest limits of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me fast.”

[Note: The manuscript Corbeiensis reads *sumpsero* (“I take up”) … *tenebit* (“will hold”), in place of *assumpsero* … *continebit*.]

No one doubts that the Son is called the hand of the Father. Of him God himself says: “Has not my hand made all these things?”

[Note: The manuscript Corbeiensis reads: “And yet.”]

Nevertheless, in order to proclaim the Trinity equally immeasurable, the prophet signified the Father, to whom he said, “Where shall I go from your Spirit?” He also signified the Spirit, from whom he testifies that he can in no way go or flee; and he demonstrated the Son when he declares that even at the farthest limits of the sea he is to be led by the hand of God. Thus it may be recognized that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one immeasurability and one presence in all creatures.

This is the Trinity, one God. Just as he alone was able to create all things, so he alone is able to fill all things. He is neither local within a place, nor temporal within time, nor bounded by the limit of a creature.

## CHAPTER XVI. God is everywhere; indeed, he hears prayers even in secret.

[Col. 0263D]

**106** The blessed martyr Cyprian, in his treatise *On the Lord’s Prayer*, affirms the immeasurability of the divinity of the Son of God by an explicit proclamation and by the testimony of the divine Scriptures, saying:

> “Finally, the Lord instructed us by his teaching to pray in secret, in hidden and secluded places, even in our rooms, as is more fitting for faith, so that we may know that God is present everywhere, hears and sees everyone, and, in the fullness of his majesty, penetrates even hidden and secret places, as it is written: ‘I am God who is near, and not a God from afar. If a person is hidden in secret places, will I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?’ (Jeremiah 23:23–24). And again: ‘In every place the eyes of God observe the good and the wicked’ (Proverbs 15:3).
>
> “And when we gather together with the brethren and celebrate the divine sacrifices with God’s priest, we must remember modesty and discipline: we must not scatter our prayers indiscriminately in unformed cries, nor noisily parade before God a petition that ought to be commended with restraint, because God is the hearer not of the voice but of the heart. Nor must he be summoned by shouting, since he sees the thoughts, as the Lord confirms when he says: ‘Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?’ (Matthew 9:4). And elsewhere: ‘All the churches shall know that I am the searcher of the kidney and the heart’” (Revelation 2:23).

The blessed Cyprian, having said that God is present everywhere, hears and sees everyone, and, in the fullness of his majesty, penetrates even hidden and secret places,

[Note: The editions of Cologne and Basel omit “in” before “hidden and secret places.”]

also asserts that he is himself the hearer not of the voice but of the heart, and that he need not be summoned by shouting, since he sees the thoughts. He also represents him as saying: “Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?” And elsewhere: “All the churches shall know that I am the searcher of the kidney and the heart.”

[Note: The manuscript Victorinus reads “kidneys.”]

Who does not know that these words were spoken by the Son of God, as the Apocalypse and the Gospel testify? The Son, therefore, as the holy Cyprian asserts, is present everywhere; he hears and sees everyone; in the fullness of his majesty he penetrates even hidden and secret places; and he does not need to be summoned by shouting, since he sees the thoughts.

The words of the evangelist John agree with this understanding. Speaking of certain people, he says: “Jesus did not entrust himself to them, because he knew everyone, and because he had no need for anyone to testify about a human being; for he himself knew what was in a human being” (John 2:24).

## CHAPTER XVII. Christ never abandons his own to solitude, because he is everywhere present to them. Everything is manifest to God.

The blessed Cyprian, writing also to the people of Thibaris concerning the immeasurability of the Son of God, bears witness in these words:

> “He is not alone whose companion in flight is Christ; he is not alone who, preserving the temple of God, wherever he may be, is not without the Lord. And if, while fleeing through solitude and mountains, a robber should overpower him, or a wild beast attack him, or hunger, thirst, or cold afflict him, or, while hastening across the sea in a headlong voyage, a storm or tempest engulf him, Christ watches his soldier wherever he fights.”

In the letter *On the Lapsed*, too, anyone who wishes will find these words:

> “He sees the hearts and breasts of individuals, and, since he will judge not only our deeds but also our words and thoughts, he looks upon the minds and conceived intentions of all, while they are still hidden within the secret recesses of the closed breast.”

The Son of God is therefore proved, both by divine authority and by the faithful and truthful judgment of the holy Fathers, to be infinite and immeasurable according to his divine nature: present everywhere, filling all things, now the witness of thoughts and deeds, and destined to be the judge and recompensor of all.

But because this same Son of God, true God born from God the Father, became true man for us from a human being—for he was made from the seed of David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3)—and because he contains in himself the truth of both the divine and human natures, he did not lose what belongs to true divinity and accepted what belongs to true humanity. One and the same person was born temporally according to the flesh from his mother, while according to his divinity he remains eternal from the Father; one and the same is a local human being from a human source and an immeasurable God from the Father; one and the same, according to his human substance, was absent from heaven while he was on earth and left earth when he ascended into heaven; but according to his divine and immeasurable substance, he neither left heaven when he descended from heaven nor abandoned earth when he ascended to heaven.

This can be known with certainty from the Lord’s own words. To show that his humanity was local, he says to his disciples: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17). After saying of Lazarus, “Lazarus has died,” he added: “And I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe that I was not there” (John 11:14–15).

Showing his divine immeasurability to his disciples, he says: “Behold, I am with you every day, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20). How, then, did he ascend into heaven, unless he is a local and true human being? Or how is he present to his faithful, unless he is likewise immeasurable and true God?

Scripture again says of him: “Truly God dwelt with human beings on earth” (2 Chronicles 6:18).
