Of him the evangelist says: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” To make it known that this Word, even when he became flesh and dwelt among us, had never departed from heaven, David says: “Forever, Lord, your Word remains in heaven” (Psalm 118:93).

Filled with prophetic inspiration and recognition, Jeremiah had spoken of this one and the same eternal Son of God, who would then also be the Son of Man, in whom true and immeasurable divinity would remain and from whom true and local humanity would be assumed:

> “This is our God, and no other will be accounted beside him. He discovered every way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36–38).

And because he had earlier said of him, “Great is he, and he has no end, exalted and immeasurable,” lest this vision of God on earth and his life among human beings be thought to have removed the immeasurable God from heaven, the Son himself, while placed on earth, demonstrated the immeasurability of his divinity. He did not show himself present in heaven according to the human being whom he had assumed, but according to God, which he always was.

[Note: The printed editions of Cologne and Antwerp and the manuscript Corbeiensis read: “and according to the human being whom he had assumed … and according to God.”]

He said: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

[Note: The edition of Basel reads “who.”]

This does not mean that Christ’s human substance had been diffused everywhere, but that the one and same Son of God and Son of Man is true God from the Father, just as he is true man from a human source. Although, according to his true humanity, he was then locally present on earth, according to his divinity—which is in no way contained by place—he wholly filled heaven and earth.

## CHAPTER XVIII. From the words of the Apostle Christ is proved both immeasurable and local. Christ’s bodily ascension. Christ dwells in us. God the Father dwells in us. The Holy Spirit dwells in us.

We also see this true humanity of Christ, which is local, and his true divinity, which is always immeasurable, indicated to us by apostolic teaching. For, to show that the body of Christ, the true human being, is locally contained, the Apostle Paul says to the Thessalonians: “How you turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God, and to await his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus” (1 Thessalonians 1:9–10). He clearly indicates that the one whom he knew to have been bodily raised from the dead would come bodily from heaven.

He therefore says again: “Our citizenship is in heaven. From it we also await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform [or: transformed] the body of our humility to conform to the body of his glory, according to the operation by which he is also able to subject all things to himself” (Philippians 3:20).

Meanwhile, since the opportunity presented by this passage must not be passed over in silence, attention should be paid to the place where the Apostle says that the Son is able to subject all things to himself, lest [or: and lest] the Father be thought to have subjected everything as though he were weak. He also says that he will transform the body of our humility to conform to the body of his glory. If this is true, Christ’s body can certainly be contained in a place.

[Note: The edition of Basel reads: “The opportunity of this passage should in no way be omitted,” and so forth.]

[Note: The edition of Basel reads: “the blessed Apostle Paul.”]

John also confirms this truth of Christ’s body, which will come from heaven, saying: “Behold, he will come with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him” (Revelation 1:7).

In the book of the Acts of the Apostles his bodily ascension is likewise made known:

> “And when he had said these things, while they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes. And as they were gazing into heaven while he was going, behold, two men stood beside them in white garments, who also said: ‘Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, whom you saw going into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven’” (Acts 1:9 ff.).

Since, therefore, Christ’s flesh is shown [or: was shown] beyond doubt to be local, his divinity is nevertheless known, on Paul’s testimony, always to be everywhere. He says to the faithful: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ” [or: “Christ’s”] (2 Corinthians 13:3)? How could he speak in him if he were not in him? Or how could he have bodily ascended into heaven and be proclaimed to be on earth in his faithful, if there were not in him an immeasurability of divinity capable of filling heaven and earth?

Paul says to the Corinthians: “Do you not recognize yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?” (ibid., 5). And to the Ephesians he says: “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts in the inner person” (Ephesians 3:16).

The Son is therefore in heaven and dwells in us on earth—namely, by that presence of his immeasurability by which the Father and the Holy Spirit also dwell in us. For the prophet showed, in these words, that God the Father dwells in us:

> “For I will dwell in them and walk among them [or: I will walk], and I will be their God, and they will be my people. Therefore come out from their midst and be separated, says the Lord; and do not touch what is unclean, and I will receive you; and I will be a father to you, and you will be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty” (2 Corinthians 6:15–17).

Paul also shows that the Holy Spirit dwells equally in us, writing to the Corinthians: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

And so that none of those who place the Holy Spirit below the Father and the Son might deny that the words “the Spirit of God dwells in you” refer here to the person of the Holy Spirit, what will he say about that passage where the Apostle instructs Timothy with the concern of paternal love?

“Guard the good deposit,” he says, “through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us” (2 Timothy 1:14).

## CHAPTER XIX. This indwelling is not local but immeasurable. Our heart is enlarged by God’s indwelling.

This indwelling of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in us is certainly not local but immeasurable; it is not comprehensible by thought but venerable through faith. The Trinity dwells in its faithful: wholly in each individual and wholly in all together. It is neither stretched out by the space of heaven and earth nor bounded by the limit of the whole creation; it is not divided into parts among separate people or [alternatively: and] separate places; nor is it absent from hell, since it is not absent from earth or heaven. For he who alone was able to make all things can alone fill all things.

Whoever, however, considers the coming or indwelling of the Son and the Holy Spirit to be local must first affirm that the Father dwells locally in us—not only dwelling, but also walking among us—whom the blessed Paul asserts, through the prophet, to have said: “For I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Corinthians 6:15).

Let it therefore be explained how the Son or the Holy Spirit may dwell [or: dwells] in us. For if we believe that these things must be measured in the human manner, the one who is said merely to dwell must be greater in quantity than the one who is shown also to walk among us. The one who dwells can fill the whole place that he inhabits; but the one who is said to walk among us is plainly shown, without doubt, to be smaller than the space in which he walks.

Yet a more absurd conclusion will follow from this foolish conception. Beyond doubt, the spaces of our heart themselves would appear larger than the Trinity, since they would contain a place that the Son and the Holy Spirit could fill by dwelling in it, and another place that the Father could not fill by walking in it.

But if these ideas do not accord with the truth, let us believe that the indwelling of the Trinity is ineffably signified according to the incomprehensible majesty of its immeasurability. When we hear that God dwells and walks among us, let us understand this spiritually, so that we do not believe that God moves locally within our heart, but that our heart is enlarged in God.

The Apostle spoke of this breadth of heart when he said: “Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart has been enlarged. Since we have the same recompense, I speak as to children: you too be enlarged” (2 Corinthians 6:11).

A little later he added the testimony of the prophet mentioned above, saying: “For you are the temple of the living God, as God says: ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them’” (ibid., 15).

## CHAPTER XX. The immeasurability of the Trinity is shown by the form of baptism. Conclusion of the second book on the immeasurability of the divinity of the Son of God.

[Col. 0268B]

**110** Nor should that by any means be omitted whereby the most evident immeasurability of the Trinity, and its presence—which is in every respect not local but divine and wondrous—is demonstrated. For, when believers are baptized everywhere in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, according to the Lord’s own command, we recognize this truth.

[Note: The word “everywhere” is absent from the editions; it is found in the manuscript Corbeiensis.]

If the whole Trinity is believed to sanctify in baptism, then the whole Trinity is certainly shown to be present. But when baptism is celebrated [or: be celebrated] everywhere at one time throughout the entire world in the name of the Trinity, if the whole Trinity is present for sanctifying [or: for signifying], behold, it wondrously displays everywhere the presence of its immeasurable majesty, since it belongs to God alone to fill all things simultaneously.

If, however, the whole Trinity is not equally present everywhere, and the Son or the Holy Spirit is thought to be absent, then that one must not be named in baptism who cannot be present for sanctification. Whoever therefore thinks that the equality of the Father’s immeasurability must be denied to the Son or to the Holy Spirit should first remove their names from the sacrament of baptism.

In this, then, the truth of the Catholic faith is recognized above all: it rightly baptizes in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, because it confidently believes that the whole Trinity is equally present everywhere.

The immeasurability of the divinity of the Son of God could still be demonstrated by countless testimonies. But we have preferred to set down a few from many, wishing also to bring the second book to an earlier conclusion. We have taken particular care that, in what we send to your Clemency, the mind happily occupied with royal concerns should not be burdened by the length of the reading, but rather instructed by the manifestation of truth.

[Note: The manuscript Corbeiensis reads “faithfully.”]

Therefore, let us conclude at this point what has been argued concerning the immeasurability of the divinity of the Son of God, so that what must be said concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion may be begun again with another opening.

# BOOK THREE. ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE LORD’S PASSION

[Col. 0267]

## CHAPTER ONE. The difficulty of the third book on the Lord’s Passion. The error of the Theopaschites. The word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing.

[Col. 0267C]

**111** Although in the second book, supported by the assistance of heavenly grace, we proved the divinity of the Son of God to be immeasurable, confined neither by time nor by place, since it fills all things, contains all things, precedes all things in eternity, and embraces all things equally in immeasurability, we took particular care to demonstrate this so that those who until now have been unable to think spiritually about God might be released from the error of suspecting locality in the Son of God.

No less concern remains for us to complete this third volume, in which we shall discuss the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, which he himself, who suffered for us, bestowed. Here we are shaken by no small fear and pressed by no light anxiety, for, so far as we are concerned, we are wholly unequal to explaining so great a depth.

But he who opened the mouth of the mute and made the tongues of infants eloquent [or: makes them eloquent] (Wisdom 10:21) will himself, as we trust, give a well-ordered and well-sounding word to our mouth. He will mercifully grant such grace for the demonstration of truth in this work, which he deigns to accomplish through us, that the rightness of Catholic doctrine and the crooked and manifold error of heretical depravity may clearly shine forth through the manifest evidence of the Scriptures.

[Note: The manuscripts Thuanensis and Victorinus read “the mouth of the mute”; the printed editions and the manuscript Corbeiensis read “the mouth of the dumb.”]

For there are certain people who think about the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion otherwise than piety requires. While seeking salvation, they incur the loss of salvation; and while attributing to God what they observe in human beings, they strike the Savior’s side, as it were, with the spear of perverse speech. Although the unbelieving soldiers did not dare to insult him while he was dying, certain people now, under the disguise of the Christian name, do not fear to disparage him while he reigns.

These are the people who, although they perhaps cannot—or certainly neglect to—consider the human and divine substance in the one Christ, true God and perfect man, according to the truth of their natures, fall into this error: they do not consider a human nature in the Son of God while the immutability of divine power remains, but dishonor the divine substance by attributing to it the passibility of divine weakness.

Foreseeing this by the divine Spirit, the Apostle said: “For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved it is the power of God” (1 Corinthians 1:8).

Those who perish through the word of the cross include not only those who think that the Son of God could not suffer in the flesh what belongs to humanity, but also those who believe that the divinity of the Son of God substantially experienced pain or passion on the cross.

But how is the word of the cross the power of God if the divine substance could become weak on the cross? Or how will Christ lead us to [or: lead us back to] the grace of immutability and incorruption if he himself is proved to have been changed for the worse according to the divine nature, when it is proper to the divine nature neither to admit deficiency nor to admit increase?

## CHAPTER II. Christ must be treated cautiously because of the two natures in one person.

Since we are about to discuss what in Christ was always impassible and what was passible before the death of the flesh, we have first judged that we must insert into this little book what we believe and hold concerning the one Christ, God and man. We do this so that, when we begin to demonstrate in the one Christ what pertains to the properties of the divine and human natures, no one may think that we believe in two Christs according to the two natures, or suppose that we are introducing a fourth person into the Trinity.

For, retaining the faith of evangelical truth, we recognize the proper character of each nature in the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, without in any way dividing the unity of his person. We know that the property of both substances remained so united in Christ that, while God remained impassible, he suffered in the flesh and, because he willed it, experienced true passion in true flesh, while remaining wholly impassible in his divinity.

No one other than the one who remained wholly impassible in the true passion of the flesh suffered in the flesh; nor did anyone other than the one who, by dying, could conquer death without being able to experience death in death, deign to hand himself over to death.

But how we say these things while preserving the unity of the person and the distinct properties of the substances in Christ, the sequence of our confession set forth below will show.

## CHAPTER III. The right faith concerning the divinity of the Son of God. The person of the Father is one and that of the Son another, in one nature. Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, full of grace and truth.

We therefore believe that the Son of God was begotten before every beginning whatsoever—that is, without any beginning to his birth—from the substance of the Father: God from God, Lord from Lord. He was not from nothing, because he is from the Father; he is not merely titular, because he has his name from the truth of his nature; and he is not from another nature, because nothing co-eternal with God existed from which an origin could be supplied to the Son.

[Note: The manuscripts Thuanensis and Victorinus read “not from another nature”; the manuscript Corbeiensis and the edition of Basel read “not from any material”; the editions of Cologne and Antwerp read “not from any nature.”]

The Son is neither later than the one who begot him nor lesser, but—as we also said in the second book—wholly equal to the Father both in the eternal nature of his immeasurability and in the immeasurability of his eternity. He is the unchangeable creator of changeable things, the timeless maker of temporal things and of times. No place contains him, and no place is without him, because the immeasurable Creator fills all things.

He is not for that reason less God because he is said to be begotten; rather, he is rightly believed to be true God precisely because he is proclaimed to have been substantially begotten from the Father.

[Note: The manuscript Thuanensis reads “true God.”]

Thus, existing eternally from the Father, he possessed one nature with God the Father, but received his own person from the begetter. For divine birth did not divide the natural unity, but distinguished the person of the Son subsisting from the Father. The designation “Father” shows that the one who was born is another, excluding the error of Sabellian confusion, as the Son himself declares when he says: “Another is the one who bears witness about me, and I know that the testimony which he bears about me is true” (John 5:32).

And to show whom he meant by “another,” he added shortly afterward: “The Father who sent me bears witness about me” (ibid., 37).

Elsewhere, likewise distinguishing his own person from that of the Father, he says: “I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 8:16).

To teach this distinction of the two persons and to establish the confession of one substance in the Father and the Son, the Son himself says: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in him who sent me; and whoever sees me sees him who sent me” (John 12:44).

There is therefore one Son, begotten from the nature of the Father. He is called the Only-Begotten so that, by the property of the Father’s nature, he may be shown to be both one and begotten. But this one who is naturally called the Only-Begotten from the Father, just as he is inseparable in unity of nature, so he remains without confusion in the distinctness of his person.

For this reason the Son of God calls himself the Only-Begotten alone, saying: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16).

And shortly afterward: “Whoever believes in him will not be judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.”

[Note: The manuscript Corbeiensis reads “because he did not believe,” in accordance with the Greek text.]

John likewise bears witness and speaks of the Son alone:

[Note: The manuscripts Victorinus and Thuanensis read simply “For John bears witness of the Son”; the editions read “For John also bears witness of the Son.”]

> “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

The Word made flesh is full of the grace of the assumption of humanity, because Christ possesses nothing lacking in human nature. The same Only-Begotten from the Father is full of the truth of the Father’s substance, because he naturally possesses in himself the entire fullness of the Father’s divinity.

The evangelist therefore recognized him as full of grace and truth: grace showed that he was one and the same true human being through the reality of the incarnation, while the truth of his eternal birth declared him to be the true God, the Only-Begotten from the Father.

But what benefit is there for the Son in being called by the name “Only-Begotten” if he is deprived of the truth of the name? For he is called Only-Begotten in vain if, in his generation, not the natural truth of his being begotten from God the Begetter but the generosity of creation from a giver is proclaimed.

For it is said of others also: “But to all who received him, he gave the power to become children of God” (ibid., 12). If, then, the only-begotten Son is also said to have become so by grace, rather than to have been truly begotten by nature, he has certainly lost both the name and the truth of the Only-Begotten once he has begun to have brothers. He is deprived of the truth of this name if, in the Only-Begotten, there is not the natural truth of the Father.

## CHAPTER IV. The adoptive sons of God differ not in names but in gifts, not in life but in glory.

For among the sons of God who do not subsist from the nature of God the Father, the adoptive sharing in dignity can possess a diversity of gifts, but not of names. The grace of the adopter, although it promises to all who are born from God the gift of different recompense according to the merit of their labor, nevertheless gives them all the one name of sons.

One heavenly life is likewise promised through true faith to all who are reborn, although differing glory is granted to those who will reign, as the blessed Paul says: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:41).

Yet to all these, on account of the power he gave them to become children of God, it will be said together at the right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34). It is likewise said of them all: “But the righteous will go into eternal life” (ibid., 46).

[Note: “Will go” is absent from the manuscript Corbeiensis; it is found in the printed editions.]

The unity of the adoptive name will therefore hold all the sons of God equally, although a difference of glory will reveal the varying quality of their merits. In this respect, that we have begun to be spiritual through the origin of a new birth, we are not distinguished by name, although by progress we are to be distinguished in reward.

For in that he voluntarily begot us by the word of truth, the grace of the Begetter has called us all equally sons.

But if that divine and eternal birth of the Son is believed to have proceeded not from the nature of God the Father but from grace, he ought not to be called the Only-Begotten but merely “begotten.” For just as the generosity of paternal adoption conferred upon him the name “begotten,” so the fellowship of paternal adoption granted to us excluded him from the name “Only-Begotten.”

The Only-Begotten is not called “among many,” although he may be called “begotten” together with the begotten.

[Note: The manuscript Corbeiensis reads this way; the editions of Cologne and Antwerp do not contain the words “among many.” In Basel it reads: “The Only-Begotten is not called [among many], although he may be called begotten together with the begotten.”]

If this is so, let what John dared to write—the name “Only-Begotten”—be erased, so that what he deserved to draw from the breast of truth may be proved false.

But if the distinctiveness of the Only-Begotten is to be demonstrated by the clear indication of its meaning, then let the many sons of God be called sons by grace in such a way that one begotten by nature may be recognized.

For who has been born as true God from true God except the Only-Begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father? The incommunicable name that distinguishes him alone from the other sons of God separates him from them precisely because in him alone remains the natural truth of the Father.

## CHAPTER V. Christ emptied himself, yet remained full of grace and truth.

115 This true God and eternal life, when he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads, “did not regard equality with God as something to be seized … but emptied himself.” The Basel manuscript reads, “to be equal.”], but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6): for the true God did not seize the equality of God, which he eternally possessed with the Father by natural unity. Therefore the only-begotten Son of God, even when he emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, remained full of grace and truth. “We saw,” says John, “his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads, “full of grace and truth.”] and truth” (John 1:14).

This is certainly what is shown in the one and same person who emptied himself and remained full of grace and truth: having received the form of a servant, he displayed the complete reality of a voluntary self-emptying, while, in the eternal form of God that remained, he manifested the fullness of grace and truth. What, then, is the self-emptying of the only-begotten, except the assumption of Christ’s passible and mortal humanity? And what is the fullness of the only-begotten, except Christ’s abiding impassible and immortal divinity? In him the perfect man is full of grace, and in him the perfect God is full of truth. To show that the term “fullness” belongs to divinity [variant: *quod* / *quo*, “which” / “by which”], let us hear the Apostle speaking of Christ: “For in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him” [variant: *in illo* / *in illa*, grammatically distinct Latin forms] (Colossians 2:9–10). What this fullness of divinity is that dwells in Christ, John shows [variant: *ostendat*, “may show,” / *ostendit*, “shows”]: “The Word,” he says, “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Of this fullness John the Baptist asserts that we have received, saying: “And from his fullness we have all received, and grace upon grace.”

## CHAPTER VI. In the one Christ there are two natures, not confused but united.

One and the same Christ, therefore, the Son of God and man, both emptied himself and remained full of grace and truth: truly made changeable while remaining unchangeable, truly suffering while not subject to suffering, truly dead while not experiencing death but extinguishing it. One Christ both performed and endured all these things, because in the one and same Christ the true nature of divinity and the true nature of humanity remained. God was not confused with man but united to him; thus, in the one person in whom both natures remained, he displayed such signs of each that the true and perfect God shone forth through true divine powers in the humanity he had assumed, while the reality of human weakness showed that he was a true and complete man in God.

For this reason the blessed Apostle both proclaims the one and same Christ crucified and declares him to be the power and wisdom of God, saying: “We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block indeed to Jews, but folly to the Gentiles; yet to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23–24). And, to display the greatness of divine power [Note: The Cologne and Antwerp editions read, “and that by weakness” (*et ut infirmitate*)], he added: “For what is foolish of God is wiser than men, and what is weak of God is stronger than men” (ibid., 25).

That Son of God, then—the power of God and the wisdom of God—at the beginning of our redemption accomplished something different [variant: *quiddam* / *quidem*, “something” / “indeed”] in man from what he had always possessed with the Father. There, his birth was one of majesty; here, the work of redemption required an act of mercy [variant: *exegit* / *exigit*, “required” / “requires”]. In the mystery of that eternal birth, the eternal and unchangeable [variant: *incommutabilis* / *immutabilis*] Father begot another who was not different from him [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads, “one birth.”]; and as great as he brought forth by begetting, so great he himself remained. He distinguished from himself in person the one whom he wholly possesses in nature. This is revealed to us in the Son’s own words: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10).

Thus nature unconfusedly unites the two, although person inseparably distinguishes the two [Note: The printed editions read, “Thus nature unconfusedly unites both natures, although person inseparably distinguishes both persons.” The Corbie manuscript reads, “unites both persons.”]. Therefore the Son himself testifies: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). By saying “one,” he does not separate divinity from God; by saying “are,” he does not confuse his birth with the Father.

## CHAPTER VII. It was fitting for the Mediator to have two natures. God became man without changing himself.

In the accomplishment of our redemption, it was fitting that the complete and true God should be united to the complete and true man, yet in such a way that, in the unity of the person, neither God in man nor man in God could be confused. No human being would ever have been capable of conquering the enemy of the human race if, in the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, there had been either something less than human or, once assumed by God, the man had been consumed by the divine assumption. Human nature could not be consumed in its restoration, since even that part of it which has been condemned will not be consumed by the eternity of punishment.

Since punishment consumes, whereas grace restores, the Redeemer of the human race must be confessed as fully God [Note: Some manuscripts read “more fully”], receiving a complete man: full of the grace by which God deigned to become man, and full of the truth by which God himself, who became man, remains unchanged [Note: The word “is” is absent from the printed editions but appears in the Corbie manuscript], just as he had already said through the prophet: “See that I am, and I have not changed” (Malachi 3:6). Of him Paul also recalls that blessed David sang: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same” (Hebrews 1:12; Psalm 101:28).

One and the same Christ, therefore, inasmuch as he was full of grace, lacking nothing belonging to human nature, was born as a complete man from a human being; and inasmuch as he was full of truth, lacking nothing of the Father’s divinity, was begotten as complete God from the Father. For the only-begotten from the Father would not be full of grace if there were something lacking of humanity in the Son of God; nor would he be full of truth if there were something lacking of divinity in that Son of man.

That ineffable God, therefore, naturally begotten from the Father without beginning, when the fullness of time came, was sent by the Father [Note: The Thuan manuscript reads, “that he might become” (*ut fieret*)] “to be born of a woman, to be born under the law, in order to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:5). He was wholly reigning in the bosom of the Father and wholly fashioning himself in the Virgin’s womb [Note: The word “is” is absent from the Corbie manuscript and the printed editions; it appears in the Thuan manuscript].

## CHAPTER VIII. Christ is wholly in the Father and wholly in his mother’s womb. Christ, rich in himself, became poor for our sake.

117 For no part of him remained in the Father while another part descended into the Virgin. Rather, while remaining wholly in the Father as what he was, he became wholly in the Virgin as what he had not been: wholly with the Father, filling and containing the whole world; wholly building for himself a house in the Virgin’s womb (for it is written, “Wisdom built herself a house,” Proverbs 9:1); wholly in the eternal Father, wholly in the man he assumed, wholly in heaven, wholly in the world, and wholly even in the underworld.

Thus the true and supreme God received the whole man into himself, and thus the fullness of divinity united itself wholly to man, while the truth of the divine and human substance remained unconfused. Consequently, since the unity of the person thereafter remained eternal, neither the man Christ could be separated from his divinity, nor the same God Christ from his humanity.

This was required as the remedy for our weakness: just as natural unity remains in the Father and the Son, so personal unity should remain in Christ; and just as personal distinction does not make two substances in the Father and the Son, so natural distinction should not make two persons in Christ. Again, just as natural unity does not confuse the Father and the Son, so personal unity should not confuse man and the Word. And just as the only-begotten Son can never be separated from God his Father by the unity of nature, so the man who was assumed could never be separated from God who assumed him by the unity of person.

Yet, although Christ could never be confused or divided, one and the same Christ, through the reality of human suffering, restored to us what had been ours, and through the reality of divine impassibility bestowed what had been his. Thus, while he became poor yet remained in possession of his riches, he made us rich from our poverty, granting us the infinite riches of his poverty. The Apostle, the chosen vessel, clearly proclaims this when he says: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that although he was rich, for your sake he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

This inseparable unity of person, in which God and man are one Christ, made it possible both for the man Christ to be born from God by grace, while the truth and fullness of human nature remained intact, and for the same God Christ to suffer voluntarily in the flesh, while the impassible fullness of the divine substance remained intact.

For just as there is one of whom the Apostle says, “whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9:5), so there is one of whom the same Apostle says: “For although he was crucified in weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4). There is therefore one Christ: in his crucifixion the true weakness of flesh was present, and in his life the power of true divinity shone forth. God possesses what is human in the truth of human nature, and man possesses what is divine in the truth of the divine substance. Hence he is proclaimed incomprehensible on the cross, inviolate in his wound, impassible in his suffering, and immortal in his death.

## CHAPTER IX. When Christ suffered, God did not suffer with him.

118 Some people fail to attend carefully to these matters and do not hesitate to subject Christ’s divinity to suffering. Hearing that Christ suffered in the flesh, they suppose that God suffered along with the flesh, paying insufficient attention to that divine and unchangeable substance of the Son of God which both assumed suffering in passible flesh and could not suffer together with the flesh.

The blessed Peter confirms this in the truth of divine inspiration and says: “Since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same understanding” (1 Peter 4:1). If he had known Christ’s divinity to be passible, it would have been enough for him to say, “Since Christ suffered,” and he would not have added, “in the flesh.” But because he knew that in the one and same Christ the human nature had been passible before death while the divine substance always remained impassible, he therefore confesses that Christ suffered in the flesh, whose divinity he knew to remain wholly impassible.

## CHAPTER X. Although Christ’s divinity assumed passible flesh, it nevertheless remained impassible because it is unchangeable.

Perhaps someone will say that Christ is proclaimed to have suffered in the flesh because the divinity, which could not suffer before the assumption of flesh, assumed passible flesh and therefore experienced suffering together with the flesh: by assuming passible flesh, the impassible divinity itself supposedly could not remain impassible in the suffering.

If this is so, Christ’s divinity is first asserted to be changeable, and the Apostle is contradicted. For, proclaiming Jesus Christ the Son of God to be unchangeable, he clearly says to the Corinthians: “For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you through us—through me, Silvanus, and Timothy—was not Yes and No, but in him it was Yes” (2 Corinthians 1:19).

To demonstrate that this “Yes” is wholly unchangeable, he says again to the Hebrews, where he clearly recalls that this was said of the Son: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; and all of them will grow old like a garment; and like a cloak you will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same” (Hebrews 1:10–11). What is it to be the same except to be unchangeable? He himself testifies concerning himself, saying: “I am who I am”; and, “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3:14).

If someone, wishing to demonstrate a difference in divinity between the Father and the Son, claims that the passage “I am who I am” applies only to the person of the Father, he should first remember that he will thereby be forced to admit that the Father appeared to Moses. Then, if the Father appeared there in his own substance, the Father was visible. If he remains visible even now, God is no longer invisible to bodily eyes. But if he was then seen substantially and is thought afterward to have become invisible, then God was previously subject to change and therefore imperfect; afterward, through progress, he became unchangeable and received the condition of complete perfection [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads this way; the printed editions read, “and afterward, having become perfect and unchangeable, received the condition,” etc.]. If he was made perfect from imperfection, another must be sought who is believed always to have been perfect, from whom this one, who was imperfect, received the gift of perfection [Note: Or, “may have received it.”].

## CHAPTER XI. The invisible God appeared visibly through a creature subject to him. As the Father is unchangeable, so also is the Son.

119 If Christian minds and ears cannot tolerate these conclusions, let it be believed that God never appeared visibly to human beings through his own substance, but through a creature subject to him, as he himself willed. Let the Son likewise be believed invisible, just as the Father is: just as, remaining outside time, he could create temporal things, so, remaining invisible, he could appear visibly in the things he created as visible.

Even if this passage, “I am who I am,” is assigned by anyone to the person of the Father, the Son must not thereby be thought separated from the equality of the Father’s unchangeability. For just as the Father says, “I am who I am,” so the Apostle says of the Son, as we quoted above: “It was not Yes and No, but in him it was Yes.” And again: “But you are the same.”

Since, then, that singular “IS” is found in the Father and likewise in the Son, either both are believed to be unchangeable or both are subjected to changeability. But since it is exceedingly impious to call the Father changeable, it is surely pious to proclaim the Son unchangeable just as the Father is unchangeable. And if the Son’s divinity is unchangeable, nothing was added to it or taken away from it in time, since nothing changeable can be received by that which subsists with the natural truth of unchangeability.

It remains, therefore, that we confess Christ’s divinity, which Holy Scripture commends as unchangeable, to have suffered in the flesh, while nevertheless believing that it did not suffer together with the flesh. God suffered in the flesh because God assumed passible flesh; but he did not suffer together with the flesh because, while suffering in the flesh, the divine nature remained impassible. The unity of person produced in Christ a common suffering of divinity and flesh—not a confusion of the divine and human natures.

## CHAPTER XII. Because of the unity of person, the Lord of glory is said to have been crucified and the author of life to have been killed.

By this unity of person the Lord of glory is asserted to have been crucified, as the blessed Paul says: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). Because of this unity of person, the author of life is said to have been killed, as Peter reproves the Jews in the Acts of the Apostles, saying: “You asked for a murderous man to be granted to you, but you killed the author of life” (Acts 3:14–15).

Who would call any human being the author of life unless God had assumed a man for our sake? From the moment God, the author of life, assumed man into the unity of person, that man obtained the name “author of life.” Similarly, from the moment the Son of God assumed a man in the Virgin’s womb, God and man together began to be called the Son of God, as the angel says to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

A little earlier he also says to the same Virgin [variant: *eidem* / *idem*, “to the same” / “the same”]: “Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High” (ibid., 31).

Not only was the Son of God called Christ according to the fact that he was born from a human being; that man too is called God because he was assumed by God. The book of Psalms shows this to us without doubt, where it says: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of equity is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44:7–8).

## CHAPTER XIII. The anointing must also be referred to the man rather than to God.

The blessed Peter shows that this anointing must be referred rather to the man, saying: “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:38). What could be proclaimed as “of Nazareth” except the human nature in Christ? For it is so clearly the humanity of Christ, not his divinity, that is proclaimed as being of Nazareth that Philip even supposed him to be the son of Joseph when he said to Nathanael: “We have found Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth, of whom Moses in the Law and the prophets wrote” (John 1:46).

This one, then, who is said to have been anointed with the Holy Spirit, is called God in David’s song. But how could that man have the name of God unless, because he was assumed by God, he possessed with him the one dignity of the name? Yet if, in the statement “God, your God, has anointed you” (Psalm 44:8), the divine nature is thought to be intended—the nature in which the Son is believed to have been anointed by God—then the true God evidently needed the gift of sanctification before the same true man was born in the flesh.

## CHAPTER XIV. There is nothing intermediate between the Father and the Son by which the Son could be anointed. God anointed Christ according to the flesh.

Let it therefore be stated what could be holier than the Son of God, by whose anointing sanctification might either be given to him when previously absent or perfected when present but incomplete. And if anything is said to be better than the Son of God—whom they consider the Father alone to surpass—they will undoubtedly admit that whatever it is must be equal to the Father. But whether it is made equal to the Father or even placed after the Father, let whatever else it is nevertheless be preferred to the Son.

It is therefore unjust that the Holy Spirit should be joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, when what ought rather to have been joined to the Father and the Son is that which, by the superiority of its sanctifying merit, should have been placed before the Son. What kind of power would that be which sanctified the divinity of the Son of God by anointing but could not sanctify his flesh? For if it could fully sanctify Christ as man, there would have been no need for him to be anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power.

Let us therefore consider whether perhaps the Holy Spirit must be believed to be more excellent and holier than both the Son of God himself and that power with which he is said to have been anointed. For, as the blessed Peter’s assertion makes clear, God anointed Jesus of Nazareth—that is, the Son of God according to the flesh—with the Holy Spirit and with power.

If Christ as man could not be fully sanctified without the grace of the Holy Spirit [Note: The editions and Corbie manuscript read *non potuit*, “could not”; the Victor and Thuan manuscripts read *potuit*, “could”], the conferral of that anointing will be called superfluous. But if he could be fully sanctified without the Holy Spirit, and if Christ as man did not possess the full grace of sanctification without the Holy Spirit—inasmuch as the Father sanctified him and sent him into the world (John 10:36), and he said of himself, “And I sanctify myself” (John 17:19), and the sanctification of the Holy Spirit is likewise recognized in him, since God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power—how does anyone dare to call the Holy Spirit lesser than the Father or the Son, without whom the perfection of sanctification is seen to be impossible?

Why, moreover, should there be any doubt that the Holy Spirit is indicated by the name “oil,” when David and Peter, using both the word “oil” and the words “Holy Spirit,” proclaim one and the same sacrament of the Lord’s anointing? David says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions,” and he clearly signifies a man when he mentions companions. For the divinity of the Son of God has no participation with any creature, since it has no natural fellowship with a creature.

God, therefore, was anointed in the flesh, so that in that man Christ, whom his mother both conceived and bore without sin, the full grace of divine sanctification might be recognized—a grace that was to be bestowed on the faithful in the name of the Trinity. For this reason the blessed Peter says: “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:38).

And yet that Jesus of Nazareth [Note: The Corbie and Victor manuscripts add: “this one who was anointed”] is called God in the Psalm. Why, I ask, except because God and man are one Christ? Therefore, since the unconfused and inseparable truth of man and God remains in the unity of person, just as Christ God assumed the name of man in the man, so the same man Christ received the title of divinity in God.

## CHAPTER XV. Christ assumed not a heavenly but a human body. One and the same Christ is both Son of man and Son of God.

For if Christ’s personal unity does not possess the name of God and man through a natural conjunction, then, consistently, the second man whom Paul proclaims to be heavenly and from heaven must be thought to possess nothing naturally from the Virgin, and, according to a heavenly nature, must be said to have the substance of heavenly flesh. This is especially so because the Lord himself also declares concerning himself: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

But if Christ is to be believed to have assumed a heavenly body rather than a human one, how can the prophecy of David’s Psalm be upheld, where it is written: “So that glory may dwell in our land; truth has sprung from the earth” (Psalm 84:10, 12)? Who would dare deny that Christ is the truth, when he himself called himself by this name, saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 1:6)?

If, then, truth has sprung from the earth, how can the second man be heavenly and from heaven, except because the material of an earthly body assumed by the Son of God passed into a heavenly name through fellowship with divinity? And again, how does the Son of man descend from heaven, except because the Son of God descended not by local movement but through an attitude of mercy? Just as he deigned to be born from a human being in the flesh he assumed, so, because of the one person of God who assumed and man who was assumed, he who was the Son of God deigned to be called the Son of man.

To make this unity of person known without any confusion of either substance, Christ questions his disciples, saying: “Who do people say that I am, the son of man?” (Matthew 16:13) [Note: The Corbie and Victor manuscripts, as well as the Antwerp and Basel editions, read in accordance with the Greek text: “Who do people say that I, the Son of man, am?” The Cologne edition reads: “Who do people say that I am? The Son of man?”].

When they immediately reported the opinion of the crowd, he then specifically asked them about the quality of true faith, so that the falsehood of human error might be removed. The Lord’s question therefore followed: “But who do you say that I am? Surely, the Son of man?”

There the apostle Peter, supported by the foundation of divine revelation, confessed the mystery of universal salvation: “You are,” he said, “the Christ, the Son of the living God.” What does this mean? As far as the uninstructed are concerned, how does the answer correspond to the question? Peter is asked about the Son of man, yet he confesses the Son of God. Did he hear Jesus, who was asking, incorrectly, or did he fail to hold to the truth in his confession? Certainly not. For how could human error be praised by the mouth of truth?

But what Christ truly was, that is what he said when he asked the question; and what Christ truly was, that is what he heard from Peter’s confessing mouth. Christ the Son of man was the Son of the living God. And deservedly he obtained blessedness by the divine voice, because with his own voice he uttered the truth of faith. Therefore he hears: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.”

Christ himself had already confessed that he was the Son of God when he asserted to Peter that this had been revealed by his Father who is in heaven. Nor should this, in my opinion, be passed over without attention: when Christ first called himself the Son of man, Peter said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” For the Son of God, having assumed the lowliness of flesh, ought to reveal in himself the mystery of great mercy; and the redeemed man ought to proclaim the true substance of divine birth in the Son of man. Thus, while the Redeemer’s benefit of gratuitous compassion is displayed, the redeemed person returns the service of divine confession.

No one, therefore, should doubt that he is the true God by nature from the Father, whom he has recognized as true man by nature from a human being. Accordingly, since it is clear that the same one is a true man through the sufferings of man, we should believe him to be the same true God through the works of divinity, as the Son himself says: “If you do not wish to believe me, at least believe the works” (John 10:38).

One and the same Christ, therefore, endured suffering through human weakness and performed miracles of benevolence through the omnipotence of divine power.

## CHAPTER XVI. In Christ there are two natures, without confusion or change. In Christ the whole man consists of a true soul and flesh. The raising of Lazarus proves that Christ possesses soul, flesh, and divinity. His divinity was neither disturbed with the soul nor separated from the dying flesh.

From the very beginning of his virginal conception, personal unity remained in Christ and the unconfused truth of both natures endured, so that neither man could be torn away from God nor God separated from the man he had assumed. Yet God did not consume man, nor did man change God in any respect. And although, at Christ’s death, the soul would leave the dying flesh, Christ’s divinity nevertheless could not be separated either from the soul or from the assumed flesh.

Since, then, that God received the whole man, he therefore truly displayed in himself the sufferings of the whole man. Possessing a rational soul, he both assumed and endured, without sin, everything that belonged to the soul’s weakness, so that, by conquering the sufferings of the human soul in the soul he had received, he might also free our souls from their weaknesses.

He also assumed human flesh and, in the truth of that flesh, possessed the reality of voluntary suffering, so that, dying in the flesh, he might put to death in himself the whole death of man, and, rising immortal to eternal life, might bestow on us the grace of eternal life.

As the Evangelist says, the true Christ in a human soul, about to raise Lazarus, “groaned in spirit and troubled himself.” The same true Christ in human flesh, when he had said, “Where have you laid him?” and they answered, “Lord, come and see,” wept; and Jesus shed tears (John 11:33–35).

The same true Christ in his divine nature did not abandon his soul when he troubled himself, because he himself troubled himself; nor did he withdraw from his flesh when he wept, because Jesus shed tears. Yet that same divinity, present in soul and flesh, while remaining unchangeable and impassible according to the divine nature, could neither produce tears nor experience disturbance at the death of a friend [Note: The Basel manuscript reads, “in the grief of the soul.” The Cologne and Antwerp editions read, “in the death of the soul.”].

Likewise, as his passion drew near, Christ was troubled according to his soul, as he himself says: “Now my soul is troubled” (John 12:27). Again, on the cross Christ dies according to the flesh, as the Apostle says: “For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

Since it has been clearly demonstrated what belonged in Christ specifically to the soul, what belonged to the flesh, and what belonged to divinity, and since the one and same Christ was both troubled and dead, the truth of God and man was nevertheless preserved in both respects. Thus, although Christ was troubled according to his soul as the passion approached, and the same Christ died according to his body on the cross, the undisturbed and immortal divinity of Christ did not depart either from the troubled soul or from the dying body. Yet it was not itself troubled by the soul’s disturbance or killed by the body’s death.

For there is one Christ, who was handed over because of our sins and rose for our justification (Romans 4:25). Just as, being truly dead, he could not die, so in true suffering he remained impassible.

## CHAPTER XVII. Christ demonstrates in himself the truth of both natures. Christ has one person, although he does not have one nature.

To demonstrate in himself both the true mortality of man and the true immortality of divinity, when the Jews said, “What sign do you show us, since you are doing these things?” Jesus answered them: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:18–19). The holy Evangelist showed what that temple was when he said: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body” (ibid., 21).

The truth of human substance was therefore displayed, which the Jews could, if he willed it, destroy in Christ; and the truth of divine nature was displayed, by which [variant: *qua* / *quia*, “by which” / “because”] Christ could raise the temple of his body. When Christ died and the soul left the flesh, that temple—which had been constructed from soul and flesh—was destroyed. When the soul returned to the flesh, that temple was raised on the third day.

Yet, because of the one person of Christ, God and man, the same one died in his body who raised the temple of his body. Thus also, when, in accordance with the prophecy of Isaiah, he gave his back to scourging and his cheeks to blows, and did not turn his face away from the disgrace of spitting (Isaiah 50:6), God suffered all these things in the flesh but did not suffer together with the flesh, because God experienced suffering in the flesh without experiencing it together with the flesh.

For the person of God and man in Christ is one, as Paul also affirms when he says: “And I also, whatever I have forgiven—if I have forgiven anything—for your sake I have forgiven it in the person of Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:10). Although Christ has one person, he does not have one substance. The true God assumed a true man in such a way that, in the truth of the human assumption, he did not lose the truth of divinity. He deigned to become what he had not been without ceasing to be what he had always been.

Thus God also willed to have one person with man, so that, although Christ God was not one person and Christ man another, true God would nevertheless remain in man and true man remain in God. Accordingly, in the one Christ there was the unconfused and likewise undivided perfection of divine and human nature.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What belonged to the flesh or the soul in Christ must not be attributed to divinity. Divinity did not in any way suffer together with him or become sorrowful. This is proved by testimonies from Scripture.

[Col. 0282C]

But the divinity of Christ did not then come into being in itself when it was born for us in the flesh. The Word was an infant according to the flesh and lacked the ability to speak; but that same Word, God, could never at any time be constrained to silence, because he is the Father’s eternal utterance. The child grew as his age advanced; but since there is no age in God, the divine majesty did not grow in the growing child. We likewise know that Christ advanced in wisdom according to his soul; but Christ, as Wisdom, could not advance along with the advancing soul. Thus the same Christ both grew in his flesh and progressed in his soul; yet, while growing in his flesh and advancing in his soul, he could neither advance with his soul nor experience an increase of age with his flesh. Likewise (another reading: *item*, “likewise”), God was sorrowful according to the soul he had assumed; but he who experienced sorrow in the soul could not, together with the soul, experience sorrow. God willed his sorrow to be in his own soul, and God willed his suffering to be in his own flesh, because inseparable God, remaining wholly in the whole man, was absent neither from the sorrowing soul nor from his own flesh in its suffering.

Yet in the sorrowful and suffering Christ, although the suffering and sorrowing humanity could not be separated from the divinity, nevertheless the divinity was not made sorrowful in the whole sorrowful man, nor did the divine nature suffer together with the whole suffering man [Col. 0282D] (another reading: “was not afflicted”). Just as, when the flesh died, not only can the divinity not be shown to have died together with it, but neither can Christ’s soul. For it is one thing to say that God suffered in the flesh, and another to proclaim that God suffered together with the flesh; one thing to say that he was made sorrowful in the soul, and another that he was sorrowful together with the soul (another reading: “was made sorrowful”).

God suffered in the man, because there is one person of God and man; God did not suffer together with the man, because in the one Christ the substance of God and man was not confused. This can be proved by clear testimonies of Scripture, so that it may be understood that sorrow and suffering are to be attributed wholly to Christ [Col. 0283A] [Note: [Col. 0283D] Basil: “to the whole.” See above in the note on chapter 13, book I, p. 81: *toto* for *toti*.] in such a way [Note: [Col. 0283D] Basil: “so that the reality of the natural functions may be shown.”] that, once the reality of the natural functions has been demonstrated, there may be no confusion of God and man.

Matthew relates that, as the time of his passion drew near, the Lord said to his disciples: “Sit here while I go over there and pray”; and, taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, “he began to be sorrowful and distressed” (Matt. 26:36). Mark, however, is known to have presented it thus: “And they come to an estate called Gethsemane, and he says to his disciples: Sit here while I pray. And he took Peter and James and John with him, and he began to be fearful and distressed” (Mark 14:32).

## CHAPTER XIX. At the recompense the righteous will be like the angels of God.

I am not unaware how closely our present discussion corresponds to the obligation of our pledge (another reading: “response”) [Note: [Col. 0283D] Thus the manuscripts Corbeiensis and Victorinus; Basil has *congruat* (“correspond”). Cologne and Antwerp have *congruet* (“will correspond”).]—not only in words but also [Note: [Col. 0283D] Basil: “in affections.”] in effects—that the distinct properties of flesh and soul must be demonstrated in the Son of God. For then the nature of divine impassibility will shine forth, when what belongs to the soul and what belongs to the flesh has become clear not only by reasoning but also by the authority of the divine Scriptures.

Matthew, then, says that Jesus was sorrowful and distressed; Mark records that he was fearful and troubled. Let those who object to the assumption of a human soul in Christ say whether they consider sorrow, grief, distress, and fear to be attributable to the divinity or to the flesh. If they answer that these belonged to the flesh, then the divinity will be excluded from every kind of suffering: it did not share in the passions of the flesh, although it was not absent from the flesh it had assumed even in its suffering. But if they assert that Christ’s divinity was shaken by sorrow, grief, distress, and fear, thereby declaring the divinity passible, they will admit that it is equal to our souls.

It remains for them to say that it is inferior to the angels, since they declare it subject to suffering. For the angels are greatly superior to our souls in this respect: just as they are alien to sins, so also they are free from sufferings. The Lord likewise promises this to those who worship him rightly and live holy lives as their recompense, saying: “They will be like the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22:30).

This will certainly be the case when, according to the testimony of blessed Paul, this corruptible and mortal body is thus clothed with incorruption and immortality [Note: [Col. 0283D–0284D] The printed editions read: “this corruptible (that is, mortal) …”], so that corruption cannot possess incorruption. Corruption consists not only in sin but also in weakness, which is known to have come upon the transgressor as the punishment of sin. The Apostle testifies that we will then be entirely free from both sin and weakness, saying: “Then the saying that is written will come to pass: Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your contention? Where, O death, is your sting? The sting of death is sin” (1 Cor. 15:54–56).

When death has therefore been swallowed up in victory, there will be no corruption of soul or flesh, because when all iniquity has been removed from us, no weakness will remain. Isaiah speaks of such people: “They will obtain joy and gladness, and pain and groaning will flee from them” (Isa. 35:10). John also speaks of them in the Apocalypse: “They will neither hunger nor thirst, nor will the sun fall upon them, nor any heat” (Rev. 7:16). And to show that they would attain this grace through Christ’s gift, he continued: “For the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne will shepherd them and lead them to the fountains of the waters of life, and the Lord will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

Since the blessed security and joy of the angels is already such today, entirely ignorant of sufferings, so that they are shaken by no fall into sin and no assault of weakness [Col. 0284A] [Note: [Col. 0284D] The manuscript Corbeiensis has *nulli* (“of no one”); perhaps this should be read instead of *nullius* (“of no”).], let those who subject Christ’s divinity to human sufferings at last consider into what abyss of blasphemy they are falling, when they attempt to demonstrate that the Lord of angels is inferior to angels in the substance he has from the Father. Is it therefore false that he himself says: “A servant is not greater than his lord” (John 13:16)?

## CHAPTER XX. An objection concerning what David says: “You made him a little lower than the angels.”

Do they think that the following should be brought forward [Note: [Col. 0284D] Thus the manuscripts Corbeiensis and Victorinus; the printed editions have “to be rejected.”]—what David says concerning the Son of Man?

“Lord, what is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:5–6). [Note: [Col. 0284D] Basil: “What is man, that …”]

But let them observe the apostle Paul referring this passage to the understanding of human death, so that he assigns this lowering not only to the nature of humanity but also excludes Christ’s divinity from participation in suffering and death. For he speaks thus to the Hebrews:

“But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels” [Note: [Col. 0284D] Thus the manuscripts Corbeiensis and Victorinus and the Greek text; the editions have “we saw.”] “because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor, so that, apart from God, he might taste death for everyone” (Heb. 2:9).

The Apostle did not divide Christ here; rather, he showed in the one Christ which substance was passible and mortal, and which remained impassible and immortal. That man therefore tasted death apart from God insofar as the condition of the flesh is concerned, but not apart from God insofar as the assumption of divinity is concerned. For when that impassible and immortal divinity deigned, in the true form of a servant, voluntarily to suffer and die for us, it was immortal in the death of the flesh alone, and so it remained entirely impassible amid the sufferings of the whole man.

## CHAPTER XXI. Sorrow and similar affections belong to the soul.

But we must now show that the suffering of sorrow, grief, distress, and fear properly belongs to the substance of the soul. Thus, when those ungrateful toward Christ’s grace seek to subject his divinity to suffering, it may become clear what belongs properly to each nature; and the Lord’s wondrous and unconquerable mercy may be recognized all the more when we have proved that he assumed the substance of soul and flesh, together with their sufferings, for this purpose: just as, while preserving the state of divine impassibility, he is known to have destroyed our death by voluntarily assuming death in his flesh, so also, by voluntarily assuming sorrow and fear, he is known to have assumed a rational soul with its sufferings, in order that he might deign to free our souls from every suffering.

Let us therefore show that Christ’s sorrow belonged neither to the divinity nor to the flesh, but to the substance of the soul. And so that this may be understood with complete clarity, let us consider what he said to his disciples at nearly the very time of his passion, in order that he might demonstrate in himself the true substance of the soul no less by its function than by its name [Note: [Col. 0285D] Basil: “in order that it might preserve …”]: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38).

Who could doubt that sorrow can neither fall upon the divinity nor belong to the function of the flesh? It is proper to the soul to fear, desire, grieve, and rejoice, as the text of David’s song also shows, saying [another reading: “who says”]: “Why are you sorrowful, O my soul, and why do you trouble me?” (Ps. 41:12). The soul is sorrowful; the soul itself is troubled.

For this reason the Savior himself, to show that this disturbance was to be attributed not to the flesh but to the soul, consoles his disciples when they were sorrowful over his future departure: “Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it fear” (John 14:1). Again he says to them:

“Now I go to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’ But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart” (John 16:5).

Who would dare assign to the flesh or to the divinity what the Lord says properly belongs to the function of the heart? For after he had said above, “Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it fear,” thereby clearly demonstrating the human soul under the name “heart,” he then said, “Sorrow has filled your heart,” showing even more clearly that both sorrow and joy belong to the soul. The Apostle says again:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: You will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you, however, will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy. A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her hour has come; but when she has delivered the child [another reading: “when she has delivered”], she no longer remembers her distress, because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world. So you also now have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.”

Here sorrow, fear, and joy in a human being are specifically assigned to the heart, that is, to the soul. Therefore the Apostle also says:

“May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God, and our Father [Note: [Col. 0285D] The manuscript Corbeiensis has “and God our Father.”], who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and good hope by grace, console [another reading: “comfort”] your hearts and strengthen them in every good work and word” (2 Thess. 2:15).

Where can consolation be applied except where sadness can intrude? Since sadness properly belongs to the soul, it is therefore written concerning Christ: “He began to be sorrowful and distressed,” and “he began to be fearful and troubled.” He himself says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” And again: “Now my soul is troubled.”

## CHAPTER XXII. Joy in Christ’s soul. Desire. Christ assumed weaknesses in order to perfect virtue in us. In Christ there was the power to lay down and take up his soul.

[Col. 0286A]

The Savior also demonstrated joy in his soul when he said to his disciples concerning Lazarus: “Lazarus our friend has died, and I rejoice, so that you may believe, because I was not there” (John 11:14).

It was the substance of the human being that rejoiced in Christ, since, through the natural fellowship of humanity, it already possessed joy at Lazarus’s resurrection; and this was also so that the disciples might understand the true God in the man whom they had learned was not hidden even when far away.

And in order to demonstrate in himself every function of the soul, Christ also did not wish desire to be foreign to his soul, saying to his disciples: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” [Col. 0286B] (Luke 22:15).

No one can attribute all these things either to the nature of the flesh or to the substance of the divinity, since flesh cannot live by itself, nor perceive, grieve, desire, fear, or mourn. The divinity fears nothing, because it rules over all [Note: [Col. 0285D] Basil and Antwerp: “because, as ruler of all, he is saddened by nothing; because …”]; it is saddened by nothing, because no suffering is inflicted upon it; it fears nothing, because it has no natural weakness; it desires nothing, because it can do all things and possesses all things.

Christ therefore endured all these things in the soul he had assumed, in order to demonstrate in himself the true and complete substance of the human being he had received, together with its weaknesses [Note: [Col. 0286D] The manuscript Corbeiensis has: “in order to demonstrate in himself the true and complete substance of the human being he had received, together with him and his weaknesses.”]. And through the weaknesses that he assumed for the weak, he perfected the virtue that he bestowed upon the weak.

For this reason he had mortal human flesh, so that he might confer upon mortals the full grace of immortality; and he assumed a human soul with its weaknesses, without sin, so that he might provide medicine for our souls. For, as Isaiah testifies, just as he was “wounded for our iniquities” (Isa. 53:5)—which properly belonged to the flesh, since the soldier pierced his side after he was already dead—so he was “made weak for our sins,” which belongs to the soul, whose weaknesses he assumed for us.

Possessing complete power to lay down and take up this soul, he said:

“For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my soul, and I will take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and [another reading: “but”] I have power to take it up again. I received this commandment from my Father” (John 10:17–18).

I ask those who say that a human soul was in every respect absent from Christ: what substance do they believe is named here by the word “soul”? Is it the divinity or the flesh? Or what substance in Christ claims for itself the power to lay down the soul?

If they assign this power to the divine substance, while saying that the flesh is called by the name “soul,” which the divinity was going to lay down in the passion—for the moment let us argue according to their position—then, if the divinity says of the flesh, “I have power to lay down my soul,” and calls the flesh “soul,” it undoubtedly assigns all the weaknesses to the flesh as well, when it says, “My soul is troubled,” and when it says, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.”

Since Christ did not say, “I am sorrowful unto death,” but said, “My soul is sorrowful unto death,” and did not say, “I am troubled,” but “My soul is troubled,” he clearly showed that these sufferings belonged to the flesh, while he taught with complete clarity that his divinity was altogether impassible.

But if they perhaps assign this power to the substance of the flesh, as though the flesh had said concerning the divinity, “I have power to lay down my soul,” are they so eager to diminish Christ’s divine substance that they subject it to the power of his flesh, so that the divinity itself obeyed the flesh, when the flesh ought to have served it?

## CHAPTER XXIII. Only the divinity possesses complete power.

The statement, “I have power to lay down my soul,” must therefore be understood as belonging to the whole man. For just as he gave himself wholly, and the whole man offered himself, of whom the Apostle says, “Walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrant aroma” (Eph. 5:2), so the whole man laid down his soul when the soul departed while the flesh was dying on the cross.

Yet the divinity did not abandon that flesh even in death, just as it did not leave the soul in the underworld. Concerning this the prophet had also said: “You will not abandon my soul in the underworld” (Ps. 15:10).

Since the man Christ received such power that, whenever he wished, he laid down his soul and, whenever he wished, took it up again, how great a power could Christ’s divinity have, for which willing is always the same as being able? Here, truly, the impassible and unconquerable divinity utterly destroyed every invention of heretical falsehood.

For if the speaker’s power was complete, the sufferer’s weakness was voluntary. But a will that proceeds from power certainly preserved the natural truth of divinity and humanity. For natural power was undoubtedly absent if there was any weakness in Christ’s divinity. How, moreover, could humanity have had the power to suffer if the divinity could not possess complete impassibility?

Let it therefore be understood that wherever power is naturally complete, there can be no weakness of suffering. Christ’s power, by which he remained immortal when Christ, dying in the flesh, laid down his soul, remained itself without sorrow when Christ voluntarily endured sorrow in his soul through that power.

That man possessed the power to lay down his soul because divine power assumed him into the unity of the person. What power is complete except the divinity alone? Of it is said: “He has done all things whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 113:11), and to it it is said: “For when you will, the ability to act is present with you” (Wis. 12:18).

Therefore complete power is rightly believed to be in him, since naturally he possesses as much ability as will and as much will as ability.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Christ truly had a soul.

Christ also deigned to show, both by its name and by its function, that he had assumed a true soul, saying: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his soul for his friends” (John 15:13).

Therefore Peter, knowing that Christ’s soul was designated by its proper and substantial name—and lest anyone think that the Lord perhaps intended the flesh by the name “soul”—desired to follow the virtue of perfect imitation, which he would later receive. When the Lord said [another reading: “was saying”], “Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward,” he replied: “Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my soul for you” (John 13:36–37).

He clearly showed that Christ would lay down his soul for him, since he said that he would follow him in this, so that he too might lay down his soul for Christ. For Peter did not share with Christ the common nature of divinity, and therefore could not say to him concerning divinity, “I will lay down my soul for you.”

Again, if he had known that Christ had laid down only the flesh for him, he could also have said, “I will lay down my body for you,” just as Paul specifically speaks of the body when he says: “If I hand over my body so that I may burn” (1 Cor. 13:3).
