But because Peter knew that Christ would lay down his soul for us, he therefore showed that he wished to follow the Lord in this respect: he demonstrated his readiness to lay down his soul for him, so that he might himself similarly lay down for Christ what he knew Christ had laid down for him.

And so that every darkness of a perverse opinion may be dispersed by the clearest light of Catholic truth, let us be instructed by the words of John. Exhorting the faithful to imitate Christ, he commands the members to do what he knew had been done in the head. He says:

“By this we know the love of God: that he laid down his soul for us, and we ought to lay down our souls for the brothers” (1 John 3:16).

To lay down the soul, then, is proper to love. Where love is absent, the body is said to be handed over; the soul is not said to be laid down. The chosen vessel, entirely filled with love, expressly testifies to this:

“If I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing.”

He shows that the body can be handed over without love, but that the soul cannot be laid down. When he seeks to signify the purity of his love, he writes to the Thessalonians:

“We were eager to give you not only the gospel of God but also our own souls” (1 Thess. 2:8).

And to show that this was an act of love, he added: “because you had become very dear to us.”

Therefore, also, Christ first invited Peter—who had promised that he would lay down his soul for the Lord—to a confession of love, so that we might recognize that the function of laying down the soul consists in love. And so that he might afterward grant his lover the ability to lay down his soul, he finally questioned him:

“Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him: “Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.” When he had said this a second time, he said to him a third time: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 21:15, 17).

When Peter had given a threefold testimony of his love in response to the threefold questioning, the Lord immediately granted Peter the ability to lay down his soul for him, saying:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (ibid., 18).

The evangelist immediately added, saying [Col. 0289A]:

“He said this to signify by what death he would glorify God” [Note: [Col. 0289D] Thus the manuscripts Corbeiensis and Victorinus and the Greek text; the editions have “him”]. “And after saying this, he said to him: Follow me.”

See how Peter wished to follow him even earlier, when he desired to lay down his soul for him, just as afterward he deserved to follow him along the right path of love, when he laid down his soul in suffering for him.

## CHAPTER XXV. Christ’s human weaknesses were real, but voluntary. It is not said that Jesus’ body was placed in the tomb, but Jesus, because the divinity was there.

Accordingly, since it has been proved by the clear testimony of Scripture that love is absent where only the body is laid down, but is present where the soul is laid down together with the body, Christ must be believed to be, from the Virgin, fully God and fully man—that is, a rational soul and flesh.

And as the truth of the Catholic faith teaches, let us believe that in the one and same Christ, according to the true substance of the flesh, there was voluntary and real hunger when, hungry, he came to the fig tree; voluntary and real thirst when he asked the Samaritan woman for a drink, or when he said on the cross that he was thirsty; voluntary and real weariness when, tired from the journey, he sat beside the well; a voluntary and real wound when the soldier’s lance struck his side; voluntary and real death when, having bowed his head, he gave up his spirit on the cross; and voluntary and real burial when Joseph and Nicodemus placed him in the tomb after he had been taken down from the wood.

Christ possessed all these weaknesses of the flesh—voluntary indeed, but real—because he assumed the nature of human flesh not in appearance but in truth. He had these sufferings in the flesh as voluntary for this reason: so that divine power, which could never suffer or die, might in the reality of the flesh conquer weakness and death, and raise his flesh to perpetual life and power.

Paul makes this declaration with truthful speech:

“Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more, and death will no longer rule over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God” (Rom. 6:9–10).

Who does not know that Christ died and was buried neither in his soul nor in his divinity, but in his body alone? [Note: [Col. 0289D] These words are absent from the editions but are found in the manuscripts Corbeiensis and Victorinus.]

John clearly shows this in the following words:

“After these things, Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, though secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate to remove the body of Jesus. And Pilate permitted it. Therefore he came and took the body of Jesus. Nicodemus also came, the one who had first come to Jesus by night, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds. They therefore took the body of Jesus and bound him [another reading: “it”] in linen cloths with spices, as is the Jewish custom of burial” (John 19:38, 40).

Here, having distinguished the divinity, the flesh, and the soul according to the properties of their substances, John says that only Jesus’ body was taken down from the cross, anointed with spices, and wrapped in linen cloths. But because of the unity of the person, since God did not abandon in death or in the tomb the man whom he had assumed from the Virgin’s womb, John therefore continued:

“Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been placed. Because it was the Preparation of the Jews [Note: [Col. 0289D] The Corbeiensis and Victorinus manuscripts read *Parasceve*] and the tomb was nearby, they placed Jesus there” (ibid., 41–42).

The holy evangelist, truly full of the divine Spirit, spoke in this way: first, showing what in Christ had died and been buried, he said that Jesus’ body had been taken and bound in linen cloths with spices. And because “what God has joined together, man must not separate” (Matt. 19:6), he therefore says not that Jesus’ body but that Jesus was placed in the tomb.

For he knew that God, who had assumed the whole man, was wholly with his flesh in the tomb, wholly with his soul in the underworld, wholly in the world, wholly in heaven, wholly [Note: [Col. 0290D] Thus the manuscript Victorinus; Corbeiensis has “into unity”; the editions have “in unity.”] through the unity of nature in the Father from whom he came, and wholly through the omnipotence of his divinity in the entire creation that he made.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The unity of Christ’s person in the words of the Apostle.

Maintaining this unity of person in Christ, the Apostle confirms the church of the Corinthians in the faith of truth as follows:

“For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose [another reading: “arose”] on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Cor. 15:3–4).

He said not that Christ’s body died, but that Christ died, in order to preserve the unity of the person of God and man. But to show the substantial distinction between divinity and humanity, he says elsewhere, as we have already cited above:

“For although he was crucified from weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:4).

The remarkable force of the apostolic words must be considered. [Note: [Col. 0290D] The Corbeiensis manuscript reads “If also Paul”; perhaps “For even if Paul” (*Etsi enim Paulus*) should be read.] If Paul had said of Christ that he was crucified from weakness but lives through power, and had not added “of God,” even then the weakness of human suffering ought not to have been confused with the impassibility of divine power. But since Paul assigns the power to the divinity, who does not see that he declares those things to belong to the human being that appear to be matters of weakness?

When he says of Christ that he lives by the power of God, he lives from his own divinity, because he himself is the Power of God. And he lives as the Father lives, because he himself is the way, the truth, and the life.

To indicate to us the one life of the Father and the Son, the Apostle John took care to place this at the beginning of his Epistle:

“What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked upon and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life—and the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and we testify and announce to you the eternal Life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us” (1 John 1:1–2).

The Son of God, whom he had earlier called the Word of God, he later called Life. But what is the Word of life except the Word of God? And since the Word is the life of Life, that Word of life and the life whose Word it is are certainly one life.

Therefore Christ, who died from weakness, lives by the power of God, because for that divinity it is the same thing to be life as to be power; and therefore for it to be able is the same as to live. Thus neither in the passion did life abandon power, nor in Christ’s death did power depart from life, because Christ’s divinity—which is both power and life—could not be changed.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Because of the unity of person in Christ, the Son of God is said to have died. Christ’s weaknesses are not to be attributed to his divinity.

Again, in order to commend most firmly the unity of the person in Christ, Paul writes to the Romans as follows concerning God [another reading: “wrote”]:

“He who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all” [another reading: “him”] (Rom. 8:32).

And to show that this handing over was voluntary and accomplished through the Son’s power, he also recalls that the Son handed himself over for us, saying elsewhere:

“The life that I now live in the flesh, I live in the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and handed himself over for me” (Gal. 2:20). [Note: [Col. 0291D] The Corbeiensis and Cologne manuscripts read *Filio* (“to/in the Son”) rather than *Filii* (“of the Son”).]

But to show what could be handed over in Christ, the prophetic book says:

“The earth has been handed over into the hands of the wicked” (Job 9:24). [Note: [Col. 0291D] The manuscript Corbeiensis has “the book of holy Job.”]

Nevertheless, because of the unity of the person, the Church not only holds and confesses that Christ’s humanity was handed over, but that Christ was handed over. For in that handing over, while the distinct property of each nature remained intact, neither could the man who had been assumed be separated from God, nor could God be separated from the man he had assumed.

Therefore, just as Scripture, because of the unity of person, wholly assigns the suffering of death and death itself to the Son of God, and yet declares the divinity impassible and immortal, so also the Son of God must be believed to have possessed the sorrow and disturbance of the soul—which he had voluntarily in his soul—in such a way that we do not deny that the sufferings of the human soul themselves were both real by his will and voluntary in their reality.

Christ’s own divinity, which according to the soul deigned to be sorrowful and according to the flesh to die for us, must be proclaimed, according to the property of its substance, to be not only immortal but also impassible. Since it assumed a true human being, it therefore endured all the weaknesses of human nature—real indeed, but voluntary—within the reality of that human nature alone.

What imprudent person would pursue such a deadly opinion concerning Christ as to believe that hunger, thirst, weariness, suffering, and death, and likewise sorrow, disturbance, fear, and distress—which no one can in any respect doubt belong to the flesh and the soul—were real in the nature of man, yet refuse to believe that the substance of the divinity was free from them, when Christ gave those who hope in him the power to overcome precisely what he himself voluntarily experienced for us [another reading: “had experienced”]?

For this reason Isaiah, inspired by God, opposes impious and deadly thoughts, saying:

“The eternal God, God who made the ends of the earth, will not hunger, nor will he grow weary, and his understanding cannot be searched out. He gives strength to the hungry and grief to those who do not grieve. Young men will hunger and grow weary, and the chosen will be without strength. But those who wait for the Lord will rejoice with strength; they will produce wings like eagles [Note: [Col. 0292D] The editions have “they will lead forward.”]; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not hunger” (Isa. 40:28 and following).

The Bread himself who descended from heaven truly promises perfect satisfaction to those who believe in him, saying:

“He who comes to me will not hunger, and he who believes in me will never thirst” (John 6:35).

I ask: how will this power be granted to human beings if God could not possess it? Or how could Christ not possess in his divinity what Paul received from him in order to possess it?

For Paul testifies concerning himself and those like him:

“We suffer tribulation, but are not distressed” (2 Cor. 4:8); and elsewhere: “As dying, and behold, we live; as chastised, and not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing all things” (2 Cor. 6:9–10).

How grave, incongruous, and utterly alien to the true faith it is to say that Paul, in one and the same substance of the soul, while sorrowful, can always rejoice through Christ’s gift, but that Christ’s divinity could not remain in itself without sorrow when the soul he had assumed was sorrowful!

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Fear is not attributed to John; therefore it must not be attributed to the divinity. What no one can take away from servants who receive, let no one attempt to take away from the Lord who bestows.

John does not fear, for he says: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear; and whoever fears is not perfected in love” (1 John 4:18). For he had heard from the Lord: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28). No one dares to attribute fear to John, yet fear of death is attributed to the Deity? David hopes in him and says: “In God I will hope; I will not fear what man can do to me” (Ps. 55:11); and again he confidently repeats: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; from whom shall I tremble?” (Ps. 27:1–2). And the Lord himself says to the apostles: “Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid” (John 14:27). Again he says: “Rejoice, because I have conquered the world” (John 16:33).

Therefore, as they await him, they take courage; they grow wings by which they may be lifted to heavenly things. Running, they know no weariness; walking, they are unaware of hunger; in tribulation they do not suffer distress; dying, they retain life; though they appear sad, they nevertheless rejoice always; though poor, they bestow riches on many; and, while striving to possess nothing, they possess all things. Filled with the love of Christ, they lack fear; illuminated by him, they confess that they fear no one; with him as their defender, they cannot tremble before anyone. Turmoil and dread are driven from their hearts; they rejoice because they see that the world has been conquered by Christ.

If no one can take these things away from servants who receive them, how does wicked blindness—or rather, blind wickedness—attempt to take away from the Lord who bestows them what he naturally possesses as divine? Who, moreover, does not see that in those sufferings of Christ certain seeds of our virtues are contained? Thus the one and the same Christ, in his humanity, experienced what belongs to humanity; but in his divinity he remained impassible and immortal.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The names of the Son of God with regard to his divinity. Christ as man, because he had no sins of his own, bore the sins of others. The complete humanity of Christ.

For the Son of God, the Word and Wisdom of the Father, is himself the salvation of which the prophet says: “Our salvation will come quickly” (Isa. 46:13). He is himself power and wisdom: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). He is fullness, because he is the bread that came down from heaven (John 6:58). He is likewise the way, he is the truth, he is the life. He is also our joy and gladness, of whom the prophet says: “Your word became for me the joy and gladness of my heart” (Jer. 15:16). He is the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1:9).

By these names, designated above, he is found to be unchangeable and impassible. Salvation cannot fall ill; power does not know weakness; fullness does not know hunger; the way cannot go astray; wisdom is not changed; life does not die; light is not extinguished; truth is not corrupted; gladness does not know sorrow; the Deity cannot be overcome. Therefore Christ’s humanity also remained without sin, because the divinity, which by nature does not know how to sin, received it into the unity [of the person].  
[Note: Ms. Corb., “into unity.”]

Christ as man, therefore, because he did not have sins of his own, deigned to bear the sins of others. He wished to bear upon himself the sins of those with whom he was bound by natural fellowship, as the Apostle says: “For the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.” For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers” (Heb. 2:11–12; Ps. 22:23).

The prophet Isaiah likewise foretells the effect of this mercy in such a way that he clearly displays in him the name of man, saying: “Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1). When he says “the arm of the Lord,” he reveals the divinity of the Son of God; and thereafter he begins to proclaim the mystery of the Incarnation and Passion:

“We announced him before his face as a child, as a root in thirsty ground. He has no appearance or glory. And we saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty; but his appearance was without honor and rejected above all men: a man under affliction and knowing how to bear weakness; for he turned away, his face was dishonored, and he was held as nothing. He bears our sins and suffers for us, and we considered him to be in pains, in affliction, and in distress. But he was wounded because of our iniquities, and he was weakened because of our sins. The discipline of our peace was upon him [or: toward him], and by his bruise we were healed. We all went astray like sheep; man went astray from his way, and the Lord handed him over for our sins. And because he was ill-treated, he did not open his mouth; like a sheep led to sacrifice, and like a lamb before the one who shears it, so he did not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away. Who will declare his generation? For his life will be taken from the earth; because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death” (Isa. 53:2 and following).  
[Note: Ms. Corb., “as a child.” Ms. Vict., “and a child.”]  
[Note: Published editions: “he resisted.”]

And so that the prophet might demonstrate in Christ the complete substance of a human being, he added a little farther on: “He himself will bear their sins. Therefore he himself will possess many by inheritance and will divide the spoils of the strong, because his soul was handed over to death [or: in death], and he was counted among the wicked. And he himself bore the sins of many, and because of their iniquities he was handed over” (Isa. 53:12).

From these words of the prophet, the Savior’s soul is recognized as having been handed over, and so is his flesh, because the whole man was led to the cross for us. For in this way the record of our sins had to be erased: while our old man was fastened together to the cross, as upon a trophy, the victory of the triumphing one might be displayed.

## CHAPTER XXX. Christ’s flesh did not experience corruption in the tomb, nor did his soul suffer punishment in hell. God’s just vengeance for the sin of the first man. Through Christ both the flesh and the soul of man are saved. Christ grieved and showed compassion for us.

There nevertheless remained, for the full accomplishment of our redemption, that the sinless man received by God should descend to the place to which the man separated from God had fallen by the merit of sin—that is, to hell, where the sinner’s soul used to be tormented, and to the tomb, where the sinner’s flesh had been accustomed to decay. Yet this was so arranged that neither Christ’s flesh would be corrupted in the tomb nor his soul tormented by the pains of hell, since a soul free from sin ought not to be subjected to punishment, and corruption ought not to spoil flesh without sin.

For because the sinning man deserved to be divided within himself by punishment, since he preferred to be separated by the guilt of transgression from God, who cannot be divided, it therefore happened that the sinner’s death brought the flesh of sin to the tomb to be corrupted, and immediately consigned the soul to hell to be tormented. But this was the equity of the avenging God, who condemned the sinner in this way because he had foretold beforehand that he should not sin. This was the recompense owed to the sinner: that he should justly pay the penalty of sin, since he had unjustly sinned against the just God.

But in order that the sinner might be freed by a gratuitous gift, it happened that the Son of God unjustly suffered at the hands of the sinner the death of the body that sinful man had justly endured from the just God. The flesh of the righteous man reached the tomb, to which the flesh of sin had descended; and the Savior’s soul descended to hell, where the sinner’s soul had been tormented by the merit of sin.

This happened so that, through the temporal death of the righteous man’s flesh, eternal life might be given to flesh, and through the descent of the righteous man’s soul to hell, the pains of hell might be released.

Holy Scripture has not kept either matter silent. Concerning the resurrection of the flesh, blessed Paul speaks thus: “By a man came death, and by a man the resurrection of the dead; and just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:21–22).

The same man, Christ, was made both priest for us, when he offered himself to suffering, and a victim, when he himself endured the Passion. To him it is said: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 110:4). Yet both “priest” and “victim” are recognized as belonging to human nature both as functions and as names.

And because this same high priest took upon himself and possessed our weaknesses, the Apostle says of him: “For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses” (Heb. 4:15). And, to teach that he was speaking about human nature, he added: “Tempted in every respect according to likeness, without sin.” A little farther on he continued: “For every high priest taken from among men is appointed for men in matters relating to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins; he is able to have compassion on the ignorant and those who go astray, since he himself is also surrounded by weakness” (Heb. 5:1–2).

In that in which he was surrounded by weakness, he grieved over our ignorance and errors; and in that same respect he showed compassion for our weaknesses. For there is unity of compassion where there is unity of nature. That high priest showed compassion for us in that in which we too suffer with him, as blessed Paul says: “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. And if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him” (Rom. 8:16–17).  
[Note: Thus Ms. Corb., in accordance with the Greek συνδοξασθῶμεν, “that we may be glorified together,” and with the Vulgate version; the published editions instead read, “so that we may also be glorified.”]

Blessed Peter also exhorts us to this grace of sharing in suffering, saying: “Beloved, do not be alarmed at the burning which is taking place among you for your testing. Do not be frightened as though something strange were happening to you; but rejoice insofar as you share in the sufferings of Christ, so that you may also rejoice and exult at the revelation of his glory” (1 Pet. 4:12–13).

Thus, in human nature, that high priest truly enduring suffering learned to have compassion on his members. Therefore blessed Paul also said: “That I may complete what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in my flesh, for the sake of his body, which is the Church” (Col. 1:24).

## CHAPTER XXXI. We too ought to suffer and die with Christ. Just as we die with Christ, so we are freed from the pains of hell. Christ’s divinity did not abandon either his flesh in the tomb or his soul in hell.

What wonder is it, then, that we share by natural fellowship in the sufferings of our own high priest, when the blessed Apostle also testifies that we have died with him, in these words: “If you have died with Christ, why, as though you were living in the world, do you still make judgments?” [Note: Thus Mss. Corb. and Victor.; the published editions instead read, “do you distinguish?”]

He also says to Timothy: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my gospel, for which I suffer hardship even to chains, as a criminal; but the word of God is not bound. I endure everything for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with heavenly glory” (2 Tim. 2:8–10).

Knowing, therefore, that Jesus Christ had risen from the dead from the seed of David—in which, naturally, the fellowship of human nature is revealed—the Apostle recalls that in the same respect in which he knew Christ to have died, we too had died with him, saying: “The saying is trustworthy: for if we have died together, we shall also live together; if we endure, we shall also reign together” (ibid., 11).

That high priest, therefore, who offered himself for us—as the Apostle says—“an offering and a sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma” (Eph. 5:2), just as he died for us, made us all die with him. Thus, when the pains of hell had been released, he freed all the faithful from those same pains, as blessed Peter bears witness, saying:

“Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God among you through mighty works, wonders, and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know—this man, handed over according to the determined plan and foreknowledge of God, you killed by fastening him to the cross through the hands of lawless men” [Note: Thus Ms. Victor., and likewise Mss. Colon., Ant. and Basil.; but Ms. Corb. reads, “afflicting him”]—“whom God raised up, having released the pains of hell, since it was impossible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2:22–24).

There too blessed Peter is shown to have set forth that testimony of David, which we included in the first book, in this manner:

“For David says concerning him: ‘I saw the Lord always before me, because he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken. Therefore my heart rejoiced and my tongue exulted; moreover, my flesh also will rest in hope. For you will not abandon my soul to hell, nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption. You have made known to me the paths of life; you will fill me with gladness in your presence’” (Ps. 16:8–11).

There blessed Peter, truly illuminated by the divine Spirit and made the light of the world according to the Lord’s word, showed with the clearest light of preaching how we ought to understand this passage, lest anyone understand the true flesh in Christ in such a way as to deny that he truly possessed a soul.

He continues, therefore: “Men, brothers, let me speak boldly to you about the patriarch David: he both died and was buried, and his tomb is among us to this day. Since he was a prophet, and knew that God had sworn to him with an oath that he would set one of the fruit of his loins upon his throne, he spoke beforehand about the resurrection of Christ: that neither was his soul abandoned in hell, nor did his flesh see corruption” (Acts 2:29–31).

In this, therefore, Christ’s divinity displayed the power of its impassibility: being everywhere always and ineffably present, it was, according to his soul, in hell without pains, and, according to his flesh, lay in the tomb without corruption. For it did not fail his flesh when it did not allow his soul to suffer in hell; nor did it abandon his soul in hell when it preserved his flesh from corruption in the tomb.

It was fitting that the place of the tomb should not corrupt the flesh that the inclination toward sin had not corrupted, and that the pain of hell should not touch the soul that the bondage of sin had been unable to hold. Therefore in the psalm, when, in the form of a servant in which Christ bore our sins, he said: “For my soul is filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to hell” (Ps. 88:4), to show that this same soul, free from sin, had descended into hell for us sinners, he added: “I have become like a man without help, free among the dead” (ibid., 5).

## CHAPTER XXXII. The Son of God is said to have died and risen with regard to the flesh. According to his divinity, the Father and the Son have one operation.

Nevertheless, since only the flesh died and was raised in Christ, because of the unity of person and name the Son of God is said to have died. The Apostle Paul clearly bears witness to this in these words: “For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life” (Rom. 5:10).

Again, that the Son of God rose is confirmed by Peter’s preaching, as he exhorts the Jews to believe in Christ in this way: “You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God established with our fathers, saying to Abraham: ‘And in your seed all the families of the earth shall be blessed.’ To you first, God, having raised up his Son, sent him to bless you, so that each one might turn from his wickedness” (Acts 3:24–25).

In this chapter also, when he mentions the seed of Abraham, blessed Peter calls the same one the Son of God; for Christ is not divided.  
[Note: This passage has been restored from Mss. Corb. and Basil. Colon. and Ant. instead had: “Yet he is understood to have risen not according to that which is from God the Father, but according to that which is from the seed of Abraham.”]

Nevertheless, so that he may be understood to have risen from the dead not according to that which he is from God the Father, but according to that which he is from the seed of Abraham, because of the unity of person in which God and man are one Christ, he is not improperly said to have been raised as the Son of God.

And, so that it might be proved that according to his divinity he has one nature with the Father, there was one operation together in the work. For just as he himself made his flesh in the Virgin’s womb, with the Father acting—for according to human nature it is written concerning Christ: “God made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 2:36); and it is also written: “Wisdom built herself a house” (Prov. 9:1)—so also, when he was handed over by the Father, he is recognized to have handed himself over. For it is written: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:32). And concerning the Son himself it is said: “The life I now live in the flesh I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and handed himself over for me” (Gal. 2:20).  
[Note: Ms. Victor., “his own Son.”]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. The Father raised the Son, and the Son raised himself.

In his resurrection also the equality of the work is found, because the majesty of the Father and the Son is one. Concerning the Father, blessed Peter speaks thus: “To you first, God, having raised up his Son, sent him to bless you” (Acts 3:25). But concerning himself the Son of God speaks thus to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). John explained this by saying: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body” (ibid., 21).

Also, when speaking to the Colossians, Paul indicates in these words that the Son of God himself raised his humanity:

“See to it that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ; for in him dwells [or: inhabits] all the fullness of divinity bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power. In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping off of the body of flesh, in the circumcision of Christ; buried with him in baptism, in which you also rose through faith in the operation of God, who raised him from the dead. And when you were dead in trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made you alive together with him, forgiving you all trespasses, erasing the record of the decree that stood against us and was contrary to us; he removed it from our midst, fastening it to the cross. Stripping off the flesh, he confidently led principalities and powers in triumph, openly triumphing over them in himself” (Col. 2:8–15).  
[Note: Thus Ms. Victor.; but Ms. Corb. and the published editions read, “God the Son.”]  
[Note: Ms. Corb., “decrees,” in accordance with the Apostle’s Greek text, τοῖς δόγμασιν.]

We are not unaware that some refer this passage to the person of the Father. But if the reader’s attention approaches it cautiously, the connection of the words shows more clearly that the meaning of this chapter is that one and the same Son should appear to be not only Christ, who was raised, but also God himself, who raised Christ.

Thus it is evident that in this passage the Apostle referred the name “God” to the Son’s eternal substance, which is from the Father, and the name “Christ” to the nature that the Son of God assumed from a human being. The Teacher of the Gentiles considered it especially fitting, in faith and truth, that just as he preached the same Christ who was raised as man, saying: “By a man came death, and by a man the resurrection of the dead; for just as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:21–22), so with no less caution he should most truly preach the same Son, who raised his flesh by that power by which he is equal to the Father, as God, as the text of this passage openly declares.

For the God who raised Christ from the dead, and who, when we were dead in trespasses and in the uncircumcision of our flesh, made us alive together with him (Col. 2:13), also forgave us all trespasses. The one who forgave the trespasses erased the record that stood against us and removed it from our midst, fastening it to the cross. The one who fastened the record to the cross also stripped himself of flesh. The one who stripped himself of flesh also confidently led principalities and powers in triumph, openly triumphing over them in himself (ibid., 15).

According to Paul’s testimony, God did all these things—the God who raised Christ from the dead. Let it therefore be considered whether the Father fastened the record to the cross; whether the Father stripped himself of flesh; whether the Father led principalities and powers in triumph, openly triumphing over them in himself. If all these things can properly be applied to the person of the Father, then the Son whom the Apostle designates here—the very God who raised Christ from the dead—will rightly be denied.

But if everything designated above belongs more suitably to the Son than to the Father, then the one and the same Christ whom the Apostle preaches is recognized: Christ who rose from the dead, and God who raised Christ from the dead.

Therefore Christ both raised himself and was raised; for just as, in what he did in himself, he deigned to be made what he did, and in what he handed over in himself, he deigned to be handed over, and in what he permitted to be killed in himself, he himself deigned to die, so in what he raised in himself, he himself deigned to be raised.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Christ’s humanity was not wholly in the tomb or in hell, but his divinity was wholly present there. The right faith concerning Christ’s humanity and his deeds. Various errors concerning Christ: the Marcionites, Ebionites, Arians, Eunomians, Apollinarists, Noesians, Sabellians, Patripassians, Valentinians and Apollinarists. Error concerning the Holy Spirit.

The true humanity of the Son of God, therefore, was neither wholly in the tomb nor wholly in hell. Rather, Christ lay dead in the tomb according to his true flesh, and Christ descended to hell according to his soul. According to that same soul he returned from hell to the flesh that he had left in the tomb. But according to his divinity, which is confined neither by place nor enclosed by any limit, he was wholly in the tomb with his flesh and wholly in hell with his soul.

Thus Christ was full everywhere, because God was not separated from the humanity he had assumed. He was in his soul so that, after the pains of hell had been released, his soul might return victoriously from hell; and he was in his flesh so that it could not be corrupted, being restored to life with speed.

The Son of God therefore took the whole man, with his weaknesses but without sin, for our sake. The same whole Christ, having been handed over, died according to the flesh alone; whole Christ descended to hell according to the soul alone; the same and inseparable Christ rose from the tomb according to the flesh alone; and the same and inseparable Christ, according to the whole man whom he had assumed, left the earth in bodily place, ascended to heaven, and sat at the right hand of God [or: sits there]. According to that same whole man he will come to judge the living and the dead, to crown the faithful and devout—those, namely, who believe him to be true, complete, and perfect in both substances, that is, the divine and the human, neither diminishing anything of the Father’s substance from the Son of God nor failing to recognize the whole man, assumed for our sake, as without sin.

But he will condemn the unbelievers who follow various errors of every kind of faithlessness and persist in them with hearts so hardened that they do not abandon them until the end of their present life. Among these are those who dare to believe that Christ possessed only an imagined flesh, while they deny that he assumed real flesh; those who, entirely denying divinity in him, think that he possessed only the substance of a human being; and also those who deny that he was naturally born God from God the Father, or who do not believe that Christ possessed the whole substance of a human being.

Likewise, he will come to condemn those who, believing the Father and the Son to be one God on account of the unity of operation, deny that one was born from the other, so that they confuse the Father and the Son personally. They assign human birth and death equally to the Father, saying that the Father himself was born from a Virgin and confessing that the Father himself suffered in the flesh.

He will also condemn with the eternal punishment of hellfire those who do not confess that Christ’s body was substantially taken from the Virgin, but fabricate that it was brought down from heaven. For the Son of God deigned to assume from a human being the nature of an earthly body precisely because he had not come to save those who were in heaven, but those who were on earth, as the Apostle says: “For he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham; hence he had to be made like his brothers in every respect” (Heb. 2:16–17).

The Son of God therefore assumed our soul—that is, what is better in us—for he is better than what is better in us. John says of him: “God is greater than our heart” (1 John 3:20). Yet he did not disdain to assume our flesh also—that is, what is lowest [or: weakest] in us—because he had come to save the whole human being. Nor could he become lower than what is lowest in us, through whom our lowliness deserved to be exalted to that name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:9–11).  
[Note: Basil., “lower than.”]  
[Note: Ms. Corb., “so that every tongue.”]

He will also consign to interminable torments those who distinguish the nature of the Holy Spirit from the substance of the Father and the Son, whether they think that he does not exist personally at all or consider him, as though he were a servant, to be entirely inferior in status. By their own profession [or: confession] they contradict themselves, confessing that they believe either in one who does not exist at all or in one who is not God.

## CHAPTER XXXV. The three persons give life together. They also regenerate together. The one love of the three dwells in us. They dwell in us. They give grace. We are the temple of the whole Trinity. A summary repetition of what has been said about the Holy Spirit. One God, threefold.

For, to append a few points pertinent to the purpose of this work: let it be said what the Holy Spirit has less than the Father and the Son—he who, together with the Father and the Son, likewise brought about the beginning of our creation, and who, together with the Father and the Son, completed the effect of our redemption. God is said to have made heaven; yet, while the Father was at work, the Son too is found to be his fellow-worker, and so is the Holy Spirit: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Psalm 32:6). What is he believed to have less than the Father or the Son, by whom all the power of the heavens is shown to have been established?

No one can give life except one who is God in substance. But just as the Father gives life, so the Son gives life, and so the Holy Spirit gives life. For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills (John 5:21). And concerning the Spirit the Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). Again he says: “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, because of his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans 8:11).

The Father regenerates, the Son regenerates, and the Holy Spirit regenerates; for when baptism is given in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, each person is regenerated in whose name he is baptized. Since, therefore, baptism is given in the name of the Trinity, the whole Trinity together regenerates—the Trinity which is one and the only God. Hence John says concerning the faithful: “They were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:13).

The Father’s love is in us, for Paul says of it: “But God commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us; much more, therefore, having now been justified in his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him” (Romans 5:8–9). Christ’s love is also in us, as the Apostle says: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Romans 8:35). [Note: [Col. 0301D] These words were absent from the Cologne and Antwerp editions; they have been restored from the Corbie and Victor manuscripts. Basil reads as follows: “Again: to know the love of Christ surpassing knowledge.”] And elsewhere: “To know also the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God” (Ephesians 3:19).

The love of the Holy Spirit is likewise in us, concerning which Paul says: “I beseech you, therefore, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Holy Spirit” (Romans 15:30). And elsewhere: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). Again he says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace” (Galatians 5:22).

The Father dwells in us, the Son dwells in us, and the Holy Spirit dwells in us, for it is written: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Corinthians 6:16). Concerning the Son the Apostle also says: “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, in the inner man” (Ephesians 3:16–17). He confirms in these words that the Holy Spirit likewise dwells in us: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). And, to show that the Spirit of God is the same as the Holy Spirit, he admonishes Timothy as follows: “Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us” (2 Timothy 1:14).

The Father gives grace, the Son gives grace, and the Holy Spirit gives grace, as the preacher of truth testifies, with Christ speaking through him: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 1:7). Concerning the Holy Spirit also it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, when Peter was sent by the Spirit himself to instruct Cornelius: “While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word; and the faithful from the circumcision who had come with Peter were amazed, because the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out even upon the nations” (Acts 10:44–45).

We are the temple of the Father, we are the temple of the Son, and we are the temple of the Holy Spirit, as we have learned from Paul the teacher, who says: “For you are the temple of the living God” (2 Corinthians 6:16). And elsewhere: “But if anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him; for the temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17). We are also the temple of the Son, whose house we are. For the Son himself called the temple a house, as the Evangelist says: “Jesus went up to Jerusalem and found in the temple those selling oxen and sheep” (John 2:13 and following). When he had immediately driven them from the temple, he said to those selling doves: “Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce” (ibid., 16).

David likewise shows in the Psalms that the temple of God is the same as his house, saying: “But I, in the abundance of your mercy, shall enter your house; I shall worship toward your holy temple” [Note: [Col. 0302D] The Cologne and Basil editions do not have “your”; the Corbie manuscript and the Antwerp edition have it.] “in your fear” (Psalm 5:8). Since, therefore, the temple of God is the house of God, the Apostle demonstrates that we are the temple of the Son, whose house he calls us when he writes to the Hebrews: “But Christ is as a Son over his own house; and we are that house, if indeed we hold firm to the end the confidence and glory of hope” (Hebrews 3:6).

Holy Scripture also calls the Son’s very body a house and a temple, when Solomon says: “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Proverbs 9:1); and the Evangelist, agreeing with this meaning, says: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:21). If, therefore, what is Christ’s body is Christ’s temple, we too are his temple, since the Apostle confirms that we are his body, saying: “You are the body of Christ and members of it” (1 Corinthians 12:27).

He also plainly declares that we are the temple of the Holy Spirit, saying: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God?” (1 Corinthians 6:19). [Note: [Col. 0302D] Basil reads: “your members are the temple.”] Thereby he also showed him to be God, adding: “And you are not your own; for you were bought with a great price. Therefore glorify and bear God in your body” (ibid., 15). Yet he testifies that this temple of the Holy Spirit is composed of the members of Christ, saying: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?”

Let it therefore be said whether he who is not God could establish the power of the heavens; whether he who is not God could give life; whether he who is not God could sanctify in the regeneration of baptism; whether he who is not God could bestow love; whether he who is not God could dwell in believers; whether he who is not God could give grace; whether he who is not God could have the members of Christ as his temple—and then the Holy Spirit will rightly be denied to be God.

Again, let it be said whether a creature can do the things that have been mentioned concerning the Holy Spirit—and then the Holy Spirit will rightly be called a creature. But if these things have never been possible for creatures, and they are found in the Holy Spirit—things that belong exclusively to God—we ought not to say that he is by nature different from the Father and the Son, whom we cannot find to be different in the power of their works. Thus, from the unity of the work, the unity of power must be recognized; and no one should doubt that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, with the Trinity of persons preserved, are naturally one God: he who was able to create all things by his sole will, who is able to govern all things by the omnipotence of his power, and who is able to fill all things by the immensity of his divinity.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Conclusion addressed to King Thrasamund the Arian

[Col. 0302D] These things, most merciful king, as the Lord has granted, I preferred to write to your piety rather than to keep entirely silent, lest by silence I should either be judged proud or be thought uncertain about the truth of our faith. For Christ wished the Catholic Church alone to be called his dove, saying: “My dove is one, my beloved is one” (Song of Songs 6:8). By the name “dove,” love and simplicity are signified [or: “are signified,” according to the alternative reading].

She alone possesses true love who does not call the Son of God, whom she loves, lesser in divinity, but confesses him equal to the Father. She alone possesses the truth of simplicity who believes the Trinity to have one true and simple substance.

We pray God to make the ears of your clemency receptive to the word of truth and to pour the light of spiritual wisdom into your devout heart, so that you may honor the Son of God, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, just as you honor the Father. He deserves this from you: that you who acknowledge him as having made you better than your father should confess him equal to his Father according to the divine nature.

I ask you, glorious king, to consider in yourself the abundance of the divine gift and not diminish the power of the giver, so that he who gave you a temporal kingdom may also grant you an eternal one. For he himself says: “Those who glorify me, I will glorify” (1 Samuel 2:30).

May the Trinity itself accomplish this—the Trinity which is one and the true God: “He who is able to do all things beyond what we ask or understand” (Ephesians 3:20). For “from him, and through him, [and in him,] are all things” (Romans 11:36). [Note: [Col. 0303] “And in him” is absent from the printed editions; it is read in the Corbie manuscript and in the Apostle’s text.]

To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0303A]

# 144. THE LETTERS OF SAINT FULGENTIUS, NOW FIRST COLLECTED INTO ONE BODY. (C, S)

## FIRST LETTER

[Note: [Col. 0303D] The Victor manuscript reads: “That even married people ought to preserve continence after the vow.”]

On the marital obligation and the vow of continence made by married couples.

[Col. 0303B]

To his lord and deservedly venerable son, Fulgentius, servant of Christ’s servants, greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I. Excuse for the delayed reply

1. A few months ago, on receiving your letter—a sign of holy concern—I wished to reply without delay. But I was suddenly seized by such a bodily illness that the violent severity of the fevers would have taken from me the course of this present life, had not the true physician of souls and bodies, who heals all our illnesses and redeems [or: “will redeem”] our life from destruction, deigned to grant the aid of his medicine for removing the scourge of so great an infirmity.

After I had recovered my health, the will to write back was certainly not lacking, but the harshness of winter prevented me from sending the reply. Now, therefore, since the Creator and governor of the seasons has deigned to grant the winds’ moderation, I have not ceased to return to your consultation [or: consolation] what I have received through the mercy and inspiration of the heavenly Giver.

## CHAPTER II. The substance of the question concerning the wife’s continence. Marital intercourse is not in itself evil, but excess is. The marital obligation

2. You say, then, that our daughter, your wife, was recently ill almost to the point of death and, as commonly happens, after receiving the laying-on of hands, performed penance according to the custom of the Christian religion. But because afterward, by the gift of divine goodness, she received full bodily health, you plead the frailty of the flesh and confess in addition the incontinence of youthful age. In this uncertainty of thought, in which you consider the flesh and fear majesty, like a sailor unfamiliar with the region and tossed by waves and winds, while you guard against the uncertainties of dangers, you ask that our reply point out to you the harbor where you may avoid the shipwreck of your soul.

3. The substance of your question therefore compels me to weigh carefully two matters that must not be considered negligently: namely, not only what the nature of marital intercourse contains in itself, but also what the promise of the person making a vow demands in each matter.

4. If, therefore, one of the faithful married people considers intercourse in itself by the guidance of reason, he will find that culpable use lies not in marital intercourse but in the excess of those who engage in it. Marital intercourse derives its guilt not from the union of male and female but from the immoderation of lust. Excess is therefore rightly censured in married people, yet the dignity of marriage is not deprived of the honor divinely bestowed upon it.

For this reason the authority of apostolic preaching cries out: “Marriage is honorable in all, and the marriage bed undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4). When Paul was instructing the Corinthians concerning the preservation of the honor of marriage, he had first said: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (1 Corinthians 7:1). But seeing the weakness of some and acting with apostolic love, like a support beneath a leaning wall or a fallen [or: displaced] fence, the excellent teacher did not neglect to provide a prop [Note: [Col. 0303D] *Destinam*, that is, a support or prop. Arnobius uses the term in Book II *Against the Nations*, near the end: “Atlas, bearer, carrier, and support of heaven.”], with Christ speaking through him.

Finally, he adds: “But because of fornications [or: fornication], let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (ibid., 2–3).

5. The substance of the apostolic reading therefore shows that wife and husband are joined by a certain sharing of obligation. The Apostle would certainly not have called it an obligation unless he knew that it was to be rendered lawfully; nor would he have commanded it to be rendered through the duty of mutual consent if the demand of the one requiring it were unjust. So entirely does the Teacher of the nations apply marriage to the divine work that he confirms, with completely equal right, the power of the woman over the man’s body and of the man over the woman’s body, saying: “The woman does not have power over her own body, but the man; likewise, the man does not have power over his own body, but the woman” (ibid., 4). [Note: [Col. 0304D] The printed editions have: “nor would he have commanded the duty of mutual consent to be rendered,” but the reading of the Corbie and Victor manuscripts appears more coherent.]

Elsewhere the same Apostle says: “There is no power except from God” (Romans 13:1).

## CHAPTER III. Marriage is to be used for offspring, not for lust

6. The use of this power is therefore blameless when it serves the divinely assigned duty of begetting, provided that a lustful excess is not allowed to cross the boundary of justice. The justice of using marriage consists in this: spouses should unite at the proper time not for the satisfaction of lust but for the purpose of bringing forth offspring.

Among those good things that God made, the chaste union of wife and husband is found; lust cannot be found among God’s works. Nor is it ever compatible with justice, since it came not to human beings from the gift of creation [or: Creator], but to sinners through the defect of the first transgression. Yet because, without it, the human race is not propagated in this body of death, chaste marriages do not desire it but endure it; and marital honor imposes a limit upon it, without which it cannot fulfill in sinful flesh the natural duty of fertility.

7. The fruit of marriage should therefore be sought in such a way that the excess of slippery pleasure is restrained. Accordingly, if marital intercourse is moderated so that the mind does not serve burning lust but looks toward the birth of offspring, and does not neglect, once the child has been born, to hasten its cleansing through spiritual generation, the intercourse granted to faithful spouses is not reckoned as a sin of the flesh. For the marital bond preserves chastity, modesty guards a temperate restraint, and marital fertility offers to God offspring destined for him, [Note: [Col. 0305D] The Corbie and Victor manuscripts read: “for the God and Redeemer.”] so that the human being already born may be reformed through the Redeemer’s help in the sacrament of baptism, by whose work he was first formed in the womb; and so that human nature may have, through the benefit of a second birth, as father the one whom it acknowledges as the author of its condition in its first birth.

8. A married person who commits fornication therefore sins damnably. But if he does not abandon fidelity to the marriage bed, and in his wife exceeds somewhat through natural use alone, being somewhat intemperate [or: more intemperate]—that is, if he seeks not only the begetting of children but sometimes also obeys the lust of the flesh—he does not do this without guilt. Yet such guilt is more quickly forgiven to one who is active in good works and prayer, because marital love itself preserves fidelity toward his spouse, although marital weakness cannot maintain restraint in it. And if marital modesty is not preserved with his wife, he nevertheless does not depart from marital fidelity through any immoderation.

## CHAPTER IV. Preserved fidelity to the marriage bed cleanses the stain of lust. All fornication is damnable, especially in a married person

9. Fidelity to the marriage bed, once retained, cleanses the stain contracted by weakness of the flesh in anyone who, joining himself to his wife not only for procreation but also because of the frailty of his flesh, does not join himself to another woman. For even if he exceeds the prescribed measure of intercourse, he nevertheless does not go beyond the marital boundary; and although bodily weakness contracts guilt, marital integrity nevertheless obtains pardon.

Such a person receives indulgence not because he demands the marital obligation from one woman more than he ought [or: demanded it], but because, content with one woman lawfully received [or: with one lawful wife], he does not seek another. Provided, however, that works of mercy are not lacking. These have such importance in the Christian religion that not only married people or those who are continent, but even virgins, cannot attain the reward of virginity if they neglect works of mercy and love.

If, on the other hand, someone intent upon good works has preserved such restraint with his wife that he joins himself to her solely for the sake of begetting children, he is undoubtedly worthy of great praise—if anyone in our times is able to fulfill this.

10. Fornication, however, can never be without grave crime. Although we do not doubt that a person separated from his wife sins damnably by committing fornication, I consider a married person’s fornication still more damnable. Holy Scripture declares both to be judged and pronounces them alien from the kingdom [or: from the reign] of God. For it is written in the Letter to the Hebrews: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Hebrews 13:4).

And in the Letter that the Apostle wrote to the Corinthians it says: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor robbers shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:9–10).

Again, among the works of the flesh the same Apostle Paul lists fornication, uncleanness, and wantonness; and at their conclusion he says: “Those who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God” (Galatians 5:21). [Note: [Col. 0306D] This is the reading of the Corbie manuscript and of the Greek text of the Apostle. All the printed editions instead have: “shall not inherit.”]

He also warns that he may not have to mourn over many of those who sinned previously and did not repent of the uncleanness, fornication, and shamelessness that they committed (2 Corinthians 12:21). [Note: [Col. 0306D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “concerning uncleanness, fornication, and shamelessness.”]

## CHAPTER V. Vows must be fulfilled to God without excuse

11. Since, then, we have spoken about the nature of marriage, which the Lord has granted, the matter that must next be examined with complete care is what the devotion of your will established—if at that time it was able to establish anything.

For the fact that the use of things granted by God is not forbidden to human beings does not mean that a person ought not to render to God what he has vowed, since it is written: “I shall render my vows to you, which my lips have distinguished” (Psalm 65:13).

And lest anyone wish to take the excuse of affliction as permission to frustrate a promise, or think himself not bound by a vow if he said that he had been compelled to vow something not by his will but by affliction, blessed David teaches that everything legitimately promised, even in affliction, must be rendered to God. After saying to God, “I shall render my vows to you, which my lips have distinguished,” he immediately added: “And my mouth spoke in my affliction” (ibid., 14).

It is also written in Deuteronomy: “But if you make a vow to the Lord your God, you shall not delay in fulfilling it, because the Lord your God will surely require it of you, and there will be sin in you. But if you do not wish to vow, there will be no sin in you. You shall keep what goes forth from your lips, and you shall do as you vowed to your God, what you spoke with your mouth” (Deuteronomy 23:24).

Solomon also says: “As soon as you make a vow to the Lord, do not delay in fulfilling it. Therefore render what you have vowed. It is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill” (Ecclesiastes 5:3–4).

## CHAPTER VI. Lawful things become unlawful after a vow. Marriage becomes unlawful for those bound by a vow of continence

12. The use of lawful things is therefore lawfully practiced with moderation so long as renunciation of the lawful thing has not been vowed, and so long as a perpetual promise of continence has not been made by the consent of both parties—that is, by the consent of husband and wife. Marital intercourse is not unlawful. For it is written: “If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned” (1 Corinthians 7:28).

Yet although the virgin who marries does not sin, some virgin is found to sin if she marries. A virgin who marries does not sin if she has not previously vowed virginity in her heart to God. But if, as the Apostle said, “she has firmly determined in her heart, having no necessity, but having power over her own will, and has decided this in her heart, to preserve her virginity” (ibid., 37), she sins gravely afterward if, after dedicating her virginity to God, she wishes to serve a human marriage.

Blessed Paul also declares certain widows bound by a bond of condemnation, because, after professing continence, they do not reject the desire to marry. Concerning avoiding them he instructs Timothy as follows: “But avoid younger widows. For when they have grown wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, incurring condemnation because they have rejected their first faith” (1 Timothy 5:11).

A promise of continence therefore removes the permission to have intercourse. Such people are forbidden not only fornication but also marital intercourse; a culpable bond holds the will that has broken faith, even if no action follows. For it is not written without reason: “When desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin” (James 1:15).

## CHAPTER VII. Married people do not have the same freedom to vow as the unmarried, because they do not have power over their own bodies. A vow of continence is binding if made with the consent of both spouses

13. Accordingly, continence dedicated to God must be preserved with fear and trembling not only by virgins but also by widows and married people. Before anyone becomes bound by a vow, no one is condemned: a virgin may lawfully marry, and a husband and wife may render to each other the marital obligation. But after someone, pursuing better things, has bound himself by a profession of continence or integrity, he sins most gravely if he thereafter thinks that what was previously lawful is still permitted to him.

In such matters, whatever the will of the person making the vow takes away from him for God, necessity does not thereafter permit him to usurp with impunity. Nor will the violator of a vow find a just excuse for his transgression, since no one compelled him to vow.

14. A distinction must plainly be made between the vow of a virgin or widow and the vow of those held by the bond of marriage. A man or woman who does not have power over his or her own body does not possess as much freedom or license to vow as any widow or virgin. A married man or woman does not have full power to vow bodily continence, because the body is not under that person’s own power but under the power of the spouse, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement quoted above: “The woman does not have power over her own body, but the man; likewise, the man does not have power over his own body, but the woman” (1 Corinthians 7:4).

A person therefore cannot assume continence without the spouse’s consent when the body is not under his own power. Each person makes a promise with right and firm devotion only concerning what he recognizes as belonging solely to his own jurisdiction. [Note: [Col. 0307D] The Corbie and Victor manuscripts read: “For it is such a thing.”]

For it is no different from someone wishing to profess continence in regard to a body that lies under the spouse’s power than if someone attempted to give alms or offer sacrifice from another person’s property. But our God, as he himself testifies, “loves justice and hates robbery in a burnt offering” (Isaiah 61:8).

15. Among married people, therefore, the promise of continence is certain only when it has been confirmed by the consent of both. When husband and wife, agreeing with each other in harmonious will, have offered it as a sacrifice of pleasing fragrance upon the altar of faith, in the temple of their heart, to the true and supreme God, neither the wife thereafter has legitimate power to demand the marital obligation from the husband’s body, nor the husband from the wife’s.

For, just as before they made the vow to God together, the offering of one was blameworthy because the consent of the lawful partner was lacking, so, when both have offered it with equal consent—what belongs inseparably to both—neither will go unpunished if he believes that a gift offered to God in voluntary devotion may be violated by an unlawful act. [Note: [Col. 0308D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “what belongs to both.”]

## CHAPTER VIII. The person who did not vow wholeheartedly is all the more culpable. Nothing may be retained or reclaimed from a vow

16. If someone should perhaps claim that he did not vow wholeheartedly, he will be all the more culpable because he approached God not sincerely but falsely. For it is written: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts without understanding” (Wisdom 1:5).

Elsewhere Holy Scripture rebukes the false-hearted as follows: “Woe to the double-hearted, to wicked lips, to hands that do evil, and to the sinner who enters the land by two paths” (Sirach 2:14).

17. How evil it is, and how carefully it must be avoided, for anyone to attempt through a deadly transgression to retain or reclaim something from what he has vowed to God is shown by the example of Ananias and Sapphira. When they deceitfully withheld part of the price of the field, the apostolic voice not only rebuked them as usurpers of what belonged to divine law [or: “rebuked”], but the severity of heavenly justice also killed them.

Finally, blessed Peter said that Ananias was liable not only for the fault of fraud but also declared that his heart had been filled by Satan, saying: “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit and keep back part of the price of the field? Was it not yours while it remained, and when sold was it not in your power? [Note: [Col. 0309D] This is the reading of the Corbie manuscript. The Cologne, Antwerp, and Basil editions have: “Since you did this, are you not...”] Why have you done this? You have not lied to human beings but to God” (Acts 5:3–4).

If, therefore, someone, overcome by the enticement of the flesh, believes that something already dedicated to the Lord ought to be reclaimed, he is not the lawful possessor of his own property but is declared an invader of what belongs to divine law. And rightly the violator of continence already dedicated to God hears the same judgment that the fraudulent miser of money heard.

## CHAPTER IX. Reply to the questions posed at the beginning of the letter. Modesty must be preserved in the marital act

18. Weigh all that has been discussed above, with your conscience bearing witness. If you have indeed vowed continence with equal consent, preserve the terms of your love with fear of God. Whenever the weakness of the flesh assails the mind, let the soul hasten to the aid of divine mercy; let it not yield to lust, but let it entreat God with complete humility and, without consenting to carnal desire warring against the soul, let it resist it.

But if one of you vowed continence without the consent of the other, let that person recognize that he vowed rashly and let him render the marital obligation to his spouse with chaste sincerity.

19. Nevertheless, so that everything you do may be honorable, in rendering the marital obligation let marital practice respond to the weakness of the flesh in such a way that the flesh does not serve lust, but the strength of the soul, divinely assisted, restrains the reins of carnal desire.

The work of bringing forth offspring should be carried out by married people in such a way that, while modesty attends them and the faithful mind inclines itself toward the work of fertility, it also preserves, with God’s help, the restraint of natural honor. Above all, faithful married people must observe that they avoid those actions which divine severity both forbids to be done and condemns when done. Apostolic teaching has not ceased to impress this upon the faithful, instructing them prudently and warning them for their salvation, so that they may preserve the rule of a good life.

## CHAPTER X. Continence is to be sought from God by all. The governance of the household and education of children. The rule of progress and perfection in marriage

20. It is therefore a great good “not to touch a woman,” which every faithful person ought chiefly to observe. Nevertheless, because of fornications, anyone—whether married or free from marriage—who has not vowed continence to God and sees himself unable to fulfill continence should, although he recognizes that he lacks the strength to abstain, remember this:

Wherever the will to abstain has been complete and true humility of heart has not ceased from prayer and good works, the one who said, “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7:7), because he is truth and cannot lie, will give to the one who asks well, prepare his discoveries for the one who seeks, and himself open to the one who knocks well, so that he may enter into the inner chambers of the better life.

Yet if someone is still more concerned about his own weakness than secure in the Lord’s power, and has not vowed continence of the flesh, let him nevertheless abstain from iniquity and use his wife as is fitting. Let him flee wickedness and greed, and he will not be condemned [or: “let him not be condemned”] if he renders the marital obligation to his spouse.

Let him not be drunken, envious, quarrelsome, false, malicious, contentious, proud, rapacious, or greedy. As far as he is concerned, let him seek to have peace with everyone; let him not hold destruction in his heart; let him slander no one; let him keep faith with his friends; let him never be treacherous or perjured toward his enemies. Let him not seize what belongs to others, nor place money above equity. Let him be just in business, devout in his works, gentle in enduring injuries, and slow to repay them; steadfast in faith and a lover of chastity and peace.

Let him heed the saying of our Savior, by which he both commands us what to do and shows us what we shall receive: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:37). Let him therefore be as generous and cheerful as he can in almsgiving, and ready and gracious in forgiving those who sin.

Yet he must not think that forgiveness is to be granted to sinners in such a way that he neglects the discipline of his household. Rather, while retaining a balance of firmness [or: severity] and clemency, let him preserve moderation in correction and judgment in remission. Let him rebuke, advise, frighten, reprove, console, and delight. Let him not do to those subject to him who sin as much as the force of anger impels, but as much as the measure of prudent counsel requires.

If a servant must be beaten for a fault, let the desire for vengeance not prevail; rather, let Christian equity mercifully provide for the one whom it chastises. Thus, even when justice pursues guilt, mercy should not be absent—mercy that knows how to lessen punishment with moderation.

21. Let children be brought up, according to the Apostle’s command, “in the discipline and correction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4). They must not be permitted to live immodestly or wantonly, since Christian offspring ought to serve not licentiousness but chastity and temperance.

Nor will the negligence of parents concerning their children’s evil works fail to be judged in that fearful examination. Even in this world the priest Eli was rejected and cast off by the Lord (1 Samuel 2:3), not because he consented to his sons’ iniquity, but because, although he admonished them with gentle words when they sinned, he failed to restrain them with appropriate severity.

Parents who truly love their children should provide for them more by doing good than by gathering riches, lest, while property is laboriously accumulated for their children, the opportunity for good works be neglected.

22. Above all, let faithful married people remember that they must always devote themselves to prayers and almsgiving. Let them not wish to lie perpetually in the weakness of the flesh itself, but hasten to ascend the step of the better life. And so that the soul may attain the virtue of continence, let the excess of carnal desire be increasingly restrained, so that, with God’s help, when they have overcome the stage at which marital weakness asks for pardon, they may laudably attain the higher stage in which the virtue of continence awaits the palm of the better life. [Note: [Col. 0310D] The Victor manuscript reads: “joy.”]

# SECOND LETTER. TO GALLA, A WIDOW

On consolation concerning the death of her husband and on the condition of widows.

To the truly illustrious lady and venerable daughter in the fear of Christ, Galla, Fulgentius, servant of the servants of Christ, greetings in the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0311D] “Fulgentius” is absent from the printed editions; it is read in the Corbie manuscript.]

# Chapter I. Galla’s Consolation on the Death of Her Young Husband. Praise of the Deceased Husband

## 1

Some months ago, on the reliable report of my returning deacon, I learned not only of the death of your husband, but also of the holy course of life you have undertaken, in which you now walk under the guidance of him who is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6). He knows how to grant his faithful, through momentary sorrow, the gift of everlasting joy, and, by the dispensation of paternal kindness, to transfer those whom he wills salutarily from earthly things to heavenly ones.

## 2

For the Lord, whose judgments are incomprehensible and whose ways are unsearchable, as the apostle Paul proclaims (Rom. 11:33), did not without purpose swiftly transfer your husband—sincere in religion, faithful, humble in heart, gentle in conduct, merciful in his works, wholly innocent in his way of life, young in age—from the pilgrimage of this life to the eternal dwelling of the heavenly homeland. He did so both to bestow eternal joys upon him and to grant you the opportunity to live better.

He granted him that, stripped of the body, he might live with Christ without end [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “dissolved”]; he granted you that you might think about the things of the Lord [Note: Thus the Corbie and Victor manuscripts; the printed editions read “that you might think”] and, in accordance with the saying of the apostle Paul, might be holy both in body and in spirit. Therefore believe without hesitation what is spoken by God, and hope with love for what is promised, so that you may be able to do well what is commanded.

# Chapter II. Christians Should Not Grieve for the Dead as Those Who Have No Hope Do. Two Kinds of Sorrow

## 3
