First, therefore, learn through the apostle Paul what you must faithfully hold concerning your husband’s death. For he says:

> We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest, who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep (1 Thess. 4:13–14).

If, then, we hold firmly to true faith; if we doubt nothing in the words of God; if we strive toward the future life with the surest hope; if we love God and our neighbor worthily; if, as Christians, we await not empty glory from human beings but true glory from God—we certainly ought not to have, like unbelievers, any grief for the faithful dead, or, to speak more precisely, for our own who have fallen asleep.

For there ought to remain in our heart a distinction between healthy and harmful sorrow. Through it, the mind devoted to eternal things neither collapses over the loss of temporal comfort nor fails to draw healthy sorrow from those matters in which it recognizes that it has done something either less or otherwise than it ought. Accordingly, Paul teaches no less by their operation than by their recompense that the two kinds of sorrow are distinct [Note: Thus the Corbie and Victor manuscripts, as well as the Cologne manuscript; the others read “retribution”]. Finally, he shows that the increase of salvation is found in one and the destruction of death in the other, saying:

> For the sorrow that is according to God produces repentance leading to lasting salvation, while the sorrow of the world produces death (1 Cor. 7:10).

## 4

Therefore, do not hold an indiscriminate grief over your husband’s death beyond the measure of Christian faith. Do not consider him lost, but sent ahead [variant: “promised”], and do not think that his youth was cut off prematurely, since you see it established in unending eternity.

For it is said to the faithful soul:

> Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s (Ps. 102:5).

# Chapter III. The Dark Day Does Not Take Away the Faithful. The Day of Christ’s Greatness Is the Day of the Final Judgment

## 5

Far be it from us to agree with the errors of unbelievers and to think or say that the young Christian was taken away by the dark day and plunged into a bitter funeral:

> The dark day took him away  
> and overwhelmed him with a bitter death.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.428.)

For the dark day takes away those who, according to the apostle John’s saying, are in darkness and walk in darkness and do not know where they are walking, because darkness has blinded their eyes (1 John 2:11).

The dark day took away those whom the true light itself severely rebukes, saying:

> This is the judgment: that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than light, for their works were evil (John 3:19).

Such are those who live in such a way that, when they hear the voice of the Son of God, they will be raised not to life but to judgment. The Lord says:

> The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, while those who have done evil will come forth to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28–29).

And since neither a short life nor a long one can benefit such people, Scripture consequently says of them in the Book of Wisdom:

> Even if they live long, they will be counted as nothing, and their final old age will be without honor. And if they die sooner, they will have no hope, nor will they have an audience on the day of greatness (Wis. 3:17).

## 6

What, then, is the day of greatness except the day on which the Lord will come not to be judged but to judge? When he came now to be judged for our sake, it was not a day of greatness but of abasement, in which he was made a little lower than the angels. But it will be a day of greatness when, according to John’s testimony, all the wicked will wish to hide themselves in the caves of the mountains, saying to the mountains and rocks:

> Fall upon us and hide us from the face of the Father who sits upon the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come; and who will be able to stand? (Rev. 6:16).

On this day of greatness the wicked will have not an audience but rebuke. They will not hear:

> Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world (Matt. 25:34),

but it will be said to them:

> Go away, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. 25:41).

Such people, however long they may live before dying, are plunged into a bitter funeral. Although their bodily age may appear mature, the deadly love of the world nevertheless preserves in their hearts the bitterness of an immature mind.

# Chapter IV. A Good Christian, Even if Young, Is Not Plunged into a Bitter Funeral. A Long Life Does Not Help, but a Good One Does

## 7

But the Christian who has lived in the fear of God, at whatever bodily age he may die, is not plunged into a bitter funeral; rather, supported by a maturity pleasing to God, he is transferred.

For we read in the same Book of Wisdom:

> Honorable old age is not that which lasts long, nor is it measured by the number of years. The gray hair of a human being is understanding, and the age of old age is an unblemished life, which, because it has become pleasing to God, is beloved (Wis. 4:8).

Indeed, shortly afterward Scripture says that a certain person who lived well and pleased God was taken away swiftly so that he might undergo no change through worldly wickedness and so that his soul might not be deceived by any falsehood [variant: “weariness”]. Thus it says:

> He was taken away, lest wickedness change his understanding or falsehood deceive his soul. For the fascination of vanity obscures good things, and the instability of desire overturns the understanding without malice. Having been perfected in a short time, he fulfilled long ages. For his soul was pleasing to God; therefore he hastened to lead him out from the midst of iniquity (Wis. 4:11–14).

By these words Holy Scripture teaches us that, in this age, it is not a long life but a good one that benefits faithful Christians. To discern, as far as possible, the merit of any deceased person, one must consider not how long he lived but how he lived.

For just as an evil life, the longer it is prolonged in time, multiplies punishment for sinners, so a good life, even if brought to an end here after a short time, obtains great and everlasting glory for those who live well. An evil life, therefore, plunges immature and bitter old people into Tartarus, while a good life brings young people who have died maturely into the kingdom.

# Chapter V. A Widow Must Be Concerned to Be Holy in Body and Spirit. Christian Marriages Are Holy

## 8

Do not, then, be sad that he went before you by a few days. Rather, be concerned to pass through the way of this mortal life in such a manner that you may be able to reach eternal life.

Therefore you must constantly remember the apostolic saying:

> The unmarried woman and the virgin are concerned with the things of the Lord, so that they may be holy both in body and spirit (1 Cor. 7:34).

Here he calls a widow “unmarried,” not because she never married at all, but because, after her husband’s death, she has been released from the marital bond. Of her he says elsewhere:

> If her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband (Rom. 7:2).

He commands her, therefore, to be holy both in body and spirit. What else is it to be holy in body and spirit except to preserve holiness both in deed and in thought?

For the woman bound by a bodily marriage is permitted to think about worldly things, as the same apostle says:

> The married woman thinks about worldly things, how she may please her husband (1 Cor. 7:34).

There, then, the necessity of worldly thought must be endured, where mortal flesh is carnally married to one who will die. And because the necessity of the flesh holds such people bound by harsher ties, the Apostle says of them:

> Such people will have tribulation in the flesh (1 Cor. 7:28).

Therefore the unmarried woman—that is, the widow—to whom it is commanded that she be holy both in body and spirit, just as she refrains—or, according to another reading, has ceased—from serving her husband bodily, so she ought not to think of carnal things in her heart.

## 9

Christian marriages are indeed holy, because marital chastity is guarded in the body and purity of faith is preserved in the heart. For apostolic authority also says:

> Marriage is honorable in all, and the marriage bed undefiled (Heb. 13:4).

Marriage, therefore, does not arise from the pollution of sin but from the institution of God. In the fact that spouses render to one another the bodily debt, insofar as they do so modestly, they keep Christ’s commandments, because they do not in any way depart from marital love and chastity.

Marital chastity condemns adulterous intercourse. Holding fast to honor and modesty, one woman seeks from one man, and one man from one woman, what each recognizes that he lawfully owes to one alone.

There, indeed, the bodily debt is rendered to the husband; but marital chastity is owed more to Christ than to the husband. For the body is truly chaste when it is not polluted by carnal fornication and when spiritual integrity is preserved through fear and love of Christ.

# Chapter VI. The Unmarried Woman Holds a Higher Rank Than the Married Woman

## 10

Nevertheless, the unmarried woman and virgin are distinguished from the married woman by no small dignity of rank. The married woman is bound by worldly thoughts, whereas the unmarried woman and virgin are not subjected to carnal tribulations, because she is not held by the bond of carnal marriage.

There—or, according to another reading, “where”—the freedom of bodily and spiritual continence is more secure, because there is no necessity arising from marital servitude.

Both, therefore, are gifts of God: marital chastity and widowly continence. For:

> Each person has his own gift from God [variant: “from God” rather than “of God”] (1 Cor. 7:7).

The former is praiseworthy in itself because it is good; the latter is more praiseworthy because it is better.

Through marital servitude, the shamefulness of fornication is overcome; through widowly freedom, the dignity of chastity increases. There, faith comes to the aid of weakness so that it does not fall into vice; here, the faithful spirit stretches itself toward an increase of virtue.

For married people it is said:

> Because of fornications [variant: “fornication,” singular], let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband (1 Cor. 7:2).

But of a widow it is said:

> She will be happier if she remains as she is (1 Cor. 7:40).

Blessed, therefore, is she who does not desire illicit intercourse because of the horror of shame; but happier is she who, through a greater love of purity, rejects what is licit.

Blessed is she who, bound to a husband, lives in such a way that she renders the debt of her flesh to her husband alone; but happier is she who, released, remains unmarried in such a way that she owes it to no one.

# Chapter VII. Consolation of the Widow

## 11

Therefore, in that you have become a widow from being married, consider God’s gift to you increased, not taken away. For he has not abandoned you who has shown you the way of a better life, a way you must follow.

The Lord wished you to ascend by stages to better things: first, to live faithfully as a married woman with one husband, and afterward to remain a widow without a husband and without difficulty.

For this purpose divine grace nourished your soul through marital chastity: you had learned, while he alone lived, not to seek another man; now you were to learn, as a widow, to remain continent from every man.

Do not neglect the grace that is in you. You know how much better it is to abstain continually from intercourse than even to have intercourse out of marital necessity.

The husband who had been given to you for a time departed at the appointed time. For he had been given to you not for the blessedness of the homeland but for the consolation of the journey.

## 12

There are, indeed, other gifts of God which God grants to his faithful in the present age in such a way that their use is necessary only in this life, so that the merit of the future life may be acquired. Such are belief that holds to the right faith [Note: Thus the Corbie and Cologne manuscripts; Basil reads “right life” or “right way”], and the practice that preserves justice and mercy.

Thus right faith is not abandoned, with the assistance of love, which is recognized in practice. For this reason the Apostle approves the faith that works through love (Gal. 5:6).

# Chapter VIII. Faith and Merciful Practice Are Necessary in This Life but Will Not Be Necessary in the Homeland

## 13

Right faith and merciful practice, therefore, will come to an end after this life, when what is now believed without being seen will be seen directly. Nor will there be any wretched person among the blessed to whom mercy must be shown.

Yet these two things—faith and practice—are not so unnecessary after the end of this life that they may be abandoned before its end. Whoever, before the end of the present life, departs from right faith or good practice, even if he previously ran vigorously and watchfully in them, loses the merit of the entire course he has run because he abandons the right path.

## 14

There are also other things which divine piety grants to human beings in this age in such a way that they ought not merely to remain continually with them in this life [Note: Thus the Corbie and Victor manuscripts; Basil reads “remain”], but also to increase in divine recompense. Such are the cleansing of sins, recognition of truth, and love of God and neighbor.

If anyone perseveringly preserves these things in himself during this age and takes care to increase what has been begun by progressing through divine gift, he will possess them in the future, where they will remain with him in eternal perfection.

Then perfect cleansing will receive perfect knowledge of the truth, and perfect knowledge will permit nothing of perfect love to be lacking in us [variant: “to perfect love”].

# Chapter IX. Some Things Are Both Given and Taken Away by God in Time. The Example of Job. The Rich Man and Lazarus: One Blessed, the Other Miserable

## 15

There are other things which God gives temporarily in such a way that they are also taken away temporarily [variant: “given” rather than “granted”]: the union of spouses, the begetting of children, abundance of wealth, bodily health, and whatever similar things there may be.

In themselves these things can make people neither miserable nor blessed. Therefore the Lord gives them both to good and to evil people, and sometimes takes them away from both good and evil people.

## 16

Job was blessed when he lived justly amid riches; but he was more blessed when he proved more just in poverty. He was blessed when he was surrounded by ten children, but more blessed when, struck by the bereavement of all of them at once, he remained unmoved in the love of God.

He was also blessed in bodily health, but he became more blessed through his wound. He was more blessed in a heap filled with filth than in a palace adorned with marble.

## 17

Consider also two men: one miserable in wealth and health, the other exceedingly blessed in poverty and wounds.

That rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day (Luke 16:19)—how empty he was amid those feasts, how poor amid the abundance of his riches, how naked amid the beauty of his clothing, how weak amid bodily health, how hungry amid the fullness of his belly, how miserable amid his joys, how desolate amid the conversation of his friends, how abject amid the attentions of his servants!

Consider also Lazarus: rich in poverty, blessed in misery, fortunate in misfortune, healthy amid wounds; indeed, without a house but not without a Lord, without clothing but not without faith, without bodily health but not without the strength of love, without food but not without Christ, exposed to dogs but a companion of angels.

He did not receive the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, but he belched forth the heavenly bread—or, according to another reading, “the bread of heavenly things”—from his innermost being.

# Chapter X. Temporal Goods May Be Possessed Well or Badly and May Be Despised Well or Badly

## 18

These, then, are the things that are sometimes possessed well and sometimes badly; sometimes despised well and sometimes badly.

They are possessed well when the fear of God is preserved in their use. They are despised well when, in despising them, one seeks glory from the supreme God and not from human beings.

## 19

Marriage, too, is such a thing: it may be entered well and it may be well rejected.

How well did Susanna preserve the work of marriage in marital chastity! How much better did Judith and Anna reject it in widowly continence! How supremely did Mary know nothing of it in virginal integrity!

## 20

Marriage, therefore, must not be reckoned among God’s principal gifts, although it must not be denied that it is a divine gift. Nor should it be called a gift of blessedness when it can be held with a good purpose but also rejected for the sake of a better purpose.

For if it were necessary to count it among God’s principal gifts, our Savior would not praise those who castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 19:12). Nor would the Savior himself command that, for his sake, father, mother, brothers, sisters, wife, children, and fields be abandoned, promising a hundredfold recompense and eternal life, saying:

> Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life (Matt. 19:29).

In saying this, Christ did not command divorce. Rather, through a just distinction, he showed that his faithful ought to place God’s gifts—though they are gifts of God—after eternal things, things that perish after things that endure, small things after great ones.

He does not condemn the good things, but praises the better things more. He does not hate the former, but loves the latter more. For whether such things are obtained or lost is not the reward of faith but its testing.

# Chapter XI. Faith Must Be Directed Toward Eternal Things, Not Temporal Ones. The Widow Must Not Be Entangled in Worldly Thoughts. The Adornment and Dress of Widows

## 21

Our faith must be directed not toward temporal things but toward eternal ones. For this reason the Chosen Vessel, exhorting us to endure present tribulation, commands us to turn the gaze of our heart completely away from contemplation of temporal things, saying:

> The momentary and light burden of our tribulation is producing for us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory [variant: “of eternal glory”], while we do not contemplate the things that are seen but the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal (2 Cor. 4:17–18).

## 22

Walk, therefore, as it is written, from virtue to virtue (Ps. 83:8). Let your spirit pass from attention to temporal things to contemplation of eternal things. Passing from the virtue of marital chastity to the better virtue of widowly continence, you must possess no less continence of heart than of body. After the death of your temporal husband, all remnants of worldly thought ought to be extinguished in your heart.

## 23

Why should a Christian widow keep her mind bound by the bond of any worldly thought when, after her husband’s death, she ought to consider the world dead along with him?

When the cause of worldly thought has ceased, worldly thought itself ought also to cease. Just as previously you adorned yourself bodily for a husband who delighted in bodily appearance, so now you must be adorned spiritually for Christ, who seeks in you only the beauty of the mind.

## 24

Consider what blessed Peter also commands married women. He forbids them the adornment of outward dress, speaking as follows:

> Let women be subject to their husbands, so that, even if some do not believe the word of God, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives, when they observe your chaste conduct in fear. Let their adornment not be external—the braiding of hair, the wearing of gold, or the display of clothing—but the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit, which is rich before God (1 Pet. 3:1–4).

[Note: Thus the Cologne and Basil manuscripts: “in which there is not external…” The Corbie manuscript reads “in which there is not,” and Antwerp reads “whose external adornment is not,” in accordance with the Greek text of the Apostle: **ὧν ἔστω οὐκ ὁ ἔξωθεν**, “let their adornment not be external.”]

The blessed apostle confirmed this command by the example of holy women, saying:

> For in this way the holy women who hoped in God once adorned themselves, subject to their husbands (1 Pet. 3:5).

# Chapter XII. Holy Women Should Be Adorned Not with Jewelry but with Conduct. The Widow’s Duty Is to Cling to God and Persist in Prayer

## 25

If, then, holy women—even married women—are not to be commended for jewelry but for conduct, and ought to be adorned more by humility than by clothing, what should be the dress and appearance of a widow who desires to please not a human husband but Christ?

Having been freed from the necessity of bodily marriage, should she not pursue only spiritual ornaments?

Let your dress, therefore, be such that it does not excite wantonness but summons to continence; does not entice to lust but restrains toward fear; does not kindle the desire of the flesh but extinguishes it; does not entice to intercourse [Note: Basil reads “entice”; the Corbie and Victor manuscripts read “incite”] but rouses to progress; from which arises compunction of heart, not lust of the flesh; by which you may please the Son of God and show yourself truly chaste to the gaze—or, according to another reading, “in the gaze”—of your heavenly bridegroom.

For that bridegroom wishes to see your flesh mortified, not polished. He enters into marriage with the soul and delights not in the beauty of the flesh but in that of the soul.

Therefore acquire beauty of heart through the discipline of the body. Let the flesh be covered with cheap garments, and let the soul be clothed in precious robes. Do not seek to please the eyes of human beings, but to avoid offending the sight of Christ.

Let him see in you what he loves, find what he gave, and recognize what delights him.

> The king desired your beauty; but all the glory of the king’s daughter is within (Ps. 44:12, 14).

## 26

The time for embracing has passed; now it is time to keep far from embraces.

Let those who are bound by the marital bond cling to their husbands. To you it must be said with the prophet:

> But for me it is good to cling to God and to place my hope in God (Ps. 72:28).

Hence the Apostle also says:

> She who is truly a widow and desolate has hoped in the Lord and persists in supplications and prayers night and day (1 Tim. 5:5).

Therefore, let prayer be frequent for you in petition, and continual in holy thought and action. In this way you will be able to fulfill what the Apostle commands:

> Let us pray without ceasing (1 Thess. 5:16).

For every good work that pleases God, who needs nothing, is prayer in his sight. And so that we may recognize that good works have a place of prayer before God, Holy Scripture admonishes us:

> Hide almsgiving in the heart of the poor, and it will itself pray for you (Sir. 2:15).

# Chapter XIII. How a Widow Should Conduct Herself in Food and Banquets

## 27

Take care not to turn care for the flesh into desires, nor always to indulge what the appetite demands. Let your nourishment satisfy not pleasure but weakness.

Your companions at table should be women who are not accustomed to praise the delicacies of the flesh but those of the heart; women who seek the bread of angels with eagerness for the inner person; women who run after your bridegroom in the fragrance of his ointments; women who perceive God through the sweetness of inward taste; women who hunger and thirst for righteousness with pure affection; women who work for food not that perishes but that endures to eternal life.

With such women you should converse and frequently dine, so that, when you feed them with bodily food, the merit of holy action may increase for you, and, when you are nourished by their spiritual words, the progress of holy conduct may grow in you.

Do not wish now to fill your table with delicacies of the sort with which you filled it when you were serving a carnal marriage.

Hear what the Teacher of the Gentiles says about a widow:

> She who lives in luxury is dead while she lives (1 Tim. 5:6).

# Chapter XIV. The Examples of the Widows Judith and Anna

## 28

In both the Old and the New Testament you have examples of holy widows by which you may be built up.

In the Old Testament, consider Judith; in the New, Anna. If, with the Lord’s help, you become their imitator, you will trample underfoot both the delicacies of the flesh and worldly boastfulness [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “the boastfulness of worldly people”] with true humility of heart.

Thus the affection of that bridegroom who is always living will always live in you, just as his resurrection was confirmed by the testimony of the angelic voice when the women were told:

> Why do you seek the living among the dead? (Luke 24:5).

Of him apostolic authority also speaks:

> For the word of God is living and effective (Heb. 4:12).

He who is the Word of the Father is therefore living, and for this reason he is the life of the faithful. Holy widows sought him through contrition of heart and discipline of body; with complete continence of heart and body they devotedly served him.

## 29

For it is written of Judith:

> Judith was a widow in her house for three years and four months. She made herself a tent on the roof of her house, put sackcloth around her loins, and wore the garments of her widowhood. Judith fasted throughout all the days of her widowhood (Judith 8:4–5).

And lest anyone suppose that this holy widow fasted not from devotion of heart but from poverty, hear what is said about her afterward:

> Judith was good—or, according to another reading, beautiful—in appearance, exceedingly lovely in face, prudent in heart, and good in understanding [Note: Thus the Corbie and Antwerp manuscripts, “good in understanding”; Cologne and Basil read “good in intellect”], and she was exceedingly honorable. For Manasseh, her husband, son of Achitob, son of Melchis, son of Heliab, son of Nathahel, son of Surisoda, son of Simeon, son of Israel, had left her gold and silver, male and female servants, livestock, and estates (Judith 8:7–8).

Behold a widow illustrious by birth, rich in possessions, young in age, remarkable in beauty: she despised wealth, rejected delicacies, trampled down the incentives of the flesh, and, clothed with virtue from above, did not seek to serve a second marriage.

Therefore, through the testimony of so distinguished a work, it became evident how greatly widowly continence is loved by God.

Finally, when Holofernes had besieged Bethulia with an enormous army and all the strength of the Israelites was shaken and failing, chastity went forth to attack wantonness, and holy humility advanced to destroy pride.

He fought with weapons; she with fasts. He with drunkenness; she with prayer.

Thus what the whole people of Israel could not do, the holy widow accomplished through the virtue of chastity. One woman beheaded the commander of so great an army and restored unexpected freedom to God’s people.

# Chapter XV. Praise of Anna. Comparison of Judith and Anna

## 30

Let us also see how the conduct of holy Anna is presented to us in the New Testament. Concerning her, the holy Luke reports:

> There was Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in age and had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity. She was a widow until she was eighty-four years old; she did not depart from the temple, serving with fasts and supplications night and day (Luke 2:37).

Although these two widows lived at different times, both served the mystery of one faith. Anna recognized Christ born in the flesh; Judith knew that he would be born.

How greatly God showed in both widows the continence pleasing to him!

Judith, girded with spiritual weapons, cut off the head of a lustful plunderer; Anna, filled with the Holy Spirit, recognized the very head of the Church.

Judith was granted the death of Holofernes; to Anna the coming of the Savior was revealed.

To the former God gave the power to drive pestilence from the people; to the latter he granted recognition of the medicine of the human race.

And because virginal holiness is followed by widowly continence at a lower degree, after the Son of God was born of a virgin, he chose to be proclaimed through the ministry of a widow’s tongue.

Yet it was not a widow devoted to delicacies who spoke of him—a woman who was dead while she lived—but one who did not depart from the temple, serving with fasts and supplications night and day.

# Chapter XVI. Praise of Proba, Galla’s Sister. Galla’s Nobility. What Is Withdrawn from Personal Display Must Be Distributed to the Poor

## 31

There is not now space to discuss at greater length those fasts and supplications. We have decided—if the Lord wills and if we live—to write something about fasting and prayer to your sister, the holy virgin of Christ Proba, whom the Lord has deigned in this age to give to the city of Rome as an outstanding example of virginity and humility.

This is contained in the promise I made in the letter that I recently sent to her [Note: The Victor manuscript reads “published”]. Her holy conduct is especially to be imitated by you in all things.

Although she was born of grandfathers and great-grandfathers who had been consuls and was raised amid royal delicacies, such humility has been infused into her as a gift of heavenly grace that, through love of submission and the practice of service, she no longer knows that she was ever a mistress. In the delight of holy servitude, she desires to have everyone as her master [Note: The Corbie and Victor manuscripts read “mistresses”].

For she knows from the Lord, to whom she vowed her virginity of both heart and body, that the humility of servant-form was accepted for our liberation. For this reason she delights to please her bridegroom in the humility of this servitude [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “the humility of this servitude”; the printed editions read “in the humility of this servitude”], so that, numbered among the company of the five wise virgins, she may be able to reign with the bridegroom in eternal brightness.

How vigorously she has despised bodily delicacies, how she makes her hunger serve the satisfaction of the poor, and how she wears cheap clothing for no other reason than to fulfill her purpose of humility and to devote continual care of holy compassion to clothing the poor—you know more fully by seeing it yourself than if you wished to hear it from me, since I can explain it less adequately in words.

## 32

Set her before you, therefore, as a mirror, and by considering her learn what you already possess and what is still lacking in you in the pursuits and works of the saints.

Although she surpasses you through the distinguished gift of virginity, she ought to have you as her companion in the other virtues.

Learn, then, not to claim anything for yourself from the nobility of your lineage. Although, through your grandfather, father, father-in-law, and husband, all of whom were once consuls, you were illustrious among worldly people, recognize that you are now to become illustrious in that which increases in you the virtue of humility.

Learn from the Lord, because he is meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your soul (Matt. 11:29).

Cast away the nobility of the flesh, which is fuel for pride, and pursue the nobility of the spirit through perfect humility of heart.

Devote yourself to prayers; persist in fasts; and whatever you subtract from your personal display, give to the hungry. Whatever you set aside for yourself, expend upon the needy.

Let your voluntary fast relieve the hunger of those who fast, so that the fruitfulness of your fasts may appear in the fruit of your mercy.

The cheapness of your clothing should also benefit you, and through you the nakedness of the poor should be clothed.

For you will then usefully flee the harmful adornment of expensive clothing if you clothe the naked, so that you may prove yourself truly a companion of Christ’s poor—not through emptiness of words or deceptive display, but through the testimony of holy action.

[Col. 0321C] **CHAPTER XVII. Vainglory in good works must be avoided.**—33. Do not consider yourself superior to those whom you feed or clothe, nor, because you give while they receive, place your merits above those of Christ’s poor, as though you were therefore better because you have despised more. For you despise your possessions in vain if you retain in your heart the harmful riches of vainglory. It is not only those who, because of the riches they possess, carry some vainglory in their hearts who sin; rather, those sin more grievously who wish to have the vainglory of having despised riches, or who wish to place themselves above the poor for the reason that they seem to distribute more to the poor. But God’s order is not the same: he considers not the amount of the property despised, but the quality of the will. Zacchaeus is said to have spent more wealth on the poor for Christ than the apostle Peter left behind in the very humble tools of the fishing trade; and yet Christ places not the rich Zacchaeus above the poor Peter, but the poor Peter above the rich Zacchaeus, so that no vainglory concerning despised riches might arise in Christ’s rich.

**CHAPTER XVIII. Treasures must be stored not on earth but in heaven.**—34. Far be it from you to store anything for yourself on earth, where you will leave behind no children of the flesh; for even those who have children from the flesh do not enjoy storing up treasures for themselves in this world without sin. Our Savior deigns to admonish all the faithful in one saying, declaring: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves neither break in nor steal” (Matt. VI, 19–20). Greatly to be feared is that rebuke of the Lord which the foolish rich man, about to die immediately, heard: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared—whose will they be?” (Luke XII, 20). [Note: [Col. 0321D] Thus in the Corbie manuscript and the Cologne and Antwerp editions; the Basel edition has *repeteut* (“they demand back”).] Send all your riches ahead to Christ; store up for yourself in heaven a treasure which you cannot lose and may possess forever. 161

**CHAPTER XIX. Human praise must be avoided so that God may be praised in us.**—35. In all good works, take care that you are not puffed up by the desire for human praise. [Col. 0322B] [Note: [Col. 0322D] The Corbie manuscript reads “Indeed to be praised”; the printed editions read “to be praised, for.”] You ought indeed to be praised for good works, but in what you do you ought not to await the praise of men. Let the human tongue praise you, certainly, but desire praise from God alone. Thus it will come about that, while you do not seek praise from men, God will be praised in your works. Remember how the Lord forbids us to perform our righteousness for the sake of human praise, saying: “Take care not to practice your righteousness before men in order to be seen by them; otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. VI, 1). Yet he says again: “Let your light shine before men, so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16). When, therefore, he says that we must take care not to practice our righteousness before men in order to be seen by them, and again commands that our light shine before men, did he give contradictory instructions? Certainly not; rather, he commands that good works be done in such a way that we desire not ourselves but God to be praised in our action. For the Apostle also avoided human glory in his works, but sought divine glory. Therefore, writing to the Thessalonians, he says: “For we were never found in a speech of flattery, as you know; nor on an occasion of greed—God is witness; nor seeking glory from men, either from you or from others” (I Thess. II, 5). Yet, recalling with joy that the churches had heard of his manner of life and glorified God, he says: “I was once unknown by face to the churches of Judea that were in Christ; they had only heard that the one who once persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once attacked; and they glorified God in me” (Gal. I, 22–23). Therefore, let the hand not cease from good work, but let the mind nevertheless not work in such a way that the reward of the good work is nullified by the intention of human praise. For the Apostle, as he himself testifies, wants us to be “sincere and without offense for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God” (Phil. I, 10–11).

**CHAPTER XX. A good work must be attributed not to one’s own virtue but to God’s grace.**—36. In devotion to good works and contempt for human praise, take care that you do not wish to attribute the good you do to your own virtue rather than to God’s grace; rather, hold firmly that you can possess no capacity for good will or good work unless you have received it as a gratuitous gift of divine mercy. Know, therefore, that God works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will. Therefore, “work out your salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. II, 12–13). “Humble yourself in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” (I Pet. V, 6). Ask from him the beginning of good will; request from him the accomplishment of good work; seek from him the gift of perseverance. Never suppose that you can will or do anything good once his help has ceased. Pray to him to turn your eyes away, lest they see vanity (Ps. CXVIII, 37); ask him to show you the way in which you should walk; beseech him to direct your steps according to his word, and let no iniquity rule over you; pray to him to direct the works of your hands over you. “Act manfully, therefore, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. XXVI, 14). “Cast your thought upon God, and he himself will nourish you” (Ps. LIV, 23).

**CHAPTER XXI. We must not despair of God’s help. Delight must be sought in the Holy Scriptures.**—37. Because I said that you ought to attribute nothing to your own virtue, do not therefore despair in any respect of divine power and goodness. For God is faithful in his words and holy in all his works (Ps. CXLIV, 13); he will not deny you help in this world, nor withhold your reward in the future. He who showed you the right way is himself your guide to your homeland. Hope in the Lord and do good (Ps. XXXVI, 3); do not suppose that you can fail if he deigns to guard you. For it is written: “Who has hoped in the Lord and been put to shame? Or who has remained in his commandments and been forsaken? Or who has called upon him, and he has despised him?” (Eccli. II, 12). Therefore do not lose your confidence, which has a great reward (Hebr. X, 35). Be steadfast and immovable, knowing that your labor will not be empty in the Lord; always desire better things, and stretch your spirit toward growth in virtue. Never cease from divine utterances, and devote all the delight of your heart to the Holy Scriptures. Do not be held in the bonds of worldly delight [or: love] [Note: [Col. 0323D] Thus the manuscript of Corbie; but the printed editions have “human delight.”], and you will triumph successfully over the devil.

38. And so that this letter may be brought to its conclusion for you with the testimony and admonition of Holy Scripture, I will add this also to everything said above: “Complete your works in gentleness, and you will be loved above all glory. The greater you are” [Note: [Col. 0323D] The manuscripts of Corbie and Victor have “The greater you are”; the printed editions do not contain the word “greater.”], “humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Eccli. III, 19–20). May the Lord direct you, illustrious lady and daughter, in the way of his virtue [Note: [Col. 0323D] The manuscript of Corbie has “in the way of his righteousness.”], and bring you to the promises of the heavenly kingdom. Amen. [Note: [Col. 0323D] “Amen” is added in the manuscript of Corbie; it is absent from the printed editions.]

## LETTER III. TO PROBA  
### On Virginity and Humility

[Col. 0324A]

163 **CHAPTER I. Congratulations on the undertaking of the spiritual life. The service of Christ is good; the liberty of sin is harmful.**—1. I wish I could adequately express in words, holy servant of God Proba, how much I rejoice and congratulate you on your spiritual desire and undertaking, if speech could equal thought in the same measure. For it ought not to be judged a small indication of purpose that, although it is clear that you are endowed with spiritual virtues through the activity in you of him from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift (James I, 17), you consider yourself as though lacking them and in need of admonition concerning the virtues. Accordingly, I greatly praise in God this zeal by which, while our holy brother Tuto, the servant of God, repeatedly presses me in writing, you earnestly urge me to offer you a discourse containing something about virginity and humility. Yet, however much I ought to praise it, I cannot praise it enough; and the more unequal I perceive myself to be to this desire of yours in offering worthy praise, the more I fear offending God in you either by a harsh refusal or by a prolonged delay. Indeed, Christ is offended whenever the service owed to his members is denied, since he once wished to free those who were wickedly enslaved from slavery to sin for no other reason than to teach us to serve one another in free love. For those whom he found oppressed by the yoke of a servile and most wretched liberty, he raised up through the gift of a liberal and most excellent service. Finally, we find that joy [possibly: knowledge] of that harmful liberty—in which one prefers to serve sin rather than God—communicated to us in the apostolic discourse; for he says: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness.” And adding, he says: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of them is death” (Rom. VI, 20–21). We also find in the subsequent words of the same teaching that service which we received after being freed, so that we might serve God our liberator generously, when he says: “But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit for sanctification” [Note: [Col. 0324D] The manuscripts of Corbie and Victor have “for sanctification,” according to the Greek text, εἰς ἁγιασμόν (*eis hagiasmon*, “for sanctification”); the printed editions have “in sanctification.”], “and the end, eternal life” (ibid., 22). See where this holy service leads and brings us: to eternal life, in which one lives forever and forever reigns; yet no human being will live there except one who is put to death to this world, and no one will reign there except one who perseveres in humility before God. That life is promised to this mortification, and that exaltation is reserved for this humility—for the very humility which you so effectively and eagerly pursue [Note: [Col. 0324D] The printed editions have “which you effectively pursue”; the manuscript of Corbie has “which you effectively and eagerly pursue.”], and in which, with God guarding you, you preserve holy virginity—and it compels me also to serve devotedly and willingly.

[Col. 0325A] **CHAPTER II. Christ’s members ought to serve one another through love.**—2. And I, holy daughter, insofar as the love of God—poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. V, 5)—urges me to serve Christ’s members both delightfully and generously, wish to fulfill competently what you have charged me to do. I know that the one truly serves Christ who serves Christ’s members through that love by which Christ himself first served on his behalf, so that he might become a member of that same Christ. Therefore the Apostle, so that we may attain eternal freedom, commands that free service be offered to Christ’s members by one another, saying: “For you have been called to freedom, brothers; only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another” (Gal. V, 13).

[Col. 0325B] 3. The more strongly, therefore, I am compelled by the command of this service to return what you demand, the more I am deterred by consideration of my own strength. For there is such a union of these two virtues, concerning which I must discuss something insofar as God grants it, that in the present life it is itself the perfection and summit of all virtues: for nothing in the body is better than integrity, and nothing in the soul is higher than faithful humility. Nevertheless, I have confidence in divine assistance, since I am helped by your prayers. For God inspires the fervor of holy desire in his sons and daughters so that, when they demand a spiritual debt from their fellow servants, they too may not cease to pray to the Lord for them; thus, through the duty of mutual love, they demand the debt owed to them in such a way that they return to their debtors what they demand.

[Col. 0325C] 4. No believer demands that love be returned to him in such a way that he himself does not owe it to his debtor. Although, according to the grace given to us, this love may seem to be returned to different people through different gifts and with different effects, in the assistance of mutual prayer it makes everyone share in one debt, making each person a debtor to all. See how the one who professes himself a debtor to the wise and the foolish both pays the debt of prayer to all and demands it from all. Writing to the Romans, he says, returning this debt: “For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I always remember you in my prayers” (Rom. I, 9). But see how greedy an exactor he is of this debt, of which he is a devoted payer. Again he says to the same people: “I beseech you, therefore, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Spirit, that you assist me in prayers for me to God” (Rom. XV, 30).

**CHAPTER III. Our sufficiency is from God. To will and to accomplish are from God.**—5. In this debt which you demand from us and return to us, I do not doubt that I am helped, so that God, who works in his people both to will and to accomplish according to his good will, may himself grant me to think worthily and speak worthily. For in good thoughts we are not capable of thinking anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves; rather, our sufficiency is from God (II Cor. III, 5). And for this reason we do not fail through want, because our sufficiency comes as a gratuitous gift from him in whom there is no want; just as he has no need of our goods, so he always abounds in order to give. By giving, he does not become needy—he gives what he is always full of. Nor is there any pleasing gift of thought, speech, or work that can be offered [or: brought] to him by us which he himself has not bestowed through gratuitous kindness. Therefore God’s holy gift is always gratuitous, because no demand based on human merits ever precedes it. For even if the merit of any human being is good, it is certainly from him from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift (James I, 17): a person can neither possess it unless it has been given by him, nor possess it perseveringly unless it has been preserved by him as guardian. From him, therefore, I ask for the ability to repay this debt, from whom I received the will to repay it. For I would not in any way wish to repay it unless the merciful one himself granted me the will. If, therefore, I say anything in this work that pleases and suffices—or, if it does not suffice, at least pleases your holy desire—it is not due to my insufficiency but to divine sufficiency. But if I should perhaps speak in such a way that it can neither satisfy your holy desire nor please it, this is not due to divine sufficiency but to my insufficiency. Therefore let Christian love perform its part in both directions, humbly acknowledging God’s sufficiency and patiently forgiving servile insufficiency.

**CHAPTER IV. The Son of the Virgin is the author and bridegroom of virginity. A virgin is like a *virago*.**—6. He who made you a sacred virgin through a gratuitous gift—he who did everything whatever he willed (Ps. CXIII, 11)—is the one from whom grace is given without preceding merits, so that pure thanksgiving may always be returned to him with humble heart. He is the only-begotten Son of God, also the only-begotten Son of the Virgin, the one bridegroom of all sacred virgins, the fruit, honor, and gift of holy virginity. Holy virginity bore him bodily; holy virginity is spiritually wedded to him; by him holy virginity is made fruitful so that it may remain undefiled; by him it is adorned so that it may remain beautiful; by him it is crowned so that it may reign eternally in glory.

7. Therefore, “guard the good deposit” (I Tim. VI, 20), and consider the worth of so great a good—which God gave so that you might possess it, and which he himself enabled you to vow to God—from the meaning of its very name. God wished the good of virginity to be so great that he deigned to name it not from anything else but from the word denoting virtue. If anyone wishes carefully to consider the word *virgin*, he will find it derived from the name of virtue: for *virgo* is said as though it were *virago*. Scripture says that *virago* was called so for no other reason than that she was taken from a man. Saint Jerome teaches this according to the Hebrew character of the book of Genesis in an explicit translation, which reads as follows: “Then the Lord God cast a sleep upon Adam; and when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs and filled the flesh in its place. And the Lord God built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam; and Adam said: ‘This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh. She shall be called *Virago*, because she was taken from man’” (Gen. II, 21–22).

[Col. 0327A] **CHAPTER V. *Virago* is said from man, and man from virtue. The Church is called both virgin and man by the Apostle. The Christian Church is from Christ, just as virgin is from man. The holy Church is called mother, virgin, and bride.**—8. Since, therefore, the name *virago* descended from the name *man*, who would doubt that *man* was called from *virtue*? And because, as Paul teaches, all those things were made figuratively for us (I Cor. X, 6), surely in that virgin who was formed from the man’s rib the future Church was already prefigured. Truly taken from the man, and joined to the one from whom she was taken, she has from him in truth the virtue from which she has the true name *virago*. For this reason Paul does not hesitate to call this *virago*, that is, virgin, not only by the name of virgin but also by the name of man. He says to the faithful: “For I have betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI, 2). Christ is the man from whom this virgin was taken. Again the same Apostle says to the same faithful: “Until we all meet in the unity of faith and knowledge of the Son of God, into a perfect man, into the measure of the fullness of the age of Christ” (Eph. IV, 13). Through holy David, too, this kind of spiritual exhortation is proclaimed jointly to men and women: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Ps. XXX, 25).

9. Thus, figuratively, the word *virgin* is derived (alternative: “is called”) from *man*, just as (alternative: “because”) the name *Christian* is derived (alternative: “is called”) from Christ. For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God; from him comes the Church, which, persisting as a virgin in faith and love, possesses both wisdom and virtue. Therefore she is neither deceived by seduction nor overcome by force, because she is supported by the integrity of inward virginity. To this virgin Isaiah says: “Because the Lord has been pleased with you, and your land shall be inhabited. For a young man shall dwell with a virgin, and your sons shall dwell in you” (Isa. LXII, 4–5). And to show that the young man is none other than the bridegroom, and the virgin none other than the bride, while the bridegroom and bride are Christ and the Church, he continued: “And the bridegroom shall rejoice over the bride; and your God shall rejoice over you.” This virgin is a mother, to whom it is said: “Your sons shall dwell in you”; and this mother is a virgin, of whom it is said: “For a young man shall dwell with a virgin.” This virgin is a bride, of whom it is said: “And the bridegroom shall rejoice over the bride.” This one Church, therefore, is the one true catholic bride, because she clings to Christ; she is a mother, because she is made fruitful by Christ; she is a virgin, because she remains incorrupt in Christ. In this bride, virginity is not corrupted by fruitfulness, nor is fruitfulness impeded by virginity. The union of this man and virgin is such that this virgin is made fruitful by this man precisely because no corruption can ever exist in this union; and such is the integrity of virginity that persists in this mother that, unless she were always a virgin, she could not be a mother. Isaiah thus foretells the new name of this mother and virgin: “And you shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord shall name” (ibid., 2). Therefore, because Christ is virtue, just as the Church took the name of virgin from virtue, so she received the name Christian from Christ.

**CHAPTER VI. The gift of grace is greater in virgins than in others. A better place in the wall is promised to eunuchs.**—10. Although the Church has different gifts in her various members, according to the grace given to her, she has nevertheless received a greater gift of grace in those members in whom she is called spiritually virgin in such a way that they also possess the integrity of bodily virginity. In the other faithful members who rightly believe in God according to the rule of Catholic faith and preserve either conjugal or widowly chastity—members who are not soiled by the pollution of actual fornication and remain free from every violation of faith—the Church possesses only spiritual virginity. But in those members in which she preserves right faith while also keeping the flesh untouched by every sexual intercourse, the more complete her virginity, the more fully and perfectly she possesses the name of that same virginity. In the former, she lacks nothing necessary for life; in the latter, she acquires something more for glory, because, as Paul says: “One is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon, and another the glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV, 41–42). Finally, under the name of eunuchs—whom the Savior also declares in the Gospel to have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven—the Lord promises virgins through Isaiah a better place in his house and in his wall. For it is written: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: Whoever keeps my commandments, chooses the things I will, and embraces my covenant, I will give them in my house and in my wall a named place better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name, and it shall not fail” (Isa. LVI, 4–5). In the Apocalypse of blessed John, too, they are the ones who follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. XIV, 4), because they remained virgins.

**CHAPTER VII. Virginity of mind and body is better than other gifts.**—11. It is therefore clear that among the Church’s other gifts the principal gift of the spiritual charisma exists where the virtue of integrity itself deserves to be designated by the perfect name of virtue. For although there may be prophecy according to the measure of faith, or ministry in ministering, or one who teaches in teaching, one who exhorts in exhortation, one who gives in simplicity, one who presides with diligence, and one who shows mercy with cheerfulness (Rom. XII, 6–8), these diverse gifts are found to be called by their own names. But bodily integrity faithfully consecrated to God, and preserved—with God helping and protecting—in virginity of heart, is therefore properly called virginity, so that it may be shown that the perfection of true virtue exists there.

12. Untainted virginal holiness is therefore better than the other active gifts. By the grace of the divine gift, it seems to derive the origin of its name from virtue, so that from the name itself it may always recognize that it is admonished to preserve the things belonging to virtue. Hence not undeservedly the Doctor of the nations [Note: [Col. 0327D] These words, “the Doctor of the nations,” are absent from the manuscript of Corbie.] and chosen Vessel distinguishes celibate and married life by such a definition that he confirms the former, being concerned with the things of God, to please God in the sanctification [Note: [Col. 0329D] Thus the manuscripts of Corbie and Basel; Cologne and Antwerp have “in sanctification.”] of body and spirit, while the latter, devoted to worldly thoughts, carries the concern to please her husband. “He who is without a wife,” he says, “is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord. But he who is with a wife is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided. And the unmarried woman and the virgin think about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit; but she who is married thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (I Cor. VII, 32–34).

**CHAPTER VIII. Holiness is also ascribed to married people, but more greatly to virgins.**—13. Nevertheless, in saying this the Apostle did not ascribe holiness of body and spirit to virgins in such a way as to deprive married women of it or deny it to widows. Above all, in an earlier passage of the same Epistle he calls the bodies of the faithful members of Christ and a temple of the Holy Spirit. For he says: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” (I Cor. VI, 15). And shortly afterward: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own? For you were bought at a great price. Therefore glorify” [Note: [Col. 0329D] The word “therefore” is absent from the manuscript of Corbie and the Cologne and Antwerp editions; it is found in Basel and in the Apostle’s Greek text.] “and bear God in your body” (ibid., 19). And to show that he was also writing to married people, he immediately added: “Concerning the matters about which you wrote: It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornications, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband” (I Cor. VII, 1–2). In the Epistle to the Ephesians he was likewise speaking to married people, to whom he said: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church” (Eph. V, 26). And shortly afterward: “He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ also does the Church, because we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones” (ibid., 29–30). The Apostle Peter, too, does not hesitate to call married faithful women holy, saying: “For thus formerly holy women who hoped in God adorned themselves, subject to their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord” (I Pet. III, 5–6). Therefore the Apostle Paul does not separate married believers from sanctification of body and spirit; rather, he says that they think about that in which he recognizes their thoughts to be more fully occupied. For who does not know that the thoughts of holy virgins turn more toward spiritual matters, while the thoughts of holy married women serve more the necessities of marriage?

**CHAPTER IX. Marriage is not sin but a gift of God. A manifold comparison between virginity and marriage.**—14. We know, therefore, that marriage is not sin but God’s work and God’s gift: he himself joined it by the bond of faith, honored it with the gift of blessing, and multiplied it through the increase of procreation. We know that marriage is honorable in all and the marriage bed undefiled (Hebr. XIII, 4); we know that it is not marriages but fornications and adulteries that are judged by God: “For God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (ibid.). We acknowledge that the fidelity of marriage, the love of spouses, and the fruitfulness of nature are from God; but because “each person has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (II Cor. VII, 7), we too distinguish the rank of the two gifts in such a way that we do not deny that both gifts are bestowed on the faithful by God. We do not therefore turn God’s lesser gift into guilt when we prefer the grace of the greater gift; nor, when we place the first gift of chastity before the second or third, do we condemn the second or third; nor, when we acknowledge the summit of virginal integrity, do we assert the guilt of conjugal chastity; nor do we ascribe virginity to the wheat in such a way that we count marriage among the weeds [or: the weed]. Marriage is not the fruit of nocturnal seed, because it was not a hostile sower who sowed this in the Lord’s field (Matt. XIII, 25), but the good Lord who instituted it.

15. Nevertheless, weighing the relative importance of both matters with suitable discernment, we say only that holy virginity surpasses holy marriage—where those who cannot contain themselves marry—in a proportionate way: as better things surpass good things, exalted things the humble, heavenly things earthly, more blessed things the blessed, holier things the holy, purer things the clean, immortal marriage mortal marriage, spirit flesh, strength weakness, and the fruit of an enduring offspring the fruit of offspring that will pass away [Note: [Col. 0330D] The printed editions have “of transient offspring”; the manuscript of Corbie has “of offspring that will pass away”]; security tribulation, tranquility disturbance, and the better eternal good accompanied by joy the momentary good accompanied by distress.

[Col. 0330C] 169 **CHAPTER X. Virginity is far superior to carnal marriage. The misfortunes of marriage concerning bodily offspring. The benefits of virginity concerning spiritual offspring.**—16. We do not hesitate to say that the intercourse of married believers—although permitted by God—with this weak and mortal flesh is as far removed from holy virginity of flesh and spirit as the likeness of animals is distinguished from the imitation of angels. In the one, the earthly desire of the flesh presses the spirit down toward the earth; in the other, the earthly flesh is lifted by the heavenly delight of the spirit toward heavenly things. To please a carnal marriage, worldly concern often troubles the mind; but to please a spiritual union, the mind, intent upon the sweetness of heavenly thought, chastises its body while growing fat on spiritual delight.

17. In the act of bodily marriage, bodily virginity is lost in order to attain bodily fruitfulness. Yet sometimes human pleasure is cheated by the fruit of uncertain hope, so that she who has ceased to be a virgin cannot become a mother; restrained by the obstacle of sterility, she can neither restore in her body what she has lost nor obtain from her body what she desires. Often—and this is more grievous—she loses with greater pain the children of the flesh whom she conceived with great pain; and she endures dangers and groans in giving birth for this purpose, that, losing those whom she had borne with groaning, she may groan still more bitterly. But in the union of spiritual marriage, when the soul is so joined to Christ the bridegroom that the flesh too is preserved intact, the more vigorously virginal integrity flourishes, the more powerfully immortal fruitfulness prevails. For there the mortal fruit does not arise from the body, so that immortal offspring is not absent from the heart. There marital intercourse [Note: [Col. 0331D] The manuscript of Corbie has “there the mortal intercourse.”] does not corrupt the body, because Christ’s spiritual embrace preserves both soul and body. In such a marriage no effect is granted to burning desire, because the fervor of holy love is nourished by spiritual refreshment. O virtue of angelic imitation, not human virtue in human beings! O ineffable honor of a heavenly and eternal gift! Those who receive it meditate in mortal flesh upon what they are going to be in immortality [Note: [Col. 0331D] Antwerp has “what they are in immortality.”]: for they choose “the good portion, which shall not be taken away from them” (Luke X, 42), but shall be perfected in them. What they now preserve inviolate in their conduct will be returned to them, increased by the glory of immortality, as a gift.

**CHAPTER XI. Virginity must walk so that it turns neither to the right nor to the left. The left-hand road is the pleasure of the flesh. The right-hand road is proud boasting of virtues.**—18. Therefore she who is not a virgin of the world but of Christ ought to be adorned not with necklaces but with virtues. The adornment of a virgin is to preserve the good of virginity no less in mind than in flesh, so that she may always show herself worthy of so great a gift and hold the way of truth without turning aside to the right or to the left. A crowd of carnal vices occupies the left; proud boasting of spiritual virtues holds the right. The former strives to delight the flesh with public pleasures; the latter never ceases to murmur praise of its own virtue into the mind. The former, flattering the virgin, tries to persuade her that, provided bodily integrity is preserved, she should love, desire, and retain everything pertaining to the pleasures of food, the splendor of clothing, the comforts of baths, the softness of bedding [Note: [Col. 0331D] The words “the softness of bedding” are added in the manuscript of Corbie.], the smoothness of perfumes [Note: [Col. 0331D] The printed editions of Cologne and Antwerp have “of sleep”; Basel has “the smoothness of dreams” [Col. 0332D]; the manuscript of Corbie has “the smoothness of perfumes,” and this is better, since below it says that “the softness of the skin is roughened by despised perfumes.”], and the gaiety of amusements, under the pretext of avoiding weakness and preserving bodily health. It shows the person walking a descent down a broader road, as though along a gentler slope—not ascending to heaven but rolling down into Tartarus—and suggests avoiding the labor of the narrow path lest one reach rest.

19. But the other prepares a precipice for the virgin, the more dangerously because it does so the more secretly, while cunningly praising the ascent. For if abstinence is maintained in food; if clothing is not elegant but despised; if fasts produce a boxwood-like pallor in the body, with its redness removed; if contempt for washing darkens the whiteness of the flesh; if harder bedding is given to the weary body for sleep; if the softness of the skin is roughened by despised perfumes; if a contracted expression always resists laughter and amusement—all these things it attributes not to divine assistance but to the powers of human capability.

[Col. 0332A] **CHAPTER XII. Christ’s virgin must flee bodily pleasures.** —20. Therefore the virgin must always keep watch with vigilant care, so as to preserve both outward and inward virginity. Let the sacred virgin wholly shun the pleasures of the flesh and bodily delights, which necessity demands of her less than pleasure does. For the spiritual bridegroom of virgins does not seek in a virgin flesh carefully pampered with delights, but chastened by fasts. When the Teacher of the Gentiles says that he does this, he also indicates that we must do so: “I chastise my body,” he says, “and bring it into subjection” (I Cor. IX, 27). And again: “In many vigils, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts” (II Cor. XI, 27). Of the widow he says: “But she who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (I Tim. V, 6). Let Christ’s virgin, then, not seek bodily pleasures, which he sees are not even granted to widows. Sodom, living in the fullness of food (Gen. XIX, 24 and following), deserved to have its food become fire; and the people of Nineveh (Jonah III, 5) drove away by fasting and tears the divine wrath that already threatened all their necks. Therefore, if visible desire is conquered in the body, invisible hostile power does not rule in the heart. We conquer the former successfully if we struggle bravely with the latter; and triumph over the former is gained when the latter is trampled down.

**CHAPTER XIII. Moderation in fasting.** —21. Fasting must be practiced with such moderation that neither fullness excites our body nor excessive hunger weakens it. Thus the virgin’s fast should be followed by such and so great a restoration that the body is neither enticed by pleasantness nor inflamed by satiety. Pleasantness diminishes almsgiving to the poor; satiety makes the body warlike. In the former case what is owed to the brethren is seized; in the latter, assistance is furnished to the enemy. For when we wish to delight the appetite of the throat with various seasonings, pleasure consumes what the needy person ought to have received. Therefore, let neither weakness snatch away the fast [Note: [Col. 0332D] Basil has “hasten” or “precipitate”]; nor let satiety remove it. Both serve our adversaries: one takes away the usefulness of the preceding fast, the other obstructs the capacity for the following fast. Satiety makes us fast in vain; weakness makes us unable to fast.

**CHAPTER XIV. What the clothing of virgins should be.** —22. The sacred virgin’s clothing should be such as to testify to her inner chastity. Let no splendor be sought in the dress of the outward person [Col. 0332D], lest the clothing [or: dress] of the inner person be sullied. The virgin who seeks adornment for her bodily garment [Note: [Col. 0332D] Basil has “of the body,” “in clothing”] strips her soul of the splendor of the virtues. Nor does she possess true chastity who prepares a temptation for those who look upon her; nor does she keep faith with Christ who seeks to please the people more than the bridegroom. Consequently, she who sows desire in the sight of human beings must reap anger in the sight of God. “For whoever sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; but whoever sows in the spirit [Note: [Col. 0333D] Cologne has “whoever sows from the spirit”] will reap eternal life from the spirit” (Gal. VI, 8).

23. But concerning these matters and similar ones, which pertain to the care of the flesh and cause the soul, under the name of virginity, to sleep amid desires, those virgins especially must be admonished who are luxurious, restless, and devoted to amusements.

**CHAPTER XV.** —Now, as we speak to the spiritual virgin, something must be said about avoiding those snares which—as I may put it—the adversary stretches not in earthly matters but in the very heavenly things; and he does not lead her astray by an open error from the road, but, as the prophet says, “On this path where I walked they hid snares for me” [Note: [Col. 0333D] The Corbie manuscript has “a snare”] (Ps. CXLI, 4). Where he sees people walking well in good works, there he resists them more vehemently and dangerously, under the appearance of pretended peace, with hidden ambushes; and, unable to destroy the virginity of the flesh in the flesh, he attempts to take away the virginity of the spirit.

24. For this reason Christ’s virgins must not consider carelessly how much the virginity of the heart outweighs the virginity of the flesh. If this virginity of the heart is preserved in faithful married people and widows through faith working by love, even without bodily virginity, in this life, then in the future they will neither be deprived of virginity of the flesh nor fail to enjoy the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom. But bodily virginity, even when dedicated to God, will profit nothing if it has not preserved virginity of heart: it is guarded in the body to no avail if spiritual chastity has been corrupted in the mind.

25. The devil attacks both kinds of virginity: that of the flesh through human beings, that of the mind through himself. **The cunning enemy’s varied temptation against virgins.** —The devil pursues both and assails both with cunning counsels. He strives to take away virginity of the flesh through a human being, but attempts to remove virginity of heart through himself. Often he does not attack the lower virginity of the flesh for the purpose of destroying it, but in order to undermine the foundations of the higher one; and he uses countless arguments, as though employing different engines of war. When he yields in open combat, he presents himself as defeated in order to conquer; he pretends to flee so that he may kill the pursuer by arrows shot from behind.

Defend yourself against such things [Note: [Col. 0333D] These words are absent from the printed editions; they are found in the Corbie manuscript]. For he provokes by manifest vices when he attacks bodily virginity; and if he is openly defeated in these, he immediately hurls pride with the greatest destructiveness. The author of vices conquers through another’s virtues in the very matter in which he cannot conquer through his own vices; he rises by the weapons with which he is struck down, and casts down by the virtue by which he himself is overthrown. He praises the virtue in which he sees himself defeated, so that, once defeated, he may capture the victor. For he injects vanity into the heart, so that he may cast a person down from a height with a more serious fall, if he sees that person fighting with firmer footing in lowliness.

For example, when he offers the delights of the appetite, if they are accepted, he supplies fuel for lust; if they are rejected, he sows pride in abstinence. He insinuates love of money [Note: [Col. 0333D] The Corbie manuscript has “delight in money”]. If he secures assent, he pierces the unwary soul with the sword of greed; but if he is repulsed, then, most wickedly, he sets through generosity the snares which he could not set through grasping. In the work of mercy he causes pride of heart to sprout, so that a person may think he has great merits because he gives to the needy.

He does this in many ways, and has especially accustomed himself to attack God’s spiritual servants and handmaids in this manner: if someone cannot be conquered by harmful and deadly things, he is killed by life-giving remedies. He makes evil out of good, harmful things out of salutary things, injustice out of what is just, and disadvantages out of advantages.

He first carried this out in himself: he did not derive the beginning of his crime from his condition, but, through the exaltation of virtue, he wished to hold the truth in injustice [Note: [Col. 0334D] The Corbie manuscript has “in injustice.” The Victor manuscript has “into injustice.” The printed editions have “through injustice”]. Having fallen through injustice, he did not stand in the truth. For how could he stand, when the One who never falls opposed him on account of his pride? “For pride is the beginning of every sin” (Eccli. X, 15); and therefore “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6).

**CHAPTER XVI. Pride is the beginning of every sin. Proud hypocrites in mind.** —26. Pride is therefore called the beginning of every sin so that every sin may be shown to sprout from it as from a root. It brings death to the wretched in many ways: it casts down carnal people in open combat, but if it finds spiritual people off their guard, it overthrows them in a more hidden conflict.

For who does not know that fornicators, those who serve idols, adulterers, the effeminate, men who lie with males, thieves, the greedy, drunkards [or: those who are drunk], the slanderous, the rapacious, and those who raise proud necks against God serve the devil more by their wicked deeds? There are others whom pride displays before human beings as its enemies, while inwardly it possesses them as most wicked soldiers. By them iniquity is cunningly practiced, so that justice may be deceitfully displayed to human eyes.

Our Lord rebukes such people in this way: “You are those who justify yourselves before human beings, but God knows your hearts.” And, to show clearly that they were proud, he immediately added: “For what is exalted among human beings is an abomination before God” (Luke XVI, 15).

27. To those also who live under the Christian profession but openly despise Christ’s commandments by sinning, Christ himself speaks thus: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke VI, 46). The Teacher of the Gentiles likewise rebukes such people in these words: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him; they are abominable, unbelieving, and unfit for every good work” (Titus I, 16).

Blessed James also says: “What good is it, my brothers, if someone says that he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him?” [Note: [Col. 0334D] The Corbie manuscript has “Can faith save him?” The printed editions have “Can faith save?”] (James II, 14). The humility, therefore, which Christ taught when he said, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29), does not consist in faith alone, but in faith together with works. For it is written: “The demons also believe and tremble” (James II, 19), yet for that reason they are not humble.

Hence the apostle Paul also declares: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be” (Rom. VIII, 7). This wisdom, according to James, “does not descend from above, but is earthly, natural, demonic” (James III, 15).

**CHAPTER XVII. Two kinds of pride. Christ’s parable of the Pharisee and the Publican.** —28. Manifest pride is detected when sin is committed openly; but when iniquity is covered with the disguise of righteousness, that plague of pride spreads more poisonously and steals in more dangerously.
