This happens when those who pursue righteousness either despise the life of others as unworthy or attribute something in good works to human strength.

That pride by which others are despised as sinners by those who consider themselves righteous is condemned in the Pharisee, as the holy Evangelist also testifies, saying: “He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves as righteous and despised others: ‘Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a Publican. The Pharisee, standing, prayed this within himself: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity: rapacious, unjust, adulterous, or even like this Publican. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I possess.” But the Publican, standing far away, would not lift his eyes toward heaven, but struck his breast, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted’” (Luke XVIII, 9–14).

In the sight of the merciful and just Judge, proud boasting of good works is not accepted, but humble confession of sins is. Those also who strive arrogantly to attribute the virtue of good will or good action to their own strength are marked out by the Apostle in this way: “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to God’s righteousness” (Rom. X, 3). Therefore, a person surely fails in his own injustice [Note: [Col. 0335D] The Corbie manuscript has “in his own righteousness”] when he does not subject his proud neck to the righteousness of God.

29. In these four kinds of pride, then, by which the devil is carried as though by a four-horse chariot and is swept by a deadly course toward Gehenna together with the wretched people upon whom he rides, he crushes two kinds of souls whom he sees lying in the flesh, and casts down by the other two those souls whom he knows to be flying away from the flesh. The former he captures through the pleasure of vices; the latter he surrounds through the exaltation of virtues. He so robs the former of their virginity that they do not hesitate to commit fornication; he so violates and stains the latter that they do not think themselves to be trampled down.

**CHAPTER XVIII. A proud virgin is not Christ’s bride.** —30. Therefore, so that virginity dedicated wholly to God may remain intact, humility of heart must be guarded much more carefully than bodily integrity. For if anyone is truly Christ’s virgin, she cannot be joined to Christ except through humility of heart. The bridal chamber of the Son of God does not admit the haughty, and the humble bridegroom drives the proud from his marriage.

Let it therefore be your endeavor, as is fitting for a sacred virgin, to pursue righteousness, piety, faith, charity, patience, and gentleness; but do not, in consideration of yourself, despise any Christian women, even those placed in a lower profession, nor exalt yourself in good works through presumption of your own virtue. Whatever spiritual gifts you possess beyond those possessed by other women, it is no small loss of virtue if, in the very chief virtue, which is humility, you do not surpass them, since you know what is written: “When you are great, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Eccli. III, 20).

**CHAPTER XIX. Christ is both Lord and bridegroom of virgins; therefore he requires both humility and integrity.** —30 bis. Consider, then, your bridegroom’s love for you; contemplate the Lord’s compassion. The Lord is compassionate, for he made you his handmaid; the bridegroom is beautiful, for he made you chaste as a bride. Yet because he is truly Lord and truly bridegroom, he fulfills the functions of both powers. From the handmaid he demands humble service; in the bride he seeks undivided chastity. Serve the Lord, then, with fear, and rejoice in the bridegroom with trembling. For because he is Lord, he causes fear; and because he is bridegroom, he is jealous.

Therefore, fearing, guard the command of the terrifying Lord; and trembling, love the affection of the jealous bridegroom. Let the thief find nothing of his own in the Lord’s handmaid; let the adulterer recognize nothing of his own in Christ’s bride. As lust does not rule in the virgin’s body, so let no arrogance rule in the virgin’s heart. “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling.” For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will (Phil. II, 12–13).

31. Whenever you think about perfection in the virtues, do not consider what other women possess less of than you possess, but what you possess less of than you ought already to possess. Do not therefore think yourself perfect in the virtues because you see someone else devoted to crimes; nor assign yourself any speed because you see some women either turning backward or walking sluggishly.

For a person with bleary eyes is not to be declared healthy merely because someone blind is seen to be wholly deprived of light. Nor is someone to be called healthy who lies half-alive from a serious wound, merely because another is found dead from a more serious wound. Nor should anyone claim glory for himself as a victor merely because, although not killed by the enemy, he is nevertheless held captive by the enemy.

**CHAPTER XX. A person ought to compare himself not with others but with himself. The help of divine grace must always be sought.** —32. Do not therefore compare yourself with others, but with yourself. Hear the Apostle doing this and healthfully admonishing us to do the same. Writing to the Corinthians, he says: “For we do not dare to class ourselves with or compare ourselves with certain people who commend themselves; but we ourselves, measuring ourselves among ourselves and comparing ourselves with ourselves” (II Cor. X, 12).

Let Christ’s virgin therefore compare herself with herself; and, in order to reach perfect health, she must not flatter herself over the greater danger of others, but must grieve over her own weakness. [Note: [Col. 0335D] The printed editions have: “If, therefore, Christ’s virgin compares herself with herself, in order to attain perfect health, she must not,” etc.; the Corbie manuscript has: “Let, therefore . . . and, in order that she may.”] The Psalmist grieved continually over this weakness when he said: “All day long I walked in sorrow, because my soul is filled with illusions, and there is no health in my flesh” (Ps. XXXVII, 7–8). To show that humility must be joined to this sorrow, he immediately added: “I am bent down and humbled exceedingly.” And to demonstrate that he did this from a desire for health, he added: “I roared from the groaning of my heart”; and: “All my desire is before you, and my groaning is not hidden from you” (ibid., 10).

The same man who said this confesses that at another time he was lifted up as though by the strength of health and experienced in that condition the danger of the gravest weakness. For he says in another psalm: “I said in my abundance, ‘I shall never be moved’” (Ps. XXIX, 7). And because, in saying this, he had been abandoned by the help of divine grace and, troubled, had failed in his own weakness, he continues: “Lord, by your good will you gave strength to my beauty; you turned your face away from me, and I became troubled” (ibid., 8).

And to show that the help of divine grace, although already possessed, must nevertheless be humbly sought without interruption, he adds this as well: “To you, Lord, I will cry, and I will entreat my God” (ibid., 9).

**CHAPTER XXI.** —No one entreats and asks who does not recognize that he either possesses something less than he ought or cannot preserve what he has by his own strength alone.

33. Whoever asks for a benefit and implores assistance must necessarily acknowledge both the evident weakness and the poverty of his condition. Our poverty asks that what it does not have be given to it; our weakness asks that what it has received be guarded for it.

Poverty hears: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. IV, 7). And: “No one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven” (John III, 27). Weakness hears: “Reveal your way to the Lord, hope in him, and he will act” (Ps. XXXVI, 5). It also hears from the very source of strength: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5). It hears from the prophet: “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (Ps. CXXVI, 1).

Let poverty therefore speak to him who, though rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich (II Cor. VIII, 9). Let it say: “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII, 73). Let weakness also speak to him who was crucified for us out of weakness but lives by the power of God (II Cor. XIII, 4), and who was so weakened for our sins that he himself is always the power of God and the wisdom of God. Let it say: “Guard me, Lord, as the apple of the eye; protect me under the shadow of your wings from the face of the ungodly who have afflicted me” (Ps. XVI, 9).

**CHAPTER XXII. Even holy souls have afflictions in this life because of intrusive thoughts.** —34. Here all the souls of those who have already been justified and live by faith are grievously afflicted; indeed, only souls understand in what affliction they have been placed when the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world, pours itself into them.

They see that, although by the gift of grace they are free from the contagion of evil works, they are nevertheless held captive by the variety of their thoughts. “Who can boast that he has a pure heart? Or who can boast that he is clean from sins?” (Prov. XX, 9). Let us consider what a great and righteous man said: “For in many things we all offend” (James III, 2). And the one who said: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 8). He also who delighted in the law of God according to the inner person saw another law in his members resisting the law of his mind and taking him captive under the law of sin that was in his members, until the grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord, freed him, conscious of his misery, from this body of death (Rom. VII, 22–23 and following).

35. From this law of sin, therefore, which is in our members, no strength of any strong person and no skill of any wise person liberates us; only the grace of the Savior does so [Col. 0338B], and this grace is given freely only to the humble: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6).

Nevertheless, just as this grace is given only to the humble, so a person cannot be humble unless grace is given. It is given so that they may begin to be humble, and it is given so that they may not cease to be humble. The grace of God therefore makes us both humble and able to persevere in humility. For he who was able to give what we did not have is himself able to preserve what we have received.

**CHAPTER XXIII. Precepts for holy virgins drawn from Scripture.** —36. Therefore, so that true humility may be in you—the inward virginity of virginity itself—you know how great a poverty of spirit must be present in a sacred virgin, so that she may deserve to receive the kingdom of heaven; how great a meekness, so that she may possess that land of the living [Note: [Col. 0337] The Corbie manuscript has “so that she ought to possess that land of the living”], in which David confidently trusts, with complete faith, that he will see the good things of the Lord (Ps. XXVI, 13).

You also know with what vigilance a virgin must flee the sorrowful joy of the present age, since, while she continually awaits the coming of the heavenly bridegroom in this life, she ought rather to mourn out of spiritual longing, so that she may obtain inward and certain consolation. You know how great a hunger and thirst for righteousness Christ’s virgin must endure, so that she may deserve to rejoice in the fullness of eternal sweetness; with what kind of entrails of mercy she must be clothed, so that she may be able to find mercy in God’s sight; and how great an eagerness for cleansing the heart must be present in a sacred virgin, so that she may deserve to see with blessed eyes that bridegroom who is “beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV, 3).

Bodily virginity cannot reach him unless it is supported by the humility of the heart through the power of inward virginity. The virgin of Christ must also possess what great virtue of peaceful tranquility, so that, clothed in spiritual armor, she may restrain the wars of carnal desires. Your bridegroom wishes you to use and enjoy such jewels: he betrothed you to himself through faith, strengthened you through hope, and joined you to himself through charity.

**CHAPTER XXIV. Every good work is preceded in us by God’s grace. The wealthy bridegroom of virgins. How virginity must be preserved. Conclusion.** —37. You would not have married such a bridegroom spiritually in the truth of faith and the integrity of the flesh if, having despised the vanity of the world, you had not loved him. Yet you would not have loved him at all if you had not first been met by the bridegroom’s gratuitous love.

I have said that you were preceded—not only by the love with which he loved you, but also by the love which he freely poured into you so that he might be loved by you. Everything, therefore, of holy love for your bridegroom that you possess is indeed in you, but you do not possess it from yourself.

The richest bridegroom received you as poor. Whatever good you have in you, you have not from yourself but from him; and whatever you do not yet have, you will have when the bridegroom gives himself—he who has already given, by a free gift, all the good things you possess. Give him humble thanks, then, for what you have received; humbly ask him for what you are to receive. For you have such a rich bridegroom that he neither lacks what he has given nor lacks abundance to give things much better [or: greater] than what he has given.

Consider these matters always with humble compunction, and preserve the virginity that you vowed to God not only through bodily integrity but also through humility of heart. Always ask him to guard your virginity and humility—him who “will neither slumber nor sleep, who guards Israel” (Ps. CXX, 4).

38. Behold, holy daughter: insofar as the Lord granted me, I have written for you this brief treatise concerning virginity and humility. I preferred to send a little to you in your desire rather than to deny the service owed to the Lord’s bride.

# EPISTLE IV. TO PROBA  
## Concerning prayer to God and compunction of heart

To the most venerable lady in Christ, and the servant of God PROBA, whose name must be spoken with every mark of honor, FULGENTIUS, servant of the servants of Christ: greetings in the Lord.

177 **CHAPTER I. Proba’s humility is to be imitated by all.** —1. I received the letter of your holiness with complete rejoicing of heart. It displayed by clear indications not only your zeal for good work but also your humility of heart. Therefore, holy daughter, you do well: for the praise of God, you are not lifted up by the wind of pride over good works, but testify that you are weak and powerless for fulfilling the Lord’s commandments.

Anyone who desires to be not a forgetful hearer of God’s word but a doer of the work (James I, 25) ought to think in this way—anyone who expects to receive his reward not here from human beings but from God on the day of recompense, and who is not carried away in the present time by the vanity of empty glory but is kindled by the holy fire of divine love.

For Christ came to cast this fire upon the earth (Luke XII, 49), so that it might burn away every sprout of pride and kindle the fervor of holy compunction in the humbled heart. Thus it comes about that we truly accuse ourselves in our sins and praise God with true humility of heart in our good works: we attribute to him what his compassion gives us, and we attribute to ourselves those things in which our weakness provokes him.

**CHAPTER II. Prayer and compunction of heart must be sought from God, so that he may pour them into us. How God is the author of our good work.** —2. And because he is frequently offended by us, it is necessary that he be appeased by frequent prayer and continual compunction of heart.

Compunction of heart awakens the affection of prayer; humble prayer wins divine assistance. Compunction of heart looks upon its wounds; prayer asks for the healing remedy. And who is fit for these things? Who can pray suitably unless the Physician himself pours into him the beginning of spiritual desire? Or who can persevere in prayer unless God increases within us what he began, nourishes what he planted, and brings to the fulfillment [or: fruit] of perfection, through the mercy that follows, what he freely gave to the unworthy through preceding mercy?

Thus the merit of good work will not be lost by us if God, its author and helper, is always glorified in the work.

3. Let us not suppose that he is to be regarded as the author of good work in such a way that, merely at the beginning of creation, God gave human nature the capacity for good work so that, once his assistance ceased, nature could by itself will or do any good thing. This was not possible even in the first human being, by his own effort alone, when he had not yet been corrupted by sin.

How, then, can a weakened person restore health without the physician’s help—one who, while healthy, was unable to preserve his health? [Note: [Col. 0339D] The Victor manuscript and the printed editions have “was able.” The Corbie manuscript has “will be able.”]

4. Therefore let earth and ashes not boast, because in his life he has exposed his inner parts. Let the wounded person not rejoice over what he considers healthy in himself as though he were healthy; rather, in the humility of a contrite heart, let him consider the corruption of his wounds, so that, crying out with the prophet, “My wounds have become foul and putrid because of my foolishness” (Ps. XXXVII, 6), he may receive healing—not by his own merit but by the gratuitous gift of divine compassion.

“For what does a person have that he did not receive? And if he received it, why does he boast as though he had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7). God alone, therefore, can give to all whom he wishes the means by which true salvation may be acquired; and therefore he alone can preserve in the recipient what he has given: “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (Ps. CXXVI, 2).

He will not permit the stealthy entrance of the most wicked robber if the assistance of the watchful Lord is not lacking to him; for he himself “will neither slumber nor sleep, who guards Israel” (Ps. CXX, 4).

**CHAPTER III. In this life we must always make progress. A person cannot do anything good from himself, without God’s grace—not even will it.** —5. Just as one who is traveling toward his homeland always has somewhere to walk until he arrives, so we too, as long as we are established in this mortal body and are pilgrims away from the Lord, have the present life as our road. On it we always have somewhere to advance, until, with God leading us, we are able to arrive at that eternal homeland of blessed immortality.

It is therefore a great blessing to live in the present age in such a way that every faithful person devotes himself to spiritual progress, yet never arrogantly attributes this to his own strength. Rather, with humble heart, let him ask God for the continual preservation of the gift he has received—from whom flows the beginning not only of every good will but also its perfection.

[Col. 0341A] 6. For the preaching of the apostle James cannot be nullified by any argument when he says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James I, 17).

No human being can be fit either to think or to do anything good unless he has been assisted by the free gift of divine help. “For it is God who works in his people both to will and to accomplish according to his good will” (Phil. II, 13), as the Chosen Vessel affirms. Through him we have also learned that “we are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as though from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (II Cor. III, 5).

He therefore supplies us with all sufficiency for good, whose fullness is not diminished when he gives, who kindly bestows every good thing on us so that we may possess it, while he himself remains full without diminution. This neither angelic nor human nature can accomplish, nor can any created substance, however spiritual.

For everything created, just as it did not exist before it was created, could not possess anything before it received it; and just as it cannot subsist without the operation of him who made it, so it cannot will or do good unless God continually deigns to help it.

From him comes the beginning of good will; from him the capacity for good work; from him perseverance in good conduct; from him, in the present age, true humility of heart; and in the future, the happiness of eternal recompense. Thus those will be happy without end who are now sincerely humble, who do not deceive themselves with empty inflation, but behold with fear and trembling the dangers of the present life [Note: [Col. 0341D] These words—“but behold with fear and trembling the dangers of the present life”—were absent from the printed editions; they have been restored from the Corbie and Victor manuscripts, since the meaning of the subsequent words requires them].

In this life there cannot be such complete security among good things that adversity does not more easily creep in when prosperity deceitfully displays itself.

**CHAPTER IV. No one can escape the devil’s snares without God’s grace.** —7. There is no time in this life when the enemy does not stretch a trap for human beings. No one can escape his snares by his own strength, unless God, through Jesus Christ our Lord, deigns to free that person by his grace.

Therefore the Chosen Vessel, when he felt himself being taken captive under the law of sin, exclaimed: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII, 24).

For this reason the prophet also declares that his feet are pulled out of the snare not by his own strength but by divine gift, saying: “My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he will pull my feet out of the snare” (Ps. XXIV, 15).

And elsewhere, speaking in the person of the saints whom the Lord has deigned to free from the snare of this age and transfer to eternal security and joy, it is said: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; the snare has been broken, and we have been set free” (Ps. CXXIII, 7).

**CHAPTER V. No one is secure in this life. We must fight through prayer and compunction of heart.** —8. Nevertheless, so that each one of us may recognize that his soul moves amid the adversities and snares of the enemy and may never grow sluggish in this age through harmful security, the same prophet says: “All day long I walked in sorrow, because my soul is filled with illusions, and there is no health in my flesh” (Ps. XXXVII, 7).

What does it mean to walk in sorrow all day long except to grieve throughout the whole time of this life at the recollection of sins? When is the soul filled with illusions except when it is shaken by frequent temptation from carnal desires? Although it does not yield to them by consent, it grows weary from exhaustion.

For although the Lord continually grants his people assistance in the struggle so that they may not fail, mortal weakness is nevertheless permitted to grow weary, weighed down by the burden of its own frailty. Thus, when it finds no support of virtue in itself, it may quickly turn to seek the help of divine compassion.

9. We conquer the adversary, therefore, if we fight with tears, [Col. 0342B] prayers, and continual humility of heart. For it is written: “The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds, and the Lord does not withdraw until he has heard” (Ecclus. 35:21). The weeping of the humble is therefore the great destruction of carnal desire. Tears that flow from compunction of heart both overcome the enemy and obtain for us the gift of triumphant joy. For “those who go forth, going and weeping, carrying their seed, will come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125:5–6). How well the holy prophet teaches that the seeds of good works must be watered by a stream of tears! For no seed germinates unless it has been irrigated; nor does fruit proceed from seed if it has been deprived of the help of water. Therefore, if we too wish to reap the fruits of our [Col. 0342C] seeds, let us not cease to water our seeds with tears, which ought to be poured out more from the heart than from the body. For this reason the prophet says to us that we should “tear our hearts, and not our garments” (Joel 2:15)—something we can do when we remember that we ourselves frequently sin, if not in action, at least in thought. For “the earthly dwelling burdens the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15), and our earth does not cease to bring forth thorns and thistles for us (Gen. 3:17); nor can we reach the eating of our bread unless we have been worn out by the sweat of our face and by toil.

## CHAPTER VI. Our weariness in resisting desires. What it means to dash the little ones of Babylon against the rock.

10. For we are wearied by our sweats when we resist our own desires. In overcoming them, the difficulty of the struggle is therefore greater because the adversity of carnal desire is generated not externally, from another, but internally, from within the person who struggles. It imposes weariness upon human weakness as it arises, although it is conquered by the aid of divine strength. For “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that we do not do whatever we wish” (Gal. 5:17). This is why we are not yet wholly subject to God: what resists the divine command arises from within us. For although, by God’s grace, there is in us a good will that makes us humble before God, the arising of wicked desire is nevertheless not absent from us, and it makes us rebellious.

11. By God’s grace, therefore, we are already subject to God in part, but because of our fault we are still in part not subject. For this reason it is said in the Letter to the Hebrews that not yet all things are subject to Christ; for it says: “In subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that was not subject to him. But now we do not yet see all things subject to him” (Heb. 2:8).

We are therefore subject to God insofar as, with him working within us, we delight in the law of God according to the inner person. But we are not yet subject insofar as we see “another law in our members opposing the law of our mind and making us captive to the law of sin, which is in our members” (Rom. 7:22–23). We are subject to God because, by his mercy, we are rescued from temptation; for we sing to him: “From you I shall be rescued from temptation” (Ps. 17:30). But we are not yet wholly subject, because “the life of man upon earth is a temptation” (Job 7:1).

We are subject to God, who directs our steps according to his word, so that no iniquity may rule over us (Ps. 118:133). But we are not yet wholly subject, because “we all offend in many things” (Jas. 3:2). We are subject insofar as, by his gift, while walking in the flesh we do not wage war according to the flesh (2 Cor. 10:3). But we are not yet wholly subject, because although, by God’s gift, we have the ability to serve the law of God with the mind, we nevertheless have, from the remnants of sin, the ability to serve the law of sin with the flesh. For this reason the Apostle says: “So then, I myself with the mind serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7:25).

[Col. 0343C] 12. Everyone who now lives justly serves the law of sin with the flesh, because he feels carnal desire being born within him; but he serves the law of God with the mind because he does not consent to that same carnal desire. We serve the law of sin with the flesh when the sons of Babylon, as they are born, disturb our soul; but we serve the law of God with the mind when those same little ones of Babylon are dashed against the rock.

For Babylon is interpreted as “confusion,” and its daughter is every carnal desire that confusion of heart generates. As long as we are exiles in the body, away from the Lord, this confusion thrusts its offspring upon us. For from that very confusion every wicked thought is born; and it is dashed against the rock when, overcome by a swift recollection and the aid of Christ, it is trampled down.

## CHAPTER VII. We must both give thanks and pour forth continual prayers to God.

[Col. 0343D] 13. Therefore, although we have reason to give thanks to God because by free mercy he has subjected us to himself so that we may be humble, we nevertheless have reason to strike upon the divine ears with continual prayers. For as long as we are in this mortal body, just as we cannot be without sin, so we are not yet able to offer perfect humility to the divine commands. Accordingly, thanks must indeed be given to God insofar as he grants us the ability to act well, lest we prove ungrateful for his gifts; and we must strive to advance toward better things, lest we fall into deadly pride by thinking that our conduct is perfect in every respect.

## CHAPTER VIII. We must weep in this life so that we may live in rest in the next. What blessedness there is in heaven.

14. Therefore let us groan and weep before the Lord, who made us (Ps. 94:6), so that he may free us from the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of the world, which is not from the Father but from the world (1 John 2:16), and bring us to that subjection in which nothing arising from the defect of mortality will resist us, but, by the gift of immortality, everything within us will be subject to God.

Then there will be in us true, perfect, and exalted humility, when no wicked desire remains either in our flesh or in our mind. The spirit will not be wearied by thoughts, nor will the body be tormented by labors. There will be no anxiety of struggle, but perfect security of peace; no need of righteousness, but complete satiety with delight. For there we shall be blessed in perfect exaltation, because in perfect humility of flesh and spirit we shall be subject to God.

There neither will our love be less than our praise, nor our praise inferior to our love. Our praise will be full, because then there will be in us perfect love of God and of our neighbor. Then we shall praise and possess; then we shall possess and love; then we shall be satisfied with delight, and delight in satisfaction.

# EPISTLE V. TO EUGYPPIUS THE ABBOT. On charity and its love.

[Col. 0344C] To the most blessed lord, most greatly venerable, and desirable with the whole affection of charity, the holy brother and fellow presbyter EUGYPPIUS: FULGENTIUS, servant of the servants of Christ, greeting in the Lord.

182 1. Would that such ability supported my utterance, holy brother, that I might find words sufficient to unfold the spiritual sweetness which I received from reading your letter. While I wish to do this and cannot, I recognize that something remarkable has happened to me: I see that the joy I drew from your words cannot be expressed by my words. Indeed, what you wrote to me, after being discovered and arranged in thought, you set forth in writing in such a way that you either wrote it with your own hand or dictated it to a scribe. How then has it happened that my mouth, in dictating, cannot render the delight which my heart conceived from the dictation of your mouth? What impoverished abundance, or abundant poverty, is this: that my speech suffices me less in proportion as affection urges me more, and that, because I speak for the very reason that I delight, I say less than I delight in? What, I ask, is this that I wish to signify by speech and cannot? It is surely something which is so signified by bodily speech and pen that it is nevertheless possessed not bodily but spiritually.

[Note: [Col. 0343D] The printed editions read “love” (*dilectionem*); but the reading of the Corbie manuscript, which has “delight” (*delectationem*), seems preferable, since a little above he had said, “to unfold the spiritual sweetness,” etc.]

## 2. Charity, the first fruit of spiritual gifts.

Among spiritual gifts, charity is the first fruit. [Col. 0345A] Therefore the Vessel of Election did not place it in that order without design: “But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace” (Gal. 5:22), and the rest. In another place too, he wished to signify something pre-eminent among heavenly charisms when he said: “Because the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). This charity, which we received through the gift of the Holy Spirit when we were unworthy, is so good, so holy, so immense, that even one who has it in his heart can never explain it in words. O what charity—greatly to be wondered at, greatly to be praised, and greatly to be loved!

## 3. He who does not possess charity does not love it.

Yet not all who admire and praise charity immediately love charity; and therefore, unless one loves it, his admiration and praise of it will profit him nothing. Admiration and praise of charity are fruitful when love is not absent in the admirer and praiser. But can those who do not yet possess charity love it, just as they can admire and praise it without possessing it? By no means; for charity itself is love. How, then, does one already love love who has not begun to possess love? For behold, with bodily sight we see many things in which sight itself is not the same thing as that which we see by it. Sight is the sense by which we see, whereas the visible object is what we see; and when that which is seen is removed from the eyes, if health remains in the eyes, what was seen is removed from the perceiving sense in such a way that the sense itself is by no means removed from the seer. Thus the faculty of seeing remains in a person, although sight itself departs from that which was seen. But when charity is loved, since it is loved only by love, a person cannot turn the attention of love away from charity, as he can turn a bodily eye away from any visible thing, and thus both fail to love charity and still possess love. For charity—that is, love—is in no way loved unless one possesses the love by which love itself is loved. Love, therefore, is loved by itself, because it is loved when possessed, and is not loved unless possessed. It can indeed be loved by us even when we ask that it may increase in us; but one who does not possess its beginning does not love its increase.

## 4. Charity is not loved as money is. Charity is not loved as the other gifts of the Spirit are.

Charity, then, is not loved as a coin or something of that kind is. [Col. 0345D] Someone may possess not even one coin and yet love and desire a multitude of coins. Thus he loves a multitude of coins while having the means of not even one coin: he finds not one coin with himself and seeks countless coins outside himself. We find the same in other bodily things: one of them can be loved while the very thing loved is possessed in no degree. There is something similar in most spiritual gifts. For example, someone may love to possess the gift of prophecy, which no one denies is included among spiritual gifts in the apostolic writings: “To one, indeed, through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom,” as the Vessel of Election affirms, “to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another gifts of healings in the one Spirit; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another interpretation of utterances. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:8, 9, 10, 11).

## 5. The other gifts may be possessed without a good will; charity cannot.

Therefore, to say nothing of the other spiritual gifts, prophecy can be loved without being possessed; charity, however, is neither possessed if it is not loved nor loved if it is not possessed. Hence the other gifts of the Holy Spirit—namely tongues, prophecy, knowledge of the sacraments, faith, distribution of resources to the poor, even the burning of one’s own body—may be possessed without a good will, so that they burden rather than honor their possessor. But charity cannot be possessed without a good will, because it does not permit the will in which charity is found to become evil. For “charity neither acts perversely nor thinks evil”; and because “it does not rejoice in iniquity” (1 Cor. 13:4, 5), it necessarily makes good the will in which it is present.

## 6. A malevolent mind neither bestows nor possesses charity.

A malevolent mind, therefore, does not bestow charity upon another because it does not possess it for itself. But once it has begun to possess, so to speak, the beginning of charity, it can be neither malevolent nor barren. And because, so long as it remains in charity, it remains in God and God remains in it (1 John 4:16), it will always possess charity if it always bestows it; but when it does not bestow it, it will not possess it. For it is characteristic of charity, as regards the course of this present life, to increase in one who dispenses it, but to depart without delay from one who wishes to possess it only for himself. Therefore he will possess it more who dispenses it more willingly; for just as a malevolent person can neither bestow nor possess it, so no one possesses it or bestows it unwillingly. A well-disposed person, therefore, is the dwelling-place of charity. This name, “well-disposed” (*benevolus*), is compounded from “well” and “to will.” If anyone wills evil to another, then insofar as he wills evil he is not well-disposed, and consequently is malevolent. “Wisdom shall not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wis. 1:4). Properly speaking, however, a malevolent person is not everyone who desires or asks for something contrary either for himself or for another, but one who harbors the will to harm, whether what he desires can be good or evil.

## 7. A good will is judged not by its office but by its end.

A will, whether good or harmful, must be assessed not by the act but by the end of the matter in each case. For each person displays the quality of his will not by what he does but by the reason for which he does it. Paul too desired something contrary to himself when he asked that the thorn be removed from him—a thorn which he had received salutarily against the vice of self-exaltation (2 Cor. 12:8). Yet he did not have a malevolent mind, although he entertained a will contrary to his own advantage. For in asking that the thorn by which he was buffeted be removed from him, he wished that the health of his body should benefit his preaching more than himself, seeking not what was useful to himself but what was useful to many, that they might be saved. Thus he wanted his health to benefit those whom, he knew, his life too would benefit. Finally, although he had “a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23), which would be far better, he nevertheless knew that it was necessary to remain in the flesh for the sake of those among whom he performed the office of apostleship. Charity, therefore, constrained him both when he asked that the thorn be removed and when, though desiring something else, he wished to remain in the flesh. He was constrained by the breadth of charity both to desire to be with Christ and to wish to fulfill the office of pious necessity. Thus in both cases he loved charity, which he always breathed forth in a good will.

## 8. In the love of one’s neighbor, charity too is loved. Love of God and neighbor is love of charity.

Whoever, therefore, loves his brother according to charity—which is God—most especially loves charity itself in him. Hence, when our Savior deigned to renew his apostles by a new commandment, saying, “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13:34), by commanding brotherhood to be loved in himself, he also commands, through the apostle Paul, that the charity of brotherhood itself be loved. For with Christ speaking in him, the Teacher of the Gentiles wills that we should have love without pretense: “Hating evil, cleaving to good, loving one another with brotherly charity” (Rom. 12:9, 10).

9. Hence, in the eleventh book of the *Confessions*, that eminent teacher, blessed Augustine, when confessing to God the love which he “had received from him in order that he might love him,” says: “I have already said it, and I shall say it: I do this through love of your love” (St Augustine, *Confessions* XI.1). Likewise, while expounding Psalm 118, when he explained the meaning of the passage which says, “I am a sojourner on the earth; do not hide your commandments from me” (Ps. 118:19), after some remarks he says: “But what lovable thing is loved if love itself is not loved? Hence this sojourner on earth, after praying that God’s commandments should not be hidden from him—the commandments in which love is commanded, either alone or above all—declares that he wishes to possess love for love itself, saying: ‘My soul has longed to desire your justifications at all times’” (Augustine, *Expositions on Psalm* 118, discourse 8). Does it not seem to you that blessed Augustine’s statement about loving love has been drawn openly from prophetic and apostolic sayings?

[Note: [Col. 0347D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “Does not the statement of blessed Augustine seem openly drawn from prophetic and apostolic sayings?” and does not contain “seem to you.” The Cologne and Basel editions read: “Does it not seem to you openly drawn from prophetic and apostolic sayings?” The Antwerp edition: “drawn from prophetic … sayings.”]

## 10. Conclusion: let us pray for one another out of charity.

Therefore love of God and neighbor—which is the fullness of the law and the end of the commandment—loves, in God, charity, which is God, and, in one’s neighbor, charity, which is from God. For then God and neighbor are rightly loved if charity itself is loved both in God and in one’s neighbor. Thus it comes about that we love God himself in God and, without doubt, God in our neighbor. For it is not without reason that, after love of God, love of neighbor alone, and no other love, is commanded to us: namely, that we may recognize that we ought to love that creature in which we can find charity itself. For every irrational animal, just as it has no reason, so has no charity; and it seems to me that reason itself is nothing other than the fitting and ordered love owed by a human being to God alone and to his neighbor.

11. You see, holy brother, how lengthy a discourse I have carried on with you concerning charity, while I love in you exceedingly charity itself—which you too surely love in us—and for no other reason than that you love this charity in us, with which, by God’s gift, you are so full that you desire those whom you love to be full in like manner. It remains, therefore, that because you love us sincerely, you may deign to pray earnestly for us: that God, who loved us first (1 John 4:10) and gave us the charity by which he is loved by us, may, just as he bestows it upon those who do not possess it by grace that goes before, consume in us all the remnants of worldly desire and perfect us in charity, serving in spirit [Mss.: “fervent in spirit”], and make us sharers in that blessedness in which, just as there is no evil delight, so no death is feared as a punishment; where no one suffers anything through the frailty of the flesh, but all the saints are always ruled in the perfect charity of God and neighbor.

12. May divine mercy preserve your holiness as you pray for us—this is my wish, holy and most blessed lord and brother. Lord Januarius greets your holiness with every affection of purity and veneration. I received, with complete exultation, the blessing sent by you. I have dispatched in quires the books which, as you commanded, were given to Monimus, that, if anything in them should please, I might recognize it to be of truth and not of love alone! These, therefore, are the offering of my littleness, which the purity of your heart will make acceptable to you. Having received the request of our common brother, I ask that the diligence of your charity may be an aid. I beg that your servants copy from your manuscripts the books which we need.

[Note: [Col. 0348D] The printed editions read “with full affection.”]

[Note: [Col. 0348D] The Corbie manuscript reads “sent to Monimus.”]

[Note: [Col. 0348D] The Corbie manuscript reads “I ask that [it] be an aid.”]

# EPISTLE VI. TO THE SENATOR THEODORE. On conversion from the world.

To the illustrious lord, distinguished by merit, and most excellent son THEODORE: FULGENTIUS, servant of the servants of Christ, greeting in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I. Occasion for writing the letter.

186 1. Since, though unknown to you in body, I venture by letter to bring my acquaintance before you in speech, I ask you not to impute this to impudence or to ascribe this work of charity to importunity. For, first, the sweet letter of the holy brother Romulus and then the persuasion of brothers coming from there, whom you graciously received in the Lord, compelled me all the more to write because knowledge of your spiritual purpose invited me all the more gladly. They reported that, impelled by affection for Christ, you had kindly mentioned my name in conversation, saying that you took delight in my letter. I therefore gladly did what I knew you gladly wished, preferring to seem uncultivated in speech rather than cold in charity, illustrious lord, distinguished by merit, and most excellent son.

## CHAPTER II. He congratulates him on his conversion and on having trampled the world underfoot.

2. Accordingly, I rejoice greatly that you are now no longer held by the bonds of worldly love, and that by despising the world you trample underfoot the world by which, when you loved it, you were trampled underfoot. Now indeed you are advanced to a consulship; now you are most certainly exalted in a blessed triumph—not one applauded by the Roman people, but one at which the angelic assembly rejoices. “Blessed are you, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but that Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:17), among which heavens you too have become a heaven. How great, do you suppose, is the devil’s grief when he sees that the world is despised by you and knows that you have been converted to Christ; when he sees you abandon the things in which you appear to be, and already migrate in heart from the love of temporal and earthly things to those heavenly and eternal things? For although Christ died equally for all the faithful and bestowed upon all an equal benefit of redemption, as the Apostle says: “For as many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal. 3:27), nevertheless the conversion of the powerful of this world greatly serves Christ’s gains.

[Note: [Col. 0349D] These words, “there is neither Jew nor Greek,” are absent from the printed editions; they occur in the Corbie manuscript and in the Apostle’s text. Other manuscripts add, “there is neither barbarian nor Scythian.”]

## CHAPTER III. By the example of the great, they draw a multitude after them.

3. For just as many brothers and friends, clients and subjects, known and unknown alike, are stirred by the authority of such persons to the ardor of worldly love, and are kindled with the fire of secular desire all the more because they see those eminent in the world willingly held captive by worldly love, 187 so whenever he “who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble, who touches the mountains and they smoke” [variant: “will smoke”] (Ps. 103:32) mercifully looks upon hearts intent on earthly things and compels them to tremble through consideration of his judgment, and touches the proud hearts of the exalted, like the heights of mountains, so that they smoke by confession of sins, very many tremble at the trembling of such persons, and in their conversion many flee to the help of divine mercy. Thus it happens that those established on the pinnacle of the world either destroy very many along with themselves or gain many with themselves on the way of salvation. Great punishment awaits such persons if they offer to many a snare of bad imitation; great glory awaits them if they show to many an example of holy conduct.

## CHAPTER IV.

For who would not despise a small cell when a senator despises a marble-clad house? Who, despising earthly things, would not provide for himself by acquiring heavenly things when a Roman consul hastens to heaven through contempt for earthly things?

4. In you we truly see fulfilled in deed what the prophet sang: “This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76:11). For who could work this in you but he who knows how to govern and order the succession of mutable things according to immutable counsel? For that individual things may change, according to the fitness of times and the diversity of causes, either for worse or for better, comes about through the immutable counsel of him who is changed neither by better things nor by worse. He has nowhere by which to advance to the better, nor any source from which to decline to the worse. He who is always is what he is, and is as he is; he does not have in himself the possibility that what is may not be, because neither does he have in himself the possibility that what is not may be. And that which thus is is neither preceded by a beginning nor bounded by an end, neither rolled about by times nor contained by places nor varied by ages. Nothing is lacking there, because all is in him; nothing is superfluous there, because nothing is apart from him.

5. Therefore, if any pass, with contempt for the love of temporal and mutable things, into love of him, they will be full in him, in whom nothing is lacking; secure in him, in whom nothing is feared; truly and forever glorious in him whose true and everlasting glory is neither taken away, diminished, nor increased. Who would not despise this present life through desire for that life? Who would not abhor the riches of passing time through delight in that abundance? Who would not despise all earthly kingdoms through love of that kingdom?

## 6. Future blessedness belongs only to the humble.

We shall receive that life, therefore, when we reckon ourselves dead to this life; we shall possess those riches when here we live as poor in spirit; and we shall attain the height of that kingdom when here we hold with true heart the humility taught by God the Teacher.

## CHAPTER V.

To those dead in this way the blessed Apostle says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, shall appear, then you too shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3, 4). Of such poor persons the Lord himself also speaks, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). Of such humble persons he likewise says: “For whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. 23:12); and elsewhere: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:29).

7. This humility is possessed neither by those who love the world nor by those who, when they despise the things that are in the world, ascribe that contempt to their own strength.

## CHAPTER VI. Two kinds of pride. Every good must be ascribed to God, not to our own strength.

The Holy Spirit indicated these two kinds of pride in one verse of the psalm, David saying: “Those who trust in their own strength and glory in the abundance of their riches” (Ps. 48:7). Those glory in the abundance of their riches who love their riches in such a way as to place in them the highest blessedness; but those trust in their own strength who despise riches in such a way as to ascribe that very contempt to their own strength. Thus both are proud: the former because they trust in riches, not in God; the latter because they wish to ascribe to themselves, not to God, their contempt for riches. The former love badly what cannot be loved well; the latter do not despise well what can be despised well. Thus the former do evil badly, while the latter do good badly.

8. Therefore, since, with the Lord mercifully working in you, you have now learned not to glory in the abundance of your riches, this remains: do not trust in your own strength. That is, do not ascribe to your own strength the fact that you despise the resources and riches of the world, count the honors of the world as nothing, are inflamed by desire for the kingdom of heaven, and delight to run the way of God’s commandments. For you could have none of these things unless you received them from God as a gift of free giving. Nature does not give this to a human being, but grace; it is not possessed by the quality of the human condition, but acquired by the kindness of divine illumination.

9. A human being was indeed made by God in such a way that he could possess these things, but he cannot possess them unless he receives them as the gift of a merciful God. The eye too was so made that it could see light, but it cannot see unless light has been poured into it. Therefore, what the eye sees is a benefit of light; if it lacks this, it will remain blind in darkness. Not everything that can be something is already that which it can be, except the one for whom it is natural to be capable of being that which always is. But this one God is the Trinity itself—that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—who alone is the creator of all things, because he alone was created by no one. But all things, because they were created by him and not from him, are by nature subject both to loss and to increase. Therefore, lest some fall back into worse things, his grace governs them; that some may ascend to better things, his grace raises them; and that they may remain forever, grace itself gives them life and preserves them.

[Note: [Col. 0351D] The Corbie manuscript reads “may not depart,” rather than “may not fall back.”]

## CHAPTER VII. God’s grace must always be sought, because it gives both willing and accomplishing.

10. The help of this grace must always be sought by us from God; but we must not ascribe even our asking for it to our own strength. For not even the disposition of prayer itself can be possessed unless it has been bestowed by God. Thus, in order that we may desire the help of grace, this very thing too is a work of grace. Grace itself begins to be infused in order that it may begin to be sought; it is infused more abundantly when it is given to those who ask. But who can seek grace unless he wills? Yet unless God works that very will in him, he cannot will at all. Therefore the blessed Apostle testifies that God works in us not only people’s good works but also their good will, saying: “For God is the one who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to good will” (Phil. 2:13). This is what, commending watchfulness and humility to the faithful, he first said [variant: “commands”]: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling”; and there he added: “For God is the one who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to good will.” In order that we may come to him, we run; and we run because we will to run.

## CHAPTER VIII.

But lest we ascribe either the will or the running itself to our own strength, the same Apostle instructs us, saying: “It is not of one who wills, nor of one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16).

11. Therefore, that you may remain and make progress in these good things which you have received from God; that you may neither stay on the way, turn back, nor turn to the right or the left: ascribe to God, who gave it, whatever good will or good action you possess, and humbly ask him both to preserve and to increase what he has given. Ascribe no good to yourself as though it were your own, lest you fail to receive what you could receive and lose what you had received. For the pride of the human heart, by which a person does what God condemns in human beings, is detestable; but more detestable is that by which a person attributes to himself what God gives to human beings. For one is held guilty of a worse pride in proportion as he is ungrateful amid better gifts. One who misuses the substance of this world is blameworthy, but more blameworthy is one who is proudly exalted by spiritual gifts.

## CHAPTER IX. Humility of mind is the Christian’s exaltation.

12. Let humility of mind, which is the true and complete exaltation of a Christian, therefore increase in you; and recognize God’s grace to be increasing in you all the more as you see humility of heart more abundant in yourself. That you may always possess it and always advance in it, work out your salvation with fear and trembling. Let reading not be absent from good works, nor good works from devotion to reading. Provide what is good before God and human beings. Devote your heart’s attention to the holy Scriptures; and there recognize what you were, what you are, and what you ought to be. If you approach them humbly and gently, there you will certainly find both prevenient grace, by which one who has fallen can rise; accompanying grace, by which he may run the way of the right path; and following grace, by which he may be able to attain the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom.

13. I beg you to greet your mother, holy and greatly venerable in Christ, who agrees with your spiritual zeal in Christian faith and truly maternal charity; and also your venerable wife, now your sister in Christ. May the inseparable Trinity preserve you by the protection of its power—this is my wish, illustrious lord and son.

# EPISTLE VII. TO VENANTIA. On true repentance and future recompense.

To the illustrious lady and daughter, venerable by merit, VENANTIA: FULGENTIUS, servant of the servants of Christ, greeting in the Lord.

[Col. 0352D] 190 **CHAPTER I.—1.** Just as true light is in no way darkened, so eternal truth never lies. God is light and truth, and of him it is written: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9). This same light and truth also says: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). And again he says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). We are also instructed by his teaching that a good tree produces good fruits, and that a tree is known by its fruits (Matt. 7:17). In him, illustrious lady and deservedly venerable daughter, although you are bodily unknown to me, I already know you; in him, although you are situated so far away, I rejoice with you.

**2.** Through the letter of my most illustrious son Junillus I learned both your purpose and your zeal for Christianity. He took such care to make known to me the grace that God has bestowed upon you that in his letter he also showed me the sign of your greeting. You would certainly not have done this unless you loved Christ with complete purity of mind in his servants; nor would you have greeted an unknown servant so kindly in the Lord unless you bore the Lord within a devout heart. Thanks be to him who multiplies our joy through the love of the faithful.

**CHAPTER II.** Love itself [alternatively, “He himself”] leads believers to God, because love itself is God. Hence the apostle John says: “God is love; and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him” (1 John 4:16).

**3. The manifold benefit of love against sins.**—When love begins to dwell here, it does not permit sin to rule, but covers a multitude of sins; and it not only causes present sins to be avoided, but also causes all past sins to be forgiven. The proud and obstinate reject this, despairing of the forgiveness of sins. In pitiable blindness they not only cast away concern for their own salvation, but, if they cannot corrupt faithful souls, do not cease to disturb them with deadly words.

[Note: Ms. Corb. reads: “although they can corrupt [them], perhaps they cannot.”]

For such people, either the enormity of their sins or the long duration of a wickedly spent life often removes hope of salvation and compels them to commit still worse deeds, so that in them the saying of holy Scripture is fulfilled: “When the sinner has come into the depths of evil, he despises” (Prov. 18:2–3). And truly the depth of evils kills those whom despair of forgiveness prejudices through detestable hardness of heart.

191 **CHAPTER III. No one should despair of God’s mercy.—4.** Who does not see how impious and sacrilegious it would be to believe that a person converted from past evils to good through repentance could not receive forgiveness for some sin? What else is accomplished by such words than that, through the vice of despair, the hand of the almighty physician is driven away from bringing about human salvation?

The physician himself says: “Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Luke 5:31). If our physician is skilled, he can heal every sickness; if our God is merciful, he can forgive every sin. There is no perfect goodness if not every evil is conquered; nor is there perfect medicine if some disease is found to be incurable.

It is written in the sacred books: “Wisdom does not overcome evil” [sic; the printed text reads *Sapientiam autem non vincit malitia*, “evil does not overcome wisdom”] (Wis. 7:30). The omnipotence of our physician is also declared in these words of the psalm:

“Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his rewards: he who is gracious to all your iniquities; who heals all your diseases; who will redeem [alternatively, “redeems”] your life from destruction; who satisfies your desire with good things; who crowns you with mercy and compassion. Your youth will be renewed like an eagle’s [alternatively, “like the eagle’s”]” (Ps. 102:1–5).

[Note: Ms. Corb. reads: “since he is gracious … since the Lord heals …”]

What, I ask, should we think cannot be forgiven in us, when the Lord is gracious toward all our iniquities? Or what should we judge incapable of being healed in us, when the Lord heals all our diseases? Or how can anything of need remain in one who has been healed and justified, whose desire is satisfied with good things? Or how can one be thought unable to receive the benefit of full forgiveness when even a crown is granted to him in mercy and compassion?

Therefore let no one, despairing of the physician, remain in sickness; let no one, diminishing God’s mercy, waste away in iniquities. The Apostle cries out: “Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. 5:6). He likewise says: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1 Tim. 1:15).

[Note: Thus read Ms. Corb. and Ms. Ant., in accordance with the Greek text of the Apostle; Colon. and Basil. instead have “into this world.”]

**CHAPTER IV. Sins committed even after baptism can be forgiven. God is abundant in forgiveness.—5.** Perhaps, however, it is said that those sinners can be saved who, after their sins, deserve to be cleansed through the washing of baptism, whereas the sins that a baptized person subsequently appears to commit remain unforgivable. Was the apostle John not speaking to baptized people when he said to them: “My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin; but if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the expiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1–2)?

**[Col. 0354C] 6.** Whatever the sin may be, it can indeed be forgiven by God when the sinner is converted; but the person who, by despairing, has closed against himself the door of forgiveness does not allow it to be forgiven. Yet Truth does not lie when it says: “Seek, and you will find; ask, and you will receive; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who seeks will find [alternatively, “finds”]; whoever asks will receive [alternatively, “receives”]; and to whoever knocks it will be opened” (Matt. 7:7).

Therefore the most holy prophet Isaiah urges the ungodly and sinners not to despair in any way of the forgiveness of sins, saying: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. Let the ungodly abandon his way, and the sinful man his thoughts; let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him; and to our God, for he is abundant in forgiveness” (Isa. 55:6–7).

Let the ungodly, then, abandon his way, by which he sins; let the sinful person abandon his thought, by which he despairs of the forgiveness of sins; and, according to the prophet’s saying, let him turn to the Lord, for he is abundant in forgiveness. Nothing is lacking in this abundance, in which mercy is both almighty and omnipotence merciful. So great in God is the kindness of omnipotence and the omnipotence of kindness that there is nothing he does not wish, or is unable, to forgive for the person who turns to him.

**CHAPTER V. A saving conversion consists in two things. Judas’s despair: repentance without hope.—7.** Saving conversion rests upon a twofold condition: that neither repentance abandon the person who hopes, nor hope abandon the person who repents. Thus, a person must renounce his sin with his whole heart and place the hope of forgiveness in God with his whole heart.

For the devil sometimes takes hope away from the repentant person, and at other times removes repentance from the one who hopes: the first he burdens and crushes; the second he lifts up and casts down. Judas, who betrayed Christ, did penance for his sin but lost salvation because he did not hope for forgiveness.

Thus the Evangelist speaks of him: “Then Judas, who had betrayed him, seeing that he was condemned, was moved to repentance and returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: ‘I have sinned by betraying righteous blood.’ But they said: ‘What is that to us? You see to it.’ And throwing down the silver pieces in the temple, he departed; and he went away and hanged himself” (Matt. 27:3–5).

He rightly did penance, because he had sinned by betraying righteous blood; but he therefore denied himself the fruit of repentance because he did not hope that the sin of his betrayal would be washed away by the blood of the very one whom he had betrayed.

**CHAPTER VI. Hope without repentance is vain presumption.—8.** The devil holds many people in their sins under a vain hope of forgiveness, compelling them not to fear God’s justice while persuading them vainly to rejoice in God’s goodness. Such people say, in accordance with the Apostle’s rebuke: “Let us do evil so that good may come”; their condemnation is just (Rom. 3:8).

**9.** From these indications we clearly recognize that a person repents in vain if, while repentance is being practiced, forgiveness is despaired of; and that it is futile to hope for forgiveness without repentance for sins. Therefore no one should sin securely under the hope of forgiveness, nor, considering the multitude of his sins, remain bound in the chains of despair.

Holy Scripture exhorts us to cease sinning and not to despair that the things we have done may be forgiven. It says: “My son, you have sinned; do not add again, but also pray concerning your former sins, that they may be forgiven you” (Sir. 21:1). Holy Scripture has given warning about both matters and has shown that we should neither remain in sin nor doubt the forgiveness of any iniquity.

Why, then, are we commanded not to add sins to sins if we are to remain in sin? Or why are we commanded to pray concerning our former sins, so that they may be forgiven us, if there are some sins that cannot in any way be forgiven those who pray? Or perhaps the length of time can prejudice someone, so that, just as after thirty years no one is permitted by human laws to reclaim what has been taken away, so under divine laws, after long periods of sinning, it is not permitted to ask for forgiveness?

Far be it from our God that he should be as human society is in lawsuits. Our God is as merciful and good as he is infinite and unconquerable. Therefore the goodness of the unconquerable one is not conquered, and the mercy of the infinite one is not brought to an end.

193 **CHAPTER VII. Every period of the present life is suitable for conversion.—10.** Every period of the present life is shown to be most suitable for conversion, when Scripture says:

“If the wicked person turns away from all his iniquities that he has committed, and keeps all my commandments, and practices justice and mercy, he will surely live, and will not die. None of all his offenses that he has committed will be remembered. He will live by his justice that he has practiced. Do I desire the death of the sinner, says the Lord, rather than that he should turn from his evil way and live?

“But when the righteous person turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, according to all the iniquities that the wicked person has committed, none of all his righteousnesses that he has practiced will be remembered; in the offense by which he offended, and in the sins by which he sinned, in them he will die” (Ezek. 18:21–22 and following).

And below he says: “When the righteous person turns away from his righteousness to commit an offense, he will die in the offense that he has committed. But when the wicked person turns away from his wickedness that he has committed, to practice judgment and justice, he has preserved his soul; and he has turned away from all his iniquities that he has committed: he will surely live, and will not die” (ibid., 24).

Both statements are true, because both are divine: whether that all the righteous person’s righteousnesses are to be consigned to oblivion when he turns away from his righteousness, or that the wicked person, when he turns from iniquity to righteousness, is to be saved and all his iniquities are not to be remembered.

**11.** It is unjust if we think that the righteous person, once turned away, can be condemned, and that the wicked person, once converted, cannot be saved.

[Note: The words “that the righteous person, once turned away, can be condemned; and that we should think …” were absent from the printed editions; they have been restored from Ms. Corb., since the context of the sermon requires them.]

God is just and merciful. Therefore, just as through justice he can condemn the one who has turned away, so through mercy he can always save the one who has turned back. No length of time prejudices either divine equity or compassion. Repentance is never late before God, in whose sight both past and future are always regarded as present.

If the duration of sins could overcome God’s mercy, Christ would not have come at the world’s final age to take away the sins of the perishing world. John says of him: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29); and the Savior himself says of himself: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10).

**CHAPTER VIII. An example of God’s mercy from the parable of the Samaritan and the wounded man.—12.** Our Samaritan would never compassionately have carried the wounded man to the inn and placed him upon his beast if he had judged any wound in him incurable. Nor, after giving two denarii, would he have promised the innkeeper that he would repay whatever more he spent, if he had not foreseen that this additional expenditure would contribute to complete health (Luke 10:30 and following). For why should the innkeeper spend anything more if the wounded man had a wound that could not be healed?

Therefore, just as no wound is incurable for our physician, so heavenly medicine cannot fail in any wound or at any time. For this reason the physician himself always testifies that he can grant salvation to the person who turns back, saying: “When you turn back and groan, you will be saved” (Isa. 30:15).

For this reason God does not cease, through Jeremiah, to rebuke the hardness of certain people as follows: “Will the one who falls not rise again, or will the one who has turned away not return? Why, then, has this people in Jerusalem turned away with a contentious turning? They have made their necks hard; they have refused to return” (Jer. 8:4–5).

God does not punish the sinner’s sins if the sinner’s neck has not been hardened.

194 **CHAPTER IX. God’s justice saves those who turn back and condemns those who turn away.—13.** It is therefore good for us to flee to his mercy, whose justice we cannot escape. For God’s justice is such that it condemns those who turn away and saves those who turn back. Hence he says: “Turn to me, and I will save you” (Isa. 45:22).

He always delights in our conversion, nor has he set any time for a person, so long as he is in this life, beyond which he cannot be reconciled to the one who turns back. Rather, he is known to have assigned the whole period of the present life to our conversion. Blessed Peter says: “The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some consider slowness, but he patiently bears with you, not wishing anyone to perish, but everyone to turn to repentance” (2 Pet. 3:9).

**CHAPTER X. The parable of the workers in the vineyard. God always delights in our conversion.—14.** If the Lord judged any age unfit for the remedy of conversion, he would not call workers to the vineyard at different times. In the diversity of the hours, the diversity of ages is appropriately understood: childhood is represented by the morning, puberty by the third hour, youth by the sixth, the maturity of declining age by the ninth, and old age itself by the eleventh, the final hour.

Therefore, at whatever age a person is called, if he does not reject the kindness of the Lord who calls him, he must receive the denarius of eternal life. For he who cries out to us through the prophet Joel does indeed always delight in our conversion:

“Thus says the Lord your God: Turn to me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning; and tear your hearts and not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, for he is merciful and patient, long-suffering, and abundantly merciful, and patient in the face of evils” (Joel 2:12 and following).

**15.** For this reason the apostle Paul rebukes hardness of heart in those who neglect to repent of their sins. He says:

“Therefore you are without excuse, O every person who judges. For in judging another you condemn yourself, since you do the same things that you judge. We know that God’s judgment is according to truth against those who do such things. Do you suppose, O every person who judges those who do such things and yet does them, that you will escape God’s judgment? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering, not knowing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? But in accordance with your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment, who will repay each person according to his works” (Rom. 2:1–6 and following).

In another passage he does not so much lament those who appeared to be committing grave sins as those who refused to repent of their sins. Thus he says to the Corinthians:

“Otherwise, when I come again, may God humble me among you, and may I mourn over many of those who sinned previously and did not repent of the uncleanness, fornication, and shamelessness that they practiced” (2 Cor. 12:21).

And the Apostle rightly mourns those who do not repent: for he knows that there is more joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance (Luke 15:7). Therefore the blessed Apostle rightly mourns over those whose impenitent hearts are not a source of joy to the angelic choir.

195 **CHAPTER XI. God calls us to repentance in various ways.—16.** God’s kindness therefore leads us to repentance. For this reason he afflicts us with tribulations, chastises us with illnesses, and instructs us through distress, so that those who sinned in bodily health may learn in sickness to abstain from sins; and those who in times of joy despised God’s mercy may, when chastised by the scourge of sorrow, fear his justice.

Thus it comes about that those who, by abusing health, have brought sickness upon themselves may, through sickness, restore the benefits of health; and those who through joy have fallen into tribulations may, through tribulations, return to joy.

[Note: Ms. Corb. adds here the words: “Listen, sinner, and rejoice”; but they are found neither in the printed editions nor do they seem to contribute anything to the sense.]

Finally, holy Scripture testifies that God’s love toward us is shown more greatly through scourges and corrections. It says: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord, and do not grow weary when you are reproved by him; for whom the Lord loves he corrects, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. 3:11–12).

[Col. 0358C] **CHAPTER XII.** The Savior himself also says that he loves those whom he rebukes: “I rebuke and discipline those whom I love” (Rev. 3:19). And the teaching of the Apostles does not cease to proclaim that we must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations (Acts 14:22). The Lord himself also says that the way is narrow and the gate constricted that leads to life.

**17.** To understand that those who take pleasure in temporal joys and despise divine commands will be burned in eternal fires, while those who patiently endure temporal evils with fear of God will obtain eternal rest, let us consider the rich man clothed in purple and poor Lazarus: the former, after his feasts, was handed over to everlasting flames; the latter, after his hardships, was secure in eternal repose in Abraham’s bosom.

When the burning rich man asked that his tongue be moistened with a drop from the finger of the blessed poor man, the blessed Abraham immediately gave him this reply: “Son, remember that you received good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now you are being tormented, while he rests” (Luke 16:25). There was no other reason why the rich man suffered punishment and the poor man obtained joy and rest, except that the one received good things during his life, while the other received evil things.

**CHAPTER XIII. It is not the same thing to possess and to receive the good things of the present life.—18.** Not all who possess the good things of the present life receive the good things of the present life; nor do all who suffer the evils of this life receive the evils of this life.

Those receive good things during their life who exult in the joy and pleasures of the present life and believe themselves blessed because they see that they are shaken by no adversity.
