Those receive evil things during their life who endure the pressures and tribulations of the present life with fear of God and, with a contrite and humbled heart, sigh not for temporal joys but for eternal ones; they desire not things that pass away but things that endure.

**19.** To those who wish to find joy in the good things of present circumstances, the psalm says: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4:3). And elsewhere: “Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire to seize by robbery. If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61:11).

[Note: The printed editions read: “Do not hope in iniquity” (*Nolite sperare iniquitatem*).]

Blessed James also never ceases to rebuke such people, saying:

“Come now, rich people, weep and howl over the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up treasure in the last days. Behold, the wages of the workers who harvested your fields, which were defrauded by you, cry out, and their cry has entered the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth. You have feasted upon the earth, and you have nourished your hearts in luxury” (Jas. 5:1 and following).

He also commanded that the laughter and joy of such people be turned into mourning and sorrow, saying:

“Cleanse your hands, sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded. Be miserable, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you” (Jas. 4:8–9).

**CHAPTER XIV. In the future retribution neither the good nor the wicked will be deprived.—20.** Let us not think that the sorrow of the humble and the joy of the proud, the mourning of the devout and the joy of the impious, can be deprived of future retribution. A fitting reward remains for each [alternatively, “for both”], to be rendered at the divine judgment, which the judge himself is known to have decreed in this sentence:

“Woe to you who are filled, for you will hunger; woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep. Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh. Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Luke 6:25; Matt. 5:5).

David also says that such people cast their seeds in tears, yet he does not fail to say that they will reap with joy and exultation. Thus he says:

“Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds. But coming, they will come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125:5–6).

He also declares that the Lord now draws near to such people, saying: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit” (Ps. 33:19).

Tribulation is so beneficial to Christians that through it our spirit becomes a sacrifice to God. For it is written in the psalm: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50:19).

**CHAPTER XV. Exhortation to prompt conversion.—21.** Instructed by these and countless similar testimonies, let us hasten above all things to turn to God as quickly as possible. Scripture says: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day, lest his anger come suddenly and destroy you at the time of vengeance” (Sir. 5:8).

Once converted, let us in no way despair of the forgiveness of sins, holding fast to the Lord’s faithful promise, in which he says: “When you turn back and groan, you will be saved” (Isa. 30, according to the Septuagint).

Let us patiently endure the pressures and tribulations of the present time, and in no way depart from the fear of God. For the Apostle commands us to be patient in tribulation (Rom. 12:12). He also testifies that correction in the present time is of great benefit to us for avoiding the punishment of the future judgment, saying: “When we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with this world” (1 Cor. 11:32).

**CHAPTER XVI. In our tribulations let us give thanks to God.—22.** In the tribulations themselves, however, let us give thanks to the Lord, and in tribulation let us say what the holy Azariah said in the furnace:

“Blessed are you, Lord, God of our fathers, and praised and glorious is your name forever; for you are just in all the things that you have done for us, and all your works are true, and your ways are upright, and all your judgments are truth. You have executed a judgment of truth according to all that you have brought upon us and upon the holy city of our fathers, Jerusalem. For in truth and judgment you have brought all these things upon us because of our sins. For we have sinned and acted wickedly by departing from you, and we have sinned greatly in all things; we have not obeyed your commandments, nor kept them, nor done as you commanded us, so that it might be well with us. And all that you have brought upon us, and everything whatsoever you have done to us, you have done in true judgment” (Dan. 3:26 and following).

And a little later he says: “And now we follow you with our whole heart, and fear you, and seek your face; do not put us to shame” (ibid., 41).

[Note: Basil. reads: “and we fear your face”; nor does it have the words “and we seek,” which are found in Ms. Corb.]

**EPISTLE VIII, OR BOOK TO DONATUS. On Orthodox Faith and the Various Errors of Heretics.**

[Col. 0360D] To the distinguished lord and most greatly desired son in the love of Christ, DONATUS, FULGENTIUS, servant of the servants of God, greetings in the Lord.

**CHAPTER I. Who shares in life; who is excluded from it.—1.** I give great thanks [Note: Ms. Cod. Colbertinus reads *Multum* (“greatly”), and the Antwerp edition gives the same reading in the margin; the other editions read *Multis* (“many”).] to the Lord, my most beloved son, whose grace has made you such that, although you are younger in age [Note: Ms. Colb. reads *minor* (“younger”).], you desire not the things of the flesh but the things of the spirit. Kindled by the fervor of faith, you have already begun laudably to meditate upon those things by which pleasure does not damnably nourish the flesh, but acknowledged truth spiritually feeds the soul.

[Col. 0361A] I do not doubt that this has come about through his inspiration: although you customarily devote yourself to the study of secular literature, you now apply your affection to divine utterances.

[Note: The word “now” is absent from the printed editions but is found in Ms. Colb.]

You wish, of course, to grasp more eagerly not the source from which inflated eloquence is learned, but the source from which eternal life is acquired. For whoever holds the true faith possesses life: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17). And whoever desires to be instructed in the mystery of that same faith desires to attain knowledge of life; in this life each person grows in proportion as he learns what is true and salutary.

Whoever has grasped the beginning of this knowledge with certainty will arrive at perfection; and whoever has not scorned humbly to receive the milk of apostolic speech will deserve to rejoice in the reception of solid food.

Whether, then, someone is nourished with milk within the Catholic Church

[Note: Ms. Colb. reads: “in the land of the Catholic Church.”]

or fed with solid food, so long as he does not withdraw from the bosom of Mother Church, he will remain a participant in life; for, holding the righteousness of faith, he will also possess life.

Neither will the person who remains in unbelief possess this life, nor the one who persists in crime, since each of them is shown to belong to those who, according to the Apostle’s judgment, “walk in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart” (Eph. 4:17–18).

[Note: Ms. Colb. reads: “of the blessed apostle Paul.”]

[Note: Ms. Ant. reads “alienated from the way of God,” while in the margin it prefers “alienated from the life of God.” Ms. Colb. and Basil. read “alienated from life,” in accordance with the Greek text of the Apostle.]

For the blindness of the heart itself does not know either what it should believe or what it should do.

**CHAPTER II. Donatus is tested by Arians concerning faith in the Trinity. We must be prepared to answer concerning the faith. The faith of the holy Trinity is explained.—2.** You say, then, that certain Arians raised a question concerning the Father and the Son, asserting that the Father was greater and the Son lesser. But because of your ignorance of the divine writings, in which you are less instructed, you did not discover what answer you should give them in defense of the true faith.

I therefore first praise this in you in the name of the Lord: although you did not possess such ability to answer [alternatively, “answering”], a firm

[Note: Alternatively, “most firm.”]

faith in the truth nevertheless remained in your heart. For not everyone who shares in Christ can also defend what he believes by answering questions. It is certainly also part of victory that, so long as a person cannot defend the truth in speech, he nevertheless avoids error with a faithful heart.

It is beneficial for us to follow the most salutary words of the apostle Peter, who commands us always to be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks us for a reason concerning the faith and hope that are in us (1 Pet. 3:15).

Therefore, wishing to be found more ready to answer, you ask to be instructed by our words so that, armed with divine utterances, you may learn how to confront heretics who wish to attack our faith.

[Note: Ms. Colb. reads: “so that you may long be able to confront them, armed with these divine utterances.”]

**3.** Above all, therefore, I urge—or, alternatively, “remind”—you to hold firmly to this: the holy Trinity, that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, is by nature the true God [perhaps, “the one God”]—supreme, true, and good—of one nature, one essence, one omnipotence, one goodness, one eternity, and one immensity.

Thus, when you hear “one God,” namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, understand one nature belonging to that supreme Trinity; and when you hear “Trinity,” recognize the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as three persons of that one supreme divinity.

For there are three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and for this reason it is called the Trinity. But there is one substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and for this reason the Trinity itself is truly proclaimed by the faithful to be one God.

**CHAPTER III. Three persons, not three natures. Equality in the Trinity. Scriptural testimonies that the Trinity is one God. Testimonies for the three persons are wrongly assigned by heretics to the Father alone. The Son is also called Lord God. Who should be called a Christian. The Son must also be worshiped.—4.** That the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three persons is shown by the utterances of Truth itself. Hence our Savior says: “I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me” (John 8:16).

He also says concerning the Holy Spirit: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16–17). He also commanded the nations to be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19).

By these and similar testimonies it is shown that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three persons, but not three natures. Hence that holy Trinity is rightly believed to exist in persons [Note: Ms. Colb. reads: “that Trinity is believed.”]; but the natural unity does not permit the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be called three gods.

And because there can be no diversity in the one nature [Note: Ms. Colb. reads: “in nature.”] of the Trinity, unconfused distinctness remains in the three persons, and substantial equality reigns immutably in the unity of nature.

Therefore it is said of the Son: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Phil. 2:6). And: “Because he not only was breaking the Sabbath, but also was calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18).

To this equality of nature and power also belongs what the Son himself says: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John 5:19).

[Note: Ms. Colb. reads: “Whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise.”]

“And just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes” (ibid., 19, 21).

Therefore, in the nature of the Trinity, everything is so wholly one that nothing there can be separated or divided; everything is so wholly equal that nothing there can be found greater or lesser.

[Note: The word “therefore” is absent from the printed editions but is found in Ms. Colb.]

[Note: Ms. Colb. reads “more or less.”]

The truthful authority of the New and Old Testaments shows us this one God. Of this one God blessed Moses says: “Hear, O Israel: The Lord your God is one God” [alternatively, “The Lord is one”]; and: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deut. 6:4, 13).

And the Lord himself says of himself: “See that I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Deut. 32:39).

[Note: The printed editions read: “I alone am, and there is no other God besides me.”]

Of him blessed David also says: “Who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God?” (Ps. 17:32).

The holy apostle James likewise, proclaiming this one God, says: “You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and tremble” (Jas. 2:19).

5. Nevertheless, we do not overlook these testimonies, nor any similar passages that occur in the divine utterances [Note: [Col. 0363D] Ms. Colb.: “or if there are any similar passages that occur in the divine utterances”]. In them God is asserted to be one and alone; but by heretics they are assigned not to the holy Trinity itself, but only to one Person, that is, to God the Father alone [Note: [Col. 0363D] Ms. Colb.: “to the Father alone”]. Therefore, insofar as, with the Lord God granting it, we are able, let us seek the meaning of the testimonies we have proposed [Note: [Col. 0363D] Thus the Ms. Colb.; the printed editions have: “the testimonies of those passages which we have proposed”]: namely, the one which says, “Hear, O Israel: The Lord your God is one God” [alternative: “The Lord is one”]; and the other in which we read, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve.” We remember that the first testimony we set forth was the one which says, “Hear, O Israel: The Lord your God is one God” [alternative: “The Lord is one”]. We thus both confess this [Note: [Col. 0363D] Ms. Colb. and Ant.: “each”] to be so utterly firm that no one should suppose that he may in any way depart from this testimony.

6. Since, then, the rule of this commandment in no way permits the faithful to worship two gods, let them either believe the Father and the Son to be naturally one God, if they wish to worship one God without violating this commandment—so that they worship neither the Father without the Son nor the Son without the Father—or, because a greater God and a lesser God cannot be one God [alternative: “could not be one God,”], it is necessary that they either call the Father alone their Lord and God and deny in every respect that the Son is their Lord and God, or assert the Son alone to be their Lord and God and abandon the worship of God the Father.

But they cannot deny that God the Father is their Lord and God, since they affirm him to be the Lord and God of all to such an extent that they even strive to subject the divinity of the Son, as though he were lesser, to him by a rightful servitude [Note: [Col. 0364D] Thus the Ms. Colb.; the printed editions have: “as though he were a lesser God, to an unwilling servitude,” or “to an unwilling servitude”]. If, however, they wish to deny that the Son is their Lord and God, they are immediately convicted by the testimony of the Father’s own voice. For through the mouth of the prophet, speaking in the person of God the Father, it is said: “And I will have mercy on the house of Judah [alternative: ‘I have mercy’], and I will save them by the Lord their God” (Hos. 1:7). The authority of evangelical truth also commends him as our Lord and God, where the confession of the blessed apostle Thomas utterly contradicts heretical depravity, as he exclaims and says: “My Lord and my God” [Col. 0363D] (John 20:28).

7. Therefore, since they undoubtedly confess the Father as Lord and are compelled by prophetic and evangelical truth to acknowledge the Son as Lord and God, let them either say that the Father and the Son, while preserving the distinct properties of their Persons, are naturally one Lord and God; or, while confessing only the Father as their Lord and God, let them consequently say that the Son is neither their Lord nor their God. Once they have said this, they will never dare to claim that they are Christians, since a Christian has received his name from Christ; and no one can in any way be a Christian who does not say that Christ himself is his Lord and God.

8. Let them therefore confess the Father and the Son not as two lords and gods [Note: [Col. 0364D] Ms. Colb.: “not as two gods,”], but as one Lord and God, if they wish to hold the truth of the faith and do not wish to be found rebellious against the legal and evangelical commandments. For in this way they will be able [alternative: “were able”] both to preserve the meaning and to fulfill the duty of that testimony which says: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve.”

For no one may worship God the Father in such a way that he does not worship God the Son [alternative: “that you do not worship God the Son”], since it is written concerning the Son himself in Deuteronomy: “Rejoice, O heavens, together with him, and let all the angels of God worship him.” The blessed David also says of him in the Psalms [Note: [Col. 0364D] Thus the Ms. Colb.; the printed edition has: “The blessed David also says of him in the psalm”]: “All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71:11).

## CHAPTER IV. No Creature Is to Be Worshiped. Idolaters Exchange the Truth of God for a Lie.

9. But if the Son, according to his divinity [Note: [Col. 0364D] Ms. Colb.: “dignity”; the printed editions: “divinity”], were not one God with the Father, he would certainly not be of one nature with him; and if he were of another nature, he would undoubtedly be a creature. If he were a creature, the authority of the holy Scriptures would not command that he be served, but rather would prohibit it.

For in the first commandment of the Decalogue, just as the worship and service of the one Lord God are most clearly prescribed, so the worship and service of every creature by the faithful are most emphatically prohibited. There it is said: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery: You shall have no gods besides me” (Exod. 20:2–3).

If this is understood to have been said jointly by the Father and the Son, let the Father and the Son be believed to be one Lord God. But if the Father is believed to have said this without the Son, or the Son without the Father, it is necessary that either the Father or the Son be denied to be the Lord God.

For concerning the one who said, “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery: You shall have no gods besides me,” the holy Moses says: “Hear, O Israel: The Lord your God is one God” [alternative: “The Lord is one”] (Deut. 6:4).

And because this God, commanding that he alone be served and ordering himself to be worshiped by the faithful, strictly forbade anyone to worship a creature or serve a creature—therefore, at the end of that first commandment, he speaks of all the things he created in this way: “You shall not worship them, nor serve them; for I am the Lord your God” (Exod. 20:5).

10. The blessed Apostle, knowing this, declares that the wrath of God is revealed against all the impiety and injustice of those who exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever (Rom. 1:18, 25) [Col. 0365A]. To hold the truth of God is to worship the one God; to turn the truth of God into a lie is to serve the creature.

True religion consists in the service of the one true God. For truth itself is one God; and just as, apart from the one truth, there is no other truth, so apart from the one true God there is no other true God. For this one truth is naturally one true divinity. Thus two true gods cannot truthfully be spoken of, just as that one truth [Note: [Col. 0365D] Ms. Colb.: “one true truth”] cannot naturally be divided.

## CHAPTER V. Scripture Proclaims Both the Father and the Son to Be the True God. Holy Men Are Sons of God, but Not in the Same Way as Christ. Who Exchanges the Truth of God for a Lie. What Must Be Concluded from the Foregoing Arguments.

11. Holy Scripture, which truly and beneficially commends to us one Lord God, makes known to all the faithful the Son as true God just as it makes known the Father as true God.

Concerning the Father, the blessed apostle Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, says: “You turned to God from idols [Note: [Col. 0365D] Ms.: “from all idols”], to serve the living and true God, and to await his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus, who delivered us from the wrath to come” (1 Thess. 1:9–10).

This Jesus Christ is not the Son of God the Father in the same way that we are. He is the proper Son; we are redeemed. He is born; we are made. He is true; we are adopted. But he who is the true Son is also himself true God—not generated by adoption, but naturally born from the Father.

In this true God and true Son there is true divinity because his birth from the Father is natural. Therefore the blessed John, in his Epistle, professes him to be the true Son of the Father, true God, and eternal life, saying: “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know what is true and may be in his true Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20).

To worship the true God, then, and to serve the true God, is certainly not to exchange the truth of God for a lie. But he exchanges the truth of God for a lie who thinks that one should serve a god who is not true [Note: [Col. 0365D] Ms.: “who thinks that one should not serve the true God”].

But the person who serves a creature and worships a creature worships a god who is not true and serves a god who is not true [Note: [Col. 0365D] Ms.: “does not worship the true God and does not serve the true God”], because wherever a god who is not true is worshiped and a god who is not true is served [Note: [Col. 0365D] Ms.: “and the true God is not served”], there the truth of God is changed into a lie.

[Col. 0365D] 12. Since, therefore, by the testimony of the heavenly utterances we know both God the Father to be true God and God the Son to be true God, let them either assert with Catholics that the Father and the Son are naturally one true God, or say that they themselves worship two true gods, contrary to the truth of the holy faith; or let them not fear to declare themselves worshipers of a creature, so that by the plain manifestation of the facts they may recognize that they have exchanged the truth of God for a lie.

For the one truth of the one true God—or rather, the one truth, the one true God—does not permit the service and worship of the true God to be joined to the creature [Note: [Col. 0366D] Ms.: “to join the worship of the true God to the creature”; the printed editions: “to God and the creature”]. True religion likewise allows the faithful to offer the obedience of worship and service to no god except the one true God.

## CHAPTER VI. No Creature Is Truth, but It Is True. In What Respect the Son Is Equal to the Father; in What Respect He Is Less. Christ’s Two Births, Eternal and Temporal.

Every nature that is less than the nature of God the Father is undoubtedly a created nature [Note: [Col. 0366D] Basil: “He permits the obedience of worship and service to no god except him who is God by nature. Whatever is not from the nature of God the Father is undoubtedly a created nature”]. What, moreover, is a created nature except a creature?

Every creature [Note: [Col. 0366D] Ant.: “every creature”; Ms. Colb.: “every nature”], since it is the work of truth, is indeed a true creature, but it is not truth. For only that which is naturally true divinity is naturally truth.

They therefore do not exchange the truth of God for a lie, but hold the saving mystery of the true faith, who believe in their hearts for righteousness and confess with their mouths for salvation (Rom. 10:10) that not the Father alone, nor the Son alone, but the Father and the Son together are one Lord and God.

Since not only the Father God but also the Son God is naturally the truthful God and God who is truth, he remains naturally with the Father one truthful God, one true God, and one truth; for the one truth, which alone is true divinity, altogether forbids two gods to be believed or spoken of.

13. Therefore God the Son, according to the divine nature, is not less than the Father but equal to the Father, because the Son is called true God in such a way that the Father is not called a truer God. For in the true God the very recognition of truth allows nothing to be considered less. Thus in the Father and the Son there remains naturally one equality of true divinity [Col. 0366C] and one unchangeable and eternal majesty.

We truthfully call the Son equal to the Father, yet we also truthfully do not deny that he is less. For we know that God the Son was born from the nature of God the Father and was also born from the nature of the Virgin mother; hence he is true God from the truth of the paternal nature and true man from the truth of the maternal substance.

The eternity of divinity shows him to have been born without beginning, while the temporal assumption of flesh undoubtedly teaches that he was made less.

The Son is equal to the Father, and the Son is less than the Father: equal in true divinity, less in true humanity. He is equal because “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1); but he is less because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 14).

He is equal because, “though he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal to God” (Phil. 2:6); but he is less because “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (ibid., 7).

The Son is equal to the Father because the Lord was born from the Lord; but the Son is less than the Father because from a handmaid he was made a servant. Hence he says: “From my mother’s womb, you are my God” (Ps. 21:11). And again: “O Lord, I am your servant, and the son of your handmaid” (Ps. 115:6).

The Son is equal to the Father because “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3); but the Son is less than the Father because “he was made from a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4:4). Therefore, just as the Son of God is truthfully recognized as coeternal with God the Father, so he is truthfully found to be later than his mother.

14. The eternity of the Father in no way preceded the Son’s first birth; yet the temporal birth of his mother preceded his second birth. In that nature of God the Father, which did not begin to exist, the Son was ineffably born coeternal with the eternal Father. In the nature of the Virgin, which began to exist in time, the same Son was mercifully generated in time from a temporal mother.

In that nature, therefore, the Son is equal to the Father in which he is coeternal with the Father before all things; and in that nature the Son is less than the Father in which he is also later than his mother.

In that nature the Son is equal to the Father in which he is the Creator of angels; in that nature the same Son is less than the Father in which he is the Redeemer of human beings. In that nature the Son is equal to the Father in which, from the beginning of creation, he is worshiped and praised by the angels. In that nature the Son is less than the Father in which he was made a little lower than the angels [Note: [Col. 0367D] This passage, mutilated through most of its length in the printed editions, has been restored here from the Ms. Colb. The printed editions read as follows: “In that nature the same Son is less than the Father in which the creature is worshiped and praised by the angels from the beginning”; everything else was absent].

## CHAPTER VII. Christ’s Being Made Less Pertains to His Human Nature.

15. Apostolic authority has not ceased to demonstrate the mystery of this being made less, saying: “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Heb. 2:9).

Earlier, however, it was clearly shown to which nature this being made less must be assigned, when that testimony of the prophet was brought forward which says: “Lord, what is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:5).

Therefore, before assuming flesh, the Son of God, though he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal to God (Phil. 2:6), because in that form of God the Son is equal to the Father. If he were less, he would not be in that same form of God; but apostolic authority testifies that the Son is in the form of God.

Therefore equality with God was not a robbery for him but his nature, because in the form of the true God he could be nothing other than true God, and the unity of the divine form is itself the natural equality of the one divinity [Note: [Col. 0368D] The printed editions have: “of this divinity”]. Where, therefore, there was unity of form in nature, equality was not robbery. The natural equality of divinity, which existed in the form of God, could not be taken away from the true God.

[Col. 0367D] 16. Hence, while retaining the truth of divinity and receiving the truth of flesh, the one and same Son of God and man was made less than the Father and remained equal to the Father. Therefore truth itself truthfully said both: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), and: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

Christ is therefore truly less than God the Father, because naturally he is descended from the fathers according to the flesh; and the same Christ is truly equal to God the Father, because naturally he is “God blessed above all forever” [Col. 0368A].

Concerning this one Christ, the Son of God, the blessed Apostle says: “To them belong the patriarchs, and from them, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever.”

Therefore the true faith, which in one and the same Christ believes and confesses the truth of both substances, proclaims the one and same Christ, the Son of God, to have been made less according to the truth of his flesh, and according to the truth of his divinity believes and confesses him equal to God the Father.

Thus the true faith worships the Son as one God with the Father, knowing that all creatures must serve the one God, yet knowing that divine service is not owed to a creature [Note: [Col. 0368D] The word “divine” is absent from the printed editions but is found in the Ms. Colb.].

204

## CHAPTER VIII. The Holy Spirit Is Not a Creature but the Creator. The Holy Spirit Is True God. We Are the Temple of the Holy Spirit, as of the Father and the Son. The Holy Spirit Is Equal to God the Father and the Son.

17. Hence the true faith also asserts the Holy Spirit to be Creator, not a creature. For how can he be denied to be the Creator, by whom the strength of the heavens is shown to have been established, when David says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their strength” (Ps. 32:6)? And elsewhere: “You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created” (Ps. 103:30).

He is the Creator of all things who is the maker of human beings. Concerning him the blessed Job says: “The divine Spirit who made me” (Job 33:4). Therefore, just as the Holy Spirit created all things, so, being boundless, he fills all things. And because he fills all things by his boundlessness [Note: [Col. 0368D] The printed editions have: “and because he fills all things”], he is naturally true God.

For it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. 1:7). The blessed David also testifies that the Spirit of God is everywhere, saying of him: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your presence?” (Ps. 138:7).

How, moreover, do the Arians deny that the Holy Spirit is God, when we are the temple of the Holy Spirit just as we are the temple of the Father and the Son? The Apostle says: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3:16).

The Apostle asserts that we are God’s temple in such a way that in the same Epistle he also calls us the temple of the Holy Spirit. For he says: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, whom you have from God?” (1 Cor. 6:19). And to demonstrate that the Holy Spirit himself is God, he immediately added: “Glorify and bear God in your body” (ibid., 20).

18. The Holy Spirit, therefore, is equal to the Father and the Son because he is the Creator of all things, just as the Father and the Son are. The Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son because, being boundless, he fills all things [Note: [Col. 0368D] Thus the Ms. Colb.; the printed editions have: “because he fills the world”], just as the Father and the Son are.

The Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son because he has the members of all the faithful as one temple, just as the Father and the Son do. Who would dare deny that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one divinity, when the bodies of the faithful, which are members of Christ, are themselves the temple of the Holy Spirit?

## CHAPTER IX. Conclusion Concerning the Trinity. In the Three Persons There Is No Diversity of Divine Nature. Baptism Is Ineffective Unless Conferred in the Name of the Trinity.

19. The Trinity, therefore, is the one and only Creator and God of all things; the Trinity is the one and only God who is naturally boundless. Human beings are recognized to have been made in the image of this Trinity, in whose name those baptized are renewed again.

Our Savior taught that the nations are to be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19), so that just as through the work of the Trinity we received the beginning of our creation, so in the name of the Trinity we might receive the grace of divine adoption [Note: [Col. 0369D] Thus the Ms. Colb.; the printed editions have: “so that we might deserve to enjoy grace”].

The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are therefore one true God, who by his omnipotent goodness creates human beings and by his freely given mercy justifies sinners. Besides this one true God [Note: [Col. 0369D] Ms.: “Besides this true God”] there is no God, because when he says, “See that I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Deut. 32:39), he teaches and warns us that it is a grave sin if anyone believes in another god besides the one God [Note: [Col. 0369D] Ms.: “believes in another”].

Without doubt, whoever considers there to be a diversity of divinity in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit believes in another god, since that God who alone possesses true divinity in no way grants permission for another god to be worshiped. Nor can anyone who is found to be alien to the nature of the one true God be named in the sacrament of human redemption.

The mystery of human redemption is in no way completed if the name either of the Son or of the Holy Spirit is removed from baptism.

[Col. 0369C]

## CHAPTER X. Excuse for Brevity.

19 bis. Since the epistolary form does not permit the discourse of our discussion to be extended, the beginnings of your affection should not be wearied by the length of the reading, but rather stimulated by brevity, so that, while you read a short work with pleasure, you may be inflamed more ardently toward longer reading.

Read attentively the few things I am about to say, understand them wisely, and hold them without doubt. From these things may you be able, in affirming the faith, to distinguish truth from falsehood and, with the help of our illuminator himself, to retain the Christian faith [Note: [Col. 0369D] Ms.: “to hold it in his name”].

## CHAPTER XI. In the Trinity There Is One God and One Nature. The Error of the Sabellians.

20. The holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is one God. For the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one nature, but not one Person.

Therefore, so that you may refute or at least reject falsehood while retaining the truth, if you see anyone confessing one nature of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in such a way that he wishes to assert one Person, do not consider him a catholic Christian, but recognize him as the heretic Sabellian.

## CHAPTER XII. The Error of the Arians. In What Respect the Sabellians and Arians Are to Be Accepted and in What Respect Rejected.

21. But if you hear anyone speak of three Persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—in such a way that he wishes to assert three natures of these three Persons [Col. 0370A], recognize him without doubt as the Arian heretic.

It is true that the Sabellians believe the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to have one nature; but it is false that there are not three Persons. It is also true that the Arians speak of three Persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; but it is false that they strive to persuade others that these three Persons have three natures.

The Arians therefore perversely divide the nature of the Trinity, while the Sabellians confuse the Persons. For the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one nature, but are not one Person, since the Person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another.

## CHAPTER XIII. The Error of the Macedonians.

22. But if you see anyone confessing that the Father and the Son have one nature while proclaiming that the Holy Spirit has another substance, so that he calls the Son equal to the Father but asserts the Holy Spirit alone to be lesser, that person does not hold the truth of the catholic faith, but follows the error of perfidy born from Macedonius [Note: [Col. 0370D] Thus the Ms.; the printed editions have: “but follows the error of Macedonian perfidy”].

Therefore, since he is not a catholic Christian but a Macedonian heretic, he must be rejected by all the faithful.

## CHAPTER XIV. The Truth of Christ’s Human Nature.

23. Now give attention to a few things concerning the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation. Christ the Son of God, who professes himself to be the Truth, is true God and, likewise, true man. In him there is the fullness of the divine nature, and likewise the fullness of human substance [Note: [Col. 0370D] Ms.: “In him, just as there is the fullness of human substance, so there is in him the fullness of the divine”].

For in him there is the natural truth of divinity, the natural truth of a rational soul, and the natural truth of flesh. Accordingly, his natural divinity is shared with the Father, while his natural humanity is shared with the Virgin mother.

## CHAPTER XV. The Heresy of the Manichaeans.

24. If, therefore, anyone proclaims true divinity in Christ in such a way that he strives to deny his true flesh, he is not a catholic Christian but the heretic Manichaeus, since Christ himself said to his doubting disciples: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have” (Luke 24:39).

## CHAPTER XVI. The Error of the Photinians. Christ Is the Mediator of Human Beings Because He Shares Both Natures.

25. Again, if anyone proclaims the truth of soul and flesh in Christ in such a way that he refuses to acknowledge the truth of divinity in him—that is, if he calls Christ a man in such a way that he denies him to be God—he is not a catholic Christian but the heretic Photinus [Col. 0370D].

For just as, according to his true divinity, Christ is the Creator of human beings, so, according to his true flesh, he is the Mediator of God and human beings. He would in no way be the Mediator if he did not possess either the nature of divinity in common with the Father or the substance of flesh and soul in common with human beings.

The man Christ Jesus is the true Mediator of human beings in that from the Father he naturally possessed the form of God, through which he would save us, and from the Virgin he received the form of a servant, which he would save in us. But no human being would ever receive from God the grace of salvation if, in the one Person of Christ, the communion of divine and human nature did not remain [Note: [Col. 0371D] Ms.: “if in the one Person Christ did not continually remain in divine and human nature”].

## CHAPTER XVII. Two Natures in the One Person of Christ the Mediator. Christ’s Two Natures Are Neither Confused nor Do They Constitute Two Persons. The Contrary Errors of Eutyches and Nestorius.

26. Thus the truth of Christ has the natural truth of divinity from the Father, just as it has the natural truth of humanity from the Virgin. For the only-begotten God deigned to become in the Virgin’s womb the bearer of human flesh and soul, so that he might be the Savior of human flesh and soul.

He is one, in whom there is a twofold, inseparable, and unconfused nature [Note: [Col. 0372D] Ant.: “undivided”], and one Person of both natures.

In him two other heretics, known to have introduced [alternative: “established”] mutually contrary errors, are exposed: Nestorius and Eutyches.

Nestorius, because he recognized two natures in Christ, attempted to proclaim two Persons in him. Thus, with a heart blinded by the darkness of falsehood, he did not hesitate to join the lie of his perfidy to the Christian faith. For just as the true faith truly proclaims two natures in Christ, so it entirely denies two Persons in him.

Eutyches, rightly believing in one Person in Christ, nevertheless appeared perversely to proclaim one nature in him, since the true faith recognizes in Christ at once the distinct properties of both natures and one Person of divinity and humanity.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Sabellius, Arius, Manes, Photinus.

27. There is one Christ, who was “In the beginning the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” He is also the one of whom it is said: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Here the Sabellian is defeated, because in the statement that “the Word was with God” it is shown that the Person of the Father is one and the Person of the Son another. Here also the Arian is overcome, because in the statement that “the Word was God” it is shown that the Father and the Son have one nature.

The statement that the Son alone is called the Word serves to demonstrate the distinct property of the Person; the statement that the Son is called God, just as the Father is called God, pertains to demonstrating the communion of one nature.

Here also the Manichaean and Photinus are simultaneously confounded by the statement: “And the Word became flesh.” In the name “Word” true divinity is recognized, and in the name “flesh” true humanity is found, so that Christ the Son of God, true God and true man, may be recognized in the natural truth of both names.

Thus neither may the Manichaean dare to proclaim flesh in him as false, nor may Photinus deprive him of his natural divinity.

## CHAPTER XIX. Nestorius and Eutyches Are Refuted from the Apostle. The Two Substances Remained Unconfused in the One Christ, and His Person Was Not Doubled.

28. Nestorius and Eutyches are convicted by the apostolic utterances: Nestorius, so that he may recognize that Christ’s one Person cannot be doubled; Eutyches, so that he may know that Christ’s twofold nature cannot be confused.

For Christ is one, concerning whom the Apostle says what was already set forth above: “To them belong the patriarchs, and from them, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5). Here, full of the Holy Spirit, he demonstrated both one Person and a twofold nature in Christ.

By saying, “From them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God above all, blessed forever,” he unmistakably showed the truth of both natures through the names of God and flesh, and he taught that there is one Person of divinity and humanity in the one name Christ.

For Christ, who is descended from the fathers according to the flesh, is himself God blessed above all forever. The nature that the Son of God has from the Father is not confused with the nature that the same God assumed from the Virgin.

Nor did Christ ever have two Persons, because the same only-begotten God was born from the Father according to his divinity and proceeded from the Virgin according to the flesh.

He who, as God the Word, was born from God is the same Word who, having become flesh, proceeded like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber (Ps. 18:6). He is one, who, while preserving the distinct property of both natures, was crucified in weakness and lives by the power of God.

## CHAPTER XX. Conclusion of the Book, Urging the Complete Reading of the Writings of the Saints.

29. Dearest son, I have sent these things to you because of your holy desire and affection. Through them may you receive a taste of instruction, and from this taste may the desire for longer reading grow in you, so that, with God’s help, you may make greater progress the more diligently you begin to seek the sayings of the holy Fathers and to review what you discover more frequently and attentively.

Thus, with God’s help, may a fuller grace of knowledge come to you, by which you may not only retain the true faith but also refute the deadly falsehood of heretics, believing and firmly holding that in the Trinity there is one nature and three Persons in God, and that in the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, there is one Person and two natures.

208

# EPISTLE IX. Victor to Fulgentius, Earnestly Requesting His Prayers and Sending Him a Discourse of Fastidiosus the Arian to Be Refuted. (C)

To the most blessed lord, equal to the apostles in merits, the holy father Fulgentius, bishop: Victor.

1. The divinely appointed time of the desired undertaking has arrived, in which our request may attain its fulfillment. For it would have been wrong for me, who had so often personally asked your blessedness to respond to the crafty scheme, to delay you when you were willing; among honorable people, whatever is promised by postponement is generally counted as a lie.

But, as your blessedness recognizes better than we do, this was not done by our will; rather, the interval between the different regions had brought an impediment, since we are led back and forth to no purpose. There is no benefit of eternal salvation found there; instead, the mind is distracted by various occupations from seeking the very benefit of the life to come, so that, even when time is available, through the prompting of diabolical fear, none of us is permitted to do anything that might advance eternal salvation.

2. For we put on various passions and desires of this world, which suddenly vanish like smoke. Our attention is so incurably devoted to worldly attractions that, as though we were going to live in this world unchangeably, we scarcely think about the danger concerning either life or death in the eternity to come, although danger lies in both directions [alternative: “in either case”]. We concern ourselves only with what we presently know will benefit our desires.

However much benefit accrues to our will, we consider it little, in accordance with the judgment of the blessed Cyprian: “What else is carried on daily in the world but a battle against the devil?” A little later he continues: “If greed has been struck down, lust rises up; if lust has been restrained, ambition succeeds it; if ambition has been despised, anger exasperates, pride inflates, drunkenness entices, envy breaks harmony, and jealousy cuts off friendship” (*On Mortality*, shortly after the beginning), and so forth.

The venerable man clearly saw that the soul is wounded daily by so many arrows of the enemy; and from this the soul cannot be rescued by its own strength, but only by divine mercy.

3. Therefore we earnestly implore you with tears to deign to entreat his mercy for us, together with all those whom you have acquired for the Lord and, rescued from the squalor of worldly affairs, have turned toward the spiritual life, so that he may show us the light of his mercy; so that he may not take vengeance upon our sins; so that we may not die in our offenses; so that we may be stripped of the snares and fetters of the enemy; so that he may not rejoice that he has won the soul whom the Lord redeemed with his own blood.

But this we beg most fervently: join our supplication to your righteous prayers, and our groans to your holy tears, so that through your intercessions we may deserve to carry away the help of the future life, and that we who are dead through sins may rise again through your holy prayers. For otherwise the prophet Elisha could not have raised the lifeless corpse unless, conforming the disposition of his limbs, he had made himself equal to that body (IV Kings 4:3–4). Greatness made itself a little smaller so that, when he kissed the dead boy, he might apply life to him and restore the boy alive. One man prostrates himself, and two arise; and suddenly he who had come back to life through another’s breath is restored unharmed to his mother. So also I trust that through your intercession I may be restored alive to the mother Church, I who seem to be held fast by the sting of death under the weight of burdensome sins.

For I know that, in the youthful season of life, many years ago, you sought the salvation of our soul and very often petitioned the Lord for this, asking that he rescue me from the temptations of this life. And because, still weighed down by the mass of my sins, I have not been able to merit this, I beseech you to deign to entreat the Lord for us with continual supplications, so that, in whatever rank or time, he may obtain forgiveness for our offenses.

4. And lest our tearful and prolonged prayer produce weariness in the heart of your fatherly affection, we must ask you once more that your promises may be followed by swift fulfillment; and that there may be a clear response to the wicked work of the man who, disdainfully scorning the spiritual life of venerable monks—and, in worldly terms, regarding it as something utterly contemptible—boasts that he has flown as far as the cedars of Lebanon. His name, unless I am mistaken, I seem to have expressed more clearly through the sequence of words in the preceding verse. I have sent you his treatise: having begged words here and there, he appears to have barked against the true faith and Catholic truth; and, as though wounding the Homoousians (as he called us) and the Donatists with the arrows of his objections, afterward claimed Catholic orthodoxy for himself, as your fatherly attention will carefully perceive from its reading.

Therefore we ask that this man’s vanity be refuted from the honey-flowing fountain of your fatherly teaching, and that a brilliant reply be made to its author, the serpent, from whom this man, feeding on evil grasses, appears to have sprouted, as it were, a kind of new error. May every wickedness devised against God be suppressed, lest those who read him suppose that he has said anything sound against the faith of the dogma. Let the cunning of the ancient serpent be confounded, because he has gathered such preachers to himself through various enticements of sedition and pleasure; and disperse his viperous, poisonous, three-forked tongue by your holy replies. At that time he was acting not as a teacher but rather as a flatterer of falsehood.

May the fabrication that he left to his descendants vanish from their minds as you reply to it—the fabrication by which he wished to wage war against the mystery of God. Therefore we ask you, with the Lord’s help, to extend in this matter the merit of a good reputation and your illustrious talent to everyone. And since the present heat seeks something fresh, I have boldly expressed the desire of my heart, possessed by the affection of our ancient friendship; and just as you shine before the minds and eyes of those who behold you more brightly than the other priests, so we desire you frequently to appear, to us and to all the nations, even more radiant through your flourishing little works.

5. Relying upon this devout love, I, unskilled in such matters, have written: thirsting with exceedingly ardent desire for the fountain of knowledge and instruction, I ran eagerly toward it with my rustic eloquence. Therefore we wish our thirst and ignorance to be satisfied, so that I may deserve not only to obtain the reward of the future life—as I sought the assistance of your prayers at the very beginning of this letter—but also to rejoice that this work has been fulfilled in every respect; so that not only we, but also all our fellow servants, your sons, whose devotion depends upon you with pious affection and expects this from you together with us, may, together with them, give thanks to the divine gift [an. *referat?* = “may give back,” “may render”].

And we ask you to pardon our rusticity, since you yourself ordered me to dare these things. Although little or no knowledge of a teacher has imbued us, there is also this circumstance: even if we retained something conceived in our heart, entangled in other occupations we have almost lost the use of Latin speech, according to that saying:

> Our hearts, admitting not two cares.

But pray that the Lord may grant and accomplish what we desire. Therefore guide and adorn the servant whom you have nurtured, and grant the teaching that you have so often taught. May eternal divinity preserve your blessedness, which prays for us; this is what we desire, lord Father.

## SERMON OF THE DISDAINFUL ARIAN (C)

[Col. 0375A]

We say, most prudent brothers, what the divinity deigns to bestow upon our littleness. God is the author of justice and of life; indeed, he himself is our justice and our life. He made man neither for sin nor for death, as Scripture says: “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living” (Wisdom 1:13).

What, then? Death befell the man whom God had made. It is not attributed to the Creator but to the deceiving devil. After man had been deceived by the devil—man who willingly committed iniquity and unwillingly fell into death—he transgressed unjustly and was punished justly.

When God therefore saw these two things in man, guilt and death—one which he had wickedly committed, the other which he had justly suffered—and when man was held bound by these two very powerful chains, he commanded that the Lord Christ assume flesh: not flesh in which he would become a debtor through sin, but flesh in which, without the debt of sin, he would undeservedly endure death on behalf of debtors. He did this not so that the Son of God would be bound by the chain of iniquity, but so that sinful man would be released from that chain.

This is what the Apostle says: “The great mystery of piety, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the Gentiles, believed on in the world, and taken up in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16). And truly, most learned Christians, what greater piety could there be than that, for the sake of carnal human beings, the Son of God—subject to his Father’s command—should assume human flesh, and that Life should endure death for mortals? That he who was begotten before the ages, established by the Father, should in the last time be born of a Virgin? That he who gives life to the world should lie dead in a tomb?

With how many tears, then, must we now lament, and with what anguish of heart must we mourn, that so many people still refuse to abandon the obstinacy of their harsh resistance, while indiscriminately they desire to serve a harmful assumption. Since they do not in any way yield to saving remedies, or reject the will to be corrected, they oppose their hands to life-giving words as though to medicinal instruments; they wound themselves by the very means through which they ought to have been healed, and turn the power of spiritual medicines against themselves. From the source by which they might have attained health, they increase the rottenness of their wounds.

For some time now a twofold error has crept in. To this day it binds the souls of the lost and does not allow them to breathe in their search for the truth. The Homoousians assert an inseparable and undivided Trinity, and that the Son was not less than the Father, nor that the Father, who is unbegotten, was the maker of his Son. The Donatists likewise proclaim that the good are defiled by communion with the wicked, while they cast far from them the gift of the holy Scriptures, the remedy of salvation.

Among them, holy mother Catholic Church is known to sing with David’s lament, as we have sung in the present psalm: “Lord, lead me in your righteousness because of my enemies” (Psalm 5:9).

For I am led in your righteousness when I believe you to be the almighty God, unbegotten and uncreated, the maker of your Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, as John the Baptist bears witness: “After me comes he who was made before me” (John 1:11). And as the apostle Peter preaches and says: “Let the whole house of Israel know for certain that God made him both Lord and Christ—this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 2:36). Solomon, too, previously declared in the person of Christ: “Before the ages he established me” (Proverbs 8:23).

Behold: Scripture testifies that the one whom those sacrilegious people abhor believing was made, created, and established. Again, as was said above, they assert that the Trinity is inseparable and undivided. And if the Son, of whom the evangelist says, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), after the power of his divinity had been concealed for a little while, entered alone into the bridal chamber of the Virgin’s womb, then without doubt he was separated from the Father and the Holy Spirit. But the Trinity could in no way be separated from the One, since according to their absurdity it is confessed to be entirely undivided.

Did the whole Trinity, then, assume flesh? Did the whole Trinity suffer the insults of the Passion? Did the whole Trinity lie in the tomb? Did the whole Trinity penetrate the underworld? Did the whole Trinity rise from the dead on the third day? Did the whole Trinity ascend into heaven on the fortieth day? At whose right hand, then, does the whole Trinity sit? Or which Spirit did the whole Trinity send upon the apostles on Pentecost? Or to which God could the whole Trinity say in heaven, “God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1)? Or to which Father could the whole Trinity say, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46)? Let them declare it, if they can.

If they cannot say this, they destroy themselves with their own arrows—those who insist that the Trinity is inseparable.

For Donatist vanity does not consider that the benefit of baptism was bestowed upon human beings so that those who were originally burdened by the errors of others, lifted up by the help of healing grace, might thereafter carry only their own burdens; and that not communion in the sacrament, but each person’s consent to sin, should condemn each one.

For just as the Lord says that he will repay the sins of parents unto the third and fourth generation, because earthly and carnal birth is shown to be subject to original sin, so elsewhere he testifies that the soul of the son is his own, just as the soul of the father is his own, so that the second, heavenly birth may be understood to be entirely absolved from the sins of others. For he immediately adds: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:20).

Solomon’s admonition agrees with this judgment and shows that one person is not burdened by another’s sins: “My son,” he says, “if you are good, it is for yourself and for your neighbors; but if you turn out evil, you alone will bear the evil” (Proverbs 9:12).

Therefore the Catholic faith, fleeing the precipices of every error and, with the Lord leading it back, walking along the path of the heavenly journey, sings with sober belief: “Lord, lead me in your righteousness because of my enemies” (Psalm 5:9).

And it asks of the Father, through the Son, for the straightness of the path by the Holy Spirit, whose free gift has granted it the ability to walk. Just as it confesses that those not yet baptized are liable not only for their own sins but also for the sins of others, since it knows that they were conceived in iniquities, so it asserts that those washed in the water of regeneration are unharmed by another’s iniquity, provided that the consent of their will is not held guilty.

“For as many as believed in him,” says the evangelist John, “to them he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:16).

Therefore, just as those who arise from the will of the flesh and from the will of man draw along with them the sins of others, although they do not yet have sins of their own, so those born of God, if there is no fault of their own will in them, are not stained by any injury of another’s iniquity.

For just as the first birth, through eating, implanted what the one being born had not committed, so the second birth, after original sin has been washed away, imputes guilt only where it lies in the will.

In this matter, therefore, we must be separated from the wicked: in baptism we who possess the first fruits of the Spirit have been buried with Christ and have risen again. In baptism also, by the grace of God going before us and accompanying us, we put off the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error, so that we may put on the new man, who has been created according to God in righteousness and in the holiness of charity. Through the Lord.

## LETTER X. Scarila proposes two questions to Fulgentius: one concerning the Incarnation of the Son of God, the other concerning the creator of lowly animals (C)

[Col. 0377B]

To the holy and most blessed lord, equal to the apostles in merit, Father Fulgentius, bishop, your servant Scarila sends greetings in the Lord.

1. The desires of the unlearned greatly desire the knowledge of your fatherhood, because it is written: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will teach you” (Deuteronomy 32:7); and because we desire to know through the teaching of your holiness what we are unable to understand.

2. While a discussion concerning the Incarnation of God arose at the table of Eventus, a Christian, a son of the Catholic Church, one of us asserted this concerning the Incarnation itself: “It was not God the Father, but God the Son, who put on flesh.” Another said: “The very God who is one in three deigned to assume flesh, so that he might lead our servitude—by which we were held bound through the transgression of our father Adam—into freedom.”

3. We wish to know whether God the Father himself descended and assumed flesh, or whether, while he remained where he was, he commanded the Word to assume flesh; for we know that “the Word became flesh” so that he himself might dwell among us. But the Word, who is God, and the Father, who is God, have one majesty shared by both, which descended to put on flesh, because we read: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him. Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36).

When we brought this testimony forward, the other man replied in opposition: “He said this about the Son, not about God the Father.” And I said at the time: “Since we are equally ignorant of this, let us have recourse to the holy father Fulgentius, bishop, to whom God has deigned to grant knowledge of such great power, so that he may show the way to our ignorance in plain speech through the disclosure of the divine Scriptures.”

Therefore, commending me to your holy prayers, I ask, by him who has endowed your holiness with such great grace, that you, as a good father, order us to be instructed in what we do not know, and that you pour over us from that fountain from which all who thirst are filled.

4. When the discussion had ended, another of us said that God had not made flies, fleas, and scorpions, nor any even fouler animals called bedbugs (*cimices*), but that after the fall of that unworthy angel, the devil, all these things had been made by the devil himself. And when we said that God had made all things, and that they were very good, he said that we ought to consult your holiness about this also, so that you yourself might order the matter to be explained to us: Were these creatures made before the transgression, when God made all things, or afterward, following Adam’s transgression?

Pray for us, holy and most blessed father, lord.

## LETTER XI. The deacon Ferrandus proposes two questions to Fulgentius concerning the salvation of an Ethiopian catechumen who was baptized when he had already lost the use of his mind through the force of illness and who died without receiving the Eucharist (C)

To the most blessed lord and father Fulgentius, bishop, worthy of all reverence, the deacon Ferrandus sends greetings in the Lord.

1. Those who lack earthly means and are not nourished by the sustained labor of prolonged work, by the skill of an honorable craft, or perhaps by respectable commerce, customarily seek food by sighing and begging at the doors of the wealthy once hunger has driven modesty away; they sometimes knock even upon the most merciful ears of noblemen with persistent requests. For they know that silence does not help beggars.

But I, who suffer from the poverty of an impoverished intellect and am not permitted to work for the food of wisdom through daily meditation upon divine reading because of the many clamorous cares that beset me, being even less capable of investigating doubtful matters, explaining obscure ones, and distinguishing and defining opposites by my own strength—that is, by the strength of my arguments and thoughts—I knock with frequent groans at the door of the heavenly master of the household.

But when I again convince myself that I am unworthy for what I desire to be opened so quickly, I then entreat in a suppliant voice those whom I see to have received, from the innermost chambers of the King’s private quarters, the money of my lord to distribute, asking that they deign to console our hunger with at least modest provisions.

Since you are one of the number of those who desire to multiply the profits of the talents entrusted to you, and since you freely share, without envious concealment, the most precious pearl of the heavenly scribe—which you, as the most faithful merchant, purchased after selling all that you had, so that it might be acquired, possessed, and enjoyed by all—bring forth, I beg you, from your treasury, excellent steward, things both new and old, by which you may enrich the needy, feed the hungry, teach the ignorant, and show the doubter what follows.

2. A certain religious man had a youthful servant, Ethiopian in complexion, brought, I believe, from the farthest regions of a barbarous province, where people are darkened by the dry heat of the fiery sun. He had not yet been cleansed by the sprinkling of the saving bath or whitened by the shining grace of Christ.

Therefore, through the diligence of his faithful masters, he was handed over to the Church to be instructed in the ecclesiastical sacraments; as customary, he became a catechumen. After some time, as the solemnity of Easter approached, he was brought among the candidates for baptism, registered, and instructed. He learned and received all the venerable mysteries of the Catholic religion; after the solemn scrutiny had been celebrated, he was claimed from the devil through the exorcism. He was heard firmly to renounce him, as the custom of the Church required, when he was about to hear the Creed.

Moreover, pronouncing the words of the holy Creed from memory in a clear voice before the faithful people, he received the devout rule of the Lord’s Prayer. Since he now understood both what he should believe and what he should pray, he was being prepared for the future baptism when suddenly he was attacked by violent fevers and became delirious as the fatal illness increased.

The shortness of the days persuaded them to postpone—or rather, to reserve—him for washing at the font together with the others. Why delay with further details? The hour desired by all had arrived, when the people of acquisition, buried with their Redeemer through baptism, would lay aside their former life and, renewed, take up the faith of the new resurrection.

Then he, standing at the last breath, without voice, movement, or awareness, unable to answer the priest who questioned him, was brought in the hands of those carrying him. When we answered on his behalf, as for an infant, he received baptism while utterly absent in mind; and shortly afterward he died, without, I believe, knowing in this present life that he had received it.

3. I now ask whether the loss of his voice harmed him in any way with respect to attaining eternal blessedness. For I am very much afraid that the Lord, to whom all things are possible, denied him the ability to speak because he judged him unworthy of the benefit of the second birth.

For I do not see how an age capable of reason could have been cleansed by another’s confession. Do we not rightly believe that only infants are saved through the faith of those who present them, since we know them to be condemned only by original iniquity? Divine justice accomplishes this in wondrous ways: where personal, that is, actual, evil is entirely absent, personal will is likewise not required; rather, through the abundance of grace, salvation is given while others believe, just as guilt is assigned while others sin.

But this man lived according to his own will. In addition to what he had drawn from the root, he had undoubtedly contracted many vices through his own desire; he was bound by the chains of numerous sins, and could be saved only by voluntary belief. Yet at the place of redemption he neither wished nor was able to confess that belief, since, perceiving nothing, he was altogether unable to will anything.

Or perhaps did a prior confession, made while he was conscious, merit forgiveness of sins even when he was unconscious? But I hesitate to say this, lest someone truthfully say to me: “Then he would have been saved even if he had not reached the washing of the body itself, since, as you assert, he had merited the benefit of purification through the mysteries already completed.”

4. Finally, why should we not also baptize the dead, whom sudden death has often snatched away from the sacred baptism, although their will and faithful devotion were known to everyone?

If I try to grant assent to one who responds in this way, a great absurdity immediately follows: it would seem that, since those mysteries alone were sufficient and conferred complete salvation, the person would receive the water of the eternal font not in order to be reborn but as one already reborn.

I see that in this matter the customary judgment of the canons might be proposed. It orders the sick to be baptized if they cannot answer for themselves but others, at their own peril, have testified to their will. Under this definition, I rather think that what the Church ought to do is commanded than that what he receives is indicated. That is, the minister of the word is to be free from the guilt of negligence, not that the sick man is thereby shown to be a sharer and participant in righteousness.

This is especially so because, although I see many being moved by this matter, I myself am often moved still more, as I hesitate about what judgment should be held concerning those who, even if they are baptized with a sound mind and according to due form, are prevented by death, which comes more swiftly, from eating the Lord’s flesh and drinking his blood.

For the Savior’s words are known to the faithful: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). Therefore we ask you to instruct us with a swift response: whether it harms, how much it harms, or whether it does not harm at all, if someone baptized in the name of the holy Trinity is deprived of the sacred food and drink.

Deign to answer both questions together—questions which, as we believe, we must ask with the presumption of charity, and which we suggest will be most useful to many. May our God deign to preserve your fatherhood for our edification, my lord and ever-father.

## LETTER XII. Fulgentius replies to Ferrandus concerning the proposed questions about the salvation of the dying Ethiopian

To the venerable lord, greatly to be desired in the love of Christ, the holy brother and fellow deacon Ferrandus, Fulgentius, servant of the servants of Christ, sends greetings in the Lord.

### CHAPTER I

1. I rejoice, holy brother, that in your heart the flame of charity, which is poured forth through the Holy Spirit, is nourished as grace continually increases. It enables you to recognize something manifest in the writings concerning matters that seem doubtful to most people, lest, while there is uncertainty about the very sacrament of salvation, the grace of the Savior be thought to be given to believers in vain.

2. You say, then, that a youthful servant of a certain religious man, Ethiopian in complexion, was handed over to the Church through the diligence of his faithful masters to be instructed in the ecclesiastical sacraments, and was made a catechumen according to custom.

After some time, as the solemnity of Easter approached, he was brought among the candidates for baptism, registered, and instructed. He learned and received all the venerable mysteries of the Christian religion; after the solemn scrutiny had been celebrated, he was claimed from the devil through the exorcism. He was heard firmly to renounce him, as the custom of the Church [of Carthage, in which, by God’s favor, you now serve as deacon] required, when he was about to hear the Creed.

Moreover, pronouncing the words of the holy Creed from memory in a clear voice before the faithful people, he received the devout rule of the Lord’s Prayer. Since he now understood both what he should believe and what he should pray, he was being prepared for the future baptism.

You say that he was attacked by violent fevers and became delirious as the fatal illness increased. You add that the shortness of the days persuaded them to postpone—or rather, to reserve—him for washing at the font together with the others.

You also say that the hour desired by all had arrived, when the people of acquisition, buried with their Redeemer through baptism, would lay aside their former life and, renewed, take up the faith of the new resurrection. Then, as you say, he, standing at the last breath, without voice, movement, or awareness, unable to answer the priest who questioned him, was brought in the hands of those carrying him. When you answered on his behalf, as for an infant, he received baptism while utterly absent in mind; and shortly afterward he died, without, as far as you judge, knowing in this present life that he had received it.

### CHAPTER II

3. After completing this account, you then ask whether the loss of his voice harmed him in any way with respect to attaining eternal blessedness. You testify that you greatly fear that God, to whom all things are possible, denied him the ability to speak because he judged him unworthy of the benefit of the second birth.

You also say that you do not see how an age capable of reason could have been cleansed by another’s confession, since we rightly believe that only infants are saved through the faith of those who present them, and know them to be condemned only by original iniquity. Divine justice accomplishes this in wondrous ways: where personal, that is, actual, evil is entirely absent, personal will is likewise not required; rather, through the abundance of grace, salvation is given while others believe, just as guilt is assigned while others sin.

But this man, as you assert, lived according to his own will. In addition to what he had drawn from the root, he had undoubtedly contracted many vices through his own desire; he was bound by the chains of numerous sins, and could be saved only by voluntary belief. Yet at the place of redemption he neither wished nor was able to confess that belief, since, perceiving nothing, he was altogether unable to will anything.

4. In these words of yours you cautiously raise another question, saying: “Or perhaps did a prior confession, made while he was conscious, merit forgiveness of sins even when he was unconscious? I hesitate,” you say, “to say this, lest someone truthfully say to me: ‘Then he would have been saved even if he had not reached the washing of the body itself, since, as you assert, he had merited the benefit of purification through the mysteries already completed.’ Finally, why should we not also baptize the dead, whom sudden death has often snatched away from the sacred baptism [F.: *baptism*], although their will and faithful devotion were known to everyone?”

You then add that if you tried to grant assent to one responding in this way, a great absurdity would immediately follow: it would seem that, since those mysteries alone were sufficient and conferred complete salvation, the person would receive the water of the eternal font not in order to be reborn but as one already reborn.

5. Finally, lest anything be thought to have been insufficiently considered by your most watchful intelligence and devout concern, you add that in this matter the customary judgment of the canons might be proposed. It orders the sick to be baptized if they cannot answer for themselves but others, at their own peril, have testified to their will.

Under this definition, you say that you rather think that what the Church ought to do is commanded than that what the sick man receives is indicated. That is, the minister of the word is to be free from the guilt of negligence, not that the sick man is thereby shown to be a sharer and participant in righteousness.
