This is especially so because, although, as you say, you see many being moved by this matter, you yourself are often moved still more, as you hesitate about what judgment should be held concerning those who, even if they are baptized with a sound mind and according to due form, are prevented by death, which comes more swiftly, from eating the Lord’s flesh and drinking his blood.

You raise this question because the Savior’s words are known to the faithful: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). Then you ask that I instruct you with a swift response, whether it harms, how much it harms, or whether it does not harm at all, if someone baptized in the name of the holy Trinity is deprived of the sacred food and drink.

Since, therefore, charity commands us to answer both questions together, it is fitting that charity willingly obey the charity that commands. We hope, moreover, that his grace will deign to be present for the payment of charity’s debt—he from whom charity itself is inspired.

### CHAPTER III

6. First, then, we must remember that judgment which the Savior’s gratuitous benevolence proclaimed generally for the salvation of the human race.

I now mean the judgment that the Lord himself wished to remain fixed in our minds all the more firmly because he deigned to proclaim it later than all his other commandments. For after the resurrection, when he was about to ascend bodily into heaven but was to remain with his own on earth in divinity, he is found to have said this to his disciples: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature: whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:15).

Here the Lord rightly foretold that the one who believes and is baptized will be saved, while he plainly showed that the one who does not believe must be condemned without question. In one who does not believe there could be no basis for a future baptism. For whoever does not believe, whether baptized or not baptized, will undoubtedly be condemned.

7. By this judgment, in which the Lord decreed and defined that every unbeliever would be condemned to everlasting punishment, it is undoubtedly established by divine decision that not only those whom the end of this life finds separated from the sacrament of baptism, but also all heretics, are to be condemned.

For if the faith that blessed Paul, filled with the divine Spirit, asserts to be one is that which is not false but true (Ephesians 4:5)—because “the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5)—how is someone said to believe when the truth of faith is not held by him?

Whatever the mind of one who believes contains that is recognized as alien to the truth of faith must necessarily be falsehood. But “the Lord hates all who work iniquity, and he will destroy those who speak falsehood” (Psalm 5:7). Therefore Wisdom also says in Proverbs: “My mouth shall meditate upon truth, but lying lips are an abomination before me” (Proverbs 8:7).

Therefore those who do not hold the truth of faith in heart and mouth do not receive salvation in baptism. And so, although they possess the form of piety, which consists in the sacrament of baptism, by denying the power of piety they receive neither life nor salvation. What remains for such people except everlasting condemnation, which false and feigned faith will bring upon them?

In such people there is no charity from a pure heart, since, according to blessed Peter’s statement (Acts 15:9), the Lord purifies the hearts of his own by faith. Nor can there be purity of heart where faith is absent, since faith cannot be called faith at all where it is not true.

Since, therefore, where there is charity from a pure heart, there is faith that is not feigned but true, and since the heart is purified not by a feigning of faith but by truth, it is evident that among heretics—among whom there is not truth but a fiction of faith—charity from a pure heart cannot be found at all.

How can they have a good conscience, when the prince of wickedness dwells in them through unbelief? Therefore, unless they convert and are saved by the truth of faith, they will be condemned for the crime of unbelief, because they did not love him in whom they did not believe according to the truth of faith; nor could there be a good conscience in those who are known to have maintained deadly faithlessness against the true faith to the end of life.

8. Let no one be troubled by the fact that the blessed Apostle called it faith, although it was feigned, because elsewhere he proclaimed one faith just as he proclaimed one God. The blessed Apostle used that expression not according to the truth of the matter but according to the opinion of believers.

For the same apostle both calls what was preached by the pseudo-apostles “another Gospel” and confirms that it is not another Gospel. This is contained in his letter written to the Galatians, in these words: “I am amazed that you are so quickly transferring from him who called you in the grace of Christ to another gospel, which is not another” (Galatians 1:6).

How, then, is it another Gospel if it is not another, unless it is another according to the error of the faithless, but not another according to the truth of faith?

So also faith is fabricated by the faithless according to their own opinion; they do not possess the true faith that the Spirit pours in divinely (variant: “the divine Spirit”). The blessed apostle likewise points out knowledge falsely so called, saying: “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and oppositions of falsely named knowledge” (1 Timothy 6:20).

Just as what is falsely called knowledge is not knowledge, so the faith that the divine Spirit does not pour in but that the human spirit invents for itself is certainly not faith. Thus, according to their opinion, it is called faith, although it is found in no way to be faith.

For we also find gods called gods in the sacred utterances, although those very divine utterances plainly testify that they are not gods. It is said in the Psalms: “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 96:5). Jeremiah likewise says: “The gods that did not make heaven and earth shall perish from under heaven” (Jeremiah 10:11).

Yet elsewhere he shows that those whom he calls gods are not gods. For he says: “Cross over to the island of Kittim (Cethim) and see; send to Kedar and understand carefully, and see whether such things have happened. Has a nation changed its gods, although these are not gods?” (Jeremiah 2:10).

9. We find the name of God in the Holy Scriptures, so far as it now occurs to us, in four ways. For God is called God according to the truth of nature, as the holy Trinity alone is one, true, and immutable God, who says: “See that I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Deut. 32:39); and of whom David says: “Who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God?” (Ps. 17:32). This is the one and only God who is naturally God.

From this one true God, certain beings received the status of gods, not naturally, but by the gift of grace. Among such gods was Moses, to whom that one true God says: “Behold, I have appointed you god to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1). Such are also those of whom it is said: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6). These gods, therefore, received the grace by which they were gods, just as they received the grace by which they became sons of God. The evangelist says: “As many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name; who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God” (John 1:12). To these same persons it is said: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6).

10. These, then, are two commendable ways of naming: one by which the true God is called God naturally; the other by which God, through grace, has bestowed this name upon whom he wished. Yet they are distinguished from one another by a great difference. For that mode by which natural truth is shown in the name “God” demonstrates one God through the very natural truth of the name, so that it never permits gods to be called gods within itself. Hence, just as the Father alone, or the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone is truly called God, so the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together are truly named not three gods, but one God. This is what that Trinity, one God, possesses: that there are indeed three persons, but that there are not three gods, because that Trinity is one true God.

Therefore the Son of God is believed and proclaimed by us to be true God not only according to his true divinity, which he has from the nature of the Father, but also according to the flesh, which he naturally has as a true reality from the body of his mother. For the Son’s eternal divinity together with his complete humanity, and that same complete humanity of the Son together with his eternal divinity, constitute one person in the Trinity; and he himself, the only-begotten Son, wholly in his divinity and humanity, is one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

The other mode, however, because it is not of nature but of grace, receives the name “gods” without any perversity of faith, because it includes only the multitude of adopted sons, to whom the one true God, the supreme Trinity, gave the power to become sons of God.

**CHAPTER IV**

In the one mode, therefore, the splendor of nature is acknowledged; in the other, the generosity of grace is found.

11. The two remaining ways in which God, or some thing or person, is named are found to be more worthy of blame than praise. In both, therefore, manifest guilt is found, because none of them can possess either nature or grace. One is according to the affection of depraved desire; the other according to the opinion of error.

For a mind devoted to carnal desire makes that its god which it loves above all else. Hence the blessed Apostle unmistakably declares that the belly is the god of certain people who are wise according to earthly things, saying: “Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame—those who set their minds on earthly things” (Phil. 3:19). I think that here the Apostle used “to set one’s mind on earthly things” in the sense of “to love earthly things.” I believe that the same meaning is contained in the passage where the aforementioned Apostle says: “Therefore, if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, [Col. 0385A] not on those that are upon the earth” (Col. 3:1).

For, showing that they ought not to set their minds on the things that are upon the earth, he added shortly afterward: “Therefore put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols” (ibid., 5). When, therefore, he commands us to put to death our members that are upon the earth, he certainly commands that the desire for earthly things be put to death within us. For this reason it is said elsewhere: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5:24). He also wishes us to consider ourselves dead to these things, saying: “Consider yourselves dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 6:11).

Everyone lives for that which he loves, and shows himself dead to that whose affection he has put to death within himself. Those, therefore, set their minds on earthly things who love earthly things; and those make their belly a god who surrender the service of their heart to the enticing pleasures of gluttony.

12. The opinion of human error has deceitfully fashioned the name of God for its own destruction in two ways. This twofold opinion of error claims no fewer heretics for itself than pagans, since it subjects both groups to itself by binding them all together with diverse bonds of manifold falsehood.

Pagans, having abandoned the true God, serve the superstition of false gods; heretics, however, holding false opinions about the true God, resist the truth of holy religion. It is therefore manifest that heretics are bound by the chain of deadly error, and that those whom the Church endures as obstinate enemies ought not to be called faithful. For it is the guilt of unbelief either to believe something false about the true God or to worship a false god under the name of the true God.

**CHAPTER V**

13. Since, therefore, we took the beginning of our discussion from that saying of the Lord which establishes that “everyone who believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16:15), let us believe that the boy was saved in whom we find that none of the things pertaining to the function and effect of baptism was lacking.

The function of the second birth consists in faith and confession; its effect consists in regeneration. “As many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12). They believe, therefore, in order to become sons of God, since they receive the grace of faith for this purpose: that, by believing, they may receive the grace of the sacrament. For it is fitting that, while one believes in the heart for justification, confession should be made with the mouth for salvation.

It is clear, moreover, that just as the function of believing and confessing belongs to the catechumen, so the effect of baptism belongs to the minister. When confession is uttered by the former through true faith, it follows that, when the latter baptizes, the grace of the saving mystery is accomplished.

14. We see this rule observed in practice in the Acts of the Apostles by the holy Philip. When he was instructed by the Holy Spirit to preach the Lord Jesus Christ to the eunuch, and when they had come to a certain water, the eunuch requested and said: “Behold, here is water; what prevents me from being baptized?” (Acts 8:30). He first elicited the function of confession, to which he would rightly administer the effect of holy baptism.

Therefore he answered the eunuch: “If you believe with all your heart, it is permitted” (ibid., 37). Since the eunuch’s confession came first, the effect of holy regeneration was subsequently fulfilled in him through Philip’s ministry.

By what justice, then, would the one who performed the function of belief and confession not obtain the effect of holy regeneration? For if the order of work and reward is considered, the work lies in faith and confession, and the reward in baptism. A person is therefore judged worthy of baptism when the merit of faith and confession precedes, and the sacrament of holy baptism is granted to it as a reward. “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7).

He who, through divinely given devotion of heart and mouth, performed the work of belief and confession ought not, therefore, to be deprived of the reward of baptism. He was not to be asked at the hour of baptism to confess what he had already confessed in the recitation of the Creed. Thus the loss of his voice did not harm him in attaining eternal blessedness, since, for as long as he was able, he remained in that confession of faith. His confession was not taken away or changed; nor was what he had said abolished when he could no longer say it, because, for as long as he could perceive, he did not change his conviction.

15. “But,” you say, “I fear that the Lord, to whom all things are possible, denied him the ability to speak for this reason: that he judged him unworthy of the benefit of the second birth.”

Rather, let us recognize there the Lord our God as one who did not forget his mercy. Although he took away the boy’s voice, he did not take away his life, so that he might receive alive what he had granted him to believe and confess.

16. But it is asked: “How could an age capable of reason be cleansed by another person’s confession?”

Rather, it is found to have been cleansed by its own confession. The confession of others could not have benefited him then if his own confession had not preceded it. The confession of others therefore benefited him in a secondary way, without doubt, when it did not forestall an unwilling person, but came to the aid of one who was failing; and what enlightened will had begun in him by believing and confessing, fraternal charity completed on his behalf.

**CHAPTER VI**

We read that the Lord said: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I will also confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:32). As long as this boy had the ability to speak, that confession was not lacking. Who, then, would dare to say that this confession was unworthy of salvation, when he sees that it was rejected not through perversity of will, but constrained by the necessity of infirmity?

His tongue was weakened, but his conscience was not corrupted. The Apostle says: “Having the same spirit of faith, as it is written: I believed, and therefore I spoke; and we also believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4:13). The one who, having received the spirit of faith, believed and spoke could have been deprived of that Spirit, by which he received the ability to believe, if he had denied the faith. Since he did not deny it, he certainly was not deprived of the Spirit.

By that same Spirit through which he spoke while believing, he was redeemed while silent, because it is through that Spirit that the second birth is completed, through which the second act of believing is granted. Therefore, since the sound will to believe and confess was not lacking in the healthy person, the necessity of silence did not harm the infirm one.

**CHAPTER VII**

17. It is true that we rightly believe that infants alone are saved by the faith of those who present them for baptism. We know that they are condemned only by original iniquity. Divine justice works this out in wondrous ways, so that, in a certain sense, where no personal—that is, actual—malice is found, personal will is not required either; rather, salvation is given through the abundance of grace to those who believe on behalf of others, just as guilt is imputed to those who sinned on behalf of others.

But you add that this boy lived by his own free choice. In addition to what he had drawn from the root, he had undoubtedly contracted many personal vices by his own desire, being bound by the chains of many sins and destined to be saved only by voluntary belief. Yet, at the place of redemption, he neither wished nor was able to confess, because, perceiving nothing, he was altogether unable to will anything.

These words, dearest brother, are yours; they are contained in the letter that you sent.

18. Accordingly, the quality of original sin must first be considered. It was committed by others, but through the fault of generation was transmitted to others. When that age is reached at which personal confession cannot be made, salvation is given to infants through the belief and confession of others, just as guilt is imputed to them through the sin of others.

Since, therefore, in those ages that already use reason a personal confession is sought—for such persons both live and understand, possessing the sin of origin from their life and the sin of their own action from their understanding—we rightly say without doubt that this boy was saved, because he believed with understanding and confirmed what he believed by his own confession. Then, although he no longer understood, he nevertheless still lived and received the sacrament of holy regeneration.

For through the sacrament of holy baptism that life was released from the bonds of original sin, having previously been bound by those same bonds. And because the power of holy baptism is so great that, wherever it finds life in which to dissolve the bond of original sin, it also washes away, through the benefit of the second birth, everything additional that it finds there, according to what the Apostle says: “Judgment from one offense brought condemnation, but grace from many offenses brought justification” (Rom. 5:16)—we rightly believe that he was saved, since before baptism he did not lack belief or a confession of understanding, and at the hour of baptism life remained in him, although he was infirm and feverish.

The life, therefore, that had contracted original sin gave testimony to its conscience and understanding when it could. Even when it could not confess, it received remission of original sin through the merit of that confession. This was especially aided by the consecration of the unity of the Church, whereby it happened that the confession offered earlier, which he could not offer at the hour of baptism because of bodily infirmity, was offered through the assistance of fraternal charity, so that he was helped by the words of those whose fellowship he was destined to share.

Once that original sin had been remitted, no believer doubts that all the sins he had contracted by his own will were also remitted.

Thus the earlier confession of one who knew what he was saying merited remission of sins even when he did not know what he was saying; concerning him, let us have no doubt.

[Note: Several manuscripts and printed editions do not have these words, *de quo* (“concerning him”), but read: “Thus the earlier confession of one who knew what he was saying merited remission of sins even when he did not know what he was saying [Col. 0388D]; let us have no doubt”—where *quod* or *quia* is lacking, thus: “that remission of sins,” etc.]

**CHAPTER VIII**

19. Nor should any suspicion withdraw our mind from this position, lest someone say that the boy “would have been saved even if he had not reached the actual immersion of the body,” since we certainly do not say that he could have been saved by confession alone without the sacrament of baptism.

“For whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.” We affirm that this young man was saved through the sacrament of baptism because we know that he believed and confessed. If he had not been baptized, he would not have been saved, whether knowingly or unknowingly.

Confession was the way of salvation; salvation was in baptism. For at that age, not only would confession without baptism have profited him nothing, but baptism itself would in no way have brought salvation to one who neither believed nor confessed. God therefore willed that confession benefit him because he preserved him in this life until holy regeneration.

The gift of holy regeneration, then, was requested by the boy because he willed it, and was given by God because God willed it.

**CHAPTER IX. Why the dead are not baptized**

20. We do not baptize the dead for this reason: every sin, whether original or actual, since it is shared by soul and body together, is remitted to neither if the soul is separated from its body. “We must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what is proper to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10).

The soul, therefore, is in no way saved without the body if it sinned in the body and did not believe while it was in the body. Consequently, it receives the evil that it did in the body, not the good that, while established in the body, it did not do.

Nor can the flesh be baptized without the soul, since it cannot receive the remission of sins. For a thing that does not live cannot have repentance for sin, just as it cannot sin. How can the sacrament of remission be given where there is no life? Or how can flesh be baptized for the remission of sins where there is no soul, when the fellowship of sin adheres to it together with the soul?

Therefore, even if there was the will and faithful devotion of a living person who nevertheless died without the sacrament of baptism, the dead person could not be baptized because the soul, whose will and faithful devotion it was, had departed from that body.

This man, therefore, about whom we are now speaking, was rightly baptized, because his soul—whose faithful will and devotion were known to all—remained in his flesh until the hour of holy baptism.

The mysteries that are celebrated in the Church before baptism cause the spiritual person to be conceived, not born again. Hence, one will reach salvation if the second birth brings him forth into the light. The person is prepared for that light by those mysteries, but is brought to it through the sacrament of baptism.

This is what I said above: in those mysteries lies the function of salvation, while in baptism lies the effect of salvation. This effect can be denied to him not by the onset of infirmity, but only by a change of will.

**CHAPTER X**

21. Therefore that judgment of the ancient canons must be held most firmly, which commands that the infirm be baptized if they cannot answer on their own, provided that others testify to their will at their own peril.

The holy Fathers saw that a will known to have been hindered, not changed, was not guilty, and that the sacrament of baptism ought not to be denied where firmness of will is recognized.

In establishing this, the holy Fathers indicated both what the Church ought to do and what the sick person receives. The Church would not do this if he received no benefit from the act. For since the Apostle testifies that the Church of God is “the pillar and foundation of the truth,” if it has any part in the mysteries of faith where firm truth is absent, then it is not in all the mysteries the pillar and foundation of the truth (1 Tim. 3:15).

Whatever firmness is taken away from its sacraments must necessarily be taken away from the Church herself. The Church, therefore, is not truly called the pillar and foundation of the truth if she is found to be weak in the principal mystery of human salvation.

But because the Apostle truly calls her the pillar and foundation of the truth, whatever is given and received within her, according to the constitutions of that Church, in the holy mysteries of human redemption and reconciliation, is given with firm truth and received with firm truth.

22. So that we may in no way reject the general constitutions of holy Mother Church—that is, those confirmed by the entirely concordant assent of all the bishops—it is thus commanded in Proverbs: “Hear, my son, the laws of your father, and do not reject the institutions of your mother” (Prov. 1:8).

Who, then, would consider useless what he hears from God must in no way be rejected?

If, therefore, the person who is baptized in this manner is not saved, there is no guilt if this is neglected; nor will the minister of the word be held guilty of negligence if he does not do it, provided that the one in whom it is done cannot be a participant in righteousness.

A person is therefore charged with negligence and found guilty wherever the effect of the work is not despaired of. Just as the person who does not perform what is useful is rightly charged with negligence, so the labor of one who expends effort on superfluous things is rightly judged vain and useless.

And if vain labor is expended in this matter, then the saying of the Apostle Paul will undoubtedly be vain: “Each will receive his own reward according to his labor” (1 Cor. 3:8), since there is no doubt that he was speaking of the ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God, as the passage of the same letter indicates.

For he had said beforehand: “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth” (ibid., 6). What was Paul’s planting and Apollo’s watering except that Paul planted by evangelizing the word of salvation, while Apollo watered by administering the sacrament of baptism?

When the Apostle had said: “Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (ibid., 7), to show that the reward of that planting and watering remains firm, he immediately added: “Each will receive his own reward according to his labor.”

Showing elsewhere in the same letter that the labor of divine work cannot be empty, he says: “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord” (1 Cor. 15:58).

23. The work of God is that which is bestowed upon each living person in such a way that it can benefit either the soul or the body of the one who receives it. Those things that benefit the soul must also benefit the body; but not everything that benefits the body pertains to the benefit of souls. Such are food, drink, clothing, and lodging, which are found not to benefit the soul of the recipient, but the soul of the giver.

The sacrament of baptism, however, is given to a person for this purpose: that the soul may be saved together with the flesh. The minister gives it in vain if he does not give it so that the one who is baptized may receive the gift of eternal salvation. For the sacrament of redemption is given in vain if the person to whom it is given is not redeemed.

But if we attend to one word in your letter, no doubt about this will remain. You said that this was defined by the ancient canons “so that the minister of the word might be free from the guilt of negligence.”

How, however, does the minister incur guilt through negligence in this matter if, through diligence, he accomplishes nothing? He does not incur the guilt of negligence in vain, except because he failed to do what he ought to have done. He ought to have done it because it could have been beneficial if he had done it.

He is therefore charged with the guilt of negligence because he caused harm by failing to do what would undoubtedly have been beneficial if he had done it.

Accordingly, in keeping with the ancient canons, that infirm person whose will is not lacking the testimony of those close to him must certainly be baptized, so that both the minister of the word may be free from the guilt of negligence and the sick person may become a sharer and participant in righteousness.

**CHAPTER XI**

24. None of the faithful should be troubled on account of those who, although they are baptized lawfully while of sound mind, are prevented by death’s more rapid arrival from eating the Lord’s flesh and drinking his blood. This is because of that saying of the Savior: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

Whoever can consider this not only according to the mysteries of the truth but according to the truth of the mystery will see that it takes place in the very washing of holy regeneration.

For what is accomplished in the sacrament of holy baptism except that believers become members of our Lord Jesus Christ and belong, through ecclesial unity, to the structure of his body? The blessed Apostle says to them: “You are the body of Christ and members of a member” (1 Cor. 12:27).

He shows that they are not only participants in the sacrifice itself, but that they themselves are the holy sacrifice, when he commands them humbly to present themselves to God as a living offering, saying: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Rom. 12:1).

Teaching the same thing, holy Peter says: “You also, as living stones, are being built into spiritual houses, into a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 2:5).

Hence, when the blessed Paul had said in one place: “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of the Lord?” (1 Cor. 10:16), he immediately added, to show that we are the true bread and the true body: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, all who partake of the one bread” (ibid., 17).

Elsewhere he says: “One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” (Eph. 4:4). And again: “Speaking the truth in love, let us grow in all things into him who is the head, Christ. From him the whole body, joined and knit together through every supporting ligament, according to the working in the measure of each individual member, makes the body grow for its own building up in love” (ibid., 15–16).

Confirming also that we are the flesh of the Lord, he says: “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, as Christ also does the Church, because we are members of his body and of his bones” (Eph. 5:29–30).

Therefore, because we who are many are one bread and one body, each person begins to be a participant in that one bread when he begins to be a member of that one body. When, in each of its members, that body is joined to Christ the head in baptism, then he is truly offered to God as a living sacrifice.

Through the gift of that birth he becomes a sacrifice, just as he also becomes a temple. Teaching this, the blessed Apostle says: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16).

When someone becomes a member of the body of Christ, how does he not receive what he himself becomes? He becomes, after all, a true member of that body whose sacrament is present in the sacrifice.

By the regeneration of holy baptism, therefore, a person becomes what he will receive from the sacrifice of the altar. We know without doubt that the holy Fathers also believed and taught this.

The blessed Augustine likewise delivered a very clear sermon on this subject, well suited to the edification and instruction of the faithful. I have preferred to append the whole sermon to the letter, because it is not lengthy and, despite its brevity, is full of great instruction and sweetness.

25. “What you see on the altar of God, you also saw last night, but you have not yet heard what it was, what it signified, or what great reality its sacrament contained. What you see, therefore, is bread and a cup, as your own eyes tell you. But what your faith demands to be instructed about is that the bread is the body of Christ and the cup is the blood of Christ.

This has been said briefly, and perhaps it is enough for faith; but faith desires instruction. For the prophet says: ‘Unless you believe, you will not understand’ (Isa. 7:9). You can therefore say to me now: ‘You have commanded us to believe; explain it so that we may understand.’

A thought such as this may arise in someone’s mind. We know where our Lord Jesus Christ received his flesh—from the Virgin Mary. He was nursed as an infant, fed, and grew; he reached youth; he suffered persecution from the Jews; he was hung upon a tree; he was killed on the tree; he was taken down from the tree; he was buried; on the third day he rose again; on the day he willed, he ascended into heaven. He took his body there, from where he is to come to judge the living and the dead. He is now sitting there at the right hand of the Father.

How, then, is the bread his body, and how is the cup—or what the cup contains—his blood?

These things, brothers, are called sacraments for this reason: in them one thing is seen, another is understood. What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has a spiritual fruit.

If you wish to understand the body of Christ, hear the Apostle speaking to the faithful: ‘You are the body of Christ and members’ (1 Cor. 10:27). If, then, you are the body of Christ and members, your mystery is placed upon the table of the Lord; you receive the mystery of the Lord. To what you are, you respond, ‘Amen,’ and by responding you subscribe to it.

You hear, then, ‘The body of Christ,’ and you answer, ‘Amen.’ Be a member of the body of Christ, so that your Amen may be true.

Why, then, in bread? Let us assert nothing of our own here; let us again hear the Apostle himself. Speaking of this sacrament, he says: ‘We who are many are one bread, one body.’ Understand and rejoice: unity, piety, truth, charity—we who are many are one bread, one body (1 Cor. 10:17).

Recall that bread is not made from one grain, but from many. When you were being exorcized, you were, as it were, being ground; when you were baptized, you were, as it were, sprinkled together; when you received the fire of the Holy Spirit, you were, as it were, baked.

Be what you see, and receive what you are.

The Apostle said this about the bread. What we should understand about the cup is also sufficiently shown by what has been said. Just as many grains are brought together so that bread may have a visible form, as though that might be fulfilled which Holy Scripture says about the faithful: ‘They had one soul and one heart toward God’ (Acts 4:32), so also, brothers, recall from where wine becomes one.

Many grapes hang upon a cluster, but the juice of the grapes is blended into unity. Thus the Lord Jesus Christ signified us; he willed us to belong to him; he consecrated the mystery of our peace and unity upon his table.

Whoever receives the mystery of unity but does not preserve [alternative: hold] the bond of peace does not receive the mystery for himself, but a testimony against himself.”

26. Holy brother, I think that our discussion, strengthened by the sermon of the distinguished teacher Augustine, should leave no one in any doubt that each of the faithful becomes a participant in the body and blood of the Lord when, in baptism, he becomes a member of the body of Christ. Nor is he excluded from participation in that bread and cup even if, before eating that bread and drinking from that cup, he departs from this world while established in the unity of the body of Christ.

He is not deprived of participation in and benefit from that sacrament when he is found to be himself what the sacrament signifies.

Pray for us always, strengthened and made steadfast in Christ, holy and venerable brother.

## LETTER XIII. Ferrandus to Fulgentius, proposing five questions

(C)

To the most blessed lord, and holy Father Fulgentius, bishop, worthy of all veneration, Ferrandus, deacon, sends greetings in the Lord.

1. I have often wished, out of a desire to learn, to ask many questions; but the rarity of messengers, because of the length of the journey, prevented me from addressing an absent teacher through frequent letters. Therefore, now prompted by the opportunity of the present occasion, I have gathered together what I could, and briefly ask what your answer may better expand. I ask and beseech Christ, from whom you inwardly hear what you teach outwardly, that you tell me truthfully:

2. Whether the inseparable Trinity, because it has one and the same nature, operation, and will, ought to be said to have separable persons, or whether it should be proclaimed wholly inseparable also in its persons.

Or whether, just as God the Son is said to have been born, to have suffered, to have died, and to have been crucified, we ought likewise to affirm that his divinity was born, suffered, died, and was crucified—although, whenever “God” or “divinity” is named, only the flesh is understood to be mutable and passible, according to which God or divinity could suffer what it could not suffer in its own nature.

Third, I further ask whether the soul of Christ, which received the divinity, has altogether a full knowledge of it; and whether, just as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit know one another, so the same Son knows himself, through that by which he is human, in that by which he is God, comprehending the Father wholly in both substances and in each substance.

Or perhaps, just as with bodily eyes he does not see God, who is spirit, lest it be believed that dignity was added to a human being rather than that nature was wholly changed, so the rational soul, although possessing a devout understanding and a most pure heart, neither sees nor comprehends the whole essence of divinity, lest any creature be found capable of containing the Creator.

Permit me, I beg, to ask again. I wish to propose several matters together, since there is no opportunity for us to inquire about each one separately.

We believe and confess that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one kingdom, understanding that they rule all creatures together. Why, then, throughout nearly all the regions of Africa, has the Catholic Church become accustomed to say in the priests’ prayers: “Through Jesus Christ, your Son, our Lord, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit”?

It seems as though only the Son possesses the kingdom with the Father, and that “in the unity of the Holy Spirit” indicates that the Son and Father are united as reigning, but does not indicate that the Holy Spirit reigns together with them.

Answer these questions, I beg you, quickly, and feed me, who consults you in unpolished speech about matters unknown, with the sweetest honey of heavenly discourse.

Also clarify what it means that the evangelist Luke, when about to narrate the Lord’s Supper, first says that he took the cup and immediately handed it around to the disciples to share among themselves; and then, after taking bread, said: “This is my body”; and after supper, having likewise taken the cup, then said: “This cup is the new Testament in my blood, which is poured out for you” (Luke 22:17 and following).

Was one cup given a second time, or was one given earlier and another afterward? And if so, what sacrament does that earlier cup concern, about which most of the others who wrote the Gospels said nothing?

Do not, I beg you, delay your answer, or keep a prepared mind suspended by a long wait. Surely we ought to earn at least a share of your occupations.

3. I also ask that you order the book *On the Rule of True Faith* [Note: [Col. 0393D] This is the book *On Faith to Peter*, below.] [Col. 0394A] to be sent to us for rereading, and the letter to John, bishop of Tharsus [Note: [Col. 0393D] This letter is not extant.], in which, as I recall, you argued at greatest length concerning not handing over a certain sorcerer to a judge. I received two codices and returned the one belonging to the child Hermias. Also order the letter *On Prayer* [Note: [Col. 0394D] Letter 4 to Proba, above.], which you graciously deigned to have sent to me here where I am staying, to be sent here again in a written copy. For since many people seek it to read because of its brilliance, we do not know with whom it has remained, owing to our forgetfulness. I humbly greet the holy presbyters, the deacons, and the blessed congregation. May our God deem it worthy to preserve your paternity unharmed for our edification, my lord and father. Amen.

## LETTER XIV. Fulgentius, replying to Ferrandus concerning the five questions proposed

[Col. 0394B]

### 1

Your letter, holy brother and fellow deacon Ferrandus, both gladdened my heart and stirred my affection, so that I might rejoice, assured of your well-being, and attentively seek from him an answer to what you ask—him, of course, to whom thanksgiving is due and from whom a true knowledge of salutary things is to be expected and requested. May the same one who grants joy through a favorable hearing also bestow understanding through the infusion of spiritual grace; and just as he himself kindles the desire to seek him, so may he grant access to those who knock at his door.

For only then shall we be able to enter into the joy of our Lord, if here he deigns to lead us by the gift of spiritual grace into that great mystery of piety, and, to prevent the weakness of this life—which frequently creeps upon us in our frailty—from overcoming us, himself grants us the bread of spiritual understanding. May he not allow us to be subjected to the aged corruption of the outward man, but make our inward man, in the pursuit of holy thought [al. understanding] and action, renewed day by day by heavenly light [al. gift]. Let us therefore now set forth the words of your letter, so that we may be able to answer each of the questions as the Lord grants.

230

## FIRST QUESTION

### 2

For you require me to tell you truthfully whether the Trinity, because it has one and the same nature, operation, and will, should be said to have separable persons, or whether it should also be proclaimed to be altogether inseparable in its persons. Without doubt you recognize these as the words of the first question.

## RESPONSE

### 3

Here we must chiefly observe that the Trinity ought not to be called inseparable if those three persons can in any way be separated. For that truly is called inseparable which cannot receive separation in any manner. What is not separated but can be separated is not inseparable.

If someone thinks that the persons in the Trinity can be separated, then it is not the Trinity but the unity that should be called inseparable. The Trinity consists in the persons; unity exists in the nature. But I do not know whether our assertion can be supported by truth when we call the nature inseparable while asserting that the persons of that same nature are separable. For surely one nature, which cannot be divided among the persons, by its own inseparability shows that the persons themselves cannot be separated either.

We find separation of nature without separation of person, to use no more distant example, in human beings themselves. No one doubts that human flesh belongs to human nature; yet it can be separated if any limb is cut off from the body. Such a cutting off, however, cannot in itself involve the separation of the person. For when a hand or foot is cut off from the body, the human person is not separated along with that limb, although a certain separation of nature occurs, since a part of nature is found cut off in the limb.

But just as that man, if he lives after losing the limb, will not lack the fullness of the natural definition by which man is called a rational, mortal animal, so, possessing the true definition of nature, he must also possess his own person together with that nature, even though he has a part of nature—that is, a part of his flesh—separated from him.

When human beings are separated as persons, however, nature is also undoubtedly separated. For the person is not separated when a hand or foot is separated from the body; but nature is separated when one person is separated from another. Therefore, the unity of the inseparable nature cannot have separable persons.

### 4

Accordingly, we must consider how that one and same nature of the Trinity fills everything in such a way that there is nothing where it is not. Hence it is wholly everywhere and is contained by no place whatsoever: wholly in individual spirits and bodies, and wholly at the same time in all creatures.

We are not now speaking of grace, by which God, through the freely given gift of his mercy, offers himself to human beings who are to be saved; we are speaking of the nature by which God both fills and contains everything he has made. Concerning this nature he says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24). In accordance with this nature, blessed David says to God:

> Where shall I go from your Spirit,  
> and where shall I flee from your presence?  
> If I ascend into heaven, you are there;  
> and if I descend into hell, you are present.  
> (Ps. 138:7)

And concerning Christ, who is the wisdom of God, it is said:

> It reaches mightily from end to end  
> and orders all things sweetly.  
> (Wis. 8:1)

Of the Holy Spirit also, divinely inspired Scripture speaks as follows:

> For the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world,  
> and he who contains all things possesses knowledge of speech.  
> (Wis. 1:7)

Here “speech” is found to signify the speech of the heart, not of the body—that is, not bodily utterance but intimate thought. It is that voice which God alone hears crying out, when he alone sees the one thinking in secret.

Therefore it continues:

> For this reason the one who speaks unjustly cannot remain hidden;  
> nor will the judgment that rebukes him pass him by.  
> (Ibid., 8)

And showing where this unjust speech exists, so that it may be understood to belong more to the conscience than to the tongue, Holy Scripture subsequently makes this clear:

> For the thoughts of the ungodly will be examined.  
> (Ibid., 9)

I have said this because it is said of the Holy Spirit that “he who contains all things possesses knowledge of speech.” For the Holy Spirit, who contains all things, is not less than the Father or the Son; and because he possesses knowledge of intimate thought, he is recognized as the true God, who is found to know hidden things.

Knowledge that comprehends hidden things undoubtedly includes the future as well. True faith attributes this to the supreme and true God, as holy Susanna invokes the true God in this manner:

> O God, who know the hidden things,  
> who know all things before they come to be.  
> (Dan. 13:42)

The Trinity, therefore—that is, the one, true, and good God, eternal, unchangeable, and immeasurable—is wholly everywhere according to the natural immensity and omnipotence, although he does not dwell in all things according to the abundance of grace.

### 5

This is why, although God says through Jeremiah, “I am God who is near, and not a God from afar” (Jer. 23:23), the same prophet nevertheless says to that God concerning certain people:

> You are near to their mouth,  
> but far from their kidneys.  
> (Jer. 12:2)

God is therefore near to the good both by nature and by grace: by nature, through which he creates; by grace, through which he saves; by nature, through which he makes human beings exist; by grace, through which he justifies sinners; by nature, through which he causes them to be born from human beings; by grace, through which he gives them power to become children of God (John 1:12); by nature, through which he causes them to live; by grace, through which he causes them to live temperately, justly, and devoutly (Tit. 2:12); by nature, through which he causes them to live for a short time in this world; by grace, through which he causes them to reign forever in heaven.

In the wicked, however, God is present only through his natural immensity and omnipotence, by which he causes them to exist, live, and perceive; to be rational; and also to possess free choice of the will—but free, not freed. Free choice still remains in human beings by nature, and in those whom God wills he deigns to set it free by grace.

From the time when the first man was sold under sin through free choice, human freedom began to be evil, because the goodness of the will was taken away from free choice itself. Thus an evil freedom began to exist in the same human choice, so that it became for him, and thereafter for all who would be born through sexual union, a hostile captivity.

Therefore, as we said above, God, through the immensity of his nature, both contains and fills his entire creation. Hence the Father fills all, the Son fills all, and the Holy Spirit fills all, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are naturally one God.

The nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that is, of those three persons—is not one in the same way as the human nature of any three human beings. Their nature is one, yet their souls and bodies are separated; and although there is natural unity in three human beings, none of them has flesh or soul in common with the other two.

Hence any creatures who are consubstantial can be separated from one another, because each of them cannot be wholly everywhere. For even when, through the grace of faith, the heart and soul of the multitude of believers become one (Acts 4:32), they can nevertheless be separated as persons by the arrangement of places, even though they are not separated in the affection of the heart. Some unbelievers can also arise from among the faithful and be separated from the fellowship of that one soul.

But the nature of the Trinity, which alone is wholly everywhere, just as it has its own one and whole being everywhere, so cannot receive the separation of its persons.

[Col. 0397A]

### 6

Those persons are indeed sometimes named individually. But the Trinity itself wished to show that it is inseparable in its persons in such a way that there is no name by which any one person is called that does not either belong to all three by natural unity or, even through the very name of singularity, show one to be referred to another.

Among the names that are properly said of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit with reference to themselves—names in which the singularity of each person is not shown, but the communion of one essence—there is no name that can belong to the Father or the Son in such a way that it cannot belong to the Holy Spirit.

The Father is naturally God; but the Son is naturally God, and the Holy Spirit is naturally God. Yet the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three gods but naturally one God.

The Father is omnipotent; the Son is omnipotent; the Holy Spirit is omnipotent. Yet they are not three omnipotent gods, but the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one omnipotent God.

The Father is eternal, without beginning; the Son is eternal, without beginning; the Holy Spirit is eternal, without beginning. Yet they are not three eternal gods, but the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one eternal God.

The Father is immeasurable; the Son is immeasurable; the Holy Spirit is also immeasurable. Yet they are not three immeasurable gods, but the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one immeasurable God.

When, therefore, any single name is such that it can equally belong simultaneously to all three and to each individual person, and is singular in nature in such a way that it cannot be plural in the persons, how can we say that the persons are separable when we do not see the plural number admitted in the name?

Whatever is said only in the singular according to nature must necessarily be signified inseparably in the persons as well. The truth itself shows that the persons cannot be divided, since whatever name is spoken of each person in relation not to another but to that person himself is spoken in the singular of one person and is likewise named in the singular of all three.

For of one person it is said, “one angel”; it is said, “one man.” But if there are three persons of angels or human beings, neither “one angel” nor “one man” can be said. For among those three persons who are found in an angelic or human nature, it is necessary to name not one angel or one man but, without doubt, three angels or three men.

Indeed, that plurality of angelic or human persons cannot be called either one angel or one man. But because those three persons of angels or human beings can be separated, those three persons do not simultaneously receive one singular designation of nature; they are unquestionably called either three angels or three human beings.

### 7

We are not unaware, however, that by the grace of God several human beings can be called by some singular name. Such is the statement already quoted above:

> The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul.  
> (Acts 4:32)

Yet they are called “one soul” in such a way that they are also called souls—namely, the souls of the faithful, not of the impious.

The Lord was speaking to faithful disciples when he said to them:

> By your endurance you will possess your souls.  
> (Luke 21:19)

Blessed Peter likewise says to the faithful:

> But believing, rejoice with inexpressible and glorified joy,  
> receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls.  
> (1 Pet. 1:8)

It is also said in the Book of Wisdom:

> The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God.  
> (Wis. 3:1)

We also know that the blessed Apostle said to the Thessalonians, whose election by God he knew:

> May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely,  
> and may your spirit, soul, and body be kept whole and blameless  
> at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.  
> (1 Thess. 5:23)

Moreover, in the hymn of the three youths we likewise read:

> Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous.  
> (Dan. 3:86)

We know that, by the grace of God, the holy Church is also called one virgin, as the Apostle says:

> I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.  
> (2 Cor. 11:2)

Yet within that one virgin, virgins are also named in the plural:

> Virgins will be brought to the King after her.  
> (Ps. 44:15)

Nor is there any doubt that there is one Church spread throughout the whole world, which the Apostle calls “the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Tim. 3:15). Yet it is both one and a Church in such a way that several churches are named within it.

For the blessed Apostle himself says:

> I was personally unknown to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.  
> (Gal. 1:22)

He also says that he sent to the Corinthians a brother whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the churches (2 Cor. 8:18). At the beginning of the same letter he also shows that he wrote to the churches of Galatia.

Our Lord, showing that his faithful are one light, says to his disciples:

> You are the light of the world.  
> (Matt. 5:14)

Yet blessed James does not hesitate to call the children of God “lights,” saying:

> Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above,  
> coming down from the Father of lights.  
> (Jas. 1:17)

In all these examples, therefore, we find both a singular name and a plural one. The plural occurs because the very quality of their nature shows that all creatures are separable; the singular occurs because that one Trinity, through its grace, has made there to be one soul, one spirit, one virgin, one Church, and one light.

The Trinity is so inseparable both in nature and in persons that whatever is said there in the singular of one person or of the three persons is not said in the plural. The persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit therefore cannot be separated, since one natural name belongs to them in such a way that it cannot be plural in the three persons.

Apart from the very term by which they are called “persons,” no other name can be found in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit that is not named only in the singular. Human speech, in its poverty, could scarcely find even this one term: at least it could say that there are three persons, lest, if even this were not said, the Trinity could in no way be believed and danger to the faith arise from that complete silence.

### 8

Accordingly, in accordance with the truth of Christian faith, we say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are naturally one God.

Just as we call the Trinity one God, so we must call it one omnipotent, one eternal, one immeasurable, one great, one most high God; and whatever name God has granted human beings to use of himself is spoken in the singular, not only of the individual persons but also of all three together.

But lest, because “Father” is the name of one person, and “Son” is likewise said to be one person in the Trinity, and when “Holy Spirit” is properly spoken the singularity of one person is likewise signified, anyone should wish to assert and affirm that these three persons are separable—for each person is associated with one of these three names in such a way that it cannot be common to the three—whoever attempts this, if he thinks as he speaks and his conscience holds what his tongue declares, pays insufficient attention to the fact that these names are unquestionably relative.

In every relative name, it is certain that one person is signified in himself in such a way that he is thereby referred to another. This occurs not only in things that are the same, as brother is spoken in relation to brother, friend to friend, and neighbor to neighbor, but also in things that are different, as father is spoken in relation to son, son to father, begetter to begotten, or begotten to begetter. From any of these names it is customary to understand two persons.

For in these names one person is not spoken of in the singular in such a way that he is not referred by the name itself to another. Through a relative name, any person is named in himself in such a way that he is not named in relation to himself.

Therefore, to make the sign of inseparability known, that one and true divinity wished to be named incommunicably [Note: [Col. 0399D] Ms. Thu.: immutably.] in the individual persons, in such a way that one person nevertheless could not be understood without another.

When the Father is referred to the Son, or the Son to the Father, although the individual names can belong only to the respective persons, and the propriety of the persons entirely refuses the sharing of those two names, the Father is nevertheless not known without the Son, nor is the Son found without the Father.

That personal relation of the name forbids the persons to be separated; even when it does not name them together, it implies them together. No one can hear any one of these names without being compelled to understand the other as well. Blessed John indicates this when he says:

> Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father;  
> the one who confesses the Son has the Father also.  
> (1 John 2:23)

He said this precisely because the Father is inseparably referred to the Son, and the Son is inseparably referred to the Father.

The person of the Father is therefore not separated from the person of the Son whenever either the Father alone or the Son alone is named. For the Father is not named unless he is referred to the Son, nor is the Son named unless he is referred to the Father. In the name “Father,” the begetter is recognized in such a way that the one who has been begotten is also signified by it; and the name of the begotten prompts recognition of the person of the begetter.

Hence, just as the Father is possessed by the one who confesses the Son, so he is not possessed by the one who denies the Son.

### 9

Therefore, whoever says that the persons of the Father and Son are separable should point out in either one of them some personal name that belongs so exclusively to one person that it cannot be referred to the other.

But since this cannot be found at all, it unquestionably belongs to the true faith that, just as we do not confuse those three persons of one and inseparable nature, so we must not dare to separate them in any way.

The Trinity itself has deigned to show this to us so clearly that even in those names by which it wished the persons to be recognized individually, it does not permit one to be understood without another.

Apart from the fact that the Father and Son are named relatively to one another—in which case one must necessarily be inseparably referred to the other—there is no less an end to every objection in the personal name “Holy Spirit.” For when the Holy Spirit is called “Holy Spirit,” he is personally called nothing other than what the Father and the Son are naturally called.

The Father is naturally spirit, and the Son is naturally spirit. The Father is naturally holy, and the Son is naturally holy.

How, then, can the person of the Holy Spirit be separated in any way from the person of the Father or the Son, when the Holy Spirit possesses in his very personal name what is recognized as common to him with the Father and the Son through natural unity?

By this name he is not referred only to the Father, as the Son is, nor only to the Son, as the Father is; rather, he is referred simultaneously to the Father and the Son, when he is called the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

When the Holy Spirit himself is called “gift,” he is likewise inseparably referred to the giver.

Knowing this inseparability of the persons, blessed David said to God:

> Where shall I go from your Spirit,  
> and where shall I flee from your presence?  
> If I ascend into heaven, you are there;  
> if I descend into hell, you are present.  
> (Ps. 138:7)

He certainly would not have said this if he had known the person of the Holy Spirit to be separable from the person of the Father.

He said that he could neither depart from the Spirit of God nor flee anywhere from God himself because he knew that God is inseparably in his Spirit and that the Spirit of God is in God—not as a creature is in God, but as his Spirit, who is not of a different nature from the God in whom he is.

The holy Apostle shows this at the passage where, after saying, “God has revealed these things to us through his Spirit—for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God,” he immediately introduces the example of the human spirit:

> For who knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him?  
> So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.  
> (1 Cor. 2:10–12)

Therefore, just as the human spirit that is in a person knows the things belonging to that person because it is of the same nature as the human being in whom it is—though here, I think, the inward person should rather be understood—so no one knows the things belonging to God except the Spirit of God because he is in God through the unity of nature, in such a way that there is nothing in God that his Spirit cannot know through natural unity.

### 10

Only natural unity possesses this fullness of knowledge. Through it, the Spirit of God is in God in such a way that he is naturally one God with him.

Yet he is in God and is one God with him in such a way that he does not have one person with him, as the spirit that is in a human being has one person with the human being.

It is certain that the blessed Apostle placed that example of knowledge on account of the unity of nature—a unity that permits no difference of knowledge in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For that one inseparable nature consists, in the three persons as well as in each individual person, of everything that is naturally in it—not as diverse but as one and whole.

To demonstrate the proper person of the Holy Spirit, the apostolic authority was truly vigilant in the same teaching of the Spirit, saying:

> We have received not the spirit of the world,  
> but the Spirit who is from God.  
> (1 Cor. 2:12)

This cannot in any way be said of the human spirit, which is said to be in a human being in such a way that it is not said to be from a human being.

The Holy Spirit is in God through unity of nature and is from God through the propriety of his person.

Through that unity of nature, by which no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God, we also understand what the Son says:

> No one knows the Son except the Father,  
> nor does anyone know the Father except the Son  
> and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.  
> (Matt. 11:27)

Through the same inseparable unity of nature, the Son testifies that he is in the Father and that the Father is in him.

For after saying to his disciples, “If you had known me, you would certainly have known my Father also” (John 14:7), Philip asked that the Father be shown to him. The Lord himself answered:

> Have I been with you for so long, and you have not known me, Philip?  
> Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.  
> How can you say, “Show us the Father”?  
> Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?  
> The words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself;  
> but the Father, who remains in me, himself does the works.  
> Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?  
> Otherwise, believe because of the works themselves.  
> (Ibid., 9 ff.)

Since, therefore, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are inseparable, it follows that they work inseparably.

If that Trinity could have separable persons, there would also be some separate works of the Trinity.

For if we consider what Holy Scripture says of Wisdom—“For she is the splendor of eternal light” (Wis. 7:26)—then, just as we see splendor inseparably clinging to light, so we should recognize that the Son cannot be separated from the Father.

The apostolic authority proclaims him to be “the splendor of glory and the figure of God’s substance” (Heb. 1:3). Following this, blessed Ambrose declares in the morning hymn [Note: [Col. 0401D] St. Ambrose, in the hymn for Monday at Lauds.] that the Son is the splendor of the Father’s glory.

### 11

We should also believe the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be inseparable on the basis of the example by which the Only-begotten God himself joined and united the divine and human nature in the unity of his person, so that they cannot be separated from him at all.

In the one person of the Only-begotten God, who “came forth like a bridegroom from his chamber” (Ps. 18:5), the union of both natures remains inseparable.

No one should therefore think that the two natures could have been divided from each other because, through the assumption of death, the lifeless flesh lay in the tomb and the soul descended into hell while the flesh was dying.

Even when the soul had departed from the flesh through the intervention of death, both natures remained inseparable in Christ, because the immeasurable divinity did not abandon either his soul in hell or his flesh in the tomb.

The two natures in Christ are so inseparable that Eutyches fell into error on this account. Seeing one person in Christ, he impiously proclaimed one nature in him as well, wishing to confuse what he saw could not be separated.

Thus, in the two natures which he recognized as belonging inseparably to one person, he incurred the crime of impiety, just as Sabellius, because of the unity of nature, erred through the blindness of deadly unbelief concerning the three persons. He did not understand that the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit subsist without confusion, although he heard that they remain entirely inseparable through natural unity.

But the inseparable Trinity overcame both; the unconfused unity crushed both. Each withdrew, alienated from the womb of Mother Church; each went astray from the belly of that most pious mother and plunged himself and his accomplices into the abyss of impiety.

For in the Trinity, true unity of nature remains, but so too does the unconfused and inseparable propriety of the persons. Likewise, in the one person of Christ, the full truth of the two natures remains unconfused and inseparable.

### 12

If, then, in Christ, because of the unity of person, the union of the divine and human nature is found to be inseparable—although the two natures do not naturally possess eternity without beginning, simplicity without mutability, or immensity without limit in common, since in the one and same Christ there is both the true divine nature, by which he is naturally God born without beginning from the Father, and the true human nature, by which he is naturally God made man in the fullness of time from a virgin; in the former he is coeternal with the Father, in the latter later than his mother; according to his divinity he is always wholly everywhere and is never enclosed by any place, whereas according to his humanity he will come on a certain day from heaven to judge the living and the dead—how great an inseparability must we believe to exist in those three persons whose natural unity, eternity, simplicity, and immensity are one?

Blessed Ambrose truly proclaims and confirms this in Book One *On the Holy Spirit* (chapter 6), saying:

> Who, then, would dare to say that the Holy Spirit is separate from God the Father and Christ, when through him we are deemed worthy to exist in the image and likeness of God?

In another passage he says:

> Who can separate the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, when we cannot even call the Father and the Son without the Holy Spirit? For no one says “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit. Therefore, if we certainly cannot call the Lord Jesus without the Holy Spirit, can we proclaim him without the Spirit?  
> (*On the Holy Spirit*, Book I, chapter 10)

Blessed Augustine also unquestionably asserts this inseparability of the three persons.

In Book One *On the Trinity* (chapter 4), after saying that only the Son was born from the Virgin Mary, that only the Holy Spirit, in the form of a dove, came upon Jesus after his baptism and, at Pentecost, came upon the disciples in divided tongues like fire, and that only the Father’s voice said, “You are my Son” (Mark 1:11; Luke 3:22), when the Son was baptized by John, and, when the voice sounded, “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John 12:28), nevertheless showing that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are inseparable, he added this statement:

> Although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are inseparable, so also they work inseparably.

You see clearly how blessed Augustine leaves no suspicion here of separable persons, when he asserts that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit work inseparably just as they are inseparable.

Confirming this statement with such a conclusion (chapter 8), he says:

> This also is my faith, since this is the Catholic faith.

### 13

Elsewhere in the same book he says:

> Finally, because of that very inseparability, sometimes the Father alone or the Son alone is sufficiently named, when he wishes to fill us with joy through his countenance; yet the Spirit of both—that is, the Spirit of the Father and the Son, who is properly called the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive (John 14:17)—is not thereby separated. This is our complete joy, beyond which there is none greater: to enjoy God the Trinity, in whose image we have been made.

> For this reason we sometimes speak of the Holy Spirit as though he alone were sufficient for our blessedness. He is sufficient alone because he cannot be separated from the Father and the Son. The Father is likewise sufficient alone because he cannot be separated from the Son and the Holy Spirit; and the Son is sufficient alone because he cannot be separated from the Father and the Holy Spirit.

This is blessed Augustine’s judgment, in accordance with the truth of the Catholic faith, concerning the inseparability of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

But lest anyone receive it as applying only to the nature and not also to the persons, shortly afterward in the same book (chapter 9, toward the end) he took care to show it more plainly and explicitly, saying:

> But for the revelation of the Trinity, certain things are said separately even when the individual persons are named; nevertheless they are not understood as separated from the others, because of the unity and the one substance and divinity of the same Trinity, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Elsewhere in the same book (toward the end of chapter 10), emphasizing this most fully, after saying concerning the Son, “By this he asks, in which he is less than the Father; but in that by which he is equal, he hears together with the Father,” he shows the inseparability of the persons and says:

> Hence, when he said, “The Father himself loves you” (John 16:27), he certainly does not separate himself from what he said; rather, he causes it to be understood according to what I recalled above and sufficiently indicated: that one person in the Trinity is often named in such a way that the others are also understood there. Thus it was said, “The Father himself loves you,” so that consequently the Son and the Holy Spirit are also understood.

Again, a little later (chapter 12, before the middle), the same holy Augustine says:

> For we have already shown through many forms of divine speech that, because of the inseparable operation of one and the same substance, what belongs to all is also said of each individual.

In Book Fifteen *On the Trinity* (chapter 25), when he was offering some lines toward understanding the Trinity from the image that exists in us, he says among other things:

> But in that supreme Trinity, which surpasses all things incomparably, there is such great inseparability that, although a trinity of human beings cannot be called one human being, that Trinity is both called and is one God. Nor is that Trinity in one God, but it is one God.

> Nor, again, is that Trinity like this image, which is a human being possessing those three as one person. Rather, that Trinity consists of three persons: the Father of the Son, the Son of the Father, and the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

[Col. 0404B]

Again, a little later in the same passage he says:

> Yet just as in this image of the Trinity these three are not one human being but belong to one human being, so in the supreme Trinity, of which this is the image, those three do not merely belong to one God, but are one God; and they are three, not one person.

In saying this, blessed Augustine understood through the revelation of the Trinity the inseparability of those same three persons. With admiration he continues:

> What is truly wondrously ineffable, or ineffably wondrous, is that, although this image of the Trinity is one person, while the supreme Trinity consists of three persons, that Trinity of the three persons is more inseparable than this one person.

14. These passages, which—as I do not doubt—we have quoted from the first and the last books of the blessed Augustine’s work On the Trinity, are entirely sufficient, especially in view of your intelligence and diligence [Note: [Col. 0403D] Ancient reading: “your office”], by which you read his statements so penetratingly and so frequently that you can discover in them many similar passages demonstrating the inseparability of the holy Trinity, not only in its nature but also in its persons. Those three persons are therefore named individually so that they may be recognized, not separated: in them there is no separation, just as no confusion can exist in them. For because those three persons cannot be confused, they must not therefore be considered separable, since they are found to be altogether inseparable both in what they are and in what they do. Nor should anyone dare to assert that those three persons are separable, when no one can find one existing or acting before another, after another, or without another. Just as there can naturally be no separability of operation, so the unchangeable unity of will remains naturally in them.

Let us consider, however, in what manner a human being or an angel has been separated from God, so that we may understand the Trinity to be unquestionably inseparable. Holy Scripture says, namely, that “perverse thoughts separate from God,” and that “wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wisdom 1:3); and that “the holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (ibid., 1:5). The prophet Isaiah also testifies that iniquities separate God and human beings (Isaiah 59:2). But the holy Trinity itself is the faithful God, in whom there is no iniquity.

The Son of God came to take away sins; “in him there is no sin,” and “sin is iniquity” (1 John 3:4–5). By taking away iniquity, he bestowed love. He therefore removed that by which we were separated from God and gave what would join us inseparably to the holy Trinity. Thus the Apostle cries out confidently: “Neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38).
