If, then, the Trinity, by pouring love into us, makes our souls cling inseparably to itself—for “whoever clings to God is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17)—how could the Trinity itself have separable persons, since the Trinity is one God and therefore one love, because “God is love”? Love never admits division; from many hearts and many souls it makes one heart and one soul in itself.

**SECOND QUESTION**

15. Your second question is then appended in the following terms: Whether, just as God the Son is said to have been born, to have suffered, to have died, and to have been crucified, we ought likewise to affirm that his divinity was born, suffered, died, and was crucified; although, whether one says “God” or “divinity,” only the flesh is understood to be mutable and capable of suffering, according to which God—or divinity—could suffer what he could not suffer in his own nature.

**RESPONSE**

16. I briefly answer your words as follows: Whatever expression is used, it prejudices nothing in the faith by which the catholic Church truly believes and proclaims that the divinity of the Son of God remains naturally impassible and unchangeable. For the blessed Apostle says: “We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23–24). The Apostle therefore calls Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, crucified.

In another passage, joining power and divinity together, he says: “His everlasting power and divinity” (Romans 1:20). If, then, Christ’s power may rightly be called crucified according to the flesh, why should divinity likewise not be called crucified according to the flesh? For when “according to the flesh” is added, it plainly shows that not his divinity was subjected to suffering, but his flesh. We see this also demonstrated by apostolic authority. When the blessed Apostle Paul had said that Christ crucified is the power of God and the wisdom of God, lest that power and wisdom be thought naturally capable of suffering, he took care elsewhere to disclose profitably the mystery of the crucified power and wisdom, saying of Christ: “For although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4).

We know from prophetic speech that Christ the Son of God is truly called the strong God, since Isaiah says: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and the government is upon his shoulder; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, the Strong God, Father of the coming age, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6). Does not the Apostle, in one passage, commend the everlasting power and divinity of this strong God? True faith does not proclaim the everlasting power and divinity of the Father in such a way that it does not believe the everlasting power and divinity of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, since the power and divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are naturally one and everlasting.

Christ, therefore, is the strong God: truly God because he is divinity, and truly strong because he is power. True faith, which truly believes and proclaims Christ to be the strong God and knows that the Apostle preached Christ crucified as the power of God and the wisdom of God, just as it confidently knows and says that power was crucified according to the flesh, so also does not hesitate to confess that divinity was crucified according to the flesh. For Christ the strong God is God in such a way that he himself is his divinity, just as he is strong in such a way that he himself is his power.

**16 bis.** You know that what I am saying has been discussed most fully by the blessed Augustine in his books On the Trinity. In them he shows that each person of the Trinity, at least in those names by which that person is spoken of in relation to itself—not metaphorically, but properly—is itself what it is naturally said to possess. For we say that the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit is the living, great, wise, strong, and good God.

In all these attributes, each person of the Trinity is named in relation to itself: because God is God by divinity, great by greatness, wise by wisdom, strong by power, and good by goodness. Thus he is God in such a way that he himself is his divinity; great in such a way that he himself is his greatness; wise in such a way that he himself is his wisdom; strong in such a way that he himself is his power; and good in such a way that he himself is his goodness.

Since the holy Augustine frequently conveys this point in the books mentioned above, I have decided to insert into this work a passage from his fifth book (Book 5 On the Trinity, chapter 10). While speaking of God and his greatness, he says among other things:

“He is therefore great by that greatness which is himself that very greatness. And therefore, just as we do not say that there are three essences, so neither do we say that there are three greatnesses. For to be God is the same as to be great. For the same reason we do not say that there are three great beings, but one great being; because God is not great by participation in greatness, but is great by the great being that he himself is, because he himself is his greatness.

“Let this also be said of the goodness, eternity, and omnipotence of God, and altogether of every category that can be predicated of God: what is said in relation to himself is said not metaphorically or by way of likeness, but properly—if, indeed, anything can properly be said of him by the human mouth.”

In the eighth book (in the preface), expressing the same judgment concerning the natural simplicity of the Trinity, he says among other things:

“Just as the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; and the Father is good, the Son is good, and the Holy Spirit is good; and the Father is omnipotent, the Son is omnipotent, and the Holy Spirit is omnipotent: yet there are not three Gods, or three good beings, or three omnipotent beings, but the Trinity itself is one God, good and omnipotent. And whatever else is said of each individually not relatively to one another but in relation to themselves—these things are said according to essence, because there ‘to be’ is the same as to be great, to be good, to be wise, and whatever else each person there, or the Trinity itself, is said to be in relation to itself.”

17. It is therefore clear from these words of the blessed Augustine that catholic truth requires us, whenever we name divinity, greatness, goodness, power, or any other attribute that is properly predicated of God in relation to himself, to understand with complete certainty not several different things corresponding to these different names—as in the case of a human being subject to qualities—but one and the same thing, namely essence or nature.

For this reason the blessed Augustine himself says in the fifth book On the Trinity that we should understand “good without quality” and “great without quantity,” because the unchangeability of the simple and omnipotent essence cannot be subject to accidents. In it divinity is the same as eternity and majesty; greatness is the same as power and goodness.

From this rule of truth, then, whatever we know to be truly said of Christ’s majesty, eternity, or power according to the flesh, let us not deny that it may likewise be truly said of his divinity. For the blessed Augustine himself, in the first book On the Trinity (chapter 12, toward the middle), showing that the Son of God according to his divinity has what he is and is what he has, speaks as follows:

“For the Son of God is not like a creature: before the Incarnation and before he assumed the creature, the Only-Begotten through whom all things were made is not one thing and has another, but is himself what he is and what he has.”

This is stated more clearly in that passage, if anyone is capable of grasping it, where he says: “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:26). He did not give this to one who already existed without life, so that he might have life in himself, since by the very fact of what he is, he is life. This, then, is what it means that he gave the Son to have life in himself: he begot the Son as unchangeable life, which is eternal life.

The same blessed Augustine, in his exposition of the Gospel according to John (Tractate 22, toward the middle), while discussing the Lord’s own words, says:

“The Son of God did not first exist without life and then receive life; for if he had received it in that way, he would not have it in himself. What does ‘in himself’ mean? That he himself should be life itself.”

A little later, in the same sermon, he confirms this by saying:

“The Apostle says: ‘For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord’ (Ephesians 5:8). After saying ‘now you are light,’ he added ‘in the Lord.’ In yourself, therefore, you are darkness; in the Lord, light. Why light? Because through participation in that light you are light. But if you withdraw from the light by which you are illumined, you return to your own darkness.

“Christ is not so; the Word of God is not so. How, then? ‘Just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself’ (John 5:26), so that he might live not by participation, but unchangeably, and might himself altogether be life.”

A little later the same outstanding holy teacher Augustine says:

“What is said, ‘he gave to the Son,’ is equivalent to saying, ‘he begot the Son’; for by begetting he gave. Just as he gave him to be, so he gave him to be life, and so he gave him to be life in himself. What does it mean that he should be life in himself? That he should not need life from another, but should himself be the fullness of life, from which other believers would live while they lived.”

18. From these words of the distinguished bishop Augustine we are taught, with all ambiguity removed, that—while the unchangeability, eternity, and impassibility of the Son of God’s divinity remain intact—it is not inappropriate for whatever is said of his majesty, eternity, and power according to the assumption of flesh likewise to be said of his divinity according to the flesh. What was assumed by the Son of God is therefore shown to have been assumed by his divinity, his majesty, his power, and his eternity.

To demonstrate this through the truthful testimony of the holy Fathers, we first produce the letter of the most blessed Pope Leo, the glorious bishop of the apostolic see. Writing to Flavian, bishop of the city of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0407D] According to the current arrangement, this is Letter 10], he expressed the true faith concerning the Lord’s Incarnation with such wonder and clarity that he destroyed every error of heretical perversity. In that letter (chapter 3), the same glorious bishop, endowed no less with the truth of apostolic faith than distinguished by the dignity of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0407D] Manuscript Thu.: “illustrious”], says the following [Note: [Col. 0408D] In manuscript Thu. “he says this” is absent; instead it reads: “While preserving, he says, the proper character”]:

“While preserving, therefore, the proper character of each nature, and with both coming together into one person, humility was assumed by majesty, weakness by power, mortality by eternity. And, in order to discharge the debt of our condition, an inviolable nature was united to a passible nature, so that—as suited our remedies—the one and same mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), could both die by virtue of one nature and could not die by virtue of the other.”

The bishop of the apostolic see continues and says:

“Thus, in the complete and perfect nature of a true human being, true God was born, whole in what was his own and whole in what was ours. By ‘ours’ we mean what the Creator established in us from the beginning and what he assumed in order to restore.”

You can see how that apostolic teacher, with the same faith by which he says that God assumed for restoration those things that he had established in us from the beginning, also says that humility was assumed by majesty, weakness by power, and mortality by eternity. When the majesty, power, and eternity of the Son of God are mentioned, nothing other than his divinity is signified. Let us not therefore doubt that Christ’s divinity assumed whatever Christ’s majesty, power, and eternity assumed.

For this reason the same letter contains once again a similar statement. The same most blessed bishop of the Roman Church confirms in the clearest proclamation both God and human being, and likewise divinity and humanity. In that letter he says:

“The nature was assumed from the Lord’s mother, not guilt; nor, because the birth of the Lord Jesus Christ from the Virgin’s womb was wondrous, is he therefore unlike us in nature. For he who is true God is likewise true human being, and there is no falsehood in this unity, since in it there are both the humility of a human being and the exaltedness of deity. For just as God is not changed by mercy, so the human being is not consumed by dignity.”

In another passage of the same letter (chapter 6), the same most blessed Pope Leo professes that the divinity was concealed beneath the veil of flesh, saying:

“When he came to the baptism of his predecessor John, so that it might not remain hidden that divinity was concealed beneath the veil of flesh, the Father’s voice thundered from heaven: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’ (Matthew 3:17).”

Thereupon he confidently calls that divinity God and unquestionably calls that flesh a human being, saying:

“Thus, the devil’s cunning tempts him as a human being, while angelic service waits upon him as God.”

Again, in another passage of the same letter (ibid.), he says:

“Although in the Lord Jesus Christ there is one person of God and human being, nevertheless the source of the common disgrace in both is one thing, and the source of the common glory is another. From us he has a humanity lower than the Father; from the Father he has a divinity equal with the Father.”

He so impresses and inculcates the firmness of this judgment upon the understanding of all the faithful that he testifies that the life and progress of the catholic Church stand upon this faith, saying (chapter 5) that the catholic Church lives and advances by this faith: that divinity is not believed to exist without true humanity.

19. The blessed Pope Gelasius likewise follows these same footsteps in every respect, preserving the continuity of the teaching, along the path of true faith and apostolic confession. In the book which that venerable bishop wrote against those who refuse to believe the undivided truth of the two natures in the Lord Jesus Christ, but confuse them by professing one nature, he confirms—preserving the very tenor of apostolic preaching—that the two natures in Christ are unconfused and inseparable, saying:

“It is necessary that these same things be brought forward [Note: [Col. 0409D] Manuscript Thu.: ‘professed’] under one and the same person, so that, undistinguished and inseparable in that union, they remain what they are.”

A little later:

“When only God is named, is the human being denied? When humanity is named, is deity thereby removed? When he is called the Son of Man, is he not consequently also understood to be the Son of God? When the Word is named, is the flesh that was made not understood at the same time? When his flesh and body are brought forward, is his divinity not also unquestionably shown?”

Again, elsewhere in the same book, speaking of those who strive to assert that there is only one nature in Christ, he says:

“For even when they say that there was one incarnate nature, wishing in this way to display it as unique, they in no way escape the implication of two. For when it is said that one nature of divinity was incarnate, there will necessarily be one nature that was incarnate and another by which it is declared to have been incarnate. The nature of deity that was incarnate will not be the same as the nature of flesh by which it is affirmed to have been incarnate; nor was the nature of deity incarnate by itself, but the nature of flesh is recognized to have been incarnate.

“Likewise, the nature of flesh did not by itself become exalted through deity, because divinity did not come incarnate from anywhere other than from the womb of the Virgin Mother; and flesh was united to deity only in that same womb, when the Holy Spirit came upon it and the power of the Most High overshadowed it.”

A little later he says:

“Let these people therefore seek by what means they may escape the pits of their madness by which they are surrounded, and openly confess either that they belong to the number of those who attack the true body of Christ, or let them not dare to deny that it is true only in this way, without which it could not be true. Likewise, when we call him the same God, or proclaim that he speaks or acts according to God, this could not be true in any other way than by confessing that there is truly present the nature of deity, remaining in the proper character of its substance.”

20. In the first book On the Faith (chapter 2), Saint Ambrose likewise professes, in one and the same passage, Christ as God and human being, and in him divinity and flesh, saying:

“The prophets speak of one God, the apostles hear of one God, the Magi believed in one God, and in supplication they brought gold, frankincense, and myrrh to Christ’s cradle: with gold confessing him to be King, and with frankincense venerating him as God. Gold is the treasure of a kingdom; frankincense is the sacrifice of God; myrrh is burial.

“What, then, did those mystical gifts intend amid the lowly manger, unless that we should understand in Christ the distinction between divinity and flesh? As a human being he is born; as God he is adored. He lies in swaddling clothes, but shines among the stars. The cradle indicates the one being born; the stars, the one ruling. It is flesh that is wrapped; it is divinity that is ministered to by angels. Thus the natural dignity of majesty is not lost, and the truth of the assumed flesh is demonstrated.”

The blessed Ambrose confirmed all these points set out above with the following conclusion (ibid.):

“This is our faith. This is how God wished to be recognized by human beings.”

Indeed, in bringing the preceding discussion to a close with this definition (chapter 4), the blessed Ambrose taught with complete clarity that this is our faith, so that just as we call him God and human being, we should likewise have no hesitation in calling him divinity and flesh.

In the second book of the same work he says:

“Let empty disputes about words therefore be silent, since, as it is written, the kingdom of God is not in persuasive speech, but in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1 Corinthians 2:4).

The same holy Ambrose continues (ibid.):

“Let us preserve the distinction between divinity and flesh: the one Son of God speaks in both, because both natures are in the same one.”

And below:

“This is he who descended; this is he whom the Father sanctified and sent into this world.”

The very text teaches us that it was not divinity that needed sanctification, but flesh.

The blessed Augustine likewise says in his book On Faith, Hope, and Charity, which you know is called by many the *Enchiridion* (chapter 34):

“For who could explain with words adequate to the matter this alone: that ‘the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,’ so that we might believe in the only Son of almighty God, born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary? Thus the Word became flesh, with flesh assumed by divinity, not with divinity changed into flesh.”

The blessed Augustine here shows divinity as the taker-up of flesh, and he likewise testifies that it took up death. For in his book On the Presence of God he says:

“Through our Head we are reconciled to God, because in him the divinity of the Only-Begotten became a participant in our mortality, so that we might also become participants in his immortality.”

Immediately commending the greatness of this mystery, he added:

“This mystery is far from the hearts of proud sages, and therefore from those who are not Christians—and consequently from those who are not truly wise.”

21. All these statements of the holy Fathers demonstrate that what is said of God the Only-Begotten may also appropriately be proclaimed of his divinity. We know, however, that in this assertion of catholic truth there are either heretics devoted to perversity or Catholics insufficiently instructed in the mystery of right belief. When they hear that what is said of God the Son is also said of his divinity, while nevertheless knowing that we proclaim one divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, they must be moved to some degree by the thought that the sharing of divinity produces a sharing in the human assumption, and consequently that, through the sharing of flesh, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit might be thought to share in human birth, suffering, and death.

So that the former may not maliciously lie in wait, nor the latter perhaps be carelessly deceived, both groups must reflect that we proclaim one substance of the Trinity without nevertheless saying that the Trinity has one person. Thus everything that belongs to the nature itself is found to be common to the three persons, while nevertheless something is found by which each person is known as possessing what is proper to it—something that is neither separable nor capable of being common.

We say that it is proper to the Father that he begot; proper to the Son that he alone was born from the one Father; and proper to the Holy Spirit that he proceeds from the Father and the Son. In these proper characteristics there is no separation of nature, but a certain recognition of person.

Although generation belongs properly to the Father alone, the Son is not separated from it, because the Son was born when the Father begot. And although birth belongs properly to the Son, he is not separable from the begetting Father, because the Son’s birth would not be naturally true unless he had been begotten from the Father.

Although, therefore, when the Son was being born the Father begot, and when the Father was begetting the Son was born, the Son did not beget together with the Father, nor was the Father born together with the Son, even though the Son was born from the Father’s nature and the Father begot the Son’s nature from himself. The personal property of the persons is inseparable in such a way, however, that neither generation nor birth can be common to two persons.

Yet unless the two persons, the Father and the Son, existed naturally, neither could one beget nor could the other be begotten. If heretics attempt to reject this in the case of God the Father and God the Son, let them either be instructed or confounded by the manifest example of human generation.

A human father naturally precedes his human son in time, because he too began to exist in time; and the son would not be born in time unless the father’s nature were subject to the beginning of time. Hence it is plainly evident that the Son of God was born without beginning from God the Father because that Father begot from himself a Son who began to exist in no way, just as he does not cease to exist [alternative reading: “will not cease”].

Yet although in human beings the father is naturally recognized to precede the son’s birth, in that same generation neither son is separated from father nor father from son, because when the father begets, the son is begotten. And although that generation is the cause of the son’s birth, and birth cannot be separated from generation, generation is not separated from birth, so that within one and the same nature one begets and the other is born.

22. That generation and birth are therefore naturally inseparable in such a way that the sharing of begetting or of being born cannot simultaneously belong to both persons. For this is what the property of the persons entails: neither does the Son beget himself together with the Father from whom he is begotten, nor does the Father, together with the Son who is born from him, himself become born.

The truth of the persons therefore remains unconfused within the unity of nature; among them there is something that is not found to be common, but proper. God the Only-Begotten, accordingly, shares one and the same nature with the Father and the Holy Spirit, while nevertheless having not a common person but an entirely proper one. For this reason he did not share the assumption of the form of a servant with the Father and the Holy Spirit, because he received the truth and fullness of the form of a servant not in the unity of nature, but solely in the unity of his own person [Note: [Col. 0411D] Ancient reading: “in the unity of his person alone”].

He who is true and complete God likewise became true and complete human being when a rational soul and flesh without sin were received by God the Only-Begotten into the unity of his person. Human nature was therefore assumed by God the Only-Begotten in such a way that there existed one person of divinity and humanity, not one nature.

Accordingly, the Son was not separated from the Father and the Holy Spirit when he assumed the full nature of our humanity; but he did not assume that same nature together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. For the nature of divinity and flesh did not become one nature in him, so that the incarnation of the entire Trinity would consequently be believed; rather, there is one person in Christ. That person is found to be inseparable indeed from the Father and the Holy Spirit, but nevertheless not to be one person with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Christ therefore possesses his own humanity, with which his divinity is found to have not one nature but one person. Since the person of God the Only-Begotten belongs neither to the Father nor to the Holy Spirit, the form of a servant is rightly believed to have been assumed by the Son alone, because the person of his divinity and flesh is one, not their nature.

In Christ there is not one person of divinity and another of humanity, but one person of both natures. Therefore, because the operation of the Trinity is inseparable, the entire Trinity made the form of a servant that God the Only-Begotten assumed. It is nevertheless certain that it was made by the entire Trinity but belongs as a person to the Son of God alone. For just as there is one operation of the entire Trinity in it, so there is not found in it a common assumption of the Trinity.

The personal property—for the Father is not himself the Son, nor is the Holy Spirit himself the Father or the Son—shows that something was made by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit which is nevertheless found to have been assumed by the Son alone.

23. No example of this matter can be found among creatures, because, apart from the Trinity, which is naturally the one true God, there is no nature that can possess three inseparable persons within itself. Since, however, in each human being we find that flesh is not the same thing as soul, and that the two are not of one nature, although the human nature is completed and constituted from both, while nevertheless in each human being they are found to have one person, let us seek something analogous in these two natures which we know to have one person.

When we find here something brought about by the common operation of soul and flesh which nevertheless belongs either to the substance of the soul alone or to that of the flesh alone, let us infer from this—and understand as much as the Trinity itself grants—that something could be done by those three persons through one simultaneous operation, in such a way that the entire Trinity would do it inseparably, while what was done would belong to one person of the Trinity.

When we take food, we plainly provide for the flesh, not for the soul. Yet in the very taking of food, by which the flesh alone is nourished, the soul works together with the flesh, because just as flesh without soul does not live, so it does not eat. Although the flesh alone receives food, therefore, one activity of both flesh and soul is found to occur simultaneously; and what the flesh alone receives by its natural property, the soul also performs together with the flesh through the unity of the person.

The operation is therefore common, but the reception is not common. The soul does not abandon the flesh in the activity of eating; yet it so mingles its own activity with the flesh that, through this common operation, the flesh alone receives vital nourishment.

Something similar is found in the same unity of person when the human soul claims for itself the activity of a person’s bodily members, if it applies the attention of the heart to the practice of divine reading [Note: [Col. 0413D] Manuscript Thu.: “with the attention of the heart it rests upon divine reading”]. Through reading, without doubt, the inner rather than the outward human being is nourished, and often, while the flesh is **FASTING**, the soul is more richly fed.

Does the soul, in order to take food from reading, not also employ the activity of bodily members? For it cannot read except through the bodily eyes; yet while it reads with the bodily eyes, it understands with the eyes of the heart [Note: [Col. 0413D] Manuscript Thu.: “what the bodily eye reads, the eye of the heart understands”]. Thus soul and flesh work together in that by which the soul alone is nourished, and the soul alone receives within itself what it does not do alone.

Here, then, two natures operate inseparably because of their one person; yet, because of their proper characteristics, one often receives what it does not do alone—indeed, what it cannot do at all without the other.

Although this is entirely sufficient for a complete outline of the matter, so that from what we see here in two natures and one person we may ascend, as far as the Trinity itself deigns to grant, to an understanding of the three persons in one nature, nevertheless a clear and indisputable recognition of this matter is also demonstrated for us in our Redeemer himself.

He joined and united both natures in the unity of his person so inseparably that, in the one person of God the Only-Begotten, neither divinity can be separated from its humanity nor humanity from its divinity. The union of the Word and flesh was made indissoluble when the Word became flesh. In it the personal unity remained in such a way that the proper character of the natures could neither be divided nor confused.

Accordingly, the activities common to both natures are found in the one Christ in such a way that, although Christ is not divided among powers and weaknesses, there is nevertheless something in the one operation of both natures that is not common to both natures.

24. Now, to say nothing at present of that ineffable conception and birth by which God, though eternal, was temporally conceived and born—so that, even in the very participation of the virginal conception and birth, it was naturally proper to the flesh alone initially to come into existence from the flesh of its Mother, to be formed into limbs, and through the passage of time and the work involved to be brought to the maturity of birth; then, as successive ages came and passed, to grow and, at the proper time, to reach the full stature of youth—what shall we say thereafter about those works and sufferings, when in him there were inseparably, by nature, true flesh, a true rational soul, and true divinity?

Nevertheless, he so dealt with those things which natural reality possessed or which he deigned to suffer that the whole Christ remained inseparable in suffering or action, while the personal unity displayed as common to divinity and humanity what nevertheless the same Christ, in himself, showed by natural reality to belong properly to each nature.

For, taking upon himself the hunger of our weakness, the whole Christ underwent that hunger, and, in order to take food, the whole Christ likewise acted. Yet, naturally, just as the flesh alone endured hunger, so the flesh alone received food through the action of the whole Christ who ate (another reading: “to be eaten”).

Wearied from his journey, Jesus sat by the well (John 4:6). Divinity, however, could not feel that weariness; nor should Christ be said in any way to have felt that weariness according to his soul. Therefore, the fact that he sat pertained naturally only to the refreshment of the flesh, which had been wearied; yet in that refreshment the operation of both divinity and soul was common.

Then, during the very time of his passion and death, who would not see that, in the same Christ and in the very sharing of his works, the proper attributes of the natures remain inseparably present? “His soul was sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38). But neither can immutable divinity receive sorrow, nor can flesh ever feel sorrow. Sorrow, therefore, belongs to the rational soul alone, and cannot naturally inhere either in divinity or in flesh. Nevertheless, the whole Christ deigned to work sorrow in himself personally: for he is found to have undergone his own sufferings in himself, since he had nothing that he suffered unwillingly.

Thus, in order to become sorrowful, the whole Christ acted; but the rational soul alone naturally received that sorrow in itself.

Now, when at one and the same time Christ lay in the tomb and descended into the underworld, who would not see the inseparable work of both natures? And who, in that one and inseparable work, would not clearly recognize what properly belongs to the flesh, the soul, and the divinity?

For Christ acted as the whole Christ in order to lie in the tomb according to the flesh; but only the flesh was naturally capable of burial. Likewise, for Christ to descend into the underworld according to the soul was one work of both natures, that is, of the divine and the human; but that descent naturally belonged to the soul alone.

At the same time Christ, wholly, did not cease to act in heaven and on earth. Yet it belonged to divinity alone both not to be confined by place and to work naturally and equally with the Father those things that pertained to the governance of the universe.

This is why, in all those works of passion and death, apostolic authority assigns to the one person acting what the whole Christ worked in himself, in such a way that it unmistakably shows what belongs to each nature. [Note: Ms. Thu. reads *operanti*, “to the one acting,” for *operantis*.] For the apostle Paul says of one and the same Christ: “Although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4).

And blessed Peter uttered the prophetic word from the Psalms in such a way that, speaking of Christ’s soul, which he knew had descended into the underworld, he said that it itself had not been abandoned there. For the same apostle Peter speaks thus concerning blessed David: “Therefore, being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn to him with an oath that he would set upon his throne one from the fruit of his loins, he foresaw and spoke of the resurrection of Christ: that neither was his soul abandoned in the underworld, nor did his flesh see corruption” (Acts 2:30).

All these things, therefore, the whole Christ did according to the one person; and the one work of both natures is recognized in such a way that it is nevertheless not denied what must be assigned to each nature. [Note: Perhaps one should read *cuique naturae*, “to each nature,” as above.] Let each person, then, be instructed by these examples, so that what he recognizes here in the consideration of the natures, he may understand there with respect to the persons; and let him not doubt that Christ’s human nature was made through the work of the whole Trinity, but belongs to the person of the Unigenitus God alone.

## THIRD QUESTION

25. Your third inquiry is this: Whether Christ’s soul, which received the divinity, possesses altogether a complete knowledge of it; and whether, just as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit know one another, so the same Son, through that by which he is man, knows himself in that by which he is God, possessing the whole Father from both substances and in both substances. Or perhaps, just as with bodily eyes he does not at all see God, who is spirit—lest it be believed that dignity was added to the man rather than that his nature was utterly changed—so the rational soul, although with devout understanding and a most pure heart, does not see or comprehend the whole essence of divinity, lest some creature be found capable of containing the Creator.

## RESPONSE

26. When I had read these words in your letter, dearest brother, I confess that I was constricted by great anxiety, because we are compelled to say what we cannot sufficiently or worthily conceive. For consideration of the distinction between Creator and creature shows to the creature’s understanding the Creator’s magnitude to be incomprehensible and inexplicable: since “the peace of God surpasses all understanding” (Philippians 4:7), and he who “ascended above the cherubim flew upon the wings of the winds” (Psalm 17:10).

You know, moreover, that “cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” What, then, is it to ascend above the cherubim except to surpass every fullness of knowledge by an incomprehensible height?

But this we confidently and indubitably say concerning holy angels and holy human beings: each of them is called a god through the gratuitous gift of divine adoption, yet the God of angels or human beings is in no way called a god.

When, however, we speak of Christ’s soul, we speak of that rational spirit to which God not only came by grace, but which divinity itself assumed in the unity of person. For that soul with the Word is one Christ; that soul with the Word is one Unigenitus God.

And because the Unigenitus God is equal to the Father, the Son cannot know the whole without knowing the whole Father. Let us therefore beware lest, when Christ’s soul is not believed to know the whole Father, knowledge not only of the Father but also of himself and of the Holy Spirit be denied in some respect to Christ, who is one person. It is exceedingly harsh, and utterly alien to sound faith, to say that Christ’s soul does not possess a complete knowledge of its divinity, with which it is believed naturally to have one person.

27. If we believe this, John the Baptist’s proclamation must necessarily be frustrated—his proclamation by which he attributes to Christ a singular and immeasurable abundance of the Spirit, saying: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3:34). For our elders receive in us a measure of this abundance, whereas in Christ they confess that the fullness of the Holy Spirit remains.

Blessed Ambrose, in the first book of his work On the Holy Spirit (book 1, chapter 6), says among other things:

> “I will pour out from my Spirit,” he says (Acts 2:17). He does not say, “the Spirit,” but “from the Spirit.” For we cannot contain the fullness of the Holy Spirit; we receive only as much as the arbiter of our affairs, according to his will, has divided from his own Spirit.

Thus, showing that we receive not the fullness but something from the fullness of the Spirit, blessed Ambrose goes on shortly afterward to say, in order to show that Christ received the whole fullness of the Spirit:

> Concerning the Holy Spirit the Father says that he pours himself out upon all flesh. For he does not pour out the whole, but what he poured out was abundant for all. Something from the Holy Spirit, therefore, has been poured out upon us. But upon the Lord Jesus, when he was in the form of a man, the Spirit remained; as it is written: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending from heaven and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33). Toward us, it is the generosity of the giver arising from abundant benevolence; in him, the fullness of the entire Spirit remains forever.

Indeed, blessed Ambrose clearly and indubitably shows that Christ’s soul possesses a complete knowledge of the whole divinity when he says: “Toward us, it is the generosity of the giver arising from abundant benevolence; in him, the fullness of the entire Spirit remains forever.”

He said this with attention to blessed John’s statement concerning the Son himself: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3:34).

Blessed Augustine also perceived and understood this through the same illumination of the Holy Spirit, and confirms that it must be understood of the person of Christ alone. For after explaining the same Gospel passage (Treatise 14 on John), and setting forth John the Baptist’s statement, “For God does not give the Spirit by measure,” blessed Augustine added:

> What does this mean: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure”? We find that God gives the Spirit by measure. Hear the Apostle saying: “According to the measure of the gift of Christ” (Ephesians 4:7). To human beings he gives by measure; to the only Son he does not give by measure.

Again, in the same homily he says:

> Thus also the gifts of the faithful are different, distributed to each according to its proper measure, as to members. But Christ, who gives, did not receive by measure. For hear what follows, since he had said concerning the Son, “For God does not give the Spirit by measure”: “The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” (John 3:34).

Blessed Augustine clearly shows by this evangelical testimony what we ought to think concerning Christ’s soul, since Christ himself, who gives the Spirit, does not receive it by measure. He is the one who gives; he is the one who receives. And because he is powerful enough to give by measure, he could not receive by measure.

Remaining in the form of God, he gives the Spirit; receiving the form of a servant, he received the Spirit. But because he himself gives by measure, he did not himself receive by measure; for he received in full the very one whom he gives by measure. He gives by measure to many sons, but the only Son does not receive by measure, because he is true man in such a way that he is also true God.

28. Blessed Augustine had once presented this Gospel passage differently in the two books he wrote On the Sermon on the Mount (Saint Augustine, book 1, On the Sermon on the Mount, chapter 6). In his Retractations, however (book 1, chapter 19), he corrected that interpretation, approving and affirming the understanding that, after later grasping it more clearly, he established in his exposition of the Gospel: namely, that it must be understood of Christ alone.

Showing this in the first book of his Retractations, he says among other things:

> Elsewhere, when I inserted the testimony, “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3:34), I had not yet understood that it was more correctly to be taken specifically of Christ. For if the Spirit were not given by measure to other human beings, Elisha would not have asked for a double portion of what had been in Elijah (2 Kings 2:9).

In these words of blessed Augustine, let us pay particular attention to his statement that the Spirit is given by measure to other human beings. He said this precisely to show that he was speaking not of Christ’s divinity but of his humanity, to which God did not give the Spirit by measure, whereas the Apostle testifies that grace is given to each according to the measure of Christ’s gift.

Why, then, did blessed Augustine say “to other human beings” rather than simply “to human beings,” unless to show that in that singular man there is not a measured portion but the whole fullness of the Spirit—he who is naturally true man in such a way that he is likewise naturally true God, receiving in the reality of his flesh the whole one whom, by the gift of divinity, he bestows by measure?

To him, therefore, who gives grace according to the measure of his gift, God gave the Spirit not by measure.

In Christ, however, according to the truth of catholic faith, we confess in the unity of person both divinity, a rational soul, and flesh. Yet divinity could not receive the Spirit, because according to divinity the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God.

The Father alone is as great as he is with the Son and the Holy Spirit; the Son alone is as great as he is with the Father and the Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit alone is as great as he is with the Father and the Son together.

Among the three persons, none is less than the other two, because in each person divinity is so complete that it is one in the three persons and whole in each individual person.

The Son’s divinity, therefore, could not receive the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father, and is given by the Son just as he is given by the Father. Nor could the nature from which the Holy Spirit has his origin either await or receive his gift.

That Spirit is wholly the Father’s and wholly the Son’s, because he is naturally the one Spirit of the Father and the Son. Therefore, he proceeds wholly from the Father and the Son, and remains wholly in the Father and the Son; for he remains in such a way that he proceeds, and proceeds in such a way that he remains.

Hence, by nature he possesses with the Father and the Son the fullness of unity and the unity of fullness, so that he has the whole Father and the whole Son, and he himself is wholly possessed by the Father and wholly possessed by the Son.

The Son’s divinity, therefore, did not receive the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit is of one nature with it and derives from it whatever he has—indeed, he is from it what he is, because what he naturally possesses is what he is.

It remains, then, that Christ’s soul received the Holy Spirit. Yet it did not receive him by measure; it received him wholly. For wherever there is said to be no measure, there is found the fullness of perfection and the perfection of fullness.

29. The prophet Isaiah shows us who this Spirit is whom Christ received not by measure. Speaking of him (another reading: “of Christ”), he says:

> “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11:1).

Christ therefore received the Spirit, but he did not receive him by measure. If God gave the Spirit to Christ’s soul not by measure, it necessarily follows that it possesses nothing less of wisdom and nothing less of knowledge. For that Spirit is the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and piety.

Accordingly, that prerogative of perfection belongs not only to Christ’s divinity but also to his soul—a perfection which the Apostle ascribes to Christ himself when he says: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). For if he received the Spirit of wisdom and knowledge not by measure, he must possess all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

If something of this fullness is taken away from him, it follows that he is proclaimed to have received the Spirit by measure. And who is there to whom God has given the Spirit not by measure, if Christ received him by measure? Insofar as the Spirit is given, to that extent knowledge of divinity is received; but where the Spirit is without measure, there must be a full knowledge of immeasurable divinity.

The whole fullness is given where the Spirit is not given by measure. We, however, have all received not his fullness but something from his fullness, “and grace for grace” (John 1:16).

This also shows that in the grace of the vision which will be given (another reading: “which is given”) in place of the grace of faith, we shall receive not the fullness itself but something from its fullness, grace for grace; and by the very fact that we have received from his fullness, we shall be filled to the extent that we are made capable through his grace.

The prophet shows this to us when he says: “You will fill me with joy in your presence” (Psalm 15:11); and again: “We have been filled in the morning with your mercy” (Psalm 89:14); and again: “We shall be filled with the good things of your house” (Psalm 64:5).

But in order to be filled, we shall receive from his fullness. Concerning Christ, however, Paul, teacher of the nations, says that “in him it was pleasing that all fullness should dwell” (Colossians 1:19); and concerning him he likewise says: “In him dwells the whole fullness of divinity bodily” (Colossians 2:9).

I therefore do not think that Christ’s soul lacks in any respect a complete knowledge of divinity, since it has one person with the Word. Wisdom assumed it in such a way that it itself is that same Wisdom. It was made lord of all things to such an extent that, together with its own divinity, it is one person in the Trinity: that is, Christ crucified, whom the apostle Paul proclaims to be “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24).

30. But if Christ’s soul possesses in some respect a lesser knowledge of its divinity, then it does not possess the whole of wisdom and the whole of power. It is therefore a participant in Christ, not Christ himself, if it possesses only part of the knowledge of its divinity.

The Apostle, however, asserts that we are participants in Christ, saying: “For we have become participants in Christ” (Hebrews 3:14). Hence it is said to Christ: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your participants” (Psalm 44:8).

There can be no doubt that the oil of gladness with which Christ was anointed is the Holy Spirit, since blessed Peter says: “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:38).

God therefore anointed him above his participants—the one to whom he gave the Spirit not by measure, in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.

Blessed Paul marvels at the height of his wisdom and knowledge when he says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33).

True faith confesses Christ to be altogether Most High not only according to his divinity but also according to his humanity. For the Mother of Zion says: “A man, and a man was born in her (another reading: ‘was made in her’), and the Most High himself founded her” (Psalm 86:5).

Indeed, who would dare deny that he is Most High whom God not only begot as Most High from himself but also exalted when he was born of the Virgin, and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:9)?

If Christ’s soul does not possess a complete knowledge of its divinity, it has not attained the full height of the wisdom and knowledge of God. Christ, therefore, would be proclaimed Most High not in his entirety but only in part, if believers proclaim that his soul falls short of the height of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge.

In what does God exalt us, except in that by which he raises our souls to himself? He raises our souls to himself to the extent that he conveys to us the truth of his knowledge and love.

Who, however, would say that Christ’s soul either perceives less of the truth or possesses less of love? Christ himself is the truth. How, then, can that soul be said to possess less knowledge of the truth, when it is found to be the soul uniquely belonging to the very truth?

Christ’s soul must not be discussed in the same way as any angelic or human spirit, which can be a participant in the true God but not the true God, who is Christ. [Note: Ant. reads: “or human [spirit]. Who can be a participant in the true God except the true God, who is Christ?”] Christ assumed perfect flesh and a perfect rational soul—that is, a complete human nature—into the eternal person of his divinity. Just as he is naturally wholly true man, so he is wholly true God.

For just as in his divinity he possesses the whole nature of his humanity, so in his humanity he possesses the whole substance, the whole majesty, the whole immutability, the whole power, the whole wisdom, and the whole omnipotence of his divinity.

The Unigenitus God deigned to assume human nature in such a way that he himself is God who is man, and the same one is man who is God.

Therefore, just as there is fullness of divinity in the man Christ, so there is fullness of humanity in God. And just as Christ, as man, uniquely possesses the reality that he is true God, so he uniquely knows his entire divinity.

31. We can certainly say that Christ’s soul possesses a complete knowledge of its divinity. Yet I do not know whether we ought to say that Christ’s soul knows its divinity in the same way that the divinity itself knows itself, or whether we should rather say that it knows as much as the divinity does, but not in the same way as the divinity.

For divinity knows itself in such a way that it naturally finds itself to be what it knows; but that soul knows its entire divinity in such a way that it nevertheless is not itself that divinity.

That divinity is naturally identical with its own knowledge; but that soul received from the divinity, which it knows completely, the capacity to know. Therefore, divinity naturally is what it knows; whereas that soul, in knowing its divinity, does not find itself to be what it knows.

Christ is therefore not known according to his divinity by his soul in the same way that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit know one another, since that soul possesses a complete knowledge of the Trinity but does not possess one nature with the Trinity.

It is one thing for each thing to know what it is by nature, and another for it to know what it is not by nature.

God, who is spirit, cannot be seen by bodily eyes. For this reason blessed Augustine, in the letter he wrote to Italica (formerly letter 6, now 82), briefly but sufficiently refutes certain people who wanted to believe that Christ sees God the Father with bodily eyes.

Bodily eyes have this property: they see not only bodies, but cannot see even those bodies if there are no intervening intervals of physical space between the eyes and the things they see. That is why, although they see many other things, they cannot see themselves; nor do they see within themselves when they see outside themselves. Indeed, the visual power itself is dulled if something to be seen is brought too close to the eyes.

Therefore, whoever thinks that God can be perceived by bodily eyes must first say that he is separated from those eyes by bodily space. But whoever wishes to recognize by what eyes God is seen should consider God himself, since he is wisdom, truth, and love.

Accordingly, by the eyes with which wisdom, truth, and love are seen, that wise, true, and beloved divinity is seen.

God therefore promises his vision not to the eyes of the body but to the eyes of the human soul, which he has made capable of wisdom, truth, and love. The rational spirit has received from God the capacity to see God—received it, certainly, through grace. Yet it cannot see him outside itself but within itself; for God is not contained by place but perceived by affection, and therefore he is not seen in one in whom he does not dwell.

God dwells much more inwardly in the soul than the soul dwells in the body, because he is the creator Spirit, whereas the soul is created.

Every holy human soul therefore possesses knowledge of that supreme God to the extent that it has received the grace of inward vision.

How, then, are we to understand the Unigenitus, full of grace and truth from the Father, if we say that some fullness of grace is lacking in that fullness of truth, or if we judge that the fullness of truth is not entirely present in that fullness of grace?

The Unigenitus is most certainly recognized as full of grace and truth from the Father when not only the full grace of humanity and the full truth of divinity are recognized in that one person, but also when the fullness of truth in itself possesses the fullness of grace, by which all humanity exists in its divinity; and when the fullness of grace possesses within itself the fullness of truth, by which all divinity exists in its humanity—so that the fullness of truth contains within itself the fullness of grace, and the fullness of grace contains within itself the fullness of truth.

33. The whole fullness of truth is not possessed when something of truth itself is unknown—something which, God forbid, we should in any way think concerning Christ.

The whole fullness of grace is in that fullness of truth, so that the full divinity completely fills its humanity. And the fullness of truth is in that fullness of grace, so that the full humanity, just as it possesses a complete and singular incorruption and immortality of flesh, also possesses, according to the soul, a complete and singular knowledge of divinity.

Christ is therefore full of grace and truth in such a way that, just as there is a complete assumption of humanity in his divinity, so there is a complete recognition of divinity in his humanity.

Let us not fear to assert that Christ’s soul knows its entire divinity, lest on that account it be said to be of one nature with that divinity. For if true reasoning demands that unity of nature necessarily follows immediately upon fullness of knowledge, then God himself, who certainly knows fully everything he has made, would be said to be of the same nature as the things he made and knows.

Anyone who believes or asserts this is not endowed with catholic truth but possessed by Manichaean impiety.

Moreover, we must also observe that, to whatever extent Christ’s soul is said to possess knowledge of its divinity, it is immediately said to possess, to that same extent, one nature with its divinity. This is plainly great madness.

We too hope, by the grace of God, to see God; and to the extent that we shall see him, without doubt we shall know him. Apostolic authority commends both truths to us. Blessed Paul says: “Now I know in part; then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Corinthians 13:12). And Christ’s beloved John asserts without hesitation: “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

That vision will not be of the flesh alone, according to which the Son alone will be seen by the wicked for their everlasting condemnation. It will be a vision of divinity, according to which the Trinity itself will offer itself to the righteous to be seen in such a way that the unceasing vision of divinity will itself be the unfailing fullness of blessedness.

“For this reason they are blessed who are pure in heart, because they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

We shall therefore see the divinity of the holy Trinity to the extent that, by the gift of grace, we receive—or, according to another reading, “grasp”—the ability to see. Yet, to the extent that we see, we shall not thereby be consubstantial with that divinity.

With the body, too, we see many things which are not of one and the same nature with our flesh. Our eyes see light, although the eyes are of one nature and the light of another.

Blessed John indeed said: “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). But by “like” he meant likeness through imitation of righteousness, not unity of nature. In accordance with this imitation, blessed Paul says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1); and blessed John says: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6).

The creature, however, contains the Creator to the extent that it receives the capacity to contain him. [Note: Ant. reads *in quantum*, “insofar as.”]

34. This is why blessed Augustine does not avoid this way of speaking but adopts it without hesitation. In the same homily (Treatise 14 on John, toward the end), in which he explained the passage, “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3:34), he says at one point concerning the Son himself:

> Remaining God with the Father, he became man among human beings, so that through him who became man among you, you might become such as can contain God. For man could not contain God; man could see man, but could not contain God. Why could he not contain God? Because he did not have the eye of the heart by which he could contain him. Something within was therefore wounded, while something outside was sound: he had sound bodily eyes, but wounded eyes of the heart. That man was made visible to the bodily eye, so that, believing in him who could be seen bodily, you might be healed for seeing the very one whom you could not see spiritually.

By these words blessed Augustine shows that in spiritual matters “to contain” means “to see,” that “to see” means “to understand,” and that “to understand” means “to know.”

For this reason, in his book On the Presence of God (Letter to Dardanus, formerly 57, now 187), when he grants the full capacity for divinity to the Son alone, he shows that the Son alone possesses full knowledge of divinity. In that book he uses these words:

> God, therefore, is present everywhere, and wholly present everywhere; yet he does not dwell everywhere, but in his temple, to which he is gracious and propitious through grace. He is contained while dwelling, more by some and less by others. Concerning our Head, however, the Apostle says: “In him dwells the whole fullness of divinity bodily” (Colossians 2:9).

Please note in these words of blessed Augustine the most certain distinction between the Head and the members. By those to whom God gives the Spirit by measure, God dwelling in them is contained—more by some, less by others.

What does it mean to be contained except to be understood and known? But when blessed Augustine wished to speak of Christ, observe what he says:

> Concerning our Head, the Apostle says: “In him dwells the whole fullness of divinity bodily” (Colossians 2:9).

Blessed Augustine himself says that God, while dwelling, is contained. Therefore, the fullness of divinity is undoubtedly contained by the one in whom the fullness of divinity itself dwells. He is contained in the one in whom he is known.

In the one, therefore, in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwells, there cannot fail to be a complete knowledge of that fullness.

This is why, shortly afterward, blessed Augustine says in the same book:

> What, then, do we think is the difference between the Head and the other members? Is it that, in any member, however distinguished—such as some great prophet or apostle—although divinity dwells there, nevertheless the whole fullness of divinity does not dwell there as in the Head, which is Christ? For in our body there is sensation in each of the members, but not so much as in the head, where all five senses are entirely present. There are sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. In the other members there is touch alone. Or, apart from the fact that the whole fullness of divinity dwells in that body as in a temple, is there something else that distinguishes that Head from the excellence of any member? Certainly there is: by a unique assumption, that man’s person was made one with the Word. For concerning none of the saints could it be said, or can it be said, or will it be said: “The Word was made flesh” (John 1:14). No saint, however distinguished by grace, received the name of the Unigenitus, so that what the Word of God is before the ages might also be said, together with the man assumed. That assumption, therefore, is unique and cannot in any way be shared with any holy human beings, however outstanding in wisdom and holiness.


It is therefore certain that the opinion of the holy Fathers agrees with the heavenly Scriptures. These most clearly testify and, inspired by God, proclaim to us that all adopted children receive through grace a share in knowing and containing divinity, according to the will of the giver; but that Christ—that is, his soul—possesses a complete knowledge of the whole divinity.

## FOURTH QUESTION

35. Your letters then contain the fourth question as follows. You say:

> We believe and confess that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one kingdom, understanding that they rule together over all creatures. Why, then, throughout nearly all the regions of Africa the catholic Church has become accustomed to say in the priests’ prayers, “Through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit,” as though the Son alone possessed the kingdom with the Father, specifically in the unity of the Holy Spirit, so that the Holy Spirit is indicated as uniting those who reign, rather than as reigning together with them?

258. RESPONSE
36. I shall state plainly what I think about this wording. Whenever I have reflected upon it since then, I have found that our predecessors intended nothing other than to safeguard the truth of the faith against many heresies. The first point to be observed is that, in the conclusion of the prayer, we say, “Through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord”; but we never say, “through the Holy Spirit.” The Catholic Church certainly does not celebrate this formula without reason, on account of that mystery by which Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings, became human—the Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek—who, through his own blood, entered once for all into the holy places, not into copies made by human hands of the true ones [Note: [Col. 0423] Thus the manuscripts Thu. and Ant., in conformity with the apostolic text; other manuscripts have *veritatis*, “of the truth.”] (Heb. IX, 24), but into heaven itself, where he is at the right hand of God and intercedes for us.

Considering this priestly office in him, the Apostle says: “Through him, therefore, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name” (Heb. XIII, 15). Through him, therefore, we offer a sacrifice of praise and prayer, because through his death we were reconciled, although we had been enemies. For through him, who deigned to become a sacrifice for us, our sacrifice can be found acceptable in the sight of God. Therefore blessed Peter admonishes us, saying: “You yourselves, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house, into a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (I Pet. II, 5).

For this reason we say to God the Father, “Through Jesus Christ our Lord.” For you know well that it is sometimes said: “Through the eternal Priest, your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.” When, therefore, mention is made of the priest, what else is revealed except the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation? The Son of God, although he existed in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; according to that form he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death; being made, that is, a little lower than the angels, while possessing equality with the Father’s divinity [another reading: “unity”]. For the Son was made lower while remaining equal to the Father, in that he deigned to become like human beings. He himself made himself lower when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Christ’s being made lower is itself his emptying; yet his emptying is nothing other than the assumption of the form of a servant.

37. Christ, therefore, while remaining in the form of God—the only-begotten God, with whom we offer sacrifices to the Father—became a priest by taking the form of a servant, so that through him we might be able to offer a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to God. Yet a sacrifice could not have been offered by us if Christ had not become a sacrifice for us; in him the very nature of our race is a true saving sacrifice.

For in order that the only-begotten Son, who is naturally true God, might also become a true priest, he did not deign to assume, in the person of his divinity, the person of our humanity, but its nature. For if, in the mystery of the Incarnation, he had assumed the nature of a human being together with a person, then the same one Christ would not be God and human in two natures, but in two persons there would be another who was God and another who was human. But Christ is one, the true Son of God and of humanity, because the only-begotten Lord, who always possessed his own person, received the reality of a servant’s nature into that same person of his. Therefore Christ remains inseparable: although one nature in him is divine and the other is a servant’s nature, nevertheless, in the one and same Christ, the person of the eternal divinity is also the person of the assumed humanity.

For this reason Christ is one and the same: the assumption of the form of a servant shows him to have been made a little lower than the angels, while natural unity demonstrates him to be equal to the Father. In this mystery the Arians so grievously erred that, observing in him the office of priest, they refused [Note: [Col. 0425D] Manuscript Thu. has *non noverint*, “they did not know,”] to acknowledge the majesty of his divinity. Hence they also say: “Glory to the Father through the Son,” refusing to say: “Glory to the Father and to the Son.”

Since, therefore, there are heretics who do not believe that the Son is of one divinity with the Father [Note: [Col. 0425D] Ant. has *non credant*, “who do not believe”;], while there are others who are not afraid to deny the reality of the flesh in the Son of God, the most holy Fathers appropriately and profitably established this wording. For when we show that our prayers are offered through the eternal Priest, the Lord Christ, we confess in him the true flesh of our race, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “Every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God, to offer gifts” [Note: [Col. 0426D] Ant. has “to offer gifts to God”] “and sacrifices for sins” (Heb. V, 1).

But when we say, “your Son,” and add, “who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit,” we recall that unity which the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possess by nature. Here it is shown that this same Christ exercised the priestly office for us, while he possesses natural unity with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Consider, I ask, how many heretics are refuted by this. Our faith is distinguished above all from the error of the Manichaeans when we offer our prayers through that Priest who is truly a Priest because he offered himself as a true sacrifice for us. The Apostle unequivocally affirms this, saying: “Be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, a fragrant aroma” (Eph. V, 1). He certainly would not have offered a true sacrifice if the reality of flesh had not been in him.

After he had risen from the dead, this supreme Priest showed the reality of this sacrifice to his disciples and offered himself to be touched, saying: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke XXIV, 39).

38. From this point our faith is also distinguished from the error of Eutyches. Although he does not dare to deny that the Word became incarnate, nevertheless, because he does not confess that the flesh of the Word was taken from the flesh of the Virgin, he utterly empties the mystery of the supreme Priest. The Apostle contradicts him with the statement I cited above: “Every high priest,” he says, “taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God” (Heb. V, 1). And elsewhere: “For he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham. Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people” (Heb. II, 16).

Thus, by this wording, through which we show that our prayers are offered through Jesus Christ, true faith resists every error that does not confess in Christ the reality of a human body. But because Christ is not only truly human, but also naturally true God, and one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, we rightly say to God the Father: “who lives and reigns with you”—in that natural unity which he displayed when he said: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30).

Here likewise our faith is distinguished not only from the error of Arius and Sabellius, but also from that of Nestorius. For in the very term “unity,” just as it is recognized that the substance of the Father and the Son is not different, so, when we say “who lives and reigns with you,” it is shown that the Father and the Son are not one person. It is also evident that the eternal Priest is himself the true Son, who reigns with God the Father in unity of nature.

When, however, we say “in the unity of the Holy Spirit,” we show that the Holy Spirit has one nature with the Father and the Son. But what does unity of nature show except that the Trinity is one God, and consequently that there is one kingdom as well? For diversity of nature can show diversity of power in a kingdom. But where there is unity of nature in a kingdom, the power of reigning remains one. In that kingdom, however, those to whom power is granted by grace, rather than supplied by nature, can possess a diversity of power.

In the Trinity there is not diversity but unity of power. The Trinity bestows that power upon each according to its own will, because it possesses ineffable unity by nature. Consider also what blessed Augustine teaches about the Holy Spirit in the sixth book of *On the Trinity* (chap. V). After saying, “Therefore the Son is equal to the Father and is of one and the same substance,” he immediately adds: “Therefore the Holy Spirit exists [another reading: ‘subsists’] in the same unity of substance and equality. For whether it is the unity of both, or holiness, or love, or unity because it is love, and love because it is holiness, it is clear that it is not one of the two by whom the two are joined, by whom the one begotten is loved by the one who begets and loves the one who begets; and that they exist not by participation, but by their essence, and not by the gift of some superior, but by what is their own, preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”

A little later, in the same place, he says: “Therefore the Holy Spirit is something common to the Father and the Son, whatever that may be; but that very communion is consubstantial and coeternal. If it can suitably be called friendship, let it be called so; but it is more appropriately called love. And this too is substance, because God is substance and God is love, as it is written” (I John IV, 16).

Again, elsewhere in the same book (the same chapter, 5), he says: “Therefore the Holy Spirit also is equal; and if equal, equal in every respect, on account of the supreme simplicity that exists in that substance. And therefore there are not more than three: one loving him who is from him, one loving him from whom he is, and love itself. If it is nothing, how is God love? If it is not substance, how is God substance?”

In these words blessed Augustine did not hesitate to call the unity of the Father and the Son the Holy Spirit, just as he called it love and holiness; nor did he hesitate confidently to proclaim that the Holy Spirit is not merely something common to them, but their consubstantial and coeternal communion. Catholics say this so that, from the very name “unity,” the faithful may recognize one essence; from this, one kingdom; and in that one kingdom, one power and one majesty of the Trinity. Thus no one may suppose that either the Son or the Holy Spirit reigns with the Father according to the divine nature as an inferior reigns with one who is superior, but that the unity of the Holy Spirit, which is the communion of the Father and the Son, by displaying the unity of divinity in that kingdom, teaches that there is one eternity of reigning, one power, one majesty, and one dominion of the supreme Trinity.

## THE FIFTH QUESTION

39. The letter contains the fifth, that is, the final question, in these words. Why is it that, when the evangelist Luke is narrating the Lord’s supper, he first says that he took a cup and immediately handed it to the disciples to divide among themselves; and then, after taking bread, said, “This is my body”; and, after taking a cup likewise after he had supped, then said: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which is poured out for you” [another reading: “will be poured out”] (Luke XXII, 17 ff.)?

After proposing this question, you add and say: Was one cup given a second time, or was one given first and another afterward? And if so, you ask, to what mystery does that cup belong concerning which, above all, the other evangelists who wrote the Gospels remained silent [another reading, as above in Ferrandus’s letter: “the Gospels”]?

## RESPONSE

40. Some have wished this passage of the Gospel to be understood in such a way that they did not assert that two cups were given by the Lord, but rather maintained that the statement was made by anticipation; in their view, there was one cup, which is mentioned as having been given to the disciples first to be divided and afterward to be drunk.

Others, however, maintain that the cup was given a second time. But whether one holds this view or the other, each interpretation is such that it is in no way found to be foreign to the true faith.

Those who think that the cup was given a second time interpreted the event symbolically. Some asserted that in the first cup the Lord prefigured his own passion, and in the second the passion of his faithful. Others said that both cups displayed what was commanded in the Old Testament (Exod. XII, 5; Num. IX, 11): whoever had not celebrated the Passover of the first month by eating the lamb was to celebrate it in the second month by eating the kid.

It seems to me, however, that another mystery appropriate to the Christian faith can also be found here: the two Testaments should be understood in the two cups. This is especially so because the Truth himself demonstrated the matter to us in such a way that no difficulty remained for those who inquire. For the Lord himself deigned to call the cup that he gave to be drunk the New Testament, as the Gospel narrative shows.

This is found in the testimony of all three evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—without any uncertainty. Matthew’s words are these: “While they were eating, Jesus took bread; and he blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat: this is my body.’ And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: ‘Drink from it, all of you: for this is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins’” (Matt. XXVI, 26).
