Mark, explaining the mystery of the Lord’s bread and cup, says: “While they were eating [Note: [Col. 0427D] Ant. has “while they were eating, however”], Jesus took bread; and blessing it, he broke it and gave it to them, and said: ‘Take this: this is my body.’ And taking the cup, giving thanks, he gave it to them, and they all drank from it. And he said to them: ‘This is my blood of the New Testament, which is poured out [another reading: ‘will be poured out’] for many’” (Mark XIV, 22).

In Luke, who is certainly found to have named the cup a second time, the account is arranged and explained in these words: “And taking the cup, he gave thanks and said: ‘Take this and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you that I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.’ And taking bread, he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying: ‘This is my body, which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which is poured out [another reading: ‘will be poured out’] for you’” (Luke XXII, 17).

This is why blessed Paul, recalling the most sacred mystery of that supper, indicates that the cup was called by the Lord nothing other than the New Testament. Among other things he says: “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘This is my body for you’ [Note: [Col. 0428D] Thus the manuscripts Thu. and Ant.; other manuscripts have “which is given for you”]; ‘do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the New Testament in my blood; do this, whenever you drink, [another reading: ‘whenever you are drinking’] in remembrance of me’” (I Cor. XI, 23).

41. In view, therefore, of this testimony from the Gospels and the Apostle, in the name “cup,” at least in this passage, we are permitted to understand nothing other than the divine Testament. Nor is there any doubt that elsewhere the Lord used the name “cup” to signify the grace of his passion.

He intended this to be understood when he said to the sons of Zebedee: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” (Matt. XX, 22). And at the very hour when he willed to be seized by the hands of the impious, he showed by these words to blessed Peter, warning him to put the sword back into its sheath, that he was going to drink the cup of his passion: “Put the sword into its sheath. Shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?” [Note: [Col. 0429D] Other copies have: “Do you not want me to drink it?”] (John XVIII, 11).

He also showed there that the cup was to be understood as his passion when, having withdrawn from his disciples about a stone’s throw, he was about to die for the sins of humanity and truly displayed in himself the feeling of human weakness. In order to remove despair from his weaker members [another reading: “lower members”], the very Power that willed to be our Head did not disdain, through divine love, to say what his members would later say through human fear.

Thus the evangelist Luke records him as saying: “Father, if you are willing, take this cup away from me” (Luke XXII, 42). Matthew likewise testifies that his words were: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI, 39). Mark, to show what we ought to understand in that cup, says: “And going forward a little, he fell upon the ground and prayed that, if it could be, the hour might pass from him” (Mark XIV, 35).

What hour do we think the holy evangelist intended here except that of which the Lord said: “My hour has not yet come” (John II, 4), and of which the evangelist John says: “No one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come” (John VII, 30)? It was the hour not of a death imposed by compulsion, but of a voluntary passion—the hour, without doubt, when he would receive a triumphant death and, releasing the pains of hell, would himself mercifully and wondrously become the death of death, as he had already said through the Prophet: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your sting, O underworld” (Hos. XIII, 14).

The blessed evangelist subsequently shows that this hour was named by the Lord in prayer under the name of the cup, adding the same Lord’s prayer: “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you; take this cup away from me” (Mark XIV, 36). It is plainly evident that to pray that the hour might pass from him was to say that the cup might be taken away from him.

Here, as I have said, our Head demonstrated that he had assumed the weakness of his members, to whom he knew he would give the power to suffer. He taught that the merit of passion is not thereby emptied if, in a human being who is about to suffer for Christ’s faith and love, a readiness of spirit is shaken by the trembling of the will arising from the weakness of the flesh. Rather, the human will itself should submit to the divine will, and from weakness should perfect strength, through the prevailing gift of spiritual grace. It retained for itself the capacity given by him whose will it would not doubt was to be preferred to its own will. Thus the human being might patiently overcome what he desired through human weakness, so as happily to reach that to which the divine will usefully calls him.

42. Christ’s will, therefore, could not have been other than the Father’s will, since natural unity always preserves one will in the Father and the Son. But he who came by assuming human nature in order to save the nature he had made uttered the words of that same nature through a real, not deceptive, assumption; and in his most merciful goodness he also assumed its feeling—that is, the feeling that the flesh has because of the fear of dying, not because of a desire to sin.

For he who knew no sin assumed, without sin, the true feeling not of our guilt but of our weakness. Indeed, blessed Peter says of him: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (I Pet. II, 22). Therefore, because he committed no sin, he did not have a will different from the Father’s will; and because no deceit was found in his mouth, there is no doubt that he uttered true words from the feeling of human weakness.

Although, then, in those sayings of our Savior in which he named the cup, the passion of both himself and his saints is to be understood—for blessed David also called it a cup, but only in the passage where he says: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXV, 3)—thereby showing that this cup means nothing other than the death of the saints, he immediately adds: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints”—nevertheless, the name “cup” also signifies the perfect grace of love, by which the strength to undergo passion is infused for Christ’s name.

Thus, even if the opportunity is lacking for someone to undergo passion for Christ, such great strength may nevertheless be present in the heart through the gift of divine grace that nothing is lacking for enduring punishment, despising life, and undergoing death for Christ’s name.

This is rightly understood in the passage of the psalm: “And your cup, which makes drunk, how glorious it is!” (Ps. XXII, 5). It had first said: “You have enriched my head with oil.” What, then, should we understand by the head enriched with oil except the mind strengthened by the gift of the Holy Spirit? The splendid richness of this oil is the inseparable strength of spiritual grace, by which holy intoxication is poured into the inner chambers of the heart, so that every affection of the flesh, consigned to oblivion, may be overcome.

Filled with this intoxication, the soul learns always to rejoice in the Lord and to count as contemptible whatever it loved in the world. We shall drink this intoxication when, having received the Holy Spirit, we possess the grace of perfect love, which casts out fear. Hence blessed Ambrose taught us to ask for the grace of this intoxication in the morning hymn, when we say: “Joyfully let us drink the sober intoxication of the Spirit” (Monday at Lauds; *Fer. 2 ad laudes*).

43. In other passages, therefore, the name “cup” may be understood in any number of ways according to the rule of true faith. In this Gospel passage, however, which we are now discussing, we are permitted to understand nothing other than what we are taught by the words of the Lord and our Master himself, who says: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood” (Luke XXII, 20).

According to this rule, by which this cup is called the New Testament, the cup that he gave first is rightly understood as the Old Testament. The Lord himself, therefore, gave both cups, since he granted both Testaments to his faithful.

For this reason, at the same supper he both ate the Jewish Passover, which had to be offered, and gave the sacrament of his body and blood, which had to be instituted for the salvation of the faithful. He ate the Passover of the Jews, in which Christ was promised, so that he might come to our Passover, in which Christ was sacrificed.

Finally, observe what the evangelist Luke records him as saying to the disciples. He says: “When the hour had come, he reclined, and the twelve apostles with him; and he said to them: ‘I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer’” (Luke XXII, 14). He therefore ate the Passover by which he was signified as about to suffer, before he voluntarily suffered for us.

There is also something in the Lord’s own words that the faithful ought to recognize with closer attention, in which the distinction between the two Testaments can become apparent. Blessed Luke says this about the cup he named first: “And taking the cup, he gave thanks and said: ‘Take this and divide it among yourselves.’” But later, speaking of the bread and cup, he says: “And taking bread, he gave thanks and broke it and gave it to them, saying: ‘This is my body, which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which is poured out for you’” (Luke XXII, 17–19).

It does not seem to me that the Wisdom of God itself made this distinction of wording without reason. For he gave the first cup to be received in such a way that he commanded it to be divided, saying: “Take this and divide it among yourselves.” But he said nothing of the kind concerning the cup that he gave with the bread. There he commends his body and blood, and declares that same cup to be the New Testament in his blood, saying: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which is poured out for you.” No mention is made of dividing the cup. The same is likewise found in the other two evangelists, Matthew and Mark, as the words we set out above clearly show.

The Lord therefore commanded that this cup, in which we have said that the Old Testament is signified, be received and divided so that the apostles, instructed by the gift of heavenly wisdom, might receive the Scripture of the Old Testament reverently and, having received the spirit of discernment, might recognize in its commandments what ought to be done and what ought to be omitted. For this is to divide rightly: that each person should know, according to the appropriateness of the time, what he ought to omit and what he ought to retain.

44. Hence, with the most careful order of division, the Church of the living God, which is “the pillar and foundation of the truth” (I Tim. III, 15), distinguishes the times before Christ’s coming from the time of his coming. It omits the sacrifices by which Christ, who was to suffer, was promised, and offers the sacrifice by which Christ, who has already suffered, is displayed.

It also divides the former time of celebrating circumcision from the present time of receiving baptism. It preserves the most salutary method of this division even in the commandment concerning the new moon. For the holy Church does not sound the Jewish trumpets without purpose; rather, it does not cease to proclaim that each person should be renewed in the spirit of his mind and put on the new human being.

The Church wisely divides all these things. It now receives them reverently in reading, but no longer celebrates them in practice, lending the ear of the heart to the apostolic words by which blessed Paul instructs all the faithful, saying: “Let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a festival, or of a new moon, or of Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ” (Col. II, 16).

Explaining the sacrament of circumcision, he also says: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ; because in him dwells bodily the whole fullness of divinity, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power. In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by human hands, in the stripping away of the body of flesh, in the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism” (Col. II, 8–12).

The Church has wisely both received and divided these things and others like them. By receiving them, it believes that what God promised has truly been promised by God; by dividing them, it recognizes that what God promised has already truly been given by him. It does not await their fulfillment in figures, but holds fast to their fulfillment in truth.

The holy Church knows that God is faithful in his words and holy in all his works. Thus, just as in the Old Testament it understands the faithful words of God who promises, so in the New Testament it recognizes the holy works of God who gives what he promised.

For some of the words of God who promised were the sacraments of the Old Testament, by which Christ was promised to us. Those words passed away when the one to whom they referred was found to have been presented. Therefore, in the very sacrifice of Christ’s body, we begin with thanksgiving, so that we may show that Christ is not still to be given, but has been given to us in truth. And in giving thanks to God in the offering of Christ’s body and blood, we recognize that Christ is no longer to be killed for our iniquities, but has been killed; nor are we to be redeemed by that blood, but have been redeemed.

True is the preaching of blessed Peter, who says: “You were not redeemed with perishable silver or gold from your futile way of life inherited from your ancestors, but with the precious blood, as of an unblemished and spotless Lamb, Christ” (I Pet. I, 18).

45. The holy Church therefore divides figures from truth and shadows from the body. The holy apostles taught this to her, for they received from the Lord that cup to be divided among themselves for their salvation.

The Lord gave the disciples the division of this cup because, through the apostles’ teaching, the holy Church received knowledge of this division. He commands them to divide it among themselves—that is, in the unity of the Spirit and the bond of peace, to distinguish the sacraments of the New Testament from the cessation of the ancient sacraments. In the cup of the New Testament, however, he does not command the apostles to perform such a division.

For in the New Testament there is not a division of sacraments, but of gifts, which rests not in human ability but in the power of the Holy Spirit. “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; divisions of works, but the same God who works all things in all” (I Cor. XII, 4).

Hence, when to one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another the grace of healings in the one Spirit, and the other gifts that the apostolic word goes on to enumerate, these are not given to be divided by human beings. Rather, one and the same Spirit accomplishes all these things, dividing particular gifts to each as he wills.

Blessed Paul shows elsewhere this division, which God did not give to human beings but reserved for the Trinity alone, when he admonishes us not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sobriety, “according as God has divided to each the measure of faith” (Rom. XII, 3).

And because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one division, Christ, who is the Wisdom of God, says in Proverbs: “I walk in the paths of justice, and move amid the pathways of equity, that I may divide substance among those who love me and fill their treasuries with good things” (Prov. VIII, 20).

46. Both cups, therefore, are given by the Lord to the apostles, but the command to divide them is not given for both. Division was necessary for the cup in which the distinction of times had to be considered.

Hence, in the Old Testament, we recognize that certain sacraments were rightly celebrated in figures at that time, and we receive them reverently; yet we do not celebrate them in the same order in which they were celebrated. For, dividing the time of promise from the time when truth was given, we now retain the sacraments handed down to us by Christ, through which we recognize and hold fast that Christ has not yet to suffer, but has suffered for us.

We show that the Old Testament too must be received under the name of “cup,” not by our own presumption, but through the tradition of the Fathers. For blessed Augustine, in his exposition of Psalm seventy-four, when he came to the passage: “For the cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine with mixture; and he has poured from this into that; yet its dregs have not been emptied” (Ps. LXXIV, 9), says among other things:

> “The cup of unmixed wine full of mixture seems to me to be the law that was given to the Jews, and all that Scripture which is called the Old Testament, in which are the weights of all the sayings. For there the New Testament lies hidden, as though in the dregs of bodily sacraments.”

And when the same blessed Augustine distinguished those sacraments of the past from the commandments concerning the life that must be lived, as though dividing the cup, after recalling the words “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Deut. V, 17, 18), together with several other commandments contained in the text of the Decalogue, holy Augustine himself added:

> “All those things belong to the wine; but those carnal things, as it were, settled down, so that they might remain with them, and therefore all the spiritual understanding might be poured out. For the cup is in the hand of the Lord, that is, in the Lord’s power; of unmixed wine, that is, of sincere law; full of mixture, that is, with the dregs of bodily sacraments. And because now he humbles the proud Jew and exalts the confessing Gentile, he has poured from this into that, that is, from the Jewish people into the Gentile people. What did he pour? The law. And the spiritual understanding was filtered out from it. Yet its dregs have not been emptied, because all the carnal sacraments have remained with the Jews.”

From these words of blessed Augustine, I think it is clear that the cup can be understood in such a way that, in the truth of the spiritual mystery, a division between the dregs and the wine can be recognized. Yet no one should therefore wish to reject the Old Testament because he sees that its sacraments have ceased.

The New Testament must be held with such reverence that the Old Testament is in no way abandoned. This seems to me to be commended under the name of an old and a new friend in the book of Ecclesiasticus, where it is said: “Do not abandon an old friend, for a new one will not be like him” (Eccli. IX, 14).

Foretelling through the holy Jeremiah this difference between the sacraments of the two Testaments, the divine word says: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will consummate a New Testament over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah, not according to the Testament that I made with their fathers” (Jer. XXXI, 31).

The New Testament is found to have been consummated by the Lord, not according to the Old Testament, in that the Lord gave the perfection of the commandments and, removing the ancient sacraments, instituted sacraments unlike them, belonging to revealed truth. Thus what he promised in the Old Testament he perfected in the New.

Therefore, since knowledge of the sacraments of the New Testament can truly be salutary and sweet only if the true promise that preceded them is recognized in the sacraments of the Old Testament, Scripture, after saying, “Do not abandon an old friend, for a new one will not be like him,” immediately adds: “New wine is a new friend; let it become old, and you will drink it with sweetness” (Eccli. IX, 15).

What does “let it become old” mean except that the type of the New Testament should appear in the Old Testament? The new wine is therefore drunk with sweetness when its meaning and promise are recognized in the Old Testament.

47. The Lord caused this new wine to grow old in the hearts of the disciples when, as the two were going to the village of Emmaus, he drew near and went with them. When they had told him, as though he were unaware, what had happened concerning his passion, he said to them: “O foolish men, and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken” [Col. 0434D] (Luke 24:25). See, I ask you, how the new wine grows old so that it may be drunk with sweetness. The Lord therefore added: “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” (ibid., 26). Then the holy Evangelist explained how the new wine grew old for them so that it might be drunk with sweetness: “And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (ibid., 27). Afterwards, they themselves displayed the fervor of novelty and sweetness conceived from the wine that had grown old, saying: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (ibid., 32).

He did this again when he said: “These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you, because it is necessary that all things written about me in the law of Moses, and in the Prophets, and in the Psalms be fulfilled.” Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:44). Thus he caused the new wine to grow old with sweetness, unmistakably showing that the promises of the New Testament appear in the reading of the Old Testament. This was so that the new friend might not be held in such a way that the old one was abandoned, since the new remains similar in faith, although it appears dissimilar in the celebration of the sacraments. For the faith of the New and Old Testaments is one. What was promised was believed among our ancient fathers; what is now believed among us has been fulfilled. The faith promised to our fathers is itself the faith fulfilled in us through the truth that has been manifested. Therefore, since this old and new friend are inseparably joined, and neither can profitably be held without the other, the new wine must grow old, so that it may be drunk with sweetness by the faithful.

269 **LETTER XV. The African Bishops Exiled in Sardinia, to John and Venerius, Concerning the Grace of God and Human Free Will**

To the most holy brothers, greatly to be embraced in the grace of God, JOHN, presbyter and archimandrite, and VENERIUS, deacon, and to the faithful men whose signatures are included in your letter: DATIANUS, FORTUNATUS, BOETHUS, VICTOR, SCHOLASTICUS, ORONTIUS, VINDICIANUS, VICTOR, JANUARIUS, VICTORIANUS, PHOTINUS [Note: [Col. 0435D] The manuscripts of Santa Croce read *Fontius*.], QUODVULTDEUS, servants of Christ, greeting in the Lord.

### 1

In proportion as the members of the ecclesiastical body are held together by the grace of Christ in the unity of faith and by the bonds of charity, so much must the members be solicitous for one another, so that, once the disease of any perverse doctrine has been driven away [Note: [Col. 0435D] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions, however, read “the word of perverse doctrine.”], constant and unwearied diligence may be devoted, through both speech and prayer, not only to preserving health but also to restoring it. For thus it comes about that, while concern for fraternal purity keeps watch, the Holy Spirit himself—through whom the love of God has been poured into our hearts—works all things together for good in those who love God and their neighbor in God.

For just as we receive love itself as a gift of spiritual grace, so, while we are solicitous for our brothers, we demonstrate not only that divine grace is present in us [Note: [Col. 0436D] The manuscripts read, “that the grace of divine reading is present in us.”], but also that, the more generously the purity of charity is bestowed by us, the more abundantly the grace of divine recompense is increased for us.

### 2

We have therefore received the letter of your charity, which has partly relieved and partly saddened our exile [Col. 0435D]. We rejoice because you hold a sound judgment concerning the grace of God, by whose gift [another reading: “light”] the free will of the human mind is illumined and by whose assistance it is governed. Yet we are affected by a certain cloud of sorrow because you have indicated that some brothers, in the question of the grace of God and human free will, do not follow the right path of the Catholic faith, but wish to exalt the freedom of human choice against the grace of God.

### 3

First of all, dearest brothers, you ought to recognize—and indeed we do not doubt that you have recognized this—that these things are permitted by divine providence so that from them the power of divine grace may be understood through a clearer demonstration [Col. 0436A]. For grace itself is in no way recognized unless it is given. As long as it is not present in a person, that person must resist it either in speech or in action. He resists the grace of God in speech when he holds a view contrary to Christian faith; he resists it in action when he does not maintain the rule of Christian life in his conduct.

For this is what divinely given grace accomplishes in a person: once the gift of faith and charity has been received [another reading: “the commandment of faith and charity”], the mind both utters good speech and applies itself zealously to good works. The blessed Apostle both demonstrated and requested that this be divinely given to the faithful, saying: “Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and good hope through grace, comfort your hearts and strengthen you in every good work and word” [Col. 0436B] (2 Thess. 2:16–17).

### 4

All grace for good speech and good action therefore comes to us from God. It is also clear that from him we are granted sufficiency even for good thought, so that a person may learn to glory not in himself but in the Lord. The blessed Apostle attributed a person’s good thought to divine grace when he said: “Such confidence we have through Christ toward God—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:4–5).

Accordingly, even if some who do not yet possess grace do not understand that they lack it, those who have received grace from God ought all the more to be strengthened in affirming that grace, insofar as they see that it is not given to everyone. It is necessary that it remain unknown to those to whom it is not given, and that it be recognized by those to whom it is granted through divine generosity.

For the Apostle testifies that the gifts of the Holy Spirit are recognized through the reception of that same Holy Spirit. Therefore he says: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God. These things we also speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. The natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him; and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned. But the spiritual person judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2:12, 13, 14).

### 3

Through the Holy Spirit, therefore, we receive grace; and once that Spirit has been received, it comes to be in us that we know what we have received. Accordingly, dearest brothers, we must know and confess with the right rule of true faith both the needy poverty of human free will and the unfailing generosity of divine grace. “What do you have,” says the Apostle, “that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

Before the generosity of grace, there is indeed free will in a person, but it is not good, because it has not been illumined. Therefore, unless grace is given, even good will is not possessed. For human free will without the gift of grace is like an eye without light [Note: [Col. 0436D] The manuscripts read “without illumination”; the printed editions, however, read “without light.”]. The eye was made for seeing, but unless it receives light, it will not see.

That, however, is the true light which illumines every person coming into this world (John 1:9); and it illumines a person by giving itself through grace. Therefore, just as the eye of the body must always receive light in order to behold the light itself, so no knowledge can assist human free will unless the infusion of spiritual grace itself is given.

### 6

Therefore, so that we might briefly explain what truth Catholic doctrine contains concerning the matters you included in your letter, we have undertaken to define each point, following the gift of that same grace, which grace itself has deigned to pour into the hearts and tongues of the holy Fathers [Note: [Col. 0437D] The manuscripts read, “which it has itself deigned to pour in order that it might be spoken concerning itself.”].

You have said that, according to your position, although Esau and Jacob had not yet been born, Jacob was chosen through gratuitous mercy, while Esau, held under original sin, was hated by the just judgment of God, whereas the others say that Esau represents the people of the Jews, to be condemned on account of future evil works, and Jacob represents the people of the Gentiles, to be saved on account of future good works.

### 7

It is good that you join these two propositions, each of which you have set forth [Note: [Col. 0437D] The manuscripts read, “which each of you has set forth.”], in Catholic agreement. Thus God’s grace is rightly acknowledged by them, and the prophetic mystery is not denied by you.

For in those two brothers the representation of two peoples is rightly understood, especially since, when Rebecca herself consulted the Lord, two peoples were foretold as destined to be separated from her womb. Nevertheless, both gratuitous goodness and just severity must be recognized in that distinction.

Since every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights (Jas. 1:17), and since all who are saved are distinguished by grace, it is clear that human works were not chosen or loved in Jacob, but divine gifts. Again, since our iniquity commends the justice of God, there is no doubt that the wickedness of human iniquity was condemned in Esau.

In Jacob God displayed the gratuitous benefit of his mercy by graciously adopting him through free grace; he did not choose him on account of the merits of any future good work, even though he foreknew that he would give him himself, faith, and good works [Note: [Col. 0437D] One manuscript reads, “he graciously adopted him freely, not on account of merits,” and so forth. Two other manuscripts read, “he graciously adopted him through free grace; nor did he,” and so forth. These words were absent from the printed editions. The latter manuscript reading, however, appears more correct and complete.].

### 8

For this reason the blessed Apostle says to the seed of Abraham, whose figure had preceded in Jacob: “You have been saved by grace through faith” (Eph. 2:8). To show that faith is not given on account of certain good merits, but that every good merit begins with the gift of faith itself, and that faith itself is the gift of God [Note: [Col. 0438D] The manuscripts of Santa Croce read, “and to show that faith itself is this gift of God,” and so forth.], he followed by adding: “and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God” (ibid., 9).

And lest anyone dare claim for himself the merit of any good works, or suppose that he received faith on account of whatever works he had performed, he added: “not from works, so that no one may boast.” To show that not only faith but also good works are divinely bestowed, he immediately added: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works,” which he testifies were not only given by God but also prepared by him, saying: “which God prepared beforehand, so that we should walk in them” (Eph. 2:10).

Jacob, therefore, was saved by grace through faith; by grace he obtained the capacity for good works.

### 9

Accordingly, since it is certain that Esau was a vessel of wrath and Jacob a vessel of mercy, this must be held with the utmost certainty: Esau justly deserved wrath, so that he might be condemned—for God is not unjust when he inflicts wrath (Rom. 3:5)—whereas Jacob received, freely, the gift of prevenient mercy, so that he might be saved.

Jacob, therefore, justified freely by the grace of God, became a vessel of mercy through unmerited grace, and through that same grace was mercifully prepared for glory. Esau, however, was justly prepared through just wrath for punishment. “For our iniquity [another reading: ‘but our iniquity’] commends the justice of God” (ibid.).

Thus in Jacob God displayed the mercy of gratuitous goodness, and in Esau the judgment of just severity. Esau, although he had received the sacrament of circumcision on the eighth day according to the ordinance of God, was free from the guilt of original sin, yet through the wickedness of his heart remained in the oldness of the earthly human being, abandoned there by the judgment of him who freely saves and justly condemns [Note: [Col. 0438D] The manuscripts read, “and justly condemns,” rather than “and justly judges.”].

In his person are signified not only those who deny the faith, but also those who, remaining within the Church until the end of their lives, persevere in evil works. Of them the Apostle says: “Those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:21).

For just as that circumcised man perished because he loved darkness more than light, so everyone who does not put off the old man, “who is corrupted according to the desires of error,” will be condemned in judgment because he did not use the sacrament of baptism worthily. To that same old man belong not only those who are ignorant of God, but also those of whom the Apostle says: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16).

### 10

Concerning little children, the rule of Catholic truth must be held without hesitation: the little child who is baptized is saved by the gratuitous goodness of God [Note: [Col. 0438D] Two manuscripts read, “by which the little child who is baptized is believed to be saved by the gratuitous goodness of God.” Another manuscript reads, “by which the little child . . . is saved.”], whereas the one who dies without baptism is condemned on account of original sin.

Nor should one say that such a child has been snatched away by some benefit of God from future impiety, since, having died without the grace of justification, he has been assigned to the company of the impious. From that impiety, whether the person is a little child or of more advanced age, each is rescued by the sole remedy only if he is redeemed by Christ’s blood.

**WHOEVER THINKS THAT GRACE IS GIVEN TO ALL HUMAN BEINGS DOES NOT HAVE A WORTHY OPINION OF GRACE**, since not all possess faith, and some peoples are still found to whom the preaching of faith has not reached. The blessed Apostle says: “How will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher?” [Col. 0439A] (Rom. 10:14).

**GRACE, THEREFORE, IS NOT GIVEN TO ALL**, since those who are not believers cannot be participants in grace itself, nor can those believe to whom the hearing of faith is found not to have reached at all.

The grace itself, however, is not given equally to all to whom it is given, but “according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4:7), and “to each as God has apportioned the measure of faith.” He does not accept the persons of human beings, but one and the same Spirit accomplishes all things, distributing his own gifts to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11).

### 11

As for what you say—that a person is saved solely by the mercy of God—while they say that no one can be saved unless he runs and labors by his own will, both positions are rightly held if the proper order of divine mercy and human will is preserved: grace must precede, and human will must follow.

The mercy of God alone confers the beginning of salvation. Thereafter the human will becomes a co-worker in its own salvation, so that the mercy of God, going before, directs the course of the human will, and the obedient human will, with the same mercy following after, runs according to its purpose toward the prize.

Thus, in the fact that the human will runs profitably and labors, it must acknowledge that the ability to run and labor is a gift from God’s mercy. It must not be ungrateful for the mercy through which it receives the beginning of salvation, since through that same mercy it reaches the full accomplishment of eternal salvation. The will is good when it is preceded by God’s gift, and it remains good when it is not deprived of his assistance.

### 12

Whoever thinks that grace is bestowed by God as though someone, having received a suitable pledge, were to hand over money, is mistaken. For the Lord himself both gives the pledge of the Holy Spirit to whomever he wills and distributes his money, to be sought from the money-changers, to the care and service of his servants, as he himself says in the Gospel (Matt. 25:27).

The Apostle’s statement, “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9:18), is better understood as spoken from the perspective of one who confirms this truth. But if someone does not wish to understand it as spoken from the perspective of one who confirms it, let him attend without dispute to what follows [Note: [Col. 0439D] One manuscript reads, “which the Apostle Paul says.”]: “Or does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (ibid., 21).

When, in making both vessels, one recognizes the potter’s power, one should understand in the vessel of honor the unmerited grace of God who shows mercy, and in the vessel of dishonor the deserved judgment of God who hardens—that is, who abandons. God is said to harden not because he compels anyone to iniquity, but because he does not rescue a person from iniquity; and because he is just, he does this justly.

When God shows mercy, therefore, a person is saved without his own merits; when God hardens, he justly receives what he deserves [Note: [Col. 0439D] The manuscripts of Santa Croce read, “the impious person justly receives what he deserves.”]. God saves through the gift of his goodness and hardens through the judgment of his severity.

### 13

As for what you say—“For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13)—while they say, “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isa. 1:19): if a mind tranquil in faith receives both statements as it ought, no question concerning grace and free will will remain [Note: [Col. 0439D] The manuscripts read, “concerning the grace of God and human free will.”].

God commands a person to will, but God works in the person both the willing and the doing. He commands the person to act, but God works in him also the action [Note: [Col. 0439D] The words “God works in him” are found in the manuscripts of Santa Croce; they are absent from the printed editions.].

Therefore the blessed Apostle joins both together, saying: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, for his good pleasure.” Thus, for each person to work out his salvation with fear and trembling is the work of a willing human being; but God works in his own people this very willing [Note: [Col. 0440D] The manuscripts of Santa Croce read, “this very willing and working.”].

Since a person possesses free will, he hears the commandments that he is to perform. Yet free will is in no way made capable of fulfilling the commandments unless it is divinely assisted [Note: [Col. 0440D] The manuscript of Santa Croce reads, “free will is in no way made capable of working” (another manuscript: “the free will of a human being”).]. Thus it comes about that a person recognizes that he ought to act when he receives a commandment, and knows that he owes every good thing that he wills and does to God. For, as the Apostle testifies, he recognizes that God works in a person both the willing and the accomplishing, according to his good pleasure.

God has deigned to promise this grace to his faithful through the Prophet, saying: “I will give my Spirit within you, and I will cause you to walk in my statutes and to observe and do my judgments” (Ezek. 36:27).

### 14

When, therefore, God begins to work willing in a person, the person is converted to God; and, with God working in him, he does what is pleasing to God. The Apostle says of God: “May he equip you with everything good for doing his will, himself doing in you what is pleasing in his sight” [Note: [Col. 0440D] Thus the manuscripts of Santa Croce, in accordance with the Greek text; the other manuscripts read, “in every good thing.”] (Heb. 13:21).

A person can stretch out his hand toward life only insofar as he has the Lord as his protection over his right hand (Ps. 120:5).

It is exceedingly absurd to think that those who possess either secular or ecclesiastical rank are vessels of mercy, but to regard clerics, monks, and laypeople as vessels of dishonor. The Apostle clearly calls those vessels of mercy which God has prepared for glory—not present glory, but future glory—and to them he says: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4). For this reason he had said to them shortly before: “Set your minds on things above, not on things on earth” (ibid., 1).

The vessels of mercy are those to whom it is said: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom.” The vessels of dishonor are those to whom it is said: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”

Vessels of mercy are therefore made not by ecclesiastical or secular rank, but by spiritual charity within the Church. Accordingly, in whatever profession a person may hold the faith that works through charity, he will be a vessel sanctified for honor, useful to the Lord, and prepared for every good work.

### 15

For anyone either to prepare for or to engage in a conflict against the predestination of the saints is an act of great obstinacy, since no one dares contradict the apostolic preaching. That preaching says not only of God: “Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. 8:29), and elsewhere: “He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, in him” (Eph. 1:5); the blessed Paul also confidently proclaims that our very head, our firstborn among many brothers, was predestined, saying: “Who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined to be the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification” (Rom. 1:3–4).

Whoever therefore denies that Christ and his saints were predestined perversely attacks the apostolic faith.

All the predestined are those whom God wills to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. They are all called “all” because people of both sexes, every human race, rank, age, and condition are saved.

The will of almighty God is always fulfilled, because his power is in no way defeated. He is the one who has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths (Ps. 134:6), and no one resists his will.

It is truly as the Son testified concerning himself: “He gives life to whom he wills” [Note: [Col. 0441D] These words, “he gives life to whom he wills,” are absent from the printed editions; they are found in three manuscripts, one of which reads “he justifies.”]. For in giving life he does not await any beginning arising from human will; rather, by making the will itself good, he gives it life.

### 16

This is the case with adults. But little children, in whom good will cannot yet arise, he causes to be saved solely through the operation of grace.

Free will, which was sound in the first human being before sin, is now indeed shaken in the children of God by its own weakness, but it is lifted up by the greater grace of divine generosity.

The question concerning souls should either be left unspoken or treated without dispute. Whether souls come from generation or are newly created for each body is not expressly declared by the authority of the holy Scriptures; it must therefore be investigated cautiously, especially since the faithful may remain ignorant of this without harm to the faith.

This in particular must be observed and held: the souls of newborn children are bound by the chain of original sin, and the sacrament of holy baptism is necessary for all. Through it the bond of original sin is broken [another reading: “forgiven”], and the adoption as sons, lost in the first human being, is received through the second human being.

### 17

You, therefore, dearest brothers, stand firm and immovable through the grace of God. While holding the true faith, show charity toward brothers who think otherwise. Do not despair of anyone, because the person who today does not recognize the truth in some matter may recognize it tomorrow when God reveals it. “It is subject to God, when he wills, to have power” (Wis. 12:18).

Let us therefore pray for them, so that God may work in them. Let us show them good will, for which we may receive a reward, knowing that whoever belongs to the number of the predestined will not perish, and that the will of the Almighty will be fulfilled in all things: they will be saved through grace and, with the Lord illuminating them, will receive the knowledge of the truth.

### 18

Above all, make every effort to place before the brothers mentioned for reading the books of Saint Augustine that he wrote to Prosper and Hilary.

The blessed Hormisdas, of venerable memory, glorious bishop of the apostolic see, included mention of these books with great praise of Catholic teaching in the letter that he sent in reply to the inquiry of the holy brother and our fellow priest Possessor [Col. 0442B]. His words are these:

“Concerning free will, however, and the grace of God, what the Roman—that is, the Catholic—Church follows and preserves can certainly be recognized abundantly in the various books of blessed Augustine, and especially in those addressed to Prosper and Hilary; nevertheless, the ecclesiastical archives also contain explicit chapters.”

### 19

These matters, therefore, dearest brothers, we wished briefly to answer in a common reply in response to your questions.

Moreover, one of us, insofar as the Lord deigns to grant his servants the grace of speaking rightly, has answered in three books dedicated in your name [Col. 0442C] all the matters that you reported the aforementioned brothers to hold or express against grace and predestination [Note: [Col. 0441D] Fulgentius, in his books *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*.]. He also published seven books against the two books of Faustus of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0442D] The same author, in his books *Against Faustus*.].

When you have read through these works, you will immediately recognize how the examination exposed the arguments of the aforementioned Faustus as contrary to the truth and utterly hostile to the Catholic faith; how clear reasoning refuted them, divine authority suppressed them, and the wholly harmonious testimony of the preceding Fathers disproved them.

### 20

We hope in the Lord that he will bestow such assistance of his grace that he will both grant an increase of holy knowledge to those who think rightly [Note: [Col. 0442D] The words “of holy knowledge” are added in the manuscripts of Santa Croce.] and give to those who believe otherwise than they ought the help of recognizing the truth.

For he himself makes those whom he predestined to life participants in his grace, so that in all their good things they may subject the freedom of human will to the grace of God. Let them recognize that every good gift and every perfect gift descends to them from him, and let them also know that they must always expect help from him who gives his predestined ones both grace and perseverance, so that they may receive grace for grace and the gift of everlasting life.

277 **LETTER XVI, OR THE BOOK OF PETER THE DEACON AND THE OTHERS WHO WERE SENT FROM THE EAST BY THE GREEKS TO ROME IN THE MATTER OF THE FAITH. Concerning the Incarnation and Grace of Our Lord Jesus Christ, to Fulgentius and the Other Bishops of Africa.** (C, G)*

To the most holy lords, worthy to be named with every honor, DATIANUS [Note: [Col. 0443D] *Ant.*, “deacon.”], FORTUNATUS, ALBANUS, ORONTIUS, BOETHUS, FULGENTIUS, JANUARIUS, and the other bishops adorned with the confession of Christ: the humble PETER, deacon, JOHN, LEONTIUS, another JOHN, and the other brothers sent to Rome in the cause of the faith.

## CHAPTER I. Agreement of the Churches in Faith; Confirmation of the Faithful

### 1

We believe it useful and exceedingly necessary, and especially beneficial to the holy Churches of God, to suggest to your holiness those things concerning the Incarnation and the divine dispensation which all the holy Eastern Churches defend with us against the heretics—those who do not cease disturbing the ancient faith of the Church with perverse and wicked arguments—and humbly to seek from your blessedness your agreement concerning them.

For we believe that your holy and glorious confession differs in nothing from ours [Note: [Col. 0443D] The manuscript reads, “we believe that the glorious confession differs.”], especially since we have no doubt that the holy Church of God is everywhere animated by one Spirit.

The Easterners will all be filled with no small, but rather great, joy if they learn that your holiness agrees with their—in fact, more properly, with Catholic—doctrines in all things [Col. 0443B].

### 2

Therefore we humbly ask and beseech your blessedness that, examining carefully the matters contained below—as befits the truest and most fearless preachers of Christ—you command that your judgment be made known to us in writing [Note: [Col. 0443D] The manuscript reads, “that you command it to be made known.”].

Then, if, by God’s favor, our exposition has been approved by you—as we do not doubt it will be—as consonant with the Catholic faith and with the apostolic traditions, we shall be able, fortified by the authority of so many men and of priests of such proven character, to silence the mouths of those who speak wickedly. Persevering in the faith of the holy Fathers, we shall give thanks to God, who has glorified you through the confession of his holiness, most holy and most worthy lords of God.

We now ask that you examine the matters that follow with the greatest care.

## CHAPTER II. In Christ, Two Natures United Without Confusion in One Person

### 3

Therefore, in accordance with the tradition of the holy Fathers, we confess our Lord Jesus Christ in two united and unconfused natures—that is, divinity and humanity—in one person or subsistence [Note: [Col. 0444D] The printed editions of Louvain, 1556, and Basel read “or substance.”].

We neither yield to those who, proclaiming one incarnate nature of God the Word, reject the faith of the venerable Council of Chalcedon, nor accept those who deceitfully pronounce two natures while refusing to confess one incarnate nature of God the Word, judging this to be contrary to the profession of two natures—as though “one incarnate nature of God the Word” signified anything other than two natures ineffably united.

The blessed Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, wrote as follows in his second letter [Note: [Col. 0444D] The words “in his second letter” are absent from the printed editions but are found in the manuscript.] to Bishop Successus:

“If, in saying ‘one nature of God the Word,’ we had remained silent and had not added ‘incarnate,’ but had seemed to reject the dispensation, perhaps their statement would not have been unacceptable, as they pretended to ask: Where is the perfection in the humanity? Or how does our substance subsist? But since both the perfection that exists in the humanity and the manifestation of our essence have been introduced through what was said—‘incarnate’—let them now cease [another reading: ‘desist’] from placing a reed-like staff beneath themselves.”

## CHAPTER III. The Blessed Virgin Is Properly the Mother of God

### 4

We believe that the blessed Virgin Mary is, not on account of the dignity of that man who was born from her—whom certain impious persons do not fear to proclaim God by grace and not by nature—but properly and truly **Theotokos** (Θεοτόκος), that is, *Mother of God*, because she truly and properly gave birth to God the Word incarnate and made human, who was essentially or naturally united to flesh.

### 5

For this reason we also confess in every respect that the union of the natures was made essentially or naturally, not as those maintain who claim that God the Word operated in Christ as in a prophet [Note: [Col. 0444D] Thus the manuscript; the printed editions read, “the Word of the Lord.”].

The blessed Gregory of Nazianzus rebukes them in his letter to Cledonius, saying:

“If anyone says that God the Word operated as in a prophet according to grace, and does not confess that the union was made essentially, let him be deprived of the better inoperation—or rather, let him be filled with the worse.”

Nor do we hold that the union of the natures was established according to illumination, love, affection, personal or subsistential relation, authority, power, or equality of honor.

The blessed Cyril, mentioned above, anathematizes those who teach this, saying against Nestorius (Anathema 3):

“If anyone divides the substances in the one Christ after the union [Note: [Col. 0444D] The printed editions read, “after the unity”; the manuscript reads, “after the union.”], joining them only by association according to dignity, authority, or power, and not rather by the conjunction that is according to natural unity, let him be anathema.”

For God the Word, not by an empty name, not as a part of himself, but by nature God, as great as the Father, equal to the Father in every respect except only that the one is Father and the other Son, united himself to human nature and became man.

6. Hence also our Lord Christ is proclaimed by the holy Fathers as composed through the union of divinity and humanity. Because Paul of Samosata was unwilling to confess this, he was condemned by the Council of Antioch, by Malchion, a presbyter of that same Church of Antioch, a man most learned in every respect, and by all the bishops who had then assembled against that same Paul and elected Malchion. Taking up the chief contest of the disputation on behalf of the aforementioned council, Malchion refuted the heretic among other things as follows:

“Certainly, what is simple becomes composite, as in Christ Jesus, who was made one from God the Word and a human body derived from the seed of David, no longer subsisting in any further division, but in unity. You, however, seem to me unwilling on this account to confess composition, so that the Son of God might not be substance in him, but wisdom according to participation. For you said that wisdom suffers loss and therefore cannot be composite; yet you do not consider that, just as divine wisdom remained undiminished before it emptied itself, so also in this self-emptying which it mercifully undertook, it remained undiminished and unchangeable. You also say that wisdom dwelt in him as we dwell in houses, so that one might be in the other [Note: The printed editions of Louvain and Basel read, ‘so that one might be in the other’—using the feminine form *altera*—whereas the manuscript has the masculine *alter*]; yet neither are we part of a house, nor is a part of the house part of us.”

Likewise, blessed Athanasius, in the treatise entitled *That Christ Is One*, refuting the vanity of the heretics, after showing that their inquiries concerning the divinity of the Son of God were superfluous, continues as follows:

“So also,” he says, “they inquire about the Incarnation: ‘How,’ they ask, ‘is God incarnated? How is he embodied? How is the uncontainable joined to a small body? How is the uncreated united to the created, the uncircumscribed to the circumscribed? Or how can that great, immense, undivided one be divided? If that magnitude has been contracted into a small place, either the small thing has been made great, or only a part, and not the whole divinity, has been united to the flesh—which it is impious to believe.’

“And from this they have fallen into saying, ‘How?’ and ‘In what manner?’ Through such a view and impiety they too have regarded indwelling as taking the place of incarnation, human operation as taking the place of unity and composition, two subsistences and two persons in place of the one substance of our Lord Jesus Christ, and, shamefully and impiously, a quaternity in place of the holy and ineffable Trinity.”

7. Again, blessed Gregory says in his sermon on the Son:

“But in one chapter of mine,” he says, “attribute the higher things to the divinity and to that nature which is shown to be superior to sufferings and to the body; but attribute the lower things to the composite one, who for your sake emptied himself and was incarnated.”

Therefore we rightly believe that God the Word, full and perfect God, suffered no increase or diminution even after assuming flesh; rather, through his union he bestowed ineffable glory upon the nature he assumed.

## CHAPTER IV. The Incarnation’s mystery did not produce a quaternity in the Godhead

8. For this reason the Trinity remained the Trinity even after the mystery of the Incarnation, because God the Word himself, even with his own flesh, is one of the Trinity—not because his flesh is of the substance of the Trinity, but because the flesh belongs to God the Word, who is one of the Trinity. For it was he himself, and not another, who ascended into heaven, the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven (John 3:13).

Therefore, following blessed Cyril, we also confess that God the Word suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, and was buried in the flesh. Cyril says (Anathema XIII):

“If anyone does not confess that God the Word suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, tasted death in the flesh, and became the firstborn from the dead, according to the fact that, as God, he is life and life-giver, let him be anathema.”

9. Likewise, we call the human Christ the Word, in accordance with blessed John’s statement: “What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have gazed upon and our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). For the Word could not, according to the nature of his divinity, be handled by human hands unless he became human.

There is also no doubt that the child whom the blessed Virgin bore, whom she wrapped in swaddling clothes, whom she placed in a manger, whom she circumcised on the eighth day, whom Simeon, a just man, embraced in his own arms, and whom the evangelists report as subject to his parents, whom they testify to have advanced in age and wisdom (Luke 2:52)—that this child was by nature God: through him all visible and invisible things were made; he is the Only-begotten and the Firstborn, in whom all things hold together (Colossians 1:16–17), according to the Apostle Paul.

The prophet Isaiah also declares this in clear words, saying:

“A child is born to us, and a son is given to us; whose authority is upon his shoulder. And his name shall be called Angel of Great Counsel, Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Ruler, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6).

10. For this reason we by no means believe that we should yield to those who assert that the Mighty God was united to that child, and do not believe that the child himself was the Mighty God—especially since the Psalmist testifies that the throne belongs altogether to the one who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary and was baptized in the Jordan by John in order to sanctify the waters, and that his throne endures for ever and ever, saying:

“Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; a scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions” (Psalm 44:7–8).

But how could God be anointed—he whose throne is for ever and ever—unless he became human?

## CHAPTER V. God became human; a human being did not become God

11. According to this prophetic statement, therefore, God became Christ; Christ did not become God, as the heretics say. They dare to assert that Christ is God through advancement, not through nature. God was anointed because he himself became human; for one is not God and another human, but the same one is God and the same one is human. He who is the natural son of the Virgin is likewise the natural Son of God.

Therefore we believe and confess two births of God the Word: one before the ages, from the Father [or, “in the Father”], according to divinity; the other in the last days, from the holy Virgin, according to the flesh. We execrate those who deny the birth of the Word of God according to the flesh, and who likewise refuse to acknowledge that the wonders and sufferings of the one and the same Son of God are what the whole Church of God confesses.

12. In accordance with this exposition of our faith, we also accept four councils: Nicaea, of three hundred and eighteen bishops; Constantinople, of one hundred and fifty, who condemned the impious Pneumatomachi; the First Council of Ephesus, presided over by the most blessed bishops Celestine of Rome and Cyril of Alexandria; and the holy and venerable council celebrated at Chalcedon.

13. We also embrace the letters of blessed Leo, anathematizing all who hold opinions contrary to the doctrines of the Church, together with all the writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia and of his disciple Nestorius, and all who share their views with that same Nestorius. We likewise anathematize all writings opposed to the twelve chapters of blessed Cyril, which he published against that same Nestorius; and in addition Eutyches and Dioscorus with their associates, together with all those whom the apostolic see has justly and canonically condemned.

## CHAPTER VI. What kind of human being was created, and what kind he became with his posterity through sin. Through sin the whole human being became worse. Without grace, only human things are conceived. What it means to believe

14. After this, it is appropriate also to declare to your Blessedness how we understand the grace of Christ, by which he rescued us from the power of Satan, according to what has been handed down to us; for your authority is also very necessary to us in this matter.

15. We therefore believe that Adam was created good by God, the Creator of all things, without any opposition from the flesh, and endowed with great freedom, so that he had it within his own power both to do good and, if he wished, to commit evil. In a certain sense, death and immortality had been placed within the freedom of his choice. He was capable of either outcome: if he kept the commandment, he would become immortal without experiencing death; but if he despised it, death would immediately follow.

Thus, corrupted by the serpent’s cunning, he voluntarily became a transgressor of the divine law. Consequently, in accordance with what had been foretold to him, he was condemned by God’s just judgment to the punishment of death. He was wholly changed for the worse—that is, both in body and in soul—and, having lost his own freedom, was consigned to the service of sin.

16. From this point, there is no human being who is not born bound by the bond of this sin, except the one who was born by a new mode of generation in order to release this bond of sin: the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.

For what else could or can be born from a slave except a slave? Adam did not beget children while he was free, but only after he had become a slave of sin. Therefore, just as every human being is descended from him, so every human being is his slave through him.

Hence the Apostle also says: “From one came condemnation upon all human beings” (Romans 5:18). And again: “Through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin, death; and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (ibid., 5:12). Therefore those who say that only death, and not sin, passed into the human race are altogether mistaken, since the Apostle testifies that both sin and death were brought into the world through him.

17. No one at all, therefore, is freed from this condemnation and death except by the grace of the Redeemer. Although he was Lord, being God, in order to free us from perpetual servitude and from the power of the devil, and to restore us to true freedom, he became a slave, taking the form of a slave (Philippians 2:7).

This is why he says to the Jews: “Then you will truly be free, if the Son sets you free” (John 8:36). They thought themselves truly free, although with utterly vain intent they were serving human occupations.

Thus, in order that false freedom might become true freedom—that is, in order that human freedom might become Christian freedom—that same freedom required a liberator, through whose grace it could turn away from human occupations and think about and desire the things that belong to eternal life.

18. Without this grace, a person can indeed think about and desire human things, but cannot think about, will, or desire divine things. The first and chief foundation of these divine things, and in a certain sense their threshold or the origin of all good things, is to believe in the Lord of glory who was crucified (1 Corinthians 2:8).

This does not arise from the freedom of natural choice, because it is not flesh and blood that reveals this, but the heavenly Father, to whom he wishes (Matthew 16:17), drawing him toward true freedom—not by violent necessity, but by pouring sweetness through the Holy Spirit—so that believers immediately say, “Jesus is Lord.” No one can say this through the natural freedom of choice except in the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3).

19. Therefore those who say, “It is mine to will to believe, but it belongs to God’s grace to help,” chatter in vain. For the Apostle testifies that the very act of believing—which is giving assent to the truth—is given to us by God, saying: “To you it has been granted by Christ not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1:29).

## CHAPTER VII. God causes some to believe through his goodness, while he abandons others by a just but hidden judgment

20. But they say: If God makes unwilling people willing to believe, while no one naturally—as you say—can believe [Note: The printed editions read, “can believe in the Son of God”; the manuscript has, “can believe, or will,” and lacks “in the Son of God”], or will anything good that pertains to eternal life, why does he not make everyone willing, since there is no partiality with God—especially since it is written of him: “He wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4)?

Either he wills this and cannot accomplish it, or divine Scripture is lying. But if it is impious to hold either of these views, it remains that he does not awaken the human will, but waits for it from the human being, so that there may be a fitting reward for those who are willing and a just condemnation for those who are unwilling.

21. If things are as the heretics boast, then God’s judgments, which are inscrutable and incomprehensible, are themselves comprehended by them. For if, as they wish, he condemns the unwilling but saves the willing, there is absolutely nothing further to investigate. So far as they are concerned, divine Scripture is mistaken when it testifies that God’s judgments are incomprehensible (Romans 11:33).

We, however, believing and declaring God’s judgments to be incomprehensible, say that from one mass of perdition some are saved by the goodness and grace of God, while others are abandoned by a just and hidden judgment.

22. Otherwise, let those who consider this contrary to divine justice and goodness say, if they can, why the one who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth performed so many miracles in Chorazin and Bethsaida, but did not wish to perform any of them in Tyre and Sidon—where, if they had been performed, as he himself testifies, they might perhaps have repented in ashes and sackcloth (Matthew 11:21).

Or why did he forbid the Apostle to proclaim the word of salvation in Asia and Bithynia (Acts 16:6–7)?

23. If these things cannot be comprehended, let them return to themselves and, recognizing that they are human beings, cease asking why he saves some by a free gift while abandoning others by a just and hidden judgment—he who has the power, from the same mass, to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor.

Let them cry out with us, or rather, in the words of the Apostle:

“O the depth of the riches, wisdom, and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen” (Romans 11:33–36).

Clearly, therefore, it is not against us but altogether against the Apostle that the person who says, “Unless I first will, grace does not come to me,” resists. For this is nothing other than saying that one must first give something to God so that God may repay him.

## CHAPTER VIII. Every movement of a good will is from God

24. But following the same Apostle, we say that the origin of all good thoughts, their assent [Note: The printed editions read, “their confession”; the manuscript more correctly has, “their assent”], and the will itself are from God, through God, and in God. He releases and corrects the perverse wills of human beings, which are entangled in earthly actions, through the inward infusion and operation [Note: So the manuscript; the printed editions read, “and activity”] of the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “The will is prepared by the Lord.”

25. Hence also blessed Basil, bishop of Caesarea, says among other things in the prayer of the holy altar, which nearly the whole East recites:

“Grant, O Lord, strength and protection. We ask you: make the wicked good; preserve the good in goodness. For you can do all things, and no one can resist you; for when you will, you save, and no one resists your will.”

See how briefly and decisively that eminent teacher once brought this controversy to an end, teaching through this prayer that wicked people are made good not by themselves but by God, and that they persevere in goodness not through their own power but through the help of divine grace.

26. Similarly, blessed Innocent, bishop of the apostolic see, writes in his letter to the Council of Milevis (V, in the chapters of Celestine, chapter 8):

“All the endeavors, all the works, and all the merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him from any other source than from what he himself has given.”

The African councils explain this judgment of Pope Zosimus more carefully and clearly in their letter to Pope Zosimus [Note: The printed editions read, “to the Roman pope”; the manuscript has, “to Pope Zosimus”], repeating it in these words:

“But what you placed in the letter that you took care to send to all the provinces, saying, ‘Nevertheless, by God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—we have referred everything to the awareness of our brothers and fellow bishops’: we understand this statement to mean that you swiftly cut down, with the keen sword of truth, those who exalt the freedom of choice against God’s help.

“For what did you attribute more to free choice than the fact that you referred everything to the awareness of our humility? Yet you rightly and wisely recognized that this was done by God’s prompting, and you truthfully and confidently said so, precisely because ‘the will is prepared by the Lord’ (Proverbs 8:35, according to the Septuagint), and because he himself touches the hearts of his children by paternal inspirations so that they may do something good: ‘For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God’ (Romans 8:14).

“Thus we do not find that our freedom of choice is absent, while in each movement of the human will toward good we do not hesitate to recognize that his grace precedes us. God works in human hearts and in free choice itself in such a way that holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of a good will are from God, because through him we are able to do some good, without whom we can do nothing.”

27. In agreement with these words, the most blessed Celestine writes in his letter to the Gauls (chapter 11):

“When the bishops of holy peoples fulfill, before divine mercy, the embassy entrusted to them, they plead the cause of the human race. With the whole Church groaning together with them, they ask and pray that faith be granted to unbelievers; that idolaters be freed from the errors of their unbelief; that, once the veil of their hearts has been removed, the light of truth appear to the Jews; that heretics may come to their senses through receiving the Catholic faith; that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed charity; that remedies of repentance may be granted to those who have fallen; and finally, that, when catechumens have been brought to the sacraments of rebirth, the hall of heavenly mercy may be opened to them.

“That these things are not requested from the Lord casually or fruitlessly is shown by the effects of the things themselves, since he deigns to draw very many from every kind of error. Rescuing them from the power of darkness, he transfers them into the kingdom of the Son of his love and makes vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath. The whole of this is so clearly understood to be the work of God that thanksgiving and confession of praise are always rendered to God, who accomplishes these things, for the illumination or correction of such people.”

A little later he says again (Celestine, chapter 12):

“By these ecclesiastical rules, drawn from divine authority and testimonies, and confirmed with the Lord’s help, we have been so strengthened that we profess God to be the author of all good affections and works, of all endeavors and all virtues by which one turns toward God from the beginning of faith. We do not doubt that the merits of every human being are preceded by his grace, through whom it comes about that we begin both to will and to do something good.

“By this help and gift of God, free choice is not taken away but liberated, so that what was dark becomes bright, what was crooked becomes straight, what was weak becomes sound, and what was imprudent becomes prudent.”

The same teacher concludes this letter and brings it to an end as follows (chapter 13):

“For confessing the grace of God, from whose work and favor absolutely nothing must be taken away, we believe that whatever the writings of the apostolic see have taught us according to the rules stated above is fully sufficient, so that we should by no means regard as Catholic anything that appears contrary to the foregoing judgments.”

Most holy brothers, we have not thought it necessary to present these things to you as though you were ignorant of them. Rather, we judged it useful to insert them into this little work of ours in order to refute the madness of those who reject them as new doctrines and as things almost entirely unheard of in the Churches.

28. Instructed by the teachings of all these holy Fathers, we anathematize Pelagius and Celestius, as well as Julian of Eclanum and all who hold similar opinions. We especially anathematize the books of Faustus, bishop of Gaul [Note: Faustus’s books against predestination], who was advanced from the monastery of Lérins; there is no doubt that these books were written against the doctrine of predestination.

In them he not only goes against all these holy Fathers, but also, opposing the Apostle’s own tradition [Note: So the manuscript; the printed editions read, “contradiction”], he subordinates grace’s assistance to human labor. Completely emptying the grace of Christ, he impiously professes that the ancient saints were saved not by the same grace as we are, as the blessed Apostle Peter teaches (Acts 15:11), but by the possibility afforded by nature.

Peter, deacon by the mercy of God, has subscribed.

John, monk by the mercy of God, has subscribed.

Leontius, monk by the mercy of God, has subscribed.

John, lector by the mercy of God, has subscribed.

286 LETTER XVII, OR BOOK OF ST FULGENTIUS AND FIFTEEN OTHER AFRICAN BISHOPS, to Peter the deacon and the others who had been sent from the East to Rome in the cause of the faith, concerning the Incarnation and Grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0451D]

To the most beloved holy brethren, most greatly to be embraced in the faith and grace of Christ—PETER the deacon, JOHN, LEONTIUS, and the other JOHN, and the remaining brethren whom you informed us by letter had been sent together with you to Rome in the cause of the faith—DATIANUS, FORTUNATUS, BOETHUS, VICTOR, SCHOLASTICUS, ORONTIUS, VINDICIANUS, VICTOR, JANUARIUS, VICTORIANUS, PHOTINUS, QUODVULTDEUS, FULGENTIUS, FELIX, and JANUARIUS, greeting in the Lord.

[Col. 0452A] CHAPTER I. Right faith is the salvation of human beings in this life.—1. Our blessed brother John, a deacon sent by your fellowship, presented to us the letter which you had sent.
