When it had been read, we joyfully learned both your faith and your well-being; indeed, in recognizing your faith, your well-being was made known to us. For what is the true salvation of human beings in this life except right faith in God, which works through love, through which apostolic authority testifies that we have been saved by divine grace, saying: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; for it is the gift of God, not from works, lest anyone should boast” (Ephesians 2:8)? And because love ought continually to cleave to right faith, love which by the devotion and effectiveness of good works covers a multitude of sins, the Teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth, lest human pride should dare arrogantly to claim anything for itself, after commending the faith through which we have been freely saved, also ascribed the grace of good works to the gifts of divine kindness, immediately adding: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them” (ibid., 10). We rejoice in the actual result that you walk in them under God’s guidance. For, being not slothful in diligence and fervent in spirit (Romans 12:11), the more devoutly you serve the Lord, the more love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith impels us, for a fuller knowledge of our common faith, to inquire into the hidden matters of your purpose [Note: Basel has “the hidden matters of your purpose”; the manuscript has “the hidden matters of our exile”; the other printed editions have “the hidden matters of your exile.” Perhaps “the hidden matters of our exile” or “of your purpose.”]. Since, therefore, the word of God is not bound (2 Timothy 2:9), and is living and effective (Hebrews 4:12), we too shall indicate to your charity in a written reply what we receive and hold, on the holy authority of the canonical books and by the teaching and instruction of the Fathers’ sayings, concerning the Incarnation and dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ, and concerning grace—which is freely bestowed upon the unworthy in such a way that it itself works in us both the beginning and the progress of good will. We trust in the Lord, from whom faith is infused so that we may believe with the heart unto righteousness, and speech is given so that we may confess with the mouth unto salvation (Romans 10:10), that he will govern alike our thought and our pen, so that our answer to your question may be such that we state concerning the Lord’s Incarnation what the truth of our redemption contains, and concerning the grace of God what the heavenly majesty itself has freely infused [or: infuses, or has infused] into us.

CHAPTER II. Two natures in Christ and one person. The Word did not assume flesh already conceived.—2. You say, therefore, that in accordance with the tradition of the holy Fathers you confess our Lord Jesus Christ in two united and unconfused natures, namely divinity and humanity, in one person or subsistence. Consequently, you also affirm that you believe the blessed Mary properly and truly to be Mother of God, because she truly and properly bore God the Word incarnate and made human, and essentially or naturally united to flesh. It is enough to have set down these points from the tenor of your letter, since the remaining matters which your profession of faith comprises concerning the Lord’s Incarnation depend on them.

3. Therefore, if anyone refuses or hesitates to believe and proclaim either two natures or one person in our Lord Jesus Christ, or if anyone refuses to confess that the same one is God and human being—that is, the Word incarnate, truly born of the Virgin Mary for our salvation—he is shown and demonstrated to be as much a stranger to the catholic faith as he is an ungrateful opponent of the mystery of human redemption. For this is that great mystery of godliness commended to all the faithful by the apostolic voice: “which was manifested in flesh, justified in spirit, appeared to angels, preached among the Gentiles, believed in this world, received up in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16). That is, the Word, which was in the beginning, was with God, and was God [Note: The manuscript reads, “and was God”; the printed editions, “and God the Word was.”], namely [or: the same] the only-begotten Son of God, the power and wisdom of God, through whom and in whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made—the same [or: that is], only-begotten God. Though he was in the form of God, that is, though in every respect equal to the begetter he possessed with him the unity of natural essence, and in that nature which he has eternally from the Father was what the Father is by nature, namely [or: the same], true, highest, and immutable God; though he was not a God other than the Father but, while personal distinction remained, was naturally one God with the Father, neither lesser than nor subsequent to the Father, nor of different power or another essence (for “he did not regard equality with God as robbery” [Philippians 2:6–7]), nevertheless he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, that is [or: the same], being made in the likeness of human beings, the same one being found in appearance as a human being (ibid.). In him there could be no thought of robbery, because the fullness of natural equality, begotten from the Father’s substance by an ineffable and eternal birth, remains in him. Therefore he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. For therein God willed naturally to be human, and the Lord of all things assumed a servile nature without loss of his own lordship, therein mercifully emptied by taking the form of a servant. How well the holy Apostle of the New Testament, as he himself testifies (2 Corinthians 3:6), having been made by God a competent minister, lest any of us, hearing that the Son of God was emptied, should conceive with harmful thought that equality with the Father’s form had been lost or diminished in the only-begotten God, and, following the crooked windings of serpentine deception, should fail to hold the path of right faith, made clear that self-emptying, removing [perhaps: revealing] all obscurities, when he immediately added, “taking the form of a servant.” That self-emptying of the only-begotten God, therefore, was the assumption of a servile form, not a loss or diminution of divinity. For the divine nature can neither in any way be diminished nor increased, because, remaining immutable, it always has being what it is. For if that true and highest God, who for our sake became poor though he was rich, so that we might become rich by his poverty (2 Corinthians 8:9), had, in being emptied, lost his fullness—which is dreadful even to say [Note: The printed editions read, “which is dreadful”; the manuscript, “which is dreadful even to say.”]—or had undergone any changeability in that assumption of a servile form, the blessed evangelist John would not have said of the incarnate Word: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). Therefore, the Word made flesh truly began to be human flesh, but did not cease to be the Word in divine truth; and the wondrous kindness of God the Redeemer effectually accomplished the mystery of the assumption and redemption of humanity because the divine majesty could never be subject to either changeability or diminution.

4. Therefore God’s Word, the same Word who is God, taking human flesh from his mother’s flesh, assumed the form of a servant in such a way that, remaining in the form of God, eternal and immutable God, he deigned through the unity of the person in which he assumed the form of a servant to become himself what he had made. For, having been made in the likeness of human beings, he was found in appearance as a human being; retaining in every respect immutable divinity from the nature of the Father, though uncreated he deigned to be created, and though not made by the Father but begotten, he willed to be made from a woman. Thus the Word was made flesh, so that there might be one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who is God over all, blessed for ever: one true Son both of God and of humanity, one and the same, always begotten God from the Father without beginning, and true human being from the mother, temporally conceived and born according to the flesh [Note: The manuscript reads, “true human being from the mother”; the printed editions, “but true God from the mother.”]. The only-begotten God did not assume this flesh as already conceived; rather, God himself was conceived in it in the deepest humility. For the same God was created in and from the Virgin according to the flesh who had created for himself the mother from whom and in whom he would be created.

## CHAPTER III. The Word not only became flesh in the virgin, but also from the virgin

### 5.

But if God the Word became flesh in the virgin in such a way that he did not become flesh from her, then plainly the same God would not possess the substance of flesh from his mother’s flesh; he would merely have passed through the virgin. Thus the mystery of the mediator would not benefit us for salvation, nor would Christ, the Son of God, unite in himself, without confusion, the full truth of human and divine substance.

Divine goodness therefore employed this remedy medicinally: that God the Only-Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, should become man not only in a woman but also from a woman. We are commanded unquestionably to believe and confess this [alternatively, to profess it: *confiteri* / *profiteri*] in the divine oracles. For the prophet did not remain silent about God’s becoming man in her, saying: “Mother Zion will say: ‘Man and man was made in her,’ and the Most High himself founded her” (Psalm 86:5).

Isaiah also, filled with the Holy Spirit, thus foretells the mystery of the future incarnation of the Son of God: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and shall bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23). Therefore, because he whom the virgin conceived and bore in her womb is called “God with us,” he is plainly recognized as God conceived and born in the virgin’s womb.

In the Gospel also it is said concerning Mary: “She was found to have a child in her womb from the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 18). Joseph likewise—whom Mary had as her husband not for intercourse and the corruption of the flesh, but for the testimony and protection of her sacred virginity and most chaste fruitfulness—is warned by an angelic oracle as follows: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife. For that which has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 20).

That he was also made from her is demonstrated by heavenly utterances. For the Apostle says: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law” (Galatians 4:4).

Writing also to the Romans, to show that he was laying down a true and firm foundation of faith, he placed this beginning at the head of his letter: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:1–2).

To Timothy also, his beloved son in the faith, he earnestly commends the remembrance of this faith above all, saying: “Remember that Jesus Christ has risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel” (2 Timothy 2:8).

To the blessed virgin herself—who was destined to become the mother of her Creator, indeed of all things—the angel Gabriel is found to have addressed these words [*alloquio*, alternatively *eloquio*, “address”]: 

“The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

### 6.

To this belongs the mystery of our salvation: our father Abraham commanded the steward of his household to place his hand under Abraham’s thigh and swear by the God of heaven (Genesis 24:2).

He must be believed to have done this only through a prophetic spirit [Note: The word *prophetico* (“prophetic”) is not found in the printed editions, but is read in the manuscript], namely at the time when the Chosen Vessel indicates that all things happened in figure (1 Corinthians 10:17).

The holy Abraham, father of the nations, therefore did this—not because he believed that his flesh already possessed some natural fellowship with the God of heaven, but in order to show that the God of heaven would be born from that flesh which would derive the reality of its descent from Abraham’s own seed [*quae*, “which,” alternatively *qui*, “who”].

There is therefore one Christ, the Son of God, in the nature of divinity and of flesh. In him the singularity of person does not confuse the human and divine nature, and the unconfused union of the natures does not make two persons exist. The truth of our reconciliation and salvation endures for this reason: God the Only-Begotten, truly God, became man for us, and the same man was conceived and born as none other than God the Only-Begotten.

### 7.

The blessed Mary therefore both conceived and bore God the Word, insofar as he became flesh. God the Word did not bring flesh into her womb in which he himself was to be conceived; nor did God, who was to be conceived, assume from her the material of flesh that had already been conceived or formed, merely in order afterward to be born. Rather, from that same virgin and in that same virgin he received the nature of human flesh, according to which the eternal God was to be conceived and born in time.

For the very reception of flesh was the virginal conception. The nature of the Word of God—spiritual and begotten without beginning from God the Father—could not have been conceived in time in the womb of that holy mother and virgin without flesh; just as flesh, without union with the Word of God, could not in any way, having been sown without intercourse with a man, have grown within the innermost part of the virgin womb.

The virgin’s nature therefore presented this flesh from herself when God, who was to be conceived, came into her. No interval of time is consequently to be supposed between the beginning of the flesh’s conception and the arrival of the divinity that was to be conceived. There was one conception of divinity and flesh in the womb of the Virgin Mary, and one Christ, the Son of God, was conceived in both natures, so that he might begin to abolish the stain of corrupted descent from the point at which it appeared to exist in every person born.

## CHAPTER IV. To abolish the sin of origin, the sinless Son of God united to himself an unstained human nature

### 8.

Since all human beings born from the intercourse of man and woman have the beginning of their conception sprinkled with the contagion of original sin—for the sin which the first man, although good by nature, committed after being deceived by the devil’s wickedness passed also to his descendants, together with its punishment, namely death [Note: Thus in the manuscript; the printed editions read “and with death.”]—it was altogether necessary that the merciful and just Lord, intending to erase the traces of human iniquity, should graciously unite to himself, at the very conception, an unstained human nature, without stain himself, precisely where the devil had been accustomed to claim it for his own dominion and possession through the inflicted stain of original sin.

God the Only-Begotten wished to assume the truth and fullness of human nature; he therefore also took upon himself its conception and birth. For let no Catholic believe or say that God the Only-Begotten, who was to redeem us by his blood in the flesh through which that same God became man, rejected the beginning of human conception, when in that same flesh God himself, while remaining immortal, was to suffer the final extremity of human mortality.

Just as, in dying according to the flesh, the true and living God did not lose his immutable and unlosable natural state, so, when that same immeasurable God was conceived in a small body, he did not lack his natural immensity; and when he was born in the flesh in time, he did not lose the natural eternity in which he is the everlasting God from the Father and in the Father. For that life willed the death he underwent in the flesh to be its own, and that eternity possessed as its own the conception he received in his mother.

### 9.

God the Word, therefore—that is, the Only-Begotten Son of God, who is, as he himself testifies, the alpha and the omega, the beginning and the end in all things (Revelation 1:11)—did not refuse to be conceived in the flesh according to human nature at its beginning, just as, dying in that same flesh, God paid the final debt of human nature.

For human nature could in no way become sufficient and capable of taking away the sin of the world unless it passed into union with the Word of God [Note: Thus the manuscript and Basil; Lovaniensis and Antverpiensis read “into the union of the Word of God”], not by a natural confusion but solely by a personal unity. For when the Word became flesh, by a marvelous union he made his own the nature that he received from us.

Yet in this deifying and wholly marvelous union, the divinity of the Word was not changed into flesh, and the true humanity of the Word retained in every respect the natural truth of our race. Therefore the virgin—something that must often be recalled—both conceived and bore God the Word himself, insofar as he became flesh in her; she conceived and bore that Only-Begotten God, namely, the power and wisdom of God, the brightness of eternal light, the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness (Wisdom 7:26), the radiance of his glory and the figure of his substance.

The immutable and eternal divinity of the Father had begotten him from its own nature, eternal and unchangeable, without any beginning; the virginal womb conceived that same one, wholly and fully God and man, in human nature at its beginning, and bore him.

## CHAPTER V. God and man in Christ signify not two persons but two natures without confusion

### 10.

When we call the Lord Christ God and man, we do not indicate a personal duality but the truest union of both natures, without any confusion having occurred. The same one is God who is man, and the same one is man who is God, because human nature was marvelously united to God the Word in such a way that he himself, true God, became true man, while true humanity did not have another person belonging to the incarnate Word.

A human substance was added to God, not a person. God, therefore, with his flesh, is one Christ, Son of God and son of man, the same Word and flesh simultaneously—indeed, the same Word made flesh [Note: These words, “indeed, the same Word made flesh,” which appear in the printed editions, are absent from the manuscript]—because he is the same God and man.

## CHAPTER VI. God is not in Christ as he was in the patriarchs and prophets. Mary’s flesh was flesh of sin

### 11.

God the Word did not receive flesh in such a way that it did not become flesh, since the evangelist says: “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14). Nor did the supreme and immeasurable [Note: The printed editions read *universus* (“universal”); the manuscript reads *immensus* (“immeasurable”)] God assume the nature of flesh in such a way that, as in one of the patriarchs or prophets, God was indeed in that man, but the same God was not man.

Nor did the supreme and immeasurable God assume the nature of flesh in such a way that, as in one of the patriarchs or prophets, God was indeed in that man, but the same God was not man. Let Christian conscience be far from holding this, and let no believer permit himself to be profaned by so great an impiety.

For when the Word became flesh, the divinity graciously united humanity to itself in a marvelous manner, so that, with the truth of both natures preserved, in one and the same God and man, Christ, that humanity of his might become a divine offering [alternatively, “victim”: *divina* / *victima*] for the life of the world.

For God, who does not contain his mercies in anger (Psalm 76:10), became man for this purpose: that whatever he had created whole in man, the same God might restore completely in himself after assuming it.

### 12.

This, then, was possessed by that truly marvelous yet true conception and birth of the God-man according to the flesh: the virgin ineffably conceived and bore the God of heaven, and the virgin mother remained inviolate. She was truly named by the angel “full of grace and blessed [Note: The printed editions read *beata* (“blessed”); the manuscript reads *benedicta* (“blessed”)] among women” (Luke 1:28).

Through the assistance of prevenient grace, and through the work of the Holy Spirit coming upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowing her, she was to conceive God the Son. She neither endured nor desired intercourse with a man in any way; instead, retaining virginity in mind and body, she received from him whom she was to conceive and bear the gift of incorruptible fruitfulness and fruitful integrity.

Thus the holy virgin conceived God the Word insofar as he became flesh: the maker of angels and human beings; and the same virgin nevertheless bore him as the Redeemer of human beings.

For the holy Virgin Mary did not conceive God without the assumption of flesh, nor flesh without the union of God, because the virgin’s conception was shared by God and flesh.

### 13.

This is the grace by which it came about that God, who came to take away sins because there is no sin in him, was conceived and born as man in the likeness of sinful flesh, from flesh of sin.

For Mary’s flesh, which had been conceived according to the universal human condition in iniquities, was indeed flesh of sin; and it bore the Son of God in the likeness of sinful flesh. The Apostle testifies: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8:3)—namely, him who, although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself [Note: The printed editions read *et semetipsum* (“and himself”); the manuscript reads *sed semetipsum* (“but himself”), in accordance with the Apostle’s text], taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings (Philippians 2:6–7).

The Son of God was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, and he was likewise made [Note: The printed editions read *idem qui in similitudine* (“the same one who [was] in the likeness”); the manuscript reads *idemque est in similitudinem* (“and the same one was made in the likeness”)] in the likeness of human beings, so that he might become like human beings in the truth of the flesh that he himself had created, and so that, created in flesh without sin, God might remove our dissimilarity, which he saw to be present in our flesh not through his work but through our sin.

The Son of God therefore appeared sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, because in his true human flesh there was not human iniquity but mortality.

When the likeness of sinful flesh is spoken of as being in the Son of God—or, rather, when the Son of God is said to be in the likeness of sinful flesh—we must believe that God the Only-Begotten did not draw the filth of sin from the Virgin’s mortal flesh, but received the complete truth of nature, so that he might be the “truth springing from the earth,” which the blessed David indicates in prophetic speech, saying: “Truth has sprung from the earth” (Psalm 85:12).

Truly, therefore, Mary conceived God the Word, whom she bore in the flesh of sin that God assumed.

## CHAPTER VII. The blessed Virgin merited to conceive and bear God and man not through human merits but through God’s gracious favor

### 14.

She merited to conceive and bear God himself made man not through human merits, but through the gracious favor of the Most High God, who was conceived and born from her.

For unless God the Word, uniquely uniting human nature to himself, were born from a virgin as true and complete man, the beginning of spiritual birth from God would never be granted to us, who are born bodily. But so that divine birth might be bestowed upon those born bodily, the divine majesty of the Only-Begotten Son was first conceived and born in the truth of flesh [Note: “from God” is absent from the printed editions but present in the manuscript].

“For salvation is far [alternatively, “was far”: *erat* / *fuit*] from sinners” (Psalm 119:155), and our iniquities had separated us from God by a great division (Isaiah 59:2). Since, moreover, we were held bound by the chain of death in the very birth of our flesh, from which we could be released only by the gift of spiritual birth, God was born from man so that human beings might be born from God.

For this reason Christ, the Son of God—that is, true God and eternal life—was born and died in the truth of flesh, so that we might be reborn spiritually in the sacrament of baptism under the one name of the Trinity.

The Apostle teaches this, saying: “All of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Romans 6:3).

### 15.

The first birth of Christ, therefore, the Son of God, was from God; his second was from man. Our first birth, however, is from man, and our second from God.

Because God, who was to be born, received the truth of flesh from the womb, he therefore granted the spirit of adoption to us who were reborn in baptism.

He became by grace through his second birth what he was not by nature through his first birth, so that we might become by the grace of our second birth what we were not by nature in our first birth.

But when God was born from man, he brought grace to us; we, however, receive grace freely [Note: Perhaps “we received,” in view of the following words; all the printed editions and the manuscript read “we receive”], so that by the gift of God born in the flesh we might become participants in the divine nature.

Because the Son of God became the son of man, therefore, “to all who received him” (as the blessed evangelist John testifies) “he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God” (John 1:12–13).

But if the Only-Begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, after his eternal birth—which he possesses as coeternal Son from the eternal Father—had not, for the sake of sanctifying [Note: The manuscript reads “justifying”] human beings, assumed a second birth, the man conceived in iniquities would not have been freed from the bonds of his first birth.

But because, according to the words of the blessed John, the Son of God appeared for this purpose, “to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8), that same God, who in his first birth—from the nature of the Father—is true God and eternal life and has no beginning of birth, took from the virgin, in time, the beginning of a second birth.

## CHAPTER VIII. Christ’s death according to the flesh destroyed both deaths in us. By the name “flesh” the whole human being is understood

### 16.

That living Word of God, therefore, while the condition of his life remained unchangeable, was naturally one life with the Father from whom he was born after his first birth—for “as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26).

The same Son of God, in the nature of flesh, was born through grace for the dead unto death, so that after the death of our first birth, which we have from flesh, we might be reborn to life in the grace of the Spirit.

But unless the true and living God—indeed, God who is truth and eternal life—became the same true man, he could not taste death; and unless the same man who tasted death were true God and eternal life, he could not conquer death.

“For, apart from him who is man in such a way that he is also God, what man has destroyed death by death? Or who has delivered his soul from the hand of the underworld?” (Psalm 88:49) [Note: Thus the manuscript; the printed editions omit “death” and read, “or who will deliver”].

Accordingly, the living and true Only-Begotten God, according to the flesh that he received from us, was conceived and born, and so also died and rose again. For he came “to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10); he was handed over for our offenses and rose for our justification (Romans 4:25).

The death of the Son of God, which he assumed in flesh alone, destroyed in us both deaths, that of soul and that of flesh. His resurrection in the flesh bestowed upon us the grace of both spiritual and bodily resurrection, so that, first justified through faith in the death and resurrection of the Son of God, we might be raised from the death of unbelief, by which we were held bound, since by nature we were children of wrath, like the rest (Ephesians 2:3); and after that first resurrection, namely of souls, which was granted to us in faith, we might also rise in this flesh in which we now live, never again to die.

God, true God and eternal life, did not graciously accept our death for destruction for any other reason than that, through belief in his resurrection, he might grant us his life, which would endure without end.

The Lord of glory likewise endured the insult of the cross for this reason: that he might give his glory to his faithful, as he himself testified, saying: “And the glory that you have given me, I have given them” (John 17:22).

The Word made flesh is one and complete Christ. By the name “flesh,” however, the whole human being must here be understood [Note: The manuscript reads, “the whole human being must be understood”], that is, the rational soul and the flesh.

For Christ, the Son of God, just as he received our true flesh without sin, so he received a true soul of his own without sin. He clothed himself with our flesh together with the condition of human mortality, but he received our soul together with its weaknesses, without the stain of human iniquity [Note: The printed editions read “human weakness”; the manuscript more correctly reads “iniquity”].

Thus the divinity of Christ, bearing our weaknesses in his soul through its own power, preserved justice without sin; and through that soul, by the gift of resurrection, removed from his own flesh the punishment of mortality.

Therefore Christ, rising from the dead [Note: The manuscript reads “from the dead”; the printed editions read “from among the dead,” or “from death”], no longer dies, and death shall no longer rule over him (Romans 6:9).

## CHAPTER IX. According to the usage of Scripture, the whole human being is often understood by the term “flesh” or “soul”

### 17.

Because it is customary in the divine utterances to designate both flesh and soul together in a human being by the word “flesh,” as it is written: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28); and: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6); and: “As you have given him authority over all flesh” (John 17:2); and: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved” (Matthew 24:22)—so, according to this usage, the whole human being is called “flesh” in the holy Scriptures.

In the same Scriptures, conversely, the whole human being is also shown to be designated by the name of “soul” alone.

When the patriarch Abraham left his land, his kindred, and his father’s house at the command and with the assistance of the God who called him (Genesis 12:1)—for he could in no way have fulfilled what God commanded unless the one who commanded had helped him—and when he departed with the people he possessed, he is said to have taken with him the souls he had acquired in Haran [Note: Basil reads “the people whom he loved”; the others read “whom he possessed”].

When Jacob likewise descended into Egypt, holy Scripture records that seventy-five souls were in his company (Genesis 46:27). The blessed Apostle Peter also says that eight souls were saved through water at the time of the flood (1 Peter 3:20).

In the Acts of the Apostles, when the Jews had been pierced by the sudden and astonishing preaching of the same blessed Peter and had been converted from unbelief to faith by the transformation wrought by the right hand of the Most High, it is written: “About three thousand souls were added on that day” (Acts 2:41).

From these testimonies we recognize that the fullness of human nature is often designated both by the name of flesh alone and by the name of soul.

The Word therefore became flesh, one and complete Christ: one from both natures and in both, that is, in human and divine nature. In him the glorious union of both natures remains wholly intact, so that whoever subtracts humanity from Christ’s divinity, or removes divinity from his humanity, dissolves Christ through sacrilegious unbelief and blasphemous teaching.

The Apostle John, full of truth, testifies that every spirit which dissolves Jesus is not from God, and that this is the Antichrist (1 John 4:3).

## CHAPTER X. Before the Word became flesh, he was not Christ

### 18.

What Christian could easily fail to know or doubt that God the Word, before he became flesh, was not Christ but God alone?

That same God the Word, who was always in the form of God, then began to be Christ when God, emptying himself, assumed the form of a servant without diminishing the fullness of his nature.

God therefore became Christ so that Christ might be God and perfect man, because the Word graciously became flesh so that flesh could be called by the name of the Word, that is, of God.

For Christ’s flesh was not Christ before that flesh was taken up by the Word; nor did that flesh—that is, that man—receive in itself the form of the living God. Rather, God, who was in the form of God, assumed the form of a servant; and God, equal to the Father, was made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a man (Philippians 2:6–7). He who was rich became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might be enriched (2 Corinthians 8:9).

The Word made flesh is therefore one Christ. But the Word without flesh was the eternal God; Christ’s flesh, however, without the Word was not only never Christ, but was not even conceived as a person.

The Word that became flesh remained eternal before it became flesh; the flesh of the Word received its personal beginning in God the Word himself [Note: Thus the manuscript; the printed editions except Basil read “in the very God the Word”].

Because the Word made flesh is one Christ, Son of God and man, and because the Word is not one and the flesh another, but the same one Word made flesh, the same one is both the eternal God begotten from the Father without a beginning and, according to the flesh, the same God made man from the virgin with a beginning in time.

He is the one Only-Begotten Son of God: from the eternity of divinity, and from the beginning of flesh. From the eternity of divinity he is the Creator of visible and invisible things; from the beginning of flesh he saves his people from their sins.

From the eternity of divinity he is coeternal with the Father, always living, born from him; from the beginning of flesh he is later than his mother, from whom he was born in time, destined to die in time.

For the Apostle testifies: “Christ died at the appointed time for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6).

### 18 bis.

Therefore it was not the Trinity—that is, not the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together—nor the Father alone or the Holy Spirit alone; that is, neither he who begot the Son nor he who proceeds from the Father. Rather, it was the Son alone, namely he whom the Father begot as his coeternal and coequal Son in unity of nature—one person of the Trinity, Christ, the unique Son of God—who was conceived and born in the flesh from the womb of the virgin mother in order to save us.

He is true and supreme God from the womb of God the Father. It was not the Trinity but Christ, the Son of God, the Only-Begotten from the Father, who was small in the flesh and grew in the flesh. The perfect and immeasurable Father [Note: The printed editions read “universal”] recognizes him, through the unity of divinity, as equal to his own perfection and immensity.

It was not the Trinity but Christ, the Son of God—“the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6)—who, through the course of time, mercifully passed through the stages of human life in the flesh, from infancy to full maturity.

Remaining eternal in unity with the Father’s nature, he marvelously made the ages and established the mutabilities of time without change in himself.

It was not the Trinity but Christ, the radiance of the Father’s glory, who suffered in the flesh for us. He alone was born from God the Father, the impassible God.

We truly believe, as cannot be doubted, that Christ the Son of God tasted death for us in the flesh, while the immortality of his divinity remained intact. We hear from the truthful preaching of the holy Apostle John that he is the true Son of God the Father, true God, and eternal life (1 John 5:20).

It was not the Trinity but Christ, the Son of God, the Word made flesh, who rose in the same flesh in which he graciously consented to be crucified and die; and he, remaining life, raised that same flesh of his from the tomb.

It was not the Trinity but Christ, who is God over all [Note: The words “not the Trinity but” were absent from the printed editions but were found in the manuscript], who ascended into heaven in the flesh, and who will come from heaven in the flesh before the eyes of his disciples.

He did not abandon heaven when he received flesh on earth, nor did he, ascending into heaven in the flesh, abandon his own on earth in his divinity [alternatively, “does not abandon”: *deseruit* / *deserit*]. For he promised this, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

That God, therefore, who, in the form of God and according to the prophecy of the blessed Jeremiah, is “great and without end, exalted and immeasurable,” concerning whom the same prophet says shortly afterward, “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him; he discovered [Note: The manuscript reads *qui adinvenit*, “who discovered”] the whole way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved” (Baruch 3:36–37)—he himself, according to the form of a servant, in which he was made a little lower than the angels, “afterward appeared on earth and lived among human beings,” as the same prophet says (ibid., 38).

Unbelievers saw that same man, mortal and mutable; those pure in heart, who now truly believe in him, will see him as God, naturally immortal and unchangeable, in the world to come.

For true faith now cleanses human hearts, so that it may present them, made capable of seeing God, for the glory of the future resurrection [Note: We have restored this passage from the manuscript; the printed editions read: “which presents hearts capable of seeing God with the glory of the future resurrection,” while Basil reads *reddendo* (“rendering”) instead of *videndo* (“seeing”)].

## CHAPTER XI. True faith believes in one and the same Christ, true God and true man. The Roman Church, the summit of the world

### 19.

What is true faith, except to believe without any hesitation in one and the same Christ, true God and true man; and to proclaim that the same one was begotten from God the Father according to divinity and from the Virgin Mary according to the flesh [Note: Thus the manuscript; the printed editions read: “to believe, and to proclaim that one and the same God was begotten”]? 

For apostolic authority testifies that one and the same is Christ from the fathers according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever (Romans 9:5); one and the same was crucified through weakness but lives through the power of God (2 Corinthians 13:4); one and the same both [alternatively, “is”: *et* / *est*] performs mighty works among human beings and endures sufferings for human beings.

When Christ the Son of God performed miracles according to divinity, his humanity was passible in that same God; and when the same Christ, the Son of God, suffered according to the flesh, his divinity was impassible in that same man.

Because in Christ, God’s Only-Begotten Son, the distinct properties of the natures do not divide the person, nor can the unity of person confuse or remove the properties of either nature—for he who naturally declares himself to be the truth preserved both in himself while natural truth remained—therefore we neither separate his impassible divinity from Christ’s humanity in his sufferings, nor consider his humanity in any way separable from that divinity in his mighty works.

We therefore neither divide nor confuse Christ in his mighty works and sufferings. He is the one whom the blessed Peter, with the Father revealing it, confessed to be the Son of the living God, although Christ himself had first truly declared himself to be the son of man (Matthew 16:16).

True faith therefore neither confuses nor divides the true Christ in his sufferings and mighty works, because personal unity admits no division in him and the truth of both natures remains without confusion.

God Christ was handed over for our offenses because he is true man; and the same man, Christ, rose for our justification because he is true God.

For unless the same true God [Note: These words, *verus Deus* (“true God”), are found in the manuscript but not in the printed editions] were true man, he could not be handed over and die; and unless the same true man were true God, he could not raise himself after the pains of the underworld had been released.

But because God is not one and man another, but the same one is Christ, God and man, it follows that the same God Christ is he who accepted death in his flesh, and the same man Christ is he who destroyed death through his divinity.

The same Christ, the Son of God, who could not die in divinity, died in the flesh, which immortal God assumed as mortal. And the same Christ, the Son of God, having died in the flesh, rose again, because when he died in the flesh he did not lose the immortality of his divinity.

### 20.

This is why, after his resurrection, just as he demonstrated the solidity of true flesh in himself through true scars and through the true eating of fish and honey, so, entering while the doors were shut, he showed in himself the true power of eternal divinity. Thus it was recognized that Christ’s weakness in dying had been natural, and that the same one, when risen, possessed natural majesty.

Therefore Thomas, when commanded to place his hand in the side of the dead and risen Christ and to examine the reality of the wound, recognized in those scars the true power of divinity in the one who had suffered and risen. When he was commanded to touch the places of the nails with his fingers, he proclaimed the same Lord and his God in a faithful confession, saying: “My Lord and my God!”

For he recognized that no other had risen in his flesh through the natural power of his divinity except the one who, from the nature of God the Father, is true God and eternal life (John 20:28).

### 21

The author and redeemer of the human race himself, the maker and participant in our nature, intimating to us the truth of this faith, after displaying in himself true flesh by true scars and true divinity by the power of the resurrection, so as to show that he himself, one and the same, must be believed and proclaimed as God and man, simultaneously named in himself the divine and human nature under the name of one Son, saying to the apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). [Col. 0464D]

Therefore the teacher and giver of eternal salvation gave this form of holy baptism so that no one, dividing the natures in the same Son of God, might be ensnared in a deadly error—whether by believing in the sacrament of baptism that the human nature of the Son of God was alien to the work of human redemption, or by confessing two persons in Christ and thus becoming no longer a true worshiper of the Trinity but an impious advocate of a quaternity. Consequently, whoever judged that the faith in Christ’s one person should in any respect be rejected would worship, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, not one Son but sons, although Jesus Christ is the one Son in the Trinity, with the Father and the Holy Spirit—the Christ who created the world and shed his blood for us. [Col. 0465A]

Therefore everyone who is washed in the sacrament of holy regeneration in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit is baptized only in the death and name of Christ, so that it may plainly appear that “we have been buried with him through baptism into death” (Romans 6:4), in whose one name, together with the name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, those baptized are established.

This the Church of Rome, which is the summit of the world, holds and teaches, illuminated by the words of the two great luminaries, Peter and Paul, as though by shining rays, and adorned by their bodies; and the whole Christian world with her believes it without hesitation as pertaining to righteousness and confesses it without doubt as pertaining to salvation. [Col. 0465B]

For these are the words of blessed Peter, preaching the Son of God to the Jews: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins” (Acts 2:38). Blessed Paul also, so that we might believe with the utmost firmness that we have been baptized into the death of Christ, set this mystery of our salvation, as though in the loftiest mirror visible to all, in the Epistle that he writes to the Romans, saying: “All who have been baptized in Christ have been baptized into his death; for we have been buried with him through baptism into death” [Note: The manuscript has this wording, following the Apostle’s text; the printed editions instead have “into death.”] (Romans 6:3). [Col. 0465D]

### 22

Whoever, then, tries to assert two persons in Christ and nevertheless confesses that he has been baptized in the one name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, according to the rule established by the Lord’s mouth and command, must either, in the clearest blasphemy, deny that he has been baptized into Christ’s death and thus show himself an enemy of apostolic preaching, or acknowledge himself a worshiper not of the Trinity but of a quaternity. [Col. 0465C]

If he fears the precipice of either impiety, let him hold with all his heart the sound judgment of the Catholic faith and not doubt that he has been baptized into Christ’s death, in whose name he has also been baptized. Recognizing also the one natural name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and considering that he has been baptized in his death and name—that one from whose side, while he hung upon the cross, the sacrament of the font and of the chalice flowed (John 19:34)—let him acknowledge as crucified for us the one whom Paul both believes and proclaims to be the power of God and the wisdom of God, saying: “But we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23). [Col. 0465D]

This is the great sacrament of godliness: namely, that the true God, the Only-Begotten, deigned to become true man; that the eternal One was born in time; that the impassible One suffered; that the incomprehensible One was crucified; that the immortal One died; and that the immeasurable One was confined not only within the smallness of a manger at his birth but also within the smallness of a tomb at his death.

All these things are true in the Son of God according to the truth of the flesh, because, while the human and divine nature remain in him without confusion and without separation, there is one person of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, in the truth of both natures. [Col. 0466A]

## CHAPTER XII  
### Through Christ not only is iniquity erased, but the capacity for holy thought, which God bestowed upon the first man at his creation, is also restored

### 23

Thus divine goodness bestowed free grace upon the human race, through which not only would all iniquity contracted through descent and added through the fault of one’s own will be erased, but also the capacity for holy thought, previously lost in the first man, would be recovered through the second man. Thus, when the God-man died and rose in the flesh [alternative reading: “flesh”] for human beings, the captivity that had been accustomed to dominate in our body while sin reigned would itself be taken captive; and where the sin of the offending man abounded, the grace of the Redeemer would abound still more (Romans 5:21). [Col. 0466B]

In this way the human will, which under sin’s domination had been wickedly free, would again recover the condition of true and healthy freedom, liberated by the gift of prevenient grace.

Concerning this grace of God—not the grace by which we are born as human beings, but that by whose working, through faith in the Mediator, we are released from the bonds of original and actual sin—we shall discourse as far as we can in the brevity proper to a letter, so that in this matter our reply may not be lacking to your question, or rather to your profession, strengthened by the help of that very grace.

### 24

Therefore whoever does not wish to bear the name of the Christian religion vainly—or rather, damnably—must firmly believe that our God, that is, the holy Trinity, which is the one supreme and true God, made the first man good by gratuitous goodness, in his own image, and implanted in him the capacity to know and love him. [Col. 0466C]

He created him not only with the gift of a good will but also with a complete and sound freedom of choice for acquiring and preserving righteousness.

Thus, if the capacity and movement of the freedom implanted in him did not abandon the grace of God assisting him, God’s goodness would grant the man the reward of eternal life; but if, despising divine righteousness, he fell away from grace, justice would repay the sinner with punishment.

Accordingly, the good and just Creator established a just condition on both sides for that man whom he had formed in an animal body and enriched with the gift of understanding and righteousness: if he preserved obedience, which is the first virtue, he would pass from the bodily condition in which he had been created into a spiritual and immortal state without bodily death—for there would be no iniquity in his soul. [Col. 0466D]

If he kept the commandments, he would receive by divine gift not only perfect and unlosable immortality of body, but also such grace in the soul for living holily and justly that thereafter he could not sin, provided that he did not sin while it was possible for him to sin.

### 25

Thus the first man, created from the earth, earthly (1 Corinthians 15:47), did receive grace by which he could refrain from sinning, if he wished [Note: Thus the manuscript; the printed editions read, “grace by which he could not sin, if he did not wish to sin.”]; but he had not yet received so great a grace that he would neither wish nor be able to sin at all. [Col. 0466D]

That grace was to be bestowed afterward by the good and just Lord, if the servant had first voluntarily preserved this commandment in action.

But if he had neglected to obey the good and just command, then, after the death of the soul which he himself had brought upon himself by sinning, he would also be punished by the death of the body with the affliction of the present life [alternative: “changed by the disadvantage of the present life”]. Nor would he be allowed continually to retain a condemnable life in sinful flesh, since he had been unwilling to preserve righteousness in his heart. [Col. 0467A]

He would thereafter be bound by the punitive necessity of bodily death, having voluntarily become subject to spiritual death by stubbornly transgressing the salutary commands.

For unless the death of the soul had preceded in sin, the death of the body would never have followed as punishment. The authority of the Apostle teaches this when it says: “The body indeed is dead because of sin” (Romans 8:10). [Col. 0467B]

Therefore, after the sin committed by voluntary transgression, the sinner deserved to hear this sentence from the punishing God: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19). Man would not, then, go into the earth in the flesh if the earth had not been made through sinning.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### Through sin man lost the capacity for good thought and good will; the beginning of good will comes only from God

### 26

That man, therefore, who was created without any necessity of sinning, sinned; and because by sinning he lost the health of his soul, he immediately lost also the capacity for thinking those things that pertain to God. [Col. 0467C]

“For he forgot to eat his bread” (Psalm 101:5), and, stripped of the garment of faith and wounded by the injuries of carnal desires, he lay so oppressed under the domination of sin that he could in no way possess any beginning of good will unless he received it as a gratuitous gift from God.

For having become a slave of sin, he was made free from righteousness (Romans 6:18); and therefore he became alienated from righteousness because [alternative: “he who”] had voluntarily surrendered himself to the dominion of iniquity.

Sold, therefore, under sin, he bound in the chains of deadly servitude all the offspring that would be born from the intercourse of flesh.

Blessed Paul clearly indicates this in these words: “Through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12).

We all endured this in that first man, the father of the whole world, in whom all sinned before they were born, though they could not sin by themselves. Hence it came about that the condemned mass propagated children of wrath; it poured both iniquity and death into the descendants of that man. [Col. 0467D]

Thus everyone who was to be born from the sinner’s seed under the law of sin—which is certainly present in mortal bodies until death—received the stain of ancestral sin at the very beginning of conception. From then on, under the heavy yoke that rests upon the children of Adam, from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all (Sirach 40:1), they would lead a wretched life, subject to brevity, sin, and death.

For it is written: “A man born of a woman is short-lived and full of wrath” (Job 14:1). [Col. 0468A] This would drag one born for the second death into mortal ruin if the death of this miserable life should find him alienated from the grace of God the Redeemer.

### 27

Therefore, so that we might be released by the grace of the merciful God from the bond of original sin by which we were held bound through the first man, there appeared one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5).

Because God is immortal and just, whereas the transgression of the first man had made us unjust and mortal, the Only-Begotten God, who was born from the Father immortal and just, was born from a human being as man, so that a remedy suited to our wounds might be applied. [Col. 0468B]

In the human nature in which he became mediator between God and human beings, he had righteousness from the Father and death from his mother, so that through him we might be freed from every sin—he who contracted sin neither by being born nor by living—and receive from him the righteousness by which we might be released from the bond of eternal death, so that through him we might be just in this life and immortal after this life.

He alone, therefore, was wondrously, because uniquely, born in the likeness of sinful flesh; he alone is the male who opens the womb and is truly called holy to the Lord. The womb of his mother was opened not by the desire of a husband’s intercourse but by the omnipotence of the Son being born.

Therefore he alone is the one in whom, when the prince of this world came, he found nothing; the only man “free among the dead” without assistance (John 14:30); the only one who “knew no sin” (Psalm 87:5). For this reason it is sufficient that he should be made sin for us—that is, a sacrifice for sins—so that we might become the righteousness of God in him (2 Corinthians 5:21). [Col. 0468C]

He alone is the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:33); and the bread that he gives is his flesh for the life of the world (ibid., 52): namely, the flesh of the just and immortal God, by receiving which righteousness and life [Note: The words “and life” are absent from the printed editions but present in the manuscript.] are bestowed upon that flesh which is born with the punishment of death and the pollution of sin.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### From the sin of the first man we inherit both punishment and guilt; whoever does not enter the kingdom of God is tormented by eternal punishments

### 28

If, then, some try to assert that only death, and not sin as well, passed from the first man into the human race, it is astonishing if they do not understand the snares into which their position entangles them.

First, they make God unjust by saying that he causes infants to die—infants whom they insist are not polluted by any contagion of original sin and whom it is plainly evident cannot, in infancy, contract any actual sin by their own will—although the Apostle defines death as the wages of sin (Romans 6:23), and again says that sin is the sting of death, by which death was inflicted [alternative: “bound”] upon man. [Col. 0468D] [Note: The printed editions read “by that drink,” while the manuscript has “by this drink,” rightly so, as is evident.]

Sin is therefore called the sting of death not because sin comes through death, but because through sin death entered the world (1 Corinthians 15:56), just as we call a poisonous drink “a drink of death,” not because the drink is given by death, but because death is compared with that drink.

By what justice, then, is an infant subjected to the wages of sin if there is no pollution of sin in him? Or how do we see him pierced by death if he has not felt the sting?

And since there is no iniquity with God, who made man in his image, what justice is it that the image of God—which could not sin by itself—should not be permitted to enter the kingdom of God unless redeemed by the blood of the Son of God, into which kingdom whoever does not enter [alternative: “enters”] will be tormented by the interminable punishments of eternal fire? [Col. 0469A]

By what justice, then, does the just God [Note: “just” is absent from the manuscript.] impose punishment upon infants born without sin, in whom he finds no cause for punishment? Is this the kindness of the Creator God: to create his image and condemn it without any iniquity, although God is not unjust when he brings wrath (Romans 3:5)?

If, therefore, they do not wish to engage in deadly impiety to the insult of that very God, let them confess that sin passed into all human beings together with death through the first man. [Note: The manuscript has this wording; the printed editions instead read, “let them confess that the first man transmitted sin into all human beings together with death.”] [Col. 0469B]

## CHAPTER XV  
### The absurd consequences that follow those who deny that infants have sin

### 29

They must also see and avoid another impiety in this position of theirs. For by saying that infants do not draw original sin from Adam, they plainly deny that they have sinful flesh, although they do not deny that they have human flesh.

But from the fact that they do not deny that they have human flesh while denying that it is sinful flesh, it follows that they deny that human flesh is sinful flesh.

They confess, compelled by the Apostle [Note: The printed editions read “with the Apostle compelling them.”], that “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” [Note: Thus the manuscript; the printed editions read “into the likeness of sinful flesh.”] (Romans 8:3). [Col. 0469D]

The blindness of their impious profession therefore drives them to this: because [alternative: “they who”] deny that human flesh is sinful flesh, while they do not deny that Christ came in the likeness of sinful flesh, they sacrilegiously invent that Christ’s flesh was not human but of another nature.

They say that the flesh in which infants are born is human flesh, while nevertheless striving to deny that it is sinful flesh; but they agree with us in confessing that Christ came in the likeness of sinful flesh.

Therefore let them either deny that Christ’s flesh was human, or agree [alternative: “have agreed”] that the flesh of all human beings—in whose likeness God sent his Son—is sinful flesh. [Col. 0469C]

When they have done this, no difficulty will remain in showing them that sin is present in the flesh of infants. For if flesh is not falsely called sinful flesh, that flesh itself contains sin. But if it does not contain sin, it bears the name “sinful flesh” falsely.

Yet the truthful disciple of Truth, Paul, calls the flesh of which we are speaking “sinful flesh.” It remains, then, that just as it is truly flesh, so it is truly called sinful flesh by the apostolic mouth. [Col. 0469D]

### 30

Perhaps they will say that the Son of God was sent in the likeness of that sinful flesh which human beings possess once they can already sin by their own will, and whose flesh is therefore not improperly called sinful flesh—not in the likeness of the flesh in which infants are born without any will to sin.

They do not notice that if the flesh of infants had differed in quality from the flesh of adults, God would have come only in the likeness [Note: The manuscript has “in the likeness”; the printed editions have “into the likeness.”] of the flesh of infants, whom they say have no original sin. [Col. 0470A]

Indeed, Christ’s flesh would be more like the flesh of infants, with which it would share the truth of substance and quality, than like the flesh of adults, with whom it would share only the nature of flesh, not its stain.

But perhaps this is what they want: that Christ’s flesh should have possessed only a likeness of nature with the flesh of adults, while it could also have shared purity with the flesh of infants.

Let them therefore confess that infants are born in the likeness of sinful flesh, although they assert that they are born in human flesh not polluted by the contagion of original sin. [Note: The manuscript has this wording; the printed editions read, “but deny that they are polluted by the contagion of original sin.”] [Col. 0470B]

They must be shown how great an absurdity follows them here as well. For while denying original sin in infants at birth, they do not deny that infants have human flesh; and while conceding that the Son of God received human flesh from the virgin without sin, it consequently follows that they must confess that there is no difference between the flesh of the Only-Begotten God born from the virgin and that of any other infant.

Hence it follows that they say that all infants whom they assert to be born without sin have no need of the Savior’s help. Thus they fall into the snare of Pelagian error while unfaithfully contradicting the Catholic faith.

For if they assert that infants are born without sin, what remains except that they should say there is nothing in them that needs to be cleansed through spiritual regeneration? And if they remove the stain of original sin from infants at birth, what else are they attempting but to charge divine truth with falsehood, when they see infants receiving the sacrament of baptism for the remission of sins?

That sacrament is therefore conferred uniformly upon infants and adults so that it may be recognized that the stain of original sin is present in all. [Col. 0470C]

### 31

Whoever, therefore, desires to attain true and everlasting salvation, rejecting the mind of heretical perversity, should not doubt that those whom he sees born with the punishment of sin were also born with sin.

Let him hear blessed Job saying: “For no one is clean from defilement, not even an infant whose life is a single day upon the earth” (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint).

Let him also consider, with the humble grief of a devout heart, the lament of blessed David, who says: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother gave birth to me” (Psalm 50:7).

Let him also see that the sacrament of circumcision was commanded to holy Abraham, not without a dreadful threat concerning the infant. For there God, faithful and just, who does not bring wrath where he finds no guilt, speaks thus to our father Abraham: “The male who is not circumcised in the flesh [alternative: “the flesh”] of his foreskin on the eighth day shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant” (Genesis 17:14). [Col. 0470D]

Whoever, then, denies original sin in infants born according to the flesh should say in what way an infant eight days old could have transgressed God’s covenant, unless he transgressed it in the one in whom all sinned.

The Apostle asserts that, before they were born, infants had done nothing good or evil (Romans 9:11) [Note: The manuscript reads, “although the Apostle asserts that, before he was born, he had done nothing,” etc.]; and yet we see that, once born—not only within the eighth day of their birth, when infants were then commanded to be circumcised, but also throughout the whole period of infancy after that day—they are so unable to transgress God’s covenant that even knowledge of that covenant cannot be imparted to them. [Col. 0471A]

### 32

Does anyone attempt to abolish original sin in infants by that saying of blessed Paul in which he says that death reigned from Adam to Moses even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression (Romans 5:14)? [Col. 0471B]

If, in opposition to this, he is confronted with what the same Apostle says—“Through one offense there was condemnation for all human beings” (ibid., 18)—and with what he says in explaining it shortly afterward—“Through the disobedience of one man the many were constituted sinners” (ibid., 19)—and when speaking of Jews and Greeks he adds universally, “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:23). [Note: “Our Lord” is absent from the manuscript and from the Apostle’s text; it appears in the printed editions.] [Col. 0471D]

Will he not immediately be driven into great difficulties unless he accepts both meanings according to the profession of Catholic belief—namely, that he says infants have committed no sin by their own works, but recognizes that all human beings generally sinned in that first man?

## CHAPTER XVI  
### Only faith in the Redeemer frees from original sin; blind nature sins without the law

### 33

From this sin, which carnal birth draws along originally, no one is rescued by natural capacity, no one by the letter of the holy law, but only by faith in Jesus Christ, the Son of God. He came [alternative: “comes”] “to seek and save what was lost” (Luke 19:10), died for the ungodly (Romans 5:6), and offered himself for us—as the Apostle says—as an offering and sacrifice to God for a pleasing fragrance (Ephesians 5:2). [Col. 0471C]

In this mediator between God and human beings, the condition of human nature was restored, and the effect [alternative: “inclination”] of fulfilling the law was brought to completion. For natural weakness, which plainly could never suffice for virtue by itself, once all our days have failed and we have failed in the wrath of God (Psalm 89:9), deprived at once of light and strength, sins, being so blind without the law, that it does not know that it is sinning. [Note: Thus the manuscript; the printed editions read, “nature sins so blindly.”] [Col. 0471D]

For this reason it is said: “I would not have known covetousness unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Romans 7:7).

Nor did hearing the law rescue anyone from the power of darkness; rather, it added to sinners a burden of transgression. Without the grace of faith, the law, once known, condemns more severely than when unknown. As ignorance of sin is diminished, so the sinner’s guilt is increased. [Col. 0472A]

Therefore the Apostle says: “The law brings about wrath; for where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Romans 4:15). He also says: “The law was established because of transgression” (Galatians 3:19), and, “Scripture confined all things under sin, so that the justification of faith in Jesus Christ might be given to believers” (ibid., 22).

How, then, can nature, so much prouder the more it is subject to the dominion of sin and death, promise itself even the smallest beginning of good will and action on the basis of the possibility of free choice alone, if it is not preceded by the help of God’s grace, through which good will is restored and preserved in a person? [Note: The printed editions read this; the manuscript instead has: “How, then, is the possibility of free choice dissolved, unless it is preceded . . . ? Or how can it promise itself even the smallest amount of good will,” etc.] [Col. 0472D]

It could neither preserve God’s command when sound nor, when wounded, obtain even the slightest remedy of healing from the law; instead, by learning the commandment, it increased sin.

“For the law entered so that sin might abound” (Romans 5:20), and no one can be freed from that sin except through the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world.

From this body of death it is not free human choice, nor the holy, just, and good commandment of the law, that frees us; only the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord frees us. “The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed us from the law of sin and death” (Romans 8:2).

## CHAPTER XVII  
### Christ frees human beings not by finding faith but by giving it

### 34

He freed them, however, not by finding faith in any human being but by giving it. For God, who justifies the ungodly, himself inspires faith in the unbeliever—faith that works through love—by the grace of his good will.

With regard, therefore, to the capacity for thinking rightly, the Apostle testifies, saying: “We are not capable of thinking anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5). [Col. 0472C]

Indeed, according to the same Apostle’s statement, God gives repentance to whomever he wills for the recognition of truth, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will (2 Timothy 2:25).

Therefore that first of the apostles, and deservedly called blessed in the language of truth, speaking of the faith of the nations, said that God had cleansed their hearts by faith; and again he said that the same grace had been divinely given to the Gentiles as to the apostles themselves (Acts 15:9), so that they might believe.

There the apostles and the elders recognized the gratuitous gift of grace in the teaching of the Holy Spirit, and all, unanimous and of one voice, adopted the judgment of blessed Peter, saying: “Then God has also granted repentance to the Gentiles unto life” (Acts 11:8). [Col. 0472D]

Although our Savior himself, by the command of his own voice, addressed [Note: Thus the manuscript; the Louvain and Antwerp editions read “addressed,” while the Basel edition reads “converted.”] the human will, saying: “Repent and believe the Gospel” (Mark 1:15), it is nevertheless clear that, for a human being to begin to believe in God, he receives from God repentance unto life. Indeed, he cannot believe at all unless he has received repentance as a gift from the merciful God.

But what is human repentance except a change of will—[lacuna]

[Col. 0473A]

Therefore God, who gives repentance to human beings, himself changes the human will.

### 35

Accordingly, if someone says, “It is mine to will to believe, but it belongs to God’s grace to help,” let him change the order of his words—or rather, let him not change it but preserve it—and let him place neither what is later in the first position nor what is earlier in the later position.

For he wrongly places God’s grace after his own will, since the latter cannot be good if the former is absent. Therefore [alternative: “for”] let him not say, “It is mine to will to believe, but it belongs to God’s grace to help”; rather, let him say, “It belongs to God’s grace to help, so that it may be mine to will to believe.”

For then his willing acts truly and rightly, when prevenient grace has begun to help him. [Note: Thus the manuscript; the Louvain and Antwerp editions read, “he says that this is his willing,” while the Basel edition reads, “he says that his willing exists.”] Faith, which works through love, makes humble the one to whom it is given, because “love is not puffed up” (Romans 13:4).

Therefore let no one doubt that faith is given to him by the help and gift of grace. Otherwise, while trying to assign the beginning of faith to himself, a human being, not strong in health but prejudiced by weakness, would also assign to himself the repentance that God gives unto life, and would be deprived of the benefit of so great a remedy, whose grace he attacks in obstinacy and ingratitude. [Col. 0473B]

The humility of the heart must be instructed, therefore, by divine utterances, in which it is principally shown that the good will itself, by which we begin to wish to believe, is prepared and directed by the Lord. Solomon says: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 8:35, according to the Septuagint). And David sings in the Psalms: “The steps of a man shall be directed by the Lord, and he shall desire his way” (Psalm 36:23). [Note: The printed editions have “he shall greatly desire,” but “greatly” is not read in the manuscript.] [Col. 0473D]

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### If the will to believe comes from ourselves, faith is not grace but the reward of good will

### 36

If, according to their opinion, it is ours to will to believe before God’s grace begins to help us, grace is unjustly called grace, because it is not given freely to a human being but is repaid to good will.

For, as they wish it, grace finds in us what it itself did not give. Indeed, if this is so, we give our will to God first and thus receive grace not through the mercy of the one who bestows it but through the justice of God who repays. [Note: The Basel edition reads “through the justice of the one who repays” and omits “God.”]

Yet “who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?” (Romans 11:35). No one, certainly, because “a human being cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven” (John 3:27). For what does he have that he has not received? And if he received it, why does he boast as though he had not received it? (1 Corinthians 4:7). [Col. 0473D]

But God’s mercy never precedes a human being if it never makes him good but waits to find a will. And where is what David says: “My God, his mercy will go before me” (Psalm 58:11)?

In what respect God’s mercy precedes us, and what kind of people it finds when it precedes us, the teacher of the Gentiles shows us not in some other person but in himself, saying: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I received mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Timothy 1:13). [Col. 0474A]

How, then, could Paul have possessed any will to believe from himself, when, blind and unbelieving, he did not recognize himself as a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent man? Considering this with a humble heart, he says elsewhere: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Corinthians 15:9).

Immediately assigning his faith not to his own will but to the grace of the merciful God, he says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (ibid., 10).

What was he already [alternative: “had been”], except faithful? In order that he might be so, he certainly received mercy, as he himself testifies, saying: “I give advice as one who has received mercy from the Lord to be faithful” (1 Corinthians 7:25).

And when he confessed that he had previously been a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent man, he did not cease to assign his faith and love to grace, immediately adding: “But the grace of God abounded in faith and love, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (1 Timothy 1:14). [Note: “Our Lord” appears in the printed editions but not in the manuscript or in the Apostle’s text.] [Col. 0474B]

### 37

If, then, the grace of God did not give Paul faith, it must not be believed that it gave him love either. Therefore—God forbid—Paul lied when he said: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

But because Paul, with Christ speaking in him, could not lie, let us most firmly confess that faith is bestowed upon us by that same Spirit through whom we cannot deny that the love of God is poured into our hearts.

When Paul was therefore a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent man, he was not helped by God’s grace because he wished to believe; rather, he received the gift of prevenient grace so that he might wish to believe. That grace found in his will not some beginning of belief but blasphemy, savagery, insults, and ignorance in unbelief. [Col. 0474C]

His will was so blind that he could not only not believe, but could not even foresee the beginning of his own belief. For he would not have acted ignorantly if he had foreseen his own ignorance.

Therefore, in Paul, the gift of prevenient mercy is rightly credited not only with the beginning of belief but also with the recognition of unbelief itself. God’s mercy bestowed this upon him so that, enlightened and assisted, he might both recognize and avoid his unbelief.

“For the Lord is our illumination and our salvation” (Psalm 26:1): he illuminates us so that we may recognize our sins, and he heals us so that, separated from our sins, we may live in righteousness.

For this reason Paul himself, who confesses that he received mercy in order to become faithful, instructs us beneficially, saying: “Therefore it is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy” (Romans 9:16). [Col. 0474D]

For truly, in order that we may will, we are illuminated by the gift of prevenient mercy; and in order that we may run, we are supported by the help of subsequent mercy.

Therefore, for anyone to attribute to himself the good will by which he begins to wish to believe is not the vigor of a living soul but the swelling of dead flesh.

# CHAPTER XIX. After sin, human free will is found capable only of serving sin without the help of grace. Freedom takes its beginning from a good will.
