**38.** From the moment when the first man voluntarily corrupted and oppressed his own nature, weakness increased [Col. 0475A] [Note: This passage, obscure elsewhere, has been restored with the aid of the manuscript, which reads: “weakness increased, so that unless,” etc., [lacuna], etc.] to such an extent that, unless free will is anticipated, healed, and continually assisted in each person by the medicine of divine grace, it is indeed free, but not good; free, but not upright; free, but not healthy; free, but not just. And the more it is free from goodness, uprightness, health, and justice, the more it is held captive in the deadly slavery of wickedness, perversity, weakness, and iniquity.

“For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII, 34); and “by whatever anyone is overcome, to that he is enslaved” (II Peter II, 19). Therefore, while sin reigns, a person does indeed possess free will, but free without God, not free under God—that is, free from justice, not free under grace—and for that reason free in the worst and most slavish manner, because it has not been liberated by the gratuitous gift of the merciful God.

The Apostle clearly indicates this when he says [Note: The manuscript reads *insinuans ait* (“indicating, he says”); the printed editions uniformly read *insinuat dicens* (“he clearly indicates when he says”)]: “For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness” (Romans VI, 20). Therefore, one who is free from righteousness cannot serve righteousness; for as long as he is a slave of sin, he is found capable only of serving sin.

No one is made free from this slavery of sin except the one whom the grace of Christ the Liberator sets free, so that, liberated from sin, he may become a servant of God. How this happens our Liberator himself shows: “If the Son sets you free,” he says, “you will truly be free” (John VIII, 35).

Therefore the Vessel of Election, indicating to us the benefit of liberating grace, testifies that we have been not merely made free but also liberated, in these words: “But now, having been liberated from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end eternal life” (Romans VI, 22).

**39.** This freedom, then, which does not arise from human choice but is bestowed by the gratuitous mercy of God, takes its beginning from a good will and, through the fruit of sanctification, attains the fullness of its result in eternal life.

But just as, in carnal birth, the formation wrought by the divine work precedes every act of will in the one being born, so in spiritual birth—by which we begin to put off the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error, so that we may put on the new man, who was created in righteousness and the holiness of truth (Ephesians IV, 22)—no one can possess a good will by his own spontaneous motion unless the mind itself, that is, our inner person, is renewed and reformed by God.

Therefore blessed Paul commands us (Romans XII, 2) not to be conformed to this age but to be transformed by the renewal of our mind. And lest we should in any way attribute the beginning of this transformation to our own ability, the Lord shows through the prophet that he himself is the fashioner of light, saying: “I am the Lord, forming light and creating darkness” (Isaiah XLV, 7).

Blessed Paul also confirms this by his preaching, saying: “God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts” [Col. 0476A] (II Corinthians IV, 6). And elsewhere he said to that same light which God had already formed: “For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians V, 6).

To some who had fallen from that honorable formation of light back into the blameworthy shapelessness of darkness, he displays the affection of a devout mind and says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians IV, 19).

But how can Christ be formed in his own people unless in the manner by which he begins to dwell in them—that is, through faith? Blessed Paul confirms this when he says: “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts in the inner person” [variant: “in our hearts”] (Ephesians III, 16). Thus, while we are reformed, we are renewed; and in that by which we are renewed, we are made alive.

# CHAPTER XX. Holy life takes its beginning from faith. Free will is not taken away by grace.

**40.** Our life takes its beginning from faith, because “the righteous shall live by faith” (Romans I, 17). Blessed Paul shows that this faith does not arise from our own will but is given to each person through the Holy Spirit, saying: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another [variant: “to one or another”] faith in the same Spirit” (I Corinthians XII, 8–9).

We therefore received the Holy Spirit not because we believed [Note: Antonius and Lovaniensis read “because we believe”; the manuscript and Basil read “because we believed”], but so that we might believe. The pattern first appeared in Christ’s flesh, which we are to recognize spiritually in our faith. For Christ, the Son of God, was conceived and born according to the flesh from the Holy Spirit. The Virgin could neither conceive nor give birth to that flesh unless the Holy Spirit had brought about the origin of that same flesh.

Thus faith can neither be conceived nor grow in the human heart unless the Holy Spirit infuses [Note: Basil reads *infundat* (“infuse”); Lovaniensis and Antonius read *effundat* (“pour out”)] and nourishes it. For we were born again from the same Spirit from whom Christ was born [Note: The manuscript reads “from whom the Lord Christ was born”].

Therefore Christ is formed according to faith in the heart of each believer by the same Spirit by whom he was formed according to the flesh in the Virgin’s womb. Hence the prophet, speaking in the person of the faithful, cries out to the Lord: “Because of the fear of you, Lord, we conceived and gave birth to the Spirit of your salvation; we did not perform righteousness upon the earth” (Isaiah XXVI, 18) [Note: Basil reads “we did not perform righteousness upon the earth”; Lovaniensis and Antonius omit “righteousness [we did] not” and read instead: “We conceived and gave birth. We performed the Spirit of your salvation upon the earth.”].

Just as Mary was called “full of grace” by the angel’s voice not only before she conceived Christ but even before she knew that she would conceive him, with no prior knowledge or will to conceive [variant: *praecessisset*, “had preceded,” or *praecederet*, “might precede”] the Son of God, so that it might be recognized that both the Virgin’s obedient will and the conception of the Lord and Savior were from the grace of God; so, before a person begins to wish to believe, the grace of the giver is infused into the heart, so that Christ may begin to be formed in the person through faith.

When Christ is formed in each person, he forms himself, because he himself initiates faith in the heart of each believer. Therefore in the Epistle written to the Hebrews [Col. 0477A] we are admonished to look to Jesus, “the author and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews XII, 2). Without doubt, he is the author of our faith when he gives faith to those who do not have it, just as he is the perfecter of that same faith when he increases and multiplies it in those who possess it and brings it to perfection through holy action.

For blessed the Apostle James says that “the faith of Abraham our father was perfected by works” (James II, 12).

**41.** Jesus is therefore the author and perfecter of our faith, because he works in us both the willing and the accomplishing, according to his good will. But if he is the author of our faith only because he waits for our will, so that faith may begin from us, it follows that he is also called the perfecter of our faith because he waits for our effort alone to bring to completion the faith that arose from us. Thus everything is taken away from God if both the beginning and the completion of our faith are attributed to the powers of human choice.

Since that is profoundly impious, if we do not resist the salutary words of the holy Scriptures [Note: So the manuscript; Basil reads *nos insistimus* (“we adhere”); Lovaniensis and Antonius read *nos resistimus* (“we resist”), but incorrectly], let us believe without hesitation that God both begins and completes in us everything that pertains to the beginning or progress of a good will. For it is he who works in us both the willing and the accomplishing, according to his good will (Philippians II, 13).

Let us therefore cry out in humility of heart and truth of faith with the prophet: “I know, Lord, that a person’s way is not his own, nor does it belong to a man to correct his way” (Jeremiah X, 23). The way that a person has from God is therefore not in the person, nor does a person correct the way that he has from himself. Accordingly, he does not possess his way within himself, nor does he correct his way, unless he has received the gift of spiritual grace together with uprightness of heart.

Therefore Solomon says: “But the Lord directs hearts” (Proverbs XXI, 2). Blessed James the Apostle also testifies that “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James I, 17)—namely, from those lights concerning which he promises through Ezekiel the grace of a new heart, saying:

“I will give you a new heart, and I will place a new Spirit within you; and I will take away the heart of stone from your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will give my Spirit within you, and I will cause you to walk in my statutes, observe my judgments, and perform them” (Ezekiel XXXVI, 26–27).

Blessed Paul, restraining the boldness of human presumption, says: “For who distinguishes you? And what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Corinthians IV, 7).

With him we must humbly and beneficially recognize and confess together that we are what we are by the grace of God [Note: Lovaniensis and Antonius read *quod et sumus* (“what we also are”); the manuscript reads *quod sumus* (“what we are”)], if indeed we are anything at all.

By this grace human choice is not taken away but healed; it is not removed but corrected; it is not abolished but enlightened; it is not emptied but assisted and preserved. Thus, in what the human being possessed weakness, he begins to possess health; where he was wandering, he returns to the way [variant: “returns in the way”]; where he was blind, he receives light; and where he was unjust, serving uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, there, anticipated and assisted by grace, he serves righteousness unto sanctification.

# CHAPTER XXI. When God makes those whom he wills into believers, he is not a respecter of persons. No one possesses from himself the will to believe.

**42.** We are astonished that some say: “If God makes people willing to believe when they are unwilling [Note: Lovaniensis, Antonius, and Basil read “when they are willing”], and no one is naturally able to believe in the Son of God or to will anything good that pertains to eternal life, why does he not make everyone willing, since God is not a respecter of persons?”

From these words, which have been set down in your writings, it is apparent that they give insufficient consideration to what they are saying. There would be respect of persons with God if—as these people wish—in any human being he found some beginning of a good will. But since he finds a good will in no one and himself grants it freely to whomever he wills [Note: The manuscript reads “to whomever he wills”; the printed editions read “when he wills”], it is recognized that there is no respect of persons when the giver’s generosity toward each person is gratuitous.

But when they ask, “Why does he not make everyone willing?”—does this mean that he does it in no one because he does not do it in everyone? Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Romans IX, 21)?

Can justice be blamed in the vessels of wrath, which justly prepared them for destruction according to their merits; or mercy in the vessels of mercy, which, without any merits, prepared them for glory solely by the gift of grace?

We have also shown from the testimony of Scripture that the will itself is prepared by the Lord. If it is not given by God but is found in a person, then what Scripture says—that it is prepared by the Lord—is false. But all Scripture, inspired by God, speaks truth in everything it says, because everything it says comes from truth: “The words of the Lord are pure words” (Psalm XI, 7).

Therefore God, who prepares the will, himself gives it. If God does not give it to a person through his grace, a person can never will to believe in God, because grace does not find that will but produces it in the person.

# CHAPTER XXII. The capacity to believe can exist in human nature, because God can heal it. Adam lost faith through sin.

**43.** When we say that no one can believe in God unless the heart is illuminated by God’s grace so that he may believe, we are not saying that the possibility of believing cannot exist at all in human nature. Rather, we demonstrate that human nature possesses the capacity by which it ought to hope and ask to receive that ability.

For, when a human being begins to believe in the Son of God, he certainly possesses this naturally. If the ability to believe had not been given in the condition of the first human being, he would never have contracted sin through unbelief. Nor is the capacity for believing implanted in any nature that God did not make rational.

“For is God concerned with oxen?” (I Corinthians IX, 9). Among oxen neither impiety is punished nor piety crowned. But we are taught by heavenly words that God is concerned with all human beings.

**44.** Faith therefore belongs to human nature. The Creator deigns to care for it so greatly that Truth says even the hairs of our head are numbered (Luke XII, 17). Thus, when human nature recognizes that it is so greatly loved by God, it may love God who loves it and cling to him through the faith of a pure heart. Faith is the way to blessedness for it, while unbelief is great misery; and unbelief is therefore justly punished when a person does not believe in the Son of God, because unbelief is its vice, just as faith is its virtue—not the kind of faith found in demons, but the kind that God gives to his saints, whom he justifies from impiety.

This is the faith that works through love. For “the demons also believe, and tremble” (James II, 19), but they do not love him from whom they departed through pride.

Because the first human being was cast down into this pride by the devil’s persuasion [variant: “suggestion”], he lost humility and lost faith; and by losing faith, he lost divine protection. For it is written: “He who does not believe God is not protected by God” (Sirach II, 15).

From that point the earth and ashes began to grow proud, because during his life he cast away his inmost self (Sirach X, 9–10). The divine word never ceases to call human beings back to that inmost self, saying: “Return, transgressors, to your heart” (Isaiah XLVI, 8).

But because they are flesh, “a passing spirit and not returning” (Psalm LXXVII, 39), a wandering sheep can never wish to return unless it has first been anticipated by the good Shepherd’s search and carried back upon his shoulders. Therefore the Good Shepherd came to seek and save the lost sheep, which cannot seek its shepherd before being sought by him, but is anticipated by the one who seeks it so that it may seek.

The shepherd would seek it in vain if the sheep, once sought, could not itself seek the shepherd [Note: So the printed editions; the manuscript reads: “if it, not having been sought, could itself seek the shepherd”]. But the goodness of the seeking shepherd grants it this: that it also possesses the will to seek the shepherd.

It is sought so that it may seek when it is illuminated so that it may believe. This, then, is what is divinely accomplished in a human being: God infuses faith into him so that, by the gift of grace, nature may recover the power of believing that it lost; and what, corrupted by guilt, it could not do, it may begin to ask for, having been formed by grace.

Thus, when that physician works—“for those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are sick”—weakness is driven out and nature is healed. The one who said this was asking for that healing: “I said, ‘Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you’” (Psalm XL, 5).

No saint would ask for healing if human nature were healthy; and anyone would ask for healing in vain if human nature could not be healed. Human nature, therefore, can be healed, but it receives the gift of that healing from the one from whom it received the beginning of its creation.

For if a human being could in no way be healed naturally, the heavenly physician would not have come to heal him [Note: The manuscript reads *non veniret* (“would not come”)]. Again, if he could heal himself, he would not need the heavenly physician.

He is healed through faith. If anyone could possess faith from himself, God would not give it to the human being. But he does give it, because “to another is given faith in the same Spirit” (I Corinthians XII, 9), as the Apostle says: “Therefore God has allotted to each the measure of faith” (Romans XII, 3).

# CHAPTER XXIII. A human being can believe naturally, although it is given to him divinely to believe.

**45.** A human being is not therefore unable to believe naturally because it is given to him divinely to believe [Note: So the printed editions; the manuscript reads: “because it is not given to him divinely to believe”]. Rather, it is recognized that the human being was created especially for possessing faith, because through faith human nature is renewed from its old condition.

Every human being has been so corrupted by the voluntary sin of the first man that God, by his good will, can heal the human will if he wills. For he created all things, as it is written, “so that they might exist,” and “made the nations of the world healable” (Wisdom I, 14). Yet, lest the beginning of healing be thought to come from the human being himself, the divine word immediately added: “And there is no medicine of destruction among them” [Col. 0480B] (ibid.).

Although the devil took faith away from the first human being, he could not take from God the power to restore what God had given. Nor could the devil corrupt human nature to such an extent that thereafter it could not receive back what it had lost, when God again bestowed it.

For the Almighty, who was able to form human nature, can also reform and preserve it when weakened, by healing it through grace. From him nature had received faith for salvation in the first human being; so now, in each individual, it receives it by the gift of divine goodness [variant: “received it”], as the same God creates from their parents those whom he has predestined and will save through faith.

**46.** Therefore, with God’s gift, a human being can naturally believe in God. What is contrary to human nature is not believing in God, because unbelief comes not from God’s creation but from the voluntary transgression of the commandment. Through that transgression, deprived of health and light, the human being can by his own choice increase his blindness and weakness, but cannot remove them.

Nevertheless, the illumination and healing of the human being are so possible for the Almighty Creator that, by his gift and for the glory of his name, an unbeliever can not only come to believe but also, through the grace of faith, attain the immortal and incorruptible state of life. There, receiving grace for grace, he will be entirely unable to sin and will be able in blessedness to see what he believed.

Hence that voice of faith resounds in the Psalms: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm XXVI, 13).

Although God did not make human nature for the purpose of its being corrupted by guilt, he can nevertheless, by his omnipotent goodness, heal through grace the nature that has been corrupted. God therefore heals and illuminates human choice so that a human being may naturally believe in God.

Thus it comes about that a human being can possess faith, but cannot possess it except as a gift from God.

# CHAPTER XXIV. We cannot possess from ourselves everything that we are able to possess.

It does not follow that everything we are able to possess we can also possess from ourselves. Our flesh, too, was made by God so that it could naturally live; nevertheless, it can possess life itself not from itself but from the soul.

Therefore, for life to begin to be naturally present in the flesh, it is clear that it is supplied by the soul [Note: The printed editions add “which lives”; the manuscript does not add it, nor does the sense require it]. Thus our flesh can live, but only if the soul, which is its life, is present.

**47.** In our soul and flesh, however, a considerable example of God’s grace is shown to us. Just as flesh does not possess life from itself but receives it from the soul, so a human being cannot possess faith unless he receives it as the gift of God who gives it.

Just as [variant: *etiam*, “also,” or *enim*, “for”] the soul alone is responsible for the flesh’s living, so it is also the work of grace alone that a human being believes. And just as flesh can do nothing if the soul ceases to give it life, so a human being can will nothing good if the help of grace withdraws from him.

Thus, in order that flesh may both live and act, it is supported by the life-giving presence of the soul; likewise, in order that a human being may will or do what is good, he is continually assisted by the support of life-giving grace.

There is, however, this difference: while [variant: *quantum*, perhaps “insofar as,” or *quandiu*, “as long as”] our flesh is given life by the soul, it receives the ability to act not only well but also badly. But when grace gives us life, it supplies assistance only for willing and doing what is good.

Let the human being therefore acknowledge that he can naturally believe insofar as he possesses a nature capable of belief and faith—a capacity not divinely given to irrational animals. Yet he must not suppose that he is so capable of possessing faith that he may regard the beginning of faith as arising from his own will.

A human being possesses faith when he wills; but God, who gives faith, himself changes and directs the human will. “For the Lord will give sweetness, and our earth will give its fruit” (Psalm LXXXIV, 13).

**313. CHAPTER XXV. The Gentiles who naturally do what belongs to the law are to be understood only as Christian believers.**

**48.** Concerning those whose nature is healed by a divine gift so that they naturally believe in God, and who, having been freely justified through faith, also receive the assistance of subsequent grace for doing good, the Apostle says:

“When the Gentiles who do not have the law naturally do what belongs to the law, these, though they do not have the law, are a law for themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts” (Romans II, 14).

Those who contradict grace strive to apply this passage of the Apostle to unbelieving Gentiles, on the grounds that even those who do not receive the grace of faith preserve, by a certain natural law, the things that pertain to moral decency and the bond of human society, so that they restrain those who attempt to violate them with the fairness and severity of their judgments.

In this they pay insufficient attention to the fact that the Apostle’s own statement is entirely weakened by the words he had previously spoken: “For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (ibid., 13).

The same blessed Apostle shows that no one can be justified without faith when he says: “Knowing that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we also have believed in Christ Jesus [Note: The manuscript, in accordance with the Greek text of Paul, reads “in Christ Jesus”; the printed editions read “in Christ Jesus”], so that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law. For by works of the law no flesh will be justified” (Galatians II, 16).

A little later, commending the grace of faith by which true righteousness is bestowed on each person, he says: “I do not reject the grace of God; for if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (ibid., 21).

Likewise, when he asserted that our father Abraham was justified not by works of the law but by faith, saying, “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (Galatians III, 6), in order to show that the Gentiles whom the divine word promised to Abraham’s seed would be justified by faith, he continued:

“Know, therefore, that those who are of faith, these are sons of Abraham. And Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, announced beforehand to Abraham, saying, ‘In you all the nations will be blessed.’ [Note: The printed editions read “Paul showed”; “Paul” is absent from the manuscript.] Therefore those who are of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham” (Galatians III, 7–9).

Confirming elsewhere that our father Abraham was justified not by works but by faith, he says:

“For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God. For what does Scripture say? ‘Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.’ Now to the one who works, the reward is not counted according to grace but according to debt; but to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness” (Romans IV, 2–5).

**49.** Since, then, when the Apostle speaks of those Gentiles who naturally do what belongs to the law and show the work of the law written in their hearts (Romans II, 14), he testifies that he is speaking of those who are justified; and since he recalls that our father Abraham was justified not by works but by faith, who would dare to understand in this passage the Gentiles whom it is clear were not justified by faith?

The Apostle himself testifies that “everything that is not from faith is sin” (Romans XIV, 23), and that “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews XI, 6).

If it is established that Abraham was justified by faith, and if the Apostle recalls that the Gentiles were promised to his seed, what remains except that anyone who asserts that the Gentiles can be justified not by faith but by works must deny that they belong to Abraham’s seed, to whom the Gentiles were promised?

For Abraham, as the Apostle says, is “the father of all who believe through uncircumcision” [Note: So the printed editions; the manuscript reads: “the father of all believers, so that faith might be counted as righteousness for them as well”] “so that faith might be counted as righteousness for them also” (Romans IV, 11).

Since, therefore, there is one God who justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith (Romans III, 30), and since the Apostle showed that he was speaking of those who are justified when he discussed the Gentiles who naturally do what belongs to the law and have the work of the law in their hearts, the interpretation consistent with the truth is that [variant: *quod*, “that,” or *quo*, “by which”] the Gentiles mentioned in that passage are those whom God justifies by the gift of faith.

By granting them the grace of faith, he writes the work of his law in their hearts through the justification bestowed on them. Thus, without the letter of the Old Testament, through the grace of the New Testament, renewed nature possesses the work of the law written in it, so that it may begin to belong to the people of God—not through the merit of preceding works but through the gratuitous gift of justification.

He has deigned to proclaim this to us through the prophetic mouth and heavenly teaching, with holy Jeremiah saying:

“Behold, days will come [variant: *venient*, “will come,” or *veniunt*, “are coming”], says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah” (Jeremiah XXXI, 31).

And a little later:

“For this is the covenant which I will establish with the house of Israel after these days [variant: *istos*, “these,” or *illos*, “those”], says the Lord: I will give my laws into their hearts, and I will write them upon their minds; and I will be their God, and they will be my people. And no one will teach his neighbor, nor each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for all will know me, from the least to the greatest of them, because I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more” (ibid., 33–34).

# CHAPTER XXVI. Knowledge of God is of no benefit without love. Faith can exist without charity, but it cannot be beneficial.

**50.** This knowledge, by which God is recognized in such a way that the forgiveness of sins is attributed to the gift of divine mercy, is entirely different from the knowledge of those who, although they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts.

Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of a corruptible human being (Romans I, 21–23).

Because they knew God without the grace of faith that works through love, they were made inexcusable by that very knowledge. But those who know God through receiving faith become unaccusable. “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?” (Romans VIII, 33). Certainly no one, for “for those who love God, all things work together for good” (ibid., 28).

Therefore no one accuses them, because God justifies and glorifies those whom he foreknew according to his purpose, predestined, and called. Thus, once boasting in the law of works—which causes the proud human being to exalt himself—has been excluded, the one who boasts may boast in the Lord through the law of faith, which works through love (I Corinthians I, 31).

**51.** If, then, knowledge profited nothing for salvation in the case of some who knew God but did not glorify him as God, how can those be righteous before God who preserve something of goodness in their conduct and works but do not refer it to the goal of Christian faith and love [Note: The printed editions read “could”; the manuscript reads “can”]? 

They can indeed possess certain goods pertaining to the equity of human society. But because these things are not done through faith and love of God [Note: The printed editions read “because [they are] not [done] through love”; the manuscript reads “because [they are] not [done] through faith and love of God”], they cannot be beneficial.

For it can happen that someone believes that God exists without loving God. But it is entirely impossible for someone to love God without believing that he exists:

**Everyone can believe that something exists without loving it; but no one can love what he does not believe exists.**

The Apostle says that faith without love, and other good works likewise, cannot benefit anyone. For he says:

“If I have all faith, so as to move mountains, and if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (I Corinthians XIII, 2–3).

If works performed with faith but without love cannot benefit, how will works performed without faith benefit?

Therefore blessed Paul rightly prays for the Thessalonians that God may fulfill in them every good purpose and the work of faith in power (II Thessalonians I, 11).

In the same passage in which he was speaking of the Gentiles who naturally do the law, he had already said: “But glory, honor, and peace for everyone who works good, for the Jew first and for the Greek” (Romans II, 10).

But how can the unbelieving possess glory, which is given only to the justified? “Those whom God justified, he also glorified” (Romans VIII, 30). Yet “the righteousness of God is through faith in Jesus Christ upon all who believe” (Romans III, 22).

Or what honor will be given to unbelievers, when blessed Peter teaches that it is bestowed only on believers, saying: “Therefore, honor to you who believe” (I Peter II, 7)?

Or how will there be peace for one who **has not been redeemed** by the blood of Jesus Christ, in whom God reconciled “the things that are on earth” and “the things that are in heaven” (Ephesians I, 10)? For he is our peace, who made the two one (Ephesians II, 14).

This peace cannot be possessed without the love and faith of Christ, because, “having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom also we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand and boast in the hope of the glory of the children of God” (Romans V, 1–2).

This hope [Note: The printed editions read *quos spes ideo*, etc.] does not put us to shame because “the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (ibid., 5). For we have received the spirit of adoption as children, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Romans VIII, 16).

Therefore, in order that human beings may become children of God, they receive the only-begotten Son of God through faith. By his gift they receive the authority both to believe in him and to belong to the number of God’s children [Note: The printed editions read “they receive from the Lord”; the manuscript omits “from the Lord,” and the latter reading is better, since “by his gift they receive” already makes the addition superfluous]:

“As many as received him, he gave them authority to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John I, 12).

In their hearts he gives his law, and in their minds he writes it—that is, the law of faith, which, when inspired, justifies; not the law of works, which without doubt condemns even those who observe it [Note: The manuscript reads “its makers,” rather than the printed editions’ “its observers”].

# CHAPTER XXVII. The law of works, which can naturally exist in the hearts of unbelievers, does not free them from impiety.

**52.** That law which is the law of works, which cannot justify a human being—for “by works of the law no flesh will be justified”—can indeed naturally exist both in the heart of the Gentiles and in the heart of unbelieving Jews [Note: So the manuscript. The printed editions read: “both in the heart of Gentiles and in the heart of believing Jews”]. Nevertheless, without the faith of Christ it does not justify its followers in any way, but holds them bound by the chain of impiety.

This law was certainly in Paul’s heart when he was an unbeliever, persecuting the Church of God according to his zeal and living without reproach according to the righteousness that is in the law (Romans III, 20).

But because he did not possess it from God, he therefore says:

“Whatever things were gains to me, these I have considered loss for the sake of Christ. Indeed, I consider everything to be loss because of the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord, for whose sake I have suffered the loss of everything and consider it refuse, so that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness that is from God, based on faith, for knowing him” (Philippians III, 6–10).

53. Who would not see from these apostolic words that the righteousness which is from the law is from man, whereas the righteousness which is from the faith of Christ is from God alone? The former, therefore, is the righteousness by which the ungodly is raised up so that he may fall into punishment; the latter is that by which the justified person is humbled so that he may be exalted to glory. Thus, although the Apostle conducted himself blamelessly in that righteousness which is from the law, he does not deny that he was ungodly, saying: “Why, then, while we were still weak, did Christ die for the ungodly at the appointed time?” (Rom. V, 6). He also truthfully confesses that he had been an enemy of God, saying: “For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved from wrath through his life” (ibid., 10).

What, then, would it have profited Paul to preserve that righteousness which is in the law of works [Col. 0485C], apart from fellowship with Christ, when our Savior himself says to the Jews: “Unless you know that I am he, you will die in your sins” (John VIII, 24)? Therefore, since the Apostle testifies that the righteousness which is from the faith of Christ is directed toward knowing him, it is evident that this is the law of faith which God promised he would write in the hearts of his own. The wording of the same passage clearly demonstrates this. For there God says: “And they shall not teach each one his neighbor, and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all shall know me, from the least to the greatest of them” (Jer. XXXI, 34).

54. This is the law that God writes in the hearts of all of them—not through the condition of nature, but through the generosity of grace; not through the free choice of man [Col. 0485D], but through the ministry of evangelical preaching; not on stone, by the letter of the Old Testament, but in the heart, by the Spirit of the living God. Blessed Paul clearly indicates this when he says: “You are a letter of Christ, delivered by us [Note: The manuscript reads, ‘delivered through us.’], and written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God; not on stone tablets but on tablets of fleshly hearts” (II Cor. III, 3).

This, then, is what God writes in human hearts through his Spirit: what the envy of the devil erased from them, through which death entered the world. He therefore writes the law of faith, by which God justifies the Gentiles [Col. 0486A], so that, by giving grace, he may renew nature. For he pours out love—which is the fullness of the law (Rom. XIII, 10)—through his Spirit for this purpose: that he may cause what he commands to be fulfilled. And he grants the grace of illumination through the spirit of faith for this reason: that faith may work through love what is pleasing to God.

As long as this love is not in a person, whatever remains written in him through the natural law, operating apart from the law of faith, does not save him in any way, because God justifies no one without faith, nor can it obtain salvation for the one who performs it, since “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebr. XI, 6). Let no one, therefore, attempt to assign to the natural law the law that God writes in the hearts of the Gentiles, not by creating nature, but by giving grace. For this is the law—not the law by which a person preserves the bond of human society even without faith [Col. 0486B], but the law by which, through believing, he knows and loves God; not the law by which anyone arrogantly claims for himself good works or even faith itself, but the law by which he submits and attributes both his faith and his good works to God, who mercifully works in him.

For this law so orders and directs the human heart that, when a person hears God’s commandments, he asks that what is commanded be given to him; and, when he acts in faith, he does not doubt that God’s grace continually assists him.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That God’s not making all people willing to believe belongs to his secret judgments

55. As for those who question God by saying, “Why, then, did he not make all human beings willing to believe, since with God there is no partiality?”—they should know that this belongs among those higher matters by which Holy Scripture restrains the boldness of human curiosity [Col. 0486C; Note: The manuscript reads “restrains boldness”; Basil reads “wards off boldness”; the Antwerp and Louvain editions read “exercises [it].”], saying: “Do not seek what is higher than you, and do not investigate what is too strong for you, but always think about what God has commanded you” (Sir. III, 22).

The one who was caught up to the third heaven was all the more terrified and trembled before these higher matters the more he was enlightened. Hence he never ceases to cry out: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, that he should be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory forever” (Rom. XI, 33, 34 and following).

IT IS THEREFORE ENOUGH FOR US to believe without hesitation that, among those who are saved, God’s mercy is gratuitous, and that, among those who are condemned, God’s justice is true; and, with contrite and humbled heart, to sing to the Lord of his mercy and judgment (Ps. C, 1). For he shows, even in the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, that no iniquity is pleasing; and he demonstrates in the vessels of mercy that his goodness is able to forgive all the sins of those whom he wills [Note: The manuscript reads: “and in the vessels of mercy, that the goodness of his power is able to forgive all the sins of those whom he wills.”].

## CHAPTER XXIX. They are mistaken who think that the divine will is equally disposed toward those who are saved and those who are condemned

56. As for the apostolic statement concerning God, “who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (I Tim. II, 4), those who think that this will of God must be understood equally with respect to the vessels of mercy and the vessels of wrath do not understand it as they ought. They pay insufficient attention to the exceedingly truthful statement of Scripture, which commends the omnipotence of the divine will: “Whatever he willed, he did, in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Ps. CXXXIV, 6). Scripture also says to God: “For when you will, having power is at your disposal” (Wis. XII, 18).

How, then, does he do everything he wills if, while willing that a human being be saved—whose salvation begins only from a good will—God does not begin that willing in the human person, but waits for it to arise from the human person? What an utterly wicked impiety is asserted when God’s grace is stubbornly resisted! Human beings deny that they are changed for the better by God’s work, even though they would not exist at all unless God’s goodness were at work.

Does the order of things really permit or allow us to believe [Note: The printed editions read “is permitted.”] that God, who is the creator of man, can make a human being but cannot change him; that he, who needs no helper in making a human being, cannot nevertheless work what he wills in the human will until he has first found in the human person the willing itself; and that, while a person has from God the fact that he exists, he has from himself the fact that he is better? Is it thus that the good will by which a person believes in God is produced not by divine goodness but by human perversity?

For every human being is perverse before believing in God. And because it is written, “The crooked things shall become straight” (Isa. XL, 4), a person is made straight from crookedness and is made faithful from unbelief. Therefore, if God does not grant goodness to a crooked will [Note: Basil’s text reads this way. Lovaniensis and Antwerp read, “does not grant a good will,” with “will” understood], but waits for it to become good from itself, then a crooked will can indeed produce goodness from itself. Thus, although it has from God the fact that it exists, it can have from itself alone the fact that it is good; and so the almighty and good God can work good from the evil wills of human beings when he wills, but, when he wills those wills themselves to be good, he is utterly unable to make them so.

57. For who does not know that Paul had an evil will when he persecuted the Church of God and attacked it? Yet God made good use of his wickedness when, while Saul was persecuting [Note: The manuscript reads “Saul”; the printed editions read “Paul.”], blessed Stephen was crowned with martyrdom. Could God, then, crown Stephen through the unbelief of Saul the persecutor, but be unable to convert Saul the persecutor to the faith? Did Paul first give his will to God, and did God then repay Paul, who was willing, with faith? And where is what Paul himself says: “Who has first given to him, and he shall be repaid?” (Rom. XI, 35). He certainly would not have said this if he had understood that he had given his will to God from himself and that God had repaid him with faith.

May God therefore keep this madness away from his faithful and remove it from unbelievers. For the person to whom grace is either not given when hardened, or taken away when ungrateful, is defiled by such a profane thought. God, who converts, gives life to those whom he wills to save; God changes human wills so that they begin to be good. Therefore it is written: “And I said, ‘Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High’” (Ps. LXXVI, 11).

The prophet’s meaning presents itself for recognition in plain speech. He did not fail to state that the change of the right hand of the Most High was not something that occurred after he began, but was precisely the fact that he began. Therefore, when these people, who maintain that God’s will—by which he wills all people to be saved—is equally directed toward the redeemed and the condemned [Note: This is the reading of the printed editions; the manuscript reads: “which they maintain must be understood alike in the vessels of mercy and in the vessels of wrath.”], are asked why God wills all people to be saved and yet not all are saved, what will they answer?

## CHAPTER XXX. God does not wait for a good will in man but grants it. Salvation is gratuitous for adults as for infants. The punishment of infants

58. Will they answer what your letter testifies that they say—that is, that God waits for the human will, so that there is a fitting reward for those who are willing, but a just condemnation for those who are unwilling?

But, to avoid prolixity and omit the other arguments that can be brought against this perverse opinion in defense of the truth of the faith, let them meanwhile be convicted and confounded by the testimony not of speaking adults but of silent infants. In these infants, to overthrow the wisdom of speech, the power of Christ’s cross shines forth greatly: it shows that the same salvation is brought about freely in all human beings who use their own will, while in infants, who possess no will, it graciously works salvation.

For in infants there is neither a good will, so that there could be a fitting reward for the willing, nor an evil will, so that there could be a just condemnation for the unwilling. If, then, as these people claim, God does not arouse or change human wills for the salvation of human beings but waits for them, how does he grant eternal salvation to infants who are baptized and die in infancy, when he neither waits for nor finds their good will [Col. 0488C]? Likewise, how does he condemn others who die without baptism to eternal punishments, when he finds in them no guilt of an evil will?

59. Does not their perversity compel these enemies of God’s grace—who are not defenders but deceivers of human free choice—to suppose that God is unjust in the death of all infants? For, when no goodness or wickedness of the will intervenes, they see some infants take possession of the kingdom and others assigned to unending fire.

Therefore, if matters are as they think, no infant ought to die before reaching an age at which he could possess either a good or an evil will, so that God would neither save baptized infants without a good will nor condemn the unbaptized without an evil will. For if God’s goodness does not begin to work salvation in a human being unless it has found his good will, it would be unjust either to condemn or redeem one who was incapable of willing or refusing what is good.

But there is no injustice with God (II Chron. XIX, 7), whose every way is mercy and truth (Ps. XXIV, 10).

60. Therefore, because the Catholic Church truly believes and confesses that God is just and good, we must most certainly believe and confidently confess that the one and the same grace of God works in the salvation of adults the beginning of a good will, while in infants, without a will, it works the effect of salvation.

That same grace redeems infants who are neither willing nor unwilling; by illuminating adults, it makes the willing out of those who were unwilling. In infants, this work of salvation is completed by God’s grace working without the assent of their own will; in adults it begins with a divinely given beginning of a good will, so that, through the work of grace alone, the will that was evil becomes good, and thereafter offers obedience as a co-worker to the grace working with it.

Thus God is not cruel in condemning infants to whom he does not grant the benefit of baptism, just as he is not unjust toward adults to whom he does not grant a good will [Note: The printed editions read, “when he does not grant a good will.”]. And just as their own evil will causes those adults to be punished, so the condemned origin of these infants rightly causes them to be punished. God, however, created in human beings neither the stain of a corrupted origin nor the wickedness of their own will.

Therefore, in the human beings whom he saves, God does not find a good will. Rather, according to the diversity required by their ages, he either freely makes good the will in adults which he finds evil, or, without a human will—whether good or evil—he perfects the grace of the sacrament in infants. He is the one whose good will no one can resist.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Which “all people” God wills to be saved. “All people” does not always mean the entire human race

61. Accordingly, we should understand those whom God wills to be saved in such a way that we neither think anyone can be saved except by God’s will [Note: The manuscript reads this way; the printed editions read, “unless God wills him to be saved.”], nor suppose that the will of almighty God is in any respect unfulfilled or impeded.

For all whom God wills to be saved are saved without doubt; and no one can be saved except those whom God wills to be saved; and there is no one whom God wills to save who is not saved, because “our God has done whatever he willed” (Ps. CXXXIV, 6). All those whom he wills to be saved are indeed saved, because this salvation does not arise in them from human will but is bestowed by God’s good will.

Nevertheless, in all these human beings whom God wills to save, the whole human race is not meant without qualification, but the entire number of those who are to be saved. They are called “all” because God’s goodness saves all these people from among all human beings—that is, from every nation, condition, age, language, and province.

In all these people the saying of our Redeemer is fulfilled when he says: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John XII, 32). He did not say this because he draws everyone without exception, but because no one is saved unless he himself has drawn that person. For elsewhere he says: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John VI, 37). And again elsewhere: “Everything that the Father has given me will come to me.” These, then, are all those whom God wills to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

62. It is characteristic of the divine utterances sometimes to say “all” while warning us that the entire human race must not always be understood by that word. Such is what the Lord says through the prophet Joel: “In the last days I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel II, 28). Blessed Peter showed that this was fulfilled in the one hundred and twenty people upon whom the Holy Spirit came in tongues of fire.

If, then, we think that “all flesh” here means absolutely all human beings, the divine utterance will begin—God forbid—to be judged false. But God is truthful, and “the words of the Lord are pure words” (Rom. III, 4; Ps. XI, 7). Therefore, just as God promised that he would pour out his Spirit upon all flesh, so he has done, so he does, and so he will continue to do until the end of the age. He pours out his Spirit upon all flesh, that is, upon all human beings—namely, upon all those whom he wills to be saved [Note: The printed editions read, “upon those human beings”; the manuscript reads, “upon all those human beings.”].

63. And so that we may know more fully who all these people are, let us listen to the words of the same blessed Peter. Filled with the Holy Spirit, he concluded his preaching with this exhortation: “Repent,” he said, “and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far away, whomever the Lord our God will call” (Acts II, 38–39).

He said “all,” then, but added, “whomever the Lord will call.” Blessed Paul likewise indicates that these are those who are called according to the purpose. Elsewhere he says that God “has imprisoned all in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all” (Rom. XI, 32).

Yet God does not have mercy in the same way on all those whom he has imprisoned in unbelief, so as mercifully to give the grace of faith to all unbelievers; although the merciful God does not grant that same grace of faith to unbelievers [Note: The words “although the merciful God does not grant that same grace of faith to unbelievers” are absent from the manuscript and occur in the printed editions.], but beyond doubt to those of whom he says to Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I show mercy” (Exod. XXXIII, 19).

Thus he displays the grace of a voluntary gift, just as the Lord deigned to say to his disciples: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given” (Matt. XIII, 11). He also says: “Let the one who is able to receive this receive it” (Matt. XIX, 13). But, to teach that this capacity itself is granted by divine generosity, he says elsewhere: “Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it has been given” (ibid., 11).

64. These, then, are all those on whom God has mercy, because they are preceded by his mercy so that they may believe and be saved freely through faith. Their belief does not take its beginning from human will; rather, faith is given to the will itself through the free generosity of the merciful God.

Blessed Paul placed this distinction among all people—which faithful understanding must preserve without exception—in one passage of his Epistle in such a way that, while speaking of all human beings without qualification, he immediately made it clear that certain people were meant as “all human beings” in distinction from others.

For he says: “Just as through one trespass there was condemnation for all people, so through one act of righteousness there is justification of life for all people” (Rom. V, 18). Since the Apostle says “for all people” with respect to condemnation and “for all people” with respect to justification [Col. 0491A], are we therefore to believe absolutely that all human beings—who are clearly condemned originally through Adam’s sin—are all at once justified through Christ? Countless deaths of unbelievers stand against this: they depart this life without the grace of justification and are swept away, without the sacrament of baptism, to the seat of death and eternal punishments.

It remains, therefore, that we should not understand that absolutely all whom the Apostle places under condemnation pass into the grace of justification, but rather that some among all those people are all these others [Note: The manuscript reads this way. The printed editions read: “some among all those people. Therefore, all these people…”].

Thus all are children of wrath through Adam, and from among them some are all children of grace through Christ. Those are “all” whom the sinful offspring condemns through carnal generation by means of the first human being. For all are earthly who bear the image of the earthly human being, and all are heavenly who receive the image of the heavenly human being for eternal life.

Again the prophet says: “All the nations that you have made will come and worship before you, Lord, and they will glorify your name” [Note: The printed editions omit “Lord” and add “forever.” The manuscript adds “Lord” and does not have “forever.”] (Ps. LXXXV, 9). The Lord also says to his faithful: “You will be hated by all nations for my name’s sake” (Matt. X, 22).

Does divine Scripture, then, contradict itself with opposing statements? Certainly not. It truthfully speaks both of “all” those people and of “all” these people: that is, of all the faithful who glorify the Lord’s name among all nations, and of all the unbelievers who persist throughout all those nations in a deadly ungodliness hostile to the name of Christ and to his faithful.

[Col. 0491C] 65. Something similar occurs in the Epistle that the blessed Apostle writes to the Colossians, where he says: “For in Christ all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones or Dominions or Principalities or Powers. All things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him” (Col. I, 16–17).

A little later he says: “For in him all fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself [Note: The manuscript reads “in himself.” The printed editions read “to himself,” in accordance with the Greek εἰς αὐτόν], making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things on earth or the things in heaven” (ibid., 19–20).

Are we to believe that all things in heaven and on earth are reconciled through him [Note: The manuscript reads this way. The printed editions read: “Are we to believe that the devil and his angels are reconciled?”]? Certainly not. For whoever wishes to think this way will fall into the twofold snare of a double impiety: either he will deny that the devil and his angels were created through Christ, or he will affirm that they are to be reconciled through the blood of his cross.

Nevertheless, whoever is entangled in the perversity of either of these opinions should beware lest he be condemned, together with the devil himself and his angels, to the punishment of eternal burning. For a person is guilty of one and the same impiety if he believes either that the devil was not created by Christ or that he will someday be restored to Christ’s reconciliation.

Since, certainly, if Christ the Lord had not created him, his damnable departure from Christ would not have occurred; and if Christ were someday going to save him, Christ would not have pronounced his eternal burning with his own mouth.

All things, therefore, were created through Christ and in Christ, because there is nothing that the Father created except through the Son and in the Son. And all things are reconciled through him and in him, because no human being obtains the benefit of reconciliation without the cross of Christ [Note: The manuscript reads, “without faith in the cross of Christ.”].

66. From this rule, therefore, which is shown to be inserted in the heavenly oracles, let us understand those whom God wills to be saved in such a way that we know that all who are saved are saved only from his gratuitous goodness [Note: The manuscript reads, “will.”].

For the salvation of any person is preceded by no good merits of human will; only God’s will is the cause of human salvation. “For wrath is in his indignation, and life in his will” (Ps. XXIX, 6). His wrath, therefore, is the merit of our iniquity, whereas our life is the gift of his will.

For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to those whom he wills (John V, 21); and he wills those same people to be given life whom he wills to be saved. Thus he saves those whom he wills, just as he gives life to those whom he wills. For he who, according to the testimony of Scripture, “has done whatever he willed” (Ps. CXIII, 11), willed nothing without doing it.

Accordingly, we do not improperly say that God may refuse something he is able to do. But it is impious if anyone says that the almighty God is unable to do something he wills: “For who resists his will?” [Note: Some editions read, “Who will resist his will?”] (Rom. IX, 19). No one, certainly, because there is no nature that is alien to his creation.

And just as nothing exists naturally that he did not make, so nothing occurs for the salvation of human beings that he did not predestine in the eternal disposition of his good will to be done. From him faith is freely infused, by which we may walk well; and perseverance is granted, by which we may attain the vision.

God always held these gifts disposed in his eternal and unchangeable will. In that will he preordained and prepared both what he would give and to whom he would give it. For by predestining he prepared the gift of grace; by giving grace, he brings the effect of predestination to completion.

## EPILOGUE

67. You have, dearly beloved brothers, a brief statement of our faith and confession concerning both the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ and grace. It most certainly contains this: that the only-begotten God was naturally born from God the Father without beginning, and that he was naturally brought forth from a virgin according to the flesh.

For one and the same is God the Word: in the first birth, the eternity of the Father begot him coeternal with itself; in the second birth, the virginal womb brought him forth in time as the Son of man.

By his grace the beginning of a good will is given to us for faith, and assistance is granted to that will itself, so that what it wills well it may perform well. For God, who created man, by his predestination prepared the gift of illumination for believing, the gift of perseverance for advancing and remaining steadfast, and the gift of glorification for reigning, to give them to those to whom he willed. He brings his work to completion in no other way than he has disposed it in his eternal and unchangeable will.

The Apostle testifies that we were predestined in Christ before the foundation of the world (Eph. I, 4). If anyone refuses to receive the truth of this predestination with the faith of his heart or to profess it with his mouth, and if, before the final day of his present life, he does not cast away the obstinacy of his impiety by which he rebels against the living and true God, it is evident that he does not belong to the number of those whom God freely chose and predestined in Christ before the foundation of the world for the kingdom.

Nevertheless, the prayer of the faithful must not cease for such people, nor must charity ever grow cold, so that God may grant them the grace of his illumination. Through this grace the seed of the divine word may bear fruit in them, for the word sounds in vain in outward ears unless God, by a spiritual gift, opens the hearing of the inner person.

## EPISTLE XVIII

Fulgentius to Count Reginus, answering the question previously proposed by him: whether Christ’s flesh was corruptible or incorruptible. Since death intervened before Fulgentius could answer the second question, Ferrandus answered it in a letter to the same man concerning the Seven Rules of Innocence [Note: See Ferrandus, among the works of Fulgentius, edited by Chifletius in 1649.]

## CHAPTER I

Having received your letter, dearest son Reginus, and recognizing the anxiety of your heart, I praised the Lord, who is able both to confer a good gift so that it may be preserved and to preserve what has been bestowed. Both things belong to the healing of our souls, so that we may rejoice in the benefits which the ineffable goodness of our physician never ceases to work for us in our weakness, so that by spiritual progress health may increase in us and weakness diminish.

The character of our weakness consists in a twofold condition: either we know something insufficiently in the faith through ignorance, or we possess in our works something that does not accord with the rule of truth. Since “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. IX, 15), both forms of weakness therefore trouble us. But we hope that he who made us, and commanded us to rejoice because he conquered the world (John XVI, 33), will perfect us in the faith that works through love.

[Col. 0493D] 2. You say, then, that a new inquiry has recently arisen in the regions of the East, with some asserting that Christ’s body was incorruptible from the very beginning of his conception, while others confess the contrary: that it was corruptible before the Passion but incorruptible after the resurrection. You, however, are greatly hesitant between the two positions and do not know how to answer; therefore you press me to explain what we ought to hold. These are the matters about which you ask.

Earlier, as a sign of your gratitude, you indicate that my letter has refreshed you. Since, then, your question has followed the path of a right heart, by which it first grasps what pertains to faith and then what pertains to works—because the Apostle commends faith that works through love, with that purpose of our salvation in view, namely, that faith without works is dead in itself (James II, 26)—,

## CHAPTER II

3. I wish you to know, dearest son, that corruption is spoken of in not one way but two, just as we speak similarly of weakness and death. For the Lord says that death is the perpetration of a crime, and also death in which the retribution of punishment is understood. Human weakness is likewise spoken of: that of the person who renders service to sin, and that of the person who bears the punishment of sin. Both belong to the weakness of the sinner: delight in sins and affliction because of sins.

So too we speak of corruption in two ways, one part of which is found in the guilt of man alone, while the other is found in punishment. That part of corruption pertains to guilt which the Apostle points out when he says: “People corrupted in mind, disqualified regarding the faith” (II Tim. III, 8). To this part of corruption also belongs what he says elsewhere: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. XV, 33). This part of corruption first seizes the soul and, through the soul, drags the flesh into sin. This part of corruption first invaded the mind of the proud angel, then the first man, and afterward the whole human race.

4. The first part of corruption, therefore, which consists in the desire for or perpetration of sin, was followed by that part which consists in the retribution of punishment, which holds both the soul and body of the sinful person. Even in that retribution there are some things in which the punishment of sin is also the sin itself, while others contain only the punishment of sin.

In those things, then, in which punishment and guilt are found together, the guilt is increased by the act through which the guilty person is punished, when God abandons him and the person continues to sin. This is the part of corruption by which sins are punished in a person in such a way that they do not cease but increase: such is the lust of heart and body, which, although it arises as the punishment of sin, multiplies sin and captivates the soul subjected to punishment through harmful delight.

The Apostle also calls the third punishment, which is repaid for this second one: “For this reason God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting” (Rom. I, 28). They are therefore handed over to a reprobate mind not merely to suffer, but to do what causes sins to multiply. Nevertheless, this handing over consists not in God’s activity but in his abandonment.

For God hands some people over but does not abandon them; others he abandons in the very act of handing them over. He hands over the good in paternal kindness, so that he does not abandon them without paternal assistance. Thus he hands them over to suffer evils by which they may be perfected, not to do evils by which they may become worse.

But the Lord hands over and abandons the wicked for this purpose: that, while he abandons them, they may follow not God’s will but their own, take pleasure in their disgrace, and bear their punishment not unwillingly but as people enticed into following it.

## CHAPTER III

5. This is the corruption of the wicked, which is both the punishment of sin and itself sin. Another part of corruption neither stains the soul nor the body of a faithful person, but afflicts it, because it serves not to defile a person but to humble the sinner.

With this distinction retained—while we distinguish voluntary corruption from penal corruption, and find that one part of penal corruption exists in human beings together with sin and another without sin—such corruption of the heart is nothing other than the deprivation of health, since no iniquity is contracted from this corruption, although weakness is present. We readily discover what part of corruption Christ assumed in his body. Although he assumed flesh for us, he nevertheless received flesh free from every original and actual sin. Yet he is known to have received that same flesh not only as weak but also truly as mortal. To the extent that the mortality he assumed was present in his body, to that extent the weakness of corruption could be present in him: namely, that corruption which is absent from all sin.

6. Hunger and thirst belong to this kind of corruption. For a mortal body is easily corrupted through hunger and thirst, since through these conditions it also reaches the very end of death. Through death one arrives at corruption, when, after the soul has departed, the body becomes so corrupted that it is reduced to decay and dust.

Christ’s flesh did not see this corruption, for it rose again on the third day. Nevertheless, he truly experienced hunger, thirst, bodily weariness, and pain. All these belong to that part of penal corruption which we draw from the punishment of sin in such a way that we do not thereby contract any punishment of sin.

The Gospel teaches that Christ hungered, thirsted, and experienced weariness (Mark XI, 13). It is clear that he hungered when he came to the fig tree and found no fruit on it. Weary from his journey, he also sat by the well (John IV, 6). On the cross he said, “I thirst” (John XIX, 28). He also endured pain, as Isaiah says: “He was wounded for our iniquities; he was weakened for our crimes” (Isa. LIII, 5).

The Apostle teaches that this weakness in the Lord was not imaginary but real: “For although he was crucified from weakness,” he says, “yet he lives by the power of God” (II Cor. XIII, 4). By “weakness” he means nothing other than corruptibility.

[Col. 0495D] CHAPTER IV.—7. It remains, therefore, for us to learn from Sacred Scripture both that Christ was in a certain corruption to which he did not return, and that he was not in that corruption which he did not see. The corruption of the animal body includes death, which precedes putrefaction, and putrefaction, which follows death. Accordingly, Christ’s body, which truly died and was raised on the third day without any putrefaction, must be said to have seen one part of corruption and not to have seen the other. For it was in the corruption of death, but not in the corruption of putrefaction, since Christ’s flesh died in such a way that no putrefaction or dissolution of its members followed. Christ, therefore, will not return to corruption, because, having risen from the dead, he dies no more, and death will no longer have dominion over him [Col. 0496A] (Rom. 6:9). Christ, therefore, did not see corruption, because his flesh experienced no putrefaction. This was caused not by the incorruptibility of that flesh, but by the swiftness of the resurrection.

In all these matters, in which Saint Augustine demonstrates in apostolic words the absolutely certain character of our sowing and resurrection, he says:

“It is therefore established, and in no way should it be doubted, that Christ’s body, although it did not experience the corruption of putrefaction in the tomb—for it is written, ‘You will not allow your holy one to see corruption’ (Ps. 15:10)—could nevertheless be corrupted by nails and a spear, but now persists wholly in incorruption; and that what was sown in the dishonor of passion and death is now in the glory of eternal life; and that what could be crucified through weakness now reigns in power; and that what was an animal body, because it was taken from Adam, is now spiritual, because it has now been inseparably joined to the Spirit” (Letter to Consentius, formerly 146, now 205).

8. In these words Augustine shows what Christ’s body is like after the resurrection and what it was like before the passion. He plainly confirms that Christ’s body now persists wholly in incorruption, is now in the glory of eternal life, now reigns in power, and is now spiritual. But a body is not wholly incorruptible if it can feel pain through wounds. Hence it is evident that before the passion—indeed, until the passion and death—Christ had a mortal and animal body; and that in this same body he truly experienced hunger, thirst, and weariness for our sake, and truly received the wounds of nails and the spear [Col. 0496C]; and that from this he experienced true pain, not by necessity but by his will, and by accepting true death he laid down his soul for us by his own authority.

It follows that the same Christ, who died through weakness but was raised through the power of God, is found to have provided an example for our bodies. For Christ humbled himself even to the assumption of our entire weakness, so that, as the Apostle says, “the body of our humility may be conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:21).

9. From this, therefore, it most clearly appears what every Christian ought to hold with firm faith concerning the condition of an animal and mortal body: it is impossible to deny that there is corruptibility wherever the mortality of an animal body is found. Christ, therefore, bore our corruption in the flesh alone, in which he truly also bore our death. In his soul, however, he preserved perfect incorruptibility, just as he neither derived sin through descent nor contracted it through contagion. Thus Christ bore the weaknesses of our souls—which he carried in his rational soul—without any corruption. For no defect of strength could exist where the perfection of love remained steadfast through the assumption of weakness: that love which caused the Only-Begotten God to approach death for us and, despising the shame, to endure the disgrace of the cross.

10. For this reason, whatever sadness, grief, or weaknesses of our souls Christ possessed, he possessed truly but voluntarily. Truly, so that he might manifest in himself the affection of a rational soul; voluntarily, so that he might show that the help of his power would be present to our weaknesses; so that we might recognize that, with his assistance, we are to be supported in the weaknesses that we suffer by necessity. He therefore accepted our weaknesses voluntarily, so that in this life he might bring help to those troubled by the necessity of weakness, and after this life mercifully remove from us every necessity of weakness.

Thus every believer, recognizing Christ as a sharer in human weakness, would most certainly hope to be a sharer in divine power, and would not doubt that he is to be strengthened by the power of him whom he had learned to have been troubled on his behalf not by necessity but by choice. In him he would possess eternal joy, in whom he saw sadness present by choice; for just as he remained tranquil in tribulation and secure in death, so he was strongest in weakness and highest in humility.

[Col. 0497A]

SAINT FULGENTIUS TO FELIX THE NOTARY, ONE BOOK ON THE TRINITY. (C)

328 CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0497B]

Since you, dearest son Felix, repeatedly ask me, inflamed by the warmth of faith, how you ought to believe concerning the holy Trinity, which is God, and how, with the Lord’s help, you can defend the catholic and orthodox faith against the errors of heretics—especially those whose fellowship you enjoy—and thereby avoid their snares, I have considered it necessary and useful to respond to your requests.

Would that the immutable Trinity itself, in whose hand both we and our words are, grant me the ability to proclaim it, right speech, and sincere faith as suitably and appropriately as I desire, so that I may fully satisfy your holy desire, aflame with eagerness to learn.

Believe, then, that we wish to make known to your most sincere mind that faith through which the patriarchs and prophets were justified, through which the apostles were justified and the martyrs crowned, and which the holy Church throughout the whole world has maintained to this day. Its splendor, illuminating the minds of believers, makes them participants in eternal life. Until now this faith has been preached through the succession of bishops in the chair of the Apostle Peter at Rome and Antioch, in the chair of Mark the Evangelist at Alexandria, in the chair of John the Evangelist at Ephesus, and in the chair of James at Jerusalem.

Compel, then, the Arians, Donatists, Nestorians, Eutychians, Manichaeans, and the remaining plagues of heresies to share communion with these Churches over which the apostles presided. They do not agree, because, divided from the unity of the Church by the perversity of their faith, they wished to remain a party apart. Hence also the Apostle John says: “They went out from us; [Col. 0497D] but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

They went out from us, certainly, because with utterly deranged hearts they separated themselves from the unity of the Church. They were not of us—that is, they were not among the predestined and chosen for eternal life. For they were not among those of whom the Lord says: “I have chosen you and appointed you to go and bear much fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15:16).

Nor are they blessed in the seed of Abraham, according to what the Lord said to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 26:4). The Apostle adds: “Not in seeds, as though in many, but in your seed, which is Christ” (Gal. 3:16). Since all nations deserve to be blessed in Christ and through Christ in the unity of faith, heretics are not blessed, because they do not possess the unity of faith. Rather, fattened on the fodder of error, they have become through pride not children of God but children of the devil.
