Therefore, having the eyes of their hearts darkened, they cannot see the whole world redeemed by Christ’s blood and united in the faith, according to what is declared concerning the primitive Church: “They had,” he says, “one heart and one soul toward God” (Acts 4:32). Thus the whole world is redeemed; thus the whole world among all nations is now called redeemed.

“And the nations shall fear your name, O Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory” (Ps. 101:16). And again: “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord” (Ps. 85:9). And again: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight. For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations” (Ps. 21:28–29).

What will the wretched people say who, cut off from the Church of God, contradict the Church itself with an impenitent heart? While they attempt to tear apart the same Church, which is the Lord’s seamless tunic, they themselves are more readily torn apart. Let them be questioned one by one.

One says that he has been redeemed by Christ’s blood. Was Christ’s blood therefore poured out only for the Arians, or only for the Donatists? Far be it. Truth does not speak in this way. God did not say to Abraham: “In your seed one nation shall be blessed,” but: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 26:4). Not one nation, but every nation. Not this one and that one, but all of them. Nor in different faiths, but in one faith, as the Apostle says: “One faith” (Eph. 4:5).

Believers are saved in this one faith; through the unity of faith the catholic Church has one heart and one soul toward God. This right faith, which makes the diverse hearts of believers one, is praised by the mouth of the Apostle Paul. “I give thanks,” he says, “to God, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Rom. 1:8). The one faith that is proclaimed throughout the whole world is the faith that must be praised and preached.

CHAPTER II.

Receive the faith in which long ago you were reborn, believing in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. The Father is not the Son; the Son is not the Father; the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son. And although there are three, what, I ask, is the one name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in which we ought to be baptized, except the name of the Godhead, which cannot be multiplied?

For although we say “God the Father,” “God the Son,” and “God the Holy Spirit,” nevertheless we do not say “three gods,” because it is written: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one” (Deut. 6:4). God is therefore one in nature, not in person, because the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another.

The Father is begotten by no one; the Son is begotten by the Father; the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Father exists not for himself but for the Son; the Son exists not for himself but for the Father; the Spirit belongs to one who breathes forth: therefore he is referred to the Father and the Son.

These relative names, then, constitute the Trinity; the essential names, however, are in no way multiplied. God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit. Good the Father, good the Son, good the Holy Spirit. Pious the Father, pious the Son, pious the Holy Spirit. Just the Father, just the Son, and just the Holy Spirit. Almighty the Father, almighty the Son, and almighty the Holy Spirit.

Yet we do not say either three gods, or three good beings, or three pious beings, or three just beings, or three almighty beings, but one God—good, pious, just, almighty—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in whom there is one nature, essence, or substance. For whatever one says of these names in that holy and supreme Trinity signifies one and the same thing.

The essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is not different. If it were, the Son would not truly be begotten by the Father, nor would the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father and the Son. But because the Son is true—that is, begotten from the essence of the Father—the Holy Spirit is also true, proceeding from the Father and the Son.

If the Son or the Holy Spirit were of another kind than the Father, the Son would not truly belong to the Father, since a different essence would make him foreign; similarly, the Holy Spirit would not proceed from the Father and the Son. It is madness to say this, because Sacred Scripture faithfully makes known both that the Son is begotten by the Father and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father.

CHAPTER III.

There are therefore three things that are co-eternal, consubstantial, and co-essential. But when the Fathers were asked, “What three?” they did not dare to say essences, substances, or natures, lest some difference among essences, natures, or substances perhaps be understood. Rather, they said “three persons, one essence,” so that the one essence would declare one God, while the three persons would manifest the holy Trinity.

Nor do we say that only God is Trinity, and not each individual person. For the Father alone is God, the Son alone is God, and the Holy Spirit alone is God. I say “alone” because the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Father, and the Holy Spirit is not the Father or the Son.

Nevertheless, the inseparable, immutable, infinite Trinity does not admit three gods, just as it does not admit three essences, substances, or natures. Therefore the Son must in no way be said to be, in that in which he is equal to the Father, created from something or constituted from nothing. For what the Father is, he begot: God, God; light, light; the immutable, the immutable; the infinite, the infinite; the eternal, the co-eternal.

We likewise believe concerning the Holy Spirit that he is what the one from whom he proceeds is. Let us next see whether we can support what we have said with testimonies from Sacred Scripture.

First, it must also be asked whether God is Trinity. “Let us make man,” he says, “in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). And again: “Come, let us go down and there confuse their language” (Gen. 11:7). The words “our” and “let us go down” indicate a plurality of persons, not of gods.

Similarly, there is Abraham’s vision of three men and his entreaty addressed to one Lord. And: “The Lord rained sulfur and fire from the Lord upon Sodom and Gomorrah, sulfur and fire from the Lord” (Gen. 19:24). And: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand’” (Ps. 109:1). And: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32:6). What else do these passages show but the Trinity?

And the Lord himself states it still more openly in the Gospel: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). And again: “A voice came from heaven, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son; hear him’” (Matt. 17:5). Likewise he says: “I saw the Spirit of God descending and remaining upon him like a dove” (John 1:32).

CHAPTER IV.

Here, in brief, you have that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another: one and another in person, not one thing and another in nature. Therefore he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). “One” teaches us to refer the statement to nature; “are” to the persons.

Likewise: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit; and these three are one” (1 John 5:7). Let Sabellius hear “are,” let him hear “three,” and let him believe that there are three persons. Let him not blaspheme with sacrilegious heart by saying that the Father is himself the Son and himself the Holy Spirit—as though he somehow begot himself or somehow proceeded from himself—when such a thing cannot even be found among created natures, namely, that anything can beget itself.

Let Arius also hear “one,” and let him not say that the Son is of a different nature, since things of different nature cannot be called one. The Son therefore cries out: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

The Apostle says of him: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Phil. 2:6). And in the Gospel it says: “For this reason the Jews sought to kill Jesus, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18).

And Arius contradicts this with blasphemous spirit: “They are not one; they are not equal,” because the Son himself says of himself: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), and frequently bears witness that he was sent by the Father.

O unhappy error and deadly doctrine, ignorant of the dispensation of the manhood temporally made for the salvation of the human race! In what respect, I ask, is the Father greater than the Son? In substance, in power, in goodness, in incorporeality, or in eternity?

If the Only-Begotten God of the unbegotten God the Father is an image, then the truth of a perfect and complete substance is in him, through which he is made to be the image of truth. The Father is powerful; but if the Son is weak, he is no longer the image of the powerful one. The Father is good; but if the Son’s divinity is of a different kind, the nature of evil will not reproduce the image of the good. The Father is incorporeal; but if the Son, according to the spirit, is bounded by a body, then the bodily Son is no longer the form of the incorporeal one.

The Father is eternal; but if the Son is not co-eternal, the name of fatherhood came to the Father temporally, and it is no longer true that all things were made through the Word, since a time is found to have existed before the Word, when the Father was without the Son. But Scripture clearly declares that the Word is the image of God the Father and that all things were made through him.

Or does Arius perhaps extend the meaning of his impious profession to the point of believing that the Holy Spirit is good, but the Son better, and the Father best? Or does he sacrilegiously assert that the Holy Spirit is powerful, the Son more powerful, and the Father most powerful? Or does he blasphemously teach that the Holy Spirit is just, the Son more just, and the Father most just?

If so, he is not held within the profession of one God, but is handed over, after the manner of the pagans, to the worship of many gods, while he rashly imagines God the Father to be greater, the Son lesser, and the Holy Spirit more than lesser. Let the error of those who refuse to be Israel have a greater God and a lesser God; let them not, with stopped ears, hear: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4); and: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (ibid., 6:13).

CHAPTER V.

But lest, with their hearts blinded, they refuse to believe that the Son or the Holy Spirit is God, and, like blaspheming Jews, deny that he is God, let them be convicted by testimonies from the Sacred Scriptures.

“Their fathers,” says the Apostle, “and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5). And again the Apostle John says: “That we may be in his true Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20).

Concerning the Holy Spirit, John the Evangelist says: “The Spirit is God” (John 4:24). And when the Apostle called the Holy Spirit the inhabitant of the Church, he says: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit? Glorify and bear the Lord in your body” (1 Cor. 6:19–20).

And in the Acts of the Apostles Peter says: “Ananias, why has Satan tempted your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts 5:3). Shortly afterward he adds: “You have not lied to men but to God” (ibid., 5:4).

Here, then, you have the Son as God and the Holy Spirit as God. It is unnecessary to prove that the Father is God, since even the one who believes in him without ambiguity believes this. But nearly all Sacred Scripture resounds with testimony concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit; for the sake of brevity, however, we have selected only a few passages.

We believe that the Son is lesser or sent according to what the Apostle also says: “God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4:4). “Made from a woman” means born from the Virgin Mary, because he who was born from the Father without beginning received a definite beginning in time by being born from his mother.

Although he was in the form of God, says the Apostle, he “did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man; he humbled himself even to death, and death on a cross” (Phil. 2:6–8).

When he says, “Although he was in the form of God,” he means that he was God in substance. He did not seize divinity, which he naturally possessed with the Father; but “he emptied himself”—that is, he did not appear to the human race in what he is as God and as equal to the Father. Rather, having assumed a human being, without the Godhead being consumed, he appeared in this world in the unity of person, endured sufferings, and underwent human affections, as was fitting and as he willed, without sin.

According to this human form he is not equal to the Father, as he himself says: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). According to that form in which he is equal to the Father, he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

According to the human form, “he came into the world to save sinners” (1 Tim. 1:15); according to the divine form, “he was in the world, and the world was made through him” (John 1:10).

Therefore we ought to believe that there are two substances, or natures, or forms—whichever of these terms one uses, the meaning is the same—in the one Son of God: one truly of God and the other of man. Thus one Son of God is believed to be true God and true man.

We must not, like Nestorius, introduce a fourth person by introducing the man born from the Virgin Mary, and so fall away from the Trinity. Nor, like Eutyches, must we refuse to believe in a true man and believe that the Son of God exists without the assumption of a human being—that is, as a single substance. Nor must we suppose that one substance could have been made from two substances.

For, as we have said, the Son of God assumed the whole man in the unity of his person: that is, a rational soul and flesh, according to what was said through the Prophet: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called [or, alternatively, ‘you shall call his name’] Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14), which is interpreted as “God with us” (Matt. 1:23).

Therefore the one born from Mary is man and God; he is man and God who grew in age; he is man and God who was fastened to the cross, who also rose again and ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. And although, because of the unity of person, God is man and man is God, nevertheless, according to his humanity, God is said to have been crucified, God is said to have suffered, and God is said to have died. For according to what he is as God, he is rightly believed to be impassible and immortal.

CHAPTER VI.

Therefore both natures remain in Christ, preserving their truth, so that neither is the human nature transferred into the divine and ceases to be human, nor is the divine transferred into the human and ceases to be God.

Thus one is begotten and the other created; one is without time and the other temporal; one is without beginning and the other has a beginning. And although the begotten and timeless nature belongs to the Father and the Holy Spirit, the temporal and created nature does not belong to them in any way. For truly, whatever belongs to the Father’s nature he gave to the Son by begetting him; but whatever of nature came to the Son in time or from outside does not extend to the Father or the Holy Spirit.

And although the whole Trinity is one substance, Christ as man belongs not to the whole Trinity, but only to the Son. For it is not permissible to believe that the Father or the Holy Spirit assumed a human being, or that they suffered according to humanity.

Although the Holy Spirit is nowhere found in Scripture to be lesser, he is nevertheless very clearly found to be sent. For this reason the heretics bind their own necks, and, with the spirit of their understanding constricted—or rather suffocated, they do not acknowledge the Holy Spirit as their creator, while defining him to be a creature.

If he were a creature, he could certainly not be the creator, because a creature does not form a creature out of nothing. And since in Genesis God says that man was formed according to his image (Gen. 1:27), while Job reports that he was fashioned by the Holy Spirit—“The divine Spirit,” he says, “who made me” (Job 33:4)—it is plainly clear that the Holy Spirit is a co-worker with the Father and the Son both in the formation of man and likewise in the establishment of the angels, according to the Psalmist: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32:6).

If he is God, if he is creator, if he consecrates baptism, why is he called sent? He is called sent because he came upon Christ in the form of a dove in the river and came upon the apostles in fire. The appearance itself is the mission. For where is one sent who is everywhere?

“The Spirit of the Lord,” it says, “has filled the world” (Wis. 1:7). And again: “Lord, where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings toward the direct path and dwell at the farthest part of the sea, even there [alternatively, ‘there also’] your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Ps. 138:7–10).

Nothing in the world has been left out where the presence of the whole Trinity is not shown to exist. Just as we believe that the Son was sent according to the human being, so the Holy Spirit was sent because of the dove or the fire.

But the Son so joined the human being he assumed to his own person for the sake of humanity that he will always possess it, never cease to possess it, and never come to an end. The Holy Spirit, however, assumed the dove or fire in such a way that those appearances, having been made in time, afterward ceased to exist.

CHAPTER VII.

Here you have why the Holy Spirit is said to have been sent. But what we have said is sufficient for strengthening your faith: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God.

He is certainly not a created nature—not earth, nor water, nor air, nor fire. For the bodies of animals are compounded from these elements [Col. 0504A]. He is certainly not an irrational spirit, such as exists in cattle, nor a rational spirit, such as exists in human beings or angels. Rather, he is the immutable God who is Trinity, creating all things through his goodness and created by no one.

Who, then, can perceive as is fitting—and as befits that uncreated form from which all things were formed—what it is, let alone express it in words, except insofar as the Trinity is believed and called God?

This uncreated Trinity has impressed upon its creature whatever traces of the Trinity it possesses. For it is written that he ordered all things “by number, measure, and weight” (Wis. 11:21). Every body, whether small or great, has a number according to the quantity of its parts, and has measure and weight. Nor could there be number without weight, or measure without weight and number. Wherever one of these is found, it cannot exist without the other two.

But in bodily things weight, number, and measure are easily demonstrated. Let us see how they can be found in incorporeal things. In the human soul there are memory, understanding, and will. You think what you will, and what you think is also contained in your memory. Your will is your love, for you remember what you bring into your thought by loving it.

There are three things—memory, understanding, and will, which we have said is love—and they are inseparable and one; one cannot exist without the other. One of the Fathers also elegantly said that these three exist in the soul when he prayed to God: “May I remember you, understand you, and love you.” In these he taught that the image of God exists.

The human soul is the image of God: not begotten, but created; not equal, but similar.

CHAPTER VIII.

I have briefly explained this to your affection in order to show that even in created things there are certain signs of that supreme Trinity, so that the magnitude of the heretics’ error may be evident: although both trinity and unity exist in created things, they refuse to believe that the Trinity which is God exists in the unity of nature.

By the power of this eternal and immutable Trinity all things were created. Yet we find that the rational nature of the angels, blessed by the gift of its God and made blessed through free will, though not continually cleaving to him, arose as the most excellent and first among creatures.

Of these angels, a certain portion, unwilling to do the will of its creator, was cast down from his contemplation and is kept for judgment, to be punished, as the Apostle Peter says: “God did not spare the angels who sinned, but dragged them down with chains into hell and handed them over to Tartarus, to be kept for judgment and punishment” (2 Pet. 2:4).

They will rightly be punished forever with the penalty of eternal fire, because, if they had wished to persevere in their blessedness, free will would certainly have assisted them. Through that will they turned toward themselves rather than toward God; made dark through pride and thrust down into the lowest regions of this air, they are kept for judgment and punishment. No trace of good will remained in them.

But those who, through the same free will, preserved what they had been made, continually cleaving to God their creator, became happier through the grace of God by which they stood. Their will has thus been made incapable both of willing to sin and of being able to sin. Although they were made changeable by nature, they have been made unchangeable by grace. Stable and certain that their blessedness will never be lost, they enjoy God, by whose contemplation they are blessed.

CHAPTER IX.

Great and learned men assert plainly that angels are composed of two substances: an incorporeal spirit, through which they never depart from the contemplation of God, and a body, through which they appear to human beings in time. They support this from the passage of the Psalm where it says: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 103:4).

They therefore say that angels have an ethereal—that is, fiery—body, while evil angels, that is, demons, have an aerial body.

After the fall of the wicked and the stability of the good, it pleased almighty God to create another rational creature, adorned with free will, through which the number of the angels who had fallen from heaven and perished might be restored.

I speak of the first human beings, constituted according to the soul from nothing and according to the body from clay: according to the soul, rational and immortal; according to the body, however, immortal if they had not sinned, but mortal if they had sinned—such that it could die. The Apostle says: “The body indeed is dead because of sin” (Rom. 8:10), because death was inflicted upon the body as the penalty of sin.

Apart from the death of the spirit, which consists in being abandoned by God, man also received death in the flesh. For just as the life of the soul is to live blessedly—that is, to enjoy God—so to die is for the body to be abandoned by the soul. He would not have experienced the unequal penalty of these deaths if he had not sinned.

Thus man was made upright and fashioned and formed according to the reason and understanding of the image of his God. He received a law, by not transgressing which he would be blessed, since he possessed free will and could be good if he wished—not indeed without the grace of God, by which his will itself was governed so that he might will; yet it was in his power to abandon that grace whenever he wished.

Because he willed and sinned, he would also justly have been condemned eternally, and his entire offspring would have been punished forever with the transgressing angels, unless grace had come through Jesus Christ our Lord.

For his death liberated the human race from the power of the devil, to whom, by a certain justice of God, it had been handed over for possession, and he ruled over them as over “children of disobedience,” as the Apostle says (Eph. 5:6). Therefore the death of Christ, which he assumed without sin, grants life to the sinner.

The Only-Begotten of God assumed a human being, and the Word became flesh, so that he might perform the office of mediator between God and human beings. Since we could not return to God through free will, we might return through God made man. Through this mediator, gratuitously slain by the devil, the devil himself, the author of death, lost those whom the same mediator, by a hidden judgment, judged.

CHAPTER X.

Let no human being therefore glory in his merits, but “let the one who glories glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17). For what does anyone have that he has not received? And if he received it, why does he glory as though he had not received it? (1 Cor. 4:7).

For the Lord himself says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36). Our liberation rests in his decision and in his will. As the Psalmist says: “There is anger in his fury, and life in his will” (Ps. 29:6).

Therefore, let the guilty person who is condemned attribute it to his own merits; let the person who is liberated attribute it to the grace of the Redeemer.

We do not say by this that the human race has lost free will. Before the grace of the Savior liberates it, it possesses free will inclined toward evil, not toward good. Therefore free will itself is liberated by the grace of God, so that it may will and be able to do good.

One of the Fathers accordingly says that the grace of God precedes the unwilling person so that he may will, and follows the willing person so that he may not will in vain (Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 32).

Thus, before a person is faithful, he has free will toward evil; once faithful, he has free will toward good also, namely, free will liberated by the grace of God. Not without reason, therefore, he receives punishment for an evil work and eternal life for a good one.

337 CHAPTER XI.

Therefore, distinguishing the grace that the first human possessed before sin from the grace by which human beings are now redeemed from the condemned mass of sin, someone said as follows: “The first is given so that a person may possess righteousness if he wills; the second, therefore, is more powerful, since through it he is also made willing, and wills so greatly and loves with such ardor that the will of the spirit conquers the pleasure of the flesh, which desires what is contrary. Nor was the former grace insignificant, by which the power of free choice was also demonstrated: for he was so assisted that, without this assistance, he would not remain in the good, yet, if he wished, he could abandon this assistance. But the latter is so much greater that through it it is little enough for a human being to restore the freedom he has lost; indeed, it is little enough that without it he cannot either grasp the good or remain in the good, even if he wishes, unless he is also made willing” (Augustine, *On Correction and Grace*, chapter 11).

What, then, is prior in this grace except faith, which will lead us to sight, so that we may see what we believe? A person will not receive this faith unless he has been baptized in the name of the Trinity, so that, having been made a believer, he may know what to ask for and from whom, may seek and knock, and may be able to find, as the Lord admonishes in the Gospel: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew VII, 7). No one is admitted among the faithful unless he has been baptized in the name of the Trinity.

Yet not all who are baptized will be saved, since many heresies in fact boast of this baptism of the Trinity and appear to be baptized in the same manner as the Catholic Church; but they are held fast in great error, while they tear apart the unity of the faith, refuse to share communion with the whole world, and therefore will rightly be condemned. It profits them nothing, then, to be immersed in the name of the Trinity when, by rash presumption, they strive to divide the indivisible name of the Godhead itself.

Nevertheless, when, pierced in heart, they return to the Catholic Church with humble devotion, the baptism that they have already received is not repeated in them; rather, they are reconciled to the Catholic Church through the laying on of hands. In this way the Lord’s command is preserved: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew XXVIII, 19), so that, whether they were baptized outside the Church or, indeed, within the Church by an evil and perverse priest according to this rule, it is in no way repeated for them.

For the faith that works through love is possessed by the holy Catholic Church. Heretics are in no way shown to possess it, since faith alone is truly insufficient unless, while believing in God, one loves God and obeys his commandments. To obey his commandments is not to do evil but to do good, and to fight against the devil, who at every moment attempts to obstruct our course directed toward God. Hence, according to the Apostle, “like a roaring lion he prowls around, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter V, 8); he must be resisted firmly in faith.

### 338 CHAPTER XII

And although, for as long as we live mortally in this world, we cannot be without sin, nevertheless, lest we become entangled in any crimes, let us return to his service and, having become his vessels, let him begin once more to dwell in us. Both divine Scripture and secular laws publicly punish the sins that are criminal; and your conscience knows them too, since it does not wish to suffer them at another’s hands. But if, after baptism, we have perhaps become entangled in certain offenses, let us not shrink from doing penance and, with heart and body contrite, asking God for forgiveness.

For those who think that they may commit sins with impunity because they perhaps give some alms to the poor are greatly deceived. They do not know that the first work of mercy is to offer oneself to God and then to show mercy to another. Thus Scripture says: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclesiasticus XXX, 24); and again: “Whoever is wicked to himself, to whom can he be good?” (Ecclesiasticus IV, 5). Therefore alms should be given, but vices must first be abandoned.

They differ greatly, then, from those who have kept their garment white—those who, having been reborn in this way, persevere, with the Lord’s help, to the end of their departure. For them daily prayer is sufficient to cancel the lesser offenses that creep in during this mortal body. The Apostle longs to be freed from this body when he says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans VII, 24).

For in the Gospel the Lord also displays three fruitfulnesses of the earth (Matthew XIII, 23), that is, he indicates three degrees of the good within the Church: thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold. Hence Noah’s ark, which signified the Church, had two chambers and three chambers; signifying, as we have said, the three degrees or orders that ecclesiastical interpreters have referred to married persons, the continent, and virgins: the thirtyfold, namely, to married persons; the sixtyfold, to the continent; the hundredfold, to virgins.

Thus the Catholic Church is also established in these degrees, so that, although there are three degrees, there are nevertheless many differences of merit. For not all virgins receive an equal reward in the kingdom of heaven, nor do all the continent, nor all married persons. “Each will receive his own reward,” the Apostle says, “according to his labor” (1 Corinthians III, 8). And the more one person has obeyed God than another, the greater reward he will receive.

And what will this reward, or prize, be, unless God himself is the reward of virtue? Someone said: “He who gave virtue, who gave victory to those contending, will himself undoubtedly be the crown.” We understand this to mean that in that life one person will see God more than another in proportion as he loved him more in this life and was obedient to his commandments.

### CHAPTER XIII

But even in the flesh of the dead who rise again there will be many differences of radiance, as the Apostle says: “There is one radiance of the sun, another radiance of the moon, and another radiance of the stars. For star differs from star in radiance; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians XV, 41).

Therefore, whatever bodies fire has consumed, a beast has devoured, or water has swallowed up, will rise at that moment of time and in the blink of an eye, each in the sex in which he died: a male in the male sex, and a female in the female sex.

That the dead will rise, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Have you not read what the Lord says to Moses concerning the bush: ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’?” (Luke XX, 37). And he adds immediately: “He is not the God of the dead but of the living. For all live to him” (ibid., 38). And again: “Then,” he says, “all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who have done good will rise to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John V, 28–29).

Elsewhere also, when counting works of mercy (Matthew XXV, 46), rebuking the good and the wicked, he says that the latter go into eternal punishment. The good, moreover, he will receive into everlasting joy; there they will reign without end with their God, and, secure in their permanence, nothing indecent will delight them. Wherever their spirit will be, immediately there will be a new heaven and a new earth.

The wicked, however, will be received by eternal fire, which will torture them forever. There “their worm will not die, and the fire will not be extinguished” (Mark IX, 44). Therefore, dearest one, we must strive and continually implore God’s mercy, so that we may live soberly, piously, and justly in this age, and thus may be able to reach the kingdom of heaven [lacuna].

---

[Col. 0507D]

## S. FULGENTIUS, *AGAINST THE SERMON OF FASTIDIOSUS THE ARIAN, TO VICTOR*, ONE BOOK. (C, S)

### 340 CHAPTER I

[Col. 0507D]

When I was reviewing, with complete delight and eagerness of spirit, your letter, dearest son Victor, which contained the sweetest fragrance of faith and charity, I found enclosed the work that you had sent to me for refutation: the sermon of Fastidiosus. After reading it, I grieved all the more over the man’s ruin because I was compelled to shudder at the blasphemer. We know that, after the Christian faith, after his profession as a monk, and after the honor of the presbyterate—which he received in the sight of human beings but did not possess before the Lord—he was turned away from the way of truth and had altogether forgotten his own redemption. He became a slave to fornication and lust and, as a result, rejected the service of divine majesty.

Thus, having changed from a Catholic into a heretic and bringing forth evil things from the evil treasure of his heart, he deservedly belches forth that sermon, stuffed with the poison of impiety, against the true faith and against Catholic truth, since he rejects the bread of life and, as the indication of his name suggests, Fastidiosus has spurned the wholesome food of true faith.

In that profane sermon, calling us “Homoousians”—as the Arians customarily call us—he wrote these words: “The Homoousians,” he says, “assert that the Trinity is inseparable and indivisible, that the Son was not less than the Father, and that the unbegotten Father was not the maker of his Son.”

Please observe in these words of Fastidiosus that some things are so badly expressed that they can never be correctly asserted, while others are so impiously stated by him that they could also be rightly said and heard, if only piety were present.

The statement by which he thought we ought to be accused—because we say that the Trinity is inseparable and indivisible—he expressed so wrongly and impiously that no one could properly make it. For who does not see with how great impiety the Arians assert that the Trinity is separable? The blessed Apostle says concerning us: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or danger, or famine, or persecution, or the sword?” (Romans VIII, 35). And shortly afterward: “I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, neither things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (ibid., 38).

### CHAPTER II

Since, then, the blessed Apostle trusts by the grace of God that we cannot be separated from his love, how can those not recognize that they are bound in the deadly snare of impiety who do not hesitate to proclaim the holy Trinity separated, although they cannot demonstrate that its works are separable in any respect?

For in what the evangelist says concerning the Son—“All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 3)—and in what blessed David sings—“How magnificent are your works, O Lord! You made them all in wisdom” (Psalm CIII, 24)—and since the blessed Apostle openly confesses Christ to be the power of God and the wisdom of God, of whom it is said, “For in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones or Dominions or Principalities or Powers; all things were created through him and in him” (Colossians I, 16), it is clear that all the works of the Father are the same works as those of the Son, and likewise the same works as those of the Holy Spirit.

For the holy Trinity works inseparably. There is no work that the Father has done which the Son has not done, nor one that the Son has done which the Holy Spirit has not done. For it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host” (Psalm XXXII, 6).

Concerning the wisdom that we say was created in the angels, we read in the book of Ecclesiasticus: “Wisdom was created before all things, and the understanding of prudence from eternity” (Ecclesiasticus I, 4). To show that the angels too were made by the Word of God, through whom all things were made, holy Scripture immediately added: “The fountain of wisdom is the Word of God, and its ways are eternal commandments” (ibid., 5). And shortly afterward, to show that the angels belong to the works of the Holy Spirit, it says: “One is the Most High Creator, almighty, a powerful King, greatly to be feared, seated upon his throne and ruling. God created her by the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 8).

What, then, will be denied to have been made by the Holy Spirit, by whom the power of heaven is read to have been established, and whose works include created wisdom?

Moreover, concerning the divine gifts that God bestows upon his Church, when the blessed Apostle was speaking and had said, “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians XII, 4), after enumerating the diversity of heavenly gifts he added: “All these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each one as he wills” (ibid., 12).

And among all creatures—in which wisdom “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom VIII, 1)—what could be found alien to the operation of the Holy Spirit, when Christ, who is the power and wisdom of God, declares that he casts out demons by the Spirit of God? For he himself said: “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew XII, 28).

How, then, does Fastidiosus deny that the Trinity is inseparable, when no Christian dares deny that the works of the Trinity are identical and inseparable in all creatures? One God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—works inseparably. For God’s Only-Begotten Son declares that his works are the same as those of his Father, saying: “Whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise” (John V, 19). And yet the Son does what he does in the Holy Spirit, in whom he casts out demons.

### CHAPTER III

But lest, because we have said that the Son also does in the Holy Spirit whatever he does, the Arians wish to assert some question of difference, thinking that the one in whom something is done must be inferior to the one who does it, let them hear our Savior resisting this perversity in every respect when he says: “But whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, which have been done in God” (John III, 20).

Here let the Arians choose how they wish to understand “God” as named in the passage: whether the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit. For if they think the Father is to be understood as the one in whom good works are done by human beings, they themselves destroy what they object against the person of the Holy Spirit when they blaspheme. For they will not dare to call the Father inferior, while they refuse to proclaim the Son equal to him according to divinity. Therefore, since a human being does good works in the Father, and Christ casts out demons in the Holy Spirit, let them recognize the equality of the Father and the Holy Spirit.

But if they say that the Son is to be understood here, on the grounds that good works are done in the Son and in the Holy Spirit, they are compelled not only to confess the Son and the Holy Spirit equal, but also to confess that the works of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are identical and inseparable. For, as the blessed Apostle testifies, “One and the same Spirit works all things” (1 Corinthians XII, 12).

If the Arians, however, judge that the Holy Spirit is meant, they must be compelled by this passage to confess that the Holy Spirit is God. For he did not say, “The Spirit of the Lord, who does the truth, so that his works may be revealed, which have been done in the Holy Spirit,” but rather, “which have been done in God.” We do not say that these works have been done in the Father alone, nor in the Son alone, nor in the Holy Spirit alone, but in the holy Trinity itself, which is one God. We confess that truth is done by the human being in whom the blessed David indicates that virtue is done by the faithful, saying: “In the Lord we shall do virtue, and he himself will bring those who afflict us to nothing” (Psalm LIX, 14).

For he is the one God of whom the blessed Apostle says: “For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory forever” (Romans XI, 36).

### CHAPTER IV

How, then, is the holy Trinity said by the impious to be separable, when it works inseparably—by those who, as far as can be understood, do not even consider in spirit the separation that is spoken of, as the truth of the matter requires?

Nothing can be separated locally from our God—that is, from the holy Trinity itself—because the same supreme, true, and good God, just as he made all things, so also contains and fills all things, being immeasurable. He is not corporeal or local, and therefore even corporeal things cannot be separated locally from God, because every body is in a place, and there is no place without God.

God is contained by no place in such a way that he himself does not contain every place. In him there is no mass, and his power is immeasurable. Since bodies, which cannot exist without a place, cannot be separated locally from God, undoubtedly neither can the spirits that God created be separated locally from God.

For every spirit that God created, wherever it may be, has God there. Although God is not present in evil spirits by grace—the grace by which he bestows holy life and blessedness upon those whom he wills—nevertheless, by his natural power he is always present in all his creatures, so that no creature, nor any part of a creature, can be found in which God is not present by his power.

That nature, therefore, can be separated from God which could or can be subject to sin. There is no other thing that can depart from God except a substance that can or could sin by its own will.

Isaiah says: “Behold, the hand of the Lord is not shortened, so that he cannot save, nor is his ear burdened, so that he cannot hear; but your iniquities separate between you and your God” (Isaiah LIX, 1–2).

The Book of Wisdom also shows that human beings are separated from God not by places but by wicked thoughts and unjust deeds. For it says: “Wicked thoughts separate from God. But tested virtue corrects the foolish; for wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins. For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wisdom I, 3–5).

Here who does not see the Trinity of persons intimated by their properties? It was said that wicked thoughts separate from God, by which name the person of God the Father is recognized. Then it was added that wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, by which name Christ is indicated, whom Paul calls the power of God and the wisdom of God. Then it was said that the Holy Spirit will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding.

But lest anyone think that any wicked or impious persons could be locally separated from this holy Trinity, which is the one, true, and good God, Scripture speaks shortly afterward as follows: “For the spirit of wisdom is kindly disposed, and he will not acquit the blasphemer because of his lips, because God is the witness of his inmost being, the true examiner of his heart, and the hearer of his tongue. For the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (ibid., 6–7).

The divine utterances, therefore, never cease to proclaim the immensity of the holy Trinity. Blessed David certainly knew this, and therefore said: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you are present” (Psalm CXXXVIII, 7–8).

Concerning Wisdom, that is, the Son of God, Scripture also says that “it reaches from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom VIII, 1).

Since, therefore, no thing is locally separated from the holy Trinity, which is wholly everywhere, but only iniquities and wicked thoughts separate from God, as we have already said, whoever attempts to assert that the Trinity is separable must necessarily say either that the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit can naturally be subject to wicked thoughts and iniquities.

Who, however, would extricate himself from the snare of such great impiety as to suspect any separation in that Trinity where there is natural unity, when Paul, the faithful Apostle, trusts that, through the grace received—as we demonstrated above—he cannot in any way be separated from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord?

The blessed apostle John confirms both that love is from God and that love is God in these words: “Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who loves is from God” (1 John IV, 7); and, “God is love” (ibid., 16).

Love cannot be separated from itself, because it is inseparable. For when human beings, who can be separated from one another, are not only possessed by love itself in an undivided state, but love also makes one heart and one soul from many hearts and souls, what madness is it to call love separable, when it customarily joins separated minds by inseparable affection?

Hence Paul said: “For although I am absent in body, I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order” (Colossians II, 5). And in the Acts of the Apostles it is written that “the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV, 32), something known only to the spirit of faith and love.

“For the love of God has been poured into our hearts” (Ephesians IV, 4). And through that same Spirit all believers become, as the Apostle says, one body and one spirit. Hence elsewhere he says: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, whether slaves or free, and we were all given to drink of one Spirit” (1 Corinthians XII, 13).

The Only-Begotten Son of God himself commanded with his own mouth that all nations be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

### CHAPTER V

Since, then, baptism is administered in the name of the Trinity, it causes all the faithful to be baptized into one body, so that from this all may become one body, as the blessed Apostle says: “We are one body in Christ, but individually we are members of one another” (Romans XII, 5).

The multitude of believers also had one heart and one soul through the love that has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.

It plainly appears with what impiety the Trinity itself is called separable, when any creature is separated from God not by place or time, but only by iniquities.

Hence God says of certain people: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matthew XV, 8). Yet he himself says: “I am a God who is near, and not a God from afar” [Note: [Col. 0513D] Read “and not God”; for so it is written above in several places.] “If a human being is hidden, will I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?” (Jeremiah XXIII, 23–24).

David himself nevertheless says: “Behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish” (Psalm LXXII, 27). And to show what it means to distance oneself from God, he added: “You have destroyed all who fornicate away from you” (ibid.).

One therefore withdraws from God in heart, and by heart also approaches him. For it is clear that God is wholly everywhere, but is in no way contained by place.

God is spirit: the creator, not created; the immutable, eternal, immeasurable, just, and good maker of all bodies and all spirits. By the immensity of his nature he never departs from any of the things he has made. For it cannot happen that God himself should be absent in power from anything that has from God the fact that it exists.

Nevertheless, through the mercy and judgment for which the Church never ceases to sing to him (Psalm C, 1), it is not unfittingly said that he is near to the faithful and far from the unfaithful.

As regards nature, since everything that has been created—whether corporeal or spiritual—was made by the holy Trinity alone, that is, by the one God who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, with one will, one operation, one power, one benevolence, and one omnipotence, just as the Father fills the whole creation—not by mass, but by power—so the Son fills it wholly, and so the Holy Spirit fills it wholly.

The Trinity does not fill the whole creation in such a way that the Father fills one part, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, nor in such a way that the whole is filled by the Father alone, or by the Son alone, or by the Holy Spirit alone.

Who would dare think this way about the Trinity—that is, about the one God—not merely if he were foolish, but if he were wholly sacrilegious, when the power and divinity of God must necessarily be naturally as immeasurable as it is naturally everlasting?

But human beings devoted to bodily senses cannot think even of God except bodily. They imagine that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit can be separated from one another just as human beings are separated from one another. Since human beings are distinguished by the form and dimensions of each body, they must likewise be distinguished by places.

But while such people roll their souls in the mud of the flesh, fashioning phantasms out of created things and weighed down by the burden of vanity, the more they occupy themselves with thoughts of those things that present corporeal mass to corporeal eyes, the less able they are to ascend toward understanding the Godhead.

They do not heed the command given by the Lord God through the holy Isaiah that we should not wish to think of him as we think of the creatures that we know were made by him, because he himself does not think as we human beings think. Hence Isaiah says: “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are my ways your ways, says the Lord. For as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so my ways are exalted above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts” (Isaiah LV, 8).

### CHAPTER VI

God the Father, therefore, and his Word, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the holy Trinity, the sole, one, true, and good God—just as there is in him no thought that changes with the turning of time—for he did not think one way before making the world and another way after making the world, nor will he think another way after the form of this world has passed away, because “the counsel of the Lord remains forever” (Psalm XXXII, 11)—so he is inseparable because he is immutable.

The Trinity, the one God, is neither a body nor a created spirit, because a body is confined by place, and every created spirit is bounded by the measure of its nature.

The Trinity, the one God, just as he is eternal, with no times coeternal with him, so is he immeasurable, and no creature can contain him. Because he is immeasurable, he is wholly everywhere; for he is neither contained by place nor extended or contracted by space.

God, therefore, is wisdom; God is truth; God is love. This is the Father, this is the Son, this is the Holy Spirit, this is the Trinity itself, which is the one, true, and good God.

If anyone can show that there is any division either in wisdom, or in truth, or in love, let him confidently dare to assert that the Trinity is divisible [Note: [Col. 0513D] “divisible and separable” is plainly missing here; [Col. 0514D] for shortly afterward it says, “the Trinity is recognized as indivisible and inseparable.”]

But if neither wisdom, nor truth, nor love can in any way be divided, then from this the Trinity is certainly recognized as indivisible and inseparable.

It is therefore clear how great was the impiety of Fastidiosus, by which he thought we were entirely to be blamed because we confess the Trinity to be inseparable and indivisible. For, as the preceding discussion has shown—and as a sufficient abundance of divine testimonies has strengthened, not reason alone—the immeasurable nature of the Trinity can neither be contained by place, nor can any person within the Trinity be subject to sin, because the Trinity itself is naturally eternal, perfect, and immutable justice.

Heretical perversity indeed attempts to assert wrongly that the Son is lesser; but, with piety preserved, Catholic truth confesses him equal.

For heretics, thinking of incorporeal divinity only in bodily terms, when they say that the Son is lesser according to nature, entangle themselves under the false appearance of the Christian name that they deceitfully assume in the unspeakable crime of idolatry.

For what is it to say that one god is greater and another god lesser in the individual persons except to place idols of different kind and different power—not on walls but, what is worse, in their hearts?

The Arians plainly show by this that they worship two gods, while they deny that the Son is equal to the Father. And when they assert that he is lesser—not because he assumed flesh, which is what the truth of faith teaches, but by the nature of his immeasurable divinity—they do so even though it was said of him that he is the wisdom of God and “the brightness of eternal light” (Wisdom VII, 26).

Concerning him it is said in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Who, being the radiance of glory [Note: [Col. 0513D] There is no doubt that there is an error here, and that “radiance of glory” should be read, as above, not in only one place; and in the Apostle’s text, τῆς δόξης, ‘of glory’], and the figure of his substance” (Hebrews I, 3).

Let them consider the brightness of eternal light and recognize that, just as that light is eternal and immeasurable, so its brightness also is by nature in no way later or lesser; rather, immeasurability is equal to eternity, and eternity to immeasurability.

### CHAPTER VII

The Christian faith, therefore, which knows the Only-Begotten God to have been born from the Father’s nature alone and created from the Virgin Mary, recognizing that both substances truly remain in him, thus truly confesses him equal to God the Father that it can also proclaim him lesser without the charge of falsehood or impiety.

Because he has one natural divinity with the Father and one natural humanity with his mother, the Son is equal to the Father in that in him he is true God from the Father; and the Father is greater than the Son in that the Only-Begotten God himself is true man.

This, then, is the true faith, this is holy piety, this is Christian belief: in the one and same Son of God, to believe both the nature of the Father’s divinity and the substance of his mother’s humanity, neither to believe the Son’s divinity different from the divinity of God the Father nor to separate the Son’s humanity from the humanity of the Virgin mother, but in the same true God to believe the true and entire humanity of our race, and in the same true and complete human being to believe the true and full divinity of the Father’s nature.

For whoever denies the unity of the Father’s substance in the Son is polluted by Arian impiety. Whoever denies the truth of flesh in the Only-Begotten God is profaned by the crime of the Manichaean plague. Whoever denies a human—that is, rational—soul in the same Son of God is immediately defiled by the sacrilege of the Apollinarians.

### CHAPTER VIII
Therefore, once the truth of the paternal and maternal natures in the Only-Begotten God has been fully believed, and the natural distinctiveness of the two substances has been preserved in the one person of Christ, the Son is piously and truthfully called equal and inferior to the Father; piously and truthfully proclaimed coeternal and later in time; piously and truthfully asserted to be both eternally begotten and born in time, both always unchangeable and changed in time. [Col. 0516A]

Thus the Son is equal to the Father because he eternally possesses this from the Father. He is also inferior to the Father because he received this temporally from the Virgin. Therefore, just as the Son is piously called equal to the Father when the humanity by which he is inferior to the Father is not acknowledged in him, so the same Son is impiously called inferior when the unity and equality of divinity that he naturally shares with the Father are denied in him.

We therefore call the Son naturally equal, and we also call him inferior. We say that he was born equal according to the form of God, but was made lower according to the form of a servant. We call him equal to the Father insofar as we recognize that he was born from the Father without beginning; and we call him inferior because, when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law (Gal. IV, 4).

Accordingly, just as we proclaim without hesitation that he was born, so we likewise proclaim that he was made. For we say that he was born without [Col. 0516B] beginning from the heart of the Father, and we say that he was made in time through the work of the Trinity. The Father both begot his own Son from his own nature and made him from the nature of the Virgin. Whatever he made, he made with the cooperation of the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Thus the Father alone begot his own Son, but did not make him alone. In the Only-Begotten Son there is the eternal generation belonging to the Father alone, and in that same Son made in time there is the one operation of the whole Trinity.

For the Only-Begotten God, Creator of humanity, was made human; and the same one who made woman from man was made man from woman. Hence it is evident that the testimonies which Fastidiosus impiously brought forward from the Gospel, the Acts of the Apostles, and Solomon do not take away from the Son the unity of the Father’s nature, but disclose the mystery of the divine incarnation.

Knowing this most certainly, John [Col. 0516C] the Baptist said: “This is he of whom I said, ‘After me comes one who was made before me’” (John I, 15). Proclaiming the truth of this mystery, the apostle Peter said: “Therefore [348] let the whole house of Israel know with certainty that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both God and Christ” (Acts II, 36).

He rightly said “made” of the one whom he proclaims crucified. For the Only-Begotten God, incomprehensible and immortal, made by no one and the eternal Maker of all things, deigned by his own work to become Christ, so that by the work of the Jews he might be crucified. For no cross could in any way have borne the world’s Redeemer unless the womb of a virgin had brought forth the world’s Creator after conceiving him.

Therefore, also intimating through Solomon the truth of his generation and creation, he said: “The Lord created me at the beginning [Col. 0516D] of his ways, in his work” (Prov. VIII, 22). But before saying this, he prefaced a clear indication of his future incarnation, saying: “If I tell you the things that happen daily, I shall recall the things that have been from the beginning of the world” (ibid., 21, according to the LXX). Then, enumerating them, he added: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways, in his work.”

This creation is from the beginning of the world, not before the world. For afterward he says: “Before the ages he founded me”; and shortly thereafter: “Before all the hills he begot me.” By saying “before the ages” and “before all the hills,” he wished eternity to be understood as the mode of the divine birth. Both “before the ages” and “after the age” signify eternity. Thus the eternity of the Son of God before the world has no beginning, just as his eternity after the world has no end.

In this way [Col. 0517A] Wisdom uses the past tense in place of the future, saying, “The Lord created me,” instead of “He will create me”; and she spoke of something as having been done which was in fact still to be done. Thus, through blessed David, she said: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves considered and looked upon me. They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots” (Ps. XXI, 18–19).

By saying, “The Lord created me,” he showed how he would be made. By saying, “They pierced my hands and my feet,” he also showed how he would be crucified. But just as what was spoken of as already done concerning his passion through David [Col. 0517B] was certainly still to come, so what Solomon prophesied concerning his incarnation as though it had already happened was likewise still to come—the one who is the Wisdom of God himself.

For Solomon himself had said shortly before: “Wisdom built herself a house, and set up seven pillars” (Prov. IX, 1), which refers to the origin of the Lord’s incarnation. Isaiah likewise speaks of Christ’s passion in such a way that he says as past what he prophesies as future. For he says of Christ: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 7).

Nor does he merely sometimes foretell the birth of the Only-Begotten God from the Virgin according to the flesh as future; at other times he speaks of it as past. Thus in one place he says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. VII, [Col. 0517C] 14). Elsewhere, intimating it as already accomplished and completed, he says: “A child has been born for us, and a son has been given to us” (Isa. IX, 6).

Who, then, does not see that everything said by the prophets concerning the humanity and passion of the Only-Begotten God was at that time truly future, just as it is now truly past? To demonstrate the unchangeability of the divine plan, prophetic Scripture was made to speak in the manner of the past about what was awaited as future [349] in its accomplishment.

For God, [Col. 0517D] of whom the prophet says, “He who made the things that are to be” (Isa. XLV, 11, according to the LXX), wished to narrate as already done the things that were still to be done because he established what takes place changeably in time through the unchangeable eternity of his disposition. Thus, even in those things whose work has not yet been accomplished, the Creator’s firm disposition remains in eternity.

Therefore, just as the Son of God was to be created through his work, he said that he had been created; and just as he was to be crucified, he did not hesitate to call himself crucified.

## CHAPTER IX

Still, with a perverse heart and sacrilegious mouth, the deranged Fastidiosus sought to assert from this that the Son was separated from the Father and the Holy Spirit, because it is established that he alone entered the bridal chamber of the Virgin’s womb. Of this it is said in the Book of Psalms: “And he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Ps. XVIII, 6).

Then, wishing to establish the proposition of his perversity, he did not hesitate to assert [Col. 0518A] that blasphemy as well, saying that the Trinity could in no way separate itself, since it is entirely indivisible. Therefore, did the whole Trinity assume flesh? Did the whole Trinity suffer the insults of the Passion? Did the whole Trinity lie in the tomb? Did the whole Trinity penetrate hell? Did the whole Trinity rise from the dead on the third day? Did the whole Trinity ascend into heaven on the fortieth day?

Does the whole Trinity sit at his right hand? Or whom did the whole Trinity send as the Spirit upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost? Or to which God could the whole Trinity say on the cross, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me”? Or to which Father did the whole Trinity say, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit”? Let them declare this, if they can.

But if they cannot say it, they themselves destroy themselves with their own weapons—those who insist that the Trinity is inseparable.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0518B]

Thus far, in that profane discourse, the words of Fastidiosus have been directed against the catholic faith. Yet, apart from those things in which he blasphemed to the dishonor of the holy Trinity, almost everything else, whether preceding or following, the most wicked man appropriated from the words of others.

Indeed, everything he set down against the Donatists was stolen from two letters. In those letters, when we were with one another in exile in Sardinia, all of us had to write a reply to Stephania, the religious daughter of the Church, against the Pelagians and the Donatists; and the very same order of words in which that most wicked man fraudulently published them under his own name is found inserted there.

But so that you would not lack knowledge of this matter, I have appended to this little work the two letters which the aforesaid Stephania sent to us and to which we replied. [Note: [Col. 0517D] These letters are not extant.] Thus you may recognize that in that discourse only those things belonged to Fastidiosus by which, leaping forth with blind heart to the injury of the holy Trinity itself, he attempted to attack the catholic truth.

## CHAPTER XI

Now, with the Lord’s help, I reply to his blasphemies. The whole Trinity did not assume flesh, nor did the whole Trinity suffer the insults of the Passion, nor did the whole Trinity lie in the tomb, nor did the whole Trinity penetrate hell, nor did the whole Trinity rise from the dead on the third day; and the same must be said of whatever other things can be shown, in that mystery of the incarnation, to belong to the person of the Son alone.

For the things which Fastidiosus, full of falsehood and perversity, brought forward against catholic truth [Col. 0518D] can truly be brought against none but the Sabellians, that is, the Patripassians. It is in them that those who insist on proclaiming one person in the holy Trinity just as they proclaim one nature are truly trapped and convicted.

Their perversity consequently drives them to this absurdity: they do not believe the divine birth at all, yet they assign to the Father, according to the flesh, the nature, passion, and death, as well as the resurrection from hell, the ascent into heaven, and all those things which in the mystery of the incarnation belong to the person of the one Son.

But the catholic Church, inspired by God and [Col. 0519A] holding the truth of the faith, knows how to assert one nature in the holy Trinity, and so, with the greatest care, assigns what belongs to each person.

Therefore, the Son of God, who was mercifully to redeem us, is rightly believed in this respect to have assumed human nature alone, because he did not receive human nature in such a way that the nature of divinity and flesh would become one nature in him.

For deity could not be in Christ what flesh is, since, while each nature retained its own property, it could not happen that either of them ceased to be or passed wholly and completely into the other. If this had happened, it would rightly be said that the flesh had been assumed by the whole Trinity, when the Son converted his flesh into that divinity which we confess remains shared by him with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0519B]

Now, because we say that in Christ there is one divine nature and another human nature, we therefore believe and confess that human nature—that is, flesh and a rational soul—was assumed not by the whole Trinity but by the Son alone.

For the Only-Begotten God assumed flesh and soul into the unity of person, not into a unity of nature, since the person of the Son is not the same as that of the Father or the Holy Spirit. Therefore, while the distinctiveness of both substances remained, the unity of person did not make Christ’s person twofold, nor did it make the assumption of human nature common to the holy Trinity.

For the Son of God does not have one common person with the Father and the Holy Spirit, as he has one nature common to them.

351

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0519C] It belongs to the Son alone, therefore, mercifully to have assumed the form of a servant. For that assumption of the form of a servant belonged to the person of God the Word [or: true God], and did not pass into the divine nature by confusion.

Therefore, the assumption of that form of a servant, according to which the Son of God—who is Lord of all things and in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwells—became true and complete man, took nothing away from him of the fullness of divinity and deprived him of none of his dominion, because in that one person the divine and human natures remained without confusion.

Hence, in one and the same Christ, the truth of human nature was made manifest, and the eternal [Col. 0519D] unchangeability of the divine nature remained. For what he possessed naturally in eternity was neither diminished in him in any respect nor changed by what he received in time.

He was made a servant in outward condition, but he did not cease naturally to be Lord of all things. He was also made poor according to the flesh; nevertheless, according to his divinity he remained supremely rich.

Hence the blessed Apostle declares that Christians have been enriched through poverty, saying: “You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: although he was rich, for our sake he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (II Cor. VIII, 9).

But he could in no way make us rich by his poverty if, having become poor, he did not possess within himself the riches of his natural [Col. 0520A] divinity. He therefore became poor according to the form of a servant and remained rich according to the form of God.

The poverty of the form of a servant is therefore not shared by him with the Father and the Holy Spirit, because, after the poverty of human nature had been assumed in the unity of person, the divine substance remained rich in him.

What, then, was the poverty of the rich Son of God, except our weakness and our mortality? Whatever the Only-Begotten God endured in weakness and death according to the flesh, the divinity did not experience.

For God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. VIII, 3): in him there was true flesh, but no pollution of sin. The likeness of sinful flesh was therefore present in Christ’s flesh because, although it was not sinful flesh, it was weak, subject to suffering and [Col. 0520B] mortal, subject to wounds and exposed to pain.

Nevertheless, all these things were common to Christ’s divinity and humanity not substantially but personally. Christ’s person, however, is entirely distinct from the person of the Father and the Holy Spirit.

This one person of divinity and humanity in Christ remains in such a way that it neither allows one nature to be separated from the other nor permits the two to be confused. Christ, therefore, who is the way, the truth, and the true life, is our way because he possessed true weakness in the truth of flesh; and he is our true life because true power remained in his true divinity.

The Apostle, distinguishing these things, says: “For although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God” (II Cor. XIII, 4).

352

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0520C]

Thus, in one and the same Christ, just as the weakness of human flesh could neither give nor restore life to itself—for the power of laying down his soul and taking it up again came not from human weakness but from divine power—so the eternity of divine power, whose natural property is to live unchangeably and unfailingly, could experience no weakness or death on the cross.

The Only-Begotten Son of God is therefore recognized as true God, born from the Father, and true man, made from his mother, because he displayed signs of weakness in the truth of flesh and showed proofs of power in the truth of divinity. He thus demonstrated that, in the unity of person, one thing is naturally shared with us and another with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Christ has a natural sharing with us of soul and flesh; with the Father [Col. 0520D] and the Holy Spirit he has a natural sharing of divinity. How, then, could the Son of God possess with the Father and the Holy Spirit things that belong to flesh [Note: [Col. 0519D] Perhaps: “could not possess”], when he in no way confuses his flesh with his divinity?

In the same way, it does not prejudice the catholic faith that we believe our nature to have been assumed by the Only-Begotten Savior in the unity of person, while we confess that the substance of the holy Trinity remains one.

The whole Trinity indeed made that humanity of the Son, but the Trinity did not assume it in the same way that the whole Trinity made it. For the person who is not common to the Son with the Father and the Holy Spirit is the one who, in Christ, is one person of divinity and flesh.

But wherever any distinction of persons or substances is found, [Col. 0521A] whatever occurs in the sharing of operation is not always referred to a sharing in assumption. Since this seems obscure when presented only in words, it is better to provide, insofar as the matter permits, a suitable example to make it easier to understand.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0521A] There is indeed a likeness readily available to the faithful for understanding, which God placed in his own likeness. This image is the human mind.

For we read that the Lord said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26). In this statement the Arian heretics are greatly to be pitied: they read the holy Scriptures but do not understand them. Confounded by the blindness of their hearts, they do [Col. 0521B] not recognize the natural unity in the holy Trinity, in which they distinguish the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit by their proclamation.

For in the testimony we set forth above, the Trinity itself—which is one, true, and good God—both displays the unity of its divinity and clearly demonstrates the indication of three persons. For it said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” lest the unity of substance be denied in the three persons; nor did it say, “Let me make man in my image and likeness,” lest only one person be believed to exist in that divine nature.

Instead, it beneficially mingled the plural with the singular [353]: and when we read that God said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” we define what we speak of as singular in nature as plural in persons.

This image—that is, the inward man—is naturally found to possess three things: memory, understanding, [Col. 0521C] and will. Memory is the power of the soul by which we remember. Understanding is that by which we turn over in thought those things that we have conceived in memory. Will is that by which we either desire or avoid something; that is, by which we are found either to love or to hate something.

Although these three do not have distinct persons in man, they nevertheless differ from one another by distinction. Thus, in these three there is one person of one man and one substance of the human mind, while within the very nature of the rational soul, in which the image of God is known to exist, we nevertheless find one memory, another understanding, and likewise another will.

For although we can think of, love, or hate nothing that we do not possess in memory—since what oblivion has taken away [Col. 0521D] from the heart cannot in any way be found there by thought or will—we nevertheless often remember what we neither turn over in thought nor desire by the will, in order to recognize the distinction between memory, thought, and will. Likewise, we think about some things that we do not love.

Our thought, therefore, which is born and formed in memory, is rightly called the inner word. For what is thought except inward speech? Hence it is written: “Be pierced with compunction in your chambers over the things you say in your hearts” (Ps. IV, 5).

In the Gospel also, when the Lord Jesus had said to the paralytic whom he healed, “Your sins are forgiven you” (Luke V, 20), the evangelist Luke added, saying: “And the scribes and Pharisees began to think, saying, ‘Who is this [Col. 0522A] who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins except God alone?’ But when Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered and said to them, ‘Why do you think evil in your hearts?’” (ibid., 21–22).
