What Luke said—“The scribes and Pharisees began to think, saying”—Matthew says in this way: “And behold, some of the scribes said within themselves, ‘He blasphemes.’ And when Jesus saw their thoughts, he said, ‘Why do you think evil in your hearts?’” (Matt. IX, 3–4).

In the Book of Wisdom also it is said of certain people: “They said within themselves, thinking wrongly” (Wis. II, 1). It is therefore evident that to think is the same as to speak within oneself.

Thus one thinks invisibly. Without the sound of bodily speech, therefore, each person says what he thinks; yet he conveys it to another’s hearing only through [Col. 0522B] bodily speech.

## CHAPTER XVI

The word, then, which is born from memory, insofar as it is found to arise from memory alone, cannot be conveyed to anyone’s ears without a bodily voice. Therefore, so that it may be expressed to others, it is clothed in the form of a bodily voice. A bodily voice from the mouth is joined to the word.

Thus it happens that the word, which existed wholly spiritually in the mind, comes to others through a bodily voice and does not depart from the soul in which and from which it remains spiritually. It is necessary for it to remain wholly in the mind even when it is wholly expressed in the voice.

Nevertheless, [Col. 0522C] we cannot say that this utterance of the word comes from memory or will alone. For everyone who speaks certainly remembers and thinks about what he is saying; and he speaks because the will operates together with memory and thought in that utterance.

Indeed, whatever a person knowingly says, he does not say unless he wishes to say it, to such an extent that whatever a person is compelled to say unwillingly, he does not say as long as the will is in no way inclined to speak.

Hence those who, now crushed by fear or pain arising from temporal circumstances, tribulations, or torments, have abandoned the truth of the catholic faith and passed over to impiety and unbelief will not be able to find any excuse by saying that they denied the true faith unwillingly, since it is evident that they did so by their own will.

For even if the mind was brought [Col. 0522D] to deny the faith by tribulation or torture, it nevertheless did not deny it unwillingly. Before denying the faith, it first thought and willed to do so, and then uttered that denial, because thought, together with the will, decided that it should happen.

## CHAPTER XVII

354

To return, then, to the matter at hand: in the image of God itself—that is, in the human mind itself—the thought that is born and formed from memory, and is rightly called a word, receives only a bodily voice so that it may be heard by bodily ears.

Thus, in that holy and divine Trinity, only the Father’s Word, which is “the spotless mirror and image of God’s goodness” (Wis. VII, 26), namely, “the radiance and form of his substance” (Heb. I, 3), although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but “emptied himself [Col. 0523A], taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 6).

Therefore the Son alone assumed flesh, so that he could be seen by bodily eyes and touched by hands; he alone assumed human nature in such a way as to make it his own and mercifully to pour through it the knowledge of his divinity as well.

Yet, in revealing himself, he also revealed the Father in himself. For, granting recognition of his own divinity, he simultaneously granted recognition of the Father. The divinity that is one in the Father and the Son makes it impossible to know the Son without the Father or the Father without the Son.

Hence he said: “I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 9).

Thus the Son, who alone assumed flesh, naturally displayed the Father in himself by virtue of the unity of divinity, just as a speaker, while speaking the truth that he remembers, shows that what he indicates as uttered by him [Col. 0523B] is stored within his mind.

The bodily voice with which the spiritual word is clothed so that it may be brought to the knowledge of those listening arises simultaneously from memory, thought, and will; but it is received from thought alone—that is, from the interior word—so that it may proceed to the bodily ears of those present through the prompting of interior thought.

That word, just as, once it has assumed the form of a bodily voice, it goes forth whole to those listening, so it is found whole in the heart, spiritually, together with memory and will.

[355] Therefore, whoever observes this image in the human mind will quickly laugh at the empty talk of the heretics. Thinking carnally about spiritual matters, they refuse to believe that in the holy Trinity something was done by the three which, by divine disposition, was assumed by only one [Col. 0523C] person.

For just as it is certain that “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1), so it is certain that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 14).

What, then, have we received? The Lord’s Word and the God with whom the Word was—not the Father and the Son.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0523D] The name “Word,” therefore, shows the distinct person of the Father and the Son; but because he was God, it teaches that the substance of the Father and the Son is one.

The flesh that belongs to the Word alone therefore belongs neither to the Father nor to the Holy Spirit, because God the Word does not share one person with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

According to the common operation of divinity, in which there is a Trinity of persons, the Father and the Holy Spirit received what the Son received. For the Son who, according to divinity, was naturally born alone from the Father alone was himself appropriately born naturally according to the flesh from the Virgin.

But in that Trinity, just as there are not two Fathers or two Holy Spirits, so there will not be two Sons. For that Trinity has within itself one Father, one Son, and one Holy Spirit: one Father and one Holy Spirit according to divine nature, but one Son according to both divine and human substance.

The Trinity is therefore distinct in persons, although the one divinity of the Trinity is neither divided [Col. 0524A] nor separated in nature. Hence humanity is found assumed in the person of the Son alone.

Because of nature, therefore, the operation of the holy Trinity is always one; because of the persons, however, the human assumption belongs to the Son alone.

Nevertheless, while we discuss these matters for the instruction of the faithful, we must also consider that heretics are indeed carnal and animal, and therefore incapable of spiritual things. Of such people the Apostle says: “The animal man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. For it is foolishness to him, and he cannot understand, because it is examined spiritually” (I Cor. II, 14).

That heretics are especially carnal or animal is attested by apostolic authority. For blessed Paul places heresies among the works of the flesh. Blessed Judas the apostle also calls those who separate themselves from the Church animal, saying: “These are the ones who separate themselves [Col. 0524B], animal, not having the Spirit” (Jude, 19).

This is precisely what we showed blessed Paul to have said: “The animal man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God.” It is therefore no wonder that those who do not have the Spirit of God cannot understand divine things.

For it is written in the Book of Wisdom: “Who will know your mind unless you give wisdom and send your Holy Spirit from on high?” (Wis. IX, 17). Hence the holy Apostle likewise asserts that the things of God are revealed only by the Holy Spirit, saying: “For God has revealed them to us [356] through his Spirit” (I Cor. II, 10).

And shortly afterward he says: “We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things granted to us by God [Col. 0524C]” (ibid., 11).

Nevertheless, it is good that we too, insofar as we are divinely assisted, should imitate the blessed Apostle and strive to become all things to all people, so that we may win them all (I Cor. IX, 20).

## CHAPTER XIX

Since the Arians therefore do not grasp what we have said—that in the one divine nature something was done by the whole Trinity which was not assumed by the whole Trinity—and since they do not believe it possible that the whole Trinity made that flesh which was nevertheless assumed by one person of the Trinity, let us become, as the Apostle says (I Thess. II, 7), like little children in their midst, and propose to them an example to nourish the breadth of spiritual understanding without tiring or disturbing the narrowness of the heretical heart.

We know that the Trinity alone [Col. 0524D] is divine, inseparable, and indivisible. Its one nature cannot be divided by the Trinity of persons, nor can its three persons be confused by the unity of the indivisible nature.

The human mind itself, in which we said that the image of God exists, received this likeness in such a way that it contains within itself a certain indication of the holy Trinity, although it does not possess within itself a distinction of three persons. This is what the divine Trinity has reserved as its own.

Thus, although there are memory, understanding, and will in the human mind, these are indeed three things, but they cannot be three persons. For in each human being—in whose mind, or whose mind itself, is the divine image—the person is naturally one, belonging not only to the mind itself but simultaneously to soul and body.

In creation, therefore, insofar as the greatness of the matter we are [Col. 0525A] discussing permits, let us seek an example in natures of something that we cannot find in persons. We have said that the whole Trinity made the humanity of the Son of God, which nevertheless was not assumed by the whole Trinity but by the Son alone into his person.

For that flesh was made by the whole Trinity—that is, by the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit—but only the Word became flesh.

Since, then, as we said above, insofar as creation is concerned we cannot find three persons in one mind, that is, in one flesh, we need not labor to discover at least two natures in one person.

For the person of every living human being consists of a rational soul and a body; yet many things are done by them in such a way that, although they are done jointly by soul and body [Col. 0525B], they sometimes pertain only to the soul or only to the body.

Who does not know that only the body is restored and nourished by bodily food, although in eating it there is a common operation of flesh and soul? The soul acts through the body—or rather, together with the body—when the body eats; and yet only the body receives what the soul performs together with the body so that it may be received.

In that eating, therefore, the operation of soul and flesh is one, but the reception belongs to the flesh alone. Indeed, only the flesh is nourished by bodily food, so much so that, if it receives it, only the flesh grows fat.

The soul’s refreshment and nourishment, however, consist not in bodily bread but in spiritual bread. [357] “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV, 4).

Yet, in receiving [Col. 0525C] this word, so that the soul may be nourished by its food, the flesh joins it in the action. This happens when the soul applies bodily ears to words in order to hear, or bodily eyes to writings in order to read.

Behold, here too the operation of flesh and soul is simultaneous, while the reception belongs to the soul alone.

Let the Arians observe these things in created beings, and let them not doubt that the divine nature of the holy Trinity is one, and that it could happen—indeed, that it did happen—that the flesh was made by the whole Trinity through one and inseparable operation, while in the mystery of the incarnation it belonged to the person of God the Only-Begotten alone.

## CHAPTER XX

[The supplied source ends here.]

Therefore the whole Trinity did not assume flesh, nor did the whole Trinity suffer the injuries of the Passion, nor did the whole Trinity rise from the dead on the third day, nor did the whole Trinity ascend into heaven on the fortieth day. [Col. 0525D] Rather, as I showed above, the one Son alone assumed flesh. Because in him there remains one unconfused property of each nature, he is therefore one and the same, who according to true divinity remained altogether impassible. For divinity by its nature suffers nothing, just as by its nature it does not change. But it belongs to a changeable nature to be subject to sufferings. Therefore no suffering could befall that nature in which natural change could not exist.

The Son alone also lay in the tomb, but that nature of the Only-Begotten God could be buried which could die. Thus, according to the nature of his flesh, the Only-Begotten God lay buried in the stone, according to which nature he hung nailed to the cross. [Col. 0526A] For how could his divinity be enclosed in a tomb, when it can be enclosed neither by earth nor by heaven? Personal unity therefore made that Passion and that burial one reality in Christ, belonging to divinity and flesh; but the distinct property of each substance in Christ caused only Christ’s flesh naturally to be subject to Passion and death, while the impassibility and immortality of the divine and unchangeable substance remained.

Thus Christ, who is not the Trinity but one person of the Trinity, truly hung on the cross according to the truth of his flesh, and lay dead in the tomb, as the Apostle says: “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,” and “he was buried,” and “he rose from the dead on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Cor. 15:3). All these things the whole Christ endured according to the unity of his person; according to the natural property of the flesh, they pertain solely to the reality of his flesh.

Thus, according to his soul alone, he descended to the underworld. For during that one and the same interval which is found to separate Christ’s death from his resurrection, the one and the same Christ truly lay in the tomb according to the reality of his flesh, and truly descended to the underworld according to the reality of his rational soul. Accordingly, according to the truth of his human nature, from the moment when Christ, hanging on the cross with bowed head, gave up his spirit until he rose from the dead after receiving his spirit again, he was not where he was according to the flesh also where he was according to the soul. According to the flesh he lay dead in the tomb; according to his rational soul he descended to the underworld; but according to his divinity, by which he is one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the Immense One filled the whole creation. According to the flesh, therefore, he was so in the tomb alone that according to his soul he was in the underworld alone; but according to his divinity, which is enclosed by no place but is ineffably found wholly everywhere [variant: in both places], he did not abandon his flesh in the tomb, nor did he desert his soul in the underworld, just as he can never be absent from earth or from heaven.

The same Son of God who lay in the tomb according to the flesh and descended to the underworld according to his soul alone—for he himself had said of his soul, “I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again” (John 10:18)—after he had laid down his soul and taken it up again, ascended into heaven according to his entire humanity and sits at the right hand of the throne of God, as the evangelist Mark testifies, saying: “The Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God” (Mark 16:19).

All these things, then, which took place temporally in the Only-Begotten God—some according to his soul alone, some according to his flesh alone, and some according to soul and flesh together—are rightly referred to the one person of divinity and humanity existing in the Son of God; yet they cannot in any way be referred to his divine substance. Accordingly, none of these things can be attributed to the person of the Father or of the Holy Spirit, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not one person.

Nor can anyone attribute the Passion or the assumption of flesh to the Father or to the Holy Spirit, because it is impious to proclaim the divine nature changeable or capable of suffering in any respect. According to that nature Christ remained eternally begotten from the Father without beginning, when he received the beginning of his conception and birth from his mother; he was incomprehensible when he permitted himself to be comprehended; impassible when he experienced the insults of the Passion; immortal when he was subject to death; undivided when, according to the flesh, he lay in the tomb and, according to the soul, descended into the lower parts of the earth; and immeasurable when he ascended from the lowliness of this earth to the height of heaven.

## CHAPTER XXI

If wretched Fastidiosus had not denied this faith, he would undoubtedly not have perished. But since he denied it both by his deeds and by his words, it is not surprising that he became utterly wicked in conduct, already perverse in speech, and, walking in darkness, proved himself an enemy of the light. Bodily fornication, which first possessed his mind and flesh, subsequently drew him headlong into spiritual fornication. For he took the members of Christ and made them members of a prostitute. Therefore he did not hesitate to lose the chastity of faith, because he did not grieve that he had lost the chastity of the body.

See how great an evil is the lust of the flesh, which was able to lead that wretched man all the way to denial of the truth! This, this was the storm that snatched the chaff from the Lord’s threshing floor and fastened it among the thorns of heretical impiety. It made him speak against his own conscience and engage in perverse speech to the dishonor of the Trinity. For he did not truly believe what he said; rather, already double-minded, he preferred to say something other than what he believed. Possessed by that despair, he wished to remove the hope of forgiveness from himself so that he might freely fulfill the pleasures of lust.

Thus, from the mouth by which he ought to have been justified, he received an increase of condemnation, when his tongue, which ought to have uttered words of repentance, uttered words of blasphemy. Wretched Fastidiosus therefore preferred to go where he could both bark against God with sacrilegious shamelessness and, since he had no fear of God, fear no human being in his fornications. Woe to that wretched man, who wished to be deprived of ecclesiastical fellowship for this purpose: that he might never be free from punishment; and who wished to sin without any fear for this purpose: that he might deserve to burn without end.

## CHAPTER XXII

Where are those two years which Fastidiosus regarded as happy, because he spent them, as he wished, in lustful fornication? How quickly they passed! Even if they had been not merely two hundred but two thousand, they would have passed just as quickly. What will the wretched man do when he comes before the judgment of the one whom he denied? What will he receive in return for such deeds and words? What will that man receive—lustful in body, blind in heart, blasphemous in error—who first violated within himself the temple of God through fornication and then departed, separated from the Church even in body? What will he receive from that holy Trinity, since he preferred to be a servant of lust and unbelief? What indeed, except eternal fire, which is known to have been prepared for such deeds?

In this present time Fastidiosus’s fornication quickly came to an end; yet his eternal burning in that fire will not end. Let Christians therefore flee both kinds of fornication into which wretched Fastidiosus fell, so that, guarding their souls, they may preserve chastity both of heart and of body. Let them hold fast to the faith within the catholic Church. Let them believe and confess the inseparable and undivided Trinity, which in its divine nature contains nothing made and nothing begun in any respect, and by whose one and inseparable work all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, were made.

Let them likewise believe and confess the Only-Begotten God, born from the Father alone according to his true divinity, created from the Virgin alone according to his true humanity; and therefore, by the work of the Trinity, flesh and a rational soul were assumed for the salvation of the world in the unity of one person. Holding this most firmly, let them advance and persevere in good works. For in Christ Jesus only the faith that works through love has value (Gal. 5:6); whoever departs from it will be answerable for his own soul. But everyone who perseveres in it to the end will be saved (Matt. 10:22).

[Col. 0527C]

# TWO BOOKS OF SAINT FULGENTIUS, *ON THE REMISSION OF SINS*, TO EUTHYMIUS. (C)

## BOOK ONE

360

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0527D]

I cannot express in words, dearest Euthymius, how greatly I rejoice with you in your devotion: not only because, while residing in your home, you devote your mind to the heavenly Scriptures, but also because you diligently frequent the holy church, so that while your bodily external hearing is struck by divine utterances, the inward affection of your soul may be nourished.

For it is recognized as a work of divine grace that in the house of God you spiritually enjoy the conversation of those whom you know to burn with love for the divine law; and that you do not take pleasure in useless conversation with certain people who gather for the living banquet of the heavenly word without deriving any benefit from it and, in accordance with the truthful statement of the accusing Apostle Paul, “turn away their hearing from the truth and turn instead to fables” (2 Tim. 4:4).

I would rightly call such people like those whose stomach, overcome by a deadly loathing, is found to take greater pleasure in hunger than in food. For this reason they see the medicinal riches set before them in vain; while they refuse to receive them, they gain from them neither strength nor health. And in the physician’s house they disdain the spiritual antidote of healing offered to them, entering with their illnesses only to leave more seriously ill.

Yet the Lord is able to grant them delight in and knowledge of his word [Note: [Col. 0529D] Manuscript and printed editions read *verbi tui*, “of your word,” but this is plainly an error], so that they may be inflamed by examples of goodness. Warned by these examples, may they cast off the negligence of their delay and seek the attainment of salvation in the healing instructions of that physician himself, so that, with those who search out the testimonies of the Lord and seek him, they too may not cease seeking for their salvation what can be found by those who seek.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0529B]

The letter that you sent me, although it disclosed nothing unknown to us about your heart, nevertheless brought to our heart a great increase of joy in the Lord. For it is known to us that divine grace is mercifully at work in you, and that you often and earnestly think about the remission of sins. Nevertheless, I said that our joy had increased because you desire to obtain the remission of sins in such a way that you frequently and watchfully seek the effect of that same remission.

You therefore say that a question has arisen among you. Although you yourself remember it, I nevertheless preferred to insert into this little work the words contained in your letter, set down in precisely the form in which you wrote them, so that you yourself may recognize them from your own dictation and, while anyone else who reads them is instructed through inquiry into the matter, may be more suitably prepared to understand the answer.

You ask, then, whether the Lord, creator of all things, forgives sins in this world only to those whom he wills, so that someone departs from this life released from them; or whether, by his omnipotence, he forgives those whose sins he did not forgive in the present world when they depart from the body before the day of judgment, or on that very day of the age to come. You surely remember that these are the words contained in your letter, as I have already said.

## CHAPTER III

In resolving this question, I see that you request the opinion of our littleness. I therefore hope in the abundance of God’s goodness—by which he is always so rich that from it our poverty too may be enriched, and from which he gives to others as much as he wills while remaining himself in it more fully—that he will graciously pour into our heart such things as it may benefit us to say and you to hear.

For the discourse that we minister to you by God’s grace benefits us also if we inwardly hear, meek and humble, what we outwardly say to you for your salvation in word and writing. The most holy David does not say in vain: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me” (Ps. 84:9). This hearing properly belongs to the humble. Therefore the same prophet says elsewhere: “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the humbled bones will rejoice” (Ps. 50:10).

Elsewhere Majesty itself speaks thus: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). Yet the Spirit of God does not rest upon the humble and quiet in such a way that he does not himself make him quiet and humble, but as though he found him already humble and quiet in order to rest upon him. He graciously rests upon the humble and quiet because he makes quiet and humble the one upon whom he rests.

The Holy Spirit therefore works this: he drives out the vice of pride and restlessness from the person in whom he rests. Thus, as the operation of the Holy Spirit anticipates and mercifully changes the human will, the remission of sins freely granted loosens every bond of past human iniquity.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0530B]

We are not therefore discussing a small matter, nor seeking something insignificant, when, as far as divine generosity assists us, we discuss the remission of sins. Through it those whom God transfers into the kingdom of his beloved Son are snatched from the power of darkness (Col. 1:13). Through it they are freed from eternal punishment so that they may possess eternal joy. Through it the burden is laid down, whether it was brought by a corrupt birth or added by the iniquity of a corrupt youth [Note: [Col. 0530D] The manuscript reads “of one living corruptly”].

Through it Christ refreshes those who labor and are burdened when they come to him, placing upon them the gentle [variant: light] yoke and light burden of his love (Matt. 11:28). Through it the ungodly is freely justified [variant: “will be justified”], so that his faith may be reckoned as righteousness. Through it he is freed from the evil life in which he had been entangled and freely receives the good life of which he was unworthy.

Through it he is enabled thereafter to walk in a good life [Note: [Col. 0530D] The manuscript reads “in a good way”], enlightened by the gift of preceding mercy, and, led along in it, to persevere through the gift of accompanying mercy. Thus the undeserved grace of living well begins in a person through the remission of sins and completes what it begins through the granted virtue of perseverance.

Through the remission of sins, human beings are freely separated from those who will be tormented eternally with the devil and joined to those who will reign without end with Christ. Finally, such is the remission of sins that for its sake the Only-Begotten became man, and for its sake his blood was shed.

One of these truths was disclosed by the voice of an angelic vision; the other the Lord himself indicated. When Mary his mother had been betrothed to Joseph and, as the evangelist testifies, before they came together she was found to have conceived from the Holy Spirit, the angel announced the cause of that conception—unknown to Joseph—in these words:

“Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife; for that which has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:18 and following).

What else is it to save from sins except to forgive sins? For our Savior himself, who came to save what had perished (Matt. 18:11), testifies that he came for this purpose: to call sinners to repentance.

## CHAPTER V

The chief benefit of this call to repentance is the freely given remission of sins. For its sake our same Redeemer, after the banquet of the Paschal supper had been completed, declares that his blood is to be poured out:

“Drink from this, all of you. For this is my blood of the new Testament, which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. 26:28).

363

I think that everyone—or nearly everyone who is called Christian in any way—desires to obtain this remission. But it matters where, when, and how each person seeks it. For no one can attain the remission of sins if he either does not hold the true faith, neglects the duty of good works, or, preoccupied by a deadly vanity, despises the divinely granted time in which the good work of right belief may be performed.

These three things—faith, works, and time—are so necessary to human beings together in this life that if any one of these three is lacking for anyone in the present world, that person cannot share in eternal life. Accordingly, he will not obtain the remission of sins, through which one reaches the reward of eternal life. With the Lord’s help, we must demonstrate this by the testimony of the divine testimonies.

## CHAPTER VI

Above all, therefore, we must hold with firm faith that the Lord our God is merciful and just. From this it can readily become clear to those who inquire to whom, where, and when God forgives sins. Once these matters are known, no one should retain a perverse opinion about God, neglect his conversion, or depart from the catholic Church. If anyone has departed, let him return quickly. Nor should anyone wish to flatter himself with foolish speculation about the time, thinking that if he refuses to turn to God in this life and serves iniquities until death, he will obtain the remission of sins after this life, when, already condemned by the time of tribulation [possibly: retribution], he will no longer be able to avoid sin by converting, but will remain condemned to eternal punishment.

By many and varied deceptions the devil attempts to block and conceal the way of the heavenly journey. His unceasing aim is, insofar as he can, either to drag a crowd of wretches into fellowship with his torments by enticement or to compel them unwillingly.

He causes some, having cast aside consideration of divine justice, to think only of God’s mercy, so that they neglect their conversion, believing that even if they lead a criminal life to the end, they will obtain the benefit of forgiveness. Others he either compels or entices, abandoning the embrace of the catholic Church, to pass over into heresies or schisms through the blindness of a corrupted heart.

He ensnares their minds by the deception of a false promise, so that they either think they are supported by correct doctrine or hope that the benefit of forgiveness will be theirs solely because of their belief in their hearts, even if, with a feigned motive, whether for convenience or fear of the present time, they remain bound until death in the deadly fellowship of heretics. They pay too little attention to the saying of our Savior:

“Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven; and whoever denies me before men, I too will deny him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:32).

And elsewhere:

“Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his majesty, and that of the Father and of the holy angels” (Luke 9:26).

But the enemy of the human race contrives to thrust the remembrance of their sins upon many sinners for this purpose: either to cast the despair of forgiveness upon those whose hearts have been hardened and exclude them from the remedy of conversion. He always carries out all these fraudulent actions under cover of deception for no other reason than to take away the time in which forgiveness can be granted to those who turn back. Thus, as far as his malignity is concerned, if it were possible, no one would attain salvation.

For he knows that God is merciful and just, and he does not fail to understand that true conversion of heart can obtain the remission of sins from God alone. He also knows that sins can be forgiven to those who turn back nowhere except within the embrace of the Catholic Mother. Nor is he unaware that in the present world alone the remission of all sins can be granted to those who turn back: here the human race is not unjustly bound by the tie of carnal birth through the divinely established order of the death of those who pass away and the succession of those who are born, and is freely released through spiritual birth.

Here, too, every guilt is either dissolved by conversion or made insoluble, whether by neglect nourished through vain hope, or by the wickedness of a hardened heart strengthened by despair and retained to the end.

## CHAPTER VII

But now the urgency of the work undertaken compels me to teach fully, through a proper discussion and the testimony of the holy Scriptures, everything that I have stated above. Indeed, the truthful sequence of both Testaments does not leave unspoken anything that pertains to the advancement of human salvation, so that the contemptuous person who is to be condemned may have no excuse in the future.

Above all, therefore, every divinely inspired Scripture proclaims that the one true God alone—that is, the Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is as merciful as he is just. To him, in the person of the Church, it is said:

“I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1).

Of him it is also sung:

“The Lord is merciful and just, and our God will have mercy” (Ps. 116:5).

Elsewhere:

“For the Lord is just and has loved justice; his face has seen equity” (Ps. 11:7).

Again it is said:

“All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 25:10).

And again:

“For the Lord loves mercy and truth” (Ps. 84:11).

In the first commandment of the Decalogue the same Lord [variant: God] declares himself just and merciful in this way:

“I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, who returns the sins of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation, among those who hate me; and who shows mercy to thousands of thousands who love me and keep my commandments” (Exod. 20:5).

Therefore Moses says:

“The Lord God, forgiving and merciful, patient and of great mercy and true, preserving justice and mercy for thousands, taking away iniquities and injustices and sins; and he will not purify the guilty, bringing the sins of the fathers upon the children’s children to the third and fourth generation” (Exod. 34:6).

Through Isaiah also the Lord recalls his mercy and justice, saying:

“I am God, and there is no other besides me, just and saving; there is no other besides me. Turn to me, and you will be saved” (Isa. 45:21).

365

## CHAPTER VIII

By these and countless testimonies of this kind, in which the Lord our God is proclaimed merciful and just, it is shown how greatly his mercy should be loved and how greatly his justice should be feared.

For just as the merciful and compassionate Lord, patient, greatly merciful, and true, knows how to remove punishment from the one who turns back, so he absolutely does not allow sin to remain unpunished in the one who refuses to turn. Therefore, if pious divine goodness does not free certain people from the dominion of sin in the present world, just severity condemns those same people in the future.

For this reason the wicked are continually and beneficially warned by the divine utterances not to remain in slavery to sin but to seek the mercy of the just God while they are in this life. The good are also commanded (Ps. 2:11–13) to serve the Lord in fear and rejoice in him with trembling, and to embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry and they perish from the just way.

The same God, who is merciful and just, therefore warns that the wicked should fear and love him because of his justice and mercy, so that, when they turn back, they may escape the punishment threatened by justice and receive the forgiveness promised by mercy. In the same way he warns that the good should love and fear him because of justice and mercy, so that those who have become good through his preceding mercy may remain in good works through love of mercy and carefully guard themselves from sins through fear of justice. Instructed by consideration of their own weakness, they should never trust in their own powers but continually and humbly ask for the help of divine strength.

## CHAPTER IX

Both the good and the wicked must therefore love mercy as much as they fear justice. Otherwise the good, loving God’s mercy, may fail to fear his justice and fall into the snares of the deceiving devil; or the wicked, considering only the severity of justice, may fail to seek—when they can find it through conversion—the benefit of mercy, and thus, hardened, not only deny themselves the remission of sins but also never cease multiplying their sins.

By this two-headed snare the devil frequently captures the unwary: either, dulled by the vain hope of future forgiveness, they refuse to turn through fear of justice; or, despairing completely of forgiveness, they neglect conversion, loosen the reins to their iniquities, and, while despairing of indulgence, rush headlong into Gehenna.

Thus that crafty enemy of the human race casts some down through the rashness of despair, while he trips up others through the deception of a false hope.

For this reason blessed Paul (2 Cor. 13:3), in whom Christ spoke, writing to those who live well, commends their obedience in such a way that he commands such people to retain the caution of salutary action with fear and trembling. For he says to the Philippians:

“Therefore, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence [variant: ‘in the presence of me’], but much more now in my absence, work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will” (Phil. 2:12).

In these words blessed Paul certainly implies that God is just, since he commands the faithful to preserve fear and trembling in good works. He also proclaims him merciful, since he says that God works in them both the willing and the accomplishing, according to his good will. The good would not rightly fear him if he were not just; nor would he himself work in them every good desire and action if he were not merciful.

The Apostle Paul again impresses this fear of divine justice upon the just with a terrible warning, saying:

“Let the one who thinks he stands take care lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12).

And again:

“Brothers, if someone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted” (Gal. 6:1).

The apostles themselves are likewise warned of their own weakness by heavenly instruction, when [Note: [Col. 0533D] Perhaps the particle *cum*, which occurs in the printed editions and the manuscript, should more properly be deleted.] the vigilance of fitting fear is shown to be maintained in humility of heart, as the Lord says:

“Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41).

[Note: [Col. 0534D] The manuscript does not contain *est*, “is,” nor does the Gospel text. Antwerp has it.]

## CHAPTER X

Nevertheless, because everything contained in the divine utterances is spoken for the preservation or restoration of human salvation, the divine word took care that, while fear of divine equity was imposed upon the just, deadly despair should not arise in sinners if the hope of forgiveness were not also displayed.

For this hope calls the wandering back to the way of truth, promising that through divine favor whatever evil a person committed before turning will be forgiven once he turns. Therefore the Apostle Paul, in the Epistle that he wrote to the Romans, terrifies the faithful and good by bringing divine severity to their attention, but likewise invites the faithless and wicked to conversion with the most certain hope of heavenly goodness, so that the good may learn not to be high-minded but to fear, while the wicked may obtain the remedy of eternal salvation without any obstacle of doubt.

Blessed Paul therefore says:

“See, then, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness; otherwise you too will be cut off. And they, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in. For God is able to graft them in again” (Rom. 11:22–23).

Since the Apostle says that the one who does not remain in goodness will be cut off and that the one who does not remain in unbelief will be grafted in, what just person would not tremble and fear justice, or what wicked person would not, strengthened by God’s mercy, hasten to him?

[Note: [Col. 0535D] It was not possible to restore this passage, which is defective in several words, with the help of the printed editions or manuscript codices.]

[The text is defective:] “Who is not compelled—concerning any good of a wicked person, if he has turned with his whole heart—to dare to despair ...?” Since heavenly medicine, through salutary commands, provides equally for the healthy and the sick—imposing the fear of justice upon the former as the guardian of the salvation they have received, and promising the benefit of mercy to the latter, so that, lifted up by the remedy of hope, they may recover the health they had lost.

The fear of justice is commanded to the one who has been healed, to whom it is said:

“Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin anymore, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14).

Hope in mercy is also shown to the sick when it is said:

“Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick; I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke 5:32).

The prophetic word also does not cease to commend God’s mercy and justice, when God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel:

“If the wicked person turns away from all his iniquities that he has committed, and keeps all my commandments, and does justice and mercy, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of all his offenses that he has committed shall be remembered. In his justice that he has done, he shall live. Do I desire the death of the sinner by my will, says the Lord, rather than that he should turn away from his evil way and live?” (Ezek. 18:21).

Having shown the benefit of divine patience and kindness for turning the wicked to conversion, the prophetic word is directed also to deterring the just:

“But when the righteous person turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, according to all the iniquities that the wicked person has committed, none of all his righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered. In the offense by which he offended and in the sins by which he sinned, in those he shall die” (ibid. 24).

## CHAPTER XI

There are innumerable testimonies of the divine Scriptures in which God is proclaimed merciful and just. Nor does the entire text of the heavenly utterance do anything else except urge the wicked, through fear of God’s justice, promptly to put an end to evil deeds, and urge the good to remain carefully and humbly in good works.

Thus every wicked person, fearing God’s equity, may run to the mercy of just goodness, and every righteous person, rejoicing in God’s mercy, may not neglect the judgment of the most gracious equity. For where mercy and justice are perfect, the righteous cannot show favor to sins, nor can the merciful deny forgiveness to those who turn back.

From the fact, therefore, that God is proclaimed just and merciful, it is most readily understood [variant: “we understand”] that forgiveness of sins is granted only to those who turn back, and that the punishment of eternal condemnation is inflicted only upon those who persist in sin.

For this reason the Psalmist sings:

“Unless you turn back, he will brandish his sword; he has bent his bow, and he has prepared it, and in it he has prepared vessels of death” [Col. 0536A] (Ps. 7:13).

Through Isaiah, too, a similar sentence is found, issued by the divine mouth against the stubborn and those who despise divine clemency. From it we learn that no one obeys the divine commands fruitlessly and that no one remains in iniquities with impunity. Thus he says:

“Wash yourselves; be clean. Take away your wickednesses from your souls, from before my eyes. Cease from your evil ways; learn to do good. Seek judgment; rescue the one suffering injustice; judge for the orphan; justify the widow; and come, let us reason together, says the Lord. And if your sins are like scarlet, I will make them white as snow; but if they are like crimson, I will make them white as wool. And if you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land. But if you are unwilling and do not obey me, the sword shall devour you. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken this” (Isa. 1:16 and following).

I ask: who is so hard or altogether foolish that, in this discourse of heavenly admonition, if he is not invited to conversion by the pleasure of the promise, is not at least compelled by the terror of punishment? The contemptuous person of the divine word will not be spared by salvation; the sword will devour him.

For this reason it is shown elsewhere in the book of the same prophet that no one will reach salvation except through conversion. For it is said:

“If you turn back and groan, you will be saved” (Isa. 30:15, according to the Septuagint).

In this conditional testimony God uses both a command and a promise. By saying, “If you turn back and groan, you will be saved,” he shows that the promise of salvation depends entirely upon the condition of conversion.

This, then, is the condition between God and humanity: between the Lord who commands and the servant who asks; between the judge who does not grant mercy without justice and the sinner who awaits the mercy of the one who judges justly.

This Lord, merciful and just, severe and compassionate, therefore says: “If you do this, you will have this; if you keep what I command, I will give what you ask; I command you to turn back, and you ask salvation from me; if you obey the command, you will obtain the benefit; if I see that the orders have been carried out, I will grant what was requested: If you turn back and groan, you will be saved.”

## CHAPTER XII
When, therefore, it is said to the sinner who desires to receive the benefit of salvation that, “if he turns and mourns, he will be saved,” it is consequently understood that, EVEN IF HE MOURNS, [Col. 0536D] nevertheless, if he has not turned, he will not be saved. For the divine word did not embrace both conditions without reason, except that we should recognize these two things—namely, conversion and mourning—as necessary for attaining the result of salvation.

Some, terrified when they consider their crimes, indeed mourn in prayer over their iniquities, yet do not withdraw from sinful conduct. They confess that they have done wrong, but do not wish to put any end to their evil deeds. They humbly accuse before God the sins under whose burden they are oppressed, yet those same sins, which they accuse with humble speech, they stubbornly heap up in their perverse hearts. The pardon they seek with tearful groans they themselves [Col. 0537A] take away from themselves by their wicked deeds. They ask the physician for a remedy, and turn the aid into a means of their own destruction. Thus, with empty words they seek to appease the just Judge, whom their wicked deeds instead provoke to anger.

Such people never wash away their sin by mourning, because they do not cease to sin after mourning. They mourn for their crimes, and after mourning return to their crimes. Concerning such people, divine Scripture says in the book of Ecclesiasticus:

> He who is baptized by a dead person and again touches him, what benefit does his washing provide? So too, the person who fasts for his sins and again does the same things: what benefit does he gain by humbling himself? Who will hear his prayer? (Eccli. XXXIV, 30–31)

Most rightly, therefore, God says to the human being: “If you turn and mourn, you will be saved.” For with God, who is severe and good, the prayer of the mourner is heard, the tears of the petitioner are heeded, and salvation is granted to the one who weeps—if he has turned to God in the humility of a contrite heart. It is necessary that God, in mercy toward the sinner, forgive him, provided that the sinner, having turned, acknowledges his iniquity.

Finally, the holy David effectively found divine mercy for this reason: having turned in the humility of a contrite heart, he condemned what he had done wrong by acknowledging it, and did not delay in punishing through repentance the desire for the evil deed into which he had fallen. For if he did not punish that for which he was held guilty, he himself would undoubtedly be punished. Having turned to repentance, he therefore acknowledged his crime; he feared that, if condemned, he would come to recognize its punishment. In repentance he himself took vengeance upon himself by acknowledging what he wished the Lord to forgive him.

Thus, after saying:

> Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy,  
> and according to the multitude of your mercies blot out my iniquity;  
> wash me more and more from my injustice,  
> and cleanse me from my sin (Ps. L, 1–2),

he immediately added:

> For I acknowledge my iniquity,  
> and my sin is always before me (ibid., 4).

He acknowledged his iniquity, not in order to increase it by sinning, but in order to wash it away through repentance; and so true conversion removed the dominion of sin, which guilty pleasure had introduced. And because David, having turned, mourned with his whole heart, he was immediately saved. Thus in him was fulfilled what is commanded through the prophet: “If you turn and mourn, you will be saved.”

## CHAPTER XIII

Conversion, moreover, is commanded both from ungodliness and from iniquity. For each provokes the wrath of God against itself, since God abhors and condemns both. Paul says:

> For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of human beings (Rom. I, 18).

Solomon also says—and blessed Peter incorporated the same words into his own preaching:

> If the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear? (Prov. XI, 31, according to the Septuagint; I Pet. V, 18)

Therefore the Vessel of Election, who was full of divine charity, just as he was shaken by great sorrow and anguish of heart on behalf of those who were sinning in the faith, so also testified that he mourned over those who, established within the Church, were living shamelessly and luxuriously without doing penance.

Concerning the Jews, whom the ungodliness of an unbelieving heart possessed, he says:

> I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me in the Holy Spirit: I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart. For I myself wished to be accursed and separated from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites (Rom. IX, 1–4).

But concerning those who, placed within the Church, persisted in evil deeds, he speaks to the Corinthians in medicinal language:

> Lest, when I come again, God humble me before you, and I mourn over many of those who sinned previously and did not repent of the impurity, fornication, and shamelessness that they committed (II Cor. XII, 21).

The Apostle would not have been sorrowful over the former or grieved in humiliation over the latter if he had believed that forgiveness was to be granted without conversion of heart to the ungodly and unrighteous who provoke divine justice. For forgiveness of sins itself takes effect only in conversion of heart—among those, that is, who, now exercising the freedom of their own will and having been turned by the aid of the divine gift so that their life is changed for the better, do not cease to hasten to seek forgiveness for sins whose commission either ignorance led them into unwittingly or, worse, the obstinacy of their will enticed them into knowingly.

For this reason the Prophet prays to God:

> Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances [or: my acts of ignorance] (Ps. XXIV, 7).

And our Savior says:

> The servant who does not know his master’s will and does unworthy things [or: things deserving of blows] will receive few blows; but the servant who knows his master’s will and does unworthy things will receive many blows (Luke XII, 47).

[Note: [Col. 0537D] Thus in the manuscript. The word “blows” is absent from the printed editions. But the Gospel text reads somewhat differently, namely: “doing things deserving of blows, he will receive many blows.”]

Accordingly, the Apostle also confesses that he sinned in ignorance, in these words:

> I give thanks to him who strengthened me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he considered me faithful and appointed me to the ministry—though previously I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man. But I obtained mercy because I acted in ignorance, in unbelief (I Tim. I, 12–13).

[Note: [Col. 0538D] The alternative reading is “in Christ”; the manuscript omits “in,” as does the Apostle’s text itself.]

Therefore, lest anyone flatter himself on account of ignorance, the Apostle’s statement must be considered. He declares that he acted in ignorance, but nevertheless does not deny that he sinned; indeed, he says that he was the first of all sinners (ibid., 15)—first, that is, not in the passage of time, but in the excess of iniquity. He therefore obtained mercy so that, once enlightened, he might recognize the sins he had committed in ignorance and immediately renounce them through conversion.

This happens so that, as the apostle James teaches us, we may recognize that every good gift and every perfect gift descends from above, from the Father of lights (James I, 17). When God finds in the sinner something for which he ought justly to be condemned, he himself freely grants conversion to the sinner, through which the torments of just condemnation may be removed.

## CHAPTER XIV

In every sinner, therefore, who now exercises the freedom of his own will, the benefit of the divine gift begins through conversion of heart. As for infants, we know that they are saved not by their own will but by the right faith of the faithful who confess on their behalf. For it accords with the judgment of truth that infants should be absolved through another’s confession, since it is established that they are bound by another’s iniquity: by the spiritual confession of others they receive the benefit of justification, while through the carnal generation of others they bear original sin. And just as the carnal intercourse of their parents harmed them at their first birth, before they were born and while they had done nothing, so, while they themselves are unaware, the spiritual affection of the faithful who confess on their behalf benefits them at their second birth.

As far as those are concerned who can now give an account of their own actions, no one will become blessed unless, renouncing evil deeds, he turns to God with complete humility of heart. For:

> Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven,  
> and whose sins have been covered (Ps. XXXI, 1).

Whoever, therefore, bears the iniquity of his own will and conduct cannot receive any blessedness unless he turns to the one who bestows blessedness.

## CHAPTER XV

The heart is blinded by sins, but by forgiveness it is enlightened. For just as being blinded is nothing other than being deprived of light, so the eye that has been healed lacks the defect of blindness to the extent that it is able to possess the sight of light. Yet that eye will in no way be able to see the light unless the light pours itself into it. Through the infusion of light, therefore, the eye can receive the vision of light.

So too, when forgiveness of sins is given to human beings, the blindness of the heart is undoubtedly driven away, so that the light of righteousness may be seen by the inner eye. But how can the darkness of shadows be removed if the infusion of light is not granted? God therefore infuses the light of true conversion into those whose sins he forgives.

[Note: [Col. 0539D] The alternative reading is “of confession”; but the reading we have substituted from the manuscript is better and more appropriate to the context.]

Accordingly, just as no blind person can see light as long as he is blind, so no unrighteous or ungodly person receives forgiveness of sins unless, preceded by the gift of gratuitous justification, he turns to God with his whole heart. For the effect of forgiveness itself consists in conversion of heart. But to one who is not granted the grace of conversion, forgiveness of sins is not given.

For what else is it to obtain forgiveness of sins than to be freed from the dominion of sin? For, as the Truth says:

> Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin (John VIII, 34).

How, then, is one believed to attain the splendid gift of liberation who is not free from the most hideous slavery of sin?

For this reason, we have learned from the Teacher of the Gentiles that the condemnation of those who say, “Let us do evil so that good may come” (Rom. III, 8), is just. From his preaching we have likewise heard:

> Neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God (I Cor. VI, 9–10).

The same outstanding teacher also warns the Galatians:

> The works of the flesh are manifest. They are fornication, impurity, lust, the service of idols, sorcery, hostilities, rivalries, anger, quarrels, dissensions, heresies, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not attain the kingdom of God (Gal. V, 19 and following).

Because God is just, therefore, as long as such people continue to do these things, they do not attain the kingdom of God. But because that same God is merciful, the wicked will undoubtedly attain the kingdom of God if they cease doing the things by which they stubbornly provoke God, and, humbled and corrected, turn to God. For just as the work of justice is not overcome, so the work of mercy is not removed. And therefore God arranged possession of his kingdom in such a way that, because he is just, he does not give it to the ungodly and unrighteous; but because he is merciful, he does not deny it to anyone who truly turns.

## CHAPTER XVI

Conversion is then proved genuine in a person if ungodliness and iniquity are driven from the heart. Nevertheless, the following distinction is usually made between ungodliness and iniquity: ungodliness either holds a perverse belief concerning God or holds none at all, whereas iniquity pollutes life through evil conduct.

Ungodliness blasphemes God; iniquity harms one’s neighbor. Ungodliness, measuring—or perhaps: falsely measuring—the Most High by the humility of the flesh, strives to proclaim the invincible mystery of piety as an insult to the divine nature; or it denies that God, the Son of God, was conceived and born in human flesh, assigning to the true God not the reality of flesh but merely the appearance of a false vision; or it confesses that Christ’s flesh came from the flesh of the Virgin while denying that he was conceived in the taking on of flesh; or impiously declares the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be one and the same person by confusion; or introduces different natures for the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit through perverse separation; or does not believe that the flesh of the Son of God was taken from the flesh of the Virgin Mary, but confidently asserts that it was brought down from heaven; or wishes to subtract something from Christ’s human nature, denying that the Only-Begotten God, having assumed human flesh, also received a rational soul—that is, a complete human soul.

It is a crime of ungodliness if anyone says that not every spiritual and bodily nature was created good by God, but instead wishes to assign a substance proper to evil. For all evil exists not from the origin or condition of natural property, but arises from the defect of voluntary thought—not because a good nature receives an evil nature, since there is no evil nature, but because, abandoning the order of love, the rational creature, which was made for love of the Creator, despises the Creator and clings either to created things or to false thoughts. Thus it becomes worse, preferring temporal things to eternal, low things to high, and mutable things to immutable.

Likewise, those who say that the righteous and the unrighteous should be judged not according to the difference of their works but according to their communion in the sacraments, wishing that it benefit no one to live justly among the unjust in the Catholic Church—as though eternal retribution, whether punishment or kingdom, were to receive each person not according to the quality of his conduct but according to his sacramental association—are guilty of the same error.

These matters, therefore, which we have explained above, and many others that heretics and schismatics advance against the Catholic and apostolic faith, are assigned to the vice of ungodliness. Their very separation reveals them as ungodly, making them not companions but adversaries of the ecclesiastical body.

For they would not be separated in body and place from the gathering of ecclesiastical unity unless they had first departed—or perhaps: fallen away—from ecclesiastical faith in their corrupted heart. Nor would they be separated by open ungodliness from the lawful marriage of the word of God unless they had conceived treacherous and perverse thoughts through the adulterous seed of diabolical defilement. Fostering these wickedly with inward assent, they later give birth to them through abominable speech, so that, in the likeness of vipers, they perish when torn apart by their own offspring.

For giving birth to vipers is equivalent to perishing. Their young, as is said, emerge into the light after tearing apart the womb in which they were conceived, and thus bring death upon their parents. Therefore, whenever any ungodly perversity is conceived either through assent or is brought forth through profession, it destroys the soul by eternal death. The soul, consenting to corruption, is for that reason swollen by the inward conception of unbelief, so that later, broken open by its own birth, it dies.

The apostolic authority describes such people in these words:

> Just as Jamnes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth: people corrupted in mind and rejected with regard to the faith (II Tim. III, 6).

If anyone, therefore, arguing for doctrines contrary to the faith and separating himself from goodness, perversely resists ecclesiastical faith, he is undoubtedly called ungodly. But if someone perseveres within the body of Catholic unity, joined by communion in the sacraments, yet is devoted to wickedness and crimes, he is customarily called unrighteous, not ungodly. This is not our present subject of discussion. We say only this: not every unrighteous person is ungodly, although every ungodly person is unrighteous.

## CHAPTER XVII

That conversion, therefore, is pleasing and acceptable in God’s sight in which both the rectitude of faith is preserved and the rule of a good life is maintained—that is, in which a right judgment concerning God is held above all, and then the charity divinely commanded is shown toward one’s neighbor.

A person loves himself rightly when, devoted and humble, he places the love of God before himself. He also loves his neighbor if, as far as he can, he looks after his neighbor so that the neighbor may reach God through right faith and good conduct.

Charity toward one’s neighbor must be preserved in two ways: namely, that one neither inflict upon another anything one would not wish inflicted upon oneself, nor deny assistance through a good work to someone in need, insofar as one is able—for one would not wish such assistance denied to oneself if one were similarly in need.

Therefore we recognize that our Savior instructed us in this way, saying:

> Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them; for this is the Law and the Prophets (Matt. VII, 12).

Christ did not say, “Whatever people have done for you, do the same for them,” lest we think that evil should be repaid with evil to the one who has done us some harm, or think that a benefit should be denied to anyone from whom we know that no benefit has been given to us. A Christian ought to offer or repay benevolent assistance to every person, so that he may repay good with good and anticipate evil with goodness.

For the Lord says to us:

> Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and rains upon the just and the unjust (Matt. V, 44–45).

The good faithful suffer persecution not only from those who, positioned outside, oppose the doctrines of the Catholic Church with treacherous and perverse barking, but also from those who appear to be within the Church yet, living badly, are found to resist ecclesiastical tradition not in word but in deed. When the good see them, they groan deeply, and the good soul is tormented by a holy feeling when it cannot escape awareness of another’s perversity, even though it cannot give that perversity its assent.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Within the Catholic Church, therefore, in the present age, the righteous and the unrighteous are held mingled together—not by communion of conduct, but by communion of the sacraments; that is, by association in belief, not by similarity of life.

[Note: [Col. 0541D] The manuscript reads “the righteous and the unrighteous.”]

Not in heart, therefore, but in body—

[Note: [Col. 0541D] Thus one manuscript. Another manuscript and the printed editions read “not in body,” but incorrectly.]

—for by profession, not by conduct.

Now, therefore, as long as, according to the preaching of blessed Paul, in a great house there are not only vessels of gold but also of wood and earthenware, and some indeed for honor, others for dishonor—

[Note: [Col. 0542D] The alternative reading is “in honor, and some in dishonor”; but the manuscript reads “for honor … for dishonor,” in accordance with the text itself, Greek εἰς τιμήν, εἰς ἀτιμίαν (“for honor,” “for dishonor”), and the Vulgate version.]

—within the Church there are both the unrighteous and the righteous; outside the Church, however, there is no righteous person.

Within the Lord’s threshing floor also, while the dreaded coming of the Winnower is awaited and the final separation by winnowing is deferred, chaff is mixed with grain through local communion. But whatever place is outside the Lord’s threshing floor, even if the farmer’s name is spoken there, only chaff, carried away by the wind, can remain there.

Yet because the omnipotence of our Farmer is so great that no one can overcome his will, whoever in the present life, having turned, returns to the proper place of the Lord’s threshing floor, if he perseveringly maintains the purpose of a right faith and a good life, will not be chaff but grain. He will not be handed over to the fires to be burned, but will be gathered into the granary, enriched with fruits pleasing to God.

## CHAPTER XIX

In the Catholic Church alone, therefore, forgiveness of sins is given and received. The Bridegroom himself calls this Church his one dove, his one chosen one. He founded it upon the rock, gave it the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and granted it the power to bind and to loose, as the Truth himself truly promises blessed Peter, saying:

> You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven (Matt. XVI, 18–19).

Whoever is outside this Church, which received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, does not walk the way of heaven but of hell; he does not advance toward the dwelling of eternal life but runs toward the punishment of eternal death—not only if, remaining without baptism, he is a pagan, but also if, baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he perseveres as a heretic.

No one attains true life through the merit of baptism if, baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, whether within or outside the Church, he does not complete this life within the Catholic Church. Nor will he live through the sacrament of ecclesiastical baptism if he does not maintain communion in ecclesiastical faith and charity. The person is saved through the sacrament of baptism whom the unity of charity has preserved within the Catholic Church until the end of his present life.

## CHAPTER XX

But if someone baptized in the Church departs from it, or if someone baptized outside the Church in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is not restored to the Catholic Church before the end of the present life, he will not lack death, but [will lack] rest. For when the flood occurred, whoever did not enter Noah’s ark (Gen. VII, 21) was not saved from the flood but killed; he did not find salvation in the water but death.

That water, in which the sacrament of baptism was prefigured, raised to heaven those whom it found in the ark, suspending them above the earth; but it overwhelmed and killed the rest whom it found outside. And when Jericho perished, Jesus commanded that whoever was enclosed in the house of Rahab the prostitute be preserved unharmed (Josh. VI, 25); but the rest, whom that house did not contain, were consumed by a single destruction of death.

In that ark and in that one house, therefore, the same Church was prefigured. But in those who perished in the flood outside the ark, and in those who died by the sword outside that house, a mystery of twofold significance may be discerned.

For the present, insofar as I can see, I think it may reasonably be believed that in the sign of the flood the baptism of Christian confession was prefigured, so that we may recognize that heretics, if they remain outside the Church, merit punishment, not life, through baptism, and that those who deny Christ and depart from the Catholic Church will perish in eternal punishment.

Blessed Peter explains the sacrament of the ark in these words:

> In the days when the patience of God was waiting, while Noah was building the ark, in which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water; and now baptism, in the likeness of this, saves you also—not the removal of bodily filth, but the appeal of a good conscience toward God (I Pet. III, 20–21).

But where is there a good conscience except where there is also an unfeigned faith? For the apostle Paul teaches:

> The goal of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (I Tim. I, 5).

Why, then, did the water of the flood not save those placed outside the ark but kill them? Without doubt it prefigured every heretic who, although possessing the sacrament of baptism, is plunged into hell by those very waters by which the ark is lifted toward heaven. Their destruction through water arises for no other reason than that the bosom of the ark does not contain them; and in that bosom alone can anyone live who does not wish to perish in the life-giving waters.

## CHAPTER XXI

Blessed Cyprian, martyr, explains the mystery of this ark in his book *On the Simplicity of Prelates*, or rather, according to the ancient copies, *On the Unity of the Catholic Church*, writing:

> The Bride of Christ cannot commit adultery: she is incorrupt and chaste. She knows one house and, with chaste modesty, guards the holiness of one chamber. She preserves us for God; she assigns to the kingdom the children whom she has begotten. Whoever is separated from the Church and joined to an adulteress is separated from the promises of the Church. Nor will he reach the rewards of Christ who abandons [or: abandoned] the Church of Christ. He is alien, profane, and an enemy. He cannot have God as his Father who does not have the Church as his mother. Just as no one who was outside Noah’s ark could escape, so also whoever is outside the Church will not escape.

[Note: [Col. 0543D] The manuscript adds, “and, so to speak.”]

It is therefore certain, both from the preaching of blessed Peter the Apostle and from the exposition of the holy martyr Cyprian, that the ark of Noah was a figure of the Church and the waters of the flood a figure of baptism.

In the house of Rahab the prostitute also, which, when Jericho perished, was the only house that Jesus ordered to be preserved unharmed with all whom it contained, the Catholic Church from the Gentiles was signified, as it seems to me, in the sacrament of Christian confession. Having rejected the filth of her former fornication, she secretly received the two spies of Jesus: that is, either the chaste knowledge of the two Testaments or the love of God and neighbor. For the love of God and neighbor is proclaimed in those two Testaments, and the whole Law with the Prophets is understood to depend upon these two commandments (Matt. XXII, 40).

This woman, who had previously been an ungodly prostitute devoted to idols, became faithful and chaste when she received Jesus’ spies. Protecting them from their pursuing enemies, she did not crush them after placing them below, but secretly hid them after raising them into the upper room of her house.

The upper room is called a *solarium* because it is flooded with the light of the sun. But what is the sun of the human heart except the one of whom it was said through the prophet:

> For those who fear my name, the sun of righteousness will rise, and healing is in his wings (Mal. IV, 2)?

Concerning that rising sun, Zechariah prophesies in the Gospel:

> The dawn from on high has visited us, to illuminate those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death (Luke I, 78–79).

The prophet Habakkuk also proclaims Christ’s ascension and the firmness of ecclesiastical order under the name of the sun and moon:

> The sun was raised up, and the moon stood in its order (Hab. III, 11, according to the Septuagint).

The heart of every believer may appropriately be called a spiritual upper room, because it is healthfully illumined by the rays of that heavenly sun.

Rahab the prostitute, therefore, hid Jesus’ spies in the upper room of her house; that is, she held them in the innermost affection of an illumined heart, in the higher realm of spiritual knowledge, so that she might sing through the truth of her deeds that prophetic saying:

> I have hidden your words in my heart, so that I may not sin against you (Ps. CXVIII, 11).

True faith, which is proclaimed in the divine words, is not handed over to persecutors and is preserved inviolate and unharmed in the hearts of the faithful if the mind remains fixed not upon earthly, passing, and carnal promises but upon heavenly and spiritual ones, and does not contemplate what is seen but what is unseen. For, as the Apostle says:

> What is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal (II Cor. IV, 18).

But whoever holds the Christian faith for the sake of acquiring earthly and transitory possessions places Jesus’ spies not in the upper room of his house but in its lower parts. Once placed there, they can more easily be found and killed by enemies. Every persecutor and enemy of the Church spiritually kills them and inflicts upon them the destruction of eternal death when he finds their hearts entangled in earthly and passing things.

For while such people either fear losing earthly wealth or desire to acquire it, they do not hide Christ’s commandments—that is, Jesus’ spies—in the upper room of the heart, but hand them over to their pursuing enemies, terrified by fear or inflamed by the fire of depraved desire.

Nor do those who do not confess the sacraments of their faith but deny them have the scarlet cord hanging from the window of their house, by whose sign that house was saved. The scarlet cord signified the mystery of Christ’s blood. He has it hanging from the window of his house who, strengthened by faith against pagans or against any heretics under God’s protection, carefully guards his faith and confesses that he has been redeemed by Christ’s blood.

For this reason the Savior himself says:

> Whoever confesses me before human beings, I too will confess before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before human beings, I too will deny before my Father who is in heaven (Matt. X, 32).

Although the enemy persecutor tries to kill Jesus’ spies in the lower parts—that is, tries through earthly promises or terrors to weaken the strength of Christian faith—nevertheless, if someone has placed in the higher realm the faith of the Trinity, by which he believes the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be one God in substance, he will fear none of the persecutor’s dark errors [perhaps: terrors], nor any of the deceiver’s snares.

## CHAPTER XXII

Therefore, not only should those bound by the guilt of repeated baptism hasten back to the Church and entreat God with tears and almsgiving for so great a crime, but also those who, perhaps without repetition of baptism, have slipped into the deadly fellowship of heretics by denying the sacrament of the Catholic faith through the attraction of gifts or fear of punishments should recover the faith they denied and quickly return to the Church. Thus, when Jesus comes, they may be found within that house outside which no one can be freed from destruction.

For just as, in Jericho, no one who was outside that house could obtain any means of life, so outside the Catholic Church no one will receive forgiveness of sins. And just as within the Catholic Church one believes with the heart unto righteousness and confession is made with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. X, 10), so outside that same Church evil belief is not counted as righteousness but as punishment, and a perverse confession does not obtain salvation for the one who confesses it but brings death upon him.
