Outside this Church, neither the Christian name benefits anyone, nor does baptism save, nor is a pure sacrifice offered to God, nor is forgiveness of sins received, nor is the blessedness of eternal life found.

For there is one Church of Christ, one dove, one beloved, one bride. In it the Trinity is believed to be one God, of one nature and substance; in it no insult of diminution is inflicted upon either the Son or the Holy Spirit; in it one and the same worship and one honor are offered to the one Trinity, which is the true God.

This is the one true Church, which believes and proclaims one essence of the Trinity in such a way that, among the three, it does not dare to prefer one person to another. For it shows that it worships nothing different in the substance of divinity by confessing the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the Trinity itself—as one true and only God. Thus it neither falls into the error of Sabellian confusion under the name of unity, nor, under the term Trinity, fails to remember to avoid the deadly ruin of Arian diversity.

For, retaining the standard of apostolic preaching, it recognizes the Trinity in the persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and likewise proclaims the right faith in one God, because it proclaims a natural unity in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXIII

If any people are outside this Church, established in various errors, they will then receive forgiveness of sins if, while they are still in this world, they turn to that same Church with right belief and the humility of a contrite heart.

Therefore let them run, while there is time, to their lawful mother. Just as she carefully embraces and nourishes the children born from her own womb, so she not only does not reject those born from a servant woman when they return, but even seeks out the wandering with the tender mercy of her heart and, in accordance with her affection, continually invites them so that she may lead them into participation in their father’s inheritance.

For she does not consider in them the condition of the servant woman’s womb, but recognizes the reality of the father’s seed. What is the reality of the father’s seed except baptism received in the name of the Trinity? Wherever she finds this, she recognizes it as belonging to her own jurisdiction, like a lawful mother.

For, like Rachel (Gen. XXX), she knows how not only to bear children from her own womb but also, as a legitimate mother, to claim in her own name those born from a servant woman.

This is what they must do: they must not neglect to recover fraternal fellowship if they wish not to be deprived of the gift of their father’s inheritance. Therefore, abandoning heresy, let them quickly return to the Catholic Church. Let them neither doubt their possession of the inheritance nor despair of forgiveness of sins.

For whoever does not believe that all sins can be forgiven within the Catholic Church denies forgiveness of sins to himself if, persevering in the same hardness of an impenitent heart, he departs from this world alienated from ecclesiastical fellowship.

## CHAPTER XXIV
Therefore, he speaks a word against the Holy Spirit that is not to be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come (Matt. 12:32). For the love of God, which covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4:8), has been poured into our hearts, as the Apostle says, [Col. 0547B] through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5). Because this love preserves the uncorrupted fellowship of fraternal unity, it therefore covers a multitude of sins and does not allow those who persevere in unity with the surest hope to perish.

If, then, someone holds the faith that works through love (Gal. 5:6) and does penance for any former error in such a way that neither the fellowship of error holds him any longer nor the deadly chain of despair binds him, he will be free from that word spoken against the Holy Spirit—a word that is not forgiven to the one who speaks it, either in this age or in the age to come. For by this word our Lord and Savior did not suggest that certain sins would be forgiven in the age to come which had not been forgiven in this age; rather, he showed those who understand correctly that, in the age to come, [Col. 0547C] only those sins will be forgiven that in this age have been forgiven to each person within the one true Catholic Church.

For to that Church alone the Lord granted the power of binding and loosing, saying: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). Therefore, whatever the holy Church has not loosed in this age remains so unloosed that it cannot in any way be loosed even in the age to come. Every person whom the Church has not loosed is bound; nor will anyone obtain the benefit of release who, without turning to the penance to be given in the Church, has hoped for the forgiveness of sins.

Thus he speaks the unforgivable word against the Holy Spirit who, despising the riches of God’s goodness, patience, and long-suffering, [Col. 0547D] in accordance with his hardness and impenitent heart stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each person according to his works (Rom. 2:4).

## CHAPTER XXV

For whether it is love, and that from a pure heart [Note: [Col. 0547D] The manuscript and edition read *et ea de corde puro*, “and that from a pure heart.” But the manuscript has, corrected by another hand, *exeat de corde puro*, “let it proceed from a pure heart.”], or the communion of fraternal unity, or the paternal possession of the heavenly inheritance, all these consist in the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Concerning love, the Doctor of the Gentiles says: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). He likewise commends the Spirit’s unity together with this love, saying: [Col. 0548A] “Therefore I, a prisoner in the Lord, urge you to walk worthily of the calling to which you have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love (variant: ‘with love,’ *cum caritate*), eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:1–3).

He also confirms that the communion itself is that of the Holy Spirit, saying: “May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Cor. 13:13). Concerning our inheritance he likewise says: “You have been sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance” (Eph. 1:13–14).

The blessed Apostle also assigns to the Holy Spirit hope itself, which drives out the vice of despair, saying: “May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy [Col. 0548B] Spirit” (Rom. 15:13).

Therefore, he will obtain an everlasting share in the heavenly inheritance who, preserving the unity of fraternal love within the Catholic Church, lays aside the deadly hardness of an impenitent heart before bringing his present life to an end, and does not despair that, in the one and truly Catholic Church, forgiveness of all sins is given through the Holy Spirit to those who turn back.

[p. 380] Our Savior himself also showed this. After he had risen, he breathed upon the disciples and granted them the gift of the Holy Spirit; he also gave them the power to forgive sins, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone’s sins, they will be forgiven; if you retain them, they will be retained” (John 20:22–23).

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Col. 0548C] Let those, therefore, who have been separated from the Catholic Church and are held fast in the error of any heresy or schism not close the door of forgiveness against themselves through deadly despair. Let them lay aside the hardness of their hearts, if they do not wish to be tormented by endless evils. For it is written: “A hard heart will fare badly at the end, and whoever loves danger will perish in it” (Ecclus. 3:27).

What, indeed, is more dangerous than refusing obedience to the divine words and scorning the will of the God who calls? For in the Book of holy Job, just as glorious eternity is promised to those who turn back, so the gifts of salvation are denied to the wicked because they do not obey. For it is written: “Those who turn from iniquity, if they listen and observe, they will complete their days in good things and their years in glory. But he does not [Col. 0548D] save the impious, because they refused to know God and, when warned, were disobedient” (Job 36:11 and following).

Let them not, therefore, despise the time granted for obedience, but return to the Catholic Church, in which alone, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, love covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4:8).

If there are also people in the Catholic Church who live wickedly, let them hasten, before ending this life, to depart from their evil way of life. Let them not think that the Catholic name is sufficient for salvation if they do not do the will of God. For our Savior says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of [Col. 0549A] my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:19).

For it is also written in the Book of Psalms: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth; he will do the will of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayers and save them” (Ps. 144:18–19).

For this reason, in Proverbs each of us is commanded both to fear the Lord and to turn away from evil. There it is said: “Fear the Lord and turn away from every evil, and there will be peace for your body and care for your bones” (Prov. 3:7–8).

And in the Book of Ecclesiasticus, each believer is likewise admonished not to do evil: “Do not do evil, and evil will not overtake you. Turn away from the wicked, and evils will turn away from you. Do not sow evil in the furrows of injustice, and you will not reap it sevenfold” (Ecclus. 7:1–3).

Again, in the same book, lest anyone, [Col. 0549B] adding sins to sins, seek to flatter himself with a vain thought about God’s mercy, salutary teaching responds in these words: “Do not add sin upon sin, and say, ‘God’s mercy is great.’ For mercy and wrath are with him, and his wrath will look upon sinners” (Ecclus. 5:5–7).

And again holy Job said: “Is there not destruction for the wicked, and alienation for those who practice iniquity?” (Job 31:3).

It is written in Proverbs: “His iniquities will capture the wicked, and each person is bound by the cords of his sins. He dies with the undisciplined; [p. 381] he has been cast out from the abundance of his life and perishes through folly” (Prov. 5:22–23).

## CHAPTER XXVII

And lest anyone think that any human sins can remain hidden [Col. 0549C] from God, let us be instructed by the words of holy Job, who says: “You have counted my thoughts, and none of my sins was hidden from you. You have sealed up my iniquities as in a bag; you have noted if I have sinned unwittingly” (Job 14:16–17, according to the Septuagint). [Note: [Col. 0549D] One manuscript omits *quasi* (“as if”), and it is not read in the Septuagint; but it is found in another manuscript and in the editions.]

And lest anyone think that he will go unpunished if he refuses to turn back, let him listen attentively to the words of the same holy man, who says: “Rather, let no one who is wicked trust that he will go unpunished, whatever he may do in anger to provoke God, as though there were to be no inquiry concerning him.”

For this reason, a salutary admonition is drawn from Ecclesiasticus: let us lack neither conversion, by which sins are avoided, nor prayer, by which past sins can be forgiven. For it says: “My son, have you sinned? Do not do so again; but pray also concerning your former sins, that they may be forgiven you. Flee from sins as from the face of [Col. 0549D] a serpent. If you approach them, they will receive you, and like a lion’s teeth they will kill you as they devour” (Ecclus. 21:1–2).

Nor is this left unsaid: the impious and sinners who refuse to do penance for their impiety or iniquity are destined at the end for eternal punishments, while our Lord grants mercy to those who have done penance. For in the Book of Ecclesiasticus it is written: “For the Most High has also had mercy on the penitent, but he will repay the impious and sinners with vengeance” (Ecclus. 12:7).

Again, in the same volume it says: “Remember that wrath will not delay. Humble your spirit greatly, for the vengeance of the impious flesh [Col. 0550A] is fire and the worm” (Ecclus. 7:18–19).

Isaiah also says: “For their fire will not be extinguished, and their worm will not die” (Isa. 66:24).

Again, it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “The assembly of sinners is a heap of gathered tinder, and their end is a flame of fire. The way of sinners is full of offenses, and at their end are the underworld, darkness, and punishments” (Ecclus. 21:10–11).

## CHAPTER XXVIII

This is the death that will receive those who live according to the flesh, as the holy preaching of blessed Paul testifies when he says [Note: [Col. 0550D] One manuscript reads, “as he writes.”]: “Therefore, brothers, we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live” (Rom. 8:12–13).

A person follows the deeds of the flesh when he either obeys [Col. 0550B] worldly desires or wishes to remain captive in impiety, since spiritual teaching instructs us in nothing else than that, having renounced impiety, we should also lay aside worldly desires. The Doctor of the Gentiles expresses this in these words: “The grace of the Lord has appeared to all people, teaching us to renounce impiety and worldly desires and to live temperately, justly, and piously in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:14 and following, as cited in the source).

Therefore, [p. 382] the blessed hope, the certain expectation, and the future happiness belong to those who, renouncing impiety and worldly desires, have lived temperately, justly, and piously in this age.

Temperance, justice, and piety must consequently be guarded with the utmost care by Christians. [Col. 0550C] Whoever orders his conduct and his life guards temperance. He lives justly who inflicts no evil upon his neighbor and, insofar as he can, offers assistance in good works. He lives piously who neither believes nor says anything perverse about God.

Therefore, whoever wishes to reach the kingdom of heaven should live temperately in himself, preserve justice toward his neighbor, and persevere in piety toward God.

## CHAPTER XXIX

These things will benefit us in the future life only if they are possessed in the life of this present age. The blessed Apostle both knew and taught this when he commanded us to live temperately, justly, and piously in this age (above), teaching that those will obtain mercy at the judgment who before the judgment have lived justly [Col. 0550D] in this age.

For this reason, divine Scripture warns us beforehand in the Book of Ecclesiasticus, saying: “Before the judgment, prepare justice for yourself, and in the sight of God you will find reconciliation” (Ecclus. 18:19).

Therefore, whoever desires to find reconciliation in the sight of God must prepare justice for himself here. For whatever a person has not stored up for himself in the present age, he will not possess at the time of future recompense.

So that this may be demonstrated as fully as is sufficient by the testimonies of the divine Scriptures, let us now bring this book to an end, so that afterward we may give an appropriate beginning to the remaining part of the question.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0551]

383

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0551A] I am not unaware that at the beginning of the preceding book we undertook, in the name and with the help of God, to treat the question of the forgiveness of sins in such a way that the discussion begun would be divided into three parts.

For when we said that our Lord—that is, the true God—lacks neither mercy nor justice, a point that we also took care to demonstrate by the clearest testimony of the divine Scriptures, we said that the truth could more easily appear to those seeking it if they asked: to what sort of people does God forgive sins, where does he forgive them, and when does he forgive them?

Since I have now completed two parts of this threefold division, I know that I remain indebted for the third. To what sort of people God forgives sins and where he forgives them, and how much help God has granted us from his goodness, [Col. 0551B] I believe has been adequately shown in the preceding book.

For it is established [Note: [Col. 0551D] One manuscript reads *constitit* (“it has been established”) for *constat* (“it is established”).] that the forgiveness of sins is granted only to those who have turned back and are established within the Catholic Church. True conversion can exist there, where true faith is adorned by the accompaniment of holy conduct and the pursuit of good living is not stained by any corruption of perverse belief.

A life is not truly called good when it is deformed by the fault of perverse belief; nor is the faith of one who believes correctly sufficient for salvation if his conduct is disturbed by shameful morals and deeds. For just as blessed James proclaims faith without works dead (Jas. 2:17), so Paul confirms by his preaching that everything that is not from faith is sin (Rom. 14:23).

384

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0551C] Now, insofar as the help of illumination is granted to us by the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1:9), we undertake to show when the forgiveness of sins is given to those who do penance.

For fruitless penance will be deprived of the fruit of forgiveness if the opportunity of the time divinely granted is neglected. For this reason blessed Peter says: “The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some consider him to be delaying, but he patiently bears with you, not wishing anyone to perish, but all to turn to repentance” (2 Pet. 3:9). [Note: [Col. 0551D] So the editions, together with one manuscript. Another manuscript reads “they consider delay” (*tarditatem existimant*), instead of *tardantem existimant*, “they consider [him] to be delaying”, [Col. 0552D] in accordance with the Greek text βραδυῆτα (the supplied damaged form, evidently “slowness” or “delay”).]

I ask you, dearest Euthymius, not to be unwilling to weigh with attentive consideration how much force there is in this virtue of the apostolic statement. For what blessed Peter says—that God patiently [Col. 0551D] bears with us because he does not wish anyone to perish but wishes all to turn to repentance—must not be dismissed as something trivial.

Here repentance benefits the sinner: God does not hasten to condemn the sinner, so that he may grant forgiveness of sins to the person who has turned to repentance. For if repentance after this life could be fruitful in any degree for the wicked, blessed Peter would not have said that God patiently bears with them because he does not wish anyone to perish—namely, [Col. 0552A] those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. 8:29).

None of these perishes. And who can resist his will? These people are freely anticipated by the mercy of God before the end of their present life; with contrite and humbled hearts they are salutarily pierced with remorse, and all are turned to repentance by the divine gift. They have been divinely predestined to this repentance by gratuitous grace, so that, having turned back, they may not perish but may have eternal life.

Without doubt, these are all those whom God, according to the proclamation of blessed Paul, wishes to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4). For since he who wishes this is the one who has done everything whatsoever he has willed, he always accomplishes what he wills irresistibly.

What is fulfilled in them is what the will of almighty God possesses as immutable and irresistible. [Col. 0552B] Just as his will cannot be changed in its disposition, so his power in its operation is neither prevented nor hindered, because no one can justly reproach his justice, nor can anyone obstruct his mercy.

For this reason our Savior rebukes the hostility of the unbelieving city in these words: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you [Note: [Col. 0552D] One manuscript reads *lapidas eos missos ad te*: “and stone them, those sent to you.”], how often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you did not want it!” (Matt. 23:37).

Christ said this to show its evil will, by which it vainly tried to resist the irresistible divine will, since God’s good will can neither be overcome by those whom he abandons nor fail to accomplish anything that he wishes.

Therefore, that Jerusalem, as far as its will was concerned, did not want [Col. 0552C] its children to be gathered to the Savior; yet he gathered all those whom he wished. Thus it wished to resist the Almighty but could not, because God, who—as it is written—“has done everything whatsoever [p. 385] he willed” (Ps. 134:6), turns whomever he wishes to himself by gratuitous justification, anticipating with the gift of abundant grace those whom he could justly condemn if he wished.

Therefore, when the Apostle Peter says that God patiently bears with us, not wishing anyone to perish but all to turn to repentance (2 Pet. 3:9), let us not understand the word “all” as though there were no one who would fail to undertake repentance appropriately. Rather, here we must understand “all” to mean those to whom God grants repentance in this life in such a way that he also grants perseverance: that is, those who are converted by the [Col. 0552D] mercy of God going before them in such a way that, with the same mercy following after, they never return to the crimes they renounce.

These are the people to whom, as Paul says, God gives repentance for knowing the truth, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will (2 Tim. 2:25). Whoever takes care to do this repentance in this age will be able to find with God the fruit of his repentance.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0553A] Nevertheless, we read in the Book of Wisdom that some will indeed have repentance on the day of judgment, but will not receive forgiveness from God. The passage reads as follows:

“Then the righteous will stand with great confidence against those who afflicted them and took away their labors. Seeing them, they will be troubled with terrible fear and will be amazed at the suddenness of their unexpected salvation, saying among themselves with repentance and groaning in anguish of spirit:

‘These are the ones whom we once held in derision and made an object of reproach. We foolishly regarded their way of life as madness and their end as dishonorable. How have they been counted among the children of God, and how is their lot among the saints?’” (Wis. 5:1 and following).

When someone reads that the wicked “will be amazed [Col. 0553B] at the suddenness of unexpected salvation,” let no one suppose that those who end their present life in crimes will at some time receive unexpected salvation by a divine gift.

For it is the salvation of the righteous that is unexpected: although the wicked despair that it will be given, it nevertheless remains for the righteous who hope. Hence blessed David sang in one of the psalms of both the hope and the salvation of the righteous, saying: “The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord, and he is their protector in the time of tribulation. The Lord will help them and deliver them; he will rescue them from sinners and save them, because they have hoped in him” (Ps. 36:39–40).

This is why the wicked, who are destined for eternal torments, will say of the righteous: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and made an object of reproach. We foolishly regarded their way of life as madness and [Col. 0553C] their end as dishonorable.”

This is the unexpected salvation: they regarded the life of the righteous as madness; although they themselves were mad, they believed that they were sane. They did not expect a recompense of divine justice, and therefore they neglected to correct their way of life. For they delighted in living luxuriously here for a few days and did not believe that afterward they would be tormented by eternal punishments. [Note: [Col. 0553D] One manuscript reads *post modicum*, “after a short while,” rather than *postmodum*, “afterward.”] Therefore, when they see the righteous in that glory of the children of God of which blessed Paul says, “in which we stand and glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 5:2), the wicked will be amazed at the glory of the righteous—that is, of the children of [p. 386] God, because the righteous themselves are the children of God.

Therefore, the wicked, having fruitlessly repented because their repentance comes too late, and groaning in anguish of spirit, will say: “How have they been counted among the children of God, and how is their lot among the saints?”

The unexpected salvation—that is, salvation [Col. 0553D] not hoped for by the wicked—will therefore certainly be given to the righteous, not to the wicked. For it will not be given to those who live wickedly because they despair of it, but to those who, hoping for it in a good manner and abstaining from carnal desires, keep the salutary commands of blessed Peter, who says:

“Beloved, I urge you, as foreigners and pilgrims, to abstain from carnal desires, which wage war against the soul, and to maintain good conduct among the nations” (1 Pet. 2:11).

Through this good conduct the righteous present their bodies as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God (Rom. 12:1), because through good conduct [Col. 0554A] they are also the temple of God. The Apostle testifies that the faithful are this temple, saying: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16).

Lest this temple be polluted by evil works, he not only gives careful warning beforehand but also greatly terrifies our minds, saying: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him. For the temple of God is holy, and that is what you are. Let no one deceive himself” (1 Cor. 3:17–18).

Who, I ask, living wickedly, when he hears from the Apostle that if anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him, would dare, if he has not turned back in this present time, to promise himself any hope of future forgiveness? Who would not tremble and fall prostrate? Who would not, before the end of his present life, hasten in remorse and humility to repentance?

[Col. 0554B] The Apostle cries out: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him”; yet a vain man deceives himself with the most wicked thought, saying: “Even if I violate the temple of God and live wickedly to the end, I will be saved.”

Does the Apostle not speak of such people when he says that they say: “Let us do evil so that good may come”—whose condemnation is just (Rom. 3:8)? Are these not the people whom holy Scripture calls wretched and declares their hope altogether empty, saying: “Whoever adds wisdom and discipline is wretched, and their hope is empty and their labors fruitless” (Wis. 3:11)?

## CHAPTER IV

That salvation, therefore, will not be given to the wicked but to the righteous—namely, to those corrected and converted before the end of this life. [Col. 0554C] That salvation will be given to the good, who have hastened through conversion to friendship with God, not to the evil, who remain friends of the world and rightly deserve to be called enemies of God according to the Apostle’s rebuke.

For blessed James rebukes such people: “Adulterers, do you not know that friendship with this world is enmity toward God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be constituted an enemy of God” (Jas. 4:4).

Therefore, whoever, turning away from evil and doing good, has done penance for his iniquities in the present life and, converted to God, has renounced evil works with his whole heart, will not have a vain hope.

But whoever thinks that he will reach life by the broad and spacious way deceives himself in vain, since the Lord commands us to walk by the narrow way and shows us the [Col. 0554D] entrance of the narrow gate [p. 387] through which one comes to the kingdom. He says:

“Enter through the narrow gate. How broad the gate and spacious the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it! How narrow the gate and confined the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it!” (Matt. 7:13–14).

Our way is the present life. If someone placed in this life does not consent to the word of God, he will not receive forgiveness of sins; rather, he will mourn punishment without end amid weeping and gnashing of teeth [Note: [Col. 0553D] One manuscript reads, “eternal punishment without end.” The others [Col. 0554D] add *aeternum*, “eternal.”]. Nor will he undeservedly fail ever to be free from torment, since as long as he lived here he refused to renounce sin.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0555A] For this reason the Savior warns each of us, saying: “Come to an agreement quickly with your adversary while you are on the way with him, lest the adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be thrown into prison. Truly I say to you, you will not come out from there until you have paid the last farthing” (Matt. 5:25).

A person makes the word of God his adversary as long as he does those things that the divine word forbids. To him it is said in the psalm: “But you have hated discipline and cast my words behind you” (Ps. 49:17).

If someone does not quickly consent to this divine word on the way—that is, in this life—once he has been sent into the prison of eternal fire, he will have no further rest.

For this is a good adversary, who continually presses upon us with salutary opposition so that he may drive away from us the opposition of deadly iniquity.

Therefore, in another passage [Col. 0555B] divine Scripture urges us to turn back quickly, lest deadly delay bring forth for the one who postpones destruction rather than salvation. It says: “Do not delay in turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day, lest his anger come suddenly and destroy you at the time of vengeance” (Ecclus. 5:8).

The divine word clearly shows that when the time of vengeance arrives, conversion will no longer withdraw evil from punishment; rather, avenging wrath will destroy the sinner through deserved condemnation. For that time will not be a time of forgiveness but of recompense, not of indulgence but of vengeance.

This vengeance is delayed by divine long-suffering so that the number of the saints may be completed. Blessed John records in the Apocalypse that the saints asked for this vengeance; their words are: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you refrain from judging and from avenging our [Col. 0555C] blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” (Rev. 6:10).

And to show that the time of vengeance is delayed by heavenly ordination on behalf of those who are to be joined to their fellowship, he continues: “And a white robe was given to each of them, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be completed” (Rev. 6:11).

Blessed Paul also knew the distinction between the present age and the future. He knew that in the present it is possible to acquire the benefit of salvation, but that in the future each person would receive only the reward of justice according to the quality of his good or evil works.

Thus, after setting forth the prophetic testimony in which God says, “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (2 Cor. 6:2; Isa. 49:8), he immediately adds: “Behold, now is the [p. 388] acceptable time; behold, now is the day of [Col. 0555D] salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2).

Concerning the future he says: “For we must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what is proper to his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10).

## CHAPTER VI

Therefore, eternal life will not be granted in the future unless forgiveness of sins has been given in this age; nor will anyone receive forgiveness of sins here except the person who renounces his sins and hastens by true conversion of heart to the supreme and true God.

That time will not be a time of forgiveness but of recompense. There mercy [Col. 0556A] will not justify the impious; rather, justice will distinguish the righteous from the impious. For it is written in the psalm: “The Lord questions the righteous and the impious” (Ps. 10:6).

And to show that iniquity brings destruction to the soul, not salvation, it continues: “But whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul.”

Lest those who persist in iniquity to the end of their present life promise themselves any mercy, the psalm next speaks of God in this way: “He will rain snares, fire, sulfur, and the spirit of storms upon sinners; this is the portion of their cup. For the righteous Lord has loved righteousness; his face has seen equity” (Ps. 10:7–8).

Therefore, whoever hears these things and refuses in the present time to seek God’s mercy through conversion will never be able to find it in the future. For the just Judge commanded this to be announced to us through the blessed Apostle [Col. 0556B] James, who says: “Judgment without mercy awaits the one who has not shown mercy” (Jas. 2:13).

The order of mercy, however, requires that the mercy a person is commanded to show to another he first show to himself, as Scripture says: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30:24).

Therefore, if someone does not wish to please God, he denies mercy to his own soul; and whoever in the present age refuses to grant mercy to his own soul will in no way be able to find mercy with God. “Judgment without mercy awaits the one who has not shown mercy.”

Accordingly, what is said next—“But mercy triumphs over judgment” (Jas. 2:13) [Note: [Col. 0555D] One manuscript reads *misericordiam judicio*, “mercy” (accusative) and “to/over judgment” (dative), instead of *misericordia judicium*, “mercy” (nominative subject) and “judgment” (accusative object); the variant changes the grammatical construction.]—will be fulfilled in the person who now has mercy on his own soul, pleasing God.

For the Lord himself says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they will [Col. 0556C] obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7).

And since the blessed Apostle urges that everything be done decently and in order (1 Cor. 14:40), for which reason it is also said in the Song of Songs, “Set love in order within me” (Song 2:4), how can someone be said to preserve the order of love or mercy who—not to mention any other person—feeds his own body with food so that it does not fail; protects it with clothing so that it does not grow cold; while it is healthy, takes care lest it become ill; while it is ill, strives to make it well; continually supplies his flesh, with vigilant attention, the assistance of food, clothing, and medicines; yet by living wickedly brings destruction upon his soul?

He nourishes his flesh with necessary foods and kills his soul with evil deeds; he denies harmful foods to his flesh but supplies [Col. 0556D] evil works to his soul as deadly poisons; he desires to prolong the life of his flesh, which ends after a few days, but procures death for his soul, [p. 389] whose punishment will have no end.

Consequently, whoever is shown to hate his own soul is also found to be its cruel adversary. For just as good actions cause the flesh together with the soul to enjoy heavenly blessedness, so evil works cause the soul together with the flesh to be tormented in eternal fire.

Therefore, whoever lives wickedly and does not change his life before ending it is his own most destructive enemy.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0557A]

For the beginning of that life depends upon the end of this one—a life in which whatever is repaid does not come to an end. Now, since the Apostle John rightly says, “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” (1 John 3:15), and since holy David says, “But whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10:6): if the one who hates his brother is a murderer, what is the condition of the one who loves iniquity and hates his own soul? And if the one who hates his brother does not have eternal life abiding in him, how can the one who, by loving iniquity and hating his own soul, brings this life to an end, attain the forgiveness of sins by which one comes to life? For our Lord himself clearly shows how each person reaches life, saying: “If you wish to come to life, keep the commandments” (Matthew 19:17).

The one, therefore, who keeps the commandments will come to life. But who keeps the divine commandments except the person who, turning to God, has departed from his former iniquities before the end of the present life? For this reason blessed Paul admonishes us: “Let everyone who invokes the name of the Lord depart from iniquity” (2 Timothy 2:19). He said this because he knew that repentance is fruitfully practiced in the present time, when forgiveness is granted to those who repent. In the future, however, there will indeed be repentance for the wicked, but it will not be fruitful, because there will be no conversion among the wicked. For they will be cast into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. There they will be tormented without end—not only their souls together with their bodies by the punishment of Gehenna, but also by the very darkness of their most evil pleasure. [Col. 0557C] For to such people the very evil will be a pleasure added to their punishment, and on account of it endless torment awaits them.

Now they despise the opportunity of the time granted to them and, in the day of salvation, do not seek divine help. God has disclosed this time to us through prophetic speech, saying: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” When blessed Paul had inserted this testimony in his Epistle, he followed it by adding: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2). In another passage the same Apostle commends this time so clearly that anyone who, enlightened by a divine gift, reads attentively and understands appropriately will not deceive himself or seek another time for conversion or forgiveness, knowing that whoever is unwilling to seek forgiveness in this time will be utterly unable to find it after this life.

Writing to the Galatians, blessed Paul says: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap. For the one who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but the one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit. And in doing good, let us not grow weary; for in due time we shall reap without growing weary. Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all, and especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Galatians 6:7–10). Who could hear these words of the Apostle and not be stirred to desire good works? Who, wandering from God, would not tremble and seek the straight path? Who would not delight in persevering in good sowing, when he knows that at the harvest he will receive nothing other than what he sows?

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0558A]

We must therefore consider somewhat more carefully this statement of apostolic preaching. For it was not without great weight that he gave the warning: “Do not be deceived”; and then added: “God is not mocked.” Afterwards he explained the matter in which he knew that some were going astray, saying: “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.” Whoever thinks that he will reap in the future retribution what he does not sow in the work of this present time is therefore deceived.

But because the difference between that sowing and harvest had to be made more clearly known, the skilled farmer, discerning between them, added in the following words: “For the one who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but the one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.” The error, then, which he prohibited at the beginning of this statement is that each person supposes he will reap something other than what he sows. Whoever sows in the flesh, from which corruption is harvested, is therefore deceived if he thinks he will reap eternal life, which is reserved for those who sow in the Spirit.

The Apostle continues: “And in doing good, let us not grow weary; for in due time we shall reap without growing weary.” This (perhaps, “Here”) clearly shows that the works of each person are designated by the name of seed. Earlier he had said: “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.” Now he says: “And in doing good, let us not grow weary; for in due time we shall reap without growing weary.” Truly a disciple of Truth, and for that reason an outstanding teacher of the nations, he taught that justice would not be lacking in the repayment of works, and likewise distinguished the time of sowing and harvest—that is, the time of action and the time of recompense—so that no one, confusing the time of sowing with the time of harvest through foolish thought, might demand the result of the future harvest during the time of sowing, or hope that the beginning of good sowing would be granted to him at the time of harvest.

Thus the idle laborer, entangled in the bonds of sloth—or, worse still, intent upon the practice of deadly sowing—will not rejoice at the harvest but will mourn when he begins to reap the due reward of his sowing, at a time when he will no longer be able to change the quality of the evil seed.

Moreover, we must attend more carefully to the fact that three things are shown to us in this passage of apostolic teaching: that we should do good, that we should not grow weary, and that in due time we shall reap without growing weary. Of these three, two are commands concerning work, while the third is a promise concerning reward. Labor is enjoined upon the worker in the first two, while in the third the spirit of those who labor is lifted up by hope of the future harvest. For one who confidently hopes for a reward corresponding to his labor is accustomed to draw greater strength from the labor itself.

The Apostle therefore joins perseverance to good work, so that whoever delights in rejoicing endlessly at the harvest may not grow weary in sowing. Accordingly, in keeping with the saying of the blessed Apostle, the one who perseveres in the seed of good work in the present time must reach the joy of the future harvest.

But he greatly deceives himself—whether it is the person who, having sent forth no seeds of good works until the end of the present life, thinks that he will one day reap good things, or the person who, corrupted and lacking perseverance in good work, hopes for joy in the repayment of his reward. For the blessed Apostle testifies that each person will receive at the harvest what he sends forth perseveringly in the seed.

Such is that most skilled winnower (Matthew 3:12), who will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor, so that in the separation of wheat and chaff he may not be deceived by any stealthy fraud; he does not put chaff into the granary to be given to the fires, nor does he deliver to the flames the grain destined for the granary.

At the time of the future harvest, good sowers—namely, those who now sow perseveringly in tears and will reap in joy, and who now go forth weeping, scattering their seed—will then come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves (Psalm 125:5–6).

Just as the person who, although he once sowed good things, did not maintain perseverance in sowing good will be deprived of the joy and fellowship of the reapers, so also the person who delights in serving and favoring the nocturnal sower, that is, the devil, to such an extent that he does not cease until death to sow those things which, gathered by the discernment of the reaping angels and bound into bundles, are assigned by the judgment of the Lord to unquenchable fire (Matthew 13:25), will be unable to share either in forgiveness or in joy.

For through the subsequent fault of iniquity all the good labor of the righteous who has gone before is rendered fruitless, while the merit of iniquity remains, whose entire labor is evil. The Apostle says: “Each person will receive his own reward according to his labor” (1 Corinthians 3:8)—namely, the labor in which each person is found when he is commanded to depart from the present age.

Therefore, as the Apostle admonishes: “While we have time, let us do good to all, and especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Galatians 6:10).

## CHAPTER IX

For in the Epistle written to the Hebrews not only is conversion indicated as necessary in the present time, but perseverance is also commanded to be maintained to the end. He says: “Take care, brothers, lest there be in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief, causing him to depart from the living God. But exhort one another each day, as long as it is called ‘Today,’ so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. For we have become participants in Christ, if indeed we hold the beginning of our substance firm to the end” (Hebrews 3:12–14).

Who would not be terrified by the Apostle’s own example, so as to depart from evil works, hasten toward God in repentance and conversion [variant: conduct], and carefully guard against becoming reprobate by abandoning the course of perseverance? All the faithful must consider with what concern blessed Paul himself ran, with what vigilance he fought, and with what severity he disciplined his body. He says: “I therefore run not as uncertainly; I fight not as one beating the air; but I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself should become reprobate” (1 Corinthians 9:26–27).

He said this because he knew what had been divinely spoken through Ezekiel: “When the righteous turns away from his righteousness and commits wrongdoing and dies, in the wrongdoing he has committed—in that he will die” (Ezekiel 18:24).

In vain, therefore, does any sinner dream of the forgiveness of sins through empty thoughts if he does not persevere in the Lord’s commandments until the end of the present life, or if he does not depart from his most evil paths before the end of the present life.

For every righteous person must work out his salvation with fear and trembling (Philippians 2:12); and every wicked person must cease to present his members to sin as weapons of iniquity, but must present himself as one alive from the dead, and his members as weapons of righteousness to God (Romans 6:13). He must cease to do those things whose wage is death, as the Apostle Paul says: “For the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23).

This death is also called the future wrath of God, which will be inflicted upon the wicked and upon those who persevere in evil. Hence John the Baptist rebukes the Pharisees and Sadducees in such a way that he also reproves Christians who live badly. He says: “Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance [variant: of penance], and do not presume to say, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid at the root of the trees. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Luke 3:7–9).

When the Lord’s Forerunner said these things, he was plainly speaking to the wicked and evil, whom he called a brood of vipers because of their imitation of serpents—that is, of the devil’s work. Yet he showed them what they should do in this age and what they should fear in the future judgment.

By commanding them to produce fruits worthy of repentance, he showed that in this life human beings can be changed and can pass, through the conversion of a repentant heart, from the merit of punishment to the merit of the kingdom. But by adding that every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire, he foretold the time of the future judgment, when those who lead a criminal life to the end, like fruitless trees, will not mercifully be granted forgiveness of sins, but will justly receive eternal burning.

For this reason also he foretells that our Savior will come to separate the wheat from the chaff: “He has his winnowing fork in his hand; he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the granary, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Luke 3:17).

Moreover, through the course of the Gospel reading he instructs every Christian to consider, with proper discernment, what was given to each person with the most compassionate generosity at the Savior’s first coming, and what each person is awaiting to receive, by just retribution, at his second coming.

## CHAPTER X

For our Savior and judge himself—who now came to save, but will then come to judge; who now came to make the good from the evil through merciful forgiveness, but will then come to separate the evil from the good through just examination—demonstrates the benefit of his first coming when he says: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10). [393]

But he makes known the fearful equity of his second coming as follows: “The Son of Man will come, and then he will repay each person according to his works” (Matthew 16:27).

Again, showing the mercy of his first coming, he says: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:16–17).

But announcing the judgment of his second coming, he says: “I have many things to speak and judge concerning you” (John 8:26). And elsewhere: “The word that I have spoken to you will judge you” (John 12:48). And elsewhere: “As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is true” (John 5:30).

Again, he expresses the benefit of his first coming, by which, finding no one alive, he freely raises the dead—making the impious righteous—in these words: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John 5:25).

But he subsequently foretells the examination of his second coming, when he will judge the living and the dead, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, and will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29).

Hearing his present voice gives life to the dead when he grants the grace of faith to unbelievers; those whom he finds evil he makes good; the impious he justifies mercifully; sinners he saves compassionately; and the blind he illuminates graciously.

But hearing his second voice will, just as it returns the crown of righteousness to the righteous, repay the wicked with punishment for their iniquity. In the hearing of his first voice, the mercy of the Redeemer goes before sinners; in the hearing of his second voice, repayment by the Judge will follow those who work.

[Note: [Col. 0561D] The manuscript formerly read operantes (“those acting”). The word was altered by another hand.]

Here everyone is told: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28). There, however, only those on the right will be told: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matthew 25:34); while those on the left will be told: “Go, accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25:41).

What an utterly certain knowledge of merits there will be in that pastoral separation by which the sheep will be divided from the goats, so that no goat will be placed on the right, just as no sheep will be placed on the left. For those merits with which human beings depart from this life will remain with them continually and unchangeably in the other life—whether the good things which divine kindness bestowed here, or the evils which human iniquity acquired here.

Accordingly, there will be no removal of evils there, although there will be an advancement of good merits. The former will remain in punishment; the latter will be perfected in glory.

This is the time of which it is written in the Psalm: “He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities. For as high as heaven is above the earth, so great is the Lord’s mercy toward those who fear him. As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us” (Psalm 102:10–12).

But in that judgment the just Judge will return the crown of righteousness, as the Apostle says, to those who love his coming (2 Timothy 4:8); while to those who work iniquity, as the Psalm shows (Psalm 27:4), he will give according to their works and according to the wickedness of their endeavors. According to the works of their hands he will repay them; he will return their recompense to them. The reason is that as each person departs from this life, so without doubt he will be repaid in the future life. No one who was not first changed in this age from iniquity to righteousness and from an evil life to a good life will be changed in that just judgment from corruption into incorruption.

## CHAPTER XI

For this reason Paul says: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51). When the blessed Apostle had said this, lest the meaning of his statement remain uncertain to some, he subsequently deemed it necessary to show which people he meant would be changed at the time of the future resurrection.

Certainly, if he had said, “We shall all rise, but we shall not be changed,” no change at all would be thought to occur. And again, if he had said, “We shall all rise, and we shall be changed,” then, just as all are believed to rise, all would likewise be believed to be changed.

But since he foretold the future resurrection of all and nevertheless did not affirm that all would be changed, he warned us carefully to investigate who will be changed in the resurrection of the future judgment. Blessed Paul did not wish to leave this ambiguous, lest the wicked sin more freely if they heard that the gift of future transformation would be shared by them with the righteous. In what follows he therefore took care to show the gift of that transformation: “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:52).

When he says “we,” he shows that those who will share with him in the gift of future transformation are those whom ecclesial fellowship and a rightly ordered life unite with Paul and his companions in the present time.

Indicating the character of that transformation, he says: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53). Thus, for transformation according to just retribution to follow in such people then, transformation by gratuitous generosity precedes it now.

Showing this transformation, blessed David the prophet says: “I said, ‘Now I have begun’; this is the change wrought by the Most High’s right hand” (Psalm 76:11).

## CHAPTER XII

The repayment of future transformation is promised to those who in the present life have been changed from evil to good. Through it, whoever has turned here to better things and changed his life will likewise be changed in that repayment and will receive the gift of equality with the angels.

The Savior himself, who is faithful in his words and holy in all his works (Psalm 144:13), promises this not to the wicked or impious, but only to those who live well and are righteous. For those who do not live well are not righteous, nor will those who, while loving God, despise his commandments be punished unjustly—God whom those who keep his commandments love.

As the Lord himself says: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments” (John 14:23).

[Note: [Col. 0562D] Perhaps “those who do not love.”]

Therefore, they truly love God—who can neither be loved unjustly nor at any time be justly despised—who obey his commands. These are the ones who, according to the Lord’s saying (Matthew 22:30), will be changed and, made equal to the angels of God through the gift of that transformation, will be incorruptible and immortal.

It is not only their souls that will be changed for the better, so that they can no longer sin; their flesh also, which they possessed as corruptible and mortal, will be changed in the resurrection, so that it will indeed be the same flesh that it is now, but it will no longer be able to be what it now is—corruptible and mortal.

Accordingly, the flesh both of the wicked and of the righteous, which now dies, is the flesh that will rise. The flesh of the wicked will rise to eternal pain, while that of the righteous will remain in eternal happiness. And just as the former will rise for torment, so the latter will rise for joy. The former will be given life so that it may be tormented with its soul in eternal death; the latter will live so that with its soul it may enjoy the blessedness of everlasting life.

The body of the righteous, according to the Apostle’s teaching, is “sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption” [Note: [Col. 0563D] The manuscript and the Antiphonary read “into incorruption”]; “it is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory; it is sown in weakness; it will rise in power; it is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:42–44).

Thus, by grace, this is brought about in them: first, through justification, in which one rises spiritually, the transformation bestowed by divine grace begins in them here; afterwards, in the resurrection of the body, through which the transformation of those who have been justified is completed, a perfect glorification that remains forever is not changed.

For grace first changes them through justification, and then through glorification, so that in them glorification itself may remain unchangeable and eternal.

Here they are changed through the first resurrection, by which they are enlightened so that they may be converted: they pass from death to life, from iniquity to righteousness, from unbelief to faith, and from evil actions to holy conduct. Therefore, the second death has no power over them.

Of such people it is said in the Apocalypse: “Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection; over these the second death has no power” (Revelation 20:6).

[Note: [Col. 0563D] The manuscript omits “and holy.” The Antiphonary has “blessed and holy.”]

Again, in the same book it is said: “The one who conquers will not be harmed by the second death” (Revelation 2:11).

Therefore, just as the first resurrection consists in the conversion of the heart, so the second death consists in everlasting punishment. Let everyone who does not wish to be condemned to the eternal punishment of the second death hasten here to become a participant in the first resurrection.

For if some people, changed in the present life by the fear of God, pass from an evil life to a good life, they pass from death to life; and afterwards, from dishonor [lacuna] “...buntur in gloriam” (“...buntur into glory”).

## CHAPTER XIII

But concerning the wretched and unhappy, who neglect to be changed from evil to good during the time of this life, holy David both condemns their stubbornness and foretells the future punishment of divine retribution, saying: “For there is no change in them, and they have not feared God” (Psalm 54:20).

And lest those who have refused to be changed should vainly promise themselves forgiveness of sins to be granted after they have crossed the threshold of this life, he immediately adds: “He stretched out his hand in repayment” (ibid.).

The beginning of this repayment occurs when the wicked person, receiving within himself the reward his error deserved, is tormented by the just judgment of eternal fire for his iniquities.

Nor should this other repayment be considered small: the wicked person, deprived of the light of righteousness, is permitted to wander in his own darkness, already condemned not in the flesh but by the blindness of his heart. It also contributes to the accumulation of his repayment if, being blind and unable to receive the light, he nevertheless eagerly strives to increase the darkness of his blindness with delight.

To such people the Lord says in the Psalms: “My people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me; so I let them go according to the desires of their hearts, and they will walk in their own pleasures” (Psalm 80:12–13).

Of such people also the Teacher of the nations says: “Therefore God gave them over to dishonorable passions” (Romans 1:26).

And again: “Therefore God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting” (Romans 1:28).

Such people are first handed over to their unjust desires, and afterwards will be handed over to just punishments. Here they are handed over to deeds that correspond to them; afterwards they will be handed over to punishments that correspond to them.

For the wicked person must not be considered exempt from the punishment of retribution merely because he sins with pleasure. Indeed, he is already severely punished by the very pleasure of sinning, because he submits himself through consent to such pleasure, by which the basis for his punishment is increased. The more completely what unjustly delights him is perfected, the more he will receive that will cause him greater sorrow.

If anyone here refuses to turn to God and to be changed from an evil life to the practices of a good life, he will not be changed there either, where immortality and incorruption are bestowed upon the righteous who have been happily changed.

Therefore the wicked or impious—that is, those who believe perversely or live wickedly—if they do not depart from their unbelief or iniquity before the end of the present life, will be neither immortal nor incorruptible in the future retribution. They will be corrupted, but not consumed; they will die, but not be extinguished.

For an everlasting awareness of torments will remain in the dead, where the wretched are not permitted to die in their punishments. There the death of the wretched will be such that it does not remove the soul from the body of the one who suffers, but continually holds it within the suffering body so that it may afflict soul and body together with the eternity of its pain.

Thus the soul will always die together with its body, and with that body it will be compelled endlessly to share eternal torments. There the death of soul and body does not die, because the torment of body and soul does not end.

This will be the eternal death of the wicked: that they will not die in the eternal fire, lest they ever be able to escape punishment. Nor will anything be taken away from the burning body, although the unhappy soul is continually consumed within its body. Rather, so that the whole body may not cease to burn, the whole body, together with the soul, will continually remain in the fire.

In whatever body the soul has lived righteously or wickedly, in that same body it will receive eternal punishment or endless joy.

397

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0565A]

It is therefore advantageous for each person, before bringing the present life to an end, to be converted through fear of future punishment, if he truly does not wish to be tormented without end after the end of this life.

For this reason it is vain to believe that the iniquity of evil people, which persists in the sight of God, will be forgiven, since in his sight the barrenness of good works will not be left unpunished.

For no one placed on the left is said to go into eternal fire because he took away bread from one who was eating, but because he did not give it to one who was hungry; nor because he stripped someone who was clothed, but because he did not provide clothing; nor because he drove someone from his own house, but because he did not receive one of Christ’s least ones as a guest.

If, then, the one who did not give his bread to the hungry will go into eternal burning, what will happen to the one who took away another’s bread? And if the one who did not cover the naked with clothing will be sent into the lake of fire and sulfur, what will the person suffer who cruelly strips someone of his clothing? And if the greedy possessor of his own property will have no rest, how can the insatiable robber of another’s property, if he refuses to be converted in this life, afterward vainly promise himself forgiveness from the just Judge?

Let us consider the wretched rich man, once clothed in purple and fine linen, burning in unquenchable flames for no other reason than that, possessed by deadly iniquity, he never wished to give even the crumbs of his table to poor Lazarus, who suffered from continual hunger.

When he had been condemned to unending torment and was left unworthy even of the cooling afforded by the poor man’s finger, while the poor man rejoiced in eternal rest, the patriarch Abraham clearly showed that after this life neither can the good cross over in any way to the wicked, nor can the wicked ever pass from punishments to the rest of the blessed.

For he says: “Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things. But now he is comforted here, while you are tormented. And in all these things a great chasm has been established between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can anyone cross from there to us” (Luke 16:25–26).

## CHAPTER XV

It is therefore good for us to do good now, while it is the time for work; and, in order to be exceedingly rich at the harvest, we must remain neither sluggish nor barren.

It is good for each person now to apply the remedy of conversion and repentance to his wounds, while, after being converted, he can receive forgiveness of sins, because the repentance of the future time will be such that it cannot earn forgiveness.

Nor will those whom God has predestined to life then undertake repentance. For in the present time, according to the Apostle’s saying, “the sorrow that is according to God produces steadfast salvation” (2 Corinthians 7:10), so that for those who repent and are converted in this time, steadfast and eternal salvation may be granted in the future.

But the repentance of those who did not practice repentance in the present life will not cease in the future. Such repentance will not arise from God’s generosity but from the torment of punishment. In such repentance there will be eternal mourning, because there will be no fruit of repentance there.

For the evil will not be converted to good through repentance there, when the wicked will have repentance in punishment for this one purpose: that he may never be without either repentance or punishment. Thus the will that kept the wicked person hardened in evil to the end will have endless repentance for its crimes, so that it can neither be converted any longer nor escape the eternity of punishment.

For not every repentance [lacuna] in which the sinner, anticipated by the grace of the merciful God, so declares his sins in repenting as to seek, through conversion, the grace of forgiveness.

[Note: [Col. 0565D] Some words are missing here; perhaps “is fruitful,” followed by “but only that in which …,” or something similar.]

Rather, the person who repents of the evils he has committed but does not hasten to God, changed through conversion, is like someone lying in a wound who suffers severe pain but does not seek the physician’s benefit. He declares the pain he suffers, but does not obtain the remedy by which he may be healed.

Therefore, not everyone who confesses sin receives forgiveness, because our God attends not only to what we carry in our heart [lacuna].

[Note: [Col. 0565D] “What we utter” should be read, or else the passage is defective and incomplete.]

For the Psalm says of him: “God, who searches hearts and reins” (Psalm 7:10). The Savior also says: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46).

This is why in the divine Scriptures we read that certain people, though equally confessing sins in speech, [Note: [Col. 0566D] The manuscript adds the word sermone, “in speech.” But the sense does not seem complete unless “and obtained forgiveness,” or something similar, is supplied, as is clear from what follows.] did not equally obtain forgiveness.

King Saul, sent by God to destroy Amalek (1 Samuel 15:3), incurred sin because he did not keep the Lord’s command at all. When the prophet Samuel came to rebuke him, Saul, terrified, confessed his sin, yet did not obtain forgiveness, because his heart was not right before God (1 Samuel 15:24).

His confession of sin arose from fear of punishment, not from hatred of sin. He did not hate what he had done, but feared what he did not want to suffer. He did not condemn his fault by reforming his manner of life [perhaps, “by conversion”], but, struck by terror of the divine anger in the present, trembled with fear.

King David too, overcome by the enticement of carnal desire (2 Samuel 11:4), not only committed adultery with the wife of his soldier but also killed the husband himself, an innocent man who was guilty of no crime and was unaware of the violation of his wife.

Yet when the prophet Nathan was sent to him by the Lord, terrified by the prophet’s rebuke, he cried out: “I have sinned” (2 Samuel 12:13). The prophet answered him: “And God has taken away your sin, and you will not die” (2 Samuel 12:13).

Behold, Saul said: “I have sinned.” David also said: “I have sinned.” Since, then, there was one voice in the confession of sin by both, why was forgiveness not granted to both alike? It was because God saw dissimilarity of will beneath the similarity of confession. He did not attend to the sound of the words, but distinguished the intention of the heart in each.

For one of them, having been converted, immediately cast away the desire to sin and, by repenting, punished his own offense; but the other indeed expressed his confession of sin in words, yet, bound by the fault of a perverse heart, did not cast away his disposition to sin.

390

## CHAPTER XVI
Then, therefore, confession of sin is beneficial if the sinner, after confessing what he had done wrongly, does not do it again and strives, by zeal for good works, to surpass the merits of his former crimes, so that, according to the Apostle’s saying, “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5:21).

Moreover, some, not knowing the power of repentance, do not undertake repentance in order that, placing their hope in the help of divine mercy, they may be converted; rather, by repenting they sin more grievously, since they despair of the forgiveness of sins. Such was the repentance of Judas the betrayer [Col. 0567B] (Matt. 27:3): it did not obtain salvation for the repentant man but brought destruction upon him in his despair. Finally, he bound himself with a worse bond of iniquity when he killed himself, guilty as he was, than when he betrayed Christ, who was innocent. For Judas’s sin of betraying Christ could have been forgiven if, while alive, he had been converted; but his own killing could in no way be forgiven once he was dead.

After Christ’s betrayal, therefore, the betrayer had time in which, through that blood which was poured out for the remission of sins, Judas’s own sin also could be forgiven. For Christ, who died for the ungodly, would not have denied his betrayer the benefit of forgiveness, had Judas not, by despairing, taken away from himself the time granted for forgiveness. He therefore did not repent rightly, nor did he endure being a just avenger of his own crime. For the unjust avenger of his own guilt increased rather than removed the punishment of his deserving: by being killed, he deprived his own slayer of the time for conversion. Thus, because he killed himself, he himself certainly took away from himself the time for conversion by killing himself.

Most wretched Judas: although he had wickedly committed the crime of betrayal, he repented of that crime still more wickedly, because he did not seek pardon at all. Thus his repentance for that grave offense was found to be worse than the offense itself. For the sin of the Lord’s betrayal had a later time in which it could be washed away; but him the sentence punishes—a sentence that contained not conversion but despair. Therefore his repentance did not help him but destroyed him, because by killing himself he took away the time for conversion, and by despairing he removed the possibility of forgiveness.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0567D]

So greatly does the opportunity of the time granted for the forgiveness of sins matter! Although betraying Christ is much more serious than killing any ordinary human being, nevertheless Christ’s killers—whoever, in the present life, have been converted with their whole heart—have obtained forgiveness of sins through Christ’s own blood.

But whoever—let me not say a heretic or pagan, concerning whom there is no doubt that they will be punished by eternal fire—whoever, even if a Catholic Christian, commits murder, or commits adultery, or plunders another’s property, or violates an oath by perjury, or does not hesitate to give false testimony, and is not converted before the end of the present life, although he appears to have sinned much less [Col. 0568A] than the one who killed Christ: nevertheless, if Christ’s killer is converted in the present life, he will be saved; whereas the other, because he is not converted in the present life, will after the end of this life be assigned to torments that have no end.

This happens not because the latter sinned more than that ungodly man who killed Christ, but because the former will attain eternal life by recognizing the omnipotence of the good physician and coming at the appropriate time to the remedy of healing. The latter, however, is condemned to eternal death because he despairs of benevolence. Thus, although his sin, compared with the killing of Christ, is declared the lighter crime, he himself is nevertheless found to be much worse in that lighter crime: for although he did not kill Christ, he sinned more grievously than if he had killed Christ in this respect—that he neglected the fitting time [Col. 0568B] granted by divine long-suffering for the forgiveness of sins.

Thus it is understood both that forgiveness of sins is not granted if repentance is not practiced in this time, and that repentance practiced in this time is of no benefit if forgiveness of sins is despaired of. In the future, however, there will be no conversion for the wicked, and the repentance of such people will continue, but in vain. For just as forgiveness will never be granted them, so their repentance will never end. They neglect the time in which repentance is salutarily practiced by sinners and in which divine mercy grants forgiveness of sins.

For this reason the Lord himself, consoling his faithful in the Apocalypse of John and threatening the wicked with the punishment of future retribution, speaks as follows:

“Let the one who does wrong continue to do wrong, and let the one who is filthy continue to be filthy; but let the righteous still do more righteous deeds, and let the holy still become holier. Behold, I am coming soon, and my reward is with me, to repay each person according to his deeds. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. Blessed are those who have washed their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the holy city through the gates. Outside, however, will remain the dogs, sorcerers, fornicators, murderers, those who serve idols, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood” (Rev. 22:11 and following).

Who, I ask, could be so stiff-necked, or who could be found so uncircumcised in heart and ears, that he would not be terrified, cast down, and converted by these words? Who would not weep? Who would not tremble in his inmost being? Who would not, shaken by fear of that just judgment, hasten to conversion in order to find forgiveness of sins and the grace of everlasting salvation?

Woe to the one who, before the time of the final winnowing, will not hasten to become wheat from chaff! Woe to the one who, before the reaping angels come to gather the weeds from among the grain to be burned (Matt. 13:39), does not take care to be changed from weeds into wheat! For the kindly warning of divine Scripture must not be despised: it salutarily commands us to convert swiftly and proclaims the future anger of divine vengeance against those who delay. For it says:

“Do not delay in turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day, lest his anger suddenly come upon you and he destroy you at the time of vengeance” (Ecclus. 5:8).

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0569A]

But in order that we may recognize more fully that only the time of the present age has been granted for human conversion, let us consider those laborers whom the Lord called to the vineyard (Matt. 20:6). Although he made their calling at different hours [variant: *they made it at different hours*], he completed it at the eleventh hour—that is, before the end of the day.

In those hours during which the laborers were called, the ages of this world are understood: during these ages God called to good work those whom he converted to himself by gratuitous justification. The morning of this day is understood as extending from the beginning of the world to the Flood. The calling of the third hour was from the Flood to Abraham. The calling of the sixth hour was from Abraham to David. From David to the deportation of the people to Babylon, the ninth hour was completed. Then the eleventh hour was at Christ’s first coming, when he came in humility in mortal flesh, in which, for the sin of the world, he deigned, though immortal, to be killed.
