This is the final calling of the laborers, which is now taking place until the end of the present age—that is, from his coming in humility to his coming in majesty; from the coming in which the good one came to be judged by the wicked, so that in mercy he might make the wicked good, to the coming in which he will justly judge both the wicked and the good; from the coming of gracious forgiveness to the coming of just recompense; from the coming in which he delivered the souls of the poor from usury and iniquities (Ps. 71:14), to the coming in which he will come to demand his money with interest from those by whom he found it consumed or not doubled through any zeal for good work [Col. 0569C] (Matt. 25:27).

This is the hour that blessed John calls the last hour: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18). After the completion of this hour, the Lord does not call laborers to the vineyard; rather, he will come to give each person the reward for his work, as he himself says: “Behold, I am coming soon, and my reward is with me” (Rev. 22:12).

Let the one, therefore, hope to receive the denarius of divine recompense who, before the day of the present age comes to an end, works commendably in the Lord’s vineyard [Note: [Col. 0569D] We obtained what follows, beginning with the words “That work also,” from two manuscripts. It is absent from the printed editions.]. For that work is nothing other than true conversion of the heart. A person is converted to God as he ought to be when, as the Apostle says, he possesses “faith working through love.”

That other diversity of hours may also properly be understood, as we explained above, as the distinction between the ages of the world [Col. 0569D]. Nevertheless, it is not inappropriate to understand in this diversity of hours also the ages of each individual person: morning is the time until a person’s infancy is completed; then the end of childhood completes the third hour; the end of adolescence carries out the sixth; the completion of youth fulfills the ninth; the course of mature adulthood fulfills the eleventh; and thereafter old age, moving toward its end, marks the setting of the entire day.

Therefore, at whatever age of the present life an ungodly or impious person may be converted to God with his whole heart, he will immediately receive forgiveness of all his former sins.

## CHAPTER XIX

[Col. 0570A]

But if anyone can find in the Gospel, or teach from it, that after the end of the day any laborer was called to the vineyard, let him rightly hope and most confidently proclaim that any wicked person who has not been converted in the present age will be granted the opportunity for good work or the grace of forgiveness in the time of the future age.

Likewise, if anyone can show that the denarius was given at the Lord’s command to someone who was not called to work in the vineyard before the end of the day, let him rightly and appropriately hope that the kingdom of heaven will, by the Lord’s generosity, be bestowed upon anyone who was not converted before the end of the present life.

But if those whom the pious labor of a full day’s work exercised in the vineyard were the only ones to receive the reward of the denarius after the end of the day, then we too, if we wish to reach the denarius of eternal life, must labor in the Lord’s vineyard in the present time. Let us not despise the command of the one who calls, if we do not wish to be excluded from the generosity of the one who rewards.

For whoever does not work in the vineyard before the end of the day will not be able to receive the denarius when the day has ended. For then there will not be a time when each person is mercifully called to work in the vineyard, but a time when reward is given for work already performed [variant: *to work already performed*]. There will therefore not be a gracious calling there, but a just repayment.

That denarius will be given neither to the idle person nor to one who works outside the vineyard. The idle person is a Catholic who does not wish to work well, because “faith without works is idle and dead in itself” (Jas. 2:17).

The person who works outside the vineyard is one who, established in any heresy, undertakes the pursuit of good works but, by believing wrongly, denies himself the outcome of salvation. For blessed Paul the Apostle says: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23), and: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6).

Each, therefore, deprives himself of the denarius; each makes himself alien to the company of the laborers: the one, because, although established within the Lord’s vineyard, he did not wish to devote himself attentively to work; the other, because he worked outside what he ought to have worked within the Lord’s vineyard before the end of the day.

Thus the one is lost because he did not work in the manner by which he could be saved, while the other is lost because he did not work in the place where he could receive the gift of salvation. Consequently, when the day has ended, the first is not permitted to enter the vineyard, and the second is deprived of the opportunity for good work.

For the bad Catholic did not have a wedding garment at the Lord’s banquet—which Paul impresses upon the faithful as something to fear when he says, “if indeed we are found clothed and not naked” (2 Cor. 5:3)—whereas the heretic disdained to come to that very banquet at the acceptable time. Therefore the former will be cast out, and the latter will not be given the opportunity to enter.

Now, therefore, is the time for chaff to be changed into wheat; now is the time for every wicked person to hasten to become wheat from weeds, if he does not wish to be burned by the eternity of unquenchable fire.

For if anyone, rejecting the grace of the present time—during which the Lord deigned to come not to judge sinners but to save them—believes that he should remain in his sins, he will find no mercy in the future judgment. For at the time of winnowing the winnower will not permit the chaff to be mixed with the grain, nor at the time when an account must be rendered will divine severity grant the power of the talent to the lazy, useless servant; but just as then unquenchable fire will consume the chaff, so eternal weeping and gnashing of teeth will receive the wicked and lazy servant, who has been assigned to the outer darkness.

For what else is meant by the command that that servant be bound hand and foot, except that in his hands the guilt of evil work, and in his feet the disposition of evil will, are shown to be destined for punishment?

## CHAPTER XX

The holy Isaiah, divinely instructed, recognized the opportunity afforded by this time. He does not cease to exhort us to conversion in these words:

“Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. Let the wicked abandon his way, and the unjust man his thoughts; let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him, and to our God, for he is rich in forgiveness” (Isa. 55:6–7).

Now, therefore, the Lord must be sought, while he can be found by those who seek him. Now he must be invoked, while he is near to the one who invokes him. Now the way of ungodliness and the thought of iniquity must be abandoned. Now the sinner’s conversion is necessary, by which, through the benefit of divine forgiveness, he can be freed from the guilt of every sin.

Otherwise, no one will see the good things of God in the land of the living (Ps. 26:13) if he does not receive forgiveness of sins in this land of the dying. For the Savior and judge of humanity himself ordained that he forgive sins to those whom he forgives in this land. Therefore he says to the unbelieving Jews: “But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins” (Matt. 9:6).

He did not say this because, when people pass from this earth, he would be unable to forgive, if he wished, the sins of this time; rather, he said it so that people might recognize that the time of divine forgiveness and recompense has been distinguished by an unchangeable ordinance, and that human vanity might not vainly hope to hear what divine truth would promise [variant: *would not promise*].

For this reason he also gave blessed Peter—that is, his Church—on earth the power of binding and loosing, so that we might recognize that in the time of this life gratuitous mercy is bestowed in the forgiveness of sins, while in the future a just reward is rendered to all according to the quality of their deeds. We should not doubt that now every sin can be forgiven, and that then whatever has not been forgiven will be demanded.

Blessed David also recognized this through the revelation of the Holy Spirit. The Lord, as David himself testifies, had revealed to him “the hidden and secret things of his wisdom” (Ps. 50:8). Before he departed from this age [variant: *before he went out from this age*], he asked for forgiveness of sins, saying:

“Forgive me, that I may be refreshed, before I go away and shall be no more” (Ps. 38:14).

Certainly, the blessed prophet would not have asked so earnestly that forgiveness of sins be granted to him before the end of the present life if he had known that after this life repentance would either benefit anyone or that forgiveness of sins would then be granted by divine gift to those who practiced repentance.

## CHAPTER XXI

[Col. 0572A]

Indeed, after this life, although there will be repentance for the wicked, they will not receive forgiveness of sins; rather, that very repentance will produce an increase of punishment. It will contribute to the accumulation of eternal torment. There the hardness of the perverse heart—which was not erased by salutary confession before the end of the present life—will burn heavily and endlessly amid avenging flames, and will be punished still more severely by its own bitter remorse.

For what is worse than to be so crushed by continual repentance for the past that the repentant person can never be freed from the torment of the crime he committed? In the case of one who ends the present life in evil works, it will not be considered that, because his evil works have come to an end, his torments will at some point also end. Rather, the perversity of his wicked will will be taken into account: he loved and held onto it until the end of the present life, even though he unwillingly lost the life he lived in the worst possible way.

By not taking care to change his evil will before the end of the present life, he unquestionably shows that he loves his iniquities so much that, if he could live here without end, he would wish to remain in iniquity without end. Therefore no wicked person will be spared on the ground that he will no longer be able to fulfill the desires of his evil will. Rather, he will be tortured without end because, for as long as he was able to sin here, he did not cease from sinning.

For this reason no end to punishment will be granted to the wicked, because before he brought the course of this life to an end he did not put an end to his crimes. Although no one who refused to be converted while living here could prolong his evil life for as long as he wished, he could nevertheless, if he wished, change it for the better before unwillingly bringing that evil life to an end, to remain without end in the evils of Gehenna.

That those who end the present life in evil habits and deeds should therefore be tormented in this eternal burning belongs to the justice of the just Judge, who repays each person according to his works. His repayment is certainly not unjust: it results in the wicked never being free from punishment, because their will in this life refused to be free from sin.

Such people take greater pleasure in sinning than in living. They do not sin in order to live forever; rather, they wish to live here forever so that, while they live, they may never cease from sinning.

No one ends the present life securely unless, before ending his life, he departs from iniquity, lest he then vainly wish to mourn his crimes when he will in no way be able to avoid the torments.

Therefore repentance is not imposed upon everyone in the present age without reason, nor is conversion preached in this life in vain. Here repentance finds the fruit of forgiveness, if the sinner, while he lives here, lays aside his desire to sin. For the merciful and just Lord has assigned the time of the present age solely to the benefit of forgiveness; the future he reserves for just recompense, in which each person will receive an appropriate reward according to the quality of his belief and work—a reward that will not end.

## CHAPTER XXII

Therefore now let every wicked person established within the Church reject his evil way of life and hasten to take up the course of a good life, so that he may be able to reach eternal life. Now let every impious person lay aside his perverse belief [Col. 0573A] and not delay coming to the Church [Note: [Col. 0573B] Manuscript: *returning*]. Now let every person acquire for himself the merit of the right-hand side, if he does not wish to endure the torments of the left-hand side. Now let him walk along the way of justice, so that he may come to the homeland where he will possess everlasting rest.

Now let everyone who provokes God by evil works pass over to a good life, by which he may acquire God’s favor and receive eternal life, which God bestows without end upon the good.

Let no one despair of God’s mercy by considering the enormity of any crime. Yet let no one remain in sins under the pretext of hoping in God’s mercy. Rather, in the confidence of hope, let him seek the harbor of repentance without hesitation, while the humility of the repentant person flees the deadly shipwreck of despair. Let him love God’s mercy in such a way that he considers God’s justice with fear. Let the converted person hope that everything may be forgiven him, but let the hardened person not suppose that anything will be forgiven him.

In this time let the wicked change his life, and he will not find punishment. Let him flee guilt, and he will receive pardon. For in this time the benefit of forgiveness is acquired, when a change of merit accompanies a change of will.

Now let everyone who labors and is burdened come to God, who calls him, to be refreshed. Now let him take upon himself the Savior’s gentle [variant: *light*] yoke and light burden. Now let him learn from him that he is gentle and humble in heart, if he desires to find rest for his soul. Now let the one who has turned away run toward conversion. Now let the wicked depart from iniquity; now let the one who has gone astray return to the way of truth.

Now let the one who does not wish to suffer misery without end seek the Lord’s mercy. Now let the one who does not wish to die eternally seek eternal life. Now let the one who does not wish to be condemned to everlasting punishment anticipate God’s presence in confession.

For now repentance is practiced fruitfully; now forgiveness of sins is granted to the repentant; now possession of the kingdom of heaven is not denied to the converted—a kingdom in which one lives without end and rejoices without end. There death does not take life away from those who rejoice, nor can sorrow take joy away from those who live.

In whatever faith and work the end of this life finds each human being, such will be the recompense given to him, and it will have no end. For just as everyone who has not been converted before the end of the present life and has ended it in his evils will have no rest thereafter, so everyone who in this time has obeyed the divine commandments and has been converted from his evils, if he perseveres to the end in right faith and a good life within the Catholic Church, will be saved. Amen.

[Col. 0573B]

**One Book by Saint Fulgentius, Author, on the Incarnation of the Son of God and the Vile Animals, Addressed to Scarila. (C)**

[Col. 0573C] 406

### 1.

After reading the letter you sent, dearest son Scarila, I rejoiced in the Lord, and my soul exulted in God my Savior, because he has inspired you with a concern for salvation and mercifully infused into your heart a desire for righteousness, so that you might wish to know the true faith.

Through this faith the abundance of life has come to humanity, as God himself testified through the prophet, saying: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17). That faith ought to be called true which is genuine, not feigned; the holy Apostle commends it when he says: “The goal of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1:5).

Since the same blessed Paul says that we have been saved by grace through faith, which he asserts is not from ourselves but God’s gift (Eph. 2:8), true salvation certainly will not exist where true faith is absent. When true faith is divinely infused, it is undoubtedly given by gratuitous generosity; and where the truth of belief exists through true faith, the truth of salvation will also accompany it. Whoever has strayed from the true faith, however, will not possess the grace of true salvation.

Therefore the faithful mind must not grow sluggish in seeking an answer if it sees something obscure in the mystery of faith—especially in the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, through which righteousness was given to the ungodly, life to the dead, salvation to the weak, and the grace of true freedom to captives.

[Col. 0574C]

### 2.

You wrote, to use your own words, that while a discussion of God’s incarnation arose at the table of Eventus, a Christian and a son of the Catholic Church, one of you asserted concerning that incarnation that God the Father did not assume flesh, but only the Son of God did so.

Another said: “The one God himself, who is one in three persons, deigned to assume flesh in order to lead into freedom our servitude, in which we were held bound through the transgression of our father Adam.”

Then you say that you wish to know whether God the Father himself descended and assumed flesh, or whether, while he remained where he was, he commanded the Word to assume flesh. You also say that we know that “the Word became flesh” so that he himself might dwell among us.

Here you also add the following words: “But one majesty belonging jointly to the Word, who is God, and to the Father, who is God, descended to assume flesh, because we read,” you say:

> “This is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36).

You add further and say that when you brought this testimony forward, the other person replied in opposition: “He said this about the Son, not about the Father” [Note: [Col. 0573D] We emend this from the letter itself, which appears above at 10; it had been read as *he did not say*, but that reading was erroneous.]. At that point you addressed him, so that you might have recourse to us concerning what both of you equally did not know.

We must now give, with God’s gift and assistance, an answer to the question contained in the first part of your letter. When that has been completed, we will not be reluctant, insofar as God grants it, to answer the other question as well.

### 3.

First and foremost, every Catholic Christian must know that the one God is the holy Trinity—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Trinity itself, which is one God, is one nature, but it is not one person.

For it is true that the Trinity is one God: the Trinity is one God because the Father does not have one nature, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. Rather, the Trinity itself, God, is one nature. Yet the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not one person. The person of the Father belongs to the Father alone; the person of the Son belongs to the Son alone; and the person of the Holy Spirit belongs to the Holy Spirit alone.

According to person, therefore, the one who is Father is not himself the Son, and the one who is Son is not himself the Holy Spirit. But according to nature, what the Father is, the Son is; what the Son is, the Holy Spirit is, because according to nature the Trinity itself is one God. There no greater or lesser is spoken of, because one is neither found to be earlier than another nor later.

There the eternity and immensity of each person are as great as those of the three persons according to their nature. Yet the Father alone is the one who begot the Son; the Son alone is the one born from the Father; and the Holy Spirit alone is the one who was neither born from the Father nor begot the Son, but proceeded from the Father and the Son.

The Father, therefore, is the Father of the Son alone; the Son is the Son of the Father alone; but the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of the Father alone or of the Son alone, but is one and common Spirit of the Father and the Son together.

### 4.

In this Trinity, therefore, there are certain properties proper to the individual persons. Although the persons are shown by their proper characteristics, they are nevertheless not separated; their nature, while inseparable, cannot be confused, but the individual characteristics remain in the individual persons precisely in order to display both the natural unity of the true Trinity and the personal Trinity of the true unity.

It is proper, therefore, to the Father alone that he was not born but begot. It is proper to the Son that he did not beget but was born. It is proper to the Holy Spirit that he neither begot nor was born, but proceeds from the begetter and the begotten.

Just as the Father’s eternal generation is without beginning, and the Son’s eternal birth is without beginning, so the Holy Spirit’s procession is naturally eternal and without beginning. For the Son’s birth and the Holy Spirit’s procession from the eternity of God the Father, which remains without beginning, are such that both that birth and that procession are coeternal with the origin in which no beginning could in any way be found.

Since that natural unity of the Trinity has this characteristic—that being born is proper to the Son alone—he alone possesses true human birth from the Virgin. For it was his to have, according to the flesh, a true natural mother, just as according to divinity he naturally has a true Father. Therefore the one begotten without beginning from the eternal Father is himself born temporally from a temporal mother. For this reason he is called the only-begotten Son of God truly not only in divinity but also in the flesh: he is found to have been begotten alone both according to divinity and according to the flesh.

### 5.

Both births, therefore, belong properly to God’s only-begotten Son alone: one from the truth of divine nature, the other from the grace of the humanity he assumed. For this reason the evangelist John declares that the only-begotten from the Father is “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

Therefore that deadly and wholly diabolical blasphemy must be avoided by which it is believed or said that the Trinity itself, as a whole, assumed flesh. The Catholic faith does not accept this; rather, it was invented by the wickedness of Sabellian error.

Sabellius recognized that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit were preached as one true God, not three gods. He heard what was true in such a way that he generated for himself what was false. Since he understood the nature of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be one, he did not hesitate to proclaim one person of that same nature. Thus, driven headlong into the madness of his error, he asserted that the Father himself was born from the Virgin.

It necessarily followed that, to the one to whom he attributed the reality of human birth, he also assigned the reality of suffering and death. For this reason the Catholic Church called the followers of that same Sabellius not only Sabellians but also Patripassians—those who say that the Father suffered—and condemned them, together with their author, under the bond of anathema.

### 6.

Therefore, may this perversity be far from the faithful, and may God not permit anyone redeemed by the blood of his only-begotten Son to be profaned by this deadly sense of unbelief.

For it is a great act of impiety if anyone wishes one person to be proclaimed in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit because of the unity of nature, or asserts three natures because of the three persons.

The one who asserts one person of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is caught in the snare of Sabellian error. Whoever confirms that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three natures is bound by the chains of Arian unbelief.

Although the assertions of the two forms of unbelief appear divided, the condemnation of both impieties is nevertheless one. The distinct properties of the persons are impiously confused because of the unity of nature; yet the natural unity is no less impiously separated because of the persons themselves.

The Father has one true Son, naturally his own: begotten from him without beginning and born temporally from the Virgin. He sent him into the world so that the world might be saved through him. The same Son, showing this, says:

> “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him. Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John 3:16–18).

### 7.

Behold, in this passage our Savior himself calls himself the Son three times, names himself the only-begotten twice, and asserts that he was sent by the Father to save the world. If the Trinity itself had come in the flesh, the Son certainly would not have said that he had been sent by the Father. But Christ could not lie: undoubtedly one person sent and another person was sent.

The true Father sent the Truth whom he begot; he sent the Wisdom in which he made all things; he sent the Word whom he uttered from his heart.

Therefore, in this other kind of mission [variant: *that mission*], his coming must not be understood locally, as though the Son of God had been sent from heaven to earth in such a way that he was not previously on earth before receiving flesh, or that he abandoned heaven when he assumed flesh for our salvation.

Since he himself is the Wisdom of God, of whom it was said, “She reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things gently” (Wis. 8:1), that divinity which is naturally one in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is not local in the way that it is not temporal. It is not confined by place, just as it is not changed by time.

That divinity, which is naturally immense and eternal, neither began with a beginning nor is confined by a place. Therefore the one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, fills everything and contains everything: wholly present in each thing, wholly present in all things, wholly present in small creatures, wholly present in the greatest creatures—so according to nature, but not in the same way according to grace; so when he creates human beings, but not in the same way when he saves them; so when he makes them, but not in the same way when he renews them; so when he makes this sun rise upon the good and the wicked, but not in the same way when the Sun of righteousness rises upon those to whom life—not of the flesh but of the heart—is infused by the gift of prevenient mercy.

For it is not the case that, just as all share in birth according to nature, so all share in rebirth according to grace.

Since, therefore, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are naturally one God, eternal and immense, there is nothing in heaven, nothing on earth, nothing above heaven, and nothing in any nature he has made where that one God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—can be absent. In him, just as there is no mutability of times, so there is no capacity or limitation of places.

Solomon is rightly found to have said this at the dedication of the Temple in these words:

> “If heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house that I have built!” (1 Kings 8:27).

### 8

Thus God is ineffable and altogether wondrous, ineffably and wondrously being, by the very immensity of his nature, wholly present in each individual thing, yet not confined by the universe. So is the Father alone; so is the Son alone; so is the Holy Spirit alone; so likewise is the Trinity together, the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: for neither is the Father alone without the Son or the Holy Spirit, nor is the Holy Spirit alone without the Father or the Son.

Therefore we must carefully consider how the Son could be sent into the world, when he could not be absent from the world; or how he came into the world, from which he never departs [Col. 0577D]—since, for one whose nature it is wholly to fill all things, it is equally impossible either to depart in any degree or to come. For that nature of immense divinity is neither extended so as to fill what had previously been empty, nor contracted so as to empty what it had previously filled. Such is the power of the Creator, and such the condition of the whole creation, that just as no substance can exist unless he creates it, so no substance can endure unless he sustains it.

Therefore, since according to his divinity God does not pass from place to place, the truth of the Christian faith is that the Son of God is believed to have come into the world in that in which he is recognized to have received the form of a servant. The Son of God came into the world when, while preserving the equality of the Father’s nature, he deigned to become a participant in his mother’s substance [Col. 0578A]—when he became man while preserving his divinity, temporal while preserving his eternity, located while preserving his immensity, mutable while preserving his unchangeability, mortal while preserving his immortality.

### 9

The coming of the Son of God, however, is not always understood in one and the same way. For he comes in one manner when sent by the Father, and in another when he deigns to come with the Father. When he deigns to come with the Father, he comes as the equal; when sent by the Father, he comes humbled, made for a little while lower than the angels. Sent by the Father, he is recognized as having come once; with the Father, he deigns to come innumerable times.

For he established neither a manner nor a number of comings when he said: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23).

Therefore, that coming by which the Son alone came once into the world from the Father was manifested not only to the good but also to the wicked: to some so that they might believe, to others so that they might crucify him; to some so that they might be able to be freed from sin, to others so that they could have no excuse for their sin.

The Apostle shows that believers have been freed from sin when he says: “But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit in sanctification, and the end is eternal life” (Rom. VI, 22). The Savior himself showed that unbelievers could have no excuse for their sin, saying: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin. But now they have no excuse for their sin” (John XV, 22). For the Jews would not have had the sin of unbelief if the Savior’s presence had not also been manifested to them.

That coming, therefore, by which the Son was sent once from the Father [Col. 0578C] into the world, was for the fall and resurrection of many; but that coming by which he comes with the Father concerns only the resurrection of many, because it is deserved by love, which covers a multitude of sins.

By the coming in which he was sent by the Father, the Son came once in the fullness of time; but by the coming in which he habitually comes with the Father, he has not ceased to come, and does not cease, from the beginning to the end of the world, to those to whom it was necessary and is necessary. Hence, before he came in the flesh, the prophets sought his coming, saying: “Stir up your power and come, that you may save us” (Ps. LXXIX, 3). They certainly would not have sought the future coming of the Son of God if they did not possess the grace of that same one who comes and remains in them.

### 10

Those who do not believe in the equality of the Father and the Son altogether reject from themselves this coming of the Son of God and of the Father [Col. 0578D]. For those who come make one dwelling with the one who loves them; but their dwelling cannot be one if their love is different. If they are unequal, they must be loved unequally. But a single dwelling cannot be prepared in a simple heart for unequal beings.

Scripture admonishes us, saying: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. I, 1). How, then, is God sought in simplicity of heart when a difference of love is shown toward God the Father and God the Son? Or how is a person’s love toward God simple if a difference is thought to exist within the divinity itself?

That divinity is loved with a simple heart which is believed to be naturally simple. But where a diverse divinity is worshiped, not simplicity of heart but duplicity is displayed; the faith there is therefore not true but feigned.

“The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. I, 5). A heart is shown to be double if someone does not think that one divinity is to be worshiped by the faithful, or if he does not believe that the Son has the same nature as the Father.

If someone who pretends goodness in his words toward his neighbor while harboring wickedness in his heart is called double-hearted, how can one who, under the pretense of truth, either believes or says false things about God not be held guilty of a double heart? To divide what is naturally one in that supreme divinity, and to imagine God as lesser and greater, most certainly belongs to the wickedness of a double heart.

Holy Scripture says: “Woe to the double-hearted, and to wicked lips, and to hands that do evil, and to the sinner who walks the earth by two ways!” (Ecclus. II, 14). And because to think that the divinity of the Father and the Son is different is not to believe in God—for the one truly worships the one God who worships no other at all, and the one believes in the one God who does not believe another to be God—therefore the same Scripture continues: “Woe to those who do not believe God, for they are not protected by him!” (Ecclus. II, 15).

Hence our Savior also, commending the one divinity and lordship, says: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI, 24). We read that “the Lord himself is God” (Ps. XCIX, 3). It is therefore certain that by true faith and sincere love no one can serve either lords or gods. For there is one God of gods and Lord of lords [Col. 0579C], who alone is to be worshiped because he alone is naturally the true Lord God, who is the Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

### 11

Therefore, if we seek God in simplicity of heart, let us not believe in our hearts that there is a difference of divinity between the Father and the Son. But so that true simplicity of heart may remain in us, let that faith remain in us by which the one divinity of the holy Trinity is believed and proclaimed without distinction.

Thus the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit deign to come and remain in us. The holy Trinity has one coming to the one who loves it: the invisible God comes invisibly and invisibly makes his dwelling. By remaining with the one who loves it, it multiplies love itself, and therefore makes its dwelling in a human being. For this reason it comes: because it is loved; and in coming it causes itself to be loved more.

### 12

I have said these things so that you may know what the coming of the Son was like when he was sent by the Father, and what the coming of the Son is like when he deigns to come with the Father. For just as in that coming, having become man, he is recognized as lesser than the Father, so in this coming he is found to remain God, equal to the Father.

The Holy Spirit is also said to come, although he is, together with the Father and the Son, one God, naturally eternal and immense, without whom neither the Father nor the Son can come. For one who has love in his heart is known to love him [perhaps: “that one,” *illum*] after the Father and the Son. “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. V, 5).

Therefore the Father and the Son do not come at all to the one who loves them without the Holy Spirit, because, in order that they may come, they bestow through the gift of the Holy Spirit the love by which they are loved.

Thus the common coming of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is always invisible: not by passing from place to place, but in this respect, that the Trinity, the one God, deigns either to give the grace of love, which it may increase, or to increase what it gives.

The Son comes in another manner when the only-begotten God became man for us. He is the one who, in the person of his own divinity, did not receive the person of a man but his nature.

We also know that the Holy Spirit came visibly in the form of a dove: in a wholly different manner—not in the manner by which the Father and the Son come to the one who loves them, never without the Holy Spirit, nor in the manner by which the Son alone came into the world, when he wonderfully and uniquely received our nature in the person of his divinity [Col. 0580B].

For the Son did not receive the form of a dove as he received the form of a servant; nor did the Holy Spirit become in the likeness of doves as the Son became in the likeness of human children. The Holy Spirit therefore came in the form of a dove, but certainly did not receive a dove into the unity of his person. For the nature of doves did not need to be redeemed through the Holy Spirit in the way that human nature was redeemed through the Son.

The Son received human nature into the unity of his person, and he would undoubtedly redeem the nature he received. And because his humanity is never separated from the Son of God, he therefore rules over all angels and all human beings in heaven and on earth.

According to his human nature, the Son of God humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil. II, 8); according to that same nature God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, “so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (ibid., 9).

When the fullness of time had come, “God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law” (Gal. IV, 4). Showing subsequently why this had been done, the Apostle says: “So that he might redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.”

Human nature was therefore assumed by the Son of God. The only-begotten God became man so that through him divine adoption might be given to us: because he is truly God and man by the natural truth of his divinity, we too, in that we are his brothers, might become children of God—not by our own merit but by his grace.

### 13

The Holy Spirit, coming in the form of a dove, did not become a dove as the Son became man; rather, through the form of a dove he showed that love was to be given to us through his gift. “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. V, 5).

He later appeared also in tongues of fire, but he did this too as a sign of the very love that he bestowed upon us. For “the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I, 5); and in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power, but only “faith working through love” (Gal. V, 6).

This is the simplicity of heart signified in the dove: we must confess with confidence for salvation what we believe in our heart unto righteousness. The dove therefore displays the simplicity of faith and love, so that we may rightly believe in God and, through God, love our neighbor as well. The fiery tongue likewise signifies the confession of true belief and the admonition of holy love.

That dove, therefore, in whose form the Holy Spirit came upon Christ when he had been baptized, was made to signify something and immediately dissolved. For the Son alone assumed human flesh and soul. To him alone, naturally, did divine birth belong. And because he alone was born from the Father, he alone could also be born from a Virgin.

Unless he became man from man, he would not have been a participant in our nature. It was therefore done so that he might receive true flesh from the flesh of the Virgin, so that true natural communion might remain between us and him. For how could he admit the ancient Fathers, or human beings of any age, into fellowship with his divinity if he did not share with them a natural fellowship of flesh?

### 14

The Son of God therefore deigned to become not merely man but also one from among human beings. Hence the Apostle, speaking of Christ, says: “For he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham.” Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make atonement for the sins of the people.

“For in that he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted.” Therefore, holy brothers, participants in a heavenly calling, “consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession, Jesus, who is faithful to him who made him” (Hebr. II, 16; III, 1).

For this reason the same Epistle says again elsewhere: “Every high priest chosen from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God, so that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins” (Hebr. V, 1).

This high priest was such that, for the reconciliation of the human race, he might offer himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, as a fragrant aroma. Hence, while we were enemies, “we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. V, 10).

To show that Christ the Son of God derived the origin of his flesh from that one man from whom the natural unity propagated all human beings, the blessed Apostle says elsewhere: “He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.” For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers” (Hebr. II, 11).

He says this about us: according to the flesh, he was both born and suffered for us; indeed, he became a participant in our nature in such a way that he came from that one from whom we all came, deriving the origin of his flesh from that one from whom we all derive our origin.

If the Trinity had assumed flesh for us, since we have become brothers of the one who was incarnate through our fellowship in the flesh, we would then be not only sons of God the Father but also brothers of the whole Trinity; and the one whom we have as Father in heaven, human birth would also have made our brother.

### 15

It is a great absurdity to suppose that he was begotten in time whose proper relation from eternity is not to have been born but to have begotten. It therefore accords with the true faith to confess that neither the Father nor the Spirit, but the Son alone, was born from God the Father, just as he alone was born from the Virgin Mary.

Since the Son alone, therefore, assumed flesh, he made us children of God and, having freed us from slavery to sin, restored us to true freedom. And because he alone was born from the Virgin, he alone was handed over for us, as the Apostle testifies: “God did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. VIII, 32).

For he also says of the Son himself: “The life that I now live in the flesh I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and handed himself over for me” (Gal. II, 20). Elsewhere he says: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins, so that he might rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be glory forever and ever” (Gal. I, 3).

Therefore, just as the Father handed over the Son, so the Son handed himself over; and just as the Son gave himself, so the Father also gave him, as the Son says: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John III, 16).

### 16

Since all these things have been established, clearly showing that the Son alone assumed flesh for our salvation, was alone handed over for our sins [Col. 0582C], and endured the punishment of suffering and death, let no believer say that God the Father was either born from the Virgin or handed over for us.

These things belong to the Son alone, who, just as he deigned to be born for us in time, so also died in time. If anyone attributes the assumption of flesh to God the Father, let him pay particular attention to this in the Gospel: the God who put on flesh very frequently called himself not only the Son of Man but also the Son of God.

To the man born blind whom he had enlightened he said: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” He answered: “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?” And Jesus said to him: “You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he.” He said: “I believe, Lord.” And falling down, he worshiped him (John IX, 35 ff.).

He also said to the Jews: “Is it not written in your law, ‘I said, You are gods’? If he called those gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—do you say of the one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (John X, 34).

Elsewhere he called himself both the Son of Man and the Son of God, saying: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John III, 14).

Immediately afterward, the Savior added concerning himself what we have placed in this work, in which he called himself the Son of God, saying: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send the Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him. Whoever believes in him will not be judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John III, 17 ff.).

And when he called himself the Son of Man, saying to his disciples, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. XVI, 13), and, after hearing the many opinions of people—those who, according to their own will, were devising a deadly falsehood about the Truth itself—said, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid., 15–16).

For this reason he deserved to be called blessed, when the Lord himself replied: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid., 17).

### 17

Hence, even after the resurrection, he testifies in these words that he is going up to his Father: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John XX, 17).

If, therefore, the God who put on flesh is asserted to be God the Father himself, it necessarily follows that another must be asserted to be the Father of that Father. Consequently, God the Father also had a Father, to whom he would say [or: “to whom it is said”]: “Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John XVII, 1).

From this impious and blasphemous understanding one also falls into the claim that there is not one Father but two: one the Father of the Son, whom the truth knows, and the other the Father of the Father, whom vanity invents.

And where is the Apostle’s confession of one God the Father: “For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we are in him” (I Cor. VIII, 6)? Elsewhere he says: “One God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in all of us” (Eph. IV, 6).

Although the Son is naturally one God with him, in respect of persons one is the Father, another the Son, and another the Holy Spirit. The blessed John clearly shows these persons, saying: “Whoever loves the one who begets loves the one who has been begotten by him” (I John V, 1).

He also says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John I, 1). A little later, to show that it was the Word alone who received flesh, he says: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 14).

### 18

God the Word therefore became flesh, not the God with whom the Word was. For the only-begotten one, who is in the bosom of the Father, is, insofar as he is flesh, full of grace, and, insofar as he is the Word, full of truth: he is the one Word made flesh who dwelt among us.

The prophet also says of him: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him, who discovered every way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III, 36).

True faith has received this testimony as spoken of the Son alone. For according to the flesh he appeared on earth and lived among human beings. Hence the holy evangelist Matthew, entirely agreeing with the prophetic statement, says that Jesus lived among his disciples. For he says: “As they were living in Galilee, Jesus said to them: ‘The Son of Man is to be handed over into the hands of men, and they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise again’” [Col. 0584A] (Matt. XVII, 21).

He had therefore come in order to be killed for us. But how could he be killed if he were not handed over? Or how could he be handed over if he were not seized? How could he be seized if he did not live among human beings? Or how could he live among human beings if he were not seen on earth? How could he be seen if he were not born? And how could he be born if flesh were not conceived from flesh?

If all these things had not taken place, the Lord’s counsel, which remains forever, would in no way have been fulfilled. With that counsel left unfulfilled, no grace of salvation would have been bestowed on us sinners. And how would the name by which he was called Jesus have been true? For this name is interpreted as “Savior.”

Therefore, when the angel told Joseph that Mary would bear the Son of God, he added: “You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. I, 21). To Mary herself the angel spoke as follows: “Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a Son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High” (Luke I, 31–32).

God the Father, therefore, was not born from the Virgin, since the one whom the Virgin bore was called the Son of the Most High. Since, then, there is one Father, one Son, and one Holy Spirit, the one who is naturally the Son of the Most High—born from the Father’s eternal divinity—is, according to the true faith, called the Son of the Most High also from the Virgin.

### 19

Nor should it disturb you that the prophet, speaking of the Son alone, said: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him” (Baruch III, 36). From his saying that no other is accounted beside him, no one should suppose that he means that the Father and the Son are the same person.

The blessed Jeremiah, filled with the Holy Spirit, says: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him,” so that in what he first said, “This is God,” we might understand that no other is accounted beside him because there is no other God apart from him.

Naturally, therefore, there is not another God apart from the Holy Spirit, because there is not one God the Father, another God the Son, and another God the Holy Spirit. Rather, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, and apart from this God of ours there is no other God.

Thus the Father is our God, so that no other is accounted beside him; the Son likewise is our God, so that no other is accounted beside him; and likewise the Holy Spirit is our God, so that no other is accounted beside him. For apart from this one God there is no other God, of whom David says: “Who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God?” (Ps. XVII, 32).

And God himself says: “See, see that I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Deut. XXXII, 39). Of this the blessed James also says: “You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe, and tremble” (James II, 19).

### 20

Naturally, therefore, no other God is accounted beside the Son, because no other God is accounted beside the Father, nor is another God accounted beside the Holy Spirit.

In respect of persons, however, the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. The Father himself is not the Son, nor is the Holy Spirit himself the Father or the Son; but they are the same one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The Son himself shows that the Father is another in person, and that the Holy Spirit is another, saying: “There is another who bears witness concerning me, and I know that the testimony with which he testifies concerning me is true” (John V, 32).

And lest anyone think that this was said about John, he says a little later: “But I have testimony greater than John’s. For the works that the Father gave me to accomplish—the very works that I do—testify about me, that the Father sent me. And the Father who sent me himself testifies about me” (ibid., 36).

He also shows the Holy Spirit to be personally another, saying: “If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John XIV, 15).

Of him he also says elsewhere: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will testify about me” (John XV, 16).

The majesty of the Father and the Son is one, and it does not descend from heaven to a place [Col. 0585B]. For the highest and true divinity cannot pass from place to place, because it is always wholly everywhere.

The one majesty of the Trinity is the same, as is its naturally one, immense divinity. But, as I said above, the nature of the Trinity is one in such a way that the person is not one.

Therefore, while the immensity of his majesty—which he shares with the Father and the Holy Spirit—remained, the Son alone received human nature into the unity of his person. For this reason the flesh he assumed is not shared with the Father and the Holy Spirit, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit do not share one person.

### 21

The whole Trinity therefore made that form of a servant, yet the Son alone received it into his person. For he alone is the Word, and the Evangelist truthfully says: “The Word became flesh” (John I, 14). Yet the Father did not command some other Word that he should become flesh. For the Father has one Word, through whom he made and makes all things, through whom he spoke and speaks all things.

This Word was sent by the Father when the Word became flesh; but the Father did not speak to him, in order that he might be sent, through passing words. For the eternal Word born from the Father is the eternal command of the Father, because the eternal generation of the Son is itself the Father’s eternal speech.

Each person hears this Word when the truth of the divinity and incarnation is recognized. For just as every human being has a word in his heart while thinking—a word that is not brought forth except when clothed with bodily speech, since through the voice it can come to the knowledge of others—when that word is revealed through the voice of the speaker, it is in no way separated from the inmost heart.

Rather, this wondrous thing occurs: the whole word reaches others through bodily speech, while the whole remains spiritually in the heart of the one speaking. So also the Word of God, born from the Father, remained in the Father. We could in no way recognize it unless it were clothed with the substance of flesh, as with a bodily voice.

Thus the whole Word came to us when the Word became flesh, while the whole remained spiritual with the Father: equal to the Father, from whom it has always been born, and, so that it could be perceived by us, made lower through the grace of the flesh it assumed [Col. 0586A].

Accordingly, the Lord from the Lord remained Lord in the form of God; and, in order to come to servants, he received from a handmaid the reality of the form of a servant.

### 22

But some, understanding less fully the mystery of this form of a servant that was assumed, when they hear us proclaiming one essence of the holy Trinity, either deny or doubt that it could have happened that the Son—who according to his divinity is proclaimed by us to be inseparable from the Father and the Holy Spirit—alone received for us the reality of the form of a servant and nevertheless remained inseparable from the Father and the Holy Spirit.

This would undoubtedly seem impossible to those who, because they do not understand the invisible things of God through the things that have been made, do not perceive them. If they would consider the common experience of human nature, they would find even in that great mystery of piety the proper lines of understanding.

Since, therefore, there is one true divinity that possesses within itself three wholly inseparable persons—for which reason the Trinity is one God—and since no nature in creation is found to be inseparable in three persons, let us consider what happens in each human being. In a human being we find not three persons in one nature but two natures in one person.

For God, by a wondrous work of power, composed one nature of a human being from two natures—that is, from a rational soul and flesh—and ordained that one human person should remain in soul and flesh. Behold: in a human being there are two natures in one person. In the same way we say that the Trinity is three persons in one nature.

### 23

Let us therefore observe that, while these two natures remain in one person, certain things are done jointly, though they are not jointly received or possessed.

Indeed, in ourselves we find something accomplished through the service of both flesh and soul, which nevertheless we attribute either only to the flesh or only to the soul.

Certainly, just as the flesh alone is nourished by bodily food, so the soul is spiritually nourished by the word of God. Yet, in order that flesh, which was made from the earth, may be nourished by earthly foods, it eats with the cooperation of the soul, since it lives from the soul. It eats because it lives, and it usefully has within itself the activity of the other working together with it—the cooperation of the soul—in which there is both, by reason of life, the capacity to eat, and, by reason of food, the capacity to live.

When food is taken, therefore, the operation of flesh and soul is common, although the food is found properly to belong only to the flesh.

In receiving the word of God also, by which the soul alone is nourished with spiritual food, it uses the service either of the eyes or of the ears in order to reach that same food. Thus, so that the soul itself may be nourished inwardly, this is accomplished not without the operation of the flesh.

Therefore, just as here the operation of both natures is found, although the reception belongs to one, so let us believe that the human nature of the only-begotten God was made together by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but was mercifully assumed by the Son alone for our salvation.

### 24

Meanwhile, you add that one of you later said at that meal that God did not make flies, fleas, scorpions, and bugs, but that after the fall of that unworthy angel, the devil, all these things were made by the devil himself.

And while you were saying that God made all things, and made them very good, he said that you should consult me about this, so that I might satisfy them on the question whether, before the transgression, when God made all things, these creatures were then made, or whether they were made after Adam’s transgression.

These are the words with which your letter concludes. Your question, however, has two parts: you asked both whether God made all those things and when he made them.

### 25

First, then, I see that we must discuss whether God made them. Here the blessed evangelist John shows us what we ought to think, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 1–3).

See how the holy evangelist, filled with the Spirit of God, has beneficially made known to us in a few words not only the Creator but also the creature.

For the statement, “In the beginning was the Word,” is rightly understood by the faith in two ways: either that the Son was in the Father, because the Father and the Son are naturally one beginning; or that not only the Father but also the Son exists without beginning.

That is most certainly called a true beginning which is preceded by no beginning of existence. Whatever began to exist in the beginning was made by the work of God the Creator and cannot have one nature with the Creator. For that is subject to a beginning which God created from nothing.

Therefore, that is rightly said to exist “in the beginning” which, by nature, always exists without a beginning of existence. This eternity without beginning is true divinity.

This is found naturally in the one Son, who was born from the Father, and in the one Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son [Col. 0587C].

What the evangelist says, “In the beginning was the Word,” is therefore as though he had said, “The Word always existed.” For whatever beginning a human being may wish to imagine, the Word is not found ever to have begun, but always to have been in the beginning.

Then, by saying, “The Word was with God,” he shows that the nature of the Word is neither temporal nor local. The Word that was in the beginning has nothing belonging to the beginning of time; the Word that was with God before every creature subject to times and places has nothing belonging to spatial extension.

Then, by saying, “The Word was God,” he shows the one nature of the Father and the Son, since he declares that the Word who was with God was naturally nothing other than God.

The evangelist first calls him “the Word,” expressing the person who truly exists—a designation that is not common to the Father and the Son. For the Son alone is called the Word.

### 26 [Col. 0588A]

Natural signification required that, just as the name of the person was disclosed, so also the name of the nature should be displayed in the Word. Therefore the blessed Evangelist subsequently added: “And the Word was God.” Thus, by indicating the only-begotten Son of God not merely personally but also naturally, he fulfilled the task of holy preaching: by calling him “the Word,” he revealed the Son of the Father by a personal name; and by naming him “God,” a common designation, he showed that he is of one nature with the Father.

Then, so that the unity of nature might be commended more fully through the unity of the work, the blessed Evangelist added: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Who said this? He who, reclining upon the breast of Wisdom and Truth, received true knowledge of the incomprehensible Majesty; who, just as he knew that the Father and the Son are one God, also knew that all things were made by the Father through the Son. Accordingly, holy John comprehended universally all those things that were made through the Son when he said: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

Whoever, then, strives to deny that flies, fleas, scorpions, bugs, or any other creatures offensive to mortal perception were made by God must either say that they were not made at all, or, if he says that they were made, must nevertheless deny that they were made by the Father through the Son. What else remains but that he should say that the Evangelist John lied in his preaching? For he says: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

### 27 [Cols. 0588B–0589A; p. 420]

There is therefore nothing that the Father did not make, since he made all things; nor is there anything that the Father did not make through the Son, without whom nothing was made. Consequently, whatever exists as a natural entity must necessarily be counted among the works of him through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made.

The Evangelist, full of truth, testifies that, in the teaching of the Holy Spirit, Paul likewise—the chosen vessel and teacher of the nations—did not cease to make this known to us in faith and truth, saying what we have already quoted above: “For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we are in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we are through him” (1 Corinthians 8:6).

In another passage he also (alternative reading: “and again”) took care to explain the same point more clearly, saying: “For in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones or Dominions or Principalities or Powers; all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him” (Colossians 1:16–17).

But lest anyone hear that all things in heaven and on earth were created through Christ and in Christ and, because the sea is not named here, suppose that the things in the waters are excluded from the work of divine creation, let him first attend to the beginning of Genesis, where, at the Lord’s command, the waters produced “the moving creatures that have life,” and the birds that fly over the earth (Genesis 1:20). Let him recognize that the one who is creator on earth of trees and plants, and likewise in heaven of the luminaries and stars, is himself the creator in the waters of fish and birds.

Just as he understands that God first made heaven, in which he would make the luminaries and stars, and first made the earth, which at his command would produce plants and trees, so also he made the waters, from which, at his command, both creatures that crawl and creatures that fly would arise. For the Word would not have created anything from the waters if he had not previously made those same waters through the Word.

For this reason the blessed David did not remain silent about the universal creation by God of heaven, earth, and sea, together with everything in them, saying: “Blessed is the man whose God is Jacob is his help, whose hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them” (Psalm 145:4–5).

How, then, while prophetic authority testifies that heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them were made by God, can the apostle Paul also assert that all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, or Powers, were created in Christ, and yet someone refuse to believe that flies, scorpions, fleas, and bugs were created on earth by God—the God whom he cannot deny to have created Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, and Powers in the heavens? Is that God, then, who established angelic legions above the heavens in creating them, to be denied as the maker of scorpions on earth, where he made human beings, beasts and cattle, birds and fish?

### 28 [Cols. 0589B–0589D; p. 421]

What, I ask, is displeasing in those scorpions, so that anyone should suppose that they were not made by God? For there is nothing in the body of a scorpion that does not proclaim the Creator’s praise. First, there is the very structure: the joining and proportioning of the limbs, their harmony and symmetry; then there is the soul that gives life to the body and enables it to sense. Who could doubt that all these things are good?

But surely the force of the venom found in the scorpion’s body, which is thought to be harmful to human beings and appears dreadful, should prompt people to consider the penalty for their transgression and cease falsely assigning God’s good works to the devil! They pay too little attention to how much natural harmony contributes to God’s works, how much proper measure benefits each thing, and how much the excess of immoderation harms it.

[Text corrupt:] “which, since almighty God did not allow [it] to be very great—who would not praise God’s works even in those servants [perhaps: ‘scourges’], when he sees a sinner chastised by the divine scourge?”

For God made, as it is written, “the human being upright” (Ecclesiastes 7:30), and established him as lord of all the things he had created on earth and in the sea, making him subject only to his own authority. He required from him the obedience due to servitude, while granting him the free choice of the will.

As long as the human being served his Lord with fitting devotion, he also retained unshaken dominion over those things over which he himself had been placed; and he lost nothing of what he had received until he himself fully repaid what he owed. But when, by transgressing the commandment, he offended the Lord, he immediately encountered in his own body the insult he had inflicted upon God. Thus he learned how evil it was to despise the commands of the good Creator, when, after he had begun to be evil, he lost his power over his generative members.

How, then, could he remain lord of all those things he had received from God, when, by despising the Lord, he had lost the rights of dominion in his own original body? From that point his body also began to be subject to infirmity and death. Thus, by a just vengeance that followed, the one who had not feared the death of the soul in sin came to fear the death of the body in punishment; and, having lost the repose in which he had enjoyed blessedness, he was miserably disturbed by the smallest animals.

### 29 [Cols. 0589D–0590B]

This is why, after the sin of the first human being, through which human nature as a whole was subjected to the reign of sin and death, the human being rules camels, horses, oxen, elephants, and other large four-footed animals, yet is tormented by the bite of a bug or flea. Although all those creatures that are larger in body and stronger in power serve human beings in a tame condition, these tiniest creatures—which could easily be killed by being crushed between two fingers—cannot in any way be brought back to gentleness.

It is clear that this happened by divine judgment, so that, from those creatures over which he rules, the human being might recognize how great a dignity he possessed before the transgression; and, from those by which he is disturbed and harmed, might acknowledge to what degradation he has descended through transgression. God left the greater creatures under his power and withdrew the lesser ones, simultaneously showing what the Creator’s goodness bestowed upon humanity and what its own wickedness inflicted upon the sinner.

Thus, through the transgression of the first human beings, because of the merit of so great a crime, a profound natural weakness befell the human race—not so that human beings would yield to certain evil natures, but so that human weakness would experience punishments and dangers arising from the disharmony of good natures.

Therefore, when a flea torments a human being and a scorpion kills him, this is not the creation of evil things, but the disharmony of good natures that followed, in accordance with the justice of the Judge, upon the prior wickedness of the rebellious human being.

For God, whose works are true and whose ways are upright, is most rightly confessed by holy Zechariah in his prayer to be one who, being supremely good, makes good everything that he makes [Note: [Col. 0589D] “Makes good” (*bona facit*), or something similar, must be supplied here.].

### 30 [Cols. 0590C–0591A; p. 422]

For this reason, in a wondrous work, immutable justice also makes fitting use of the very disharmony of natures by which human sins are punished. It does this by assigning to each its due, so that it makes the disharmony of one nature toward another universally correspond to the works of each nature.

A particular nature, when it is less suited to another nature for the purpose of preservation, must not on that account be considered evil because it causes harm—for every nature, insofar as it is a nature, is good. Rather, adversity is often inflicted by one nature upon another because weakness yields and succumbs to incompatibility.

Indeed, often even those very things—those very natures—in which alone undeniable danger is usually found, when tempered by suitable moderation from other things, are transformed from the danger of death into remedies for health. We find this first of all in poisonous animals themselves.

Some people say that whenever a sharp fever arises in the body, it is quickly extinguished by crushing scorpions and applying them. But even if some perhaps consider this doubtful or false, no one is permitted to deny what is found wonderfully in snakes.

No one is unaware that vipers are naturally poisonous, or of how scorpions kill with their poisonous sting [perhaps: “with which they kill…”]. Yet, to show that it is not the wickedness of natures but their incompatibility that causes harm, we know that medicines are prepared against viper bites from viper flesh suitably tempered with other substances; and these medicines are beneficially applied not only to those struck by scorpions but also to those bitten by vipers.

Who would not marvel here at God’s wisdom? Who would not magnify his goodness and praise his prudence? He does not restrain his mercies in anger; rather, from the very source from which he caused dangers to arise for sinners, he ordained that remedies should be supplied to those in peril. Thus, from his goodness, we might experience benefits where we feel hardships because of our wickedness.

Who could express the Creator’s praise in words sufficient for the occasion, when he created one and the same viper in such a way that it simultaneously carries within itself both destruction and remedy; and when, while alive, it brings death, yet when dead, restores health; both inflicts and repels the destruction of life; and the venom poured in by the serpent’s tooth is extinguished by the flesh of that same serpent? Thus the viper, while alive, served human weakness and death, but when dead, serves life and health.

Who, I ask, does these things except the one to whom the Church sings, “Mercy and judgment” (Psalm 101:1)?

### 31 [Cols. 0591B–0591C; p. 423]

Who is unaware how harmful the plant called scammony is to healthy people if taken alone, and how beneficial it is to the sick if suitably mixed with other substances?

And, to speak of things always desired by everyone, things whose daily use is needed not only by weakness but even by human bodily health itself, let us consider bread and wine, neither of which suits a person suffering from fever. For we see physicians prohibiting the sick from drinking at all times, and sometimes also from eating bread.

This is done not because bread or wine is evil, but because it is unsuitable for the sick. Once they begin to be suitable, they nourish strength and preserve health. Yet their excessive consumption deprives the strong of their vigor, forcing healthy people to become ill.

See how much moderation and suitability of things matter in God’s creatures, to which excess and incompatibility are found to be contrary. When these are called natural, what is found is not natural wickedness but an accidental weakness. Anyone who considers all creatures as good, created by the supreme Good, readily recognizes in them the inexpressible and indescribable praise of the Creator.

Accordingly, he above all must be loved who is found both merciful and just even in those things we experience as punishments for our wickedness: from the very place where he restrains the rebellious, he raises up the weak. And because misery immediately followed pride in humanity, the merciful and just Lord places the weight of pride upon us from the very place where he applies the relief of mercy.

### 32 [Cols. 0591D–0592A]

Nevertheless, whoever is a son of the Church and, as you say, proposed the view that flies, scorpions, fleas, and bugs were made not by God but by the devil should take care not to be deceived and led astray by the deadly cunning of the Manichaeans. These people, themselves established in darkness, attempt to introduce a god of light and a god of darkness, and to preach two principles naturally opposed to one another.

Because they say that the nature of light is good but the nature of darkness evil, their own error leads them to assert without hesitation that among all things in the world some natures are good and others evil. They call those natures evil by which their senses are offended, and those good whose enjoyment delights them. They do not understand, as the Apostle says, either what they are saying or the matters about which they make assertions (1 Timothy 1:7).

To say something about light and darkness, whose natures they principally regard as opposed, is not their assertion found to be false at the outset in this respect: darkness, which they say is naturally opposed to light, is found to possess no nature at all? For light and darkness are not two natures. Rather, where light is absent, that very absence of light is called darkness; just as the absence of sound is called silence, and the absence of clothing is called nakedness, and an empty vessel is called empty when no substance—whether liquid or anything else—has been poured into it. So, among ourselves, hunger is spoken of where there is no food, and thirst is spoken of where there is no drink.

### 33 [Cols. 0592B–0592D; p. 424]

All these things I have mentioned, and similar things that I have now left unmentioned in order to maintain moderation in the discussion, are certainly opposed to one another, but not through their own natures. They are opposed through disposition and privation—that is, through the kind of opposition by which something is either possessed or not possessed.

Therefore, although they are opposites, their effects are not always found to be contrary. This bodily light, which the Manichaeans consider the principal good, is indeed good because it was created by the supreme Good; yet it is good in such a way that the substance of life is naturally preferable to it.
