Although it is good, it sometimes becomes not beneficial but punitive for those who use it improperly: it invigorates healthy eyes but torments diseased ones; it refreshes sound eyes but dulls painful ones.

Conversely, eyes afflicted by pain obtain some relief from darkness. With doors and windows closed, they experience some alleviation of the pain they suffer from light, and through a certain suitability of darkness they are nourished so as to see the light.

See how, the less light suits them, the more it harms them; and the more darkness suits them, the more it benefits them. Just as the brightness of light ordinarily assists healthy eyes, so the obscurity of darkness ordinarily assists painful eyes. Thus, when each is received in a suitable way, the effects of both light and darkness are found to aid the eyes. For just as the healthy are helped by light, so the sick are restored by darkness.

When tired eyes close in sleep, they are in a certain way helped by darkness, so that they may again be restored to strength and vigor for seeing the light. For unhealthy and fatigued eyes, removal from beneficial light for the restoration of health and strength is like the suspension of customary food from the entire body when it becomes ill.

These things are not contrary and harmful to the sick because they are naturally evil, but because they are unsuitable for their weakness. For not everything that health accepts can sustain illness. Hence, sometimes the very things by which a healthy body is restored weigh down a sick body; and sometimes even a healthy body is harmed by excess in things whose use benefits it. When something is received improperly, illness is found where health was being sought.

Even the use of clothing, if unsuitable, is found to be not healthy but harmful. Who, whether because of poverty or bodily weakness, would not be harmed by wearing winter clothing when overheated, or summer clothing when chilled?

### 34 [Col. 0593A]

It would take too long to demonstrate the judgment of suitability through many examples, since examples cannot be lacking for those who observe carefully.

All natures that exist, that live, that sense, and that understand are good, because they were made by God—that is, by the supreme Good. If they were not made by the supreme Good, they would not be good; and if they were not good, they would possess nothing good in themselves.

First, because life is something good, and a good of such a kind that living human beings love it, if there were any nature that was not made by the supreme Good, it would in no way live. I say this of animals—that is, of a substance that lives and senses. But even those natures that neither live nor sense possess their very being through the creation of him who supremely is; for not only living but also existing is good, and what supremely is is the supreme Good.

### 35 [Cols. 0593B–0593C; p. 425]

Therefore no nature is evil, whether living or not living. Consequently, all natures, insofar as they are natures, are good. But some of them, although good by God’s creation, have become punitive for human beings because of the punishment of sin—not because of their own nature, but because of human guilt.

Here it was shown to the human being made in God’s image what evil he had brought upon himself, when he was reduced to the point that the destruction of death could be inflicted upon him by tiny creatures. Therefore, among all animals, all plants, and all creatures universally, whatever a human being sees to be deadly to him, he should not say that those creatures possess an evil nature, but should recognize in them the retribution for his own wickedness.

We became like fleas and bugs after we rebelled against God; and the scorpion’s sting became deadly to humanity after humanity willingly chose to be wounded by the sting of death. For “the sting of death is sin” (1 Corinthians 15:56). With this sting the human being first wounded himself unto death, in such a way that he made it pass through his whole offspring as well. Thus, even for those in whom God’s grace prevents sin from reigning, frequent and manifold danger arising from the punishment of sin is not absent.

For this reason even just and holy people in this mortal life are not free from such troubles and dangers: as long as they live mortally, they are not without sin. Hence the blessed John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). The holy apostle James also testifies: “We all offend in many things” (James 3:2).

### 36 [Cols. 0593D–0594A]

Yet the sins of the saints are not like those of the wicked. The sins of the saints are light; the sins of the wicked are grave.

In the sins of the wicked, human perversity either thinks wrongly about God, or human desire leads a person toward the cravings of the flesh, or human cruelty harms one’s neighbor. Concerning those who sin against God, Wisdom says: “Those who sin against me act wickedly against their own souls, and those who hate me love death” (Proverbs 8:36).

Concerning those who live luxuriously, the Apostle says: “If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple. Let no one deceive you” (1 Corinthians 3:17–18).

Speaking also about hatred of a brother, the blessed John says (alternative reading: “in the light” for “in the light”): “Whoever says that he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness. Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no cause of stumbling in him. But whoever hates his brother is in darkness, walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2:9–11).

### 37 [Cols. 0594A–0594D; p. 426]

The sins of the wicked are therefore committed in three ways (alternative reading: “in all ways”). They are involved either in sacrileges, shameful acts, or crimes.

They commit sacrilege when they do not think rightly about God and depart from the true faith, whether through fear of temporal advantages (alternative reading: “through” for “toward”)  [Note: [Col. 0593D] Something is missing here, and the reading seems to be: “whether through fear of temporal punishments, or through hope of temporal advantages, or through mere …”], or through the mere blindness and perversity of the heart.

They sin through shameful acts when they live disgracefully, immoderately, and obscenely in themselves. They sin through crimes when they cruelly harm others through losses or any other forms of oppression.

The blessed Apostle calls both groups—those who sin mortally in faith and those who sin mortally in conduct—reprobates. Concerning those who contradict the true faith, he says: “Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these people also resist the truth: they are corrupted in mind and reprobate concerning the faith” (2 Timothy 3:8).

Rebuking in the same way those who live in evil works and crimes while professing the true faith, he says: “To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure. Their minds and consciences are defiled. They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him, being detestable, disobedient, and reprobate for every good work” (Titus 1:15–16).

When the saints sin, they succumb in some sin through human weakness or human pleasure [alternative reading: “affection”] in such a way that they neither stubbornly contradict the true faith, nor defile themselves with shameful acts, nor harm their neighbors through crimes. The blessed Apostle shows this when he says: “The grace of God our Savior has appeared to all human beings, instructing us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires, and to live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this present age” (Titus 2:11–12).

The same blessed Apostle admonishes us elsewhere, saying: “Do not think more highly than one ought to think, but think with sober judgment” (Romans 12:3).

Nevertheless, in this threefold division—“that we should live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this present age”—it seems to me that the person lives soberly who does not pursue the pleasures of lust; justly who in no way harms his neighbor and bestows benefits upon him insofar as he is able; and devoutly who for no reason departs from the fellowship of ecclesiastical unity, and, remaining within the Church, holds without hesitation those things he knows with certainty to belong to the knowledge of the true faith. As for those things he does not know or about which he has doubts, he investigates them humbly and patiently until, if he holds some different opinion, God reveals the truth to him.

### 38 [Cols. 0594D–0595A]

This sobriety, justice, and piety [alternative reading: “peace”], which ought to be present in all the faithful, are so interconnected that, if one is absent, the other that appears to be present is of no benefit.

For sobriety (alternative reading: “is saved”), by which someone abstains from shameful acts in himself, does not save unless it is also pious and just—that is, unless he believes rightly in God and willingly bestows upon his neighbor what charity requires. Nor is that justice fruitful by which each person gives his neighbor what he himself enjoys receiving, unless it is also sober and pious.

Piety is likewise dead if one believes rightly in God but does not maintain either sobriety of conduct or charity toward one’s neighbor. True salvation of the soul is acquired when piety in faith, justice in charity, and sobriety in chastity and moderation are maintained together.

### 39 [Cols. 0595A–0595B]

The divine Scriptures teach us that the saints sin in one way and the wicked in another.

Hagar, Sarah’s servant, would not have been driven out if she had not become proud (Genesis 21:11); and Sarah herself would not have been reproved if she had not laughed (Genesis 18:11). The former became proud when she saw that she had conceived; the latter laughed because she doubted that she would conceive.

Both are found to have sinned, but their sins are not found to have been equal. In one, human weakness doubted; in the other, human rashness raised itself up rebelliously. Therefore Hagar deserved to be expelled at the command of divine severity, whereas Sarah deserved to be reproved by the gentle mildness of the divine word.

And because her sin in that doubt was light, once strengthened by the word of the divine promise she cast off her doubt and received the firmest faith. Through that faith she also received the power to conceive, as apostolic authority testifies: “By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even beyond the proper time of her age, because she considered him faithful who had promised” (Hebrews 11:11).

### 40 [Cols. 0595C–0595D; p. 427]

Elsewhere we find that the sins of the saints and of the wicked are not equal: the former are light and require purification through temporal correction, while the latter are grave and deserve punishment through the perpetual burning of eternal fire.

At the waters of contradiction, the children of Israel sinned in one way (Numbers 20:13), being entirely rebellious against God; Moses sinned in another way. He did not contradict God through rashness, but through weakness presumed too little upon God’s work. He became like the blessed Peter, who heard from the Lord: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matthew 14:31).

Therefore the Israelites’ rebelliousness deserved condemnation to eternal punishment. In Moses, however, the vengeance for that sin extended only to the denial of entry into the promised land. Moses himself testified in Deuteronomy that the Lord was angry with him not because of his own sin but because of the people, saying: “The Lord was angry with me also because of you, and said: ‘You also shall not enter there’” (Deuteronomy 1:37).

The holy David also showed that Moses was afflicted on account of that same sin of the people, saying: “They angered him at the waters of contradiction, and Moses suffered because of them” (Psalm 105:32).

The people therefore angered the Lord, while Moses doubted the Lord’s work. Because the sin of that anger and the sin of that doubt were not equal, holy Moses, although he was afflicted on their account, was nevertheless not condemned with them to eternal punishment.

### 41 [Cols. 0596A–0596B]

To observe something briefly also in the conduct of ordinary human life, so that we may take an example more easily, let us regard the souls of baptized people as women joined in marriage. For the Apostle commends the great sacrament of marriage itself in Christ and in the Church (Ephesians 5:32).

Thus every soul faithfully cleaving to Christ is like a wife living faithfully with her husband. Within the chastity of marriage she may often grieve her husband, yet she preserves the fidelity of the marriage bed in pure chastity and prudently and temperately manages her husband’s property. In this way she sins against her husband, yet still lives chastely and faithfully with him; and the human weakness that sometimes causes her to offend her husband is counterbalanced by marital chastity, which makes her cling sweetly to him.

But a woman who, whether she has left her husband’s house or remains in the same dwelling, becomes involved in adultery or squanders her husband’s property is judged unworthy of pardon and is held liable to a deadly offense.

So it is with the soul that consents to the devil and is either overthrown by infidelity or entangled in crimes.

### 42 [Cols. 0596B–0596D]

Concerning such people the Apostle says: “Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who have intercourse with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:9–10).

But concerning those who sin lightly it is said: “The righteous man falls seven times and rises again” (Proverbs 24:16). Such a person is said to sin and yet is truly called righteous. For he does not fall in such a way that he ceases to be righteous, because it is written: “When the righteous man falls, he shall not be shaken, for the Lord strengthens his hand” (Psalm 36:24).

The Lord is therefore present even with the righteous person who falls, because he does not sin in such a way that the Lord departs from him. He possesses desire arising from the weakness of the flesh, but he does not consent to that desire, being strengthened by the power of spiritual grace.

That desire is the law of sin established even in the members of the saints. Yet God’s grace delivers his righteous ones from it through Jesus Christ our Lord. For this reason he bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, separated from our sins, we might live in righteousness (1 Peter 2:24).

When the righteous person falls, therefore, he incurs debts; but they are such debts of the righteous as can be forgiven in daily prayer, when he truly says: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

### 43 [Cols. 0596D–0597A; p. 428]

The sins of the righteous therefore arise from the necessity of weakness; the sins of the wicked arise from the deliberate intention of an evil will. In the former, sin is found to arise without being followed by its full effect. Although it is born through weakness, it is overcome through God’s grace.

But evil will casts down those deprived of the help of grace [alternative reading: “fittingly”], wherever depraved desire leads them. Therefore the faults of the saints are called sins, not crimes. For these they are corrected by the Father in such a way that they are not condemned by the Judge. This correction nevertheless pertains to judgment, but to paternal judgment, by which God mercifully both judges and chastises his children in order to rescue them from the punishment of eternal condemnation.

The blessed Apostle demonstrates this when he says: “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged. But when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (1 Corinthians 11:31–32).

The blessed Peter also affirms this, saying: “The time has come for judgment to begin from the house of God. And if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the gospel of God? And if the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” [The final wording is grammatically corrupt in the supplied text: *peccator et impius ub parebunt*; the intended sense is evidently “where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?”] (1 Peter 4:17–18).

### 44 [Cols. 0597A–0597B]

Let no faithful and wise person therefore say that the faith of the saints is weak if he sees some trouble caused by adversity befalling them during the time of this life.

Bodily health and bodily illness occur alike to the faithful and the unfaithful, to the good and the wicked. For this reason the adversity of bodily weakness touches both alike, since health too is sometimes granted temporally to both alike.

The righteous are distinguished from the wicked not by bodily condition but by faith and life. They therefore endure together, bodily, the troubles and dangers of the present life, but they bear them with entirely different intentions.

They do not groan equally under the evils of this life because they do not love the goods of this life equally. The wicked want the present life to be tranquil and free from troubles so that they may not lack perishable and temporal goods. The righteous, however, hate the dangers and troubles of the present life so that they may enjoy God, whom they love (perhaps *Deo*, “in God”). In him they seek true rest, in whom they will possess everlasting blessedness.

Therefore they do not love temporal goods, knowing that they will soon pass away. In using them, they do not seek the satisfaction of desire, but the renewal of charity and the support of weakness. From them they seek not joy as from a familiar delight, but a modest consolation as from provisions for a journey, according to the needs of circumstances [alternative reading: “according to the needs of the guilty”].

### 45 [Cols. 0597C–0598A; p. 429]

And because we are now discussing the opinion of the person who does not believe that flies, scorpions, fleas, and bugs could have been made by God, we must also take care lest he have conceived this sense—which is altogether foreign to the Catholic faith—not from the error of the Manichaeans but from reading the divine Scriptures.

“For the law is good, if one uses it lawfully” (1 Timothy 1:8). But the person does not use the law lawfully who does not understand from the words of the law what he ought to understand.

I say this because we read in Exodus that the staff of Moses, which Aaron carried, was transformed into a serpent by divine action (Exodus 7:10). There it is also said that Pharaoh’s magicians—whom the Apostle calls Jannes and Jambres—did something similar, so that their staffs were changed into serpents by magical incantations (2 Timothy 3:8).

Then, when Aaron struck the waters of the river and they were turned into blood (Exodus 7:20), sacred Scripture also records that the same thing was done by their incantations (Exodus 7:22). Later, when Aaron struck the waters and brought forth frogs, which immediately covered the land of Egypt, those sorcerers too are said to have done something similar by resisting with their wicked arts (Exodus 8:6–7).

But when the time came for gnats to be produced after the earth had been struck (Exodus 8:17–18), the wickedness of magical art could accomplish nothing of the kind.

Here let the person who asserts that flies were made by the devil recognize that he is a liar: although the devil and his angels were permitted to do other things, they failed in the work of making flies. Who does not see that the transgressors produced either serpents from staffs or frogs from waters because God permitted it, whereas they were unable to make gnats—that is, flies—because God did not permit it?

46. Sometimes, however, by the hidden and incomprehensible judgment of God, evil angels are permitted to do certain things, in order to test the good and lead the wicked astray. Yet they themselves do not create what they do; rather, from the hidden bosom of God the Creator—which we cannot see—they are permitted to produce something that we can see. Thus the devil could not be the creator either of the serpents or of the frogs, although he produced them with God’s permission; just as he was not the creator of fire when, in order to test Job, it fell from heaven and consumed his sheep together with their shepherds (Job 1:16); nor was he the creator of the winds when a great wind, rushing in from the wilderness, struck the four corners of the house and crushed all the children of holy Job in one simultaneous ruin.

God alone, the almighty, created the various natures—that is, the elements of this world. Within their hidden and inaccessible depths he established certain seeds of things, concealed from us but manifest to the angels. From these, as the needs of the work and of time require, God, by the hidden counsel of his wisdom, either commands certain things to be produced through good angels or permits them to be displayed through evil ones. By permitting these things, God demonstrates what great power he has placed in the holy angels, since he grants even the wicked the ability to perform certain marvels from the bodily creation itself.

For this reason our Savior also does not cease to warn his faithful, saying: “For false Christs and false prophets will arise and will give great signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, even the elect might be led astray” (Mark 13:22). Blessed Paul likewise, speaking of the Antichrist, says: “That wicked one will be revealed, whom our Lord Jesus Christ will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation of his coming. His coming is according to the working of Satan, with every power and signs and lying wonders, and with every deceit of wickedness for those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved. Therefore God will send them a working of error, so that they may believe the lie and all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to wickedness” (2 Thess. 2:8 and following).

47. By these and similar testimonies we shall understand that all natures were created by divine action, and that whatever harms us ought not to be called evil by nature, but should be recognized as unsuitable for us because of our weakness. Nevertheless, from this we receive a fitting warning, so that with humble hearts we may fear the justice of divine power.

As for the natures themselves, no wise person either believes or says that not only evil angels but even good angels are their creators. For God, as we said above, made all things in wisdom, and “wisdom reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1). He orders all things because in that wisdom the Father made all things.

Therefore, just as God created the angels in heaven in wisdom, so in that same wisdom he created the little worms on earth; and he who established Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, and Powers above made scorpions, fleas, and bedbugs on earth. He who created the hen also created the fly: he gave the one to humble the proud person, and the other to refresh the weak. Hence a person willingly receives food from the one, but unwillingly suffers disgust from the other, so that, even if he does not see God’s consolation in the former alone, he may at least be compelled to see in the latter the desert of his own sin.

48. Therefore let this person take care not to be led astray even by the name by which the prince of demons is called Beelzebub in the Gospel, a name interpreted as “prince of flies.” This was not said because the devil was able to create flies. For an angel, speaking to the prophet Daniel, says: “And behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came first to help me” (Dan. 10:13); and a little later: “No one is my helper in all these matters except Michael, your prince” (ibid., 21).

We find not only angels but also human beings called princes. For it is written: “The princes of the peoples have gathered with the God of Abraham” (Ps. 46:18); and it is said to the Church: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. 44:17). In the book of Moses also we know that the tribal leaders are called princes (Gen. 25:16).

Yet because human beings or angels are called princes, they should not for that reason be called creators—not only of angels or human beings, but also of any irrational souls or any bodies whatsoever. Beelzebub himself, whose name is interpreted as “prince of flies,” is certainly called the prince of demons; yet he rules over them as the first author and instigator of wickedness, not as the creator and founder of their nature.

For evil angels have God as the maker of their nature, but the devil as the prince of their wickedness. The whole multitude of the apostate angels was made good by God, by whose gratuitous kindness they came into existence; but by their own will they adhered to the devil and fell. Therefore he is called their prince, not because he created them, but because he drew them with himself into the abyss of perdition.

Thus, in the statement that the devil is called “prince of flies,” he is shown to be the prince of the wicked, whom another Scripture signifies by saying: “Dying flies destroy the sweetness of the oil” (Eccl. 10:1). Who are those who destroy it, unless they are those who grieve the Holy Spirit either by the sin of unbelief or by the foul obscenity [variant: obscurity] of unclean works, defiling themselves either through perverse belief or through depraved conduct? The Apostle earnestly forbids this, saying: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4:30).

49. Therefore those who do not live according to the proper order of life destroy in themselves the oil of sweetness, the sacrament of spiritual grace. Yet when they destroy it, the oil itself cannot be destroyed; just as, when they grieve him according to their evil will, the Holy Spirit cannot experience any grief.

Of the Son of God himself it is said in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “How much worse punishments do you think he deserves who has trampled underfoot the Son of God?” (Heb. 10:29). The Son of God is Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God; he is in no way trampled underfoot, because he is in no way defiled. For of this wisdom it is said in the Book [variant: Books] of Wisdom: “For because of her purity she reaches everywhere; therefore nothing defiled enters into her. For she is the radiance of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness” (Wis. 7:24 and following).

The wicked, then, grieve the Holy Spirit, but the Holy Spirit cannot be grieved; the wicked trample upon the Son of God, but the Son of God is in no way trampled upon.

50. It is in this sense that the wicked are said to grieve the Holy Spirit and trample upon the Son of God, even though both the Son of God and the Holy Spirit [variant: of God] remain incapable of grief and impossible to trample upon. Thus the Savior says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). Yet if, while he commits adultery, she remains chaste, how much more, when the wicked grieve and trample, does the divine substance of the Son of God and the Holy Spirit remain without grief and blessed!

51. Therefore let no believer say that any nature could originally have been created by the devil. For if he affirms that any animals came into existence through the devil’s creating them, he will consequently attribute to the devil even those things from which they derive their origin.

Certain kinds of flies arise either from bodily waste or from rotting herbs or meat. We often see some flies born even from vegetables. The weevil, too, commonly comes into existence from grain. Therefore, whoever asserts that such animals were created not by God but by the devil, why should he not also assert that the wood, grain, vegetables, herbs, and meat from which they arise were made by him?

Further, when he sees that worms originate not only from human corpses but also from living bodies—where the carnal sense of human mortality is sometimes displayed in worms—he will undoubtedly proclaim the devil the author even of human bodies. But if, believing and understanding rightly concerning the good, he would not dare to assign the origin of any creature even to the good angels, how does this person assign the power or authority to create any animal to an angel who was cast down and excluded from his dignity through the fault of his own perversity? No one would dare assign this to him even if he had remained in angelic dignity and goodness without any fault.

52. It is not without reason that, at the very beginning of Genesis, Scripture, speaking of all that was made, confirms that God made everything, saying of each thing: “And God made it, and God saw that it was good” (Gen. 1). He completed all these things on the sixth day, and nothing that might later be made could have been lacking among them.

Since God, who foreknows the future, knew that the human being would sin, he mercifully prepared for him from all that he made not only comforts but also scourges. For one is the hand of a good father, which gives a child both food and the rod: one for the child to live, the other to live well; one lest he fail through weakness, the other lest, being undisciplined, he despise his father’s commands. “For the Lord disciplines the one whom he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6).

Nor does it profit anyone to abound in temporal goods if, by living wickedly, he is deprived of eternal ones. Once deprived of those, he must be consigned to everlasting evils from which he cannot escape.

53. Therefore let each person restrain the rashness of his thinking, and let him not doubt that, just as the things in which he delights, so also the things by which he is offended, were naturally made by God. His wisdom reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly; and even in those things that corruption destroys it displays the beauty of its work. In the smallest animals as well it shows the distinctive excellence of each kind: he made the tiniest flies all the shorter than great elephants and therefore all the more agile; and although the size of their limbs differs in both, the praise due to their works of God is not therefore different.

For what healthy-minded person, contemplating the invisible things of God through the understanding of the things that have been made, would not praise God himself as their maker in the worm, just as he praises him in the elephant? Or would not praise the same one in the flea whom he praises in the ox? Even in the signs that the skill of artisans customarily forms in gems, the mind tends to praise the work all the more as the eye observes it to be smaller.

54. We must therefore confess that God created everything. But concerning these things by which human transgression is scourged at the divine command, when the question is asked whether they were created by God before Adam sinned or after he sinned, the appropriate answer is that those which arise from water or from earth were established originally when God created them, by that Creator who knew not only the nature of the human being he was making but also wonderfully foreknew that the human being himself would sin.

He did not make these things in such a way that, before sin, the human being would experience them as harmful or fear them. For no action of any earthly animal could harm him, since by God’s gracious gift he had been established as lord of them all. Thus transgression made these things harmful and destructive to the human being himself; it was not the condition imposed by the Creator. For this was wrought not by the kindness of the creator but by the justice of the judge.

55. As for those things that we see arising from the corruption of flesh or of fruits, we do not say that they existed at the time when, during those six days, God made all things “very good”; rather, those things were made temporally in such a way that these others would later be born from them.

Human flesh, too, descended into this corruption, as it is written: “The human being, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13). Thus necessity came to possess the body of sinful humanity with corruption and death. From these two evils the bodies of the righteous are to be freed by God’s grace—not in the present age, in which, just as God makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked and rains upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45), he caused not only the unbelieving Herod to be consumed by worms (Acts 12:23), but also permitted his servant Job to boil with putrefaction and worms (Job 2:8).

In the future, however, the bodies of the righteous will feel no discomfort of corruption or mortality, when “this corruptible body will put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53). In that life of the good and misery of the wicked, whatever there will be for the good or the wicked will be full and eternal. There, comforts will not be mixed with torments, nor torments inserted into comforts. There the eternity of joys and punishments will remain without end; the wicked will not hope for joys, and the good will not fear sorrow. In the good there will always remain eternal exultation; in the wicked, weeping and gnashing of teeth will always remain. The fellowship of demons will hold the wicked in misery forever, while the likeness of the holy angels will receive the righteous as blessed forever.

56. Therefore, singing of God’s mercy and judgment, let us not despise the time of mercy, so that we may come to judgment without fear. Let us hope in the judge whom we know as Redeemer. Let our works be such that eternal rewards may be given to us. From the fact that we fear and avoid the troubles of the present time, we must consider how greatly we ought to flee eternal punishments.

Let us therefore turn away from evil and do good. For at the time of divine recompense every person will find there what he has possessed here in his works, as the Apostle says: “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap; for the one who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but the one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Gal. 6:8).

For this reason the same Apostle admonishes us, saying: “If you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live” (Rom. 8:13). Here, then, let us put to death by the Spirit the deeds of the flesh, and, having died to sin, let us live for God.

Let neither the prosperity of the world corrupt us nor its adversity break us. In our hearts let us depart from the dwelling of this world, from which we shall soon depart bodily as well, so that that heavenly house may receive us, of which the Apostle says that “we have an edifice from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5:1).

Of this it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 85:5). There, just as the dwelling is eternal, so also is the praise eternal. Those who dwell there always praise God, because they always exult from the Lord and in the Lord. And just as the eternity of the holy dwelling is sweet to those who praise, so the sweetness of praising remains eternal for those who dwell there.

[Col. 0603]

**St. Fulgentius, On the Truth of Predestination and the Grace of God, to John and Venerius (C)**

**Book One**

**CHAPTER I**

[Col. 0603A] 1. I give thanks to God, holy brothers John the presbyter and Venerius the deacon, through whose help you are such men that you contend with great spirit and fervor for the grace by which we are saved.

I have been saddened because certain of our brothers, under the Christian name, are striving to oppose the Catholic faith—transferring the gifts of God’s grace to the power or merit of human free choice, as though our effort, without God’s help, could obey the divine command; as though God’s only role were to command us what we must do, without himself working in us what he commands; and as though, if God grants anything good to a human being, he should not be thought to give it as a gift but to repay it [Note: Here and in many places below the manuscripts read “God,” where the editions have “the Lord”].

They think that the gifts of divine goodness depend so entirely on the quality of human actions that they even assert that infants are divinely foreknown and predestined in such a way that, in those who are chosen, no gratuitous good bestowed from above is found [Note: Two manuscripts read “gratuitous”; the editions do not have these words here or below, “eternal recompense.”]. Nor, they say, does gratuitous mercy precede anyone by gracious favor; rather, the eternal recompense of punishment and reward is to consist solely in each person’s own future will [Note: The editions omit “future”; but the manuscripts more correctly add it, since the discussion concerns infants, for whom the works of the present or past life can in no way provide assistance.] and action.

2. I am greatly surprised and grieved that another absurdity has also crept into the thinking of certain people. They do not hesitate to be so hostile to God’s grace as to assert that infants are baptized on the basis of the merit of future works. Conversely, they say that divine goodness also provides for those infants who die without baptism, so that they are snatched away from the course of the present life [variant: lives] and carried off to punishment without the grace of sacred washing—claiming, evidently, that God foreknew their future evils had they lived somewhat longer here and, in his goodness, removed them from this present life; as though anyone could, without the benefit of holy redemption, either be withdrawn from everlasting punishments or obtain the gifts of eternal life.

Thus, while they obstinately contradict the truth, they stab themselves with deadly perversity. They appear to want to distinguish the merits of Esau and Jacob—twin brothers born from one seed and one act of intercourse—in such a way that, while asserting that Esau was condemned on the basis of foreknowledge of future works, they also maintain that Jacob could have been saved not by a gratuitous gift of divine goodness but only by foreknowledge of future works. In this way, they claim, God may be acknowledged as just in both cases, and no one may believe that he granted anything to either by gratuitous mercy.

But especially in this question concerning infants, in which the guilt of the sinful origin itself is made known—not anyone’s personal wickedness in actual sins [Note: One manuscript reads “stain”]—everyone who does not wish to depart from the truth of the apostolic faith, and who, with God’s illumination, desires to preserve the rightness of Catholic doctrine in unbroken faith and confession, must truly believe and confess, with every ambiguity of hesitation removed, that the one [Note: Thus one manuscript; the others read “the living God”], true, and good God—that is, the highest and ineffable Trinity of one nature and essence—created the nature of the first human being wholly good and upright, without natural evil and without any defect; that he did not create in the flesh a necessity of dying, nor insert into the soul any stain of sin.

Therefore human nature has from God the good of creation, but from the voluntary transgression of the first human being it has original sin, which those being born draw with them; and from the one unjust transgression, through the most just condemnation, both the stain of iniquity and the punishment of death have spread simultaneously to all.

For the human being, made in the image of God, received uprightness both of will and of action.

**CHAPTER II**

3. Thus the human being was created in such a way that, by his own will, he could either sin or not sin. Therefore the fall into voluntary transgression was rightly punished in him, because he was not constrained to sin by any natural necessity of flesh or soul.

Although, as the Apostle teaches, he himself was not deceived (1 Tim. 2:14), nevertheless, by agreeing through a perverse will with the woman who had been deceived into transgression, he inflicted upon himself, through his lack of foresight, a deadly wound. Thus, in that one human being whose soul had died through sin and whose body had died because of sin, all who were to be born from that first sinful human being through the intercourse of male and female became subject originally to sin and death.

After the father of all human beings had sinned by his own will, he experienced the truth of the divine command that he had heard: “On whatever day you eat from it, you will die” (Gen. 2:17), and he experienced the justice of God’s vengeance. By one taste of the forbidden tree, because he abandoned righteousness, he fell into punishment; voluntarily dead in his soul spiritually, he also received bodily death unwillingly.

4. The voluntary death of the soul therefore brought forth a punitive death for the body. Because death through guilt took possession of the first human being, the death of retribution immediately followed. As a result, guilt bound his entire offspring—not only those who could sin by their own free choice, but also infants who did not yet use their own will—and, with sin prevailing, punitive death claimed for itself passage and dominion over all human beings.

For this reason the Apostle says: “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). Again he says: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (ibid., 14).

By sinning, therefore, the human being subjected his entire offspring to sin, when through transgression he lost true freedom: “For by whatever anyone is overcome, to this he is enslaved” (2 Pet. 2:19); and, “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34).

5. From this slavery, by which infants are held bound from birth [Note: So read three manuscripts; the editions have the entire phrase in the singular], only one—the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus—is born free [Note: The editions do not have “one”; the manuscripts do].

Although he was born a true human being, he was not born through the intervention of fleshly desire or through the intercourse of male and female, but from the Holy Spirit. Thus he received true flesh from his mother’s flesh, yet, being true God, he assumed not the guilt of human origin but its nature; and he did not receive sins to be committed in his body, but bore sins to be removed.

For the authority of apostolic preaching teaches truthfully that “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22); and, “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, freed from sins, we might live for righteousness” (ibid., 24).

His mother alone, just as she was a virgin before conception, remained an undefiled virgin after childbirth. She experienced neither lust when she conceived God, who had wonderfully become human in her womb, nor any corruption when, in true flesh of our race, she gave birth to the Redeemer of the human race.

For true God, taking true flesh from a virgin, received from her the perfection of a human body without removing from her the grace of virginity. It was not fitting that God the creator should grant bodily integrity to human flesh in its creation, and that the same God, who assumed human flesh in order to redeem what he had made, should remove virginity from the flesh from which he was born.

He is “the second human being from heaven” (1 Cor. 15:47). He is not called from heaven because he wished to bring down from there the substance of his body, but because the form of a servant that God the Creator of heaven and earth assumed into the unity of his person could contain nothing of earthly desire.

**CHAPTER III**

6. God therefore did not bring a heavenly body down to earth; rather, in himself he raised the true nature of an earthly body to heaven. Receiving the truth of this earthly body from the earthly body of his mother, he bore our sins in his flesh, although he had no guilt either of origin or of action.

Isaiah says: “He himself bore our sins” (Isa. 53:11). Thus, so that grace might abound all the more in human beings where sin abounded, he not only washed away the sin by which the earthly human being polluted the whole of his offspring, but through this grace he also forgives every believer whatever has been added to original sin by the voluntary impulses or actions of human beings.

Blessed Paul teaches this when he says: “Judgment followed from one transgression to condemnation, but grace followed from many transgressions to justification” (Rom. 5:16). This is the grace of God that frees us through Jesus Christ our Lord. The Liberator himself, revealing the work of this grace to us, says: “If the Son makes you free, you will truly be free”; and elsewhere: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10).

[Col. 0606B] 7. This grace of God, by which we are saved, is not given to anyone on account of a preceding good merit; yet it is not denied except on account of a preceding evil merit.

For the first human being transmitted to all human beings the merits of his sin, and their flesh is conceived under the law of sin. Therefore, although in infants there is no sin arising from their own will, there is nevertheless in the children of wrath, carnally begotten, a parental stain. This does not disrupt the well-ordered arrangement of divine creation, but it inflicts upon those being born the grim defilement of the father’s transgression.

No one is separated from that condemned mass by foreknowledge of future works; rather, he is separated by the help and action of the merciful potter. Therefore the vessels of mercy, which are freely made from the same mass for honor, are separated from the vessels made for dishonor by the gift of gratuitous justification.

To demonstrate the grace that freely justifies sinners, apostolic preaching calls them not vessels of justice but vessels of mercy, as blessed Paul says: “What if God, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, so that he might make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory?” (Rom. 9:22–23).

This mercy finds no one worthy, but finds all unworthy, and from among them makes worthy whomever it wills.

**CHAPTER IV**

8. Prevented by this mercy, Jacob was chosen before he was born, not according to the merit of any past or future human work, but according to the purpose of God who predestines.

For the Apostle says that, while they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain, it was said to Rebecca—not on the basis of works but on the basis of the one who calls—“The elder will serve the younger” (ibid., 11 and following).

Therefore, when the younger brother was preferred by God to the elder, there was no merit of any past deed or future work, since the guilt of those conceived from one lawful and righteous intercourse remained equal. Grace, then, accomplished this through divine goodness. Grace was never given in such a way that it found some good merits in a human being; rather, it was given so that it might itself bestow them upon those who did not possess them.

For if, when grace was absent, the distinction between choosing one infant and rejecting the other had been made solely through foreknowledge of human works, the Apostle would never have said that it was not on the basis of works but on the basis of the one who calls that it was said to him, “The elder will serve the younger.”

The Apostle would certainly have said “on the basis of works” if he had recognized there at least the good merits of future human works. But because he knew that in both there were only merits deserving condemnation, he attributed the cause of election solely to the purpose of divine goodness.

Accordingly, of these two brothers, whom our father Isaac received as one seed conceived from one intercourse and whom one birth brought forth into the light, divine mercy alone separated the one whom it willed from the condemned mass. It was aided by the predestination of gratuitous gifts, not by foreknowledge of future merits.

Thus God’s purpose according to election remained, so that election might be gratuitous according to God’s purpose. The will of God is the cause of election; election is not the cause of his will.

God was gratuitously merciful in the one who was chosen, while he was not unjust in the one rejected. He freely took up one and justly abandoned the other. For “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10).

9. The goodness of God, who freely shows mercy, and the severity of God, who judges justly, brought it about that neither did both receive the gratuitous gift of mercy nor did both together meet the same destruction, although the original cause had been one for both.

For this reason, before the prophet said, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated,” he mentioned not any past or future work but their shared origin, with Malachi speaking as follows: “Was not Esau Jacob’s brother? And I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau, says the Lord” (Mal. 1:2).

Why, then, is not some difference of works mentioned here, but only the brotherhood of those being born, when the good works of the one who was loved and the evil works of the one who was hated ought rather to have been recalled? In that way, neither personal favoritism in the one who was loved nor unjust condemnation in the one rejected would be suspected.

Brotherhood signifies no difference of works by which one might be distinguished from the other through comparison of merits. Therefore, God showed that he loved one and hated the other of the twin brothers without mentioning works for no other reason than that we might recognize that, through their shared conception and birth—which established their brotherhood—both were bound by equal merit in that condemned mass. From it merciful goodness freely separated one in such a way that just severity did not unjustly leave the other there [Note: One manuscript reads, “the just severity of God.”]

The cause of condemnation would indeed be unjust in the case of any infant if mortal offspring had received no contagion of sin from its paternal root. But divinely inspired Scripture testifies that not only can no human being be clean from defilement, even if his life upon earth is only one day (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint), but that even the legitimate and marital conception of the human race is not free from the guilt of iniquity.

10. Here no one should think that any accusation can properly be brought against the truth. Following the teaching of the holy Fathers, with God’s help, we say that the stain of original sin is in the conception of infants, not in the legitimate intercourse of marriage, whose goodness we know was divinely instituted at the beginning of the human race.

For this reason apostolic teaching also commends honorable marriage in all respects and the undefiled marriage bed without hesitation (Heb. 13:4). Although marriage, laudably bestowed by God, possesses clean offspring in faith and love, it nevertheless produces children defiled by the sin of the first human being.

Therefore, the good that a human being receives from good marriages is so truly good that it is not evil even if he is born from adultery or fornication. God bestowed upon human nature the gift of fertility; the evil of lust, however, is not God’s creation but the punishment of sin.

Accordingly, a human being is not born clean from the purity [Note: The editions read “from the impurity”; the manuscripts’ “from the purity” is preferable, since it was said shortly before that marriage possesses offspring made clean for it by God] of marriage, because he is conceived through the intervention of lust [Note: Two manuscripts read “through the intervention of sordid lust”]. The honor of marriage certainly does not love this lust, but the necessity of mortal propagation tolerates it within marriage.

Lust itself pollutes those conceived, even if it cannot draw faithful parents into and drive them toward the consummation of an illicit union. For this reason holy David, born from a lawful and faithful marriage, laments the stain of carnal generation with profound sorrow: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins [variant: transgressions] my mother nourished me in the womb” (Ps. 50:7).

**CHAPTER V**

11. Since these things are so, whoever is conceived in iniquities cannot be born without the obligation of iniquity. In order that Jacob might be freed from it, while Esau was rejected, there were no human merits, but only the grace of divine goodness.

Both were circumcised in the body with visible circumcision, which in earlier times was divinely given to our fathers as “a sign of the righteousness of faith” (Rom. 4:11). But circumcision of the heart, which is in the spirit and not in the letter, whose praise is not from human beings but from God (Rom. 2:29), Jacob alone received from God, freely justified.

Although Esau too was circumcised in the flesh, he was nevertheless not rescued from the mass of perdition by the gift of divine love and election. In him there was carnal circumcision, but it did not profit him because spiritual circumcision did not at all remove him from the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God (Rom. 8:7).

In Esau, therefore, before the ages God hated the enduring wickedness of the earthly human being and justly assigned him to punishment. But in his brother he did not foresee any good works that would come from the human being, by which he might choose and love him. Rather, before the ages he prepared for him the grace of justification, through which he would grant him not only the beginning of a good will but also the fulfillment of good action.

He did not find good merits in him, but freed him through the gratuitous gift of mercy. For he says to Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I will show mercy.” Therefore, it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy (Rom. 9:15–16; Exod. 33:19).

## Chapter VI

### 12

Therefore God freely bestows his grace upon one who has been born, because he had freely prepared it for one who was to be born. For whatever good things good people possess in will or deed, God bestows them—the one who also preserves the gifts he has bestowed. But for the wicked and ungodly God could never have prepared or given evil works, by which they would serve damnably [Note: The manuscripts read “by which they would live damnably.”]; nor did he implant evil desires in them, by which they would culpably will every sort of injustice. Rather, he prepared for them the punishment of eternal fire, so that in everlasting burning they might experience retributive justice.

The evil will of human beings [Note: The editions omit “of human beings”; two manuscripts include it.] is therefore not from God. For this reason the just Judge punishes it in human beings: in it the good Creator does not recognize the order of his creation. And the persistence of iniquity and the obstinacy of a proud neck, since they are not possessed through God’s generosity, are for that reason condemned by God as their avenger.

But for those whom God makes heirs of his kingdom, he freely prepares a good will and freely grants it [Note: Two manuscripts read “he grants by grace”]; to them he also supplies perseverance. For mercifully and freely he prepared the merits of gifts to be bestowed, by which he might justly repay the gifts of merits.

### 13

There is no doubt that the figure of two peoples was prefigured in those two brothers: one destined to be saved, the other destined to be condemned. Yet salvation was not repaid to this people on account of works in the same way that condemnation was requited to the other on account of works. One received the gift of saving grace, which he had not deserved; the other received, according to his merit, the destruction of just condemnation. In the one, merits deserving condemnation were found; to the other, merits deserving glorification were freely conferred through justification. The former possessed in himself what would make him displeasing; the latter received from the one to whom he was destined to be pleasing what would make him pleasing to God.

Therefore, in all who are handed over to the fire of Gehenna [Note: Two manuscripts read “who will be handed over”], strict justice finds an evil merit to punish [Note: The editions read “their evil”; the manuscripts read “an evil merit”]: in some, one inherited from the beginning; in others, one added through the fault of their own will. For, except for infants, who cannot yet possess free choice for choosing justice and fleeing sin, because at that tender age reason lies sluggish and dormant, all the others who can use reason, with the guilt of their own will added, either do not come to faith or depart from faith.

But in order that someone may become just from ungodly, God’s friend from his enemy, acquitted from guilty—whatever bodily age he may be living, from the very beginning of birth to decrepit old age—no one is found worthy of justification; rather, the unworthy person is justified by gratuitous goodness. No one is rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of God’s beloved Son unless the Lord has freely deigned to go before him with the gift of glory—he who freely saves and justly condemns.

The merciful and just Lord justly punishes the perverse will that he does not mercifully correct, because he finds in it a perversity that he himself did not make. But he himself freely prepares the good will, freely grants it, himself assists it, and himself brings it to completion.

## Chapter VII

### 14

Let us therefore all hold with the greatest certainty that human beings, by themselves, can attain not only no perfection of justice, but not even its beginning. Rather, all who become good are preceded by divine justification; and, so that they may not fall away after receiving a good will, God grants them progress and perseverance through his assistance. Grace is not given on account of any past or future merits of human beings; instead, through the gift and assistance of grace itself, all good human merits are both begun and brought to completion.

But the wicked, whom God in his just judgment abandons in their wickedness—even if they are said to lack the sacrament because of the guilt of original sin—are nevertheless brought down to the punishment of eternal fire on account of the merit of subsequent sins, that is, their own sins. For the merciful and just God justly punishes the sins of human origin and will, whether in infants or in adults, which he does not mercifully wash away. He is the good and true God who made the human being but did not create sin in the human being. Nor has he ever found in any human beings good merits or works for which he might save them; rather, when he justifies them by gratuitous mercy, he himself changes both their wills and their works.

By the certain and unchangeable firmness of his foreknowledge, he foreknew in the vessels of mercy nothing except the gift of his grace, which he knew he would bestow both in the merits of gifts and in the gifts of merits. [Col. 0610C] For he himself gives gratuitous goodness to the human will and assists the good will in its works. He likewise foreknew in the vessels of wrath those works of human wickedness that would unquestionably follow in their outcome.

### 15

According to right faith and evident truth, then, with regard to an infant who is taken from this life without the benefit of a second birth: just as we must confess that God foreknew the infant’s future death, which truly was going to occur, so it is absurd to say that God foreknew the infant’s future sins, which were not going to occur. For God, the Creator of all things, would not have foreknown as destined to be done things that were not destined to be done.

We know that God’s foreknowledge is so true and unchangeable that the things it foreknows as future truly are future; nor does it foreknow anything as destined to be done that does not take place according to his foreknowledge. Only the mutability of the creature admits of futurity; such futurity in no way belongs to the immutability of the Creator.

Therefore, nothing is past or future for God. Everything that he foreknows as destined to be done is present to him in such a way that, once it has been done, it cannot be past for him—for just as he knows the past, so he also knows the future. Whatever things change or pass away with time remain in his knowledge without the passage of time or mutability. [Note: One manuscript reads, “all things remain in his knowledge,” and so forth.]

But that God possesses foreknowledge not of things that will not be future, but of things that are destined to be done, is testified by the book of the prophet Daniel in these words: “O God, knower of hidden things, who know all things before they come to be” (Dan. 13:42). God therefore knows in his eternal foreknowledge what is future, so that it may come to be in actuality.

## Chapter VIII

### 16

It is therefore absurd to say that God foreknew an infant as destined to become ungodly if he lived, when he certainly did not foreknow that infant as destined to live any longer than he actually lived. He foreknew, rather, that the infant would not reach the age in which he would live impiously, because he truly knew that he would be taken from the world in infancy.

Since no sinful age was foreknown in him, how could the wickedness of an age that was not going to exist have been foreknown, when the age of a reborn infant can exist entirely without any act of sin, whereas a human act of sin cannot exist without some age of life? Works, whether good or evil, may properly be said to have been foreknown as belonging to a future age; but it is absurd to assert foreknowledge of a human work in an age in which the future human being himself is shown not to exist.

Just as we rightly say that God foreknew only the beginnings of those who were to be conceived, so we say that he foreknew the actual sins only of people who were to live. [Note: The editions read “of that one”; this is less satisfactory.] God is therefore rightly called the foreknower of the works of those whose eventual outcome is not denied to follow.

### 17

Moreover, whoever thinks that God foreknew future works that nevertheless were not going to occur must conclude that, in the foreknowledge of God—which he certainly does not deny to be truthful—there is, God forbid, some falsehood. For it is false that something will be future if it will not be present. But God’s knowledge can contain nothing false, because falsehood cannot exist in truth.

The foreknowledge of truth, therefore, which admits no falsehood, foreknows as destined to be done what is destined to be done, and as not destined to be done what is not destined to be done. God therefore did not foreknow any sins in the infant that the infant did not commit before dying. For if he had foreknown them as destined to be done, they would certainly have occurred. He would not know future things that he foreknew as not destined to be done.

Accordingly, we must acknowledge that, just as the infant died, so God foreknew that the infant would die. God’s foreknowledge is in no way deceived. Just as he foreknew the world as destined to be made, and made it in the manner in which he foreknew it was destined to be made, so also each individual thing in the world—whether it has been made, is being made, or is destined to be made—has always been destined to be made in God’s foreknowledge in the manner in which it has come to pass or will come to pass in actuality. [Col. 0611D]

God therefore did not foreknow as destined to be done by any human being something that the human being was not going to do; nor did anything escape his foreknowledge of the things that human beings have done, are doing, or will at some time do. The true God is rightly said to foreknow in human works those things that begin in relation to actual circumstances, persons, and times. But where neither the circumstance, nor the person, nor the time is shown to exist, there is certainly no work that can be asserted to have been divinely foreknown.

It is not consistent with truth to say that something is future in God’s foreknowledge when it is shown to be so entirely nothing that it cannot in any way be shown to become or to have become present from the future. Indeed, what cannot at some point be designated as present cannot properly bear the name of “future.”

## Chapter IX

### 18

From an infant who did nothing, therefore, God foreknew that nothing was destined to be done. Why he did not remove original sin from the infant, however, we cannot know; nevertheless, we must have no doubt that he acted justly. For the height of God’s incomprehensible counsel is closed to us—not only to us who were created from nothing, but also to us who bear the stain of sin, which, just as grace repeatedly washes away in God’s children living a mortal life, infirmity also frequently produces. Yet this is clear to us: there is no iniquity in God.

For it is written of him: “God is faithful, in whom there is no iniquity; the Lord God is just and holy” (Deut. 32:4). And elsewhere: “The judgments of God are true, justified in themselves” (Ps. 18:10). We believe that the negligence of parents or of any other human beings belongs to the hidden depth of these judgments—for “the judgments of God are a great abyss” (Ps. 35:7). Likewise, in the case of an infant who reaches baptism, we do not doubt that the care of the parents must be attributed to the gifts of divine grace.

If the parents are not endowed with piety and good conduct, God—who makes good use even of the evil wills of human beings—works the benefit of his grace in the infant through the solicitude of wicked parents. But if the parents are good [Note: Two manuscripts read “faithful parents”], the parents’ good will benefits not only the infant; it also contributes to the parents themselves toward their future reward. [Note: These words, “the parents themselves toward the merit … for their good will,” have been restored from two manuscripts.]

For God, who works both willing and accomplishing according to his good will, himself bestows on believing parents the grace of a good will, so that they may exercise pious care for the infant until it reaches the saving remedy of holy rebirth. Yet neither their efforts nor the very solicitude of their good will can suffice unless God deigns to precede them with the gratuitous gift of his mercy.

Indeed, the good will that the Lord inspires in parents for the infant’s rebirth urges them to run, so that the infant may reach the washing of saving water. Nevertheless, the effect of that rebirth is not of anyone who wills or runs, but of God who shows mercy. He both arouses the parents’ will and grants assistance to those who are willing.

### 19

[Note: From the words “Therefore, in order that” to “who also,” this entire passage is found in two manuscripts of the Holy Cross. In the other manuscript only these words occur: “Thus therefore he granted [the gift] of a truthful preacher, who also [granted] opportunity,” and so forth.]

Therefore, in order that the infant may be redeemed through the work of rebirth, the Redeemer mercifully acts. He prepares opportunities, supplies wills, provides persons, and grants places. And he works this not only in infants but also in adults.

Thus we read in the Acts of the Apostles (8:26) that an angel suddenly instructed Philip, who was stationed in Samaria, to descend by the road leading from Jerusalem to Gaza. There he not only preached the mystery of the Christian faith to a passing eunuch, who nevertheless was not in any way seeking the benefit of rebirth, but also administered the sacrament of baptism.

See how the Holy Spirit, by his grace going before the eunuch, granted him the person of a truthful preacher. He also gave Philip the opportunity to preach when he mercifully stirred the eunuch’s mind to read Isaiah. He himself likewise supplied the place, leading them by gratuitous goodness to a pool. In the eunuch he completed the work of saving grace. By its illumination the eunuch believed that Christ was the Son of God; and, coming to the pool, he requested the effect of holy washing. He departed not only baptized but also filled with the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0613B] ### 20

Who instructed the centurion Cornelius to send for the apostle Peter by sending an angel (Acts 10:5), except the one who freely infused into that same centurion the gift of his fear and of good works? So that God might remember his prayers and almsgiving, he first remembered Cornelius himself—not on account of any particular good work of his, but according to his own good pleasure, so that he might infuse into him the gift of his fear and inspire in him both devotion to almsgiving and affection for holy prayer.

He therefore conferred on him the grace of pleasing God, who found in him what was pleasing before himself. For he is the God of whom the Apostle says: “The God of peace [Note: Thus the manuscripts read, in accordance with the Apostle’s text; the editions omit “of peace”], who brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep through the blood of the eternal covenant, our Lord Jesus Christ, equip you in every good thing so that you may do his will, doing in you what is pleasing before him” (Heb. 13:20).

So great, however, was the work of divine grace in the instruction given to Cornelius to send for Peter that, when those whom Cornelius had sent came to him, the Holy Spirit not only commanded Peter to go with them but also removed all fear and doubt, assuring him that they had been sent by him. Thus the Holy Spirit said to Peter: “Behold, three men are seeking you. Rise, descend, and go with them, doubting nothing, because I have sent them” (Acts 10:19).

We also read that the apostles wished to go into Bithynia and Asia but were forbidden by the Holy Spirit (Acts 16:7). And after the Lord had struck Saul down by his own voice (Acts 9:4), he himself visited Ananias and sent him to baptize that same man (ibid., 11). Paul, too, writing to the Corinthians, clearly affirms that the holy solicitude of his disciple Titus, by which he cared for them, had been divinely inspired. For he says: “But thanks be to God, who gave the same solicitude for you in the heart of Titus” (2 Cor. 8:16).

## Chapter X

### 21

Since the testimony of the holy Scriptures makes it clear that God—whose will no one resists, whose decree no one changes, whose judgments no one comprehends—according to the abundant riches of his grace, which he possesses in goodness above all, procures or withholds from human beings who use reason appropriate persons for salvation, distinguishing some whom he makes vessels of mercy from the condemned mass for honor and glory, while maintaining justice toward some and granting mercy to others, why should we not also most certainly believe and freely proclaim that, in the baptism of infants, the diligence of the parents belongs to the grace of the redeeming God, while their negligence belongs to the justice of the judging God?

This is not because negligence in a good work comes from God, from whom no cause of an evil work could ever arise. Rather, the good will that is bestowed by God, in proportion as it advances in love [Note: Thus two manuscripts read; the editions have “advanced”], displays that much greater solicitude for the salvation of any soul. But the evil will, which by its own merit either does not receive or loses the grace of love, does not lay aside the torpor of its negligence; and, while it is abandoned in its darkness, it becomes increasingly blind.

### 22

When God therefore works mercifully in human beings, assistance through persons and opportunities is also provided [Note: Thus two manuscripts read; the editions and one manuscript have “when he provides”], and the very opportunity for the work is found for baptizing the infant when the Lord has determined that the work of holy washing is to be accomplished in that child.

For God, who cleanses an infant who does not will or run, who knows nothing of faith and is ignorant of his salvation and benefit, in whom there can be no request for rebirth and no confession of faith, through the gratuitous power of the sacrament—he himself arouses, for the infant’s redemption, the minds of the parents or the wills of any believers. Thus, while they work out their salvation with fear and trembling, it benefits them toward the reward of a good recompense; through their pious care the infant is brought to salvation.

For if the person who gives one of Christ’s least ones a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple will not lose his reward (Matt. 10:42)—a gift by which only the flesh of a human being is nourished [Note: The words “of a human being” are absent from the editions and from one manuscript but are present in two manuscripts]—how could the person who runs and labors with pious solicitude so that an infant’s flesh and soul may be saved fail to receive a reward?

## Chapter XI

### 23

Accordingly, this good will also must be believed to be given by God to pious parents: that they may not neglect to have the fruit of their flesh—whom they know, having been carnally born, to be polluted by the contagion of original sin—cleansed by spiritual regeneration; that they may desire, and diligently strive, not merely to have a temporal heir, but to have him become with them a co-heir of Christ; and that the son whom they have from mortal seed, destined to pass away mortally, they may have, reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, as an everlasting brother under God the Father.

Yet God undoubtedly gives this praiseworthy will to those parents into whom he has poured, through the Holy Spirit, the grace of holy love. They too attain eternal life, not because they beget children who are to die in the body of this death, but because, living in the fear of God, they do not neglect to hasten with them to the benefit of the second birth, and until it is completed in them in deed, bring forth in Christian love those whom they bore by human fertility. Nor do they allow those who have been baptized to run to ruin through crimes and wicked deeds; rather, according to the Apostle’s command, they endeavor to nourish and bring them up in the discipline and correction of the Lord (Eph. 6:4), desiring more that they please God than that they be rich or distinguished in the world.

### 24

Indeed, it is so manifest that the grace of baptism ought quickly to be brought to children by their parents that not only good and conscientious believers are accustomed to do this, but also those who do not belong to the number of God’s children: those, that is, who, though reckoned by the name of the faithful, are convicted by their works of denying the faith, while they do things that cannot accord with faith.

For, to say nothing of others, do we not see certain little women carefully bring to the grace of baptism children conceived not in wedlock but in fornication, and take great care that those born of them carnally not be deprived of spiritual birth? Thus, with those whom they commonly conceive and bear unwillingly, they run voluntarily and tremblingly to the church; and though they neglect the sin of their fornication and so remain in their iniquities, they nevertheless desire that their children be released from the bonds of original sin.

Thus the good God makes the pious will of good parents contribute to the effect of grace, not only for infants but also for the parents themselves; but he makes the solicitude of wicked parents serve the benefit of the children upon whom he bestows grace. For even those who nullify in themselves the benefit of baptism by evil works do not fail to know what the grace of baptism confers; and though in their own flesh they yield to deadly lust, in the fruit of their flesh they yield rather to acknowledged truth.

### 25

But if any Christian parents of infants [Col. 0615C]—a thing which, since it is greatly abhorrent to religion, is for the present hard to believe—forgetful of Christian love and of the salvation of their own souls no less than of their children’s, take no care for the regeneration of their infants, let them hear, concerning this crime, not our judgment but that of the Apostle, and would that they tremble at his words: “But if anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8).

Just as no one has it from God that he should deny the faith, so no one is permitted to impute negligence in any good work to the divine will. And just as it pertains to the work of divine grace that parents exercise pious solicitude for the regeneration of their children, so too it pertains to divine judgment that God abandons evil wills, when parents so love the bodily welfare of their children that they neglect the soundness of their souls; and take care that those who are to die may live, yet do not fear if their children perish under the guilt of everlasting damnation. Here they incur the gravest guilt and become, spiritually, most cruel murderers of their children. For by the very sluggishness of their neglect they serve the devil’s gains, and, pleasing their most wicked enemy, provoke the good King by evil works.

Therefore, just as we ought humbly to praise God, whose every way is mercy and truth (Ps. 25:10), when he gives grace, so no one can justly accuse him when he withholds it. For such are his goodness and justice that by gratuitous mercy he can redeem whomever he wills: “For who resists his will?” (Rom. 9:19). Yet he can neither ever will nor be able unjustly to condemn anyone, because “the Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him” (Ps. 92:16), and “our iniquity commends the justice of God; God, who inflicts wrath, is not unjust” (Rom. 3:5).

## Chapter XII

### 26

Therefore, whoever wishes to consider the wonderful and incomprehensible power of divine grace should rather consider with a humble and devout heart how pious, faithful, energetic, and solicitous parents often run swiftly with their little children to baptism, and yet the infants die without baptism in the hands of their hastening parents.
