Let us therefore consider two infants who died without baptism: one whom the harmful negligence of his parents neglected; the other, for whom the pious solicitude of his parents was indeed not lacking, but was unable to help because he was snatched away by the swiftness of death. While being carried in the hands of those who were taking him to baptism, before he reached the benefit of the life to come, he met the end of this present life [Note: The editions and one manuscript read “the present [end].”]; he was deprived of life before he was deprived of stain, and was snatched away to punishment before he could be brought to grace.

If, of these two, parental negligence is said to have harmed one, let it be said why the effect of salvation was denied the other, whom neither his parents’ will nor their running could assist. Or is it said that God even provided for this one, so that he who was foreseen to be going to become ungodly was thought to have been helped by the benefit of a lamentable death? Who would say this? Or who would not see that such a death did not snatch the dying infant from condemnation but from salvation? His condemnation was certainly not lightened, but redemption was denied him; provision was not made that he might be tortured less, but he was snatched away lest he be set free.

Was not here both the pious will and the running of the parents from God, yet of no avail because it was not from God that the infant should be baptized? In his deep and just judgment God indeed poured into them a religious affection for their son, but was unwilling to grant the infant the life-giving remedy. Thus he poured into holy David (2 Sam. 18:5) the gift of love, so that he commanded Absalom his son to be spared, lest he die in his impiety; but it was not from God that the ungodly Absalom should be preserved for future repentance. The pious will of the holy man therefore displayed what it ought; but divine justice accomplished what it knew ought to be done.

### 27

If anyone also considers this with a devout mind, will he not be both soothed by the sweetness of divine mercy and terrified by the depth of divine judgment? For sometimes an infant is born to believers who, as we have already said, are solicitous in devout faith and love for the redemption of their child, yet dies before being washed in holy baptism. Another, however, is born of unbelievers whose parents do not desire his salvation even tepidly, but do not desire it at all. Yet this same infant, by the ordering of heavenly providence, is either violently taken from his parents or stolen away, is brought by the pious love of any believers to holy baptism, and, as soon as he has been baptized, departs this life.

If the cause of original sin in these infants is considered, both are equally children of wrath, because they are bound together under one and the same bond of original sin. But where the cause of two persons is entirely equal, their merits surely cannot be declared unequal. Therefore there is no diversity of cause in infants which makes one chosen and the other rejected.

But if the will of the parents is considered, those who are Christians earnestly wished and most urgently ran [Note: Thus two manuscripts read; the editions read “took care”] that their child might be baptized; yet their child, forestalled by death before he was baptized, was assigned to eternal fires. The other, born of unbelievers, was brought to the grace of baptism against his parents’ will and was made an heir of God and co-heir of Christ. What did God foresee to occur in these cases, so that parental love could benefit one not at all, while hostile cruelty could benefit the other greatly? Who can penetrate this depth of God’s judgments? Yet who does not recognize here both the mercy of gratuitous goodness and the justice of divine severity? For where, in two infants, there are no merits in acts and no dissimilarity of cause in origin, it is manifest to us indeed that both were bound by the chains of original sin, but hidden why both were not set free.

## Chapter XIII

### 28

Let us therefore know that it is inscrutable to us why, one being left behind, God freely rescues the other from that mass of perdition. Yet we must know with complete certainty that the compassionate and merciful Lord, patient, very merciful, and true, so grants mercy to the one whom he frees that he by no means passes over justice and truth in the one whom he condemns. Thus the person released receives grace, which he should always praise; but the person condemned finds justice, in which he has nothing to accuse, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world become subject to God (Rom. 3:19), when one recognizes in his good things God’s preceding grace, while the other finds in his condemnation not a false foreknowledge of future works which he was not going to do, but the true guilt of the first parent.

### 29

Someone will say: “Why did God not grant gratuitous mercy to both, when one man bound both in guilt?” To him, while preserving the incomprehensible height of God’s judgments, we reply: Because God neither can ever will evil nor do it, he commanded that the debt be exacted from one in just severity, but that it be remitted to the other in gratuitous goodness. For in two equally ungodly persons, of whom one is released and the other condemned, the one released displays God’s gratuitous kindness, which can freely forgive every sin without any merits of works; while in the one condemned appears the justice of God, to whom no sin can ever be pleasing. Therefore neither merciful acquittal can be blameworthy nor punishment unjust. Goodness, which is overcome by no malice, acquits the guilty; equity, which delights in no iniquities, punishes the guilty.

Therefore, when God saves human beings, he bestows grace upon their good works; and when he punishes sinners for their iniquities, he renders justice in return for human evil works: in the former, indeed, restoring what they were made to be, but in the latter judging what they did. For all have sinned and need the glory of God (Rom. 3:23). For even those who have not sinned by the particularity of their own acts inherit original sin from the transgression of the first human being [Note: Two manuscripts read, “all inherit original [sin].”]

### 30

But we must not judge the secret of the divine will, by which he justifies one ungodly person and condemns another, to be unjust because we see that it is hidden from us. Rather, no one should doubt that it is divine and just precisely because no human being can investigate it. Therefore, simply displaying humility of heart, let us sing with the prophet, “Mercy and judgment,” to the Lord (Ps. 101:1), restraining the purpose of our inquiry so far that we do not wish to investigate what we cannot comprehend.

For Holy Scripture admonishes us, saying: “Do not seek things higher than yourself, and do not search into things stronger than yourself; but always consider the things that the Lord has commanded you, and do not be curious about his many works” (Sir. 3:22). Indeed, the labor of superfluous inquiry is expended in vain where no abundance of discovery lends aid; and harmful curiosity immediately falls into guilt when human weakness does not measure its own limit.

Rather, in this most profound mystery of the divine will, let us know that nothing else suits our salvation except that each of us humbly say with David: “Your knowledge has become wonderful from me; it has been strengthened, and I shall not be able to attain it” (Ps. 139:6). Let us also join the utterance of religious exclamation with blessed Paul, who says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. 11:33–34).

In this place blessed Paul fittingly [Note: Two manuscripts read “not vainly”] prefaced the height of God’s wisdom and knowledge before calling his judgments incomprehensible. By these words he surely stopped every presumptuous utterance of a human voice that complains against the just judgment of God [Note: The manuscripts read *querulam*, “complaining,” except that one reads *querelam*, “complaint”; the editions read “the rashness of the human voice”]. For it is certain that it belongs to the person and office of a judge both not to neglect knowledge in ascertaining a case and not to abandon the straight path of wisdom in judging, lest he be proved, through ignorance, rashly to pass judgment against an unknown truth, or be found through foolish perversity to suppress a truth that has been recognized [Note: One manuscript omits “rashly”]. Therefore God is neither ignorant, so as to judge rashly, nor foolish, so as to condemn anyone unjustly; of him prophetic authority cries: “The Lord is just and has loved righteousness; his countenance has seen equity” (Ps. 11:8).

## Chapter XIV

### 31

Therefore God is worthy of eternal praise in all his works: because to all whom he calls and justifies according to his purpose he freely forgives iniquity; but in all whom he punishes he preserves irreproachable equity. The case of adults and infants [Note: Thus two manuscripts read; the editions read “minors”] who complete the course of this present life in unbelief without baptism is one, as concerns their participation in original sin; and on account of this both will go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels, because in them the grace of the Savior has not erased the written bond by which the wickedness of the deceiver subjected them to itself.

But the case of adults is worse in this respect: having received the capacity to use reason, they reject or neglect the saving remedy of regeneration, without which they will not merely be unable to obtain the kingdom, but will also be subject to more severe punishments. For such persons, despising God’s kindness, according to their hardness and unrepentant heart store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works (Rom. 2:5–6). Thus they burn in eternal fires not only for original sin—the fires in which infants too, dying without baptism, who have done nothing good or evil, will burn—but also are tortured more severely for their own evil will, in proportion as they add more of their own iniquity. For in that original sin eternal death embraces both alike; but for the wickedness of their wills and acts punishment is added to these. It is worse to refuse to seek the benefit of redemption through an ungodly will than to be wholly unable, through tender age, to attain it; and the one who adds his own burden to that inherited from the first parents is weighed down more heavily than the one who bears only another’s burden.

[Col. 0619C] 32. No Christian ought to doubt that those who are stripped of the burdens of either original or even their own sins are preceded by the grace of God. In the abundance of this grace, some, having given too little consideration to the matter, fall into no slight error, supposing that it is given equally to all human beings—so that it is given even to those who greatly diminish the benefits of this grace, as though of themselves, while they do not believe that the work of grace is required in a person in order that grace may be received by that person.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] One manuscript reads: quam ipsi, “than they themselves”; the others: tanquam ipsi, “as though they themselves.”] Yet grace is divinely given for no other reason than that it may first produce a good will in a person; and it is present in each recipient in the measure that God, by gratuitous mercy, pours it into the recipient’s heart.

## CHAPTER XV

### 33. 

It is therefore fitting, dearest brothers, that whenever, in individual propositions, we are uncertain amid the fog of some obscurity, we should cling to the definitions of the holy Fathers: God’s mercy went before them and freely enlightened them so that they might believe, and then instructed them spiritually so that they might teach. Holding throughout to the truth of apostolic preaching, they recognized with complete certainty—and left this to be recognized in their books and letters—that the grace of God is not given universally to all human beings. For grace is the gratuitous gift of God. Therefore the Apostle says: “Each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that” (1 Cor. 7:7).

This grace, which God freely gives to the vessels of mercy, begins with the illumination of the heart; it does not find the human will good, but makes it good; and, so that it may be chosen, it first chooses it itself. Nor is it received or loved unless it itself works this in the human heart. Thus both the reception and the desire for grace are the work of grace itself. No human being can desire or ask for this grace—or even recognize it—unless he first receives it from the One who bestows it without any preceding works or good wills, so that he may prepare, grant, illuminate, awaken, preserve, and bring to completion the will in which grace itself always remains.

[Note: [Col. 0620D] These words are absent from the printed editions but are found in the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XVI

### 34. 

Therefore, in order that God’s grace may be recognized, loved, desired, and requested, it is first given to a person who does not recognize, love, desire, or request it. Thus grace itself causes itself to be recognized, loved, desired, and requested. For when the Lord, as he speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, removes the heart of stone from human beings and gives them a heart of flesh (Ezek. 11:19), he surely changes the human will through the illumination of his grace.

This is “the change” not of human free choice but “of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76:11); through it, the children of men who are “heavy of heart,” who “love vanity and seek falsehood” (Ps. 4:3), do not themselves bring a good will to the love and pursuit of truth, but receive from the Lord the gift of a good will. For it is written: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8:35, according to the Septuagint).

From the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world, a good will is given, so that a person may believe in God and faithfully love God. From him this will is continually governed and directed, so that neither the person’s faith may fail nor love grow cold. Hence the Savior says to Peter: “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32).

This faith is that of the saints, and it works through love. Therefore, just as no one can possess the beginning of a good will unless he has been enlightened by God’s preceding mercy—for “the will is prepared by the Lord,” and again it is written, “My God, his mercy will go before me” (Ps. 58:11)—so no one can retain that same good will to the end unless he is continually preserved by the same mercy following after him. For blessed David says to God: “Your mercy will follow me all the days of my life” (Ps. 22:6).

Thus mercy freely goes before the evil person so that he may be changed for the better, and, by following after the person it has made good, governs him so that he may not be changed for the worse.

[Note: [Col. 0620D] The printed editions read: mutet, “may change.”]

### 35. 

Every good will and work can therefore exist in a person only if it is given through the abundance of preceding grace and preserved through the assistance of that same grace following after. Grace goes before the evil person so that, with God’s generosity, he may begin to possess a good will—a will which previously he did not possess because he could not possess it by himself. It follows the good person so that he may persevere and progress in the good will which he could not possess from himself but received freely.

It therefore goes before by directing the human heart when it is perverse, for it is written: “The Lord directs hearts” (Prov. 21:2). It follows by guarding the heart once corrected, for similarly it is written: “My just help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart” (Ps. 7:11). Grace therefore works in both: in the one who is straying, so that he may live once corrected, and in the one who has been corrected, so that he may not depart after being corrupted.

## CHAPTER XVII

### 36. 

Anyone who devoutly seeks to know whether this grace is not given to all, and whether, among those to whom it is given, it is not given equally to all, learns this from the testimony of the holy Scriptures. For what good can exist first in a person by which he may tend toward eternal life, other than a good will? Yet concerning this it is said in Proverbs: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8:35, according to the Septuagint).

The Lord, therefore, who prepares a good will in us, himself grants us the beginning of a good will. The Apostle also teaches that God works in us not only so that we may will, but also so that we may do what we rightly will, saying: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will” (Phil. 2:12–13).

That the beginning of this good will consists in faith is shown by the book of the Song of Songs (4:8, according to the Septuagint), where Christ says to the Church: “You will come and pass over from the beginning of faith.” Yet blessed Paul asserts that this faith is not given to all, saying: “For faith is not possessed by all” (2 Thess. 3:2); and again: “Not all obey the Gospel” (Rom. 10:16).

That it is not given equally to those to whom it is given, we learn from the same Apostle, who says: “For by the grace that has been given to me I say to everyone among you not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sobriety, and to each according as God has apportioned the measure of faith” (Rom. 12:3).

### 37. 

For this reason the very company of the apostles, which had received not the spirit of this world but the Spirit who is from God, “so that it might know the things granted by God” to it (1 Cor. 2:12),

[Note: [Col. 0621D] Two manuscripts read: donata sunt, “are given.”]

knowing that the beginning of faith had been conferred upon it by the Lord, asked him to increase that same faith in them. For the evangelist Luke records that the disciples said to the Lord: “O Lord, increase our faith” (Luke 17:5).

If the human will could obtain the beginning of faith from itself, it would surely have taken its increase from itself as well. But blessed apostles knew that they had received from the Lord the beginning of faith, which they had not possessed; from that same source they asked for its increase. For the grace that had conferred upon them the beginning of faith itself awakened in them the desire for its increase.

Although, in this desire, their will was already faithful, it could in no way suffice for them unless the One who had given the beginning of faith to those who did not ask for it also, in his kindly mercy, conferred its increase upon those who asked for it. Thus, for the apostles to believe, the will was not absent; rather, the Lord himself had prepared that will in them.

For a person’s not believing arises from himself as unbelief; but for a person to believe in God, he receives faith from God; and for faith to be perfected in him through subsequent increase, this is accomplished not by the power of the human will but by divine grace. For just as God prepares the will to believe through grace, so, by the working of grace, he brings that will to completion; and just as he himself gives faith to those who do not have it, so he himself also multiplies it in those who do have it.

For this reason the Epistle written to the Hebrews says: “Therefore, laying aside every weight and the sin that clings closely to us, let us run with perseverance the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Heb. 12:1–2).

Accordingly, if a person has faith from himself, Jesus is not the author of faith; and if a person perfects faith by his own strength, Jesus is not the perfecter of faith. But apostolic authority confesses the Lord Jesus to be the author and perfecter of our faith. It is therefore certain that faith can neither exist nor grow in us unless he grants it to us, increases what he has granted, and perfects what he has increased—he whom apostolic authority proclaims to be the author and perfecter of faith.

For this reason the Apostle Paul, in the Epistle he wrote to the Ephesians, just as he proclaims that grace is given by God, so he testifies that it is not given equally to all, but according to the measure in which he mercifully grants it—he who is accustomed not to repay it as something owed according to merits, but to bestow it freely. For he says:

“To each of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4:7).

[Note: [Col. 0621D] Two manuscripts read: “The same Apostle therefore says.”]

These and similar testimonies show that grace is neither given to all nor given equally to those to whom it is given, but according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Hence, concluding the same Epistle, blessed Paul divinely wishes peace, love, and faith to be granted, saying: “Peace to the brothers, and love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Eph. 6:23).

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 38. 

Therefore, in order that we might will to believe in God, he bestowed upon us a good will; in order that we might believe in him, he himself gave us faith; and in order that we might also love him, he poured the grace of his love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.

It is not because we willed that we received grace; rather, grace was given while we did not yet will.

[Note: [Col. 0621D] The printed editions read: “Not indeed because we will.”]

We could have possessed this grace so that we might receive grace; but while we were unbelievers, faith was given to us by grace.

[Note: [Col. 0622D] The printed editions read: gratis, “freely.”]

The chosen instrument plainly testifies to this, saying: “By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God” (Eph. 2:8).

Grace alone therefore makes a good will in us; grace alone grants faith to that will. But when the good will has faith—without which it cannot be good, since “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6)—it begins to do good, provided that the help of grace is never absent from the one who works.

For this reason the grace of God makes the will good in us: so that it may have something in us which grace can assist—not only the one who wills but also the one who acts. And for this reason grace pours the gift of belief into our will, so that it may not be lacking to that same will when it believes and acts. Thus, in order to possess faith, the human will must recognize that the abundance of faith is present in it not from itself but from God’s grace.

[Note: [Col. 0622D] Two manuscripts read: “Thus, so that the human will may have good merits through faith.”]

[Col. 0623A] ### 39. 

It is not enough for us to know that faith is divinely given to each person unless we know with complete certainty that each person is granted as much faith as God deigns to give, not as much as the human will deserves. Before it receives faith, the will can by itself deserve punishment, but not faith.

For everything that is not from faith is sin, and without faith it is impossible to please God (Rom. 14:23; Heb. 11:6). Whoever does not please God is undoubtedly displeasing to him; and whoever displeases God does not appease him but rather provokes him.

The will that does not have faith can therefore possess no merit for receiving faith, because not to have faith is to displease God. The evil of unbelief merits not justification but condemnation.

The distribution of faith is therefore gratuitous. It is granted to each person not according to the faith of unbelievers—which is no faith at all—but according to the voluntary generosity of God, who justifies. Teaching this, the Doctor of the Gentiles admonishes us “not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sobriety” (Rom. 12:3), and “to each according as God has apportioned the measure of faith” (1 Pet. 4:10).

Blessed Peter also testifies that God’s grace is manifold. For this reason he commands each believer to serve according to the quality of the grace received, saying: “Be hospitable to one another without complaining; as each has received grace, administer it among yourselves, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1 Pet. 4:9–10).

Blessed Paul likewise says: “Though we are many, we are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another; but we have gifts differing according to the grace that has been given to us” (Rom. 12:5–6).

## CHAPTER XIX

### 40. 

Furthermore, lest anyone attempt to attribute the difference among these gifts to any human works or merits, the same Apostle shows that they are granted by the voluntary generosity of spiritual grace.

[Note: [Col. 0623D] Thus one manuscript. The printed editions read: “the voluntary generosity … is granted.”]

Grace finds no merit to which it can give the gift; rather, it itself grants the beginnings of merits. He therefore says:

“There are varieties of graces, but the same Spirit; there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of works, but the same God, who works all things in all” (1 Cor. 12:4–6).

And after enumerating the spiritual gifts he says: “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills” (ibid., 11).

Every Christian ought therefore to know that the beginning of saving grace rests neither upon the powers of nature nor upon legal commands, but upon the illumination of the heart and the voluntary gift of divine goodness. Through this grace what God commands can be not only recognized by us but also loved and accomplished.

For human nature by itself can never recover a good will that pleases God, since it lost that will in the first human being when, its will corrupted from the rectitude it had received from God, it consented to the devil. It lost it then in such a way that thereafter no human being could possess it from himself, unless each received it freely from the One from whom the first human being received it when he was created. If the first human being had not lost it, every human being thereafter would naturally possess it.

### 41. 

The commands of the law can also sound externally in the ears of the flesh; but inwardly no one perceives them in a salutary way through the hearing of the heart unless he has received the gift of spiritual grace within.

The letter increases sin by prohibiting it if the help of spiritual grace is absent from the hearer; and once the law is recognized, a person becomes a transgressor unless his will is prepared by the Lord to fulfill the law. For “the law brings wrath, and where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15); and “Scripture confined all things under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to believers” (Gal. 3:22).

The law without grace can therefore show sickness but cannot heal; it displays wounds but does not supply medicines. Grace, however, supplies inward assistance so that the command of the law may be fulfilled. Thus the law reveals guilt, while grace grants pardon. It belongs to the law that we recognize sins; it belongs to grace that we avoid them.

The Apostle says: “I did not know sin except through the law. For I would not have known covetousness unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Rom. 7:7). Concerning grace he also says: “Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid., 24–25).

It is therefore a defect of corrupted nature that a person sins; the function of the law is to show a person the sin of which he is ignorant; but it is the gift of grace to heal the person’s defect, which nature brought upon itself and the recognition of the law intensified.

[Note: [Col. 0623D] Thus two manuscripts. The printed editions read: “which guilt brought upon itself.” [Col. 0624D] We have preferred the earlier reading because it is more suitable to the context itself.]

Grace therefore works both illumination and salvation in human beings. Thus, assisted by grace’s preceding help, a person comes to know that the commandments of the law—which, until he could fulfill them, he heard not only uselessly but also to his condemnation—are holy, just, and good; and he also receives love, by which he can both love and fulfill what he learns.

## CHAPTER XX

### 42. 

Let us not therefore suppose that the grace of God is given to all human beings. “Faith is not possessed by all,” and some do not receive the love of God so as to be saved.

Yet in those who do not believe in or love God there is a defect of the human will. As long as that will is not changed by the grace of the divine gift, it either does not understand the commandments or, having understood them, despises them—that is, it either sins through ignorance or, through the fault of transgression, increases its sin.

Concerning those whom the darkness of ignorance surrounds, it is said: “They did not know, nor did they understand; they walk in darkness” (Ps. 81:5). As the Apostle says, they “walk in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their hearts” (Eph. 4:17–18).

Concerning those who know, he says that, “although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts” (Rom. 1:21). And concerning the servant who despises, it is said: “A stubborn servant will not be corrected by words; even if he understands, he will not obey” (Prov. 29:19).

What else is meant by “he will not be corrected by words” than this: by the command of the law alone, if grace is absent, he will not be converted? For “God, who converts us, gives us life, so that his people may rejoice in him” (Ps. 84:7). “He himself shows us his mercy, and he himself gives us his salvation” (ibid., 8).

Thus, for a person not to believe in God, he has the defect of unbelief from himself; but for him to believe in and love God is a gift of divine generosity.

For if one asks what sort of people grace finds, it certainly finds them as the Apostle describes them: “foolish and unbelieving, wandering, serving various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another” (Tit. 3:3). From all these vices, he proclaims that we are saved not by nature’s capacity or by knowledge of the law, but by the kindness of our Savior God (ibid., 4).

By his help we “deny ungodliness and worldly desires and live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this age” (Tit. 2:12).

## CHAPTER XXI

### 43. 

This, then, is what the grace of God through our Lord Jesus Christ accomplishes: it makes the foolish wise; grants faith to the unbelieving; calls the wandering to life and also recalls them from perverse desires; once earthly desires have been expelled, inspires a desire for the heavenly kingdom; removes the craving for carnal pleasures and pours in the gift of spiritual delight and will; uproots malice and replaces it with goodness; drives out envy through the gift of kindness; and grants the gift of holy love even to those who are hateful and hate one another.

[Note: [Col. 0625D] Two manuscripts read: terrenis desideriis, “earthly desires”; the printed editions read: pravis desideriis, “perverse desires.”]

[Note: [Col. 0625D] Two manuscripts read: infundat, “pours in,” in place of attribuat, “grants.”]

Thus, for us to become good from being evil, and for us to burn with the fire of holy love, the work of spiritual grace is begun in us and is brought to completion in us through its operation.

“For the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, goodness, kindness” (Gal. 5:22–23), and the other things commended by apostolic teaching. When this Spirit works salutarily in us, we recognize what must be done, because he himself works in us so that we may do what we have recognized.

“For we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Cor. 2:12). We are also led by the same Spirit so that, by doing good, we may be children of God: “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. 8:14).

### 44. 

Therefore, obeying the heavenly utterances, let us hold most firmly that the beginning of every good is conferred upon us by divine generosity. We cannot, by ourselves, possess either the beginning or the progress by which we restrain ourselves from doing evil and begin to will or do good.

For just as it is written concerning self-control, “No one can be self-controlled unless God grants it” (Wis. 8:21), and the Apostle counts it among the fruits of the Spirit (Gal. 5:23), so love—which “does not act wrongly” (1 Cor. 13:4), insofar as this pertains to self-control, and which “covers a multitude of sins” through good works (1 Pet. 4:8)—is the means by which God works with us not only to turn away from evil but also to do good; by it we love not only our neighbors but also our enemies, do good to those who hate us, and pray for those who persecute and slander us (Matt. 5:44).

This love therefore neither begins nor grows in us from our own will; rather, through the action of God’s grace, it is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

## CHAPTER XXII

### 45. 

Whoever therefore does not wish to be deceived or to deceive others concerning the name of grace should listen to the Apostle, who carefully suppresses the arrogance of human pride that attempts to claim for itself the beginning of a good will. He says:

“For who distinguishes you? What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

Let him also follow, with sincere humility of heart, the judgment of James, which recalls us from error and leads us into the way of truth. He says: “Do not err, my brothers: every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:16–17).

Our Creator and Redeemer himself, when he spoke to the crowds in parables, wished to show that the capacity for inward recognition belonged only to those to whom he himself chose to grant it. For he is the one “who teaches human beings knowledge” (Ps. 94:10). When the disciples asked him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?” (Matt. 13:14),

[Note: [Col. 0625D] The printed editions read: intelligentioris, “of more intelligent recognition”; three manuscripts more suitably read: interioris, “of inward recognition.”]

he disclosed the gift of heavenly grace in an explicit reply, saying: “Because it has been given to you to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables” (Luke 8:10).

His own confession directed to the Father also clearly shows that all the wisdom of the human mind is powerless to understand divine preaching unless God—who teaches externally through a speaking human being—teaches inwardly through himself, illuminating and assisting the hearer. For he says:

“I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25).

How can grace be claimed to have been given to all when, as the giver himself testifies, it is shown to have been hidden from the wise and prudent?

[Note: [Col. 0626D] Two manuscripts read: ipso donatore, “the giver himself”; the printed editions read: ipso donante, “he himself giving.”]

In the words that follow, he also shows that the knowledge of God rests not in human power but in divine revelation, when he says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (ibid., 27).

Who here would not see that a person hears the discourse of heavenly teaching from another person to no benefit unless God, by mercifully revealing himself, speaks to him as teacher in his heart?

## CHAPTER XXIII

### 46. 

This revelation is particular to the children of God. Through it they receive not only the gift of knowledge but also divine love. For this revelation or knowledge is not like that of those concerning whom the Apostle says: “What can be known of God is manifest among them. For God manifested it to them” (Rom. 1:19)—namely, so that they might be without excuse, because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks (ibid., 20–21).

That manifestation by which they knew God, whom they did not love once they knew him, did not contain the grace by which God is known in such a way that he is loved. Because they did not receive grace, therefore, although they knew God, they did not give thanks; and because they were vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, that manifestation by which they knew God worked in them so that, through knowing, they might become proud, not so that, by humbling themselves, they might love him whom they had known.

[Note: [Col. 0627] Two manuscripts read: “so that they might recognize that he ought to be loved, not so that they might have loved the one whom they had known.”]

Thus, when such knowledge is taken away, there is excuse, not salvation bestowed. But in this revelation, which the grace of God works in the vessels of mercy, knowledge of God and love of God are conferred upon a person together.

Those who are not chosen are without excuse; the chosen, however, become unaccusable. For the Apostle says:

“Who will accuse God’s elect? God, who justifies. Who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who was also raised—who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:33–34).

### 47. 

In the vessels of mercy, therefore, the guilt of nature is released through the humble faith and love which spiritual grace grants; but in the vessels of wrath it is nourished by proud knowledge.

Through that former knowledge the blind heart is puffed up by itself toward death; through this latter knowledge it is divinely illuminated and humbled toward life. Through the former knowledge the foolish heart is darkened, when a proud person claims for himself what belongs to God; through the latter he receives light, so that he may not doubt that the very fact that he knows and loves God is present in him not through nature’s capacity, nor through hearing the law, nor through his own will, but through God’s gift.

He should always remember to be humble, lest, by becoming proud, he lose what he received undeservedly. That knowledge therefore adds the guilt of transgression to the sinner; this removes punishment from the sinner. The former justly condemns; the latter freely justifies. There, knowledge that puffs up nourishes and increases sin; here, love that builds up covers a multitude of sins.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0627]

[Col. 0627B] 458 ## CHAPTER I

### 1. 

In the preceding book, with the assistance of God’s grace—which alone can pour the gift of holy thought into the human heart and grant the mouth the capacity for right speech, since both we and our words are in God’s hand—I discussed Jacob and Esau sufficiently and more than sufficiently.

[Note: [Col. 0627D] The printed editions read: cognitionis, “of holy knowledge,” in place of cogitationis, “of holy thought.”]

[Note: [Col. 0627D] Thus two manuscripts. The printed editions read: “we demonstrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently”; the earlier reading is fuller and more harmonious.]

I showed, on the authority of the apostolic judgment, that holy Jacob was chosen before he was born, without any merit of preceding or subsequent works requiring it, and was distinguished solely by the kindness of the divine purpose.

Blessed Paul is plainly understood to have asserted this in the statement where he says: “For when they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil, so that the purpose of God according to election might remain” (Rom. 9:11).

The Apostle said this in order to show that the purpose remained not according to human merit but according to the purpose of the one who calls, and that election was understood to arise not from any merit of the one who was to be born but from God’s will.

For God’s calling would truly have been an election based on human merit and not on God’s grace if some good or evil action could have been found in the infants. But since there were no merits of their own works in those not yet born, conceived from a single act of intercourse, by which their difference might cause one to be chosen and the other rejected—because, if such merits existed, God’s purpose would not remain according to God’s election but according to human works—since, therefore, there was no difference in those brothers of their own good or evil work that could confer the merit of election upon one and impose the punishment of condemnation upon the other, God’s purpose was according to election.

For the will of the one choosing did not remain on account of the merit of the one to be chosen; rather, the distinction of the one chosen was gratuitous, arising from the purpose of the one choosing. For this reason the Apostle went on to add: “Not from works, but from the one who calls, it was said to her: ‘The elder will serve the younger’” (ibid., 12).

### 2. 

Once, insofar as the Lord granted it, this question concerning the twin brothers had been treated, the course of our work brought forward a general inquiry concerning infants who die without baptism. After this had been examined more carefully and, as I think, resolved more clearly, we finally undertook, with careful investigation, a discussion of that very grace by which all who are saved are freely preceded.

It became clear that grace is not given universally to all, and that, among those to whom it is given, it is not given equally. It belongs to the one who chooses both whom to give it to and how much to give, since he does not repay it as something owed to human wills or works, but freely and mercifully pours it into hearts to be illuminated.

Therefore he certainly gives it to whomever he wills and in whatever measure he wills, since he is invited neither by any beginning of a good will nor by the accomplishment of any good work before he grants grace.

## CHAPTER II

### 3. 

Nevertheless, because we know that many people, in the question of God’s grace and human free choice, do not preserve the distinction between them but assert one in such a way that they attempt to remove the other—or, when they hear one asserted, suppose that the other is being taken away,

[Note: [Col. 0628D] This wording, as far as the words “suppose that the other is being taken away,” is found in two manuscripts.]

although the grace of piety permits neither to be denied but commands that the proper order be preserved in confessing both—we, supported by the protection of divine grace by which the human free choice is both illuminated and governed, have taken care in this second book to assert both God’s grace and human free choice in such a way that we remove neither while defending both.

Rather, we intend to show which of these needs the other, and what one freely bestows upon the other through the gift of goodness; what it is that always awaits healing, and from where the benefit of medicine continually overflows.

For the Creator and Savior of mortals says that “those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick,” and that he did not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (Matt. 9:13).

From this, then, we learn what the same physician finds in the sick and what he himself provides for those he is to heal. He finds the free choice of the human being—at least in that age which is already capable of rational use—either completely unaware of its own sickness or puffed up by the disease of harmful thought.

That is, the person either does not know what ought to be done, or, knowing what ought to be done, trusts that he can fulfill it by his own strength. Thus the ignorant person either embraces the disease, or is more seriously ill because he does not ask the physician but attempts to apply a remedy to himself.

It follows that, weighed down by the fatal disease either of ignorance or of pride, he neither seeks the physician nor finds in himself the effect of true health.

Yet free will is not absent from a person before he is healed by the work of divine conversion merely because he prefers to obey the disease rather than the physician. For by the very fact that a person obeys or does not obey, he clearly shows that free choice is present in him.

## CHAPTER III

### 4. 

Free choice therefore exists not only in righteous people but also in the ungodly. In the former it is raised up and directed by the goodness of God the Redeemer; in the latter it is abandoned and punished by the justice of God who takes vengeance.

Thus, in the righteous, free choice clings to the truth not only by knowing it but also by loving it. In the ungodly, however, it either does not know the commandment, and therefore does not possess knowledge of sin in its own sin, or it can know sin without the help of God’s grace only in such a way that, presuming it can fulfill the commandments of the divine will by itself, it does not humbly obey God’s will but, doing good badly, serves its own error instead.

For, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish its own, it is not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:3), since “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (ibid., 4).

## 5

Our physician, therefore—skilled and good—who freely restores the dead to life and returns the sick to health, himself the salvation of the languishing and the resurrection of the dead, in his unsurpassable goodness provided for the enlivening and healing of human beings by making himself our medicine. But in order that the Wisdom of God might wisely complete the order of his healing, he first gave a commandment through the law of righteousness, by which the sick person might recognize his weakness [Col. 0629D], intending to give him affection [Note: [Col. 0629D] So the manuscripts. The editions read *effectum*, “effect.”] through grace. Thus the infirm person, made salutarily aware of his infirmity, would no longer swell with confidence in his own strength; rather, recognizing the very fountain of life and salvation, he would ask that source itself for the benefit of healing. Nor, vaunting his own righteousness with a proud heart, would he suppose himself free from disease, as though he did not need the help of treatment [hence the Pharisee’s saying: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity—robbers, unjust, adulterers—or even like this tax collector” (Luke 18:11)]; but, looking upon his wounds with the humility of a contrite heart, he would truthfully cry out [Col. 0630A]: “I said, ‘Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you’” (Psalm 40:5).

Yet that heavenly physician would not heal our weakness through knowledge or love of the commandment unless he had given human beings free choice. Rather, weakness was multiplied through knowledge of the commandment alone, so that, through grace, the health of faith and love might begin to be established. Through knowledge of the commandment, therefore, the free choice of the human being is summoned to do what is good—not because a person can fulfill what the law commands by will alone or by strength alone, but so that, through knowledge of the commandment, he may become conscious of his weakness and seek the aid of medicinal grace. Once this has been received, he can both love what is commanded and do it; he can recognize what he can and cannot do, ask that he may be able to do it, attribute the misery of his weakness to himself, and assign the grace of health to the benefits of healing.

## CHAPTER IV

### 6

All these things that we have set forth above ought rightly to be confirmed by heavenly utterances. Through Isaiah God speaks as follows: “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and do not listen to me, the sword shall devour you” (Isaiah 1:19). In the words “If you are willing” and “If you are unwilling,” the freedom of the human will is plainly declared. No one is unaware that willing and unwilling belong to the will.

What, then, is said through the prophet—“If you are willing and listen to me”—summons our will, by which we ought always to desire what is good and persist continually and willingly in good works. But when the Apostle says that “God is the one who works in us both to will and to accomplish, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13), he clearly shows that the human will itself is directed toward willing what is good only by a divine gift and is divinely helped to do what is good. When, therefore, we are commanded to will, what we ought to possess is shown; but because we cannot possess it from ourselves, we are admonished to ask help from the one who gives us the command. Yet we cannot ask this unless God works in us the willing itself.

For the will that is made good [Note: [Col. 0629] The word *bona* (“good”) is read in two manuscripts, but not in the editions.] in us by the gift of the merciful God is itself assisted in us so that it may be able to act well. It rises from the evils in which it lies before justification, and in which it fails with delight, not by its own strength but through the operation of God who goes before it. After it has risen, however, it cannot suffice by itself to avoid falling; just as it is raised to rise by the benefit of prevenient mercy [Col. 0630D], so it is guarded in perseverance by the help of subsequent mercy.

## CHAPTER V

### 7

Blessed David, therefore, recognizing both the will of human choice and the power of divine grace, summons us to do what is good; yet what he commands us to do, he asks from the source from which he does not doubt that we can possess it. Calling human choice to conversion, he terrifies it with salutary preaching, saying: “Unless you are converted, he has brandished his sword, bent his bow, and prepared it” (Psalm 7:13). But to show that the conversion we are commanded to undertake and which he proclaims to us is assigned to the gift of heavenly operation, he says: “O God, you will turn us and give us life, and your people will rejoice in you” (Psalm 84:7).

So that each person might have mercy on his own soul and please God, human choice is admonished in divine speech as follows: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Sirach 30:24). But since no one can have mercy on his soul unless, anticipated by God’s mercy, he has received the ability to be merciful, the giver of mercy himself teaches us, saying: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I will show mercy” (Exodus 33:19). Therefore blessed David also says: “My God, his mercy will anticipate me” (Psalm 58:11).

And because no one can please God unless God works in that person what pleases him, it is plainly stated in the Epistle written to the Hebrews. For there it says: “But may the God of peace, who brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, our Lord Jesus Christ, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you in every good thing so that you may do his will, doing in you what is pleasing in his sight” (Hebrews 13:20–21).

### 8

We therefore please God only if we are willing; but it is from him that we are granted the ability to will. Unless he changes the human will so that it is good, it either always desires evil or never properly desires the good; and thus, while it does not maintain right order in good things, it in no way pleases God, who is himself good.

We therefore please God only through a good will; but in order that we may please him, he himself equips us in every good thing [Note: [Col. 0631D] These words—“but in order that we may please him … he himself does it”—are absent from the editions but are found in two manuscripts.]. When we do his will, we do it willingly; yet in order that we may do it, he himself works in us what is pleasing in his sight.

For David says: “To do your will, my God, I have willed” (Psalm 39:9). But in order to do that will itself, he asks the help of spiritual grace, by which he may be taught so as to know and directed so as to act. Hence elsewhere he prays as follows [Note: [Col. 0631D] Two manuscripts add here: “Thus he prays to the very author of knowledge and ability” [Col. 0632D].]: “Teach me to do your will, for you are my God” (Psalm 142:10); and immediately he adds: “Your good Spirit will lead me on a straight path” (ibid.).

Isaiah likewise commands, saying: “Let the wicked abandon his way, and the unjust man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord” (Isaiah 55:7). The apostle Paul also urges us to be renewed in the spirit of our mind and to put on the new human being, who has been created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth (Ephesians 4:23–24).

## CHAPTER VI

### 9

Nevertheless, lest our conversion or renewal [Col. 0631D] be attributed to human choice, holy Jeremiah asks both from the Lord for us in these words: “Turn us to yourself, and we shall be converted; renew our days as in former times” (Lamentations 5:21).

Again the Psalmist [Note: [Col. 0632D] One manuscript reads, “Again the prophet.”] says: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80:11). Here we understand the mouth of the heart to be signified, not the bodily mouth. Of this mouth he says elsewhere: “When the Lord brought back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted. Then our mouth was filled with joy” (Psalm 125:1–2).

Yet, lest anyone proudly attribute the opening of the mouth to himself, the book of the Acts of the Apostles shows that, for receiving the word of Christian preaching, the mouth of the human heart is opened by the generosity of the divine gift. For it is written there concerning a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple: “The Lord opened her heart to attend to what was being spoken by Paul” (Acts 16:14).

Again it is written that Wisdom “opened the mouth of the mute and made the tongues of infants eloquent” (Wisdom 10:21). It opened the mouth of the mute so that unbelievers might believe, and made the tongues of infants eloquent so that they might proclaim what they had believed. Hence Paul rightly ascribes both his believing and his speaking to the gift of the Holy Spirit, saying: “But having the same Spirit of faith, as it is written, ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’; we also believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Corinthians 4:13).

A human being believes willingly and speaks willingly; but the will of the human being cannot have this from itself unless God gives it. For, so that the unbelieving person [Note: [Col. 0632D] The editions read, “so that the believing person.”] may believe, Wisdom opens the mute mouth; and so that the believer may speak, it makes the tongues of infants eloquent.

### 10

The commandments, therefore, by which we are admonished through the prophets and apostles what we ought to desire and what to avoid, summon our choice, so that we may willingly serve the Lord’s commands. But since the prophets and apostles themselves—who, filled with the Holy Spirit, lived holy lives and taught holy things—never ceased asking for divine help (for, in order to fulfill what God commanded, they sought help from him), they plainly did not deny that human beings possess free choice of the will; at the same time, they testified that, without the help of God’s grace, it is insufficient and powerless not only to do but even to think what is holy.

Hence the holy Apostle, showing that human beings possess free choice of the will, exhorts the Philippians through saving commands to think about and do what is holy and just, saying: “Whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are holy, whatever things are just, whatever things are good in reputation, if there is any virtue, if there is any praise, think about these things, which you have learned, received, heard, and seen in me. Do these things, and the God of peace will be with you” (Philippians 4:8–9).

Does he not both command them to think about and do what is holy, and yet clearly show from where the ability both to think and to act is given to us? Concerning thought he says: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves” (2 Corinthians 3:5). What does he mean by “from ourselves” except “from free choice of the will”? From where, then, does it come, if it is not from ourselves? “But,” he says, “our sufficiency is from God” (ibid.).

Regarding action also, he proclaims that we are led by the Spirit of God: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God” (Romans 8:14).

## CHAPTER VII

### 11

This, then, is the distinction between the commanding letter and the life-giving spirit—that is, between law and grace: the law summons the human will, while grace converts it. The law cries out that we should will what is good; grace grants it. Through the law, divine righteousness instills terror in the will of the human being; through grace, mercy pours in love. Through the former, the will receives [Note: [Col. 0633D] So one manuscript, here and shortly afterward; the other codices read “received.”] the spirit of slavery in fear; through the latter, it receives the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry, “Abba, Father.”

This free will, therefore, naturally possesses within itself the capacity to desire good or evil spontaneously; but it desires good by advancing and evil by declining. To decline, it can suffice by itself; but to advance, it always needs the help of divine compassion.

Unless it is lifted by prevenient grace, it does not rise at all, because “the Lord raises up those who are bowed down” (Psalm 145:8). Unless it is helped by that grace as it leads, it does not run at all, because it is written of God: “He led me along the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake” (Psalm 23:3); and to him it is said: “Lord, lead me in your righteousness because of my enemies” (Psalm 5:9).

Unless it is brought to its destination by grace guarding it, it does not arrive at all. For holy David says: “Send forth your light and your truth; they themselves have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles” (Psalm 42:3).

Nor, once it has rejected evil, will the human will be able either to choose the goods that lead to life or to love them unless it has received from God the grace of discernment and love. For blessed Paul included discernment among spiritual gifts, saying: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another the grace of healings in one Spirit, to another the working of powers, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits” (1 Corinthians 12:8–10).

Of which spirits is discernment bestowed by spiritual generosity, if not of good and evil spirits? Thus, enlightened and helped by the grace of the Holy Spirit, we may know and be able both to preserve the gifts of the Holy Spirit with fear and trembling and to repel the suggestions of diabolical wickedness with salutary discernment. The blessed apostle John commands us to observe this, saying: “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1).

## CHAPTER VIII

### 12

In order that we may know what is given to us by God, it is not the spirit of the world that works in us, but the Spirit of God—that is, not the spirit a human being possesses in order to be born into the world, but the Spirit received in order to be reborn to God. The Apostle clearly teaches this, saying: “We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit that is from God, so that we may know what has been given to us by God” (1 Corinthians 2:12).

The Apostle testifies that this is given not only so that we may know but also so that we may understand. He writes thus to Timothy: “Understand what I say” (2 Timothy 2:7). By this statement he certainly summons human choice to understand; if a human being did not possess it, he could in no way understand what is said. But to show from where understanding is given to human choice, after saying, “Understand what I say,” he adds: “For the Lord will give you understanding in all things” (ibid.).

The most holy David likewise asks God for understanding so that he may learn God’s commandments, saying: “Your hands made me and fashioned me; give me understanding, and I shall learn your commandments” (Psalm 119:73). The Proverbs also testify that “the Lord gives wisdom, and from his presence come knowledge and understanding” (Proverbs 2:6).

The apostle James likewise commands that, if anyone lacks wisdom, he should ask it from God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach (James 1:5). But to show that the very will to ask is also divinely given, he adds: “Let him ask in faith, doubting nothing” (ibid., 6). Paul shows that God cannot be invoked without faith when he says: “How, then, will they invoke one in whom they have not believed?” (Romans 10:14).

Since no one invokes God before believing, and no one believes in God unless he has received faith, it is certain that the one who awakens us to ask for wisdom is the one who enlightens us so that we may believe.

## CHAPTER IX

### 13

A human being therefore wills what is good by the will and does what is good by the will, but without God’s gift and help he can never will or do what is good. He is summoned to know and admonished to act because he always possesses free choice of the will. Yet he cannot possess holy knowledge unless he has received it from above through the gift of grace, from the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes (James 1:17). And, once he knows, he either does not do what he already knows ought to be done, or, while attempting to attribute to himself the things he does, he is weighed down by the burden of his own pride.

I have therefore spoken above of “holy knowledge” because there is also an unholy knowledge—namely, that which puffs up a human being and does not possess the love that builds up. Some who knew God through that knowledge did not glorify him as God or give thanks. If anyone thinks that he knows something through this knowledge, he does not yet know how he ought to know (1 Corinthians 8:2).

### 14

For living well, knowledge of the commandment never suffices for anyone unless love is the guardian of the commandment; and in order to love, one loves only by one’s own will. Therefore the love of God and of one’s neighbor is commanded to each of us in the language of the law: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:37–38). In these two commandments our Savior says that the whole law and the prophets depend.

But in order that we may love God with all our heart, we do not possess that love from our own heart [Note: [Col. 0634D] These words—“we do not possess it from our own heart, but”—are not found in the editions but are found in two manuscripts.]; we possess it from God. “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.” And in order that we may love one another, God grants us love. For blessed John says: “Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who loves his brother has been born from God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love” (1 John 4:7–8).

### 15

Since the divine utterances make clear that God is love, it is plainly evident that no one can possess God unless God himself gives himself to that person. Our free choice is therefore made capable of loving God and neighbor precisely when love is divinely given to it. Without love, neither God nor one’s neighbor can be loved.

In order that God may be loved, he gives himself, because God is love, and we love God only through love. Unless we receive God, we are unable to love God.

Fire and water, life and death, have also been set before the human being, so that he may freely extend his hand toward whichever he wishes by the choice of his will (Sirach 15:17–18). For if free will is absent, the hand is extended nowhere; but a human being never extends that same hand toward life unless God has held it by his gracious goodness.

Therefore the prophet also says to him: “You have held my right hand, and in your will you have led me” (Psalm 73:24). Elsewhere he says that this right hand of ours is saved by divine protection. For he says: “The Lord guards you; the Lord is your protection over your right hand” [Note: [Col. 0635D] The words “over your right hand” were lacking in the editions. We have restored them from two manuscripts.] (Psalm 121:5).

Again he prays that the Lord, by the illumination granted over us, may direct the works of our hands. Therefore he says: “Let the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us, and direct the works of our hands for us” (Psalm 90:17).

## CHAPTER X

### 16

By these and similar testimonies, with which both the New and the Old Testament are filled, the human will is shown to be such that, whether it is beginning what is good, it can do nothing unless divine grace has first anticipated it, or whether it is bringing good to completion, it cannot suffice for itself unless the grace that anticipates it also continually helps it.

Yet it must not be said that free choice does not exist merely because it needs help; nor, merely because it exists, should it be believed capable of sufficing for itself at the beginning or in the progress of what is good.

Accordingly, if a humble and gentle mind approaches the divine utterances—which it can do only if the gift of humility and gentleness is divinely bestowed upon it—then, once the veil has been removed by which the inward—or, alternatively, the more discerning—and loftier understanding is covered, wisdom and knowledge are granted to a contrite and humbled heart. For it is written that “the Lord gives wisdom, and from his presence come knowledge and understanding” (Proverbs 2:6).

### 17

Since there is no commandment that God has not given to human beings precisely so that it may benefit those who act willingly and humbly; and since the good will begins only through faith and is perfected through love; and since faith and love are divine gifts of the will [Note: [Col. 0635D] Two manuscripts read “gifts of goodness.”], which, unless a human being willingly received them when given, would neither be present nor beneficial in him—for God prepares the human will for this purpose, so that there may be someone into whom he can pour the gift of faith and love—therefore we must confess that what we are taught by the holy utterances is true: a human being is saved by God’s mercy alone, because it is written, “Save me in your mercy” (Psalm 30:17); and that a rational human being reaches eternal salvation when he has run and labored with his own will.

For the Apostle does not say without reason: “Run in such a way that you may obtain” (1 Corinthians 9:25); and, “Each person will receive his own reward according to his labor” (1 Corinthians 3:8); and, “Labor as a good soldier of Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 2:3); and elsewhere: “Therefore, brothers, be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not empty in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 15:58).

Yet a certain person asks help for this labor in the Book of Wisdom, saying from the depths of his heart: “God of our ancestors and Lord of your mercy, who made all things by your word and established the human being by your wisdom, so that he might rule the creatures made by you and govern the world in equity and justice, and render judgment in uprightness of soul: give me the wisdom that sits beside your thrones” (Wisdom 9:1 and following).

A little later he says: “Send her from your holy heavens and from the throne of your majesty, so that she may be with me and labor with me, so that I may know what is acceptable in your sight. For she knows and understands all things; she will lead me prudently in my works, and she will guard me by her power, and my works will be acceptable” (ibid., 10).

## CHAPTER XI

### 18

Nevertheless, lest anyone suppose that even the very inclination to pray by which he asked God for wisdom was not divinely infused, a little earlier he says that he knew that he could not be continent in any other way unless God gave it (Wisdom 8:21); yet he also says that knowing whose gift this was was itself wisdom.

From where, then, was he instructed to know? From there he was also awakened to pray. Yet (alternatively, “Again”) he knew only willingly, and prayed only willingly, because the grace of Christ, going before the ignorant and sluggish human choice, instructed and awakened it both to know and to ask [Col. 0636C] [Note: [Col. 0636D] “And awakened it” is absent from the editions but is better supported by two manuscripts.].

It is therefore a work of divine mercy that the free choice of the human being is enlightened, so that the human being both recognizes what pleases God and joins voluntary devotion in labor to the work of assisting grace. To the illumination of human choice the following is said: “My God, his mercy will anticipate me” (Psalm 58:11). To assistance is referred: “Your mercy will follow me all the days of my life” (Psalm 23:6).

It would not be enlightened by anticipation if it did not exist; nor would it be helped by following it if, once enlightened, it could be capable by itself of any good thought or work.

Divine speech shows this inability where it says: “Who among human beings can know the counsel of God? Or who can conceive what the Lord wills? For the thoughts of mortals are fearful, and our plans are uncertain” (Wisdom 9:13–14). The thoughts of mortals are fearful—not with praiseworthy fear, but with blameworthy fear; not with good fear, but with evil.

From this fear we have been freed by the one who, through death, destroyed him who held the power of death—that is, the devil—so that he might free those who throughout their whole life were subject to slavery through fear of death (Hebrews 2:14).

467

## CHAPTER XII

### 18 [repeated]

Our Redeemer clearly shows this slavery from which he rescued us, and the freedom that he freely bestowed upon us, saying: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” [Col. 0637A] (John 8:31–32).

When the Jews replied that they were Abraham’s offspring and had never been slaves to anyone, he immediately showed, in his answer, both the deadly condition of their slavery and the truth of the freedom he was about to grant to his own, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. A slave does not remain in the house forever; but the son remains forever. Therefore, if the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (ibid., 34–36).

The “fearful thoughts of mortals,” therefore, are designated as those by which people serve sin—people who throughout their entire life are subject to slavery. Paul teaches that we have been freed from this slavery by God’s grace, saying: “For when you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness. What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now, having been freed from sin and having become slaves of God, you have your fruit for sanctification, and the end is eternal life” (Romans 6:20 and following).

### 19

Behold what God’s grace has bestowed upon us. It has freed the fearful, of whom Scripture says: “The thoughts of mortals are fearful” (Wisdom 9:14)—plainly subject to that fear of which divine speech rebukes certain people, saying: “There they feared with fear where there was no fear” (Psalm 14:5).

This is the fear that worldly desire brings upon people for guilt and nourishes for punishment. This fear possesses those captives whose thoughts it holds entangled in uncertain and unstable things. Therefore the one who said, “The thoughts of mortals are fearful,” immediately added: “And our plans are uncertain” (Wisdom 9:14).

A plan is uncertain when it is directed toward uncertain things, and things are uncertain when their secure possession cannot be maintained. Each day we can unwillingly lose what we cannot possess forever. The plans of mortals are therefore uncertain when the mind is held bound by love of things whose possession can be taken away from their possessor against his will, or whose possessor can be taken away from the possession against his will.

From where this uncertainty of human plans arises is shown immediately afterward, when Scripture says: “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks about many things; and we scarcely judge the things that are on earth, and we discover the things that are before us with difficulty” (ibid., 15–16).

## CHAPTER XIII

### 20

After Scripture has shown us the misery of our mortality [Col. 0637D], it next discloses to us the grace of divine goodness, so that we may recognize from where both the gift of knowledge and the benefit of correction and healing are bestowed upon us.

It continues [alternatively, “But”] by saying that the things that are on earth are difficult to judge and that the things before us are found with labor, and it says to God: “But who will investigate the things that are in heaven? Who will know your mind, unless you give wisdom and send your Spirit from the heights? And thus the paths of those who are on earth were corrected, and human beings learned what pleases you, and through wisdom they were healed” (ibid., 17–18).

What does “they learned” and “they were healed” mean? What is he saying has been bestowed upon human beings through the Holy Spirit and through the Wisdom of God, which is certainly Christ, except that we learn salutarily what we ought to do when prevenient mercy enlightens us, and we are healed so that we may do, through the same mercy following us, what we learn through its anticipation?

It anticipates us when the Lord becomes gracious to all our iniquities (Psalm 103:3); it follows us when he heals all our diseases. Mercy anticipates human free choice when, in one who does not yet will what is good, it alone brings about the beginning of a good will; it follows when it supplies help to one who wills what is good, so that by doing good he may reach the fulfillment of a good will.

### 21

Prevenient mercy, therefore, prepares the human will alone so that it may cooperate with it; subsequent mercy helps the will that cooperates with it. Thus prevenient mercy freely leads a person established in darkness out into the light—not only by admonishing outwardly but also by bestowing inwardly the grace of illumination.

For “the Lord enlightens the blind”: that is, he makes a believer out of an unbeliever, a humble person out of a proud one, a gentle person out of a harsh one, a chaste person out of a fornicator, a benevolent person out of a malicious one [Note: [Col. 0637D] So two manuscripts. The others read “a kindly person out of a malevolent one.”], a peaceful person out of a savage one, a lover of God and neighbor out of a lover of the world, and afterward a giver of his own possessions out of one who seizes the possessions of others.

Thus, when God’s mercy anticipates a person and works wondrously in his heart, the person who had been carnally exalted in pride by temporal riches is gladly made humble in the fear of God and poor in spirit. The person who had previously been harsh [Note: [Col. 0637D] In some manuscripts it reads “was harsh”; the better reading omits “was.”] and disobedient and had resisted the divine words approaches the hearing of the word and obedience [Note: [Col. 0638D] “And obedience” is absent from the editions.] with gentleness and peace. The person who had long belched forth the cruelty of injustice, having drunkenly indulged in undigested perversity, hungers and thirsts for the fullness of righteousness.

Thus it happens that he also mourns for the sins in which he had previously rejoiced with deadly pleasure. Then, continually devoting himself to works of mercy, he too obtains mercy, through which he may reach the crown. And when faith works commendably through love in holy things, he acquires purity of heart for seeing God—the person whose thoughts had previously been soiled by obscene imaginings.

### 22

This is “the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 77:11), through which human choice is enlightened; these are “the great works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Psalm 111:2).

Thus God prepares his designs in us, because he himself prepares in us what he will find in us. He makes the bow of the mighty weak and girds the weak with strength (1 Samuel 2:4)—that is, in those whom he freely saves, he weakens the presumption of human strength [Note: [Col. 0638D] Two manuscripts read “restrains”], so that they may recognize themselves as weak and receive the help of divine strength.

God mercifully does these things in us: he repays good for evil; through prevenient mercy he gives good things to the evil, so that through subsequent mercy he may preserve those good things in us. When he supplies help to those who have been justified and who will what is good, he adds increase to his own gifts; and thus he confirms what he has worked in us (Psalm 68:26), since he does not permit the good will that he himself has bestowed to grow sluggish or fail in us.

## CHAPTER XIV

### 23

Therefore, in accordance with the Apostle’s command, let us work out our salvation with fear and trembling, knowing that “God is the one who works in us both to will and to accomplish, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13).

Nor should we misuse the benefits of grace by becoming sluggish without good works. Grace certainly departs from those whose love grows cold. Let us therefore hear the Apostle, a participant in grace, demonstrating grace’s works to us.

For in one place he says: “What shall we say, then? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound?” (Romans 6:1). Immediately he answers: “By no means! Since we have died to sin, how shall we still live in it?” (ibid., 2). This, then, is what grace works in us: that, having died to sin, we may live for righteousness.

For this reason the same Apostle again says that we should consider ourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord (ibid., 11). Divine grace therefore works in human choice both death, salutarily, and life: the death of sins and the life of virtues.
