Therefore God says: “I kill and I make alive” (Deuteronomy 32:39). Just as, when we were living to sin, our perverse works followed our perverse will, so now, having received the benefit of grace and thereby having had our will changed for the better, let us not live to sin but to God.

For this purpose, when we were cold under the sentence of death, the life-giving fervor of the Holy Spirit was given to us. We received it freely so that, through God’s grace, we might be able both to will what is good and to do what is good. Therefore the Apostle commands us to be fervent in spirit, serving the Lord (Romans 12:11).

We must not therefore cease from holy labor, since not only is the reward of divine grace promised to us, but its help also supports us. And because “each person will receive his own reward according to his labor” (1 Corinthians 3:8), it is right that, while doing good, we should not grow weary either in work or in prayer (Galatians 6:9). Nor should we attribute any of the good things we do to the powers either of our will or of our ability, lest we rightly be counted among those who, “not knowing the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Romans 10:3).

This is plainly the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God; it does not submit to the law of God, nor indeed can it (Romans 8:7).

## CHAPTER XV

### 24

Let the humble will of the human being therefore follow the mercy of the Redeemer that goes before it and accompany the mercy that follows it. When mercy goes before us, we forget what lies behind; when it follows us, we stretch toward what lies ahead. Thus grace itself both directs us by granting the desire for what lies before us and, by removing remembrance of what lies behind, does not allow us to be held back from the course we have begun.

Prevenient grace makes us follow toward the prize of God’s heavenly calling (Philippians 3:14). Subsequent grace makes us glory in tribulations, knowing “that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans 5:3 and following).

It is grace itself that ensures that we are neither captured by enticement into desires nor overcome unwillingly by adversities. Thus, in proportion as we are made dead to the world through the work of subsequent mercy, we are increasingly renewed in the spirit of our mind.

25. Therefore, obeying the heavenly commands, let a person strive with voluntary efforts insofar as he is divinely assisted. But whatever he does not fail to accomplish in his labor, whatever he runs with upright steps, whatever he fights well, whatever faith he keeps, let him attribute not to his own strength but to the gift of grace working in him and with him. Let him devote the zeal of a good will to holy labor; and that will is good if it does not doubt that its zeal is a gift of divine generosity.

For the Apostle urges Timothy to the virtue of this labor, saying: “Labor as a good soldier of Christ Jesus” (II Tim. II, 3). He also testifies that he himself labored more than all the others, saying: “I labored more abundantly than all of them” (I Cor. XV, 10). But to show that he had obtained both the gift of faith and the virtue of laboring through the gift and assistance of divine grace, he likewise says: “Though formerly I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent; nevertheless I obtained mercy” (I Tim. I, 13). He shows the work of that same mercy in these words: “But I give this advice as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful” (I Cor. VII, 25).

Therefore, when he had said that he was unworthy to be called an apostle because he had persecuted the Church of God, he displayed in himself the work of prevenient mercy and said: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Cor. XV, 10). And to show that the gift of laboring also (alternative reading: “indeed”) had been bestowed upon him through the generosity of grace, he continues and says: “And his grace toward me was not empty.” What is “empty,” however, except idle? Therefore he adds: “But I labored more abundantly than all of them.” “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XVI

26. Therefore, for Paul to become faithful from unbelieving, grace alone accomplished this: it turned him from his former direction and granted faith to the unbeliever, although, by the merit of his unbelief, he did not deserve to receive faith. Thus Paul believed voluntarily, and voluntarily labored more abundantly than all the others; but he could neither believe nor labor unless he received from above the gift of grace working in him and with him.

Just as grace therefore preceded Paul when he was unwilling and unbelieving, so that he might have a good will, so, with Paul himself cooperating, it bestowed a good will and, having bestowed it, assisted that will in all things. Paul’s labor was therefore fruitful because he attributed his labor not to his own powers but to the grace of God, by whose assistance he was strengthened. He knew that he would have neither the effort nor the achievement of that labor if the help of prevenient and subsequent mercy had been lacking.

Thus, as he labored, he did not lack will; grace did not cease to assist the will it had given. And so that Paul would not fail in his labor, grace supplied strength to him who willed. Such a will therefore deservedly merited a reward both for itself and for its labor [Note: [Col. 0641D] The printed editions have “and through itself”; two manuscripts have “for itself.”], because both in itself and in its labor it recognized not its own strength but the generosity of divine grace.

For this reason, whatever he was able to think or do that was good—namely, that he used prosperity temperately and also resisted adversity courageously—he humbly and truthfully attributed not to himself but to God, by whom he was strengthened. For he says in one place: “I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound. Everywhere and in all things I have been instructed, both to be hungry and to be filled, both to abound and to suffer want. I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Phil. IV, 12–13).

Paul could therefore do all things by free choice, but in him who had clothed him with strength from above. Of this he says in another place: “For which I labor in struggle according to his working, which he works in me in power” (Coloss. I, 29).

Blessed Paul therefore did not conceal that he had been preceded by mercy so that he might become faithful; nor did he attribute to his own merit the grace of Christ working in him, so that he would not cease from holy labor. For grace worked in him so that, by failing, he would not become sluggish, nor, by becoming proud, be ungrateful to grace itself.

27. Accordingly, as we are salutarily admonished in the Psalm, “Let us serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. II, 11), knowing that it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will (Phil. II, 12–13).

The greatest assistance and benefit of divine grace is that the human mind, once enlightened, continually considers both that it has been preceded by gratuitous grace and that it must be unceasingly assisted by divine strength. Thus a person will fittingly humble himself before God, the giver and guardian of all good things; he will continually give thanks and will not cease to pray.

Let him give thanks because he was preceded by grace so that, though turned away, he might be converted; though blind, he might be enlightened; though unbelieving, he might receive faith. But let him pray that the sick may be healed and the weak strengthened by the assistance of grace.

Therefore, let him ask with his whole will, so that he may receive; let him seek, so that he may find; let him knock, so that it may be opened to him. He will by no means do this unless he has the will to receive, to find, and to enter. Yet when, by asking, he receives; by seeking, finds; and by knocking, enters, let him not attribute the activity of asking, seeking, and knocking to his own powers. For although a person voluntarily asks, knocks, and seeks, he will never be able, by asking, to receive; by seeking, to find; or by knocking, to enter, unless he has first received a holy will.

For some, as Saint James says, ask and do not receive because they ask wrongly, intending to spend what they obtain on their desires (James IV, 3). And Wisdom says of certain seekers: “The wicked will seek me and will not find me” [Note: [Col. 0641D] The printed editions omit the word “wicked”; it is found in two manuscripts.]. Therefore those who ask do not receive, and those who seek do not find, because they possess a will devoted to earthly pleasures. The wisdom descending from above is not in them, but rather wisdom that is earthly, natural, and demonic (James III, 15).

But in order that a person may ask for and seek that highest and unchangeable good, the will is prepared and given by the Lord. Once it has been given, the beginning of asking, seeking, and knocking itself rises from the human heart through God’s working there [Note: [Col. 0641D] Two manuscripts read thus. The printed editions have: “because the beginning of asking, seeking, and knocking arises not from the human heart but from God.”]. For it is written: “With all vigilance guard your heart, for from it flow the springs of life” (Prov. IV, 23).

## CHAPTER XVII

28. We guard our heart, however, if he guards us to whom it is said: “Guard me, Lord, for I have hoped in you” (Ps. XV, 1). For this reason the only-begotten God himself, having assumed the humility of the flesh and sympathizing with our weaknesses, deigned to entreat the Father for us, saying: “Father, preserve them in your name, whom you have given me” (John XVII, 11); and again: “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil” (ibid., 15).

Therefore a person never guards his heart with fitting vigilance unless that heart itself has been preserved by God’s guarding. For “unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it watch in vain” (Ps. CXXVI, 1).

For this reason the Apostle Paul prays that divine guardianship may be present in our hearts [Note: [Col. 0642D] The printed editions read “divine peace.”], saying: “The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Phil. IV, 7).

And although God says to us through Jeremiah, “Guard your souls” (Jer. XVII, 21), blessed David, knowing that he could not accomplish this by himself, asks for divine guardianship of his soul, saying: “Guard my soul and deliver me” (Ps. XXIV, 20). Again he says: “You, Lord, will preserve us and guard us from this generation forever” (Ps. XI, 8).

And, wishing divine guardianship to be granted to every believer, he says: “The Lord guards you from every evil; may the Lord guard your soul” (Ps. CXX, 5). And so that we might know that the guardianship of divine grace is necessary to us continually, he continues and says: “May the Lord guard your going out and your coming in, from this time forth and forever” (ibid., 8).

What is said in the same Psalm—“Behold, he will neither slumber nor sleep who guards Israel” (v. 4)—refers to this grace of God, which continually guards us. Therefore, just as we receive all good things, including the will itself, only because God gives them, so we preserve all that we receive only because God guards them.

Whatever gifts of a good life there may be in a person are preserved by him only if a good will perseveres in that person. But that will itself, through whose goodness the other good things are possessed and rightly preserved, perseveres as good and just in a person only if the divine grace guarding it does not abandon it.

For just as no one can possess a good thought in himself unless it becomes good through the assistance of grace, so he can in no way preserve by his own strength what he receives unless the one who freely makes it good preserves it through the support of his grace.

The progress of a good will is certain when a person vigilantly and carefully guards what he receives from God, so that he seeks the assistance of divine guardianship through frequent prayer and devotion to good works. Thus, while help is granted to the one who prays, the one who labors will not be deprived of the reward of good work.

29. Nevertheless, God will grant perseverance in praying and in doing what is good to those whom he has predestined to life. For “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James I, 17). He, possessing eternal foreknowledge of his works, prepared by the unchangeable counsel of his disposition not only the things he would give but also the things he would reward.

Therefore he fulfills his decrees in no other way than he decreed that they should be fulfilled. For just as the ordering of divine disposition has always existed, so the order of things proceeds in divine works. In them are “all his ways mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10): one of these grants good things to the wicked, while the other repays the good and the wicked with what is due; one justly crowns and justly condemns, while the other justifies by gratuitous goodness.

For whoever receives righteousness through prevenient grace reaches the crown only through that same grace when it follows afterward.

If our brothers receive these things according to sound teaching, with God’s help, they will never attempt in their disputes to defend the power of human free choice in such a way that they are shown to hold opinions opposed to God’s grace [Note: [Col. 0643C] The printed editions read “to understand.”]. Rather, all who desire to become participants in eternal life ought to be instructed by and adhere to the judgments of the holy Fathers, inspired by God. They were so enlightened by the gift of divine grace that they asserted without hesitation that no good thought arises in the human will except what is infused by the benefit of prevenient grace; that nothing is increased for the better except what is strengthened by the assistance of subsequent grace; and that no good is brought to completion by a human being except what is accomplished through that same grace working and assisting [Note: [Col. 0643C] The printed editions read: “nothing is brought to completion well.”].

## CHAPTER XVIII

30. This doctrine, therefore, handed down through the apostolic teachings of the Catholic Fathers, remains in the Churches without any doubt. The Greek and Latin pontiffs, strengthened by the infusion of the Holy Spirit, have always held it with one and inseparable agreement [Note: [Col. 0643C] Thus one manuscript reads. The printed editions read indissonabili, and indisso in some places.].

In this doctrine blessed Augustine, clothed with power from above, labored more abundantly than all the others; “yet not he, but the grace of God with him” (I Cor. XV, 10). Through his ministry the Lord provided his faithful with richer instruction concerning this matter.

For while Augustine was still in the body, the Pelagian heresy rebelled against the grace of God with deadly audacity. Nor was the invincible kindness of the merciful God absent: it girded his soldier all the more powerfully with the weapons of spiritual grace, the more fiercely the devil stirred up against that grace the vessels of wrath.

Accordingly, the renowned pontiff of God, Augustine, holding grace itself as a tower of strength and, from that position, shattering all the devices of the hostile armies by the power of heavenly assistance [Note: [Col. 0644C] The printed editions read “weapons.”], not only triumphed by carrying away a perfect victory over the enemy, but also showed posterity the method of fighting and conquering should wickedness ever attempt, after defeat, to raise its abominable head again.

Having the mind of Christ, he distinguished both the functions and the merits of divine grace and of human free choice, always subjecting human things to divine ones. He taught truthfully that God grants to a human being, freely and divinely, the gift of justification, the beginning of a good will, and the complete fulfillment of glorification.

Let everyone who desires to attain eternal salvation read him, humbly praying to the merciful God [Note: [Col. 0644C] The printed editions read “the Lord of mercy.”] that, as he reads, he may receive the same Spirit of understanding that Augustine received in order to write, and that he may obtain the same grace of illumination in order to learn that Augustine received in order to teach.

31. We marvel, and not without great sorrow, that these brothers of ours, who evidently do not understand the grace of God and seek to empty it of its power, have discovered for themselves such an absurd comparison [Note: [Col. 0644C] The printed editions read “an absurd likeness.”]. They say that the gift of God’s grace is like someone who lends money after receiving adequate security, and who cannot collect the debt unless he preserves that security.

But whoever applies this comparison to God is undoubtedly either attempting to deceive or is deceived. For our God, in the parable he proposed (Luke XIX, 13), said that the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who, when departing, entrusted money to his servants to be increased through suitable commerce. Yet he showed that he had given the money in such a way that he said he had received no security.

Indeed, blessed Paul, bearing Christ speaking in himself, testifies that the grace of the security was also granted by the one from whom he knew that the money had been given to us. For he says: “We who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. Now the one who has fashioned us for this very purpose is God, who has given us the pledge of the Spirit” (II Cor. V, 4–5).

Writing also to the Ephesians, he indicates the same pledge in these words: “You were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance” (Eph. I, 13–14).

Therefore, so that we would not be sluggish but prudent in preserving and multiplying the money of our Lord, we have been fortified with a spiritual pledge. The servant who neglected to multiply the money he had received from his master certainly did not possess this pledge (Luke XIX, 20).

God therefore gives his money and his pledge as a gratuitous gift to whomever he wishes. For our part, we gave him nothing for which we might receive a pledge—“For who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?” (Rom. XI, 35). Nor did we give him a pledge in exchange for the money. Rather, we possess both the pledge and the money because he himself has given them to us. Through the pledge that guards us, we do not lose what we possess; and through it we are continually assisted so that we may multiply the money we have received through profitable commerce.

## CHAPTER XIX

32. We understand that passage of the blessed Apostle in which he says of God, “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wishes, and whom he wishes he hardens” (Rom. IX, 18), more correctly if we refer it not to the sense of a question but to the conclusion of an argument.

For blessed Paul the Apostle was discussing the gratuitous mercy by which God saves those whom he wishes without merits, and the just judgment by which he condemns the others with irreproachable equity.

First, speaking of the little ones Esau and Jacob, he proposed the question to himself. Without any merit arising from their own works—for before they were born they had done nothing good or evil—and while both were held bound by the guilt of original sin, one received love freely through unmerited mercy, while the other received condemnation justly through deserved judgment.

In this question, therefore, putting forward the objection that his opponents might raise, he says: “What shall we say, then? Is there injustice with God?” (Rom. IX, 14). Immediately he answers: “Certainly not.” Confirming his answer by the testimony of the Law, he says (v. 15): “For he says to Moses: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.”

And, explaining the meaning of his promise, he concluded as follows (v. 16): “Therefore it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy.”

Having resolved the question he had proposed concerning the little ones, he then showed through the example of Pharaoh that the wills of people who already possess the use of reason are also converted solely by God’s mercy. For he says (v. 17): “For Scripture says to Pharaoh: For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.”

He confirmed in one conclusion the twofold judgment he had pronounced concerning the gratuitous salvation of the little ones and of adults, saying: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wishes, and whom he wishes he hardens.”

In saying this, he knew that he was supported by the words of the Law, in which he had learned that God said to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy” (Exod. XXXIII, 19), and that he had said concerning Pharaoh that he would harden his heart.

## CHAPTER XX

33. Finally, so that it may be recognized that this sentence was not introduced as an objection but offered as the conclusion of the preceding argument, blessed Paul the Apostle, immediately after that conclusion, put forward for himself the speech of an objector:

“You will say to me, then: Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” (Rom. IX, 19).

When people wandering [Note: [Col. 0645D] The printed editions read “standing out” (exstantes).] in the darkness of their own blindness hear that the wills of human beings are preceded and changed by God’s grace, and see themselves condemned because of the perversity of their dark hearts, they habitually seize upon God’s just will as an unjust support for their excuse, so that they may thereby receive a greater increase of punishment.

They accuse God, from whom they do not receive grace, and excuse themselves, although by the fault of their own wickedness they offend the just God. They inflict wounds upon themselves with their own hands and do not hesitate to bring an accusation against the physician, as though the cause of their death lay not in the one who kills himself but in the one who did not assist him sufficiently with salutary treatment.

Medicine is the cause not of death but of healing. Death cannot rightly be attributed to it if it is not provided for the grievous wound that a person has inflicted upon himself. It is a matter of justice if the wounded person is abandoned, so that he may meet the death he has acquired for himself by voluntary deeds; but it is a matter of mercy if the physician excludes from him the destruction of death through the benefit of gratuitous healing [Note: [Col. 0645D] The printed editions have “gratuitous prayer,” but this is incorrect.].

34. The physician’s kindness is therefore defamed all the more unjustly the less attention is paid to the voluntary destruction of the person who wounds himself. If the complaining sinner looked upon that destruction in himself, he would learn not to set God’s will against his own wickedness as an excuse, but humbly to ask for mercy.

The Apostle answers: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (ibid., 20). Here blessed Paul did not, as some think, fail in his response; rather, he restrained the pride of the hardened heart with a sufficiently useful rebuke.

By saying, “O man, who are you?” he admonished the proud sinner to look at himself. Finding nothing in his works that might please God, yet seeing that the command to live well proceeded from God, he should implore help from that same God in the humility of a contrite heart.

He should know that he alone must be blamed for whatever he sins in thought or action; and that the will and ability to live justly and holily in faith and love never arise in a human being from the human being himself, but are granted divinely through gratuitous generosity.

This generosity, by preceding evil human wills, changes them into good ones, so that it may forgive sins to the ungodly and wicked. By assisting those same good wills, it follows them afterward, so that it may give to those who live well the crown of righteousness, which the Lord will bestow on his faithful not in this age but in the age to come, when he grants glory to the vessels of mercy [Note: [Col. 0645D] The printed editions read “when he grants grace.”] and assigns the vessels of dishonor to an eternal fire in which they will always burn.

35. Regarding these vessels of mercy and dishonor, the understanding of those brothers differs greatly from the truth. They think that the vessels of mercy are those who possess in this age the dignity of ecclesiastical or secular service, while clerics and monks, or any laypeople, are vessels of dishonor.

They pay too little attention to the goodness of God, which distinguishes the vessels of mercy that he prepared for glory from the vessels of wrath and dishonor by gratuitous love. This distinction consists in the illumination of the heart—that is, in faith, hope, and love. “Whoever perseveres in these until the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22).

## CHAPTER XXI

36. For this reason blessed Paul does not testify that glory, honor, and peace can be granted to someone possessing any secular or ecclesiastical dignity, but to everyone who does good (Rom. II, 10).

Speaking of the vessels that are in a great house, he does not say that some dignity will make anyone a more excellent vessel of honor. Rather, he asserts that true honor is to be bestowed on those who have been cleansed. For he says:

“In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; some indeed are for honor, others for dishonor. If anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work” (II Tim. II, 20–21) [Note: [Col. 0646D] This passage of the Apostle is not found in the printed editions but is found in two manuscripts.].

Again he says of God:

“He will repay each one according to his works: eternal life to those who, by perseverance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption; but wrath and indignation to those who are contentious and do not obey the truth, but believe in iniquity. Tribulation and anguish upon every soul of a human being who does evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek; but glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, for the Jew first and also for the Greek” (Rom. II, 6 and following).

Blessed Peter likewise shows that through God’s mercy, according to which all who are saved are called vessels of mercy, it is not the dignity of the present age but the gift of regeneration in faith, hope, and love that is bestowed. For he says:

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has regenerated us into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, into an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance, preserved in heaven for you, who are guarded by the power of God through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.

“In this you will rejoice, though now for a little while, if it is necessary, you are distressed by various trials, so that the testing of your faith, much more precious than gold which is tested by fire, may be found to result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ. Though you have not seen him, you love him; and though you do not now see him, you believe in him. Believing, you rejoice with inexpressible and glorified joy, receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls” (I Pet. I, 3–4 and following).

37. You see the holy shepherd providing wholesome nourishment of spiritual teaching for the sheep whom he received for feeding from the very Prince and Lord of shepherds. He clearly shows what God works here through his great mercy in his faithful: regeneration not into the hope of some passing secular or ecclesiastical dignity, but into the hope of eternal life; not into an inheritance of imperial, pontifical, or military service, but into an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance, neither to be sought on earth nor possessed there, but preserved in heaven.

This inheritance is not for those who temporarily attain the height of secular or ecclesiastical dignity, but for those who are guarded by the power of God through faith for salvation—not a salvation already perfectly granted in this age, but one ready to be revealed at the last time.

“In this,” he says, “you will rejoice,” and immediately, indicating the character of the present life, he adds: “Though now for a little while, if it is necessary, you are distressed by various trials.”

Then, indicating the purpose for which these things happen to the faithful, he says: “So that the testing of your faith, much more precious than gold which is tested by fire, may be found to result in praise, glory, and honor.”

He soon reveals when this honor and glory are to be expected: “At the revelation,” he says, “of Jesus Christ.” The chosen vessel also indicates this when he says:

“For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Coloss. III, 3–4).

## CHAPTER XXII

38. As far as the life of the present age is concerned, it is clear that in the Church no one is higher than the bishop, and in the world no one is more exalted than the Christian emperor. But it must not therefore be thought that every bishop is a vessel of mercy prepared for glory merely because he performs pontifical service.

Rather, he is such if he is always watchfully concerned for the flock entrusted to him; preaches the word; insists in season and out of season; reproves, entreats, and rebukes with all patience and teaching (II Tim. IV, 2); does not arrogantly attempt to usurp authority over it; and, instructed by apostolic words, presents himself as an example to all.

Nor is he such merely because he rejoices in the temporal rank bestowed on him at some height, but if he offers himself to the faithful with a humble heart as an example of good conduct (Tit. II, 7).

The most merciful emperor is likewise not a vessel of mercy prepared for glory merely because he has received the summit of earthly rule. He is such if he lives with right faith at the imperial height; if, endowed with true humility of heart, he subjects the summit of royal dignity to holy religion; if he serves God more in fear than he delights in ruling the people in pride; if gentleness in him moderates anger and kindness adorns power; if he shows himself to all as more worthy of love than of fear; if he prudently provides for his subjects; if he upholds justice in such a way that he does not abandon mercy; and if, above all, he remembers that he is a son of the holy mother Catholic Church, so that he may make his rule beneficial to her peace and tranquility throughout the whole world.

The Christian empire is governed and extended more truly when care is taken for the ecclesiastical order throughout the earth than when war is waged in any region for the sake of temporal security.

39. Therefore, it is not through any dignity of the world or of the Church, but through faith working through love, that each person becomes a vessel for honor by the gift of the merciful God.

Our Savior did not call blessed those who possess secular or ecclesiastical dignity, but the poor in spirit, the meek, those who mourn, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake (Matt. V, 3 and following).

Nor did temporal honors or riches lead Abraham our father to friendship with God. Rather, because he believed God, it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he was called God’s friend (James II, 23).

Nor did poverty and lowliness exclude the poor Lazarus, afflicted by the misery of poverty and hunger, from eternal rest. Rather, Lazarus received the same virtue that Abraham, rich in earthly goods, had received from God, so that he might live holily while poor in spirit. Lazarus, the poor man, bore fruit with perseverance and, carried by angels, reached the bosom of the rich Abraham (Luke XVI, 22).

This happened because, according to the world, Abraham the rich appeared to possess one kind of abundance and Lazarus the poor another kind of want. But according to God, rich Abraham shared with Lazarus in holy poverty, and poor Lazarus possessed with Abraham the holy riches [possibly: “holy wealth”] in undivided communion.

For “God chose the poor of this world, rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom which he promised to those who love him” (James II, 5).

All who know that “the form of this world is passing away” (I Cor. VII, 31), who are dead to sin but live to God (Rom. VI, 11), and who glory with the Apostle not in temporal dignity but in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (Gal. VI, 14), become rich through that faith.

Vessels of mercy and vessels of dishonor may temporarily attain secular or ecclesiastical dignity [Note: [Col. 0649D] One manuscript reads: “For they may attain secular dignity for themselves, and ecclesiastical dignity.”], because these things are common to the good and the wicked. But to glory truly in the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ belongs to the vessels of mercy, which God prepared for glory and called not only from the Jews but also from the nations (Rom. IX, 23–24).

Blessed Paul declares that these vessels truly belong to Christ, saying: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. V, 24).

40. Whoever considers this, enlightened by divine mercy, will in no way dare to place any laypeople, however much secular dignity they possess, above clerics and monks who live holily while despising the world, so as to call the latter vessels of dishonor. By the gift of divine grace he sees that they have despised and trampled upon the world itself; nor will he judge the former to be vessels of mercy on account of their temporal power, when it is evident that those established at the summit of the world—namely, the religious rulers of this world—have genuinely and commendably submitted themselves, under the pretext of Christian religion, not only to bishops but also to monks who despise the world.

41. Could any Christian call the emperor Constantine a vessel of mercy in such a way as to call Antony and Paul vessels of dishonor? If the Augustus Constantine of blessed memory were still involved in human affairs, would he not count such a harmful praise of his name among the greatest insults?

Or could anyone call the blessed emperor Theodosius a vessel of mercy prepared for glory in such a way as to separate the monk John of Thebes from the vessels of mercy and perversely declare him a vessel made for dishonor? The most glorious emperor Theodosius, to whom God subjected even untamed nations because of the merit of the faith that God himself had given him, is said to have shown such great honor to that man of God that he did not dare to enter into any of those conflicts before being strengthened by the monk’s prophetic response.

Could so religious an emperor have believed that such a great man was a vessel of dishonor, when he humbly consulted God through him and, with the actual outcome of events confirming it, immediately recognized that God had answered him truthfully through that man?

42. Who, then, could deny that the blessed bishops Innocent of Rome, Athanasius of Alexandria, Eustathius of Antioch, Gregory of Nazianzus, Basil of Caesarea, Ambrose of Milan, Hilary of Poitiers, John of Constantinople, Aurelius of Carthage, Augustine of Hippo, and the other pontiffs are vessels of mercy that God prepared for glory?

They governed the Churches of God with the greatest vigilance. With the Holy Spirit dwelling in them, they resisted heretics either at their birth or after they had arisen; they did not permit the old wolves to creep into the ecclesiastical flock, nor allow new ones to lie hidden dangerously within the Lord’s sheepfold.

But who could be so hostile to divine faith and love that he would not fear to call Paul, Antony, John, Hilarion, Macarius, and other monks of similar life and holiness—men in whom the truth of right faith and the integrity of holy conduct shone forth—vessels of dishonor?

Far be it from all Christians to believe such things about the good servants of God.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### 43.

All who are led by the Spirit of God consider such things unworthy—not only of monks who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, but not even of married laymen who rightly believe and live rightly.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “regard these things unworthily” (haec indigne).] The fruit of the seed is indeed diverse, for when the Son of Man sows it, the good earth receives it into its fertile bosom to nourish it; yet it is not only a hundredfold, but also sixtyfold and thirtyfold, and, so that it may be gathered into the granary, it is nourished while God now grants the increase inwardly.

For God says through the prophet that he will give eunuchs—that is, virgins—honor in his city and in his wall, and a better place than to sons and daughters (Isa. 56:5). But he himself, speaking through his Apostle, also granted, by the generosity of his goodness, the honor appropriate to widowly continence and to marital chastity, when Paul says: “Honor widows who are truly widows” (1 Tim. 5:3); and again: “Marriage is honorable in all, and the marriage bed undefiled” (Heb. 13:4).

Would the Apostle, who says that in a great house there are some vessels for honor and others for dishonor, command that widows and married people be honored if he counted them among the vessels of dishonor? No faithful person dares deny that all who, having despised their possessions, serve in faith and love are vessels for honor. But who would dare call vessels of dishonor those whom the Lord, placing them at his right hand, will therefore give the kingdom because they fed him when he was hungry and thirsty among his least ones, clothed him when naked, received him as a stranger, and visited him when sick and imprisoned (Matt. 25:35)? Who would dare call all these vessels made for dishonor, when the Potter himself testifies that they will enter eternal life?

[Note: Two manuscripts have the present reading. The printed editions read: “for this the Lord will say, because they …”]

### 44.

Or perhaps these people say that monks and laymen who devoutly serve the Lord in their respective ranks and professions are vessels of dishonor only in this present age, because they see them afflicted by insults and tribulations? But those who think this will immediately be led into such an absurdity that they will first be compelled to call the blessed apostles themselves—those most glorious rams of the Lord’s flock and most vigilant shepherds—vessels of dishonor.

For whom, according to their view, could these brothers more certainly call vessels of dishonor in Christ’s house than those whom they know, on the testimony of Scripture, to have endured insults for Christ’s name? Let them therefore hear blessed Paul speaking thus to the Thessalonians: “You yourselves know, brothers, that our entrance among you was not empty, but that, after suffering and being mistreated—as you know—in Philippi, we had confidence in our God to speak to you the gospel of God amid great struggle” (1 Thess. 2:1–2).

Writing also to the Corinthians, he says (12:10): “I will gladly glory in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me. Therefore I am pleased with weaknesses, with insults, with necessities, with persecutions, and with distresses for Christ.”

[Note: The manuscripts, following the Greek εὐδοκῶ, read complaceo mihi, “I am pleased”; the printed editions read placeo mihi, “I please myself.”]

And so that they may know that enduring insults in this present age is common to all the saints, let them hear what the book written by the evangelist Luke concerning the Acts of the apostles also testifies about the other apostles. There it is recorded that the Jews sent the apostles into the public prison; when an angel opened the prison doors and released them, they brought them back again, tortured them with blows, ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and then let them go.

There blessed Luke indicates with joy that they had suffered insult, in these words: “They went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41).

[Note: One manuscript reads “for the name of Jesus.” The printed editions read “for the name of Christ.”]

## CHAPTER XXIV

### 45.

But perhaps they will say that the blessed apostles were not vessels of dishonor for this reason: the insults they endured for Christ’s name were seeds of future honor and glory, since through those insults they were deprived neither of the truth of faith nor of the virtue of holy conduct.

Let them therefore recognize that those are vessels of dishonor—not those who endure insults in the world, but those who, placed bodily within the Church, which the Apostle calls a great house, either stubbornly hold contrary to right faith until the end, or cast aside the ordinances of holy conduct.

Let them also understand, according to blessed Paul’s judgment, that if anyone cleanses himself from these things, then, whatever his rank, whatever his honor, whatever profession he belongs to, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work (2 Tim. 2:21). From the Judge who in this world grants gratuitous justification to whomever he wills, and supplies the justified through faith with the assistance of grace, he will receive the eternal blessedness of future recompense; and by the gift of glorification he will be brought into the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom, to the equality of the angels.

# BOOK THREE

[Book 3, chapter 1]

## CHAPTER I

### 1.

The order of the work undertaken now requires that we discuss those whom God predestined for adoption as sons.

[Note: The printed editions read “compels [us] to discuss” (cogit disputare).] According to the rule of true faith, firmly established by the authority of the holy Scriptures, no Christian should doubt that they were predestined before the foundation of the world, by God’s gratuitous goodness, not only to the reward of glorification but also to the grace of justification; not only to eternal blessedness, which does not change, but also to the faith that works through love; not only to eternal rewards, but also to the gratuitous good merits bestowed by God’s goodness. By the benefit of this predestination they were called according to his purpose and justified.

For whoever strives to deny the truth of divine predestination undoubtedly proclaims God mutable, perversely assigning to him a temporal knowledge of temporal human actions. For if God is immutable—and this cannot be doubted—he knows all future things immutably from eternity and has arranged all his works by an immutable ordinance.

Nor could there ever have been a change in his arrangement, since the eternal knowledge of the things arranged remains without beginning.

[Note: Two manuscripts read dispositorum ordinum, “of the arranged orders,” for dispositorum, “of the things arranged.”] Therefore, just as God’s foreknowledge of future things was never absent, so the eternal and immutable predestination of future works and gifts was never absent.

For in him, in whom eternal immutability and immutable eternity remain, just as knowledge of things to be begun could never itself have begun, so the eternal arrangement of mutable works could never have been changed. Thus, just as God was never ignorant of future things, so he was never ignorant of his mercy or judgment. Rather, just as he always foreknew all future things, both good and evil, so he arranged all the works of his grace and justice by immutable predestination.

## CHAPTER II

### 2.

Great indeed is the depth of God’s wisdom and knowledge. Full of these riches, he both knowingly understood all future things as one who is wise and wisely ordained them as one who knows.

[Note: The words “as one who is wise … as one who knows” are absent from the printed editions but occur in two manuscripts.]

To him it is fittingly said: “You, O Lord, have known all things, the last and the first” (Ps. 138:5). Blessed Isaiah truthfully proclaims that he had already made his future works, saying: “He who made the things that are to be” (Isa. 45:11, according to the Septuagint).

He made his future works already in this sense: he immutably ordained that they should be made. Hence whatever he is going to do is rightly said to have already been done by him, in whose works that are to be done an eternal and immutable arrangement is found.

For from eternity the power and wisdom of God immutably knew all future things; he irreproachably arranged all his future works; and thus he irresistibly accomplishes everything he has arranged.

[Note: The printed editions read “he irreproachably accomplishes”; other manuscripts read “he accomplished.”]

God does not alter what he has predestined, because his wisdom neither errs nor is reproved in its arrangement. God completes what he has predestined, because his power is neither impeded nor overcome in its work.

This is why our God—whose every way is mercy and truth, and to whom the Church truthfully sings of mercy and judgment (Ps. 24:10; Ps. 100:1)—not only foreknew, by immutable and perpetual knowledge, all his works, which are certainly good and are searched out according to all his purposes (Ps. 110:2), but also foreknew certain evil works of human beings and angels, although they were to be done in time.

He arranged not only those things that, as a good God, he would freely give to whomever he wished, but also those things that, as a just God, he would repay to both the good and the wicked.

### 3.

Therefore he gratuitously predestined the wicked to be justified and the righteous to be glorified, those whom his mercy would both precede and follow. These are the ones called according to his purpose; these are those whom God foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. 8:29).

But by whom are they made so, if not by him who promised them to Abraham? Abraham, strengthened by faith, gave glory to him, knowing most fully that whatever he had promised, he was also powerful enough to accomplish (Rom. 4:21).

Thus he himself, who predestined them, made and makes them conformed to the image of his Son, who is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works (Ps. 144:13).

Of these the Apostle says: “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8:30).

All these predestined people are called in such a way that they may be justified; they are justified in such a way that they may be glorified. Accordingly, he predestined those whom he willed [Note: Two manuscripts add here, “because he willed it”] both to good works and to eternal rewards; he predestined them to a good life, he predestined them to eternal life; he predestined them to faith, he predestined them to vision; he predestined them to be adopted in this world, he predestined them to be glorified in the kingdom; he predestined them by grace to be made brothers of the Firstborn, he predestined them by grace to be made coheirs of that same Only-Begotten Son.

## CHAPTER III

### 4.

All these things, just as the eternity of predestination contains them in itself, so the mercy and just majesty of the predestining God fulfill them. For he could never have been ignorant of his future sons who prepared brothers of predestination for his only Son, whom he begot coeternal with himself and without beginning.

He prepared grace for us freely and gave grace to us freely; choosing those whom he would justify in him before the foundation of the world, not on the basis of human merits but according to the gratuitous purpose of his will. He made his good will the cause of our justification, rather than finding our righteousness to be the cause of his will.

For the Apostle testifies that “God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1:4). And to show that we did not merit being chosen on the basis of works, but received good merits as the gift of election, he immediately added: “That we should be holy and blameless in his sight” (ibid.).

This election existed in God’s eternal preparation, to be fulfilled through his grace in time. This eternal preparation of election is itself divine predestination, in which everything is rightly ascribed to the gratuitous benefit of divine goodness, because there is found there only the love of God who shows mercy toward us.

Therefore the Apostle, following this and impressing it clearly upon us [Note: Two manuscripts read, “impressing this sufficiently upon us”], says: “Who predestined us in love for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ unto himself” (ibid. 1:5).

And to teach that everything proceeds solely from the purpose of God’s good will, he added: “According to the purpose of his will.” And to show that this purpose of God’s good will is gratuitous, he continued: “To the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he favored us in his beloved Son” (v. 6).

### 5.

The predestination of God’s sons is therefore usefully not only known but also proclaimed, so that in all the good acts of the human will and in every good work, when divine predestination is recognized in the eternal preparation of grace, the effect of that same predestination may likewise be acknowledged in the actual bestowal of grace.

Accordingly, in this adoption of God’s sons—which God both prepared from eternity by predestining it and grants in time by calling and justifying them—God’s grace is glorified and praised.

For God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, “that we should be holy and blameless in his sight” (Eph. 1:4).

## CHAPTER IV

God therefore did not find, or foreknow that he would find, those whom he would choose already holy or blameless; rather, he chose them before the foundation of the world in order to make them holy and blameless.

He did not choose us because we were going to be holy and blameless, but so that we might be holy and blameless. And he predestined us in love because, in predestining us, he freely bestowed upon us the effect of love.

He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ unto himself (ibid. 1:5), not according to the merit of our will or work, but according to the purpose of his will.

And because we received this adoption as sons freely from God, by whom we were freely chosen to be holy and blameless, blessed Paul therefore proclaims in all these matters the praise of the glory of God’s grace. Thus everyone enlightened by the gift of that same grace may both understand the true gift of grace from the eternity of predestination and recognize God’s eternal predestination from the gift of spiritual grace.

### 6.

The eternal firmness and firm eternity of this predestination remain not only in the arrangement of works but also in the number of persons, so that no one may lose the grace of eternal salvation from the fullness of that number, nor may anyone outside the measure of that number attain the gift of eternal salvation.

For to God, who knows all things before they occur, the number of the predestined is no more uncertain than the outcome of arranged works is doubtful to him.

That one who predestined them for adoption as sons through Christ possesses within himself the most certain number of the predestined, because he arranged all things “by measure and number and weight” (Wis. 11:21).

For he promised these very people to Abraham, saying: “Look up to heaven and number the stars, if you can number them”; and he said: “So shall your offspring be.” And Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness (Gen. 15:5).

Of these it is said to the prophet Daniel: “At that time all your people who are found written in the book will be saved” (Dan. 12:1). To these our Savior says: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

Of these it is said in the Book of the holy Daniel: “Those who instruct many in righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever” (Dan. 12:3).

Spiritually these people are understood in the psalm where it is said of God: “He numbers the multitude of the stars, and calls them all by name” (Ps. 146:4). Therefore he who numbers the multitude of the stars cannot be ignorant of the number of his sons.

## CHAPTER V

### 7.

No one is added to that number, and no one is taken away from it.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “is diminished”; they then add “because the same number …” before the words “For since,” which are not found in the printed editions.]

For that same number is fulfilled according to the purpose of the predestining God. Since God predestined his saints according to the purpose of his will, and it is written that “whatever the Lord willed, he made” (Ps. 113:3), no one can alter his predestination any more than anyone can overcome his will.

But if that number is not certain with God, then either divine knowledge is mistaken, or the divine will changes, or divine power is overcome by some adversity.

If only the wicked can say any of these things—or perhaps no wicked person dares say any of them—then no one should deny divine predestination, since the predestination of that God is altogether asserted to be true whose knowledge is irreproachable, whose will is immutable, and whose power is unconquerable.

To this predestination belong both the Redeemer’s gratuitous justification and the Judge’s just recompense. To this predestination belongs the mercy that Paul received so that he might be faithful (1 Cor. 7:25), and the crown of righteousness that the Lord, the just Judge, will render to him on that day—not only to Paul, but also to all who love his appearing (2 Tim. 4:8).

For all whom God predestined for adoption are freely justified here from ungodliness, because Christ died for the ungodly (Rom. 5:6); and “all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace” (Rom. 3:23).

[Note: Freely (gratis) is absent from the printed editions but occurs in two manuscripts.]

Just as through mercy he prepared for them the gratuitous gift of justification, so through justice he prepared the reward of eternal justification.

[Note: Perhaps “eternal glorification.”]

Thus the work of grace is begun in all the predestined by gratuitous mercy and completed by just recompense.

### 8.

God therefore predestined his saints both to the grace of a good life and to the grace of eternal life.

[Note: These words are found in the manuscripts but not in the printed editions.]

“The grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

Therefore, by the grace of God the ungodly are justified so that, renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, they may live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this present age; and so that, justified by his grace, they may be heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

God therefore gives the prepared grace so that people may be justified, live well, and receive eternal life for their right actions.

Eternal life is also called the grace of God by the Apostle (Rom. 6:23) because a good life is given freely to human beings, so that eternal life may justly be repaid to it.

God also prepared eternal fire for the wicked—those whom he justly prepared to undergo punishments, though he did not predestine them to commit sins.

God predestined what divine equity would repay, not what human iniquity would commit. Therefore he predestined for the guilty person not the fault that he hates, but the judgment that he loves.

For it is written that the Lord “loves mercy and judgment” (Ps. 32:5). And therefore God will punish the wicked for not only original sin but also every actual sin, because he neither provides the beginning of evil works nor ever gives his consent to them.

Evil works therefore do not please God because they do not come from him. For if they came from him, they would not be evil.

Accordingly, God mercifully gives good works and justly crowns them; but the works he himself does not bestow he justly punishes. In the former, divine generosity is crowned; in the latter, human transgression is condemned.

A human being therefore possesses beneficially what he has received from God, and disastrously what he has had from himself.

## CHAPTER VI

### 9.

It is exceedingly wrong to say that, if there is predestination, we ought neither to pray nor to keep watch, but should do every desire of the flesh because we have already been predestined.

For the grace that was prepared for us by divine predestination is given to us by God precisely so that we may keep watch and pray, and so that, as in the daytime, we may walk honorably—not in feasting and drunkenness, not in sleeping chambers and indecency, not in quarrels and rivalry; but that we may put on the Lord Jesus Christ and make no provision for the flesh in its desires (Rom. 13:13–14).

For how can it happen that someone receives grace but does not perform the works of grace, when grace itself is working in him?

Grace is given through the Holy Spirit, but “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control” (Gal. 5:22–23).

Who, then, after receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit, would not pray, keep watch, and with the support and assistance of grace resist carnal desires? Our Savior commands us to keep watch and pray (Matt. 26:41), and blessed Paul testifies that “those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5:24).

### 10.

It is the same as if someone said: “If a person has been predestined, he ought neither to pray nor to keep watch,” as it would be if he said that someone to whom life had been divinely promised ought not to seek the means of sustaining life.

For we read that fifteen years were added to the life of King Hezekiah as a gift of divine mercy (2 Kings 20:6). Should Hezekiah therefore have said that, since God’s promise to him was certain, he consequently ought neither to take food nor drink nor think about the things that contribute to the support of life?

Certainly the use of life is given precisely so that the desire to persevere in living may remain in the heart of the living person; and when someone loves his life, he does not reject the means of sustaining life.

From life itself, therefore, we have the ability to be concerned about preserving the condition of that life.

Accordingly, the grace that God predestined—that is, prepared for his faithful from eternity—does this in us once we have received it: it causes us to ask, as a divine gift, that it be preserved in us, and to have in our works what we have received through its generosity.

The gifts of that grace remain in those for whom they were prepared by the gift of divine predestination.

Therefore it must not be said: “If we are predestined, let us neither keep watch nor pray.” Rather, when we keep watch and pray, let us recognize the benefits of God’s grace. Let us not deny the eternal origin of these good things, whose divine generosity we see in ourselves. Their predestination cannot be uncertain, since their eternal preparation is recognized.

For this reason the Apostle says: “We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we might walk in them” (Eph. 2:10).

## CHAPTER VII

### 11.

Far be it from us that, while predestination is affirmed, the evangelical and apostolic commands should be abolished.

Jesus knew from the beginning who would believe and who would betray him (John 6:65), and the Creator’s knowledge could not have been false. Therefore, just as he foreknew his betrayer—and no one else betrayed him except the one he had foreknown—so he certainly knew from the beginning that those whom he knew, by his preparation, to be predestined for faith would believe.

How do we abolish the apostolic commands by asserting predestination, when we know, on the preaching of the Apostle, that not only the members of Christ but Christ himself was predestined?

For blessed Paul says of him: “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined to be the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification” (Rom. 1:3–4).

In another place he says: “We speak wisdom among the mature—not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed—but we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom that God predestined before the ages for our glory” (1 Cor. 2:6–7).

Therefore, what is it to criticize the assertion of predestination except to condemn apostolic teaching with deadly impiety?

Paul had most certainly learned and taught divine predestination. What he did not deny in the Head, he did not deny in the body. For he knew that the eternal and immutable God, according to his eternal and immutable will, foreknew all the things he had arranged to do, and predestined all the things he foreknew that he would mercifully and justly do in his saints.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 12.

Therefore, whoever denies predestination should first erase it from the apostolic Epistles; then, once he has shown that he has rightly reproved the Apostle Paul, let him present himself to human beings as unquestionably worthy to be heard.

The blessed Apostle Paul did not wish what he wanted written to be kept silent. Just as he reproved error when he recognized it among human beings in his Epistles, so he wanted the truth he inserted into his letters to be proclaimed to all people.

Without doubt, then, the person abolishes the apostolic commands who strives either to deny or to oppose the apostolic statements.

Just as the blessed Apostle proclaimed predestination with confidence and truth, so he commanded us to proclaim it with confidence and truth. Nor did he fear that he might seem to introduce genesis (nativity), fate, or constellation.

If these brothers foolishly fear this, they tremble with fear where there is no fear (Ps. 13:5); and while they fear being reproved along with the ungodly, they do not hesitate to think impiously about God.

For who can think more wrongly about the eternal God, the true God, the good and blessed God, than one who denies that from eternity he knew what he would do in time; or who attributes a chance course to divine works, denying that the plan of his future action remains eternal in the immutable will of God?

This assertion, which is truly hostile to the divine plan, denies altogether that human beings’ good wills and works are held in God’s eternal predestination, and thus confirms that God’s knowledge depends upon human wills and actions.

For if God foreknew all his future works from eternity, without doubt he prepared those same works according to the purpose of his good will and arranged what he would do through the firmness of his immutable counsel. The order of divine works cannot proceed otherwise than as it is found established in the preparation of his immutable knowledge.

## CHAPTER IX

### 13.

Whatever is carried out mutably in time exists naturally, eternally and immutably, in the depth of God’s riches of wisdom and knowledge. In the fullness of his knowledge he foreknew all future things, and in the depth of his wisdom he prepared all his works, in a wondrous order, before they came to be.

Otherwise human thought and action would precede divine wisdom, if divine knowledge had not comprehended them from eternity.

But if God is immutable and eternal, it is necessary that his knowledge also be immutable and eternal. Nothing temporal happens to immutable and eternal knowledge.

For if it is known that something happened to it in time, it must be subject to a beginning and to mutability; and a nature cannot be without beginning if its knowledge is found to be subject to a beginning.

He began to exist who had not existed, and his knowledge began to exist although it had been absent. Nor can he contain everything simultaneously in the fullness of knowledge if he was at some time able to be ignorant of something.

Therefore he was always mutable who needed the fullness of knowledge. Nor does his wisdom “reach mightily from end to end and order all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1); nor does it reach everywhere because of its purity (Wis. 7:24), if either some future work escaped it or he did not possess in his eternal arrangement and predestination what he does.

Nor does he retain the complete state of his immutability if, in his temporal works, he can apply not an eternal but a temporal plan.

### 14.

Therefore, knowing that God is immutable, eternal, and perfect; the all-powerful creator of creation; and the eternal knower and arranger of everything he was going to do, let us confess that from eternity he preordained all his works and from eternity prepared his gifts and judgments.

For the one to whom the prophet says, “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24), in the same wisdom in which he created all things arranged from eternity everything he knew he would do, because he was ignorant of none of the things he was going to do.

Therefore, before the foundation of the world, God chose all those whom, placed here at whatever age and in whatever period, he calls and justifies according to his purpose. He also grants perseverance to these same people and brings all of them to eternal life.

For he wills all these people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4).

The will of the Almighty must necessarily be fulfilled in all things. Whatever he wills to happen therefore happens, and no one resists his will. For God’s power is not less than his will, and therefore he is found to will nothing that he cannot accomplish.

God could indeed do certain things and does not do them; nevertheless, there is nothing that he wills to happen and does not at some point bring about: “Whatever the Lord willed, he made, in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths” (Ps. 134:6).

Therefore, since he has done whatever he willed among human beings, he saves those whom he wills to be saved. And since the Truth itself truly says, “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44), he brings all those to the knowledge of the truth whom he mercifully deigns to draw.

## CHAPTER X

### 15.

They are called “all” because they are gathered from every human category: from all peoples, from all nations, from all masters, from all servants, from all kings, from all soldiers, from all provinces, from all languages, from all ages, and from all ranks.

Thus all whom God wills to be saved are saved, because no one is saved except the one whom he wills to save by gratuitous justification.

For when our Savior said, “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27)—which he clearly said to show that he wills to reveal himself to some and not to others—how can it be said that he wills to save those to whom he did not wish to reveal his Father and himself?

The Gospel shows that he spoke to some people in parables in such a way that he wanted his words to be heard but did not want them to be understood.

The Lord himself unquestionably disclosed this. For when the disciples questioned him, Matthew records that he said: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to them it has not been given” (Matt. 13:11).

Mark likewise reports a similar response from the Savior and testifies that these were his words: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but for those who are outside, everything is in parables, so that seeing they may see and not see, and hearing they may hear and not understand, lest they should ever turn and their sins be forgiven” (Mark 4:11–12).

Luke also confirms that the Lord gave the same response, saying: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand” (Luke 8:10).

### 16.

Clearly, then, the Lord spoke to the crowds in such a way that he nevertheless did not wish to open to them the mystery of the kingdom of heaven.

In doing this, he did not want his words to be understood because he did not want himself to be recognized in that mystery.

The Apostle Paul testifies that this recognition is recognition of the mystery of Christ, saying: “Instructed in love and in all the riches of the fullness of understanding, in the knowledge of the mystery of Christ Jesus, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2:2–3).

For elsewhere it is also said: “That God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ” (Col. 4:3).

Indicating the earnestness of his prayer for the faithful, he says: “I do not cease giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him” (Eph. 1:16–17).

If, then, God generally wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, what does it mean that the Truth itself conceals from some the mystery of its own knowledge?

Certainly, to those from whom he withholds the knowledge of himself, he also withholds salvation. For people are saved in this very thing: that they come to the knowledge of the truth.

It was said of Christ that “he himself will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21). Blessed Peter also says of him that “there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

How, then, could there have been a will of God to save those from whom the very knowledge of the truth was hidden?

## Chapter XI

**17.** Or is it perhaps said that, because of the hardness of their hearts, our Savior did not wish to reveal to them the mystery of the knowledge of himself? Here we could give a fuller response. But, to use a brief summary for the sake of concision, let those who say that Truth itself did not wish to reveal the mystery of the knowledge of himself because of their hardness of heart recognize meanwhile this point: it cannot possibly be said of all human beings, since God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth—unless they acknowledge that Christ did not wish to save those whom he saw to be hard-hearted, since because of the hardness of their hearts he did not wish to reveal to them the mystery of the knowledge of himself.

They must therefore either deny that God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth—those who acknowledge that our Savior did not wish to give certain people knowledge of the mystery of the kingdom of heaven—and declare the Apostle Paul a liar; or, if the Apostle’s statement is understood universally of absolutely all human beings, they will be compelled to declare the holy Evangelists liars. For how could he not have wished to give certain people knowledge of the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, when he wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth? For if he wills absolutely all, he certainly wills no one not to be saved; and if he wills all to come to the knowledge of himself, he ought to show all the mystery of the knowledge of himself. Yet he did not give certain people knowledge of that very mystery.

**18.** What kind of willing to save was it, then, while refusing to reveal the mystery of salvation? What kind of thing was it, I ask, if Truth wished all human beings to come to the knowledge of him, yet did not wish to show them the way by which they would come? What is this—that he denies life to those whom he invites to their homeland? For he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV, 6).

How, then, does he wish those to come to the knowledge of himself to whom he denies the knowledge of himself? For what is refusing to show the mystery of the knowledge of himself except refusing to save? Therefore he does not will all human beings to be saved if, because of their hardness of heart, he refused to reveal to certain people the mystery of the knowledge of himself, without which no one reaches salvation.

Yet the Apostle could not have lied when he said that God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (I Timothy II, 4). Nor did the Evangelists lie when they said that the Lord himself gave his disciples knowledge of the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but did not give it to others. Certainly, because he wished to give it to the former, he gave it to them; but because he did not wish to give it to the latter, he did not give it to them. And because he gave it to the former so that they might be saved, it is understood that he did not give it to the latter so that they might not be saved. He therefore wished those to be saved to whom he gave knowledge of the mystery of salvation; but he did not wish those to be saved to whom he denied knowledge of the saving mystery. For if he had wished both groups to be saved, he would have bestowed on both the knowledge of the saving mystery.

## Chapter XII

**19.** Since, therefore, both Scriptures are true, both holy, and both divinely inspired—and for that reason both must be reverently preserved and heard and accepted without hesitation—let all those people whom Christ did not grant knowledge of the mystery of the kingdom of heaven be removed from that universal category. Let all those human beings whom God wills to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth be rightly understood as belonging to it, because the will of the one who saves is truly recognized in those to whom the grace of recognizing the truth is not denied.

Thus God, because he does everything whatever he wills, fulfills his will in all: for all whom he wills to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, he grants a right knowledge, joined with love, of the saving mystery. Blessed Peter shows that all these people are to be understood in this way when he calls “all” those whom God deigns to call. For these are his words, spoken to the Jews: “For the promise is to you and to your children and to all who are far away, whomever the Lord our God shall call” (Acts II, 39).

**20.** Blessed Paul too says “all” in one passage, although he does not wish “all” to be understood universally. For, writing to the Philippians, he says: “For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Philippians II, 21). If no one among all these is excepted here, then it is necessary that all the Apostles and the other believers of that time also be counted among those “all”—something that no one, however impious, will suspect.

It remains, therefore, that we must understand “all” as referring to certain people: that is, not absolutely all human beings, but all who sought their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ. For earlier in the same Epistle, indicating that some were good, he says: “Some indeed preach Christ because of goodwill, but some out of rivalry, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the Gospel” (Philippians I, 15). Those who preached Christ because of goodwill and out of love, since “love does not seek its own interests” (I Corinthians XIII, 5), did not seek their own interests but those of Jesus Christ. They therefore were not among those “all” who sought their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ.

At the end of his Epistle he calls these good people holy; and just as he calls the wicked “all,” so likewise he calls these good people “all.” For he says: “All the saints greet you” (Philippians IV, 22). Behold: in one and the same Epistle of the blessed Apostle there are both “all the saints” and “all who seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ,” although certainly all who were holy did not seek their own interests, and all who sought their own interests were not holy.

Let both these groups and those groups therefore be accepted—not confusedly, but distinctly. Let both be called “all” in such a way that, according to the proper order of truth, all of the one group are distinguished from all of the other, and all of the other from all of the one.

**21.** The same meaning is found in all the tribes whom God promised to Abraham’s offspring and showed would be blessed in him, saying: “And in you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis XXVIII, 14). Blessed Peter also confirms this when he says to the Jews: “You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant which God established with our fathers, saying to Abraham: ‘In your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed’” (Acts III, 25).

Then, showing that Christ is the offspring of Abraham in whom the blessing of all the tribes was promised, he immediately added these words: “God, having raised up his Son first for you, sent him to bless you” (ibid., 26). Christ, therefore, is the offspring of Abraham in whom all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.

Certainly God’s promise is true, because “the Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works” (Psalm CXLIV, 13). In this promise Abraham did not waver through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God and being fully convinced that whatever he promised, he was also able to do (Romans IV, 20).

## Chapter XIII

Since no Christian doubts that all the tribes of the earth are blessed in Christ, blessed John, speaking in the Apocalypse about Christ—that is, about the offspring of Abraham in whom all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed—nevertheless truthfully says: “Behold, he will come with the clouds, and every eye will see him, including those who pierced him; and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him” (Revelation I, 7).

Behold: all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in Christ, yet when he comes all the tribes of the earth will mourn.

**22.** How, then, can both statements stand for us, if the universal fullness of all the tribes is understood either in a good or in a bad sense in such a way that nothing is left for the other group?

But the same blessed John, who had drunk from the breast of Truth the abundance of truthful preaching, shows that these “all” are the tribes that will mourn at Christ’s coming, while demonstrating that all the tribes whom the truthful God promised would be blessed in the offspring of Abraham are gathered from among all those tribes.
