For in the same book he introduces those who have been redeemed by the blood of the Lamb singing a new song and saying: “Worthy are you, Lord, to receive the book and to open its seals, because you were slain, and you redeemed us by your blood from every tribe and tongue and people and nation; and you made us a kingdom and priests for our God, and they shall reign upon the earth” (Revelation V, 9–10).

Elsewhere in the same book, after mentioning twelve thousand sealed persons from each of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel, in order to show an innumerable multitude of the faithful from all the tribes of the earth, he speaks as follows: “After this I saw a great multitude which no one could number, from all nations and tribes and peoples and tongues, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palms in their hands” (Revelation VII, 19).

These are all the tribes gathered from all the tribes. These are all the tribes that are blessed as they believe in Christ, from all those tribes that will mourn because they did not believe in Christ.

Thus are understood all the faithful and all the unfaithful; all the good and all the wicked; all whom God saves in his most merciful goodness, and all whom he condemns in his most just severity. To some he justly does not grant the knowledge of the truth; to others he mercifully reveals the truth so that they may recognize it; and in all he fulfills his all-powerful will.

## Chapter XIV

**23.** Whoever wishes to review the divine Scriptures with the right eye of the heart will be able to find very many testimonies in the divine utterances according to this most salutary rule of interpretation.

When, however, human will is under discussion, insofar as it concerns either the beginning or the effect of salvation, this is certainly true: among those who use reason, those who will are saved, and those who do not will are not saved. But those who are saved will to be saved when divine grace precedes them so that they may will it; indeed, they will to be saved precisely when they receive the very act of willing as a gift of divine generosity.

For Holy Scripture cannot in any way lie when it says: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs VIII, 35, according to the Septuagint). Accordingly, the Apostle also truthfully says, with Christ speaking in him: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will” (Philippians II, 12–13).

The Apostle assigns to God not only the beginning of good will and good action, but also testifies that both are fulfilled by him, saying: “May our God deem you worthy of his calling, and may he fulfill every good purpose of goodness and the work of faith in power” (II Thessalonians I, 11). To show that this happens through grace, he immediately added: “So that the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ” (v. 12).

Thus, in those who are willingly saved, divine grace works so that they may will; but in those who do not will, human hardness persists so that they may not will. Yet a human being will not have that hardness when God wills to remove it. For God can effortlessly fulfill whatever he wills, since he says of certain people: “I will remove from them their heart of stone, and I will give them a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel XXXVI, 26).

He therefore removes the heart of stone by taking away hardness of heart; he gives a heart of flesh by infusing the grace of holy faith. Thus the heart that had been hard is softened, so that the beginning of holy faith may be granted to it.

## Chapter XV

**24.** The free choice of the human mind was created upright in the first human being, though not without the assistance of grace—of such grace that, if he willed, he could remain in that same uprightness, and from which, if he willed, he could depart by a contrary will.

Now, however, prevenient grace works in every human being so that the freedom of choice may be corrected. Human choice is liberated to the extent that it is corrected; but it is led captive to the extent that it is still entangled in the necessities of harmful servitude.

These necessities oppress not only the children of the world unto death, but also frequently afflict the children of God—“the children of God” being repeated in the source. This is that law of sin which dwells in the members and resists the law of the mind. It pursued that vigorous soldier, the Apostle Paul, who delighted in the law of God according to the inner person, seeking to take him captive through the suggestions of desire, although it could not subject him to itself in deed.

Accordingly, the same Apostle says: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person, but I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin which is in my members” (Romans VII, 22–23).

Nor did he remain silent about the fact that he could be liberated only by the help of grace. Therefore he continues, saying: “Wretched man that I am! Who will liberate me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (vv. 24–25).

Thus, in his mind he possessed the strength of grace, but in the flesh he felt the weakness of choice—a weakness Adam did not have before he was corrupted by voluntary transgression of the commandment. Hence the Apostle, although already established not under the law but under grace, and although he served the law of God with his mind, was nevertheless compelled in the flesh to serve the law of sin: what had been divinely given to him was present in his will, while what remained in him by necessity was something else.

For he was unwillingly pressed by those necessities from which every holy person both longs and asks to be rescued, saying to God: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Psalm XXIV, 17). Feeling in himself the distress of these necessities, the Apostle said: “For I do not do the good that I will, but the evil that I hate, that I do. But if I do the evil that I hate, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Romans VII, 19–20).

## Chapter XVI

**25.** These necessities do not cease in the body of this death for the saints who live mortal lives. They are shaken by them in a pitiable way so that they may recognize that, by the desert of the first human being’s sin, they lost that grace of holy freedom and of the first peace, and that they can receive it again only through the grace of Christ—in that life, at least, in which the saints will have no anxiety of conflict but perfect security of peace.

Then, certainly, when death is mocked and every struggle of sin has been uprooted from the members, it will truly be said in that peace: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? The sting of death is sin” (I Corinthians XV, 54–56)—the sin into which we fell through the transgression of the first human being, and without which we are not in this life.

For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us (I John I, 8). We must therefore keep watch in the struggle so that we may rest in peace. We must always consider the weakness of free choice that the wickedness of the first human being generated in us. And, to summon the help of strength, we must humbly beseech the divine majesty to grant strength to those who labor and to lead us, as victors, into peace, where we shall possess the freedom of choice made perfect and fully liberated from every sin.

This will be when every creature—which is now being renewed in Christ—will be liberated from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Romans VIII, 21). When it is liberated, it will undoubtedly enjoy the gift both of free peace and of peaceful freedom.

But if that peace and that freedom were even now present in a human being to the same degree as they were in the first human being before sin, he would not see in his members another law that stubbornly resisted the law of his mind and violently carried him captive to the law of sin.

**26.** The free choice of the human mind, then, before the first human being sinned, was truly free to the extent that he felt nothing in himself opposed to himself. He therefore possessed health and happiness; he did not feel any misery existing in himself, because he held justice through upright freedom. For justice served freely, and therefore he rejoiced in true freedom.

## Chapter XVII

The first human being, as long as he served justice, had no sin whatsoever. We, however, although liberated from sin and made servants of God (Romans VI, 18), nevertheless, if we say that we have no sin, deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us (I John I, 8).

Before sin, Adam did not have upon him the heavy yoke that has been upon his descendants from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in “the mother of all” (Sirach XL, 1). In Adam before sin, the flesh had no desire that resisted the spirit. For he ruled the body as easily as he faithfully obeyed the Creator. That soul had a body subject to it, because a pure disposition subjected it to God.

Now, however, we recognize that we do not obey God perfectly in this respect: the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that we do not do what we wish.

**27.** The freedom of the first human being therefore had greater peace; but now, through grace, the freedom of the faithful receives greater love. For the former had justice wholly at rest in peace, while the latter are granted a glorious victory in combat.

A greater grace is therefore now given, since free choice is restored through faith; and when God restores the freedom of our choice by the gift of faith and the infusion of love, he perfects strength in us in weakness.

For ruin crept into the sound choice of the first human being through vice; but, in order that choice might be healed in human beings, greater grace was given after the vice. Thus it happened that where sin abounded, grace also abounded all the more. Accordingly, choice is restored by God’s gift.

And although it does not possess as much health and peace as it possessed earlier, it nevertheless receives greater strength from generosity, so that the human will—which had departed from God solely through the persuasion of the deceiver—now, supported by the help of grace, may be separated from Christ neither by persuasion nor even by tortures.

Thus Christ God wondrously demonstrates what human strength can accomplish and what divine strength can accomplish: the human being who, while sound, was defeated by his own will is not defeated, once weakened, after receiving greater grace.

The human strength that had received lesser grace fell of its own accord when conquered; but human weakness receives through the greater help of grace the victory it had lost.

The power to act well or badly can certainly be present in a rational human being. But the power to act badly is possessed solely through the choice of free will; the power to act well is present in free choice when it is given by God.

The Evangelist John testifies that this power is given divinely in these words: “But to all who received him, he gave the power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John I, 12).

## Chapter XVIII

**28.** The question concerning the soul, which you placed second to last in your letter, I have placed last in this response. I judge that among you it has more the character of a conflict than of a conclusion: in it contention can increase more than knowledge can provide assistance.

For each side relies so firmly on its own assertions that it is nevertheless refuted by objections from the opposing side. The blessed Augustine, seeing the depth of this question to be inscrutable to him, wished to pronounce no definitive judgment on the matter. He considered it wholly inappropriate to affirm without hesitation what another person could overturn with an opposing answer.

His discussion of this question shines forth as no less extensive than profound—and all the more praiseworthy because it was moderated with fitting restraint—in the tenth book of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, in the books addressed to Vincentius Victor *On the Origin of the Soul*, and also in the first of the two books that he wrote to Saint Jerome (Epistle formerly 28, now 166), as well as in the three letters composed for Bishop Optatus on this question (fifth letter of that collection, formerly 157, now 190).

There he investigated and examined individually whatever he saw needed to be sought and discussed by acuteness of intellect, by orderly reasoning, or by the weight of authority. Nevertheless, he refrained from committing himself to either definition, lest he undertake the labor of so great a discussion in vain, a rash definition of either opinion rendering it worthless.

He saw that both the position which asserts that the soul is propagated from soul as body is from body and the position which asserts that new souls are made for each person at birth could be overcome by opposing arguments. The individual replies to these positions will be inserted, for the sake of brevity, throughout the sequence of this work.

## Chapter XIX

**29.** Those who assert that new souls are made for each individual, when they are confronted with the question by what justice the soul newly given to a body bears original sin, since it does not come through the propagation of human seed, are entirely at a loss. They are constrained by a twofold absurdity: they are compelled either to pronounce God unjust or to deny original sin.

For a soul that is not propagated as flesh is propagated ought not to be held, together with the flesh, in the fellowship of original sin; and consequently it is found not to need the sacrament of baptism.

If, in the child who dies without baptism, only the flesh is polluted by the contagion of original sin, while the soul of the unbaptized infant is thought to depart this world without iniquity, let them say where that child will be in the resurrection: in the kingdom of God, because of the purity—or perhaps “innocence”—of the soul; or in eternal fire because of the impurity of the flesh?

Wherever they say the child will be, God is asserted to be either a liar or unjust. He is a liar if he introduces the unbaptized child into the kingdom, since the Savior himself established this most firm judgment: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 5).

But he is unjust if he sends into eternal fire, together with the flesh, a soul that does not share sin with the flesh. Yet it is clear that everyone who has not been baptized either with sanctified water in the name of Christ or with his own blood for the sake of Christ and his Church must be condemned to the burning of eternal fire.

By what justice of divine judgment, then, will the soul be sent into eternal fire together with its flesh if it is not held by the guilt of original sin?

**30.** Or will someone perhaps try to seize upon this absurdity and say that the soul, on account of its purity, will exist separately in blessedness forever—perhaps a word such as “happy” is missing—while the flesh will burn in eternal fire because of the guilt of original iniquity?

But the truth of the catholic faith, which most certainly believes and proclaims that there will be a resurrection of the flesh in all human beings, destroys the utterly foolish falsehood of this invention. For if the flesh does not receive the soul, it will not rise; and if it does not rise, it certainly will not live.

How, then, can what cannot live without the soul, being lifeless, feel the torments of that fire? Those who wish to place the soul of the unbaptized child in the kingdom because of its purity must therefore deny that the flesh will rise.

They themselves see how absurdly and impiously this is said. For it is a great impiety either to deny that the dead flesh of a human being will rise, or to say that the soul, apart from the flesh in which it lived, will after judgment share either misery or happiness.

Our Savior showed that there will be a resurrection of the flesh when he said: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, and they will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John V, 28–29).

When the body rises, therefore, there must be a common recompense for soul and flesh according to their works. For when the flesh has risen, neither will the body remain without the soul nor the soul without the body. There will therefore be either eternal rejoicing or eternal affliction shared by soul and flesh, when the eternal connection of flesh and soul remains indissoluble.

Yet they ought not to have a punishment in common if they do not have sin in common, because it is inconsistent with God’s justice that a soul given to a new body, and not propagated together with that body, should be compelled to share the guilt of propagation with a body with which it has no common origin.

## Chapter XX

**31.** Those who assert that souls are propagated together with bodies can indeed use this to establish, in order to demonstrate God’s just judgment concerning infants, that original sin is common not to the flesh alone or to the soul alone, but to both, so that, through the commonality of their origin, the guilt of sin too may rightly be believed to be common.

But when they consider seeds that perish without being conceived, they become completely silent—perhaps the source reads “they fall silent.” It is certain that the human soul received immortality as a gift from the very act of its creation; and it is necessary that, in the resurrection, it receive again the body in which it lived here for however short a time.

Who, then, would say that animate seeds have flowed forth—whether those that are not conceived or those emitted in nocturnal emission? Every wise person sees how absurd this is and how entirely alien to reason.

**32.** While the two sides therefore overcome each other with these and similar propositions, neither can be victorious. Each becomes victorious over the other’s position in such a way that it is defeated by its own; and when it destroys the opposing proposition, it is itself unable to establish what it proposes.

How much better, then, that we refrain from the combat of this question, in which we recognize that we labor in vain—especially since we see that what was not defined at all by the holy men who came before us ought to be sought by us with all the more caution and restraint, insofar as we see that those distinguished men did not reach its conclusion.

Let this therefore be firmly established for us without hesitation, what the catholic faith both believes and proclaims: namely, that the human soul is a rational spirit, not a body; that it is not a part of God but a creature of God; and that it was not sent into the body as into a prison because of whatever sins it had committed before the body, but was inserted into the body by the work and ordering of God, so that through it the body might live and feel.

Let us not doubt that the soul draws original sin together with the flesh in which it is born, and that for this reason it needs the benefit of holy baptism.

## Chapter XXI

**33.** Omitting these true and clear statements of the catholic faith that we set out above, many people have fallen disastrously into various errors.

Tertullian, saying that the soul is not a spirit but a body, was seriously mistaken. He went so far in his folly as even to say that the supreme and true God is a body, although we read not only concerning God, the Creator of all things, that “God is spirit” (John IV, 24), but also concerning the angels whom God created: “He makes his angels spirits” (Psalm CIII, 4).

No wise person doubts that the human soul is a rational spirit. Concerning this spirit the Apostle says: “For who knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him?” (I Corinthians II, 11).

Therefore the holy Evangelist also taught that the rational soul which Christ assumed together with flesh is not a body but a spirit. For the Savior himself had said: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John X, 18). Without doubt he laid it down when the Evangelist says that, having bowed his head, he gave up his spirit (John XIX, 30).

The human soul is shown to be rational in that it is said to have been made in the image and likeness of God. Hence human beings are divinely admonished not to become like horse and mule, which have no understanding (Psalm XXXI, 9).

**34.** The blind impiety of the Manichaeans holds that the soul is a part of God—that is, that it shares one nature with God. They consider God’s substance to be enclosed not only in the bodies of human beings, cattle, birds, and fish, but also in wood and herbs, in trees and vegetables.

In their misery they do not know and do not attend to the fact that a creature is not the same as the Creator, since God is unchangeable while the soul is changeable. At one time it knows and at another does not know; at one time it declines and at another advances; at one time it is wise and at another foolish; at one time it remembers and at another forgets; at one time it hates what it had loved, and at another loves what it had hated; at one time it falls into the snare of deception, and at another, even without being deceived, nevertheless gives its consent to error.

The blessed Apostle most certainly shows this in Adam and his wife when he says: “For Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression” (I Timothy II, 14). The woman, therefore, was deceived and sinned, while the man, who was not deceived, consented to her through voluntary perversity.

It is therefore impious to believe that the soul is a part of God. From the fact that it is sometimes changed for the worse, it is found to be not a part of the divine nature but a certain part of the divine works. For it belongs to those works that God made, each of which is good individually, while all together are very good.

## Chapter XXII

**35.** It is also wholly contrary to the faith to say that, before it existed in a body, the soul committed some offense in heavenly or earthly places and, on account of some sin, deserved to be thrust into a body. Origen is said to have held this view.

The Apostle Paul wholly opposes it when he says that, before they were born, they had done nothing either good or evil (Romans IX, 11). The acts of those being born are not peculiar to them, although we are born bound by the ancient sin of the first human being.

“For through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin death; and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans V, 12). Hence they were made by nature children of wrath and slaves of sin; but, while serving sin, they were made free from righteousness—since they were conceived in iniquities and since their mothers nourished them in sins in the womb (Psalm L, 7).

**36.** From this original bondage of sin, that good freedom of choice was lost, when, through the vice of an evil freedom, the human being began voluntarily to serve sin.

Therefore, for all human beings at every age—from birth itself out of the mother’s womb to the end of decrepit old age—the blood of Christ is necessary. It was poured out for the remission of sins and alone can destroy every sin.

“For there is one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (II Timothy II, 5). Whoever has not been buried with him in baptism into his death will neither be able to obtain the kingdom nor escape the punishment of eternal fire.

For Truth says that “unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 5).

Accordingly, the statement that the teacher of the Gentiles truthfully makes in faith and truth must be understood of all human beings, small and great, infants, children, adolescents, young adults, and the elderly: “For there is no distinction. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace, which is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as an expiation through faith in his blood, to demonstrate his justice because of the remission of previous sins” (Romans III, 22 and following).

When previous sin is sought in infants, without doubt the first sin of the first human being is found: it entered this world through the first human being and, in that original author, claimed his entire offspring for itself by inheritance.

This offspring needs to be redeemed by the blood of that mediator who, while remaining the true God in the form of God, so emptied himself by taking the form of a servant that he could have no stain either of original or of actual sin.

## Chapter XXIII

**37.** In him, therefore, true freedom has been restored to us—he in whom there could be neither original nor actual iniquity. Hence he himself says: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV, 30).

He is just and the one who justifies, free and the one who liberates. By justifying, he liberates; and by liberating, he justifies.

He liberates human beings from the power of the devil, and he liberates human choice from slavery to sin, so that human choice may be truly free because it has been salutarily liberated, and so that true freedom may exist in it, with no iniquity ruling over it.

Our Liberator himself testifies in these words that he will give this freedom through grace: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.” And shortly afterward: “If the Son therefore liberates you, you will be truly free” (John VIII, 34, 36).

The Son therefore liberates from that slavery to sin, so that free choice, liberated by the grace of Christ, may commendably serve righteousness, whereas it had wickedly served sin.

Thus sin does not reign in the mortal body through human choice but through the grace of the Liberator (Romans VI, 12), while we are justified by faith. Through the help of grace, God works in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good will. He himself gives us good will; he himself supplies the ability to do good. From him comes “every good gift and every perfect gift” (James I, 17).

Without him we can do nothing, and in him we can do all things, insofar as we have received from him the grace of strength. This the blessed Apostle confidently presumes in righteousness when he says: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Philippians IV, 13). And again: “In him I labor, struggling according to his working, which he works in me in power” (Colossians I, 29).

## CHAPTER XXIV

**38.** Holding all these things faithfully and without hesitation, we are safe, even if we do not know how souls are given to bodies. It is enough for us to know that by our first birth we were polluted, and by our second birth cleansed; by our first birth captives, and by our second birth free; by our first birth earthly, and by our second birth heavenly; by the fault of our first birth carnal, and by the benefit of our second birth spiritual; [Col. 0670D] by our first birth children of wrath, and by our second birth children of grace; by our first birth children of the world, and by our second birth children of God.

Therefore, even if we cannot know how the soul is given to bodies, let us rightly believe this and live well, and let us strive with the utmost earnestness for this: that in the kingdom [Page 499] of God both our soul and our body may rejoice. If we cannot know that matter, let us patiently remain ignorant of it; but let us seek the kingdom of God ardently and persistently, where, without doubt, God will also reveal to us what is not uselessly hidden from us here, except perhaps because in this life it is not fitting that it should be known.

**39.** But if anyone, enlightened by God, or enabled by indications of the most certain reasoning, or by testimonies of holy authority, should be able either to recognize or to teach that human souls are given newly to individual bodies, or that they are propagated together with those bodies, let him meanwhile assert what the faith of the Church has made clear: namely, that all human beings, from the very moment of conception, draw original sin, which in each person being born must be remitted by the blood of the one Mediator, so that the bond of impiety contracted in the first birth may be loosed in the second birth.

And through the Son of God, who was made of a woman, made under the law (Gal. 4:4–5), so that we might receive adoption as sons, let each person receive the grace of that adoption, which each had lost through the fault of the sinful man, by the benefit of the Redeemer. Whoever asserts this without hesitation will rightly do well not to remain silent about whatever he may subsequently be able to demonstrate concerning the origin of souls in accordance with the truth.

[Col. 0672A] The question concerning the soul is rightly treated, then, if there is no doubt about the original sin of the human race and about the benefit of holy baptism, which was given by the grace of the Savior to captives—he who deigned both to assume the whole nature of our race without sin and to abolish all the guilt of our wrongdoing.

[Col. 0671A]

## SAINT FULGENTIUS, ON THE FAITH, OR ON THE RULE OF TRUE FAITH, ONE BOOK, TO PETER

[Note: [Col. 0671C] Earlier printed editions bear this title: *On the Faith, to Peter the Deacon*. We, however, judged that this title should also be added, *or, On the Rule of True Faith*: first, because this is how the book is called near its beginning and in Ferrandus’s letter to Saint Fulgentius, above, no. 11; and also because it is so read in the most ancient manuscript [Col. 0671D] of Corbie. We also thought that the name “deacon” should be removed. First, because from the entire structure of the book it can easily be inferred that this Peter is plainly a different person from the deacon to whom the book *On the Incarnation*, or Letter 16 above, is addressed, since many matters are treated there that would not have needed to be repeated to the same person here. Furthermore, he is called neither “brother” nor “fellow deacon,” although he ordinarily addresses priests or deacons by that name, as is clear from Letters 5, 12, 14, and 17 above. Finally, if one does not mind drawing some argument from this as well, below, in chapter 45—in a passage attributed to an author who, as will be said there, differs from Fulgentius—we read: “In the service of the world, render faithful service to the earthly king, because God loves this and the Apostle commands it.”]

[Col. 0671B] [Page 500]

## PROLOGUE

**1.** I received, my son Peter, the letter expressing your affection, in which you indicated that you wished to travel to Jerusalem, and asked to be instructed by our writings concerning the rule of true faith that you ought to maintain [Col. 0672C] in those regions.

[Note: [Col. 0672C] One Vatican manuscript reads: “that you should maintain the faith in those regions.” All the other manuscripts and printed editions read: “the rule of true faith.”]

Thus no notion of heretical falsehood could creep into you.

[Note: [Col. 0672C] One Vatican manuscript reads: “so that no notion of heretical depravity could creep into you.” Two others read “creep in” for “creep into you” and “falsehood.”]

I rejoice, indeed, that you are concerned to preserve the true faith without any fault of faithlessness, since without it conversion can neither profit nor even exist. For the apostolic authority says that without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11:6).

Faith is the foundation of all good things.

[Note: [Col. 0672C] The ancient Corbie manuscript, of excellent quality, has: “For divinely inspired faith itself is the foundation of [Col. 0672D] all good things.” The other manuscripts have the wording found in the text.]

Faith is the beginning of human salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0672D] Two Vatican manuscripts read: “and the judgment and beginning of all human salvation.”]

Without it,

[Note: [Col. 0672D] The printed editions read: “Without this faith.” The word “faith” is absent from the Corbie manuscript and four Vatican manuscripts.]

no one can belong to the number of God’s children.

[Note: [Col. 0672D] The printed editions read: “can arrive.” Five manuscripts read: “can belong.”]

For without it no one in this age obtains the grace of justification, nor will anyone [Page 501] possess eternal life in the age to come. And if anyone here does not walk by faith, he will not attain to sight.

Without faith all human labor is empty. Such indeed is the case if anyone wishes to please God through contempt of the world without true faith.

[Note: [Col. 0672D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “Such indeed is it to wish to please God without true faith,” and so forth; another reads, “if anyone wishes without true faith.”]

For it is just as though someone, setting out for his homeland, in which he knows he will live blessedly, should abandon the straightness of the road and heedlessly pursue an error, by which he would not reach the blessed city but fall into a precipice—where no joy would be granted to the one arriving, but destruction would be inflicted on the one falling.

[Col. 0672B] **2.** Nevertheless, although a sufficient discourse concerning faith should be produced, time does not support us, because you eagerly desire to have our answer quickly, and the task of this discussion is so great that it could scarcely be completed by extensive discourses.

[Note: [Col. 0672D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “so that it could scarcely be completed by great men.” The other manuscripts and printed editions read: “by great discourses.”]

For you did not ask to be instructed about faith in such a way that you would identify one particular heresy against which the purpose of our discussion would specifically keep watch.

[Note: [Col. 0672D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “that you should be instructed about the faith in such a way that I would identify …”]

Rather, since you ask without specifying for a definition of faith and desire that it also be confined within brevity, you plainly see how impossible it is for us fully to comprehend in a short space so great a matter, for which we cannot be sufficient—even if we had so much time and such an intellect that we could produce many volumes on the subject you ask of us. [Variant: *valeremus* (“we could”) or *valeamus* (“we may be able”).]

But because God is near to all who call upon him in truth (Ps. 144:18), he who, completing and abbreviating his word, made it prevail upon the earth (Rom. 9:28), I hope that, just as he has given you a holy concern for this faith, so he will also grant me sufficient ability to serve your desire, so good and praiseworthy.

Thus, even if I should not be able—or, in the variant, be able—to say everything by which every heretical error could be recognized and, once recognized, either refuted or avoided, nevertheless, in the name and with the help of the holy Trinity, who is the one and only true and good God, I shall say those things in which, at least for the most part, it is evident that the principle of the Catholic faith is contained without any obscurity of error.

Once you have retained these things, you will also be able to detect and flee those errors which, although they do not appear to be refuted here by a special discussion, nevertheless are shown by the matters set forth here generally and absolutely to be what faithless people wish—or, in the variant, are accustomed—to whisper into the ears of the faithful. [Variant: *appareat* (“it may appear”) or *appareant* (“they may appear”).]

[Note: [Col. 0673D] One manuscript adds “and unbelieving people.”]

They have not been handed down as the rule of divine truth, but invented by the wickedness of human error.

## CHAPTER I

**3.** Therefore, wherever you may be established, since according to the rule promulgated by the command of our Savior you know that you were baptized in the one name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,

[Note: [Col. 0673D] Two manuscripts read: “in the name of the Father,” and so forth.]

[Col. 0673B] hold this principally and without hesitation with your whole heart: God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit—that is, the holy and ineffable Trinity—[Col. 0673A] is naturally one God. Concerning him it is said in Deuteronomy: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your [Page 502] God, God—or, in the variant, Lord—is one” (Deut. 6:4).

And: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (ibid., 6:13).

Nevertheless, because we have said that this one God, who alone is naturally the true God, is not the Father alone, nor the Son alone, nor the Holy Spirit alone, but simultaneously the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, we must beware lest, just as we truthfully say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God with respect to natural unity,

[Note: [Col. 0673D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “with respect to natural truth.”]

[Col. 0673C] we should dare personally to say or believe that he who is Father is the same person as the Son or the Holy Spirit; or that he who is Son is either the Father or the Holy Spirit; or that he who is properly called the Holy Spirit in the confession of this Trinity is personally either the Father or the Son. That is wholly unlawful.

**4.** For the faith which the holy patriarchs and prophets received divinely before the incarnation of the Son of God, and which the holy apostles also heard from the Lord himself when he was present in the flesh, and which, instructed by the teaching of the Holy Spirit, they not only preached in words but also left embedded in their writings for the saving instruction of posterity—that faith proclaims one God, the Trinity, that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

But the Trinity would not be true if the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit were said to be one and the same person. For if, just as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one substance, they also had one person, there would be absolutely nothing in which the Trinity could truthfully be called a Trinity.

Again, the Trinity would indeed not be true,

[Note: [Col. 0673D] Two manuscripts give this passage differently: “Again, the true Trinity would not exist if the one God were not himself the Trinity; but just as …” One of these has only “just as …”]

but the one God would not himself be the Trinity, if, just as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are distinct from one another by the particularity of their persons, they had likewise been distinguished by diversity of natures.

But because in that one true God who is Trinity it is naturally true not only that he is one God but also that he is Trinity, [Col. 0674A] the true God is therefore Trinity in persons and one in nature.

[Note: [Col. 0674D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “He is Trinity, one in nature.”]

Through this natural unity, the whole Father is in the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the whole Son is in the Father and the Holy Spirit, and the whole Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son. None of these is outside any of the others.

(*Sentences* I, distinction 19, chapter “And from this.”)

For none precedes another in eternity, surpasses another in greatness, or exceeds another in power. For, insofar as the unity of the divine nature is concerned, the Father is neither earlier nor greater than the Son or the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0674D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “For the Father is not greater, nor, insofar as the unity of the divine nature is concerned, is he earlier than the Son or the Holy Spirit.”]

(*Sentences*, same distinction, chapter “Now after.”)

Nor can the eternity and immensity of the Son, as though earlier or greater, naturally precede or surpass the eternity and immensity of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0674B] Therefore, just as the Son is neither later nor less than the Father, so the Holy Spirit is neither later nor less than the Son.

For that the Son came forth born from the Father’s nature is eternal and without beginning.

[Note: [Col. 0674D] Six manuscripts and the Master’s *Sentences*, distinction 19, read “came forth.” The printed editions and the English manuscript read “exists.”]

And that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the nature of the Father and the Son is likewise eternal and without beginning.

Therefore we rightly believe and say that the three are one God, because the three persons have, naturally, [Page 503] one eternity, one immensity, and one divinity.

**5.** Let us therefore hold that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are naturally one God; yet let us not hold that the Father himself is the one who is the Son, nor that the Son himself is the one who is the Father, nor that the Holy Spirit himself is the one who is the Father or the Son.

(*Sentences* I, distinction 2, chapter “But all Catholics.”)

For the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one [Col. 0674C] essence, which the Greeks call *ousia* (οὐσία, “essence”); in this there is not one thing that is the Father, another the Son, and another the Holy Spirit, although personally the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.

This is shown to us especially at the very beginning of the holy Scriptures, where God says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26).

When he says “image” in the singular, he shows that the nature according to whose image man was to be made is one. But when he says “our” in the plural, he shows that the same God according to whose image man was made is not one person.

For if in that one nature

[Note: [Col. 0674D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “in that one essence.”]

of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit there were one person, he would not have said “in our image,” but “in my image”; nor would he have said “Let us make,” but “Let me make.”

But if three substances were to be understood or believed in those three persons, he would not have said “in our image,” but “in our images,” since one image could not belong to three unequal natures.

Yet, when man is said to have been made according to the one image of the one God, the essential divinity of the holy Trinity is made known.

Then, shortly afterward, in place of what God had earlier said—“Let us make man in our image and likeness”—[Col. 0675A] Scripture narrated the making of man as follows: “And God made man; in the image of God he made him” (Gen. 1:27).

**6.** The prophet Isaiah did not remain silent about this Trinity of persons and unity of nature having been revealed to him,

[Note: [Col. 0675D] Three manuscripts read: “noted as having been revealed to him.”]

when he says that he saw Seraphim crying out: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. 6:3).

There, plainly, in the fact that “Holy” is said three times, we recognize the Trinity of persons; but in the fact that “Lord God of hosts” is said once, we recognize the unity of the divine nature.

In that holy Trinity, which is therefore repeated by us

[Note: [Col. 0675D] The printed editions read: “which is repeated so many times.” The words “so many times” are absent from six manuscripts.]

so that it may be fixed more firmly in your heart,

[Note: [Col. 0675D] Two manuscripts read “in your heart”; the printed editions read “in our heart.”]

there is one Father,

[Note: [Col. 0675D] The printed editions read “God the Father.” Three manuscripts omit “God.”]

who alone essentially begot one Son from himself;

[Note: [Col. 0675D] One manuscript reads *sed unicum* (“but an only Son”) instead of *sed unum* (“but one Son”).]

and one Son, who alone was essentially born—or begotten—from the one Father; [Col. 0675B] and one Holy Spirit, who alone essentially proceeds from the Father and the Son.

All of this could not belong to one person—that is, both to beget himself, to be born from himself, and to proceed from himself.

Since, therefore, begetting is one thing, being born another, and proceeding—or, in the variant, having proceeded—is different from either begetting or being born, it is clear that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.

Thus “Trinity” refers to the persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; “unity” refers to the nature.

[Page 504]

## CHAPTER II. THE HUMANITY OF CHRIST

**7.** Therefore, just as, according to that divinity by which the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one, we believe that neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit was born, but only the Son, so also, [Col. 0675C] according to the flesh, the Catholic faith both believes and proclaims that only the Son was born.

For in that Trinity it would not be proper to the Father alone that he himself was not born but begot the one Son; nor would it be proper to the Son alone that he himself did not beget but was alone born from the Father’s essence; nor would it be proper to the Holy Spirit that he himself was neither born nor begot but alone proceeds from the Father and the Son,

[Note: [Col. 0675D] The Corbie manuscript adds: “he proceeds in unchangeable eternity,” and so forth.]

if, according to the divine nature, God the Father were born from no God, but according to the flesh he himself were born from a virgin (*de*, or in the variant *ex*).

For if the Father were born from a virgin, the Father and the Son would be one person. But that one person, because he would be born not from God but only from a virgin, would truly be called not the Son of God but merely the son of a human being.

Nor would that one himself, the Son of God, say: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3:16);

[Note: [Col. 0675D] One Vatican manuscript reads, and more correctly than the others: “But the Son of God himself says, ‘God so loved …’”]

and again: “For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved [Col. 0676A] through him” (ibid., 3:17).

Nor would blessed John have said: “Whoever loves the one who begets loves also the one who has been born from him” (1 John 5:1); nor would the Son himself have said: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17).

For if the one who is called the Son were also the Father, he would not truly be called the Son of God, since he would be born not from God but from the virgin alone.

Finally, the Father himself would not testify from heaven and point out his Son with a bodily voice, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17).

[Note: [Col. 0675D] The Vatican manuscript adds: “Listen to him.” The others do not.]

The Apostle Paul likewise would not have said of God the Father: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:32).

[Note: [Col. 0675D] Two manuscripts read: “He did not spare his own Son.”]

**8.** But since all these things were spoken divinely for our instruction, and since they were spoken as divine truths,

[Note: [Col. 0675D] This is the reading of the printed editions and four manuscripts. The Corbie manuscript reads: “and since those things which were spoken are divine.” One Vatican manuscript reads: “and since they are divine.”]

[Col. 0676B] they are certainly true.

It is therefore true what the Catholic faith proclaims: that, according to his divinity, the Son alone was born from the Father—eternal with the Father, immortal, incapable of suffering, and unchangeable God; and that, according to the flesh, not the Father but his only-begotten Son was born in time, while preserving his eternity;

[Note: [Col. 0676D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “and according to the flesh, not from the Father but from the mother, the Father’s only-begotten Son, while preserving his eternity.” The others read uniformly as in the text.] suffered while preserving his incapacity for suffering; died while preserving his immortality; and, while preserving his unchangeability—for he is true God and eternal life—was truly raised from the dead.

The Son possesses in common with the Father everything which, as eternal by nature and without beginning, he had; but he possesses nothing in common with the Father of those things which that eternal and exalted one assumed temporally and humbly into his own person.

[Note: [Col. 0676D] Some manuscripts add here “from the virgin,” but this seems superfluous; it is absent from three manuscripts and the Antwerp manuscript. Some manuscripts also redundantly add here: “For the Father and the Son would be one person; but that one person, because he would be born not from God but only from a virgin, would not be the Son of God.” These words are absent from three manuscripts and the Antwerp manuscript.]

[Page 505] **9.** Again, if it were not he who is the proper and [Col. 0676C] only-begotten Son of God the Father, but the Holy Spirit, who were born from a virgin, the holy Church would not receive in the Creed, believe with the heart for justification, and confess with the mouth for salvation, that the very Son who was made of a woman, made under the law, was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.

But if the Holy Spirit himself, who is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, were to assume the form of a servant, the Holy Spirit himself would not descend from heaven in the form of a dove upon himself, made human.

**10.** God the Father, himself begotten from no God, once begot from his own nature, without beginning, God the Son, equal to himself,

[Note: [Col. 0676D] One Vatican manuscript reads “co-equal to himself.” All the others read “equal to himself.”]

and, in the same divinity by which he himself is naturally eternal, co-eternal with himself.

But although this same Son of God is eternal and true God,

[Note: [Col. 0676D] This is the reading of the Corbie manuscript. One Vatican manuscript reads: “although he is the eternal and true Son of God.”]

and, with the Father according to his divinity, naturally one God, in accordance with what he says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), he was made for us a true and complete human being.

[Col. 0677A] He was true in that the God who is spoken of possesses a true human nature.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] One manuscript omits the words “the God who is spoken of.”]

He was complete in that he assumed both human flesh and a rational soul.

Yet the same only-begotten God was born a second time:

[Note: [Col. 0677D] Five manuscripts read: “was born a second time.” The printed editions omit “a second time.”]

once from the Father, once from his mother. For he was born from the Father as God the Word; he was born from his mother as the Word made flesh.

**11.** There is therefore one and the same Son of God, born before the ages and born in the age; and both births belong to the one Son of God.

The divine birth is that by which he is Creator, God in the form of God, co-eternal with the Father. The human birth is that by which, emptying himself and assuming the form of a servant, he not only formed himself, when he became human, in the conception of his mother’s womb through that same assumption of the servant’s form, but also, having been made the God-man, came forth from that same mother’s womb.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “from the womb of that same mother.”]

[Col. 0677B] The same God-man hung upon the cross.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “the man who had been made [God-man] died.”]

The same God-man lay in the tomb.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “and for three days the same God-man was in the tomb.”]

The same God-man rose on the third day from the dead.

But in the tomb the same God lay according to the flesh alone, and he descended into the underworld according to the soul alone. [Variant: *qua* (“in which”) or *quae* (“which”) in the following clause.]

When that soul returned from the underworld to the flesh on the third day,

[Note: [Col. 0677D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “When the soul returned from the underworld to the flesh on the third day.”]

the same God rose from the tomb according to the flesh in which he had lain in the tomb.

On the fortieth day after the resurrection, the same God-man ascended into heaven and sat at the right hand of God.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] Four manuscripts read: “sits at the right hand of God.” The remaining manuscripts read: “sat.”]

From there he will come at the end of the age to judge the living and the dead.

**12.** The Word made flesh is one Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] One manuscript reads “our Lord.”]

He is mediator because he is the same true God and true human being, [Col. 0677C] possessing with the Father one nature of divinity and with his mother one substance of humanity; possessing from us, even unto death, the penalty of our iniquity; possessing from God the Father unchangeable righteousness;

[Note: [Col. 0677D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “possessing unchangeable substance from God the Father.”]

[Page 506] temporally dead because of our iniquity, yet, because of his righteousness, himself always living and destined to bestow immortality upon mortals.

He preserved his perfect humanity within the very perfection of his divinity. But through the assumption of death he absorbed the reality of his mortality into the truth and unchangeability of his immortality.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] Five manuscripts read “the reality of his mortality.” The printed editions read “the reality of our mortality.” [Col. 0678D] In one or another Vatican manuscript the whole passage reads: “But he absorbed the reality of his mortality in the assumption of death; and he absorbed death in truth …”]

**13.** This is what blessed Peter testifies: Christ swallowed up death so that we might become heirs of eternal life (1 Pet. 3:22).

Blessed Paul also teaches that Christ swallowed up death, but brought life and incorruption to light (2 Tim. 1:10).

Christ therefore tasted death because he is a true human being; and the same Christ swallowed up death because he is true God.

[Col. 0678A] For the same one, as the Apostle says, died from weakness

[Note: [Col. 0678D] The Corbie manuscript reads “was crucified”; one Vatican manuscript reads “from our weakness.”]

but lives by the power of God (2 Cor. 13:4): one and the same, who, according to the prophecy of blessed David, both was made human in Zion and himself founded it, the Most High (Ps. 86:5).

[Note: [Col. 0678D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “according to the prophet David.”]

**14.** Thus Christ’s divinity is not foreign to the nature of the Father, in accordance with what is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1).

Nor is his humanity foreign to the nature of his mother, in accordance with what is written: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 1:14).

That nature which remains eternally begotten from the Father assumed our nature without sin, so that it might be born from a virgin.

[Col. 0678B] For eternal and divine nature could in no way be conceived and born in time from human nature, unless the ineffable divinity had assumed within itself, through the assumption of true humanity, a true conception and birth in time.

Thus he is eternal and true God, truly conceived and born from a virgin in time.

[Note: [Col. 0678D] One Vatican manuscript has a fuller reading: “Therefore, just as the eternal and truly timeless God is immortally living in the essence of his divinity, so, if according to time he was conceived by a virgin mother and born as a human being, he is truly God. For when …”]

For when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made—or born—of a woman, made under the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons (Gal. 4:4–5).

[Note: [Col. 0678D] The printed editions read: “so that we might receive adoption as sons of God.” Five manuscripts omit “of God,” in agreement with the Greek text of the Apostle, where the expression is a single word, *huiothesia* (υἱοθεσία, “adoption as sons”).]

This was that God who was naturally made the son of a human being, although he is naturally the one Son of God the Father.

[Col. 0678C] The evangelist John confirms this when, after saying, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), he immediately adds: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (ibid.).

Thus he, the Creator and Lord of all spirits and of all bodies—that is, of all natures—created the virgin in order to be created from the virgin. He who himself is her maker made her his mother, when, in order to be conceived and born from her flesh, immense and eternal God received from her the true matter—or nature—of flesh. [Variant: *quando* (“when”) or *quomodo* (“how”).]

In this way God mercifully became human according to the truth of the servant’s form; and, according to the form of God, the same God-man, remaining so in natural truth,

[Note: Some manuscripts read “in natural power.”]

did not cease to be what he was.

[Page 507] **15.** Therefore believe Christ, the Son of God—that is, the true God, one person of the Trinity—in such a way that—or, in the variant, and—you do not doubt that his divinity was born from the nature of the Father.

And believe him to be a true human being in such a way that you do not think his flesh is heavenly, airy, or of any other nature, but of the same nature as the flesh of all [Col. 0679A] human beings.

That is, it is the flesh which God himself formed from the earth in the first human being

[Note: [Col. 0679D] One manuscript reads: “in the first human being.”]

and forms in all other human beings whom he creates through propagation from human beings.

But although Christ’s flesh and the flesh of all human beings are of one and the same nature, this flesh, which God the Word deigned to unite to himself from the Virgin Mary, was conceived without sin

[Note: [Col. 0679D] This is the reading of three manuscripts. The printed editions read: “was assumed without sin.”]

and born without sin, since according to this flesh the eternal and just God was mercifully conceived and born, and the Lord of glory was crucified.

**16. THE LUST OF INTERCOURSE**

In what words can the unique excellence of that flesh be explained? Its divine person exists from the very moment of its conception,

[Note: [Col. 0679D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “from the moment of its formation.”]

and its origin by birth is extraordinary. The Word became flesh in such a way that the only-begotten and eternal God was one person with his flesh, being himself conceived through the conception [Col. 0679B] of his flesh.

It is certain that the flesh of other human beings is born through ordinary human intercourse: the man sowing, and the woman conceiving and giving birth.

And because, when a man and a woman join together in order to beget children, the intercourse of the parents is not without lust, the conception of children born from their flesh cannot be without sin.

Sin is not transmitted to infants by the propagation of nature, but by lust. Nor is it the fecundity of human nature that causes human beings to be born with sin, but the foulness of lust, which human beings possess as a consequence of the just condemnation of that first sin.

Therefore blessed David, although he was born from a lawful [Col. 0679C] and righteous marriage—in which, naturally, neither the guilt of unfaithfulness nor the stain of fornication could be found—nevertheless, because of original sin by which the children of wrath are naturally bound, cries out and says: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me.”

[Note: [Col. 0679D] Four manuscripts read: “and in sins my mother bore me.” The printed editions and one Vatican manuscript read: “and in sins my mother conceived me.”]

Saint Job also says that a human being is not clean from defilement, even if his life upon the earth should last only one day (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint).

**17.** Therefore the only-begotten Son of God, who is in the bosom of the Father, became incarnate through the assumption of flesh and a rational soul, in order to cleanse human flesh and soul.

He who is true God became a true human being—not so that there would be one God and another human being, but the same God and the same human being.

In order to remove the sin which human generation contracted through intercourse of mortal flesh, he was conceived in a new manner: God was incarnate in a virgin mother, without intercourse with a man and without lust on the part of the conceiving virgin.

Thus, through the God-man whom the inviolate womb of the virgin brought forth, conceived without lust, the sin which all human beings acquire at birth might be washed away. For those born in this body of death have such a condition of birth that their mothers cannot fulfill the work of fecundity unless they first lose the virginity of their flesh.

[Page 508] [Col. 0680A] Therefore the only-begotten God alone removed the sin of human conception and birth. In being conceived, he received the reality of flesh from the virgin; in being born, he preserved the integrity of virginity in his mother.

This is why God became the son of the virgin Mary, and Mary the virgin became the mother of the only-begotten God: so that the one whom the Father begot from eternity the virgin, having conceived him, might bring forth in time.

She was the virgin whom God—he who was to be born from her—so anticipated and filled with singular grace that she possessed as the fruit of her womb the one whom the whole universe has had as its Lord from the beginning; and she saw subject to herself, in the solemnity of his birth, the one whom every creature, not only human but also angelic, recognizes and worships as the Most High in the unity of the Father’s substance.

[Col. 0680B] **18.** Thus sin and the punishment of sin, which entered the world through the crime of the corrupted woman, are taken away from the world through the childbirth of the inviolate virgin.

[Note: [Col. 0679D] One manuscript reads: “It happened that through the childbirth of the inviolate virgin it was taken away from the world.” Three manuscripts read: “through the inviolate childbirth.”]

And because, in the condition of the human race, through the woman who was made from the man alone, it happened that we were held bound by the chain of death, divine goodness brought this about in the redemption of the human race: through the man who was born from a woman alone, life would be restored to human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0680D] One manuscript reads “from a virgin woman.”]


There the devil joined human nature to himself through the most wicked deception in the likeness of sin; here God assumed human nature into the unity of his person.

There the woman was deceived so that she might become the daughter of the devil; here the virgin was filled with grace so that she might become the mother of the highest and unchangeable only-begotten God.

There the angel cast down through pride gained possession of the mind of the deceived woman.

[Note: [Col. 0680D] A manuscript reads: “corrupted the mind of the cast-down woman”; and shortly afterward three manuscripts read: “of the incorrupt woman who was a virgin.”]

[Col. 0680C] Here God, humbling himself through mercy, filled the womb of the incorrupt virgin, intending to be born from her.

For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was in the form of God—which he could not be unless he had been born from the nature of the Father—

[Note: [Col. 0680D] This is the reading of the Corbie manuscript. Three Vatican manuscripts read: “who was in the form of God, which he could not be unless he had been born from the nature of the Father.” Another Vatican manuscript reads: “who was the form of God, which he could not be,” and so forth.]

according to the teaching of the Apostle, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7).

Thus God himself took the form of a servant—that is, the nature of a servant—into his own person. In this way the maker of human beings became in the likeness of human beings, was found in appearance as a human being, and humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross (ibid., 2:8).

**19.** Consider this statement of the Apostle attentively, and in it you will understand how to believe the Lord Jesus Christ to be the same God and human being.

Yet do not confuse or divide in him the reality of both natures in one person.

When, therefore, you first hear concerning the Lord Jesus Christ that he was in the form of God, you must recognize and hold most firmly that by the name “form” the fullness of nature is to be understood.

The Lord Jesus Christ was therefore in the form of God because he was always in the nature of God the Father, from whom he was born.

[Col. 0681A] He is therefore of one nature with the Father, and equally eternal and immense with him; equally immortal and unchangeable; equally invisible and indescribable; equally good and just; equally compassionate and merciful, patient, abundantly merciful, and truthful; equally strong and gracious; equally wise and almighty.

20. Therefore hold with the firmest faith all these things that we have said about the Son of God, because [or: who], possessing all these things in unity of nature with the Father, he is undoubtedly equal to the Father. For this reason the Apostle immediately adds: “He did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God” (Phil. II, 6). The Son’s equality of divinity with the Father was not a matter of robbery (rapinae; alternatively rapina), but of nature (naturae; alternatively natura). The Apostle also continues by saying that “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being”; and that “he humbled himself, becoming obedient” [Note: [Col. 0681D] The printed editions have “obedient to the Father.” The word “to the Father” is absent from the Corbie manuscript and from the Apostle’s text.] “unto death, even death on a cross.” All these statements concern that only-begotten God, the Son of God; that Word who is God, of whom the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1); that power of God and wisdom of God, of which it is said to God: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII, 24); that Beginning with which the Father himself, the one Beginning, is one, and in which, co-eternal with himself, he made heaven and earth—that is, every spiritual and bodily nature.

Receive all these statements personally concerning the only-begotten God, who is, as I have said, in the bosom of the Father, while nevertheless preserving the eternity, immensity, immortality, immutability, and invisibility of his divinity. The Son of God possesses these qualities naturally and equally in common with God the Father, so that, although he truly became human for our sake, he nevertheless remained equal to the true God the Father, from whom the true God and Truth was born. He therefore emptied himself [Note: [Col. 0681D] In one Vatican manuscript, “taking the form of a servant” is added; it is not added in the others.], but “from his fullness we have all received” (John I, 16). If, when he was emptied, he had lost that fullness, he would have had nothing to give us from it. If he did not possess it, we certainly [or: indeed] could receive nothing. “From his fullness, then, we have all received.” By what he gave us from his fullness, he also showed that, when he emptied himself, he did not lose the fullness that he possessed; for if he had lost his fullness, he could in no way have given from it. He therefore took the form of a servant: for that emptying of the supreme God was nothing other than the taking on of a servile form—that is, of human nature.

21. Thus Christ possesses both forms, because in Christ there is true and complete substance in both respects. For this reason the holy Evangelist proclaims him “full of grace and truth” (ibid., 14): he is full in the divine nature, in which God is Truth, and he is full in the human nature, in which the true human being was made by grace. In that fullness he is God, equal to God in the form of God; in this fullness he is a servant, in the form of a servant, because he was made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being.

He therefore emptied himself and took the form of a servant in order to become a servant; but he did not lose the fullness of the form of God, in which the Lord is eternally and immutably. Made a true human being according to the form of a servant, he was of the same nature as his servant mother; and remaining true God in the form of God, he was of the same nature as the Lord Father.

In the form of God, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he is the one and sole God, maker of all things; according to the form of a servant, he alone was formed by his own operation and by that of the Father and the Holy Spirit. What he is as Creator he possesses naturally in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit; what he is as created, he alone possesses personally in himself according to the form of a servant by which he was created [Note: [Col. 0682D] The words “according to the form of a servant by which he was created” are absent from all the manuscripts. And indeed, their omission is not inappropriate.].

The Law and the Prophets never ceased to foretell his future birth according to the flesh, his death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, just as he himself commanded them, obedient [Note: [Col. 0682D] “Obedient” is absent from the printed editions; it is found in the manuscripts.] in words and deeds.

22. For even in the sacrifices of bodily victims, which the Holy Trinity itself—the one God of the New and Old Testaments—commanded our fathers to offer, the most gracious gift of that sacrifice was signified: the sacrifice by which God the Son alone would mercifully offer himself for us according to the flesh. For, according to apostolic teaching, “he offered himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma” (Eph. V, 5). He is the true God and true high priest who, not in the blood of bulls and goats but in his own blood, entered once for all into the holy places (Heb. IX, 12). This was signified at that time by the high priest who entered the Holy of Holies every year with blood.

This, then, is the one who displayed in himself everything that he knew to be necessary for the accomplishment of our redemption: the same one both priest and sacrifice, the same one both God and temple. He is the priest through whom we were reconciled; the sacrifice by which we were reconciled; the temple in which we were reconciled; and the God to whom we were reconciled. He is nevertheless alone priest, sacrifice, and temple, because all these things are God according to the form of a servant [Note: [Col. 0682D] Three manuscripts read “because all these things.” The printed editions read “and all these things.”]; but he is not God alone, because in the form of God he is this together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

23. We have therefore been reconciled through the Son alone according to the flesh, but not to the Son alone according to divinity. For the Trinity reconciled us to itself by the fact that the Trinity itself made the Word alone flesh. In him the unchanging truth [Note: [Col. 0682D] One Vatican manuscript reads “truth and immutability.”] of the human and divine nature remains, so that, just as his divinity—which he has immutably from the Father—is always true, so his humanity, which the supreme divinity bears united to itself, is always true and immutable.

24. I have inserted these few observations about the faith of the Holy Trinity, which is naturally the one and true God, as far as the brevity of time and discourse permitted. Now I shall explain what you ought to believe without hesitation concerning creation.

CHAPTER III

25. From what created natures advance and decline.—First of all, therefore, hold that every nature [or: creature] that is not God the Trinity was created out of nothing by the Holy Trinity itself, which alone is the true and eternal God. Thus everything in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible—whether Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, or Powers—is the work and creation of the Holy Trinity, which is the one God, Creator and Lord of all things, eternal, almighty, just [Note: [Col. 0683D] Four manuscripts do not have “just.”], and good, naturally possessing the quality of always existing and of never being able to change.

This God, who has always existed without beginning because he supremely is, gave existence to the things he created. Yet they are not without beginning, because no creature is of the same nature as the Trinity, the one true and good God, from whom all things were created.

And because he is supremely good, he gave all the natures [or: things] he made the quality of being good. Yet they are not as good as the Creator of all good things, who is not merely supremely good but the supreme and immutable good, because he is eternal good. He has no defect, because he was not made from nothing; he has no progress, because he has no beginning [Note: [Col. 0683D] Six manuscripts read this way. The printed editions instead have: “because he has no lack.”].

Created natures can therefore advance because they began to exist; they can decline because they were made from nothing. The condition of their origin leads them toward decline, but the Creator’s activity carries them toward advancement.

In this first property of the Trinity, which is the true God, its natural eternity without beginning is recognized: he made certain things in such a way that, although they began to exist, they can never cease to exist. His omnipotence, however, is understood in this, that he made every visible and invisible creature—that is, every bodily and spiritual creature—from nothing. The very diversity of things thereby greatly commends the goodness and omnipotence of the Creator. For if he were not almighty, he would not have made the highest and the lowest with the same ease [or: faculty]; and if he were not supremely good, he would not have extended himself even to the governance of the lowest things.

26. Heavenly and earthly bodies differ.—Thus, in both the greatest and the smallest created things, the goodness and omnipotence of the Creator are great. For he made everything wisely, with supreme and true wisdom, for which being is naturally the same as being wise, and doing the same as doing wisely.

The simplicity of God’s manifold wisdom therefore commends the greatness of its exalted height not only in the magnitude of sublime creatures but also in the smallness of the lowest. All the good things he created are not only far lower and unlike their Creator—since they were not brought forth from him but made wholly from nothing—but are also unequal among themselves. Each thing remains as it received from God the quality of being [Note: [Col. 0683D] The Corbie manuscript reads this way. The printed editions have: “although it did not exist, it received [from God].” Two other manuscripts read: “although it existed,” perhaps referring back to God.], one in this way and another in that.

Bodies were not given existence in the same way that spirits received it. Bodies themselves are not equal, and even among heavenly and earthly bodies there is some diversity. Heavenly and earthly bodies differ not only in the unequal quantity of their mass but also in the dissimilar brilliance with which they shine. For, as the Apostle says, “the glory of heavenly bodies is one thing, and that of earthly bodies another.” Among the heavenly bodies themselves there is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: “star differs from star in glory” (I Cor. XV, 41).

The diversity of bodily natures therefore shows that each of them is not what it could always have possessed from itself, but what it received [or: because it received] from the ordering and work of the almighty, immutable, and supremely wise Creator.

27. God is everywhere.—If any bodily creature were of the same nature as the Holy Trinity, which is the one God, it would neither exist locally in a place, nor ever experience temporal change, nor pass from place to place, nor be bounded by the quantity of its mass.

All these things show that the maker of such natures is one for whom no place is broad or narrow, because he is wholly present no less in narrow places than in broad ones. He is not changed by time, because he alone can order the cycles of time—not by temporal rotation [Note: [Col. 0684D] The Corbie manuscript reads “not by temporal will.”], but by eternal stability. He does not think within time about how the sequence of times runs through the departure and succession of things; nor is he bounded by any quantity of mass, because he is enclosed by no limit [Note: [Col. 0684D] The printed editions read this way. Four manuscripts have “because he is enclosed by no boundary,” with “by mass” understood. One Vatican manuscript reads “because by no place”; another, “because by no one.”].

Nor is he spread through the parts of the world by his own parts, so that he might fill the larger parts of the world with his larger parts and the smaller with his smaller parts, while nevertheless never pouring himself forth wholly anywhere. For he is the God who says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII, 24).

Therefore the Lord God, wholly and ineffably present everywhere, both fills and contains everything he made: spirits and bodies, the highest and the lowest, heavenly and earthly things, living beings and those to which he did not give the capacity for life. He is not divided among things that are divided, nor is he altered by any change among things that change. For unless he himself were immutable by nature, a certain immutable order of his plan and arrangement would never remain among mutable things.

28. God is the life of all things.—God, then, the immense Creator of bodily and incorporeal things, first shows that he is no body by the fact that he did not give life to certain bodies, although he himself created all bodies. He himself, however, is naturally life, because, if he were not life, he would not have made bodies that do not live [Note: [Col. 0685D] Five manuscripts read: “he would not have made living bodies. For he does not make a living thing.” The reading of the Corbie manuscript and the printed editions agrees better with what follows.]. For he does not make a nonliving thing unless he is himself a living thing.

Bodies that cannot live at all are therefore not of one nature with God. Nor are those bodies of one nature with God into which he inserted individual brute and irrational spirits, so that those same bodies might be enlivened and endowed with sensation.
