Nor are the brute spirits themselves of one nature with God. Although they are known to have been inserted into bodies in order to enliven and sensitize them, he did not grant those spirits any light of understanding by which they could know or love their Creator.

28 bis. As for the spirits whom there is no doubt are rational and intellectual, who would dare, with blasphemous spirit and blind heart, either to think or say that they are of the same nature as God? God is naturally altogether immutable and immense. Although he can have no diversity within himself, he nevertheless displays the diversity of his activity in those same spirits whom he made rational and intellectual.

Among these spirits—namely, those inserted into earthly and mortal bodies—there is no local movement, because, while they are in bodies, they are not distributed in parts through the parts of bodily places, but, just as they are wholly in whole bodies, so they are wholly in the parts of those bodies. Nevertheless, the variation of their thoughts displays in them a diversity of a certain temporal movement and change: at one time they do not know something, at another they know it; at one time they will, at another they do not will; at one time they are wise, at another foolish; at one time they are unjust after having been just, at another just after having been unjust; at one time they are illumined by the light of piety, at another corrupted by the darkness of impious error.

29. As for those whom no muddy matter of earthly bodies burdens—that is, angelic spirits—who does not see that they are not of one nature with God, but were made from nothing? Their natural mutability is recognized in this: a part of their nature has been changed for the worse.

Furthermore, those who have not been corrupted—although, by the gift of him from whom they were made when they did not exist, they continually receive, with perfect love, contemplation, and exultation, as far as was freely granted to angelic creatures, an abundance of the sweetness of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0685D] All the manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have “they perceive.”], and although, by their natural condition, they do not decline from him—have nothing of temporal variation within them while they cling to God, because, having received the gift of eternal incorruption and immutability, they experience no change within themselves.

Nevertheless, each possesses a natural limit [Note: [Col. 0685D] One Vatican manuscript reads “the end of a natural boundary.”], by which they are distinguished from one another, because none of them is in another. And when some task is entrusted to one of them, another is likewise assigned by the decision of divine power to fulfill another task.

All these things show that even the holy angels are creatures [Note: [Col. 0685D] Four manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have “are works.”] of the Holy Trinity. In each of the things he made, as he willed, there appears both wondrous wisdom in arrangement and power in execution.

29 bis. God created certain spirits in such a way that they would always exist; others he created so that at some time they would cease to be spirits. Some of those destined to cease he produced from water, and some from earth, because the Almighty so willed. But he made the higher spirits have no natural association with bodily elements [Note: [Col. 0685D] One Vatican manuscript reads “no association with a body, no association with bodily elements.”]. He created them eternal and implanted in them the capacity and understanding to think about, know, and love the divinity.

Yet he created them in such a way that they would love above themselves the one whose work they recognized had made them what they were, although no merits had preceded their being made such. In order that this love might receive a just and fitting praise, he also granted them freedom of will, so that it would be possible for them either to raise the intention of holy love toward him who is above them, or to incline themselves by the weight of perverse [or: grave] desire toward themselves or toward the things beneath them.

30. There is therefore no nature that can subsist eternally, whether in misery or in blessedness, unless it is able, by God’s gift, to think about God himself. This intellectual nature exists in human souls and angelic spirits. For God has given the capacity to know and love him only to angels and human beings.

Because of freedom of choice—which ought especially to have been conferred upon intellectual creation by the Creator’s kindness [or: goodness]—he gave them the capacity and will to know and love him in such a way that each could possess it and lose it; yet, if anyone willingly lost it, he could not thereafter recover it by his own choice.

It belonged to the gratuitous gift of his goodness to renew again in whomever he wished the beginnings of holy thought [Note: [Col. 0685D] Three manuscripts read this way. One Vatican manuscript has “the beginning,” another “in the beginning.” The printed editions have “to call back again.” Four manuscripts have “to renew.”]. It was also his prerogative, at the beginning of creation, without any preceding merits, to arrange spirits and bodies, places and conditions, wondrously according to fitting circumstances [Note: [Col. 0686D] The printed editions have “fittingly and wondrously.” Six manuscripts read “fitting circumstances, wondrously.”], as he himself in his wisdom willed.

Angels and human beings, therefore, insofar as they were made rational, received from God, at the very creation of their spiritual nature, the gift of eternity and blessedness [Note: [Col. 0686D] So read three manuscripts and the Anticodex. Other printed editions have “within themselves from the Creator of the spiritual nature.”]. They received it in such a way that, if they had continually clung to the love of their Creator, they would have remained eternal and blessed together; but if, by the choice of their own freedom [Note: [Col. 0686D] The printed editions have “of their own will.” Five manuscripts have “of their own freedom.”], they had striven to do their own will against the command of the supreme [or: their] Creator, blessedness would immediately have departed from the rebellious, and miserable eternity would have been left to them for punishment, to be tormented thereafter by errors and pains [Note: [Col. 0686D] The Corbie manuscript reads “subdued by pains.”].

With regard to the angels, he both decreed and fulfilled this: if any of them lost the goodness of his will, he would never restore it by the divine gift [Note: [Col. 0687D] Three Vatican manuscripts read “without the divine gift.” But the reading of the other manuscripts is more likely, where the word “without” is absent.].

31. The part of the angels that departed by wholly voluntary aversion from God their Creator, by whom alone it was blessed, found the beginning of its condemnation in that very aversion of the will, by the judgment of supreme justice. Thus its beginning to be punished consisted in being deprived of the love of that blessed good. God decreed that this entire angelic company should remain in eternal punishment, and he also prepared eternal fire for it.

In that fire all those transgressing angels can never lack either evil will or punishment. The evil of their unjust aversion remains in them, and with it remains the eternal condemnation of just retribution.

The prince of these evils, the devil, who out of envy led the first human beings into the precipice of sin [Note: [Col. 0687D] Two manuscripts read this way. The Corbie manuscript has “into participation in sin.” The printed editions have “to the beginning of sin.”], implanted in them—and not only in them but also in their entire offspring—the deserving of death together with the defect of sin.

But God, merciful and just, just as, when the devil and his angels fell by their own will, he established the other angels in the eternity of his love, so also did not permit the whole mass of the human race to perish forever. Rather, by his gratuitous goodness, he predestined those whom he willed to be brought back to the light, when the darkness in which every human birth is involved through the condemnation of original sin had been driven away [Note: [Col. 0687D] The Corbie manuscript reads “but if he predestined some.”].

In this he especially demonstrated that those whom the undeserved grace of the Liberator would free from the bonds of original sin were not freed by their own merits, while others—and especially infants, in whom no merits of their own will, whether good or evil, can exist [Note: [Col. 0687D] The Corbie manuscript lacks “of their own”; three Vatican manuscripts contain it. Another Vatican manuscript reads “the merit of their own will.” The printed editions have “their own merits.”]—would be held by eternal condemnation in an unbreakable bond.

32. God clearly shows that the beginning of a good will and thought does not arise in human beings from themselves, but is divinely prepared and bestowed, by the fact that neither the devil nor any of his angels, from the time when they were thrust down into this lower darkness on account of the merit of their fall, has been or can be able to recover a good will.

If it were possible for human nature, after turning away from God and losing the goodness of its will, to regain it from itself, this would be far more possible for angelic nature, which, the less it is burdened by the weight of an earthly body, would possess that capacity all the more. But God shows from where good will is given to human beings: the angels lost it even though they possessed it, and after losing it they cannot possess it again.

33. Since the same good will is worthy, through God’s grace, of the reward of eternal blessedness, while angelic and human wickedness ought not to remain unpunished, we faithfully await, according to the rule of the Catholic faith, the coming of the Son of God to punish all sinful angels and to judge the living and the dead.

For blessed Peter testifies that “God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but thrusting them into the prisons of gloomy hell, he handed them over to be kept for punishment in the judgment” (II Peter II, 4).

Regarding the judgment of living and dead human beings, blessed Paul says: “I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, both by his coming and by his kingdom” (II Tim. IV, 1) [Note: [Col. 0688D] One Vatican manuscript reads this way, in accordance with the Greek text of the Apostle. The others do not have the preposition “by.”].

At his coming, from the body of the first human being, which [alternatively: whom] God formed from the earth, to the bodies of all human beings, which at some time began to live after being animated, all will be raised by him through whose activity they were created. Each body will be restored in the resurrection to its own soul, which it began to have in the mother’s womb in order to begin living.

Thus, in the judgment of the just Judge, souls will receive retribution in those same individual bodies of theirs—whether the reward of the kingdom or punishment—in which they possessed either the good or the evil quality of their present life.

34. The origin of an evil life.—The evil quality of life begins with unbelief, which takes its beginning from the guilt of original sin. Whoever begins to live in such a way that he finishes his life before being released from that obligation—even if that soul lived in the body for only one day or one hour—must endure with that same body the endless punishments of Gehenna, where the devil will burn eternally with his angels.

The devil both sinned first and persuaded the first human beings to sin. There, together with him, fornicators, idol-servants, adulterers, the effeminate, those who have intercourse with males, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, slanderers, the rapacious [or: robbers], and all who perform the works of the flesh will be burned in eternal fires if they have not turned from their evil ways before the end of this life—concerning whom the blessed Apostle says that “they will not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal. V, 21).

For every human being who remains in this world until the end in delight in wickedness [Note: [Col. 0688D] Five manuscripts have “in love of wickedness … the harmful love of crimes.”] and hardness of heart will be held by eternal torment without end, just as the harmful delight of crimes held him here.

35. The bodies of the wicked.—There will also be a resurrection of the wicked, but without the transformation that God will give only to the faithful and to those who live justly from faith [Note: [Col. 0688D] One Vatican manuscript reads “and in faith.”]. For blessed Paul says: “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be transformed” (I Cor. XV, 51). Showing that the just will be changed by a divine gift, he says: “And we shall be changed” (ibid., 52).

The wicked, therefore, will share with the just a common resurrection of the flesh, but they will not have the grace of transformation [Note: [Col. 0688D] One Vatican manuscript reads “the transformation of the flesh”; another, “the transformation, however.”] that will be given to the just. For corruption, dishonor, and weakness—the conditions in which the bodies of the wicked are sown—will not be removed from them. For this reason they will not be extinguished even by death, so that that continual torment may be the punishment of eternal death for body and soul.

But the just souls whom God the Redeemer freely justified here through faith, and to whom he granted perseverance in living well to the end [Note: [Col. 0689D] One manuscript reads “he granted the grace and perseverance of living well to the end”; another, “he gave it.”], will possess the eternal blessedness of the heavenly kingdom in those same bodies in which they received here the grace of justification from God and in which, justified through faith, they lived in the love of God and of their neighbor.

Their bodies too will be glorified. Without doubt, the nature of the flesh that God created will truly remain, but they will then possess bodies that are spiritual rather than animal, as here. For “the animal body is sown; the spiritual body will rise.” In these bodies, through that transformation which will be given only to the just, what the Apostle says must happen will be fulfilled (I Cor. XV, 53): “This corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality.”

The male and female sexes will remain in them, just as the same bodies were created; their glory, however, will differ according to the diversity of their good works. Nevertheless, all bodies, whether of males or females, whatever bodies will be in that kingdom, will be glorious. The Judge knows how much glory he is to give each one, because by mercy he freely preceded with justification in this life those whom he has determined [or: determined beforehand] to glorify there by justice.

36. God has given human beings the time for acquiring eternal life only in this present life, in which he also willed repentance to be fruitful. Repentance is fruitful here because here a person can lay aside wickedness and live well, and, having changed an unjust will [Note: [Col. 0689D] Five manuscripts do not have “unjust.”], can change his merits and works at the same time, and perform in the fear of God those things that please God.

Whoever does not do this in the present life will indeed have repentance in the future age for his evil deeds, but he will not find forgiveness in the sight of God. For although there will be there the goad of repentance, there will no longer be any correction of the will. Such people will condemn their own wickedness in such a way that they will in no way be able either to love or desire righteousness.

Their will will be such that it will always contain within itself the punishment of its wickedness, yet will never be able to receive an affection for goodness. For just as those who will reign with Christ will have no remnants of evil will within themselves, so those who will be assigned with the devil and his angels to the punishment of eternal fire will have no rest thereafter and will in no way be able to have a good will.

And just as the perfection of grace will be given to Christ’s co-heirs for eternal glory, so wickedness itself will heap up punishment upon the devil’s companions, when, assigned to outer darkness, they will be illumined by no inner light of truth.

37. The keys of Peter.—Therefore repentance can be useful to every human being in this life. Whenever a person undertakes it—however wicked or advanced in years he may be—if he renounces his past sins with his whole heart, sheds before God tears not only of the body but also of the heart for them, and takes care to wash away the stains of evil works by good works, he will immediately receive forgiveness for all his sins.

For the Lord promises this to us in prophetic speech, saying: “If you turn back and groan, you shall be saved” (Isa. XXX, 15, according to the Septuagint). And elsewhere it is said: “My son, you have sinned; do not add to it again, but pray concerning your past sins, that they may be forgiven you” (Ecclus. XXI, 1). Prayer for sins would never have been prescribed to the sinner if forgiveness were not to be granted to the one who prays.

But repentance benefits the sinner only if he practices it in the Catholic Church. To the Church God, in the person of blessed Peter, granted the power of binding and loosing, saying: “Whatever [or: Whatsoever] you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 9).

Whenever, therefore, a person of any age undertakes true repentance for his sins and, with God’s illumination, corrects his life, he will not be deprived of the gift of forgiveness. For, as God says through the prophet, he does not desire the death of the one who dies [Note: [Col. 0689D] Six manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have “he does not desire the death of the sinner, or of the one who dies, but rather”; two Vatican manuscripts have “but only that.”], but rather that he turn back from his evil way and that his soul live (Ezek. XXXIII, 11).

38. Nevertheless, no one ought to remain longer in his sins under the hope of God’s mercy, just as, even in the body, no one wishes to remain ill longer under the hope of future health. For those who neglect to withdraw from their iniquities and promise themselves forgiveness from God [alternatively, Dei: of God] are sometimes overtaken by God’s sudden wrath in such a way that they find neither time for conversion nor the benefit of forgiveness.

Therefore Holy Scripture kindly warns each one of us, saying: “Do not delay turning to God, and do not put it off from day to day; for his wrath will come suddenly, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you” (Ecclus. V, 8). Blessed David also says: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Ps. XCIV, 8).

Blessed Paul likewise agrees with him in these words: “Take care, brothers, lest perhaps there be in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief” [Note: [Col. 0690D] One Vatican manuscript reads “infidelity of the carnal.”] “in departing from the living God. But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called ‘Today,’ so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Heb. III, 12–13).

The hardened person therefore lives [Note: [Col. 0690D] So read the printed editions. Two manuscripts have “The person hardened in heart therefore lives”; another, “He therefore lives in hardness.”] either by failing to turn back and despairing of forgiveness for his sins [Note: [Col. 0690D] The Corbie manuscript reads “by despairing of forgiveness for his sins.”], or by hoping for God’s mercy in such a way that he remains [or: persists] until the end of his present life in the perversity of his crimes.

39. **Sin against the Holy Spirit.**—Therefore, let us love the mercy of God and fear his justice; let us neither despair of the forgiveness of sins nor remain in sins, knowing that the equity of the most just Judge will exact all those debts of human beings which the mercy of the most merciful Redeemer has not remitted. For just as mercy receives and absolves those who turn back, so justice will reject and punish the hardened. These are those who sin against the Holy Spirit and will receive no forgiveness of their sins, neither in this age nor in the age to come.

The human soul is therefore an intellectual spirit so that it may seek, recognize, and discern both the time of its actions, for which it is to receive recompense at the judgment ordained by divine justice, and the time of that same recompense, when it will no longer be permitted either to change its deeds or profitably to ask divine mercy for the forgiveness of its sins.

The other spirits of all animals, however, which possess no understanding, since some of them derive their origin from the earth and others from the waters—for reptiles and birds are from the waters, while from the earth arose some creatures that creep and others that walk—are spirits only so long as they live in bodies. For a soul that was not divinely made capable of reason begins and ends its life together with its flesh: when it no longer gives life to the body, it too does not live. Thus, although the soul is in a wondrous way the cause of life for all flesh [Note: [Col. 0691D] Vatican manuscript: “although every soul in flesh is the cause of life.”], an irrational spirit lives only as long as it can remain in the flesh; and when it is separated from its flesh, it is extinguished [Note: [Col. 0691D] Three manuscripts: “is weakened.”]. Thus it happens that, although it is itself the life of its flesh, it cannot live when it ceases to supply life to the flesh; and if there is no flesh to which it can give life, it too immediately no longer possesses life.

Therefore neither was eternity given to irrational spirits, nor is any judgment prepared for them in which blessedness for good deeds or condemnation for evil deeds might be repaid to them. For this reason no distinction of deeds is required of them, because they have received from God no capacity for understanding. Their bodies therefore will not rise again, because their souls possessed neither justice nor injustice for which eternal blessedness or punishment should be repaid to them.

40. [Note: [Col. 0691D] “Therefore” is absent from four manuscripts.] Those animals carry out the course and ornament of the present age according to the incomprehensible will of the Creator; they will give no account of their deeds, because they are not rational. For is God concerned with oxen? (1 Cor. V, 10.)

Human beings, however, because they were made rational, will give an account to God both of themselves and of all the things they received for the use of this present life, and according to the quality of their actions they will receive either punishment or glory. For “we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to him according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. V, 10). This will occur, of course, when, according to the utterance of our own Creator and Redeemer: “All who are in the tombs will hear his voice; and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John V, 28–29).

Thus those who have done evil will go into eternal fire, forever to burn with the devil, the prince of all evils; but those who have done good will go into eternal life, to reign without end with Christ, the King of all ages. Those will reign with Christ whom God, by his gratuitous goodness, predestined for the kingdom. For because, by predestining them, he prepared them to be such that they would be worthy of the kingdom, he prepared them to be called according to his purpose, so that they might obey; he prepared them to be justified, so that, having received grace, they might believe rightly and live well; he also prepared them to be glorified, so that, having become coheirs with Christ, they might possess the kingdom of heaven without end.

[Col. 0692B] **41. Baptism is not to be repeated.**—To that kingdom, at various times, through the sacraments that Christ instituted for faith in his incarnation, came those whom God saved freely, with no merit of good will or good work preceding. From the time when our Savior said, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 5), no one can receive the kingdom of heaven or eternal life without the sacrament [Note: [Col. 0691D] One Vatican manuscript: “without the sacrament”] of baptism—except those who, in the Catholic Church, shed their blood for Christ without baptism.

For whether someone receives the sacrament of baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit in the Catholic Church, in any heresy, or in a schism, he receives the sacrament intact; [Col. 0692C] but he will not have the salvation that is the power of the sacrament if he has received that sacrament outside the Catholic Church. Therefore he must return to the Church, not in order to receive the sacrament of baptism again—for no one ought to repeat it in any baptized person—but in order to receive eternal life within the Catholic fellowship. No one can ever be fit to attain that life if, while possessing the sacrament of baptism, he remains alienated from the Catholic Church.

Even if he gives abundant alms and sheds his blood for the name of Christ, he will not have eternal salvation because in this life he did not maintain the unity of the Catholic Church. For wherever baptism can benefit someone, there almsgiving too can benefit him. Baptism, however, can exist outside the Church, but it cannot benefit anyone unless it is within the Church.

[Col. 0692D] **42. The Catholic Church.**—Therefore, only in the Catholic Church can baptism, the performance of works of mercy, and the glorious confession of Christ’s name benefit anyone, provided that he lives well in the Catholic Church. [Page 520.] For just as, without fellowship with the Catholic Church, neither baptism nor works of mercy can benefit anyone—unless perhaps so that he may be tortured less severely, though not so that he may be counted among the children of God—so within the Catholic Church eternal life is not acquired through baptism alone if one lives wickedly after baptism.

Those who live well must also devote themselves continually to works of mercy, knowing that, although light, they nevertheless contract certain sins every day. For these sins even holy and just people must always say to God in this life: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12). The more frequently these sins creep upon human beings even in things that are lawful and granted by God, and the more the body is filled with stronger foods and the human heart is entangled in carnal actions and desires, the more frequently guilt is contracted in this mortal life.

**43. Abstinence.**—For this reason the humble servants of Christ, who desire to serve their Lord without hindrance and without harmful occupation of mind, do not desire marriage at all and abstain from meat and wine insofar as bodily health permits. This is not because it is a sin to have a spouse or to consume wine or meat. For the blessed Apostle also says: “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (1 Tim. IV, 4–5).

God both instituted and blessed marriage among the first human beings (Gen. II, 22). Therefore the Apostle says: “Marriage is honorable in all, and the marriage-bed undefiled” (Heb. XIII, 4). Thus [Note: [Col. 0693D] The printed editions have “Therefore”; seven manuscripts have “Thus.”] the servants of God, in abstaining from meat and wine, do not shun them as unclean things, but follow the discipline of a purer life; and in not marrying they do not consider the goodness of marriage to be a crime, but do not doubt that perpetual continence is better than good marriage—especially in the present time, when it is said concerning continence: “He who is able to receive this, let him receive it” (Matt. XIX, 12), while concerning marriage it is said: “If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry” (1 Cor. VII, 9).

In the one case virtue is raised by exhortation [Note: [Col. 0693D] The printed editions read, “For in one reasoning virtue arises.” The better reading restored here is based on the Corbie manuscript. Two Vatican manuscripts have, “For in one prayer virtue arises” (two others: “of prayer”). Two English manuscripts have, “by prayer virtue is exercised.”]; in the other, weakness is relieved by a remedy. Since one must always take account of infirmity, therefore, if someone first happens to be deprived of a spouse and wishes to enter a second or even a third marriage, he will have no sin from those marriages if he preserves them chastely—that is, if one man and one woman, joined lawfully, keep faith, so that neither man has intercourse with a woman other than his wife nor woman with a man other than her husband.

In such matters, even if some marital excess has occurred, provided that it does not violate the lawful marriage-bed, there will be some sin, but venial sin [Note: [Col. 0693D] One manuscript: “he will have not mortal but venial sin.”].

**44. The vow of continence.**—But these provisions concern those who have vowed no continence to God. Whoever, however, has made himself celibate for the sake of the kingdom of heaven and has vowed continence in his heart will incur condemnation, according to the Apostle’s judgment (1 Tim. V, 12), not only if he is stained by the deadly crime [al. wound] of fornication, but also if a man wishes to take a wife or a woman to marry, because he has nullified his first faith.

Therefore, just as, according to the Apostle’s judgment (1 Cor. VII, 3), it is right for a husband to render the marital debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband—for if someone takes a wife, he does not sin, and if a virgin marries, she does not sin—so, according to the same Apostle’s statement, whoever is firm in his heart, having no necessity but possessing power over his own will, and vows continence to God, must guard it with complete attentiveness of mind until the end, lest he incur condemnation by nullifying his first faith.

Likewise, married men or married women who, by mutual consent, vow perpetual continence to God should know that they are bound by their vow [Note: [Col. 0693D] One Vatican manuscript: “that they are held by the bond of their vow.”]. They must no longer claim for themselves the intercourse of the flesh, which they formerly possessed lawfully, but must understand that they owe God the continence they vowed [Note: [Col. 0693D] One Vatican manuscript: “but must understand that they must preserve the continence they owe to God.”].

Then each person will possess the kingdom of heaven, which is promised to the saints, if, forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, he vows willingly what he knows to be lawful and to pertain to the advancement of a better life, and quickly fulfills it, according to what is said in the Psalms: “Vow and pay to the Lord your God” (Ps. LXXV, 12), and if, in fulfilling his vow, he continually advances with ever better effort [Note: [Col. 0694D] One Vatican manuscript: “and faithfully fulfills it.”]. For to everyone who vows to God and fulfills what he has vowed, God himself will also repay the rewards of the heavenly kingdom that he promised.

**CHAPTER IV, or FIRST RULE. The divine nature.**—45. [Col. 0694C] [Note: [Col. 0694D] Up to this point the text is read as continuous prose in the Corbie manuscript. From here to the end, each of the forty rules is designated by its own number.] Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are naturally one God, in whose name we have been baptized. For although “Father” is one name, “Son” another, and “Holy Spirit” another, nevertheless “God” is the one name of the nature of these three. He says in Deuteronomy: “See, see that I am God, and there is no other” [Note: [Col. 0694D] Three Vatican manuscripts and the Corbie manuscript read “See, see”; the others read it only once.] [Note: [Col. 0694D] Two Vatican manuscripts: “there is no other God”] besides me (Deut. XXXII, 9). Of him it is also said: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord” [al. “one God”] (Deut. VI, 4); and, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (ibid., 13).

**CHAPTER V, or SECOND RULE. One God.**—46. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the holy Trinity—are the one true God by nature. Although it is not permitted us to worship three gods, but only one true God [Note: [Col. 0694D] One Vatican manuscript: “the true and almighty God”], nevertheless, just as the Father is called true God, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “You turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God and to await his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus” (1 Thess. I, 9), so the apostle John commends the Son as true God, saying: “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and be in his true Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John V, 20).

Since he is certainly true God, he is also Truth, as he himself teaches us, saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). The apostle John also says of the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit is truth” [Note: [Col. 0695D] One manuscript: “because he is truth.”] (1 John V, 6). Certainly, he who is Truth cannot by nature fail to be true God.

The apostle Paul also confesses him as God, saying: “Your members are a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own. For you were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. VI, 19–20).

[Col. 0695B] **CHAPTER VI, or THIRD RULE. The eternal God.**—47. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the holy Trinity—are one true God, everlasting and without beginning. Therefore it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. He was in the beginning with God” (John I, 1–2). This eternity is again declared in the Psalm where it says: “But God our King is before the ages” (Ps. LXXIII, 12); and elsewhere: “His eternal power and divinity” (Rom. I, 20).

**CHAPTER VII, or FOURTH RULE. The immutable God.**—48. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the holy Trinity alone is the true God and, just as eternal, is naturally alone immutable. For this is what he signifies when he says to his servant Moses: “I am who am” (Exod. III, 14).

Hence it is also said in the Psalms [Note: [Col. 0695D] So four manuscripts. The printed editions read, “Hence the Psalm also says.” The Corbie manuscript has, “To this it is also said in the Psalms.”]: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain, and all of them will grow old like a garment; and like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail” [Note: [Col. 0695D] Three manuscripts omit these words] (Ps. CI, 26–28).

**CHAPTER VIII, or FIFTH RULE. God, creator of all things.**—49. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the holy Trinity alone is the true God, creator of all visible and invisible things. Of him it is said in the Psalms: “Blessed is he whose God is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them” (Ps. CXLV, 5–6). Of him the Apostle also says: “From him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory forever” [Note: [Col. 0695D] One manuscript: “forever and ever. Amen.”] (Rom. XI, 36).

**CHAPTER IX, or SIXTH RULE. The Trinity in unity.**—50. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one nature, but are three persons. The Father alone is the one who said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17). The Son alone is the one over whom the voice of the Father alone resounded when the only-begotten God, who alone assumed flesh, was baptized in the Jordan according to the flesh.

The Holy Spirit alone is the Spirit of the Father and the Son who descended in the form of a dove upon Christ as he was baptized and rising from the water; and on the fiftieth day after the resurrection, he came upon Christ’s faithful gathered in one place and filled them in the division [Note: [Col. 0696D] The Corbie manuscript has this reading; the printed editions have “vision.”] of tongues of fire.

That voice, therefore, by which God the Father alone spoke; that flesh by which the only-begotten God alone became human; that dove in whose form the Holy Spirit descended upon Christ; and those tongues of fire (Acts II, 3), in whose division he filled the faithful gathered in one place [Note: [Col. 0696D] The printed editions read “the faithful apostles.” Five manuscripts omit “apostles”]—all these are works of the entire holy Trinity, that is, of the one God who made all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible.

[Col. 0696B] **CHAPTER X, or SEVENTH RULE. The distinction of the persons.**—51. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that God the Son, that is, one person of the Trinity, is the Son of God the Father alone; but that the Holy Spirit, himself also one person of the Trinity, is the Spirit not of the Father alone but of the Father and the Son together.

For, showing that he alone was begotten of the Father, the Son of God says [Note: [Col. 0696D] One manuscript: “For he shows ... when he says”]: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John III, 16); and shortly afterward: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (ibid., 18).

The Apostle teaches that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of both the Father and the Son when he says: “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Rom. VIII, 9). And he continues [Note: [Col. 0696D] Three manuscripts: “and, continuing, he says”]: “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his” (ibid.).

**CHAPTER XI, or EIGHTH RULE. The Holy Spirit.**—52. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the same Holy Spirit, who is the one Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeds from the Father and the Son.

For the Son says: “When the Spirit of truth comes, who proceeds from the Father” (John XV, 26), thereby teaching that the Spirit is his, because he himself is Truth (John XIV, 6).

Prophetic and apostolic teaching also commends to us that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. Isaiah says of the Son: “He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he will slay the wicked” (Isa. XI, 4). Of him the Apostle also says: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thess. II, 8).

The only-begotten Son of God himself also signified that this Spirit was the breath of his mouth when, after his resurrection, he breathed upon the disciples and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX, 22). John says in the Apocalypse concerning the mouth of the Lord Jesus himself that a two-edged sword proceeded from it (Rev. I, 16). Therefore that breath of his mouth is itself the sword that proceeds from his mouth.

**CHAPTER XII, or NINTH RULE. The Trinity confined by no boundaries.**—53. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the Trinity is God immeasurable in power, not in bulk, and that every spiritual and bodily creature is held together by his power and presence.

For God the Father says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII, 24). It is also said of the Wisdom of God, who is his Son, that “she reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII, 1). We also read of the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. I, 7). The prophet David says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 7).

**CHAPTER XIII, or TENTH RULE. The person of the Son.**—54. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that one person of the Trinity, namely God the Son, who alone was born from the nature of God the Father and is of one and the same nature with the Father, was himself, in the fullness of time, voluntarily conceived in the Virgin and born from the Virgin through the assumption of the form of a servant, the Word made flesh.

He is also the one who was born essentially from the Father [Note: [Col. 0697D] One manuscript: “and who was essentially born from the Father and temporally conceived and born essentially from the Virgin mother; the same ...”], and who was essentially conceived and born from the Virgin; and he is one and of one nature with the Father and of one nature [Note: [Col. 0697D] These words, “with the Father and of one nature,” are absent from the printed editions and are supplied from the Corbie manuscript] with the Virgin.

Of the God the Father he says: “Before the ages he established me, and before all the hills he begot me” (Prov. VIII, 22, 26). Of him the Apostle also said: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law” (Gal. IV, 4).

**CHAPTER XIV, or ELEVENTH RULE. The humanity of Christ.**—55. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that Christ the Son of God, just as he was begotten from God the Father as complete and perfect God, was begotten from the Virgin mother as complete and perfect human being [Note: [Col. 0697D] The Corbie manuscript: “God-man”]—that is, the Word God possessing, without sin, true flesh and a rational soul of our race [Note: [Col. 0697D] One Vatican manuscript: “the same Word of God, possessing without sin the true flesh of our race”].

The Son of God himself clearly shows this when he says of his flesh: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke XXIV, 39). He also shows by these words that he has a soul: “For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my soul, and I take it up again” (John X, 17) [Note: [Col. 0697D] Four manuscripts: “I shall take it up.”]. He shows that his soul also possesses understanding by saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29).

And God says of him through the prophet: “Behold, my servant will understand, and he will be exalted and raised up, and he will be very high” (Isa. LII, 13). The blessed Peter also confesses, according to the prophecy of holy David, that Christ possesses flesh and a soul.

Speaking of the blessed David himself, he says [Note: [Col. 0697D] One Vatican manuscript: “Speaking of the blessed David himself, the prophet says: ‘For you will not abandon my soul in hell.’”]: “Since he was a prophet and knew that God had sworn to him with an oath that one of the fruit of his loins would sit upon his throne, he foresaw and spoke of the resurrection of Christ, that neither was his soul abandoned in hell nor did his flesh see corruption” (Acts II, 30–31).

**CHAPTER XV, or TWELFTH RULE. The divinity of Christ.**—56. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the one and the same is God the Word [Note: [Col. 0698D] The printed editions read, “one Son, and the same is true God.” The reading of three manuscripts seems more coherent], who, together with God the Father and God the Holy Spirit, made all times, and on Mount Sinai gave Moses the law (Exod. XX–XXI), arranged through angels (Gal. III, 19); and that this same Word, God made flesh, when the fullness of time came, was sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit, and alone was made from the woman whom he made, and alone was made under the law (Gal. IV, 4) that he had given.

**CHAPTER XVI, or THIRTEENTH RULE. The two natures in Christ.**—57. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the two natures of the Word of God who was made flesh remain without confusion [Col. 0698B] and without separation [Note: [Col. 0698D] The Corbie manuscript and three Vatican manuscripts have “and inseparably.” The others omit these words and have “the Word of God ... in two natures,” but corruptly].

One is the true divine nature, which he shares with the Father, according to which he says: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30); “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 9); and, “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (ibid., 10). According to this nature the Apostle calls him “the radiance of glory and the figure of God’s substance” (Heb. I, 3) [Note: [Col. 0698D] Three manuscripts have this reading. One Vatican manuscript has, “according to which the Apostle also says, ‘the radiance of glory and the figure of his substance.’”].

The other is the true human nature [Note: [Col. 0698D] Two Vatican manuscripts: “the other, however”; another Vatican manuscript: “the other, however, true”], according to which the same incarnate God says: “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28).

**CHAPTER XVII, or FOURTEENTH RULE. The unity of the person in Christ.**—58. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the Word of God made flesh has one person of his divinity and his flesh.

For God the Word graciously united the complete human nature to himself truly and in such a way that, while his divinity remained [Note: [Col. 0698D] One Vatican manuscript: “the nature of his divinity”], the Word became flesh. Although the Word is not naturally identical with the flesh, since the truth of two natures remains in Christ, nevertheless, according to one person, the same Word became flesh from the beginning of his mother’s conception.

God the Word did not assume a human person but a human nature; and into the eternal person of his divinity he assumed the temporal substance of flesh. Therefore there is one Christ, the Word made flesh (John I, 14), who is from the fathers according to the flesh and “God blessed above all forever” (Rom. IX, 5).

There is one Jesus, to whom the Father also says: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 3). Here an eternal birth without beginning, before all time, is signified. Of him the evangelist also says that his name was called Jesus, as the angel had said, before he was conceived in the womb (Luke II, 21) [Note: [Col. 0698D] The printed editions repeat “one Jesus”; it is absent from six manuscripts].

**CHAPTER XVIII, or FIFTEENTH RULE. The union of the Word and the flesh.**—59. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the flesh of Christ was not conceived in the Virgin’s womb without divinity, before it was assumed by the Word; rather, God the Word himself was conceived through the taking of his flesh, and the flesh itself was conceived through the incarnation of the Word (III Sent., dist. 2, chapter “Si autem”).

**CHAPTER XIX, or SIXTEENTH RULE. Sacrifices. The sacrifice of bread and wine.**—60. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the only-begotten God the Word made flesh offered himself for us as a sacrifice and victim to God “for a fragrant odor” (Eph. V, 2). To him, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, animals were sacrificed by patriarchs, prophets, and priests during the time of the Old Testament; and to him now, that is, in the time of the New Testament, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, with whom he has one divinity, the holy Catholic Church does not cease to offer throughout the entire world, in faith and charity, the sacrifice of bread and wine.

In those carnal victims there was a sign [al. figure] of Christ’s flesh, which he himself, without sin, was going to offer for our sins, and of the blood that he was going to pour out for the remission of our sins. In this sacrifice, however, there is thanksgiving and commemoration of the flesh of Christ, which he offered for us, and of the blood that the same God poured out for us.

The blessed Paul says of this in the Acts of the Apostles: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to rule the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood” (Acts XX, 28).

In those sacrifices, therefore, what was to be given to us was signified figuratively; but in this sacrifice what has already been given to us is shown plainly. In those sacrifices it was foretold that the Son of God would be killed for the ungodly; but in this sacrifice it is proclaimed that he has been killed for the ungodly. The Apostle testifies that “while we were still weak, at the appointed time Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. V, 6), and that “while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (ibid., 10).

[Page 526] **CHAPTER XX, or SEVENTEENTH RULE. The humanity of Christ.**—61. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the Word made flesh always possesses the same true human flesh in which God the Word was born from the Virgin, in which he was crucified and died, in which he rose again and ascended into heaven, and sat [al. sits] at the right hand of God, and in which he will also come to judge the living and the dead.

Therefore the apostles heard from the angels: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I, 11). The blessed John says: “Behold, he will come with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him” [Note: [Col. 0699D] So five manuscripts. The printed editions have “crucified him”], “and all the tribes of the earth will see him such” [Note: [Col. 0699D] One Vatican manuscript adds: “namely, as the one they despised”; the others do not add this] (Rev. I, 7).

**CHAPTER XXI, or EIGHTEENTH RULE. Nature is wholly good.**—62. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the Trinity, God—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is naturally the supreme and immutable good; and that all natures were created by him. They are good, because they were made by the supreme good [Note: [Col. 0699D] One manuscript: “made good by the supreme good”], but mutable [Note: [Col. 0699D] These words, “but mutable,” and what follows are absent from two Vatican manuscripts], because they were made from nothing. There is no nature of evil [Note: [Col. 0699D] So six manuscripts. The printed editions have “an evil nature”], because every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good.

But because the good in it can be diminished or increased, it is called evil insofar as its good is diminished. For evil is nothing other than the privation of good.

Hence it is established that rational creation has a twofold evil: one by which it voluntarily fell away from its supreme good, its Creator; the other by which, unwillingly, it will be punished with the penalty of eternal fire. It will suffer the latter justly because it committed the former unjustly; and because it did not preserve within itself the order of divine institution [Note: [Col. 0699D] Five manuscripts: “and because it did not preserve ...”; one Vatican manuscript: “of the divine constitution”], it will not escape the order of divine retribution.

**CHAPTER XXII, or NINETEENTH RULE. No creature is identical with God.**—63. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that neither angels nor any other creature is of the same nature as that which the supreme Trinity possesses according to its natural divinity—that Trinity which is naturally one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

For the maker and the things he made could not be of one nature [Note: [Col. 0700D] Seven manuscripts read *esse poterant* (“could be”) for *esse potuerunt* (“could have been”).].

**CHAPTER XXIII, or TWENTIETH RULE. The angels made steadfast.**—64. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that every creature, naturally mutable, was made by the immutable God. Nevertheless, none of the holy angels can now be changed for the worse, because they received eternal blessedness, in which they enjoy God steadfastly, in such a way that they cannot be deprived of it.

But this very inability to be changed for the worse from the state of blessedness in which they are was not naturally implanted in them; rather, after they were created, it was bestowed by the generosity of divine grace [Note: [Col. 0700D] Three manuscripts: “this very thing by which ...”]. For if the angels had been made naturally immutable, the devil and his angels would never have fallen from their fellowship.

**CHAPTER XXIV, or TWENTY-FIRST RULE. Rational creatures.**—65. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that among every creature, spiritual and bodily, made by the supreme Trinity, only angelic and human spirits received from God the capacity for understanding. The other spirits, those of brute animals, received neither reason nor understanding, nor can they possess these at all.

Therefore it is said to human beings: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. XXXI, 19). For this reason the souls of human beings and the souls of animals are not of one nature; nor can the souls of animals ever pass into human beings [Note: [Col. 0700D] So four manuscripts. The printed editions have “into human souls ... into animal souls”], nor the souls of human beings into animals.

**CHAPTER XXV, or TWENTY-SECOND RULE. Adam’s free will.**—66. Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the first human beings—that is, Adam and his wife—were created good, upright, and without sin, with free will, by which they could, if they wished, always serve and obey God with humble and good will [Note: [Col. 0700D] These words, “always serve God,” are found in the Corbie manuscript but not in the printed editions].

By that same will they could also, if they wished, sin of their own accord. They sinned not by necessity but by their own will; and through that sin human nature was so changed for the worse that not only did death gain dominion in the first human beings themselves through sin, but the dominion of sin and death also passed to all human beings.

## CHAPTER XXVI, or RULE XXIII. Original Sin

**67.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that every human being conceived through the intercourse of a man and a woman is born with original sin, subject to ungodliness, subjected to death, and therefore born by nature a child of wrath. Of this wrath the Apostle says: “For we too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3). No one is freed from this wrath except through faith in the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus [Col. 0701B], who was conceived without sin, born without sin, and died without sin, and was made sin for us—that is, he was made a sacrifice for our sins. For in the Old Testament the sacrifices offered for sins were called “sins”; in all of them Christ was signified, because he is “the Lamb [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “the one, immaculate Lamb.”] of God who takes away the sins” (or: “sin”) “of the world” (John 1:29).

## CHAPTER XXVII, or RULE XXIV. The Punishment of the Unbaptized

**68.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that not only human beings who already possess reason, but also infants—whether they begin to live in their mothers’ wombs and die there, or, having already been born from their mothers, depart from this world without the sacrament of holy baptism, which is administered in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit—are to be punished by the everlasting torment of eternal fire. For although they have committed no sin through their own action, they have nevertheless drawn the condemnation of original sin through carnal conception and birth.

## CHAPTER XXVIII, or RULE XXV. Judgment

**69.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that Christ the Son of God will come to judge the living and the dead in order to raise up and glorify at his coming those human beings whom here, by the gift of his grace, he freely justifies through faith, and to whom, once justified, he grants perseverance in faith and the love of holy Mother Church unto the end; and, according to his promise, to make them equal to the holy angels and bring them to that state in which they will be perfectly good, insofar as God grants this to each one, and thereafter cannot be changed from that perfection. There the glory of the saints will be diverse, but the eternal life of all will be one.

But Christ will send the devil and his angels into eternal fire, where they will never be without the punishment that divine justice has prepared for them. With the devil himself, he will send the ungodly and unrighteous human beings of whom Scripture says: “But those who are on his side imitate him” (Wis. 2:25), because they imitated him in evil works and did not perform fitting repentance before the end of this present life; after receiving their bodies again, they will burn in the punishment of eternal conflagration.

## CHAPTER XXIX, or RULE XXVI. The Resurrection of the Flesh

**70.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that at the Lord’s coming there will be a common resurrection of the flesh for all human beings, both good and evil; but that God’s retribution in justice will be unlike for the good and the evil, according to what the Apostle says: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51).

The righteous, however, who will go into eternal life, will be changed. The Apostle demonstrates this when he says: “And the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (ibid., 52). Showing what this change will be, he added: “For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” (v. 53).

In the bodies of the righteous what the Apostle himself says will take place: “It is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it will rise in glory; it is sown in weakness, it will rise in power; it is sown an animal body, it will rise a spiritual body” (ibid., 42 ff.). He called it “spiritual” not because that body itself will be a spirit, but because, being made alive by the Spirit, it will remain immortal and incorruptible. A body will then rightly be called “spiritual” when it is not a spirit but remains a body, just as it is now called “animal” even though it is found to be not a soul but a body.

## CHAPTER XXX, or RULE XXVII. Faith and Baptism

**71.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that, except for those who are baptized in their own blood for the name of Christ, no human being will receive eternal life who has not here been turned away from his evils through repentance and faith [Note: One manuscript reads: “through mercy and faith”] and freed through the sacrament of faith and repentance—that is, through baptism.

For adults it is necessary both to repent of their evils, to hold the Catholic faith according to the rule of truth, and to receive the sacrament of baptism [Col. 0702C]. But for infants, who can neither believe by their own will nor repent for the sin that they bear originally, the sacrament of faith and repentance—which is holy baptism—is sufficient for salvation for as long as their age is incapable of reason.

[Note: One manuscript omits “and repentance,” as do the printed editions. Four manuscripts read it. One manuscript has: “which is the second baptism.”]

## CHAPTER XXXI, or RULE XXVIII. Grace

**72.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that no human being can practice repentance here unless God has enlightened that person and converted him or her through his free mercy. For the Apostle says: “Lest perhaps God may grant them repentance for the recognition of the truth, and they may recover from the devil’s snares” (2 Tim. 2:25).

## CHAPTER XXXII, or RULE XXIX. Nothing Is Accomplished without Grace

**73.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that a person whom neither ignorance of letters nor any weakness or adversity prevents can indeed read the words of the holy Law and the Gospel, or hear them from the mouth of some preacher [Col. 0702D]; but no one can obey the divine commandments unless God has first come to that person with his grace, so that what he hears with the body he may also receive with the heart, and, having received from God a good will and strength, may both desire and be able to fulfill God’s commandments.

“For neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7); he also works in us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will (Phil. 2:13).

## CHAPTER XXXIII, or RULE XXX. Nothing Is Hidden from God

**74.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that for the immutable God not only all past and present things but also all future things are immutably known, to whom it is said: “O God, knower of hidden things, who know all things before they come to be” (Dan. 13:42).

## CHAPTER XXXIV, or RULE XXXI. Predestination

**75.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that the immutable Triune God, the most certain knower of all things and works, both his own and human [Note: Two manuscripts read “creator”], knew before all ages to whom he would bestow grace through faith [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “through faith inspired by him”]. Without this grace no one from the beginning of the world to its end could be absolved from the guilt of either original or actual sin.

“For those whom God foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” [Note: Six manuscripts read: “his Son.”] (Rom. 8:29).

## CHAPTER XXXV, or RULE XXXII. The Blessed Are So through Predestination

**76.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that all whom God makes vessels of mercy by his free goodness were predestined by God, before the foundation of the world, for adoption as the children of God; and that none of those whom God predestined to the kingdom of heaven can perish, nor can any of those whom God did not predestine to life be saved by any means.

For that predestination is the preparation of a free gift, concerning which the Apostle says that we were “predestined for adoption as children, through Jesus Christ, in him” (Eph. 1:5).

[Note: The word “of God,” found in the printed editions, is absent from the Corbie manuscript and from the Apostle’s text.]

## CHAPTER XXXVI, or RULE XXXIII. Baptism

**77.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that the sacrament of baptism can exist not only within the Catholic Church but also among heretics who baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; but outside the Catholic Church it cannot be beneficial [Note: One manuscript reads: “cannot benefit those who have been baptized”]. Indeed, just as within the Church salvation is conferred through the sacrament of baptism upon those who rightly believe, so outside the Church those who have been baptized, if they do not return to the Church, accumulate ruin through that same baptism (I, question I, chapter “Firmissime”).

The unity of ecclesiastical fellowship has such value for salvation that baptism does not save a person when it is not given there where it ought to be given. Nevertheless, baptism is present in a person baptized even outside the Church, but it is present for judgment in one separated from the Church [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “Nevertheless, baptism is present in a person baptized outside the Church … but … is present.”].

And because it is clear that, wherever it has been given, this baptism is to be given only once, therefore, even if it has been given by heretics in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, it must be reverently acknowledged and for this reason must never be repeated. For the Savior says: “The one who has bathed once does not need anything except to wash the feet” (John 13:10).

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “does not need to be washed except to wash the feet.”]

## CHAPTER XXXVII, or RULE XXXIV. There Is No Salvation Outside the Church

**78.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that no one baptized outside the Catholic Church can become a participant in eternal life if that person has not, before the end of this life, been restored to and incorporated into the Catholic Church. For the Apostle says: “If I have all faith and know all the mysteries, but do not have love, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2). For in the days of the Flood also, we read that no one outside the ark could be saved.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII, or RULE XXXV. Those Who Are to Be Condemned

**79.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that not only all pagans, but also all Jews, and all heretics and schismatics who end their present life outside the Catholic Church, will go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. 25:41).

## CHAPTER XXXIX, or RULE XXXVI. Heretics

**80.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that any heretic or schismatic baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, if that person has not been joined to the Catholic Church, cannot in any way be saved, no matter how many alms he or she may have given, even if he or she has shed blood for the name of Christ.

For no human being who does not maintain the unity of the Catholic Church can benefit toward salvation from baptism, from any amount of almsgiving, or from death undertaken for the name of Christ, so long as there persists in that person the heretical or schismatic perversity that leads to death.

## CHAPTER XL, or RULE XXXVII. Christians Who Live Badly

**81.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that not all who are baptized within the Catholic Church will receive eternal life, but only those who, having received baptism, live rightly—that is, those who have abstained from vices and the desires of the flesh. For just as unbelievers, heretics, and schismatics will not possess the kingdom of heaven, so criminal Catholics will not be able to possess it.

## CHAPTER XLI, or RULE XXXVIII. No One Lives without Sins

**82.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that even righteous and holy human beings—except for baptized infants—no one can live here without sin; and that it is always necessary for every person to cleanse his or her sins until the end of this present life by almsgiving, fasting, prayer, or tears [Note: The words “by fasting, prayer, or tears” are found in the Corbie manuscript], and humbly and sincerely to ask God for forgiveness [Note: One manuscript reads: “to redeem”].

## CHAPTER XLII, or RULE XXXIX. Food and Drink; Marriage; Second Marriages Permitted

**Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that every creature of God is good and that nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving [Col. 0704D]; and that God’s servants who abstain from meat or wine do not reject them as though they were unclean things made by God, but abstain from richer food and drink solely for the chastening of the body.

Marriage too was divinely instituted and blessed. It is indeed better if someone remains without marriage, so that he or she may think more freely and fully about the things of God—how to please God (1 Cor. 7:34). Nevertheless, for those who have not vowed continence, there is no sin if a woman marries or a man takes a wife.

Not only did God institute first marriages, but he also permitted second and third marriages because of the weakness of those who cannot remain continent. But for those who, whether married or free from marriage, have vowed continence to God, it is exceedingly condemnable if the married seek the marital act from which they had professed, by free decision, that they would abstain, or if those free from marriage seek to return to what they had professed they would leave.

## CHAPTER XLIII, or RULE XL. The Wicked Are Mixed with the Good in the Church

**84.** Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatsoever, that the Catholic Church is God’s threshing floor, and that within it, until the end of the age, chaff will remain mixed with the grain—that is, the wicked will be mixed with the good through participation in the sacraments [Col. 0705B]. In every profession—whether of clergy, monks, or laypeople—there are both good and wicked persons.

The good are not to be abandoned on account of the wicked; rather, the wicked are to be tolerated for the sake of the good, insofar as the order of faith and love requires this—that is, provided they neither scatter seeds of unbelief in the Church nor lead their brothers and sisters to some evil deed through deadly imitation.

Nor can any person within the Catholic Church who rightly believes and lives well ever be stained by another’s sin, provided that he or she gives neither consent nor favor to anyone who sins. It is beneficial for the wicked to be tolerated by the good within the Church if this is done by living well and admonishing them well, so that, seeing and hearing what is good, they may reject their evil deeds and tremble at the thought that God will judge them for their evil works; and thus, by the gift of grace going before them, they may be ashamed of their iniquities and, through God’s mercy, be converted to a good life.

The good, however, are not to be separated from the wicked within the Catholic Church except by the dissimilarity of their works [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “are to be separated by the dissimilarity of their works”], so that those with whom they share the divine sacraments may not have in common with them the evil works by which those persons are criminal.

At the end of the age, the good will also be separated bodily from the wicked, when Christ will come holding a winnowing fan in his hand, will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor, and will gather his wheat into his granary [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads, in accordance with the Greek text: “his wheat into the granary.” The printed editions instead read: “the wheat into his granary”], but will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matt. 3:12).

Then, by a just judgment, he will separate the righteous from the unrighteous, the good from the wicked, and the upright from the perverse. He will place the good at his right hand and the wicked at his left; and from his mouth will proceed the sentence of eternal and unchangeable judgment, and all the unrighteous will go into eternal burning, while the righteous will go into eternal life (Matt. 25:45): the unrighteous will burn forever with the devil, while the righteous will reign without end with Christ.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Perseverance in the Faith

**85.** In the meantime, believe faithfully, hold firmly, and defend truthfully and patiently these forty chapters, which pertain most firmly to the rule of the true faith. If you discover anyone teaching doctrines contrary to them, flee from that person as from a plague and reject him as a heretic.

For what we have set forth agrees so fully with the Catholic faith that if anyone wishes to oppose not merely all of them but even individual points, then, in stubbornly resisting any one of these and not hesitating to teach the contrary, that person will appear to be a heretic and an enemy of the Christian faith and, for this reason, subject to anathema from all Catholics.

Although the shortness of time and the haste of the bearer compelled us to pass over in silence certain matters that ought to have been inserted for recognizing and avoiding various heresies, nevertheless, if you do not neglect to review everything contained in this little work and make it thoroughly familiar, you will be able, with prudent discernment, to judge spiritually from it also concerning other matters.

For the Apostle says that “the spiritual person judges all things” (1 Cor. 2:15). Until each of us reaches this state, let each walk in what he or she has attained—that is, let each faithfully persevere in what has been received as certain. “And if anyone thinks otherwise, God will reveal this also to him.” Amen.

## 532 ADMONITION CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING CHAPTER XLV

No one will deny that the following chapter was not truly produced by Fulgentius, but was appended to this completed work by some other and unknown author, if, on reading Fulgentius’s entire book, he pays even moderate attention to the final words of the last chapter.

For, after setting forth forty chapters, or rather rules, of the true faith, he says that the shortness of time and the haste of the bearer compelled him to pass over in silence many matters that ought otherwise to have been inserted. Therefore, especially with the manifest conclusion of the entire work already added, it is not plausible that he enlarged a work already completed with this longer chapter, which contributes nothing or almost nothing to the subject, or repeated in briefer speech rules that are already sufficiently condensed in themselves.

[Col. 0706C] Moreover, even if these considerations were insufficient to prevent us from attributing this chapter to Fulgentius, all the manuscripts examined by us—the four Vatican manuscripts, the two English manuscripts, and the one very ancient Corbie manuscript, whose script itself indicates an age of a thousand years or more, that is, one written almost in Fulgentius’s own century or in the immediately following century—omit everything that is read in this chapter.

That last manuscript, at the end, after the words “And if anyone thinks otherwise, God will reveal this also to him. Amen,” has, in exactly the same hand: “Here ends the book of Fulgentius, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of Ruspe, On the Rule of the True Faith.”

Nevertheless, because it seemed irreverent to print here anything less than what had already been printed, it appeared appropriate to append this entire chapter to the work as a separate appendix.

## CHAPTER XLV

[Col. 0706D]

**1.** The truly firm foundation of faith is principally to believe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are naturally one God: so that we believe that the only-begotten Son was truly born from the nature of the Father, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds truly and naturally from the Father and the Son. We must also believe that the holy Trinity itself is one, sole, true, eternal, and immutable God.

For salvation it is also fitting to believe that one person of the Trinity—that is, the only-begotten God—alone was made human for our salvation; and that he is one true God and one true human being: according to his divinity, possessing one nature with the Father and the Holy Spirit; but according to his humanity [Col. 0707A], Christ’s rational soul is of the same nature as the souls of all human beings, and Christ’s flesh is of the nature of all those who derive their origin from the first human being.

Therefore neither Christ’s soul nor his flesh is of one and the same nature with his divinity, because according to his humanity he was truly created. But just as his divinity shares the divine nature with the Father and the Holy Spirit, so his soul and body have a natural communion with our souls and bodies.

By his divinity, taking away sin, he freely rescued from the dominion of sin and from the punishment of eternal death the flesh and soul of those who believe in him.

**2.** Strengthened by this belief, do not forget to implore divine mercy day and night, entreating Christ the Lord, the blessed hope of all who believe in him, that you may hold firmly and preserve inviolate the truth of this faith. For the Holy Spirit supplies abundant assistance to the faithful who pray to him, as the prophet says:

“The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth. He will do the will of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayers and save them. The Lord guards all who love him, but he will destroy all sinners” (Ps. 144:18–20).

And again he says to God himself: “Behold, all who distance themselves from you will perish; you have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you” (Ps. 72:27). But concerning himself he says: “For me, it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord” (ibid., 28).

**3.** Cling, therefore, to God, dearest son, and place your hope in him with all your heart, in faith and love. In the service of this world, render faithful service to the earthly king, because God loves this and the Apostle commands it.

But in the matter of the faith by which Christ redeemed us in his blood, let all fear depart from our hearts. We owe our souls to the one by whose blood we were redeemed. We ought to love above all the one whom we know to be the most merciful Redeemer of our souls. Above all, we ought to fear the eternal and true power of the one whom we hope will come as the most just judge.

We ought with the whole affection of our hearts to desire the promises of the one who can give eternal life to soul and body. We ought to fear the anger of the one who can send soul and body into Gehenna. In his judgment, without respect of persons and without the influence of earthly powers, masters and servants, kings and soldiers, rich and poor, lowly and exalted will be judged equally.

There, whatever servant has held the faith of God in truth here will possess an eternal kingdom, while the unbelieving master will be burned with everlasting fire. There, the life of faithful servants and masters will neither end nor their joy cease; but concerning unbelievers, whether servants or masters, according to the truth of the prophetic word: “Their fire shall not be quenched, and their worm shall not die” (Isa. 66:24). For the unrighteous will go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

**4.** Let us consider, moreover, whom the Savior foretold would go there—namely, those to whom he will say:

“I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was naked, and you did not clothe me; I was a stranger, and you did not receive me; I was sick and in prison, and you did not come to me” (Matt. 25:42).

If the person who did not give bread to Christ, hungry in his least ones, will rightly be sent into eternal fire, what will happen to the one who, through the vice of unbelief, deprives himself of the very bread that came down from heaven?

And if the person who did not give Christ, thirsty in his least ones, a cup of cold water will be burned in everlasting flames, what will happen to the one who, having been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, allows holy baptism—which he received once for salvation and as the sacrament of holy rebirth—to be repeated in him?
