And if we believe that the person who neglects to receive Christ, a stranger in his least ones, with love and hospitality must be subjected to everlasting torments, what will the one think he will suffer who excludes the Lord Christ from the house of his heart, receives the devil into himself through utter blindness of unbelief, and, having been ensnared by heretical falsehood, departs from the holy Church, which is “the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Tim. 3:15)?

And if the person who does not visit Christ’s servants who are sick or imprisoned is assigned to everlasting fire, what do we say should be repaid to those who violently afflict God’s servants—those in whom they persecute only the truth of the faith—either through the squalor of prisons or through deportation into exile?

Yet in all these matters, though unbelievers rage, God nevertheless supplies assistance to his own. While the enemies of the faith seek to corrupt someone either by cunning seduction or by violent compulsion, Christ, who is the power and wisdom of God, grants strength so that they may despise the promises of deadly persuasion and resist human terrors with the strength of divine fear. The essential thing is that the will not be turned away from God and that it obtain the reward of faith. For to the will either eternal punishment is inflicted for unbelief, or everlasting joy is granted as the reward of preserved faith.

[Col. 0707C]

# ONE BOOK OF ST. FULGENTIUS, *FOR THE CATHOLIC FAITH, AGAINST PINTA, THE ARIAN BISHOP* (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0707D] 534

**1.** After Christ, the apostles are the most trustworthy foundation of the Catholic faith; the integrity of the faith bears certain witness to this. Even when preaching itself perhaps ceases, some hidden operation of the Holy Spirit, sown and established in the minds of the faithful, suggests this truth.

Yet who among those who believe rightly is unaware that all heresies have gone out from the Catholic Church, like useless branches cast off from the vine? But she remains in her own root, in her own vine, and in her own love, and “the gates of hell shall not prevail against her” (Matt. 16:18).

The Church is one, the true Church, the Catholic Church. She fights against all heresies; she can fight, but she cannot be conquered. Concerning her, Solomon says in the Song of Songs, speaking in the person of Christ as he praises his bride, whom we believe to be the Church:

“Behold, my close companion is like a lily among thorns” (Song 2:2).

For the integrity of the Church is daily pierced as though by thorns through the doctrines of various heresies, so that she may be trained in vigilance against her enemies, until, rising like a lily upon the head of her bridegroom, she is adorned by that very whiteness.

**2.** But because someone, moved by his own spirit, presumed that those who honor the Church’s faith should be called *Homoousians* or *Consubstantialists*, his ignorance must be answered.

The almighty God is so great and so powerful that through wicked people he proclaims good things, just as through an evil high priest he deigned to foretell the mystery of our redemption (John 11:49).

The person who composed that little book, conceived in a savage mind, thought that a collection of divine testimonies from both the New and the Old Testament ought to be brought against *homoousion*. Concerning such people the Apostle foretold long ago, saying: “Understanding neither what they say nor what they affirm” (1 Tim. 1:7).

If he knew what *homoousion* expresses from Greek into Latin, he would strive to praise it rather than reproach it. For our fathers—the three hundred and eighteen who prepared the antidote of this term to exclude Arius’s poisons—did not use words foreign to the Gospel. Rather, word for word, they took care to introduce the meaning of the true faith to those who did not yet understand it easily.

For in Greek, *homos* means “one,” while *ousia* means “substance.” Consult the saying of the Gospel, and you will find this uttered by the divine mouth: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

Examine the plural expression and return to the singular truth of the substance. By saying, “I and the Father are one,” he proclaimed the distinction of his person and the Father’s against Sabellius, whom he foresaw would become a heretic: by saying “we are,” he distinguished his person from the Father’s.

By saying “one,” he likewise foresaw Arius, who did not hesitate to divide the substance of the deity. Sabellius wrongly united, while Arius more wickedly separated. For Sabellius ought to have distinguished the person of the Father from that of the Son, while Arius ought in no way at all to have separated the substance of the deity.

They think that a grave crime against the faith is attached to the Catholic Church when they call its disciples *Homoousians* or *Consubstantialists*, as though *homoousion* contained the name either of the substance of the deity or of some human being, just as the founders of various heresies judged that their sect should be proclaimed to their disciples under their own names.

Thus the Simonians were named from Simon, the Menandrians from Menander, the Marcionists from Marcion, the Valentinians from Valentinus, the Manichaeans from Mani, and the Nepotians from Nepos. To pass over ancient heresies that are now almost dying out, I will mention more recent ones: the Sabellians from Sabellius, the Arians from Arius, the Eunomians from Eunomius, the Macedonians from Macedonius, the Apollinarists from Apollinaris, the Nestorians from Nestorius, the Donatists from Donatus, the Maximianists from Maximianus, and the Rogatists from Rogatus—and any others who are called Christians in name only, not in deed, who have abandoned God and revere the names of their founders.

Let the person who thought *homoousion* should be brought as an accusation against Catholics show that *homoousion* is the name of some human being [Col. 0709D]. It would seem to me that, unless the Gospel’s brightest summit were known to all nations more clearly than daylight, the Arians, in deciding how their heresy should be fostered, might even erase the Lord’s own words from the Gospel [Note: The Port manuscript reads “erase” in the sense of “scrape away”]: “I and the Father are one”—the very words that, as stated, the Fathers translated word for word and established as *homoousion*.

**3.** As for what they assert among the uninstructed—whether many or few ought to be believed, since the Council of Nicaea was held with three hundred and eighteen Fathers, while they boast that the Council of Ariminum assembled eight hundred and thirty, where cunning men attempted to corrupt *homoousion* among the uninstructed—I will give a brief account.

Behold, *homoousion* prevailed among the few, so that it became known to the other bishops established throughout the entire world, and they rejoice to be honored by confessing it. If the later council of Ariminum [The word “assembly” appears to be missing] had been gathered in such great numbers, as they claim, its sect’s bishops would have multiplied throughout the world, its peoples would have increased, and such a faith would itself have taken possession of the empires.

But once the cunning of that fraud had been recognized by prudent and highly approved men, *homoousion* was confirmed so firmly that we scarcely see any remnants of Ariminum left for testing Catholics.

Let us, if it pleases, consult the city of Ariminum itself, where this fraudulent business was conducted—or rather contrived. I do not know whether it has a bishop belonging to that sect. For I will speak more freely about Milan, where Auxentius poured out the poisons of his sect like a cunning craftsman. His successor Ambrose so destroyed the doctrine, filled with the Holy Spirit, that after his death Auxentius’s name was erased from the memory of the living in that very city, and his name was regarded as a kind of contagion.

Through this Ambrose, the faith of the emperor Gratian was then strengthened, and its growth increased more and more among bishops and peoples. For almighty God, who through all the Scriptures promised the growth of his Church, could not abandon his promise and allow falsehood to grow. Let this have been said concerning all heresies.

**4.** In what follows, with God’s help—he who instructs the heart and governs the tongue—testimonies will be set forth concerning the one God, his power and invisibility, the equality of the Son with the Father, and the divinity of the Holy Spirit: testimonies concerning the Trinity, which, though they do not wish it, is nevertheless one God, such that, if they do not love the darkness of contention, they must see the light of truth.

And lest anyone be troubled because we said that the growth of the Church had been promised throughout all the Scriptures, and lest they claim that it was granted through this oppression, let them know that it is written in Jeremiah:

“The partridge cries out; it gathers what it did not hatch; it makes its riches not with judgment” (Jer. 17:11).

This is also a most certain proof that the Catholic faith has grown only through tribulations and persecutions, so that what was said might be fulfilled: “Through many tribulations and afflictions we must see the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21).

The growth of that faith is attested by the exiles of the innocent, the confiscations of the wretched, and the tortures and oppression of captives.

But I see certain contradictors giving birth [Note: The Port manuscript reads “contradictions”] and throwing the persecutions of the Donatists in our face. Their fury did violence through the laws, and they suffered these things because of the laws. For if the Catholic mother received any of them into her pious embrace, this happened without any injury to baptism, without any loss of burden, and without any insult to the Holy Spirit, so that those who were converted by their own will might grieve that love had remained hidden from them for so long.

## Catholic Testimonies Concerning the One God
## 5.

The first word of God is: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI, 4). In Deuteronomy: “The Lord alone led them, and there was no foreign god with them” (Deut. XXXII, 12). Again there: “See, see that I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Ibid., 39). Likewise in Exodus: “You shall have no other gods besides me” (Exod. XX, 3). Again: “Whoever sacrifices to other gods besides me shall be rooted out” (Ibid., 5). Again: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deut. VI, 13). Again: “For there is no other god either in heaven or on earth who can do your works or be compared with your greatness” (Deut. III, 24).

In the prophet Hosea: “You shall know no one but me as Lord, and there will be no savior besides me” (Hos. XIII, 4). In Isaiah: “I am God, and there is no savior besides me. I announced it, and I saved, and there shall be no stranger among you” (Isa. XLIII, 11). Again above: “Thus says the Lord, who made heaven; this is God who stretched out the earth and made it. He did not make it in vain, but [Col. 0711B] so that it might be inhabited. I am, I am, and there is no other. I am God, and there is no other” (Isa. XLV, 18). “By myself I swear: unless righteousness has gone forth from my mouth, my words shall not return; for every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall swear by God” [Note: [Col. 0711D] Above, in the response to the tenth objection of the Arians, more than once, ‘by God.’] (Ibid., 22–24).

Again above: “From of old we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen a God besides you” (Isa. LXIV, 4); and: “Before me there was no God, and after me there shall be no other” (Isa. XLIII, 10). “I am the first God, and I am with the things that are to come” (Isa. XLIV, 6). In the body of the Psalms: “Who is God besides our Lord?” (Ps. XVII, 32). Again: “Who is a great God like our God? You are the God who alone works wonders” (Ps. LXXVI, 15). Again: “Let the nations know that the Lord is your name; you alone are Most High over all the earth” (Ps. LXXXII, 16).

[Col. 0711C] This applies even more fittingly to the Son. In the Books of Kings, Hezekiah, against Sennacherib: “Lord God of Israel, you alone are God of all the kingdoms of the earth” (IV Kings XIX, 15). Again above: “O Lord our God, save us from their hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are Lord” (Ibid., 19). Solomon, in prayer, stretched out his hands toward heaven and said: “Lord God of Israel, there is no god like you, neither in heaven above nor on earth below” (III Kings VIII, 23).

Although two or three testimonies concerning the one God would suffice, nevertheless let those who introduce two gods among us listen. They confess God the Father and God the Son; this, indeed, is true. But whoever does not honor the Son as he honors the Father is impious. For if sacrifice or honor is owed to the Father, it is owed also to the Son. But when you assert that the Father is greater and the Son lesser, you introduce two gods: in both respects you are sacrilegious—by refusing to hear, “The Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI, 4), and by failing to honor the Son as you honor the Father.

The Son introduced no degrees. Ask what honor belongs to the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0712D] In the Portus manuscript the following is added here: “There is no distinction between the honor of the Son and that of the Father.”]

You strive to insult both: the Father, because his Son is not heard, although the Father says, “Listen to him” (Matt. XVII, 5); and the Son, whom you dare to despise in his command. But now let other testimonies concerning the equality of the Father and the Son be brought forward.

## Testimonies concerning the equality of the Father and the Son

[Col. 0712A]

### 6.

In the Apocalypse: “And on his garment, or on his thigh, he had written: King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. XIX, 16; I Tim. VI, 15). If the Apostle says this concerning the Father, here it is plainly said concerning the Son.

Again above: “Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection. Over these the second death has no power; but they will be priests of God and of his Christ, and they will reign with him” (Rev. XX, 6).

Again above: “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. I will give the thirsty person the spring of the water of life freely. Whoever conquers will possess these things, and I will be his God, and he will be my son” (Rev. XXI, 6).

Again above: “I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb” (Ibid., 22). There is no distinction.

Again above: “And he showed me [Col. 0712B] the bright river of the water of life, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Rev. XXII, 1). There is one throne, not two.

Again above: “The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and they will serve him” (Ibid., 3).

In the Epistle of John: “Everyone who does not remain in the doctrine of Christ does not have God. Whoever remains in the doctrine has both the Son and the Father” (II John, 9). The Son is named first.

In the Epistle of Jude: “Denying our ruler and God, Jesus Christ” (Jude, 4). He is both God and Lord.

In the Apocalypse: “They say to the mountains and rocks, ‘Fall upon us and hide us from the face of the one seated on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb, because the great day of their wrath has come, and who will be able to stand?’” (Rev. VI, 16). There is one judgment, or an equal judgment.

Again above: “Salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb” (Rev. VII, 10).

Again above: “The kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our Lord God and of his Christ, and he will reign for ever and ever” (Rev. XI, 15). It says “he will reign,” not “they will reign.”

Again above: “And I heard a loud voice in heaven saying, ‘Now salvation and power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come’” (Rev. XII, 10). There is no division.

Again above: “And I saw, and behold, the Lamb was standing on Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand, having his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads” (Rev. XIV, 1). Does it prejudice the matter that the Son is named first, when there is one power?

Again above: “These have been purchased from among humanity as first fruits for God and the Lamb” (Ibid., 4).

Again above: “These will wage war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings” (Rev. XVII, 14). What more does the Father possess? Let it be said.

To the Hebrews: “For when God made his promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom he could swear, he swore by himself, saying…” (Hebr. VI, 13). If this is understood of the Father, he will be visible; if of the Son, there is none greater than he.

The Father in the Gospel: “So that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father” (John V, 23). And because he has the one who sent him, this sending is not from one place to another. The sun, too, sends forth its rays without being separated from itself.

Again: “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes” (Ibid., 21). Behold the Son: he gives life to whomever he wishes. Behold the Spirit: he wills where he wills.

The Son says to Philip: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 9). And again: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John XIV, 11). Behold the equality of the Father and the Son.

Again: “Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John XVII, 1). Equal power. But these testimonies concerning the equality of the Son with the Father are sufficient.

## Testimonies concerning the deity of the Son

### 7.

In Job: “He alone stretched out the heavens and walks upon the sea as upon the earth” (Job IX, 8).

In Jeremiah: “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him. He found the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared upon the earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III, 36–38).

Does the fact that the Son’s person is expressed here—when it says, “No other shall be reckoned beside him”—mean that we separate the Father from deity?

[Col. 0713B] In Isaiah: “Egypt has grown weary, and the commerce of Ethiopia. Many will come to you, and they will be your servants; they will walk behind you, bound in fetters; they will worship you and entreat you, because God is in you, and you are God alone, and we did not know it: God of Israel, our Savior” (Isa. XLV, 14–15). In this most clear testimony not only the Son’s deity is shown, but also his complete equality with the Father. For what it says, “God is in you, and you are God,” is said in the Gospel as: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 11).

To the Romans: “Their fathers are theirs, and from them is Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever” (Rom. IX, 5). The Son’s deity is his own.

The Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “Who is the image of the invisible God” (II Cor. IV, 4). If he is the image, he is the reality.

Again above: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V, 19). If God was wholly present, he was not present only in part.

To the Ephesians: “To proclaim the unsearchable riches of Christ” (Eph. III, 8). Are they Christ’s alone and not the Father’s?

To the Colossians: “Because in him he was pleased to have all the fullness of deity dwell bodily” (Col. II, 9). Observe here both “all the fullness” and “deity”: there is nothing that can be added.

Again above: “That God might make known among the nations the riches of his mystery, which is Christ” (Col. I, 27). Behold: Christ is the riches of God.

Again above: “So that they may attain the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II, 3). The fullness is complete.

To the Philippians: “Who, being established in the form of God…” (Phil. II, 6). You hear “form,” and yet deny equality?

Again above: “But God the Father himself and our Lord Jesus Christ direct our way to you” (I Thess. III, 11). Behold, both direct: equal power.

In the First Epistle to Timothy: “That you keep the commandment without reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, which the blessed and only Sovereign will display at the proper times” (I Tim. VI, 14), and so forth. Does the fact that he says “only Sovereign” exclude the Father from sovereignty?

To Titus: “The grace of God and of our Savior Jesus Christ has appeared to all” (Tit. II, 11). Again above: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (v. 13). If the Son is the great God, he possesses nothing less.

Again above: “But when the kindness and humanity of our Savior Jesus Christ appeared” (Tit. III, 4). Here he did not conceal either his humanity or his divinity.

John [Col. 0714A] to the Parthians: “That we may believe in his true Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life” (I John V, 20). In this testimony whoever denies the Son the perfection of God is Antichrist.

The Second Epistle of Peter: “For in this way the entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will be richly supplied to you” (II Pet. I, 11).

Although these few testimonies concerning the Son’s deity are like a drop drawn from the great sea of the Scriptures themselves, since all Scripture bears witness both to his deity and to his humanity assumed in the flesh, as he himself says in the Gospel according to John: “Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and they are the ones that bear witness concerning me” (John V, 39). He did not say, “Concerning us,” lest he introduce two gods.

In Luke Jesus said to them: “These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you: that everything written in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms concerning me must be fulfilled” (Luke XXIV, 44). Does he exclude the Father from the testimony of the Scriptures because here also he says “concerning me”?

Concerning the Son’s omnipotence, in Solomon: “Your almighty word, O Lord, came from the royal throne of heaven” (Wis. XVIII, 15).

In Zechariah: “O flee from the land of the north, says the Lord, for I will gather you from the four winds of heaven. Says the Lord: Be saved, you who dwell in the daughter of Babylon. For thus says the Lord Almighty: After glory he sent me to the nations that stripped you. For whoever touches you is like one who touches the apple of his eye. Therefore [Col. 0714C] I will raise my hand against them, and they will be plunder for those who plundered them; and you will know that the Lord Almighty sent me” (Zech. II, 2 and following).

Above, the Almighty speaks; below, the Almighty sends. Are there therefore two Almighty ones?

The prophet Amos: “The Lord who touches the earth and shakes it, and all who dwell in it will mourn; and it will rise like the river of Egypt, who builds his ascent upon heaven and establishes his vault upon the earth; who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth: the Lord Almighty is his name” (Amos IX, 5).

Are not all these things understood to apply to the Son? Descending, he touched the earth; by his passion he shook it; from the earth he ascended into heaven; and upon the earth he descended from heaven, as he himself promised in the Apocalypse (chapter III, 14): “Thus says the one who is the faithful witness, the beginning of God’s creation: He who is and who was and who is to come, the Lord Almighty” (Rev. I, 8).

Let it trouble you because it says, “the beginning of God’s creation”; let it trouble you because it is said, “the Lord Almighty”—so that the latter refers to his deity, and the former to the fact that he was born of the Virgin Mary.

## Testimonies concerning the Trinity

### 8.

In the Gospel: “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). It says “in the name,” not “in the names.”

Again: “The kingdom of heaven is like a woman who hid leaven in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened” (Matt. XIII, 33). Here the woman signifies the Church, which hides in the hearts of believers, in equal measures, faith in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

In the Apocalypse: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Rev. IV, 8). Three times I hear “holy,” and yet one Lord God.

Again above: “And the angel said to me, ‘These words are true words of God.’ And I fell before his feet to worship him; but he said to me, ‘See that you do not do this. I am your fellow servant and one of your brothers who hold the testimony of Jesus and the spirit of prophecy’” (Rev. XIX, 9–10). What could be clearer for demonstrating the Trinity than the Father’s true words, the Son’s testimony, and the Spirit’s gift of prophecy?

In the Psalms: “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV, 10). With God the Father, Christ is the fountain of life; and because light is in him, the Holy Spirit is seen as the illuminator, since “whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. VIII, 9).

In Psalm LXVI, 8: “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him.” Three times I hear “God,” and yet he proclaims one whom they must fear.

In the Epistle of John: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit; and the three are one” (I John V, 7).

What shall I say about the patriarch Abraham? When he saw the appearance of three men, he recognized one God in them, saying: “Master, Lord” (Gen. XVIII, 3). In bodily service he offers hospitality to three, but from one he receives the benefit of offspring, when it is said to him: “At this time I will come, and Sarah will have a son” (v. 10). He did not say, “We will come,” but “I will come,” lest he appear to introduce a multitude of gods.

But so that you may know that the Trinity dwells together and together avoids impurity, hear what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him” (John XIV, 21); and: “We will come, I and my Father, and we will make our dwelling with him” (v. 23). Behold, the Father and the Son inhabit one dwelling.

What of the Holy Spirit? Hear the Apostle saying: “You are God’s temple, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (I Cor. III, 16). The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have been shown to dwell together; let the Trinity itself also be shown to avoid impurity together.

In Solomon you find: “But perverse thoughts separate from God”: this concerns the Father. “For Wisdom will not enter a malicious soul”: this concerns the Son. “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts without understanding” (Wis. I, 3–5): this concerns the Holy Spirit.

But so that you may gather, in brief, the meaning of Scripture speaking with one voice about the nature of the Trinity, you also find in Exodus: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. III, 6).

In the Psalm: “The Lord lives, and blessed is my God, and exalted is the God of my salvation” (Ps. XVII, 47).

Paul: “The same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God” (I Cor. XII, 4–6). Does it offend the Catholic understanding that the Spirit is named first?

Again, if you seek the Lord spoken of as the Trinity itself, hear: “Ascribe to the Lord glory and honor; ascribe to the Lord glory due to his name” (Ps. XXVIII, 2).

Because the King is the Trinity itself: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory” (Ps. XXIII, 9).

A testimony is given: “God” is repeated three times, and “Lord” is called three times, as King. Gods, lords, and kings are not distinguished, because in the three names and persons they are discerned: for there is one deity, one lordship, and one royal sovereignty.

Whoever contradicts this truth out of a desire to prevail wickedly will not merely be condemned; he is already condemned.

## Testimonies that the Holy Spirit is God

### 9.

At the beginning of the book of Genesis: “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. I, 2)—so that he might sanctify the waters in the figure of baptism, not so that he might pause from weariness.

In Job: “The divine Spirit is the one who made me, and the Spirit of the Almighty is the one who teaches me” (Job XXXIII, 4). In divinity there is perfection.

In the Gospel: “God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” [Col. 0716B] (John IV, 24). Again: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John III, 31). Behold, the Spirit is immeasurable.

To Nicodemus: “For the Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (Ibid., 8). When you hear “where he wills,” this is proper power.

Christ speaks of himself: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Luke IV, 18). Unless pious understanding qualifies these words, the Spirit will be greater than the Son.

Again: “Jesus, filled with the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Ibid., 1). The same understanding applies.

Again: “If therefore you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before: it is the Spirit who gives life; for the flesh profits nothing” (John VI, 63). The one who gives life lacks nothing of deity.

Again: “When the Paraclete comes, the Spirit of truth, whom the Father will send in my name, he will lead you into all truth and will teach you” (John XVI, 13). He is God who will lead into all truth.

In the Acts of the Apostles, Peter to Cornelius: “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit” (Acts X, 38). He was anointed as a human being, not as God.

Again, to Ananias: “Why has Satan tempted your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts V, 3). And he adds: “You have not lied to human beings but to God” (v. 4).

Again: “Thus says the Holy Spirit: Set apart for me Saul and Barnabas for the ministry to which I have called them” (Acts XIII, 2). Here he does not introduce the person of either the Father or the Son, although sound understanding does not separate them from the command.

Again, the Apostle to the nations in the Epistle: “It seemed good,” he says, “to the Holy Spirit and to us not to impose upon you anything more than that you abstain from sacrifices to idols, from fornication, and from blood” (Acts XV, 28). Was this command made without the Father and the Son?

Again there: “The Spirit said to Peter, ‘Rise and go with them, because I have sent them to you’” (Acts X, 19). Does anyone command a creature unless he is the Creator?

Again there: “From Miletus Paul sent to Ephesus and summoned the presbyters and elders” (Acts XX, 17); and after much exhortation he added: “Take heed to the flock of Christ, over which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops” (Ibid., 28). Are the Father or the Son separated from this appointment of a priest?

Paul to the Romans: “The Spirit is eternal life and peace” (Rom. VIII, 6). This is the Father, this is the Son, this is the Holy Spirit—but one life, not three.

Again above: “The Spirit is life because of righteousness” (Ibid., 10). This is the Father, this is the Son.

Again above: “But if the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you” (v. 11). What kind of God is this who raised the Creator’s flesh from the dead?

Again above: “For you have not received a spirit of slavery” (v. 15). No one is free except God, which is the Holy Spirit.

Again above: “May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope through the power of the Holy Spirit” (Rom. XV, 13). Just as Christ is the power of God, so is the Holy Spirit.

Again above: “So that the offering of the nations may be sanctified in the Holy Spirit” (Ibid., 16). As the Spirit gives life, so also he sanctifies.

Again above: “For I will not dare to speak of anything that Christ does not accomplish through me for the obedience of the nations, by word and deed, through the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Holy Spirit” (Ibid., 18–19). The Son is power, the Spirit is power, the Father is power—but one power, not three.

In the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “The Spirit searches everything. No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (I Cor. II, 10–11).

Again above: “You are God’s temple, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (I Cor. III, 16). He who dwells in his temple is God.

Again above: “You were washed and sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (I Cor. VI, 11). Behold: the Son and the Holy Spirit cleanse and sanctify together.

Again above: “One and the same Spirit accomplishes all things, distributing to each one as he wills” (I Cor. XII, 11). Whoever freely does what he wills is subject to no one.

In the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “An epistle written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God” (II Cor. III, 3). A human spirit is not lesser than a human being; how much more is the Spirit of God not lesser than God?

Again above: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (Ibid., 6). Whoever gives life is God, since “the Lord puts to death and gives life” (I Kings II, 6).

To the Galatians: “That we might receive the blessing of the Spirit through faith” (Gal. III, 14). He who blesses is God.

Again above: “We live by the Spirit; by the Spirit let us also walk” (Gal. V, 25). He who again blesses also gives life as God.

Again above: “Whoever sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Gal. VI, 8). In these three testimonies to the Galatians, the Spirit blesses, gives life, and grants eternal life.

To the Ephesians: “In him, when you believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit” (Eph. I, 13). We are sealed in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Again above: “In him you are being built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit” (Eph. II, 22).

Again: “It was revealed to his holy apostles by the Spirit that the nations are co-heirs” (Eph. III, 5). One and the same Spirit accomplishes all things: he makes them heirs.

Again above: “That he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power [Note: [Col. 0717] Perhaps ‘by power,’ as in the Greek text and in the Vulgate version.] through his Spirit” (Ibid., 16). No one strengthens except God.

Again above: “Eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. IV, 3). Christ is peace. Are there therefore two peaces?

Again above: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI, 17). Christ is the Word of God; the Holy Spirit is the Word of God. Are there therefore two Words?

To the Philippians: “Whether absent, I may hear about you that you are standing firm in one Spirit” (Phil. I, 27)—that is, in God.

To the Thessalonians: “God chose you from the beginning for salvation through sanctification by the Spirit” (II Thess. II, 12).

In the First Epistle to Timothy: “Great is the mystery of godliness: he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit” (I Tim. III, 16). Behold, the Holy Spirit also sanctifies Christ’s incarnation.

In the Second Epistle to Timothy: “Guard the good trust committed to you through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us” (II Tim. I, 11). If the Spirit were not God, the Apostle would not dare to adjure his disciple by him. Moreover, he says that he dwells in us.

To Titus: “He saved us through the washing of regeneration, through the Holy Spirit” (Tit. III, 5).

Peter to the nations: “These things have been announced to you through those who preached the gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, into which angels long to look” (I Pet. I, 12). He whom the angels desire to behold is God.

Again above: “Christ died for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might offer us to God, put to death indeed in the flesh but made alive in the Spirit” (I Pet. III, 18).

Again above: “That they might be judged according to human beings in the flesh, but live according to God in the Spirit” (Ibid., IV, 6).

Again above: “If you are reproached in Christ, because the Spirit of the Lord’s glory rests upon you” (Ibid., 14). Christ is the glory of the Father; the Holy Spirit is glory. Are there therefore two glories?

In the Second Epistle of Peter: “Understanding this first, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from private interpretation. For prophecy was not brought forth at any time by human will, but human beings spoke from God, moved by the Holy Spirit” (II Pet. I, 20–21). No one inspires the gift of prophecy except God.

John to the Parthians: “By this we know that he remains in us, from the Holy Spirit whom he has given us” (I John III, 24).

Again above: “By this we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us from his Spirit” (I John IV, 13). “He has given,” as you hear, refers to the operation of power, not to a separation of deity.

In the Apocalypse: “After three and a half days, the spirit of life from God entered them, and they stood upon their feet” (Rev. XI, 11). Whatever proceeds from God is God.

Again above: “Write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From now on the Spirit says that they should rest from their labors” (Rev. XIV, 13). It does not say the Father; it does not say the Son; it says the Spirit, who is shown by this command to be God.

To the Hebrews: “For if the blood of bulls and goats and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled upon the defiled, sanctify for the cleansing of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleanse…” (Hebr. IX, 13–14). This testimony teaches what power the Holy Spirit possesses, through whom Christ’s flesh is presented unblemished.

Again above: “Anyone who sets aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, regarded the blood of the covenant as polluted, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” (Hebr. X, 28–29). Behold the vengeance exacted for an injury against the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Again above: “God the judge of all, the spirits of the perfected righteous, and Jesus the mediator of the New Testament” (Hebr. XII, 23). This testimony accords with the Trinity, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are all named here.

Because the Holy Spirit is omnipotent, Solomon says: “The Holy Spirit is manifold, subtle, eloquent, secure, undefiled, possessing every power” (Wis. VII, 22). And you deny that he is omnipotent?

Because the Holy Spirit is judge, the Lord says: “If I go, I will send him to you; and when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment” (John XVI, 7–8). You see the judge, who even, if it may be said, vindicates the Savior himself. And does anyone dare to take deity away from him?

And what more shall I say about the deity of the Holy Spirit, whom David fears, saying: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, O Lord, or where shall I flee from your presence?” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 7)?

And to conclude: so great and so mighty is the Holy Spirit that, if anyone blasphemes against him, he will find that the Spirit does not forgive him, either in this age or in the age to come.

## The Catholic faith

[Col. 0719B]

### 10.

It is impossible to express in human words that ineffable substance or nature of the Divinity: unchangeable, immutable, impassible, simple, uncompounded, indivisible, inaccessible light, indescribable power, boundless greatness, glory invisible, goodness to be desired, incomparable beauty—which touches and moves the affection of a pure mind, but cannot be indicated or explained.

Where the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are, there is the one uncreated nature, the power of lordship, and natural goodness.

The Father is the beginning of all things, the cause of everything, the root of the living: from him proceeds the fountain of life, the power and unchanging image of the invisible God, who is the Son begotten from the Father.

The Word, or living Reason, who always was, and was with God, and was God; not made from the Father before the ages, nor later received or adopted as a son, nor by possession or creation, but the Creator and Maker of all things; he is everything that the Father is. The Father gave him, by begetting him, everything that he has.

And therefore, where the one who gave gave by begetting, and the one who received received by being born, help was not given to one in need; rather, abundance itself was born. For the one who received cannot be unequal to the one who gave, because in being born he also received that he should be equal.

He who said, “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John XVI, 15), possesses nothing less than the Father.

And because he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant—not losing the form of God—and in that same form of a servant became obedient unto death, even death on a cross; in that condition he was made for a little while lower than the angels, so that in the form of God he might remain equal, because that form is not changeable.

He who in heaven, among pure intellectual spirits, exists in the form of God and equal to God, provides an example as God, so that he might also provide that same example to the fallen human being returning to God—one who, because of the uncleanness of sins and the punishment of mortality, could not see God.

He emptied himself not by losing his divinity, but by assuming our humanity; and taking the form of a servant, he came to us in this world, although he was in this world, because the world was made through him (John I, 10). He became an example above for those who see God, and an example below for those who marvel at the human being; an example to the healthy for perseverance, to the weak for recovery, to the dying for freedom from fear, and to the dead for resurrection.

He himself holds primacy in all things, so that, since the human being ought to follow none but God toward blessedness, yet could not perceive God, by following God made human he might at once follow the one whom he could perceive and the one whom he ought to follow.

Let us therefore love him and cling to him, through the love poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

This Spirit is both life and life-giving and illuminating light; good, and goodness; the upright Spirit, the sovereign Spirit, who is Lord of all; sending apostles, setting ministers apart for himself, establishing temples for himself, breathing where he wills, and distributing the gifts of the Spirit as he wills.

He is the Spirit of adoption, the Spirit of truth, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of knowledge, counsel, power, and fear of God; through him the Father is recognized and the Son is glorified.

For it is not fitting that the Son should ever have been absent from the Father, or the Spirit from the Son. Otherwise the Divinity would have been defrauded in the greatest matters, and it would be considered inglorious and unworthy if God had reached the fullness of perfection as though through repentance and a backward-looking plan.

“Let the one who can receive it receive it” (Matt. XIX, 12); whoever cannot yet receive it, let him pray that he may receive it, let him believe that he may receive it, because it is written: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VII, 9, according to the Septuagint).

[Col. 0719C]

# The Sermons of Saint Fulgentius (C, G, S)*

## Sermon One: Concerning the Lord’s stewards

[Col. 0719D]

### 1.

The Lord’s word—which we must all hear not only diligently but also wisely, and which we ought to obey humbly and gladly—maintains everywhere the balance of its moderation, so that neither the sheep lack pasture nor the shepherds nourishment. It commands some things specifically to us alone, [Note: [Col. 0719D] These words are absent from the Cologne, Mainz, and Basel editions. They are found in the Colbert manuscript and in the Antwerp edition.] and other things generally to both us and you.

For us—that is, for the servants whom the father of the household, the lord of all things, established in his great house for this purpose, that we might minister the word of grace to his people—the duty of holy preaching is specifically imposed. But upon both us and you alike the saving [Note: [Col. 0720D] Basel: ‘of the Savior.’] obedience to the commandments is generally enjoined.

In these commandments, again, as in very rich dishes, such an abundance of spiritual heavenly delights overflows that in the word of God there is enough for the perfect to eat, and enough also for the little one to suck.

For there are found there both milk to nourish the tender infancy of believers and solid food by which the vigorous youth of the perfect may receive the spiritual growth of holy virtue.

There, assuredly, provision is made for the salvation of all whom the Lord deigns to save; there is what suits every age, what corresponds to every vocation. There we hear commands that we are to carry out; there we learn the rewards that we are to hope for. There is the injunction that teaches and instructs us through the letter for knowledge; there is the promise that draws us by grace and leads us to glory.

[Col. 0721B] 547

## 2

Therefore, concerning the servants whom the Lord has placed over his people [Note: Col. 0721D. Basil: “has put forward”], wishing to make their special office clear, he says what we have just heard from the Gospel:

“Who, then, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord has appointed over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom, when the Lord comes, he finds doing so” (Luke 12:13).

[Note: Col. 0721D. Mainz and Cologne: “not to be made manifest, but to make manifest.”]

[Note: Col. 0721D. Basilianus: “Who is he?”]

[Note: Col. 0721D. Thus the Colbertine manuscript and Antwerp edition, in accordance with the Greek text of the Gospel and the Vulgate version of Luke 12:43. The Mainz, Cologne, and Basel editions have “watching.”]

Who is this Lord, brothers? Without doubt, Christ, who said to his disciples: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am” (John 13:13).

And what is this Lord’s household? Surely it is the one which the Lord himself redeemed from the hand of the enemy and subjected to his lordship. This household is the holy Catholic Church, which spreads throughout the world in abundant fruitfulness and glories in having been redeemed by the precious blood of its Lord.

For, as he himself says, “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many” (Matthew 20:28).

[Note: Col. 0721D. This is absent from the Mainz, Cologne, and Basel editions. It is found in the manuscript and the Antwerp edition.]

He is also the good Shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep. The flock of the good Shepherd, therefore, is the household of the Redeemer.

Who, then, is the steward who must be both faithful and prudent? The apostle Paul shows us, speaking of himself and his companions:

“Let a person regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of God’s mysteries. Here, moreover, it is required among stewards that one be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:1–2).

## 3

But let no one among us suppose that only the apostles were made stewards, and, neglecting the duty of spiritual service, let the lazy servant sleep faithlessly and foolishly. The blessed Apostle also shows that bishops are stewards, saying: “For a bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward” (Titus 1:7).

We are therefore servants of the master of the household; we are the Lord’s stewards. We have received the measure of wheat which we distribute to you. If we ask what this measure of wheat is, the blessed apostle Paul also shows us, saying: “To each one as God has allotted the measure of faith” (Romans 12:3).

The measure of wheat which Christ calls by that name, Paul calls the measure of faith, so that we may recognize that spiritual wheat is nothing other than the venerable mystery of the Christian faith.

We give you this measure of wheat in the Lord’s name whenever, enlightened by the gift of spiritual grace, we discuss matters according to the rule of the true faith. And you receive this same measure of wheat through the Lord’s stewards when, day by day, you hear the word of truth through God’s servants.

Let us therefore now speak of this measure of wheat [alternatively: “let us speak”]. From it, as God distributes it, let us all be nourished; from it let us take the food of a good life, so that we may be able to attain the rewards of eternal life—believing in him, hoping in him, and loving him above all and in all things. He gives himself to us both as nourishment, so that we do not fail on the way, and as the reward he preserves for us, so that we may rejoice in our homeland.

For Christ is our nourishment; Christ will be our reward. Christ is the food and consolation of travelers who are running onward; he himself is the satisfaction [Note: Col. 0722D. Antwerp: “she is the satisfaction”] and exultation of the blessed who are at rest.

The measure of wheat also includes what the Lord says:

“Sell what you possess and give alms. Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven, where no thief comes near and no moth destroys” (Luke 12:33).

It is a great good, dearest brothers, highly fitting, very beneficial, and especially to be desired by all Christians, that no one should take pleasure in declining toward what is worse, but that we should all strive to advance toward what is better.

[Note: Col. 0722D. Antwerp: “my brothers.”]

## 4

We are trees, brothers, planted in the Lord’s field. [Col. 0722C] God is our farmer: he drenches us, he cultivates us, he himself grants fertility, and he himself supplies the grace of bearing fruit.

God’s rain is the word of holy preaching; God’s cultivation is the infusion of spiritual grace. God therefore drenches us through his commandment and cultivates us through his assistance.

When he drenches us, he removes from us the dryness of ignorance; when he cultivates us, he grants the abundance of a good life. When he rains, he irrigates the soil of our heart; but when he cultivates, he uproots from that soil the thorns and thistles of worldly desire.

We must therefore be made fruitful by heavenly rains; we must respond with fitting fruitfulness to the hands of our heavenly cultivator. And even if all the trees cannot bear equal fruit, nevertheless no tree ought to remain barren in the Lord’s field.

## 5

We must greatly fear, brothers, that threatening sentence in which it is said:

“Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3:10).

If barrenness is cast into the fire, what does rapacity deserve? Or what will the one who has taken what belongs to another receive, if the one who has not given from what is his own will burn forever?

And if “judgment will be without mercy for the one who has not shown mercy” [alternatively: “does not show mercy”] (James 2:13), what judgment will there be for the one who has committed robbery?

Let us therefore fear our deeds, brothers; let us fear them.

A person obedient to Christ should sell what he possesses and give alms, so that he may lift his heart from earth to heaven; so that he may trample avarice; so that with the full intention of his mind he may hasten toward the summit of perfection; so that he may not be anxious about the things of the world but about the things of the Lord [alternatively: “of God”]; so that he may have the world crucified to himself and present himself crucified to the world; so that he may be altogether poor in the world and rich in Christ.

Who could fail to recognize the greatness of this good?

## 6

Yet we see that not everyone possesses the ability to sell his possessions. For each person has his own gift from God, one in one way and another in another way (2 Corinthians 7:7).

Behold: few can fulfill this very great good, while many cannot. Does it follow, because this perfection is granted to few, that all who cannot yet be perfect in goodness should therefore be utterly wicked?

Does a Christian therefore have to persist in the vice of rapacity because perhaps he cannot yet distribute all his possessions to the poor? Or should he covet what belongs to others because he is not yet able wholly to despise what belongs to himself?

Far be this from all Christians; may God turn it away from his faithful people. For the Apostle truly says that neither the avaricious nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:9).

It is evident, moreover, that all who will be excluded from the kingdom of God will be condemned with the devil and his angels in eternal fire.

## 7

Therefore, beloved, if not everyone can fulfill what the Lord says—“Sell what you possess” (Luke 12:33)—nevertheless what he added, saying, “Give alms” (ibid.), is possible for everyone, provided there is good will; easy for everyone, provided dreadful greed is absent; beneficial for everyone, provided love is fervent.

Therefore it ought to be common to all that eternal happiness be granted to everyone.

Whoever receives from the Lord such great virtue that, for love of the heavenly kingdom, he despises everything in the world should sell what he has and spend it on the needy. But whoever does not yet possess such virtue should give alms from what he has, to the extent that he has it.

Let good will work as much as ability permits. Let the perfect occupy the first place of virtue; let the imperfect at least reach the second. Let the former become gloriously worthy; let the latter be praiseworthily generous.

Let the former be the most ardent lover of holy poverty; let the latter be the most devout comforter of the holy poor. Let the latter have the poor as patrons before God, while the former rejoices to have them as companions in virtue.

Let the latter be such that he may sit with the Lord when he judges; let the former be such that he may stand at the right hand when he is judged. Let the former be such that he may possess the eternal dwelling places by perpetual right; let the latter be such that the former may receive him.

For the Lord admonishes us, saying:

“Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that they may receive you into the eternal dwelling places” (Luke 16:9).

[Note: Col. 0723D. Manuscript: “he admonished us.”]

## 8

This, then, brothers, is necessary for all of us: that no one be sluggish in good works, that no one be barren, that no one, through love of present things [alternatively: “through delight in present things”], despise the future; that no one, despising eternal things, perversely look only upon temporal things; that no one prefer bodily things to spiritual things, or earthly things to heavenly things.

Let us place our treasure in heaven, brothers, so that we may also be able to have our heart in heaven. For it is necessary that wherever the treasure of our love has gone ahead, the affection of our thought should follow there as well.

Therefore the Truth says: “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21).

If, then, we wish to store up treasure in heaven, let us love heavenly things. Do you wish to know where you are storing up treasure? Pay attention to what you love. Do you wish to know what you love? Pay attention to what you think about.

Thus it will happen that you recognize your treasure from your love, and understand your love as an indication of your thoughts.

Showing how we can store up treasure in heaven, the Lord says:

“Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12:35).

## 9

If we wish to understand this saying of the Lord according to the letter, we can find no spiritual benefit in it. For what does it contribute to the salvation of the soul if someone physically girds his loins or lights a lamp?

A different spiritual meaning must therefore be sought in the girded loins and burning lamps—a meaning worthy of the divine command and found to be fitting and beneficial for our salvation.

For the Lord himself did not say without reason in another passage: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:63).

[Note: Col. 0723D. Manuscript: “For he who …”]

In the loins, therefore, carnal desire is signified; in the lamps, Christian faith and love are shown.

[Note: Col. 0724D. Manuscript: “Christian is shown.”]

When the Lord commands us to gird our loins, he undoubtedly commands that the desires of the flesh be restrained [alternatively: “he commanded that they be restrained”]. But when he orders us to keep burning lamps, he certainly commands that we shine with the light of true faith and burn with works of holy love.

When he commands our loins to be girded, he orders us to flee evil desires and deeds; when he commands our lamps to be burning, he urges us to love and do good.

## 10

Let us compare what we have put forward from the Gospel with the prophetic sayings. For one God established both Testaments [Note: Col. 0724D. The editions read: “God established.” The manuscript reads: “The one God established”]; one Lord gave them both. And although the sacraments of the two Testaments differ according to their times, nevertheless the judgment concerning human salvation agrees in both: it commands that we not sin and orders us to devote ourselves to good works.

The Lord therefore commands through the blessed David:

“Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 33:15).

Through Isaiah also he admonishes everyone in these words:

“Remove the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes; cease to act perversely; learn to do good” (Isaiah 1:16).

What the Lord now commands through himself, therefore, he also commanded us through the holy patriarchs and prophets.

For what is meant by “Let your loins be girded” except “Turn away from evil”? What is meant by “Let your lamps be burning” except “Do good”? What is meant by “Let your loins be girded” except “Cease to act perversely”? What is meant by “Let your lamps be burning” except “Learn to do good”?

## 11

The loins of the faithful are therefore girded when evil desire is restrained; when an iniquitous thought is held back; when the mind resists lust; when desire is denied to wantonness; when luxury is trampled; when avarice and robbery are despised; when injury to one’s neighbor is avoided; when pride is conquered; and when envy is overcome.

The lamps of the faithful burn when they preserve the rule of right faith; when they persevere patiently in the bosom of Mother Church; when they despise earthly things and desire heavenly things; when they carefully guard peace; when they love one another purely; when they anticipate one another in mutual honor; when they advance in gentleness of heart and humility; when they willingly and cheerfully perform works of mercy; and when in good works they strive to please not human beings but God.

## 12

Every Christian should have girded loins, so that he may flee lust; he should have a burning lamp, so that he may preserve chastity.

He should have girded loins, so that he neither seize nor steal anything belonging to another; he should have a burning lamp, so that he may mercifully act from what is his own.

He should have girded loins, so that he may not oppress the weaker; he should have a burning lamp, so that he may provide the oppressed with the help of just defense under the covering of justice.

[Note: Col. 0725D. Thus the Basel edition. The manuscript has only “that he may provide the oppressed with the covering of justice” (perhaps for “of just defense”). The Mainz, Cologne, and Antwerp editions read: “that he may provide the oppressed, under the covering of justice, with the help of defense alone.”]

He should have girded loins, so that he may not take food from one who has it; he should have a burning lamp, so that he may give nourishment to the hungry.

He should have girded loins, so that he may not strip the clothed; he should have a burning lamp, so that he may clothe the naked.

He should have girded loins, so that he may not invade anyone’s house; he should have a burning lamp, so that he may gladly receive the strangers of Christ.

He should have girded loins, so that he may flee arrogance; he should have a burning lamp, so that he may preserve humility.

He should have girded loins, so that he may drive envy and ill will from himself; he should have a burning lamp, so that he may show pure love to everyone.

He should have girded loins, so that he may not present his members as weapons of wickedness to sin; he should have a burning lamp, so that he may present his members to God as weapons of righteousness (Romans 6:13).

## 13

This, brothers, is the true and sound doctrine of the Catholic faith. This is the measure of wheat with which the household of the Lord the Redeemer is to be fed.

From it we give you [alternatively: “give ourselves”] as much as the Lord grants, and we continually entreat the Lord himself to deign, by his aid, to feed both us and you in the fear of grace [Note: Col. 0725D. The Mainz, Cologne, and Basel editions: “in the fear of his grace”].

May he remove from us the domination of perverse desire and grant everyone progress and perseverance in love. May he himself gird our loins, make our lamps burn, and preserve them burning, so that neither our love grows cold nor any iniquity rules over us.

But may our Lord and Redeemer grant grace to all and pour into everyone the gift of holy illumination and virtue. May he grant us rightly to understand what we hear from him and to do it as we ought, and may he grant us to preach to you, in sufficient and fitting speech, what must be done.

May he also grant you to understand in your hearts and fulfill in your works what you hear from him through his servants.

May divine mercy accomplish this in all of us [Note: Col. 0725D. The manuscript reads “in all”; “of us” is absent]: may it make us, whom he has willed to be stewards, faithful and prudent; and may it make you obedient and humble, so that we may have with you, for your health and benefit, the Lord’s measure of wheat which we give you [Note: Col. 0725D. Basel: “so that you may have with us, for your health and benefit, the common measure.”].

# SERMON II  
## On the Twofold Birth of Christ: One Eternal, from the Father; the Other Temporal, from the Virgin

[Note: Col. 0726D. Two manuscripts have: “On the Nativity of the Lord.”]

## 1

Desiring to say something about the solemnity of this day, and at the same time considering that one Word about which we intend to speak, we find no words with which we can adequately say anything.

For this Word is not one that ceases once uttered, but one that remains after being born; not transitory, but eternal; not made by God the Father, but begotten; and not merely begotten, but only-begotten.

For God the Father begot one Word from himself, through whom he created all things from nothing:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3).

In the fact that God the Father [alternatively: “the Almighty”] made all things through that Word, it is shown that he begot this Word; he did not make him. That Word, therefore, is God from God, Creator from Creator. Hence he naturally possesses in himself that being which the Father possesses.

## 2

The Son, God, was therefore born from God the Father: another in person, but not another in nature.

He is always with the Father, always with the Father, always from the Father, always in the Father: always with the Father, with whom he possesses one natural immensity; always with the Father, with whom he possesses one natural eternity; always from the Father, from whom he naturally has eternal birth; always in the Father, with whom he naturally possesses one equal divinity.

One is the Father, the other the Son; yet neither is another God, because Father and Son are one God.

[Note: Col. 0726D. Thus the Antwerp and Basel editions. The Mainz and Cologne editions omit the relative “who” in the first occurrence. In the later occurrence, Mainz and Cologne have “who is the Son.” The manuscript has “which” in both places.]

Therefore, when discourse arises concerning God the Father and God the Son, we rightly say that the one is the Father and the other the Son; and nevertheless we rightly say that the Father and the Son are one God.

When we say that one is the Father and the other the Son, we indicate the distinct persons of the begetter and the begotten. But when we say that the Father and the Son are one God, we show the one nature of their undivided divinity. The person of the begetter and the begotten is different, but the nature of the begetter and the begotten is one.

[Note: Col. 0726D. Thus the manuscript and Antwerp edition. Basel, Mainz, and Cologne have “because.”]

## 3

But who could speak sufficiently or worthily? About what? A human being about God; a mortal about the immortal; the visible about the invisible; the changeable about the unchangeable; a work about its maker; a creature about the Creator; a thing made about its maker; a little one about the immeasurable; the temporal about the eternal; the humble about the Most High; one fashioned from clay about him who created all things from nothing.

His omnipotence is indescribable, by which in gratuitous goodness he made us; yet no less indescribable is his grace, by which in almighty compassion he saved us.

He freely made us as the work of his creative omnipotence, and omnipotently completed us as the work of saving grace: there he had the power to establish and govern his creature; here he had the power to lay down and take up his life for us.

[Note: Col. 0727D. The words “for us” are absent from the manuscript.]

By this omnipotence [alternatively: “now”] we mean that by which the Word who was in the beginning, who was with God, and who was God, made everything that did not exist.

[Note: Col. 0727D. The printed editions have “everything that he knew.” The manuscript has “everything that did not exist.”]

By grace we mean that by which the Word became flesh and came to seek and save what was lost; omnipotence by which he made every day; grace by which he deigned to be conceived on a particular day and born on a particular day.

## 4

The same one, made for a little while lower than the angels, became human on a certain day—he who, coeternal and coequal with God the Father, is always the day of the holy angels.

For concerning him the prophet says:

“Announce the day from day, his salvation” (Psalm 95:2).

What is “day from day” except “Son from Father”?

[Note: Col. 0727D. The printed editions have: “What is ‘day from day’ except ‘Son from Father’?” The manuscript has: “What is ‘day from day’ except ‘Son from Father’?”]

The Son is therefore from the Father, day from day; yet the Father and the Son are not two days but one day. The Son is from the Father, God from God; yet the Father and the Son are not two gods but one God.

We therefore recognize the Father and the Son together as one day of eternity; but on the day of time the Son alone is found.

For the eternal day, the Father and the Son, made our body and soul; but on the day of time the Son alone assumed our body and soul.

Christ is the eternal day, the only-begotten one remaining in the form of God; Christ is, on the day of time, the only-begotten one taking the form of a servant.

Christ is the eternal day, remaining rich in order to create us; Christ is, on the day of time, made poor in order to redeem us.

Christ is the eternal day, God from God the Father; Christ is, on the day of time, God-man from a virgin mother.

Christ is the eternal day, the Word poured forth from the heart of the Father (Psalm 44:1); Christ is, on the day of time, the Word made flesh from the womb of the virgin mother.

Christ is the eternal day, true God from true God; Christ is, on the day of time, the bridegroom proceeding from his chamber (Psalm 18:6).

As the day of eternity, Christ creates the angels; as the day in time, Christ saves human beings.

As the day of eternity, Christ feeds the holy angels in heaven; as the day of time, Christ refreshes human beings on earth.

For, so that human beings might eat the bread of angels, the Creator of angels became human, feeding both and remaining whole.

How good is that bread which feeds the angels through vision, so that they may be satisfied by it in their homeland, and feeds us through faith, so that we do not fail on the way!

That bread, which gives itself to the angels for the joy of stability, gave itself to human beings as a remedy for healing; and he who is the food of angels became medicine for us.

## 5

Nevertheless, beloved brothers, consider here the greatness of grace and recognize what God has deigned to bestow upon humanity.

Christ, the Son of God, true God from the true God, and naturally one God with the Father, always feeds the holy angels from himself.

[Note: Col. 0728D. “Holy” is absent from the manuscript.]

Yet the Son of God did not assume the nature of angels. But, so that God might commend his love to us, his Son assumed our nature from us. And the only-begotten God, who is the bread of angels, in order also to make himself the bread of human beings, assumed both a human soul and human flesh.

He assumed both as true, both as holy, and both as clean. He assumed our soul without iniquity; he assumed our flesh with mortality. He assumed a righteous soul, through which he might restore righteousness to our souls; but he deigned to have mortal flesh so that, dying according to it, he might conquer death and, according to it, rise again, through which he would also raise our bodies.

## 6

A great mystery, beloved brothers, a great sign of divine love!

Humanity, despising God, departed from God; God, loving humanity, came to human beings. He loved the impious in order to make him righteous; he loved the weak in order to make him well; he loved the perverse in order to make him upright; he loved the dead in order to make him alive.

And what more shall I say? The only-begotten God loved human nature so greatly that he not only freed it from the power of the evil angel, but also placed it in himself at the right hand of the Father, above all good angels.

For the nature that in the first human being had been taken captive by the evil angel now reigns in the second human being above all good angels.

[Note: Col. 0728D. The passage beginning “The nature that …” and ending “above all good angels” is found in the Antwerp edition and in the Thuane manuscript. It is absent from the Colbertine manuscript and the other printed editions.]

The nature that in the first human being polluted the world with sin has, in the second human being, cleansed the world from sin.

“The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:47).

A woman, corrupted in mind, deceived the first human being; a virgin, incorrupt in virginity, conceived the second human being.

In the wife of the first human being, wickedness, having seduced her, corrupted the mind; but in the mother of the second human being, the grace of God preserved both an intact mind and flesh. It gave the mind the firmest faith and removed lust entirely from the flesh.

Since, therefore, humanity was miserably condemned because of sin, God-man was wondrously born without sin.

## 7

Consider, brothers, the lines of healing grace shown to us by divine kindness.

Then the evil angel came to Eve, so that through her he might separate from God the human being whom God had made. But now the good angel came to Mary, so that in her the only-begotten God might be united to human nature.

The devil came to Eve in order maliciously to take life from us; Gabriel came to Mary to announce that life would be restored to human beings.

Through the fault of the first human being, the devil began to rule over humanity; through the grace of the second human being, he began to be conquered by humanity: proud over the first, captive under the second.

Through the first he held us captive; through the second he lost us after we had been set free.

The first Adam became for us the author of guilt; the last Adam became for us the author of grace.

The first, fashioned from clay, produced earthly people; the latter, born from the Holy Spirit, made heavenly people.

Through the first we lost the earlier grace; through the latter we received the greater grace.

The first brought upon us the stain of sin, with which we would be born for punishment; the latter bestowed upon us the grace of justification, so that we might be reborn for the kingdom.

Through the first, carnal generation made us children of the world; through the latter, spiritual generation presented us as children of God.

The first subjected us to vices; the latter made us flourish in virtues.

The first cast us down through the vices by which he first fell; the latter raises us through the virtues by which he first ascended.

For the first was the first to fall into hell; the latter was the first to ascend into heaven.

## 8

Meanwhile, brothers, it is fitting that on the day of the Lord’s Nativity you should also solemnly hear of the day of the Lord’s Resurrection.

For the only-begotten God, just as he deigned to be born for us, so also for us, according to the flesh, he deigned to die and likewise to be raised.

This is the day of visitation; that is the day of redemption.

The work of grace by which the only-begotten God saved us began when he was conceived in the womb; and he completed that same work of grace when he was raised from the tomb.

Conceived in the womb, he became a participant in our death; rising from the tomb, he made us participants in his life.

Now, therefore, let us all entreat the Lord that, just as on this day he granted joy to his people, so he may lead us all with joy and peace to that other day, and preserve his people in faith and love.

Amen.

# SERMON III  
## On Saint Stephen the Protomartyr and the Conversion of Saint Paul

[Note: Col. 0729D. The manuscripts have “Dearest brothers,” and do not contain “eternal.”]

## 1

Yesterday we celebrated the temporal Nativity of our eternal King; today we celebrate the triumphant passion of his soldier.

Yesterday our King, clothed in the military robe of flesh, deigned to emerge from the court of the virginal womb to visit the world; today the soldier, leaving the tabernacle of the body, migrated as a triumphant victor to heaven.

He, preserving the majesty of eternal divinity, assumed the servant’s girdle [Note: Col. 0729D. The manuscripts: “tent of flesh”] and entered the battlefield of this world to fight; the other, laying aside the corruptible garments of the body, ascended to the palace of heaven to reign forever.

He descended veiled in flesh; the other ascended crowned with blood [Note: Col. 0729D. The manuscripts: “crowned”].

The latter ascended while the Jews were stoning him, because the former descended while the angels rejoiced.

Yesterday the holy angels sang in exultation, “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2:14); today, rejoicing, they received Stephen into their fellowship.

Yesterday the Lord came forth from the virgin’s womb; today the servant [Note: Col. 0729D. Thus the manuscripts. The editions have “soldier”] came forth from the prison of the flesh.

Yesterday Christ was wrapped in swaddling clothes for us; today Stephen was clothed by him in the robe of immortality.

Yesterday the narrowness of a manger bore the infant Christ; today the immensity of heaven received the triumphant Stephen.

The Lord descended alone in order to raise many; our King humbled himself in order to exalt his soldiers.

For the one who prepared the womb of the virgin for his body deigned to open heaven for his martyr. The Lord Christ did not disdain to enter the narrowness of the womb, so that the breadth of heaven might receive Stephen’s soul.

## 2

It is necessary for us, dearest brothers, to recognize with what weapons Stephen, girded for battle, was able to overcome the savagery of the Jews, so that he might thus deserve to triumph happily.

For such virtue and such a triumph must not be considered insignificant. He could not have been fortified with cheap weapons, since he could not be overcome by many.

For in him the mark of unconquered virtue shone forth: it neither feared the savagery of those who raged [alternatively: “of those who thronged”], nor, defeated by the blows of the stone-throwers, yielded.

[Note: Col. 0730D. The manuscripts: “For unconquered, the signs of virtue shone forth in him, because he neither … was overcome and succumbed.”]

Indeed, he remained so fearless [alternatively: “undaunted”] among those who raged and so secure amid the torments of stones that he confidently reproved the unbelief of the Jews and kindly prayed for those who were stoning him.

What, then, is that great and unconquerable kind of weapon by which, fortified, he reproved those who raged and did not fear [Note: Col. 0730D. The words “and did not fear” are found in the manuscripts]; by which he overcame the stone-throwers, not by striking back but by enduring; and, moreover, though killed, entered alive and crowned into the court of the heavenly kingdom?

Without doubt he was surrounded by royal protection and was in no way overcome by his adversaries. For our King, although he is Most High, came humbly for us, but he could not come empty-handed.

He brought a great gift to his soldiers, by which he not only enriched them abundantly but also strengthened them invincibly for battle.

For he brought the gift of love, by which he would lead human beings into fellowship with divinity. What he brought, he distributed; nor did he diminish anything of himself. Rather, he wondrously enriched the poverty of his own people [Note: Col. 0730D. The manuscript and Antwerp edition: “of his faithful people”], while he himself remained full of inexhaustible treasures.

## 3

The love, therefore, which brought Christ down from heaven to earth itself raised Stephen from earth to heaven.

The love that went before in the King itself shone forth afterward in the soldier.

O admirable power of the Savior everywhere! O grace of the Redeemer, worthy to be proclaimed without cease!

In the mother he displayed the miracle of eternal virginity; in the martyr he demonstrated the sign of unconquered love.

For inviolate integrity remained in the virgin, and the power of love remained unconquered in the martyr. And just as virginity could not be violated in the Lord’s mother, so Christ’s love could not be overcome in the martyr’s mind by such a great mass of raging enemies.

Stephen, therefore, in order to deserve to receive the crown signified by his name, had love as his weapon, and through it he conquered everywhere.

Through love of God he did not yield to the raging Jews; through love of neighbor he interceded for those who were stoning him.
