Through love he reproved those who were in error, so that they might be corrected; through love he prayed for those who were stoning him, so that they might not be punished.

Supported by the power of love, he conquered Saul raging cruelly, and the one whom he had as a persecutor on earth he deserved to have as a companion in heaven.

That holy and tireless love desired through prayer to gain those whom it could not convert through admonition.

For we must not suppose, brothers, that Stephen loved his enemies when he prayed for them, but did not love them when he rebuked them by reproving their unbelief.

Far be this from the soul of a martyr hastening to the palace of heaven.

That holy love preserved steadfast patience in prayer, while it maintained strict severity in correction. And therefore gentleness deserved to be heard in his prayer, because severity in his correction was not without love.

Thus, whether praying or correcting, blessed Stephen preserved love, because in both cases he considered the salvation of those in error. By the evidence of his holy prayer he showed that his rebuke had not arisen from hatred but from love.

[Note: Col. 0731D. In one manuscript the words “that he loved his enemies when he prayed for them,” and the following words “Far be this,” etc., are absent.]

## 4

In doing this, the blessed martyr both showed love to those present and left a very useful example for posterity.

For he demonstrated the twofold diligence of an ecclesiastical steward: in correcting anyone’s error, correction must not be absent from the mouth, and humble prayer for that person must be poured out before God.

The one who has done evil should be brought to shame concerning his evil deeds through rebuke, and should be helped before God through prayer. Thus love itself should speak justice with the mouth, in order to correct the one in error, and preserve patience in the heart, in order to pour out prayer for the erring person with a pure affection of love.

For whoever does not rebuke the one in error is judged for negligence [Note: Col. 0731D. The manuscript: “will be judged … will be condemned”]; but whoever does not pray for him is condemned for his destruction.

Therefore, brothers, whenever someone is rebuked for the salvation of his soul, let him not receive the admonitions of love disdainfully. Let him not consider the present sadness of his own will, but let him reflect on the gains of usefulness that he is acquiring.

He is rebuked for this reason: so that he may be corrected from evil deeds. Yet when he sees correction burning with some harshness of words, let him not suppose that love is growing cold in the heart.

Thus correction keeps watch in the mouth, so that prayer does not sleep in the heart.

Accordingly, the sinner is wisely cared for in both respects: while the rebuked person is brought to shame by his sin, he is separated from evil deeds and, through prayer, saved by God’s mercy.

For holy Scripture also says:

“For the Lord reproves the one whom he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives” (Proverbs 3:12).

### 5

Compelled, therefore, by the charity of Christ, we both exhort the good to remain in goodness and compel the wicked to depart from wickedness—especially since in these two holy men a twofold sign of salvation is shown to us: if someone is good, let him imitate the perseverance of charity in Stephen; but if someone is wicked, let him follow Paul’s example of conversion. Let the good hold fast to uprightness to the end; let the wicked depart from his perversity as quickly as possible. Let presumption in his righteousness not make a good man negligent, nor consideration of his wickedness make a wicked man despair. Let the former hold firmly to the good, and let the latter quickly abandon the evil. Let the good fear lest he fall; let the wicked strive to rise.

Whoever, then, is wicked, let him fall with Paul in wickedness, so that with him he may be raised up in goodness; for he too fell as a wicked man and rose as a good one. The unrighteous man was cast down, and the righteous man was raised up; the most savage persecutor fell, and the truthful preacher rose [Note: The manuscript reads, “the most faithful preacher was raised up.”]. In falling, the impious man lost the light of his body; in rising, the justified man received the light of his heart. Thus he was joined to Stephen and became a sheep from a wolf.

And now Paul rejoices with Stephen, enjoys with Stephen the glory of Christ [Note: The manuscripts read, “the charity of Christ.”], exults with Stephen, and reigns with Stephen. For wherever Stephen went ahead—slain by Paul’s stones—there Paul followed, aided by Stephen’s prayers.

### 6

How true a life [Note: The manuscripts read, “How truly blessed a life.”], my brothers, in which Paul is not confounded by Stephen’s killing, but Stephen rejoices in Paul’s fellowship, because charity rejoices in both! For charity in Stephen overcame the savagery of the Jews; charity in Paul covered a multitude of sins; charity in both together merited possession of the kingdom of heaven.

Charity, therefore, is the source and origin of all good things, an excellent defense, the way that leads to heaven. Whoever walks in charity can neither go astray nor be afraid. It directs; it protects; it brings us to our destination. Therefore, brothers, since Christ established the ladder of charity by which every Christian can ascend to heaven, hold firmly to pure charity, show it to one another, and advance upward in it by making progress. Devote yourselves to good works, so that you may reach eternal rewards, aided by the grace of the Savior [Note: One manuscript reads, “of our Lord and Savior”; another, “with the Lord cooperating”], who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON IV. On the Epiphany, the Slaughter of the Innocents, and the Gifts of the Magi

### 1

You know, dearest brothers, that this day, which we celebrate each year in honor of the Lord, is reverently called Epiphany by the mouth of all the faithful. Since it is evidently a Greek word, it is unknown to many Latins. Hence all Latins indeed pronounce this name, but not all are found to know what they are saying.

It is therefore good that all who call the present day Epiphany, yet do not know why it is so called, should learn the mystery of this day through an interpretation of its name. For the solemnity of this day ought to be celebrated by the faithful, and therefore the reason for the solemnity ought not to be unknown.

This day, then, as we have said, the Christian religion calls Epiphany. Epiphany is interpreted as “Manifestation.” We have received from the Fathers the tradition that, after the Only-Begotten of God had been born temporally according to the flesh, on this day he was manifested to the Magi when they came, and was humbly worshiped by them after they had offered their gifts.

Since he himself is the God who commanded that firstfruits be offered to him in the Old Testament (Exod. XXV, 2), that same God, having been born as man, dedicated the firstfruits of the nations to his worship. Apostolic authority also bears witness that there is one God who justifies circumcision by faith and the uncircumcision through faith (Rom. III, 30), plainly showing by the name “circumcision” the Jews, and by the name “uncircumcision” the nations.

### 2

These are the two walls that came from different directions and came together in the unity of faith in the stone that was made the cornerstone. One wall came from the Jews, the other from the nations. They were far apart when they believed different things. The cornerstone was placed in the middle to draw both walls to itself and to call both by one name, so that they might be one through sharing a name, and might become one through sharing the one grace of the sacrament.

Through Christ, who is our peace and who made both one (Eph. II, 14), Jews and Gentiles became one; the unity of faith gave them one name, the name “Christian” [Note: The manuscripts read, “both,” instead of “one”]. Each wall, therefore, came to the cornerstone, and the unity of faith made the true corner.

One of these two walls was brought in when the angel announced to the Jewish shepherds that Christ had been born; the other wall was brought in when a new star appeared to the Gentile Magi.

### 3

The former were the firstfruits of the Jews; the latter became the firstfruits of the nations. The former were brought from nearby; the latter were brought back from far away. The Jews were near, because they worshiped God; the nations were far away, because they served idols.

This was signified by the shepherds, who were found nearby when Christ was born, and by the Magi, who were brought from distant regions [Note: The manuscripts and the ancient version read, “from the distant regions of the East.”]

Yet when they came, although they were not Jews, they professed that they were seeking the king of the Jews and said that they had come to worship him. For the evangelist says that Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East, and we have come to worship him” (Matt. II, 1–2).

What does it mean, dearest brothers [Note: The manuscripts read, “What does this mean, beloved brothers?” One manuscript lacks “to be worshiped”], that these Magi sought to worship the king of the Jews when they themselves were not Jews? And which king? Certainly not Herod, but Christ.

They desire to worship a king newly born, yet they do not worship the king established several years earlier. They desire to worship an infant at the breast, yet they do not worship the king ruling the peoples. For sons had already been born to Herod, king of the Jews, who were to reign after their father’s death. When this Herod died, Archelaus reigned in Judea, and the younger Herod obtained rule over Galilee.

### 4

Archelaus was born in a palace; Christ in an inn. When Archelaus was born, he was placed on a silver bed; when Christ was born, he was laid in a very humble manger. Perhaps the former was wrapped in costly silks, while the latter was wrapped in the cheapest cloths.

And yet the one born in a palace is despised, while the one born in an inn is sought. The former is not mentioned at all by the Magi; the latter, when found, is humbly worshiped. The firstborn son of a king is utterly scorned, while the firstborn son of a poor woman is worshiped with gifts [Note: The ancient version reads, “honored”].

Who is this king of the Jews, poor and rich, humble and exalted? Who is this king of the Jews who is carried as a little child and worshiped as God? A little child in the manger, immeasurable in heaven; lowly in swaddling clothes, precious among the stars. When his birth became known, Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him (ibid., 3).

### 5

Why are you so troubled, Herod? Because you heard that a king of the Jews had been born, you are troubled, agitated by suspicions, inflamed by the goads of envy, and for this reason you attempt to kill the king who has been born.

Your disturbance is empty, and your thought is utterly vain. This king who has been born did not come to overcome kings by fighting, but wonderfully to subjugate them by dying. He was not born in order to succeed you, but so that the world might faithfully believe in him.

He came not to fight while alive, but to triumph when killed; not to seek an army for himself from other nations with gold, but to pour out precious blood for the nations that were to be saved. In vain, through envy, you feared a successor whom you ought to have sought as a Savior through faith. For if you believed in him, you would reign with him; and just as you received a temporal kingdom from him, you would also receive an eternal one.

The kingdom of this child is not from this world; rather, through him one reigns in the world. For he is the Wisdom of God, which says in Proverbs: “Through me kings reign” (Prov. VIII, 15). This child is the Word of God; this child is the Power and Wisdom of God. If you can, devise something against the Wisdom of God. You are working your own destruction, and you do not know it.

You would have had no kingdom at all unless you had received it from this child who is now [another reading: then] born. The child whom the Magi now call the King of the Jews [Note: The manuscripts read: “This child, who is now worshiped by the Magi, is called the King of the Jews; he is the same, and so forth”] is himself the Creator and Lord of the angels.

Therefore, if you fear the infancy of the one who is being born, you ought much more to fear the omnipotence of the one who judges. Do not fear him as the successor to your kingdom; fear him as the most just condemner of your unbelief.

### 6

Would that, while the Magi were worshiping him, you too had worshiped him with them, instead of sending the Magi to him with deceitful cunning! “Go,” he says, “and inquire carefully about the child; and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and worship him” (Matt. II, 8).

O feigned cunning! O impious unbelief! O deceitful wickedness! If you had certainly resolved to worship this child, why did you kill so many children because of him? The blood of the innocent whom you poured out in your credulity bears witness to what you desired concerning this child.

And yet you not only failed to find this child, but you did no harm to those children either. Indeed, without knowing it, you did what benefited them. Through your savagery they became martyrs, though through their infancy they had been innocent: by the grace of this child they merited to die for him before they could confess him before human beings.

This child, therefore, who created the world, who governs the world, who does everything whatever he wills [Note: The manuscripts read, “who did everything whatever he willed”], who orders all things in a wondrous and unconquerable order [Note: The manuscripts read, “with unconquerable divinity”], arranged and brought about this: through your mad envy those children should receive a precious death, and what you could not provide for them as a friend, to their salvation [another reading: your salvation], you should do as an enemy, to your condemnation.

For this reason he allowed you to kill the infants: so that he might make them triumph over you. He allowed you to proceed to wickedness; he led them to the palm of victory.

One and the same is the almighty Lord who was a little child crying; one and the same is he who deigned to flee from your cruelty, though you cannot flee from his majesty. He fled not from human fear but by divine dispensation; he fled not from necessity but by power.

He deigned to flee into Egypt so that afterward he might deign to ascend the cross. By the same power by which the child hid in Egypt, the young man hung upon the wood. One and the same is the receiver of death and giver of life; one and the same is immortal from the Father and mortal from his mother, dying by his own power and rising again by his own power.

### 7

This child, therefore, who was born is not found among the number of the dying infants because he is himself the expectation of the nations. The blood of this child is not poured out together with the blood of those children because he alone is to be poured out for the remission of sins; and all those children would die in vain unless they were saved by his blood.

This child, indeed, will certainly die, because if he did not wish to die, he would not have been born at all. But he will die not to fulfill your savagery, but to perfect his gentleness: his own goodness, not another’s wickedness, will cause him to die.

He will die not so that you, an unbeliever, may reign in this age, but so that he may make the faithful reign with him in heaven. [Note: These words are found in the manuscripts and in the ancient version, but not in the other witnesses.] He will die not so that he may lose his kingdom, but so that he may gain those who are to reign. He will die not to lose a brief life, but to bestow eternal life. He will die not as a servant of iniquity, but as the Lord of majesty. He will die not by the bond of necessity, but by the resolve of his will.

He will die wondrously, mercifully, uniquely, by his own power, so that he may fulfill his will in all things. For he will die mercifully for this purpose: that, rising again, he may rule over all nations.

He will die as one [Note: This passage seems defective, and we have been unable to restore it from the manuscripts], and indeed as the one whom the virgin’s faith conceived as God-man, and virginal fruitfulness bore as God-man.

### 8

If you do not know the true divinity of this child, consider the star shining in heaven, going before the Magi, and showing the way to those who did not know it. This star had never appeared before, because this child created it now and appointed it to go before the Magi as they came to him.

This child is indeed placed as a little one in the manger, but works wondrously as the great one in heaven. He allows himself to be carried by human hands on earth, yet commands the heavenly things to serve him.

Why, then, do you attend to his infant age and fail to understand his divine power? Thus the natural divinity and natural humanity of this child were truly to be proclaimed: both naturally true, both united, neither confused into the other nor separated from the other.

Mary had as her son the one born from her, for whom the star rendered the service owed to him. Mary gave birth in Bethlehem to that same one, God-man [another reading: Lord-man], whom the star announced to the Magi who were in the East. The Magi therefore came and recognized the Virgin’s son as one and the same God-man [another reading: Lord-man].

### 9

Finally, consider what they offered, and recognize what they believed [Note: One manuscript reads, “what they offered, and you will recognize what they believed”]. For the evangelist reports that, entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother; and falling down, they worshiped him; and opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh (Matt. II, 11).

Through these three kinds of gifts, the divine majesty, royal power, and human mortality of one and the same Christ are signified. Frankincense belongs to sacrifice, gold to tribute, and myrrh to the burial of the dead.

Holy faith does not cease truly to offer all these things to Christ, while believing him to be one and the same true God, true king, and true man, and truly recognizing that he died for us [Note: The printed editions read “so that … he may recognize”; one manuscript reads “so that”—which should be read as “and”—“he recognizes …”].

### 10

In the offering of frankincense, Arius is confounded, for he contends that sacrifice ought to be offered to the Father alone [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts and the ancient version; the other witnesses have “that sacrifice should be owed”]. In the offering of myrrh, Manichaeus is confounded, because he does not believe that Christ truly died for our salvation. In the gold, both are confounded together: Manichaeus does not believe that he was born king from the seed of David according to the flesh, while Arius strives to assign natural servitude to the Only-Begotten God.

Therefore neither will experience the king by whom he is ruled through faith [another reading: by whom he reigns], but by whom he is punished for the crime of unbelief, because one denies the truth of his divinity and the other the truth of his flesh.

In these same gifts Nestorius too is confounded, for he strives to divide Christ into two persons, although he sees that the Magi humbly offered not one set of gifts to God and another to the man, but the same gifts to the one God-man. Let him not be divided in persons who is not found divided in gifts. For this one and the same person is honored by these gifts so that he may be recognized as one and the same God and man.

The offering of the Magi also confounds the madness of Eutyches, who does not wish to proclaim both natures as true in Christ. He removes the truth of these gifts when he insists on proclaiming one nature in Christ.

### 11

We, therefore, dearest brothers, should offer Christ without hesitation in faith what the Magi are known to have offered in their gift, so that the confession of true divinity and humanity may itself be our faithful offering to Christ.

Let us offer these gifts with the Magi in complete agreement, and let us strive toward the region of the saints with wholehearted devotion. Let us not remain on the way of our former life, but, humbly obeying the divine commandments, let us change our way and walk on the path that the Lord has commanded, so that we may be able to reach our homeland, where we may rejoice with the Lord himself without end.

For a person’s way is his life. Whoever lives badly follows the way of error; whoever lives well walks along the way of truth. Therefore, let the one who used to walk the way of fornication now follow the way of chastity; let the one who followed the way of greed now follow the way of mercy; let the one who walked by the way of deceit now follow the way of purity.

Let us walk well through faith, so that we may reach the vision [another reading: hope], where our joy will be complete, because our desire will be fulfilled in good things [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts; the ancient and printed editions have “in us”], through him who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON V. On the Charity of God and Neighbor

### 1

As much as I desire to render to your holiness the sermon owed concerning charity, so much more do I see myself becoming a debtor of charity. Nor do I find how I can express in words the praise of charity, in which, as long as we live in this age, we ought to grow by loving one another, just as we are commanded always to repay it while always remaining in its debt.

For the blessed apostle Paul, when he had commanded us to be released from all debts, wished us to remain forever bound by the one debt of mutual charity, saying: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Rom. XIII, 8). This is the sum of apostolic teaching. These are the counsels of paternal charity: that we owe no one anything except that we love one another.

Therefore, when we hear that we are to owe no one anything, let us not stop at this phrase, but let us also hear and do what follows: that we love one another. Then we shall find holy charity, which we always repay by remaining in its debt, and by repaying which we are savingly indebted.

Charity is a great thing, dearest brothers. The Apostle teaches us to repay it always while nevertheless commanding us to owe it without interruption. O good debt of charity, holy debt, debt filled with heavenly benefits, debt altogether full of eternal riches!

### 2

By this debt, brothers, we acquire great profits; by such interest we obtain immeasurable benefits. For while charity is repaid and owed by us, all our iniquity is forgiven and erased.

Indeed, blessed David asked that charity itself be restored to him for the erasure of his iniquities, when he tearfully implored the Lord for his grave sin. Once he had been captivated by a seductive sight, committed adultery with the wife of his soldier, and, doubling his crime, killed her innocent husband. After the sin had been committed, he was rebuked through the prophet’s oracle; after his confession, he was restored by a healing response. While, prostrate, he uttered the words of repentance in humble supplication, by which he might quickly appease God, the just King of kings and Lord of lords, he is known to have said among other things: “Turn your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities” (Ps. L, 11). And because he saw that this could not be done without the gift of charity, he immediately added: “Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me” (ibid., 12).

That a clean heart is the dwelling place of charity the Apostle commends in these words: “For the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. I, 5).

### 3

Therefore, we ought to consider two things more carefully in the prophet’s words: one, what he asked to have taken away from him; the other, what he requested to be bestowed upon him. He asked that his iniquities be erased, that a clean heart be created within him, and that a steadfast spirit be renewed in his inward parts.

What, then, is iniquity except perverse desire? And what is purity of heart except holy charity toward God and neighbor? When the prophet says, “Turn your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities,” and immediately adds, “Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me,” what else does he say but: “Erase from me the stain of perverse desire, and grant me the grace of charity”?

Take away from me the desire through which I can be condemned, and grant me the charity through which I may deserve to be crowned. Take away from me the desire because of which there is continual pain and groaning in torment, and grant me the charity through which one reigns in heaven without end.

For if I possess charity, which I repay while remaining in its debt and owe while repaying it, I shall not fear the iniquity that I would have to pay for by grieving without end. The Apostle therefore rightly commands that we owe no one anything except to love one another. Through this debt the accumulation of all offenses is taken away from us, because “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. IV, 8).

But no one should think, brothers, that charity ought to be repaid by us in such a way that, once repaid, it eventually ceases to be owed. For when it is repaid, more is owed; and it is acquired all the more when it is repaid while it is owed.

Whoever does not always consider himself a debtor of charity should not rejoice that he has been released from the debt, but should mourn that he has been deprived of the gift of charity. For he does not possess the charity that he has ceased to possess: by failing to repay it, the wasteful debtor has lost what he received so that he might always repay it and always possess it.

Therefore, let him know that he lost what he had received when he failed to repay what he owed.

### 4

But someone says: “To whom do I owe this charity? Or to whom ought I repay it?”

We answer that charity must be repaid to all human beings—that is, to those known and unknown, to the good and the wicked, to friends and enemies. For when the blessed Apostle says, “Therefore, while we have time, let us do what is good to all, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith” (Gal. VI, 10), he clearly shows that in the work of charity one person (*alius*) may indeed be preferred to others (*aliis*) [another reading: to another (*alio*)], but that no one is to be excluded from the benefits of charity.

That holy, pure charity—or, to speak properly, Christian charity—which is patient, which is kind, which does not envy, which does not act improperly, which is not puffed up, which is not ambitious, which does not seek its own, which is not provoked, which thinks no evil, which does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth, which bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things, charity which never falls (1 Cor. XIII, 4 and following), should embrace friends in such a way that it expands even to enemies.

Let it offer itself to friends who desire it; let it press itself upon enemies who do not desire it. Let it hold the former and win the latter; let it delight the former, so that from friends they do not become enemies; let it invite the latter, so that from enemies they may become friends.

### 5

Let us remember, brothers, the words of the Lord: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. V, 44).

Behold, the Lord commands that charity be extended even to enemies and that the benevolence of a Christian heart be enlarged even to persecutors. What reward, then, will be given for such great works? Or what gift is bestowed upon those who obey this command?

Let the one who, through the Holy Spirit, deigns freely to pour charity itself into us show the reward prepared by him for charity; let him tell us what he will repay to those worthy of charity, since he deigns to give that same charity to the unworthy.

Let the Lord speak, then; let him speak and, in his own words, show us the greatness of his promise: “So that you may be,” he says, “sons of your Father who is in heaven” (ibid., 45).

When he commanded that enemies be loved, what was commanded to the hearer may perhaps have seemed bitter; let what is promised to the obedient be sweet. Let the sweetness of this sweetness be held in the heart, and the difficulty of that bitterness will be overcome. Those who love their enemies and do good to those who hate them will be sons of God.

### 6

What these sons of God will receive the Apostle declares, saying: “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God. And if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ” (Rom. VIII, 16–17).

Hear, then, Christians; hear, children of God; hear, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ. In order to possess the paternal inheritance, show charity not only to friends but also to enemies. Let charity be denied to no one, for it is commonly possessed by all good people [perhaps: by all people]. Possess it all together; and in order to possess it more fully, show it both to the good and to the wicked.

This is a common possession of the good—not an earthly possession, but a heavenly one—and therefore the person who shares it with another does not make it narrower for anyone. Charity grows as desire is diminished; and charity always makes the person free whom worldly desire has not held captive.

Charity is the gift of God, as the Apostle says: “The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V, 5). Desire is the snare of the devil—not merely a snare, but also a sword. Through it he captures the wretched; through it he kills those whom he has captured.

Charity is the root of all good things; desire is the root of all evils (1 Tim. VI, 10). Desire is always tormented, since it is not healed by seizing. Charity, however, always rejoices, because the more it multiplies, the more generously it is distributed.

Thus, just as the seeker of iniquity becomes poorer by acquiring, so the giver of charity becomes richer by repaying. Desire is disturbed while it seeks revenge for an injury; charity is tranquil while it delights in granting forgiveness.

## SERMON VI. On Saint Cyprian the Martyr

### 1

The illustrious birthday of so great a martyr, the blessed Cyprian—that day on which, stripped of his earthly and mortal limbs, he migrated to the rewards of eternal life—has commended to us both the teaching of his priesthood and the victory of his martyrdom, and has made us freer from the former temporal sadness.

While the bishop suffers by his confession amid the danger of bloody death and the glory of devoted struggle, the Church suffers with him through prayer. Who does not know—or rather, who does not recognize through wise reflection—that this very day, which now returns to us each year as a festival, was at that time a source of anxiety to Christian and religious minds, while the devout expectation of the people trembled as their bishop, having assumed the dignity of a prelate, confronted the devil?

Thus faith resisted the persecutor, lest the flesh yield to the tempter; thus the shepherd went before, lest he abandon the sheepfold and the wolf invade the deserted flock—which God forbid. The Church grieved that so illustrious a priest had meanwhile been taken away from her fellowship; yet she rejoiced that, when the adversary had been struck down, he had become Christ’s victorious martyr.

His praiseworthy teaching remained in memory; his wondrous virtue stood before their eyes. So great was the God who preserved what he had taught and showed by deeds, no longer by words, what the others ought to do, confirming the faith of his words with the firm solidity of his actions. He believed and trusted that Christ had died for the salvation of all, and did not withdraw from being killed for Christ’s name.

By whose blood he had once been unworthily redeemed, for him he poured out his own worthy blood; and he had believed that the one whose blood he had faithfully drunk in this life could restore eternal life to him.

### 2

He who had given the law gave them a blessing, so that they might go from strength to strength: from the strength of most sincere faith to the strength of most steadfast struggle; from the strength of most ardent charity to the strength of most glorious suffering.

He believed, and he spoke; he loved, and he followed. For he had heard the Lord say: “Whoever loves me follows me” (John VI, 26); and again: “Whoever believes in me will never die.” And the faithful father [another reading: likewise the faithful man] followed the footsteps of the Savior.

Undaunted, he despised the commands of rulers and the edict of judges. Ready, he received the executioner’s blow, and death itself preserved unconquered the spirit that was subject to God alone.

Finally, nothing recalled him from guarding the shepherd and the flock: neither the place of exile, nor the violent officer, nor the time of persecution, nor fear of the judge, nor the threatening sword, nor the approach of death.

For while he was in exile, separated in body—but not in mind—from the Church entrusted to him, he guarded the nourishment of the poor; while hidden in secret, the rigor of discipline; while detained by the ruler, the chastity of virgins; while brought before the tribunal, the protection of the clergy; while driven by threats, a steadfast conscience; while subtly worn down, spiritual vigilance; while unjustly judged, Christian patience.

Admonishing the people by frequent letters, he supported the needy with more generous alms, encouraged the martyrs by exhortations as well as examples to undertake the battle, and did not abandon his care until he laid down his life.

### 3

In the end, he is both guarded and guards: a secure despiser of his own pain, an anxious guardian of another’s modesty; fearing lust more than sorrow, and taking greater care to avoid the devil’s pleasures than to dread many torments.

For the faith, he keeps watch against the roaring lion; for chastity, he fights against the hissing serpent. In his own body he conquers the wickedness of the raging persecutor; in the flesh of young women, the softness of the tempter. Trampling the persecutor’s threats, he avoids the deceiver’s fraud. He yields to no one in fury, nor does he allow the violent man to steal anything.

Therefore, considering his struggle, perseverance, victory, and crown, and sweetly recalling in the mirror of our minds what he escaped and where he arrived, let us sing with annual devotion:

“Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us as prey to their teeth. The snare has been broken, and we have been set free” (Ps. CXXIII, 6–7).

## SERMON VII. On the Thief Crucified with Christ

### 1

We celebrate the Lord’s Pascha, a mystery to be admired and revered above all the other holy festivals. For *Pascha*, in Hebrew, is interpreted in Latin as “Passage.”

Our iniquity had blocked this passage until the small key of the cross opened it. For our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ had mortal flesh, but he did not have a sinful soul. By accepting punishment without guilt, he caused guilt to pass over without punishment.

At his Passion all the stars were shaken, and the elements trembled at the outcome of the Lord’s wound. Day was terrified by an unfamiliar night, and the world encountered darkness that was not its own. Day stood enclosed beneath uncertain light, and almost the very light of the world appeared to die with God.

For this purpose all brightness had passed into night, lest it be forced to look upon the sacrilege. Heaven had closed its eyes, lest it behold the Lord upon the cross. And the world itself was no longer worthy to be a witness, so that only the one who struck him might look on.

The persecutor struck with a spear, and the Redeemer poured out our price. For when the Lord suffered, all the apostles fled; all of them abandoned him. Where is that crowd that went before the Lord—that crowd, I mean, which said: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. I, 29)?

### 2

The Lord suffered, and all fled. They all became mute, lukewarm in love, constrained by fear, and shortly afterward they fled.

Others did not recognize the one performing miracles; the thief recognized him hanging on the cross, transfixed in all his limbs. His hands were transfixed, his feet transfixed, all his limbs transfixed. The whole body was fastened to the cross, yet his tongue confessed Christ.

There was one place for the three crucified men: in the middle was the Lord, who was reckoned among the wicked (Isa. LIII, 12). Two thieves were placed on either side, but they did not have a similar cause. They were attached to the sides of the one who hung there, but they were far separated from him.

Their crimes crucified them; our sins crucified Christ. Yet in one of them it became sufficiently evident how powerful was not the torment of the one hanging there, but the devotion of the one confessing.

The thief acquired in suffering what Peter had lost through fear. He committed a crime, ascended the cross, changed his cause, and gained paradise. He truly deserved to change his cause because he did not despise in Christ the likeness of punishment.

The Jews despised him performing miracles; he believed in him hanging there. He recognized the Lord as his companion on the cross, and by believing the thief violently seized the kingdom of heaven. The thief believed in Christ at the very time when apostolic faith trembled.

He deserved to hear: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43). He himself had not promised this to himself. He was indeed commending himself to great mercy, but he was also considering his own merits. “Lord,” he said (v. 42), “remember me when you come into your kingdom.”

Until the Lord should come into his kingdom, he expected to remain in punishments, and at least he pleaded that mercy be shown to him at the Lord’s coming.

### 3.

Therefore, thinking of his own merits, the thief was putting it off; but the Lord was offering the thief what he had despaired of, as though he were saying: “You ask that I remember you when I come [Col. 0742C] into my kingdom, and I say to you: Today you will be with me in paradise. Recognize whom you are entrusting yourself to, whom you believe will come. Before I come, I am everywhere. Therefore, although I am going to descend into hell, today I shall have you with me in paradise—not entrusted to someone else, but with me. For my humility descended to mortal human beings and to the dead themselves; but my divinity never departed from paradise.”

Thus three crosses were made, and three cases: one of the thieves was insulting Christ; the other, having confessed his own evil deeds, was entrusting himself to Christ’s mercy. The cross of Christ in the middle was not a punishment but a tribunal. It condemned the one who insulted him and freed the one who believed. Fear, you who insult; rejoice, you who believe. May Christ do in glory what he did in humility. Divine gifts come forth from the depths of judgment. [Col. 0742D] We can marvel at them, but we cannot investigate or explain them.

## 569. SERMON VIII. On the holy day of Pentecost

### 1.

We are celebrating the annual solemnity of the day on which our Lord Jesus Christ sent the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, whom he had previously promised to the disciples. For he had said: “He cannot come unless I depart” (John XVI, 7). Therefore, on the fortieth day after his resurrection—we celebrated that solemnity ten days ago—he ascended into heaven; and, mindful of his promise, today he sent the Holy Spirit, whom he had promised to the one hundred and twenty who had gathered together and were faithfully awaiting the Lord’s promise. [Col. 0743A] They spoke in all languages. For at that time it pleased God to indicate the presence of the Holy Spirit in this way: whoever had received him would speak in all languages.

Let us first briefly consider when he promised the Spirit and why he said, “He cannot come unless I depart.” For the Holy Spirit is not separable from the Son of God, nor was he unable to come while the one from whom he cannot depart was present. But because the Lord was still displaying to his weak disciples the form of a servant, in which the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and because even carnal people could behold the cause—or perhaps, “the form”—of a servant, that is, the Lord’s flesh, whereas the form of God, in which he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God (Phil. II, 6), can be contemplated only by spiritual people, therefore he said: “He cannot come unless I depart,” as though he were saying: “As long as your carnal affection is occupied with my flesh, your spiritual vision does not receive my divinity.” For he had promised that through the gift of the Holy Spirit they would be led into all truth, as it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts XV, 9). “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. VI, 8). Therefore the Lord’s bodily form withdrew from their bodily eyes, so that through the Holy Spirit the Lord’s divinity might be implanted in their hearts.

### 2.

Next, let us consider why at that time this was a sign of the Holy Spirit’s presence: that those who received him spoke in all languages. For the Holy Spirit is certainly given even now, yet those who receive him do not speak in all languages, by which evident miracle he manifested himself at that time.

Understand, dearest brothers, that this is the Holy Spirit through whom charity is poured into our hearts. And because charity was going to gather the Church of God throughout the whole world, what one person was then able to do by receiving the Holy Spirit—namely, to speak in all languages—the unity of the Church itself, now gathered by the Holy Spirit, does. Therefore, if someone says to one of us, “You have received the Holy Spirit; why do you not speak in all languages?” he ought to answer: “I certainly do speak in all languages, because I am in the body of Christ, that is, in the Church, which speaks in all languages.” For what else did God then signify through the presence of the Holy Spirit, except that his Church would speak in all languages?

### 570

Therefore what the Lord had promised was fulfilled: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins, but they put new wine into new wineskins, and both will be preserved” (Matt. IX, 17). Rightly, then, when they were heard speaking in all languages, some said: “These men are full of new wine” (Acts II, 12). For they had already become new wineskins, renewed by the grace of holiness, so that, filled with new wine—that is, the Holy Spirit—they might burn with fervor as they spoke in all languages and, through the languages of all nations, prefigure by that most evident miracle the future Catholic Church.

Accordingly, heretics are rightly believed not to have the Holy Spirit, since they are separated from the body that has deserved to resound through all nations in every language.

### 3.

Celebrate this day, then, as members of the unity of Christ’s body. For you do not celebrate in vain if you are what you celebrate: clinging to that Church which, filled by the Lord with the Holy Spirit, recognizes him as her own while the whole world grows, and is recognized by him as his own. As a bridegroom has not lost his own bride, no one substitutes a stranger for her.

To all of you constituted from the nations—that is, to the Church of Christ, the members of Christ, the body of Christ, the bride of Christ—the Apostle says: “Bearing with one another in love, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. IV, 2–3). See that where he commanded us to bear with one another, there he placed love; where he mentioned the hope of unity, there he showed the bond of peace.

This is the house of God, built from living stones, in which it should please such a householder to dwell that the ruin of division ought not to offend his eyes.

## SERMON IX. On Saint Vincent

### 1.

I wonder, brothers, whether you still wish to hear anything. After the martyr’s passion that has just been read to us—so great a passion—the speaker is superfluous and the listener wearied. We have just heard of a savage judge, a bloodthirsty torturer, and an unconquered martyr: on whose body, marked by varied punishments, the tortures had already failed, yet the limbs still endured.

Impiety persisted, though convicted by so many miracles; weakness did not yield, though tormented by so many punishments; divinity was recognized beneath its covering. For when would corruptible dust have endured such monstrous tortures unless Christ had dwelt in it?

[Col. 0744C] Certainly, brothers, after such a spectacle as the unfolding sequence of the reading has displayed to our minds, I would not entrust my sermon to your ears, were it not that “my mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord” (Ps. CXLIV, 21). In all these events, therefore, he must be recognized, glorified, and praised—the one who at the first calling gave faith, and in the final passion gave strength.

Do you wish to know that both were granted? Hear the Apostle Paul: “It has been granted to you by Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. I, 29). Vincent had received both of these things.

### 571

He had received them; therefore he possessed them. For if he had not received them, what would he possess? He possessed confidence in his speech and endurance in his passion. Let no one, therefore, presume upon his own heart when he speaks; let no one trust in his own strength when he endures temptation. For our wisdom, by which we speak good things prudently, also comes from him.

### 2.

Recall the Lord Christ admonishing his disciples in the Gospel. Recall the King of martyrs equipping his troops with spiritual weapons, showing them the battles, supplying assistance, and promising rewards. When he had said to his disciples, “In this world you will have tribulation” (John XVI, 33), he immediately added, to console those who had been frightened: “But be confident, because I have conquered the world” (ibid.).

Why, then, dearest brothers, do we marvel if Vincent conquered in the one by whom the world was conquered? “In this world,” he says, “you will have tribulation.” Although the world presses, it does not crush; although it attacks, it does not conquer.

The world brings a twofold battle line against Christ’s soldiers. It flatters in order to deceive; it frightens in order to break. Let one’s own will not hold him captive, and let another’s cruelty not frighten him. May Christ meet both avenues of attack, and the Christian is not conquered.

If you consider that human strength was present in this passion, it begins to seem incredible; if it is recognized as divine, it is recognized as marvelous. Such cruelty raged against the martyr’s body, and such tranquility was expressed in his voice. So many tortures’ harshness raged in his limbs, and such security sounded in his words.

### 3.

In a remarkable way, we might have thought that someone else was speaking while Vincent suffered, or certainly that someone else was being tortured while Vincent spoke. And truly, brothers, that is how it was—entirely so: someone else was speaking. For Christ also promised this to his witnesses. You have just heard it. In the Gospel he was speaking and said to those whom he was preparing for such contests: “Do not think about how or what you will speak. For it will be given to you in that hour how or what you should speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 19–20).

The flesh, therefore, was suffering; the spirit was speaking. And while the spirit spoke, not only was impiety convicted, but weakness was also strengthened. The tortures made the martyr more glorious to us. Pierced by a multiplicity of varied wounds, he did not abandon the battle but renewed it with greater vigor.

You might think that, while the flame continued, it did not burn him; rather, like a potter’s furnace receiving soft clay and making it hard earth, it hardened him. Our martyr could have said to Datian: “My flesh no longer cares about your fires, because my strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. XXI, 16). For it is truly written: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation in tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. XXVII, 6).

Vincent was tested and fired in that flame. Datian, however, burned and crackled. For if he was not burning, why was he smoking? What were the words of the enraged man except the smoke of one who was burning? Thus, while he brought flames upon our martyr, who possessed coolness in his heart, he himself, kindled by the torches of fury, burned inwardly like a furnace and scorched the devil who inhabited him.

Through the furious cries of Datian that you heard, through his savage eyes and threatening expressions, through the turbulent movements of his whole body, that inner inhabitant was moving; through these visible signs, like the crackling cracks of the vessel he had filled, he was revealing himself.

### 572

The flame did not torment the martyr as much as madness ravaged Datian.

### 4.

But now, brothers, all those things have passed away: Datian’s anger and Vincent’s punishment. Datian’s punishment remains, however, and Vincent’s crown.

Finally, setting aside for the moment the ultimate outcomes of future tribulation, let us also demonstrate in this world the glory of the martyrs. What region today, what overseas province, as far as either the Roman Empire or the Roman name extends, does not rejoice to celebrate Vincent’s birthday? Yet who would have heard Datian’s name today, except one who had read it in this passion?

And when the Lord preserved the martyr’s body with such care, as you have heard, what else did he demonstrate except that he had governed the victorious man, whom he did not leave lifeless? Vincent therefore conquered Datian while alive, and conquered him when dead: alive, he trampled upon tortures; dead, he swam across the seas.

But the one who gave an unconquered spirit amid the claws of the torturer himself guided the extinguished corpse amid the waves. The torturer’s flame did not bend his heart, nor did the sea’s water sink his body; but in all these things there is nothing belonging to him except that “the death of his saints is precious in the sight of the Lord” (Ps. CXV, 15).

## SERMON X. On what the prophet Micah says: “I shall show you, O man, what is good”

### 1.

Concerning the present prophetic reading, which contains great benefit for our souls, we have resolved to speak to your charity, asking from him an appropriate ability for speech, from whom we have freely received a good will. For who gives this except God, who works in his people both the willing and the accomplishing, according to his good will (Phil. II, 13)?

Therefore let us together review the words of the holy Micah, which we have likewise heard. Would that, brothers, just as we review them in speech, so we might fulfill them in our works!

For we heard the words of a holy man, a just man, a pious man, a man concerned for his salvation; a man who knew that he had been created by God and who considered himself subject to God; a man who awaited the divine judgment with great fear and trembling, knowing that before the tribunal of the just Judge he would have to render an account not only of his deeds and words but also of his very thoughts.

Therefore, thinking about God’s future judgment—a judgment which all of us must fear and about which we must think in all our works with great trepidation of heart—this holy and just man asked what he should do, or with what gifts he should entreat God the Judge. He knew that almighty God, who created all things and made everything from nothing, who established nothing out of the want of poverty but all things out of the abundance of goodness, does not seek only our gifts but also our works.

Indeed, he knew that God is especially pleased by our gifts when we please him through holy conduct and good works. Thus, seeking what a human being ought to offer to God, this man said: “What worthy offering shall I make to the Lord?” (Mic. VI, 6). By this wording—he did not say, “What shall I offer to the Lord?” but “What worthy offering shall I make to the Lord?”—he taught us that whenever we wish to offer a gift to God, we should seek something worthy and offer it.

What, however, can be worthy in an offering to God except what is preeminent among creatures? Among all the creatures that the Lord made upon the earth, none can be found better than the creature whom God made in his own image. This creature on earth is the human being.

### 2.

Therefore, whoever wishes to offer something worthy to God should offer himself before anything else. For God, who made the human being in his own image, is pleased to have his image offered to him, and commands that it be presented to him pure and clean.

That is why our Savior answered certain people who were testing him: “Give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII, 21). This means: “O human being, just as you return Caesar’s image to Caesar on a coin, so return God’s image to God in yourself.”

Return, human being, his image to your Creator; return it just, not unjust; humble, not proud; not made foul by greed, nor disfigured by rapacity, nor fickle through the vice of anger, nor crushed by earthly love, nor soiled by envy, nor polluted by fornication; but complete through the weight of prudence, clean through the truth of faith, and shining through good conduct and works.

The most holy prophet admonishes us how we should return God’s image to him in ourselves, saying: “I shall show you, O man, what is good and what the Lord requires of you: namely, to do judgment and justice, to love mercy, and to walk carefully with your God” (Mic. VI, 8).

### 3.

Let us first inquire what it means “to do judgment,” which the blessed prophet placed first. A judgment is called an assembly in which the accusation and defense of some person are contested; hence it is necessary that the guilty person depart condemned, while the one proved innocent withdraw victorious.

Return, therefore, to yourself, human being. Seek the accusation in yourself, the defense in yourself, the judgment in yourself. Indeed, be yourself both accuser and defender and judge. Enter the secret chamber of your heart, where the eyes of the Lord your God alone see you.

There accuse yourself, so that you may be able to be defended by your accusation. There convict yourself, so that you may obtain victory. There condemn yourself, so that you may deserve to be acquitted. There punish yourself, if you wish to be freed from the punishment of eternal punishment.

Christian, carry out a true and just judgment within yourself; carefully attend to the secrets of your heart. Place your evil deeds before your own eyes. Frequently review and reread whatever you have erased in the innermost book of your memory. Examine yourself by yourself without overlooking anything, and afflict yourself with the tortures of thought.

Pronounce a just sentence upon yourself. Whatever evil you have done by sinning, punish by truly repenting; and, having become the judge of your sins, do to your iniquities what judges customarily do to persons charged with capital crimes. Do not favor yourself when you judge your own case.

But examine your evils with severity; with rigor [or: “with vigor”] pronounce the sentence of condemnation upon your sins, and kill the sins that you condemn in yourself.

### 4.

To kill sins means henceforth in no way to obey sins. Therefore, do not be a perpetrator of sins, and you will be their killer. If you are a just judge of your sins, you will emerge acquitted from God’s just judgment.

But in order to be able to carry out a just judgment upon yourself, hear the Apostle Paul, who teaches what works you must put to death within yourself so that you may reach life. For he says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols; because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience” (Col. III, 5–6).

There you have, human being, what you must judge in yourself; you have what you must condemn and what you must put to death in yourself. Judge these things, and you will not be judged. Condemn these things, and you will not be condemned. Put these things to death, and you will not die.

Here be a most severe judge; here be a most forceful executioner. Judge these things by considering them rightly; put them to death by casting them away. For if you consider your sins rightly, you have judged them; if you cast them away, you have killed them.

Therefore, in order to defend yourself, accuse yourself; in order to acquit yourself, judge yourself; and in order to lead your case to victory, examine your conscience. Recognize your iniquity, put your desire to death, correct your life, and by judging rightly you will free your soul.

### 5.

Behold, brothers, how much the Lord has granted: we have said what it means to do judgment. Let us now say what it means to do justice.

To do justice means that you should not do to another what you do not wish to be done to you, but also that you should do to another what you are pleased to have done to you by another. You wish every person to do good to you; for it is just that every person do good to another, because one who does evil to another acts against justice.

By evil I mean the deed by which one sins through perverse desire, not the deed by which punishment is inflicted upon sinners through charity. I now call evil not what recalls one’s neighbor from guilt, but what provokes the just God to anger. I call evil not what severity rightly inflicts, but what iniquity habitually perpetrates wrongly. I now call evil what can never be just but is always found to be unjust. I call evil that by which one sins against God, not that by which one takes care of one’s neighbor.

I therefore call evil that which is evil to all who do it, so that it is good to none who suffer it. A human being will therefore do justice if he does evil to no one and does good to everyone. Let him do no evil to anyone, against which the blessed Apostle forbids us when he says: “Returning evil for evil to no one” (Rom. XII, 17).

By these words he commended complete benevolence to us. For he did not say, “Doing evil to no one,” but “Returning evil for evil to no one,” showing that it is not enough for a Christian not to inflict evil unless he also learns not to return it. From this it is understood how exceedingly bad it is if we do evil to someone, since when others do evil we ought not to return evil for evil.

### 6.

Therefore, Christian, observe justice according to its rule. Do good to every person; do not do evil to anyone, nor return it. For if you return evil for evil, you will undoubtedly also be evil.

Then the one who first did evil to you will not be the only evil person, because he will have you as a companion in wickedness. But when you begin to return evil for evil, you will be more blameworthy in this respect, because you imitate the evil that you condemn in others.

Having become evil, you do not conquer evil but are conquered by evil—and what is worse, you are conquered not by another’s evil but by your own. For there is no way for you to become evil except by departing from goodness. Thus you will remain in yourself condemnably defeated if you have been corrupted by the fault of your own will.

You will most certainly overcome an evil person when you yourself remain good, when you return not evil for evil but good for evil. Therefore the Apostle, who says, “Returning evil for evil to no one,” says a little later: “Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good” (ibid., 21).

### 7.

To ensure that we return evil for evil to no one, we have heard the Apostle together; let us also hear from that same Apostle that we should do good to everyone. He says: “Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all” (Gal. VI, 10).

We do justice, then, when we do to people what we wish people to do to us. The Savior himself, commending this justice, says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. VII, 12). What do you wish people to do to you except good things? But if they do evil to you, they are not doing what you wish.

Therefore, if you return evil for evil, because you do not do to people what you wish them to do to you, you are certainly not doing what Christ commanded but what the devil persuaded you to do.

Accordingly, in order to do the justice that Christ commanded, give to each person what you desire to receive from all people. Thus you will do judgment and justice, about which the blessed prophet admonished us.

You will do judgment if, by repenting, you condemn your sins and, by condemning them, live well. You will do justice if you return evil for evil to no one but do good to everyone. This is what the Apostle commends when he says: “See that no one returns evil for evil to anyone, but always pursue what is good for one another and for all” (I Thess. V, 15).

### 8.

But because good works are then done well and profitably when they proceed from a good will, therefore, after the prophet had said that we ought to do judgment and justice, he added: “And to love mercy.”

For those who are exalted ought especially to show mercy to the humble, and the rich ought to provide for the poor. This mercy is exercised in two ways: when forgiveness is granted to one who sins and promises correction, and when what is necessary is not denied to one in need.

It belongs to this mercy that a superior should not oppress an inferior but defend him with justice; that the rich should take nothing from the poor but feed and clothe the poor; that he should not lie in wait for the poor but rather console him by his benefactions.

What, then, makes a fragile and mortal human being puff himself up? Why does earth and ashes grow proud? Why does the proud rich man exalt himself over the poor? Why does he despise the poor? Why does he oppress the poor? Why does he either fail to give the poor bread through stinginess, or take it away through rapacity, and, to the one to whom he ought to give generously something of what he possesses, cruelly attempt to take away the little that he has?

[Note: [Col. 0749C] The word “something” appears to be redundant.]

He thinks that when he burdens the poor he lightens himself; he supposes that when he afflicts the poor he provides some good for himself. He does not know that when he oppresses the poor he imposes the heaviest burden upon himself, nor does he realize that if he considers anything concerning the poor, he is considering himself.

For he does good to himself when he does good to the poor. But if he thinks of doing evil to the poor, he will harm himself more than the poor.

### 9.

Let the rich, then, do good to the poor, and it will benefit him. Let him love mercy and always show it to the poor, so that he himself may find mercy on the day of tribulation [or: “retribution”].

Let him consider himself placed above the poor person in such a way that he remembers himself to be placed beneath the rich God. Therefore let him not hesitate to show mercy to the poor person, since he is pleased to receive mercy from the rich God.

Let him remember that God is the judge, who has eternal power over all things. For he sees the deeds of everyone, and he will repay each according to his works (Matt. XVI, 27). Hence it is truly said: “Judgment without mercy awaits the one who has not shown mercy” (Jas. II, 13), and: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V, 7).

### 10.

Therefore let us do judgment and justice; let us love mercy. When we do judgment and justice and love mercy, we walk carefully with our God.

The one who advances in good conduct and works walks with God; he who places heavenly things before earthly things and eternal things before temporal things walks with God. But everyone must walk carefully—that is, he must not be high-minded but must fear; he must flee pride and attribute no good to his own merits, but in everything good that he has done recognize God’s grace.

This carefulness makes a person walk with Christ along the path of humility and reach the height of the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore, turning together to the Lord, let us beseech his mercy, that he may bestow upon us his grace, by which we may be able to maintain right judgment within ourselves, show justice to others, and, loving mercy, not oppress the poor but support them; so that in the sight of God—to whom we sing of mercy and judgment (Ps. C, 1)—we may be able to find mercy exalted above judgment.

[Col. 0749C]

# DOCUMENTS OF THE CATHOLIC FAITH, EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOKS OF SAINT FULGENTIUS Against the Acts that the heretic Fabian falsely concocted against him (C)

## FROM BOOK I. On the One Most High, the Paraclete, the Messenger, the Teacher, and the Judge

### 577. FRAGMENT I. The Son is both God and Most High, and life like the Father; he also does the same things as the Father and does them similarly

[Col. 0749D]

I wonder, then, since according to your own inclination you measure the merits of the Son and the Holy Spirit from those names and works, why you do not also consider those names and works by which the one natural exaltation of the Father and the Son is demonstrated.

For when it is said, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1), the name of the Son is understood to be in no way less than the name of the Father, since the Son, just as the Father, is not deprived of the name of God.

Likewise, we know that the Father is called Most High, but it is also certain that the Son is called by this name. For the angel Gabriel is found to call the Father Most High when, speaking to Mary, he says: “Behold, you will receive in your womb and give birth to a son, and you will call his name Jesus. He will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High” (Luke I, 31–32).

Concerning the Son himself, blessed David, filled with divine inspiration, sang as follows: “Mother Zion says: ‘A man was made in her, and he himself, the Most High, founded her’” (Ps. LXXXVI, 5).

Who, moreover, would dare deny the unity of works in the Father and the Son, when the Son himself shows that the same works are both his and the Father’s? For he says: “Whatever the Father does, the Son also does in the same way” (John V, 19).

Here he shows that between the Father and the Son the functions of divine operation are in no respect dissimilar or divided. For the one who does the same things in the same way, just as he does not do different things, so he does not do them differently. But since whatever the Father does, the Son also does in the same way, just as nothing is divided in the work, so nothing is different in power.

The one nature of the Father and the Son therefore agrees in the unity of the work, and in the similarity of operation the one omnipotence of the divine nature shines forth. If the Son were another God, he would not himself do the same things that the Father does; and if the Son’s divinity were lesser, it would not have done the same things in the same way. But since the works of the Father and the Son are the same and are done similarly by the Father and the Son, the one nature of the Father and the Son is recognized without doubt.

Hear further the natural unity of the Father and the Son, both in names and in works. For the Son says: “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has also given the Son to have life in himself” (ibid., 26).

To give the Son life is the same as to beget the Son as life. For the Father gave the Son to have life in himself, but as the Father has it—as a right belonging to generation, not as a gift of generosity. And observe how he gave the Son to have life in himself: just as the Father certainly has life in himself.

The Father has life in himself because he is life by nature. Accordingly, he also gave the Son to have life in himself because he naturally begot the Son as life.

Therefore blessed John does not cease to proclaim the Son as life, saying of him: “He is the true God and eternal life” (I John V, 20). In another passage also, just as he calls the Father life, so he calls the Son life. For he says: “What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked upon and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life” (I John I, 1).

We know that the Son is the Word of the Father. Therefore, when the Son is called the Word of life, we see the Father proclaimed by the name of life. He names that very Word of life as life in what follows, saying: “And the life was made manifest, and we have seen and testify and proclaim to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was made manifest to us” (ibid., 2).

Behold: the Father is called life, and the Son life, because the Son is proclaimed both as the Word of life and as life. Accordingly, the unity of the name in the Father and the Son does not naturally differ; hence, consistently, the unity of works also agrees through natural majesty.

The Son himself says: “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes” (John V, 21). In saying this he shows both the unity and the perfect power of the Father’s will and his own.

Here, then, there is no will belonging to one who is weak; there is no work belonging to one who is unwilling. For the Son gives life to those whom he wishes; but without doubt the Son gives life to those to whom the Father gives life, since whatever the Father does, the Son also does.

Likewise, the Son gives life to those whom he wishes, just as the Father gives life to those whom he wishes; for whatever the Father does, the Son not only does the same things but also does them in the same way.

In this unity of work there is one natural will. For if the Son is said to do unwillingly those things that the Father does willingly, he does indeed do the same things, but he does not do them in the same way. Yet the Truth says that he does both the same things and does them similarly.

Let the natural unity and equality of majesty therefore be recognized, where there can be no difference either in work or in will. Why, then, do you assert a difference of nature and some inequality—I do not know what kind—between the Father and the Son on the basis of those names and works you have set forth, and fail to recognize the equality of the Father and the Son on the basis of these names and works that I have recalled?

## FRAGMENT II. God the Father is also the Paraclete
You have indeed said that God the Father, who is inferior to no one and subject to no one, is entirely without that humility of works and names. First, then, recognize that God the Father is not without the work of the Paraclete, so that from this you may learn not to quarrel over the name. For if we find in the Father the work signified by this name, there will be no need to dispute about proving the name.

*Paraclete* in Latin means not only “Advocate” but also “Comforter.” Hear, therefore, what the Apostle says about God the Father, and recognize from the true work of consolation the truth of God the Comforter. The Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says:

> Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who comforts us in all our tribulation (II Cor. I, 3).

In Greek this is written as follows:

> Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς καὶ Πατὴρ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ὁ Πατὴρ τῶν οἶκτιρμῶν καὶ Θεὸς πάσης παρακλήσεως, ὁ παρακαλῶν ἡμᾶς ἐπὶ πάσῃ τῇ θλίψει ἡμῶν  
> “Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who comforts us in all our tribulation” (in the Bible: ὑμῶν, “your tribulation”).

Joining the Father’s consolation also to the consolation of the Son, shortly afterward he says:

> For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so also through Christ our consolation abounds (ibid., 5).

And lest you suppose that the consolation of the Father and the Son is different or divided in us, hear what that blessed Apostle himself writes to the Thessalonians. He says:

> May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us everlasting consolation and good hope by grace, comfort your hearts and strengthen you in every good work and word (II Thess. II, 16).

The word I have rendered here as “comfort” is found in some Latin codices as *exhortetur*, “may he exhort.” But whether this reading or that one is accepted, since among the Greeks both consolation and exhortation are called παράκλησις (*paraklēsis*), we have rendered it this way in order to show that the Father and the Son have one consolation, or one exhortation. Among the Latins, too, although the two expressions differ in sound, they agree in meaning. For every comforter does nothing other than urge the soul of the person whom he comforts toward the hope of a better outcome. Thus, although there may be exhortation that does not seem to require consolation, there is no consolation that does not need the language of exhortation.

That passage is expressed in Greek as follows:

> Αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ Κύριος ὑμῶν (in the Bible: ἡμῶν) Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς, καὶ ὁ Θεὸς καὶ Πατὴρ ἡμῶν, ὁ ἀγαπήσας ἡμᾶς, καὶ διδοὺς (in the Bible: δοὺς) παράκλησιν αἰωνίαν, καὶ ἐλπίδα ἀγαθὴν ἐν χάριτι, παρακαλέσαι ὑμῶν τὰς καρδίας, καὶ στηρίξαι ὑμᾶς ἐν πάντι λογῷ καὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ.  
> “May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us everlasting consolation and good hope by grace, comfort your hearts and strengthen you in every good word and work.”

Consider carefully also that passage in which the Apostle, writing to the Philippians, says:

> If, therefore, there is any consolation in Christ (Phil. II, 1),

and you will find it written thus:

> Εἴ τις οὖν παράκλησις ἐν Χριστῷ.  
> “If, therefore, there is any consolation in Christ.”

Divine Scripture has not kept silent about the consolation of the Holy Spirit, bestowed upon the holy Church. For it is said in the Acts of the Apostles:

> The Church throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace; and, being built up and walking in the fear of the Lord, it was filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit (Acts IX, 31).

In Greek it is written as follows:

> Αἱ μὲν οὖν Ἐκκλησίαι καθ᾿ ὅλης τῆς Ἰουδαίας, καὶ Γαλιλαίας, καὶ Σαμαρείας εἶχον εἰρήνην, οἰκοδομούμεναι καὶ πορευόμεναι τῷ φόβῳ τοῦ Κυρίου, καὶ τῇ παρακλήσει τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος ἐπληθύνοντο.  
> “The churches throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace; and, being built up and walking in the fear of the Lord, they increased through the consolation of the Holy Spirit.”

How, then, is the Father denied to be the Comforter, when he comforts his own people? For he is, as was said above, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who comforts us in all our tribulation (II Cor. I, 3). Recognize, therefore, God the Father as our Comforter in his work, and learn not to quarrel vainly over the name. But if you persist in stubbornly denying this, you will deny yourself the benefit of his consolation. Take care lest, by denying one whom you call the Comforter, you find him to be the avenger.

## FRAGMENT III. The functions of angel or messenger, teacher, and judge are common to the Father and the Holy Spirit. Assistance differs from ministry.

I am astonished that you wish to prescribe to the Son and the Holy Spirit concerning the name “messenger,” as though someone thereby showed himself inferior if, in any work, he announces his will to those who are ignorant. Yet the name “messenger,” which in Greek is called *angelos*, is found properly in the Son alone. For he is called the Angel of Great Counsel (Isa. IX, 5).

As for the Holy Spirit, although you may find the work of announcing, I think you will be unable to find that the Holy Spirit is called an angel. The Son, therefore, was called the Angel of Great Counsel; yet that counsel was not the Father’s alone, but was the counsel of the Trinity. For the Son himself, just as he is called the Angel of Great Counsel, is also called “Wonderful, Counsellor.” The Holy Spirit likewise is himself the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and strength (Isa. XI, 2).

The Son alone, therefore, is called the Angel of Great Counsel; but the work of announcing is neither foreign to the Father nor to the Holy Spirit. For the things that pertain to our salvation are shown to have been announced by God the Father. What could have been more beneficial to the world than the coming of Christ the Savior? Yet the Father testifies that he announced him among human beings. For through the prophet Amos he says:

> For behold, I am the one who establishes thunder, creates the spirit, and announces his Christ among human beings (Amos IV, 13).

Plainly, this is understood to refer only to the person of God the Father. Hence the holy evangelist Luke says that when the Son of God had asked, “But you—who do you say that I am?”, Simon Peter answered, “The Christ of God” (Luke IX, 20).

But lest anyone, hearing God say, “For behold, I am the one who establishes thunder and creates spirit,” should wish on this basis to assert that the Holy Spirit was created—although it is established that he is the creator of all things—let him observe that if something concerning the Holy Spirit were to be understood in this passage, thunder would certainly not have been named first. It says, “Behold, I am the one who establishes thunder and creates spirit.” If anyone wishes to understand this according to the letter, there is nothing else that can be understood here by the name “spirit” except wind, which is also called “the spirit of the storm” in the psalm (Ps. X, 7), especially since thunder is mentioned first, which ordinarily occurs when clouds are gathered by winds blowing.

Nevertheless, because a spiritual interpretation is more appropriate to this prophetic passage—especially since, after saying, “Behold, I am the one who establishes thunder and creates spirit,” it immediately adds, “and announces his Christ among human beings”—let us rightly understand this as a prophecy of the ministry of apostolic preaching. For he called that preaching “thunder,” of which blessed David also says:

> The voice of your thunder is in the wheel (Ps. LXXVI, 19),
