that is, “The voice of your preaching is throughout the world.” By the name “wheel” he signified the world; for a wheel is a circle, and small wheels are called little circles. The path of a wheel is called an orbit, that is, the pathway of a circle.

God therefore established thunder by establishing the preaching of the Gospel; he created spirit by making spiritual preachers of the Gospel; and he announced his Christ among human beings through the dispensation of the New Testament.

Since, then, you see that the work of announcing belongs equally to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, why do you seek to demonstrate a difference by means of names, when you find that only the Son is called an angel? As for the person of the Holy Spirit, one can scarcely find this title applied to him.

If you raise a question about the name, you have no grounds for using it against the Holy Spirit in order to assert that he is inferior to the Son, since Holy Scripture is more readily found to call the Son “angel.” But if you claim that the title “angel” is assigned to the Son not according to his divinity but according to the flesh, then do not say that the divinity of the Son differs from the divinity of the Father, since you do not say that the title “angel” belongs to his divinity but to his flesh.

If, as is more fitting, you consider not the name of the work but the work itself, the announcement is found to be common to the Trinity.

Consider, therefore, that saying of the Lord and Savior which he addressed to the disciples when he promised them the coming of the Paraclete; and understand in it the purpose for which you recognize that he came. Before his Passion, the Lord foretold in that passage that the Spirit Paraclete would come to teach the disciples, where he promised that the Paraclete himself would be sent by both the Father and the Son. He says:

> For the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, whatever I have said to you (John XIV, 26).

He plainly says, “He will teach you,” not “He will plead for you.”

Again, in the same discourse:

> But when the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me (John XV, 26).

And again:

> I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth (John XVI, 12).

Here the communion of the Godhead is shown by the very similarity of the work.

The Father teaches us, as the Lord says:

> It is written in the prophets: “And they shall all be taught by God.” Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me (Isa. LIV, 13).

The Son also teaches, concerning whom it is written:

> His disciples came to him, and opening his mouth he taught them (Matt. V, 1–2).

The Holy Spirit also teaches us, as we have shown above from the words of the Son of God.

For this reason blessed Paul also assigns the whole work of his preaching to the teaching of the Holy Spirit, saying:

> For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God. But we have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things granted to us by God. And these things we speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit (I Cor. II, 11–13).

Blessed John also makes this teaching of the Holy Spirit known to us, signifying the Holy Spirit himself by the name “anointing.” For he says:

> I write these things to you concerning those who deceive you. And as for you, let the anointing that you received from him remain in you. And you have no need for anyone to teach you; but just as his anointing teaches you about all things, and is true and is not a lie (I John II, 26).

We have said these things because you wished to bring against the Holy Spirit the name “Advocate,” on the ground that the Lord Jesus called him the Paraclete. We have therefore shown for what work the Lord said that the Paraclete would come.

For since the Teacher himself was departing bodily from the disciples, he was plainly promising them a teacher. And consider what kind of teacher: one who would grant them both knowledge and strength. For he said to the disciples:

> But you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high (Luke XXIV, 49).

And again he says:

> You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you (Acts I, 8).

When that Spirit came, therefore, just as he granted knowledge, so also he bestowed firmness. Hence it is written of the disciples:

> They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God with confidence (Acts IV, 31).

Call him an inferior teacher if some philosophy has overcome his teaching; call him an inferior teacher if the savagery of kings has overcome those whom he strengthened.

I do not know whether you will be able to find the Holy Spirit called a “minister” anywhere. And do not expect to obtain any support for your assertion from that passage of the Apostle in which, writing to the Philippians, he says:

> For I know that this will turn out for my salvation, through your prayer and the assistance of the Spirit of Jesus Christ (Phil. I, 19).

I think that, since you claim expertise in Latin, you certainly know that to assist (*subministrare*) is not the same as to minister (*ministrare*). For in the one there is shown the service of humility, while in the other an indication of abundance and power. From one who ministers, service is rendered; from one who assists, aid is supplied.

Tell me, please: when the Apostle had said to the people, “I know that this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer”—in which prayer he was plainly expecting not their ministry but their assistance, as he shows elsewhere when he says, “I appeal to you, brothers, through the love of the Spirit, to help me in prayers for me to God” (Rom. XV, 30)—when, as I have said, blessed Paul was expecting the prayer of the faithful as assistance, why was it necessary for him to add, “and the assistance of the Spirit of Jesus Christ”?

It was because he wished to show that the Holy Spirit supplies effectiveness to the prayer of the faithful, while he supplies help to those by whom or for whom prayer is made—not doing this by the service of a servile condition, but by the command of divine power, which he naturally possesses as one with the Father and the Son.

To make this clearer to you, I shall also bring forward the truth of the Greek reading in this passage. Writing to Timothy, blessed Paul says, among other things:

> Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for ministry (II Tim. IV, 11).

In Greek this is written:

> Μάρκον ἀναλαβὼν ἄγαγε (in the Bible: ἄγε) μετὰ σεαυτοῦ· ἔστι γάρ μοι εὔχρηστος εἰς διακονίαν.  
> “Take Mark and bring him with you; for he is useful to me for ministry.”

You see, then, that here the Apostle calls ministry διακονία (*diakonia*). But in the other passage, “through your prayer and the assistance of the Spirit of Jesus Christ,” the Greek reads:

> διὰ τῆς ὑμῶν δεήσεως, καὶ ἐπιχορηγίας τοῦ πνεύματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.  
> “Through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ.”

Is it not clear that διακονία (*diakonia*) is not the same as χορηγία (*choregia*)?

Hear also a clearer proof from the Epistle of blessed Peter, by which you may recognize that administration—that is, χορηγία—is not a work of a creature but of the Creator, and may understand, without any obscurity of doubt, that from the name of administration the Holy Spirit is none other than God.

Blessed Peter says:

> Be hospitable to one another without grumbling. As each has received a gift, minister it among yourselves, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. If anyone speaks, let him speak as the oracles of God; if anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength that God supplies (I Pet. IV, 9).

In Greek this is written:

> Φιλόξενοι εἰς ἀλλήλους ἄνευ γογγυσμῶν, ἕκαστος καθὼς ἔλαβε χάρισμα, εἰς ἑαυτοὺς αὐτὸ διακονοῦντες, ὡς καλοὶ οἰκονόμοι ποικίλης χάριτος Θεοῦ. Εἴ τις λαλεῖ, ὡς λόγια Θεοῦ· εἴ τις διακονεῖ, ὡς ἐξ ἰσχύος ὡς (in the Bible: ἧς) χορηγεῖ ὁ Θεὸς.  
> “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling. As each has received a gift, minister it among yourselves, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. If anyone speaks, let him speak as the oracles of God; if anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength that God supplies.”

From these passages, which are distinguished more clearly in the Greek than in the Latin expression, it is understood that ministry belongs to human activity, whereas administration or assistance belongs to divine grace.

For the Holy Spirit to supply assistance, therefore, is to give sufficiency. For when God supplies strength, he grants sufficiency. Blessed Paul teaches that this sufficiency is not from us but from God:

> Our sufficiency is from God, who also made us competent ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit (II Cor. III, 5–6).

While showing his own ministry, he also took care to demonstrate the assistance of the Holy Spirit, saying:

> For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life (ibid.).

You have also thought it proper to call God the Father a judge, as though the Son and the Holy Spirit were not judges as well. Do you not know that the Apostle said:

> I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom (II Tim. IV, 1)?

Concerning the Holy Spirit, the Son himself says:

> He will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment (John XVI, 8).

## FROM BOOK II: ON THE FUNCTIONS OF PETITIONING, GROANING, AND PRAYING IN CHRIST AND THE HOLY SPIRIT

[Col. 0757]

## FRAGMENT IV. In Christ there are two natures, but one person.

We confess Christ as the Son of the living God—the confession by which the Apostle Peter confessed him and, for this confession, deserved to be called blessed by the Savior himself (Matt. XVI, 16–17). We believe him to be one and the same Son of God and of humanity, recognizing with complete certainty in him the natural truth of both the paternal and maternal substance. Just as we do not divide the two natures in him, so in no way do we separate them.

For this is what the catholic Church censures and condemns in the Nestorians. They err especially in this: because of Christ’s twofold substance, they wish to make two persons in him, saying that one belongs to the Son of God and another to the Son of humanity, although he is one and the same Son of God and of humanity—God the Word from God the Father, and the Word made flesh from the Virgin Mother, that is, truly born as God and human.

When he accepted the form of a servant, in which he became a true human being from his mother, he lost nothing of the form of God, in which he is naturally one God with the Father. When he emptied himself, he remained full of his own riches; and when he humbled himself, he did not cease to be what he was, always the Most High.

Thus he also became obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II, 8), in such a way that in the work of obedience he did not lose the rights of his own power. Therefore, even when he died, he nonetheless did not cease to be true God and eternal life; and when he bore the shame of the cross with humble heart, he remained the Lord of glory and majesty.

## FRAGMENT V. How the Holy Spirit groans or petitions.

According to the right rule of catholic faith, therefore, the statement that the Holy Spirit groans must not be understood as though groaning belonged either to the divine nature possessed by the Holy Spirit or even to the blessedness of the angels, which the holy angels are known to possess as a gift of the Trinity.

It is rightly understood in the manner by which what is effected is signified through the one who effects it: that is, the Holy Spirit is said to groan, desire, and petition because he causes us to groan, desire, and petition, inspiring in our hearts the disposition to groan and petition.

The Holy Spirit is thus said to groan, desire, and petition in the same way that God is said to know, because he causes someone to know. For it was said to Abraham:

> Now I know that you fear God and have not spared your beloved son for my sake (Gen. XXII, 12).

Since the unchangeable and eternal knowledge of all things naturally remains in God, and since it is impious to believe that the everlasting divinity came to know something temporally, the rule of truth requires that when the divinity says that it has come to know, we recognize that it makes someone know.

Blessed Paul maintained the same manner of expression when writing to the Galatians:

> At that time, when you did not know God, you served those who by nature are not gods. But now, since you have known God—or rather, have been known by God (Gal. IV, 8–9).

It was not false when the Apostle said that they had known God, as though he wished to remove this in the sentence that follows. Rather, lest they assign that knowledge to themselves instead of to the divine gift, the Apostle subsequently said, in the manner of expression we have described—where what is effected is shown through the one who effects it—that they had been known by God. He thereby showed that it was brought about by God that they should know God.

You cannot deny that the Apostle said:

> But because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba, Father” (ibid., 6).

How, then, does this Spirit, who is not the Son but is nevertheless the Spirit of truth, cry “Abba, Father,” unless it is in the manner by which he makes us cry? Blessed Paul clearly indicates this elsewhere, saying:

> For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII, 15).

You plainly see that for the Spirit to cry “Abba, Father” means that he makes us cry. The Holy Spirit is therefore said to groan and petition because he makes us groan and petition.

Just as the Apostle explained more clearly and plainly what he had said about the Spirit crying “Abba, Father,” saying, “in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father,’” so he similarly explained elsewhere what he had said about the Spirit petitioning, saying:

> Praying at every time in the Spirit, and keeping watch in him with all persistence and supplication (Eph. VI, 18).

See, then, how the Spirit petitions for us: when we pray in the Spirit. See how he intercedes for us: when, with all persistence and supplication, we keep watch in that same Spirit.

The Holy Spirit, through whom the love of God is poured into our hearts, makes us groan and petition for our sins. He makes us groan by making us grieve over our iniquity, ask forgiveness, and desire righteousness. He had received this desire and groaning as a gift of the Holy Spirit who said:

> I roared because of the groaning of my heart; and all my desire is before you, and my groaning is not hidden from you (Ps. XXXVII, 9–10).

## FRAGMENT VI. Christ intercedes for us as a human being and as a priest. What it means that the angels desire to look upon the Holy Spirit.

The Holy Spirit does not, therefore, groan, since in his divine and unchangeably blessed nature there can be no misery that causes groaning. But you object to us that Christ prays for us. We in no way deny this, knowing that the Apostle said:

> Who will accuse God’s elect? God, who justifies. Who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who also rose again, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us (Rom. VIII, 33–34).

Christ therefore intercedes for us according to the nature he received from us. Since the Holy Spirit did not receive this nature, he in no way intercedes or petitions for us.

But what the Son alone does according to the form of a servant, the Holy Spirit gives together with the Father and the Son according to the one common nature of the divinity. Indeed, Christ Jesus himself would in no way pray for human beings if he had not become human. He prays for us in the function of a priest.

But the true person of a priest cannot be found where there is no true humanity. For apostolic authority testifies:

> Every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins (Heb. V, 1).

That High Priest, taken from among human beings, offered himself as the only sacrifice in order truly to offer a pure sacrifice for us. That offering—of the holy and undefiled High Priest—is itself the Savior’s prayer heard on our behalf.

Therefore, according to the testimony of blessed John the Apostle:

> We have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he himself is the expiation for our sins (I John II, 1).

Yet when he rose from the dead, since he does not die and death will no longer rule over him, he was without weakness and mortality and was likewise without grief and pain. Accordingly, he truly performs the function of praying for us, and yet he does not groan.

He intercedes for us without anxiety, since he asks on behalf of those to whom he has determined to give salvation. Christ therefore in no way groans while he intercedes for us: what he possesses from the humanity of the flesh in order to ask, he possesses from the majesty of divinity in order to grant.

But if you desire to recognize the dignity of the Holy Spirit from divine Scripture, see what the Apostle Peter says about him:

> Through the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, into whom angels desire to look (I Pet. I, 12).

When you hear that the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven, you can understand no one other than the Spirit Paraclete.

Remember also what the Son of God says about the angels: they always see the face of the Father (Matt. XVIII, 10), yet they desire to look upon the Holy Spirit.

If you heard that the holy angels see the face of the Holy Spirit and desire to look upon the Father, would you not on that basis assert that the Father is much greater, because the Holy Spirit is seen while the Father is desired more than seen?

Divine Scripture did not say that the Father is seen and the Holy Spirit desired in order to show that the Holy Spirit is superior—which it would be impious to say—but by saying this it indicated to us the equality of the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Thus, from the fact that the angels are said to see the Father but desire to look upon the Holy Spirit, let this statement benefit us by teaching that, since true faith cannot believe the Holy Spirit to be superior to the Father, profane unbelief must not dare to judge him inferior.

For there is one unfailing vision and desire of the Trinity among the holy angels; they always behold it and always desire to behold it. They live forever in the highest good—that is, in the one true and blessed God—because he is always seen and always loved.

Just as love causes that vision not to fail, so vision causes love to remain. Love is not laid aside because the vision is not changed; and the vision is not changed because the good that is seen is unchangeable.

That desire to behold, therefore, is not without the joy of possessing. For nothing is sweeter than the Holy Trinity, nothing more delightful, because nothing is better. From it the angels have eternity, so that they may live without failing; from it, truth, so that they may see clearly; from it, love, so that they may desire faithfully.

## FROM BOOK III: ON THE ONE IMMENSE LORD OUR GOD

[Col. 0759]

## FRAGMENT VII. What belongs properly to each person of the Trinity.

We can truly say something about each individual person that we cannot say about the Trinity as a whole. For we rightly profess that the Father alone begot, that the Son alone was born from the Father, and we also rightly say that the Holy Spirit alone proceeds from the Father and the Son.

The Trinity did not beget the Son; the Trinity was not born from the Father; nor does the Trinity proceed from the Father and the Son. There are therefore certain things which, although they do not pertain to the Trinity, nevertheless pertain to individual persons within the Trinity.

Thus also the voice that sounded from heaven over Jesus after he had been baptized (Matt. III, 16–17) belongs so exclusively to the Father that it cannot belong to the Son or to the Holy Spirit. Likewise, the seeing of the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him belongs so exclusively to the Son that it cannot in any way be attributed to the Father or to the Holy Spirit. And the descent in bodily form like a dove upon Jesus belongs so exclusively to the Holy Spirit that it cannot be attributed to the Father or to the Son.

There are therefore certain things that correspond to individual persons and do not belong to the three together. Yet there is nothing that does not belong to one person and can belong simultaneously to all three persons.

For within the Trinity, although it is one thing for the Son to be born from the Father and another for the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father—since the procession of the Holy Spirit is not the same as the birth of the Son—it is nevertheless common to the Son and the Holy Spirit to be naturally from the Father, although it belongs to the Holy Spirit alone to be from the Father and also from the Son.

But it is proper to the Father to be from no one, that is, to have no author of his natural essence.

## FRAGMENT VIII. The Holy Spirit fills the whole world while also always being in heaven. The immensity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one.

Do you not know that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (I Cor. I, 24)? The sequence of divine speech testifies concerning this wisdom that it is from the Lord God, that it was always with him, and that it exists before the age (Ecclus. I, 1).

Because his invisible attributes are perceived through the things that have been made, Scripture, after saying:

> Who has counted the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of the age? Who has measured the height of heaven, the breadth of the earth, and the depth of the abyss? (Ecclus. I, 2)

so that from created things we might recognize the magnificence of the Creator, immediately adds:

> Who has investigated the wisdom of God that precedes all things?

And rightly so. For concerning this wisdom it is said:

> She reaches everywhere because of her purity, and no defilement enters into her (Wis. VII, 24, 26);

and again:

> She reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things sweetly (Wis. VIII, 1).

What does “reaches everywhere” mean except “fills everything”? She fills everything in the same way that the Father and the Holy Spirit also fill everything.

For this reason blessed David says:

> Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you are present (Ps. CXXXVIII, 7–8).

Elsewhere it is said:

> The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world (Wis. I, 7).

Do you suppose that the Holy Spirit fills the whole world in such a way that he is not in heaven when he fills the earth? But see what the same Book of Wisdom contains elsewhere. It says to God:

> Yet who has searched out the things that are in heaven? Who has known your mind, unless you have given wisdom and sent your Spirit from on high? (Wis. IX, 16–17).

Recognize, therefore, that the immensity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, because the Trinity is one God, who created all things; and everything he made is surpassed by the eternity and unchangeability of his wisdom and power.

Seeing this, blessed Paul said:

> May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus (Phil. IV, 7).

## FRAGMENT IX. The three persons are one Lord our God.

If, then, we ought to think as you say—that the Son is our God, while the Father is the God of our God, and yet the Father and the Son are not naturally one Lord our God—see how by your own words you are compelled to deny God the Father the service owed to God.

For it is said to us:

> Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord (Deut. VI, 4).

And elsewhere:

> You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve (verse 13).

It is certain that the first commandment is also contained in the Decalogue:

> I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery (Exod. XX, 2).

David also says:

> Who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God? (Ps. XVII, 32).

This Lord our God commanded that an altar be constructed for him alone and ordered sacrifices to be offered to him alone, saying:

> You shall make an altar of earth for me, and upon it you shall offer your burnt offerings and your peace offerings (Exod. XX, 24).

In the same book it is also said:

> Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be destroyed, unless it is to the Lord alone (Exod. XXII, 20).

Therefore either, abandoning unbelief, recognize the Father and the Son according to their divine nature as one Lord our God; or say that what we are commanded to offer to the Lord our God alone is not to be offered to God the Father.

You have said that the Son is our God but is not naturally one God. Tell us whom you think should be worshiped and to whom you think sacrifices should be offered: to the one whom you call our God, or to the one whom you assert to be the God of our God?

According to your view, you must either reject the commandment of the Law if you think sacrifice is to be offered to the Father alone, or, if you obey the Law, say that sacrifices are to be offered to the Son alone. For according to your position, the Law commands sacrifice not to the God of our God, but to our God.

## FRAGMENT X. God the Father is the God of the Son from the womb of his mother, not from the womb of his begetter.

Recognize, therefore, that according to divinity the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God; and that to this one God, whom he commands the faithful to worship, all acts of service are rightly and inseparably rendered.

Recognize also that God the Father is the God of the Son, not from the eternity of his divine birth, but from the time of the humanity he assumed. The Son has God the Father as his God, but from his mother’s womb, not from the womb of his begetter.

If you do not believe this, hear from the Son himself the truth of this mystery. In the psalm he says:

> From the womb of my mother you have been my God (Ps. XXI, 11).

Because God the Father is by nature the Father of the only-begotten Son, but is our God, he brought this about through indescribable goodness and according to the purpose of his will: so that, for our salvation, the Father who is naturally the Father of his only-begotten Son might be God to him by grace; and so that he, who is naturally our God, might graciously deign to be our Father.

## FRAGMENT XI. Christ truly our God. “Estimation” in Scripture has two senses: uncertain knowledge and certain understanding. Christ is not the God of the Manichaeans, Jews, or Arians.

Let us accept and embrace the opinion of the blessed Cyprian, who, writing to Quirinus in the second book, chapter six, under the title “THAT CHRIST IS GOD,” among other testimonies also brought forward this one:

“This is our God, and no other will be reckoned besides him, who discovered every way of prudence and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After these things he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36–38).

Recognize, on the testimony of so great a martyr, that this was said of Christ: “This is our God, and no other will be reckoned besides him”; and learn to understand divine statements correctly, so that you do not rebel against the Son of God. For the blessed prophet wished to show the mystery of the divine incarnation. Hence it was necessary for him both to call Christ “our God,” besides whom no other would be reckoned, according to his divinity, and to prophesy that the same one had appeared on earth in the true substance of flesh.

For among the faithful no other God is reckoned—that is, believed, accepted, or considered—besides the Son of God, because “God” is not the name of a person but of a nature. If, then, we attend to nature, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God—that is, one nature—then just as no other God is reckoned besides the Father, so no other God is reckoned besides the Son, and likewise no other God is reckoned besides the Holy Spirit. Therefore no other God can be reckoned by the faithful besides the Son of God, because entirely outside the nature of the Son of God—which he shares as one nature with the Father and the Holy Spirit—no other God can be found.

Thus the blessed Jeremiah, by this testimony refuting the Arians, at the same time refuted with them the Manichaeans and the Jews: the Manichaeans, so that they might believe that Christ—the God whom they believe to have appeared on earth and lived among human beings—himself gave the law to the Jewish people; and the Jews, so that they might recognize that the one whom they both believe and proclaim to have given the law to the people of Israel is the Son of God, and that the same one, having appeared on earth and lived among human beings, must be acknowledged in the mystery of the incarnation.

For the blessed Prophet did not say without reason, “After these things he appeared on earth,” unless certainly to show that after these things—that is, after he had given the way of instruction to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved—after these things, certainly, he appeared on earth. He wished to show that he had not appeared at the time when he gave the law through angels, which the Apostle says was “ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator” (Galatians 3:19), but that he appeared when “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” For he took the form of a servant so that he could be seen, and so that this God of ours, besides whom no other can be reckoned, might live among human beings.

The word “reckoning” is ordinarily used in Scripture in two ways. Someone is said to reckon either when he considers something to be what it is not, or when he knows with complete certainty that something is what it is.

To reckoning based on uncertain cognition belongs what the blessed Stephen says concerning holy Moses in the Acts of the Apostles: “He supposed that his brothers understood that God would give them salvation through his hand” (Acts 7:25). To show that this reckoning was uncertain, he added: “But they did not understand.”

Likewise, in the same book, when an angel had led the blessed Peter out of prison, it is said: “He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought that he was seeing a vision” (Acts 12:9).

But in the Book of Wisdom the term “reckoning” denotes the most certain knowledge, where it is said of Wisdom herself: “If anyone desires a multitude of knowledge, she knows the things of the past and reckons concerning the things to come” (Wisdom 8:8). What does it mean for Wisdom to “reckon,” except to know with complete certainty?

Hence Paul also, possessing the mind of Christ, certainly knew what he said he reckoned, when he stated: “For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18). For in Paul this cannot be called uncertain cognition of these matters, but certain knowledge.

Such, then, is also what the blessed Jeremiah said of Christ: “This is our God, and no other will be reckoned besides him” (Baruch 3:36). For what does “will not be reckoned” mean except “will not be known”?

Hence the blessed Isaiah says: “Lord, besides you we have known no other; we have invoked your name” (Isaiah 26:13).

He, therefore, is our God—that is, the God of Christians—who reckon no other God besides him. He is not the God of the Manichaeans, who do not believe that he gave the law. He is not the God of the Jews, who do not believe him to be the living God but a dead human being. He is not the God of the Arians, who do not believe him to be, together with the Father, naturally one God.

For those who proclaim one nature of the Father and another of the Son reckon another God besides Christ; and because this is not a Christian but a heretical understanding, among those who reckon in this way neither the Father can be God nor the Son. For Christ is recognized as God by those for whom no other God can in any way be reckoned as naturally existing.

## FROM BOOK IV. ON THE WORSHIP OF THE FATHER, THE SON, AND THE HOLY SPIRIT.

### FRAGMENT XII. We are the temple of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Service is owed to them by us.

We are the temple of God the Father and of the Holy Spirit in such a way that we are also the temple of the Son. For it is certain that the temple of God is also called the house of God. Hence the prophet says: “But I, in the abundance of your mercy, shall enter your house; I shall worship toward your holy temple in your fear” (Psalm 5:8).

The Savior himself, when he drove the sellers and buyers from the temple, calling that temple a house, said: “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you have made it a den of thieves” (Matthew 21:13).

The apostolic authority also testifies that we are the house of Christ, where it says: “But Christ is as a son in his own house; and that house are we” (Hebrews 3:6).

It is therefore evident that the Holy Spirit is God by nature, since we are the temple of the Holy Spirit just as we are the temple of the Father and the Son. And since we cannot be the temple of two or three gods, nor are we permitted to worship or serve a creature—that is, to offer λατρείαν [latreian, worshipful service]—we rightly worship one God: not the Father alone, nor the Son alone, nor the Holy Spirit alone, but the Trinity itself, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Otherwise, distinguish the temples, so that you may also distinguish their worth, and say in whom the Father has his temple, in whom the Son, and in whom the Holy Spirit. The Apostle certainly did not make this distinction: in one and the same Epistle he said that those people are the temple of God, and he said that they are the temple of the Holy Spirit; and, calling them members of Christ, he showed that they are the temple of Christ.

For he says again in the same Epistle: “You are the body of Christ and members” (1 Corinthians 12:26). For this reason he says elsewhere: “Because we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones” (Ephesians 5:30).

But observe how our Savior himself calls his body a temple, saying: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). The blessed Evangelist, showing of which temple he had spoken, says: “But he was speaking of the temple of his body” (John 2:21).

Therefore we are the temple of God because we are members of the body of Christ. We are the temple of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—not a temple differentiated among three, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit conceived as a creature, but of the one Trinity, the one God, to whom, as his temple, we offer the service of obedience.

We must not in any way deny this service either to the one God whose temple we are, or offer it to a god whose temple we are not. We must observe in every respect what was said: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deuteronomy 6:13).

This service is called λατρεία [latreia] in Greek. It is owed rightly and legitimately to the true God alone, and is offered not by the faithless but by Catholic believers.

Hence the Apostle censures certain people who “exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25). This passage appears in the Greek wording as follows: καὶ ἐσεβάσθησαν, καὶ ἐλάτρευσον τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα—“and they worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.”

You plainly see that the Apostle gravely marks those who offered to any creature the λατρεία [latreia] owed to the Creator alone—or, according to another reading, “who offered” it.

Moreover, the blessed Apostle, showing that this worship of the creature, which is called λατρεία, consists especially in the offering of sacrifices, wished to restrain the Corinthians from feasting on sacrificial meat and said: “Therefore, my beloved, flee from the worship of idols. I speak as to prudent people; judge for yourselves what I say. The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not participation in the blood of Christ? And the bread that we break, is it not participation in the body of the Lord?” (1 Corinthians 10:14–16).

A little later, showing what worship of idols he had meant when he ordered them to flee from it, he says: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (ibid. 20–21).

It is therefore evident that the worship called λατρεία is found especially in sacrifices. For the statement that we mentioned shortly before—that the blessed Apostle said, “Flee from the worship of idols”—is expressed in Greek by the word idol-worship, εἰδωλολατρεία. The passage reads: φεύγετε ἀπὸ τῆς εἰδωλολατρείας—“flee from the worship of idols.”

### FRAGMENT XIII. How λατρεία and δούλευσις differ.

Therefore true divinity alone claims λατρεία for itself; δούλευσις [douleusis, service] is to be rendered to God in the measure required, and to human beings in the measure appropriate.

Because of λατρεία it is said: “Sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness to God” (Psalm 4:6); and: “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be destroyed, unless it be to the Lord alone” (Exodus 22:40).

Because of δούλευσις the Apostle says: “Serve the Lord Christ” (Colossians 3:24); and again: “Serve one another in charity” (Galatians 5:13).

Again, when the same Apostle was speaking about foods sacrificed to idols, he said, with reference to λατρεία: “But for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we are in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we are through him” (1 Corinthians 8:6).

With reference to δούλευσις he says: “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus” (Romans 1:1); and, speaking to the faithful, he says: “For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants through Jesus” (2 Corinthians 4:5).

### FRAGMENT XIV. When the Son of God is named, not only Christ’s divinity but also his humanity is signified. Christ and Jesus Christ are the same.

What you thought fit to insert under my name into false records, I neither perceived nor said. May God turn away and keep far from the hearts of the faithful this perverse and deadly understanding.

For who, I do not say a fool, but someone utterly insane, would dare to believe or say that, when the Son of God is named, only Christ’s divinity is more clearly signified? Certainly this same Son of God is proclaimed in the prophetic writings not only according to divinity but also according to the flesh—not merely as the Son of God but also as God.

For it is clear that the Son of God, not according to divinity but according to humanity, was anointed with the Holy Spirit; yet the blessed David calls the one who was anointed “God,” saying: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44:8).

Or who would say that where Jesus is named, only the person of a human being is indicated, whereas where Jesus Christ is named, the share of humanity already exceeds that of divinity? Certainly the blessed Apostle says: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus: who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being” (Philippians 2:5–7).

Do you see Jesus Christ in the form of God? Jesus Christ emptying himself and taking the form of a servant? Jesus Christ made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being? Who did all these things except the only-begotten God?

The Apostle also says: “One Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we are through him” (1 Corinthians 8:6). Who, then, is Jesus Christ through whom all things exist, except the one of whom the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3)?

Since, therefore, Jesus Christ is one God and human being, whether he speaks about himself or the apostles speak about him, they nowhere make the distinction that you pointlessly wished to make in that falsification of your records. For our Savior himself calls himself wholly the Son of God, just as he calls himself wholly the Son of Man.

When he had said to the man blind from birth whom he had healed, “Do you believe in the Son of God?” and the man had replied, “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?” the Son of God himself answered him: “You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he” (John 9:35–37).

Did only his divinity speak to that man then? Or did the man see and worship only his divinity? Certainly not. For the Lord Jesus himself, in both natures, is one Son of God.

He says again concerning himself: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). Yet he did not say both things according to the flesh alone. At that same time he did not have his flesh in heaven but on earth; and yet he was the Son of Man not only on earth but also in heaven: according to the flesh alone, on earth alone; according to divinity, both in heaven and on earth. Nevertheless, in both respects he is inseparably one Son of Man.

For Jesus Christ himself is one Son of God and of a human being. Pointlessly, therefore, you multiplied superfluous words, wishing to show that the apostles were servants not only of Jesus Christ but also of Christ. Yet Christ himself is Jesus Christ, possessing both natures in one person, in whom the divine and human substance remains undivided and unconfused.

### FRAGMENT XV. In Scripture neither the Father nor the Son is called “Spirit” without qualification, nor is the Holy Spirit called the Father or the Son. The Spirit of God, the Holy Spirit, and the Paraclete are the same.

At least now acknowledge that the apostles and prophets proclaimed the Spirit of the Paraclete—that is, the Holy Spirit—as the very Spirit of God. Therefore, when the Apostle wrote, “We who serve the Spirit of God” (Philippians 3:3), he taught that we must serve none other than the Holy Spirit, that is, the Paraclete.

We cannot understand this passage, as you suppose, of God the Father or of God the Son. For although the Father is also Spirit, the Father or the Son is never found to be named simply “Spirit,” that is, without some additional qualification.

Thus, in the statement “God is Spirit” (John 4:24), the word “God” has been added. And when the Son is called Spirit, we find that Jeremiah said: “The Spirit before our face is Christ the Lord” (Lamentations 4:20).

But the Father and the Son are never found to be called Spirit absolutely, as we find with the Holy Spirit. Thus, where the Apostle says, “I appeal to you, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Spirit” (Romans 15:30), he plainly speaks of the Holy Spirit—or, according to another reading, “it is said” of the Holy Spirit.

Again: “In whom you also are built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22). And the Apostle Jude says: “These are the ones who separate themselves, natural people, not having the Spirit” (Jude 19).

Thus, when “Spirit” is said absolutely, it must be understood as the Holy Spirit, just as when only “Father” is said, we understand only God the Father; and when only “Son” is said, we can understand only Christ.

We hold this rule, promulgated in the words of divine Scripture. When it names the Father, it shows that no one other than God the Father is to be understood; when it names only the Son, it shows that Christ is to be recognized; and when it names only the Spirit, it teaches that the Holy Spirit is to be understood—except in those passages where a human spirit is intended, or some creature inferior to that human spirit itself.

Such is the statement of the Apostle: “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness” (Romans 8:10). And such is what the Lord said through the prophet: “The spirit shall go forth from me, and I have made every breath” (Isaiah 57:16). For he showed what he meant by “spirit” when he also said “breath.”

He called the human spirit “breath” because it is written that God breathed into the face of the human being the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul (Genesis 2:7).

Other similar passages are found in which not the Creator but some created spirit—whether rational or irrational—is indicated.

Whenever the Spirit is named with honor, however—as in the statement of the Apostle, “through the love of the Spirit” (Romans 15:30), and in all similar passages—it is not permitted to understand anything there except the Holy Spirit. This is the Spirit of whom our Savior said: “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings, but blasphemy of the Spirit will not be forgiven” (Matthew 12:31).

In this passage we must understand that the genitive case is being used, that is, “of this Spirit,” not the nominative, as many are deceived into thinking. The distinction is found in the Greek, where it does not say τὸ Πνεῦμα [to Pneuma, “the Spirit,” nominative/accusative], but τοῦ Πνεύματος [tou Pneumatos, “of the Spirit,” genitive].

Indeed, the Greek Gospel codex reads: ἡ δὲ τοῦ Πνεύματος βλασφημία οὐκ ἀφεθήσεται—“but the blasphemy of the Spirit will not be forgiven.”

There the Son of God, to show who the Spirit is whose blasphemy he declared unforgivable, added these words (verse 32): “And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come.”

Therefore, not only when “Spirit” is stated absolutely, but also when the apostles call him “the Holy Spirit,” the Father or the Son is nowhere signified. We do not, however, deny that, with respect to nature, both the Father is Spirit and the Son is Spirit, and both the Father is holy and the Son is holy; for the Trinity has one nature, and its natural holiness is one. Yet with respect to the property of person, the Holy Spirit is nowhere so designated that the Father or the Son may be understood by the same name. Rather, that Spirit is signified who is properly called the Holy Spirit in the Trinity: the Paraclete Spirit, who is certainly not the Father or the Son, but is one and the same Spirit of the Father and the Son.

### FRAGMENT XVI. We are the temple, sacrifice, and priests of the Holy Spirit, as of the Father and the Son.

This in no way prejudices the divinity of the Holy Spirit, whom the blessed Paul most certainly shows to be God when he says that our bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, whom we have from God (1 Corinthians 6:19).

Here you cannot in any way demonstrate the person of the Father, since the blessed Apostle said that we have the Holy Spirit from God. Nor can you in any way demonstrate the person of the Son in the name “Holy Spirit,” which the Apostle distinguished above when he said: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” (ibid. 15).

In this way the Apostle clearly displayed the Holy Trinity: naming Christ, that is, the Son of God; also naming the Holy Spirit; and likewise naming God, that is, the Father, from whom we have the Holy Spirit himself. You pointlessly inserted the contrary into your lies; but we have him from God.

In this we recognize his true divinity: we do not make a temple for him out of stones and wood, but we ourselves are his temple. And certainly the one who dwells in a temple not made by human hands is the exalted God, as the blessed Stephen says: “The Most High does not dwell in things made by hands” (Acts 7:48).

After saying this, that same most blessed martyr added the testimony that reads: “Heaven is my throne, and earth the footstool for my feet. What house will you build for me? says the Lord” (Isaiah 66:1). Shortly afterward he added: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did, so do you” (Acts 7:51).

There is therefore one exalted God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—who does not dwell in things made by human hands; rather, through the grace he grants us, he mercifully made us his temple.

And we are not only a temple but also a sacrifice. For it has already been sufficiently shown by us that our bodies are the temple not of the Father alone, nor of the Son alone, nor of the Holy Spirit alone, but of the Trinity itself, the one God, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

The blessed Apostle teaches us to present these bodies as a living offering to God, saying: “Therefore I appeal to you, brothers, through the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans 12:1).

To the extent that each person offers a sacrifice to God, to that extent he spiritually performs the office of a priest. Hence the blessed Peter also showed that we are at once temple, priests, and sacrifices, saying: “You also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house, into a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 2:5).

For he himself was made a priest for us and offered himself for us, as the Apostle says: “An offering and sacrifice to God for a pleasing aroma” (Ephesians 5:2).

But what we offer through Christ according to the humanity alone of the Son, we offer simultaneously to the supreme Trinity itself.

Therefore we rightly owe λατρεία [latreia] to the Holy Spirit, whose temple we know our bodies to be; and for this reason we spiritually present those same bodies to him as a living sacrifice.

Since we are the temple of the one to whom we offer our bodies as a sacrifice, it is necessary that we owe him priestly service. Hence the Catholic Church, which is the one temple of the Holy Trinity—that is, of the one God—does not cease to offer a spiritual sacrifice to that same Holy Trinity, the one God, because it certainly recognizes that it owes priestly service to the Trinity itself, the one true and good God.

### FRAGMENT XVII. The Holy Spirit is no less the one and true God than the Father and the Son.

For no one serves the true and living God, nor ministers to the living and true God, if he attempts to build a temple in human bodies not for the living and true God but for an uncertain deity. Such a building certainly does not come from God.

And how could he have said above to those whom he called the temple of the Holy Spirit, “You are God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3:9)?

You must therefore hold to one of two alternatives: either acknowledge that the temple of the Holy Spirit has been built in us by God, and from this recognize that the Holy Spirit is the true God; or, if you do not believe that this is God’s building, declare Paul to be a liar.

But if you refuse to hear this preaching of Paul, you will remain entirely alien to the truth. Paul, however, will not be a liar, for, full of truth, he cries out: “I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness with me in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 9:1).

Since Paul therefore taught the truth, and by saying that our bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit made his divinity most certainly known to the faithful, whoever denies the true and certain divinity of the Holy Spirit should recognize that he in no way belongs to the Church of the living God, which Paul calls “the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15).

This holy Church knows that it is the temple of that one God whom it recognizes as God by nature and, for this reason, recognizes his divinity as true and certain. It casts away the worship of false gods, since, because they are not gods by nature, they cannot possess a certain divinity.

Therefore, because that divinity is certain which is natural, those who are not gods by nature do not possess a certain divinity; and those who do not possess a certain divinity possess none at all.

But right faith does not hesitate to offer λατρεία [latreia] to the one true God, knowing that it is not owed to any other god. Nor can it establish a temple in the bodies of the faithful or offer a sacrifice to any god who has not been God by nature.

For it knows that this service is owed to the God who commands that he alone be worshiped and who alone ought to be honored spiritually by the faithful with a temple, priesthood, and sacrifice.

Therefore the holy Church rightly believes and confesses the Holy Spirit to be the true God and, together with the Father and the Son, the one God. Knowing that it is the temple of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, it understands one divinity in the Trinity and humbly offers one service to the Trinity.

## FROM BOOK V. ON THE IMAGE OF GOD.

### FRAGMENT XVIII. The Son does not imitate the Father, nor does he do similar things with him, but the very same things. The human being is said to have been made in the image of God because he is the image of the divine Trinity in memory, understanding, and will.

In something superior, an example of a good work can indeed be found. For insofar as there is equality of nature and power, we see that imitation is lacking, but we find unity of action. An example is proposed where there is inequality either of nature or of power. Hence the Son of God, showing that he has one nature with the Father and therefore equal power in action, said: “Whatever the Father does, [Col. 0770D] the Son likewise does these same things” (John 5:19). Since, then, he does the same things, no example of a superior is found; and since he does them likewise, no indication of a different operation is discovered.

Nor can what he said be referred to an example: “The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing” (ibid.). For he said this as an indication of one nature and power, not as an example of imitation. He added: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does these same things.” Certainly, if he had wished to show imitation of the Father’s work in himself, he would have said that he did such things, not the same things. But the Father does nothing in which he might provide an example [Col. 0771A] for the Son, since he did everything he made through the Son. He would then have shown something for the Son to imitate if there were some work that he had not done through the Son. But there is nothing that the Father did or does without the Son. The operation of the Father and the Son is therefore one in all things.

Accordingly, when the Son acts, he sees the Father acting—not through imitation, but through the natural unity of power and action. When he does the same things, this is not imitation but unity of action; and when he does them likewise, this is not inequality but natural equality.

The blessed Apostle clearly shows that imitation, insofar as it pertains to an example, is found only among those who are diverse and unequal, whether in nature or in wills. Although he knew that those whom Timothy governed were equal in nature, he indicated that they were unequal in will [Col. 0771B] when he said to him: “Be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in love, in faith, and in chastity” (1 Tim. 4:12). Surely, unless he knew and wished Timothy to be superior to the others in all these respects, he would never have commanded him to be an example to the faithful. [p. 600] He wished those whom he knew to be unequal in will and virtue to be built up by Timothy’s example.

He likewise exhorts Titus to present himself as an example to the faithful, saying: “In all things show yourself an example of good works” (Tit. 2:7). Demonstrating something similar in his own case, he says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 11:1). The Apostle said this because Christ left us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps (1 Pet. 2:21).

The explanation for understanding the Trinity in some measure must be sought where we were made in the image of God, and where, insofar as we can, for as long as we walk by [Col. 0771C] faith and not by sight, we now see with the difficulty of great labor, through a mirror in an enigma. For just as God has given human beings an example of good works in himself, so he has placed in human beings a testimony to his own recognition, so that when his image is contemplated, the recognition of the one whose image it is may be grasped.

For if no indication of divine knowledge were present in created things, the blessed Apostle would not have said: “For his invisible attributes have been clearly seen since the creation of the world, being understood through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20). Hence that supreme Trinity, which has no equal, has wonderfully impressed the image of itself as a testimony to its recognition—not upon any animal, nor upon any living creature incapable of rational understanding, nor even upon the human body itself, but upon our inner human being. There is neither male [Col. 0771D] nor female there, because in the spirit no distinction of sex can be found.

If, therefore, you truly wish, guided by reason, to know in some measure the mystery of the supreme Trinity, contemplate the human mind—not with the eye of the body, but with the inward gaze. Return to yourself, so that you may recognize the one who made you. Look deeply within yourself precisely where you possess some rational capacity, and immediately the recognition of the Trinity will shine forth for you in its image, as in a mirror.

Thus, in contemplating an image that is not begotten but created—that is, one belonging to a far inferior and very unequal nature—you will discover, insofar as it can be seen through a mirror in an enigma, the true unity and Trinity of the supreme Creator. For there are three things in the human mind that contribute to the recognition of God, provided that the hardness [Col. 0772A] of the human heart does not conceal from itself the light of truth. These are the three I have mentioned: memory, understanding, and will. They are distinguished by their proper names in such a way that there is no natural diversity among them.

Memory is one thing, understanding another, and will another; yet although these are truly three, the nature of the mind is not diverse but one, because these threefold things [*trina*; alternatively *tria*, “three things”] exist in one human mind. Thus, although these three are found within the one nature of the human mind, the mind itself is not divided among them, as though it possessed memory in one part of itself, understanding in another, and will in another. Rather, whatever it remembers, the whole mind is found to remember; whatever it understands, the whole mind understands; and whatever the mind itself loves, the whole human mind is recognized as loving by its own will.

Fabianus, [Col. 0772B] if you can, attend to these things; think about them; consider them with rational concentration. From contemplation of the image, ascend to understanding the truth. Having found here a distinct Trinity of names, understand there a Trinity of persons; and recognizing that in one human mind there is one undivided nature of memory, understanding, and will, recognize that in that true divinity [p. 601] one essence of the holy Trinity remains.

Then, certainly, through the apprehension of this reasoning, the knowledge of the Trinity will be given to you. If in this life you see it through a mirror in an enigma, then in that life you will see it face to face. For this is what the Apostle says: “For now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).

In this mirror of human creation, therefore, recognize the image of the Creator, if you wish afterward to recognize [Col. 0772C] the very truth of the Creator. Walk by this faith, so that you may reach sight. At the same time, attend in it to the mystery of the divine Incarnation, so that you may recognize both that the whole Trinity has one substance and that the assumption of flesh belongs to the person of the Son alone.

For memory itself, which is in the human soul, when it wishes to speak of something, brings forth a thought from itself, and in a certain manner a spiritual word is born from it. Thus that one rational and indivisible nature of the soul is found wholly to remember what it understands, and wholly to understand what it remembers; and whatever it beholds with the eye of memory, it embraces entirely in thought.

When this thought is brought forth for the knowledge of others, it is conveyed by bodily speech. For that thought is nothing other than an inward utterance. Hence the rational soul speaks within itself [Col. 0772D] while turning over in thought what is contained in memory; and therefore it is rightly called a word even before it is brought forth through the body and the office of the voice.

That spiritual word, then—that is, the thought formed from memory—takes on, in a certain manner, a bodily form when it receives a bodily voice. Thus, wonderfully, that word both proceeds to others once it has received a voice and does not depart from the memory from which it is born. Nor is it subject to division. When one word is emitted from the mouth of the speaker, all who hear it are instructed in such a way that each receives in its entirety, without division, what all hear once spoken.

Thus, insofar as the word is found in all, it is found in each. It remains wholly in the memory from which it is born; [Col. 0773A] it is wholly uttered by the bodily voice; it is wholly spoken once to many hearers; and it is found wholly in each individual hearer, no less than in all of them.

So also the Son of God, who is the Word of God, “went out from the Father and came into this world,” as he himself testifies (John 16:28). Yet he was also always with the Father, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1); and before he came into the world, “he was in the world, and the world was made through him” (ibid., 10).

For the Word, God, was always in the world, because through unity of nature, just as the Father fills every creature, so also does the Son. Thus he did not depart from the Father when he went out from the Father, nor did he then begin to be in the world when he came into the world. Rather, going out from the Father, he remained with the Father as he had always been; and coming into the world, [Col. 0773B] he then willed to be present there by grace where he could never be absent by nature.

Behold, insofar as I have been able, although briefly, I have given the explanation by which we call the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit one God; and in the image of God itself I have shown a certain indication of divine knowledge. In this image, however, memory, understanding, and will do not possess individual [Col. 0774A] and proper persons. For this is an image, not born but made, not begotten but created.

The purpose is that, just as [p. 602] in this one image a certain distinction of names is found, so in that one divinity a distinction of persons may be recognized; and that natural unity may show that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, while the particularity of the persons may demonstrate that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.

The Father is another—not insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is Father; the Son is another—not insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is Son; and the Holy Spirit is another—not insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is the Spirit of both the Father and the Son.

Thus the Father who begot [In the witness abbreviated *Theod.*, *quia*, “because,” instead of *qui*, “who,” here and below] is another, the Son who was born from the Father is another, and the [Col. 0774B] Holy Spirit who proceeds from the Father and the Son is another. Yet the Father is not another God, nor the Son another God, nor the Holy Spirit another God; rather, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God.

For unity does not confuse the Trinity, nor does the Trinity separate unity, because what is distinguished by the particularity of the persons is shown to be one naturally through the communion of the one essence.

## FROM BOOK VI: ON THE ONE ETERNAL

[Col. 0773]

### FRAGMENT XIX. The Son Is Coeternal with the Father

[Col. 0773B] The faith of the Catholic Church is not unreasonable, since it both believes and proclaims the Son coeternal with the Father, knowing that every god in whom any beginning of existence [Col. 0773C] is found is a recent god. God promised this to his people: if they listen to him, a recent god will not be among them, and therefore they will in no way worship a foreign god. For it is said through the prophet: “Israel, if you listen to me, there will be no recent god among you, nor will you worship a foreign god” (Ps. 80:10).

The Son, therefore, is not a recent god, because he is naturally coeternal with the eternal Father. For this reason he is worshiped by us as one God with the Father, because he is in no respect found to be later than the Father.

When the cause of the Son’s eternal birth is sought, the Father’s eternal substance alone is found. For a nature that knows no beginning of existence could not have a beginning of begetting. What could be clearer for recognizing the Son as born from the Father’s nature and naturally coeternal with the Father than that passage of Scripture [Col. 0773D] where Wisdom is called “the brightness of eternal light” (Wis. 7:26)?

For brightness is found neither to be foreign to the nature of light nor, just as it is not less than the light itself, can it be later than it. The eternity of the light most certainly commends the coeternity of its brightness.

Apart from the fact that each human being begets a son in the manner in which he himself was begotten, and therefore is found to be earlier than his son because he was later than his own father, let us nevertheless return to the first human being, to whom alone in the entire human race it was granted that, although he himself was not a son, he should bring forth a son from himself, possessing one born from himself [p. 603] although he was not born, and being able to beget although he was not begotten.

That natural generation preserved the unity of nature in father and son. But [Col. 0774B] the son’s birth had a beginning because the begetter’s substance was not without a beginning. Thus that nature truly had a beginning of birth in the son because it did not lack a beginning of existence in the begetter. Hence [Col. 0774C] it is evident that this birth in the son would have been subject to no beginning if the father’s nature had had no beginning of existence.

Accordingly, where the father’s natural eternity is found to be without beginning, the offspring’s birth cannot have a beginning. Thus, when God the Father is called unbegotten and God the Son begotten, just as the natural generation of the unbegotten Father makes the unity of nature recognizable in the Father and the Son, so the Father’s natural eternity forbids any beginning of the divine generation from being understood.

Both Father and Son are therefore without beginning, and for this reason the Father and the Son are one true principle. Hence God the Father himself says to his own Son in the psalm: “With you is the principle, on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3).

What is “with you is the principle” except what is said elsewhere about Wisdom: that she is from the Lord God, has always been with him, and is before [Col. 0774D] the age (Sir. 1:1)? The Son therefore rightly professes himself to be the principle, because he knows himself to be so coeternal with the Father, the Principle, that he knows himself to be naturally one principle with the same Father.

And when the Son asserts that he is “the alpha and the omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1:8), he confirms that he himself is without beginning and without end. For just as no letter exists before alpha, so no nature could exist before the Son. The Son therefore calls himself alpha to show that he is the principle of things, which no principle can precede.

Hence the holy Evangelist also, wishing to express the eternity of the Word without beginning, found nothing more suitable or more fitting, when filled with the Holy Spirit, than to say: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). [Col. 0775A] For the Word did not begin to exist in the beginning, since he knew that the Word was not naturally subject to a beginning of birth. Rather, he says, “In the beginning was the Word,” so that, hearing this, the rashness of human curiosity may restrain itself from the impiety of supposing that the generation had a beginning. Whatever it wishes to conjecture through unrestrained thought as existing before that generation, it can find in the Word nothing other than what always was.

For that truly was in the beginning which was without a beginning of existence; it would not truly be in the beginning if it had begun to exist. That is truly said to be in the beginning in which existence itself is naturally found without beginning.

Therefore, when the holy Evangelist said, “In the beginning was the Word,” he said something equivalent to saying, “In eternity was the Word.” For true eternity, which did not begin to exist, alone is found to be the true beginning.

[Col. 0775B] The Evangelist did not say, “In the beginning was God,” but “In the beginning was the Word,” because no one doubts that God the Father is eternal without beginning. But it was necessary for us to be told this about the Son, as the blessed John most fully shows when he says, “In the beginning was the Word”: so that from this we may know that the Son is without beginning. Whenever we wish to conceive of some beginning, we will always find that the Word was in the beginning, lest we ever say that what we always hear was in the beginning once began to exist.

The Son was therefore with the Father, as [p. 604] God with God, as the immeasurable with the immeasurable, and as the naturally coeternal with the eternal.

### FRAGMENT XX. The Eternal Father Was Able to Beget Without Beginning

[Col. 0775C] The very terms themselves protest against you: the Father was certainly able to beget the Son, and because he was able, he begot him. Therefore, since God the Father is omnipotent, just as he was able to beget, so he was able to beget without beginning; indeed, just as he begot, so he begot without beginning.

For his nature, which is without beginning, just as it has no beginning of existence, so it could not have a beginning of begetting. That nature always exists; and therefore what is naturally born from it exists equally always. Natural unity could not be changed by generation, since natural birth recognized in itself both the nature and the natural eternity of the God who begets.

Yield, then, at last to the proper meaning of the terms and believe; and in the one whom the Apostle proclaims to be the Father’s own Son, [Col. 0775D] recognize the eternity without beginning of the Father’s generation.

### FRAGMENT XXI. Humanity Was Made in the Image Not of One Divine Person Alone but of the Whole Trinity. Scripture Shows Both the Trinity in the Persons and Unity in the Nature of God

Return to the beginning of the holy Scriptures, where, whether you wish it or not, you will hear that humanity was made in the image of the Trinity. For there it is written: “And God said: Let us make humanity in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26).

In the fact that it does not say “They said,” but “God said,” the one essence of divinity is recognized. Likewise, in the fact that it does not say “in images,” but “in the image,” the one image that is made [*quae fit*; alternatively *quam fecit*, “that he made”] [Col. 0776A] shows the one nature of its maker [*factoris*; alternatively *auctoris*, “author”].

But when it is said in the singular, “in the image,” without saying “in my image” or “in your image,” but “in our image,” the plural number is joined to the singular, so that the Trinity of persons may be recognized within the unity of the divine nature.

If, then, the Trinity is not naturally one God, why did he say not “in images” in the plural but “in the image” in the singular? But if humanity was not divinely to be made in the one image of the whole Trinity, why did he say “our” rather than “my”?

A little later, to indicate the [p. 605] one divine essence, Scripture says: “And God made humanity; in the image of God he made him” (ibid., 27). Confirming this also by his preaching, the blessed Apostle says: “Stripping off the old human being with his deeds, and putting on the new, [Col. 0776B] who is being renewed unto knowledge” [*in agnitionem*, accusative; alternatively *in agnitione*, “in knowledge,” ablative], “according to the image of him who created him” (Col. 3:9–10).

And lest you think that he is asserting that humanity was created in the image of God the Father alone, hear what the Apostle immediately adds: “Where there is neither gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all” (ibid., 11).

Behold, in this passage the blessed Apostle, wishing to show who it was by whom and in whose image humanity was created, says that Christ is all and in all. But if you wish to assign to humanity the image of Christ alone, consider how you will answer concerning the passage where it is said: “Let us make humanity in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26).

Whether you insist on assigning this statement to the person of the Father or to the Son, if you do not say that humanity was [Col. 0776C] made in the image of the Father and the Son, you must either declare the Father or the Son to have lied.

Recognize, then, in humanity not the image of the Father alone, nor of the Son alone, nor of the Holy Spirit alone, but the one image of the holy Trinity, so that you may truly confess the three persons to be the Trinity and one God.

Moses also, to teach the mystery of the one God who is Trinity, is known to have blessed the people of Israel by God’s command in this way: “May the Lord bless you and keep you. May the Lord illuminate his face upon you and have mercy on you. May the Lord lift up his face upon you and give you peace” (Num. 6:24–26).

Behold: the Lord is named three times, so that both the distinction of the persons and the unity of the nature of the holy Trinity may be recognized.

The Trinity itself, [Col. 0776D] which is one, true, and good God, also taught through the prophet Isaiah that we ought to believe and confess this. The Seraphim cry out to one another three times: “Holy, holy, holy,” and then once add: “The Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Isa. 6:3).

From this proclamation of the heavenly powers, therefore, recognize the holy Father, the holy Son, and the holy Spirit, the Paraclete; and believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. Hear “Holy, holy, holy” three times, so that you may recognize that there are three persons; hear once, “The Lord God of hosts,” so that you may understand the unity of the divinity.

The blessed Apostle also confirms this when, to distinguish the persons, he says: “There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and [Col. 0777A] we through him” (1 Cor. 8:6). And he says that the faithful are being built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit (Eph. 2:22).

Showing that the Trinity is one God, he says: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. 11:33). And shortly afterward: “For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory forever” (ibid., 36).

The blessed Apostle John plainly says: “And the three are one” (1 John 5:7). This was said of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as we showed above when you demanded an explanation.

[p. 606]

### FRAGMENT XXII. Fire Is Not Prior to Its Brightness or Vapor; So Neither Is the Father Prior to the Son or the Holy Spirit

What, then, did you mean by saying: “Can it really happen that the one who begets [Col. 0777B] comes into being at the same time as the one whom he begets?” You wished to say this foolishly, as though we also claimed that the Father was born because we call the Son coeternal with the Father.

We know that the Father was begotten by no one; we know that the Son was begotten from the Father. For that eternity, which is not found to have an origin from anything else, begot offspring coeternal with itself.

The Father, therefore, is the eternal source; the Son is the offspring coeternal with the eternal source. The Father could not therefore come into being at the same time as the Son whom he begot, but the Son could be born without beginning from the unbegotten Father.

The comparison with fire that you proposed under my name often greatly undermines your arguments, since something is found in creation that produces something from itself and yet does not precede what it has produced. From this, those who consider the matter rightly can recognize the Son’s birth from the eternal Father [Col. 0777C] as no less eternal.

To take some likeness of divine generation from fire, there is the authority of apostolic preaching, which says: “For our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. 12:29). This follows the preaching of the holy Moses, who says in Deuteronomy: “For the Lord your God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24).

This also pertains to what is said about Wisdom herself in the Book of Wisdom: “For she is the brightness of eternal light” (Wis. 7:26). The same is expressed in apostolic preaching when it is said of the Son himself to the Hebrews: “Who, being the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance” (Heb. 1:3).

When these things are said, corporeal things are not being compared with God, who is not corporeal. Rather, because “his invisible attributes have been clearly seen since the creation of the world, [Col. 0777D] being understood through the things that have been made,” divine kindness, taking account of our weakness, placed in various things certain indications of its own knowledge, so that we might be instructed by the evidence of familiar things concerning matters that we are too weak to grasp directly.
