Although it is said of Wisdom that she is “a vapor of the power of God” (Wis. 7:25), the Holy Spirit, in the nature of fire, may also be compared to vapor—not incongruously, insofar as the knowledge of the divine matter requires it—because of what the Apostle says: “Fervent in spirit.”

This is not to be understood as allowing anyone to ascribe to the Holy Spirit a birth from God the Father, but only so that he may recognize the one nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and understand the one eternity naturally belonging to the divine Trinity.

Consider, therefore, that [Col. 0778A] in fire there is the origin of brightness and vapor, and yet fire is not prior to its brightness or vapor. From this, confess the Son and the Holy Spirit to be eternal, just as you confess the Father to be eternal—not [p. 607] comparing a creature with the Creator, but recognizing the invisible things of God as understood through the things that have been made.

### FRAGMENT XXIII. Wisdom Is the Brightness of Eternal Light. There Is No Eternal Light Without Eternal Brightness

I believe that what we have recalled concerning Wisdom was said in the holy Scriptures: that she is “the brightness of eternal light” (Wis. 7:26). You will never dare to declare the brightness to be in any way later than the light.

And since that light of which Wisdom is the brightness is [Col. 0778B] naturally eternal and therefore without beginning, it is necessary that the brightness of that light also be eternal, naturally coeternal without beginning with the very light whose brightness it is.

This testimony of holy Scripture is not only full of the force of authority but also illuminated by reason. For it is right reasoning that, if this testimony of holy Scripture is accepted, the one eternity of the light and its brightness should be believed.

God would not have wished without purpose that, in the passage where Wisdom is shown to be the brightness of light, that same light should be called eternal by the testimony of Scripture. Rather, he did so so that, from recognizing that light as naturally eternal, we might also believe without hesitation that its brightness is naturally coeternal with it.

### FRAGMENT XXIV. The Father Was Not Before the Generation, Nor the Son Before the Birth

[Col. 0778C] I say that the Son was always born, and I confess that the Father begot without beginning. How, then, could the Son have existed before he was born, when his birth could not have had a beginning?

For he could not have existed before his own birth, by which birth he is eternal in such a way that he is naturally not later than the Father. The Son therefore did not precede his own birth; that natural birth showed him to be coeternal with the one who begot him.

I also affirm that the Father begot, but I do not declare that he could have existed before he begot. For he did not exist before the birth of the Son, because just as the divinity of God the Father is eternal, so also is his fatherhood eternal; and wherever the eternity of fatherhood is recognized in the begetter, [Col. 0778D] eternal birth is also found in the Son.

The Father therefore did not begin to exist from the time he begot, since neither the Father’s essence nor his generation began in any respect. The eternity of essence [p. 608] and generation in the Father is one. In this eternity essence and generation remain in such a way that it would be impious either to consider the generation later than the Father’s divinity or to believe the divinity earlier than the generation.

God the Father, who did not begin to exist, therefore begot without beginning; and the Son’s birth is without beginning, because this is what the eternity of the Father’s generation entails.

You have heard that the Son always exists and was born without beginning, and that nothing can be said to have existed before his birth, since both his divinity and his birth are naturally recognized as never having begun.

Search the holy Scriptures, and you will find that the divine birth of the Son [Col. 0779A] has no beginning to such an extent that wherever his divine birth is mentioned, “before” is always said. Thus it is written in the psalm: “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 109:3). There the Father also says that he and his Son are one principle, because that is the true principle which is naturally found to be eternal without beginning.

In the Book of Proverbs, Wisdom herself says of the Father: “Before he made the earth, before the springs of waters came forth, before all the hills he begot me” (Prov. 8:23–25).

You say that the divine birth of the only-begotten God cannot be known because it cannot be narrated. Yet if it could be narrated, it would not be divine. Therefore, because it is divine, it is true; because it is divine, it is eternal; because it is divine, it is ineffable.

That thoughtless reply you made to yourself—that [Col. 0779B] the Son could not have existed before he was born, while the Father certainly existed before he begot—is a thought of flesh and blood, which cannot possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 15:50). For you think of divinity as you observe it in human beings.

But it is not so. God the Father, eternal and without beginning, has an eternal generation by which he begot his only-begotten Son—not as flesh is generated from flesh, but as God is born from God, one from one, true from true, coeternal from eternal; distinct in person, not different in nature; God born from God the Father, and naturally one with God the Father—eternal, immortal, and unchangeable [Col. 0780A] God.

Let us therefore acknowledge that the Son is the Beginning and the Principle, because it is written: “The Beginning, and what I am speaking to you” (John 8:25); and again: “I am the alpha and the omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1:8). But this is the principle that is one principle with the Father, and therefore the true principle, because it is before every principle.

For just as he is true God because God was born from the Father’s nature, so he is the true principle because he was born without beginning from that Father who is the true principle. Thus the Son has no beginning of being born, just as the Father has no beginning of existing.

The Son is therefore in the beginning with the Father, because the Father and the Son are one principle—and that one true principle has no beginning of existence.

The Ancient of Days is the Father and the Son together, because [Col. 0780B] that is true antiquity naturally which is natural eternity without beginning. For just as the length of which God says, “I will fill him with length of days” (Ps. 90:16), and of which the prophet says, “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days” (Ps. 22:6), is true length because it is not destined to be ended by any limit, so that antiquity is true which is recognized as having begun from no beginning.

Thus antiquity knows no beginning just as that length admits no end. Therefore, the one who said that he was the alpha and the omega neither began to exist nor ceases to exist, because just as he does not possess in himself the possibility of at some time not existing, so naturally he does not possess in himself the condition of having not existed.

## FROM BOOK VII: ON THE EQUALITY AND UNITY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT WITH THE FATHER AND THE SON

[Col. 0779]

[p. 609]

### FRAGMENT XXV. The Holy Spirit Is Neither Less Than nor Subject to the Father or the Son

[Col. 0779C]

Against the points you proposed concerning names and functions, we have already given you as much of an answer as the matter required, with the Lord’s help: demonstrating that the Holy Spirit is not thereby found to be in any respect subject or subordinate, as you suppose. But in that passage of the Gospel where you think he is shown to be lesser and subject, there it is recognized that the Holy Spirit is not by nature alien from the unity of the Father and the Son. Consider what Christ says:

> “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:12–13).

[Col. 0779D] Here our Savior first deigned to commend the power of the Holy Spirit, since the things which, while he was present and teaching according to the flesh, the disciples could not bear, they would undoubtedly bear once strengthened by the gift of the Holy Spirit. Here he certainly did not show that the power of the Holy Spirit was greater than his own; rather, he demonstrated that the power of the Holy Spirit and his own are one, so that the one who would bestow upon them the fullness of power might not be lesser in power.

This was necessary on account of the distinction of the persons, not on account of any difference in their works. It belonged to the order of things that, through the inward illumination and confirmation of that one, the gift of spiritual understanding and wholly unconquerable power might be perfected in the apostles—[Col. 0780C] without whose name the sacrament of baptism cannot be complete.

Christ therefore did this, not because he was able to give less than what the Holy Spirit gave—for in every gift there is one gift of the Holy Trinity, just as in every work there is one function of the Holy Trinity—but God the Son did this to show the one nature and the one power of the Holy Trinity. Thus no one would in any respect consider lesser than the Father and the Son the one by whom it was established that the apostles should be taught all truth, with the Savior himself proclaiming it.

There is therefore no indication of subjection here, where natural unity is manifested. Rather, Christ, who is true Wisdom, is found to have reserved the full teaching of truth for the coming of the one whose substance he wished to demonstrate as one with himself and with the Father. [Col. 0780D] He showed this in the words that follow, saying:

> “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John 16:13–14).

Behold: first he shows that the Holy Spirit possesses nothing other than what belongs to the Son. Then, to show that everything belonging to the Father is his, he added:

> “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine” (v. 15).

Let us first attend to what he says: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak.” Who, however, can comprehend what the speech of that simple nature is like, or what its hearing is like? There, just as knowing or understanding is not something other than being, so hearing is not [Col. 0781A] something other than being.

The Holy Spirit therefore hears whatever the Father and the Son says (Theodulphus: “say”), and he likewise says these same things, just as the Son sees what the Father does and likewise does these same things. For in that nature, where there is supreme and true simplicity, the Son sees what the Father does, and the Holy Spirit hears what the Son says with the Father, because through communion in the natural essence the Son has come forth born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

For the Holy Spirit, hearing means proceeding from the nature of the Father and the Son; and speaking means inwardly conveying ineffably to our hearts through grace. Yet the blessed David calls that same Holy Spirit, who spoke both in the apostles and in the prophets—for our Savior said not only to the apostles, [Col. 0781B] “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20)—and blessed Peter likewise said, “No prophecy was ever brought forth by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21)—the Lord God, as I have said, saying:

> “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Psalm 84:9).

For the Holy Spirit, then, hearing means being; and for him being is nothing other than knowing.

## FRAGMENT XXVI. How the angels always see the face of the Father and long to look into the Holy Spirit

Next, remember that the apostle Peter said of this Holy Spirit that the angels long to [Col. 0781C] look into him. For he says:

> “The things now announced to you through those who preached the gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven are things into which angels long to look” (1 Peter 1:12).

What, then, is the angels’ looking into something except understanding? For a rational creature understands what it looks upon spiritually, since its eye is its understanding.

If, therefore, the Holy Spirit knew something less—which he certainly would have known less—he would understand less. The holy angels, therefore, who are attested by the testimony of Truth itself to see the face of the Father according to the fullness of knowledge, ought not to have longed to look into him.

For, speaking of the little ones, he says:

> “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10).

Who, then, so perverse would dare to suppose this concerning the holy angels: that they always see the face of the Father—whom you say is greater than the Holy Spirit [Col. 0781D]—and yet long to look into the Holy Spirit, whom you assert to be lesser?

[p. 611]

## FRAGMENT XXVII. What it means that the Holy Spirit does not speak from himself, but speaks what he hears from the Father and the Son; and what it means that he is sent by them

Therefore, if you rightly consider what it means that the Holy Spirit is said to hear, you will recognize from this that the Holy Spirit has one nature with the Father and the Son. The Holy Spirit hears the Father and the Son speaking, just as the Son sees the Father acting: he hears through the communion of one nature. For from the same source from which he has the natural origin of eternal divinity, he possesses eternal hearing. Thus he speaks what he hears, because in the very fact that his divine teaching is recognized, [Col. 0782A] his one substance with the Father and the Son is recognized at the same time.

The speech of the Holy Spirit is perceived there where one thinks rightly concerning his divinity. But those who resist his majesty with the hardness of blind hearts in no way perceive that the Holy Spirit teaches all truth. To those who did this, the Son of God replied:

> “You are seeking to kill me, because my word finds no room in you” (John 8:37).

They could not receive his word because they did not at all recognize his divine majesty. Therefore he says to them:

> “What I have seen with the Father, I speak” (v. 38).

For he spoke what he had seen with the Father, thereby naturally confessing himself equal to the Father. For the evangelist had also said above:

> “For this reason the Jews sought all the more [Col. 0782B] to kill him: not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was also calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18).

And afterward, when he had given sight to the man who had been born blind, he replied to the indignant Jews:

> “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish forever” (John 10:27–28).

To show what voice of his his sheep hear—for those sheep truly hear the voice of this good shepherd who recognize one power and, from this, one essence of the Father and the Son—he immediately displayed by a truly divine voice his own one power and essence together with that of the Father, saying concerning his sheep:

> “No one snatches them from my hand. What my Father has given me is greater than all, and no one can [Col. 0782C] snatch anything from the hand of my Father. I and the Father are one” (ibid. 10:28–30).

This, then, is the voice that his sheep hear: namely, that in the fact that no one snatches them from the hand of the Son or from the hand of the Father, they understand the one power of the Son and the Father; and, hearing from him that he and the Father are one, they recognize the true unity of the natural essence in the Father and the Son.

This is the voice of the Son; this is the speech of the Holy Spirit. The Son and the Holy Spirit heard this from the Father, because the Son was born from the Father’s nature and the Holy Spirit proceeds from it. The Holy Spirit also hears this from the Father and the Son, because he proceeds from the equality of the common divinity of the Father and the Son.

The Holy Spirit therefore does not speak from himself, because he is not from himself. Rather, he possesses natural speech from the Father and the Son; and, proceeding naturally [p. 612] from them, he possesses the truth of his origin. [Col. 0782D] This is certainly related to what he says:

> “He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John 16:14).

For is “he will receive” to be understood—as it is perhaps worded—as though the Holy Spirit had not yet received the things he was going to teach the apostles? I demonstrated above how absurd and impious that would be.

It was therefore said, “He will receive from what is mine,” as though it were said: “When he begins to teach you as God, he will show that everything he teaches you comes from what is mine.” For what is proper to God’s teaching except both to bestow understanding upon the ignorant and to inspire strength and confidence in the fearful? The Spirit truly does this—he who is by nature the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude.

[Col. 0783A] Hence it is also said in the Acts of the Apostles concerning the believers:

> “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God with confidence” (Acts 4:31).

But because the Father is the natural origin of the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Son, assigning everything to the Father, says:

> “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine” (John 16:15).

How faithfully Truth itself preserved the truth of its teaching! If he had not said this, he would have seemed to show that the Spirit was his alone. But by saying, “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine,” he showed that the Holy Spirit is one, belonging both to the Father and to himself.

He also preserved the same line of thought in the preceding passage, saying:

> “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything that I have said to you” (John 14:26).

[Col. 0783B] The Father sends him, but sends him in the name of the Son. The Spirit, sent by the Father, teaches; but the Son speaks.

This is also demonstrated in the passage where the Lord says:

> “But when the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26).

Behold: the Paraclete whom the Father sends in the name of the Son, the Son himself sends from the Father. He sends the Spirit of truth from the Father; therefore he sends his own Spirit from the Father, because he himself is the Truth.

The Father sends him in the name of the Son because there is one Spirit of the Father and the Son. The Son sends him from the Father because he proceeds from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father. The same Spirit of the Father is also the Spirit of Truth.

Therefore he received from the Son (variant: “from the Son’s”), and everything that the Father has belongs to the Son—things which the Holy Spirit received—because he proceeds not from the Father alone, nor from the Son [Col. 0783C] alone, but from both together.

The designation “procession from the Father” is found to have been granted to no creature, so that this distinctive procession may be shown to belong solely to the natural essence. For we read that the Son was begotten from the Father. Although, in the designation “Only-Begotten,” natural generation alone is demonstrated, nevertheless, on account of the grace of adoption, God the Father also voluntarily begot us by the word of truth (James 1:18).

[Col. 0784A] The Only-Begotten, therefore, is the one and only Son born from the essence of the Father. Yet we too are called, through adoption, sons of God and born from God, as the blessed Evangelist says:

> “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God” (John 1:12–13).

Although the divine utterances thus show us both to be children of God and begotten from God and born from God, no one can demonstrate that the term “procession from God” has been granted to any creature.

[p. 613]

Why is this so, except because natural birth could show the Only-Begotten Son to be true [Col. 0784B] God, and unmistakably demonstrate him to be not adoptive, nor of a different nature, but consubstantial with the Father?

No creature is therefore said to proceed from God, so that the one who proceeds from the Father and the Son may be believed to be God just as the Father and the Son are God. This property of procession from the Father and the Son belongs solely to the Holy Spirit, whose nature is shared with the Father and the Son.

For he proceeds from the Father and the Son, but does not depart from them. Nor is he in any respect lesser or subject, who proceeds inseparably and wholly as one from the immeasurable Father and the immeasurable Son.

Thus the Holy Spirit cannot be commanded concerning what he speaks, any more than he can be commanded concerning what he wondrously does. For:

> “One and the same Spirit accomplishes all these things, distributing to each one individually as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11).

The Holy Spirit [Col. 0784C] therefore does not do anything under the command of another power, but accomplishes everything according to the judgment of his own will. The will of the Holy Trinity is one, and its power is one; its divinity is naturally one.

## IX. BOOK VIII. ON THE SENDING OF THE SON AND THE HOLY SPIRIT

[Col. 0783]

## FRAGMENT XXVIII. The Trinity has one speech and one will. The Holy Spirit is not sent like the angels: he is one and immeasurable. Baptism is also given in his name. He does not depart from those who ask that he be sent to them. What the Church asks when it asks for the Holy Spirit

[Col. 0783C]

Nor is the Spirit therefore a betrayer of the divine secret, because he speaks what he says by his own will. For the one holy Trinity always has one utterance, just as it has one will in all things; and in the fact that the Holy Spirit hears from the Father and the Son what he speaks, this is an indication solely of origin, not of any inequality. By this it is not shown whom he obeys as a subordinate, but from whom he proceeds as the exalted one.

You would by no means have judged the sending of the Holy Spirit comparable to the missions of angels, if you had sought these matters with humble heart and had not, in arrogance, rushed forward in insult to the Holy Spirit. Since you desired to investigate this question, you ought to have examined what divine Scripture says about the Holy Spirit: first, whether it asserts that there are many or one; next, whether it calls him local or immense; finally, considering his works, you ought to have recognized whether they belong solely to divinity or could also befit some creature, so that from all these considerations a correct understanding of the sending of the Holy Spirit might support you.

Thus I do not believe that you can in any way doubt that, just as there is one Father and one Son, so also one Holy Spirit is proclaimed everywhere in the divine utterances. The blessed Apostle says:

> “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of works, but the same God, who works all things in all” (1 Cor. 12:4–6).

And shortly afterward (v. 11):

> “But all these things the one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills.”

But lest you be unwilling to understand here that the Holy Spirit is the one who distributes each thing, and suspect that there is another Spirit for you, hear what is said in the Epistle to the Hebrews:

> “God bearing witness with signs and wonders and various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will” (Heb. 2:4).

In another place the same blessed Apostle says:

> “One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” (Eph. 4:4).

There he immediately joined one Father and one Son to the one Spirit, adding:

> “One Lord”—clearly signifying Christ—“one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in us all” (Eph. 4:5–6).

In another place he says:

> “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or gentiles, whether slaves or free, and we were all given to drink of one Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:13).

Our Savior likewise showed that the Holy Spirit is one, saying:

> “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

Recognizing the immensity of this Spirit, and understanding that he is always wholly present throughout all things, the prophet says to God the Father:

> “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138:7).

Here he clearly signified that God is always everywhere with his Spirit, from whom he declared that he could not flee at all.

Perhaps you contend that there is one Spirit of God and another Holy Spirit. Here you must immediately be overcome by the divine utterances. The blessed prophet testifies that the Holy Spirit is that very Spirit—the Spirit who is God—saying:

> “Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 50:13).

And because one Holy Spirit was given to the apostles and prophets—as the blessed Apostle testifies when he says:

> “Having the same Spirit of faith, as it is written: ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’; and we also believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4:13)—

he unmistakably shows that the Spirit of God is the Holy Spirit when he says:

> “But whoever rejects these things rejects not man but God, who also gave his Holy Spirit in us” (1 Thess. 4:8).

On the day of Pentecost also, when the Holy Spirit had come upon the apostles, the blessed Peter showed by prophetic utterance that this Paraclete himself, whom the Lord promised and sent to them, is the Spirit of God. He said that this was what had been spoken through the prophet Joel:

> “And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord, that I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh” (Acts 2:16–17).

And shortly afterward (v. 18):

> “And indeed upon my male servants and upon my female servants in those days I will pour out from my Spirit, and they shall prophesy.”

Joel the prophet therefore also unmistakably asserted the immensity of this one Spirit—an immensity that only true divinity can naturally possess, indeed that only true divinity naturally possesses—when he said in the person of God speaking:

> “I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28).

For this reason it is also said in the Book of Wisdom:

> “For the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (Wis. 1:7).

He is therefore nowhere absent, but is wholly and immeasurably everywhere—he who is said both to fill the world and to contain all things. He is said to contain all things so that, when he is said to fill the world, he may not be thought absent from heavenly things.

Yet a little earlier divine Scripture calls him the Holy Spirit, saying:

> “For the holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (ibid., v. 5).

The natural immensity of the Holy Spirit is also recognized in this: throughout the world, just as people are baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son, so they are baptized in the name of the Holy Spirit. And lest anyone perhaps think that the name of the Holy Spirit is indeed pronounced everywhere in baptism, but that his presence is not always everywhere, the Apostle says to the faithful:

> “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4:30);

and elsewhere:

> “He who establishes us with you in Christ, and who anointed us, is God; he who sealed us and gave us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts” (2 Cor. 1:21–22).

And again:

> “God himself has prepared us for this, who gave us the pledge of the Spirit” (2 Cor. 5:5).

In another place he says:

> “In him you also, having believed, were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance” (Eph. 1:13–14).

By these words he showed not only that the Holy Spirit is immeasurable by nature, but also that he is the true God, whom he asserted to be the pledge of our inheritance. Since the Lord God alone is the portion of our inheritance, as the whole Church says:

> “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup” (Ps. 15:5),

it is evident that the Holy Spirit is immeasurable by nature. He does not merely fail to exist locally in a place; he cannot even pass from place to place.

All rational spirits whom God created, although they are not locally contained in places, nevertheless pass from places to places. They would certainly not do so unless, leaving the place in which they had been, they came to a place in which they had not been. Who does not know that the angel Gabriel came into the temple when he appeared to Zechariah, and departed from the temple after completing the service of his announcement, and that while he was in the temple he was not elsewhere? For no creature can fill the whole creation with its presence at once; this belongs solely to the Trinity, whose natural immensity is without limit, just as its eternal divinity is without beginning.

Hence even all the holy angels—of whom blessed Peter says that they desire to gaze into the Spirit—would not at all desire to gaze into him if they did not possess that same Holy Spirit within themselves. They desire to gaze into him through love, because no one desires what he does not love; but they received the love with which they love the Holy Spirit only through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

> “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

Through that same Spirit love has been poured into the hearts of human beings, through whom it has also been poured into the minds of angels.

The Holy Spirit is therefore immense: the one and the same Spirit fills the world and also fills the spirits of the heavenly angels. For he is, as Scripture says:

> “The Spirit of understanding, holy, one, manifold, subtle, mobile, eloquent, undefiled, manifest, sound, loving what is good, sharp, unhindered, doing good, humane, steadfast, certain, secure, possessing every power, observing all things, and entering through all intelligent, pure, subtle spirits” (Wis. 7:22–23).

Who does not see that the works of the Holy Spirit belong only to the supreme Godhead? For:

> “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6).

The Lord Jesus manifests that he casts out demons by this Spirit; and the power of signs and wonders, which Paul says Christ himself performs through him, he declares to be effected in the power of the Holy Spirit, saying:

> “For I will not dare to speak of anything that Christ does not accomplish through me for the obedience of the gentiles, in word and deed, in the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 15:18–19).

Thus, when through the Spirit one person is given a word of wisdom, another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, another faith in the same Spirit, and the other gifts contained in the text of the Apostle’s discourse, the one and the same Spirit accomplishes all things, as we recalled above, distributing to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11).

Believers are baptized in his name, and in him they are sealed. He descended upon Jesus when he was baptized and remained upon him. Showing through Isaiah that the Spirit was upon him, that he was anointed by the Spirit, and that he was sent by the Spirit, the Lord Christ says:

> “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor” (Isa. 61:1).

When he reviewed this passage of the prophetic book in the synagogue, he said to the Jews:

> “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21).

After the Spirit had descended upon him when he was baptized, the Evangelist said:

> “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (v. 1).

Then, after the devil had departed from him when the temptation was completed, until the appointed time, the holy Evangelist says:

> “Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee” (v. 14).

Consider, then, all that we have mentioned, and you will recognize that the Holy Spirit is one, like the Father and the Son; that he is immense, filling every creature; and that he performs works which only divinity performs. This same one, taught to be naturally immense, cannot be sent from place to place; nor is anything commanded him as a subordinate, because he has done and does those works voluntarily which no one can do except God.

The sending of the Holy Spirit must therefore be considered wisely. He is not sent like an angel, whose duty is to carry out due service, but like God, whose task it is, through voluntary goodness, to bestow gifts of sanctification and holy operation.

For the Holy Spirit, as we taught above, fills the world. This is never stated of any angel, but only of God, to whom the blessed Azariah, placed in the furnace, says:

> “Blessed are you, Lord God of our fathers, and praised and glorious is your name forever” (Dan. 3:26).

And shortly afterward he says:

> “Let them know that you alone are the Lord God throughout the whole world” (v. 45).

Here he taught that the true Lord God is the one who is throughout the whole world. Whoever does not fill the world cannot be in the world; and therefore he is neither the Lord nor God. We must therefore confess that the Holy Spirit is the Lord God, of whom Scripture says:

> “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. 1:7).

I could say many things about the Holy Spirit, which I pass over because I intend to bring this work to an end. Yet I would have you say this: why is it necessary that the sacrament of baptism be given not in the name of the Father alone, nor merely in the name of the Father and the Son, but in the name of the entire Trinity—that is, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit—if the Holy Spirit is not of the same nature and power as the Father and the Son?

What does the single mention of the name in the sacrament of baptism mean, if there is not there a single operation of the Trinity? Why is it necessary that a person cannot be saved in baptism without the name of the Holy Spirit, if the Holy Spirit did not create the human being? Or consider more carefully what is greater: why did he come upon the Son of God, if he is created and not creator? Or how did he fill him, if he must not be believed equal but inferior?

For certainly neither was his operation necessary for renewing the human being, since he did not make the human being; nor would the Spirit come upon Christ, whom you say the Father made through the Son; nor would he fill one to whom he could not be equal.

But you, who revive the question concerning the sending of the Holy Spirit and say that the Holy Spirit is taught to be sent and directed like an angel and minister, recall what was said above, and you will find that the Holy Spirit is not sent like an angel. An angel is sent from one place to another and is sent there where he was not. But the Holy Spirit, who fills all things and is absent nowhere, deigns to be sent by the Father through his grace there where he is always present through his immeasurable divinity; he comes there by the bestowal of his gift, from which he is never absent through the greatness of his deity.

Therefore, as you answered yourself according to your own will in my name, the sending of the Holy Spirit should not be called his appearance. He was sent visibly when his sending had to be announced to the faithful in such a way that, from what they visibly perceived with their eyes, they might recognize the gifts of invisible grace.

You thought that, from the prayer in which the coming of the Holy Spirit is requested at the time of the sacrifice, you wished to demonstrate a local sending of him. But you will be able to think rightly about the Holy Spirit only if you do not follow the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God (Rom. 8:7).

First of all, you must attend to what blessed Paul says to the faithful:

> “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16).

In saying this he was certainly mindful of the promise of our Savior, who says:

> “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may remain with you forever: the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it does not see him or know him. But you know him, because he remains with you and is in you” (John 14:16–17).

Behold, the Lord Jesus gave the Holy Spirit to his faithful so that he might be with them forever and remain in them. If the Savior’s promise is true—as no Christian doubts—the Holy Spirit must not depart from the faithful. He is taken away only from those whom God has cast away from his presence. For this reason blessed David says:

> “Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 50:13).

Since, then, the Holy Spirit rests with truly eternal dwelling in those who rightly worship God, how do they ask that he be sent to them? They would certainly not be worthy to stand at the offering if they did not have the Holy Spirit within themselves. In this matter the holy Apostle also admonishes us to pray, saying:

> “Praying at every time in the Spirit, and watching in him with all perseverance and supplication” (Eph. 6:18).

How, then, do they ask that he be sent to them when they do not fail to know that he has been divinely given to them and continually remains in them? Or perhaps, before holy people pour out their prayer, the Holy Spirit rests in them, but when he senses that they are about to pray, he immediately departs? If this were so, it would be better for holy people never to pray and to have the Holy Spirit continually within them than for him to abandon them at some time when they are about to pray. Consequently, the statement of the Evangelist that one must always pray (Luke 18:1) would not be beneficial but harmful. He commands prayer at all times.

Who, then, in his right mind would say that the one who prays in the Spirit does not have the Spirit within himself? Or perhaps, at the time when the sacrifice is offered, do you think that the Holy Spirit is in those who pour out the prayer but is not in the very place where the sacrifice is placed? Who would think this way except one who is foolish?

Or who would regard the coming of the Holy Spirit as local except one who, possessed by carnal thought and therefore excluded from spiritual thought, wishes to think about divine things as he thinks about human things, and to think about the Spirit of God, who fills the world, as he can think about a human or angelic spirit? The Holy Spirit fills the whole creation in such a way that he alone is always wholly everywhere.

Recognize, then, what takes place in the offering of sacrifices, so that from this you may understand why the coming of the Holy Spirit is requested there. Indeed, what our Savior himself commanded is fulfilled in the offering of sacrifices, as the blessed Apostle testifies:

> “The Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and giving thanks broke it and said: ‘This is my body, which will be delivered for you; do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood; do this, whenever you drink it, in remembrance of me.’ For whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you will proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes” (1 Cor. 11:23 and following).

The sacrifice is therefore offered so that the Lord’s death may be proclaimed and remembrance may be made of him who laid down his life for us. He himself says:

> “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

Since Christ died for us through love, when at the time of the sacrifice we make remembrance of his death, we ask that love be granted to us through the coming of the Holy Spirit. We earnestly beseech this: that through the very love by which Christ deigned to be crucified for us, we too, having received the grace of the Holy Spirit, may be able to have the world crucified and to be crucified to the world.

Imitating the death of our Lord, just as Christ, in that he died, died to sin once for all, but in that he lives, lives to God (Rom. 6:10), may we also walk in newness of life (v. 4); and having received the gift of love, may we die to sin and live to God (v. 11).

> “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

The very participation in the body and blood of the Lord, when we eat his bread and drink the cup, also suggests this to us: that we die to the world, have our life hidden with Christ in God, and crucify our flesh with its vices and desires.

Thus it comes about that all the faithful who love God and neighbor, even if they do not drink the cup of bodily suffering, nevertheless drink the cup of the Lord’s love. Intoxicated by it, they put to death their members that are upon the earth; and, having put on the Lord Jesus Christ, they do not make provision for the flesh in its desires. They do not contemplate what is seen, but what is not seen.

The Lord’s cup is therefore drunk when holy love is guarded. Without this love, even if someone hands over his body to be burned, it profits him nothing. Through the gift of love it is granted to us to be in truth what we mystically celebrate in the sacrifice.

The Apostle says:

> “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body”;

and he added:

> “For we all partake of the one bread” (1 Cor. 10:17).

We have the most salutary example of our Savior showing that we should request this at the time of the sacrifice. In remembrance of his death, he wished us to ask for what he himself, the true High Priest, requested for us when he was near death. Among other things he said:

> “Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one as we are” (John 17:11).

And shortly afterward:

> “I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, so that all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they too may be one in us, and that the world may believe that you sent me. And the glory that you gave me I have given them, so that they may be one as we are one. I in them and you in me, so that they may be perfected into one” (ibid., vv. 20 and following).

This, then, is what we ask for when we offer the body and blood of Christ: what he asked for us when Christ deigned to offer himself for us. Review the Gospel, and you will find that our Redeemer entered the garden after completing this prayer and was immediately seized by the hands of the Jews.

Nevertheless, after the supper in which he gave the sacrament of his body and blood to the disciples, the Savior poured out this prayer for his faithful. He showed that at the time of the sacrifice we ought especially to pray for what he, as the supreme High Priest establishing the rule of sacrifice, deigned to request.

What we ask for—that we may be one in the Father and the Son—we receive through the unity of spiritual grace. The blessed Apostle commands us to preserve this carefully, saying:

> “Bearing with one another in love, taking care to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”

We therefore ask that the Holy Spirit come, not according to the substance of his immeasurable divinity, but according to the gift of undivided love. For if you think that the Holy Spirit comes from one place to another, it follows that you must also confess that the Father and the Son come from one place to another. For the Son of God says:

> “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

The Father and the Son therefore come to the one who loves them, although they are loved only by one in whom they deign to dwell. For God is love (1 John 4:8), and God is loved through love; God is therefore loved when he is possessed.

Just as the eye cannot see light at all unless it receives light, so God begins to be loved by a human being when the human being begins to be visited by the Lord. How, then, do the Father and the Son come to the one who loves them, by whom they could not be loved if they were not in him? They are said to come rightly when they increase in him the grace they grant, adding to it the progress of a better life.

They therefore come to the one who loves them not by approaching a human being in whom they were already present, but by increasing in that human being the gifts they had given. The Spirit is likewise said to come when he is requested by the faithful, whenever he deigns either to bestow or to increase the gift of love and unity.

It is especially in this gift, and, so to speak, properly in this gift, that the Holy Spirit is recognized. He can bestow any other gift through his omnipotence and himself not be present through grace; but he shows himself present through grace when he grants love.

Thus, if someone speaks in the tongues of human beings and of angels but does not have love, he will become like a resounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. If he has prophecy and knows all mysteries and all knowledge, and if he has all faith so as to move mountains, but does not have love, he is nothing. And if he distributes all his possessions as food for the poor, and hands over his body to be burned, but does not have love, it profits him nothing (1 Cor. 13:1 and following).

Who could deny that all those things are gifts of the Holy Spirit, since the Apostle testifies that they are given through the Spirit? Yet none of them profits where love is absent. The Holy Spirit gives all those things even to those in whom he does not dwell; but from those to whom he grants love he does not depart.

Therefore, when the holy Church prays in the sacrifice of the body and blood of Christ that the Holy Spirit be sent to her, she is asking for the gift of love, by which she may preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4:3). And because it is written:

> “Love is strong as death” (Song 8:6),

she asks for that love for the putting to death of the members that are upon the earth—the love through which she remembers her Redeemer, who freely died for her.

The Holy Spirit therefore sanctifies the sacrifice of the Catholic Church. Thus the Christian people remain in faith and love, while each of the faithful worthily eats and drinks the body and blood of the Lord through the gift of the Holy Spirit, because he both holds a right faith concerning his God and, by living well, does not abandon the unity of the ecclesiastical body.

**FRAGMENT XXIX. Why the Holy Spirit is requested in the blessing of the font. What is meant by Elijah’s double spirit; what is meant by the manifold Spirit; what are the seven spirits before the throne of God in the Apocalypse. The Holy Spirit is master of his own will. What it means for the Son to be sent by the Father, and for the Holy Spirit to be sent by the Father and the Son. The Son, as man, was sent by the Father and by the Holy Spirit.**

[Col. 0791D]

And so, in the blessing of the font we do not ask that the Holy Spirit be sent as though we were requesting his local arrival. Rather, knowing that the Holy Spirit has his natural origin in God the Father, we ask from God the Father the abundance of the spiritual gift, naming his gifts by his name. We do this not without the authority of Holy Scripture. For there are many examples of these expressions in the canonical books, in which the gifts of the Holy Spirit are recognized as being designated by his name. We read that, when the holy Elijah was about to be taken up into heaven, he told Elisha to ask for whatever he wished before he was taken away from him. Elisha replied: “I beg that a double portion of your spirit be upon me” (2 Kings 2:9). Here, clearly, we see a spiritual gift designated by the name “spirit.”

For the simple nature of the Holy Spirit, in itself—as it is always full and remains unchangeable—is neither diminished nor increased. It is indeed said in the Book of Wisdom: “The Holy Spirit, unique, manifold” (Wisdom 7:22). But what is called “manifold” is found not in the Spirit himself, but in his gifts. Thus, in the ancient books, the Spirit of God is called “manifold,” just as in the apostolic Letters the wisdom of God is called “manifold” (Ephesians 3:10); yet it is manifold not in itself, but in its bestowals. Blessed Peter makes this most clearly evident when he says: “As each has received a gift, minister it among yourselves, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1 Peter 4:10).

The nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is therefore one and simple. According to this nature, the Wisdom of God and the Spirit of God are likewise simple. But since we have gifts differing according to the grace that has been given to us (Romans 12:6), we find that the Wisdom of God and the Spirit of God—whom we know to be simple in his nature—are manifold in their various gifts.

Blessed John likewise designates spiritual gifts by the name “spirit” in the Apocalypse, saying: “John to the seven churches that are in Asia: grace to you and peace from him who is, and who was, and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne” (Revelation 1:4). By mentioning seven spirits, he certainly intended one Spirit, the giver of sevenfold grace, to be understood. Isaiah, enlightened by his grace, recognized him as the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of God (Isaiah 11:2).

Wherever, therefore, the seven spirits are named in the Apocalypse of blessed John, let the seven gifts of the one Holy Spirit be understood. But if perhaps you do not believe that in these seven spirits the grace of the sevenfold spiritual gifts itself is meant, and instead think that there are actually seven spirits distinct in their individual persons, tell us whether you consider them equal to, inferior to, or superior to the Holy Spirit—that is, the Paraclete of whom we are now speaking. Or perhaps do you think that this Holy Spirit is one of those seven?

For if you say that those whom you suppose to be the seven spirits are equal to the Holy Spirit, then you will undoubtedly be naming not seven but eight holy spirits of one dignity. What reason, then, did blessed John have for wishing grace from those seven spirits for the churches, while excluding from them the grace of the Spirit Paraclete? The Book of Acts says that, when blessed Peter was speaking the word of faith to Cornelius and the others who were with him, “the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word, and the faithful of the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished, because the grace of the Holy Spirit had also been poured out upon the nations” (Acts 10:44–45).

Did blessed John know this grace of the Holy Spirit to be lesser, and therefore ask for grace from other seven spirits for the churches that were in Asia? If there were indeed eight spirits, he ought to have asked those churches for the gift of spiritual grace from all of them together, so that there would be no separation in the bestowal of those whom you assert to be equal.

But if you say that those seven spirits are inferior to the Paraclete, the question arises again: why did blessed John wish the grace of inferior spirits to be given to the faithful, and not seek the grace of the superior one? Surely the one who is higher in nature can be the giver of the better grace.

If, however, you declare those seven spirits to be superior to the Holy Spirit, why is the Holy Spirit alone named with the Father and the Son in baptism, and why is he also called by the Apostle the “Spirit of adoption” (Romans 8:15), while those whom you say are seven spirits—being, according to your view, both better in nature and more numerous—ought to have been named with the Father and the Son in the sacrament of baptism? By their numerical plurality and the superiority of their nature, they would be able to bestow upon those being reborn a better and more abundant grace.

If matters were as you say, holy baptism ought therefore to be given not in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, but in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the seven spirits. The same rule ought to be observed in baptism if one of those seven spirits were the Holy Spirit. If you think or say that this should be done, consider Christ, whose rule you contradict.

Or perhaps, in order to show the Holy Spirit to be inferior to the Father and the Son, you remove him from the sacrament of baptism and introduce another Spirit of God there? For some of you, when they begin to be convicted concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit, turn to this perversity: since it is certain that people are baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, according to the rule of the Lord and Savior, they say that it is not this Spirit, the Paraclete, but another Spirit of God in whose name believers receive the sacrament of baptism—and they undoubtedly place that Spirit above the Spirit Paraclete.

If this is so, tell us whether you believe this Spirit to belong to the Father alone, to the Son alone, or to both. If you say that this Spirit belongs to the Father alone, you unquestionably proclaim him superior to the Son. We ask, then, whether at least you say that he is of one nature with God the Father. If you say that God the Father and this Spirit have one nature, you must necessarily place him above the Son of God.

If this is so, then, according to your view, Christ placed the order of the names incorrectly in the sacrament of baptism. For if the Son is not of one nature with God the Father and his Spirit, the Son’s name ought not to be inserted between the name of the Father and that of the Holy Spirit, since the natural unity of the Father and the Holy Spirit teaches that their names ought to be joined together.

Nevertheless, you should remember that the Spirit Paraclete of whom we are now speaking descended upon Jesus after he had been baptized. Consider, then, whether you ought to call that Spirit superior who descended upon Christ in the Jordan rather than the other Spirit whom you now suppose to be given to the faithful in holy baptism.

But in every respect the supreme divinity refutes and overturns you. God the Father testifies that he gave his Spirit upon the Son. The holy Evangelist, commending what was spoken through Isaiah in the person of Christ, says: “That what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul has been well pleased: I will place my Spirit upon him’” (Matthew 12:17; Isaiah 42:1).

He also took care to indicate this at Christ’s baptism, saying: “When he had been baptized, immediately he came up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him” (Mark 1:10).

Do you see that it is the very Spirit of God whom you blaspheme without reverence and strive to make inferior? Or perhaps you say that this too is the Spirit of God, but nevertheless another Spirit of God, who is named with the Father and the Son in the sacrament of baptism?

But, as I said above, since this Spirit descended upon Christ, you ought not to consider him inferior to that Spirit, but superior. Next I ask whether the Spirit whom you call the Spirit of God is one Spirit common to the Father and the Son, or whether he is said to belong to the Father alone.

For if this Spirit is one Spirit of the Father and the Son, and this same Spirit is of one nature with the Father, he is plainly also of one nature with the Son. The Father and the Son therefore have one nature and one divinity, because the one Spirit of both has one nature with the Father and the Son.

But if you say that this one Spirit belongs to the Father alone and not to the Son, consider what the Apostle says: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9). Either deny that you belong to Christ if his Spirit is not in you, or say that not the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but the Father and the Son and two spirits dwell in you.

But since no one can serve two masters (Matthew 6:24), how will you rightly claim to be servants of four masters? Do you say that the Father with his Spirit is one master, and the Son with his Spirit another? Even so, you wish to be servants of two masters, so long as you refuse to confess that the Father and the Son are one Lord.

Nor will you be able to be servants of the Father and the Son until you believe in the one lordship of the Father and the Son. Consequently, as long as you call the Father and the Son two lords, while you cannot serve two masters, you will not be free from servitude but from salvation.

Therefore, Fabian, recognize the majesty of the Holy Spirit and cease at last to blaspheme him. He is requested to come for the blessing of the font precisely so that, by granting the remission of sins, he may bestow the gift of adoption as sons. He comes in the abundance of his gifts, although he never ceases to fill the whole world.

The Father sends him because he proceeds from the Father; yet he sends him by the origin of majesty, not by the command of an order. Thus the Holy Spirit, who is wholly everywhere, comes just as the Son is accustomed to come with God the Father.

The mission of the Holy Spirit is therefore the bestowal of an invisible gift, not a personal appearance, because the mission itself is not to be understood locally where the one who is sent is found by nature to be immeasurable.

To recognize his mission clearly in his gifts, consider what blessed John said in the Apocalypse: that the seven spirits of God had been sent throughout the world (Revelation 5:6). Yet in the Gospel he said that our Savior had promised that not seven spirits would be sent by him and by the Father, but one Paraclete, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father (John 15:26).

Could blessed John, then, have forgotten his own Gospel, so that there he said one Spirit had been promised, while here he said that seven spirits had been sent? Or ought the Lord not to have given the apostles all seven spirits, whom he was appointing as the leaders of his Church? Do you also assert that seven spirits were sent to the apostles? Holy authority absolutely does not permit you to say this.

For on the day of Pentecost the apostles received the same Holy Spirit whom the Lord had promised them, and they testified that one and the same Holy Spirit had been given to all the faithful and obedient to God, saying: “And we are witnesses of these words, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him” (Acts 5:32).

This one Spirit was given to all the faithful, concerning whom the Apostle says: “And we were all given to drink of one Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:13). When blessed John therefore says that the seven spirits of God were sent throughout the world, he wished to show how the one Spirit of God is sent—not in himself, for he is always immeasurable everywhere—but in the abundance of his gifts.

He therefore said that the seven spirits of God had been sent throughout the world in order to show that the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit had been bestowed upon the Church, which is spread everywhere throughout the world.

The Holy Spirit, then, who both gives and preserves the Church’s charity, sanctifies both the sacrifice and baptism through the operation of divine power. Therefore our baptism is not—as you say—of no importance and of no substance. For baptism, when it is given within the Catholic Church in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, contains within itself both the form and the power of piety.

The form of piety is conferred through the visible washing; the power of piety is infused through the gift of true faith and charity. Heretics and schismatics, however, when they depart from the Church, have lost the power of piety because they have neither held the true faith nor preserved ecclesiastical charity. But they did not lose the form of piety—the visible sacrament of washing—when they left the Church.

It remained in them as a testimony to condemnation, not as an aid to salvation. Thus, outside the Church, they gave what they had received and could not in any way lose: the visible sacrament of baptism.

Baptism should not therefore be said to lack the form of piety among heretics merely because it does not possess there the power of piety. The power of piety must be restored to the form, and this power is possessed by Catholic unity alone, in which there is both the truth of right faith and the unbroken fellowship of charity.

The one Spirit gives life to this one body of the Church. For this reason blessed Paul says: “One body and one Spirit” (Ephesians 4:4). In every member that remains within this one body, both form and life are found to be present.

But every member that is cut off from this body, whether by unbelief or by hostility, retains its form but lacks life. A member separated from the body loses invisible life, yet does not lose visible form.

You say that by this the Holy Spirit is shown to be subordinate and inferior, because he himself is not requested to descend or come if he possesses his own power, or free will. But how does Fabian deny freedom of will to the Holy Spirit, when the Apostle Paul assigns it to him above all, saying: “The Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17)?

Does Fabian therefore deny freedom of will to the Holy Spirit, who is given to us so that through him the freedom of our own will may be restored by a gracious gift? For who has ever been able to escape the deadly slavery of sin without the grace of the Holy Spirit? Who, I ask, without the gift of the Holy Spirit, has been able even in some measure to aspire to the beginnings of recovered inner freedom?

What outrage! How far human recklessness plunges itself by its pride, and, while striving to rush into insult against its Creator and Liberator, fails to attend to the benefits of divine goodness.

For the Son of God says: “If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free” (John 8:36). In being freed, we are made sons of God, because, having been freed from sin, we become servants of God (Romans 6:22). In receiving the gift of divine adoption, we also receive the grace of freedom.

The blessed Apostle says: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15). How, then, does a human being dare to take away from the very Spirit of adoption the freedom that, without that Spirit, he can neither recover once lost nor retain once bestowed?

And what is worse, Fabian, you dare to say that free will is not lacking in human beings, but that the Holy Spirit does not possess free will. The Apostle says to us: “You were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love of the Spirit serve one another” (Galatians 5:13).

Behold, the love of the Spirit has caused us to be called to freedom. How, then, is that Spirit denied to be free in will? But since that Spirit convicts the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment (John 16:8), when you come to judgment on account of this sin, you will experience the free will of the Holy Spirit.

Meanwhile, you say that the Holy Spirit is inferior and subordinate because he is not requested to descend or come, nor to send and direct himself; yet you do not deny that the Son was sent by the Father, and on this account you attempt to assert that he is inferior.

If, therefore, you learn from the testimony of the divine books that the Son was requested by the prophets to descend and come, at least from this you will confess that he is not subordinate and will say that he possesses free will and power of his own.

For to whom except the Son, whom he knew would descend, did the blessed prophet say: “Lord, bow the heavens and descend” (Psalm 144:5)? Or whose arrival, except that of the Only-Begotten of God, did he request when he said: “You who feed Israel, attend; you who lead Joseph like a sheep. You who sit upon the cherubim, appear before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. Stir up your power and come to save us” (Psalm 80:1–3)?

Recognize, then, that when the Father was requested, as the prophet says, “Send forth your light and your truth” (Psalm 43:3), and, “Command, O God, your power; confirm what you have worked in us” (Psalm 68:29), the Son was sent by the Father. But when the Son himself was asked by the prophets to come, he came by his own will.

The Son would never have been requested by the prophets if his coming had not been in his own power. The Father was therefore asked to send the Son because he begot the Son. Yet the Son would not have been asked to descend and come if he did not naturally possess the same power as the Father.

The holy prophets therefore knew that they were asking the Son when they asked the Father, and likewise that they were asking the Father when they asked the Son. Thus, whether they directed their prayer to the person of the Father or to the person of the Son, they asked the whole Trinity by addressing one person, because they knew the Trinity to have one substance.

The Son, therefore, was sent by the Father, not the Father by the Son, because the Son was born from the Father, not the Father from the Son. Similarly, the Holy Spirit is read to have been sent by the Father and the Son, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

But because Scripture speaks of “mission” in more than one way, in the sacrament of the Incarnation the Son was sent not only by the Father but also by the Holy Spirit, because Christ Jesus, the man who is mediator between God and human beings, was formed through the operation of the whole Trinity.

In another way the Holy Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son: namely, because he proceeds naturally from the Father and the Son. The Holy Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son when the effect of spiritual grace is bestowed by the Trinity itself, the one God.

In yet another way the Son was sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit when, emptying himself, he took the form of a servant. For to assume flesh into his own person and to become the Word made human is not the same as invisibly bestowing some gift. The Holy Spirit did not truly become a dove or truly become fire when it was necessary for him to be signified by the appearance of such things—[Florus reads: “to be marked/signified”]. But the Word became flesh when the Only-Begotten God assumed flesh.

Yet he did this not by another’s power but by his own; nor by his own alone, since that sacrament of piety was accomplished by the one will and power of the whole Trinity.

I am astonished that you do not believe an angel to be sent by the Holy Spirit, from whom you read that the Lord of angels himself was sent.

We invoke the Father because of his origin, and because of the natural and indivisible unity of the Godhead. The holy Church preserves this, in any case, by the gift of divine inspiration. For she could not ask the Trinity in the plural number, lest unbelievers suppose that the Christian religion served not one God but gods.

The holy Church therefore asks the Father in her prayers, recognizing by right faith that he is the origin of the Son and the Holy Spirit. But she concludes her prayers and petitions in the name of the Son and of the Holy Spirit in order to show that the Holy Trinity is of one nature and majesty.

I have already answered you above concerning the power of the Holy Spirit, which you are not afraid to deny him over creation, although you cannot escape his power and justice. For it is evident that he possesses full power over all things, because “he works all things, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11).

Do not therefore, in your pride, deny the power of the Holy Spirit, lest, when condemned, you experience his justice. The Holy Spirit is naturally Lord because he is naturally the Spirit of the Lord—not the Spirit of the Lord Father alone, nor of the Lord Son alone, but of the one Lord, namely, the Father and the Son.

And because he is naturally the one Spirit of the Father and the Son, he is naturally one Lord with the Father and the Son. For this reason he does not come unless he is sent by the Father and the Son: the power of his voluntary coming derives from the same source as his naturally eternal divinity.

## FRAGMENT XXX

Not every mission is an appearance. The Holy Spirit appeared only in the dove and in the tongues of fire, and was often sent on other occasions without an appearance. The devil was not sent to Job but permitted. Angels are sent as ministering spirits. The Holy Spirit does not pray for us in the same manner as the Son.

**[Col. 0798B]**

Behold, I say again what I said above: not every mission is an appearance, and this is especially true of the mission of the Holy Spirit. His mission needed to be shown visibly only twice—not through his own nature, but through a subordinate creature, a creature that would signify something and, once its significance had been fulfilled, pass away.

Thus the Holy Spirit had to be signified in that dove and in the tongues of fire—although we do not believe that he was sent locally—just as the voice that came over Jesus after he had been baptized had to signify God the Father. In that voice, however, we understand the person of the Father to have been signified, without in any way daring to attribute a temporal utterance to his divinity.

The spirits who are sent from heaven appear when God commands them to do so, and they do not appear when they are not divinely commanded. Nevertheless, they are sent to a place where they had not been before they were sent.

This cannot rightly be believed or said of the Holy Spirit, whom we know to be wholly everywhere always, because “the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wisdom 1:7).

What you said is false: “When the Devil was sent to Job, why did he not appear?” Holy Scripture did not say that the devil was sent to Job, although it did say that he was permitted. You therefore uselessly multiply pointless words about the mission and appearance of angels, and by turning them over multiply them again, as though we denied that angels were sent because they have often made themselves visible.

In fact, whether they are sent and appear to human eyes or hide themselves from human sight, they are sent in the manner proclaimed by apostolic authority: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent for service, on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1:14).

But the mission of the Holy Spirit can never be of this kind. He cannot have a mission resembling that of angels, because wherever the holy angels are, they are all filled with the one Spirit, who is wholly in each and one in all.

The Holy Spirit, however, is never called an angel or a minister. Although in the work there is one proclamation of the Trinity, in the Spirit’s assistance there is not the service of slavery but the aid of divine majesty. Blessed Peter unquestionably demonstrates this when he says: “Whoever speaks, as the words of God; whoever ministers, as from the power that God supplies” (1 Peter 4:11).

Here it is shown that the assistance of supplying power belongs not to any creature but to God alone.

Regarding that objection in which you said that the Holy Spirit requests, groans, and intercedes, insofar as the Lord helped me I gave an answer, showing how the Apostle’s statement must be understood according to the rule of truth.

For in truth Christ, who is at the right hand of God, does intercede for us (Romans 8:34), but inasmuch as he deigned to be Priest and offered himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a pleasing fragrance (Ephesians 5:2).

Prayer, then, comes from the same source as offering; priestly supplication from the fact that he shares our nature with us. Thus he is the one who both prays for us and is prayed to by us.

He prays for us insofar as he is our Priest and the head of the body, the Church, the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. He is prayed to by us insofar as he is naturally one God with the Father.

The Holy Spirit, however, performs no office of petition for us either with the Father or with the Son. Rather, with the Father and the Son he grants one hearing of benevolence to our petitions, bestows one mercy, supplies one aid, and grants one forgiveness of sins.

For when we ask the Father, the whole Trinity is asked together, because whatever is beneficial to us is bestowed by the whole Trinity through inseparable power and goodness.

## FROM BOOK IX, ON THE INVOCATION OF THE TRINITY

## FRAGMENT XXXI

The Father alone is not invoked; the Son also is invoked. In invoking one person, the whole Trinity is invoked. Whatever one person is asked for, the whole Trinity accomplishes.

**[Col. 0799B]**
You say that whether the Lord’s Prayer or all common prayers and supplications are properly addressed only to the person of God the Father. We, however, say that the Lord’s Prayer must always be offered to the person of the Father alone, since in it we begin to pray by naming the Father first. Therefore, following this rule established by the Savior, the Church, which is his body, has been accustomed to offer her prayers to the person of God the Father.

Nevertheless, so that we may recognize that, in the invocation of one person, the whole Trinity is likewise honored by the service of faithful invocation, we find that the Son too was invoked by patriarchs and holy martyrs—men whom you surely will not dare accuse either of ignorance of the truth or of some crime of irreligious error. In the case, then, of him whom God appointed “Father of many nations” (Rom. IV, 17), receive the first evidence of this matter. Of him, while he was still called Abram and had not yet, by divine favor, been called Abraham, the following is written in Genesis:

“And the Lord God appeared to Abram and said to him: ‘To your seed I will give this land.’ And there he built an altar to the Lord who had appeared to him. And he departed from there to the mountain east of Bethel, with Ai toward the sea, eastward; and there he built an altar to the Lord God, and invoked in the name of the Lord God who had appeared to him” (Gen. XII, 7–8).

Choose now one of two alternatives: either say that God the Father appeared to holy Abraham, or assert that the Son was invoked. See what Scripture emphasizes: “And he invoked in the name of the Lord God who had appeared to him.” Here it is acknowledged that the God who had appeared was himself invoked. Or do you perhaps think that, because it does not say, “He invoked the Lord God who had appeared,” but rather, “in the name of the Lord God who had appeared,” one was the one who appeared and another perhaps the one who was invoked? Say, then, whom the holy patriarch invoked, or in whose name you think that he invoked him. Without doubt, you must assert either that he invoked the Father in the name of the Son, or the Son in the name of the Father.

But whichever you choose, you must be overcome by the force of truth. For if you assert that the Son was invoked in the name of the Father, on account of the statement, “I have come in my Father’s name” (John V, 43), then for the present you must admit that the Son was invoked by the holy patriarchs. Now what is it to invoke except to pray? Abraham therefore prayed to the one whom he invoked. Does it please you, or does it displease you, that the Son was invoked by holy Abraham? If it pleases you, either say that the Father was not invoked there, or acknowledge that, in the invocation of one person, the honor is shared by both. But plainly, if you say that the Son was invoked in the name of the Father, you cannot separate the Father from this invocation.

Why, then, when the Son is invoked do you believe that the Father too is invoked, but when the Father is invoked do you not believe that the Son is also invoked? For just as there the invocation proceeds from the offspring back to the source, so here it must likewise proceed from the source back to the offspring. Thus the God who is invoked in the name of the Lord God is invoked in his own name; and to invoke the Lord is nothing other than to invoke the name of the Lord.

Otherwise, to whom does Isaiah say: “Lord, apart from you we have known no other; we have invoked your name” (Isa. XXVI, 13)? Or to whom does Jeremiah say: “And you are among us, Lord, and your name has been invoked over us” (Jer. XIV, 9)? David too, praying, says: “O God, save me in your name, and judge me by your power” (Ps. LIII, 3).

Finally, if you think that the rule of faith does not allow the Son to be invoked, you must necessarily condemn blessed Stephen, of whom it is written that, while the Jews were stoning him, he invoked and said: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts VII, 59). You must also reject the teaching of the apostle Peter, who says:

“Grace with all who invoke Jesus Christ in perpetuity. Peace to all of you who are in Christ” (I Pet. V, 14).

[Note: [Col. 0799D] The preceding words are not found in the Vulgate.]

Why, then, does blessed Stephen direct his prayer to the Son, if the Son is never to be entreated? Or whom else does David invoke when he says what we quoted above: “You who shepherd Israel, attend; you who lead Joseph like sheep” (Ps. LXXIX, 1)? He also asks for his coming when he says (v. 3): “Awaken your power and come to save us.”

Acknowledge, therefore, that when the Father is invoked, the Son too is invoked together with him; and that when the Son is invoked, the Father is likewise invoked; and that the Holy Spirit is in no way separated from the same invocation. For we owe one service of prayer to the holy Trinity, in whose name we were baptized and received the grace of redemption.
