When we pray, therefore, we say to the Father, “Through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son,” asking that through him he may accomplish what we pray for—through whom he deigned to bring it about that we should exist. For the Father made and makes all things through the Son, since there is “one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (I Cor. VIII, 6). Of him it is likewise written: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 3); and that “all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all, and all things hold together in him” (Col. I, 16–17).

But because you think that the expression “through our Lord Jesus Christ” is an adjuration, recognize even in this respect that the Son is equal to the Father. For apostolic authority says: “When God promised Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom he could swear, he swore by himself” (Heb. VI, 13). Therefore the God who swears only by himself is adjured only through the one who is recognized as being of one nature with him.

Although that conclusion of the prayer more clearly shows through whom the Father acts, it does not contain the language of adjuration. However it may be expressed, it is sufficient, since it is said for this purpose: that every prayer and every supplication may be concluded in the name of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Since, then, we have shown that blessed Stephen, at the very moment of his passion, directed his prayer not to the person of the Father but to that of the Son, while the whole Church always directs her prayer or supplication to the person of the Father, you must recognize that the entire rule of our faith, although it appears to be directed to one person of the Trinity, nevertheless contains in that person the honor of the whole Trinity.

For he who says, “Whoever hates me hates my Father also” (John XV, 22), and of whom blessed John says, “Whoever loves the one who begot loves the one who was born from him” (I John V, 1), just as he is commonly hated or loved together with the Father, so, when the Father is entreated, he is understood by the faithful to be entreated together with him.

And since the Spirit of the Father and of the Son is one, it is necessary that, when the Father or the Son is invoked, the one Spirit of both should also be invoked in the Father and the Son.

There is one Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, in whose name we conclude every prayer that we direct to the Father; yet not without mentioning the Holy Spirit, so that we may show that we humbly petition the whole Trinity. For we do not say to the whole Trinity, “Through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son,” but to the Father alone, whose only-begotten Son is the Lord Jesus Christ.

For this reason, as we have already said above, when we pray to the Father we add the name of Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit, so that we may show that whatever we ask, we ask from the whole Trinity. Otherwise, show us how what our Savior himself is known to have commanded in the final discourse that, according to the Gospel of John, he delivered to his disciples can be fulfilled.

At one point in that discourse he says: “If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, whatever you wish you will ask, and it will be done for you” (John XV, 7). Here he said that something should be asked, but he did not indicate whether it should be asked from him or from the Father.

Shortly afterward, however, he took care to disclose that the person of the Father should be asked, saying: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give you” (ibid., 16). Repeating this, he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, if you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you” (John XVI, 2).

Nevertheless, hear how he also took care to make clear to his disciples that he himself should be asked, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you, whoever believes in me will himself do the works that I do, and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father; and whatever you ask in my name, I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask me for anything in my name, I will do it” (John XIV, 12–14).

Behold, the Son of God indicates that he himself is also to be asked. If the Father is asked for anything in the Son’s name, he will undoubtedly give it, because the Son, who is faithful in his words, promised this. If the Son too is asked for anything in his own name, he promises that he will certainly do it.

Therefore either say that the work of the Father and of the Son is one and that the persons are united in prayer; or, if you separate the persons so that you do not believe that when the Father is asked, the Son is asked, you must, if you think that the service of prayer belongs to one alone, attribute to that one alone also the effect of the action.

Accordingly, by your position, there is found among the holy apostles and martyrs a great diversity in their prayers: one prays to the Father, another invokes the Son. For we read that the blessed Paul invoked the Father on behalf of the faithful, as he himself says:

“For this reason I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, and that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Eph. III, 14–17).

The Father unquestionably accomplished this. Blessed Stephen, however, invoked the Lord Jesus so that he might receive his spirit (Acts VII, 59), and the Lord Christ unquestionably fulfilled this when invoked.

What, then, do you say? Did the Son, together with the Father, do what Paul asked of the Father, and did the Father, together with the Son, do what Stephen invoked the Son to do? Or, just as Paul asked only the Father, did the Father alone do it, and just as Stephen invoked only the Son, did Christ alone accomplish it?

For if you say that what Paul, according to your position, asked only of the Father was done by the Father alone, you will nevertheless admit that what Stephen asked only of the Son was accomplished by the Son alone, without any cooperation of the Father. Thus you assert that the works of the Father and of the Son are separate—contradicting the Son of God himself, who says: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John V, 19).

But if you say that the Father and the Son have one work in fulfilling the petitions of the martyr Stephen and the apostle Paul, acknowledge that their work could not possibly be one except through unity of nature: so that the Father might see himself invoked by Stephen in the Son, and the Son might recognize himself entreated by Paul in the Father.

But so that you may recognize that apostolic teaching requires both the Father and the Son to be invoked by us, see how the blessed Apostle commends Christ as one to be invoked. He writes to the Corinthians:

“Paul, called an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Sosthenes, our brother, to the Church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called saints, together with all who invoke the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, theirs and ours: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (I Cor. I, 1–3).

You plainly see that the Apostle divinely asks grace and peace for those who invoke the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. What, then, remains except that whoever does not invoke the name of the Lord Jesus Christ can have neither grace nor peace from him? Whoever does not receive grace from God will undoubtedly receive eternal punishment; and whoever does not receive peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ will in no way attain salvation.

For blessed Paul commends the invocation of this very name in prophetic language, saying: “Everyone who invokes the name of the Lord will be saved” (Rom. X, 13; Joel II, 32).

It is therefore certain, according to the rule of true faith, in which the one substance of the holy Trinity is believed, that no separation of the Father and the Son occurs, whether the Father or the Son is invoked by the faithful.

But those who do not believe that, in the invocation offered to the Father, the Son is naturally invoked together with the Father, invoke neither the Father nor the Son. For the natural unity of the Trinity has this character: that the services of holy religion are rendered inseparably to all three persons, in whom there is one inseparable and unchangeable nature.

In the prayers that the one true Church offers to God, the unity of nature is preserved and the distinction of persons is maintained: when the prayer is directed to the Father, who is the source of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, the one nature of the Trinity is shown; but by mentioning the Son and the Holy Spirit, the very conclusion of the prayer displays the true Trinity.

Thus the impiety of Sabellius and Arius is overcome, while in the prayers and supplications themselves Catholic priests proclaim both the truth of one nature and the truth of three persons.

## FRAGMENT XXXII. Jesus Christ is not the Son of the Trinity, although according to the flesh he is the work of the whole Trinity; but according to his divinity he is the Son of the Father alone, and according to his humanity the son of the Virgin Mary alone.

For who could ever be found to possess such madness as to dare proclaim Jesus Christ the Son of the whole Trinity? The Church of the living God, “the pillar and foundation of the truth” (I Tim. III, 15), knowing one Father of one Son and knowing one Holy Spirit of the Father and of the Son, can never call Jesus Christ the Son of the Trinity, because it cannot in any way proclaim either two Fathers, or two Sons, or two Holy Spirits.

Jesus Christ, therefore, not only according to his divinity—in which he is naturally equal to God the Father—but also according to soul and flesh—in which the same God is consubstantial with his mother—is not merely the Son of God the Father, but also the only-begotten Son.

Accordingly, we not only altogether refuse to call Jesus Christ the Son of the Trinity, but also confess Jesus Christ to be the Son of God the Father alone, without in any way separating him. For it is a great impiety to regard Christ as one person and Jesus Christ as another, since Jesus Christ is one and the same Son of God and man: namely, the Son of God the Father alone, and not, of course, of the whole Trinity.

For the same Jesus Christ is recognized according to the flesh as the work of the whole Trinity, but he is nevertheless not found to be the Son of the whole Trinity. The human nature of the Son of God—that is, the form of a servant—was made simultaneously by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, that is, by the holy Trinity itself; but it was assumed by Jesus Christ alone, as the blessed Apostle says:

“For have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus: who, although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 5–7).

That same Jesus Christ, therefore, both in the form of a servant and in the form of God, is the one Son of God the Father alone, because, in taking the form of a servant, he did not assume a human person but a nature.

In the Virgin’s womb, when the Word became flesh, the conception of the Word and the flesh was made one; and in the one person of the Word, the divine and human nature were conceived together—not so that the two natures would become one, but so that, from the two natures, the one existing person of Jesus Christ might be constituted.

The truth of this matter, just as it does not permit a fourth person to be added to the fullness of the divine Trinity, so it altogether forbids Jesus Christ to be called the Son of the Trinity.

This is also shown by the wording of the holy Creed, where it says: “I believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.” The very one whom we call the Son of God we also confess to have been born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.

Therefore, when we say “Jesus Christ, his Son”—that is, Jesus Christ the Son of God the Father—we indicate the birth of his divinity, by which he is eternal, without beginning, from the Father. But when we say that he was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, we confess the birth by which that same only-begotten God, according to the flesh, temporally took his beginning from the Virgin.

Accordingly, Jesus Christ, as was said above, is according to the flesh the work of the whole Trinity, but according to both births he is the Son of God the Father alone, because the same only-begotten God alone is the true man temporally produced from the Virgin, who was born the true God without beginning from the Father alone.

## FRAGMENT XXXIII. Jesus Christ is not a designation belonging only to man but also to God; and in Scripture he is sometimes understood according to the divine nature alone, sometimes according to the human nature alone, and sometimes according to both. From one and the same Holy Spirit, the Son of God deigned to become the Son of man, and we were granted adoption as sons of God. The Arians are not worshipers of one God but of several.

First, then, concerning what you falsely said in my name—“Jesus Christ is a designation of man”—Paul, the teacher of the nations in faith and truth, proves that this is contrary to truth and contrary to faith, for he demonstrates Jesus Christ to be both God and man.

Thus, under one and the same name, Jesus Christ, in one and the same person, Scripture sometimes intends the divine substance alone, more often the human substance alone, and at other times both together.

For he himself says: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus: who, although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. II, 5 ff.).

Writing also to Timothy, he says: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David according to my gospel” (II Tim. II, 8).

Behold, in both passages one Christ Jesus is named, but the two passages are not understood according to one nature in Christ Jesus. For it is one Christ Jesus who, although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and who rose from the dead from the seed of David.

But Christ Jesus, emptying himself in the form of God and taking the form of a servant, is understood according to the divine nature alone. He is understood according to that nature also where he says: “And one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (I Cor. VIII, 6).

The same Christ Jesus, however, rising from the dead from the seed of David, can properly be understood according to the human substance alone.

Again the Apostle says: “I appeal to you, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Spirit” (Rom. XV, 30). And elsewhere: “I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead” (I Tim. I, 4).

In these passages we understand the Apostle to have named the whole Christ Jesus, not according to the divine nature alone or according to the human nature alone, but according to both natures.

Do you see that Jesus Christ is not to be understood in every passage of Scripture merely according to the fact that he is God, nor merely according to the fact that he is man? Rather, in each passage of Scripture he must be understood according to what the Truth teaches.

For Christ Jesus is one, the Son of God and man in both natures, one and true in both. Hence what you say also cannot stand: “When we say ‘Son of God,’ we signify God the Son himself, that is, Christ the spiritual one.”

For our Redeemer himself was not without a body when he said to the man born blind, to whom he had mercifully and wonderfully given eyes: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” When the man said to him, “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?” Jesus said to him: “You have seen him, and he who speaks with you is he” (John IX, 35–37).

It is clear, however, that what was visible to bodily eyes in him was not divinity but humanity.

Consider also the confession of blessed Peter, who says: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI, 16), and recognize that this Son of God is not God alone but God and man—especially since Christ himself called himself the Son of man, whom Peter confessed as the Son of the living God.

Therefore, since Christ is one, the Son of God and of man, just as we do not always find him called the Son of God according to divinity alone, so neither do we always find him called the Son of man according to the flesh alone.

For the same one who said to his disciples: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes; and they will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles, and they will mock him and spit upon him and scourge him and kill him, and on the third day he will rise” (Matt. XX, 18–19), also said: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven” (John III, 13).

Who of sound understanding would think that in both passages the Son of man spoke according to one substance, since according to divinity the Son could not undergo all those sufferings, while according to the flesh he would not then have been in heaven when he spoke such words on earth?

Thus it is one and the same Son of man who, according to the flesh alone, was truly handed over, truly killed, and rose on the third day; and who, according to divinity alone, was wholly on earth and wholly in heaven when, while according to the flesh he was present only on earth, he truthfully said these things about himself.

It is therefore true that in Christ there is one person of divinity and flesh, while the distinctive property of each nature is preserved. For Christ is sometimes spoken of according to divinity alone, sometimes according to flesh alone, and sometimes according to both substances.

The Apostle showed that Christ is to be understood according to divinity alone when he said:

“Do not lie to one another: strip off the old man with his deeds, and put on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of his creator. There is no Gentile and Jew, circumcision and prepuce, Barbarian and Scythian, slave and free, but Christ is all and in all” (Col. III, 9 ff.).

What he says here—“Christ is all and in all”—has the same force as the statement, “that God may be all in all.”

We likewise know Christ to have been named by the Apostle according to the flesh alone where he says:

“For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures” (I Cor. XV, 3–4).

Another passage of the same Apostle is also found to correspond to this understanding, where he says: “All of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death” (Rom. VI, 3); and shortly afterward: “Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him” (ibid., 9).

Yet he is also known to proclaim Christ according to both natures when he says: “Their fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. IX, 5).

It is therefore clear that those rules which you wished to establish from the terms mentioned above have no strength to support them, since they in no way accord with Christian truth.

For not only when he is called the Son of God, or the Son of man, or Christ, or Jesus Christ, but also when he who is the only-begotten Son of the Father, full of grace and truth (John I, 14), is called God in holy Scripture, we must consider which substance is rightly to be understood in the one person of the Son of God, without any error.

For in that passage of the Acts of the Apostles where the same apostle Paul says to the elders and leaders: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood” (Acts XX, 28), we understand “God” here to mean none other than the Son of God.

Yet he is understood to have acquired the Church with his blood not according to his eternal and unchangeable divinity, which he has unchangeably from the Father, but according to the humanity by which he became true man from the Virgin.

We therefore do not say that Jesus Christ is the name of humanity and of man alone; rather, we say that the one Jesus Christ is God and man, in whom the true nature of man from the nature of his mother remains just as the true and eternal substance of divinity from the nature of God the Father remains.

For he who is the Truth is the true Son both of the Father and of the mother. Of him blessed John says: “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true one and be in his true Son Jesus Christ” (I John V, 20).

And because the true Son of God is naturally true God—and he would not be true God if he were not the true Son from the Father’s nature—blessed John immediately added: “This is the true God and eternal life” (ibid.).

In the statement that Christ the Son of God was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, the Holy Spirit is none other than the Paraclete, who is the one Spirit of the Father and of the Son. For the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father (John XV, 26) is the same Spirit who is habitually called the Holy Spirit most explicitly in the holy Scriptures.

For the Father is naturally spirit, and the Son is spirit; the Father is holy, and the Son is holy. Yet no passage is found in the divine utterances in which the Father or the Son is called “the Holy Spirit” absolutely and without some addition.

It is written, “God is spirit” (John IV, 24), but “God” is added there, where without doubt the Father is understood as God.

Therefore, when holy Scripture signifies the Father or the Son, it is accustomed either to say merely “Spirit” or merely “holy,” and to add a name by which the Father or the Son may be understood; or, if it does not add a name, the preceding or following context indicates whether the expression should, according to the rule of true faith, be applied to one person or to the holy Trinity together.

He, then, is the one Holy Spirit from whom Christ was born according to the flesh, and from whom every Christian is spiritually reborn. By that grace of the Holy Spirit through which the only-begotten God deigned to become the Son of man, we were granted adoption as sons of God.

Jesus Christ is not the Son of the Trinity but of God the Father alone. He is rightly called coeternal with God the Father even after assuming his flesh, because in him there is one person of divinity and flesh; and the Son of God himself, who assumed flesh into the person of his divinity, naturally possesses a divinity coeternal and without beginning with God the Father.

Nor is there any other Holy Spirit whom we name with the Father and the Son in our prayers besides the one Spirit, the Paraclete. We know him as the one Spirit of the Father and the Son, and we know with absolute certainty that he is consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son.

We demonstrate that we worship one God because we believe and confess one substance of the Trinity.

You, however, are in no way worshipers of one God, since you say that the Father has one nature, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. Yet, although you do not worship one God, neither do you worship three gods; rather—and this is worse—you say that you do indeed worship two gods: God the Father, the greater, and God the Son, the lesser. Together with them, you worship, as it were, the Holy Spirit, from whom you entirely remove the name “God” and whom you call a creature without any reverence.

Since you thus show yourselves to be worshipers of a creature, you could, if you wished, worship not merely three but even five gods.

## FRAGMENT XXXIV. The Church does not sacrifice to the Father alone, nor give glory to the Father alone, but to the whole Trinity. Christ made his body both a temple and a sacrifice for us. We give thanks to the Father and the Son as God, but to the Father through the Son as man. The Holy Spirit has no place among the works of God.

[Col. 0808B]

But your lie must next be refuted, in which you say that I have always maintained that every sacrifice is offered to the Father alone—for I have neither ever said this nor do I say it now. For the holy Catholic Church sacrifices not to the Father alone, but simultaneously to the holy Trinity; and just as, directing its prayer to the person of the Father alone, it invokes the whole Trinity together, so whatever it offers in sacrifice to God the Father, it sacrifices simultaneously to the Trinity. For whether in prayer or in sacrifice, true faith makes no distinction in the offering, because there is no diversity of power within the Trinity. Consequently, whatever is offered to one person must necessarily be offered equally to the Trinity.

This is demonstrated by the examples of the holy patriarchs and prophets. [Col. 0808C] Here we must chiefly observe that an altar was always built for God so that God might be honored with the due service of sacrifice. The altar is first mentioned in the sacred books where holy Noah, coming out of the ark, is said to have offered victims to God. For it is written:

“And Noah built an altar to the Lord, and took from all the clean cattle and from all the clean birds, and offered a victim upon the altar to God” (Genesis 8:20).

The Lord also, showing that an altar is built for this purpose, speaks thus to Moses his servant:

“You shall make an altar of earth for me, and upon it you shall sacrifice your burnt offerings and your peace offerings” (Exodus 20:24).

Let us therefore inquire for whom our fathers built an altar, so that we may recognize that they also offered sacrifice to him. After that altar which [Col. 0808D] Noah made for the Lord, we read that an altar was built by holy Abraham. For it is written:

“And the Lord God appeared to Abraham and said to him: ‘To your offspring I will give this land.’ And Abraham built there an altar to the Lord, who had appeared to him. And he departed from there to the mountain that lies toward the east of Bethel, and pitched his tent there, with Bethel toward the sea and Hai toward the east; and he built there an altar to the Lord God, and invoked the name of the Lord God, who had appeared to him” (Genesis 12:7–8).

When we were previously discussing the invocation of God, I remember that we already cited this passage; let us now repeat its meaning. For, wishing to demonstrate that the Son is lesser than the Father, you are accustomed to say that the Son appeared to the holy Fathers. What, then, do you say now? For our Abraham built an altar to the God who appeared to him. There could have been no necessity for building an altar except for offering sacrifices. Therefore holy Abraham offered sacrifice to the God who appeared to him, for no other reason did he build an altar than to sacrifice to him. He also invoked him, since he is said to have invoked the name of the Lord God who had appeared to him.

Accordingly, either confess that the Father and the Son are invoked together in the service of one prayer, and that one sacrifice is offered simultaneously to the Father and the Son; or, if you do not wish this, you must either say that it was the Father who appeared, or admit that sacrifice was offered by the holy patriarchs to the Son alone, and thus be compelled to take away from the Father what you are trying to take away from the Son.

We read similarly about Isaac, of whom Scripture says:

“But from there he went up to the Well of the Oath, and the Lord appeared to him that night and said: ‘I am the God of Abraham [Col. 0809B] your father. Do not be afraid, for I am with you; I will bless you and multiply your offspring, because of Abraham your father.’ And Isaac built an altar there, and invoked the name of the Lord” (Genesis 26:23 and following).

Observe carefully that it is the same God of Abraham who appeared both to Abraham and to Isaac, and that an altar was built for him by Abraham and Isaac; consequently, sacrifice was offered to him by both. Let us come also to Jacob, so that we may show that he too, possessing the same faith, built an altar to the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, and likewise invoked him. For it is written of him:

“Jacob came to Salem, a city of the Shechemites, in the land of Canaan, when he had returned from Mesopotamia of Syria; and he approached the front of the city. He bought a portion of the field where he pitched his tent from Hamor, the father of Shechem, for one hundred lambs. And he set up an altar there, and will invoke the God of Israel” (Genesis 33:18 and following).

Again, a little later, holy Scripture says:

“Then God said to Jacob: ‘Arise, go up to Bethel, and dwell there, and make there an altar to the God who appeared to you when you were fleeing from the face of Esau your brother’” (Genesis 35:1).

And a little later:

“Jacob came to Luz, which is in the land of Canaan—that is, Bethel—he and all the people who were with him; and he built an altar there, and he called the name of that place the House of God. For there God appeared to him when he was fleeing from the face of his brother Esau” (ibid., 6–7).

It is certain that the holy patriarchs offered sacrifice to the God for whom they built an altar and whom they are known to have invoked in supplication. I think you will not dare to say that the patriarchs invoked one God and the holy apostles and martyrs another. For they invoked one God, because the apostles and martyrs believed in the very one in whom the patriarchs believed.

Since the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac, at the appointed time, gave the Old Testament, in which the promises of the New Testament were held concealed beneath fitting figures—for although there were other sacraments belonging to that period, the faith of the Christian religion was never different—the one true divinity of the Trinity ordained that, also through prophetic utterances, the true sacrifice to Christ the Lord should be declared as destined to be offered by the faithful in the time of the New Testament.

The prophet Zephaniah, filled with the Holy Spirit, intimates this in these words:

“Wait for me, says the Lord, on the day of my resurrection, for testimony. For my judgment will be upon the assembly of the nations, so that I may receive kings and pour out upon them the anger of my wrath; for in the fire of my jealousy the whole earth shall be consumed. For then I will transfer a language among the peoples into their generations, so that all may invoke the name of the Lord and serve him under one yoke. From beyond the rivers of Ethiopia I will receive those who observe me. Those who have been scattered will offer victims to me on that day” (Zephaniah 3:8–10).

Who is he who says that victims are to be offered to him, unless it is he who commanded that he be awaited on the day of his resurrection? And who foretold that he would rise again, unless it is the one who was handed over because of our sins and rose again for our justification (Romans 4:25)?

But who will doubt that the holy patriarchs and prophets also offered one sacrifice to the Father and the Son in the time of the Old Testament? For at the very beginning of the birth which Christ received from the Virgin, he consecrated to himself the sacrifice of the nations destined to believe, when the Magi offered it—making them, as it were, the firstfruits of the nations, and displaying in their gift the firstfruits of the immolation owed to him.

For the Magi, worshiping Christ the Lord, also humbly offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh. It is certain that frankincense is always offered in sacrifices to God; gold is paid with annual devotion to royal power; and myrrh is applied to the bodies of the dead for burial. In this threefold kind of offering, therefore, the complete mystery of Christian faith is contained: through it were to be recognized in Christ both the weakness of the assumed flesh and the eternal and royal omnipotence of the Godhead.

For in one and the same Christ they believed in mortal flesh, royal power, and exalted divinity above all things; and thus they taught that the true death of the Redeemer was to be believed, that royal power was to be rendered to the very King who created and renewed his image in us, and that to this same highest and true God was to be offered what the Greeks call λατρεία (*latreia*), the service of sacrifice.

Thus there was found written in their hearts, not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God:

“You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deuteronomy 6:13);

and:

“Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be destroyed, unless it be to the Lord alone” (Exodus 22:20).

And, to offer you something from your own writings, so that you may easily remember that frankincense is customarily offered always in sacrifice, let us review Virgil singing:

“And a hundred of Sabaean …”

“Altars glow there.” (Aeneid, book I, verse 425.) [Col. 0810D]

And do not doubt that to Christ, whom you recognize as having received frankincense, the Church, one and true, offers a sacrifice also in the unity of the Father and the Holy Spirit. For blessed martyr Stephen offered himself as a sacrifice to Christ the Lord, whom he invoked so that he might receive his spirit, saying: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59). It is written, moreover: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (Ps. 50:19); and holy Azariah said to him: “With a contrite soul and a spirit of humility may we be received, as with the holocausts of rams and bulls and the multitude of fat lambs; so may our sacrifice be made in your sight” (Dan. 3:39–40). Stephen offered his spirit to that Lord whom he invoked to receive his spirit. No holy man, however, is said to have invoked anyone except God. In particular, the holy patriarchs are then said to have invoked the name of the Lord whenever they built altars, on which they offered sacrifices to that God whom they invoked; indeed, scarcely anyone among them is ever said to have invoked the name of the Lord without constructing an altar.

Hence, very suitably and appropriately, blessed martyr Stephen is said in this passage not to have asked, but to have invoked the Lord Jesus, when it is understood that he offered himself as a sacrifice to God. Here it becomes evident that, while he was being stoned, he undoubtedly invoked the one to whom he was offering himself as a sacrifice and as a truly living victim. True faith offers one sacrifice not only to the Father and the Son, but also to the Holy Spirit—that is, to the holy Trinity itself, the one true and good God—and renders one service of adoration to him. The whole Church is therefore one temple in all the saints, just as, in the one name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, it knows itself to have been delivered from the kingdom of death and sin.

For this reason the blessed Apostle, demonstrating that the majesty of the holy Trinity is naturally one, says: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). And to show that the Holy Spirit dwells in us, in his temple, not as a servant but as the true and supreme God, he says again: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” (1 Cor. 6:19). And to demonstrate that the Holy Spirit is the true God, he added: “Glorify and carry God in your body.” The Holy Spirit, therefore, cannot be foreign to the Father and the Son in the sacrifice of the holy Church, since, together with the Father and the Son, he possesses the whole holy Church as one temple. Nor can we fail to offer a sacrifice to him whose temple we are, since the Apostle Paul commands that our very bodies, which are the temple of the Holy Spirit, be presented as “a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Rom. 12:1).

How, then, is the Church’s sacrifice in bread and wine not offered to the Holy Spirit, when the Spirit himself is understood to possess the Church as both temple and sacrifice? For our Savior himself, who suffered for us, leaving us an example, and who is the head of the body, the Church, displaying in himself what we should recognize in ourselves, made his one and same body not only a temple but also a sacrifice. He himself says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). The evangelist John, explaining this, says: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body.” The Apostle Paul likewise recalls that Christ offered himself for us: “Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma” (Eph. 5:1–2).

Christ, therefore, made his body a temple for us and offered it as a victim. Blessed Paul testifies that the whole Church is his body, saying of the Lord himself: “He is the head of the body, the Church” (Col. 1:18). He says again (v. 24): “I complete in my flesh what is lacking of Christ’s sufferings for his body, which is the Church.” Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow in his footsteps. Thus Christ taught us by his example and showed that the sacrifice belongs to the one whose temple we are.

We are the temple not only of the Father and the Son, but also of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, with supplication, we offer one sacrifice to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And since in a temple human beings are found to serve that supreme, one, true, and good God chiefly through two duties—prayer and sacrifice—for this reason our Savior, entering the temple, said: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. 21:13); and he says that two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector (Luke 18:10). Therefore, just as we offer one sacrifice to the Trinity itself, that is, to the one God, so we humbly render to the Trinity itself one service of prayer and supplication.

Consequently, whoever denies to the Son and the Holy Spirit the sacrifice that is offered to the Father should recognize himself as alien to the members of Christ. For the holy Church, which is the true body of Christ, knows that there is one temple and one sacrifice of the holy Trinity; accordingly, in the truth of faith, hope, and charity, it is accustomed to offer one sacrifice to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

To the holy Trinity, to whom we owe one and undivided service in all things, we offer one sacrifice, and so with faithful devotion we also sing one glory. Since the holy Trinity is acknowledged to possess one nature, it is fitting that one glory should be spoken by the faithful to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in hymns and psalms.

Nevertheless, because of the assumption of the form of a servant and the office of our High Priest, we rightly and faithfully give thanks to the Father through the Son, because according to the true faith we recognize in the Only-Begotten the reality of both natures. Thus, confessing him truthfully, we acknowledge him not only as equal to the Father according to the truth of eternal divinity, but also as lesser than the Father according to the grace of the humanity assumed, since, as the holy evangelist teaches, we know with complete certainty that the Only-Begotten came from the Father, “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

We rightly give thanks to the Father and the Son, because with the Father the Son is naturally one God; and we rightly give thanks to the Father through the Son, because he who by the Father’s nature is the one Son of God is also, by the mother’s nature, made the Son of man. We therefore give thanks to the Father through the Son insofar as he has granted himself to us in humility; we give thanks to the Father and the Son insofar as he will bestow—or, according to Florus, bestows—himself upon us as Most High.

We give thanks to the Father through the Son because the eternal and immortal Only-Begotten God became mortal man in time for our sake; and we give thanks to the Father and the Son because that same Only-Begotten God remains naturally coeternal with God the Father. We give thanks to the Father through the Son because he completed the work of our redemption; we give thanks to the Father and the Son because he promised us the gift of future blessedness. For he redeemed us through the humility of the flesh, and he will make us blessed through the exaltation of divinity.

We do both, therefore, because we find both prescribed in the sacred writings. That we ought to give thanks to the Father through the Son, we learn from apostolic speech; and that we ought to give thanks to the Father and the Son, we find not only in apostolic sayings but also in angelic praises. The apostolic message, however, has handed these things down to us because God himself showed them to his apostles for our instruction.

We know that blessed Paul said, when writing to the Romans: “First, I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you” (Rom. 1:8). He also says to the Colossians: “Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him” (Col. 3:17); and similar passages may be found in the apostolic writings. We also read that the same Apostle said: “I give thanks to him who strengthened me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful and appointed me to the ministry” (1 Tim. 1:12).

The Apostle therefore gives thanks through Christ and gives thanks to Christ. He gives thanks through Christ according to that by which Christ is from the fathers according to the flesh; and he gives thanks to Christ according to that by which Christ himself is “God blessed above all forever” (Rom. 9:5). The same blessed Apostle shows even more clearly that thanks are to be given to the Father and the Son when he both prays for and recalls that God’s grace is given to us not only by God the Father but also by Christ Jesus our Lord.

Teaching that grace is given to us by God through Christ, he says: “According to the Spirit of sanctification through the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom we have received grace and apostleship for obedience to the faith among all the nations for his name” (Rom. 1:4–5). And again he says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24–25).

The same Apostle, in all the openings of his letters, does not cease to ask that grace be given to us by God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. If you examine the beginnings of the apostolic Epistles, you will find this in nearly all those in which the Apostle’s name is included: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 1:7). Therefore, we must give thanks in the manner in which it is certain that we have received grace.

Since we have received grace from God through Jesus Christ our Lord, by this rule of truth we give thanks to the Father through the Son. But because we have received grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord, by this further rule of truth we give thanks simultaneously to the Father and the Son. For just as we have received grace not only from the Father through the Son but also from the Father and the Son, so it is necessary that, with the humility of the service owed to them, we pay the debt of thanksgiving not only to the Father through the Son but also to the Father and the Son.

Our giving thanks to the Father through the Son pertains to the mystery of the Incarnation; but in our giving thanks to the Father and the Son, the recognition of one divinity is made clear. For just as the Son assumed our flesh in such a way that he did not lose the natural truth of unity with the Father, so he granted us both things: that through the Son we should give thanks to the Father, and that we should give thanks simultaneously to the Son and to the Father.

The grace that the Father granted us through the Son, the Son also granted us, the Father granting it together with him. Therefore, just as we received the gift through him, so we must render the service through him; and just as grace is given to us by God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord, so thanksgiving must be paid by us to the Father and the Son.

For just as it is right and consistent with faith to give thanks to the Father through the one through whom it is certain that we received from the Father, so it is impious and contrary to true religion if someone reads in the apostolic writings that grace is given to the faithful by God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, yet refuses to have thanksgiving paid simultaneously to the Father and the Son.

Whoever does not wish to give thanks to the Father through the Son does not understand the true humanity in the divinity of Christ; but whoever does not give thanks to the Father and the Son does not wish to recognize the true divinity in Christ’s humanity. Since both positions are impious and profoundly harmful to the soul, the rule of true faith must be maintained: because of the form of a servant, by which the Son is lesser than the Father, we rightly say that thanks are to be given to the Father through the Son; nevertheless, because of the form of God, in which the Son is equal to the Father, we must know that thanks are to be given to the Father and the Son.

Since one grace has been bestowed on us by the holy Trinity, one thanksgiving must jointly be paid by us to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For just as the Apostle says to the faithful, “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 1:7), so it is written in the Acts of the Apostles (10:4): “For the grace of the Holy Spirit has also been poured out among the Gentiles.” We have therefore received one grace of the holy Trinity. It is fitting, then, that with the truth of faith and simplicity of heart we pay one thanksgiving to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

The one glory that is to be sung to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, just as holy Scripture never ceases to urge, every Christian must both know and render. In the apostolic writings we find glory spoken not only to the Father but likewise to the Lord Jesus Christ.

We know that blessed Jude the Apostle said in his Epistle: “To him who is able to preserve you without offense and to set you immaculate in the presence of his glory with joy, to the only God our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be honor, might, splendor, and power before all ages, and now, and forever and ever. Amen” (Jude 24–25). This is rightly understood according to the mystery of the Incarnation, by which the Son of God is found to have become both High Priest and sacrifice for us.

The truth of both natures—namely, the divine and the human—must be acknowledged in the Son of God, so that, without the error of any unbelief, the Son may rightly be recognized as both lesser than the Father and equal to the Father. Therefore blessed Peter says that glory is to be given to Christ not only in this present time but also in that eternity; for he concluded his Second Epistle with these words: “Grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be glory both now and unto the day of eternity” (2 Pet. 3:18).

Since one spirit of faith was given to the apostles and prophets—as blessed Paul affirms when he says, “Having the same spirit of faith, as it is written: I believed, and therefore I spoke; and we also believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4:13)—blessed David, expressing a harmonious judgment in faith and truth, says: “Let all your works give thanks to you, O Lord, and let your saints bless you. They shall speak of the glory of your kingdom, and they shall proclaim your power, to make your power known to the children of men and the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom” (Ps. 144:10–12).

And lest anyone think that this in no way concerns the person of the Son, elsewhere he says that glory is to be given to that God who ascended above the heaven of heavens. For he says: “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord. Sing psalms to God, who ascends above the heaven of heavens toward the east. Behold, he will give his voice, the voice of power; give glory to God” (Ps. 67:33–35).

If the darkness of unbelief does not close your eyes in this passage, the truth of the right faith must become known to you. For we give glory to the Son when we sing and chant psalms, just as we give glory to the Father. But when you sing, you do not give glory to the Father and the Son; you give glory to the Father through the Son. The most holy prophet, filled with the Spirit of God, acted so that he might show us, when singing and chanting psalms, rightly to give glory to the Father and the Son, and might expose you, who sing and chant psalms but do not give glory to the God who ascended above the heaven of heavens, as ungrateful and defiant.

Blessed David foresaw that glory would be sung to God the Father not only by catholic Christians but also by heretics. He therefore took care to admonish and correct those whom he knew would deny glory to the Son in their songs and psalms. For this reason he says: “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord. Sing psalms to God, who ascends above the heaven of heavens toward the east. Behold, he will give his voice, the voice of power; give glory to God.”

It is as though he were saying: “I know that you all sing and chant psalms to God the Father, and that in singing and chanting psalms you give glory to him; but while singing psalms to God the Father, sing psalms also to God the Son; and while giving glory to the Father, give glory to the God who ascended above the heaven of heavens.” In doing this we obey the prophetic oracles; in refusing to do it, you stubbornly oppose the faith of the prophets.

It is certain, therefore, that glory must be spoken not to the Father alone but also to the Son. But lest, being wholly convicted by these testimonies, you should say that glory must indeed be given to the Son, though not together with the glory given to the Father, divine authority also resists you in this matter, for it shows that one glory is spoken to the Father and the Son by the holy angels in heaven.

Blessed John the Apostle is witness to this. Speaking in the Apocalypse about the four living creatures, he says: “The four living creatures each had six wings around them, and within they were full of eyes; and they had no rest day or night, saying: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty, who was, and is, and is to come.’ And when those living creatures gave glory and honor and thanks to him who sat upon the throne, who lives forever and ever, the twenty-four elders immediately fell on their faces before the throne and adored him who lives forever and ever, casting their crowns before the throne and adoring him who lives forever and ever, saying: ‘You are worthy, O Lord our God, to receive glory and honor and power, because you created all things, and by your will they were established’” (Rev. 4:8–11 and following).

Perhaps you will answer that all these words must be understood only of the person of the Father. First, however, you must consider that what we read as spoken by the four living creatures—“who was, and is, and is to come”—applies more aptly to the Son than to the Father. Both the Old and the New Testament testify that the Son is to come.

It is then said: “And when those living creatures gave glory and honor and thanks to him who sat upon the throne, who lives forever and ever.” You cannot deny that the Son sits upon the throne, since blessed David says to him: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever” (Ps. 44:7). If you wish to deny that the Son is here called the one who lives forever and ever, you are refuted by the Son’s own words, for he said to that same blessed John: “Do not be afraid. I am the first and the last, and the living one; I was dead, and behold, I am living forever and ever” (Rev. 1:17–18).

If you still think that you must resist and do not wish this to have been said of the Son, hear what the same blessed Apostle John says in what follows: “And I saw,” he says, “and I heard a voice like that of many angels around the throne, and around the living creatures, and around the elders. Their number was thousands upon thousands, saying with a loud voice: ‘Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honor, and glory, and blessing.’ And every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and those in the sea and all that are in them, I heard all saying: ‘To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb, blessing and honor and glory and power forever and ever.’ And the four living creatures said: ‘Amen’” (Rev. 5:11 and following).

At least now, Fabian, recognize how great an impiety it is to resist not only apostolic voices but also angelic voices. Hear the thousands upon thousands saying with a loud voice: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honor, and glory, and blessing.” And hear every creature that is in heaven, on earth, under the earth, and in the sea, and all that is in them.

And lest you think that thanks are to be given or glory spoken separately to the Father and separately to the Son, hear what blessed John immediately added: “I heard all,” he says, “saying: ‘To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb, blessing and honor and glory and power forever and ever.’ And the four living creatures said: ‘Amen.’”

Here the testimony of angelic devotion makes it known that glory must be spoken to the Father and the Son, that thanks must be given to the Father and the Son, and that one power must be spoken of the Father and the Son. For blessed John heard them all saying together: “To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb, blessing and honor and glory and power forever and ever.”

By the expression added here, “forever and ever,” it is clearly shown that those who recognize one honor of the Father and the Son, who pay one thanksgiving to the Father and the Son, who sing one glory to the Father and the Son, and who proclaim one power of the Father and the Son will attain the eternal fellowship and blessedness of God’s angels.

Whoever in this age refuses to give all these things simultaneously to the Father and the Son will not remain in the fellowship of all the angels who, as mentioned above, say them forever and ever. For in that eternity all those of whom blessed David says to God, “Your altars, O Lord of hosts, my King and my God; blessed are all who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83:4–5), will say nothing else.

Since they will be equal to the angels of God (Luke 20:36), it is certain that they will say forever and ever what the holy angels always say in praise of God. And lest anyone think that the praise of the Father is one thing and the praise of the Son another, the same blessed John, speaking in the aforementioned book about those who dwell in that heavenly Jerusalem above, which is the house of God, and who will praise God forever and ever, says:

“After this I saw a great multitude which no one could number, from every nation, tribe, people, and language, standing before the throne and before the Lamb. They were clothed in white robes, and palm branches were in their hands; and they cried out with a loud voice: ‘Salvation belongs to our God who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb’” (Rev. 7:9–10).

Immediately afterward he showed that God the Father and the Lamb are one God, saying: “And all the angels who stood around the throne, and around the elders, and around the four living creatures, immediately fell on their faces before the throne and adored God, saying: ‘Amen. Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and virtue and strength to our God forever and ever’” (ibid., 11–12).

Is it not recognized that what they had earlier said—“To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb, blessing and honor and glory and power forever and ever”; and the four living creatures said, “Amen”—all these angels have now confirmed under the profession of one God, adoring that very God?

Pay attention to what they said—or rather, consider carefully what they say: “Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and virtue and strength to our God forever and ever. Amen.” All these things the same angels had earlier said were to be given to the Lamb, in that great voice of theirs: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom and strength, and glory, and blessing.” They immediately gave all these things to God, saying: “To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb, blessing and honor and glory and power forever and ever.”

Recognize that they gave these same things again under the name of one God, since they adored God, saying: “Amen. Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and virtue and strength to our God forever and ever. Amen.”

Consider these three passages, and you will find the truth of our faith confirmed by angelic devotion. First, honor, glory, blessing, and power are said to be given by all the angels to the Lamb, that is, to the Son. Then blessing, honor, and power are given as one to him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb—which means nothing other than the Father and the Son. After this, blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, virtue, and strength are given to the one God; these are the very things previously given to him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb, that is, to the Father and the Son.

Recognize, therefore, that glory must be given to the Son, that one glory must be given simultaneously to the Father and the Son, and that our one God is the Father and the Son. This is what that free Jerusalem above, which is our mother (Gal. 4:26), continually sings. Its portion that struggles through the pilgrimage of this age strives toward its delightful countenance and sweet fellowship by a straight course because it imitates that mother not only in good works but also in these praises.

While singing this, the earthly portion walks in faith; while singing, the heavenly portion rests in vision. While singing, this portion of that Church is refreshed by the bread of its pilgrimage; that Jerusalem is satisfied by perpetual and tireless fullness.

How, then, does that Church dare to believe or say that it is the daughter of the holy heavenly Jerusalem when it does not think that it should say on earth what that holy mother never ceases to say in heaven? Or how can it share blessedness with her when it does not share the praise of God himself? Whoever does not now imitate the service of that holy Jerusalem can in no way attain fellowship with it, since the heavenly host itself, when the Son was born according to the flesh, sang nothing else on earth than: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2:14).

If anyone asks, “To which God?” that angelic multitude immediately answers: “To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb.” This is said by the angels in the highest heaven and sung on earth by people of good will, so that the one and same Christ might be shown: the one to whom the angels say, “Glory to God in the highest,” and the one who was made on earth “peace to people of good will.” For he is our peace, who made both one (Eph. 2:14).

From the one from whom we have peace, we received good will, through which, by the gift of gratuitous justification, we give glory to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the one God, so that we may be able to reach the fellowship of the angels. There, having received the gift of glorification, we shall be able to say glory to him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb, our God, forever and ever.

Let no one be troubled by the fact that in all these passages nothing was said about the Holy Spirit. For evangelical teaching shows that whatever service it commands to be rendered to the Father and the Son is likewise to be rendered to the Holy Spirit. What did our Savior demonstrate by one command when he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19)?

By saying this, he certainly indicated that every service of religion is owed by us simultaneously to the same Trinity, in whose name the beginning of salvation is conferred upon those who believe and are baptized. Above all, however, the one glory of the Trinity is recognized in that passage of the prophet Isaiah where the Seraphim cry: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. 6:3). There they show one Lord God to be the Trinity, and immediately add: “The whole earth is full of his glory.”

Blessed David also intimates something similar to us when he sings: “The voice of the Lord preparing the stags, and he will reveal the thickets, and in his temple all shall say glory” (Ps. 28:9). The apostolic authority confirms that we are the temple not only of the Father and the Son but also of the Holy Spirit, as we have already mentioned in this work. Blessed Paul says: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” (1 Cor. 6:19).

How, then, can it happen that the glory spoken in the temple of the Holy Spirit is not spoken to the Holy Spirit himself? Surely whatever is said in the temple of God for the praise of God cannot be foreign to the God whose temple it is. Blessed David said this so that the Trinity, to whom glory is spoken in his temple, might be recognized as naturally one Lord.

To make this clearer, observe the divine praises in the Psalms and attend carefully to the blessing of the three youths in the book of the prophet Daniel (Dan. 3:57 and following). When you find that the Holy Spirit is nowhere named among all the things that have been made, recognize that the Holy Spirit is the creator, not created; the maker of all things, not made. From this understand that he is naturally one Lord God with the Father and the Son.

For in the Psalms, where all created things are summoned to praise the Lord, the summons begins with the angels—that is, with the very wisdom of whom it is written: “Wisdom was created before all other things, and the understanding of prudence from eternity” (Ecclus. 1:4); and of whom it is said shortly afterward: “He himself created her by the Holy Spirit” (Ps. 148:1).

The blessed prophet says: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights.” Beginning with that first and chief creature, above which the substance of the Creator alone exists naturally, he places the angels at the beginning of this praise, saying (v. 2): “Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers.” Then he says (vv. 3–4): “Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light. Praise him, heavens of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord.” Showing the reason for this praise, he says (v. 5): “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.”

All these things are therefore said to have to praise the Lord because they were made by him. If the Holy Spirit too had been made, the prophetic word would have placed him in that order of praise before the angels and powers.

Does it please you that the Holy Spirit, whom according to your opinion you say was made through the Son, should be left without the service of divine praise? And that he, whom you maintain was made through the Son more excellent than the other creatures, should, while all things praise the Creator, persist ungrateful without praise? And that the Lord should not be praised by him, in whom, according to your belief, his Creator is found more worthy of praise?

Attend prudently also to the blessing of the three youths, as I said above. In it the maker of all things is first blessed in such a way that they say to him: “Blessed are you, Lord God of our fathers, and worthy of praise, and glorious forever” (Dan. 3:52). Behold, those three, as though from one mouth, do not cease to bless, praise, and glorify the Lord God.

Here the authority of divine Scripture does not permit only the Father to be understood. For at the beginning those three youths say: “Blessed is the name of your glory, which is holy and worthy of praise and glorious forever” (ibid.). This holy name is not the name of the Father alone but the one natural name of the Trinity. We demonstrated this above by the testimony of holy Isaiah, who recalls the Seraphim crying to one another: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Isa. 6:3).

If you do not affirm that this holy name is one name of the holy Trinity, it remains that you must, whether you wish it or not, assign the holy name to the Holy Spirit alone; for in the Trinity he is specifically called the Holy Spirit, although according to the right faith it is not denied that the Father and the Son are naturally both Spirit and holy.

Therefore the blessed Apostle, knowing that there is one holy name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, testified that believers are sanctified in that name, saying: “But you were washed, but you were justified, but you were sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Cor. 6:11).

Recall, then, in whose name holy baptism is given, and you will find that everyone who rightly believes in the same name is justified and sanctified in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, being washed into the one substance of the Trinity. Whoever understands that the gift of true sanctification is conferred—or, according to Florus, that it is confessed—in the same name recognizes that the holy name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is naturally one.

The blessing then says: “Blessed are you in the holy temple of your glory, and worthy of praise and glorious forever” (Dan. 3:53). We have already shown sufficiently in this work, by the testimony of the holy Scriptures, that we are the temple not of the Father alone but of the holy Trinity itself.

The Trinity, therefore, is one Lord God, blessed and worthy of praise and glorious forever. Those who recognize themselves to be one temple of the holy Trinity truly bless him in the temple of his holy glory.

Then the three youths say: “Blessed are you who behold the abysses, seated upon the Cherubim, and worthy of praise and glorious forever” (ibid., 55). The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each see the whole equally, just as the Trinity itself fills the whole. Therefore the sight of the abysses is denied neither to the Son nor to the Holy Spirit, since the holy Trinity itself simultaneously embraces all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, by the knowledge of its natural omnipotence. It beholds all things with the clearest vision, because by the fullness of its knowledge it knows all things, past and present as well as future.

When the blessing then says: “Blessed are you above the throne of your kingdom, and worthy of praise and glorious forever” (ibid., 54), who would be so foolish as to try to separate the Son or the Holy Spirit from this blessing? Blessed Isaiah indicates that the throne of the holy Trinity is one, saying: “I saw the Lord seated upon a throne, high and exalted” (Isa. 6:1). He recalls that this Lord was proclaimed in the following words, as the Seraphim cried to one another: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.”

The prophet therefore recognized that the one Lord seated upon one throne is called a third time in the mystery of the Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0819] Florus reads, “Therefore the Spirit … whom in the sacrament …”]
holy, and heard him called once as Lord God, by the revelation of spiritual grace. Hence it is that apostolic authority does not cease to proclaim one kingdom and one throne of the Father and the Son. For blessed Paul, demonstrating that the Son and the Father have one kingdom [Col. 0821A], says:

> “For know this and understand: no fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person—which is the service of idols—has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Ephesians 5:5).

The holy John also clearly shows that there is one throne, saying of the angel by whom he testifies that the holy city was shown to him:

> “And he showed me a river of living water, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb. In the middle of its street, and on either side of the river, was the tree of life, bearing twelve fruits and yielding its fruit each month; and the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations. And there will no longer be any curse, and the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it” (Revelation 22:1–3).

The Trinity, therefore, is to be understood as one God in the blessing of the three youths, where it is said [Col. 0821B]:

> “Blessed are you above the throne of your kingdom”;

for just as there is one throne, so there is one kingdom of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Then, concerning what follows—“Blessed are you in the firmament of heaven, and praiseworthy and glorious forever” (Daniel 3:56)—who does not see that this was said in praise of the Trinity? For the firmament of heaven itself is one work of the Trinity: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Psalm 32:6).

But in order to show that the Lord God of our fathers—not the Father alone, nor the Son alone, nor the Holy Spirit alone, but the holy Trinity together, one Lord God—is to be blessed, praised, and glorified by all his works, let us see from where those three men took the beginning of their divine works. For when they said, “Bless the Lord, all the works [Col. 0821C] of the Lord” (Daniel 3:57), they showed that nothing should be counted among the works of the Lord unless it could be found among the works included here.

Then all things whatsoever that are works of the Lord God are understood to be summoned by this beginning to render to God the Creator the service of due blessing:

> “Bless the Lord, heavens” (verse 59);  
> “Bless the Lord, angels” (verse 58);  
> “Bless the Lord, all waters that are above the heavens” (verse 60);  
> “Bless the Lord, all the powers of the Lord” (verse 61);

and so forth, whether the things in heaven or those on earth, visible or invisible [p. 651].

Yet among all these works of the Lord the Holy Spirit is not found. Indeed, if it were necessary to reckon him among the divine works, neither the angelic creature nor any other creature whatsoever ought to have been named before him [Col. 0821D].

What, then, is the meaning of the fact that the Holy Spirit neither praises the Lord among all the things made by the Lord, nor blesses God among all his works? Or perhaps forgetfulness stole upon the prophets, so that they failed to remember the Holy Spirit when they summoned to praise the Lord all that had been made by the Lord, and to bless the Lord all the works [Col. 0822A] of the Lord?

But blessed Peter permits no one to believe this, saying:

> “For prophecy was never brought forth by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21).

In another passage he likewise records the following concerning these same prophets:

> “Searching into what person or what time the Spirit of Christ who was in them was signifying” (1 Peter 1:11).

Accordingly, if the Holy Spirit—by whom the holy men of God were moved and spoke—had known himself to be not the maker but something made, and if he had understood himself to be not God the worker but a work of God, he would unquestionably have placed himself first, before all those things that were made and are called the works of the Lord. Thus preeminent praise would have been rendered to God the worker, since in him the excellence of a divine work above the angels would have been recognized.

But this does not happen because [Col. 0822B] there is one God, the Creator of all things: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. He is rightly praised by all that he has made and is likewise blessed by all his works, because he is found to be himself the Creator and Maker, the Lord God of all things. One blessing, therefore, one praise, and one glorification are owed by all his works to the one God, the Trinity, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit alone are found to be God, the Maker of all things, not made; and God alone is the Creator, not created.

## FRAGMENT XXXV. The Father is not the author of the whole Trinity, but only of the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Who, moreover, would not detest the absurdity of that lie of yours by which you falsely represent me as having called God the Father the author of the whole Trinity in those false and deceitful Acts? This is as far removed from the faith of truth as it is contrary to holy religion. For God the Father is not the author of the Trinity, but is the author of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, in that the Son was born from him and the Holy Spirit proceeds from him. For whoever correctly understands the term “author” will find it to be a relational term, not one of nature. No one, indeed, is said to be the author of himself, but of another; hence he is truly called an author not in relation to himself but to another. No one, however, can be referred by any relative name to his own person in the same way as to another’s; for whatever is said of one’s own person is in no way found to be said according to relation. We therefore confess God the Father to be not the author of the whole Trinity, but the author of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, from whom the only-begotten Son has the origin of his eternal birth and the Holy Spirit the origin of his eternal procession. Natural unity, however, indicates that the Son, the Creator, came forth from the Father, the Creator, by natural birth, and that the Holy Spirit, the Creator, proceeds from the Father and the Son.

## FROM BOOK X, WHICH CONTAINS A DEFENSE OF THE APOSTLES’ CREED AGAINST THE ARIANS

[Col. 0821]

## FRAGMENT XXXVI. What the Creed is. For its proper use, the believer’s mind must be rightly disposed. When the Father is called almighty and creator in it, this must be understood of the whole Trinity. The Trinity is immortal and invisible in a manner different from an angel or the human soul. All the articles of the Creed are expounded.

[Col. 0821D]

[Col. 0822D] The Creed of the Christian faith—which in Greek usage is customarily called both a “compact” and a “collation”—was indeed arranged by the apostles in a holy, correct, and altogether wise manner according to the rule of truth. For the Lord, who made upon earth a word that brings to completion and shortens, just as he brought all the precepts of the Law to completion in brevity (Rom. 9:28), saying that the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon those two commandments, love of God and love of neighbor (Matt. 22:40), and just as in the brevity of prayer he perfected whatever pertained to the assistance of the present life and to the attainment of the future life, so also in the brevity of the Creed he willed that, through his apostles, the complete pattern of the holy faith should be established, so that it might bring salvation to those who believe rightly.

The Creed is a certain true compact and a true collation, in whose brevity the sum of the whole Christian faith is contained. Yet the believer’s mind must be rightly disposed, lest he himself wish to turn what he hears away from its saving effect and toward the punishment of death. For the Law is good, if one uses it lawfully (1 Tim. 1:8). Therefore it seemed pointless to you, through misunderstanding, to wish to bend the uprightness of the Creed toward your own meaning and on that basis to prescribe against the holy catholic faith that, in the Creed, not everything said of the Father is said of the Son, since surely the fullness of divinity ought to have been commended in its source as far as was necessary, because it could not otherwise be recognized in the offspring.

For when anyone says that he believes in God the almighty Father, by saying “in God the Father” he displays both the truth of natural divinity in him and the truth of natural fatherhood, and from this also the truth of natural generation. For God the Father is naturally God and naturally Father, since in him both divine fatherhood and paternal divinity are natural. That divine generation therefore possesses in itself whatever the eternal substance of God the Father possesses in itself. Consequently, it was sufficient that whatever was to be understood equally of the Son should be said of the Father alone.

For the Father begot the Son almighty in the same way as the Father himself is almighty; the creator of all things in the same way as he himself is creator of all things; King of the ages in the same way as he himself is King of the ages; immortal and invisible in the same way as he himself is immortal and invisible. Everything, therefore, that is ascribed to God the Father in the Creed is naturally ascribed to the Son also by the single name “Son.” For the Father is the creator of all things, but all things were made through the Word, and without him nothing was made (John 1:3); and: “In him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones or Dominions or Principalities or Powers; all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him” (Col. 1:16–17).

Thus there is one God the Father, from whom are all things, and we exist for him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we exist through him (1 Cor. 8:6). The Father is King of the ages, but the Son too is found to be King, to whom the Prophet says: “Your kingdom is a kingdom of all the ages” (Ps. 144:13).

The Trinity itself, which is one true and good God, is at once immortal and invisible—not, of course, immortal and invisible in the same way as the human soul or an angel. God is called especially invisible in that he is not seen except by grace. No created spirit sees the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit by its own power, unless God himself grants this. God the Trinity must be seen not by the body but by the spirit, if he grants this gift of his goodness; otherwise, how will it be true that the holy angels always see the face of the Father? And: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8)?
