An angel, therefore, and a rational soul, because they are spirits created by God, cannot be seen by bodily eyes. The Trinity, however, who is God, the creator of all things, and truly invisible, is certainly not seen even by the eye of the heart unless grace is granted by him. For God is the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:9); by enlightening freely, therefore, he grants purification, so that he may bestow the capacity to see.

God is also called immortal not in the same manner as either the soul or the angel is found to be immortal. For although there is no natural extinction in an angel, natural change can nevertheless be found in it; and that nature which receives a quality receives, through mutability, a kind of death. We, however, call God good without quality, since for him “to be God” is not one thing and “to be good” another. Hence, when we call him good, we show his very divinity; and when we call him divine, we undoubtedly demonstrate his goodness.

Our God is therefore truly recognized as immortal in that he is not naturally changed. No creature could or can possess this by nature, although some creature is known to have received it by grace. For everything that God made derives its origin from nothing; consequently, it is recognized as having begun to exist at a definite beginning and as not having existed before it began to exist. Hence every being whose nature is not one with God the Father has this characteristic: that by itself it is subject to mutability, while it obtains immutability as a gift from that nature in which natural immutability is found.

The nature of the Trinity alone is incapable of natural change, because it did not begin to exist. In every substance that is not of one and the same nature with God the Father, just as an origin derived from nothing is recognized, so natural mutability is found. The divine nature of the Trinity alone does not possess this mutability: it did not begin to exist, and it made everything that it made from nothing. For this reason it willed that belief should be directed toward itself alone, because it alone is sufficient for the renewal of human nature by its natural power and goodness, just as it is sufficient by itself for the creation of all things.

We therefore rightly and salubriously believe in that nature of the holy Trinity which we recognize as almighty, creator of all things, king and singular possessor of the kingdom of all the ages, invisible by nature to bodies and spirits but visible by gratuitous grace to righteous spirits, and immortal through the eternity of natural immutability.

Accordingly, since all these attributes were recalled in relation to the Father, in whom the divine nature had chiefly to be commended, it was sufficient that his only Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, should then be named, since by the very term “only Son” the full natural communion of the Father and the Son is found to be signified.

Jesus Christ would rightly be believed to possess another omnipotence, dominion, immortality, and invisibility if he were not called the only Son of God the Father. He is called “only” because he alone is the true Son; and he is the true Son alone because he alone was born from the nature of the Father. The truth of his birth therefore demonstrates the natural fullness received from the Father in the Son, in whom the fullness of the paternal nature remains through natural generation.

It was fitting for our faith and salvation to confess not only the mystery of creation but also that of redemption. For in everything said above about the Father, his majesty by which he made us was proclaimed, but the goodness by which he redeemed us was not shown. Since this was bestowed upon us, it was fitting that, after the sole name of the Son had sufficiently demonstrated the divine majesty by which we were created, there should follow the word of the cross, which is foolishness to those who are perishing but the power of God to those who are being saved (1 Cor. 1:18).

[Note: [Col. 0825D] It seems that “should be added” is missing here.]

This was all the more difficult to believe. For it was not difficult to believe that the Son was of one nature with the Father and therefore possessed, by natural unity with the Begetter, everything that has been mentioned. For this reason, in order completely to destroy the wisdom of the world—because Christ crucified is a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to gentiles, but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:23)—it had to be emphasized more insistently and thoroughly that the true God, the proper and only-begotten Son of God the almighty, immortal, and invisible Father, was also born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, which means nothing other than that he was born by the grace of God and from a virginal womb.

What is more wondrous and salutary than to recognize that the only-begotten God, born without beginning from the nature of the Father and naturally coeternal with God the Father, became what he became not for his own advantage but for our salvation, and was wonderfully and mercifully created in order to redeem what he had created?

But because that same proper and only Son of God at once assumed our nature and our punishment, and demonstrated in himself the reality of a human soul and of flesh by assuming the reality of sorrow and death—for he says, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:33)—therefore in the Creed we also say that the only Son of God, whom we confess to have been born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, was crucified and buried. Thus the reality of both natures is recognized in him: the majesty of eternal divinity shows him to be true God, while the humility of divine kindness teaches that he is true man.

For that God who is from the Father, the creator of all things, became from the Virgin the mediator between God and human beings. He could not be mediator unless he possessed in himself the truth of both paternal and maternal substance. For just as we were reconciled in him through the death of his Son, because that mediator truly possessed flesh in himself, according to which he could undergo true death, so in him he granted us the benefit of true reconciliation, in whom there is one natural divinity with the Father.

Christ, who is the truth, is true man from the nature of his mother, and likewise true God from the substance of the Father. His divine nature is no more different from the Father’s than the natural distinction between soul and flesh is absent in relation to the Virgin.

Therefore, because he accepted death in the reality of flesh, which he swallowed up in the reality of divinity, we confess that, after being buried, he rose on the third day. Divine kindness accomplished this for the confirmation of our hope, so that in the one in whom the punishment of our death was overcome, the example of our resurrection might shine forth. And because Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies, and death shall no longer rule over him (Rom. 6:9), just as the true flesh of Christ will never die, so let us believe that our bodies too will live forever through the eternity of the resurrection.

Then we confess that Christ ascended into heaven and will come from there to judge the living and the dead. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father (John 5:22).

One honor, therefore, is to be offered to the Father and the Son, because the Father, who judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son, showed that his judgment and the Son’s judgment are one. He gave it to the Son so that all might honor the Son just as they honor the Father. To remove any difference of honor, the unity of judicial power was displayed, so that we may offer equal honor together with the Father to the Son, to whom we know that all judgment was given by the Father; nor should we separate the service of honor where we do not see judgment separated.

After completing the confession of the true divinity and true humanity of the only Son of God, we confess that we believe in the Holy Spirit, who is the one Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeding from the Father and the Son, and naturally [variant: faithfully] abiding in the Father and the Son; having the origin of divinity from the Father and the Son, and naturally possessing with the Father and the Son the truth of one deity.

But in the Holy Spirit, what more could or should have been proclaimed for the perfection of the divine majesty than that, when the Son of God is said to have been born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, the Holy Spirit himself is found to be the maker of that holy body? In what respect, then, can he rightly be called less than the Father or the Son, who is the almighty creator, according to the flesh, of that very only Son of God?

This is the Trinity, one God, whose mystery is contained in the holy Creed. For this reason holy baptism is administered in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

The forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life are therefore added in the Creed after the commemoration of the holy Trinity, so that the usefulness of that confession may be shown by the addition of this reward. The faith of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—namely, of the one eternal, true, and good God—is useful for this purpose: that we may receive forgiveness of sins and, rising in this flesh in which we now live, live blessedly forever.

This is the devotion that is useful for all things, possessing the promise of the present life and of the future life (1 Tim. 4:8)—of the present life, certainly, insofar as it is good, and of the future life, insofar as it is eternal and blessed.

The holy Church is also added, so that it may be recognized as the house of God the Creator and the eternal city of the Redeemer. Without its fellowship and unity, forgiveness of sins is not obtained, and through the resurrection of the flesh one arrives not at the joys of eternal life but at the punishments of eternal death.

The holy Creed is therefore beneficial to the person who believes that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are naturally one God. Such a person has received forgiveness of sins and, through the resurrection of this flesh in which he now lives well, will undoubtedly possess eternal life. We do not, however, believe in the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life in the same way as we believe in the Holy Spirit.

With the distinction between the giver and the gift preserved, we believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; but we believe and hope that forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life will be given to us by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

For our Savior himself clearly showed in whom we ought to believe when he said to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

In the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the proper distinction of the persons had to be indicated, lest in the Trinity, in which one nature is most salubriously believed, one person should also be believed—a most destructive error.

I am astonished that you confess that nothing other than God could be born from God, yet fail to consider that in the very nature and name of God all those things said of God the Father are contained. For if nothing other than God could be born from God, then nothing other than almighty God could be born from almighty God; nothing other than God the creator of all things could be born from God the creator of all things; nothing other than the King of the ages could be born from the King of the ages; nothing other than immortal God could be born from immortal God; nothing other than invisible God could be born from invisible God.

Since, therefore, God was born from God—Son from Father, almighty from almighty, creator of all things from the creator of all things, King of the ages from the King of the ages, immortal from immortal, invisible from invisible—what remains except that the Son be believed equal to the Father in all things?

## FRAGMENT XXXVII. The Father is truly Lord, Christ is truly God, and the whole Trinity is truly Lord God. How are we baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and yet saved in the name of Christ alone? Whether baptism in the name of Jesus Christ is good.

[Col. 0827D]

The wording of the Creed does not attribute divinity to the Father alone; rather, in God the Father it displays the natural origin of the Son and the Holy Spirit. In him true divinity had to be demonstrated by the name of omnipotence, because he would not be God if he were not almighty. True generation also had to be demonstrated by the name of fatherhood, so that the common nature of the Father and the Son might truly be signified.

And because it naturally belongs to God to be Lord of all things, in saying that Christ is Lord the wording of the Creed also truthfully indicated that he is God. For it is proper and natural to the true God that he be nothing other than Lord, and to the true Lord that he be nothing other than God.

That is why blessed Paul the apostle also says: “For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we exist for him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we exist through him” (1 Cor. 8:6). Thus, just as he did not take away from God the Father the rights of true lordship, so he should not be understood to withdraw from the Lord the Son the unity of divinity.

We are permitted to confess one God and one Lord. For there is one lordship of the one divinity, and one divinity of the one lordship. Thus, just as besides the one God there is no other God, so besides the one Lord there is no other Lord.

The one lordship of the one God is therefore recognized in his one divinity, and the one divinity of the one Lord is naturally found in his one lordship. Besides the one God the Father there is no other God, and besides the one Lord Jesus Christ there is no other Lord.

Yet God the Father is not one God without God the Son, nor is the Lord Christ one Lord without the Lord Father. For God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ are naturally one Lord God, possessing the fullness of divinity naturally in the fullness of lordship, and the fullness of lordship in the fullness of divinity.

Therefore blessed David says: “Who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God?” (Ps. 17:32).

The wording of the Creed therefore shows the unity of divinity and lordship in the Father and the Son, when it rightly makes known to those who believe that the Father, whom it called God, is nothing other than Lord, and that Christ, whom it called Lord, is nothing other than God.

For one God Jesus Christ, born from one God the Father, could be born as nothing other than God. Yet he would not naturally be one Lord if he had not been born from the Lord.

The Father, therefore, who is God and begot the Lord, is recognized as the true Lord; and Christ the Lord, begotten from God, is recognized as the true God. The Holy Spirit, likewise, the one and same Spirit of the Father and the Son, because he is of one nature with the Father and the Son, is the true Lord God.

For naturally he has with the Lord God the Father and the Lord God the Son one divinity of true lordship and one true lordship of divinity.

This is why every catholic Christian, when asked whether God the Father is Lord and whether the Lord Jesus Christ is God, undoubtedly confesses both, yet is found to be a truthful preacher not of two gods or two lords, but of one Lord God.

For what remains for one who is not permitted to preach two gods or two lords except to confess fearlessly, when asked, that God the Father and the Lord Christ are one Lord? Nor should he answer otherwise concerning the Holy Spirit, because he is one Lord God with the Father and the Son, who is the one Spirit of the Father and the Son.

Whoever either denies or doubts that this is true must necessarily say either that only God the Father is to be worshiped or that he is a worshiper of both the Creator and the creature.

But the Christian faith therefore proclaims the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one Lord God, because it is not lawful to believe in two or three lords or gods; nor may anyone worship the creature together with the Creator; nor can the Christian faith exist without the worship of the Son or of the Holy Spirit.

There is therefore one God and Lord of all things, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. “God” is not a name belonging to the Father alone, but one common natural name of the Trinity.

For this reason our Savior commanded his disciples, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

Consider what you will answer blessed Peter, who placed the effect of human salvation in the name of Christ alone, asserting that we could be saved in no other name.

In the book of the Acts of the Apostles, after the man who had been lame from his mother’s womb was healed, when Peter and John were questioned by the chief priests about by what power or in what name they had done this, it is written as follows:

“Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them: Rulers of the people and elders, if we are judged today concerning a good deed done to an infirm man, by what means this man has been made well, let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, whom you crucified and whom God raised from the dead, in this name this man stands before you healed. This is the stone rejected by you builders, which has become the cornerstone; and there is salvation in no other. For there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:8–12).

Behold, Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, says that we are saved in the name of Christ in such a way that there is no other name under heaven given to human beings by which we must be saved.

Now compare Christ’s command, by which he commanded that the nations be baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, with this statement of blessed Peter, in which he commends human salvation in the name of Christ alone, so that he altogether denies that there is another name under heaven given to human beings by which we must be saved.

Compare, then, Christ’s words with Peter’s words; compare the teaching of the master with the teaching of the disciple; compare what Peter heard from Christ with what he said when filled with the Holy Spirit. Christ commanded that people be baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; Peter, however, said that the name of Christ alone had been given to human beings by which they must be saved.

Tell me, then, whether what Peter heard from Christ and what he preached when filled with the Holy Spirit agree. If both agree, it is necessary that the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit be one, and that this be the one name given to human beings by which they must be saved.

But if you say that Peter’s teaching disagrees with Christ’s command, this remains for you: to say that it was not so much Peter as the Holy Spirit who lied. For he said this filled with the Holy Spirit, and he certainly heard from the Spirit what he was to preach.

When you call the Holy Spirit a liar on account of Peter’s lie, you will immediately also call Christ a liar. For Christ himself promised that he would send the Spirit of truth to his disciples, so that the Spirit would teach them all truth.

If the Holy Spirit led them into some lie, you assert not only that he himself lied by teaching something contrary to the truth, but you must also say that Christ is a liar if he did not send the kind of Spirit he promised.

For if you deny that blessed Peter’s preaching is true, you must confess Christ himself—that is, the Truth—to be the author of a lie. For he says concerning the Holy Spirit: “He will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John 16:13–14).

If the Holy Spirit received from Christ what he was to say and spoke a lie, then Christ gave a lie to the Holy Spirit. But if he did not receive this from Christ, and the Holy Spirit spoke from himself what he had not received from Christ, then, according to your position, Christ lied either knowingly or unknowingly when he said, “He will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak.”

But neither Christ nor the Holy Spirit could lie, because the holy Trinity is naturally one truth. For just as we confess God the Father to be truth, so we naturally recognize the Son and the Holy Spirit also to be truth. The Son says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Blessed John also testifies that the Spirit is truth, saying: “And it is the Spirit who testifies, because the Spirit is truth.”

[Note: [Col. 0829] So read the Syriac and Greek texts, and some ancient Fathers. In the Vulgate editions it reads, “Because Christ is the truth.”]

Since, therefore, the Father is truth, the Son is truth, and the Holy Spirit is truth, there are not three truths, but the holy Trinity itself is naturally one truth. Whatever the holy apostles taught, they spoke in the fullness of truth. It is therefore necessary that both what Christ taught Peter and what Peter taught when full of the Holy Spirit be true.

For just as no one is saved unless he has been baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so, apart from the name of Christ, there is no other name given to human beings by which we must be saved.

There is one natural name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, namely, God. This is the one name given to human beings, in which those who believe rightly attain salvation through the sacrament of baptism.

Therefore, if believers do not receive holy baptism in one and the same name, which is naturally common to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but—as you think—are baptized in three different names when, according to the rule established by the command of Christ our Savior, believers are baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, answer us whether, when the name of either the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit has been removed, baptism administered in two names can stand with Christian validity.

You will certainly not dare to say this, because the statement of Truth himself will prevent you from saying it. What remains, then, except that you answer that the sacrament of baptism is complete when it is administered according to the Lord’s command in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?

Now let the book of the Acts of the Apostles come to mind, in which blessed Peter is found to have said to the Jews: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38).

Next consider what is contained in the same book, where it is written:

“When the apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they had come, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit. For he had not yet come upon any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 8:14ff.).

Likewise, in the same book, when the apostle Peter, sent by the Holy Spirit, was preaching to the centurion Cornelius the great sacrament of divine mercy, and while he was still speaking the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word, the Scripture records that the holy apostle Peter answered as follows:

“Can anyone forbid water, so that these should not be baptized who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” And he ordered them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ (Acts 10:47–48).

Consider also that passage in the same book where it says:

“It happened that, while Apollos was at Corinth and Paul, having passed through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found some disciples, he said to them: ‘Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?’ But they said to him: ‘We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.’ He said: ‘In what, then, were you baptized?’ They said: ‘In John’s baptism.’ Paul then said: ‘John baptized with a baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus.’ When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied” (Acts 19:1ff.).

Behold, in so many passages bearing witness, we find that certain people were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ by apostolic authority.

Tell me, then, whether those who are said to have been baptized in the name of Jesus Christ were also baptized in the name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, or whether you will deny this altogether.

If you say that in the name of Jesus Christ the name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit must also be understood, you will undoubtedly confess one name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and from the one name you will necessarily confess the holy Trinity to be one God.

But if you say that those baptized in the name of Jesus Christ were not baptized in the name of the Father and the Holy Spirit, what remains except that you do not consider that baptism true, but declare the holy apostles themselves guilty of transgression?

When you say this, consider how you will dare to call yourself a Christian, once you have begun to oppose Christ in his apostles, whom you know to have said to those same apostles: “Whoever receives you receives me,” and, “Whoever despises you despises me” (Matt. 10:40; Luke 10:16).

Hear, therefore, the apostolic teaching, and reverently offer obedience to the doctrine and work of the apostles.

The person who hears Christ commanding that the nations be baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and also hears blessed Peter saying that, apart from the name of Christ, there is no name by which we must be saved, encounters no difficulty in these words of the apostle Peter. He most certainly believes and unhesitatingly confesses that the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one and natural.

Therefore you must either confess that holy baptism is administered in the one name of the Trinity, or else not believe that the name of the Father and the name of the Holy Spirit are necessary for human salvation, and thereby attempt to empty Christ’s most salutary teaching of its force.

But consider what Christ said, whose teaching Peter held faithfully. He commanded that the nations be baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Peter guarded this command most steadfastly and fed Christ’s sheep with this teaching even unto the shedding of blood.

Guarding the truth of the Christian faith and knowing that the name of the Trinity is one, he rightly said that, apart from the name of Christ, there is no other name under heaven given to human beings by which we must be saved. And when he taught that they should be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, he baptized in the one name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

For there is no natural diversity of name in the Trinity, where there is natural unity.

## FRAGMENT XXXVIII. The Son is almighty like the Father, and possesses all things as the Father does.

You add and say: “The Son is therefore almighty, but not like the Father, because the Father gave and conferred omnipotence itself upon the Son; but no one conferred or gave omnipotence to the Father.”

Yet the Son is recognized as equal to the Father all the more on this account, because what he is he does not have from elsewhere but from the Father; nor does he subsist from nothing, but from the eternal Begetter.

The nature of the Father therefore preserved what was its own in the Son, because that natural generation could not produce from itself anything of a different divinity. The Father gave all things to the Son and denied him nothing, in whom he ineffably begot his whole nature.

That the Father gave omnipotence to the Son pertains solely to origin, not to any diversity of omnipotence or nature. Whoever seeks what was “given” there will find that it means nothing other than “begotten.”

That generation, which is naturally divine and eternal, demonstrates the Father’s having given the Son the fullness of all that he possesses; and in this it naturally demonstrates the Son’s equality with the Father. Thus the Son possesses all things as the Father does, because wherever natural generation is recognized, no natural difference between the Begetter and the Begotten is found.

## FRAGMENT XXXIX. The Holy Spirit is naturally one Lord God with the Father and the Son.

[Col.

[Col. 0832D]

Bear in mind, then, that with the Lord’s help we have given a response to all your objections. Do not believe that the Holy Spirit is found in the divine utterances as subordinate or lesser; do not conceive of his sending in a carnal manner, nor suppose it local, nor assign to him the obedience of a servile condition. For the Holy Spirit is naturally one Lord and God with the Father and the Son. This is clearly recognized both in the creation of all things and in the redemption of the faithful. For if he were not God, he would not have works in common with the Father and the Son; if he were not God, he himself would not strengthen the powers of heaven; if he were not God, the angels would not desire to gaze upon him; if he were not God, he would by no means have descended upon Jesus when he was baptized; if he were not God, he would not have one name with the Father and the Son; if he were not God, he would not have bestowed the grace of divine adoption; if he were not God, our bodies would not be his temple; if he were not God, Christ would not have cast out demons through him; if he were not God, he would by no means have filled heaven and earth. If, therefore, you rightly consider these things and others like them, you will immediately hold the right faith concerning the Holy Spirit.

## From Book III of Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims, Against the Objections of the Greeks, to Odo of Beauvais; and also from Book III of Ratramnus, Monk of Corbie, Against the Oppositions of the Greeks

[Col. 0833]

**663** Bishop Fulgentius, exceedingly learned in literary studies and conspicuous for the holiness of his life, who also suffered much at the hands of the Arians for the catholic faith, says the following in his book *Questions on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*:

Thus everything that belongs to the very nature is found to be common to the three Persons, while nevertheless something is found by which each Person is properly recognized—something that is neither separable nor capable of being common. We say that what the Father properly possesses is that he has begotten; we say that what the Son properly possesses is that he alone was born from the Father alone; and that what the Holy Spirit properly possesses is that he proceeds from the Father and the Son. In these proper characteristics there is no separation of nature, but rather a certain personal recognition.

Likewise, in what follows:

The divinity of the Son, therefore, could not have received the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit himself proceeds from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father, and is given by the Son just as he is given by the Father. Nor could that nature from which the Holy Spirit has his origin either await or receive generosity. That Spirit is wholly the Father’s and wholly the Son’s, because he is naturally the one Spirit of the Father and the Son. Therefore he proceeds wholly from the Father and the Son, and remains wholly in the Father and the Son: for he remains in such a way that he proceeds, and proceeds in such a way that he remains. Hence, by nature he possesses with the Father and the Son the fullness of unity and the unity of fullness, so that he is wholly from the Father and wholly possessed by the Son. The divinity of the Son, therefore, did not receive the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit is of one nature with it and has from it whatever he possesses—indeed, since this is what he is from it, because what he possesses naturally is his very being.

## Two Sermons of Saint Fulgentius, Hitherto Unpublished (C, G, S)*

### Preface to the Two Sermons That Follow

**664** Since these two sermons, hitherto unpublished, were once copied from a Vatican manuscript by the distinguished Luca Holstenius and sent here by the most eminent Cardinal Barberini, and since it was not possible to publish them in their proper order together with the other sermons of Saint Fulgentius, it seemed appropriate to append them here at the end of his works. We scarcely doubt that the first of them is genuinely Fulgentius’s; but we judge that the second should be attributed to another author, and indeed to a reputable one, although perhaps later than Fulgentius. Who that author is, however, we have not yet discovered.

## First Sermon: On the Circumcision of the Lord

### 1

The mystery of the divine Incarnation, that outstanding sacrament of our reconciliation, is celebrated and honored by us in its annual recurrence so that the commemoration of so great a benefit may show what has been bestowed upon us, though unworthy, and remind us what we owe to such great glory. Therefore, brothers, the more we have heard that the Lord Jesus Christ was mercifully humbled for us, the more let us recognize that he is ineffably glorious. For the only-begotten God clearly displayed his unconquerable love toward us in this: that for us he assumed the humility of true flesh and true death, not compelled by necessity but moved by merciful goodness.

What good had we done, brothers, that so great a benefit should be granted to us? What good merits of ours existed, so that the only-begotten God should deign to become human, that the Most High should be humbled, that the unfailing bread of angels should be nursed at a woman’s breasts, that the King of the ages should be subjected to insults, and that eternal Life should most patiently deign to die?

### 2

Consider, then, O human being, the condescension of such great kindness, so that you may offer humble thanksgiving in return. Know, however, that you would return not honor but insult to divine grace if you began to doubt the greatness of so great a benefit. Rather, let us believe without any hesitation that everything we have heard about the Lord Savior’s humility and humanity is true. And therefore, brothers, let us give greater thanks: although we deserved punishment, we received grace; and by that grace it came about that, while death was justly owed to the lost, life was freely given to the unworthy.

**665** The humility of the Most High Savior brought no loss to him but conferred great increase upon us; it did not cast down the exalted but raised up the fallen. For, in order that the Son of God might accomplish the full work of our redemption, the Creator of all flesh deigned not only to be naturally born from the flesh of the Virgin, truly according to the reality of flesh, and the God who made humanity to become a true human being from a human being; he also deigned to be wrapped in swaddling clothes, placed in a very narrow manger, circumcised on the eighth day, and carried by human hands to his own temple.

O most merciful kindness of God! O exalted humility of the Most High God! He who, immense, created a mother for himself was nourished as a little infant by his mother. He who, as the great God, was entreated in that same temple by holy men was carried as a little child by his parents to his own temple. And he commanded a sacrifice to be offered for himself, although without sin he had come to be sacrificed for our wickednesses. Consider, then, O human being, what you owe to the exalted one who was humbled for you: to your exalted Creator and your humbled Redeemer.

### 3

Nevertheless, dearest ones, the integrity of the Christian faith has always been accustomed to hold this: if we read or hear that anything was done by Christ according to the canonical account of the Evangelists, let us first believe without doubt that the history is true, and then, within the historical truth, let us also seek a spiritual understanding.

For when the text of the divine history is believed to be true, Manichaeus is confounded in his severity: while he does not believe in the reality of flesh in Christ the Son of God, he strives to accuse the holy Scriptures, both Old and New, of falsehood. The wretched man curses the divine history of the Old Testament; in the New Testament he denies himself its medicine. He does not wish to believe that human flesh was fashioned by God, nor that circumcision of the flesh was commanded by God to our holy fathers, nor that in ancient times a sacrifice from the flesh of animals was offered to the living and true God, nor that the Sabbath was observed by God’s command and will, nor that a temple was built for the Lord at God’s command. Thus, because he does not distinguish the character of the times in the holy Scriptures, he rejects and despises the most salutary truth of the Lord’s Incarnation.

Therefore, so that Manichaeus may be defeated and converted by the clearest reasoning, may we, overcome by today’s Gospel reading, defend the truth of the Old Testament, and thereby prove most manifestly that the God of the Old and New Testaments is one!

### 4

Behold: as the holy Gospel narrates, we have learned that Christ the Son of God was truly circumcised, and that a sacrifice from flesh was offered for Christ the Son of God according to the custom then established by divine institution. Circumcision of the flesh and the regulation of fleshly sacrifices are both known to have been instituted in the Old Testament.

Why, therefore, dearest ones, should you not most justly believe in the Old Testament that humanity was fashioned by God’s hands, when in the New Testament the only-begotten God himself became true man for us, so that humanity would not perish forever? Why should it not be believed that God commanded circumcision to be performed at the proper time to signify something, when the Son of God caused it to be celebrated in his own body? Why, moreover, should you not believe that our God formerly commanded the Jewish people to offer typical sacrifices of flesh, when God himself, the only-begotten one, born temporally from the Jews, deigned according to the flesh to be sacrificed for our sins?

Let Manichaeus therefore attend to the most manifest and perfectly harmonious truth of both Testaments and, converted, cast away his vanity. Let him see in the Old Testament the signification of future things, and in the New the revelation of past things; but let him recognize Christ as the God of both Testaments: in the Old Testament promising what he was going to bring about, in the New bringing about what he had promised—not a liar in his promise, nor deceptive in his gift, but everywhere good, everywhere just, everywhere holy, everywhere powerful, everywhere merciful. In the Old Testament he is the most powerful Creator of flesh and soul; in the New, the most merciful receiver of that same flesh and soul; and thus first the Savior of flesh and soul.

Let Manichaeus hear, compare, acknowledge, and believe these things; and, believing, let him return to the catholic Church, in which he may find the benefit of true salvation.

### 5

Through these things that the Lord did while established in the body, he deigned not only to demonstrate the harmony of both Testaments but also wished profitably to shape Christian conduct, so that what we behold as having been done bodily in him for our salvation, we too might imitate spiritually.

Christ was born as a little child on earth so that the Christian might learn humility. He was subject to his fleshly parents so that every Christian might always show honor to father and mother. Christ was wrapped in mean garments so that the Christian would not delight in costly clothing. Christ wished to appear poor on earth so that wealthy Christians might learn not to love earthly riches but, by distributing alms to the poor, might store their riches in heaven.

Christ was placed in a narrow manger, though he is not bounded by the breadth of his whole mind, so that those who believe in him might have spiritual nourishment and Christians might learn not to covet the houses or possessions of others. For what Christian, however humble his house or limited his means, should not be satisfied, when the narrowness of a small manger was sufficient for Christ the Son of God?

### 6

By the circumcision that the Son of God received in the flesh, he foreshadowed the circumcision of our heart in the spirit. The legal word commands this circumcision to us, as Moses says: “Circumcise the foreskin of your heart, and be circumcised for your God” (Deut. 10:16). The blessed Apostle agrees with this command, saying: “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart in the spirit, not in the letter; whose praise is not from human beings but from God” (Rom. 2:28–29).

Christ therefore had circumcision in his body so that the Christian might have it spiritually in his heart. For this reason he who could not have any sin at all removed the foreskin of his flesh, so that we might cast away desires of depravity.

Christ was carried by hands to the temple so that the Christian might ascend into heaven by good works. Christ wished a sacrifice to be offered for himself so that the Christian might offer himself at the Lord’s altar. Above all, let him hasten to offer himself by living well.

But if he delights in presenting a pure sacrifice to the divine gaze, we recognize that by the very kind of that sacrifice a certain spiritual sacrifice is also indicated to us: “A pair of turtledoves and two young pigeons,” it says (Luke 2:24). In this kind of bird, dearest brothers, a great sacrament of the catholic faith is commended to you. In the dove, love is recognized; in the turtledove, chastity is found. The turtledove preserves undefiled fidelity to one mate, while the dove does not abandon the unity of those dwelling together.

A catholic Christian, therefore, truly becomes a spiritual turtledove if he preserves the true faith of the Trinity with firm belief and rejects the mind of heretical depravity as the pollution of fornication. He will truly be a dove if he remains patiently to the end within catholic fellowship and stands firm with immovable constancy against temptations and scandals, so that neither heretical fornication corrupts the chastity of faith in his heart nor bitter dissent abandons the unity of ecclesiastical chastity. For this is the legitimate Church: it keeps faith with the one God as with a legitimate husband and multiplies the gathering of children in love.

### 7

In this turtledove and dove, dearest brothers, remain attentively; guard it with all your prayers, so that neither the Arian may violate it, nor the Donatist trample it, nor the Manichaean defile it. For they, like evil hawks, desire to scatter the dove’s unity and violate the turtledove’s chastity.

Manichaeus does not believe that Christ has true flesh; Arius diminishes his true divinity; and the Donatist scatters the unity of the catholic body. Manichaeus does not see the sacrament of the Redeemer; Arius does not consider the greatness of the Savior; and the Donatist, like a ravening wolf, did not hesitate to scatter the flock of the good Shepherd. Thus, if—as I have said—they pursue the love of the dove like evil hawks, wishing to kill wretched people who are desirous of vanity or ignorant of the truth, and if they curse the chastity of the turtledove, then those whom they can seize they either devour with their mouths or tear with their claws.

You, therefore, most holy brothers, guard catholic truth in faith and preserve catholic peace in love.

### 8

He offers a sacrifice pleasing to God who preserves the true sacrament of the catholic faith together with brotherly love. There one God and one Trinity are worshiped; the Father is not proclaimed greater than the Son, nor the Son, according to divinity, less than the Father; nor is the substance of the Holy Spirit distinguished from them, for with the Father and the Son he is naturally one God.

The power of the holy Trinity is one, because one natural substance remains in the three Persons; its authority is one, because its majesty is one; its eternity is one, because its divinity is one; the dominion of the Creator is one, because the condition of the creature is one. For whatever the Father created, he fashioned through the Son and established in the Holy Spirit.

The Son was born from the one who begets; the Holy Spirit proceeds from the one who remains. Yet the Son did not divide the Father by being born, nor did the Spirit diminish God by proceeding, because he does not increase by abiding. Therefore the Son was not diminished by being born, nor was the Spirit separated by proceeding.

That blessed Trinity itself remains, because substantial unity remains there; and since nothing created exists in the divinity of the Trinity, nothing there is separated.

### 9

Hold these things faithfully, dearest brothers, and remain constantly in them. Let this be the thought in your heart and the confession of your mouth. Hold the faith that you received in the name of the Trinity. Preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace, and of the turtledove and the dove, so that you may always be spiritual in the house of God.

May he himself deign to grant this, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Son.

## Second Sermon  
*(as it appears in the manuscript, although the title is doubtful)*

### On the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary

### 1

If the faithful carefully consider the solemnity of this day, they should undertake its celebration with the same devotional feeling with which they observed the solemnities of the Lord’s Nativity, Circumcision, and Manifestation. For this solemnity is that of the same Lord as those are; yet this one is no less than those. We shall demonstrate this openly with proofs in the present sermon.

The solemnity of this day is as unknown to some Christians as it is honored by many above the other solemnities of the year. Especially in that place where the catholic Church has received primacy in the Shepherd, it is held by them in such great reverence that on this day the entire crowd of the city gathers together, glittering with immense lights of candles, and celebrates the solemn rites of Mass together. No one enters the public station without carrying a light in his hand, as though they were about to offer the Lord in the temple—or rather, to receive him—and were showing outwardly, through the religious observance of their offering, the light of faith with which they shine inwardly.

Today, according to the law and the Gospel, forty days after Christ’s Nativity have been completed, and that same Lord was presented by his parents in the temple. Today he was received by the holy Simeon and offered to the Father with sacred gifts. Today, by that same Simeon and by Anna, he is publicly proclaimed to those awaiting the redemption of Israel.

O what a devout spectacle, one in which only the devout are shown to delight! Here stands a virgin and mother—not of just anyone, but of God; here the infant son of a virgin is received, he whose divinity the world cannot contain. Prophets come from both sides, and each sex prophesies concerning the child. An offering is made for the child, not one that cleanses sins, but one that declares mysteries.

### 2

Because I wish to exalt the proclamation of this day, I am pleased to pass through the Gospel reading itself in conversation, in which I know these things are narrated, so that it may respond to what I say—or rather, so that the voice of my exhortation may respond to what it narrates.

Accordingly, Luke the Evangelist, setting forth the historical truth of Christ’s Incarnation more fully and orderly than the other Evangelists, after his annunciation by the angel, after his birth was declared by angelic voices, and after his circumcision on the eighth day in his parents’ house, follows this sequence, saying:

“After the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were fulfilled, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: ‘Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord’” (Luke 2:22–23).

It is clear to all the faithful that the mother of the Redeemer did not in any way contract a stain through his birth, as though she were purified by abstaining from the holy buildings during those days. For she gave birth as a virgin without human desire and without any corruption of the flesh, and she remained a virgin forever; consequently, no male born from her opened her womb.

Yet the Evangelist, weaving together the narrative of the law, does not close the mystery of the divine Incarnation to the impious; rather, he introduces the mother as observing the law. Nor is it surprising that the mother observed the law which her Son had come not to abolish but to fulfill. For she knew in what manner she had conceived and who he was whom she had borne. But, observing the common law, she awaited the day of purification and concealed her Son’s majesty.

This is why, when she found him in the temple at twelve years of age, she called him Joseph’s son, saying: “Child, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I, grieving, have been seeking you” (ibid., 48). She certainly knew that she had conceived him without intercourse with Joseph and brought him forth without violation of her virginity.

### 3

But why did she conceal the mystery of his conception and birth when she knew him to be the immeasurable God? Did she begrudge him to others, when she brought him to the temple and handed him over to the hands of the holy old man? Far from it. Rather, filled with the spirit of prophecy, she did not disclose the redemption of the world to the impious.

For, already full of grace and breathed upon by the spirit of divinity, she knew that, if the rulers of this age had known him, they would never have crucified him for our salvation. Offer, therefore, most blessed Virgin, as one observing the law, in the temple the one whom you brought forth, so that it may not be revealed to everyone, but only to a few, who he is whom you bore.

For the time being, let the humble stone appear, cut from the mountain without hands, so that it may be rejected by the builders, until, striking the statue upon its feet, it grows into a great mountain and fills the whole globe.

### 4

O how small, O how great, is he whom you bore! Small in humanity, great in divinity; small in the kingdom of the Jews, great in the kingdom of the nations. Yet he is not regarded as small by everyone in the kingdom of the Jews. For you yourself, who bore him, grew from that people of Israel into a rod.

You arose as a rod from the root of Jesse and blossomed. You put forth leaves as Aaron’s rod and produced a nut. And because you recognized his immeasurability above all others, although you saw him born from you as the tiniest child, beyond doubt you tremblingly adored as almighty God the infant whom you bore, and in adoring him you trembled. Yet because you recognized him as your son according to his humanity, you nursed, embraced, and nourished him.

Who, do you think, can make known to us the feeling of your soul amid such acts of service, O most blessed Virgin? Here you saw the tiny infant born from you; there you regarded the immeasurable God; here the created one, there the Creator; here the weak one, there the strongest; here the one needing nourishment, there the one who nourishes; here the one who did not speak, there the one teaching angels.

Who, I ask, could unlock for us the secrets of your breast, and in what manner you inclined your thoughts toward both realities, when, holding in your hands the one and the same Son of God and man, you adored him here as Lord and kissed him there as a little child?

### 5

Who would not be astonished at so ineffable a miracle? Who would not become almost speechless? A young woman gives birth to her own Creator and the Creator of all; she nourishes her own Nourisher and the Nourisher of all; she carries to the temple its own Lord and the Lord of all.

O wondrous spectacle, at which not only human nature but even the angelic nature is astonished! To this, dearest brothers, raise the eyes of faith; for this, assemble with devout affection. There receive Christ, humbled for you in the flesh, but worship the exalted God in his divinity. Embrace the little child, but consider the immeasurable one. Love the humbled one and fear the exalted one.

### 6

Now, dearest ones, if it is asked what was mystically signified by the fact that our Redeemer wished to be carried by his mother and parents from his own city to Jerusalem, to the Lord’s temple, we find that the glorious mother and virgin herself, together with her relatives, represented that Church which believed from the Jews through the Apostles.

For when is the Church not a virgin, whose members the Apostle addresses, saying: “I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2)? When is she not a mother? But since it is said through the Psalmist, “Mother Zion will say, ‘A man’” (Ps. 86:5), and the Lord says in the Gospel, “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. 12:50), when are the elect not relatives, since they are called brothers and sisters?

The mother, then, and the relatives of our Redeemer carry him from Nazareth to Jerusalem, to the Lord’s temple, because that primitive Church, believing first in the first disciples, was rejected by the Jews and brought the dispensation of the same redemption to the knowledge of the nations.

That Church itself is rightly called Jerusalem—not only from the nations but also from the Jews—Jerusalem meaning “Vision of peace.” Of it the Psalmist says: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in the same thing” (Ps. 121:3). It is also the temple, as Paul says to the faithful: “The temple of the Lord is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3:17).

And so, when the Apostles come from Judea to the nations proclaiming Christ, Jerusalem meets Jerusalem, and temple encounters temple, since all of them are one city, Jerusalem, and one temple. In this city and in this temple Christ, offered by the Apostles, is received. Hence the Church herself speaks in the words of the Psalmist, saying: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple” (Ps. 47:10)—that is, in the midst of the Church, which is your temple.

### 7

Whether according to the historical account or according to the mystical understanding, the reason why Christ is led by his parents to the holy city and temple is made clear when the text adds:

“To offer a sacrifice, according to what was said in the law of the Lord: a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (Luke 2:24).

The command of the law was that, if someone happened to lack a lamb but found one of these alternatives—that is, either a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons—he should offer it to God at the offering of his son; and the person who offered either of these alternatives would not be disadvantaged because of the other.

Finally, in this offering of birds was prefigured that offering which was made for the salvation of the world in the evening of the day, namely the Lord’s Passion, through which we were reconciled to God. Concerning this sacrifice Paul says to the faithful:

“Walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a pleasing aroma” (Eph. 5:2);

and again: “He loved me,” he says, “and handed himself over for me” (Gal. 2:20).

### 8

Since all the elect are members of Christ—turtledoves in the turtledove and doves in the dove—this offering of birds also signifies the mortification of the elect, to whom the same Apostle says:

“I appeal to you through the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living, holy, pleasing sacrifice to God” (Rom. 12:1).

But there can be no sacrifice of mortification acceptable to God in those in whom there is not the chastity of true faith and the harmony of true chastity. Therefore it is not without reason that the sacrifice said to have been mystically offered for the Lord is reported to have consisted of turtledoves and doves.

In the turtledove chastity is found; in the dove unity is commended. The turtledove preserves undefiled fidelity to one mate, while the dove does not abandon the unity of those dwelling together.

A catholic Christian, therefore, truly becomes a spiritual turtledove if he preserves the true faith of the Trinity with firm belief and rejects the sense of heretical depravity as the pollution of fornication. He will truly be a dove if he remains patiently to the end within catholic fellowship and stands firm with immovable constancy against the scandals of temptation, so that neither heretical fornication corrupts the chastity of faith in his heart nor bitter dissent scatters the unity of ecclesiastical chastity.

For this is the catholic Church: it preserves faith with the one Lord as with a legitimate husband and multiplies the gathering of many in faith.

### 9

The text continues:

“And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon; and this man was just and devout, awaiting the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was in him. And he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death unless he had first seen the Christ of the Lord. And he came in the Spirit into the temple” (Luke 2:25–27).

Nothing less than holiness is specifically attributed to this man, who dwells in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace—who is just through the activity of faith, devout through reverence, astonished at the consolation of Israel *(possibly: “attentive to consolation”)*, and said to have been filled with the Holy Spirit and strengthened by his response concerning the command *(possibly: “mission”)* of the incarnate Word.

O with what ardent desire this man awaited, according to the promise of the Holy Spirit, seeing the Redeemer in the flesh! What, we suppose, was the persistence of his prayer, which deserved to be confirmed by a divine response concerning what he was asking? What were the continual words of his sighs in holy preaching? For he did not cease asking until he received a response concerning what he sought.

### 10

In former times there were many inflamed by a similar desire, as the Lord testifies to the disciples, saying:

“Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Luke 10:24).

But of all those, this was granted only to him, who appeared as the last of them in the fullness of time.

Yet if we attend with vigilant care to the desire of the saints who followed, for whom “to live is Christ and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21), we find that they wished to behold the divinity of that same Savior with no less anxious ardor than Simeon desired to see him in the flesh.

Hence Paul says: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ, which is much better” (ibid., 23). Hence the Psalmist says in his own person: “My soul thirsted for the living God. When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:3).

Who, then, can see even here that in the one Simeon many are signified, and through one all the elect, who are now found to be just through faith and action, devout through expectation of what is to come, and astonished by the consolation that is coming?

The Holy Spirit is also recognized to be in them, since it is said through the Apostle: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5); and again it is said to the faithful: “Your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God” (1 Cor. 6:19).

They also receive from the Holy Spirit the answer that they will not see death unless they first see Christ the Lord, because, while still in this corruptible life, with the grace of the same Holy Spirit revealing him, they behold with the open eyes of faith the one who promised that he would remain with them until the end of the age (Matt. 28:20)—no longer as a little one in the flesh, but as immeasurable in divinity.

They too say with the Apostle: “Even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him so” (2 Cor. 5:16).

They also dwell in Jerusalem and come in the Spirit into the temple into which Christ is introduced. For they are Jerusalem who dwell in Jerusalem; they are also the temple who come into the temple, and in whom and by whom Christ is received.

### 11

Briefly, brothers, we have passed through these matters, lest, while striving to indicate the mysteries of this day and its holy and pure proclamation, we become tedious to anyone.

The text continues:

“And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law, he himself received him into his arms, blessed God, and said: ‘Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace’” (Luke 2:27–29).

He who lives, and so forth.

# Appendix to the Works of Saint Fulgentius

## Book and Letter

### Preface on the Book *On Predestination and Grace* and the Following Letter of Ferrandus to Egyppius

We should by no means attribute the book that follows immediately to Fulgentius. Apart from the judgment of the theologians of Louvain and the agreement of learned men, who find nothing in it worthy of Fulgentius but rather much that is strongly contrary to Fulgentian teaching, this is also shown by the fact that the author of the book does not agree even with himself.

For although he had said in chapter 3:

“It could more easily happen that, although sin passes from the first human being to his descendants, punishment would not follow at all, than that, without any communication of sin, one who has no guilt should share in punishment”;

nevertheless, in chapter 16 he says:

“If the human race, which is known to have been originally created from nothing, were not born with the due origin of death and sin, and yet the omnipotent Creator wished to condemn some of them to eternal destruction, who would say to the omnipotent Creator: ‘Why did you make me thus?’”

How much these statements conflict with one another can be detected more easily than it can be demonstrated at length.

How greatly this opinion also opposes the teaching of Saint Fulgentius—and indeed of the bishops who were exiled with him in Sardinia—is clear from these words of their fifteenth letter to John and Venerius, p. 272, no. 9:

“Since it is certain that Esau was a vessel of wrath, but Jacob a vessel of mercy, it must be held with absolute certainty that the former justly deserved wrath so that he might be condemned; for God is not unjust when he inflicts wrath,” and so forth.

I pass over other passages of this book, already noted as deviating from the mind and teaching of Augustine and therefore also from those of Fulgentius, his disciple in all things.

We have caused the letter of the Deacon Ferrandus to Egyppius to be printed here in the Appendix because, since it was written neither by Fulgentius nor to Fulgentius, it ought not to have a place among his works, except so that it might not altogether perish, and because it seemed fitting in this edition to reproduce everything that has hitherto been published from Fulgentius or together with his works.

## Book on Predestination and Grace (C, G, S)

## CHAPTER I

When, in the sacred books—whether they pronounce future events in the prophetic spirit, recount past events with historical truth, or deliver counsels for living with apostolic authority—the reader is disturbed or the hearer troubled by a statement that seems to sound different, it must be held as known with certain and unshakable faith that one and the same Spirit, apart from whom there is no truth, speaks more openly in one place and somewhat more obscurely in another about the mysteries. Therefore, if something is suspended under a hidden meaning, or briefly indicated by the writer and explained less fully than the dullness of the human heart required, one should recognize that truth appears more clearly here, lies more deeply hidden there, and is nowhere absent. But if, because of the greatness of the matter under inquiry, understanding does not readily present itself to the mind of the seeker—especially if, concerning the unchangeable will of almighty God, the two statements of canonical authority sound different—then everything must be directed according to the rule of piety, so that it may be held with unshakable conviction that God is neither unjust, nor one who assesses individual merits with some confused partiality, nor weak, as though he were unable to accomplish whatever he willed.

## CHAPTER II

Under the yoke, then, of this definition, lest ill-controlled necks stretch themselves into sacrilegious presumption, let us recall, as far as God grants us to do so, the hidden matters of this question, which the blessed apostle Paul, in various places and with words that differ considerably, sets before diligent investigators and addresses through the truth itself. Having completed an exceedingly broad and powerful discussion of preceding grace, he concludes it thus: “Therefore he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills” (Rom. 9:18); while elsewhere, speaking of divine benevolence, he says: “Who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:4).

The question arises why some of these people perish, although almighty God wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth; and then, again, why he hardens some while having mercy on others—or how he can will all people to be saved when he himself hardens certain ones so that they may not be saved. In relation to human justice this seems unjust. But who would be so foolish—or rather, who would blaspheme so greatly—as to say that God’s justice is to be judged according to the rule of human justice? If the latter conflicts with God’s justice, it is plainly unjust. For it is evident that everything that is just in any way proceeds from him who is supremely just.

Who, then, will subject the wisdom of God—which remains unchangeable and creates, governs, and preserves all that exists—to the judgment of human wisdom? Concerning this same wisdom the apostle says: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God” (Rom. 8:7). And elsewhere: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3:19). Therefore, the majesty of divine wisdom must not be debated according to the judgment of human vanity.

## CHAPTER III

If anyone, by nourishing his sins, is deceived by the figure, shadow, or flattering image of pride, so that he says that certain people will make the objection which the blessed apostle Paul immediately foresaw, he added: “Someone will say: If he has mercy on whomever he wills, and hardens whomever he wills, why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” (Rom. 9:19).

Let him know that this statement compels and constrains us all the more toward humility and piety. For when the most eminent Teacher refers everything to God and denies it to human powers, what else does he exhort us to do but, hanging upon God with our whole heart, seek from him the aids of salvation?

If anyone is troubled by this diversity in the dispensation of divine grace and considers it unjust that one person should be denied what another has received, let him understand how the Psalmist spoke divinely: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10); and let him recognize that God directs human affairs by such a judgment that he either justly exacts deserved punishments or mercifully remits them.

For the stain of the corrupted root has been spread through the branches of descent by the succession of generations in such a way that not even an infant of one day is free from the guilt of the first transgression (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint), unless he has been liberated by the undeserved grace of the Savior.

If even this person is not without sin—one who could not have a sin of his own—it follows that he has contracted another’s sin, concerning which the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12).

Whoever denies this certainly denies, first of all, that we are mortal. For if, as the Apostle says, “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death,” death could not have entered unless sin entered with it. And since death is not a condition of nature but the punishment of sin, it necessarily follows that sin accompanies the punishment. But because death passed to all people, sin must necessarily have passed to all.

We cannot see with the eyes of the flesh how original sin is born with infants. But because we see that all who are born bodily from Adam—even those who have already been reborn in Christ—are held under the law of death, by observing that infants always die we are compelled to confess that infants are always born with original sin.

It would more easily be possible for punishment not to follow, although sin had passed on, than for one who has no guilt to share in punishment without any communication of sin. Therefore, if, as has been shown, we are all born debtors from the seed of the transgressor, since, as the Apostle says, all sinned in him, and since the very mass from which we descend was already condemned at the beginning, let no one dare complain about his hardness or his punishment, which is owed even in the absence of personal sins solely by the condition of birth.

But that God grants to others, converted by a gratuitous calling, an undeserved mercy must, according to the reason of truth, be attributed not to the justice of the dispensation but to the most merciful generosity—or, as another reading has it, liberty—of the giver.

Would a debtor dare accuse a creditor of injustice if, after remitting another person’s debt, he demanded from him what he was owed? If, then, among human contracts there is no ground for such a plea that a debtor should say he is unjustly required to pay because he knows that the same creditor has remitted to another debtor what that debtor owed, who would burst forth into such madness of profane speech as to accuse God of injustice if he granted one person undeserved grace and repaid another with deserved punishment?

## CHAPTER IV

Accordingly, regarding the earlier part of this statement, which says, “He has mercy on whomever he wills,” I think that no one except one unworthy of mercy would dare dispute it. But in what follows—“He hardens whomever he wills”—the attention of the human mind is somewhat confused by the novelty of the expression.

It must not be understood as though God produced in a person a hardness of heart that had not existed. For what else is hardness than opposition to God’s commands? Hence the blessed Stephen said to the people: “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7:51).

Whoever thinks that this hardness is made by God because it is said, “He hardens whomever he wills,” should contemplate the beginning of the transgression and attend to the command given by God, through which the guilt of transgression was produced in the heart—although even by the tempter he could not have been compelled if he had refused consent.

Therefore, whatever punishment a person born into that transgression suffers, let him confess that it is justly and deservedly repaid. For God is said to harden the one whom he does not wish to soften. Likewise, he is said to blind the one whom he does not wish to enlighten. Likewise, he is said to reject the one whom he does not wish to call.

“For those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified” (Rom. 8:30). For he himself gave us existence, and he himself gave us the ability to be good.

## CHAPTER V

His divinity foreknew us; his wisdom created us; his justice condemned us; his grace liberated us. Although the world began in time from the moment when it was made, it could have no beginning in the light of that divine foreknowledge when it was to be made. All the people who have been born from Adam to the present day, and all who will be born after our time through the succession of generations, were already born before God and, while remaining in that light of divine vision, have passed through the whole course of their lives.

For God, who is confined neither by place nor preceded by time, is full of the memory of all past things and the knowledge of all things that are imminent. He is not carried backward by remembering, nor stretched forward by hoping. Whatever exists and is moved by the changes of time exists from that beginning in which “the Word was, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), to the end of all ages.

Concerning that end, when the blessed Moses said, “Lord,” he said, “you who reign for age and age” (Exod. 15:18)—while future things are not yet hoped for and past things have not yet passed away—all things are nevertheless seen in the ever-present light of the divine presence.

Therefore, because he is eternal and foreknowing, just and compassionate, exercising deserved severity and displaying undeserved kindness, and because in creating and choosing human beings he possesses authority like a potter over clay, some vessels were made for honor and others for dishonor.

Before he made us, he foreknew us; and in that very foreknowledge, before he had made us, he chose us. But by whom could this have been done except by him who “calls into existence things that do not exist as though they did” (Rom. 4:17)? For the Apostle says: “He chose us before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1:4).

We were made within the world and chosen before the world. Thus, in one and the same time—which neither passes away nor is future, but is continuous—or, if it can be expressed in some other way, provided that this is so with God, there are foreknowing, making, and choosing; and, with his foreknowledge remaining unchangeable, he chooses as those to be made those whom he was going to choose.

Let these matters, insofar as they concern the rule of faith, be stated in this way with God’s illumination.

## CHAPTER VI

But now I see what malicious perversity can bring forward even here. It follows, they say, that if those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified (Rom. 8:30), then those who were neither predestined nor called, and therefore not justified, ought to be innocent of every fault; and it would be unjust for punishments to be demanded from them on the day of judgment for the wickedness of their lives.

Let the apostle Paul answer them: “Is there injustice with God?” (Rom. 9:14). Let him immediately answer himself: “Certainly not.” When this has been established in a human mind sound with piety—that there is no injustice with God—let it understand the words, “He has mercy on whomever he wills, and hardens whomever he wills” (ibid., 18), as though he were saying: “He has mercy on whomever he wills, and he does not have mercy on whomever he does not will.”

Let it likewise understand the same statement as though it said: “He grants to whom he wills, and from whom he wills he demands what is owed.” Whoever persists in calling this unjust should hear from the Apostle: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (ibid., 20).

The apostolic authority rightly rebukes such impiety, imposing such weight through the force of these names when it says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” O man before God, clay before the potter! For the same Apostle adds: “Does the molded thing say to the one who molded it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (ibid., 21).

If the potter has this authority—or rather, because he has the authority—to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, then, O man, who are you to answer back to God because he has mercy on whomever he wills and hardens whomever he wills?

But before the blessed Apostle reached this conclusion in the order of his discussion, he took the following example above all from the ancient Scriptures, in which he was to teach the hardening that is said to be done by God:

“Scripture says to Pharaoh,” he writes, “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth” (ibid., 17; Exod. 9:16).

God is also most plainly said in the same Scripture to have hardened Pharaoh’s heart when he spoke to Moses about the signs that were to be performed through him against the Egyptians. Thus he says: “But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, so that he will not let the people go” (Exod. 4:21).

Now let the clever calumniator, boasting openly, weigh God’s justice according to his own judgment and answer with all the shouting he can muster: “If he has mercy on whomever he wills and hardens whomever he wills, why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?”

To this arrogance let the Apostle answer: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9:19–20).

But whoever desires to find something through pious inquiry should reread the passage of that same Scripture where fire first appeared to Moses in the bush and kindled his heart with the heat of divine love, so that, as David says, he might speak his testimonies without shame before kings (Ps. 118:46). There he will find that everything which Scripture says beforehand about God hardening Pharaoh’s heart pertains not to God’s action but to his foreknowledge.

For, speaking from the bush, the Lord says: “I know that Pharaoh, king of Egypt, will not let you go unless by a mighty hand. But I will stretch out my hand and strike the Egyptians with all the wonders that I shall perform among them, and afterward Pharaoh, king of Egypt, will let you go” (Exod. 3:19–20).

This is God’s first statement, by which he indicates Pharaoh’s future will, just as he had foreseen it. Later, amid the very showers of miracles, he is read to have said: “But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, so that he will not let the people go” (Exod. 4:21).

Here it is clearly understood that he repeated his first statement. For what is “I will harden the heart” except “I will not soften it”?
