The statement of Scripture was fulfilled: justice remained toward some, while grace flowed toward others, because God said to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth” (Exod. 9:16).

Since God makes use even of the wicked for good, what else was accomplished through Pharaoh’s hardening, the plagues of Egypt, and so many great miracles performed together and in succession among that people, except that the power of God—which is great in itself and complete in itself—might come to the knowledge of the human race, benefiting not God but those who would later read and believe?

God foreknew, in that lofty light of his providence, that Pharaoh would not change, nor that entire nation which, after so many blows, scarcely having allowed God’s people to escape, attempted even by force of arms to pursue them and wage war against them.

But he willed the destruction of those destined to perish to be an argument for the vessels of mercy predestined by him for salvation. He used the perdition of some for the salvation of others, because “the potter has authority over the clay to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor” (Rom. 9:21).

## CHAPTER VII

The blessed Apostle had recalled somewhat earlier this same judgment of divine power in the election of human beings, and he demonstrated it with very powerful examples when, speaking of Rebecca’s offspring still enclosed within the womb, he referred everything to the grace of God.

Thus he says: “Rebecca also had conceived by one act of intercourse with Isaac our father; and when the children had not yet been born and had done neither good nor evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works but from the one who calls—it was said: ‘The elder shall serve the younger,’ as it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.’ Immediately he added: ‘What shall we say? Is there injustice with God?’” (Rom. 9:10–13; Gen. 25:23; Mal. 1:2).

He answered with a denial: “Certainly not,” so that the other matters that follow might be referred back to this statement and resolved in light of it—namely, his denial that there is injustice with God.

Here the purpose of this apostolic argument is quite clear. He compared not merely brothers, but twins; not merely twins, but children conceived from a single act of intercourse and poured together into the womb. Since they had not yet been born and had not yet done anything, there could be no consideration of merits; nor could any obstacle be left against grace arising from the merits of their parents, which might have differed at different times.

Even if we allow that divine assistance might either have been withdrawn from or granted to the children because of the merits of their parents, whether for good or for evil, those merits ought to have been equal with respect to the twin offspring, who were conceived in the same act of intercourse and brought into the light at the same moment.

But if it is said that the divine judgment distinguished their future conduct, then what the Apostle stated beforehand is certainly nullified: “Not from works but from the one who calls it was said: ‘The elder shall serve the younger.’” For he did not say, “not from past works”; rather, when he said generally, “not from works,” he intended both past and future works to be understood: past works, which did not exist, and future works, which did not yet exist.

Jacob was predestined as a vessel for honor because it was said, “Not from works but from the one who calls: ‘The elder shall serve the younger.’”

## CHAPTER VIII

And lest the vessels predestined for honor should deny the grace of the Creator by attributing something to their own powers, the Apostle called them elsewhere “vessels of mercy,” so that they might recognize that everything they were, they were according to mercy.

Thus the same Apostle says elsewhere: “And this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Eph. 2:8).

The blessed Moses also says to the people in Deuteronomy: “Do not say in your heart, ‘My strength and the power of my hand made this great power for me’; but you shall remember the Lord your God, because he gives you strength to accomplish power, in order to establish his covenant which he swore to your fathers” (Deut. 8:17 and following).

Again, shortly afterward in the same place he says to them: “Do not say in your heart, when the Lord your God has destroyed these nations before your face, ‘Because of my righteousness the Lord has brought me in to take possession of this good land.’ It is not because of your righteousness, nor because of the holiness of your heart, that you enter to take possession of their land; but because of the wickedness of these nations, the Lord will destroy them before your face” (Deut. 9:4–5).

Behold how ancient is the doctrine of the Holy Spirit, preached not only in the apostolic writings but also proclaimed in the prophetic writings and confirmed by the voice of the Holy Spirit at the very beginnings of the Israelite people—yet the assault of novel presumption attempts to overthrow it.

In one and the same passage of Scripture, the blessed prophet clearly shows the goodness and severity of God, saying that the inheritance of that land was not granted to the people because of their righteousness, but given solely by the grace of the merciful one, while the others were driven out because of their unrighteousness.

In those people iniquity is justly punished; in these, no righteousness is rewarded, but grace is freely given. Nor was it enough for the blessed Moses to have said that the inheritance of the land had not been granted to the Israelite people because of their merits; he also had to add what he did add, by which he showed them to be unworthy of every good thing.

For after what we mentioned above, it follows: “And you shall know today that the Lord your God does not give you this good land to inherit because of your righteousness, for you are a stiff-necked people” (ibid., 6).

Who could say here that a reward had been given according to the due measure of preceding merits? Who would not confess that the grace was undeserved?

How often does the prophet say: “They tested him in the desert” (Ps. 94:9)? How often did they deserve God’s anger by turning away their hearts, and yet he saved them because of his mercy, so that he might make his power known (Ps. 105:7–8)?

The Apostle says this again: “He endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order to show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory” (Rom. 9:22–23).

## CHAPTER IX

But lest, once more, a person, reduced to the lowest dregs of sluggishness, should suppose that the arduous path of virtue—which, even with the help of God’s grace, must be traversed only by labor—could be bestowed upon him in his idleness, and should therefore apply no industry of labor in pursuit of his own progress, God distributed times and duties between himself and the human being in such a way that we should begin with the calling itself, while, once called and illuminated, we should recognize the ways of his commandments through the understanding of a good disposition and freely choose either to follow or abandon them.

If, however, supported by his assistance, we followed these ways with continual devotion, then at the end he would crown in us an obedience that was not resistant but subject to his commandments.

The free will that we have from him flows with an inclined slide toward wickedness. Since, when God’s help withdraws, it can do nothing toward the nature of virtue, it nevertheless remains equipped with sufficient power for every kind of sin.

For the law of sin, born in the members, drags us along; and God, according to his justice, abandons those who withdraw from the easy yoke and light burden of his commandments and, by the free choice of their will away from righteousness, flow down into the harshest slavery of sin.

But those who receive the gift of calling with fitting piety, who are not subjected to carnal allurements, who have been free from the vice of boasting, the flames of avarice, and the wind of pride, and who, insofar as human beings can, preserve God’s good things within themselves and devote every effort to spiritual exercises—he both assists them as they contend in the contest of this life and grants eternal crowns to those who conquer.

Again, he abandons those who sin, hardens those who resist, and condemns those who despise him.

## CHAPTER X

Concerning the distribution of these stages—what God works in us and what he commands us to work—let us ask him from whose words the question arose, which, if the Lord is present, we are attempting to unravel. The statements arranged through various books in differing language but with one and the same intention may disclose, by comparison with another statement, whatever lies hidden in this passage.

That the apostle Paul was called by God we read either in the book where his deeds are narrated with complete truth, or he himself confesses it in his Epistle, saying: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle” (Rom. 1:1).

In a second place, having followed his calling and having accomplished everything that had been worked in the human being, he himself says: “I worked harder than all of them” (1 Cor. 15:10). But lest he attribute even this to himself, he added with attentive piety: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (ibid.).

Now, having been called and having followed his calling through works of righteousness, what else remained for him except, once delivered from this body of death, to reach the blessedness of that other life which has been promised to all the saints by the mouth of Truth?

That this is not repaid by any human merits but bestowed by the grace of God the giver, he himself answers after the groans in which he had said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” He replies: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24–25).

The Apostle shows this distribution—that people are called by God when no merits yet exist, and that those who have been called need God’s assistance in order to do anything good—by taking an example from the ancient writings. He had attributed the election of the two twins entirely to God’s grace and judgment, excluding every praise of merits; then, seeing what impious chatter might blaspheme, he said: “Is there injustice with God?” (Rom. 9:14). And it follows: “Certainly not.”

As though someone had said to him, “How do you prove this?” he considered the authority of his own teaching insufficient unless he also taught his statement by an example from the Law.

Thus he intended Moses’ words—“I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion” (Exod. 33:19)—to be understood so that we believe the first mercy is granted to people through calling. This mercy alone is not sufficient for right living if the one who called does not remain with them.

Therefore it was added: “And I will show compassion to whom I show compassion,” so that it might be clear that even the works of mercy themselves are received from God, although, when we appear to perform them, we merit God’s mercy.

Thus he says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them” (Matt. 5:7). If the Apostle had not understood this in that way, he would never have taken care to insert this testimony in his discussion concerning the benefits of grace.

## CHAPTER XI

But if anyone is troubled that not all, even among those who have already been called to the second grace—that is, to the gift of right living—deserve to reach it, as the Lord says in the Gospel, “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16), let him understand what sort of thing the person is trying to defend against God’s grace who takes pride in his free will.

For all who, abandoning the gift of the divine calling, have flowed back again into impious unbelief possess sufficient free will to fulfill what they have willed, since they themselves have abandoned God’s grace.

The Psalmist, as the Apostle interprets it from Moses’ meaning, sings in the truth of the prophetic spirit the order of God’s mercies. “Hear,” he says, “my people, and I will testify to you” (Ps. 80:9).

What did he want them to hear, when he spoke with testimony? What else but the commandments of life, as another prophet says: “Hear, Israel, the commandments of life” (Baruch 3:9)?

But the Psalmist adds and continues by showing what these commandments of life are: “For I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Ps. 80:11).

That these are the commandments of life he also shows in the prayer by which the Lord commended his disciples to the Father, saying: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

After this calling comes what he both wishes to belong to human efforts and shows cannot be accomplished without him. This is what the Apostle says: “For from him we have both the will and the accomplishment, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13).

From him we have the will because he calls and illuminates; from him we have accomplishment because it belongs to us to strive toward the good things whose willing he has also granted.

Nor was it carelessly added by the Apostle, after he had said, “From him we have both the willing and the accomplishing,” that this is “according to his good pleasure.” Thus they may see again and again where, according to God’s justice, the free will of which they boast is to be found.

Let us also observe, in the continuation of this psalm’s prayer, the order by which the Lord distributes various mercies through the administration of time, just as the Apostle understood Moses to have said.

What does the Psalmist say after he had instructed the called, saying, “For I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt”? “Open wide your mouth,” he says, “and I will fill it” (Ps. 80:11).

Here it once again appears that something has been reserved for human beings to do through free will. They are commanded to open their mouth, but God promises to fill it.

Thus he had also said to his disciples in the Gospel: “Do not consider how or what you will speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:19–20).

He attributed this one thing to them: that they willingly accept every necessity of tribulation for the sake of truth; but he promised that the result would belong to himself.

What place, then, is left to free will, if human nature, though supported by rational dignity, is not sufficient of itself to accomplish what it wills without God’s help? The Psalmist immediately shows: “But my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me” (Ps. 80:12).

The one who, when he called, had said, “Hear, my people, and I will speak; Israel, and I will testify to you,” had commended to the minds of his hearers that he was the Lord their God.

What else had he commanded them to do? He had liberated them from the land of Egypt and the darkness of ignorance and led them into the light of his commandments, in the splendor of his calling. “Open wide your mouth,” he says.

Immediately, as though he were saying, “If you wish to open it while I have abandoned you, it will accomplish nothing,” he added: “And I will fill it.”

What, then, does the one who had called them and instructed those who were called say afterward in a complaining voice concerning those same people? “My people did not hear my voice,” he says, “and Israel did not attend to me.”

Let the defender of free will now come forth against God and hear the Apostle, when he speaks of his good labors: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

Let him hear God’s voice in the psalm, speaking of those whom he had abandoned: “So I let them go according to the desires of their hearts; they shall walk in their own wills” (Ps. 80:13).

Let him hear the same Apostle attributing to himself alone the evils of the various periods of his life, but all good things to grace: “I who formerly was a blasphemer and a persecutor,” he says (1 Tim. 1:13). And elsewhere: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10).

When he said, “I who formerly was a blasphemer and a persecutor,” no mention of grace was joined to the evil deed, because human freedom’s nature, as has been said, is sufficient for itself in wickedness.

But when he spoke of the blessedness of his present life, he said: “By the grace of God I am what I am.”

The blessed apostle Paul also preserved, in a continuous account, the order by which God has mercy when calling and afterward has mercy by assisting those who have begun to strive, just as it has been narrated and arranged in the sequence of the psalm.

For if the cited testimonies are reread in the order in which he placed them, he speaks as follows: “By the grace of God I am what I am.” This is the first mercy, which the works of free will follow.

But so that good works might follow the calling of the apostle Paul, what does he say? “And his grace toward me was not empty” (1 Cor. 15:10).

What did you do? “I worked harder than all of them,” he says.

Do not become too proud, defender of free will, when you hear Paul boasting of his labors. Attend to what follows: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me.”

I certainly think that none of those who, with a heart exalted before ruin, as it is written (Prov. 16:18), blaspheme against God’s grace will assume so shamelessly arrogant a posture as to consider himself equal or even superior to the merits of the blessed prophet David.

Let me pass over for the moment that first reward—the bestowal of the kingdom—which no one fails to acknowledge as undeserved; let us consider the earnestness and devotion of David’s prayers and confessions.

He himself declares in the psalm: “Blessed is the person whom you instruct, Lord, and whom you teach from your law” (Ps. 93:12).

But let us see whether this alone was sufficient for blessedness for one who had already been instructed and adequately trained, according to Jewish teaching, in all knowledge of the Law.

Why, then, did the same man again cry out to the Lord: “Give me understanding, and I will search out your law and keep it with all my heart” (Ps. 118:34)?

It was not enough that he had asked for understanding in order to search out the Law, unless he also indicated that help was necessary for keeping it, when he said, “And I will keep it with all my heart”—as though he were saying, “I will keep it with all my heart if you give me understanding.”

## CHAPTER XII

Let that proud defender of his own will now respond that the prophet asked for divine assistance only in order to understand the divine commandments, which he would nevertheless fulfill by his own power.

If this is so, blessed David, I wish to search out for a little while the hidden matters of your thoughts. From where, I ask you, comes the struggle between flesh and spirit? From where comes the apostolic combat, as you yourself confess?

Although you have certainly been illuminated and instructed by the gift of understanding which you had asked for from God, you cry out and say: “Turn my eyes away, that they may not see vanity” (Ps. 118:37).

Since you received, as you requested, the understanding by which vanity is certainly to be distinguished from truth, why do you not turn your eyes away from the vanity that displeases you?

If you condemn avarice, why do you not, separated from it by your own free will, incline your heart toward the commandments of salvation? Why, instead, do you cry out to God as though weak in every respect: “Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to avarice”?

It is because the law of sin, born in the members, suggests avarice, and the holy man still wishes to turn away his eyes but cannot do so by himself. Thus “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). No one frees us from this conflict except grace, which is granted through our Lord Jesus Christ to the small and the great (Rom. 7:25).

“For to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find” (Rom. 7:18). Yet even the willing itself does not come from us but is the gift of God, since “from him we have both the will and the accomplishment, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13).

Therefore you are blessed, because you agree with the apostles of Christ in the equality of both doctrine and struggle: in your writings we recognize the battles of the apostles, and in the apostolic writings we find your contests.

[Col. 0851D] **CHAPTER XIII.** Hence, whence in one and the same human being, who consists of soul and body, comes this diversity of things and of wills, unless it is because, despising the just judgments of God, human beings find within themselves the penalties of disobedience and the defiance of the inferior part: human being against God, creature against Creator, the lowly against the Most High? For by what justice would a creature, though inferior to a better creature, nevertheless serve a creature, if that creature itself refused to serve the Creator, whatever sort of creature it might be?

But even this is not sufficient as a punishment: that the inferior part should resist the better affections of the heart, unless it also frequently prevailed, led one captive, and took possession—not only of human beings born in Adam, but unless the law of sin itself claimed them for the service of its impulse, and unless, even in those reborn in Christ, it continued to assail them while its prompting remained. For truly, through the gift of regeneration, guilt has been forgiven; the condition of grace has not been abolished, since it erases the written acknowledgments of former debts; nor does it yet separate a human being living in the flesh from carnal passion, so that every person [Col. 0852A] may in the future continually implore divine assistance.

And since the law was able less to remove than to reveal sin—sin which, as people were born into it, claimed them indiscriminately for itself and plunged those possessed by agreement with desire into everlasting destruction—our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, the Word of the Father, equal and coeternal with the Father, “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 7). Although he himself was not sin, by taking flesh he was made sin, so that, by healing the human being from the sin of the flesh, he might condemn sin in the flesh. He came “to seek what had been lost” (Luke XIX, 10), to heal what was sick, to raise what was lying fallen; having the power to forgive sins, to give what he did not owe, to forgive what was owed to him; and, after erasing all the stains of the former guilt, to restore the nature that he had made.

Of those for whom just severity had decreed punishment, according to the ineffable mercy of his hidden disposition, he chose vessels to make for honor; and by the gift of a gratuitous calling he released some from the coming wrath, while leaving others for the judgment of equality. Yet he deprived no one of the capacity to acknowledge the truth. Thus the fullness of divine foreknowledge was completed, with justice flowing into some and grace streaming into others, so that the Church, spread throughout the whole world, might be multiplied both through those perishing whom God had foreknown to be destined to perish and through those being saved whom, in that secret election, he had foreknown to be destined for salvation.

**CHAPTER XIV.** Rejoice, therefore, whoever you are who have been illumined, and acknowledge the grace that you did not deserve. Mourn, whoever you are who have been hardened, and confess justice. Say, whoever you are who rejoice that you have been cleansed from original contamination by the washing of grace:

> “The Lord is merciful and gracious, patient and rich in mercy. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities” (Psalm CII, 8 and 10).

Say, whoever you are who have been condemned:

> “You are just, O Lord, in all that you have done to us, and all your judgments are true, because in truth and judgment you have brought all these things upon us, on account of our sins” (Dan. III, 27–28).

And do not attribute the blame for your hardening to the injustice of God, because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm XXIV, 10). Thus those who have obtained mercy from God should not boast of anything in their merits against the judgment of truth; nor should those who have been hardened and condemned imagine that they can derive an excuse for their guilt from the fact that they received no mercy by which they might be converted.

Pharaoh, then, did not receive this mercy, and therefore his free choice was sufficient for him to perish. Yet no one will be so ignorant of the divine Scriptures as to dare say that he suffered all those things unjustly. Or perhaps, if we think devoutly about God as we ought, we shall find that mercy was also given to Pharaoh? For God’s patience ought to have been effective for his salvation: by postponing the deserved and just punishment, God repeatedly intensified the blows of the miracles.

Could Pharaoh not, just as he drove out the people by blows, have recognized through the miracles and believed in God, who possessed such great power? If it is said that Pharaoh could no longer be changed because God had foreknown that he would not be changed, the answer is that God’s foreknowledge does not compel a human being to be such as God foreknew him to be; rather, it foreknows that he will be such as he is going to be, although God did not make him so. If God compelled him to be, he would certainly compel him to be what he is not. But if he had foreknown that what is not would be destined to be, then it would not be foreknowledge—a conclusion whose impiety toward God is perceived by anyone who flatters himself in his sins on the ground that God foreknew him to be destined to become a sinner.

**CHAPTER XV.** Nevertheless, I suppose there may be someone who says that the way to salvation is less adequate if someone, without being inwardly summoned by any calling, is nevertheless scourged. How, then, did Nebuchadnezzar gain fruitful repentance (Dan. IV, 33)? Was he not scourged after countless acts of impiety, repented, and received again the kingdom that he had lost?

Pharaoh, however (Exod. VIII and following), became harder through the very scourges and perished. Let the person who judges the divine plan with a supposedly wise heart because it is too profound explain to me why the medicine prepared by one physician benefited one person unto destruction and another unto salvation—unless it is because “the fragrance of Christ” is “for some the fragrance of life unto life, for others the fragrance of death unto death” (II Cor. II, 15–16).

In nature, both were human beings; in dignity, both were kings; in circumstance, both possessed God’s captive people; in punishment, both were mercifully admonished by scourges. What, then, caused their ends to be different, except that one, feeling the hand of God, groaned in remembrance of his own iniquity, while the other, by his free choice, fought against God’s most merciful truth?

Whoever replies that divine assistance was present for the first so that he might be changed, but absent for the second so that he might be hardened, and contends that this was unjust—because the Apostle, establishing the outcomes of these matters in God’s will, said, “He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (Rom. IX, 18), while the Lord says, “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5)—let him understand that all these things are accomplished either with the Lord’s help or permitted when he abandons, yet let him know that, when the Lord does not will it, absolutely nothing is admitted.

**CHAPTER XVI.** But let us return to the little ones; let us return to the twins. What I have said is too little: let us return to those not yet born, who had been conceived in the same intercourse and were destined to be brought into the light at the same moment. The apparent difference and divergence of the divine will’s judgment concerning them confounds human understanding, because human beings argue with excessive pride about God’s will in the face of so great a question.

Now raise your voice with all your strength, unjust accuser of the Just One, and tell me: what evil did the one commit, and what good did the other deserve? And the Apostle Paul, not I, answers you:

> “Neither had they deserved anything; but the potter has power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor” (Rom. IX, 21).

You will say, “Why? What is the reason for this judgment’s confused diversity?” Let him again refute this presumption and say:

> “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Ibid., 20).

Especially since, when attention is again turned to the comparison of human actions, the reply is that a creditor cannot be accused of injustice if he chooses to exercise such a judgment over two debtors that he forgives one and exacts from the other what both owe.

And certainly, in all the acts and transactions of human society, whenever we distinguish or judge anything, it is evident that this justice which we seem to recognize flows into the hearts of our humility from the ineffable fullness of divine justice. Blessed John confirms this in his Gospel, saying that “we have all received from his fullness” (John I, 16).

If this is so, with what impudence will a human being judge God, or clay the potter—not only saying, “Why have you made me thus?” but also probing the case of others with condemnable curiosity and saying, “Why, from the same lump, have you made one thus and another otherwise?”

If the human race, which was originally created from nothing, had not been born with the due origin of death and sin, and yet the omnipotent Creator had wished to condemn some of them to eternal destruction, who would say to the omnipotent Creator, “Why have you made them thus?” For he who, when they did not exist, had granted them existence also possessed the authority to determine the end for which they should exist. Nor would the others say why the divine decision differed despite equal merits in all, because “the potter has power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor” (Rom. IX, 21).

But now, since just punishment is repaid to the condemned while undeserved grace is given to the saved, who is so forgetful of the human condition as to investigate the secrets of the divine mind? Having himself deserved punishment, how can he ask why another received grace that was not owed to him?

Moses therefore showed that this divine election is not repaid according to merits but bestowed upon human beings solely by the generosity of the will, even though at that time he was teaching a carnal people. For he says clearly in Deuteronomy to the people:

> “Behold, the heaven belongs to the Lord your God, and the heaven of heaven, the earth, and all that is in it; yet the Lord chose your fathers to love them, and chose their descendants after them—you above all nations.”

And he added:

> “Circumcise, therefore, the hardness of your heart, and do not harden your neck any longer” (Deut. X, 14–15).

But that the hardness of heart remained in them, as we have already said above, blessed Stephen demonstrated when he rebuked the Jews. For in the Acts of the Apostles he says:

> “You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts VII, 51).

Whence came the stiff neck in that people, which had been chosen from the whole world, which had deserved liberation from slavery through ten miracles, to which the law had been given, for whose salvation the mouths of all the prophets had fought, from whom Christ was made according to the flesh and to whom he was sent? It came from the fact that “a hardening in part has happened to Israel, until the adopted Israel should enter the kingdom from the fullness of the Gentiles” (Rom. XI, 25). And the Lord shut all up in unbelief, so that all might need the mercy of the Savior.

Touching briefly upon the mysteries of this divine plan and the mystery of its majesty—although he knew it through the greatness of his revelations, nevertheless, overcome by human weakness—even he who, because of persecutions and blasphemies, deserved to be called the Chosen Vessel, cries out in amazement:

> “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Ibid., 33),

confessing that his ways are inscrutable and that God’s judgments are unsearchable.

With him, then, whenever such matters are questioned, let us wonder. While the judgment remains that there is no injustice with God, if there is something being asked that exceeds the measure of our understanding and does not fit within the narrowness of our intellect, let us confess it with unshaken equity, remaining within that fullness of divine justice, mercy, and foreknowledge.

Let us not, while disputing about the higher secrets of the divine will in a way exceeding the measure of our condition, abandon God’s justice and, wishing to establish our own, fall into the deepest abyss of defiance.

[Col. 0853C]

**LETTER OF THE DEACON FERRANDUS TO EGYPPIUS: ON THE ESSENCE OF THE TRINITY AND THE TWO NATURES OF CHRIST (S)**

[Col. 0853D] To his most blessed lord and brother, the presbyter Egyppius, Ferrandus, the least of all, sends greetings in the Lord.

My dearest, consider what force the question recently proposed by the Arian count possesses; but first let us deliberate on the ways in which Arians and Catholics differ from one another in their opinions and doctrines.

The Arians wish to proclaim the Trinity as undivided, just as the Scriptures proclaim one God; but the Catholics, hearing salutary precepts of the law, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0853] For the remainder, see among the works of the Deacon Ferrandus, which we shall publish shortly. EDITOR.]

**[EIGHTY SERMONS.]**

[Col. 0855]

**APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF SAINT FULGENTIUS. NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING EIGHTY SERMONS**

[Col. 0855A] As we read through all the sermons of Saint Fulgentius, it seemed to us that they could easily be reduced to three classes. The first consists of those that certainly acknowledge Fulgentius as their author, or at least come as close as possible to his style and character. The second class contains several sermons by an author different from Fulgentius and indeed certainly identifiable—no one other than Augustine, as will become clear from what we shall say by way of preliminary notice about each of them in its proper place below. Finally, the third class comprises all the remaining sermons by a different but altogether uncertain author.

To the first class belong those which we published above as genuine productions of Saint Fulgentius from previously printed editions, as well as the first of those which we are now publishing for the first time from a Vatican manuscript. To the second belong several of those which we shall present below in their order; they plainly claim Augustine as their author and are read among his works. To the third class we assign all the rest, which are about to follow immediately in this appendix.

With the exception of a few that may be attributed to some African, though not uneducated, man, they scarcely contain anything worthy not only of Fulgentius but of any other approved writer. Unless one should prefer to attribute them to the same author through whom most of them slipped into the works of Saint Augustine and are read in the appendix to volume five of the present edition, or volume ten of the earlier editions. If anything concerning particular pieces seems worth noting individually, or perhaps deserving correction, it will be indicated in the brief notice prefixed to each.

[Col. 0855A]

**OF SAINT FULGENTIUS, BISHOP—UNDER A FALSE TITLE—ON THE FOLLOWING HOMILIES OR SERMONS (C, G, S)**

**PREFACE**

[Col. 0855B] When he wishes to exercise his charity toward us, he has not displayed to you the customary clarity of his holy discourse. Therefore it is fitting for us obediently to do what he has willed, and for you willingly to endure it because he has willed it. Pray, then, for us, that our deeds may correspond to our words; for we desire rather, aided by your prayers, to grow rich in the fruits of our deeds than to be shaded by the leaves of our words.

We exhort your charity, dearly beloved brothers, not to be reluctant to listen eagerly and attentively when brothers and fellow presbyters minister the word of God to you. For our Lord and God, the very truth whom you hear, speaks through whomever he chooses; what he says must be heard devoutly and attentively. For among us no one is greater except the one who has become lesser.

We wished to speak to you in the customary manner so that you might do with love what we say. Salt is indeed a wholesome seasoning for all foods, if measure is not lacking. Otherwise, the salt itself is wasted, and it ruins what it has salted. Excessive quantity makes bitter what measure could have made flavorful.

So, too, the understanding within us, if it keeps to proper measure, gives good sense, produces understanding, generates prudence, enlarges the heart, increases intelligence, matures what is to be said, and orders what is to be heard. It becomes sweet to itself and, to those who taste it, becomes the fullness of all sweetness. That understanding will also plainly be honey-sweet if nothing bitter comes forth from the mouth from which it is spoken.

We have prefaced this so that in evangelical sayings our understanding may be restrained by a definite measure, lest it violate the living food, the divine nourishment, and the heavenly flavor, but may guard them for us with the utmost sobriety, according to the Apostle’s saying:

> “Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sober judgment” (Rom. XII, 3).

Therefore, let us now hear what the Lord said in the Gospel. Among the principal stars—the Great Bear, Orion, and the morning stars—the lesser star is always dimmed by the brightness of the greater ones. But it is not so in the new heaven of Mother Church, in which the star of Abraham’s offspring shines with the splendor of faith.

There, although I proceed like a very small star among the constellations, with the Fathers themselves shining upon me and instructing me, I trust that I shall not be obscured but illumined. Thus, for whatever I lack from the orbit of my own star, I may deserve something from the splendor of the paternal oracle, from your hearing, and from your attentive heart—which is to me like the heaven in which the star of my discourse, aided by it, proceeds, while paternal intercession advances together with your favor.

The archer of arrows fights securely when he is protected by a fortified line of shields covering him. Since, then, I see the Fathers strengthening me with the shield of their kindness, I am not afraid to shoot very slender sermons from a small quiver. When the arrow of my heart’s unadorned speech is shot from the ark of trembling lips in a weak voice, it will not fear, protected by the armor and shield-bearing circle of the holy Fathers.

For even those are the arrows of the Mighty One, shot from the bow of a little discourse. Together with coals that lay waste, they will cause our words to fail [Latin reading uncertain: *deliquent*] and illumine your hearts, so that the flaming arrows of the enemy may be extinguished and your wisdom may willingly hear, without the labor of battle, from the victory of the Fathers.

I see, dearly beloved brothers, the alacrity of your spirit, your tireless zeal, and your luminous fervor. But lest I myself be found sluggish amid your energy, let me not seem superfluous when I rouse the watchful and encourage those already aflame. Even if the discourse finds in you such a great contest that it cannot kindle anything more, it nevertheless wishes itself to burn together with you.

The ancient teaching of the holy Fathers and your luminous attention, brothers, terrify my small and inexperienced ability; yet again both their command and your kindness encourage me. For although you weigh what is said with highly learned examination, you nevertheless love everyone in Christ with such rich charity that you willingly listen not only to the strong and the moderately gifted, but also to the weak and the poor.

It is a great confidence born of charity to speak the word of God to those whom one knows and loves, where the fruit of devotion is expected. If something is presented in less polished speech, a friend readily forgives one whose speaker is not unknown to him.

In this respect, almighty God strengthens the prophet Ezekiel, who hesitated to carry out his proclamation, lest, tremblingly excusing himself on account of his inexperience, he should falter under the great burden of prophecy with his small shoulders. The Lord says to him:

> “Why do you hesitate? I am not sending you to a foreign nation; you will go to your own people, not to a people of an unknown language, but of a known one” (Ezek. III, 5).

Nor will you say, “I heard a language that I did not know.” The language is one, the words are alike, and the audience is fellow-citizens. And lest anything that was reprehensible in a known friend should appear in him to those who knew him, God handed him a book written within and without with heavenly pens and commanded him to swallow it with eager jaws, so that he might belch forth the delights he had tasted. He received it and devoured it. His tongue was instructed, his members were sweetened, and the skill of divine teaching that had been sweetly swallowed began to resound from the human being.

May the Lord likewise deign to grant us the delights of this book, so that he himself may teach what no human being has taught. I do not fear your familiar, civic assembly, trusting that you will rejoice to hear whatever sort of sermon it may be.

Whenever the word of divine command is spoken and royal doctrine is discussed in public, the ministering angels of the word of God are present: advocates of eloquence and interpreters of the mystery. Gabriel the interpreter was present to blessed Daniel when the emperor Cyrus stood at his right hand and said to him:

> “Gabriel, make him understand this vision” (Dan. VIII, 16).

May that same Lord now command, amid holy and great conversations, that we be commended by so great an angel, so that we may deserve to receive the meaning of angelic interpretation. Then we shall be able with confidence to offer a discourse somehow suited to your charity.

I know that your hearts are always filled with holy, sweet, abundant discourse and with very great affection. And because, through the assistance of the lord, my brother and fellow priest, you have often been accustomed to be filled with great banquets of spiritual things, it cannot be comprehended with what boldness or confidence you will be able to take pleasure in these words.

Presenting this to myself as such a very little human being, I dare less than I presume. But since I am summoned by the common vote [Note: [Col. 0857D] Here something is missing, such as “I am summoned,” or something similar.], I do not refuse to obey the commands, even though I blush. And therefore, like a kind of small advocate, I offer something mediocre—not to satisfy the heart, but to remove weariness.

Therefore, if whatever it may be is not altogether distasteful, I ask that you deign willingly to receive it. Lend attentive ears, you who love the word of God, and consider more carefully what, with the Lord’s gift, we shall be able to say.

For in proportion as the word of God is entrusted to us preachers, the abundance of the sacraments is increased for you. But just as one who enters the sea in a small boat fears less while he is near land, yet when he has gradually advanced into the deep and, as the waves swell, begins to be dragged down into the depths, fear immediately invades his mind and dread strikes him because he has entrusted a tiny craft to immense waves, so we too seem to suffer this, who, small in merits and weak in ability, dare to enter so vast a sea of mysteries.

But if, at your prayers, the Lord deigns to give us a favorable breeze from his Holy Spirit, we shall enter the harbor of salvation with the word proceeding on a prosperous course. The beginnings of our boldness would never easily break forth if your primacy and affectionate love toward me did not deign to grant me the license to speak. Whatever, therefore, we can draw from the divine springs and spiritually convey to your hearts for drinking, I ask that you deign to receive willingly.

## SERMON I. On the Nativity of Christ

The instruments of heaven are lowered, instruments that can sing the glory of the One who is being born. For as the angels descend, the heavenly Church is carried through the winds, so that the model of the heavenly homeland may now be transferred alive to earth.

Silence is everywhere, because all things yield to the instruments of heaven. The prophets are silent, the priests are quiet; only the melody of the angels is now fitting. Zechariah is silent in the temple; the angels have begun to sing a hymn from heaven. They cause the star to shine, the night to be bright, the shepherds to watch, the sheep to chew their cud, and the lambs to leap for joy.

A clear messenger, a sweet song, a gentle Lord born, strength for the shepherds, food for the flocks, song for the angels.

Blessed John describes one hundred and forty-four thousand singing a sweet hymn on Mount Zion, in the manner of harpists (Rev. VII, 4); but the sound of the angels is different. The shepherds’ hanging mouths were astonished; the lambs and sheep were silent, as though before a pastoral pipe, when the angels announced in a soothing hymn the One lying in the manger to the shepherds.

Father Abraham desires to receive in truth the Trinity whom he had received symbolically beneath the tent that sheltered him. Isaac rejoices beneath the Bethlehemite hut, as beneath a hundredfold ear of grain; he is illumined by the wheatlike medicine and is no longer visited.

The patriarch Jacob, beneath the ladder, beholds the Lord—not reclining upon the ladder, but being born from the earth, lying in a manger, and suckling at his mother’s breasts.

Moses leads the Israelite peoples (Deut. XVIII, 15), because a Prophet has been raised up for us from among our brothers. Isaiah, beneath the beloved vine, sings along with him, making the Church beneath thorny branches, because “a child is born to us, a son is given to us” (Isa. IX, 6).

He who invites the shepherds to the manger will choose fishermen from the shore, making earthly instruments by bending down the heavenly ones.

Already Matthew paints God as man, whom the Holy Spirit painted upon the tablet of virginal limbs. Already Mark the evangelist begins to bring forth the lion—not from a hunter’s cage, but from a stable’s cavern. Already Luke the evangelist carries the calf, fattened upon episcopal shoulders, so that the human race may feed upon it. And now the whole earth is plowed by the furrow of the cross, in the seed of tears and in the sheaves of joys; and calves are fattened for the banquet of Christian marriage.

Behold, the eagle already flies, and John bends the oarage of his little wings as far as the Lord’s breast, so that he may receive fragrance from Christ’s breast and extend his flight to heaven, sweeping through heaven in flight and song:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John I, 1).

For the evangelists delight to walk upon earth with Christ the Lord as he is born, to roar with him as he suffers, to sacrifice with him as he dies, and to fly with him as he rises and ascends.

From East and West they bring forth the eagle’s wings, leaving the earth, surrendering their limbs, and enduring torments. The wings of the martyrs have sailed as far as our shores and taught us to fly toward the Lord on the wings of righteousness.

The bones of the martyrs, the limbs of the saints, are the wings of eagles. The song of the angels invites them, as does the flight of the heavens, so that there may be joy for the shepherds, rumination for the sheep, and nourishment for the sweet lambs, because the Lamb of God has been born, the one who takes away the sin of the world.

## SERMON II

[Note: [Col. 0859D] It is read among Augustine’s Sermons I “On the Saints”; it appears in volume V of our edition, column 2145. We have not hesitated to publish it and several others that occur in this appendix, although they had previously been published among Augustine’s works, because, on comparing the two editions, we detected variant readings. EDITOR.]

**On the Nativity of Saint Stephen**

Yesterday we celebrated the nativity on which the King of martyrs was born into the world; today we celebrate the nativity on which the first-ranking martyr departed from the world. For it was fitting that the immortal One should first assume flesh for mortals, and that then a mortal should despise [variant: “assume”] death for the sake of immortals.

The Lord was born to die for the servant, so that the servant would not fear dying for the Lord. Christ was born on earth so that Stephen might be born in heaven. The Lord entered the world so that Stephen might enter heaven. The exalted One descended to lowliness, and the lowly one ascended to high things.

The Son of God became the son of man so that he might make the sons of human beings sons of God. Christ worked miracles, and Stephen did so as well. Could Stephen have done so without Christ? Stephen lived from Christ, as a branch lives from the vine. Do you marvel at fruit hanging from the branch? Look also at the branch remaining in the vine.

Come, Saint Stephen: say something about the Jews, so that you may begin to be stoned and thus be able to be crowned. Shoot forth words and receive stones. Say something about uncircumcised hearts, and you will die by stones. Say something about him whose name they do not wish to hear, and “let deceitful lips become ashamed and enraged and fall silent” (Psalm XXX, 19).

Tell them where you see alive the one whom they mocked as crucified. Tell them where you see him, and here you will not live, but you will live better with him. Tell them that what they did is nothing, for the one whom they killed is alive. Tell them that you see him in heaven standing at the Father’s right hand, the one whom they mocked as he hung upon the cross.

And Saint Stephen said:

> “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.”

But crying out, they stopped their ears (Acts VII, 56). They closed their ears and ran toward the stones; they all rushed upon him. And they were stoning Stephen as he called upon the Lord and said (Ibid., 57):

> “My soul has clung to you, because my flesh is being stoned for you.”

Christ prayed for his crucifiers, and Stephen prayed for those who stoned him. The Lord Christ prayed fastened to the wood, while Saint Stephen prayed on bended knee. The one who, standing, commended his spirit to the Lord prayed for their offense with knee bent.

He prayed to the Lord for his enemies as a friend, saying:

> “Certainly I am suffering, I am being stoned; they rage against me and roar against me. But do not hold this sin against them” (Ibid., 60),

because, in saying this to you, I first heard it from you. I, your servant, suffer, but there is a great difference between me and you. You are Lord; I am servant. You are the Word; I am a hearer of the Word. You are teacher; I am disciple. You are Creator; I am created. You are God; I am human.

There is a great difference between the sin of those who are stoning me and that of those who crucified you. Therefore, when you said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34), you asked forgiveness for a great sin and taught me to ask it for a small one.

“Lord,” he said, “do not hold this sin against them.” It was as though he were saying: “I suffer in the flesh; let these not perish in the mind.”

They were throwing stones, while Saint Stephen poured out prayers. Great is the piety, brothers; great is the clemency. Indeed, what he ate at the table of his Lord, he himself prepared at his own banquet.

It is written in the law:

> “You have sat down at a great table; know that you must prepare such things” (Eccli. XXXI, 12).

Thus he displayed in prayer things such as he had eaten at the table of his Lord. The Lord Christ said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing”; Saint Stephen said, “Do not hold this sin against them.” And after saying this, he fell asleep in the Lord.

O sleep of peace! What is more tranquil than that sleep? What is quieter than that sleep? How he went to his friends, since he loved his enemies in such a way!

So that your holiness may know how powerful the prayer of Saint Stephen the martyr was, return with us to that young persecutor named Saul, as we heard when the book was being read. While Stephen was being stoned, Saul guarded the garments of all those who were stoning him, so that he himself seemed to be stoning Stephen in the hands of them all.

As Saul was traveling on the road, suddenly a light from heaven surrounded him, and he heard a voice saying to him:

> “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.”

And he said:

> “Who are you, Lord?”

And the Lord said to him:

> “I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting” (Acts IX, 3–5).

“What have I to do with you? Why do you rise up against me to your own harm, rather than humble yourself for your own good? For the great evils that you have committed against me, I ought long ago to have destroyed you. But my Stephen prayed for you. Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? But because you rage against my name, I shall make you my servant.”

O Saul, ravening wolf: you have eaten—wait a little, and you will digest.

Let me say it plainly: the son of perdition was struck down, and the Chosen Vessel was raised up. For if Saint Stephen had not prayed, the Church would not have had Paul. But Paul was raised up because Stephen, bent down upon the earth, was heard.

Therefore what Saul did, Paul suffers; what the persecutor did, the preacher suffers; what the wolf did, the lamb suffers. For in such a person punishment must be inflicted in such a way that he learns to suffer what he was doing and himself feels what he was inflicting upon others.

The Lord Jesus Christ said to Ananias:

> “Go to him and mark him with my sign” (Ibid., 11).

Ananias went, baptized Saul, and made a lamb from the wolf. We began to have as our preacher the man whom Saint Stephen had had as his stoner.

Thus Saint Stephen was heard, so that through his prayers the sin committed by Saul might be erased. Let us therefore commend ourselves to his prayers; for he is heard all the more now on behalf of those who honor him, since he was then heard on behalf of those who stoned him.

## SERMON III

[Note: [Col. 0860D] It belongs neither to Augustine nor to Fulgentius nor to any other learned man, as is clear from the fact that below it says that Christ, hanging on the cross, said, “Amen, amen, I say to you, from now on you will see…” Nevertheless, it appears in volume V of our edition of Augustine, column 2143.]

**On the Nativity of Saint Stephen**
Our Lord Jesus Christ, the good, gentle, and merciful shepherd, mingles his sheep among wolves in this world, so that he may help them from his throne. Do you wish to see, whoever you are, Christian, the Lord Jesus Christ mingling sheep among wolves? In the reading of the present Gospel he himself cried out, saying: “Behold, I am sending you as sheep in the midst of wolves” (Matt. 10:16). Do you wish again to see the Lord Jesus Christ leading his sheep out of the hands of wolves? He himself cries out and says: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10:14). The wolf is destroyed when the shepherd is killed. The sheep is redeemed when the shepherd is crucified.

The sheep sent into the midst of wolves ought not to fear. For they are mingled with wolves for this purpose: not that they should be changed into the wolves’ wickedness, but that the wolves should be converted to the innocence of the sheep. But if they do not wish to become lambs, let the sheep not fail, following the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world.

Behold the first sheep, Saint Stephen: how, by the testimony of faith, he drives away the wolves while they cry out, and with his own eyes sees the heavens opened! A most excellent sheep fighting in the midst of wolves, following—and not yet having reached—the Lord, he is already the friend of the angels. How manifestly was he familiar and friendly with the angels, he who appeared like an angel in the midst of wolves! For when the heavens were opened, the appearance of the confessor was changed; and he began to shine like the sun, illumined by righteousness, so that he no longer had a human appearance while the heavens themselves stood open and his enemies themselves bore witness. For he stood in the midst of wolves, and his face was like the face of an angel standing in the midst of the Jews (Acts 6:15).

What are you doing, O Jews? Do you not fear Christ’s first sheep and foot-soldier, who bears upon his forehead the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? This is the sign that shone upon you from Stephen’s forehead. The heavens saw this sign and were opened; and, as though a seal had been displayed in the form of an angel, the gates of heaven were opened. For Saint Stephen came with the keys of faith, and opened for himself what he had faithfully believed and gladly beheld.

What he saw, therefore, he did not keep silent about. “Behold,” he said, “I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the Father” (Acts 7:15). But what remained for him to see, once the heavens had been opened, except the very Lord and Savior who had ascended into heaven? We all see these heavens, but closed, not opened; shining with stars, not sparkling with angels. But this man, now no longer merely human but an angelic man, does not look upon the seat of his Lord’s palace as closed, but as opened. He sees not angels but archangels; indeed, he sees them too, but proclaims the one to whom he was a witness. He exalts the one whose servant he is, perfected in the contest.

For how great was the grace granted to Saint Stephen! He saw the army of the heavenly host standing; he saw the Son of Man seated at the Father’s right hand. Behold, he sees the Lord while he himself was already departing to the Lord; and, by the merit of his confession, he beholds the assembly of the heavenly powers, though he was already about to depart to the realm of the dead. But among the dead he cried out, while among the wolves he shone.

“Behold,” he says, “I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the Father.” Let friends rejoice if enemies blaspheme. Let the sheep not be silent in giving testimony, even if the wolves cry out in blasphemy. For they closed their minds and said, “He has blasphemed.” The Jewish high priest Caiaphas said the same about the Son of Man, who was suffering and enduring all things.

When our Lord Jesus Christ, suspended on the cross, said, “Amen I say to you, from now on you will see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the Father” (Matt. 26:64), Caiaphas cried out, saying, “He has blasphemed” (ibid., 65). Caiaphas tore his garments; these men closed their minds. Caiaphas did so in order to remain naked; they did so in order to remain in their wickedness.

O great miracle! The gates of heaven are opened, and the Jews have closed their impious minds. But Saint Stephen did not keep silent, did not falter, and did not yield to those who blasphemed. He kept his attention fixed where he opened the eyes of his heart.

“Behold,” he says, “I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” But why are you angry with me, Jews, for so great a testimony? Were the heavens opened at my command or by my power? They were opened not to proclaim my glory, but to show my shepherd standing to assist me. Consider, then, and see how far I am from heaven, placed with you here on earth. Could I have reached it and opened the gates of heaven? The Lord of angels himself opened his palace for me.

Rightly, in a certain sense, I see; and what I see I do not keep silent about. I did not despise him hanging on the cross; therefore I see him seated at the right hand of the Father. This testimony from heaven has been given to you; but if you do not believe, what have I done to you? “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:1), and shall I be silent about the mercy of my Christ? I see Christ seated in his glory and standing to assist me in my salvation. He himself is my witness in heaven; shall I not be his witness on earth? If I confess him before men, he too will confess me before his angels. But if I deny him on earth, he too will deny me in heaven.

Yet for such faithful testimonies you throw stones, close your minds, and refuse to hear what is said plainly and openly to you. Strike, strike with stones the one who confesses; I have my helper at the Father’s right hand. You strike my head; I commend my spirit to him.

“Lord Jesus,” he says, “receive my spirit” (Acts 7:58). They curse; you bless. They persecute; you receive the one who is persecuted. Not without cause, my Jesus, my Lord, do you deign to stand at the Father’s right hand for me, whom I know and believe to be seated at the Father’s right hand. It is for me that you deign to stand; standing, you do not fail, and you do not abandon those whom you must help.

You, my Lord, sent me into the midst of enemies; you deigned to make me the first martyr after your ascension. If you wish me not to fail you, help me. Let the crushing of the stones cease, lest the strength of my limbs fail within me. For me, my Lord, you speak while standing: I hear the embassy of your voice; I believe, I accept, I recognize you as asking the Father on my behalf, giving and assisting, so that my faith may not fail as I follow you.

What does my Jesus, my Lord, say as he asks the Father on my behalf?

“Father, behold this first foot-soldier has entered a new contest on my behalf in the world. Grant mercy; let him reach victory. Let my sheep feel that you are assisting him, lest he think that I have handed him over among the wolves.”

Behold, I see him standing; I dare to believe that he is asking on my behalf. And therefore, my Lord, who behold my contest, receive my spirit. But because I do not fear, Lord, though my limbs are being stoned, place my spirit in everlasting rest. Among these men I have been reckoned as a sheep for slaughter; with you let me be placed in the rest of sweetness and peace.

The Jews were stoning; he was groaning. The Jews were striking his head; he was commending his spirit. But once he had become secure concerning the spirit he had commended, he became an advocate for his enemies; and he does not plead for his enemies in the same way that he had pleaded for himself. He was standing when he saw Christ; he bent his knees when he prayed for his enemies.

For advocacy was necessary for such numerous and such terrible enemies. He knew that the Lord Jesus could not quickly hear him on their behalf, because he was asking for their sin, not on the basis of his own merit. Therefore, for the great wickedness of the Jews who were stoning him, he bent his knees and shed tears, saying: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (ibid., 59).

See, whoever you are, Christian, how this sheep follows and imitates the shepherd in everything. The Lord Christ, suspended on the cross, cried out: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit”; this man says: “Lord, receive my spirit.” The Lord Christ cries out for his enemies: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing”; this man says: “Do not hold this against them as sin.”

And plainly, my brothers, in the midst of these stoners—among whom he raged most fiercely—the blessed apostle Paul was present. If vengeance had then been granted to Stephen against the one who was stoning him, how would the Church have had such a teacher?

After saying these things, he gave up his spirit, ascended into heaven, and obtained forgiveness for his enemies. He deserved to rejoice in heaven over the friendship of the blessed Paul who followed him, because he is the Lord who makes the barren woman rejoice in her house of children (Ps. 112:9).

Behold what Saint Stephen merited: he saw the Son of Man standing, whom we know to be seated at the Father’s right hand. Let us ask that he intercede for us and for our sins, and rescue us from all such dangers and all birth-pangs, through his goodness, not on account of our conscience. For what, or how many, sources of our sin can extinguish the flame? May he himself deign to bury our crimes, so that, just as he briefly entrusted his limbs to a new tomb, so he may bury our sins in the fountain of forgiveness, that together with him we may always rejoice in the holy Church.

[Col. 0863A]

## SERMON IV. On the Epiphany of the Lord and on the Innocents

Christ has been born; heaven and earth rejoice together, because the star rejoices and the Magi offer gifts. The Magi offered a great gift, because they sang a new song in the midst of the shepherds, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). The stars of heaven also offered a gift. For behold, a star proceeded from the midst of the stars, sent forth as though on a great embassy. It looked upon the Magi traveling, not knowing the way, and seeking the Lord.

The star was told: “Go, show them the way. This is my grace for those who love me: let them have a forerunner in the star.” Behold, while the Magi considered the road—ready with their gifts, ignorant of the way, and insufficiently instructed about the Lord—he gave them a star to serve as a lamp during their nighttime journey. He provided them with a torch, so that they would not suffer harm in the night.

They began to follow the star, becoming certain, instructed as ambassadors, and guided as far as the place. From there the star withdrew, once it had shown the Lord to the Magi. For when someone begins to know the Lord, he has no need to fear any enemy.

Behold how much they merited who offered gifts to the Lord. In the same way angels lead us when we offer glory to the Lord, the everlasting King; we offer him glory and honor. The angels provide us with the sweetest service of their guidance.

But the gifts must be weighed according to the dignity of the person. He is emperor: he must be adorned with gold. He is Lord: incense must be offered to him. He became human for us, so that he might dwell in us: myrrh must be used for his burial, so that a living memory may remain in our hearts and he may always appear to us in glory.

The Magi were also warned in a dream by an angel not to return to announce anything to Herod, but to travel back to their own region by another route. Then, when Herod saw that he had been deceived by the Magi, his face changed and his mind was troubled. He sent for the scribes and elders and questioned them, saying: “Where do you know that the future king is to be born?” They answered: “In Bethlehem; for it is written: ‘And you, Bethlehem of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers, for from you will go forth a King who will rule my people’” (Matt. 2:4–5).

Then Herod sent armed soldiers and, threatening them with a terrible command, said: “Go to Bethlehem of Judah, and whatever you find there, from two years old and under, kill the male child, but let the female live.”

At that very moment I saw the Lord choosing friends for himself and calling the innocent to himself, so that the friend might be innocent, just as the Lord is innocent—the spotless Lamb who took away the sin of the world. The innocent became his friends, as it is written: “The innocent and upright have clung to me, because I have awaited you, Lord” (Ps. 24:21).

He awaited him while fleeing into Egypt, and made for himself armies of infants, to whom he granted martyrdom without pain: for the mothers felt pain, while the infants, without knowing it, rejoiced. The conscience of the innocent did not fear the sword of the executioner, because the innocent flight of the Savior rejoiced together with them.

The Lord is sought, and his friends are slaughtered, so that innocent blood might mourn those whom the shameless sword separated. O shameless right hand of the executioner! It has nothing to strike among the limbs, yet it stretches out the arms of savagery. The sword had no proper place, and the executioner felt no shame: the sword was broader than the entrails, so that the sword might bear the crime, not innocence.

When they were torn from their mothers’ embraces by the severe hand of the torturers, while they clasped their mothers with tender fingers and lamented with pitiful groans, one mother cried out:

“O son, why do you hold me back, while the executioner separates you from me? You clasp my hands, while my affection is tortured. The king has ordered you to be separated from me, but there is an eternal King through whom you will be joined to me. Son, I bid you farewell. The earth drinks your blood, but God will receive your spirit.”

From another side one mother cried out, and another mother wept from elsewhere: everywhere mourning, everywhere groaning. The decree was one not of desire but of bereavement.

The mothers cried out from every side:

“Executioner, do you hasten to tear my little one away from me? Grant a delay, if you have any compassion. You take my son from me, and am I not to have even a moment with him? I conceived him; I gave birth to him. But I have found you a stepfather of cruelty.

“At least let my little one not depart from me hungry. I will give him the provisions of milk, so that he may have rich entrails on which you may fatten the sword of cruelty. Let a little blood join the nourishment of milk, so that your sword may be satisfied and my son’s soul be made radiant with milk and blood. Just as blood was purple like a tunic with a central stripe, so milk was a shining, precious robe.

“What was it like to see the milk and blood of murdered infants mingled and not separated from one another?”

And the mother cried out to the executioner:

“I am going with you; I am coming with you. I accompany you, about to watch my sweetest son. I plant a kiss, and you plant your sword. You strike, and I receive the blood of the innocent. You slaughter without cause, and I receive my own entrails. If I was not permitted to give milk, at least let me be permitted to prepare the grave.”

Amid the lamentation of the mothers and the wailing of the children, the Lord was in flight. The swordsmen were striking, the mothers were burying, the angels were receiving the spirit, and Christ was saying: “The innocent and upright have clung to me.”

If we wish to cling to Christ, let us be free from wickedness and hold fast to simplicity, so that we may deserve mercy from the Lord.

## SERMON V. On Abraham

It is a pleasing spectacle for those who gaze upon the painting shaded by the curtain, when the painter’s brush forms a sword in the father’s hand over the son whom he loves. There the father is painted standing upright, the son bent down. How the viewer’s gaze is moved, pierced by a certain stimulus of compassion, when it sees a child on bent knees, bound with hands twisted behind him! No foreign captor binds him; only the paternal affection that disregards its own entrails does so.

This painting on the shaded curtain is pleasing to those who look at it. Yet the truth of the sacrificed Lamb, whom God the Father offered for the world, is regarded by few and despised by some—though the entire army of angels beholds it both on the wood and on the throne.

Some say: “What kind of one is he who demanded a sacrifice of blood?” It was not a desire for blood, but a testing of love and affection.

Look, then, upon the hanging curtain of this reading; and with your eyes gladly fixed upon it, see Abraham, the father, saddling the ass, setting out on the journey, and accompanying his son—not to a feast, but to a sacrifice; or rather, to a feast, so that he might present to them the ram as a sacramental sign.

What does the altar that has been constructed signify except the cross raised upon the mountain? What is the bound son except Christ fastened with nails, so that he himself might carry the chain, though he had no debt-bearing conscience?

The father raises his right hand. The angel, with a mighty cry, moves the earth, so that he should not grieve over the slaughtered boy but rejoice over the Lord’s slaughtered Lamb:

“Abraham, Abraham!”

He raises his face, which had bent toward the sword.

“What is it, Lord?” (Gen. 22:11)

“I have taken care to fulfill what you commanded; you delay my joy by interrupting me with your cry. What do you command, Lord? Let there be no delay at all in what I am doing with joy.”

For he was doing it with joy. Inwardly, the spirit was prophesying that an innocent one had to be slaughtered for the salvation of the world, and he believed that salvation for the world would come through the slaughtered son.

“Do not stretch out your hand over the boy,” he says (ibid., 12). What you suppose is one thing; what you rejoice over is another. Behold, you have the prince in the ram. For your son belongs to that flock.

He turns his face so that he might receive the hidden sacramental meaning. Behold, the ram was held fast by thorns, and its forehead was covered in their shade. Its face was free, its gaze clear. Those thorns served as ribbons around its horns and as jeweled ornaments. There were no sins in those thorns, so that a crown might be prepared for the head of the flock from the precious head of the shepherd.

He seizes the ram and releases the child. The ram that took his place is silent, and the angel who cried out from heaven is silent. Where is the angel’s voice that forbade the sacrifice of the child? Why does he not cry out in the same way for the ram? He must not allow the world to remain in guilt if the Lamb were to cease from the cross.

In Isaac there had been a testing of love; in the ram, a prefiguration of the truth. There was obedience in the one, mercy in the other. There the will gave; here gratuitous grace.

The angel is silent because, while the Lamb was suffering, the angelic host rejoiced. If the angel had cried out from heaven, “Abraham, spare the Lamb,” just as he had said, “Spare your son,” the Lamb, wearied by the approach of his passion, might have abandoned it, and no one would have suffered the scandal of his death on the cross.

“My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38). He did not cry out from heaven, because the Emperor was suffering by his own choice.

“Father,” he says, “if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (ibid., 39).

And no angel cried out from heaven; but an angel descended, conversing with his Lord and strengthening him—not by his own counsel, but rather through the sacramental mystery of the Lord himself.

Isaac returned unharmed to his home, and the glorified Lamb returned to heaven. Abraham led his son to death so that he might receive him back resurrected in a better state. Abraham offered the Son; and you, from righteous works and labors, offer the Lord a sacrifice, so that together with Father Abraham you may have one joy in the kingdom of heaven.

[Col. 0865B]

## SERMON VI [Note: [Col. 0865D] In a Vatican manuscript it is attributed to Augustine.]

On the only son and the centurion’s child

Blessed is the Lord, who alone works wonders. The centurion is a witness on behalf of a child; the widowed mother is a witness in her son. In the one case there is power; in the other, compassion. There a great embassy; here a pitiable abandonment [manuscript: miserable abandonment].

The centurion sent elder ambassadors, while she sought bearers for her dead son. He said: “My child lies paralyzed in the house and is being grievously tormented” (Matt. 8:6); she said: “I grieve with bitter indignation over the fruit of my womb, taken away from me. My son has indeed rested in peace, and my womb has been left in sorrow.” [Note: Other copies: “Where is the fruit of my womb?”]

The centurion commanded: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (ibid., 8); she was thinking of preparing a pitiable tomb for her only son.

Between these two persons—the centurion and the mother, the rich man and the needy woman, the powerful soldier and the lamenting widow—the Lord practiced his customary mercy [Note: So the manuscript reads. Other copies: “the Lord practiced his own care of his hidden purposes.”], for he accepts no one’s person. He sent his word quickly and healed the paralyzed child [Col. 0865C], so that he might hasten to go and raise the only son.

He did not wait for an embassy, for he knew that the wretched mother had no ambassadors, but was hiring workers to dig a grave. He proceeded silently toward the city, he who opens the gates of Jerusalem to believers. At the gate of her homeland, the woman approached with her dead son, and Christ opened the door of healing.

The apostles followed him, and rejoicing angels, while weeping crowds accompanied the mother, moved by their shared human condition. Between the dead man and the Lord a gate stood in the way. He went out through the gate and found life.

The streets of the city resounded with the mother’s mourning, and heaven resounded with the groan of compassion. Cry out, Raphael, angel accompanying the coming Lord:

“Do not, do not weep, mother; joy is near you.”

But she who was wailing—what complaints she uttered, filling heaven and earth with her cries! She had lost the son whom she possessed:

“Where is he, where is my only son, born in vain [manuscript: born in old age]? He was quickly snatched away; your place is in peace, but dreadful mourning has remained for me. You are carried on a bier, while I have already become a burden to the world [manuscript: I have become dishonored in the world].

“Why did you not survive me and close your mother’s eyes in death? Why, with your eyes pressed shut by the ruin of death, did you not precede me, wretched as I am? Why was I not found worthy to be buried by your hands—as is always desirable—but was found worthy to be bound by the most cruel chains of your death?

“You ought to have handed me over to the earth, because you came forth from my womb. There is no father, no brother. Do you think it is true that ‘a brother will not redeem, a man will redeem’ (Ps. 48:8)? Where is that Lord, the judge of widows and father of orphans? Why does he not regard my mourning, he who promised joy to those who mourn?
