“I heard him saying: ‘Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted’ (Matt. 5:4). Behold, I am a widow; where is my judge? Behold, you are an orphan; where is your father?

“If only, Lord, you had brought sudden judgment upon me for my sin, and made a tomb for my only son within my womb, so that my womb might be a domestic grave and a hidden burial! In the light of this air and under this heaven, the funeral oration of my dear dead one has gone forth.

“Let those who have children and shine with a many-child crown look upon this. Let them see that one little flower of my head, one jewel of my crown, has fallen from my head, and that I remain bald instead of possessing a crown of joy.

“Let no one condemn my tears. I mourn one only son; I am not guilty, because I have no other. And if there is someone who reproves me, would my comforter come to me?”

And immediately, before she had finished these complaints and lamentations with heaven as witness, behold, the Lord of the city had already come to the gates. He approached the gate, opened life, and closed hell. Dark mourning came forth from the gate, and light shone when Christ arrived. He flashed his lightning and dispersed the crowds that followed him.

Before doing so, however, he stood [manuscript: he looked attentively] and felt compassion. For “we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses” (Heb. 4:15). He sympathized with the only son, he who as the only Son hung upon the wood.

“Stand,” the Lord said; “stand; let the bearers labor no longer. Set down the dead man; await the miracle. Fill the tomb with earth, for when the dead man is raised, earth and heaven will rejoice.”

They stood, set him down, and provided silence [variant: time]. They were awaiting some action, but they heard nothing except one word, and they were terrified at the dead man now alive. He who spoke, and all things came to be, spoke, and the young man received life again.

He cast off the linen wrappings [manuscript: he broke through them], tore apart the fatal chain, sat up, rose, and worshiped.

“Thank you,” he said, “my Lord and God. How terrible you are, and how gentle! That you are terrible is witnessed by unbridled hell; that you are gentle is witnessed by my mother and by my life.

“I saw the terrible power of your name when I saw death trembling, recognizing you as you approached me in mercy. You commanded, and it trembled. It gave back one whom it had not borne, and it closed its open jaws.

“I thank you, Lord, because the pit did not open its mouth over me, but you wiped away my tears through the springs of the waters of life.”

Then the Lord, who had said, “Young man, I say to you, arise” (Luke 7:14), answered his mother:

“Woman, behold your son; and know that I am the judge of widows and the father of orphans” (Ps. 67:6). I saw your tears and recognized your complaints. I did not condemn the woman who mourned; I consoled the one who lamented.

And the mother, her voice shaken with joy, said:

“My Lord and God, what thanks shall I give you? Your compassion bears witness. With what praises ought I to honor you, since you did not permit me, desolate and wretched, to beg? Let the angels give thanks to you on my behalf, since they ascend and descend, and let the entire expanse of heaven rejoice for me.

“May the gate of heaven be opened for you, because before the gate you restored to me the pledge of my funeral. O good and great miracle! Outside the gate the Lord raised the dead man, he who outside Jerusalem redeemed the human race.

“Behold, the only son went forth on a bier, but together with the reproach of the cross.”

The women were mourning, while he himself rejoiced, because that cross was not a reproach but rather an ornament, by which the whole world was adorned, and through which the army of peoples faithful with the mother shone forth.

## SERMON VII. On the Two Blind Men

What great gain it is to sit beside the road through which Christ is pleased to pass! It is a royal road, full of holy angels, so that the sight of blindness may be illumined by the salve of brightness. Our Emperor is passing by. Carriages do not precede him with splendor; miracles precede him with power, while the lame are enabled to run and the blind to receive light.

[Col. 0867A]

This is the road of our Emperor, the road by which one comes to life, because he himself is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6). Whoever sits on the road along which Christ passes cannot be ruled by a tyrant, nor can a person remain sick when Christ the physician passes by.

These two blind men believed this about the Lord. Sitting beside the road, they cried out in a strong voice to the physician, desiring that sight be restored to them. At their cry, the crowds of the peoples preceding them roared; the army of angels rejoiced; and the one who illuminates the blind himself prepared the cure.

What were those blind men crying out, who desired to see the light?

“Have mercy on us, Lord, Son of David” (Matt. 20:30).

But the crowds thought that our physician was being annoyed and commanded them to be silent as Christ passed by. They cried out more forcefully and paid no attention to the crowds rebuking them. They repeated their cry even more, so that by their very voices they might penetrate to the Savior:

“Have mercy on us, Lord, Son of David” (ibid., 31).

We pay no attention at all to human voices. You have mercy, who heal human errors.

The Lord therefore walked along his road, he who is eternal life. He passed by and healed; he saw the thoughts of the blind beforehand and rejoiced at their cry. He took no pleasure in the opposition of the crowds, but rejoiced in the desire of the blind men who cried out in a loud voice.

He stood still, so that healing might travel farther than footsteps. And, with the crowds following, he commanded the blind men to come to him and fear nothing beneath heaven. The crowds rebuked, compelled, invited, and wonderfully urged them forward.

How delighted they were, those whom the Lord was calling! Their cry achieved this for them: the opposition of the crowds did not frighten them. They saw the Savior first through desire, before they saw the brightness of light.

Sight and blindness stood before the Lord. The road stood still for those sitting beside the road. Those who remained in darkness stood still while the light of eternity stood there—the light that causes light to rise in darkness.

The crowd that followed and preceded became a theater, and the Church of the angels rejoiced.

Jesus says to them: “What do you want me to do for you?” (ibid., 32).

Hearing the physician’s voice, they fell prostrate in voice and heart:

“Lord, you see our condition; grant us your healing, so that our eyes may be opened and we may deserve to be companions of your journey, because on the road we have deserved to be healed by you, the physician.”

The Lord, who raises those who are bowed down and gives light to the blind (Ps. 145:8–9), heard them, had mercy, and healed them. No remedies intervened, and the blind began to see by the word alone. No regulation of foods was required; only the authority of medicinal commands intervened.

Jesus says to them: “Let it be done for you according to your faith” (Matt. 9:29).

Immediately blindness fled and brightness was restored. They looked upon the face of the Savior, whom they had not known as the one healing by his power. With their eyes they learned who he was, though by their words they had already presumed to know him.

They fell at his knees, now knowing how to touch Christ’s footsteps—those who, sitting beside the road, had cried out with their voices alone—and they began to accompany Christ the Lord along one road. Rejoicing in his company and now joined to him in brightness, they would never wholly depart from Christ.

So let us also, brothers, sit on that very road along which we hope that Christ the Lord may pass. For he does not walk on the road of the impious, since he did not stand on the road of sinners.

Christ the Lord is now making his passage from the world, while he intercedes for us in heaven. But he walks only on a clean road, because his way is undefiled. Let us sit there; let us cry out there. He passes by every day, because he never departs from us.

But if someone sees us among the world’s murmurers, sees us crying out more forcefully to Christ, and begins to blaspheme us because of his own scandal, we must pay no attention at all to his envy. Let us keep our gaze fixed there, from where we hope for help.

## SERMON VIII. On the Three Boys

The liberation of the redeemed is near, because already the free captivity of the boys is triumphing. It is already near that, just as the bonds of the saints melt in the fire, so the sins of the elect may be dissolved in the font.

In both places a pleasant tranquility breathes like dew, because warm charity refreshes them. In the font, however, burning iniquity is extinguished, because in both the furnace and the font the Angel of Great Counsel will descend from heaven, so that what he granted to the boys in refreshment he may give to believers in the sacrament.

Behold how many trumpets of the saints sounded one by one; now three horns resound together in one pleasant field of flames. It is beautiful to see three golden lampstands. It is beautiful to behold the bodies of the three boys assailed, because they were one soul while they pressed forward toward the crown.

The flame did not divide them, and their songs joined them together, because the Angel of Great Counsel embraced them and sheltered them in his overshadowing arms.

What are royal palaces compared with the furnace of the singing boys? The king’s hall became a sanctuary of holiness, so that the king might delight in looking upon them there more than in dwelling in his royal house.

O those streets paved not with marble but with fire, not with mosaics but with flames! Proud kings walk upon purple carpets, playing with delicate steps; but on the fiery street our men proceed while singing.

Who would not delight in accompanying them with equal steps, when it delights the angel to be joined to them in equal song?

One thing the sight revealed, another the senses supplied; one thing the sense of touch showed, another was within and another without. For the angels were within and the enemies without: within they were singing, outside they were burning.

See, my brothers, how much it matters to be inside the great house in which there are vessels of gold and silver (2 Tim. 2:20), rather than to burn outside among wooden vessels, among wood, hay, and stubble.

But the furnace of God’s temple contains you as tested gold. Your vessels are produced from gold, in which Jerusalem, the eternal homeland, may rejoice. And may the Savior himself, rather than Nebuchadnezzar, marvel at you; from the flames of the world, amid the refreshing pleasantness of life, may he console you with us from heaven.

## SERMON IX. On the Woman Caught in Adultery
The Son of God must be feared and loved. Feared as judge, loved as king: for he did not come first to judge, but initially to set free, and afterward to judge justly. Meek [Col. 0868C] and true—but the Jewish slanderer did not recognize this. They sought to condemn his meekness, and in their own crime they found its strength. They sought to assail Christ’s meekness and either to violate justice or to criticize justice on account of meekness. They stood in the narrow space between two walls, besieging the Savior, who was to be handed over like a robber. They bring an accusation and are found guilty in their own conscience. They accuse so that they themselves may be accused and the adulterous woman set free. It was not the deed that displeased them, but the Lord. For they were all adulterers. They find an occasion in the adulterous woman so that they might attach to it an accusation seemingly colored with justice.

They find a wretched woman darkened by the stain of recent adultery, so that before the Lord’s feet they might see her whitened by the snow of forgiveness. Many slanderers and sinners, plotters and thieves, gather and bring her. They place themselves with the adulterer in his portion (Ps. XLIX, 18), and lead the adulterous woman away. Many bring one woman before the indulgence of the one Lord.

Drag her, Jews, drag her; drive the adulterous woman out of iniquity [Col. 0868D]. Free from the open waves the ship whose planks have been split apart. You have taken counsel concerning the shattered ship; the Lord, its craftsman, knows how to join it, close it, chastise it, and caulk it. He has drained from it the bilge that rose up to its sides, while a foul residue remains in your conscience. You did not wisely wish to hold the oars of malice against the wretched ship; behold, you will begin to struggle in the inner waves of your accusation, while she will begin to sail with the sails of chastity.

Go, woman: you are being led to mercy, not severity; you are being dragged before an emperor, not a judge. An end has come both for them and for you: for you, so that you may not live wickedly; for them, so that they may recognize that they are living wickedly. A great crowd gathers. The trembling woman is seized and brought forward by the hands of many. She is set in the middle. As though they had not come to ask a question but already to issue a condemnation, they raise their cloaks and tunics violently aloft; their faces are disturbed, their eyes bloodshot, their voices confused and mingled. Standing before one who was seated, they shouted at one who was silent but silently judging:

“Woman,” they say, “this woman was caught in adultery [Col. 0869A]. Moses commanded that such women be stoned. What do you say about her?” (John VIII, 5–6).

They ask a judgment of the Judge who is the Judge of judges. But he, sitting with his head bowed in humility, was writing meekness with his finger on the ground—not Jewish meekness, but Christian meekness. They prepared stones, while he wrote with his finger on the ground. The questioners received no answer. Shamelessly they repeat their question, thinking that he could find no answer. In their fury they press him, demanding a sentence, wishing to snatch neither a quick sparrow nor an eagle flying high in the sky.

Lifting his face in compassion, he replied with deliberate and measured pace, giving both what she wanted and what they did not want.

“What do you say? You demand Moses’ judgment? You ask justly; let what you desire be done justly. The woman must be stoned. You who are her accusers, be her executioners—if you presume yourselves innocent. Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (ibid., 7).

O great sentence, which he wrote with the finger of his spirit upon the ground! He recited it, and the Jew fell silent. No one first, no one last, no one in the middle: every person was guilty [Col. 0869B]. They began to examine themselves, and one after another went out.

You entered with violence; you depart in silence. Stay—why are you leaving, you who registered the woman as guilty? Satisfy the laws, if you are confident about your morals. What unjust thing have I said? You stone her. If you are guilty, learn meekness from me, because you too need the mercy of judgment.

Where are those who wished to corrupt meekness and criticize justice on the grounds of justice? He both maintained meekness and preserved justice. If he had said, “Let her be stoned,” he would have seemed not to be meek. If he had said, “Let her not be stoned,” he would have seemed not to be just. He answered in such a way that judgment remained for the tempters, while only shame remained for the accusers.

The woman remained standing before the Judge; the accuser remained nowhere. She is not dismissed so that she may wander again, but she is taught by most merciful chastity. She is not freed so that she might be released into sin.

“Woman,” says the Lord, “where are those who accused you? Has no one condemned you?”

And she: “No one, Lord” (ibid., 10–11).

Then the just Judge said:

“Your accusers have fled from you; let sin flee as well. You have escaped the Jews who accused you; fear the angels who will drag you to my judgment [Col. 0869C]. Nor will I condemn you, because I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world through me. Learn to live well, and now sin no more. Learn justice, because you have already been freed from the sentence.

“Woman, I will not sit upon the throne of judgment in the manner in which I now sit, bent toward the earth. Another terror will be present then; the Jewish accusers will not be there. They accuse themselves, those who come in this manner to the judgment where the fire will not be extinguished and the worm will not die” (Mark IX, 44). “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. VIII, 12). There will be a terrible trumpet; the heavens will be shaken; angels will hasten and sound the great trumpet; the sun will be darkened, the moon confounded, the stars falling, the guilty trembling, a fiery judgment, a throne of fire, and before him a mighty storm (Ps. XLIX, 4).

“I grant mercy; I allow delay. Therefore learn chastity, so that in the future you may deserve perpetual joy.”

[Col. 0869D]

## SERMON X. On Solomon’s Judgment

Since, at the command of our holy father, we are now ascending the highest throne of sacred preaching, intending to sacrifice the sacrifice of the word of God to your understanding, we first await the utterance of God, who makes the speaker mute, so that, as we ascend the steps of the apse, he himself may descend from the throne of heaven—he who bent the heavens and descended (Ps. XVII, 10)—because the human being who descended wrongly could not ascend by himself. Nor can the preacher ascend alone, unless the Lord of angels deigns to kindle with him the radiant majesty of his present glory.

Therefore, brothers, let us hear what is being said, so that we may deserve to receive the heavenly promises. When Solomon had ascended the mountain, he was escorted by the splendid service of soldiers and surrounded upon the shining mountain by heavenly protection. He rests upon his bed and keeps vigil with God, saying: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song V, 2). Or, when he offered sacrifice [Col. 0870A] and slaughtered thousands of lambs, the army of angels was present. The palace became radiant on the mountain when the Lord visited it. A throne was established, and the servant was admonished to ask from the altars of his Lord, where he had offered sacrifice, a special written response to his prayers.

“Why,” he says, “are you resting? I am present, the giver of gifts, and you sleep, a negligent petitioner. Solomon, ask something of me, so that I may do it for you. Expect from me the throne of David your father, who deigned to bear great things in his own flesh, and for whom I made you a successor by my foreknowledge. I gave you the kingdom; shall I not also give you a household? I placed the purple upon you; shall I not also give you glory? Ask something of me: he who knows all things requires this.

“Was not the almighty Lord already aware of his secrets, so that he might learn from him what he should grant? But he wishes us to become more distinguished advocates of our prayers and vows, interpreters of the inner heart, so that our petition may be made known to God, and free choice may be preserved through preceding grace: so that what the tongue requests, heavenly grace may confer [Col. 0870B], or indulgence grant.”

Thus Solomon too is told: “Ask something of me, so that I may do it for you.”

And he says:

“Lord, you have bestowed royal dignity, and yet you ask me what my desire wishes? Blessed are you, Lord, who have placed me upon the throne of David my father. You have given me great glory, but I possess little wisdom. The radiance of jewels surrounds me, but the judgment of the peoples who bring their pleas presses upon me with the greatest burden.

“This is what I ask, Lord, and what you yourself have come to give, because you deigned to inspire me to ask it. Your people, whom you have given me, as numerous as the sand of the sea, trouble me with petitions of many kinds, and I do not know how to enter or depart, or with what justice I ought to answer your people. Give me, Lord, wisdom and understanding” (III Kings III, 9), “so that I may know how to divide justly between the just and the unjust by a discerning judgment, lest my sentence begin to displease you, and lest your people begin to suffer under my small and insufficiently instructed examination.”

And the Lord:

“Because you asked for wisdom, and not riches or the deaths of your enemies—and I will grant you even what you did not ask for, and I will add to it” (ibid., 11).

“But I will give you wisdom beyond the wise men of Egypt, so that you may know how to reveal the hidden secret of the petitioner and descend into the depths of every profound question, so that the judgment of your throne may be suffused with the splendor of penetrating knowledge, and no shifting darkness of those who obscure the truth may deceive you.”

Behold, he is visited and instructed; he asks and receives. He ascends insufficiently instructed and likewise inexperienced, but descends a disciple of the teacher of heavenly law, made a judge for those who bring petitions and an advocate for the peoples.

Behold, as he suddenly descended from the sanctuary of the mountain, two women met him face to face—women who, as it concerns the matter, were prostitutes. A great mystery is signified here: after a chaste visitation, he was to receive the pleas of prostitutes. For our Lord too, the truly peaceful Solomon, descending from the holy mountain of heaven, brought salvation to sinners and a merciful judgment to prostitutes, when the Judge of mercy cries from the throne of indulgence: “Prostitutes and tax collectors will go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. XXI, 31).

[Col. 0870D]

What, then, did one of these women say?

“Lord king, hear me” (III Kings III, 17 ff.). “I and this woman shared one dwelling and lodged together. When both of us had retired for the night, this woman devised a new theft against me, attempting to alter by nature what conscience would not permit. A careless mother crushed her own son beneath the ruin of her sluggish body. Sleepy affection did not hear him crying beneath his mother’s weight until the infant’s groaning faded into the faint whimper of death.

“This woman, awake for fraud though she slept against compassion, arose and found her son dead, crushed by the ruin of her own body. She arose and wished to make a grave beside me for her dead child, so that she could transfer my infant to her side. I was awake. I offered my breast, but he did not offer his lips. I sensed that he was dead, but I did not understand the exchange of the fraud. The light was present as a witness, and nature was present as an advocate, proclaiming that he was not my son.

“This was the domestic dispute between us: I did not acknowledge the dead child and claimed the living one, while she considered her own child alive and said that mine was dead [Col. 0871A]. Nature herself stands present as witness, lord. Deign to pronounce a just sentence between us.”

At once the Lord who had visited Solomon, who had promised wisdom, entered into Solomon’s secret places. He established his seat there and began to judge through him, as through his temple, with only the cloud of the body intervening, so that he might understand this dispute between nature and nature.

“What do you say?” he asks. “The living son is yours?”

“Mine, lord,” she cried.

“No, he is mine alive, and hers is the dead one.”

As they repeated these claims by turns, the women produced an uncertain darkness. The light flashing from Solomon began to disperse that cloud, and he burst forth into such a declaration, thundering with royal authority:

“Bring a sword,” he says, “and give the living infant to be divided by the blade” (ibid., 24).

So that no part of the child’s body might be separated from either woman, he orders them to cut the living infant with a sword and divide him according to nature.

The affection of the true mother cries out; her inward organs are shaken [Col. 0871B] when the sword is armed.

“No, no, lord! I brought my plea for gain, not for my loss. I presented my complaint so that I, a sinner, might not become a parricide. Do not, lord; do not cut him. While you divide the little child, if you deign, I bring the whole question to an end. Let her possess the innocent child entirely; let her take the infant whole. Let him live, and let him be hers. If he belongs to both, he will belong to neither.

“Do not make my eyes mourn with the innocent blood of my child, lest this woman begin to rejoice at my bereavement. Indeed, lord, if she herself possesses the little child, I too shall have a share in his eyes. I shall see him possessed under another mother. I shall watch him walking, growing, and running; at some time I shall hold him as he passes through the street in the secret embraces of his true mother.”

But the woman whom nature did not admonish and whose inward organs did not plead cried out:

“Certainly, lord, you have judged rightly. Let him be divided; let him be divided.”

“Certainly you are the mother. Earlier you said, ‘The living child is mine’; now you say, ‘Let him be divided.’ Certainly you are the mother.”

The true mother was turned away in tears.

Immediately the king said:

“Spare him, spare him. Do not cut the whole child, because I have recognized the mother’s whole affection [Col. 0871C]. Pain bears witness; the groaning proves it. The false mother accuses herself. This is the true mother: she declares that the innocent child must not be divided, but wishes to lose her own portion of him intact. Give him to her. She is his mother.”

She receives the child with outstretched arms and begins to praise the heavenly judgment. Having taken the child, she embraces him and, fixing sweet kisses upon him, cries out and says:

“According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. XCIII), because you have displayed your clear justice to me, and I shall always bear gratitude for your grace; because your sword divides between me and the mother [lacuna]lsam, so that where other judges are accustomed to inflict death, you defended the true mother through the sword. You know well, king, how to draw a sword from the sword, and not blood but love, because your sword, lord, is not wounds for me, but rather medicine.”

[Col. 0871D]

## SERMON XI. On the Same Subject

Solomon sat in the house of David his father, and two women appeared before him face to face. While David’s offspring, infused with heavenly teaching, was bearing fruit, and was about to ascend the throne of the royal court in order to reign justly, there was—if I am not mistaken—a lofty seat, an image of the Temple. Roofs of outstanding height bore the wealth assigned to it, and gold fixed into the beams, enclosed by the craftsman’s hand, was carved more beautifully than the unbuilt mass of the walls. Marble and purple stones, cut and laid on both sides, shone, so that the splendor of the royal house might gleam; everything precious was trodden underfoot.

Ebony, radiant in the ornament of its own beauty, shone fixed into the doorposts, bringing as much magnificence as beauty to the court. Ivory was clothed in adornment; the throne was decorated with distinguished jewels; and golden foil, laid out as though purple-colored, rattled.

Amid these things the wisest Solomon sat, raising his head that glittered with a radiant diadem and, so to speak, covered with a flashing mantle of metal. [Col. 0872A] By the light of the jewels he surpassed the true daylight. In all these things the name and merit of the king were displayed: all were as great, as brilliant, and evidently as precious as could be. Yet more precious was the splendor of the wisdom bestowed upon him. Shining with prophetic inspiration, it taught the past, revealed the present, and sang of the future.

When he had taken possession of the power of his father’s kingdom, the first and more difficult matter presented for his consideration was the dispute of two women whom the birth of children at the same time had made mothers of equal standing. Held beneath one roof and overcome by the sleep that resembles death, one of them, weighed down by the burden of her own body, crushed the child she had miserably borne into death.

The other, entrusted to wakeful care, preserved her son through maternal devotion and was destined to live. But the first, armed with the deceit of falsehood, took the living son from the sleeping mother and deceptively brought him to her own side, destined to possess no remedy for what she had done.

When the darkness of night was broken by the light and the darkness of shadows, together with sleep, had for a time passed out of the world with the coming of day, the mother, anxious in her love for her child, saw that the dead son was not her own, while she was astonished that her living child had been joined to another’s side [Col. 0872B].

The two women—both deceitful and truthful—rise up. Their quarrels resound; words and arms are brought into combat. But the compassionate mother, who had preserved the child in her flesh and bosom, appeals to the royal mind with this prayer:

“I know indeed that you are both heir and divine power of your father’s kingdom, and that heavenly justice and wise judgment have been granted to you; nothing is hidden from your understanding. Now undertake the case of my wretched child, whom I seem to have brought into the light for this reason: while he is claimed by this liar, she piles up accusations and laments with sobs that her innocent child has been taken from her maternal breasts.

“I therefore hold to my claim, and with you as judge I will not withdraw it: I who preserved a living son will not accept another’s corpse.”

Amid these circumstances the justice drawn forth by King Solomon is troubled, and he fixes his judgment upon the women’s dispute. Rising as though in equal grief, they look at the dead child with judicial agitation. Both say that he is not theirs; both defend the living child with their cries.

No witness or advocate is produced [Col. 0872C]. The case is argued in the silence of night, and only the theft of the wicked bed is brought forward. Suddenly, by that sign of divine power in which truth is established, he orders the infant to be cut into pieces, so that the judge’s sword might separate the mother who preserved her child from the murderous woman who had given birth to her own offspring.

When the true mother saw the wound about to be inflicted upon the wretched body of the child, tortured in her inner organs she burst into speech:

“O harsher necessity of nature! To what end do you compel, or to what end do you force mothers to love their children or to bear offspring? Behold, as the infant’s body is divided, the mother’s breast is cut apart; and those who deserved to bring forth a son in this way are themselves torn apart in the son by the bond of nature.

“Therefore, most merciful of kings, complete the case of the most righteous compassion. If I do not deserve to have the son whom I bore, if falsehood thus brings bereavement, let her have the child’s full body; let her possess intact the one whom she did not bear. While he is fed, while he is nourished, while he is advanced toward maturity, perhaps, if he ever recognizes maternal affection within himself, he will recognize the legitimate mother in his grown years.”

But the other woman, growling with a justly cruel grief [Col. 0872D], at once deprived of what she had wrongly lost and struck by jealousy, because she saw that the good mother might gain the child, cried out indignantly with such words:

“Most just of kings, you have pronounced an excellent and fitting sentence, lest you seem to favor one and oppress the other. Let the child’s body be divided in half, so that it may benefit neither me nor her—the one who seemed to remain from the two.”

But wise Solomon, in royal justice, issued this sentence in rebuke:

“Savage woman, more cruel and more severe than an infanticide of every kind of criminal, why do you wrongly unite a stepmother’s hatred with a son well preserved? Let the woman whom compassion has proved to be the true mother have the child intact. Let this other woman make use of her own corpse, since she did not give birth to what she might nourish, but found what she had killed.”

## SERMON XII. On Joseph

All who bear the mystery of God are illustrious [Col. 0873A], but especially those who foretold the Christ who was to come. Yet Joseph is more magnificent than all the rest, for he displays an image of Christ’s glory and passion in a complete figure.

In the figures and images of the saints we recognize the Lord Christ; their past or present sufferings bear witness to a similar testimony, as it is written: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not trouble my prophets” (I Chron. XVI, 22). For it is easy for each person to bear his own burden, but difficult to bear another’s. Thus all the righteous and holy endured particular punishments in their sufferings.

But when the Lord Christ came, he alone bore whatever all the others had suffered, as examples drawn from many of them demonstrate. Daniel (Dan. XIV, 28), after interpreting dreams, after marvelous honors, after repeatedly rejecting the gifts of kings, and after proving the emptiness of idols to kings, is crushed by the fury of the pursuing people and, against the king’s will and almost against his safety, is handed over to the people.

The king, who had found him faithful through the divine Spirit, released him to the raging people, not without tears and grief of heart. Did Christ not suffer similarly? The Jews persecuted him fiercely and demanded with wicked cries that Christ be handed over to them, even to the envy of Pilate the king (Matt. XXVII, 24). At once the king, reflecting upon the people’s wickedness and the silence of the divine man before him, took water to wash his hands and declared himself innocent of his blood.

Isaiah likewise was loved by the king but hated by the king’s son. Having been commended together with the king’s son, he spoke to the king in this way:

“Your commendation, king, does not last, but it is beneficial. For Belial has already begun to rage in Manasseh’s heart.”

Did Christ himself not endure a similar deed, because [Note: [Col. 0873D] It would be better to read “who” (*qui*). EDITOR.] although the Son was loved by God the Father, he was betrayed by Judas?

Indeed, he spoke thus to his disciples: “Amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me” (Mark XIV, 18).

Let us now come to the passion of holy Joseph, whose beginning presents the marked chastity and nobility that arose from servitude and does not allow us to remain silent. When he [Col. 0873C] simply explained to his brothers the repose of his vision, he encountered the fuel of jealousy: in his dream he saw himself being worshiped by the heavenly luminaries and twelve stars, and his sheaf raised above the sheaves of the other brothers (Gen. XXXVII).

What fault did he commit by seeing this? Or what benefit came from the brothers’ desire for his blood? Rather, they ought to have cared for his future dignity, which they did not know how to hate. Thus calamity fostered the righteous man from the very source from which the brothers’ destructive cruelty harmed him.

As it is written: “Do not fear, because I have called you by your name” (Isa. XLV, 4).

This blessed Joseph went on; he went through unknown passages, he went alone, and everywhere he was safe. When he came as a brother to his brothers, he did not know that they would become robbers. For he did not seem to them to be coming as a brother, since their minds were possessed by a deadly thought.

Once their criminal plan had been conceived, he was thrown into a deep pit (Gen. XXXVII, 23), in which he was safer than he would have been with his brothers. Then he was sold in Egypt, and there, amid the harsh duties of slavery, the chaste man was desired by an immodest woman [Col. 0873D], as though the example of the first man could emerge in every respect: through a woman he suffered shipwreck, as it is written: “Lord, the woman whom you gave me deceived me” (Gen. III, 12).

When Joseph, the father of chastity, sought to avoid the woman’s persistent advances and was fixed in her husband’s mind as guilty of a fabricated crime, he endured prison for three years. He deserved prison who lived commendably. He deserved prison who rejected what he deemed disgraceful. He deserved prison who preserved her honor without the husband’s knowledge.

But that higher guardian of innocence was not absent: once the righteous man had been placed in prison, he sent him the wisdom to interpret dreams. He revealed the dreams of two eunuchs imprisoned with him, foretelling life for one and death for the other, and thus he came into the king’s presence (Gen. XL). When the king’s dream was more clearly explained, he revealed the coming famine.

Made superintendent of the supplies [Col. 0874A], he deserved the key to the storehouses, and, received in the chariot as second to the king, was declared prince over all. Already the abundance of heaven had first flowed forth, and heavenly fruitfulness, spread abroad with the generosity of the rains, had fertilized the lands. The harvest, swollen by a richer furrow, undulated. Seed was gathered into overflowing storehouses, destined to provide help in future need.

Then an incurable famine followed. When the rains were withheld, summer possessed a season alien to it. The plants dried up at their roots, destined to refuse seed in the years to come, while amid all peoples disfigured by pallor, Joseph’s people alone exulted in wealth.

As it is written: “I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring begging bread” (Ps. XXXVI, 25).

He always provides, shows mercy, acquires, and gladly distributes grain to those who come. He preserved his own in need, though he could not be preserved by his own in abundance, and he bestowed the mercy he had not received. Poverty returns upon its authors, and God’s servant is honored. He loads them with grain, heaps it up, and hastens to provide before he is recognized.

Even in providing, he creates delays, so that he may see his brothers longer. O slanderous compassion! He places his silver cup among their goods so that he may at last be recognized by his brothers. He falsely threatens terror; they look upon the king in the storehouses. With lowered eyes they adore the ground. The whole brotherhood lies beneath vengeance, yet, though they are detained as guilty not of theft but of fratricide, he grants them as much pardon as they had deserved punishment.

Nobility is usually quick to forget the miseries of one’s parents. Joseph, however, forgot nothing in his brothers except their injuries. In place of hatred he brings mercy; in place of cruelty, joy; in place of swords, kisses. He makes lords from enemies, illustrious men from the lowly, stronger men from the starving, and gathers together into one the whole race of his blood.

We too, dearly beloved brothers, if we imitate these things, will be as it is written in the Gospel: “If you do what I command you, I shall no longer call you servants, but friends” (John XV, 14).

[Col. 0874C]

## SERMON XIII. On the Exodus

Ruin falls badly when obstinacy raises a proud head. Thus the spirit of the obstinate leaps forward, so that it neither sees that it is about to fall nor recognizes that it is about to collapse. The Egyptian arrogance raged under savage commands and tormented the fuel of envy with inflamed minds. With such cruel spirits it tore apart the divine people; it oppressed those condemned to labor, believing that the punishment would be less recognized if it did not see the innocent being killed.

Nowhere is justice safe against a king’s hatred, because the innocent is not safe where he is recognized as guilty. A terrible power rises into madness, and immense fury swells with the insane gnashing of teeth. When it harms, it is inflamed. When the spirit pants, the breast swells. The inward parts burn; the limbs grow hot. Nor can the tyrant understand himself, whom future condemnation had made fearful.

He orders destruction to be brought upon future males [Col. 0874D] and orders them to be slaughtered by hidden wounds at nature’s impending descent. He orders those he does not know to be killed; he orders those of whom he is ignorant to be destroyed.

Alas for the race! Alas for the tears of compassion! If the living could have been feared, what had those yet to be born done?

Thus the authority of Scripture confirms it:

“And Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying: Every male child that is born to the Hebrews, throw into the river; but every female keep alive” (Exod. I, 22).

O unspeakable flame of lust! O conflagration of an insane mind! Anger endures those whom it may strike; punishment seeks those whom it does not know. It wishes to possess those whom it may torture, and does not know whom it may kill.

Consider, natural compassion, how impious he was who ordered infants to be cast into devouring waters and newborns thrown upon rapacious waves. Consider, I say, what the living could suffer there, where the unborn were ordered to be killed. What disasters then did the maternal name fear? What griefs did that impious and deadly decree bring upon parents, whether in the very wretchedness of childbirth or in the condition imposed by nature [Col. 0875A]?

Recognize the dangers by which those who were giving birth to murder could be enclosed. The king’s attendants surrounded the womb near to delivery, so that every male might be born not for life but for death, not for the joy of parents but for the brutality of the attendants.

That was not a birthday, but destruction born from mourning. The birth is celebrated, yet there is no son. The eyes of the pitiable mothers grow wet; tears trickle down their cheeks; and the woman who had given birth wastes away in the mournful rites of her face. A famished filth rises upon her limbs; her appearance is squalid in grief; stains cling amid raging tears; and a shadowy sadness knots the brow, fixed into and woven through every bone by painful creases.

What disasters would he now wish for the wretched man who forced himself to perish? Vengeance presses forward; a vindicator is born, and compassion is compelled by advancing punishments to exact vengeance.

The Lord sends Moses, demanding his own people. Pharaoh, however, refuses what belongs to another. O stubborn presumption and harsh destruction! God demands; he despises. He despises the Judge [Col. 0875B]. He neglects the one who commands.

Observe what kind of man he could rush forward as: he had first been warned by miracles, and afterward refused to obey even the plagues. The exhausted cruelty of tyrannical savagery rages, and, dying, grows numb in its attacks upon its own people.

Yet, defeated by the deaths of his firstborn, he expelled those whom he had refused to cast out and drove away those whom he had neglected. Punishment made him devoted when grace had not. He orders them to depart and compels them to be driven out. Now he too fears for himself what he sees happening to others.

But because ready anger condemns its own guilty subjects, he resists because he has suffered loss; he repents because he has been deprived.

“What have we done,” he says, “that we let the children of Israel go, so that they should no longer serve us?” (Exod. XIV, 5).

Pharaoh therefore harnessed his chariots, took his entire army with him, and took six hundred chariots, together with all the Egyptian cavalry and all those armed upon them. He took up weapons, rushed forward with his chariots, went out, pressed on, and raged. He prepared disasters to announce to the fugitives, terrors to bring upon their parents.

He stood terrifying, so that he might fall; he had come trembling, so that he might perish. A credulous multitude went forward in flashing armor. The crowd surpassed the breadth of the land; the abundance of forces overcame the armed host.

[Col. 0875C]

The revolving chariots rolled light through precious fires, and fires spread over the pole shafts blazed with gleaming reins. The army lived amid flames, though it was destined to perish in the waters. A terrible radiance rose upon the helmets, and a flame kindled upon red rays flashed with jewel-like brilliance. Light was spread across the open fields, and the stretches of hidden roads grew red with poured-out splendor.

The clear prospect of the eyes wavered, and the crimson brilliance of the sun blushed against its paling rays. Beautiful destruction had overcome the light, and bronze crests with shining scales radiated the brightness of the sun.

Recognize what kind of man could rush forward who had come to fight against God.

But after the marvelous powers of heaven and earth, Moses was also commanded to stretch out his hand over the sea and display the Lord’s power among the waves. That glorious Moses therefore trod upon the bosom of the avenging sea and entered the murmuring storms amid the storytelling sounds of the shrieking waves.

He forced up masses of swimming foam; the playful sea [Col. 0875D], in its waves, led away the whirlpools formed by the storms as the waters moved. It shuddered at the blow that came and feared the hand that struck. The divine army seized a path through the open waters and opened the door of the avenging sea after it had been struck.

It enters, emerges, and closes. He who could not know justice learned that the sea too must serve him.

That furious enemy follows, inflamed by inescapable punishment, and tramples the avenging paths with burning spirits. The sea bent its rippling locks into whirlpools, and between liquid walls and fragile supports, with soothing sounds, invited the living guilty man onward.

The anxious storm hung amid stable movements, and suspended punishment stood amid motionless attacks. But when Pharaoh rashly entered, the waves returned; the sea joined together; and, with the seas shattered against themselves and their crashing sounds mingled, the waters bound him with contending foam.

At the command, the sea thrust his limbs into the restraining waters, and the seas, bending back upon themselves with twisting waves, laid down their curved whirlpools headlong. The sea rages against the enemy [Col. 0876A]; the waves fight. Punishment had stood within itself; punishment moved together with itself.

Now the water, fastening the chariots, lifts those hanging beneath them; now the devouring wave twists them amid gaping heaps. Now the deep upheaval spits out those it has seized; now the changed sinking casts them headlong. It displays them to the underworld and extends them toward heaven; it digests those thrown into it and swallows those it has carried away.

The sea is torn open, the waters are shattered, and the shores, driven back upon their own assault, roar against them with resounding waves.

For what did he lack in glory, through whom God wished to exact vengeance? Consider now, Egypt, once so furious; learn how to perish, learn how to sin. Slay the righteous; scourge captives. What crime did you commit too little, when, tearing life from the righteous at their birth, you denied them what is worse: burial?

## SERMON XIV. On the Same Subject
He who does not understand that he is a human being does not acknowledge the Lord as his maker. He who does not recognize his own frailty—how will he be able to know the divine benefits? He who refuses to listen when admonished will be subjected to repentance. He who despises the one giving orders will grievously stir up against himself the indignation of the one commanding. He who refuses to obey God’s commands will remain liable to punishment.

For that gentile tyrant of Egypt resisted the Lord with supine efforts, and, his breast weighed down by insane arrogance, had made himself hateful through his own evils. He was carried along, surrounded by raised hair and armed for fury by the terror of weapons; and, with sin itself militantly assailing him, he had become alienated from his own mind. But because grievous envy itself suggests punishments to itself when it grows hot under the goad of slander, so he learned to be tormented by a punishment he had deserved. He was hurled by his burning evils into fury; and as the savagery of his obstructed breast grew stronger in his torments, he rebuked them while destined to perish.

While the Hebrew offspring flourished through the gift of blessing, he, inflamed by the ardor of a blind mind, crushed the afflicted life of the righteous by toil and oppression. The fruitful wombs of the mothers were being cherished, and the offspring of the holy seed, once brought forth, was growing. The more the Egyptians oppressed them, the more numerous they became. A new glory of holiness—and new are the destructions of the persecutor. While the enemy exulted in harsh afflictions, the people of God grew all the more, with punishment itself helping them.

For the afflicted were driven on through harsh sorrows, and their wombs, shut off from the work of childbirth, were compelled by savage beatings to submit. A new plan is devised against the enemies, so that mourning might be inflicted on the children through punishment. The wretched are ordered to die before they have learned to live; and, though they had not been condemned, they were sought out for killing.

What sort of groans were there among the mothers, who, in their grief, were giving birth while funerals hastened on? For how did the royal anger condemn the fathers, who did not even have time to mourn their sons? He had ordered the males to be killed for this purpose: that, as the people increased, he might conquer the innocent by killing them.

Alas! The mothers were forced to lament burial within the womb, and, before she had seen the child born, the wretched mother lamented the deaths that were to fall. But while they were shaken by long-continued blows, as savagery gained strength, and a hard succession of torments entangled them in grief-inspiring terrors, they beat upon the doors, mourning their lives in silence with a terrible murmur.

For they murmured in silent pains, fearing, and with their breasts obstructed by wounds they were crushed beneath hidden sorrows. What were the endings of those who murmured, since they did not even dare to trust their voices to such great griefs? Consider with what showers of tears the eyes could break forth—when one was not even permitted to weep in sorrow.

At last the Lord heard, though struck without a cry, and heaven recognized the message of grief without a voice. For that glorious Moses was sent, so that, when the wounds had been weighed again, he might return upon the Egyptian what the Egyptian had inflicted.

And receiving the rod, the teacher of virtues, God entered battle through a human being. The powers of God passed into human hands, and Moses, secure, carried the heavenly offices in the rod. The enemy is compelled to listen patiently, and, hardened in his evils, is made such that the torments themselves might preserve him for his appointed steps. For no guilty person can die before he has been tortured, and no one can bring forth the truth of his end unless he has first been led to the destruction of punishment and vengeance.

Thus tyrannical error had also invaded him, so that, when the ranks had been counted, it found the one whom punishment would torment. Royal treachery, once revealed, struck those whom it had held; and, exhausted and cooling in its own judgments, it feared those whom it had possessed.

That Moses, therefore, the craftsman of virtues, went forth, appointed leader of the host in the wilderness, to lead the people of God out from their enemies. They were led through dry stretches of the fields, and, advancing through pure regions of the road, were preserved under the Lord’s guidance.

But when they approached unknown shores, the enemy regretted having let the people go, so that he might find them together with the necessity of death. At once he rises, inflamed by fire and armed with fury; with himself he shuts out the prospect of the power destined to die. He had risen again for his own destruction, doomed to perish.

Chariots are fitted to the strongest teams, and, swift for punishment, they hasten toward ruin together with their own master. Thus they were borne along, surrounded by the terrors of weapons, so that perhaps the Egyptian clamor might threaten them. Israel hears the murmur of the enemies growing louder and, confused by the crashing of wheels, loses courage through fear.

For recognize what kind of enemies they were—enemies whom Moses himself seemed to fear. Immediately, struck by the powers of the rod, the seas vanished, and the sea, disturbed from its own laws, was restrained by the captive chariots. The waves rose, avoiding human hands, and the waters stood fixed against the watered rock. He enters boldly, animated by insolent plots, and, secure amid dangers, followed them through the whole peril. He enters confidently, as though the waves would also be servants to them through fear.

He wishes to return, but now he is no longer permitted to return. The waters are ordered to celebrate their own retreat; and, when their powers were released, the commanded seas took up again their proper function.

What is this, faithless Pharaoh? You were hastening splendidly toward death. Where do you think you are, unjust enemy? They do not die by the wound with which you struck them. No labor is imposed upon your punishments; no cloud pours down a storm of swords. There is nothing that you would feel as grievous. A single rod has been preserved for your destruction.

## SERMON XV. On the foregoing.

Since the people of Israel had long since forgotten the divine benefits, had been rescued by the heavenly arm from the service of tyrannical power, and had crossed the deep sea on dry feet, while the walls of water hung restrained, the fiercest tyrant was offered by his own savagery to the deepest recesses of the sea. He was to perish there with all his men—the man who had previously girded himself and hastened to capture the innocent.

With the waves arched overhead, a wall is established amid the perils of the waters; and God enters with the peoples, about to display the victory of salvation. The wave is trampled beneath their footsteps, and there is no moisture on their soles.

Mad Pharaoh enters, blind in his own counsel and destined to perish among the waves. Finally, he frenziedly compresses the seething waters, which recognized the madman inspired against them. But he understood that he could not escape when the Lord God granted the people a passage; and while the waters raged, restrained within their hidden masses, the waves of burial rolled back upon themselves against Pharaoh. A place was prepared for him and his armies, while the Lord brought his own people unharmed to the shore. Pharaoh and his men remained buried in the sea, overwhelmed by shipwreck.

The people of God plowed through the wave across the sea’s floor, and shipwreck provoked Pharaoh toward his approaching death. Moses stood beside the sea and stirred heaven with cries, because he saw Pharaoh engaging him in battle.

And the Lord said: “Moses, Moses, why are you shouting? Soon you will rejoice over your enemies. Moses, Moses, why are you crying out? I have measured heaven with a span and enclosed the world in a handful, and you think that I do not fight with Pharaoh?”

The people enter the sea, and the devil arms Pharaoh for shipwreck. The Lord brought the Hebrews unharmed to the bank. For he left Pharaoh submerged in the sea with six hundred chosen chariots.

Pharaoh enters the sea presumptuously, as though the waves were saying to him: “It is a great thing, traveler, that you have come safely; it is a great thing, presumptuous one, that you have emerged. It is a great thing that sweat has carried you through while you raced. Greater still is it that rigidity now carries you through while you swim. You came with us to fight; just now we carried God’s people to the shore, and so we return with you to battle. We prepare for you the field of the sea, and bring ruin upon your soul. Come confidently, never again to return to your own men. From where do the waves of the deceptive sea feed upon tranquillity? He arms the four-footed beasts, and the swift ones are not lacking—those whom anger inflames against the enemy.

“By your command, Lord, the people of Israel, fleeing the rage of Egypt under Moses’ leadership, at last escaped happy and free, so that the fury itself might fail at the sea’s boundary.”

The people stand amid conflicting waves, surrounded by threats of weapons, and seek flight in the waters. The sea was struck apart by the prophetic blow, and the rod rebuked the waters it had scourged. The sea’s hidden depth fell silent, its frozen structure settling into stability; the structure stood firm, and the sea came forward to fight with the enemies.

The sword of the shipwrecked cruelty swam forth; the presumptuous man enters the sea with the chariots’ surging hooves, from which they suffer violence. And suddenly the wave, as if awakened from sleep, becomes a dreadful image of night, most terrible against the Egyptians, mournful and premature. The wave binds the boundaries, prepares its folds to receive the people’s adversaries, and, with its waves curling, overwhelms them all at the morning watch.

“Ho, traveler upon the waters, why do you suffer the violence of the waves? No one is fighting, yet you perish, traveler. Strike the waves, if you can. Slaughter the surf, if you prevail. O harmony of the waters! It has submerged the Egyptian army, and fury has gone astray.”

The people of Israel cross the sea on dry feet, and Pharaoh follows, seated in his chariots, destined to be submerged in the waves. The wave is trampled by footsteps; it is struck by the hooves of the chariots. And the wave willingly endured the slaughter of its adversaries, for it itself was preparing shipwreck for them.

The tyrant enters, surrounded by a multitude of armed men, and, upon the soft waves, dares to direct the steps of chariots and horses.

O most impious darkness of blindness! Peter stumbled with Christ and was submerged; Pharaoh thought that he alone could cross. But against the apostle, who was sinking, a hand was stretched out by Christ, and he was lifted up. Pharaoh, abandoned by Christ, is devoured by the raging waves.

Who would not be overwhelmed by such a spectacle? On one side the water foams, on the other weapons flash. On one side the sound of the waters, on the other the clamor of weapons. Thus God is accustomed to work and thus to be present: where human counsel has ceased, there divine aid intervenes all the more swiftly.

Immediately, with Moses’ hand raised, the sea is split by the blow of the rod, and the sea’s hidden depths are opened. A shore is made where the sea had been. The wave turns over on its back, and the shores are filled with corpses. In death itself their punishment was greater because, after their life had been torn from them by the avenging waters, they did not even deserve burial.

Pharaoh went out to the bank before all the others; but, his life already lost, no one continued the battle, and the whole victory emerged from the enemies.

## SERMON XVI. On Jonah.

When Jonah was sent to preach destruction to the Ninevites, wicked vanity immediately introduced into him the plan of flight. He hurried down to Joppa and took a ship in order to flee to Tarshish, despising God—as though he could escape divine knowledge, or as though there were any region outside God’s sphere, which is impossible.

The whole world is a small place for God, since it is smaller than his arm; and it cannot conceal the fugitives of its maker in any hidden shadows, beneath whose gaze the trembling world is seen. No place is empty of concealment; everything is occupied by its creator.

As the most holy Isaiah says, speaking of how God holds all things within his handful (Isaiah 40:12): “He measured heaven with a span, enclosed it in his fist, and gathered the world within the enclosure of his right hand.” And again: “With his hand, as with a nest, he holds the world.”

Could he hide from the one who holds the world in his fist, who possesses the fixed boundaries of heaven, earth, and the abyss, who shakes the world with muttering thunder when heaven is split by flashing fire? No one can flee his power; nothing is hidden from him. And, to put it more plainly, he sees whatever he does not fail to see.

All things are naked before God, as he himself testifies: “I am God who is near, and not God from afar. If a man is hidden in hidden places, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?” (Jeremiah 23:23–24). The prophet also testifies: “The eyes of the Lord behold everywhere the good and the wicked” (Proverbs 15:3). David says: “Your eyes saw my unformed substance, and all things are written in your book” (Psalm 138:16). And again: “A human being sees what is before his face, but God sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). And: “All the churches shall know that I am God who searches the kidneys and the heart” (Revelation 2:23).

Therefore, for the one who knows beforehand the secrets of hearts, there are no hiding places that escape his gaze. Though absent, he sees everything; though present, he is seen by no one.

In vain, therefore, did the most holy prophet, despising God’s profound command, flee. He could not flee without God as his companion; he thought he had fled from the one who followed him joined to him—or rather, from the one who went before him.

And when he had boarded the ship and sailed as a guilty man from the presence of the present God, at once, by the divine will, the gulf was overturned. Torn from its channels, it seethed with uplifted crest and overshadowed the ship’s sides. The ship’s timbers were battered amid the raging dangers, and the gaping wave hesitated to swallow what had been cast into it with fiercest violence.

For the discord of the waters, raging, struck the ship with repeated blows. The sea roared through its channel and, growling amid conflicts, raged against the fugitive. Restless and turbid, the swelling of the sea wandered furiously through the air with its head rippling. A dreadful disorder had seized the gulf.

As the sea also fought, the ship’s enclosure was shaken. The rabid waves growled against the fugitive in conflicting combat and, rising up, ran barking toward the ship. The entire sea around the fugitive was impatient.

Under the blows of the turbulent waters, therefore, the keel trembled with shrieking timbers. The sea, beating from one side and the other, loosened the joints of the planks through its destructive assaults.

Thus, finally, we read: “And the Lord stirred up a wind upon the sea, and there was a great storm upon the sea, and the ship was in danger of being broken apart” (Jonah 1:4).

The sailors therefore expressed themselves not only with their voices but with tears. Showers of tears poured forth; joined by groaning, they flowed abundantly down their cheeks and drenched the whole region of their eyes. They also stretched out their hands in supplication and pleaded with their various gods in pious speech.

All of them, therefore, seized the whole burden and threw it into the deadly abyss, striving together to overcome the dangers and to discover whether, through losses or rewards, they could calm the swollen waves of the quarrelling sea. While attempting to defeat the danger, they offered up their property.

There too we read: “And the sailors were exceedingly afraid, and each man cried out to his neighbor, and they cast the objects that were in the ship into the sea, so that it might be lightened for them” (ibid.).

The wretched men did this while lamenting; even after losing their merchandise, they could not be secure. More and more the ship was flooded by the thickest waves and the harshest blows.

But the fugitive knew nothing of this. He was below deck, so to speak, steeping the limbs of his fugitive body in sleep beneath the covering of the ship.

The shipmaster approached him amid lamentation, shook him, and said: “Why are you snoring? Rise and call upon your Lord, so that God may save us and we may not perish” (ibid., 6).

At last the guilty man awakens when the shipmaster strikes him, and the lot reveals what has happened. The lot declares it; the guilty man does not deny it. They considered what they should do with such a man.

When, awakened, he saw the keel roaring amid tearful cries, and the sea, torn up from its depths by the waves, accusing him of its cause, and the sky confused for him by a black mass, he asked to be thrown into the raging sea by the sailors themselves.

“Take me,” he said, “and throw me into the sea, and the sea will become calm for you. For I know that because of me this great storm has come upon you” (ibid., 12).

But they, trembling before the danger, considered it just to yield to him; they struggled to turn back and delay their voyage. Yet the harshness of the cries would not be bent, nor would the whole region allow the balance of the ship to be restored.

Therefore the trembling mast was uncontrollable beneath the blow, while the waves, raging much more fiercely, swelled and, seizing the sky, struck it. The sky becomes deep with the sea, while the sea becomes near to the sky.

Then, as the waves cried out and battled, the prophet is thrown overboard. And now the monstrous, voracious whale (Jonah 2:1), rising from the depths, hastened toward him. Cutting through the fiercest waves, understanding, evidently by divine command, that prey had been thrown from the ship, it swallowed him with terrible jaws—but it neither tore him with its teeth nor killed him by its bite.

Jonah was brought down unharmed through the dangers of the savage mouth, now blunted, into the deep belly; and there he was held captive, enclosed for three days in the innermost recesses of its organs.

Even then he bore the glorious and extraordinary figure of the Lord Christ: in his Passion, hidden for the span of three days, he was to search out the depths of the earth, as we read in the Gospel:

“An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Matthew 12:39–40).

Yet he whose command had moved the waters calmed the sea’s rugged dangers. As the grief of darkness fled, the air became clear and the sky was made bright. When the dangers had also been quieted, the ship sailed like marble upon the serene sea; running with its canvas swollen by the wind, it cut through the waves and sailed securely.

The prophet, buried in the waters, a stranger to the waves, cuts through the waters while remaining dry beneath the waters. The whale’s monstrous size, which had enclosed its captive in the inner hospitality of its organs, preserved him immune from digestion. The sea beast is consumed because it is denied what it carries in its own belly. The whale, fattened yet unable to digest, hungers. The fury of its belly consumed the satiated beast for three days.

“You are consumed by indigestion, beast. What you hold is denied to you.”

Thus the creature, seething as it sailed pregnant through the vast sea, could neither take in nor digest its food. Then the monstrous whale, loaded with its meal and dried out by fasting, hastened at the command of its inner ruler toward the boundaries of the sea. Cutting through the ranks of the waters as though through a ship’s passage, it brought forth the fugitive prey from the dark, black prison of its organs and poured him out unharmed upon the shore.

## SERMON XVII. On the man born blind.

The mirror passes; the mirror is wiped. For he is the true mirror of the Father, who enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:9).

Christ, I say, passes as the mirror of the Father, and wipes the mirror of blindness from the one who did not see. Christ passes, coming from heaven, so that all flesh might see him, according to the prophetic voice of that blessed old man Simeon, who received the infant Word into his hands, looked upon him joyfully, and said:

“Now dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30).

The blind man alone, therefore, did not possess the mirror by which to see the Father. And where was the faithful proclamation of the prophets?

“Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear; then the lame shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be clear” (Isaiah 35:5–6).

Thus the blind man’s mirror, and the beggar’s face, seemed to have a kind of closed case that covered his darkened face. Christ opened that case, wiped the mirror, and the blind man saw the Father’s mirror in Christ.

A great medicine against nature! His eyes were not impaired but entirely denied him: he had been born blind, not made blind. And because the first human being was created luminous but departed from the serpent blinded, he began to be born again already blind, believing; for nature, corrupted and weakened in the body, had need of a double light—he who had not blushed at his own nakedness.

The blind man, therefore, sat beside the public thoroughfare, clothed yet naked through the constraint of poverty, deprived of natural light. He sat, I say, and asked nothing; he requested no collyrium from any physician. Since his condition was contrary to human nature, it undoubtedly had no need of ordinary medicine.

The craftsman came to the mirror of the image. He saw the misery of the blind man sitting and humbly asking alms.

O miracle of divine power! What he sees, he heals; what he visits, he illuminates.

Finally, the disciples ask and say: “Who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind?” (John 9:2).

The Lord says: “Neither did this man sin, nor his parents; but that the glory of God might appear in him. I must work the works of my Father” (ibid., 3–4).

All things, therefore, were held beneath sin, beneath harsh punishment. The blind, the lame, the deaf, the bleary-eyed, and the dead were held, I say, under the custody of the first punishment.

The liberator came—the one who had been the judge. He looked upon the blind man and he saw; he touched the deaf man and he heard; he cleansed the leper and he shone again; he raised the lame man and he ran; he descended to the dead man and he rose from death. And now the prisons of punishment began to be emptied, when the gates and wooden bars of hell were broken by the wood on which the Lord of heaven hung.

Therefore, he who made the globe of the earth opened the globes of the blind man’s eyes.

O revolving potter! The wheel revolved at his word, and sight was given to the blind man. For when a potter turns vessels to be formed from clay, he touches the revolving wheel with his feet. And our potter saw the vacant wheels of the blind man’s eyes and touched them—not with his foot, but with his voice. He touched them by stirring them, and formed eyes by placing mud upon them.

What is this? From where did such collyrium come? It was not collyrium made from the pigments of herbs, nor was it crushed in a mortar through the labors of physicians. A human being was made from mud; collyrium was made from clay.

For just as a goldsmith does not renew a broken necklace with the appearance of silver, nor a silversmith repair silver vessels from gold metal, so our craftsman and potter, the Lord Christ, restored from clay the vessel that he had made from clay. From the same material from which he formed the first eyes, he renewed the second eyes.

Which is the greater glory: to form the globe of the sun, or to reform the eyes of one born blind? He caused the sun to be illuminated while sitting upon his throne; he granted the blind man sight while walking through the streets of the world.

Thus brightness came without being requested, and natural blindness departed without the labor of prayers. He is sent to the pool, washes his eyes, receives brightness, and is led into conflict.

O illuminated mirror! Before, he could neither fight nor conquer; now, with illuminated eyes, he worships Christ. The blind man’s mirror was illuminated, while the Jews were covered in darkness. They do not wish to see in another’s light; therefore, in their pride, they could not behold the true light in God.

A contest is prepared after the light, and the author of light does not abandon the contest of his illuminated servant.

O delightful arena, the battle of brightness against the darkness of blindness! At the command of the elders and rulers of the Jews, he is brought in. Light is surrounded by darkness, and he raises the torch of his answer on behalf of the Savior’s miracle.

He is questioned and answers; he is surrounded and not confined; he is attacked and not ensnared.

“Who,” they say, “opened your eyes?” (ibid., 10). “Were you not blind, sitting and begging along the road?”

“I was a beggar along the road before the one who is the road passed by. My eyes were opened because he passed by who is the way, the truth, and the life. I am he—I am he. I do not conceal my blindness, so that I may confess the freely given medicine. I was healed in a unique place. I testify beneath the light of heaven that it is Christ who made me see.”

“Tell us,” they say, “the nature of your physician.”

“I will tell you; I am not ashamed. It is a new Gospel: to illuminate the blind. I will tell you, I will tell you—would that you too might embrace his love, you who ask about the nature of the physician! He made clay, mixed with the spittle of his mouth; he smeared my eyes and sent me to the pool. What I have obtained is testified by my eyes.”

“What do you say? This is a strange thing; you are lying. We have never, never known of a blind man’s eyes being opened by clay.”

“You speak truly, because you do not know what you have not seen. I know—the one who sees, the one who believed, sensed, and saw.”

There was a great dispute, because a great light had come. Some said, “He is not the same man.” Others said, “He is the same man.” All spoke the truth: he was the same man, and he was not the same man.

“If you consider the human being, he was the same; if you consider the eyes, he was not the same. If you consider the mirror, he was the same; if you contemplate the light in the mirror, he was not the same. For his physician was the Word in the beginning, and the Word was with God and was God.”

“We are not satisfied with your testimony,” they say, “nor with your own image.”

“It is not the same, I know, as my former image. But the one who made me according to his own image and likeness came to me.”

“You are lying; you are not the same man.”

“I am not the same man, because I have been changed.”

They order his parents to be brought in, so that they may become witnesses for their son. His parents are brought in; the testimony grows, and the accusers are put to shame.

O wickedness! They gather witnesses against themselves, so that a complete victory might be achieved over the blind man.

They come and stand in the midst of the elders. They ask: “Is this your son, who sat blind and begging along the road?”

And they answer: “He is; we know that he is our son. And if we deny it, our affection accuses us. Yet we see his eyes opened, and we ourselves marvel: our womb brought forth a blind man. But we do not know who made him illuminated from blindness.

“He is indeed our son, but we would rightly be compelled to speak for the child if he could not speak for himself. But he is of age: formerly he spoke, and now he sees. We have known him blind from birth; we formerly heard him speaking, and now we see him seeing. Ask him himself, so that you may be instructed. Why do you question us maliciously? He is of age; let him speak for himself” (ibid., 21).

He was judged not to be of childish age but legally mature, so that the triumph of his testimony might emerge in its fullness.

He is returned to the struggle and battle, until he should behold the one who would crown him.

“Tell us,” they say.

“What shall I tell you? I have already told you. Why do you wish to hear it again? Do you also wish to become his disciples?”

And they reply: “You be his disciple” (ibid., 27–28).

O great insult! Do you say this from desire, and rebuke without cause? You do not separate me from the light.

“But we,” they say, “are disciples of Moses.”

And he says: “I have listened to Moses, and I have listened to the prophets. From the beginning of the world it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one born blind” (ibid., 32).

O great defender! He already defends the truth before he believes. In the midst of the clouds he stands as a single drop, and from the living fountain he wins a triumph.

They are angered and cast him out.

Blessed is he who goes out from the synagogue of the wicked. As he leaves the arena victorious, an army of angels escorts him.

He fought, defended, conquered, and departed without a crown, because it was necessary for him to be crowned by the Lord.

The Lord, the one who crowns the innocent and illuminates the blind, meets him and wipes the sweat from his forehead. He consoles him with a word, having healed him with clay.

“What do you say, my mirror?” the Lord says. “You see outwardly; do you suppose that you see inwardly? You see me as I appear to you; do you suppose that you see in me what does not appear to you? You see that I am a human being; do you suppose that you see that I am the Word made flesh? Do you believe in the Son of God?”

“Lord, who is he, that I may believe in him?” (ibid., 36–37).

“I am he,” he says, “the one speaking with you.”

And he replies: “I believe, Lord. I have perceived your majesty and received the brightness that I had lacked through nature. I heard your voice; I recognize your glory. I believe, I believe, I believe, Lord.”

And falling down, he worshiped him (ibid., 38).

He worshiped what he saw; he believed what he had sensed. Once illuminated, he worshiped the light and gave thanks to the Lord, saying with the prophet:

“With you, Lord, is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35:10).

## SERMON XVIII. On Elisha, where he multiplied the widow’s oil.

Since the Lord has come, to humble the slanderer, let the Church not fear the moneylender, because he has made the woman secure.

O great mystery, sacrament of the oil that comes to our aid, by which a debt is paid, life is brought to completion, and security before the coming Judge is confirmed!

O great mystery, which is enclosed in a horn! From where priests are anointed, greedy creditors are defeated. From where prophets were anointed, there the mother with her sons does not fear the moneylender. From where priests were anointed, there the greater priest is made, together with the sweet Church of his children.
