And just as one ointment is poured from many ingredients, so this mystery caused brothers to dwell together with their mother in unity.

O grace of oil, by which help is brought to the mourning mother and violence is taken away from the moneylender! O preparation by which healing has been accomplished! From there wounds, once smeared, are comforted; from there proud hearts are softened, so that necks anointed with chrismatic oil accept the gentle yoke.

Who would not attend to the sacrament of oil, by which the woman wins the freedom of her children? For it makes everyone see, because without oil a lamp cannot shine.

In the sacrament of oil, therefore, is the grace of the Holy Spirit. The richness of illumination drives away the onset of night’s succession of darkness.

For this widow was amid darkness. A mother bereaved of her husband, burdened with debt, and subjected to a double yoke, she had lost sight of the light through weariness. She suffered darkness because of the agreement of cruel moneylenders. Outside, violence; within, misery.

Mercy is sought, and there is no one to provide it except the prophet. The woman, distressed, appeals to Elisha:

“Help me, lord, servant of God. The matter is brought forward and explained, and the tears cannot be held back. You know, lord, your servant, my husband, because he was a man who feared God” (2 Kings 4:1).

“He has died while a debt remained outstanding, which he himself was unable to repay. I am compelled to pay it. All my wealth consists of my two sons, the sighs of my womb. The moneylenders expect nothing else than to make my sons, born with heavenly freedom, subject to their own lust.

“Silver was not what they wanted; that is clear, for even if it had been available, the impious moneylenders would have hastened only to enslave the free status of my children. They want to take away those whom God has deigned to grant me. Can they pay their father’s debt? Is it not the soul that sins which alone shall be punished?

“They do not desire me as a maidservant; they claim my womb itself to be enslaved. Why did I give birth? Why did I give birth amid groaning? Why were the gates of my womb opened, and why did I pour into the light those whom I see now in another’s power?

“They seek them; they despise me. And what comfort can my sons have in the house of the moneylenders? No mother to cherish them when fevered, no mother to console them when weak. They will weep, and there will be no one to console them.

“I offer them to your sight, blessed prophet. Make them servants of their Lord. If you help me with my debt, let profane moneylenders not take them away, but let angelic powers nourish them.”

And the prophet said: “Stop mourning. Give me an account from your stores. What do you have in the house?” (ibid., 2).

And she replied: “It is shameful to say, lord, what I possess; because of it I suffer this misery and violence. I have nothing except a little oil in a vessel.”

And the prophet said: “Woman, what you have is not little. It will overcome the darkness of the moneylenders and bring about the light of the angels. I can advise you about oil, because no one can belong to God without oil.”

See, brothers, where the prophet directs the mourning mother: to the anointing of chrism, that is, to the exceedingly rich compassion of Christ.

John cries out: “I am not the Christ. Attend and see: Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:20, 29).

Isaiah cries out: “Behold, our Lord himself will come, and he will save us” (Isaiah 35:9).

David cries out to the mourning mother: “If you wish to be free from the violence of the moneylenders, take holy oil, so that your sons may be able to dwell with you as brothers in unity” (Psalm 112:9).

“And what shall I do,” she says, “with the little oil that remains in the vessel of the Church coming from both peoples?”

This is the figure of the worshiper; and truly only a little oil remained for Israel in the Jewish vessel. The prophet was already coming to his end, hoping for the Lord Savior, who is in the little oil that remained.

“For unless the Lord had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom” (Isaiah 1:9).

“Take counsel,” he says, “woman, concerning that vessel. Do not despair completely. Take for yourself as many new vessels as possible. Enter, you and your sons, into an inner room in silence, and shut your door. Enter your storerooms; hide yourself for a little while, until the fury of the moneylenders passes.”

The woman did as the prophet commanded. She took new vessels; the Church took members of the human race from all the neighboring nations, from the Lord’s pottery. The mother and her sons enter within.

What takes place in that room? There I see the sacrament of Passover. It is the Holy of Holies. There the horn flourishes; there the moneylender withers. It is Passover with the mother and her sons, with the Church and the peoples.

I see a fountain; I contemplate chrism; I worship Christ.

The woman received vessels from her sons as they ministered, and poured into them; she brought another vessel and poured again, and the oil did not cease.

Is it not obvious what is happening, when new vessels are filled? The woman became wealthy and secure. She who had poured out tears gives thanks.

“Go,” he says, “sell it, repay the debt, and live on what remains—you and your sons.”

One must live from what remains. One must pass through life by the grace of Christ, because Christ came in humility and is sufficient for the Church, since oil never grows dark.

O sacrament of oil! From there wise virgins were approved; from there mothers too are made secure. From there virgins deserve to enter their homeland; from there the mother deserves to offer service to the Lord and to rejoice with her sons in perpetual freedom.

## SERMON XIX  
[Note: Attributed to Augustine in the manuscript codex of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, in the city.]

Also on Elisha.

[Col. 0884A]

Sweetly the word “freedom” sounded in our ears as it was recited, while bitter captivity raged against us. Just as good fragrances are kindled amid foul odors, and the arrival of a physician is announced in a house of the sick, so the groaning of those in chains found relief because the resurrection of the dead was proclaimed. Hence David cries out, appropriately expressing the judgment of divine vengeance: “Avenge, O Lord, the blood of your servants that has been poured out; let the groaning of those in chains enter your presence” (Ps. 88:10–11).

Here a pitiable mother, embracing a funeral while excluding death, heightens her grief before Elisha, with the mountains as witnesses, and seeks again her son, already dead, whom she had not expected suddenly to conceive. Hence the devout sisters conclude their embassy: “Lord,” they say, “behold, Lazarus, whom you love, is ill.” Between sisters and a mother, Death, how can you fulfill the purpose of your cruelty? [Col. 0884B] Your dreadful condition is emptied, whether in a bed or—even more so—in a tomb, because a fraternal and maternal embassy has succeeded. You poured out your poison without cause; through the mercy of tears it has been brought to nothing. You hasten to bend your sting: the servant from the mountain will crush it, the Lord from the cross— the servant by sending, the Lord by foreknowing; the servant descending to the house, the Lord coming to the tomb. Everywhere your dreadful condition is emptied, whether in a bed or, what is more grievous, in a tomb.

But we have shared in the joy of Lazarus restored to life, together with the compassion of his sisters. Let us now turn to the mother’s grief and to the raising of her only son.

That woman who approached the prophet concerning her dead son had previously received him with fitting hospitality [variant: “with recognized dignity”]. The merit of resurrection was the progression of hospitality. For since the prophet frequently had his comings and goings among them, and had been content with their common dwelling, intending to be a pious guest and a better advocate for them, the woman conferred with herself, wrestled with her conscience, prepared her mind together with her hospitality, and asked her husband:

[Col. 0884C]

“Behold,” she said, “the man of God frequently comes to us, and he greatly surpasses us. He is righteous; we are sinners. He is heavenly; we are earthly. He is singular in hope; we, joined together without fruit. It is hard that he should share the walls of a common dwelling with us when we do not share his character. Let us make him, my husband, a room above, so that when he comes he may retire as though to his own lodging. Our dwelling should be lower, because our merits too are lower. The martyrs lie beneath God’s altar. Should we not remain [manuscript: ‘lie’] beneath the dwelling of a man of God?”

The holy plan pleased them, and, with common counsel [reading uncertain] and in the likeness of bees, they began to build a lodging for their guest. That good woman, who loved hospitality, did not disdain to pour water or carry beams [manuscript: “wood”]. The labor was sweet, for the love of charity had prompted it. She conceived the plan in her mind and built it through her labor. She prepared the room with adornments. She placed a table, a chair, a bed, and a lamp, and prepared a worthy lodging for the one who was coming.

[Col. 0884D]

“Where are you,” she said, “servant of my Lord? A house prepared with your adornments awaits you, so that the sweet affection of your guests may rejoice.”

He is received, cherished, and honored, and he considers how to return the favor.

“Tell me, Gehazi,” he said; “tell me, boy; call that Shunammite woman, so that we may return some recompense to her who has shown us such great charity.”

The boy came and called the woman. And the prophet said:

“Tell me, woman, what pressing need you may have, so that you may receive the fruit of your devotion? Nor should our embassy on your behalf have to act before a king or rulers, lest some troublesome disturbance affect you.”

And the woman replied:

“Nothing, lord, is troublesome to me. I dwell in the midst of my people; public litigation is far from us, since you deem it worthy to be our guest. We impose no burdensome labor upon you. From you, before the Lord, we ask only one choice prayer.”

[Col. 0885A]

And the boy said:

“Lord, certainly she has no son, and her husband is already old.”

And the prophet said:

“By this time next year you shall see yourself with a son conceived.”

Filled with desire and modest in her thoughts, she trembled with fear and quivered with joy, yet she received the fruit. A son was born to her, conceived late and destined to die soon. For, overcome by the heat of the summer sun, he sighed upon his mother’s knees and closed his eyes in death.

She patiently placed her dead child upon the bed of the man of God, and asked her husband to hasten to the man of God, concealing the emergency lest one hope should become desperate grief.

“I know,” she said, “that fathers grieve the death of their sons more bitterly, and sometimes, through grief, blaspheme the Lord with bitter lips. Better that I remain silent and not provoke my husband into the sin of sorrow, lest, losing my son, I begin to lose my husband as well.”

Having made her arrangements in silence, she went upstairs and tearfully bade farewell to her son:

“My son, conceived late and mournful, before you I learned to weep rather than to nourish. Forgive me; I proceed in such a way that I may soon come to you. I leave you alone, going [Col. 0885B] alone, but I shall return to you not alone, nor shall I find you alone without the Lord. I am coming quickly; I shall not delay, lest I create a pitiable reproach for my guest. Why should I prepare a place for your burial, not knowing what pleases my lord? Your body is small; if the outcome is not achieved, a place for your burial can be prepared for you in a moment. What labor is there in a grave when the limbs are small? Yet I shall not pass by my guest, lest he charge me with the sin of silence.”

She went by a sorrowful road, intending to return with mercy. Grief drives the journey swiftly; the road will be swift, so that the remedy may be swift.

But when she reached the mountain, she began from afar to display her tearful face and to testify to her maternal grief:

“Did I ask you for a son, Lord? Did I make some troublesome request of you? Yours was the promise; yours, through God, was its fulfillment; yours must also be the healing. My womb had been empty, and my mourning was empty too. Through you I learned to weep; through you may I deserve also to rejoice.”

The prophet, preceding the mother, hastened and [Col. 0885C] wondered within himself and considered:

“Why has the Lord God concealed this from me? The Holy Spirit reveals everything to me from heaven, yet he kept silent with me about my little guest.”

He sent the boy ahead as a forerunner, so that he might touch the dead child with his staff and he might live. But she said:

“As the Lord lives and as your soul lives, I will not leave you. Restore what you gave, for you did not promise through a disciple that I should have him. As testimony I have your bed, where I placed my dead child, if you disregard my grief. Come with me, or raise the dead, or at least commend the deceased.”

When the prophet descended from the heights to the heights below, from the mountain to the house, from the wilderness into silence, he groaned before the Lord, who is judge of the living and the dead:

“Lord,” he said, “look upon me and upon this woman, your guest. Let me not be accused in your mercy, so that you may be praised in your healing.”

He climbed onto the bed, constrained by the child’s contracted limbs. He breathed upon the one lying there seven times and restored him alive to his mother.

[Note: [Col. 0885D] We add the remainder from a manuscript.]

What joy there was in the house! How humble and gentle the healing had to be! Whoever wishes to heal one who suffers should take up humility. There is no fruit in the proud, because God humbles the proud. The prophet was humbled, and he restored life to the child.

Thus also our Savior Jesus Christ, making his word brief upon the earth, was humbled, becoming a worm and not a man, the reproach of men, although he is Lord of angels. He rose, ascended into heaven, and the entire host of angels rejoiced. Amen.

## SERMON XX. On Elijah and Elisha

The Jordan opens to those who presume to cross it, because the fountain of life opens to believers. It is good and delightful to see the channel of the Jordan divided by the withdrawal of its waters, and the company of deer, when herds of the thirsty cross over—those who desired it like a deer longs for springs of water. It is familiar for the Jordan to be divided by a staff and separated by a sheepskin.

[Col. 0886A] Joshua divided it when the ark of the covenant shone forth (Josh. 3:15); Elijah divided it while a goatskin inspired fear. Joshua divided it with the angel standing there with a sword; Elijah divided it (2 Kings 2:8) when a fiery chariot came to meet him in great triumph. He passed through water and reached flame. Yet the water did not cleanse him, nor did the fire scorch him: the wave withdrew, the flame bore him. There was baptism with victory; here, fiery triumph with a crown. Thus he might sing amid the winds and the heavens:

“We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (Ps. 65:12).

For after water and fire he was carried to paradise.

Elijah and Elisha, the master and the disciple, the Lord Christ and the acquired people, stood at the bank of the Jordan with the disciple of charity. For when Christ passed through the channel of the Jordan, the entire people of the candidates began to cross the waves of the waters. The Lord ascended from the Jordan and emerged into fiery temptation, a flaming contest in the wilderness, so that through his victorious victory he might make the whole burning world beautiful,

[Col. 0886B] and refresh by the triumphs of temptation the world growing green amid its heat. A fiery, cloud-bearing chariot met him, while God’s chariots descended, the rejoicing angels, and ministered to the victorious Lord after his triumph, as the evangelist Matthew testifies (chap. 4:11). The candidates follow the Lord, crossing through the midst of the Jordan. And at the bank they are met by flame—that is, fiery combat—so that a beautiful crown may blossom from the flames.

“My son,” Scripture says, “when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Sir. 2:1).

But let us return to Elijah the triumphant and Elisha, his dearest follower: the former a testator, the latter an heir. This one asks for a testament; that one dictates it. The pen was the tongue, not a reed; the inkwell was not black smoke but the brightness of baptism.

What does the master, the willing testator, say?

“Ask something of me before I am taken away from you.”

And he replied:

“Let the spirit that is in you become double in me.”

And the master said:

“What you have asked is difficult, but what is requested amid the waters is not denied” (2 Kings 2:9).

What do they not receive when they pass through fountains of water, so that they may enter the kingdom of heaven?

[Col. 0886C] What, then, did Elijah reply to the covetous disciple, without the fault of covetousness? For the covetous person is not reproved in the kingdom of God but praised.

“If you see me being taken away from you,” he said, “it will be granted to you.”

The one promises; the other follows. The master strikes the Jordan’s wave with the skin, and the disciple does not abandon the living charity of his master.

The prophet’s garment, carried into the fire, was not silk with a moth in it but a dead skin with new life. He wore a skin because he mortified his limbs upon the earth. It was the skin of a dead goat, which Christ carried, having come in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:3).

The asker and the promiser pass through; the one who offers and the one who presumes pass through. The wave receded, and a chariot with flame appeared before them. The air is disturbed, the winds are stirred, storms grow quiet, demons flee, and the rulers of darkness are scattered. The disciple is suspended, and the master is lifted up.

O wondrous conveyance, in which there are not Cappadocian horses but burning horses!

[Col. 0886D] A chariot made from fire, not wood. The chariot of the righteous man’s strength will not be clothed in a mass of silver but in a golden curtain of flame.

I ask: what sort of horses were they? They appeared to be animals, but the fire could not be touched. The one seated was lovely in chastity. Where did the wheels run? Where did the horses’ hoof strike? What sort of meadow was there? The air and the wind—where the revolving wheels shone and resounded with spiritual motion. The air was his meadow, fire his ascent, paradise his homeland.

But just as it delights the master to receive the one ascending, so it delights the disciple to behold him, hanging back in mournful expectation after his master. He cried out, addressing him:

“Father, Father, driver of Israel!” (2 Kings 2:12).

And he cast down the skin in order to console the one who loved him. He received the great treasure of his inheritance: the skin of the mighty testator. Through that skin he received the power to divide the Jordan himself, to cut through the stream, to cleanse a leper,

[Col. 0887A] to raise two dead men, to free a widow from the debt of interest, and to rescue orphans from the chains of slavery. These were the riches of the skin, from which the testator stripped himself, while the heir was clothed.

For Christ the Lord also, whose prophet Elijah was, stripped himself of flesh through living death, and through the Jordan the whole world was clothed in the newness of grace.

## SERMON XXI. On the sons of Zebedee

Blessed is the Lord, who alone works wonders, who sits upon the throne of his kingdom. He deigned to visit the abyss of our sin, so that he might rescue us from the throne of death and place us with himself and in himself at the Father’s right hand.

But who could reach the one seated, unless we saw the one passing by, whom Stephen saw standing? Blessed David asked this, as we have just sung and then answered in harmonious voice while singing the psalm:

“You who sit upon the cherubim, appear before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh” (Ps. 80:2).

[Col. 0887B] The blessed mother of the sons of Zebedee had heard this and learned it by reading. She understood that the Lord sat upon the cherubim because he possessed great dignity. She approaches to be enlightened and worships like a maidservant. She asks not for earthly gifts but for heavenly wishes. For he is Lord of the heavens, from whom she demands a heavenly desire.

“Say,” she says, “that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left, in your kingdom” (Matt. 20:21).

“Say it,” she says, “by your word, and the fulfillment will advance my request. You spoke, and heaven came to be; speak, and a throne, the splendor of thrones, will be prepared for my sons.”

O woman by condition! But because you are a mother in devotion, you have surpassed human dignity. Christ preached from the cross, and she understood sovereignty. He said:

“Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified” (ibid., 18).

And she approached as an intercessor for her beloved sons.

O blessed mother of holy sons! You surpassed the merit of the blessed and went beyond the honor of angels. Is it not enough for you that I have made your sons exalted preachers, whom you had raised as needy fishermen?

[Col. 0887C] After nets, you ask for heaven; after the hook, the Gospel; after the little boat, you ask for a throne?

Have you not read in the books of the fathers what he said concerning the angels of glory? Raphael says:

“I am one of the seven angels who stand and move about before the glory of the Most High God” (Tob. 12:15).

And you say, “Let my sons sit”?

Have you not heard what Daniel said?

“I saw, and behold, a throne was set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat. Thousands upon thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:9).

And you say, “Let my sons sit”?

The prophet Isaiah sees the Seraphim standing around the altar before the Lord (Isa. 6:2), and you ask for your sons to sit on thrones?

As though it were little for you if they stood, mother. Or if you did not know the order of angels, why did you not read the merits of our fathers? It is not fitting that your sons should be made equal to our father David, who drove away demons with the lyre (1 Sam. 16:23), who sang an angelic Alleluia with a human tongue, who defeated the foreigner Goliath by innocence, not armor (1 Sam. 17:49), and who said in prayer to his Lord, who was to come from his seed according to the flesh:

[Col. 0887D] “In the morning I shall worship you, Lord; in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I shall stand before you, and I shall contemplate you” (Ps. 5:4–5).

What shall we say of Elijah, who, carried upward in a heavenly chariot, deserved triumph before he received his reward? And what did he say when he raised his hand toward heaven?

“As the Lord lives, before whom I stand today” (1 Kings 17:1).

And you ask for your sons to sit upon a throne?

The voice of the Lord also belongs to the one who remains, terrifies, and confirms:

“Watch and pray, that you may be worthy to escape all the things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man” (Luke 21:36).

And you ask thrones of majesty for your sons?

Forgive us, mother: we have said these things in wonder, not in condemnation.

“Do not, do not,” says the blessed mother, “judge me desirous of impossibilities. The Lord has granted me this eager will. He loves those who use force to seize his kingdom and hates only those who seek to wield power over the needy. He says, ‘The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it’” (Matt. 11:12).

[Col. 0888A] Because he deigns to love this, I have dared to ask it of him. From him I heard:

“Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7).

While it is open, I knock; while it is permitted to receive, I ask; while there is time, I seek. For I heard it said:

“Seek the Lord while he may be found” (Isa. 55:6),

lest you seek him then, when he cannot be found. Now—now, while he appears in the form of a servant, while he is patient even unto the death of the cross, while he bears an unrecognized face and the sparks of coals have not yet been kindled by him. But when the angels begin to go before him with a trumpet and a loud voice, when the powers of heaven are shaken, what will a woman’s intercession accomplish there? When fire is shaken around him and a mighty storm rages, how will my desires prevail? Shall I be able to approach the fiery throne when legions of sinners have gathered for judgment? Therefore, now, seeing him in this humility, I desire to seize this promise in advance, but I shall hear my Lord responding.

[Col. 0888B] “Say now, Lord, that my sons may sit with you at the sides of your kingdom.”

And the Lord replied:

“Great is what you ask, but you do not consider the merit of the contest. You want the reward for your sons before they begin to undergo the labor. Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” (Matt. 20:22).

The mother asks, and the Lord demands faith from the sons. The mother was not competent to pledge faith on behalf of her children, whose will she did not control as her own. But the Lord, as just and wise, demanded faith from those to whom he proposed the contest of martyrdom. For the cup of passion is drunk in the bloody draught of martyrdom, so that the bloody poison of death may be expelled, by which the whole human race had perished through Adam.

When questioned, they themselves replied:

“We can” (ibid.).

What should we say, Lord? “We can.” Through you, Lord, may we be able, through whom we ask for what we desire. Our ability is in your power. May our request be according to your will.

[Col. 0888C] “You ask well; you promise well. May truth follow your promise. But your request surpasses the grace of human merits. You will indeed drink my cup” (ibid., 23): mine, not yours; your drinking, but my granting. Since this is granted to you who drink by my gift, hope well. But what you ask, because it is reserved for those who contend, await with certain understanding.

“To sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give you, but it belongs to those for whom it has been prepared” (ibid.).

He did not say for whom it had been prepared. He places the honor in concealment, so that he may show everyone the labor. He wants all to be prepared, since he desires none to be separated. Therefore he suspended the request of the two, lest he stir resentment in the others. This was always the practice of our Lord: not weakness in power but wisdom in justice, so that he would not incite the human spirit of the disciples to jealousy.

Thus far he sends all equally toward glory, granting grace to all by one way. For when the apostle Peter presumed upon a special grace for himself, he did not receive it favorably but warned him in advance, when Peter said:

“Even if all are scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized.”

He replied:

[Col. 0888D] “Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times” (Matt. 26:33–34).

Peter, you presume yourself superior to the others; you will immediately discover yourself inferior.

But when he looked out for all in common, and asked life and glory both for himself and his fellow disciples, saying:

“Behold, we who have followed you—what will there be for us?”—

the Lord answered equally, without separating them:

“Amen, I say to you, you who have followed me, in this generation, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also will sit with him upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:27–28).

Consider the reason for what he said: “It is not mine to give you.” He did not want the honor of two to create discord among the others over precedence, because he prepares one crown for all. Reason itself testifies to the greater promise, for the Son of Majesty is not powerless. He who promises twelve thrones in response to a common request—did he not have power over two thrones for his own purposes?

[Col. 0889A] He who established the thrones with power wants his disciples always to be in harmony, because God is love. Behold, he does not promise them to the two, and the ten disciples became sorrowful. What would happen if the ten had grieved that they were placed behind the two? But as a wise ruler, he removed pride from the two and took envy away from the ten, so that he might preserve the souls of all unharmed. For he can grant the thrones not in the human form in which the Father is greater, but in that form in which the Father and I are one.

Let the Christian understand this, and he will be eternal.

## SERMON XXII. On Lazarus raised

Lazarus, the friend of the Savior, when he had already been removed from human affairs, already committed to burial, indeed already returned to the earth from which he had been taken, immediately at the Lord’s word was summoned from the tomb and came out alive, having shortly before been carried there dead.

All the common people marvel at so many and such great wonders. Christ speaks, and [Col. 0889B] power follows. Lazarus himself is astonished that he has been made alive again from death. Twice two days had already passed, but he who had been deprived of light did not perceive the day. The gloomy whirlwind of night had already possessed him in the horror of the dark, foul-smelling cave. Already the powerful prison of hell, hostile to light, had enclosed him. His limbs lay there, putrefying and exhaling a heavy odor. After four courses of the sun had passed, his body, covered with the decay of death, was besieged by a flesh-eating host of worms, and the earth produced little beasts of the grave to prey upon the abandoned corpse.

His sisters mourned with grief and lamentation, deprived of their brother’s help. His parents and relatives also shared their sorrow in a cloud of sadness. All wore mourning clothes; their hair was unkempt and covered with a black veil. Their faces were wet with tears, their vital beings strained by sobs, and a mournful wailing had disturbed their entire appearance.

But when Christ, who is ignorant of nothing that happens—for nothing is inaccessible, distant, or obscure to him; neither distance of place, remoteness of regions, nor abyss restrains him—announced to the disciples through his foreknowing divinity that Lazarus was dead, [Col. 0889C] the disciples themselves became sorrowful and said:

“Let us go, and let us die with him” (John 11:16).

O indissoluble covenant of friendship! O effect of unconquered charity! Those whom charity had made harmonious in this life desired to become companions in death.

When Jesus therefore stood beside the tomb of the one who rested there, while the surrounding crowd of peoples made a tumult and the wailing of ululating voices offered grief to his most merciful ears, Jesus himself was moved in spirit and groaned (ibid., 33), and shed tears.

Here let every religious understanding be vigilant: what did Christ grieve over, and what did he weep for? For he who held complete power over life and death could not have mourned Lazarus as a dead man. He wept, but certainly he did not weep for the reason the Jews supposed, that he loved Lazarus greatly. Rather, he wept because he was bringing him back again to the miseries of this life.

[Col. 0889D] Death, dearest brothers, is the recovery from sorrow, the release of captivity, the harbor of sailors, the homeland of travelers, the end of miseries, and the termination of sins. For this thing called life is not life, where there is neither rest from labor nor security from fear; where there are frauds and accusations; where another’s property is taken without regard for mercy; where the rich are lifted up and the poor oppressed. Everything is conducted in iniquity, so that nothing at all may be reserved for justice.

Therefore Jesus wept for Lazarus, not because he was dead, but because he was going to rise again. For how could he mourn the dead when he himself had come to raise him?

But you will say to me: If it is evil to return again to this life, what of Jesus Christ, who died and rose again? Christ rose in such a way that he would die no more; Lazarus, however, rose again in order to die again. As the apostle Paul says:

“Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more, and death shall no longer rule over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God” (Rom. 6:9–10).

And therefore he raised Lazarus on the fourth day, because he reserved for himself the third day on which he would rise.

[Col. 0890A] After Jesus had seen the stone closing the enclosure of Lazarus’s tomb, he ordered it to be rolled away. When it had been rolled away, he looked toward heaven and declared that he had already been heard. In the presence of the people he prayed to the Father in these words:

“Father, I thank you because you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me; but because of the people standing around I said this, so that they may believe that you sent me.”

And when he had said these things, he cried:

“Lazarus, come out!” (John 11:41 and following).

How great was the power of the cry, that its sound reached the wretched? How powerful was the force of fear, that fear invaded the dead? Immediately, at the Lord’s command, death broke through the law it had possessed and, at Christ’s command, dissolved the rights it had held for so many ages. The royal keys of hell gave way, and the barred entrances of the foulest prison opened before the Lord’s command. All custody vanished, and the person who had been torn away emerged. Lazarus was restored once more to the light, and once again he shared a meal in the body with Christ, because he had already been delivered over to hell.

## SERMON XXIII. On the washing of feet

[Col. 0890B]

All error came to a standstill because the Lord washed the feet of servants. He directed them into a new course, so that he might make their footsteps firm like those of deer.

What should I proclaim more: joy or miracle? Rather, both joy and miracle. Joy, because our footsteps were offered and the Lord’s right hand touched the feet of servants. But it is more truly a miracle that the one whom the armies of angels attend with fear should wash, with hands bent down, the feet of fishermen.

Heaven was terrified, earth was terrified, that the Lord should humble himself in this way and that the human being should be exalted above God.

What does the heretic mean by saying that the Son was humble before the Father in honor, not in fear? When you see the Lord bent down in servile fashion, it is not through fear but through love, not through servitude but through dominion. For in order to restore freedom to servants, he showed them a servant’s devotion.

Will the one who is greater than all therefore be lesser than servants because he washed their feet?

“For the one who is lesser among you is greater in the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9:48).

The Lord serves, and the servant murmurs. The Master and Lord freed and taught when he did [Col. 0890C] what he taught.

“For,” he says, “the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve” (Matt. 20:28).

He did what he taught.

But blessed Peter did not understand the mystery. He was more afraid than unwilling:

“Lord, are you washing my feet?” (John 13:6).

You, Lord, whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is the earth, will you be the servant of my feet? Is the cross you accepted small, the wounds you endured, the gall and vinegar you drank? Is it a small thing that, while alive and dying, you hid in the tomb? Have you come, Lord, even to my feet?

Your appearance terrifies me. Your hand disturbs me. My footsteps are unworthy.

And the Lord said:

“Let it be, Peter. You do not know what I am doing, but afterward you will understand” (ibid., 7).

You are like a child, one of these little ones who weep childishly when their feet are washed, not knowing the mystery but not refusing the service. Such are you; then you will be little; you will be, Peter, the last.

“Unless I wash your feet, you will have no share with me.”

“Lord,” he said, “not only my feet, but also my hands and head” (ibid., 8–9).

[Col. 0890D] Let all who think otherwise take an example here; let them come to judgment. Let some not mock Christ’s humility; let others not repeat the simplicity of baptism. For:

“The one who has bathed once has no need to wash; he is entirely clean” (ibid., 10).

Why, then, are the feet washed, if he is entirely clean? This is not the mystery of baptism but the service of charity, so that the little ones may learn what the fishermen learned, and so that all may be the ready-footed heralds of Christ, for it is said of them all:

“How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Rom. 10:15).

These are the feet in which Mother Church rejoices, she who is now gathered in the basin, as though baked in the potter’s vessel. She is gathered throughout the whole world, as water is gathered in the basin. There the footsteps of servants are cleansed, so that throughout the world the grace of baptism may be seen and the clean proclamations of all priests may run forth, because:

“The voice of his thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. 77:19),

because the earth belongs to the Lord, together with the whole redeemed Church, in which we all sing Alleluia.

## SERMON XXIV. Another sermon on the same subject

[Col. 0891A]

Today’s mystery is a journey toward the kingdom of heaven, where the footsteps of little ones are washed, so that they may themselves be able to run with cleansed feet and the dragon may not be able to insert its poisons into them.

How beautiful are their feet, whose feet the Lord of angels washes! What a great spectacle, in which the human race trembles to see the Lord bend down to the footsteps of servants.

He who bent down the heavens and descended, with darkness beneath his feet (Ps. 18:10), now bends himself to serve the disciples. Let the whole world rejoice. For Christ’s bending down is the bending of Antichrist’s pride, so that he himself may walk bent over, while the apostles’ course is upright and the whole world rejoices.

For this basin is the whole redeemed earth, into which water has been poured, so that those who dwell upon the earth may pass through water to life. The potter who made the basin and redeemed the world adorns earthen vessels in the muddy basin, so that they may bear the treasure in earthen vessels—with washed feet, rejoicing waters, and trembling apostles.

[Col. 0891B] But Peter, steadfast in his faith, wanted to object—not through disobedience but through fear.

“Lord,” he said, “are you washing my feet?” (John 13:6).

You, Lord, whom angelic powers tremble before; you who sit upon the cherubim (Ps. 80:2)—you bend down to the basin! You bend toward your servants, you who raise up the fallen and release those in chains (Ps. 146:8)!

“Lord, this great mystery exceeds me. I think heaven itself could tremble with me, and the angels would not permit you to do what I, trembling, try to excuse. It is enough for me that you have granted your presence, given grace, and bestowed power, so that sight may be restored to the blind, hearing to the deaf, movement to the lame, and life to the dead—and yet you bend toward my feet! This is not fitting for my merits or ours.”

“Let it be, Peter,” he says. “You need not oppose me, lest you begin to hinder yourself. Unless I wash your feet, you will have no share with me—and you excuse my service? For this reason I took the form of a servant while remaining in the form of God: so that I might bend down and exalt you; so that I might put my hand into the water for your footsteps, in order that you may learn a new way and walk along it with beautiful course.”

[Col. 0891C] Peter heard this and, though he had been fearful, became eager:

“Lord,” he said, “not only my feet, but also my hands and head” (John 13:9).

“No, Peter. I know the measure, I who gave my grace. You are already clean, since you have been washed once; for the one who has been washed once has no need to wash, but is entirely clean. I am teaching you the service of humility, not a repetition of baptism. I am showing you what you should do in life. I am Master and Lord, as your confession declares. My humility will hand this on to you. As Lord, I cleanse you; in the form of a servant, I teach you, so that pride may not exalt you.”

We have therefore learned the Lord’s humility. Let us rejoice on the eighth day of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Let people learn that they ought to be reborn once, and let them desire to be cleansed by Christ’s hand. For whoever is not cleansed by Christ’s hands cannot run the road to heaven.

Thus the apostles ran through all the directions of the world; thus the martyrs, with their feet cleansed, came forward,

[Col. 0891D] so that they would not fear treading upon the flames of the burning griddle, the boiling pot, or the seething furnace. For he made firm the soles of his servants, so that the word of the Lord might run and be glorified, and so that his humility and divinity might reign forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXV. Also on the washing of feet
The Head has risen, and the whole body has shone forth; yesterday the apostolic choir of those sitting behind closed doors was illumined. Today the feet of the elect are washed, prepared for the race like deer. How fittingly the Head has bent down, so that the body might rise again! And because the feet could not ascend to the Head, may the Head deign to bend down to the feet.

Today he filled the basin, so that in his Trinity he might gather the unity of our calling. He who gathered the sea filled the basin: the sea with fish, the basin with fishermen. There he said to Peter, “Come after me, and I will make you a fisher of human beings” (Mark 1:17). Here he admonishes and terrifies, obeys and threatens. “Unless I wash your feet,” he says, “you will have no share with me in the kingdom of heaven” (John 13:8). Are you still, like a delicate invalid, pushing away the physician’s hands? Do you wish to refuse good care? Do you not wish to have a share with me? For if you reject my humility, you will not see my exaltation. If my hands do not wash you, your hands will not touch me. If I do not wash your feet, Peter, how will you be able to enter paradise? Your feet will not be free from the serpent’s poison if you resist my hands. My hands made you; let my hands wash you. Let your hands not push me away, lest you fight against me with those hands.

O astonishing miracle! O great spectacle! The Emperor of heaven lies bent down at the feet of soldiers, while a human being, dust and ashes, swollen with pride, fights against the Lord. Some proud man, resisting from the opposite side, says to me that the Son of God, who was sent by the Father and honors the Father, is lesser. Is he lesser than the Father not because of unequal dignity, but because of indivisible love, since he glorifies the Father? What are you saying? What kind of judgment is this? And what of the one who says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9)? Is he therefore lesser than the Father because he glorifies the Father? Is he also lesser than his servants, to whom he displayed such humility that he deigned to attend to their footsteps?

For the one who gives thanks to his Father and by his own power raises Lazarus from his own tomb himself washes the feet of Peter, his fisherman-servant. What wonder, then, if he rose from supper and laid aside his garments (John 13:4), since, though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself? Yet, although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized. This chosen vessel cries out concerning God the Potter and says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Philippians 2:6).

I ask—I ask the apostle Paul: [Note: [Col. 0891] The pronoun *qui* (“who”) seems to need to be added, although the syntax does not altogether require it. EDITOR.] if he is proclaimed equal to God in the form of God, how is he described with sacrilegious presumption as lesser than the Father? What wonder, then, if he girded himself with a towel (John 13:4), since, taking the form of a servant, he was found in appearance as a human being? What wonder if he poured water into a basin (ibid., 5), with which he might wash the feet of the disciples, since he poured out blood on earth with which he might cleanse the uncleanness of sinners? What wonder, I say, if with the towel with which he was girded he wiped the feet he had washed, since with the flesh with which he was clothed he established the footsteps of the evangelists?

To gird himself with the towel, he laid aside the garments he had. But to take the form of a servant, when he emptied himself, he did not put down what he had; rather, he took what he did not have.

He therefore came to Peter, and Peter protested: “You will not wash my feet.” Lord, you have laid aside your garments for my sake, and will you wash my footprints? You are girded at the waist for my sake; gird me in my conduct for your sake. And do not humble yourself so far as to lie before me. Your humility is my trembling. You are in the form of God, and for my sake you have become in the form of a servant. I saw your feet walking upon the sea. I cannot bear your hands upon my feet. You suffer insult, and you kindle the awareness of my guilt.

And the Lord said: “Unless I wash your feet, you will have no share with me” (ibid., 8). It does you no good to make excuses, lest afterward you begin to accuse yourself. “What I am doing you do not know now, but afterward you will understand” (ibid., 7).

This was a dispute concerning the Savior’s piety and humility, between the fisherman and the Redeemer, the redeemed and the Redeemer, the one who obeyed and the one who feared, the Lord and the servant, the Teacher and the disciple—so that the venerable apostles might be taught to serve one another. Explaining the meaning of this action, he addressed them in these words: “Do you know what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am. If therefore I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, so that just as I have done to you, you also may do to one another” (ibid., 12 ff.).

What the Lord deigned to do for his servants, we servants likewise did today for our fellow servants. Girded with towels, we washed the feet of baptized infants, so that their paths might also be directed in the preparation of the gospel of peace (Ephesians 6:15), and so that their names, recorded with the pen of the swiftly writing scribe, might be kept in the register of the heavenly kingdom.

## SERMON XXVI. On the foregoing

Behold, the Lord of majesty has undertaken the office of servitude, because, although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6). Let us all say, “Blessed is the Lord,” we who are hearers of the evangelical reading and beloved spectators of the washing of feet.

Behold, he bends down to the footstool of his own feet, he whose throne is heaven. He has deigned to descend to his own feet, because we cannot reach his Head. Who can speak of the mighty deeds of the Lord (Psalm 105:2), which he carried out in the form of a servant?

Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth exult, and let the tender feet of infants tremble. For the Lord who stretched out heaven like a skin (Psalm 104:2)—behold, he has also filled a basin. Who can speak of the mighty deeds of the Lord?

When he made the stars, his angels praised him with a loud voice. He himself bears witness through his servant Job, in that splendid account of the creation of the stars. “When I was making the stars,” he says (Job 38:7), “my angels praised me.” When he established thrones and strengthened Principalities, Powers, and Dominions, he was powerful in the form of God. Now, as he arranges seats and looks upon the apostles sitting girded, he who is powerful in the form of God has become patient in the form of a servant.

The heavens rejoice, the angels tremble, the archangels are afraid, and the disciples do not dare to make excuses. If we were to say that at that spectacle the angels, descending from heaven to the basin, sang a hymn of peace, I would not think it absurd to say so. There he was wrapped in cloths; here he was girded with a towel. There the Magi lie at his feet; here he himself, in the form of a servant but girded with power, lies at the feet of servants—he who troubles the depth of the sea (Psalm 65:7).

He rejoices over his little basin, he whose roar of waves no one can withstand; he himself offers servitude to his servants. But the apostle Peter wishes to remain restless—not resisting, but trembling in conscience. He came to Peter first, as I believe, because he had assigned the last place to the washing of the feet, lest Peter’s excuse make them all excuse themselves. The other servants could not make excuses—not because they received this confidently when the Lord bent toward their feet, but because, shaken by trembling, they did not dare to object.

A frightening burden had fallen upon them: the ruler of the world had deigned to bend toward servant-like footsteps. Peter alone, first among the legion, steadfast in confidence, held the Lord’s hands and brought forward his own tears with devotion. The one bent down with the One bent down; the servant bowed with the Lord. God stretches out his hands to wash the feet, and Peter stretches out supplicating hands to make excuses.

“Lord, are you washing my feet?” (John 13:6) If you commanded an angel, it would somehow be a burden for me. Are you washing my feet—you who created earth and heaven? Did you not gather the sea into one place? And for my sake will you fill a basin? My iniquities have risen above my head, and you bend toward the uncleanness of my feet. If heaven is not clean before you, can the contact of my soles be clean? “You shall never wash my feet” (ibid., 8).

You spoke well, Peter: “I shall never wash your feet.” For I do not wish to repeat a unique and singular mystery, nor have I commanded a sacrament to be repeated twice. “I shall never wash your feet.” Nevertheless, one thing is necessary: if you now make excuses for the service being offered, you will have no share with me in the kingdom of heaven (ibid.).

Let me fulfill all righteousness. In the same way your fellow servant John made excuses at the Jordan, and you make excuses at the basin. “Let it be so for now”; what I am doing you do not know, but afterward you will understand.

Blessed Peter still seemed to bear the figure of an infant rejecting the Lord’s hands. Likewise, when we were washing the feet of infants, the sweet spectacle of the innocent children’s gentle resistance anticipated us: they pushed away, cried, wailed, and screamed, because they did not know what we were doing. So it was with Peter, to whom it is said, “What I am doing you do not know now, but afterward you will understand.”

Knowledge of the heavenly kingdom was displayed; understanding grew in the infant. He cries out, offering himself to the Lord: “Not only my feet, but also my hands and my head” (ibid., 9). Wash all of me, so that I may reach your grace whole. If I knew this, I would not object; but for the sake of your inheritance, fulfill whatever will of yours you wish.

O blessed saying! O precious mystery! O sweet service! “Unless I wash your feet, you will have no share with me.”

Why are your feet—that is, those of the whole human race—still held in the oblivion of terror? Have they not been cleansed for the way to the kingdom? Therefore I wash your feet, so that you may walk the straight road and reach my kingdom. On the road there are many robbers and many dragons, abundant serpents and watching scorpions.

If you wish what I have said to you to be fulfilled, you will tread upon serpents and scorpions, and nothing will harm you. Let me wash your feet and clothe them with the sandals of the gospel of peace, so that you may be a good runner and a beautiful announcer; and, as though dressed in the evangelical sandals like pearls, it may be said of you: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce good things, who announce peace” (Romans 10:15)!

Therefore we washed the feet of infants. They received a new sandal, and their feet became beautiful, so that wherever they enter, the sight of their feet upon royal sandals may be beautiful. When they say, “Peace to this house,” peace will rest in your worthy home, because the washed feet of your infants are dear to the solemnity, for eternal life.

## SERMON XXVII. On the woman who poured ointment over Jesus’ head

The Lord reclined in the house, he whom heaven contains. He is covered with ointment, he who, from his own name, gave the ointment of chrism; he who nourishes all trees with liquid and condenses within the inward parts of olives the richness of highly fragrant oil; he who commanded an olive branch to hang from the lips of a flying dove.

He does not reject the woman’s ointment, he who created cinnamon, balsam, spices, chosen myrrh, stacte (*gutta*), and cassia. He is covered with ointment at a new table, because it was something new that he who made heaven and earth should recline with fishermen. The ointment was precious, because he himself was beautiful, more beautiful in form than the sons of men (Psalm 45:3), as he reclined among little stones.

The Passion was approaching; the woman, the Church, ran with ointment. She stood behind him, because she understood Christ when he would rise again. Earlier she anointed him for burial; afterward, at the angels’ announcement, she worshiped him.

The house was fragrant with ointment; the world gave off its scent, because the unclean one had been cleansed. Judas is jealous and says, “Why this waste? Could not this ointment have been sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” (Mark 14:4–5).

What are you saying, Judas? You are understood: this is not piety, but greed. There is no waste in such an act; your betrayal will be hostile. She pours out the ointment through the good affection of her mind; you sell your Lord while loving money. What are you saying? “It could have been sold for three hundred denarii,” yet you hand over your Lord for thirty pieces of silver? Is ointment worth more than Christ, the Christ of christs, the Holy of holies, King of kings, and Lord of lords? You rightly judge the chrism to be precious; why do you demand a cheap price for Christ?

Sweet spices composed that ointment; Christ was breathed forth from the Father’s heart, and from him came a fragrance: the illumination of the blind, the hearing of the deaf, the raising of the lame, and the resurrection of the dead. And you bargain over him for a cheap price in the marketplace of the Jews?

But the Lord, who gladly accepted the ointment, himself rebukes the murmurer. “Why do you trouble her? Nothing has been lost through the woman’s service. Why are you angry about the poor? You always have the power, if you nevertheless intend to show piety; and I am poor, I am before you, and you do not understand me? I recline with you, and you sell me?”

The Jews paid the price; Judas accepted the silver, but he himself did not possess the price, because he ran to the noose; nor did they possess the one whom they bought. Let Christ the Redeemer sing; let Judas the seller groan; let the Jewish buyer blush. Behold, Judas sold, and the Jew bought. They conducted a wicked transaction; both were ruined, they destroyed themselves.

O Judas! O Jew! You wished to be seller and buyer. How much better would it have been for you to be redeemed by Christ! Judas sold; the Jew bought—an unhappy transaction! Neither has the price, nor has the one whom he bought, Christ.

Come all to this transaction, you who purchase the Lord not to keep him, but to crucify him; not to embrace him, but to fasten him with nails. If you wished to conduct a transaction, you would not have given silver in vain. You are false; you arranged a cruel bargain, devised a false plan, destroyed yourselves, and [destroyed] the wretch to whom you paid the money.

Behold, we are redeemed in a transaction of graces; here the bodies of many dead are redeemed, and they are raised from their own tombs. They cried out to the Redeemer, while you shouted against the one hanging on the cross. They obeyed in Jerusalem, while you led the Lord outside Jerusalem. They said, “The dead will not praise you, Lord, but we who live bless you” (Psalm 115:17–18); and you were saying, “Crucify him, crucify him” (Luke 23:21).

You fastened the nails; they opened their eyes. They abandoned their tombs, while you sealed Christ’s tomb, placing a great stone; with a futile guard you sealed the Lord lying in the tomb. Did you seal him against the one reigning in heaven? Can the one who descended from heaven with the heavens bent down not drive away the stone of the tomb? Can the one who leads captives out by his strength (Psalm 68:7) not strike your guards with blindness?

At the cross the dead bore witness: made alive, they announced the rising Lord; the soldiers confirmed it. And you arranged another bargain, giving money to the soldiers so that they would say, “His disciples came and stole him” (Matthew 28:13). O Jews, always foolish! The mystery of the risen Christ could not be hidden.

You lost the silver for no reason—there to the betrayer, here to the soldiers. But the angels laughed at you as they announced him. The nations rejoiced, and the angelic powers believed concerning the Lord. Where is the one whom you bought? Where is the one to whom you paid the money?

You could have been redeemed freely; but even now, if you wish to be redeemed, drink the blood that you poured out. We too drink it; if you wish, drink it with us as you sing, “And your cup that intoxicates—how splendid it is!” (Psalm 23:5). It is that blood which redeemed us in the world and now shines in heaven in the living Lamb.

## SERMON XXVIII. On the thief crucified with Christ

It is read above among the genuine sermons of Saint Fulgentius with this beginning: “Wonderful above all others,” and so forth.

## SERMON XXIX. Also on the foregoing

Among the praises of the righteous and those commendations with which we ought to accompany the testimony of those who act well, and encourage the confession of the sinner, this same protection is also ours: by every figure we may teach that our Lord, the Creator, Founder, and Ruler of all things, is generous in granting rewards and merciful in forgiving errors. The present evangelical reading reasonably persuades me to praise the thief, who left sinners an example of his faith and confession.

For thus we read: while the Lord was suffering for us, two thieves were hanging with him on the cross; one of them confessed, and the other blasphemed. The one who blasphemed said: “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us.” But the other answered and rebuked him, saying: “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? We indeed are suffering justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong” (Luke 23:39 ff.). And to commend his confession with a prayer, he himself said to the Lord: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (ibid., 42).

The Lord quickly answered the one who quickly recognized him, quickly confessed him, and quickly prayed for himself, with a fittingly brief response: “Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (ibid., 43). Thus was fulfilled what he had said through the prophet Isaiah: “You will pray, and he will answer you quickly; you will cry out, and he will say, ‘Here I am’” (Isaiah 58:9).

Behold, brothers, the Lord chose to be with the one who confessed him in paradise, he who has his own kingdom in heaven. “You will be with me,” he said, because it belongs to the superior to honor the inferior by union with himself. If he had said, “I will be with you,” the Lord might have seemed to have raised the sinner into pride rather than rewarded him, just as the evangelist says: “It is enough for the servant to be like his master, and for the disciple to be like his teacher” (Matthew 10:25).

“You will be with me” is therefore said to the sinner—that is, it is as though he were saying: “I am not hurrying to heaven for a little while, so that I may not deny the kingdom you have requested, since you have confessed.” But he said, “You will be with me in paradise,” not “You will sit with me in heaven.” For the one who alone descended from the Father’s bosom is the one who alone sits at the Father’s right hand. And the one who alone descended from the Father is the one who alone ascended to the Father.

This thief, by confessing, surpassed the martyrs on the way to paradise; by praying, he surpassed the apostles on the way to the kingdom—violent in the world, violent in reward. To Peter it is said, “Follow me” (John 21:19); to the thief it is answered, “I will not abandon you.” By one confession and one praise, he offered faith to Peter and bestowed knowledge upon Paul. Peter had been a denier; Paul had been a persecutor. The thief alone, in a similar passion and on a similar cross, was found to be the true preacher of the Lord.

The Lord is therefore always laboring for sinners and merciful among sinners; praying for sinners and granting gifts to sinners. For either the advocate prays or the judge grants. Stephen saw the Advocate standing; Paul recognized the Judge seated.

Thus, my brothers, so that the confessing thief might be rewarded, the Lord came to paradise; so that Adam might be rescued from punishment, the Lord descended to the underworld as a complete human being. He honored the one and freed the other. For this one he established a place without punishment in paradise; the other he freed from the punishing abyss. This is what he said: “Today you will be with me in paradise,” because the Lord first went to paradise with the thief, before he descended to the abyss for Adam.

On the first day, descending, he placed that one in rest; on the third day, ascending, he led this one into the light. But I cannot determine which of the two was happier after sin. Paradise first had a resident without sin; afterward it received a thief after sin. And because throughout creation the voice of praise to God is heard and understanding is recognized, I think that paradise was astonished that it had excluded Adam the sinner but received the thief the sinner. Hence I believe it said:

“If there is certainly one condition for sinners, why, after Adam was cast out because he sinned, does the thief dwell in me? I recognize that one as snatched up to me, another as transferred to me, and this one as placed within me.”

The thief’s just confession of sins became blessed. He who had been guilty in the world becomes a third inhabitant in paradise. And while Enoch and Elijah will come to die for the Lord, the thief alone dies with the Lord and enters paradise with the Lord.

## SERMON XXXIV

[Note: This is Augustine’s sermon, as Fulgentius himself testifies; he reproduces the sermon in full in his Letter to Ferrandus, now numbered the twelfth, at the end, from a manuscript of the Vatican codex. Although some things are lacking here, since this text is read somewhat differently here than it appears there, we likewise present in full what earlier printed codices had at this place.]

### On the sacrament of the altar

These things, brothers, are called sacraments because in them one thing is seen and another is understood. What is seen has a bodily form; what is understood has a spiritual fruit.

If therefore you wish to understand the body of Christ, hear the Apostle saying: “You are the body of Christ and members” (1 Corinthians 10:2, 7). If therefore you are the body of Christ and members, your mystery has been placed upon the Lord’s table; you receive your mystery, corresponding to what you are. You answer, “Amen,” and by answering you assent. For you hear, “The body of Christ,” and you reply, “Amen.” Be a member of Christ’s body, so that your “Amen” may be true.

Why, then, in bread? Let us bring nothing of our own into this. Let us hear the Apostle himself again and again. When he was speaking about this sacrament, he said: “One bread, one body—we who are many” (ibid., 17). Understand, and rejoice. Unity, piety, truth, love: one bread, one body—we who are many.

Recall that bread is not made from one grain, but from many. When you were exorcised, you were, as it were, ground; when you were baptized, you were, as it were, sprinkled together; when you received the fire of the Holy Spirit, you were, as it were, baked. Be what you see, and receive what you are. The Apostle said this about the bread.

What we should understand about the cup, even though it was not stated, he sufficiently indicated. Just as, for visible bread to exist, many grains are mixed together into one, as though that were fulfilled which Holy Scripture says concerning the faithful, “They had one soul and one body in God” (Acts 4:32), so also with wine, brothers. Recall from where wine comes. Many grapes hang upon a cluster, but the juice of the grapes is blended into unity.

Thus the Lord Christ, signifying that we belong to him, willed to consecrate the mystery of our peace and unity upon his table. Whoever receives the mystery of unity but does not hold the bond of peace receives not the mystery for himself, but a testimony against himself.

## SERMON XXXV

[Note: This is Augustine’s sermon 140, *On Time*.]

### On the second day of Easter

Yesterday the Resurrection was read from the Gospel, and it was read from the Gospel according to Mark. Today, as you heard the reader announce, the Resurrection of the Lord was recited for us from the Gospel, as the evangelist Luke wrote it—something you must often be reminded of and retain in memory.

You should not be troubled if one evangelist says something that another omitted, because the one who omits what another said also says something that the other omitted. Some things one alone says, and the other three do not say. Some things they say about the Lord, and others do not say. Some things three say, and one does not say. Yet the authority of the holy Gospel is so great that, because one Spirit spoke in them, what one has said is also true.

What you have just heard—that after the Lord Jesus had risen from the dead, he found two of his disciples on the road speaking with each other about what had happened, and said to them, “What are these words that you are speaking to one another, and why are you sad?” (Luke 24:17)—was said only by the evangelist Luke.

Mark touched on it briefly (chapter 16:12), saying that he appeared to two on the road, but he omitted what they said to the Lord and what the Lord said to them.

What, then, did this reading bring us? Something great, if we understand it. Jesus appeared; he was seen by their eyes, but he was not recognized. The Teacher walked with them on the road, and he himself was the road. Yet they were not walking on the road; rather, he found them wandering from the road.

When he had been with them before the Passion, he had foretold everything: that he would suffer, die, and rise on the third day. He had said everything, but his death became their forgetfulness. They were so disturbed when they saw him hanging on the wood that they forgot the Teacher, did not expect him to rise, and did not hold fast to the one who had promised.

“We had hoped,” they said, “that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21). O disciples, you had hoped? Then you no longer hope? Christ lives, and hope has died in you?

The living Christ found the disciples’ hearts dead. He appeared to their eyes and did not appear, and yet he was seen. For if he was not seen, how did they hear him asking questions and answer the one who questioned them? He walked with them on the road as a companion, and he himself was their guide.

Certainly they saw him, but they did not recognize him. Their eyes were held, as we heard, so that they would not recognize him (ibid., 16)—not held so that they would not see, but held so that they would not recognize.

Come, brothers: where did the Lord wish to be recognized? In the breaking of bread (ibid., 35). We are secure: we break bread, and we recognize the Lord. He did not wish to be recognized except there, for our sake—we who would not see him in the flesh, yet would eat his flesh.

Therefore, whoever is faithful, whoever is not called a Christian in vain, whoever does not enter the Church without cause, whoever hears the word of God with fear and hope, let the breaking of bread console you. The Lord’s absence is not absence. Have faith, and the one whom you do not see is with you.

When the Lord was speaking with them, they did not have faith, because after he had risen they did not believe and did not hope that he could rise. They had lost faith; they had lost hope. The dead were walking with life itself. Life walked with them, but life was not yet in their hearts.

And you, therefore, if you wish to have life, do what they did: they recognized God when they received him as a guest. The Lord appeared as though he were traveling farther away. But they held him, and before they came to the place they urged him, saying: “Stay with us now; evening is approaching and the day is already declining.”

Hold on to the guest, if you wish to know the Savior. What unbelief had taken away, hospitality restored. The Lord therefore presented himself in the breaking of bread. In the breaking, the unknown one speaks with human beings; in the breaking of bread he is recognized, because there eternal life is received.

He is received as a guest who prepares a dwelling in heaven. For he says, “There are many dwelling places with my Father” (John 14:2). Meanwhile, the Lord of heaven wished to be a guest; he deigned to be a guest so that you might have a blessing by receiving him.

Let no one be proud because he gives to the poor. Christ was poor here. Learn where to seek the Lord; learn where to have him; learn from what to recognize him when you eat.

For the faithful know something that they understand better. The Lord Jesus was recognized, and after he was recognized he appeared nowhere else. He withdrew bodily from them, while he was held in faith. He is absent for this reason: so that faith may be built up. For if you see, where is faith? But if you believe what you do not see, when you see it you will rejoice.

Let faith be built up now in regard to what you believe, because appearance will be restored. What we have not seen will come. See how it finds you. For when people say, “Where is he? When will it be? When will he come?” Be certain: he will come. And if you do not wish it, he will come.

There will be a great trembling for those who did not believe, and great joy for those who believed. The faithful will rejoice; the unbelieving will be confounded. The faithful will give thanks to the Lord, because what they believed was true; the unbelieving will be confounded, because they thought it false.

I praise those who do not see and yet believe, because when they see, they will rejoice. For the sake of our salvation the Lord took flesh, and in it he also took death. He rose on the third day, never again to die, and, having taken back the substance of the flesh he had laid aside, he first gave us an example of incorruptible resurrection.

Ascending in that same body to the Father, he sits at the right hand of God, sharing in the Father’s judgment through mercy. We hope that he will come to judge the living and the dead, so that we too may believe that we shall receive from this dust the same flesh, the same bones, and the same restoration of the members, which will always remain.

We shall all rise, but we shall not all rejoice. “The hour is coming,” he says, “when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who have done good will come out to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29). Thus he will act, so that punishment will be given to shame and reward to joy. “They will go into eternal burning, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46).

## SERMON XXXVI

[Note: The following sermon belongs neither to Fulgentius nor to Augustine; it has already been rejected as Augustine’s by the theologians of Louvain. It reflects the mind and style of neither of them. In the Basel edition, where it says below that the Virgin Mary assumed all these courses of nature in the Lord Jesus Christ so that she might aid all women fleeing to her, and thus restore the whole race of women who come to her as a new Eve while preserving virginity, just as our Lord Jesus Christ, the new Adam, restores the whole race of men, these words are written in the margin of the book: “These things must be tempered and corrected with the salt of piety. For they do not taste of the pure milk of truth.” It is read in Augustine, volume 5 of our edition, column 1990.]

### On the praises of Mary from the birth of the Savior

The birth of our Lord Jesus Christ has today illumined the whole world with the new light of his coming. Today God descended from heaven to humanity, so that in heaven he might prepare an ascent for humanity.

Today we have received the one born as God, the Son of the Virgin, the Savior of all believers: God from the Father, human from his mother; God hidden, human manifest. And because the devil spoke to Eve through the serpent and through Eve’s ears brought death into the world, God conveyed the word to Mary through an angel and poured out life upon all ages.

The angel uttered the message, and the Virgin conceived Christ. O union accomplished without defilement, in which the husband is the word and the wife the little ear! By this splendor the Son of God is conceived; by this purity he is born. No heaviness could occur for the one conceiving, no sadness for the one giving birth. For the one who had come to gladden the sorrowful world did not make the lodging of the womb sorrowful.

The physician passing from heaven through the Virgin caused the Virgin to remain unharmed after his passage. For the one who could restore the ruptured limbs of others by touching them could much more, in his own mother, avoid violating what he found intact by being born.

By his birth, bodily integrity increased rather than diminished, and virginity was enlarged rather than driven away. In the narrow members of the body she sustained whatever the heavens sustain. Her womb was full, yet the virgin’s conscience knew no contamination.

While she was pregnant, she rejoiced with healing lightness, for the light she carried within herself could not have weight. Mary became a window of heaven, because through her God poured true light upon the ages. Mary became a heavenly ladder, because through her God descended to earth, so that through her human beings might deserve to ascend to heaven.

Those will be permitted to ascend there who believe that God descended to earth through the Virgin Mary. Mary became the restoration of women, because through her they are shown to have been withdrawn from the ruin of the first curse.

Finally, three evils of Eve are shown to have been excluded by three goods of Mary. For it was said to Eve: “In pain and sorrow you will give birth, your turning will be toward your husband, and he will rule over you” (Genesis 3:16). Women who do not follow Mary are therefore subjected to these three evils: pain, sorrow, and servitude.

But listen to how Mary, by contrast, is exalted by three most splendid goods: the angelic greeting, divine blessing, and the fullness of grace. For the angel is read to have greeted her in this way: “Hail, Mary, full of grace; blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:28).

When he said “Hail,” he offered her a heavenly greeting. When he said “Full of grace,” he showed that the anger of the first sentence had been completely excluded and the grace of full blessing restored. When he said, “Blessed are you among women,” he expressed the blessed fruit of her virginity, so that every woman who perseveres as a virgin may be called blessed among women.

For Eve had been accursed; now we believe that through Mary she returned to the blessing of glory. Come, virgins, to the Virgin, and rejoice. Lay aside the curse of transgression and take up the blessing of restoration. Cast away the pains that Eve received through the serpent, and assume the honors that Mary received through the angel.

Drive away the sorrow of the one conceiving and cast off the groans of the one giving birth, so that this Son of the Virgin alone may rule over you. Come, virgins, to the Virgin; come, women who conceive, to the one who conceived; come, women giving birth, to the one who gave birth; come, mothers, to the mother; come, nursing women, to the one who nursed; come, young women, to the young woman.

For this reason the Virgin Mary assumed all these courses of nature in our Lord Jesus Christ: so that she might aid all women who flee to her, and thus restore the whole race of women who come to her as a new Eve while preserving virginity, just as our Lord Jesus Christ, the new Adam, restores the whole race of men. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVII

[Note: In Augustine, sermon 146, *On Time*, but truncated here.]

### On the third day of Easter
Today the Gospel according to Mark was read, as you heard when it was recited. What, then, did we hear Mark saying? That the Lord appeared on the road to two men, just as Luke also said, whose Gospel we heard yesterday: “He appeared to them in another form as they were walking” (Mark 16:12). Luke said this same thing in other words, but did not depart from the same meaning. What did Luke say? “Their eyes were held back, so that they would not recognize him” (Luke 24:16). What did Mark say? “He appeared to them in another form.” What Luke said—“Their eyes were held back, so that they would not recognize him”—Mark said as “in another form.” For another appearance was seen by eyes that were restrained, not opened.

What then, brothers, since Luke said—and I believe you very recently remember this from yesterday’s reading—that when he blessed and broke the bread, their eyes were opened and they recognized him. Since Luke said this, what are we to think? If their eyes were then opened, were they accompanying him on the road with closed eyes? And if they had closed eyes, could they know where to place their steps? Their eyes, then, were opened for recognition, not for seeing.
