Our Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, speaks with men unknown before the breaking of the bread and is recognized in the breaking of the bread, because there eternal life is received. He is received as a guest who prepares a dwelling in heaven. For he says through the holy evangelist John: “There are many dwellings with my Father. Otherwise I would have told you, for I am going to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself” (John 14:2–3).

The Lord of heaven wished to be a guest on earth, a stranger in the world through whom the world was made. He deigned to be a guest so that you might have a blessing by receiving him. Not because he himself was in need when he entered as a guest. The Lord always fed Elijah through a raven in a time of famine (1 Kings 17:6), and birds served the man whom human beings were persecuting. The raven brought the servant of God bread in the morning and meat in the evening. He, therefore, whom the Lord fed through serving birds was not in need. Yet although Elijah was not in need, he was sent to the widow of Zarephath: one who was not in need was sent to one who was in need—not so that he might be sustained, but so that she might be satisfied. And she, who did not hesitate to receive him and offered refreshment, earned a blessing.

Let no one be proud because he gives to the poor: Christ was poor here. Let no one be proud because he received him as a guest: Christ was a guest here. The one received is better than the one receiving; the one who accepts is richer than the one who gives. The one who received possessed everything; the one who gave had received from the one to whom he gave what he was giving.

Let no one, therefore, my brothers, be proud when he gives to the poor. Let him not say in his heart: “I give, he receives; I receive him, he needs a roof.” Perhaps he possesses more of what you need; perhaps the one whom you receive is righteous. He needs bread, but you need truth. He needs a roof, but you need heaven. He needs money, but you need justice. That poor man, therefore, has been received as a guest as though he were poor. It was the receiving person’s condescension, not the needy person’s misery.

Perhaps you say to yourself: “O blessed are those who deserved to receive Christ! If only I had been there then! If only I had been one of the two whom he found on the road!” Be the road, and Christ the guest will not be absent. Do you think that you are no longer permitted to receive Christ? “How,” you ask, “is it permitted?” He has now risen and manifested himself to his disciples. He has ascended into heaven; there he is at the right hand of the Father. He will not come until the end of the age, to judge the living and the dead. He will come in glory, not in weakness. He will give a kingdom, not seek lodging, when he gives the kingdom.

Is this what you say? Have you forgotten what he will say: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40). That rich one is needy until the end of the age, and he is truly needy—not in his head, but in his members. Where is he needy? In those concerning whom he grieved when he said: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

Let us, then, serve Christ; he is with us in his own people, he is with us in us. Nor did he say without reason: “Behold, I am with you always, to the consummation of the age.” By doing these things we recognize Christ in good works—not with the body but with the heart, not with the eyes of the flesh but with the eyes of faith. “Because you have seen, you have believed,” he said to one of his disciples who had been unbelieving and declared: “I will not believe unless I touch.” And the Lord said: “Come, touch, and do not be unbelieving but faithful” (John 20:27). He touched and cried out: “My Lord and my God!” (ibid., 28). And the Lord said: “Because you have seen, you have believed” (ibid., 29).

Is your entire faith this—that you have believed what you see? I praise those who do not see and yet believe, because when they see, they will rejoice.

## SERMON XXXVIII

Also, concerning the foregoing.

How beautiful a shore appears when it is filled with merchandise and trembles with merchants! Bundles of various garments are unloaded from ships; countless sailors rejoice in the delight of their singing, and the rich bosom of the sand dances. What does this mean? How much more delightful it is to contemplate the shore of the Lord’s resurrection and to see the harbor of the risen Lord glittering with precious merchandise!

Who are the porters? Angels and archangels, who lead the bundles of souls released from the bonds of hell with palms of joy to the harbor; and on their bearing shoulders they bring them to the shore of the land of the living. Thus, when the Lord rose, the bank shone while the shipwreck of Gehenna mourned.

In that vessel of the body of Christ returning from the underworld are placed the wares recently seized by piracy: the souls of all the captives groaning in the underworld. When the groans of hell were released, they rejoiced on Peter’s shore. Let that Mary also rejoice, carrying the necessary spices, and bringing back from the tomb precious joys and the living merchandise of the dead from the shore.

The angels were the porters and delightful bearers who most powerfully escorted the Lord as he descended to Gehenna and most joyfully preceded him as he returned. One sat upon the stone of the tomb, to display the merchandise of both death and life to the women and to announce it to the shepherds, while in the morning dawn of paradise the Lord Jesus Christ himself shone (John 20:12). Other angels—one at the head and another at the feet of that new tomb—presided there, not to sell Christ’s linen wrappings but to offer them.

They say to the women who are purchasing, offering the price of their tears: “Why,” he says, “are you weeping? You are seeking Jesus; he is not here. He has risen from the dead, just as he told you.” The merchant has ascended from the underworld with bundles of mercy. If you do not believe in the merchant who is rising, behold the merchandise shining in the tomb. Behold the burial linens, which no one should wish to possess without paying the price. Behold the head-cloth. Behold the merchant’s bundle. Go, announce it to the disciples, so that the bundle of mercy may be opened to all merchants. He rose in linen who, through Lazarus’s linen, broke the chains of burial; he made a burial out of the linen of sins, in order to restore the life of angels.

A pleasant garden came to be on the shore, because the swollen waves had ceased. The meadows began to flower, and the wave ceased to roar. The tumult in hell fell silent, and Christ was recognized in the garden. And Mary says: “Lord, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have placed my Lord” (ibid., 15).

The despoiler of hell is thought to be the thief of his own body, as though he himself had stolen away his limbs—the one who raised buried limbs and opened tombs without number. But this merchant was rich in the merchandise of the rising dead. Unless he gives a sweet answer with his voice, no one can resume his commerce, possess his business, purchase the mystery, or obtain joy when he ends the shipwreck and returns to the harbor.

Let him answer willingly; let him say to Mary: “Mary.” The merchant speaks piously. Let no one hesitate to buy the merchandise of the resurrection without cost. Perhaps he is a merchant. Let us say to him with Mary: “Rabbi”—which means “Lord”—“where is your merchandise? How far do your dealings extend? At what price are your wares purchased?” “All authority,” he says, “has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28:18).

Let us buy peace from him freely on earth, so that we may possess saving joy in heaven. We believe the Lord risen, we behold him ascending, and we greet him coming in judgment—not so that he may display merchandise, but so that he may inspect it; not so that he may sell, but so that he may collect. Let us prepare our merchandise for him.

What merchandise? Not gold, not silver, not shining threads of gems, but faith, hope, charity, birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension. These are our wares.

Will he himself come empty-handed in the cloud? Behold, the Lord will come, and his merchandise will be with him, as it is said: “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your Savior will come, carrying his merchandise, and his work is before his face” (Isaiah 62:11). Hell did not rule him; his body ascended in the clouds; and from the dead and the living one song resounds: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalm 117:24). For behold, the dead dance from the underworld, and the angels rejoice in heaven, so that we too may rejoice in this temple.

## SERMON XXXIX

[Note: This is Augustine’s Sermon 155, “On the Season”; it is also found in volume V of our edition, column 1151.]

On the fourth day of Easter.

Today also the Resurrection of the Lord was read from the holy Gospel. The Gospel according to John was read. We heard things that we had not heard in the other books of the Gospel. The proclamation of truth is indeed common to all, and all drank from one fountain; but in proclaiming the Gospel—as I have often reminded your Charity—all included some things, three included others, two others, and individual evangelists still others.

What we heard now according to John—that Mary saw the Lord, and the Lord said to her, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17)—is reported by John alone among the evangelists. Concerning this, then, I must speak to your holiness.

Even after they had seen the linens in the tomb, they had not yet believed that he had risen, but thought that his body had been taken away from the tomb. John himself—for he says that he was “the one whom Jesus loved” (ibid., 2)—when he heard the women announcing, “They have taken my Lord from the tomb,” ran with Peter. Looking into the tomb, he saw only the linens, and believed.

What did he believe? Not that Christ had risen, but that he had disappeared from the tomb. The following words testify to this, for this is what we have just heard written: “He looked, saw, and believed.” For he did not yet know the Scriptures, “that he had to rise from the dead” (ibid., 20:9). It therefore became clear what he believed: he believed something that was not a matter of faith. He believed, but he believed falsely. The Lord later appeared to him: he drove away the falsehood and implanted the truth.

Yet because the statement “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” has often troubled the reader and the attentive, not careless, listener, let us see—with the Lord himself assisting us—what should be said about it.

What does “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” mean? When did he ascend to the Father? As the Acts of the Apostles indicates (chapter 1:3), on the fortieth day after his resurrection, the day we will celebrate in the Lord’s name on the fortieth day after Easter. Then the disciples, who had touched him with their hands and followed him with their eyes, heard the angelic voice: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

If he then ascended to the Father, what are we to say, my brothers? Could Mary not touch him standing on earth, but could she touch him seated in heaven? If she could not touch him here, how much less could she touch him there?

What, then, does “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” mean? The words sound as though he were saying: “Touch me when I have ascended; before I ascend, do not touch me.” “O Lord, you are here, and I am not to touch you? When you have ascended, shall I touch you?”

Furthermore, if before he ascended to the Father he recoiled from human touch, how did he present himself to the disciples not only to be seen but also to be handled, when he said: “See my hands and my feet. Behold, touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have” (Luke 24:39)? That unbelieving disciple, Thomas, also touched his pierced side and exclaimed, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). When he touched him, Jesus had not yet ascended to the Father.

Or perhaps some foolish person might say that before he ascended to the Father men could touch him, but women could not until he had ascended? That is an absurd thought and a perverse judgment. Whatever Mary heard, let the Church hear. Let everyone hear this, everyone understand it, everyone do it.

What, then, is “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father” (ibid., 17)? You see me as merely a human being; you do not yet know that I am equal to the Father. “Do not touch me”: do not believe that I am merely the human being whom you see, but understand me as the Word equal to the one who generated me.

What does “Do not touch me” mean? Do not believe that I am only what you see. I will ascend to the Father, and then touch me. I ascend to you when you understand that I am equal. For when you think me lesser, I have not yet ascended for you.

To touch, I think, means to believe. We can easily understand this from the woman who touched the fringe of Christ’s garment and was healed. Recall the Gospel. When the Lord Jesus Christ was going to visit the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, a woman who suffered from an issue of blood touched him. The Lord said, “Who touched me?” The disciples replied: “The crowds press around you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” He said to them: “Someone touched me. I know that power has gone out from me” (Luke 8:45).

And they said: “The crowds are pressing around you, and you have perceived one person?” “Someone touched me.” What does “touched me” mean? They press; she touched. The Jews afflict; the Church believed.

According to this understanding—by which we saw that the woman touched in order to be healed, which means that she believed—Christ said to Mary: “Do not touch me. I will ascend, and then touch me.” You will touch me when you understand: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

But because you see merely a human being, because “the Word became flesh” (ibid., 14), you do not see the Word alone. Do not believe in the flesh and abandon the Word. Let the whole Christ appear to you. “Do not touch me now,” he says, “because you do not yet see who I am.”

Let the Church, therefore—of which Mary bore the figure—hear what Mary heard. Let us all touch, if we believe. He has now ascended to the Father and sits at the Father’s right hand; the whole Church confesses this today. Let those who are being baptized hear this; let those who are about to be baptized hear it. When they believe, Mary touches Christ.

The understanding is obscure but sound, opened to faith that knocks. Our Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, is there, is with us, is with the Father, and is in us; he does not depart from him, nor does he abandon us. He teaches us to pray as a teacher, and with the Father he hears us as the Son.

## SERMON XL

[Note: Attributed to Augustine in the manuscript of the Cistercian Fathers of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem in the city.]

On the fifth day of Easter.

We see that the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, according to the truth of the four evangelists, was completed yesterday. On the first day the Resurrection according to Matthew was read; on the second day, according to Luke; on the third, according to Mark; on the fourth—that is, yesterday—according to John.

But since Luke and John wrote more extensively about the resurrection itself and the events that occurred after the resurrection, and these cannot be recited in a single reading, yesterday we heard something according to John, and today further readings still remain.

What, then, did we hear today? That on the very day on which he rose—that is, on the Lord’s day—when evening had come, and the disciples were in one place, and the doors were shut because of fear of the Jews, the Lord appeared in their midst (John 20:19). On that day, therefore, as the evangelist John testifies, he appeared twice to the disciples, morning and evening. The reading concerning his morning appearance has already been recited (alternative reading: “also”). But that he appeared again in the evening of the same day, we have just heard when it was recited.

It was not necessary for me to recall these things, except so that you might pay attention, because of some people’s limited understanding or greater negligence, and so that you might know not only what you heard but also from which Scripture what you heard was read.

Let us see, then, what today’s reading proposes for us to discuss. The reading itself admonishes us and, in a certain way, speaks to us, so that we may say something about how the Lord, who rose in the solidity of his body so that he might not only be seen by the disciples but also touched, could appear to them while the doors were closed.

Some are so disturbed by this that they nearly endanger themselves, bringing the prejudices of their reasoning against divine miracles. They argue in this way: “If it was a body, if it was flesh and bones, if what rose was what had hung upon the wood, how could it enter through closed doors? If it could not, they say, it did not happen. If it could, how could it? If you comprehend the manner, it is not a miracle.” And if it does not seem miraculous to you, you are approaching a denial that he also rose from the tomb.

Look from the beginning at the miracles of your Lord and give me an account of each. A man did not approach, and a virgin conceived. Explain how a virgin conceived without a man. Where reason fails, there the building of faith begins.

Behold, you have one miracle in the Lord’s conception (alternative reading, textually uncertain: “in the one God conceived”); hear also of one in his birth. A virgin gave birth, and remained a virgin. Even then, before he rose, the Lord was born through closed doors.

You ask me and say: “If he entered through closed doors, where is the condition of the body?” And I answer: “If he walked upon the sea—or, in the alternative reading, through the sea—where is the body’s weight?” But the Lord did that as Lord. Did he cease to be Lord because he rose (manuscript: “when … he ceased”)—the one who also made Peter walk upon the sea (alternative reading: “What of the fact that,” etc.)? What divinity could do in him, faith fulfilled in Peter. Christ did it because he could; Peter did it because Christ helped him.

If, then, you begin (manuscript: “attempt”) to examine the reason for miracles with human understanding, I fear that you will lose faith. Do you not know that nothing is impossible for God?

Therefore, if someone says to you, “If he entered through closed doors, he was not a body,” answer him in return: “Rather, if he was touched, he was a body; if he ate, he was a body.” He performed the former by miracle, the latter by nature.

Is not the daily course of nature itself worthy of wonder?

[Note: Manuscript: “nature’s course itself.” Everything is full of miracles.]

Nature itself is full of all miracles, but they have become cheap through constant repetition. Give me an explanation; I am asking you about familiar and ordinary things. Explain to me why the seed of so large a fig tree is so tiny that it can scarcely be seen, while the lowly gourd produces such a large seed. Yet if you consider that tiny, scarcely visible seed with the mind rather than the eye, within that smallness and narrow space the root lies hidden, the strength is uncertain, the future leaves are concealed, and the fruit that will appear (manuscript: “because it produces”) on the tree is already sent ahead—or, in the alternative reading, promised—in the seed.

There is no need to examine many examples. No one will give an account of everyday things, yet you demand an account from me of miracles? Read the Gospel, then, and believe the things that are wondrously accomplished. Greater is what God has done, and yet you do not marvel—or, according to another reading, we do not marvel—at what surpasses all works. There was nothing, and the world exists.

“But,” you say, “the mass of a body could not enter through closed doors.”

[Note: Manuscript: “pass through the doors that were closed.”]

How great was that mass of body? Was it like that of a camel? Yet the Lord, wishing to show the difficulty of a rich man’s entering the kingdom of heaven, and when the disciples considered this impossible and were saddened that no rich person could be saved, answered: “What is impossible for human beings is easy for God” (Luke 18:25).

God can make a camel pass through the eye of a needle, and can bring a rich man into the kingdom of heaven. Why do you accuse me concerning closed doors? The doors had a crack—or, according to another reading, a fissure. Compare the crack in the doors with the eye of a needle; compare the mass of human flesh with the size of camels; and do not accuse the divinity of miracles.

## SERMON XLI

[Note: This is Augustine’s Sermon 148, “On the Season”; it is also found in volume V of our edition, column 1158.]

On the sixth day of Easter.

Today a reading was recited about the things that happened after the Lord’s resurrection, according to the evangelist John. Your Charity heard with us that the Lord Jesus Christ showed himself to his disciples at the Sea of Tiberias, and that he who had already made them fishers of men found them still fishers of fish. They had caught nothing throughout the entire night (John 21:1).

When they saw the Lord and, at his command, cast their nets, they caught the number you heard. The Lord would never have commanded this unless he wished something to be signified. What, then, could it have mattered greatly to Jesus Christ whether fish were caught or not? But that fishing signified us.

Let us therefore recall the two catches of the disciples at the command of the Lord Jesus Christ: one before the passion and the other after the resurrection. In these two catches the entire Church is signified—what it is now and what it will be in the resurrection of the dead. Now it contains countless people, both good and bad. After the resurrection, however, it will contain a definite number, only the good.

Recall, then, the first catch; there let us see what the Church is in this present age. The Lord Jesus found his disciples fishing when he first called them to follow him. At that time they had caught nothing all night. When they saw him, they heard him say: “Cast out the nets.” “Lord,” they said, “we have worked all night and caught nothing, but at your word we will cast out the net” (Luke 5:5).

They cast them at the command of the Almighty. What else could happen except what he wished? Yet by that very deed he deigned to signify something, as I said. The nets were cast, and they caught such a multitude of fish that two boats were filled and were breaking under the weight of the multitude.

Then he said to them: “Come, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:19). They received from him the nets of the word of God; they cast them into the world as into the deep sea; and they caught the great multitude of Christians whom we see and marvel at.

Those two boats (alternative reading: “the Lord”) signified two peoples: Jews and Gentiles, the Synagogue and the Church, circumcision and uncircumcision. For the cornerstone of those two boats, like two walls coming from opposite directions, is Christ.

But what did we hear there? The boats were being pressed by the multitude. So it happens now. Many Christians live badly and weigh upon the Church. It is not merely that they press upon it—according to another reading, “live badly”—but they also tear the nets. For if the nets were not torn, schisms would not have been committed.

Let us pass, then, from this catch, which we endure, and come to the one for which we ardently hope. Behold, the Lord died, but he rose again. He appeared to his disciples by the sea and ordered them to cast out the nets. Do not cast them indiscriminately. For in the first catch he did not say to them, “Cast the nets to the right or to the left.” If he had said “to the left,” only the wicked would have been signified; if he had said “to the right,” only the good would have been represented. Therefore he did not say “to the right or to the left,” because the good are caught mixed together with the wicked.

But now, after the resurrection, what the Church will be like, hear, distinguish, rejoice, hope, and understand. “Cast the nets,” he says, “on the right side.” Now those on the right are being caught.

You know that he said he would separate the sheep from the goats: he would place the sheep on the right and the goats on the left; he would say to those on the left, “Go into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25:41), and to those on the right, “Receive the kingdom” (ibid., 34). Hence: “Cast the nets on the right side.”

They cast them, they caught fish, and the number is definite; no one there is supernumerary. But now how many supernumeraries approach the altar who appear among God’s people but are not written in the book of heaven? There, therefore, the number is definite.

Strive to be among those fish—not merely by listening and praising, but by living well. The nets are cast, and large fish are caught. For who will then be small, when they will be equal to the angels of God (Luke 20:36)?

A hundred and fifty-three are therefore caught. Someone may say to me: “Will there be only that many saints?” Far be it from us to think that there will be so few saints in the kingdom of heaven. The number signifies thousands upon thousands (Revelation 14:1) of saints and faithful people.

Why, then, did the Lord deign to signify by this number the thousands who will be in the kingdom of heaven? Listen. You know that the law was given through Moses to God’s people, and that in the law the Decalogue—that is, the ten commandments of the law—is especially mentioned. One commandment concerns worshiping the one God; the second, not taking the name of your God in vain; the third, observing the Sabbath, which Christians observe spiritually, while Jews violate it carnally. These are the three commandments pertaining to the Lord.

The remaining seven concern human conduct, because of those two principal commandments: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind,” and “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” “On these two commandments depend the whole law and the prophets” (Matthew 22:37–38).

Since there are two commandments, therefore, in the Decalogue three pertain to the love of God and seven to the love of neighbor. No one fulfills them by his own strength unless he is helped by God’s grace, unless God helps him by his Spirit.

Now recall how the Holy Spirit is commended through the number seven. Isaiah says that a person is to be filled with the Spirit of God: “wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of God” (Isaiah 11:2). These seven operations commend the Holy Spirit through the number seven. The Spirit, as it were, descends to us beginning with wisdom and ending with fear. We, however, ascending, begin with fear and are perfected in wisdom: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110:10).

If, then, the Spirit is needed so that the law can be fulfilled, let seven be added to ten, and let the number be seventeen. If you count from one through seventeen, the total is 153. There is no need to count it now; count it yourselves. Compute it in this way: one and two, and three, and four; then add the remaining numbers up to seventeen, and you will find the sacred number of the faithful and the saints who will be with the Lord in the kingdom.

## SERMON XLII

On the closed doors.

The door is secure wherever the master of the household enters. For he himself is the door and the gate. He enters directly and subtly, so as to instruct rather than remind, and to bring joy by inspiration rather than make a noise by visiting.

God descends from heaven, the deaf man hears, the mute speaks, the heart of the doubting person believes, and there is no sound when the Savior enters, because he knows how to enter through closed doors. He enters the heart of a person who previously did not believe and blasphemed everything good. When that person begins to believe, he begins to marvel. He is awestruck as he becomes a believer, and at Christ’s merciful entrance into his heart.

Is the structure of the limbs opened? Is the body’s framework, joined together within itself, separated from its joints or from its necessary ligaments? Thus, through the closed doors where the apostles were confined (John 20:19), he entered in the truth of his body, not merely by the presence of his majesty. He customarily enters in such a way that he promises joy before making any noise.

He entered the womb of the Virgin; the Holy Spirit came upon her, and the power of the Most High overshadowed her (Luke 1:35). He was generated, and that gate was closed—the gate through which no one enters except the prince alone—and, it says, “it shall remain closed forever” (Ezekiel 44:2).

Behold, then, the one who has now risen from the guard of the tomb enters the apostles through a closed door. An angel, as we read, rolled away the stone from the tomb and sat upon it. If the angel had not descended, would Christ not have risen from the tomb? Or did the stone impede the Lord unless it was removed by the angel? Rather, the Lord rose so that the angel would not be necessary. The angel was present in service, not in assistance.

Rising from the tomb and recognizing Mary in the garden, he asks Mary: “Why are you weeping?” And she: “Rabboni,” which means “Lord” (John 20:15–16).

He now enters the apostles through barred doors. Tell us, evangelist, how did he enter? From where did he come? He entered powerfully, opened Gehenna, and seized its spoils. He entered through the doors and greeted the apostles. He did not say that the cracks in the doors had opened, nor that the structure of the doors had been loosened.

“How,” says the heretic, “did a true body, as you say, enter through closed wooden boards?” He would rightly say this if he were arguing before the passion, when Christ still bore a mortal body destined to undergo suffering, to be seized by enemies, nailed with nails, pierced by a lance, and committed to burial.

By then all the density of the body he had assumed had been absorbed and transformed into divinity, though it had not been annihilated. O great mystery! He enters through closed doors and displays open scars. Nothing hindered him as he entered; unbelief hindered Thomas as he doubted.

What do you say, Thomas? “Unless I see the marks of his nails and put my hand into his side, I will not believe” (ibid., 25). This is the faithful testimony of one who seeks and demonstrates, touches and offers. Did the Lord say, “You seek my wounds in vain”? He willingly accepted what the doubter had presumed.

“Put your hand into my side” (ibid., 27), and let your touch not be deceived. Although the doubter did not touch, the Savior offered what he had sought. A spirit can neither be touched nor handled; but because it was a true body, and a true body entered through closed doors, he himself said: “Thomas, put your hand into my side.”

What is this, Thomas? Do you recognize the Lord by touching the wounds of his passion? And he: “This is enough for me to believe in my Lord: if I touch the healing power of his scars.” There is all power there; there is all mercy there.

I know you better, Lord, through your passion; I touch you better in your cross, because you were lifted up for my salvation. “Be exalted, Lord, in your strength; we will sing and praise your mighty acts” (Psalm 20:14). How shall we sing? “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28).

He opened the doors of divinity, he who entered through closed doors, and he gave everyone peace through the truth of his body.

## SERMON XLIII

Concerning the foregoing.

The earthly emperor does not visit his dependents who are held in fear, as the Lord Christ visited the apostles who were afraid. For if, on account of the safety of an earthly king, his companions are shut up under the sieges of tyrants, the emperor himself does not deign to come to the confinement of his frightened servants: he can send an army to bring assistance, but he does not humble his own imperial dignity. Our Lord, however, is King of heaven, Lord of angels, raiser of the dead, salvation of the despairing. He did not send angels to the apostles who were afraid—those who feared the Jews, the crucifiers of the Lord—but came himself, rising from the dead; he entered through closed doors, so that he who had poured out his blood for them might give them security through his presence. The heavenly Emperor entered, destroyer of death and liberator of the human race, not through purple hangings, nor passing through gilded curtains, but himself, with angelic legions preceding him in spirit, entered as the everlasting Emperor. No one lifted the veil; no one opened the door. Thus he entered through a closed door, he who opened the hell of death, who loosed our chain, who opened the heavens, descended, and with his body again ascended into the heavens, penetrating the inner side of the veil that is set before our eyes. For he, true God and true man, was able to enter through a closed door, to open the book with its seven seals, and to enter the hidden treasuries of wisdom.

Good was his entrance, accompanied by the messenger of peace and bringing the effect of security. What does he say to those who fear? “Peace be with you” (John 20:19). Peace greets them in peace, because the disciples could now be afraid and yet dared to examine his wounds. He says to those whom he comes to help: “I said, ‘Peace be with you,’ and unbelief has remained fixed in you. I received your wounds, and you make contests out of my Passion? Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24:39).

Thomas was absent from the flock and began to be in danger with respect to his faith, because he had not yet seen the Savior. The disciples said to him, “We have seen the Lord” (John 20:25); but he said to them: “You have seen the Lord crucified! A great miracle! Unless I see the mark of his nails and put my hand into his side, I will not believe” (ibid.).

Thomas doubted, and Christ was entering. Peace entered, and unbelief departed. Thomas, what do you desire? Touch, if you can touch. Touch my wounds, so that you may not falter in your faith. You wish to put your hand into my side; would that you wished to enter wholly! My openings stand open, so that my door may stand open to heaven for you.

He heard the sweetest voice and received complete faith. From the wounds of the physician he received the message, and the sick man drank the antidote. “You are,” he said, “my Lord and my God” (ibid., 28). He entered into the openings of Christ, and the door of the heavenly kingdom was opened. May those wounds always heal us and restore our strength—the wounds that gave medicine to the world—so that we may always sing, “Alleluia.”

## SERMON XLIV. Where Christ appeared after the Resurrection to Mary Magdalene in the garden

The enclosed garden flourishes, watered by the joyful rush of the stream; the firstborn of the dead, after the disgrace of the cross and the outrage of the Passion, deigned to visit it, crowned with honor and glory. The tall palm displays the freshness of its beauty, because Christ’s flesh, unaware of corruption, rose imperishably from the underworld. For concerning him it had long before been foretold in the oracle of the singing David: “You will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Psalm 15:10).

Behold, the flower of the field breathes its fragrance sweetly in the meadows. Everywhere the grace of the catholic mother is spread, and the lily of the valleys gleams around the mountain of the sacred altar, while a banquet of angelic Passion is prepared for all the faithful clothed in the white garment of righteousness.

After the resurrection of the saints, therefore, with shoots lifted together with him from the hollows of the tombs, and walking with graceful steps, the Lord entered the paradise of delight. And because, at the beginning of the world, that transgressing Eve had made the head of her body an exile from Paradise together with herself, Mary deserved first to behold in the garden of delight the Redeemer of her salvation returning from the underworld to the tomb as victor, carrying the spoils of death. She watched attentively; she was called by her Creator, turned away from unbelief, and firmly confirmed by the calling of her name.

For when, with the most devout affection and an anxious heart, she visited the tomb of the Lord’s body with impatient zeal, she first saw two angels in white sitting at a distance, one at the head and one at the feet, where Christ’s body had been laid. The heavenly angels had not descended so that the flesh of the resting Lord might be guarded by them, but so that Mary Magdalene might be shown that he had risen from the dead. The fact that the two angels sat at the head and at the feet, from which the Lord had already risen alive with his resurrected body, undoubtedly signified that the resurrection of Christ, proclaimed from east to west, would fill the whole world as if from head to feet.

They say to her: “Woman, why are you weeping?” (John 20:13). You see angels clothed in white descending from heaven, and yet you remain occupied with womanly tears? Stop, woman; set a limit to your empty weeping. The tears have already been wiped from the eyes of the wretched, because, when the bonds of groaning had been loosed, the Lord of angels, the triumphant one, ascended on high: “He ascended on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to human beings” (Ephesians 4:8).

“Tell me, blessed ones whom I see but whom I do not know who you may be. Tell me, I say, good comforters, how will I not be able to weep when such a teacher has been taken from me? I desire to see his face, yet I do not even find his buried corpse. Who is this adversary who envies me so greatly that he attempted to carry away by theft the venerable body of the Lord lying here? Was it not enough that Judas sold him, a Jew bought him, Pilate condemned him, a soldier pierced him on the cross with massive nails, looked upon him dead, and transfixed him with a sharp blade? Were these things too little—what the sacrilegious committed against my Lord while he was still alive and afterward willingly gave up his spirit? He is fastened alive to the gallows, and stolen dead from the tomb?

“For our consolation, that wealthy Joseph received from Pilate the body requested for burial and carefully embalmed it in this tomb-chamber (Luke 23:55). We marked the place of the buried body and prepared spices, so that, by anointing even the lifeless body of our Teacher, we might nourish the ardor of our burning heart. And behold, suddenly, with every precaution, watching and searching, I come in haste and find the tomb in the morning. These are my complaints, my tears running down amid the bitterness of my inward anguish. Attend to my grief, weigh the thorn of my wounded heart, and grant to me who weeps the sweetest remedy of our conversation.

“Handle this matter more carefully, I beg you; handle it as faithful patrons, with tranquil ears receiving the matter of your salvation entrusted to you, and offer the wisest counsel about finding the pledge of so great a treasure.”

You ask well, Mary; you seek well; you knock well. No one has taken from you the one you seek: he raised himself by his own power. While you speak with us, he will quickly appear to your eyes. For the Lord will always be with you, and you will be satisfied according to what your soul desired; your bones will become rich, your heart will be like a watered garden and like a spring whose water does not fail, because the luminous pupil of your eyes keeps watch like a glowing torch.

The messengers sent by divine command depart, and immediately the Lord of the messengers appears. He sees her standing and asks her, weeping: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” She, supposing that he was the gardener, says to him: “Lord, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have placed him, and I will take him away” (John 20:15).

Consider, I beg you, the groaning of the grieving conscience, and do not despise the torment of my breast. I perceive that you are the cultivator of this garden. I am seeking my Lord, buried in this garden. You alone are both the master and the cultivator and the guardian of this garden. It cannot be otherwise than that you yourself should show me where I may find the one whom my soul loved. Either I find him through you, or perhaps you yourself are the one whom I seek. My eye gazes upon you, and my sight is inflamed. Are you perhaps the Lord and my God, toward whom my thirsty spirit keeps watch by night like a deer?

O Mary, who directed the full attention of faith within me, you quickly found the one whom you desired with pure purpose. Her request was not delayed any longer: she received the true answer to her petition and deserved to obtain recognition of the Savior through the calling of his name.

Let us now briefly ask why, when the Lord called Mary and, called by him, she recognized him as Lord and Teacher, she heard from him: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (ibid., 17). This means, certainly: “Do not merely think me a human being, Mary, whom you see walking in the garden after rising from the dead; but touch me when I have ascended to the Father, so that you may believe me equal to the Father. Go instead to my brothers and say to them: ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God’” (ibid.).

He is my Father by origin, not by adoption; by nature, not by grace. For he himself said: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7). “Today” in God is eternal. It has no beginning and no end, neither rising nor setting. Nor is tomorrow ever contemplated with God, where yesterday never existed. In this way, therefore, he is my Father.

But he is your Father, to whom, having received the gift of my teaching, you have deserved to say in prayer: “Our Father who are in heaven” (Matthew 6:9). He is my God, to whom, because for your sake I assumed humanity in order to be mediator between God and human beings, I said while placed upon the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). This was not because I was ever separated from the fellowship of the Father, or because the Father could in any way depart from the indivisible love of the only-begotten Son—“I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10)—but so that, by submitting to the death of punishment in the flesh of a true human being for the expiation of sin, I might on this occasion be shown more openly to the doubtful and the weak, and especially to unbelieving Manichaeans.

Behold how he is my God. But he is your God because, in the first human being, with my majesty cooperating with him, he created you; and now, through the profound mercy manifested in the price of my blood poured out, he has recreated you for the possession of the heavenly kingdoms.

## SERMON XLV. On the one baptism

The psalm has sung for us, and the water has resounded, because the Lord thundered over the waters. And if the thunder from the clouds shakes the earth with its voice—“the voice of the Lord over the waters” (Psalm 28:3)—what creature is not warned, except the heretics who violate the sacrament of water when they repeat the mystery after the Holy Spirit?

What, then, is so great about “the voice of the Lord over the waters”? What sort of one is he himself who gathered those waters, when he gave them their name and law, when he uttered such a voice: “The one who has been washed once has no further need to wash; for he is entirely clean” (John 13:10)?

If, at the voice of the Lord over the waters, the whole world was shaken, is the whole human being not clean at the sacrament of the Holy Spirit over the waters, when the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit wash him? The voice of the Lord, which cannot be repeated, can be heard with trembling. For when he said, “The one who has been washed once…,” he said this at the basin, when he washed the disciples’ feet and entrusted to us the singular sign of the mystery.

The basin is the whole world, and the basin’s rounded vessel is the circuit of the earth, where we are like vessels made by the hands of Christ the potter, because Jesus is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit and fire (Luke 3:16). If fired vessels return to the furnace, they are immediately shattered beyond repair. Yet heretics lightly bring back to a second washing of their presumption the fired vessels of souls, baked in the baptism of grace, making themselves greater than the Holy Spirit.

Tell me, heretic: who said in Genesis, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things, living souls” (Genesis 1:20), and who caused all the living birds to come forth from the womb of the waters, except the one who said, “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19)? It is one voice: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things, living souls,” and “Go, baptize the nations.” Therefore, because it is the same voice in the waters, when human beings are reborn from spiritual waters and brought forth toward heaven like flying birds.

Thus the Spirit deigned to descend over the waters in the form of a dove (Matthew 3:16), and to remain over the author of baptism in united love, dwelling there, so that you might understand that the kingdom of heaven belongs to those who are reborn through water and the Holy Spirit.

Show me another place where the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove, except once, when Christ was baptized, and once, when the world suffered the Flood. Show me a second Flood or a second dove. One Flood, one dove, one branch, one baptism, one Spirit, and one sacrament of chrism.

That dove, content with carrying one leafy branch, accuses you. It was sent out again from the ark (Genesis 8:8), and it did not carry another, because one is sufficient for it, once, under one sacrament. The raised lips of the dove holding the branch signify, as it were, the two Testaments, holding forth in foliage the mystery of Christ’s chrism.

And for you, heretic, is it a small matter to repeat many floods? The Lord preserved eight souls unharmed in the Flood; you, in the second flood of unlawful baptism, destroy all the souls, badly submerged, whom Christ saved by washing them.

Then the Lord said, so that human beings would not hope that the Flood would be repeated: “I will no longer make a flood over the earth; I will set my bow in the clouds” (Genesis 9:11, 13). You have seen the bow in the clouds. Understand that there will not be a future flood. You have heard the voice of Christ, like a bow in the clouds, that is, defining and declaring by the highest judgment: “The one who has been washed once has no need to wash.” Do not repeat the Flood, because you cannot find another Holy Spirit.

As I see it, over the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, you attempt to boast of a fourth—or of a first—so that you may say that where you are not present no one is to be baptized. The Father is present, the Son is present, the Holy Spirit is present, because what has been commanded can be celebrated only in the Trinity. And you say that it is not valid because you were not present. Therefore our God is present where you are absent.

It is said of the Lord: “The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Israel” (Isaiah 4:4). It is said to the Lord: “You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Psalm 50:9). He did not say, “That one washes me, and that one,” but, “You will wash me,” because both priest and people are washed by one, and the priest presents sacramentally what he receives.

The Father is present, and that is not enough for you? The Son is present, and it has not benefited you? The Holy Spirit is present, and still it is not enough for you? It is enough for those whom Peter and Paul baptized.

Paul, however, said when he was administering the sacrament: “Were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Corinthians 1:13). Perhaps, taking an opportunity from Paul’s name, you will say that he baptized more through the blessed John. This argument is useless; it does not support your case. Tell me, which of the two was holier, John or Paul? I confess that both were. Yet I can say that Paul was stronger than John.

Do not help yourself by burdening yourself, as though you might seem to do this rightly by saying it, lest you appear to bring a charge against the blessed Paul. Saint Paul found twelve men and asked them whether they had received the Holy Spirit. They said: “We do not know; we have never even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” And Paul said: “Into what, then, were you baptized?” They replied: “Into John’s baptism” (Acts 19:2–3). And he baptized them with Christ’s baptism. He did not rebaptize them, because the former was servile, whereas this is the Lord’s baptism.

John has his baptism; Paul has Christ’s baptism, not his own, not John’s, but Christ’s baptism. That preliminary baptism of repentance passes away, because John himself cried out: “I baptize you in repentance, but the one who comes after me baptizes you in the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 3:11). For after Judas the betrayer, no one baptized, because he had a baptism that was not his own but the Savior’s. John had his own baptism. Therefore Paul, so that they might receive the Holy Spirit, washed them in Christ’s baptism.

And you insist on washing again someone who confesses to you and says, “I was baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”? Because you were not there, is the sacrament of the Trinity not complete? Where were you when the Son of God said, “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19)? Until your most recent and filthy time, was the name of the Trinity empty, so that your separation should have more force than the united conjunction of the Trinity?

“But I am righteous,” you say, “and you are sinners.” “The wicked son justifies himself, but he will not cleanse his departure” (Proverbs 24, according to the Septuagint), just as you justify yourself and empty the Trinity without yourself.

How many false witnesses—prophets and wicked priests—circumcised the sons of Israel under the old law, but did not perform a second circumcision according to the law? And you wish to gather a second abyss, so that you may assert yourself to be a righteous practitioner, rather than acknowledge the Trinity itself, which perfects everything.

Once the sea was gathered into one gathering (Genesis 1:9); once the waters brought forth living creatures; once our fathers crossed the sea in baptism.

## SERMON XLVI. On the true vine

Because the branches of our vine are cut off by the sickles of cruel harvesters, and the courts of the churches have been polluted, the chambers of spiritual things grow weak because of the small number of those left and have no shelter, let us run to Christ, who is the true vine (John 15:1), whose blood-red foliage casts shade over the Church oppressed by heat.

For he is the true vine planted for us from the Father’s substance, whose power covered the heavens, and whose praise filled the earth (Habakkuk 3:3). Ascending from there to the right hand of the Father, the vine, ever lovely and giving green grace to those suffering heat, extended its branches—clothed either in the white flower of its birth or in the bloodstain of its Passion—and spread them over the earth like shoots, its hands extended on the cross, so that it might be a cooling shade for Christians who believe rightly.

Let us run beneath this shade, woven from the heavenly true vine, and let us say amid the temporal heat: “Behold Christ our Lord, who was handed over for our sins” (Romans 4:25); “under his shadow we shall live among foreign nations.” And touching the harp of David, let us sing beneath the vine: “In the shadow of your wings I will hope, until iniquity passes away” (Psalm 56:2).

For behold, iniquity does not pass away but grows; it does not rest but rages. When the boar from the forest ravages it and the solitary wild beast feeds upon it (Psalm 79:14), the true vine is at rest on its throne and the Father, the cultivator, is angry, because the vine has become bitter and alien.

Let us run to the purple stock of this vine, marked by the blood of the Passion, and, like a statue of the cross, let us hold the reed until the Father, the cultivator, having removed the sickle, restores his mercy. Protected by the consoling shoot of one prayer, let us say to him: “Father, Father who are in heaven, why do we labor so greatly on earth? Are you not the cultivator of the true vine, while the boar from the forest, a barbarian ignorant of mercy, harvests us? Did you not transplant the vine from Egypt, renew it, and cause it to fill the earth?” (ibid., 9).

Golgotha bears witness, where beneath the cross you made a trench. There you planted the true vine with blood and water. Then, as the vine spread from the gallows through the tomb to heaven, its shadow covered the mountains; and now an intrusive barbarian has occupied the mountains to cut off its branches.

Its branches covered the cedars of God (ibid., 11), and now powerful enemies cut us down, showing no mercy to infant or old person, because they did not blush before the faces of the elderly and had no mercy on those suckling at the breast. Where is the tower of strength against the face of the enemy? The angels abandoned it, and the barbarians mounted more lightly than eagles.

“God,” he says, “the nations have come into your inheritance; they have polluted your holy temple” (Psalm 78:1). Intercede for us, true vine, because our sins have become bitter, so that we seek shade and find nothing but sickles and spears.

The boar from the forest walks about, snarling, and the solitary beast feeds upon it, because the Lion from the tribe of Judah is quiet on his throne and will give no voice in the light until the nocturnal beasts of blindness flee. Therefore we have been made a desolation.

Do not, Father, hand over the sickle of your moderation to foreign nations. They do not know how to prune, but only how to cut off. You know how to cleanse well, you who deigned to make us whiter than snow. Cut us off in such a way that you preserve us at the root, not so that our memory perishes from the earth, but so that our traces remain in the true vine; and when the bloodshed of slaughter has ceased, let the dried vine grow green again, with its branches restored from captivity. We think this applies to all the saints who are brought forth from this vineyard.

Do not the grieving saints now walk beneath its roots, afflicted and alive, mourning for the dead who have been cast down? When we say, “Why does the boar from the forest harvest us?” does Isaiah, the good vinedresser, perhaps answer us: “Why? Because I waited,” he says, “for you to produce grapes, but you produced thorns” (Isaiah 5:4). Why? “Because I waited,” he says, “for you to practice equity; you produced not justice but a cry.”

But let us turn again to the good Father, the cultivator, whose heart poured forth a good word (Psalm 44:1). He alone cleanses the branch of his vine, not with a sharp sickle but with measured grace. Angel and archangel do not dare to prune this vineyard, for they are ministers, not cultivators. The Father alone knows the Son, because no one knows the Father except the Son.

[Note: Thus in Augustine. In the editions the words inserted here were: “but cultivator according to what he says.”]

Let us pray only that we may not perish when cut off, but that, once the branches have been cleansed, we may bear abundant fruit.

## SERMON XLVII [Note: This is a treatise of St. Augustine on the Gospel of John, 80]. Also on the true vine and the branch

This Gospel passage, brothers, in which the Lord declares himself to be the vine and his disciples to be the branches, says this because he is the head of the Church and we are his members: “the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

The vine and the branches are of one nature. Therefore, although he was God [variant: Lord], whose nature we do not share, he became human, so that in him human nature might be the vine of which we human beings could also be branches.

What, then, does “I am the true vine” mean (John 15:1)? Is “true” added to the vine because it refers to that vine from which this likeness has been transferred? For he is called a vine by likeness, not by proper identity, just as he is called a sheep, a lamb, a lion, an eagle, a rock, the cornerstone, and other things of this kind—things that are themselves more truly what they signify, from which these likenesses are drawn, rather than proper identities.

But when he says, “I am the true vine” (Jeremiah 2:21), he certainly distinguishes himself from the one to whom it is said: “How have you been changed into the bitterness of an alien vine?” (Isaiah 5:4). For how is it a true vine that was expected to produce grapes but produced thorns?

“I am,” he says, “the true vine, and my Father is the cultivator. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will remove; and every one that bears fruit, he will cleanse, so that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:1–2).

Are the cultivator and the vine one? According to what he said, therefore, Christ is the vine in the sense expressed by “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28); but [as the note records, the editions inserted here: “cultivator according to what he says”] according to what he said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), he himself is also the cultivator.

He is not such as those who, by working outwardly, perform a ministry; rather, he is such that he also gives growth inwardly. “Neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7). And certainly Christ is God, because “the Word was God.” Thus he and the Father are one; and although the Word became flesh, which it was not, he remains what he was.

Finally, after he had spoken of the Father as the cultivator, saying that he removes the unfruitful branches but cleanses the fruitful branches so that they may bear more fruit, he immediately showed himself also to be the cleanser of the branches: “Now you are clean,” he says, “because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15:3).

Behold, he too is the cleanser of the branches, which is the work of the cultivator, not of the vine; and he made the branches his laborers. For although they do not give growth, they nevertheless provide some assistance—but not from themselves, because he says, “Without me you can do nothing” (ibid., 5).

Hear them also confessing this. “What, then, is Apollos? And what is Paul? Ministers through whom you believed, and each as the Lord gave. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.” He does this not through them but through himself. This surpasses human humility, surpasses angelic exaltation, and belongs entirely to the Trinity, the cultivator.

“Now you are clean,” that is, clean and yet to be cleansed. For unless they were clean, they could not bear fruit; and yet the cultivator cleanses everyone who bears fruit, so that he may bear more fruit. Who in this life is so clean that he does not need to be cleansed more and more? For [Augustine: or, “Where”], “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us; but if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (1 John 1:8 and following). He cleanses the clean—that is, the fruitful—so that they may be more fruitful in proportion as they have become cleaner.

“Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15:3). Why did he not say, “You are clean because of the baptism with which you were washed,” but instead say, “because of the word that I have spoken to you,” unless it is also in the water that he cleanses through the word? Remove the word, and what is water except water? The word is added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament, itself as it were a visible word.

For he had certainly spoken of this when he washed the disciples’ feet: “The one who has been washed does not need to wash, but is entirely clean” (John 13:10). Whence comes such great power of water that it touches the body and washes the heart, unless it is through the word? Not because it is spoken, but because it is believed.

For even in the word itself one thing is the passing sound, and another is the abiding power. “This is the word of faith that we preach,” says the Apostle: “If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:8 and following).

Hence also it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). And blessed Peter says in his Epistle: “So also baptism now saves you—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience” (1 Peter 3:21).

This is the word of faith that we preach; through it, without doubt, baptism is consecrated so that it can cleanse.

[Note: Alternatively: “which, without doubt, can also cleanse the consecrated, and baptism.”]

Christ, the vine with us and the cultivator with the Father, loved the Church and gave himself for her. Read the Apostle and see what he adds: “That he might sanctify her,” he says, “cleansing her by the washing of water in the word” (Ephesians 5:26). Cleansing would in no way be attributed to the flowing and unstable element unless the word were added.

This word of faith has such power in the Church of God that through it—even through him [variant: her], the believer who offers, blesses, and dips—it cleanses even a tiny infant, although the child is not yet able to believe with the heart unto righteousness or confess with the mouth unto salvation.

All this takes place through the word of which the Lord says: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.”

## SERMON XLVIII [Note: Formerly it was read under Augustine, Sermon 179, On the Season. But it is neither Augustine’s nor Fulgentius’s. It appears in volume V of our edition, column 2085]. On the Ascension of the Lord

With how many ornaments of joy the halls of heaven shone forth today! For the angels received at last what they had long desired and sang a hymn as the gates were raised. Light was in the heavens, splendor at the doors, because the bridegroom ascended, proceeding from his bridal chamber to sit upon his throne.

Therefore holy David sets his instrument at the gates of heaven, singing a new song, because the one who descended is himself the one who ascended above all the heavens (Ephesians 4:10). Touching the instrument, therefore, with happier plectrums, he sounds forth and speaks of the *protoferus* (“first-bearer”) of the eternal consul, seeing him not adorned with gold and jewels but made white with the ice of the clouds: “He makes the cloud his ascent, and walks upon the wings of the winds” (Psalm 103:3).

For he has already walked upon the asp and the basilisk and trampled the lion and the dragon (Psalm 90:13)—with the foot of death and the applause of resurrection. Wonderful in our eyes, glorified, he flashes forth in an ascent of power, seated upon a light cloud, sprinkling the apostles with the inheritance of peace and testamentary love: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14:27).

Invited by the melody of the sounding instruments before the heavenly hall and royal palace, the apostles accompany him as they set out along the path of blessing, the sons of the bridegroom going with the Lord to receive the pledge of the Holy Spirit.

And raising his hands, he blessed them (Luke 24:50). He gave them, as the pledge of the bridal gift, a precious token—not one decorated with gold and jewels, but a chain woven from the links of love, by which they, bound to him, might follow him to the bride of the Lamb, Jerusalem, their everlasting homeland.

“Lord,” they say, “why do you leave us as you ascend, you who chose us while going before us on the riverbank? Lord, when shall we receive your words, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, from a distance, and taste the balm of your dripping grace falling from your lips and throat? Either instruct us where you are ascending, or do not abandon us when you ascend.

“We remain exposed, stripped of the shield of your kindness, like chicks deprived of the winged covering of an embracing mother. When will you come to us, you who redeemed us? May your death be our price; may your ascent be our pledge, lest we, overwhelmed by excessive sorrow, sink—those whom you lifted from the groans of the underworld.”

As the Lord ascended, therefore, looking down from the lofty cloud upon the sadness of his dependents, he sent forth the comforter of their grief: messengers of the one departing and heralds of the one returning. “Men of Galilee,” they say, “why do you stand looking toward heaven? This Jesus, whom you see, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

He will come in this way: there will be one ascent, one cloud-bearing litter, one appearance, gentle yet glorious and to be feared by sinners. His coming will not terrify you, whom his ascent consoles. He will come showing unharmed the wounds of the nails and the bloody jewels of his openings. To you, sons of the bridegroom, he will display the cross as the crown of heavenly rule; he will not change his wounds, because “the sign of the Son of Man will shine in heaven” (Matthew 24:30).

After receiving, therefore, the command of the ascending one and the precious pledge of the Holy Spirit, who was to come from above, the apostles were in the temple, united in praising the Lord, so that the fiery crown of gracious gifts might find them united as one.

In the temple, therefore, brothers, let us always remain united; walking in the house of the Lord with the harmony of his peace, let us await his coming, and in his temple let us all give glory. And may the crown of grace rest upon us like fire—not kindled by fire, but moistened with dew.

## SERMON XLIX [Note: This too is not Augustine’s, although it was formerly read under him as Sermon 180, On the Season. It appears in volume V of our edition, column 2086]. Also continuing the preceding subject.

It is delightful to behold Christ the Lord ascending, borne by clouds, when, rising from the dead, he began to return to heaven, from which he had come to save the human race. Who are those awaiting the one who ascends? Those who saw him rising, fled from him as he hung [on the cross], and follow the one ascending with their eyes. Fear was on the cross, love in the cloud, a delightful sight in the air. O sweet affection of the one descending! O delightful sight of the one flying upward! He takes leave and blesses them in peace. They commend themselves to him, [Col. 0915D] and he leaves them the grace of his blessing. He blesses them with outstretched hands, and clouds are prepared and placed in his path to receive him: he finishes his speech and now returns to heaven. For suddenly a white cloud appeared, a conveyance prepared from heaven. A cloud appeared, and he entered it who brings up the clouds from the end of the earth (Ps. CXXXIV, 7), so that the pleasantness of the cloud might delight their eyes and the sweetness of the one ascending from heaven might refresh them like dew, lest the empty anxiety of those who longed for him remain alone.

Behold, in the shield of the Acts of the Apostles, the painted lights of the fishermen who hang there live. The Consoler is present, because the Savior has ascended. [Col. 0916A] He immediately sends two heavenly officers, to make his disciples, who were afraid, secure and to turn those who were weeping into joy. For heavenly consolers had to be sent, lest the trembling fishermen remain without comfort. Indeed, when an emperor passes from one city to another and his arrival is announced, no one is sent except household officers and palace officials to announce to the provinces the king’s arrival or return. So also, when the Lord approached, a multitude of heavenly officers (or: protectors) shone forth in song, so that an angel might, as it were, cause the hearts of the provincials—the shepherds—to breathe again after their fear. When he also suffers and rises, household angels are sent, and in the city and palace of the tomb they announce that the Lord of heaven has risen. And now, when he ascends, from the choir of the Powers proceeding and from the multitude of those singing in the air among the camps, two palace officials of the heavenly empire are dispatched, so that the tearful eyes of the fishermen might find rest.

The fishermen recite a heavenly hymn:

“Men of Galilee, why do you gaze at Jesus going into heaven? He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I, 11).

His departure was desirable; he will not come to you in terror. A cloud met him; a cloud will accompany his return. He bore his wounds; he will bear them back again. He carried back the cross in triumph; the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven. He will come in that same body, in that same cloud, in that same reality: to you in love, to the ungodly in trembling. Blessed are those to whom it is truly said: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.” Will he come in this way to the eyes of sinners? It will be the same reality, but not the same security. It will be the day of terrifying judgment, the descent of angels, the resurrection of the dead. The angels will approach and, as though with a finger of the sounding trumpet, touch the tombs of the trembling earth, so that they may restore their charges to the fiery throne of the Judge.

The angels will approach the tombs of the prophets and of the apostles themselves, and of all the saints, and will say: “Behold, he is here who returns in the manner in which he ascended again.” Did we not say that he would come in the way in which you saw him going into heaven? You who escorted him as he went, receive him as he returns. This address is not in the seventy languages, but rain-bearing clouds are prepared as chariots, to meet in dew and cooling pleasantness those whose consciences do not fear examination. Let us therefore ask our Lord God that, just as today we celebrate the day of the Ascension, so we may deserve to receive the morning mercy of the one who returns, so that we may say to him in the morning: “In the morning I will pray to you, Lord; in the morning I will stand before you, and I will contemplate you” (Ps. V, 5).

## SERMON L

[Note: [Col. 0915D] We printed this sermon above among the genuine sermons of St. Fulgentius, beginning, “The anniversary solemnity,” and so forth. But because we later found it transcribed from a Vatican manuscript, in several places fuller and more accurately corrected than we had then been able to print it, and because in that manuscript it is attributed to Augustine, we did not hesitate to insert it here, in this appendix, exactly as it appears there.—It appears in volume V of our edition, column 2091.]

### On the holy day of Pentecost

Dearest brothers, today the anniversary solemnity is celebrated on which our Lord Jesus Christ sent the Holy Spirit, whom he had previously promised to his disciples. For he had said, “He cannot come unless I depart” (John XVI, 7). Therefore, on the fortieth day after his resurrection, the solemnity of which we celebrated ten days ago, he ascended into heaven; and, mindful of his promise, today he sent the Holy Spirit. The one hundred and twenty who had previously been gathered together were filled with him, and they had faithfully awaited the same promise of the Lord. It is written (Acts II, 2) that suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent wind being carried along; and there appeared to them divided tongues as though of fire, which also rested upon each one of them; and they began to speak in all languages, as the Spirit gave them utterance.

That wind cleansed their hearts of the straw of the flesh; that fire consumed the hay of their former desire. Thus it pleased God at that time to signify the presence of his Holy Spirit: those who had received him spoke in every language. [Col. 0917A]

Let us first briefly see why God, when he promised him, said, “He cannot come unless I depart.” For the Holy Spirit is not separable, nor was he powerless to come while the one from whom he cannot depart was present. But because the Lord was still displaying to the disciples the form of a servant, in which the Word became flesh and dwelt among us—and even carnal people could behold the Lord’s flesh—while the form of God, in which he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God (Phil. II, 6), can be contemplated only by spiritual people, for this reason he said, “He cannot come unless I depart.” It was as though he were saying: “As long as your carnal affection is occupied with my flesh, your spiritual vision does not receive my divinity.”

For he had promised that by the gift of the Holy Spirit they would be led into all truth, as it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts XV, 9). “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. VI, 8). Therefore the Lord’s bodily form withdrew from their bodily eyes, so that through the Holy Spirit the Lord’s divinity might be insinuated into their hearts. [Col. 0917B]

Now let us see why at that time this was a sign of the presence of the Holy Spirit: those who had received him spoke in every language. For the Holy Spirit is not even now withheld, yet those who receive him do not speak in every language; therefore by that evident miracle he was manifesting himself at that time. Understand, dearest brothers, that this is the Holy Spirit through whom the love of God is poured into our hearts. And because the love of God was destined to gather the Church throughout the whole world, what one person could then do—namely, receive the Holy Spirit and speak in every language—the unity of the Church, now gathered by the Holy Spirit, does by speaking in every language.

Therefore, if someone says to one of us, “You have received the Holy Spirit; why do you not speak in every language?” he ought to reply, “Indeed I do speak in every language, because I am in that body of Christ, that is, in the Church, which speaks in every language.” For what else did God signify then except that, by the presence of the Holy Spirit, his Church would speak in every language? [Col. 0917C]

Thus what the Lord had promised was fulfilled: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins; but they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved” (Matt. IX, 17). Therefore, when they were heard speaking in every language, some said, “These men are full of new wine” (Acts II, 12). For they had already become new wineskins, renewed by the grace of holiness; filled with new wine—that is, with the Holy Spirit—they overflowed in the fervor of speaking in every language and, through that most evident miracle, foreshadowed the Catholic Church that would exist among all the languages of the nations.

Therefore, beloved, celebrate this day as the unity of the body of Christ. You do not celebrate in vain if you are yourselves what you celebrate: clinging to that Church which, filled by the Lord with the Holy Spirit, the Lord recognizes as his own as it grows throughout the whole world, and which is recognized by her own. Like a bridegroom with his bride, he did not lose his own, because no one substitutes a stranger for her. To you, who are established among all nations—that is, to the Church of Christ, the members of Christ’s body, the bride of Christ—the Apostle says: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. IV, 2–3). See that where he commanded us to bear with one another, there he placed love; there he named the Spirit of unity; there he showed the bond of peace. This is the house of God, built from living stones, in which such a master of the household rejoices to dwell, and whose eyes the ruin of division ought not to offend.

## SERMON LI

[Note: [Col. 0917] It is found among Augustine’s works as Sermon 187, *On Time*.—It appears in volume V of our edition, column 1245.]

### On the same subject

A welcome day has dawned for us, brothers, on which the holy solemnity shines upon the eyes of the faithful and burns in their hearts. [Col. 0918A] For we celebrate the day on which the Lord Jesus Christ, glorified by his resurrection and ascension, sent the Holy Spirit.

As it is written in the Gospel, when he said, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink; rivers of living water will flow from his belly,” the evangelist explains the saying and declares: “Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII, 37–39). It therefore remained that, once Jesus had been glorified, when he had risen from the dead and ascended into heaven, the Holy Spirit should be given—sent by the one by whom he had been promised—as indeed happened.

For forty days after his resurrection the Lord lived with his disciples and ascended into heaven; and on the fiftieth day, which we celebrate today, he sent the Holy Spirit, as it is written (Acts II, 2 and following): “Suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a violent wind being carried along, and there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, which rested upon each one of them; and they began to speak in every language, as the Spirit gave them utterance.” [Col. 0918B]

That wind cleansed hearts of the straw of the flesh. That fire consumed the hay of former desire. Those tongues, by which they spoke while filled with the Holy Spirit, foreshadowed the future Church through the languages of all nations.

For just as, after the flood, the proud impiety of human beings built a lofty tower against the Lord (Gen. XI, 7), when the human race deserved to be divided by different languages, so that each nation spoke its own language and was not understood by the others, so humble piety brought that diversity of languages into the unity of the Church: so that love might gather what discord had scattered, and the scattered members of the human race, as of one body, might be joined together and brought back to one head, Christ, and fused into the unity of the holy body by the fire of love.

Therefore those who hate the grace of peace and do not preserve the fellowship of unity are wholly alien to this gift of the Holy Spirit.
