Although they too gather solemnly today, although they hear these readings in which the Holy Spirit is promised and sent, they hear them for judgment, not for reward. For what benefit is it to them to receive with their ears what they reject in their hearts, and to celebrate the day whose light they hate? [Col. 0918C]

But you, brothers, members of Christ’s body, offspring of unity, children of peace, keep this day joyfully; celebrate it securely. For what was foreshadowed in those days when the Holy Spirit came is fulfilled in you. Just as then the person who received the Holy Spirit—even one person—spoke in every language, so now unity itself speaks in every language among all nations. You possess the Holy Spirit because you have been established in that unity, in which the Church of Christ speaks in every language and you are divided by no schism.

## SERMON LII

### Also on Pentecost

In this most solemn gathering we celebrate the coming of the Holy Spirit descending from heaven, for we have already frequently celebrated the ascension of the Mediator returning to heaven. [Col. 0918D] For the only-begotten Son of the Father, while he bore human form on earth and the blessed apostles adhered to him, had promised, saying: “Unless I depart, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John XVI, 7).

*Paraclete* in Greek speech is called “consoler” in Latin. Christ consoled the fainthearted: God dwelling with human beings in human form, by the instruction of the gentleness he had assumed, offering the weak the benevolent assistance of his strength. He promises the Holy Spirit as Consoler, so that the disciples would not remain sad after his ascension, since the Spirit would remain with them forever.

O unity of indivisible operation! O power of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, alike and coeternal with the omnipotent Father! The Apostle Paul proclaims God the Father to be the Father of consolation when instructing the Church of the Corinthians: “Blessed,” he says, “be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation.” Concerning the Son, he adds in the following passage: “As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds” (II Cor. I, 3–5). [Col. 0919A]

Behold, the Father consoles; likewise the Son consoles; behold, the Holy Spirit consoles, he who is called the Paraclete. How is the sacred unity of the Trinity torn apart by some, when it possesses both inseparable power in dominion and, in the gift of consolation, displays a common love toward those who have been adopted?

Therefore the Holy Spirit, proceeding principally from the Father and not departing from the Son, descended today upon the apostles and the other one hundred and twenty gathered together in one dwelling. They were holding fast to the truest promise; they rejoiced in secure hope and demanded its fulfillment by continual prayer. With unshakable patience they endured most firmly; they dwelt in the upper room, destined to receive the gifts of the higher dignity. They believed the one who promised faithfully, and, with hearts cleansed by preparation, they deserved to receive the one who was coming.

Then there was a sound from heaven, as we have just heard read, as though a mighty spirit were arriving; it filled the entire house where they were sitting; and divided tongues appeared to them as though of fire, and it sat upon each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in various languages, as the Spirit gave them utterance (Acts II, 2 and following). [Col. 0919B]

The fact that the Holy Spirit, arriving in fire, sat upon the blessed apostles manifested by judgment that he is God. For, as the chosen Vessel writes to the Hebrews, “Our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. XII, 29).

O saving fire! Desiring to kindle it in his elect, the Son of Majesty cried: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke XII, 49). O, I say, saving fire, burning up the straw of vices and flashing with the flame of virtues! In the heavenly furnace of that dwelling it somehow purified the blessed lips of the fisherman apostles; and, like a most skilled goldsmith, by repeatedly heating them carefully it wiped away every impurity, so that gold polished in such a workshop might be brought forth, to be distributed to the army of Christ and to benefit the whole world by the most generous distribution of its resources. [Col. 0919C]

A radiant face in the apostles displayed the distinguished beauty of the Holy Spirit, and the tongue, proclaiming inward riches, with the sweetest eloquence of preaching delighted the multitude of the various nations gathered together. They were astonished and confused in mind, because each of them heard them speaking in his own language. And they said to one another: “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how do we hear them speaking in our own languages the great things of God?” (Acts II, 7–8).

Today the Holy Spirit unlocked the great chambers of the heavenly palace, hidden through the ages. How many treasures were brought forth from them thereafter! How many precious stones were given to deserving servants! How many were enriched with the noblest gold, comparable to no visible metal!

For he did not employ miners banished into exile, who, after undertaking penal labor, with failing arms and bodies blackened by smoky grime, would strike the hidden veins of the earth with a hammer in order to reach the purest gold; rather, the Spirit of truth rested upon the chosen apostles, filled their breasts and mouths, and, as though fastening royal ornaments of gems upon them, distributed knowledge of various languages. Thus, while one person spoke in various languages, the unity of beauty destined to reign in all the Churches was represented.

But among the others who were then present at Jerusalem and giving glory to God, men from every province, some blinded by the folly of their minds, enviously mocked the blessed apostles as drunk and full of new wine, and said derisively, “These men are drunk and full of new wine” (ibid., 12). [Col. 0919D]

Answer me, hard-hearted toward belief and eager to slander: can any human being, rendered drowsy by drinking hot new wine, become most eloquent in an unknown language? How can a drunken man take up the mastery of a language he has not learned, when lips disturbed by wine begin to stumble even in their own speech? In your delirium you do not know what you are saying. The vanity of such an accusation blunts your deceit and refutes your falsehood, while it confirms and establishes our most simple truth.

All the venerable apostles, new and whole, not patched with any shreds of antiquity, foaming with new wine—that is, overflowing with the richness of the Holy Spirit—give off a sweet fragrance to others and preserve within themselves incorruptible sincerity. Return, therefore, transgressors, to your hearts; bring the nostrils of your souls near; receive the ineffable sweetness of so great a fragrance; and, by a draught from your inner lips, drink the honeyed taste, untouched by blood.

This wine heals the inward parts, gladdens hearts, makes one soberly drunk, and invites its drinkers to the banquet of the eternal master of the household.

But we, my brothers, rejoicing with spiritual gladness in this most sacred feast, worshiping the one God of the eternal Trinity and praying to the one Name, should ask that the serene fire of the Holy Spirit, with which the apostles were filled, be breathed from heaven into our marrow. May it drive every cloud from our innermost dwelling and illuminate the senses of our understanding with the brightness of its radiance, so that, by the light of its power flourishing within us, we may enter the Church of the firstborn with blazing lamps and, singing the angelic Alleluia, cleave in perpetual happiness to the choirs of the shining saints.

## SERMON LIII

### On the Nativity of John the Baptist

The splendid nativity of this day has gathered us together, on which the truthful authority of the Catholic Church bears witness that holy John, the forerunner of Christ the Lord, was born. [Note: [Col. 0919] Alternatively, “how much according to.” We correct the reading from the beginning of the following passage, which is plainly similar.]

His venerable father Zachariah, during the time of his priesthood, when he entered the Holy of Holies in order to burn an incense pleasing to the Lord of virtues—as the Gospel according to Luke, now read to our ears, [Col. 0920C] has taught—suddenly feared an angel flying through the air in the snowy splendor of divinity and standing at the right side of the altar amid the sacrifices, descending in a flash.

O proclamation of the burnt offering of salvation, and offering of sincere sacrifice pleasing to God! The most ardent sweetness of prayer rose upward; the Lord of Majesty, dwelling in the heights, was delighted; and, according to the inscrutable plan of his will ordained before the ages, the simple priest’s petition received an answer.

But when the angel Gabriel saw the priest terrified by his arrival and visitation, he immediately encouraged the trembling man with a gentle address. “Do not fear, Zachariah,” he said, “for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John; and you will have joy and exultation, and many will rejoice at his birth. For he will be great before the Lord; he will drink neither wine nor strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” (Luke I, 13 and following), and so forth. [Col. 0920D]

Zachariah was astonished. He had not entered the temple’s secrets to ask for a child, but had stood there as an envoy, commending the people to the Lord. He wavered amid conflicting thoughts, changed in appearance until his face was flushed, and first began to consider the time already measured out in his own life; then he thought of Elizabeth, his barren companion, already advancing toward the extreme old age of her days. Moved by this double doubt, he became—although he ought not to have done so—unbelieving toward the angelic promise.

“How shall I know this?” he said. “For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years” (ibid., 18). It was as though he were saying: “O blessed messenger, the assertion of your promise seems impossible to me. The power of sowing has withered in my loins; nor has any hope of bearing ever appeared in my wife; the age suitable for childbirth has passed from the bodies of both of us. How can an aged husband and a decrepit old woman [Col. 0921A] conceive, or can a barren tree put forth shoots from the dried root of an ancient trunk covered with hard bark?”

Do not, do not, Zachariah, resist the heavenly will. The word of God runs swiftly wherever it is sent. No obstacle hinders it from accomplishing the commands of the divine ordering. Have you not read (I Sam. I, 20) that Anna, barren after the passing of many years, bore Samuel as a son? Did merely carnal desire prevail in her, or did only male implantation sprout? Rather, did not faith obtain power in the conception of the seed?

Rachel, joined in marriage to your father Jacob (Gen. XXX, 23), groaned because she had been granted no fruit of offspring. It pleased the Creator, and she became the mother of the patriarchs and was deemed worthy to give birth to Joseph, that most chaste and industrious man, who, refusing the defilement of adultery and forgetting the injury inflicted by his brothers who had sold him, generously supplied grain during the famine to his father and to the whole household of his plotting kinsmen.

Likewise Abraham, as you too are aging with the dignity of whitening hair and the maturity of age, [Col. 0921B] when he had already completed many years of a hundred, while the heat of the incitements of desire was growing cold and he hoped for no future heir of his legitimate line—did he not receive Isaac, conceived from himself, as a sacred heir from a ninety-year-old woman (Heb. XI, 11)? The devout father attained the possibility of begetting because he believed the one who promised faithfully.

Therefore, because you, O Zachariah, said that what you heard from the words of my mouth was incredible, your lips will be held bound in the prison of silence until your once-barren side becomes fruitful. And when Elizabeth, contrary to your despair, has borne you the promised son, then the function of your tongue, freed for speech, will be restored to your mouth.

O punishment pregnant with mystery! O beneficent vengeance filled with miracle! The father is deprived of the voice of speech, and the sentence of retribution lasted in the father for as long as the Voice of the Word was being born from the mother. For John is the Voice; Christ is the Word.

Hear John himself confessing that he is the voice: “I am,” he says, “the voice of one crying in the wilderness: [Col. 0921C] Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Matt. III, 3; Isa. XL, 3). You have heard John proclaiming as a voice in the wilderness; understand the Word, Christ, reigning with the Father in indivisible eternity.

But so that you may both believe and grasp this, listen to another John. I mean John, son of the fisherman Zebedee, formerly occupied with mending nets, intent upon the waves of the sea and devoted by his inherited craft to drawing fish from the deep, but now a disciple of Christ, chosen by Christ with the others and loved by Christ above the rest, compared by Christ to an apostle and evangelist in the noble likeness of an eagle: cutting the air in a swift flight, penetrating all heights as he flies with powerful screeching, passing beyond heaven and the stars, leaving behind the powers of invisible thrones, transcending the angelic dominions, and contemplating with fearless mental gaze and unobstructed vision the Word, God from God and remaining in God.

For he alone thundered in this manner about Christ at the beginning of his preaching: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word [Col. 0921D] was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 1–3).

Behold what sort and how great a herald of the Judge was born today in greatest splendor, announced before his father’s presence, through whom the Judge was to be carried in his mother’s womb. What ineffable grace is this? What incomprehensible riches of generosity are these? He is enclosed and held in the secrets of the womb, and there he is adorned by the gift of the Holy Spirit. He has not yet begun the principles of life among human beings, and he is designated the Prophet of the Most High.

Thus the illustrious chancellor of the heavenly palace, Gabriel, confirms: “He will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and he himself will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of fathers toward their children, and the unbelieving to the prudence of the righteous, and to prepare for the Lord a perfect people” (Luke I, 16–17).

Since the Savior of the world [Col. 0922A] was going to come in the purest womb of a virgin, not conceived by lust but by faith, the one born of a barren woman went before him, chosen as the one greater than whom none has arisen among those born of women. This great surveyor went before the magnificent one, wondrous before the exalted one; the friend of the Word, the bridegroom’s attendant, who, seeing the Virgin of virgins—that is, the Lamb of God—as though he were a bridegroom crowned with a royal diadem and about to proceed from the virginal bridal chamber, recognized that the marriage of Christ and the Church, long and ardently desired by the fathers, had arrived.

And observing his own Creator being carried from the bond of a chaste womb into the palace of the consecrated uterus, he did not greet him with bodily steps but, with every movement of his soul, rejoiced in singular delight, the conscious mother exulting while the child, late in the process of childbirth, exulted in the womb and greeted him from the womb.

For thus Elizabeth replied to holy Mary as she entered to her: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And whence is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, as the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy” (Luke I, 42–44).

Therefore, because Christ—the King and physician of the earth, God and man—was coming among human beings, offering the most precious [Col. 0922B] antidote of his body for the restoration of humanity wounded by the long illness of sins, the noble forerunner of so excellent and skilled a chief physician prepared a level road and a perfectly straight path, not in the valleys of the earth but in human minds. Rejecting royal dwellings with ivory houses, disregarding golden ceilings and abandoning marble palaces, he prepared a royal residence for the Lord of heaven in the souls of believers.

Rejoice, rejoice, blessed Zachariah, priest and father, because although you were unable to speak for the brief period of the three-month discipline imposed as correction, you received back what you had lost with increased interest. You doubted a little when you heard the archangel announce the pledge who was to be born; leaving the sanctuary, you came forth mute to the people and endured the tolerable punishment of corrective silence; when the appointed limit of the day had passed, you received a son, born from an aged womb, who was great before the Lord.

When the child had been born and you were asked by what name he should be called, you wrote the name “John” [Col. 0922C] on tablets, just as the angel had announced to you. Immediately the bond of your silence was loosed, and the service of a melodious voice, crowned with the Lord’s blessing, was restored to you.

Let us also rejoice, brothers, celebrating with devoted attendance on this most solemn day the wondrous birth of the servant, and awaiting with complete reverence the ineffable birth of the Lord. May those to whom the generation of the forerunner who came through a barren woman brought joy be granted, through the subsequent fruit of the undefiled Virgin, the Redeemer’s everlasting security.

## SERMON LIV

### Also, on the above subject.

The splendid solemnity of this day has gathered us together, on which the authoritative testimony of the catholic Church declares that holy John, the precursor of Christ the Lord, was born. His merits are shown by the circumstances of his birth, since the Lord testifies and says that “among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11:11). Indeed, no Church celebrates the day on which a person assumed flesh; rather, it observes the day on which he abandoned all carnal things. Thus the glorious and blessed birth of the Lord is celebrated—the birth announced by the star and feared by Herod—which the same holy John, filled with the Holy Spirit from the womb and even while still in the womb, recognized with joy and greeted with profound reverence. Therefore a herald is sent to announce the Judge, and a precursor is dispatched to proclaim the Savior. For it was said of him: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way” (Malachi 3:1). Of him also the prophet Isaiah prophesies, saying: “A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; the crooked places shall become straight, and the rough places into level roads, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isaiah 40:3–5).

Behold, a voice sounds in the wilderness; humility is commanded to the mountains, and straightness and level ground are required from the higher roads and from the crooked paths. The herald of faith is arranged within human hearts, and human mortality is terrified. O carnal weakness, what will you do at the coming of the most serene Judge, when you begin to render an account of your deeds—when now you are unwilling to receive the preaching of so great a herald, crying out and saying: “Behold, the axe has already been laid at the root of the tree. And every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Luke 3:9)?

How great the dignity of this herald was at his birth became evident in this way. While his mother was barren, his father had been appointed the most eloquent advocate for the people. But when the barren mother was made fruitful, the father became mute and without a voice. During his priestly ministry, while he entered the Holy of Holies on behalf of the people to offer incense to the Lord, suddenly, disturbed, he saw Gabriel—the most intimate confidant of divine mysteries—flying through the air and standing among the altars. When he saw him with tranquil countenance, Gabriel encouraged the trembling man with this address:

“Zechariah, do not be afraid, for your prayers have been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. He will drink neither wine nor strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb, and he will convert many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God” (Luke 1:13 and following), and so forth.

But Zechariah began to consider the matter within himself and, changed even to the flushing of his face, said in amazement: “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days” (ibid., 18).

And the angel said: “Believe, Zechariah; believe the angel, believe the heavenly minister. Give faith to the message, if you do not wish to lose your voice. Behold: when you incurred the guilt of unbelief, at once you received a chain at the doorway of your tongue. Here the angel brings both joy and restraint; he guards faith and voice. If you believe, you have earned joy; if you do not believe, you have incurred the restraint of your tongue.”

And Zechariah said: “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days.”

And the angel said: “Is God, then, powerless to produce a son from the barren, when he made the first human being from the substance of clay?”

And Zechariah said: [Col. 0923C] “How shall I know this?” And he said: “I am Gabriel, who stand before the Lord, and I have been sent to speak to you and to announce these things to you. And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day on which all these things come to pass, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their proper time” (ibid., 19–20).

O wondrous power! Zechariah does not believe that the barren woman will give birth at the Lord’s command, and by divine decree he deserved to receive the restraint of his tongue. It is taken from the father until the child is generated from the mother, so that he may receive speech at the moment when he receives his son. The instrument of the voice was struck silent on the body’s lyre, and while all the limbs lived within the body, the tongue alone lay in the tomb of the teeth.

Thus there were in the angel’s hands both a gift and a sword. Zechariah denied his mind to the gift, and the angel exercised punishment upon his tongue. He did not believe, and he fell silent; the angel spoke, and Zechariah was bound at the palate of speech. He faltered over the promised son, while the angel awaited faith. When Zechariah did not believe, he immediately received the fetters of silence in his mouth. Speech rolled about within the rib cage of his breast, but could not be heard outside, because the doors of his mouth had been closed with the keys of authority.

Behold, the angel placed a prison upon Zechariah’s lips and shut up the dwelling of the word. He ascended to the place from which he had come, confirming what he had bound by divine command. It was released when John was born. His tongue received release when Elizabeth gave birth to the voice. For John himself was “the voice of one crying in the wilderness,” who, though he had not yet come forth from his mother’s womb, was already displaying an example to the unbelieving.

Thus the prophet is present in the light; a lamp is led forth from the mother’s womb, and there is uncertainty about his name. The father is asked what the child should be called; and because he could not speak, he asks for writing tablets. He wrote the name “John,” and the knot of his voice was immediately broken. And when a name was assigned to the Voice, the door of the voice that had been closed was opened.

Zechariah begins speech in the presence of the Voice. The son is born, and the father is released from muteness. The voice is brought forth by the mother, and speech is created in the father’s mouth. The birth of the son at daybreak granted the gift of speaking to the one whom unbelief had made mute.

[Col. 0924A]

The Voice preceded the Word; the lamp went before the Sun of justice. A voice is born from a barren old man, and the Word is born from a most pure virgin. In Elizabeth, within dryened entrails, the Creator renews youthful vigor; in the virgin’s members, Christ changes the law of nature. In Elizabeth the heat of sexual desire came upon her, but in Mary the fervor of virginity did not depart, because the Holy Spirit, coming upon her, prepared the divine temple.

The servant is born before the Lord; the surveyor runs ahead of the Judge. In John the condition of the marriage covenant is changed; in Christ it is abolished. For the union of barren old people brought John into the world, whereas virginal integrity gave the Savior to the age. Yet in John’s mother, carnality is discerned to have been infused, while in the mother of Christ the majesty of the Holy Spirit was at work.

Let us therefore celebrate this day, beloved brothers, in the increase of faith, hope, and charity—not of foolishness, wickedness, and vanity—lest, after having grieved the Lord’s precursor, we find the Judge himself angry when he comes.

[Col. 0924B]

## SERMON LV. On the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist

Brothers, the narrative of today’s Gospel reading offers our minds an appropriate comparison. We heard virtues confronting vices, when the wickedness of Herod and the lust of Herodias were set against the venerable justice of holy John—to such an extent that he willingly accepted death lest he appear to despise the truth.

Consider what three things have come together in one cause: a matter worthy of wonder, if you rightly examine the prophet’s seriousness, the woman’s lust, and Herod’s most savage ferocity. Tell me, what have you to do with John the Baptist, Herod and Herodias, whom the impurity of your crimes has brought together in a partnership of names? Do you fear that, although joined to one another in name, you may perhaps be separated in lust? Be certain that, just as you fall into lust with one consent, so you will receive your sentence under one name.

You hold the righteous man in prison because he lawfully forbade your incest—as though truth could be bound. Even if all his limbs were fastened with the bonds of chains, his tongue alone could not be restrained, since it is free to prevent the truth from being polluted by the wicked.

But you will say: “Why does he obstruct our desire?” He may obstruct desire to whom it is permitted, at the proper time, to remove crimes. Yet when the prophet declares to you that this displeases the Lord’s will, scarcely anyone who is wise is ashamed to hear what he was not ashamed to commit without embarrassment.

O human madness! So that Herod might indulge his lust, John is killed. Did the prophet frighten you by his own merit, and not by divine judgment? It is the height of madness to hate the one who speaks and not fear the one who judges—as though you should no longer fear the Judge if you can kill the herald who cries out, of whom Isaiah testified, saying: “This is the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight his paths” (Isaiah 40:3).

Now we must come to the culmination of the passion. The banquet theater is prepared, and a lascivious female executioner is brought forward to overthrow the prophet not with a sword but with a dance. The tender girl comes forward with gentle steps, about to demand a murder and please an adulterer; she carries another’s blood on her feet and is about to demand the reward for her crime. She dances in such a way as to please; she pleases in such a way as to kill. Alas for the crime—that a woman should use the luxury of her body to seek danger for another’s head!

What shall we do, John? The vast solitude of the wilderness did not frighten you; will this woman’s dance frighten you? The woman is about to demand your head. But the Lord says: “It is better for you that one of your members should perish than that your whole body should be thrown into the fires of Gehenna” (Matthew 5:29). And again: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matthew 10:28).

Behold, with the devil arranging it, the girl began to take pleasure in playing, solely so that she might be able to kill the prophet. I do not know what the female name has always had in common with holy men. Elijah also, in whose spirit the Lord testified that John had come (Luke 1:17), suffered the queen Jezebel as a grievous enemy (1 Kings 19:1). While fleeing from her, he consumed his entire life in flight; he feared her sword so greatly that, alive, he fled into heaven.

In whatever way a woman pursues someone, if he pleases her, she slaughters him; if he displeases her, she torments him even worse. Yet it is better to displease her with the death of the body, lest she take away from the soul what is greater: its health.

What I have long dreaded saying was also pleasing to the dancer. But what wonder, if amid abundant dishes and frequent storms of cups, a wanton girl should charm the senses and bend the affections? Wine and dancing are a double conflagration of pleasure. In addition, lust is offered the promise that whatever reward she might demand would immediately be granted—even if the woman had asked for half the kingdom.

Solomon bears witness that “there is no head above the head of a serpent, and there is no wickedness above the wickedness of a woman.” And again: “It is better to dwell with a lion and a dragon in the wilderness than to live with a wicked woman” (Ecclesiasticus 25:22–23).

Therefore, despising the height of the kingdom, she asked for John’s head on a dish—hating more deeply the one who forbade incest than she loved the one who had promised the kingdom. She curses the teacher of discipline and presumes upon the merchant of lust. O wickedness of a woman! She chose to despise honor in order to make a profit from blood. Truly, she gives no thought to empire, for what is disgraceful is dearer to her.

The blood of the freshly severed head flowed upon the dish, provoking the good to pity and striking terror into the wicked. This alone, plainly, was lacking from the royal tables. I believe that many heads of fish and cattle had already preceded it; but what is that in relation to royal desire? Perhaps even a private table could have witnessed such a thing. Nothing had been done, nothing at all accomplished, if a human head had been absent from the royal banquet. And it was not some random or ordinary head, but a prophetic head brought from prison to the table.

Kings usually seek great and earthly banquets for their celebrations; for Herod, even the prison began to provide delicacies. Therefore poverty is always pleasing to God: its food has no blood, but a cheap vegetable supplies a gentle hunger. For the three boys (Daniel 1:16), the food was vegetables and legumes. Otherwise they would never have overcome the flames if they had wished to love delicacies.

Truly, you do not know what wickedness does, when you honor more highly the one whom you hate than you condemn him. When you order a head to be presented at the table on a silver dish, it is not, as you think, a memorial of cruelty; rather, it already reveals the honor due to that person. So it will also be carried to heaven, so that from there it may stir up against you God the Judge, who is angry with you. To him be glory forever and ever.

## SERMON LVI. On the Birth of Saint John the Baptist

Today a good banquet of the precursor has been prepared for us at the table of the confessor. Cyprian provided hospitality for a friend, but John has prepared a heavenly meal for us—John, I say, and Cyprian. The former is the “child prophet of the Most High” (Luke 1:76); the latter is an aged priest of Christ. The former was sanctified in the womb; the latter was sanctified in his own blood. The former is a herald; the latter is robed. One Christ is the advocate for both. The former leaped in the womb; the latter triumphed beneath the sword. The former is the precursor; the latter is the confessor.

The former is at the table, and the latter beneath the table. The former lost his head at the table but did not lose it; the latter did not lose his head at the table but found it. For the former’s head is in a dish; the latter’s head is in the temple. Both are at the table, but both are also beneath the table, since he says: “I saw the souls of the righteous beneath the altar of God” (Revelation 6:9).

John is beneath the altar, the one of whom his barren mother was ashamed; and Christ is placed above the altar, the one over whom his virgin mother rejoiced. But since God’s gifts are not our private possession, we have taken from a friend what belongs to the honor of a friend.

Let us set aside for a little while the glorious passion of both, content with their palms and triumphs, and let us believe in their wondrous birth. Today the herald is born. But because their dignity is different and their arrivals are unequal, the herald comes in an aged chariot, while the Judge comes in a virginal carriage.

This carriage was not born for a man alone, but for the Lord. Earthly emperors are said to have, among their various carriages in which they ride, one in which no one sits; it is called the angelic carriage. This carriage is not only angelic but also lordly, for in it sits not merely a human being but God and man.

Behold the carriage; behold the coming. What sort of herald has been sent? The herald went ahead of the carriage of the coming Lord, who is common to all. What did he say?

“Lord, I go before your steps, because you possessed my kidneys” (Psalm 153:13). Thanks be to you, Lord: you knew my ways from afar, and you entrusted your ways, which were near, to me. Thanks be to you, Lord: you placed my condition before its proper order and promised me your grace. Your mother went to my mother, and I go before your face.

Thanks be to you, Lord: you received me from my mother’s womb so that I might recognize you in your mother’s womb. My mother’s womb held me enclosed within the hidden chamber of its narrow uterus; you sent your Christ, you illumined the maternal heart. You sent your shining lamp within, so that I might recognize your mother.

O good lamp—not one that loves the world, but one that loves heaven. If you wish to call the day of lamps by its proper name, love the Holy Spirit. But this grieves us: there are many who call the day a lamp and yet remain in the midst of darkness.

[Col. 0926B]

Thus we have described the character of the carriage and the lawful service of the one who goes before it. Let us come to the dignity of the Lord’s own arrival. Before the carriage of an emperor come the surveyors, palace guards, protectors, tribunes, generals, and counts; standards, dragons, and banners; those little streamers rejoicing in harmonious variety of cloth; sounding trumpets; cities trembling; the innocent rejoicing; the guilty fearing.

Before the carriage of our King, let us see what comes first: venerable sacraments, the temple, the Holy of Holies, the golden altar, the mercy seat where there is remission of sins; the golden urn containing the judgment of divine allotment, not the decision of human choice; the cherubim protecting the mercy seat with their wings and fixing their eyes upon it; the flowering rod; manna as an example of compassion, because “he gave them the bread of heaven” (Psalm 77:24).

There also were the tablets of heavenly instruction, given to good disciples but made for the hard-hearted. There is the priest; there is the altar; there incense burns. There the angel stands together with the human being at one altar.

[Col. 0926C]

Thanks be to you, Lord: you have begun to reconcile both what is in heaven and what is on earth through the blood of your cross. Today the angel stands with the human being at the altar. Would that Gabriel stood with us, so that through angelic fellowship paternal purity might drive away fraternal discord and the ancient harmony might be restored.

Let us therefore see the angel coming and the priest standing in fear: the one announcing, the other hearing and not believing. Suddenly the heavenly being stood there, coming in spiritual flight as spirit and burning fire, because “he makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire” (Psalm 103:4). He came, stood, and drew near; he removes terror and gives security.

“Do not be afraid,” he said, “Zechariah. Your incense, springing forth from the golden censer in sweet smoke, burned upon the golden altar in heaven and gladdened the entire angelic host. From that court I, Gabriel, a courtier, have come to you, with heaven already rejoicing together with the world in one incense. Do not be afraid, Zechariah” (Luke 1:13). I see that the priestly garment has been shaken and bent in fear upon you. Do not be afraid, Zechariah: a messenger of peace, not of fear, has come to you.

“Do not be afraid; your prayer has been heard” (ibid.), and may you love my presence. Lay aside for a little while the ancient service; hear from me a new answer. Lay aside this service of the ancient bondage in the observance of the law, where the priest entered once each year with another’s blood.

Behold, a Priest will come who will enter once with his own blood. What kind of priest? The High Priest of the things to come, building a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands (Hebrews 9:11), which a virgin bore and which no man knew. He does not enter by the blood of goats and calves, in which there is no remission of sins; rather, he enters the holy places once by his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption (ibid., 12).

Thus the High Priest will come—but before then you will receive a son in your old age.

“How will this happen, Lord?” he said. “The condition of old age denies it; I hear a great announcement of novelty. How? I am old, and my wife is advanced in her days” (Luke 1:18).

It would have been a great thing if you had heard me with grace; punishment would not have followed, but glory. Because my mouth spoke and your heart did not believe, your mouth withers.

Within, the angel was mingling heavenly speech with the priest’s human voice like a trumpet: he was condemning the unbeliever, while outside the praying people were thinking intensely about the priest’s delay. The priest came out mute and unbelieving, though he would speak better with the new tongue of faith. The people awaited an answer, not understanding the mystery. A great miracle astonished them. He was signaling with his fingers, wishing only through gestures and movements to indicate what he had not believed with his senses.

The High Priest will not come in this way from the holy heavens. He will not come mute, because “our God will come and will not be silent” (Psalm 49:3). Behold, now the entire age is a temple. All this world is a temple; throughout the courts of the world, as of a temple, this entire crowd dispersed everywhere awaits the hour when the priest will come out from the Holy of Holies—not to bring a new message, but a judgment to be feared.

How will he come? The windows of heaven will be opened; all creation will be in fear. The very offices of the angels will begin to seethe in the heat of trembling dread when the human race begins to be heard in terror. Heavenly attendants will go before him, as though before the cloud-bearing carriage of the Judge coming from his throne: fire, storm, flames, worms.

Flames that are not extinguished, worms that do not die, a river of fire, a fiery throne. Angels with voice and a great trumpet; tombs burst open, not a confused tongue. What will he himself be like, the one who visited us, “the dawn from on high” (Luke 1:78), and ascended above the heavens of heavens toward the east (Psalm 67:34)?

He will come and give a great voice, a voice of power. The prophet will go before him, saying: “Let all flesh fear before the face of the Lord, because he has risen from his holy dwelling place” (Zechariah 2:13). Therefore, remaining secure in the matter of his judgment, let us do what is required of us: serve the Lord in piety and righteousness before him all our days (Luke 1:75).

[Col. 0927C]

## SERMON LVII. On Saint Peter, where the Lord says: “Feed my sheep”

The entire salvation of the heavenly flock lies in the care of the shepherd who descended with the heavens bowed down, in order to raise up the sheep that lay fallen, whom the prey of the ravening wolf had scattered. He gathers them from sickness, healing wounds, binding them with the sweet chain of his love, applying a bandage to broken bones, and laying on a medicinal poultice. While he heals the lame, he visits the sick, gives sight to the blind, cures the infirm, and raises the dead.

Love was the reason for the great shepherd’s care of the flock. He still cares for the flock through his own passion; he lifts them upon the cross so that they might pluck the shoots of his wounds and hang in sweet rumination upon the shepherd’s love.

He commends them to the Father; he commends them also to Peter. He commends them to the Father as one about to suffer; he commends them to Peter as one about to return to heavenly things. For at the moment of his passion, when he commends the little sheep of the chosen flock to the Father, he also commends Peter to the Father together with the others (John 17:6). The twofold commendation was beneficial where there was one protection.

[Col. 0927D]

The Father protects Peter from heaven, and Christ visits Peter in the governor’s palace. For if he had not been visited, he would not have wept; and his wounds would not have been wiped away unless they had been watered by tears.

The ascension is at hand, and Peter is required to confess the mark of love, as you heard in the Gospel. Christ the Lord of the angels was commending you, the sheep, to the shepherd. “Simon, son of John,” he said, “do you love me?” (John 21:15). And he said: “I love you, Lord.”

You are gracious and gentle, and I do not love you? In you all the sweetness of eternal life resides, and I do not love you? I give you thanks for asking me. For while I love you, love comes from you. If your love had not gone before, my love would not have followed.

The angels love you, singing your glory; the heavens love you, because “the heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18:1); the earth loves you, drenched by the drops of your blood dripping from your side; those given life love you; the dead whom you raised love you.

What shall I repay you? You healed my wounds, and I do not love your medicine?

“Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). What you profess in love, demonstrate from the flock. You too were a sheep, and you remain one. I appoint you shepherd over the sheepfold. I release you to my sheep as their deputy caretaker. Feed my sheep.

Before the pasture he plants, and thus he entrusts the sheep to Peter. I planted pasture upon the living wood, upon the unfading cross. He planted wounded shoots; he opened the human being as a spring—or rather, the true spring, the cross.

Behold, you have a field of meadows, the passion of wounds and scars. Out of concern for my little lambs, lead them to pasture, to my passion. Teach them to pluck the shoots and to believe in my wounds. Teach them to pluck the most burning roses, the scars opened up in the Sun of justice. There let my sheep flourish in diverse professions, so that the Church redeemed by this attentive pasture may not be violated.

He commends them a second and a third time, and returns to heaven, seated upon his own throne. Let us appeal to him; nor is Peter silent—the legate, the shepherd, the deputy who wept over his denial and grieves over human hardness.

Let us say to him: “Lord, you entrusted them to us; have you departed completely? If you do not defend the shepherds, the sheep would not be safe either. Look, then, upon the raging wolves and the lambs groaning in compassion. Why has the cruel pirate scattered your sheep, whom you redeemed like a sheep led to sacrifice? Like a lamb beneath the shearer, you did not open your mouth; the tongue of the suffering one was silent. There was no guilt, and a great silence—so that heaven marveled, earth was astonished, and the heavenly lights fled.

“And now you are silent while your sheep are being shorn by swords and by the storms you sought through the purple passion of your body. Do not let those whom you brought forth from your side be devastated upon the shore.”

Let us approach the most faithful Redeemer with these prayers by the correction of our deeds, not by a mere embassy of words.

## SERMON LVIII. On the Birth of the Apostles Peter and Paul

The birth feast of the apostles Peter and Paul has dawned—a birth not one that entangled them in the world, but one that liberated them from the world. Through human weakness a human being is born for hardship; through the living love of Christ the martyrs are born for the crown.

Today Peter suffered first; today Paul suffered first. Their merit made their passion equal, and love came to meet the day. This day has therefore been set before us because of their merit, for the celebration of solemnity and the imitation of holiness, so that, loving the glories of the martyrs, we may be able to imitate their footsteps.

O blessed merits of the apostles, that one grace was granted to two, so that you seem to invoke both their names! For if you say Paul, you do not keep silent about Peter; and if you say Peter, you do not fall silent about Paul. Indeed, both names are held by each as cognomens.

For good reason the Savior wished to name Saul “Paul,” so that by a cognomen he might join them together. Their fellowship was united in life, and one day’s passion confirmed it.

Paul, therefore, is loved by God while he persecutes God’s law. And he who did not wish to be humble before God in order to be saved suffers God humbly. For while he traveled on his destructive mission, the Savior came in a cloud and, by his weight, struck down the man who was oppressed—not to harm the one he loved, but to raise him, cast down in carnal pride and made humble in spirit as though reborn, so that the enemy who had fallen might rise as a Christian.

A voice from the cloud answered him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). This means: “Proud man, proud man, destructive man, why are you persecuting yourself in me? You grieve the Maker while destroying his work within you. You injure the Creator while ruining his creature. The craftsman does not lack vessels necessary for worthy use, but in a work he approves the master does not wish to suffer loss.

“You acquire for me those whom, by injuring them in the world, you perfect in me; what you lose is what you abandon by turning away from me. I cry out now in grief before you perish entirely. I will laugh now if, hardened, you do not listen.”

God entreats a human being and shows the hope of mercy to the humble, since he easily has mercy upon the proud.

And Saul says to this: “Who are you, Lord?” (ibid., 5). Horrible was Saul’s pride; Paul’s ready belief is worthy of imitation, when with one word he utters the voice both of the ignorant man and of the believer. No one asks the name of one who cries out except the one who does not know by whom he is being called; and no one says “Lord” except the one who promises service.

Thus no distinction was made between the ignorant and the consenting. For the one who had wished Saul to remain unknown for a long time suddenly made Paul known to himself.

And the Lord said to him: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:5)—certainly it is hard for the fragile to contend with the solid, for when you collide with it, you are immediately broken. Your resistance is grief to me and death to you. If you perish, it is evil for you; but if you advance, it is good both for me and for you.

Paul therefore proceeds, no longer Saul, to be of service to the divine law, although he had come to persecute that same law. He is baptized in the hope of resurrection, though he had prepared death for those proclaiming the resurrection.

He teaches the law that he did not know and forgets the one he had learned. For this reason he rightly recalls the praise of his deeds in his own words, saying: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. There remains for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord will repay me on that day” (2 Timothy 4:7).

He does not say “he gives,” but “he will repay.” If he will repay, then it was owed. Had he received a loan, so that something should be owed to him? God did not become a debtor through our merit, but through his promise. I dare even to say that he owed the apostle a crown.

Therefore, if someone promises us something, we use this expression when we approach him and say: “Repay what you promised.” We demand a debtor when we say “repay,” but we acknowledge his benevolence when we say “what you promised,” not “what you received.”

## SERMON LIX. Also on Paul

Saul was a Jew who was awaiting the time when he would become Paul the Christian. While persecuting what he was destined to become, he deserved to be an apostle.

He was therefore sent by his elders to the one whose punishment would save him; he was sent to be blinded. He is blinded, therefore, so that he might see the true way, which does not deceive the eyes but directs the steps. He is blinded in the flesh and illumined in the heart, so that the eyes of the heart—and those of the flesh—might be illumined.

He was sent so that Paul might believe in the one whom Saul had persecuted. He was sent into himself to seek himself. He was wandering with himself, an ignorant traveler, and did not find himself because he had lost the way within himself.

Therefore he hears a voice saying to him: “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). That is: “Saul, why are you persecuting Paul? He is mine, the one you carry with you, and you do not see him because you have the eyes of one raging, not of one seeing. That is, you do not believe in the one in whom you are destined to believe, and you persecute the one whom you will later preach.”

Correct, then, correct your feet from Saul’s paths, so that you may find Paul’s faith. Strip off, Paul, the tunic of blindness, and at last put on the Savior’s robe. Cast off what you are, so that you may be able to become what you are not.

For your blindness is not the punishment of blindness; rather, it is the cause of blindness. I wished to show you in the flesh what you possess in your heart, so that you might see what you did not see and not be like those who “have eyes and do not see, have ears and do not hear” (Psalm 113:5–6).

I endured you as an adversary and sinner of the Law while you were armed by the foolish and deceitful elders of the Synagogue. Therefore I wished to show you your usefulness while you were wavering, so that you might love the struggle of a good soldier.

Let Saul return with his superfluous letters, so that Paul may write necessary Epistles. Let Saul’s blindness return to the blind, so that Paul’s light may benefit believers.

Go, Saul; return, Paul. Go to Ananias, my father (papam), where you may render the apostle you owe. Go—why do you delay returning what must contribute to your punishment? Go to Ananias; there you have the fountain where you may erase the bond.

And therefore, Saul, see your way, so that Paul may see the heavenly homeland. Where are you, vanity, which persecuted me in order to hold my soldier? Behold, the one who did not know me is learning me. Behold, the one who hated without knowing is loving.

Here is the chosen vessel, the one who had been a storehouse of iniquity. Behold, there is Siloam, Saul: wash your eyes. Behold, there is the fountain, Paul: restore your eyes. You, Saul, wash the mud; you, Paul, see Christ. Wash, both of you; see, both of you, so that you, Saul, may see that you are in the mud, and you, Paul, that you reign in Christ.

Now then, elders, ask the blind Saul of your origin who made him Paul of his light. “Who made you Paul?”

“Do you wish to hear who made me Paul? A man called Christ. When he made me, he made mud.”

“What is mud?”

“The medicine of the flesh, because from it he anointed my eyes and said to me: ‘Go to the pool of Siloam, wash, and see.’ And I went, washed, and I see” (John 9:7).

But why are you astonished? The one who made me himself remade me; from what he made me, from that he healed me; from what I had sinned, from that he cleansed me.

Come, therefore, Paul, from the old Saul, for it is not far off that you may deserve to find Peter also. Come; let Ananias touch you, so that the Christian may no longer fear the wolf, but the Jew may grieve over the apostle.

Touch Saul, Ananias, and give us Paul. Drive out the persecutor and send forth the preacher, in whom the lambs may not fear but Christ’s sheep rejoice. Touch the wolf who was ravaging Christ, so that now he may feed the sheep with Peter; let the one who was accustomed to destroy cruelly learn to acquire mercifully.

You discovered the loss arising from the gains of the one who made not our losses but his own. You were sending out one whole in appearance who was broken in every respect. Let him return reformed from the potter’s wheel, he who had grown old in his character through the counsel of his ways.

Let him be restored to suffer what the persecutor had done, when in his own evils he rejoiced in another’s good, when he secretly rewarded Stephen with his name, and when in violent fury he exercised himself against Christ’s martyr.

Let the pursuer flee; let the persecutor fear. Let him love what we feared, so that we may possess a teacher of patience. Let him be shipwrecked, beaten, scourged, and imprisoned, so that through the punishments of the flesh he may deserve the grace of the cross.

Come, see, and hear, you who inhabit the earth in the place of those who grieve: Paul is a citizen in the city of those who rejoice. See the works of God: Paul, headlong through his pride, a fugitive in a basket, disfigured as he is lowered over the wall—the preacher of Christ whom he hated, now the wolf of the Jews and the sheep of Christians, snatching goats from the synagogues and making them lambs of the Church; persuading the executioner to show compassion, promising forgiveness to the guilty, patience to the harsh, grace to the pagan, and concord to the Jew.

See him beaten for Christ and not failing because of Christ. He is beaten and preaches, so that through necessary punishment he may acquire the gains.

He is shipwrecked and becomes a harbor; he is needy and feeds others; he is sick and heals. Behold, as though a sinner, he liberates sinners. For by the bite of the viper he was indicated as a sinner, when he was bitten for sinners; but unless the serpent had bitten his hand, he would not have laid on hands.

And now observe the devil placed between Paul and Peter. Observe also the crown of the world beneath Peter’s feet, in which Saul gloried when Paul did not yet know himself. Peter was owed to him for fellowship—not by the merit of a debt, but by the grace of Christ. Without that grace he was sent to kill, hand over, and destroy; now, however, he redeems, saves, and acquires—those to whom Peter may open, whom Christ may receive, and in whom Paul may rejoice.

## SERMON LX. On Saint Lawrence
We who celebrate the martyrdom of blessed Lawrence should carry his trophy with joyful necks. Upon the standards shines the triumph of the earthly king, the martyr and confessor. [Col. 0930D] For in his triumph pearls and gems do not shine; rather, the blind who see and the needy who have been fed flash forth. O standard of the Lord’s cross, which he carried upon his neck and placed upon closed eyes, opening the gates of blindness! For the standard did not have a purple cloth fastened with gems; rather, with the wounds of the Savior, it had a purple cloak dyed in the blood of the grape—that is, made precious by blood.

What praise shall we offer to blessed Lawrence? We are weak; we are poor. He himself is a column of the heavenly altar. May he restrain our tongue, so that we may be able to praise his crown. A precious column: a deacon in the Church, a martyr upon the gridiron. A true column supports walls, and blessed Lawrence sustains the needy. You are rich: feed the poor, leave your heirs behind, and gladden the angelic powers. He followed his testator and, himself enduring suffering, left an heir. That testator was Father Sixtus, and blessed Hippolytus follows the same testator. For [Col. 0931A] while he stood beside the glorious bed of Father Sixtus—the pontiff hanging beside the torture-rack—the testament was written with a pen of blood. The son mourned, and the father promised precious riches. “Son,” he said, “do not be sad; you will follow me after three days.”

The martyr’s testament is the resurrection of the Savior. The torture-rack was the pen, just as the cross was a pen. The Lord was writing a testament for the thief; Sixtus was speaking it: “You will follow me after three days.” And the Savior said to the thief, “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). A trustworthy testament: neither does the testator lie, nor is the heir defrauded. The thief follows Christ to paradise in one chariot, and blessed Lawrence, from Father Sixtus, proceeds to the gridiron.

A fiery chariot, preceded by precious attendants—not men clad in cloaks, shields, and silk, but the blind illumined, the poor enriched, and the wretched fed. The impious emperor was terrified: “What do these men mean? Where are the treasures you promised?” “Here are my treasures, my good bearers, who carried my riches there, where you cannot stretch out your hands. [Col. 0931B] I have no gold or silver, but what I have, this I give you. My gold was eaten by the bellies of these people, but their bellies received it: your gold is the idols of the nations; my gold is the satisfaction of the poor. From your gold they do not see images; from my gold the blind see, and the poor rejoice.”

He himself is placed upon the cooling bed of the gridiron and leaves Hippolytus as his heir. He handed him jewels of coals and the opened eyes of the blind, so that, through contempt for torments, Hippolytus too might make himself an heir and fashion an ornament for himself. O pearls of embers, with which Lawrence’s entrails are adorned! The fires breathed, the gems glittered, and the martyr’s limbs shone.

Those bars of the flaming gridiron were pens—the tongues of the martyr writing his testament. With them the pen threatened hell to the impious judge, and a crown was written for Hippolytus, who followed him. The sparks hissed amid the crackling flames, and the persecutor’s ministers groaned, because the angels of the Savior rejoiced. They themselves had persecuted the one who rose again, whom the poor would precede as he came from the gridiron.

From the gridiron they led him down to the city of Rome. From the tomb they lead him down to his everlasting homeland. Christ the Lord will meet him in the air, he who helped him in the fire, because he himself deigned to appear with the three youths in the furnace (Dan. 3:92). He will give him a chariot of cloud after the gridiron of blazing fire. The gridiron had flaming wheels; the clouds will have pleasant drops and cool rains, so that, just as he slept rejoicing in the Lord’s peace upon the bed of the gridiron, he may sing and say in the Lord’s Jerusalem, “This is my rest; here I will dwell, for I have chosen it” (Ps. 131:14). And what did the angels sing at this triumph? “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; for ever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83:5).

## SERMON LXI. On the Man Who Fell among Robbers

Let the roads of the world rejoice, because the Creator of heaven passes by with angelic powers before him, so that he may cause robbers to cease their attacks in the ravine [Col. 0931D] and raise up the innocent who lie half-dead along the road. Behold, the road’s mourning is gone; the groaning of the half-alive man lying there is silenced. The physician passes by: the one who mourned is silent, the one who lay there rises. Struck down by robbers, he begins to be carried upon the Lord’s shoulders.

He, he is the one whom the Gospel showed us lying there, and whom the Lord in heaven displayed to the angels, breathing again upon his shoulders. “A certain man” (Luke 10:30). His name is not mentioned, because he had been erased from the book of the living. He had abandoned the vision of peace—for this is how Jerusalem, from which he had descended, is interpreted. He had abandoned the temple of peace, the dwelling of rest, the court of the angels, the Church of the firstborn (Heb. 12:23); and, descending, he began to lie exposed in the hands of robbers.

O man, you who lie there, how well you had been stretched out, how well you entered through gates of pearls and rejoiced! How well you were sheltered beneath the medicinal shade of the trees along the banks of that crystal river! Those leaves do not fall; why did your footsteps fall away from there? There was no one there to terrify you: no lion in the forests, seizing and roaring; no bear lying in ambush; no leopard on the road of the Assyrians, because there is the delight of the angels. There are no robbers there, because nothing unclean is in it; no ravines, because nothing in it is hidden, but everything shines with a light seven times brighter. Everything there is gentle.

There is no sickness there, no plague, no poverty or need. Why did such a city displease you, where there is no slanderer and no wicked moneylender? No quarrel of an exactor occurs there, nor does the litigant’s clamor resound, because “peace is in your strength, Lord, and abundance in your towers” (Ps. 121:7). Its streets utter a song of joy, and all its lanes sing alleluia. Why did such a precious homeland displease you?

You descended and fell into the hands of robbers; you lie there. Rise, you who wished to leave without being compelled by any necessity. No one pushed you. Who calls you back except the one who did not push you but receives you? How often, when you saw armed men hiding with swords of malice in the ravine, did you turn your face toward the beautiful summits of those towers, toward the sweet entrances of the gates—and yet you displeased yourself and blamed yourself; and [Col. 0932B] you did not help yourself unless the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, descended.

“Come, come, Lord Jesus of Nazareth. Descend to the one who lies there; console the mourner; refresh the one who sighs. Bow the heavens and descend” (Ps. 143:5). Your dominion is upon your shoulders; let the wounded man be taken up upon your neck; let the one pierced by the sword breathe again upon the wood. You who determined to heal and permitted him to be wounded, and you did not wish him to die completely, so that, while half-alive, he might mourn, recognize his condition through repentance, and not, having died that day, be deprived of tears.

“There is no one, Lord, to come to my aid; there is no one to bring medicine; there is no one to lift the wretched man from the road, except you alone, who are the way, the truth, and the life.” The priest passes by in his appointed order and does not offer his neck to the wretched man. The Levite passes by; he felt compassion and passed on.

But you, who became obedient unto death, death upon a cross, hang upon the wood the wounds of the one who laments. This was done by the one who descended to see the groans of the imprisoned: he stood still, took pity, lifted up the delicate man, and placed the wounded man upon his shoulders. He made himself a beast of burden, like a sheep, becoming like a silent lamb. He placed him upon his own beast, not another’s; he tended him with oil bearing his own name and poured wine from his own blood.

And the merciful Samaritan began to walk with another’s burden, because “he himself bore our infirmities and healed our wounds” (Isa. 53:4). He brought the restored stranger to an inn. He calls the innkeeper, the overseer of his inn, and entrusts to him the deposit he had been carrying. And he says, “Receive my pledge into your care. Guard my deposit. He has just been healed; for a long time he lay there, for a long time he was confined by robbers. Cherish in your heart the man whom I have carried to you upon my shoulders. I hand over the expenses; I commend him to you for healing. Restore the inner being of the hungry man at my expense.”

“Behold,” he said, “you have two denarii.” He did not say gold ones or silver ones, because no metals can be compared with the two Testaments—not gold, nor silver, nor electrum—because they were written by the finger of God and of the Holy Spirit. They are the expenses of our journey. Medicines are supplied to the Lord; two denarii are entrusted. And he says to the innkeeper, “Whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return” (Luke 10:35). What more does one expend who receives what he expends? This is charity, which spends more than is commanded, because “it does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13:5); charity has no limit.

And the innkeeper, spending something beyond what he had received, says, “But concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord; I give advice” (1 Cor. 7:25). Therefore, when the Holy Spirit came, he led the one who lay there into all truth, so that he might receive health from the present physician; and, with the Holy Spirit’s approval, learn chastity; and, returning to the Jerusalem he had abandoned, not leave the city.

## SERMON LXII. On the Only Son of the Widow of Nain

Where heavenly life deigns to enter, death has no power there as an enemy. Christ is our life. Let us all say, “Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Cor. 15:55). Christ by his death saved our death. Let us say again, “Where, O hell, is your victory?” (1 Cor. 15:55).

Behold, our physician enters the gates of the city. Let the widowed mother cease her tears. From where and to where does he come—the one who by his own death gives aid to the dead? From the centurion to the wretched mother, from the servant to the son, from the rich man to the only son. There he is asked to come; here he deigns to come of his own accord.

There was someone to send him, so that the one who was suffering might not perish completely. Here there is only a mother and an only son, with whom her affection alone had departed, while the wretched mother considered and pondered with herself that the time of burial was already approaching, and there was no one to run to the Lord of healing.

“Whom shall I send?” she cried, “and who will go to my Lord? Not a parent, not a relative, not a servant, nor another son. If I let him go, my dead son will accuse me. He knows my funeral, wherever my Lord is. How has the mother remained alone in her very entrails, alone in her grief? Would that the gates of my womb had been closed, so that I had not created one whom I would mourn! Would that he had been formed like an aborted child in the hidden places of my womb, so that he would not have seen the light, from which he would make a double blindness of grief for me! I have neither husband nor son; only my Lord remains to me. I know that he sees the woman who mourns, but if he comes quickly with power, he will destroy the death that is near. For behold, the grave’s pit is ready. Where is my life? Do I suppose that I am burying this man, or shall I hope in my Lord?”

While she weeps and weeps, and her tears are upon her cheeks, and there is no one to console her (Lam. 1:2), behold, the commander of life arrives. He was entering; she was going out. Death and life meet each other. Angels, sympathizing with the mother’s grief, go before them with spiritual service.

Faith cries out through them: “Say to the daughter of Zion, ‘Let the apple of your eye be silent. Behold, your Savior comes, having his reward with him, and his work before his face’” (Isa. 62:11). What is his work? What is the Lord like? “The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the dead are raised” (Matt. 11:5). Behold his work.

What is his coming like? Behold, he comes with his holy companions, his twelve apostles, as a commander—not in a golden chariot to frighten the living, but through the labor of his feet, to raise the dead. [Col. 0933C] He draws near, though he was not far away. He comes to the gate and finds a double misery: an only son and a widow.

He is moved because of the only son, since he too is the only Son. He is moved because of the widowed mother, he who makes the barren woman in the house a rejoicing mother of children (Ps. 112:9). He looks upon the wretched widow following the bed of her funeral, tearing her cheeks and scattering her hair with her hand. She looked only to her son; she had no other to whom she might look. She does not see the Lord, but he himself sees her mourning. He became the spectator of those who mourn, the one who commands the bearers to stop, and the consoler of tears.

He does not first address the mother, nor does he initially pour out words of consolation to her, for he knew that she was overwhelmed by tears. He warns the bearers of the funeral to stand still. “Put down,” he says, “your burden. You too, observe my medicine. The burden will not return to you again. Hell will remain hungry, and the bed will be carried back empty. But you have labored by carrying it too long. The fruit of your labor is sweeter: carry alive to his homeland the one whom you were carrying dead.”

The bearers of the funeral hurry to become spectators of the miracle. They obey the one who commands and attend to their own labor. They set the bier down, stand still, and all raise their eyes toward the Lord. A great theater was formed, a sweet spectacle for angels and human beings. The clamor of tears fell silent; mourning remained with the dead man in the midst of the crowds.

He approaches who never departs, drawing near to the bier. Descending from heaven, he cries out to the dead man, “Young man, I say to you, arise” (Luke 7:14). “To you,” I say, lying beneath death—not to the people perishing beneath the arrogance of life. “Young man, I say, arise.” Let there be no delay—not for your sake, who lie there, but for the sake of your mourning mother.

“Behold, the hour is coming, and now is, when those who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of Man and come forth to life.” Receive hearing; recover your spirit; break the bond of burial; look upon your grieving mother. He called him, raised him, lifted him up, and restored him to his mother, saying, “Receive, mother, your son.” Your dead son [Col. 0934A] will be a pledge of faith, not a fruit of hell.

She receives him as though new—the young man whom she had lost—feeling that she had received a better birth through the Lord’s word than she had received in her mother’s womb. “I give you thanks, Lord. I have received him from you better than I brought him forth from myself. I do not know how I conceived him; I do not know how I gave birth to him, just as I do not know how I received him again. You know how his body was joined together in the womb by your word alone. I did not give the spirit; I did not assemble the bones. You gave him; you took him away; you restored him.”

Piety clung to piety; the new son embraces his mother.

## SERMON LXIII. On the Paralytic

Behold the fountain, dearest brothers, draws near to the pool; healing now hastens to the wretched. Behold the fountain at the pool, so that the pool may receive water from the fountain. It is not the fountain that receives from the pool, because the pool offered healing to one man, whereas the fountain watered the whole earth and offered free medicine to the entire languishing world, excluding no person.

The pool is constructed; the fountain, however, is not fashioned by human hands. The fountain does not receive its beginning from the pool, nor is Christ generated from a human being; rather, he himself regenerates the human race. The fountain does not receive water through a channel, because it directs water itself into its passage: for he was not born through a man and woman, but through the Holy Spirit and the virgin mother.

The pool had a boundary; the fountain has no end. The pool was enclosed by porticoes, but the fountain of life is enclosed neither by heaven nor hidden by earth. It “reaches mightily from one end to the other and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1).

So that the sick man, after many years, might receive healing, the fountain came and filled the pool. Only one received medicine. No one knew from where the fountain flowed. Neither the north nor the south, neither the east nor the west: the hidden fountain made one man well, because “God is known in Judah” (Ps. 75:2).

But when all flesh saw the salvation of God, the world learned that the fountain did not flow from the pool; rather, the pool shone, filled from the fountain, when the fountain stood beside the pool without being asked and healed without the pool.

What were those porticoes like! It is pleasing to look upon the columns, but compassion is moved even more when it looks upon the sick, who were to become columns of the Church when they received healing.

Porphyry columns: human beings who would drink Christ’s blood.

Lacedaemonian columns: the insane who would be freed from the demon, which, with Christ present, no longer had power over human beings.

Parian columns, shining in ordered ranks: lepers and paralytics who would pass through the fountain, so that they might leave behind their diversity and receive unity from the fountain.

Carystian columns: people laboring under punishment but placed under grace, so that, in accordance with the name of the columns, the healing of the sick might be given freely.

There were twisted limbs and lame people. The limbs were healed by their maker, and the paralytic was tormented without his maker. The architect came, and the temple was raised through the stability of its limbs. The architect encountered his own fallen structure beside the pool, which received only a little water.

The fountain stood, filled by nothing but filling everything, because “from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace” (John 1:16). It did not look toward the pool, but asked the sick man, “Do you want,” he said, “to be healed?” (John 5:6).

He answered, “Lord, the length of time bears witness to my desire. After being sick for so long, do I not wish to be well for even one hour? Lord, I have long desired this. Wearied by lying here, I have been carried and borne along, but I have no bearers—not human beings, not even angels. I have no bearers to take me to the pool, and I am badly carried on my bed beneath punishment. I know when the pool is stirred, but I grieve when another gets to the medicine first, and I, weak, return to my bed.

“I raise my head, but still I do not see the Head. In the pool, beneath the splendid light of the smiling waters, their motion trembles, while my mournful senses tremble. I see how another ascends from the pool, radiant, while I descend alive into hell. If you are the one who lives and gives life to the dead, I shall not die, but live, and I shall recount your works” (Ps. 117:17). You did not ask me without reason, unless you came to help me. Let the Lord come to my aid, since a servant has not helped me.”

And the Lord said, “Arise, take up your bed, and go to your house” (John 5:8). He immediately rose from the pool, and through the fountain of grace directed a path of joy toward his own dwelling. He carries the bed of sickness back to his house, so that, without the bed of disease, he might enter the heavenly Church.

The sick man, now well, carries the bed, because the physician of the world bore sin. He carried his own burden upon his shoulders, but the Lamb of God carried another’s burden upon his neck. That bed was the cross. Yet the paralytic’s bed was woven with the garments of sins; the cross had no interweaving of garments, because it had no bonds of sins.

The healed man rejoices, and the Jew begrudges the Christian’s joy in the fountain. “What are you doing?” the Jews cry. “You are carrying your bed on the Sabbath!” O open blasphemy! I would rather carry my bed on the Sabbath than have my bed carry me on the Sabbath. On the Sabbath I had lain there for thirty-eight years; I had no servant to minister to me.

The Lord of the Sabbath came, and I received the Lord’s sacrament. O Jews, if you knew where you lie, you too would carry your pallets on the Sabbath, because the Sabbath did not hinder the Lord, nor did my physician wait for the pool’s assistance.

He abandoned mourning, set down the bed, bade farewell to the pallet, and repaid it its service, lest the ungrateful bed perhaps accuse him. The Lord meets the man carrying the pallet. The one who receives meets his receiver, the healed paralytic. The Savior sees him rejoicing and does not tolerate negligence. “Behold,” he says, “you have been made well” (ibid., 14). Rejoice in health, but be attentive to sickness, so that a second death may not have power over you.

Do not think that I corrected and chastised you for so long without reason. You were guilty, not I; you did not heal yourself, but I did. “See that you do not sin, lest something worse happen to you” (ibid.).

The Lord said this, not the angel, when one descended into the stirred pool and the paralytic sighed. For the angel stirred the water in the pool, and only one was saved. Christ came, did not look at the pool, and the nations flowed in.

Sinners no longer depend upon a single pool, because throughout the whole world infants who were candidates for baptism are reborn. The reception places of the fountain are no longer enclosed by porticoes but surrounded by prophetic and apostolic writings, so that the crowds of thirsty deer may not suffer from the heat. For the fountain itself cries out, “Let the one who thirsts come and drink” (John 7:37).

Nor is it now the time for an angel to stir the water, because the Holy Spirit makes beautiful the fountain of grace, just as it was said, “The Spirit of God was moving over the water” (Gen. 1:2). Then he moved over the water; now he dwells in the earth with sweet rest. His movement is not seen but believed.

It is not only bodies that are saved; souls too are set free.
