All who are baptized are raised on the course toward the kingdoms of heaven, so that, always looking upon the pallet, they may strive to avoid sins of conduct and, without the bed of sickness, live as righteous people for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0935D]

## SERMON LXIV. On the Man Whose Field Produced an Abundant Harvest

You have heard, brothers, how the blessed evangelist today presented us with a parable, saying: “The field of a certain rich man produced abundant crops, and he thought within himself, saying, ‘What shall I do, because I have nowhere to store my crops?’ And he said, ‘This I will do: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will gather my crops; and I will say to my soul, You have many goods stored up for many years. Rejoice and be merry.’ But the Lord said to him, ‘Fool, this night your soul is demanded of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’” (Luke 12:16 ff.).

O blindness of greed, dearest brothers! Only one night remained, and he was laboring over storing things for many years. He rejoiced at how much he saw being born for himself, and he did not know that he would take nothing with him, but would leave everything here. The night denied him life, and he was thinking about tomorrow. What he observed in others, he did not expect for himself. Surely he had seen people possessing things; he had seen them dying. [Col. 0936A] He had seen that no one took the earth with him, but that all were rather consumed and swallowed up by the earth.

How many people now say in this way, “I have this much; I possess this much; I produce this much”? To them one must respond according to the Gospel: “Fool, this night your soul is demanded of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?”

However widely greed may spread its roots, however much it may seize, it must leave everything in a single hour. But you will say, “I have children for whom I labor; I have children for whom I must take the greatest care.” How great a care do you take for your children, so as to overwhelm them with the tears of the wretched? This is not loving children, but rather killing them.

Do you not know that every tree is recognized by its fruit, and that what is hidden in the root is revealed in the branches, and what lies hidden in the leaf shines forth in the fruit? I do not want your children to recognize you as such a father. I do not want you to provide for them in such a way that you become more envious.

O how many are born poor and later become rich! And how many are left a great inheritance and later reduced to poverty! For holy Scripture does not lie when it says, “God makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and exalts” (1 Kings 2:7).

If, then, it belongs to God to make poor and to enrich, why do you act as though you were the prudent provider for your children? Why do you seize whatever you can? You do not know whether it will remain. You nourish perpetual punishment for yourself and leave the greatest grief to your children.

For Scripture says, “He who gathers what belongs to others leaves grief to his children.” And again it says in the Psalms: “Yet man walks about as an image; surely he is troubled in vain. He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers” (Ps. 38:7).

Why do you store up treasure? Why do you hide away talents of gold and silver? Why do you preserve the image of the king engraved on coins, while you despise the image of God the Creator in human beings? Let what belongs to God also belong to God.

Our ancestors therefore abounded in every resource, because they gave tithes to God and paid tribute to Caesar. But now, because devotion to God has departed, Caesar’s levy has increased. For the treasury takes what Christ does not receive. To the barbarians is given what is not distributed to the poor.

You greatly err, greedy man, if you think you are acquiring something in this world. It slips away daily; it fails daily. The world threatens its own ruin and bears witness to its end. And there you delight in remaining; there you continue to build—the place from which the saints desire to depart?

Build what stands, not what falls. Build what remains, not what remains here. Acquire paradise for yourself; acquire heaven for yourself, where you may remain forever. But if you wish to acquire heaven, do what has been commanded.

“Do not spare,” says Solomon—alternatively, “do not obey”—“your treasures.” Alms, however, are to be given according to the measure and quantity of one’s possessions, as it is written: “My son, according as your substance shall be, so give alms from it. If it is abundant, give more from it; but if you have little, share even that little with the poor” (Tob. 4:8–9).

When the equality of the law is observed, human grasping ceases. In the work of almsgiving there is no distinction of persons. The two small coins of that poor widow went before the great offerings of the rich. She who was sustained by the mercy of others practiced mercy herself, and what ought to have been done to her, she herself did even more.

Although all her possessions amounted to two coins, she did not give one and keep the other for herself; rather, she placed everything she possessed into the gifts of God. She is the one who did not think about tomorrow.

And you, brothers, have received the widow’s deed as an example of so great an act. If you cannot give everything, give at least a little from everything. Know this: “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; but he who sows in blessing will reap eternal life from blessing” (2 Cor. 9:16).

## SERMON LXV. On the Woman Who Suffered from an Issue of Blood

Dearest brothers, we understand more fully by believing what we have learned well by reading, because Christ alone applied medicine to human beings, and divine majesty gave him the power. For he does not heal with medicines and the knife; he heals by power and by the word.

Indeed, by his power he healed the woman’s illness, and by his word he raised the centurion’s boy. For twelve years the woman spent her possessions on physicians (Mark 5:25–26), hoping to escape; but if Christ had not come, she would have remained in her condition. Thus the woman had set aside the protection of modesty in order to disclose to human beings the pain of her secret.

The physicians promised health; the woman dissipated her resources. She gave away her possessions, and health withdrew farther. The chief physicians left her begging, though they had not restored her to joy. The woman was now wearied in two ways: she endured poverty and suffering. The physicians of the flesh were unable to restore her by healing; instead, by plundering her, they wished to exhaust her through poverty.

Therefore, burning with want and thinking for a long time about health, she did not lack a counselor: faith, which would drive away her need. “Behold, all my possessions have been dissipated by physicians, and they have not benefited me, because I have not been healed.”

Silent faith found a plan. She sees the physician; she also sees the crowd. Pain compelled her to seek medicine, but modesty prevented her from declaring her condition in the presence of men.

“I will extend my hand,” she said, “and touch the fringe of his garment, and I shall be made well” (ibid., 28). She dared to receive what she had not dared to request.

The disciples and the crowds were standing together, and we likewise heard Christ teaching. Yet those who heard about this event had not been strangers to it. Jesus said, “I perceive that power has gone out from me” (Luke 8:46). And the disciples said, “Lord, the crowds press around you” (ibid., 45).

“Peter,” he said, “I perceive that power has gone out from me. What do you mean, ‘The crowds press around you’?”

The woman, therefore, made healthier by touching the fringe of the garment, feared to conceal the benefit she had received, lest she be condemned because she had not asked. In silence she received what she had silently sought. Touching Christ’s fringe with the tips of her fingers, the woman deserved to be freed, though, consumed by the physicians and their demands, she had been unable to be freed by her entreaties.

Faith provided the woman’s illness with a divine physician, so that he himself would not need to ask the cause, nor would she disclose the secret of her modesty. But when Christ displayed the fruit of faith to everyone, the woman then declared her condition in the presence of men.

Jesus said to her, “Go, daughter; your faith has saved you.” And the woman was made well from that hour (Matt. 9:22).

Entrust the secrets of your conscience to this physician as well, and you will quickly be healed. But if you neglect him, you will be deceived for a long time. He heals everyone without the violence of the knife; he healed the woman without payment. All physicians heal bodies, which are dissolved; Christ, however, heals souls, which never decay.

Indeed, you see him by reading, but you have also seen him by hearing, because he has been revealed to you through believing. The centurion lost his dying servant but was not seized by mental anguish; rather, he sought the master of healing.

“Lord Jesus,” he said, “my boy is now dying, but if you wish, he will quickly be restored to me” (Matt. 8:6). He asked boldly because he knew that Christ could do everything. Or rather, it was not boldness but trust.

Jesus said to him, “Do you believe that I can do this?” And he said, “I believe, Lord” (Matt. 9:28). Then Jesus said to those following him, “Let us go and raise his boy.”

Then the centurion, with an even louder voice, dared to say before the entire people, “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word, and my boy will be healed. For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it” (Matt. 8:8–9).

It was as though he had said to God, “I command soldiers; you command powers.”

The woman’s trust was greater, but the centurion’s faith was praised. And who praised him? The one who healed both the boy and the woman. The evangelist showed us how he praised him: “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel” (ibid., 10).

Faith, then, had not departed from the woman; as the centurion hurried toward Christ, it had gone ahead of him. Thus the centurion came and pleaded even for the boy; faith asked and obtained. Therefore, once again faith went before the centurion toward the gift—not because it had abandoned him, but so that it might reveal the divine gift to many.

It touched the boy’s side, suggesting life to him with joy, and, as though awakened from sleep, restored him to his home in gladness. A great physician, my brothers! It is little that he gave healing to the wound; in addition, he restored the soul to the dead man.

“And he believed,” it says, “and his whole household” (John 4:53). Behold the order in which one believes rightly; in this way one withdraws more effectively from unbelief.

## SERMON LXVI. Also on the Same Subject
The temporary clinic seems to be fixed in place, where medicines of herbs give off their fragrance and instruments enclosed within the roof of the treatment-room gleam. If the physician should happen to be accosted by a sick person in the street, he cannot administer an immediate remedy unless he has brought the necessary instruments with him from the clinic. Christ, however, went forth wholly himself, because he was a physician not by skill but by power, not by expertise but by mercy. The physician walked about carrying his clinic with him—that is, his flesh, which he had mercifully assumed.

O clinic of mercy, purity of flesh from the Virgin’s womb, by which every affliction of the sick world is healed! The father, pleading for his daughter, holds the handles of this medicinal clinic [Col. 0938B] (Luke VIII, 42). Another woman, bashful, strikes one of its handles with a furtive touch (ibid., 43). It is opened to the woman who steals, but delayed for the one who asks. The father, touching the handle, makes a sound through his pleading: the crowd waits, the people follow, heaven is astonished, and death trembles. But the woman, modest in her cause and secure in her faith, touched the handle of the clinic in such a way that the flow of blood stopped before the voice of her confession became known.

The clinic is opened; the sick woman perceives it, but the crowd does not understand. The handle does not sound, and medicine goes forth from the doorway. The Holy Spirit emerges from the temple of majesty; subtle, he makes no noise, yet produces the effect of healing. The physician and creator cries out, “Who touched me?” (ibid., 45)—not so that there might be punishment for the woman who touched him, but so that public praise might be given to the one who had dared. Spiritual faith went before, and the touch produced bodily healing. She too confidently presumes upon him, and he who healed willingly accepted it. For this purpose he descended: to be touched, to be handled. He who touches the mountains and they smoke (Ps. CIII, 32) is touched by a woman and gives life.

For if the little body had not been made by him, he would not willingly accept the touch. And if the structure of the limbs had not been made by him, the woman’s faith would never have reached such a spectacle; heaven would never have opened in order to assemble such a theater. The sick woman struck the clinic—the Lord’s flesh, the fragrant garment. Power went forth, and immediately the flow stopped. And he says, “Woman, your faith has saved you” (Luke VIII, 48).

Here a difficult road, a narrow path crowded by the peoples, but opened by the angels, is made available to the woman. Faith comes forward and cries, “Make way! Let the foster-child of my virtues pass, and let the faithful servant of heavenly payment reach his Lord, who desires by the price of his own blood to condemn punishment.” He himself healed, and he was not ashamed of the touch of his body—he who established the blood of the human body and made the ancient murderer an innocent thief upon the cross.

The Manichaeans and Venustians go before him and are ashamed. [Col. 0938D] They see and say that it is not a human body but a divine work. He himself who heals cries out and says, “Did not the one who made what is within also make what is without?” O shameful argument, but liberating medicine! If the work of human flesh were alien to him, would he have established blood? Would he have proclaimed that power had gone forth from him and driven back tyrannical death?

In the street there is healing; in the house, resurrection. In the street the slayer is confounded, because the blood stopped and the accuser of the blood lay prostrate. Was it not he himself who raised the girl lying on the bed? He enters the house and takes hell captive. He calls the soul back from Tartarus and raises the body from the bed. Why, then, does he command that the girl who has been raised be given food, unless because the bodily limbs were his, and food was necessary for them?

Therefore the ruler’s faith, the woman’s chastity, and the girl restored by food rejoice in the maker of the human body, and the woman is praised together with them, so that heaven and earth may rejoice over the small and the great alike.

[Col. 0939A]

## SERMON LXVII. On the solemnity of the holy apostles

It is delightful to handle the pearls of such great saints; it is delightful to gaze upon the gems of the beloved fishermen. There is no uniformity of color, no sameness of number in virtue; their radiance is varied and their adornment diverse. If a blind person looked upon these stones, he shone forth illumined; if a deaf person wore one, he received clear hearing through the word of the Lord. If a lame man looked upon these stones at the Beautiful Gate (Acts III, 2), he recovered his ability to walk and entered the temple boldly.

Peter is witness, in the case of Tabitha (Acts IX, 40), to the radiance of these pearls, when so great a number of widows exulted. Let each of us, then, contemplate them one by one. Who, in choosing Peter, would reject Paul? Who, seeking Andrew, would despise James and John? There is no difference among the names, because there is one crown of gems, one birthday of the apostles, and one joy of the peoples.

Every shipwreck is removed, and fear of pirates is excluded, because the boats of the beloved fishermen come to our aid. [Col. 0939B] The shores are safe through the apostles’ nets. Peter, at the prow of the heavenly skiff, triumphs on the shore. If you despise Andrew, there is one womb, one service, one innocent catch. Through the fishermen’s fish, poverty was removed; through the souls enclosed in the catch, grace is revealed, and the riches of the kingdom of heaven are made public.

Who counts the fish in Peter’s skiff? Who counts the nations in Paul’s Gospel? The names are different, but the catch is one. Behold James and John: abandoning their father, disregarding their mother, and leaving their net, they followed the most loving Redeemer.

Let such a great banquet therefore take place at the solemnity of the saints. Behold Matthew prepares a meal, and Christ the banqueter enters with a multitude of sinners. The innocent banqueter and the guilty guests: through the fellowship of his banquet he made sinners rejoice in his sacrament. The Jews were saying, “Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?” (Matt. IX, 11). No sinner is separated; no guilty person is excluded. All are Christ’s guests; the banquet is common to all. The solemnity of the apostles prepares a meal of joys: the righteous is fed by grace, and the sinner is restored by pardon.

And although the Jews murmur, the guilty are enriched and made secure: “You have prepared a table before me, against those who afflict me” (Ps. XXII, 5).

That Simon the Cananaean, who changed the name of his nation and grafted his flower onto the crown of virtue, fitted by the Savior’s hands, shines from this crown, adorned with fiery vigor. Judas the Zealot, zealous for the Lord, did not seek profit by selling Christ; he was zealous for him, not bargaining over him.

For there we find a little stone separated by its blackened color: Judas, the Lord’s betrayer, defiling the appearance of the crown through a commercial transaction. O name! He too was called by that name: “With zeal I have been zealous for the Lord almighty” (III Kings XIX, 14). But Judas the betrayer was carrying out cruel agreements: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” (Matt. XXVI, 15). The former was zealous with the Lord’s devotion; the latter is excluded from the mark of the Lord’s banquet. Yet it is more pleasing to look first upon Peter the fisherman, because one shudders to look last upon the betrayer.

He was excluded from the crown; the crown itself must be completed. He who chose ascended; he who betrayed wickedly hung. Who should complete the number in this crown of gems? The judgment of the divine lot is proposed. Christ loves Matthias from heaven (Acts I, 24), who appointed twelve (Luke VIII, 13) in the palace of the open country.

The Holy of Holies is opened; a golden urn is brought forth, truly adorned with heavenly gold. O good lot, which chose a disciple so that the crown of gems might remain complete, because Judas alone hung from the noose!

Behold, the twelfth crown shines painted before your eyes; at its sight your congregation, as though fanned by living sparks [reading uncertain: *visa flata*, perhaps *vivis afflata*], shines forth. Where is that “vessel of election”? Let him complete the crown of piety and the stone of the Gospel that thunders throughout the whole world. Good is the last, whom the first and the last chose. Saul, harsh, became Paul, gentle.

By what goldsmith’s tools was this stone fitted? [Col. 0940A] The foundations of the prison, shaken at night; the prisoners’ bonds, loosed; grace granted to the request; and the apostle’s crown proved it. His feet were in the stocks, and his steps were in heaven. Through the darkness of the prison he sang a new song, so that, as the final string of the thirteen-stringed harp, he might sing eternal joy to you through the apostolic crown of the saints.

## SERMON LXVIII. On the martyrs

It is delightful to see fields of grain with golden ears ripened on their stalks; more delightful still to contemplate the fields of the Church, their martyr-plants sparkling through the one blood of the innocent Lamb.

For the sufferings of the martyrs are crops “beside streams of water” (Ps. I, 3), watered by fountains of tears. Thus blessed David now sang of the purple shoots of the martyrs, as though he were a reaper and, before the harvesters of joy, were sounding his reaping lyre: “Those who sow in tears,” he says, “shall reap in joy” (Ps. CXXV, 5).

Where do they sow in tears, if not beside the tree of the cross, where the Savior’s fountain is near? From there drops of blood dripped from his side, and a rain of blood and water was sown as the endurance of the confessors. From that wood of the living cross, beside the fountain of blood, virginity planted there flourished in chastity. From there the planted endurance of the martyrs began to gather the purple shoots of its seed.

For from where do martyrs endure, if not through the Lord’s cross? From where come the martyrs, in whose hearts is the law of God, who do not fear the curses of men, except because Christ the Lord patiently endured the insults of the Jews? From where did martyrs delight to enter prison custody, except because the Lord was led to the praetorium of the chief Caiaphas and did not disdain to endure the cruel prison of the night? Yet he said, “I was handed over, and I did not go out” (Ps. LXXXI, 9).

From where did martyrs care nothing for chains and iron bonds, except because Christ the Lord allowed himself to be held and bound by the Jews, since, already buried among the dead, he broke the chains of death [Col. 0940C], and said to those who are in bonds, “Come out,” and to those who are in darkness, “See the light” (Isa. XLIX, 9)? And after Lazarus had been buried for four days, he said to him, “Come outside” (John XI, 43). The one who had been handed over did not go outside because he was free within and without.

From where did martyrs not dread blows upon the face, except because Christ offered his cheeks to the blows of the impious? From where did the martyrs remain unharmed by the sharp violence of vinegar or mustard poured upon them, except because Christ’s lips tasted vinegar and gall—lips not worthy of such a drink from impious cupbearers—he who struck the rock and waters flowed, and gave them drink as from a great abyss (Ps. LXXVII, 15)?

From where did martyrs endure being stripped naked, and not weep when scourged, except because the Lord was stripped and scourged, and girded before Pilate the judge, whom he himself will come to judge? From where, when placed upon the rack and furrowed with hooks, did they make the ordeal seem sweet through their most delightful songs, causing shame to their torturers, except because Christ the Lord ascended the cross, did not accuse his enemies, did not weep over his injury, but sought forgiveness for his enemies, singing in pious song upon the wood, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34)?

This sowing of Christ’s blood therefore caused the seeds of the martyrs to sprout in the field of Mother Church, as David says: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy.” Going, they went; they wept, and did not stop, but went weeping and journeyed toward their eternal homeland. The city prolonged their journey, and they wept so that they might reach the place they desired.

Thus they went forth. How do they return? Not weeping, but rejoicing; not still sowing, but carrying their sheaves upon their joyful necks. They will come, not with their heads covered by a cloak or veil because of the heat, but with light upon their heads and precious joy. “Coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. CXXV, 6), which they sowed beside the Lord’s cross and harvested more happily from his resurrection. They met him in the clouds, offering him their shoots and receiving eternal things.

O shoots [Col. 0941A] that flame cannot scorch! They are beside the glassy river in Jerusalem, and forever remain green with the flower of immortal, eternal life. They do not know how to wither, because they did not fear to burn in flames for righteousness. For the Lamb will lead them to the fountains of the waters of life, and will wipe away every tear from their eyes (Rev. VII, 17), and they will flower like lilies in the midst of the angels.

## SERMON LXIX. On the birthday of the holy Maccabees

Boötes sparkles in heaven, shining brightly through its cluster of stars; but today the Church shines more brilliantly with the mother through the seven stars of her sons (II Macc. VII). Here there is not one star great in splendor and another faint in light; all shine with brotherly love because they surround the Savior’s cluster upon the cross.

Here no star of the beloved brothers changes its station into something faint, like a torch vanishing when its radiance is extinguished. All preserve a united confession, so that they may not abandon their brotherly love. Brothers from the womb, brothers in martyrdom, blood brothers rejoiced in heaven.

What is it like to see the blessed mother who, though barren, gave birth to seven, and departed for the city of Jerusalem with the seven spiritual stars crowning her head? What shall we say? Seven angels rejoice with us in the precious fellowship of the solemnity. The Son of Man walks and moves in the midst of seven golden lampstands (Rev. I, 13), in the midst of the blessed martyrs, while the mother sings a hymn with the legions of angels.

There is no foreign wall among the seven; there is no silver lampstand there; there is no lampstand mixed with the lead of sin. All the lampstands are golden, melted in the furnace of passion. Always burning and shining before the throne, the heavenly Church and that blessed mother rejoice.

O truly golden womb, praised by the angelic host! Blessed David says to her, in the pleasant sweetness of the spiritual lyre, while the mother watches among burning cauldrons: “He makes the barren woman rejoice in her house as the mother of children” (Ps. CXII, 9). “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked.”

O devotion of the mother’s milk, in which brotherly kinship was not divided! The eagle rejoices in its lofty little nest among mountains and rocks over the offspring of its dear young. It nourishes them like an eagle and remains as a widow when the fledglings fly off toward corpses.

This eagle, whose flesh covered her young with the shelter of her wings and placed them upon her shoulders through the speech of good persuasion, flew with her young into the field and rejoiced with them in heaven among the meadows of paradise. None of these fledglings, beneath their mother’s wings, sought the corpses of the dead, because they all contained the Holy Spirit within themselves. All were spiritual doves, knowing nothing of brooding over corpses.

The tyrant wished to make even one of them a raven that did not know how to return to the ark, and all the doves with silvered wings groaned heavily, because they did not seek a corpse like ravens. Instead, with their mother the dove, they carried purple branches in their scarlet mouths to the Lord.

What were these corpses that they rejected for the sake of the temporal reward proposed to the eaglets of this eagle? They were unclean meats, polluted altars, and defiled vessels. But they were golden vessels, tested in the furnace, shining seven times over in the furnace.

“Eat,” he said, “of the flesh of your sacrifices.” And they replied, “We are clean birds, not unclean. We have the heavenly meadows of sweetness; we do not want the rotten flesh of the tempter. Food from corpses does not suit doves, but the chaste shoots of meadow fields.”

The tyrant grows angry, while the mother’s affection rejoices. He cuts off a hand with an axe, and they raise their minds upon the cross. A tongue is cut out, and fraternal instruments resound, which the mother-teacher had touched. The brothers burned with the Spirit, while the boiling cauldrons cooled; the frying pans blazed, and the sweet brothers’ unleavened breads were baked.

The skin was stripped from the head, and crowns were prepared for the head. Blessed, they went forth bald; crowned, they returned. But the fowler of temptation wished to snare these most chaste offspring with the traps of everlasting death. [Col. 0942A] Yet one of them runs back to his mother and seeks the sweet nest again.

He speaks to his mother in the Lord, and the mother receives the remaining one beneath the sweet shelter of her wings—the seventh, still tender and immature in bodily strength. She bares her breasts and shows her beloved son his nourishment.

“My son,” she says, “do not defile my crown, and do not violate brotherly harmony. Christ wove my crown; let the enemy not unravel it. Little children, my son, usually make themselves a red crown from flowers and crown their innocent heads with yellow marigolds. If a petal should fall because the hand of another child struck it, how the child’s devoted soul is twisted! How much more so for me, who have not field flowers, but hold spiritual flowers? I do not want, I do not want, my son, to defile my crown by removing a single gem. There will be two evils: Gehenna will swallow you, and I shall not be fully crowned.”

The mother joined a precious stone to the gems through her words and made a sevenfold garland, which the whole host of angels carried with her to heaven. Who is sufficient to praise this mother? The womb itself bears witness, for there was never a womb like that of this Maccabean mother.

O mother of the sons of Zebedee (Matt. XX, 20), she offered James and John to Christ as disciples; but the Church’s seven martyrs came forth from one womb. The good mother promised her fledglings and flew like an eagle. Let our congregation rejoice over the mother and her sons.

## SERMON LXX. On Job and blessed Perpetua

One who wishes to rejoice in triumph ought not to fear in combat, nor should one who wishes to gain everlasting victory fear a temporal struggle. Let him not despise exile who desires heaven. Let him regard prisons as praetoriums who desires the joy of paradise.

Blessed Perpetua, sent into prison and confined by darkness, was enlarged by the light. Because she ventured forward, she changed the prison, dispelled the darkness, and, innocent, triumphed not in a prison but in a royal court.

For all the holy martyrs were bound with chains, and they themselves inserted their hands into the bonds of love toward heaven. They were amid darkness, yet the joys of light flashed forth. The blessed endured squalor and stench together through strong patience, because “blessed are those who suffer persecution, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 10).

We shall act appropriately and rightly if, by the examples of the martyrs, we come to blessed Job (Job ch. II), because almighty God praised and honored him as a martyr. He was amid squalor; dung stank, but heaven burned within his heart. Through opened doors and heavenly gates he received the fragrance of sweetness: patience, endurance, and love.

The one who tested him himself helped him; the one who had handed him over himself delighted him, pointing out to him, as it were with the finger of love, the treasures of the heavenly kingdom. The righteous saw what he loved and despised various losses, because he always counted them as nothing.

“What are you doing, enemy? You take away gold—but do you take away the Lord? You take away silver—but do you cut heaven from my eyes? I know the court of my Lord, the retreats of my Creator. How broad there is the expanse of riches! How many the treasures of joys in which the present orders of angels delight through their daily allotment!

“You have taken from me thousands of bulls, herds of goats, and the flesh of lambs. I have a greater and purer sacrifice with which to please my Lord, who will not eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats, but I sacrifice to him a sacrifice of praise (Ps. XLIX, 13–14), because he himself has established for me an altar of love, and he himself is my priest of devotion.

“I see his altar and do not shudder at a heap of dung. Do you not know, enemy, that my Lord raises the poor from the earth and lifts the needy from the dungheap, to seat him with princes (Ps. CXII, 7–8)? You have seated me among worms in this way; he will seat me upon the tribunal of honor.

“I shall not fear the pus flowing from my wound. You touch my flesh; he guards my soul. For me the royal court of the King is a heap of dung upon the streets of the most beautiful city. You apply dung, and I do not wither. He supplies fountains, and I flower.”

Thus the righteous spoke through lips of patience, by the strength of combat, and through love of the crown. Ashes caused his wounds to fester, and patience destined for a crown blossomed forth. The one who crowned patience was present, because the combatant had fought lawfully.

What was the battlefield? Nothing but a heap of dung. There were the army lines of the tempting fallen angel, false friends, a deceitful wife, and flattering deception; worms and wounds, pus and decay, dung and bitterness. They were not divided by nightly rest, nor was the struggle lulled when the days arose and the battle became clear.

Victory and life were hidden, because, he says, “your life is hidden with Christ. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. III, 3–4). Behold, what was hidden is revealed. Behold, the crown, once concealed, has blossomed forth from the heap of dung now exposed, because patience had reached maturity.

The one who prepared the crown was present; he tested and praised him. He did not disdain to remain upon the heap of dung and show the crown to the victor—the one who, in the paradise of delights, sat to pronounce judgment upon the first cultivators, and did not let the place prejudice the purity of the devotion.

Therefore God the one who crowns was present: he restores, praises, and multiplies. He speaks from the cloud of the whirlwind (Job XXXVIII, 1; XL, 1), so that he might water the victor with rains of honor. He wiped him, cleansed him, and likewise adorned him.

He who made the victor flourish also appointed him priest, so that he might admonish his enemies to become friends, and so that the righteous victor might slaughter a victim on his behalf (Job XLII, 8). With his wound changed and his appearance renewed, he stood in splendor at the altar—the one who had sat putrid in dung. For he had already been a priest in his struggle, had offered a sacrifice from his victory, had earned a crown for himself, and had sought pardon for his friends.

Behold how great is the good of enduring an inflicted temptation, so that through Christ we may deserve to be tested. To him we say, “Do not allow us to be led into temptation” (Matt. VI, 13). He himself will deign to rescue us from present scourges and make us rejoice through the renewed grace of freedom. To him we must always proclaim our thanks.

Let us turn to the Lord almighty and everlasting Savior.

[Col. 0943C]

## SERMON LXXI. Also on Job

Whoever is God’s friend is the devil’s enemy. The transgressor against righteousness hates devotion to divine worship. He tries to bind the person whom he finds righteous, so as to make him his slave. He stretches out and prepares a manifold line, so that he may seize and bind the soldier of God at the same time. He desires to make captive the one whom he finds made fruitful by God’s joy. For he does not wish to see the form of the divine image.

The illustrious patriarch Job, a citizen of the East, noble in righteousness, fortunate in nobility, exceedingly rich in abundance, extremely wealthy in property, and exalted in the height of humility—him the swelling of pride had never lifted into a fall, because he possessed strength through humility alone.

The enemy, inflamed against him for his destruction and drawing near to royal thrones, extorted by deceitful subtlety the power to harm the divine majesty. Therefore the Lord, foreseeing the enemy’s design, praised the worship of his majesty in his own voice, saying, “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a blameless man, a true worshiper of God?” (Job I, 8).

Behold what confusion there was for the enemy who was plotting, when the support of majesty went before him. As I suppose, he already stood guilty—the one who vehemently desired to make another guilty. Behold, the Lord praised the innocent and exposed the pious robber.

Power therefore having been granted from heaven, he went forth into the world and violently extorted Job’s possessions through various blows, rages, and savage fury. He himself had been the author of the crime. He himself was also the messenger, as though fallen away from the spoils, deceiving and reporting them. He said, “I alone escaped, and I have come to tell you” (Job I, 15, 17, 19). He reported the events to the patriarch’s ears and recounted the cruel losses.

The devil reported, but the patriarch praised the Lord. Amid the enemy’s frenzy, no impatience disturbed his faith. In devotion he stood firm against the losses with the shield of endurance through unconquerable strength. He remained strong, established within the bounds of righteousness on a tenacious foundation, supported by deep roots and fortified; in his breast glory alone was at war.

Then, when everything had been taken away, a sudden onslaught overwhelmed him, and one death seized them all. Then, mingled with grief, he tore the hair from his head, prostrated himself upon the ground, and burst forth in praise with these words: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (ibid., 22).

Within, dangerous fury raged; amid the blows, faith remained unharmed. Patience did not yield to any blow or withdraw before any tongue’s assault. Losses did not turn aside the stout soldier, nor did the greatest grief over his children. In losing everything he lost nothing, because the devil did not separate him from the Lord. He lost little and gained much.

The enemy therefore saw himself defeated around the stout soldier by the heavenly army. Then the enemy again approached heaven and the cherubim, received power, and returned to engage one fit for combat, though not to conquer him. He thought that the man who could not be overcome by the loss of possessions might perhaps be defeated by the pain of wounds.

Then the most savage dragon spewed the poisonous virus of his entire ferocity upon the patriarch’s limbs and turned his whole body into a wound. No limb remained that the plague had not seized with the spray of wounds. He had wounded his limbs so severely that the bones remained stripped of flesh—except, of course, for the precious soul, which was not wounded.

For patience was surrounded by a wall and enclosed within the chamber of prison-like danger. It slaughtered dangers, crushed the warrior peacefully, and killed the robber without iron. Then pus streamed forth, and horrible beasts burst from the recesses of the ulcers, which he patiently drove back without pain. Armies of worms pierced the flesh with the savage wedges of their legions.

In the body of the innocent there were the accoutrements of battle between the enemy and the righteous, between the foe and the innocent, and between the devourer of the inward parts, the worms, and the flesh.

O steadfast vigor of the warfare of the flesh! Though suffering, it endures against the devil’s poisonous powers. Yet the victor never shudders at the endurance of the flesh; he flees the proximity of putrefying wounds; he despises the kinship of brothers and the consolation of his wife; he is avoided by God’s servants; and he is willingly regarded by God alone.

For whoever has been humbled for God’s sake, almighty God must look upon him. “Upon whom shall I look,” he says, “if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 2).

O patience, mother of victory! Endurance acquired a palm-bearing life when the devil’s power had been defeated. Yet the one whom the Lord had praised before the victory could not be conquered. It was not the one who fought who was defeated; the one who struck was defeated. Job conquered by being beaten, while the devil grew exhausted by striking. He saw himself weary because of the weary man, and fatigued because of the fatigued man. The devil withdrew in grief, while the patriarch was found strong.

When his bodily health was restored, he received what he had lost. Everything he had lost was doubled. O loss that produces profit! Service is never dismissed without a gift. The patriarch rejoiced most joyfully, and the devil fell, defeated and mournful.

[Col. 0944D]
