This sermon was printed above, beginning, “Yet the illustrious birthday of the martyr,” and so forth.

## SERMON LXXIII. On Saint Vincent

This sermon too is read above, among the sermons that we judged to be by Fulgentius, beginning, “I wonder, brothers, whether anything still remains,” and so forth.

## SERMON LXXIV. On Goliath

The reading that has now been recited from the Book of Kingdoms (I Kings XVII, 1 and following) undoubtedly remains fixed in the understanding of your charity. It concerns Goliath and David, a most holy man, most devout, pleasing to God, and, to say more, a forefather of Christ, in whom righteousness, truth, piety, and the love of Christ shone forth most conspicuously.

When he was challenged to battle against his adversaries, he raised his eyes toward heaven. He did not presume upon his own strength; rather, confident in his innocence and in Christ’s righteousness, he humbly cried:

“God, attend to my help. Lord, hasten to assist me. Let my enemies be confounded and put to shame, who seek my soul in order to take it away. Let them be turned backward and confounded who seek evil for me” (Ps. LXIX, 2 and following).

And after he had won the victory:

“Who is God besides our God? God who girded me with strength for battle and overthrew all my enemies” (Ps. XVII, 32–33).

And again:

“All the nations surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance upon them” (Ps. CXVII, 10).

You see, my brothers, how innocence of purity is always greater than the malicious strength of power, because “wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul” (Wis. I, 4). For “from the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Ps. VIII, 3); they produced greater glory than warrior boys.

How great was the difference between Goliath and blessed David? The former was a young man; the latter a little child. The former was a warrior; the latter a shepherd of sheep. The former stretched a bow; the latter prepared a shepherd’s pouch (*saxiperium*)—simple in feeling but heavenly in understanding—one of those children who praised the Lord with the instrument of piety. Of them he himself said, “Praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXII, 1).

He was a shepherd and fed sheep, but God, who feeds Israel, helped the little one. For his innocent armor-bearer, God himself fought as companion and commander. David carried a shepherd’s pouch (*saxiperium*), in which he bore the mysteries of curdled milk. There he also carried five stones, so that through the milk and the stone he might display the Old and New Testament. The little one carried milk for little ones, and in the five stones he carefully carried the five books of the Law. By these means he overcame the enemy, not by fighting but by rejoicing.

The enemy saw and mocked. But the most holy David saw and lifted his eyes toward heaven. The former cursed; the latter prayed. The former presumed upon his own strength, while the latter grieved for Israel, on whose behalf the Lord compelled him to fight. The former poised a hundredweight; the latter set in motion the hand that whirled the sling. The former presumed upon himself; the latter asked for an angel as his helper.

The stone was directed by the boy and carried through the air by the angel. The enemy stood secure against the little warrior, unaware of the Lord’s help from above. The enemy immediately felt the stone upon his forehead, because he did not possess the Lord’s mark. There he lost his life with shame, where David had perceived the angel as his helper.

He fell with a great collapse, the one who had insulted with great pride, because “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6); he gives victory and prepares a crown.

David ran ahead, taking joy before the battle began; he was joyful over victory before he had completed the fight. He stood over the lifeless corpse of the fallen man, drew out the sword, struck him with it, cut off the enemy’s head, and triumphed with his right hand raised. Leaping for joy, he began to cry out:

“Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and makes my fingers ready for war” (Ps. CXLIII, 1).

He restored the stone to its companion and set down the severed head, the head of his joy.

For David, sent against Goliath, signified nothing other than Christ against the devil for the salvation of the human race. In him was fulfilled:

“Sinners have unsheathed the sword and bent their bow, to deceive the poor and needy and slaughter the upright in heart; their sword shall enter their own hearts” (Ps. XXXVI, 14).

Behold how much gentle innocence avails with God, rather than the lofty power of evil will: because the Lord loves innocence and abandons wickedness, so that the righteous may obtain the victory owed to his innocence and receive a gratuitous crown from heaven.

## SERMON LXXV. On Absalom
Usually nature provides faithfulness, and kinship creates affection. Parents take delight in children being born, in their growth increasing their joy, in the labor of their anxieties ending when their offspring reach maturity, and in fatherhood being relieved by the succession of children. But in Absalom, David’s son, a new overthrow of wickedness arose: it grew not through assistance, but through the devastation of his own kindred. The mind shudders to recount the history of his monstrous cruelty, lest fathers regret having begotten children. The sacred name does not recall him; the care bestowed in rearing him does not come to mind; and for so great a gift he learned to persecute his parent. Desire broke faith, and avarice overcame affection.

What an outrage! With impious hand a son strikes the man from whom the father had hoped to receive comfort. When his mother’s womb had poured him forth into the light of life, the father, unaware of what was to come, rejoiced at the first beginnings of so promising a youth, thinking that he had received rest in his son. He was eager to watch over him more carefully and to raise him with the greatest concern, intending later to count this affection to his credit. He loved him, cherished him, and watched over him; thinking he had begotten a son, the pious father embraced the future parricide. The devout father kissed the sacrilegious one, and, ignorant of the disasters to come, rejoiced in him daily.

For when this boy had advanced from childhood into manhood, he displayed brutality before filial obedience. To recall the beginnings of this most savage man, I shall not pass over the bereavement caused by his brother’s death. When he demanded vengeance for his violated sister, he made his way to his father through the murder of his brother (II Kings 13:26 ff.). It is worse to find a remedy for such cunning than to commit the sacrilege of the crime itself: thus, for an impious war, he sought the aid of peace.

He prepared a banquet, summoned his brothers, and summoned the incestuous offender. He composed his expression, lest his color betray his anger; he even set royal delicacies before the mourning man. And, lest the young man be delayed long in carrying out what he had begun, he showed the enemy still greater attentiveness. He moved through the rooms of the house, calm in a feigned peace, bringing forth the moment of crime. When he saw him already made ready by much wine amid cups and goblets, he offered both wine and the sword.

And what kind of banquet was it, where anger supplied the service and grief prepared the meal? I do not know what spirit he bore who so flattered in order to strike, or so served in order to kill. After this, therefore, through an impious peace and the sacrilegious vengeance of an executioner, he attempted to destroy the innocent man—and, shameful to say, his father.

Happy and blessed would the life of mortals have been if desire and jealousy did not exist! O roots of crimes and material of vices, by which fear is neither quieted nor the multitude of crimes satisfied; and from the very point at which they seem to be restrained, they are stirred up in far greater number! For behold, Absalom, glutted with the murder of his brother and drunk with kindred blood, is stirred more and more toward evil, as though he became hungry from that very satiety. He declares war on his father—now no longer a son—as though it had been too little to kill his brother. He brought destruction to those whom he ought to have helped. Who could have been dearer to one who hated his nearest relatives so greatly? Or what faith did he possess who committed such crimes against his own people? He revealed to the ages a new kind of madness, exercising more than anger had dictated.

Suddenly they proclaim the war with the trumpet’s cry. The sacrilegious rush forward; parricides march; affection is turned into fury. The outrage was brought to the father, but anger did not destroy his paternal devotion. The father orders his allies to go out to battle and begs that severity not break their loyalty. Those whom he was accustomed to encourage greatly, he restrained by his prayers from attacking the monstrous enemy, his son.

“Go,” he said, “my commanders; go quickly, sons of valor—but beware, I beg you, lest you conquer. Calm the madness of righteous fury, lest in the death of my son you wound me, miserable as I am. If he himself refused to have a father, his father nevertheless deserved bereavement. Spare, therefore, spare my child; spare, fellow soldiers, the madman. And if I have begotten a bad son, I still watch over him all the more, so that affection may overcome anger and justice may not carry out an outrage.

“I renounce the prize of this contest. I do not want—I do not want victory accompanied by grief. If the madness of a perverse mind made him what he is, will not your vengeance make you parricides? Restrain your grief; forbid punishment. The injury you inflict is mine, and you grant it to me. The most devoted father preferred to be defeated rather than deprived of triumphs. He commends his enemy to his commanders and, lest he lose his son, asks that the enemy be preserved.”

But when the battlefield received both armies, the father, bereaved yet faithful to his sacred duty, conquered.

What place did the battle occupy in the divine outcome, so that neither father became impious nor son escaped guilt? War thundered with savage blasts, bringing forth a rain of tears. Kindred battle lines stood with right hands brandished, demanding license for crimes. Suddenly the shrill standards of the commander cry out [the reading is uncertain]; the trumpets are shattered; voices form the ranks; the armies carry out slaughter, and there are no enemies.

O most accursed battle, in which wars are waged without enemies! O unjust contest, in which neither victory follows nor triumph! Brothers arm themselves against brothers. For the defeated and the victors there is one mourning. Affection wept, and nature lamented the loss inflicted upon it by the fury of one man. Love was divided by the sword; devotion was nowhere. Desire drove some, injury drove others.

From one side the clamor of weapons thundered; from the other, wounds flew on feathered arrows. From one side hail hastened along the ground; against the others, leaden missiles sped through the air. The former were crushed by whirling stones; thus, in nearly a thousand ways, one death overwhelmed almost everyone. And the one who ought to have rejoiced in brotherly harmony offered himself the bond of death because of one man’s crime.

The clear sky rained wounds, darkened by the density of the heavens. The night of the crime stood in the air amid weapons; in the darkness it gleamed, thrust forth [the text is uncertain]. War rejoiced in its functions, woven into a seething cloud. O how accursed were the clouds whose iron rain poured down wounds! Streams ran in channels of blood, and the fields drank gore from the gushing veins of corpses; neither affection nor shame was spared.

Rage grows amid crimes, and from the very things by which strength is usually weakened, its power increases through calamities. The sword rages against kindred, and cruelty knows no limit. Where are you now, affection? Where is faith, if enemies are brothers?

But after the battle’s dreadful disasters and fatal shipwrecks, how wonderfully vengeance came upon the criminal! For when Absalom was carried upon a mule through the battle (II Kings 18:9), the sight of the slaughter tore the rider from the war, as though the outrage itself seemed to recoil in horror. He fled swiftly through the secluded places of the neighboring forest, destined to destroy the author of his crimes. And while, among the very thickets of the trees, the scorned animal rushed on unheeding, a trunk transfixed the young man who was to die, leaving him suspended from the tree’s scaffold by no human hand.

Without a battle, the enemy received his wound, taken captive by his own treachery; the sacrilegious man preferred to die rather than reign with his father. For God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6). For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11).

## SERMON LXXVI. On Isaiah

God speaks through Isaiah, saying: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me, and my people have not understood me” (Isaiah 1:3).

The ox recognizes its owner, while the owner despises the Lord. The Lord’s donkey watches over its manger, while man corrupts the divine commands. Learn, therefore, you who despise, an example from mute beasts, you who do not fear divine judgment. Be toward the Lord such as you recognize the beasts to be toward you. Be instructed by the example of animals: nature equipped you for obedience, and the Lord subjected you to service.

And yet, although animals lack reason, in this respect they cannot be without reason. But you, human being, though ordered with reason, offend your Creator by living without reason. Let human faithlessness blush; let human folly be confounded. Beasts, therefore, preserve obedience to human beings through divine instinct, while human beings, with obstinate minds, avoid God’s commands. Animals serve the rational human being, while human beings irrationally despise God. The beasts to whom God the Creator denied reason strive not without reason to obey man. Human beings, however, who excel in reason, persist in folly by refusing to worship God. Oxen receive the human God, and human beings reject the divine rule.

By whose judgment beasts diligently serve human beings, by that same judgment human beings abandon and despise God’s commands. What great evil is this madness, which could not even be equaled by beasts, since it cannot compare with mute animals in obedience to the Lord? For beasts, while serving man, are known to serve God; human beings, while neglecting God, show that they hate themselves.

Therefore, if beasts had received reason, they would both worship and fear God rationally. Yet now, without reason, they are what human beings with reason cannot be. You are judged, human being; you are judged by the example of an animal; you are condemned by the obedience of cattle. Nor can an excuse benefit you, since you desire to obey neither divine authority nor the example of the beasts.

For divine service is great, and it is the good economy of life: here punishments for evil deeds are not feared, but divine rewards for good merits are awaited. God desires that those whom he rewards should be good, rather than that those whom he condemns should be wicked without sorrow. For he now punishes unwillingly those whom he would rather reward, if they wished to escape through a good life.

Flee sins, Christian, if you desire to win God’s favor; hate offenses, if you long to please him. The devastation caused by sins must be feared as poison. The destruction caused by crimes must be avoided as a weapon and sword. Let no offense be loved which has destroyed the human race. Let sin be fled, since it has always prepared ruin for humanity. What appears to others to have brought destruction must be dreadful to God’s servant; and where you see another has perished, there you must take greater precautions yourself.

Let no one promise himself immunity because many are sinning. Let no one, while transgressing with the crowds, claim to be free from danger. Adam did not fall into death merely because he sinned alone with his wife, nor did Cain deserve destruction merely because he alone committed fratricide. God loves a few innocent people more than countless sinners. In one righteous person he rejoices and is glad over what makes him sorrowful and mournful in many sinners.

Therefore, when the Lord judged the world by the flood, he alone saved Noah with his household (Genesis 7:1); and when he destroyed Sodom with a rain of fire, he preserved Lot alone with his children (Genesis 19:12). The people of Nineveh too would have been destroyed for their crimes unless their repentance had tempered the Lord’s anger (Jonah 3:5). For the Lord himself loves this even when he threatens: he threatens those whom he desires to restrain from offenses with the severity of judgment.

God rebukes in order to save, chastises in order to correct, and reproaches in order to reform. For some people, whose condition is desperate, say: “In his mercy God will not desire the destruction of so great a multitude, nor will he allow the peoples whom he did not wish to be captives but redeemed to perish. Otherwise he will seem to have redeemed them for this purpose: that someone might be condemned by his judgment. Either he redeemed them in order to save them, or he would not have redeemed those whom he later destined for judgment.”

This pernicious persuasion must be avoided entirely. For just as these people are entangled in crimes, so they wish to involve others in their own crimes; and while, by refusing to seek pardon, they promise themselves indulgence while sinning, they entangle the wretched in the same persuasion.

But the Lord Christ has already given us, the redeemed, forgiveness; he has already washed and cleansed the defiled and polluted, and corrected them. Therefore the redeemed may no longer sin, and the cleansed may no longer become defiled. “Behold,” he says, “you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14).

He who made you whole imposed upon you a rule for living; he who cleansed you from defilement did not wish you to become defiled again. If you have consented to God the Father, observe the Father’s admonitions. If you profess yourself Christ’s servant, demonstrate Christ’s commands in your deeds. The promises made concerning anything are shown more by conduct than by a name.

A man cannot prove himself a physician if he could not cure the sick; he is not a pilot who cannot steer a ship; he cannot be a philosopher who practices vices rather than virtues. Thus, too, he cannot be a Christian who has disgraced what he professes.

Therefore, either do what is commanded if you wish to receive what is promised; or, if you do not do what is commanded, you will receive what is destined for sinners. For if punishments for offenses are not repaid to sinners, neither will the merits of righteousness be rewarded to the righteous. But the merits of righteousness must necessarily be repaid to the righteous, and the punishments destined for sinners must necessarily be imposed.

Let no one deceive himself; let no one cheat himself. Whoever despises heavenly commands cannot remain unpunished. “If you wish to enter into life,” he says, “keep the commandments” (Matthew 19:17). The contrary is understood: “If you despise the divine commandments, you cannot remain unpunished.”

No one despises the commands of the world without penalty. Unless someone appeases his father’s anger, he will be disowned; and we do not allow contempt shown to servants to go unavenged. Therefore, since you do not patiently tolerate contempt from a human being, how do you think that, when you sin, God can be appeased toward you?

So cease sinning, if you wish to obtain pardon for the past; or, if you think you must continue to sin, you will necessarily be subjected to divine judgment. Therefore, while it is permitted, while there is time, while repentance is allowed, while the one who has sinned can still reject his own sins, let past offenses be repaired by a holy life.

Let us not postpone this until tomorrow, since we do not know whether we shall see tomorrow. This delay has killed many: once unexpectedly taken away, it did not restore them to eternal life but rather handed them over to everlasting death.

As grievously as we have sinned, so humbly let us beseech the Lord. Let the vice contracted in the world be left here in the world. The offense of the indignant Lord; the patience of the Lord, which has preserved us for repentance and correction. The garment stained through the sin of the first man must now be carefully cleansed anew by us through faith in Christ, so that we may happily be admitted to the wedding feast in the shining garment of the bridegroom.

Let these things be fulfilled by us; let these things be accomplished by all. Let man not be summoned to the example of beasts, but rather follow the deeds and merits of the saints, so that we may not perish after death in the manner of beasts, but may be pardoned through divine gifts for everlasting ages.

## SERMON LXXVII. On the Trouble Caused by the Tongue

The most wise Solomon spoke thus: “Life and death are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 18:21).

The tongue is the key of the breast, the testimony of the heart. Within the court of its mouth it presides over a great tribunal, either of gracious salvation or of bitter death. By denying God, it commits sacrilege in a single word; or, by one utterance, it completes martyrdom with courage.

Who can explain the riches of the tongue? Through it, if a person remains silent, there is a funeral; but when it speaks eloquently, it produces dignity for a human being; when it runs benevolently, it secures salvation. It acquires friends and restrains enemies. It is the coloring of bodies and the health of souls. It directs every work and completes actions; by the command of its mouth it filled seas and lands.

Every deed ceases where the authority of speech is absent. You spend a word and receive a benefit. You ask on earth and are heard in heaven, as the Lord says through the prophet: “Who cried out to me and was not heard?”

Behold, the twenty-four elders pray before God, saying: “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Revelation 4:8). They have no bodily members, yet a tongue speaks. The martyrs suffer, and even after burial they live through their own words, saying: “How long, holy and true Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” (Revelation 6:10).

Speech alone has no end, because it has no blood. The clouds themselves speak when the eloquence of majesty resounds. The dense air in the clouds tells its tale, as John testifies in the Apocalypse, saying: “Do not write what the seven thunders have spoken” (Revelation 10:4).

Why is the apostle forbidden to record the language of heaven? So that the voice which made the world tremble might not appear commonplace. If it were contained within human articulations, or if man had nothing to behold when he recognized what he hoped for, the fire would not burn in the bush. And the flame received a tongue, saying to Moses: “Do not come nearer. Remove the strap of your sandals. The ground on which you stand is holy” (Exodus 3:5).

The seas themselves speak when they bless the Lord, as Scripture says: “Bless the Lord, seas” (Daniel 3:78). For what do we think the crashes are, when they converse with the Lord, as the prophet says: “His voice is like the voice of many waters” (Ezekiel 1:24)? What shall we say of the wind, the straits, the thunder, the rivers?

Through this voice of blood Cain could be exposed as a murderer (Genesis 4:10), because Solomon says: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice” (Wisdom 1:7).

Therefore, if what lives makes a sound, and what moves speaks, the tongue is a blessed possession of a human being if it has discipline in its use. It saves or slaughters all things; it helps or accuses; it heals or kills. In either case it labors, when it troubles another, so that it may perish first through its own misfortunes.

Thus Judas, the lying apostle, while greeting the Lord Christ, committed sacrilege with a single word. The salvation of the world received the Lord Christ, and Judas himself entered the snare.

Therefore, Christian, impose a bridle upon your tongue and confine its freedom within the cave of your mouth. Bind thousands of words with restrained powers, lest it strike its author. Hear the Lord threatening such people through the prophet: “Why do you boast in wickedness? Why are you mighty in iniquity? Your tongue devised injustice all day long; like a sharp razor you practiced deceit” (Psalm 52:3–4), and so forth.

You have teeth for this purpose: bite your tongue if it cannot remain silent. Confine the undisciplined tongue of your mouth within the cave, inside its prison, lest, when it comes out wickedly, the sword strike it. Command it while you can, because once speech has gone out, it does not return. If you cannot speak well, at least be permitted to remain silent.

For the devil would never have perished from paradise if the tongue had kept silent when the thieving serpent wounded the infancy of the first man and the garden of majesty. The neighboring thief, the serpent, with a single tongue conceived and produced an enemy conversation that brought death to man, and gave birth to bereavement for the whole world when it struck the Creator.

O sword of the tongue, by which the whole world was struck with a wound! The mother bears what she must mourn; the father begets what he must lose. The whole human race either mourns or is mourned, while all flesh returns to its origin, the dust.

## SERMON LXXVIII. To the Candidates for Baptism after the Delivery of the Creed

Behold how Israel, the spiritual people, is led out of the present world as from Egypt, and how the house of Jacob, which is the household of the heavenly King, is liberated from the barbarian people.

Moreover, Egypt was struck by ten plagues so that, released from Pharaoh’s domination, the Hebrew people might become free. We read that these plagues were completed in order (Exodus 12:29), when, in the middle of the night, the destroying angel passed through the Egyptians, saw those who had been marked, passed them by unharmed, and guarded them by the blood of the Lamb; then he compelled the children of Israel to hasten out toward the promised land.

So too the devil, who can figuratively be compared with Pharaoh, has in a certain manner been driven back from us by ten blows, slaughtered most severely by a heavenly scourge. He received the first plague when you gave your names, so that you might be enrolled there from which he had been erased. His second plague is the daily persistence of your prayer; the third, fasting; the fourth, vigils; the fifth, terrible exorcisms; the sixth, the prayer of the Lord’s priests descending upon you; the seventh, the delivery and confession of the apostolic Creed; the eighth, instruction in the Lord’s Prayer.

The ninth plague strikes him when renunciation is made of the world and its pomp, and of the apostate angels. The tenth comes when Egypt is destroyed with its firstborn, when the one approaching the font of rebirth is brought near, stripped of the old man, and turned with the whole conviction of faith toward the living God.

After this he entered the Red Sea, which was of course made red by the blood of Christ in consecration. And while he is immersed there in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, believing, the waters of the Jordan are divided to the right and left by the rod of the mediating cross. The ancient enemy who pursues is drowned; the new Israel is revealed; and from there the Church proceeds in splendor, adorned with the drums and choirs of the radiant ranks of the reborn.

## SERMON LXXIX. On Consolation at the Assumption of a Bishop

You, brothers, are seeking a consoler; but we too must be consoled. Our consolation is not any human being, but the one who makes human beings: for the one who made them restores them, and the one who created them renews them.

Through weakness we can do nothing but grieve; but through hope we ought to be consoled. We wish all good people to live with us longer, and in this most harsh life we do not wish to be abandoned by our companions. Yet those who lived well and have gone before us encourage us by their example, so that whether we live here a long time or depart from here soon, we may live in such a way that we come to them.

For living here a long time is nothing other than enduring troubles for a long time. But to live with God and in God is to live without any trouble and without any fear that happiness may perish, since it has no end.

Nor should we think that your bishop, our brother, departed from here too soon or lived too little. There is rightly no short life there where, though much is said, it does not end. Here, even what is long, once it has ended, will be counted as nothing.

Nor did he live too little here if we consider his works rather than count his years. How much that others perhaps did not accomplish in many years did he fulfill in a few years? Therefore, to wish to keep him here any longer would be nothing other than to envy his happiness.

In this we have grief concerning a human being as human beings. What, then, shall we do so that we may not be human? As human beings, therefore, we grieve humanly over the departure of a human being. But we have heard the divine reading: “Though he was perfected in a short time, he fulfilled long ages” (Wisdom 4:13).

Let us therefore reckon time there as the day is reckoned. Whatever he did among you by exhorting, speaking, offering himself for imitation, and praising and worshiping God—retain it, and you will be most beautifully adorned by his memory. For it is not a great thing for him to be enclosed in marble tombs, but to be enclosed in your hearts. Let him live buried in living tombs. His burial is your memory.

He lives with God so that he may be blessed; let him live among you so that you may be blessed. We could perhaps exhort you to faithful prudence at length, if human grief did not scarcely allow us to speak. Therefore, because God granted us to be present for a time at the death of one who was dying, because he granted us to escort his funeral, the escort owed to affection adds nothing to his happiness.

He also granted us to see your holiness and to address you, so that, according to our limited ability, we might console you by consoling you. Whatever grief does not allow us to say, supply by reflection. Our spirit, in recalling so great a man, has human sorrow, but it does not have faithless despair.

## SERMON LXXX  
*[Note: This sermon is read in Augustine, volume V of our edition, column 1909.]*

### A Sermon to Be Delivered at All Times, or Rather, On Prayer

The Lord is gracious and gentle. He keeps the door of his mercy open and does not reject those who knock there; rather, he accuses those who are negligent. For no one asks for anything that he does not possess, so that, when he has not given it, he may blush with shame.

The Lord is rich and compassionate, abundant and kind. He gives and does not reproach (James 1:5). Indeed, the treasures of his house suffer grief when the delights of petitions have become wearisome. The Lord himself says: “Until now you have asked nothing” (John 16:24). “Ask, and it will be given to you. Knock, and it will be opened to you” (Luke 11:9). “I am the door and the gate” (John 10:9).

Why does your hand tremble as it knocks, and why does your conscience grow drowsy in its poverty? I am the gate of life. I do not shudder at the filthy knocker; I do not reject the poor petitioner. Let each person only beware of neglecting his own poverty.

“Knock,” he says, “and it will be opened to you.” The angels stand at my door to bring people in, not to drive them away or terrify them. There is no pomp at my door. I am the door, I who endured the disgrace of the cross. Why does the needy person fear want, when my mercy has never been denied to anyone? “Who has hoped in the Lord and been forsaken?” (Sirach 2:12).

If those who desire chastity of body knock at the door, he immediately gives them the holiness of grace. And he says to them: “Do not walk polluted; do not proceed stained. Be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44).

If an orphan approaches and knocks with a small hand at his father’s door, an angel announces him and says: “Lord, an orphan is knocking; he awaits the protection of your mercy.” Answer him, Lord: “The poor man is left to you; you will be the helper of the orphan” (Psalm 10:14).

The Lord answers, he who is rich, who is the merciful Father: “I am the father of orphans and the judge of widows” (Psalm 68:6). Let no one harm those whom I receive; let no one despoil those whom I defend.

And if some approach this door, although they are divided by unequal places, nevertheless all receive the equal mercy of one rich father of a household in response to their prayer. This is what the saving door loves: that it abound in petitioners, both timely and importunate. Therefore the Lord himself, by the voice of the petitioner who knocks and by his silent cry, invites everyone to prayer, ready to grant mercy to all.

Even if you do not receive, ask; persevere; knock. Do not grow weary; do not yield. The Lord does not kill the righteous soul with hunger, though such souls have chosen to be agreeably importunate.

He sets forth in a parable (Luke 11:5) a man to whom an unexpected guest comes, and a poor host receives his guest. Ashamed, he immediately goes to the house of a rich man to ask for loaves—not without a sacrament, but for three loaves, because the guest is the grace of mercy, yet contains the substance of the Trinity.

Was not one guest present in three persons when he came to Father Abraham (Genesis 18:2)—a friendly guest, a diner, and a promiser—and were not all the duties of hospitality offered to him in the Trinity? Father Abraham brought a threefold calf; the future mother who was to bear a son mixed three loaves of fine flour; and for that son the father sacrificed a lamb, so that he might already behold the sacrament of Christ’s body in the Trinity.

So too this friend, when a guest arrives, goes to the rich man and pleads the need for three loaves. He knocks, and none of the doorkeepers answers, because sleep had overcome them all. Not angels, not archangels, not prophets, not ministers—and yet he knocks, although no one answers.

At last the rejoicing master of the household answers the persistent knocker from within the sacred chambers: “Why do you knock at an unsuitable time, you who were lazy when there was time? It was day, and you did not walk in the light. Night has come, and you have begun to knock?” The unforeseen urgency of his need excuses the time.

And he says: “Lord, Lord, I ask you; I knock at you; I seek you yourself. You rise and give me mercy, because you did not disdain to form my entrails from the clay of mud. You do not need a servant, because you can do everything; but your servants are sleeping, Lord. You do not sleep, nor do you slumber, you who guard Israel” (Psalm 121:4). I ask freely; under grace I beg; I do not presume under the law.

“Even if the law and the prophets lasted until John” (Matthew 11:13), your grace has no end. Your servants, your prophets, have rested, and I know this, Lord. But you, who are beginning and end, first and last (Revelation 22:13), do not grow weary of me, who ask at the final hour of the night, you who at midnight led captivity captive.

What can the master of the household do, constrained by the voice of such a persistent petitioner? He does not rouse a servant, a prophet, or send an angel or archangel. Rising himself, he gives him an answer—not because of friendship, but because of his persistent plea for mercy, shamelessness having removed his modesty.

With what joy that determined petitioner, that nocturnal beggar, returned to his own guest, whom the poor man had received and the rich man had welcomed after making him rich! And the guest never departed from his host without having been fed.

Was this not the guest who says: “I stand at the door; if anyone opens to me, I will enter, and I will dine with him, I and my Father” (Revelation 3:20)? How good is the house into which the Father and Son enter as friendly guests, where the Holy Spirit himself provides different dishes for the Lord’s supper!

What are the dishes of the Holy Spirit? Peace, joy, kindness, goodness, self-control, faith, love (Galatians 5:22). Let us only not be reluctant to receive the Lord as a guest. He himself carries with him an abundance of delights, so that he may feed the rejoicing armies of angels there.

Would that this blessed guest might come to us, and that the guest among us might no longer be a Goth and a barbarian! For those guests bring weapons and arrows; with this guest there is peace accompanied by joy. He comes not to torture his host but to spare him; not to strip him but to clothe him; not to strike him but to heal him.

Let us receive this guest through the open doors of our hearts, and the enemy will never rule within us. By his gift, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## List of Manuscripts Used for the New Revision of the Works of Saint Fulgentius, Together with Certain Variant Readings Selected from Those Omitted

*(Those marked with an asterisk are apparently to be referred to the text.)*

### Books Addressed to Monimus

The works have been corrected against the manuscripts of Corbie, namely the Corbie manuscript, eight hundred years old, formerly belonging to the monastery of Corbie and now belonging to the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

Variant readings have been taken from the manuscript of Saint Victor near Paris; the manuscript of the Thuan Library; and the manuscript of Port, that is, from the manuscript of the Charterhouse of Portes, extracted by the Reverend Father Pierre-François Chifflet, priest of the Society of Jesus. They have also been compared with the older and more carefully corrected editions: Cologne, that is, Cologne in 1526; Antwerp, or Antwerp at Plantin’s in 1573; Mainz, or Mainz in 1515; and Basel, Basel 1621.
