# IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 439–533. SAINT REMIGIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

[Col. 0961]

# NOTICE (from Galland)

[Col. 0961A] I. In arranging the events in the acts of Saint Remigius, bishop of Rheims, according to their chronology, distinguished men of learning and scholarship disagree: Baronius [Note: Baronius, under the year 471, § 34.], Pagius [Note: Pagius, under the year 471, § 13, and under the year 541, § 10.], Henschenius [Note: Henschenius, *Acta Sanctorum*, September, volume I, p. 783, no. 1, and p. 785, nos. 12–13, and June, volume II, p. 90, note 6.], Cointius [Note: Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of France*, under the years 486, § 12, and 512, § 2, volume I, pp. 117 and 292.], Labbeus [Note: Labbeus, *Historical Chronicle*, under the year 523, volume I, p. 387.] and Sammarthanus [Note: Sammarthanus, *Gallia Christiana Nova*, volume IX, pp. 10 ff.], to omit others. In our judgment, however, we have preferred the chronology established by the writers of French literary history [Note: *Literary History of France*, volume III, p. 155, note 1.], who assign the blessed bishop’s birth to the year 439, place his ordination in 461, and state that he died on 13 January 533, in the ninety-fourth year of his age, after completing seventy or more years in the episcopate, as Gregory of Tours writes [Note: Gregory of Tours, book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 79.]. For Remigius himself testifies, in a letter that he wrote in 512, after the death of King Clovis, concerning the case of the presbyter Claudius, [Col. 0961B] as almost everyone agrees, that he had then already presided over the episcopal see for fifty-three years [Note: Remigius, Letter 3.]. He must therefore have been ordained in 461. And since, according to Hincmar [Note: Hincmar, *Life of Remigius*, chapters 6 and 60.], followed by Flodoard [Note: Flodoard, *History of Rheims*, book I, chapters 11 and 17.], he was twenty-two years old when he was carried—rather than elected—to the height of the pontificate, it follows that he was born in 439. Again, we have just learned from Gregory of Tours that this same prelate completed more than seventy years in the episcopate. Moreover, it is known that Flavius, Remigius’s successor after Romanus, subscribed to the Council of Clermont on 9 November 535 [Note: Sammarthanus, at the place cited, p. 13.]; consequently, it does not seem that Remigius lived beyond the beginning of 533, when he is said to have died on 13 January. This opinion is considered the most plausible of all.

[Col. 0961C] II. Of the distinguished deeds of this prelate of Rheims, it will be enough to mention one thing: namely, that he baptized Clovis, king of the Franks, in the year of Christ 496, on the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, as Avitus, bishop of Vienne, reports, writing to Clovis himself on this matter as follows [Note: Avitus, Letter 41.]: “In the western regions, the light of a new radiance shines forth in a king who is not new. Its splendor the nativity of our Redeemer appropriately inaugurated, so that it may consequently appear that you were regenerated from the water for salvation on that day on which the world received the Lord of heaven born for its redemption.” Gregory of Tours discusses Clovis’s conversion and baptism at greater length [Note: Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book II, chapters 30–31]; among other things he says: “More than three thousand of his army were baptized.” In Hincmar’s *Life of Saint Remigius*, however, Clovis is said to have been baptized with his entire people. An ancient author agrees, saying [Note: Anonymous, *Deeds of the Kings of the Franks*, chapter 15.]: “Afterward all the Frankish people were baptized.” Thus blessed Remigius was rightly called the apostle of the Franks. Nor should that famous utterance recorded by Gregory of Tours be passed over here [Note: Gregory of Tours, at the place cited, chapter 31], by which our bishop of Rheims, as though invested with a certain divine majesty, addressed King Clovis as he approached baptism: “Bend your neck gently, Sicamber; adore what you burned, and burn what you adored.” The remaining deeds of blessed Remigius should be sought from the authors mentioned above; Sammarthanus presents them briefly [Note: Sammarthanus, at the place cited.].

III. “Saint Remigius,” says Gregory of Tours [Note: Gregory of Tours, at the place cited.], “was a bishop of outstanding learning and thoroughly trained in rhetorical studies.” What kind of man our prelate of Rheims was, and how great he was in cultivating the disciplines, as well as how exceptional his learning, is abundantly testified by Sidonius, bishop of Clermont, who wrote to Remigius himself [Note: Sidonius, book IX, Letter 7.]: “Rare, or perhaps no one, is the man for whom, when he is preparing to speak, there is an equal arrangement through arguments, arrangement through letters, composition through syllables. To this are added aptness in examples, trustworthiness in testimonies, precision in epithets, urbanity in figures, force in arguments, weight in meanings, a stream in words, and thunder in clauses. The structure is strong and firm, its very graceful conjunctions joined by unbreakable caesuras; yet it is no less smooth and light, rounded in every way, and so pleasantly loosens the reader’s unimpeded tongue that, having encountered no rugged joints, it does not stammer as it rolls through the vault of the palate. Finally, it is wholly fluid and pliable, as when a finger without a striking fingernail glides over crystalline or onyx-like crusts—for no tenacious fracture, caught in fissured obstacles, delays it. What more can I say? There is no living person’s speech at present that your skill could not, though only with effort, surpass and outstrip.” This is what the bishop of Clermont says.

After reporting this, our Baronius adds [Note: Baronius, under the year 471, § 37.]: “Would that Sidonius himself, who wrote these things, had fulfilled what he threatened in the same letter sent to him, in these words: ‘If you delay enriching our barrenness with eloquent conversations, we shall hunt down the markets of flying thieves, and, while we close our eyes and act as accomplices, the clever hands of burglars will plunder your writing cases of their own accord. Then, robbed by theft, you will begin uselessly to be distressed if, when asked, you are not moved by duty.’ But, to use Sirmond’s words [Note: Sirmond, on Sidonius, Letter 7, book IX.], the declamations of Remigius, whose eloquence Sidonius praises so highly, have not reached us; nor is this a recent loss, since Hincmar himself [Note: Hincmar, *Life of Remigius*.] and Flodoard, who inserted this letter of Sidonius into his *History* [Note: Flodoard, *History of Rheims*, book I, chapter 12.], seem to have been entirely unaware of them.”

In Baronius’s interpretation [Note: Baronius, at the place cited.], “we are not permitted to enjoy these works of Remigius, which, while he was alive, he preferred to bury in oblivion through humility of spirit rather than dedicate to posterity.” On this matter, see the writers of the *Literary History of France* [Note: *Literary History of France*, at the place cited, pp. 161 ff.].

IV. Yet not all the literary monuments of the blessed prelate of Rheims have completely perished. For four of his letters still survive, and whether one considers their eloquence, their judgment, or especially the priestly vigor of spirit with which they defend ecclesiastical rights, they are acknowledged to be worthy of so great a bishop. Concerning these letters, and the others appended to them, nothing further can be said here beyond what we have noted in the accompanying notes. As for the *Explanations of the Letters of the Blessed Apostle Paul*, formerly published under the name of Remigius of Rheims by Jean-Baptiste Villalpando, learned men long ago warned that they had been falsely attributed to him. Among them are Cointius [Note: Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of France*, year 533, § 49, volume I, pp. 405 ff.], Pagius [Note: Pagius, under the year 471, § 14.], the authors of the *Literary History of France* [Note: *Literary History of France*, at the place cited, p. 162 ff.] and, most recently of all, Dom Abbé Lebeuf, in the work entitled *Collection of Various Writings Serving to Clarify the History of France* [Note: Lebeuf, *Collection*, etc., volume I, pp. 278 ff., Paris edition, 1738.]. It is therefore truly surprising that Huet [Note: Huet, *Origeniana*, book II, chapter 2, question 8, § 2, p. 128.], adhering to Villalpando’s opinion, attributed that work to blessed Remigius, bishop of Rheims, whereas others more correctly proved that it should be ascribed to Remigius of Auxerre.

[Col. 0963C]

# LITTLE WORKS OF SAINT REMIGIUS

The notes for which we have placed numbers in parentheses are taken from the work entitled *The Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Rheims*, recently published by Th. Gousset, archbishop of Rheims. PUBLISHED.

## FIRST LETTER

[Note: The beginning of this letter is reported by Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book II, chapter 31. From this letter we learn that Albofled, the sister of Clovis, died consecrated to God as a virgin. For Remigius writes that she had received the blessing of virginity and says that a consecrated woman ought not to be mourned. Hence Hadrian Valesius, *Frankish Affairs*, book VI, volume I, p. 261, rightly wonders that neither Gregory, who had read this letter, nor the other historians of Gallic affairs noticed this; and he thinks that Albofled was baptized and consecrated by no one other than Remigius. This letter appears in *Collection of Councils*, volume V, p. 396, Venice–Labbe edition, and Ruinart quotes it in the appendix to the works of Gregory of Tours, p. 1326.]

# TO CLOVIS, KING OF THE FRANKS: A CONSOLATORY LETTER ON THE DEATH OF HIS SISTER ALBOFLED, WHO DEPARTED THIS LIFE NOT LONG AFTER RECEIVING BAPTISM

[Col. 0963D]

To the illustrious Lord King Clovis, distinguished by merits, Remigius, bishop [Note: “Bishop,” *évêque*. Saint Remigius was a metropolitan bishop, an archbishop. The title “metropolitan,” for the bishop of Rheims, goes back to the establishment of that city’s episcopal see. Under the emperors, Rheims was a civil metropolis. In apostolic times, civil metropolises that embraced Christianity generally became ecclesiastical metropolises. See Thomassin, *The Discipline of the Church*, part I, etc. Nevertheless, in the West metropolitan bishops did not begin to take the name “archbishops” until the end of the sixth century.]

Your sister Albofledis [Note: Thus indeed Gregory of Tours. But Valesius reports that Remigius wrote “Albochledis”; Ruinart’s copy reads the same.], of glorious memory, has died, and this cause of your grief troubles me—indeed troubles me greatly. [Col. 0964D] Yet we can be consoled, because she departed this light in such a manner that she ought to be received in remembrance rather than mourned. For her life was such that she may be believed to have been taken up by the Lord, since, chosen by God, she departed to the heavens. She lives for your faith, although she has been taken from your sight into longing. Christ fulfilled his purpose, so that she might receive the blessing [Col. 0965A] of virginity. She who was consecrated is not to be mourned; in the Lord’s sight she is fragrant with the flower of virginity, and is indeed clothed with the crown which she received for her virginity. Far be it from the faithful to mourn her, since she deserved to be the good fragrance of Christ, so that through him who is pleased to do so she may be able to bring help to those who ask.

My lord, drive sadness from your heart. With your spirit properly composed, govern the kingdom more wisely, adopting more elevated counsels through the practice of serenity. Strengthen your limbs with a joyful heart. Once the sluggishness of sorrow has been shaken off, you will watch more earnestly over your salvation. The kingdom remains for you to administer and, with God’s auspices, to govern. You are the head of peoples and bear the burden of rule. Do not let those who have been accustomed to seeing happiness through you see you afflicted by the bitterness of mourning. Be yourself the comforter of your soul, preserving the vigor of its innate foresight, lest sadness draw the brightness from your mind. Because of her present departure, she who, as I believe, has been joined to the choirs of virgins, the King in heaven rejoices.

In greeting Your Glory, I commend to you my associate, the presbyter Maccolus, whom I have sent. I ask you to forgive me for presuming to send words of exhortation when I ought to have come in person. Nevertheless, if you order me through the bearer of this letter to come, I shall strive, with the Lord’s help, to reach you: disregarding the severity of winter, paying no heed to the cold, and trampling underfoot the hardship of the journey.

# LETTER II

[Note: It appears in *Collection of Councils*, volume V, p. 539, and in Ruinart, at the place cited. On this expedition of Clovis, see Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book II, chapter 37, as well as the *Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions*, volume X, p. 529, and volume X, pp. 178 ff.]

# TO KING CLOVIS: AN EXHORTATION, WHEN THE KING WAS PREPARING FOR WAR AGAINST THE GOTHS

[Col. 0965C] To the illustrious and meritorious, magnificent King Clovis, Remigius, bishop.

A great rumor has reached us that you have undertaken [Col. 0966A] a second administration of military affairs [Note: [Col. 0965D] This refers to the war that Clovis undertook against the Goths, who still occupied part of Gaul.]. It is not surprising that you have begun to be as your parents always were. This above all must be done: that the judgment of the Lord concerning you should not falter, since your merit has reached the highest summit through the industry of your humility; for, as the common saying goes, a man is judged by the outcome of his deeds.

You ought to appoint counselors [Note: [Col. 0965D] Kings should have counselors who are prudent, fearing the Lord, and honorable in conduct. Council of Calchut, 787, canon 11.] who can adorn your reputation. Your beneficence too ought to be pure and honorable; you must show honor to your priests and always have recourse to their counsels. If you are in good agreement with them, your province can stand more securely.

Raise up your citizens, relieve the afflicted, cherish widows, nourish orphans—if it is preferable, educate them—so that all may love and fear you. Let justice proceed from your mouth; let nothing be demanded from the poor or from strangers, lest you should wish to receive gifts or anything else. Let your court be open to everyone, so that no one may depart from it sorrowful.

Whatever paternal wealth you possess, use it to free captives and release them from the yoke of slavery. If anyone comes into your presence, let him not feel himself a stranger. Play with the young [Note: [Col. 0965C] Ruinart has *joca* in the active form; this form is also used by Plautus, *Casina* IV, 4, 20.], converse with the old, if you wish to reign nobly and to be judged noble [Note: [Col. 0965D] Labbe, vol. IV, col. 1401. We read in a short work by Hincmar addressed to Charles the Bald:

“Intellectually, the name ‘king’ retains this meaning: that he should administer the office of ruler for all his subjects. But how will he be able to correct others who does not correct his own conduct, lest it be unjust? For ‘in the justice of the king his throne shall be exalted, and in truth the governance of peoples shall be established.’

“Now the justice of a king is to oppress no one unjustly through power; to judge justly, without respect of persons, between a man and his neighbor; to be a defender of strangers, orphans, and widows; to restrain thefts; to punish adulteries; not to exalt the wicked; not to support the immodest and the stage-performers; to destroy the impious from the land; not to allow parricides and perjurers to live; to defend churches; to feed the poor with alms; to appoint just men over the affairs of the kingdom; to have old, wise, and sober counselors; not to attend to the superstitions of magicians, diviners, and prophetesses; to defer anger; to defend the fatherland courageously and justly against adversaries; to trust God in all things; not to raise his spirit in prosperity; to endure every adversity patiently; to hold the Catholic faith in God; not to permit his children to act impiously; to devote himself to prayers at fixed hours; and not to taste food before the appropriate hours. ‘Woe to the land whose king is a child, and whose princes eat in the morning’ (Ecclesiasticus 10).

“These things bring prosperity to the kingdom in the present life and lead the king to the better kingdoms of heaven. But whoever does not administer the kingdom according to this law will certainly endure many adversities of the realm. For this reason the peace of peoples is often broken, offenses are also stirred up against the kingdom, the fruits of the earth are diminished and the services of the peoples impeded, [Col. 0967C] many and varied sorrows infect the prosperity [Col. 0967D] of the kingdom, the deaths of dear ones and children bring sadness, the incursions of enemies lay waste the provinces on every side, wild beasts tear apart the herds of cattle and flocks of sheep, storms disturb spring and winter, prevent the fertility of the earth and the services of the sea, and sometimes flashes of lightning burn the crops, the blossoms of trees, and the vines.

“Above all, the injustice of the king not only darkens the appearance of the present kingdom but also obscures his sons and grandsons, lest they hold the inheritance of the kingdom after him. Because of Solomon’s offense, the Lord scattered the kingdom of the house of Israel from the hand of his sons; and because of the justice of King David, he always left a lamp from his seed in Jerusalem.

“Behold how greatly the justice of a king benefits the world: it is plainly evident to those who observe it. For it is the peace of peoples, the protection of the fatherland, the security of the populace, the defense of the nation, care for the sick, joy for humanity, moderation of the air, calmness of the sea, fertility of the earth, consolation of the poor, inheritance of children, [Col. 0968C] and hope of future blessedness for himself.

“Nevertheless, let the king know that just as he has been placed first among men on the throne, so also, if he has not practiced justice, he will hold first place in punishments. For all the sinners whom he has had beneath him in the present life he will then have above him, in that punishment, in an implacable manner.” (*Works of Hincmar*, Sirmond edition, vol. I, p. 5.)].

While preserving the authority of government, let us return unceasingly to our heart and constantly consider that we have been created equal with others, not that we have been temporally placed above others. For the more power externally rises above others, the more it ought to be pressed down inwardly, lest it conquer the mind, lest it carry the spirit away in delight at itself, lest the mind, already beneath it, be unable to rule it—the mind which has subjected itself to the desire to dominate.

David knew well how to govern the power of kingship: by repressing himself, he overcame the arrogance of that power, saying: “Lord, my heart is not exalted” (Psalm 130). And, as an increase of that humility, he added: “Neither have my eyes been lifted up,” and further: “Neither have I walked in great matters.” Still examining himself with the most subtle scrutiny, he says: “Neither in marvelous things above me.” And, drawing all his thoughts from the depths of his heart, he adds: “If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul …”

For the most subtle art of living is to hold the summit while restraining glory; to be powerful, yet not know oneself to be powerful; to recognize one’s power for granting benefits, but to disregard entirely whatever power one possesses for reclaiming harmful things. Thus it is rightly said of such men: “God does not cast away the powerful, since he himself is powerful” (Job 36). For he desires to imitate God who administers the height of power, intent upon the usefulness of others and not elated by his own praises; who, placed above others, seeks to benefit rather than to rule them (ibid., p. 7).].

## LETTER III [Note: [Col. 0965C] It appears in the *Collection of Councils*, vol. V, p. 748, and Cointius likewise cites it in the *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks* under the year 512, section H.] TO THREE BISHOPS

Concerning the presbyter Claudius, whose case he complains that they treated with contempt.

To the truly holy and deservedly most blessed lords in Christ and brothers, Heraclius, Leo, and Theodosius [Note: [Col. 0966D] Heraclius—Heraclius, bishop of Paris; Leo—Leo, bishop of Sens; Theodosius—Theodosius, bishop of Auxerre.], Remigius, bishop.

[Col. 0966C] The apostle Paul says in his Epistle: “Charity never fails” (1 Corinthians 13:8). Yet charity did not remain in your hearts when you sent me such a letter. For Claudius I offered a simple prayer, but you write that he is not a presbyter, thereby revealing the indignation of your hearts against me.

I do not deny that he has committed a grave offense; but you ought to have shown consideration for my age, even if not for my merits. May this be said with the favor of God: for fifty-three years I have presided over an episcopal see, and no one has ever addressed me with such insolence. You say that it would have been better had you not been born [Note: [Col. 0967D] Cointius is correct here. The negative particle is inadvertently absent from the *Collection of Councils*, where immediately afterward one also finds *Ergo Cl.* incorrectly.]. That would have suited me, so that I would not have heard the reproach of a transgressor.

I made Claudius a presbyter, not corrupted by a bribe, but on the testimony of the most excellent king, who was not only a preacher of the Catholic faith but also its defender. You write that what he commanded was not canonical. You exercise the highest priesthood. The governor of regions, guardian of the fatherland, and conqueror of nations imposed this command. You burst forth against me with such angry bitterness that you did not even show consideration for the author of your episcopate.

I asked that Claudius, the perpetrator of sacrilege, be preserved for penance. For we read—we read that the Ninevites escaped through penance the destruction foretold by heavenly proclamation (Jonah 3:5–10); that John, the Lord’s forerunner, preached this in the Gospel (Matthew 3:2), so that, as the kingdom of heaven drew near, the people might do penance and not perish. In the Apocalypse (chapter 2:5 and following), the churches’ angels are instructed by command of the Lord and Savior to correct by the satisfaction of penance what they had done less worthily.

From the angry wording of your holiness I understand [Note: [Col. 0967C] Cointius has the inferior reading *interrogo*, “I ask.”] that you do not pity the fallen after their ruin. Rather, I see that you wish him not to turn and live, although the Lord said: “I do not desire the death of the dying, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 33:2).

It is expedient for us to follow this, not to neglect but to hold fast to the Lord’s will, because he appointed us not for anger but for the care of human beings, and to serve mercy rather than fury.

In your letter you state that a certain Celsus, who trusted Claudius, was led away by him, and that you do not know whether he is alive or dead; yet you order me to search for him. You do not know whether he is to be sought in this world or among the dead, and you wish me to restore his property, although I do not know that it was taken away. You command impossibilities in order to carry out impious acts.

You write that, by the number of my years, I am a “Jubilee” [Note: [Col. 0967C] Those bishops insultingly called Remigius “Jubilee” on account of his advanced age, since he had spent fifty or more years in the episcopate. Hincmar, in the *Life of Remigius*, and Flodoard, *Ecclesiastical History of Reims*, book I, chapter 17, near the beginning, testify that the blessed bishop was commonly called by this name, contemptuously, because of his old age.], mocking me rather than rejoicing out of affection. Once the bond of charity has been broken, you neither spare nor respect me in sincerity.

## LETTER IV [Note: [Col. 0967C] It appears in the aforementioned *Collection of Councils*, vol. V, p. 749. Cointius also cites and reports it in the place mentioned, under the year 495, section 4.] TO FALCO, BISHOP OF TONGRES [Note: [Col. 0968D] Tongres, whose see had already been established at Liège.]

He accuses him of having usurped jurisdiction in the church of Mouzon against the rights of the Church of Reims.

[Col. 0968B]

To the truly holy lord and most blessed brother in Christ, Falco, bishop, Remigius, bishop.

As far as I have learned and proved by the facts, your first concern was to inflict an injury upon me rather than to offer a greeting. What a fitting beginning you made, injuring a bishop before seeing me as a bishop yourself! Too quickly you have flown on tender wings, through lightness of mind rather than mature judgment.

At the very beginning of your episcopate you attempt to enter upon another’s right, when you ought still, with modesty, to have entered upon your own. Was it therefore permissible for you to believe that the Church of Mouzon [Col. 0969A] could be occupied by your unlawful ordinations [Note: [Col. 0969C] Since Mouzon belonged to the diocese of Reims, Foulques could perform no episcopal act there without the consent of Saint Remigius. On this point see the councils of Constantinople, 381, canon 2; Carthage, 397, canon 20; Rome, around 400, canon 15; Orange, 441, canon 10; Ireland, around 450, canon 30; Chalcedon, 451, canon 20; Tours, 461, canon 9; Epaon, 517, canon 5; Lyon, 517, canon 4; Clermont, 535, canon 10; Orléans, 538, canon 15; Herford, 673, canon 2, and others.]—the Church which the metropolitans of the city of Reims have always governed by their own ordination, with Christ’s help?

You still do not know your own affairs, I think, and already you invade those belonging to another. In it, then, you have made levites, consecrated presbyters, appointed archdeacons, and installed a first master of the illustrious school and of the corps of readers. I do not complain that you did not consult me in these matters—would that you had consulted yourself!

For if your holiness was ignorant of the canons, it was most rash to transgress before learning them. But if you knew the statutes of the churches, then your folly has trampled upon the decrees of ancient and magnificent pontiffs with all the greater gravity and danger [Note: [Col. 0969C] Remigius did not rely upon empty authority. Among the apostolic canons, the thirty-sixth according to the old edition of Dionysius Exiguus, it is established that a bishop must not dare to perform ordinations outside his own boundaries, in cities and villages subject to him by no right. If he is convicted of having done so, without the knowledge of those who hold those cities and villages, both he and those ordained by him are to be deposed. The disagreement between these holy and distinguished prelates did not last long; the church of Mouzon remained in the parish of Reims. Cointius, in the place cited.].

Beware, you who presume upon what belongs to another, lest you lose what you appear to possess. Since the rights of the ordination you performed are not secure, by what counsel will you defend the beginnings of your priestly office, if you mingle obstinacy or incapacity with the admission of a rash transgression? It will be a more serious danger that an ancient sanction has been violated than it will be praise to stand in a place against canons you yourself have created.

But why should I speak of the orders of those whom your blessedness was permitted to promote? This is more serious: if we examine the matter according to the statutes and severity of our predecessors, your episcopate will be called into question no less than their status.

The Lord says to Peter in the Gospel: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” And Peter: “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you” (John 21:15). Under this answer the Lord commands him twice and three times: “Feed my sheep.”

Since I am wholly unskilled and unable to feed Christ’s sheep with the abundance of heavenly nourishment, I, instructed by sacred learning, admonish you to feed those entrusted to me by Christ’s command, and I forbid you to invade them. Always act so that things worthy of you accompany you. Serve the Church which by divine dispensation you have deserved to govern, and as an attentive shepherd keep watch for the salvation of the Lord’s flock.

Would that my modest ability possessed the things which I desire you to have in the name of the Lord! But though my own resources are lacking, I do not seek a hireling for the Savior’s service entrusted to me.

John in the Apocalypse (chapters 2 and 3) addressed his writing to seven angels and wrote to each Church. He examines the deeds and merits of those set over them, and rebukes what, once examined, requires correction. Since the form of pontifical action is therefore conveyed under the name “angel,” I grieve over the audacity of your presumption: you exchange ancient rights for new ones, caution for rashness, and divine things for earthly.

Let them hear us—let those whom you have chosen as priests hear us. Let your priests themselves hear us. I trust that the sentence of the Creator will be pronounced by those who judge, not for you but against you. For who, in the uprightness of his judgment, would not condemn one who has broken forth against the rule of the Church, when he ought to have guarded that rule?

You order, as I hear, that the taxes of tenant farmers be brought to you, and command that the revenues of the estates be delivered. It is evident that you desired the property of the Church, not the Church itself, since you eagerly and insistently demand what I, to whom it rightly came, returned rather than sought.

I do not want you to be unaware that the levites and presbyters whom you made, contrary to proper order, have already been removed from their order. I considered that it was not fitting for me to admit those whom it had not been lawful for you to ordain.

Alas, how greatly you have driven me away from the purpose of honoring you, preferring to act wrongly rather than to preserve brotherly agreements! For I had wished you to remain a cleric, since you had been made a priest by force. But if this concern does not touch your mind, I nevertheless sincerely confess that it troubles me no less that you have erred without excuse than that I have been treated with contempt by you.

## THE TESTAMENT OF SAINT REMIGIUS [Note: [Col. 0969D] This Testament, enlarged by various interpolations, appears in Flodoard, *History of Reims*, book I, chapter 18; Brissonius also cites it in *De Formulis*, book VII, as does Miraeus, *Diplomatic and Historical Works*, vol. I, near the beginning. But an authentic exemplar of this Testament was finally brought to light through the work of Joannes Jacobus Chifflet in his *Inquiry into the Rheims Ampulla*, though disfigured by several errors, which Philippus Labbe corrected with the help of a sounder copy in *New Bibliotheca of Manuscript Books*, vol. I, p. 806. It also appears in Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, under the year 533, section 50, vol. I, pp. 407 and following. In transcribing it here, we have followed Labbe’s edition. On the integrity of this monument, see Pagi under the year 524, section 9, and under the year 541, section 11.]. (C)

[Col. 0969D] In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Glory to the Lord. + Amen.

I, Remigius, bishop of the city of Reims, having received the priesthood, have drawn up my Testament according to praetorian law, and have ordered it to have the force of a codicil if anything should appear to be lacking in it legally.

Whenever I, Remigius the bishop, depart from this light, you shall be my heir, holy and venerable Catholic Church of the city of Reims. And you, my brother’s son, Bishop Lupus, whom I have always loved with special affection. And you, my nephew Agricola, the presbyter, who have pleased me by your service from childhood: in all my property which came to me by my share, except what I may give, bequeath, or order to be given to anyone before I die, or what I may wish each of you to possess as a special portion.

You, my holy heir, the Church of Reims, shall possess the tenant farmers whom I have in the territory of Portus, whether from my paternal and maternal property, or those whom I exchanged with my brother, Bishop Principius of holy memory, or those whom I hold as gifts. You shall claim as your property Dagaredus, Profuturus, Prudentius, Tenuaicus, Maurilio, Baudoleifus, Projunciolus, Niviatena, Lauta, Suffronia, the female tenant farmers, and also Amorinus, the slave. Likewise, by the authority of this Testament, you shall reclaim the fields which I possess [Col. 0971B] on Portus soil, with their appurtenances, pastures, and woods.

To the future bishop, my successor, I leave a white paschal *amphibalum* [Note: [Col. 0971C] This designates a garment, from the Greek *amphiballō* (ἀμφιβάλλω), “to place around,” “to cover,” or “to clothe,” as Colvenerius observes in his notes on the first book of Flodoard. Octavius Ferrarius, book II of *De Re Vestiaria*, chapter 12, writes that it was a kind of garment resembling a *laena* and not greatly unlike a *chlamys*, which the ancients called an *amphimallum*. Andreas Saussaius, in *Panoplia Clericalis*, part I, book V, chapter 5, interprets it as a *planeta*. In former times the *planeta* was completely round and surrounded the entire minister, so that, when he was performing the sacred rites, it was necessary to fold both edges over the celebrant’s right and left arms. From this seems to have arisen the custom by which even now we are accustomed to lift the edge of the priest’s *casula*, *planeta*, or *paenula* when he raises the divine host and the cup of perpetual salvation, lest its weight inconvenience the celebrant; although this is scarcely necessary now, since the *planeta* has been cut on both sides, right and left, so that he who performs the fearful mysteries can move and extend his arms and hands freely, without any obstruction. Cointius, in the place cited under the year 533, section 52.], two dove-colored coverlets, and three curtains which, on feast days, are placed at the entrances of the dining room, the chamber, and the kitchen.

I have distributed, with the Lord’s assent and as I wished, a silver vessel weighing eighteen pounds, fashioned into plates and chalices for the sacred ministry, between you, my heir, and your diocesan Church, the Church of Laon [Note: [Col. 0971D] In many copies of the aforementioned Testament, *Lugdunum* and *Lugdunenses* are read; in others, *Laudunum* and *Laudunenses*. We have retained *Lugdunum* and *Lugdunenses*, but wish to point out that *Lugdunum Clavatum*, Laon, is meant, since it lies under the metropolitan Church of Reims—not Lugdunum of the Segusiani, Lyon, which is the chief city of Celtic Gaul. The same author, in the same place, section 51.].

I order that another silver vessel, which the illustrious King Chlodowicus of blessed memory, whom I received from the sacred baptismal font, graciously gave me so that I might do with it whatever I wished, be made for you, my heir, the Church mentioned above, into a little tower and an image-bearing chalice [Note: [Col. 0972C] Labbe reads *thuribulum*, “censer.” Colvenerius, in his notes on Flodoard, book I, chapter 18 of the *History of Reims*, reads as we have printed it. Cointius likewise reads so, and observes at this place, under section 53:

“Difficulty arises concerning the little tower and the image-bearing chalice. For *turriculum* some substitute *thuribulum*; others read *turriculam*, contrary to the testimony of the ancient copies, which we think should be followed with Colvenerius. For a *calix turriculus* is the same as a tower-shaped or turreted chalice, so called from its form; and it is *imaginatus*, ‘image-bearing,’ because it is adorned with carved sacred images. What we now call a ciborium, the ancients called a tower. Gregory of Tours bears witness, when he says in book I, chapter 86, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*: ‘The deacon began to carry to the door the tower in which the mystery of the Lord’s body was held.’ Flodoard himself also bears witness in his *History of Reims*, book II, chapter 6, where he praises Lando, bishop of Reims, for placing upon the altar of Saint Mary’s church at Reims a golden tower which he had had made according to his vow.”].

I shall have this made myself if I have sufficient time left in life. If I close my final day before that, you, my brother’s son, Bishop Lupus, mindful of your order, shall have the aforementioned objects made.

To my fellow presbyters and the deacons who are at Reims I leave twenty-five solidi, to be divided equally among them [Note: [Col. 0972D] The solidus is reckoned as forty denarii, as solidi were then calculated; this is contained in the Salic Law of the Franks and generally continued in payments until the time of Charlemagne, as is found in his Capitularies. Labbe, in the place cited, p. 806.].

They shall likewise possess jointly, with Melanius the vinedresser, the vine planted above my vineyard in the suburb; I give Melanius in the place of the ecclesiastical man Albovicius, so that Albovicius may enjoy complete freedom.

I order two solidi to be given to the subdeacons, two solidi to the readers, and two solidi to the doorkeepers and junior clergy. Two solidi shall be brought to the poor listed in the church register who wait before the church doors for alms, so that they may refresh themselves.

From Vaculiacum I order Frunimius, Degaleifus, Dagaredus, Duction, Baudovicus, Uddulfus, and Vinofeifa to be free. Tennaredus, who was born of a freeborn mother, shall enjoy the status of liberty.

You, my brother’s son, Bishop Lupus, shall claim as your property Nifastes and his mother Nucia [Note: [Col. 0972D] We read this with Cointius; Labbe has *mutam*, apparently incorrectly.]; also the vineyard cultivated by Enias the vinedresser. I order Enias and his younger son Monulfus to enjoy freedom.

You shall assign to your right Mellovicus the swineherd and Paschasiola his wife; Vernivianus with his sons, except Widragasius, to whom I grant freedom. I order my slave from Cessurnicum to belong to you. You shall reclaim for yourself the portion of land which my brother, Bishop Principius, held, with its woods, meadows, and pastures. I leave to you my slave whom Mellonicus held, Viteredus [Note: [Col. 0972D] I have restored the pronoun *tibi*, “to you,” which is absent in Labbe, from Cointius.].

I transfer to your right and ownership Teneursolus, Capalinus, and his wife Teudorosena. Teudonivia, too, shall be free by my command. You shall retain Edoveifa, who was joined to your man, and her family.

I order Aregildus’s wife and her family to be freeborn. You shall reclaim my portion of the meadow which I possess at Laon [Col. 0973A], situated near the mountains, and the small meadows called Jovia, which I held.

To you, my nephew Agricola the presbyter, who spent your childhood within the walls of my household, I give and transfer Merumvastus the slave, his wife Menatena, and their son named Marcovicus. I order his brother Medovicus to be free.

I leave to you Amantius and his wife Daero; I order their daughter Dasovinda to be free. I assign Alaricus the slave to your portion; his wife, whom I bought and freed, I commend to you to defend as a free woman. You shall claim as your property Bebrimodus and his wife Mora. Their son Monacharius shall rejoice in the benefit of freedom.

You shall reclaim Mellanricus and his wife Placidia for your ownership; their son Medaridus shall be a freedman. I give you the vineyard which Mellaricus cultivates at Laon, my slave Brittobaudes, and also Gibericus.

I leave you the vineyard which Bebrimodus cultivates, on this condition: that on feast days and all Sundays my offering be made upon the holy altars, and that annual banquets be provided for the presbyters and deacons of Reims.

I assign to my nephew Praetextatus Moderatus, Tottion, Marcovicus, and Innocentius the slave whom I received from Profuturus, my hereditary tenant; four large spoons; a small dish; the cloak which Tribunus Friaredus gave me; and a decorated silver plate.

To his little son Paronius I give a small dish, three spoons, and the *casula* whose fringes I exchanged.

To Remigia I transfer three spoons bearing my name; also her tablecloth which I have for everyday use; I also give her the *hichinaculum* [an uncertain item], concerning which I spoke to Gundobad.

I assign to my blessed daughter Helaria, the deaconess, a female servant named Nora, and I give her the *vitis pedatura* [a vine-plot measure], which is joined to her vineyard, the vineyard cultivated by Cattusius. I transfer to her my portion of Talpusciacum in return for the services which she continually renders me.

To my nephew Aetius I give the portion of Cessurnicum which came to me by lot in the division, with every right which I held and possessed; I also transfer to his right and ownership Ambrosius, a boy.

I order Vitalis the tenant farmer to be free, and his family to belong to my nephew Agathimerus. To him I give the vineyard which I planted at Vindonissa and established through my labor, on this condition: that from his ancestors, on all feast days and Sundays, an offering be made upon the holy altars in memory of me, and that annual banquets be provided, with the Lord’s permission, for the presbyters and deacons of Laon.

I give eighteen solidi to the Church of Laon, to be distributed equally among its presbyters and deacons. Let the Church of Laon reclaim my entire portion of Secia.

I commend to your holiness, my brother’s son, Bishop Lupus, those whom I order to be free: Carthusio and his wife Auliateva; Nonnio, who cultivates my vineyard; Sunnoveifa, whom I bought as a captive and who was born of good parents, and her son Leuberedus; Mellaridus and Mellateva; Vasanta the cook; Cesaria; Dagaraseva [Col. 0974A] and Baudoroseva, the niece of Leo; and Marcoleifus, the son of Tottion. You, my brother’s son, Bishop Lupus, shall defend all these as free persons by priestly authority.

To you, my heir, the Church, I give Flavianus and his wife Sparagildis; I have decreed that their little daughter Flavaraseva shall be free.

The presbyters and deacons of Reims shall possess Fedamia, the wife of Melanius, and their little daughter.

I order Cispiciolus the tenant farmer to be free, and his family to belong to my nephew Aetius. The tenant estate at Passiacum shall come to both of them, that is, to Aetius and Agathimerus.

To my great-niece Praetextata I give Modoroseva. To Profuturus I hand over the boy Leudocharius. I order Leudovera to be given to Profutura.

I leave four solidi to the subdeacons, readers, doorkeepers, and junior clergy of Laon. One solidus shall be given to the poor listed in the register, for their refreshment.

I assign eight solidi to the Church of Soissons for the commemoration of my name; six solidi to the Church of Châlons; five solidi to the Church of Mouzon; to the Church of Vong, a field near the millworks established there; and four solidi to the Church of Catariga, with an equal amount to the Church of Portus, for the commemoration of my name.

Since I have enjoyed the customary services of the household of Ursus the archdeacon, I give him at home a fine textile *casula* and another fuller one; two delicate cloaks; the rug which I have on my bed; and the tunic which I leave behind at the time of my death, the better one.

My heirs, Bishop Lupus and the presbyter Agricola, shall divide my pigs equally between you.

Friaredus, whom I bought for fourteen solidi so that he would not be killed, shall have two solidi granted to him; he shall give twelve for the construction of the chamber of the basilica of the lord martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris.

Thus I give, thus I bequeath, thus I testify. As for all the rest, let all of you be disinherited—let you be disinherited. No fraud is present in this Testament of mine, nor shall there be. If any erasure or scratching is found in it, it was made in my presence while it was being reread and corrected by me.

Executed at Reims, on the day and in the consulship written above, with the witnesses and signatories intervening and present.

+ I, Remigius, bishop, have reread, signed, and subscribed my Testament, and, with the help of the Lord, have completed it in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Vir clarissimus Pappolus was present and subscribed. Vir clarissimus Rusticolus was present and signed. [Col. 0974D] Vir clarissimus Eulodius was present and signed. Vir clarissimus Eutropius was present and signed. Vir clarissimus Eusebius was present and signed. Vir clarissimus Daweus was present and signed.

After the Testament had been drawn up—or rather, signed—it came to my mind that I should assign to the basilica of the lord martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris a silver dish weighing six pounds, so that from it a future resting place for my bones might be fashioned.

[Note: [Col. 0973] Flodoard cites these verses in *History of Reims*, book I, chapter 10.]

## VERSES DEDICATED TO REMIGIUS BY A. B., AND ENGRAVED AT HIS COMMAND ON A SILVER VESSEL FOR THE USE OF THE VENERABLE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST

From this may the people drink life from the sacred blood,

which eternal Christ poured out when the wound was inflicted.

Remigius the priest renders his vows to the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0975] This epitaph appears in Aimoinus, *On the Deeds of the Franks*, book I, chapter 25. Baronius likewise copied it from Aimoinus under the year 514, section 28. On it, see Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, under the year 511, section 60, and Pagi under the year 514, section 10.]

## EPITAPH OF KING CLOVIS

Reportedly composed by Saint Remigius. (C, G, S)*

Rich in wealth, powerful in virtue, and renowned for triumph,

King Clovis founded this seat; and the same man,

A patrician exalted by great honor, shone forth.

Full of love for God, he scorned to believe in the thousand

Gods whose monstrous forms bristle with varied shapes.

[Col. 0976A] Soon cleansed by water and reborn from Christ’s font,

He wore fragrant hair, anointed with chrism.

And he gave an example which a great multitude

Of the gentile people followed; rejecting the error of their ancestors,

He worshiped God the Author and the true Father.

Blessed by these merits, he surpassed the deeds of those before him:

Always formidable in counsel, in the camp, and in wars;

A good leader by exhortation and brave in heart,

He first strengthened the battle line in its ordered formation.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 534. MARCELLINUS COMES

### A
## A

**ABRAHAM**, faithful friend of God and father of the faithful nations, 29. Abraham and Lazarus, the poor and the rich, 477. Why Abraham commanded his servant to place his hand under his thigh and swear by the God of heaven, 289, 290. He is to be believed to have done this in the prophetic spirit, ibid. Abraham built an altar, intending to sacrifice not to the Father alone but also to the Son, 28. Abraham built an altar to that God who had appeared to him, 29. The Arians said that this was the Son, ibid. The sacrament of Abraham’s circumcision was commanded with a dreadful threat against little children, 303. Abraham was justified, not by works, ibid. God swears to Abraham by himself, 66.

There is no partiality with God, 282 and following.

He would not have died unless he had sinned, but would have passed into a spiritual and immortal state with sinlessness, 299. The condition of innocent Adam, 336. His fall and deliverance, ibid. and 14. He consented to the woman without being deceived, 435, 497. By sinning he lost faith and God’s protection, 310, 311. Adam’s sin was transmitted to his descendants together with death, 290, 437. By sinning, Adam subjected himself and his descendants to sin, 436. The condition of sinful Adam and his descendants, 435. The multifaceted comparison of the first and second Adam, 554.

For God’s adopted sons there is one name of sons and one glory, although their functions and their splendor are different, 114.

What it means to adore on the mountain, 103.

God’s advent is the manifestation of grace, 99. It does not occur locally, 32. To whom Christ’s advent in his own person is to be attributed, 105. The advent of the Holy Spirit is not local, 33.

There are two kinds of estimation in Scripture: uncertain knowledge and certain understanding, 591.

**HAGAR** sinned grievously through exalting herself, 426.

Christ is our nourishment, 547.

The word *alius* (“other”) distinguishes the persons, but does not divide the essence of the Trinity, 62, 63.

An address used in place of a blessing, 152.

An altar is built for no other reason than to offer sacrifice to God, 29, 638. Abraham built an altar intending to sacrifice not to the Father alone but also to the Son, 29, 638 and following. Isaac [Col. 0976] and Jacob likewise built an altar to the same God who had appeared to them, 30.

**AMBROSE** succeeded the Arian Auxentius in the episcopate of Milan, 536. Through Ambrose the faith of the emperor Gratian was strengthened, ibid. What he thought about Paul’s supererogation, 39.

What it means to walk with God, 576.

**Amen.** When receiving the Lord’s mystery, the faithful heard the Body of Christ and answered “Amen,” 227. What each of the two things signifies, ibid.

Why God’s friends are never abandoned by God, 106.

Love of the Creator is the true blessedness and wisdom of a rational creature, 15. Disordered love is the beginning of sin, 16. Why love of the world is vicious, ibid.

Satan filled the heart of Ananias and Sapphira because each retained something from his vow, 149.

Although the name “angels,” or “messengers,” properly belongs especially to the Son, it is appropriated to the Father and the Holy Spirit, 580, 581.

The creation of the angels, the fall of the evil angels, and the confirmation of the good, 14, 335. Angels are superior to our souls, 125. According to the opinion of some, they consist of a twofold substance, 335. They say that the bodies of the good angels are ethereal, but those of the evil angels aerial, ibid. Angels are free from sins and passions, 125. They are immutable by God’s gift, not by nature, 89, 526. The stability of the good angels comes from God’s gift, 90. Good and evil angels are not creators, 431. Why angels are permitted to produce certain unheard-of things, 419. Human beings were created to fill the number of angels who fell from heaven, 335. In the evil angels, turning away from God is the beginning of damnation, 514. Angels and human beings are immortal because they are rational, ibid. Those who teach the law but do not practice it are said to speak in the tongues of angels; why, 35. Comparison of the evil angel who deceived Eve with the good angel sent to Mary, 554. How angels and human beings received the gift of blessedness, 514. In the wicked there will never cease to be an evil will, ibid. The mutability of angels, 513. All could have fallen, 90. The angelic nature is insufficient for the restoration of humanity, 89, 90. How angels long to look into the Holy Spirit, 586, 587.

The soul is the image of God: not begotten but created, not equal but similar, 335. Faith teaches that it is a rational spirit, not a body, 496. In Scripture, “soul” is used for the whole human being, 294. Various opinions concerning the origin of souls, 494, 495. Saint Augustine did not wish to put forward any settled opinion concerning the origin of souls, 494. Fulgentius thought that one should refrain from contention over this question, 275, 496. In what the soul of human beings differs from that of animals, 518. What are the soul’s refreshment and fatness? 356, 357. The passions of sadness, grief, fear, and so forth belong to the substance of the soul, 126, 127. The soul draws original sin along with the flesh in which it is born, 496. The soul, rather than the flesh, is Christ’s bride, 77, 78. How the soul is in the body, 513. Why the soul must be cared for much more than the body, 389. Everything that benefits the soul also benefits the body, but not conversely, 225. Neither is the flesh nourished without the soul, nor is the soul spiritually nourished without the flesh, 356. God is to be understood as entering souls when he is said to transfer himself into them, 46. The soul consenting to the devil is like an adulterous wife, 427. In the body the soul will receive either everlasting punishment or everlasting joy, 396. To lay down one’s soul is proper to love, 130. The soul’s first death is in sin, its second in the lake of fire and brimstone, 23. The soul dies, and through what, 49. What it means for the soul to be filled with illusions, 179. The soul could not have been saved if the soul had been absent from the Savior, 77. Why the soul was assumed together with the flesh, 51. On what basis it is asserted that Christ truly had a soul, 125. How the soul is to be hated, 389. The Apollinarists denied that Christ possessed a rational soul, 347.

The apostles are the beginning of God’s creation, 55. They were not made dispensers alone, 547. How certain it is that after Christ the apostles are the foundation of the Catholic faith, 534.

**Apud** is used in place of **in**, 42 and following. To be with God and to be in God are the same, 46. In human beings also, insofar as substance is concerned—the substance by which they are human—to be with is no different from being in, 48. In Scripture this preposition does not always denote something external, 45 and following; just as God, remaining with the faithful, is in them, so the Son of God, when he is said to be with the Father, must be understood to be in the Father, 46. How many blasphemies follow from the false interpretation of these two prepositions, 44.

We are trees in the Lord’s field, 548.

Noah’s ark is a figure of the Church, 375. No one was saved outside it, 530. Augustine’s various interpretations of Noah’s ark, 40. It is commanded to have two chambers because of the twofold multitude that the Church gathers from all nations; and three chambers because of Noah’s three sons, from whom the whole world was filled, ibid. Noah’s ark is a figure of the three stages of perfection in the Church, 330.

Archelaus, son of Herod, ruled after his father’s death, 558. Various comparisons between the birth of Archelaus and the birth of Christ, ibid.

The Arians think correctly about the divine persons, but wrongly assert three natures, 205. The Arians involve themselves in the crime of idolatry, 346, 637. They served two masters, 623. The Arians posed to the young Donatus a question in which they asserted that the Father was greater and the Son lesser, 198. The Arians say “Glory to the Father through the Son” in such a way that they refuse to say “Glory to the Father and to the Son,” because in Christ they regard the priestly office in such a way that they refuse to acknowledge the majesty of divinity, 259, 644. The Arians customarily said that the Son had appeared to Abraham, 29. The Arians say that not the Father but the Son swore to Abraham; hence they are refuted by the fact that the Son is God, because the one who appeared to Abraham swore by himself, since he had no greater by whom he could swear, 66. The Arians deny in Christ the unity of substance with the Father, 347. Some of them said that people were baptized not in the name of the Spirit Paraclete but in the name of another Spirit, 622. They are refuted, ibid. The Arians should be asked whether God gave his Church the faith by which Abraham pleased God through believing in him, or whether they judge that the faith of the patriarchs and prophets should be rejected, 28. A new invention of the Arians in defense of their heresy, 42. The Arians called the Trinity separable because only the Son was incarnate, 349. The Arians denied not only that the Son of God was of the substance of the Father but also that he possessed a human soul, 51. The Arians acknowledged a greater God and a lesser God, 345. They called the Son lesser not because of his assumption of flesh but by the nature of his divinity, 345. To teach that the substance of the Father and the Son is different, they suppose that all bodily forms of things must be assigned to the Son alone, 29. The Arians wrongly concluded that the Holy Spirit was lesser than the Father and the Son because he himself was not asked to descend but was to be sent by the Father and the Son; yet they did not call the Son equal to the Father on the grounds that he himself is asked in Scripture to descend, 625, 626. The Arians explained the words “And the Word was with God” in such a way that they denied that what is said to be with God is in God, 42. The Arians asserted that what is in God is inward, while what is with God is outward, 44. A dispute between two Arians concerning the prepositions **in** and **with**, 42 and 43. The Arians’ inept definition of these prepositions, **in** and **with**, 43. The Arians do not understand that what was made by the whole Trinity was not assumed by the whole Trinity, 356. In the offering of incense the Arian who maintains that sacrifice is owed to the Father alone is confounded, 562. The Arians deny that the Holy Spirit is God, 294. The Arians’ reasoning is contrary to reason and hostile to the law of God, 43. The Arians called Catholics “Homoousians,” but themselves did not wish to be called “Triousians,” 63. [Col. 0978] Hardly any remnants of the perfidy of Rimini remained in Fulgentius’s time, 336.

## AUGUSTINE

Augustine was divinely instructed in the holy Scriptures, 38. The praise and grace of Saint Augustine by which he was strengthened should be sought, 473. Saint Augustine triumphed over his enemies and showed posterity the manner of fighting and conquering, should conquered wickedness ever attempt to raise its impious head again through renewed assault, 473. Saint Augustine should be consulted above the other Fathers on questions concerning grace, 473. Saint Augustine’s modesty in doubtful matters, 494. Let everyone read Saint Augustine who desires to attain eternal salvation, 473. In what spirit Saint Augustine should be read, 473. Saint Augustine’s sermon on the sacrament before the altar, 226, 227. Fulgentius calls Saint Augustine’s book *On the Predestination of the Saints* most lucid, 25. The book *On the Presence of God*, Letter 187, 245. Augustine’s books to Prosper and Hilary are to be read above all by those who oppose grace, 275. What many call Saint Augustine’s *Enchiridion* is the book *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, 245. Saint Augustine’s book *On the Perfection of Human Justice*, 4. Augustine, overtaken by an early death, did not reply to the Gauls, 25.

## B

**BABYLON** is interpreted as “confusion,” 180. The daughter of Babylon is every carnal desire, ibid.

Baptism is given in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, 141. Baptism conferred by any heretics and in any place, provided it is given in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, is not to be repeated, 520. For it is valid, although it does not contribute to salvation, 624, 625. It possesses the form of godliness but not the power of godliness, 624. Why the form of Baptism is this, 298. On Baptism in the name of Jesus Christ, 660, 661. The mystery of human redemption is in no way completed if in Baptism the name either of the Son or of the Holy Spirit is omitted, 205. Each person is regenerated in the name in which he is baptized, 141. The immensity of the Trinity is shown by the words of Baptism, 110. Through Baptism all, even heretics, become subject to the Church’s jurisdiction, 378. Baptism conferred by heretics in the name of the Trinity is the truth of the paternal seed to which the Church attends, 378. Heretics baptized outside the Church are born of the slave woman, 373. If heretics remain outside the Church, through Baptism they merit punishment, not life, 375. For heretics who do not return to the Church, Baptism increases their ruin, 529. The sacrament of Baptism exists outside the Church, but benefits no one except within the Catholic Church, 529. Baptism does not benefit heretics unto salvation, 337. Although validly conferred, it is not to be repeated, ibid. Baptism received from heretics benefits a person when the baptized person returns to the Church, 519. Outside the Church neither Baptism, nor almsgiving however abundant, nor death undertaken for Christ’s name can contribute to salvation, 530. Such is the power of holy Baptism that it washes away even all the sins it finds superadded to original sin, 223. The necessity of Baptism, 275, 519. In Baptism, the adoption of sons lost in the first man is restored through the second man, 275. Everyone who is not baptized, even if he dies as a little child in his mother’s womb, is to be punished with the torment of eternal fire, 525. Baptism is the reward of faith and confession, 221. Just as good works do not benefit anyone outside the Church, so in the Church Baptism without a good life does not benefit, 520. Baptism does not contribute to salvation for those who do not believe, 218. In adults, neither confession without Baptism nor Baptism without confession is beneficial, 223. Philip first requires a confession of faith from the eunuch before granting Baptism, 221. Why the Canons command that the sick be baptized on another person’s testimony, 224. How the person who is baptized eats the flesh of the Son of Man, 225 and following. Why the dead are not baptized, 223. It is a matter of divine judgment that God abandons evil wills in such a way that parents do not care about the regeneration of their children, 446. He himself sometimes instills in parents a holy concern that their little children be baptized, but does not always bring it to fulfillment, 447. Why sometimes the child of unbelieving and impious parents is saved through Baptism, while the child of faithful and devout parents is condemned without Baptism, 447. God does not bring about the negligence of parents by which an unbaptized infant perishes, 446. The concern of good parents for their children’s Baptism benefits both parents and children unto salvation, 445. The faithful are ground as though by exorcisms, sprinkled as though by Baptism, and baked as though by the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that they may become what they receive, 227. What is done in the Church before Baptism causes a person to be conceived, not reborn, 224. The scrutiny and exorcisms before Baptism, 214. The recitation of the Creed and of the Lord’s Prayer, 214. We were reborn by the same Spirit by whom Christ was born, 308. The sacrament of Baptism was prefigured in the water of the Flood, 375. Just as those outside the ark perished through the waters, so also heretics perish through Baptism, ibid.

**Blessedness.** No other blessedness could, can, or will exist for a rational creature than that, recognizing from whom it was made rational as well, it should show greater love to the Creator than to itself, 14, 15. Who will be eternally happy, [Col. 0979] 382. In the heavenly homeland there will be no want or labor, but perfect rest and satiety, 181. The eight beatitudes are jewels of holy virgins, 176. Christ’s virgin ought to possess the eight beatitudes in their perfect degree, 175, 176.

**Beelzebub** is interpreted as “prince of flies,” 430.

**Benevolent.** The word “benevolent” is composed of *bene*, “well,” and *velle*, “to wish,” 184.

**BOETHUS**, bishop, 286.

The good grieve over the perversity of their elders, 373. Neither should the good be presumptuous nor the wicked despair, 557. Good faithful people also suffer persecution from Catholics who oppose ecclesiastical tradition not in word but in deed, 373. Good is to be done for others, 574, 575 and following. What is supremely good is the highest good, 424. Of whom and of what good it was said, “There is none who does good,” 4. What it means to receive good things in one’s lifetime and to receive evil things, 195. The good and evil things of this life are common to the good and the wicked, 428. Not everyone who possesses the good things of the present life receives them as good things, 195. Whatever is good and just in the just and the unjust is to be attributed to God, 12. Every good thing we do comes about through God working in us, ibid. We will persevere and progress in good things when we attribute to God whatever good will and good action we possess, 189. No created substance, whether human or angelic, can supply us with the complete sufficiency of goodness, 178.

The arm of the Lord is the divinity of the Son of God, 134, 135.

## C
### Blindness

There is nothing else to be blinded than to be deprived of light, 371. Blindness of heart neither knows what it should believe nor what it should do, 198. Just as blindness of the eyes is driven away by the infusion of light, so blindness of the heart is driven away by the remission of sins, 371.

### Cup

The Lord gave the disciples the division of the cup, because the holy Church learned the knowledge of this division through their teaching, 266. He says that they should divide it among themselves—that is, in the unity of the Spirit and the bond of peace, ibid. Various interpretations of the cup that Luke says was given to the disciples, and what each signifies, 261. For Fulgentius it signifies both Testaments, ibid. The first cup, not the later one, is commanded to be divided; why, 165. By the name “cup” perfect charity is also understood: if the opportunity to endure death is lacking, nevertheless nothing is lacking for enduring punishment, despising life, and undergoing death for Christ’s name, 264. Because the New Testament is to be understood in the later cup, and the Old in the earlier one, ibid. In other passages the name “cup” signifies the grace of suffering, 262. The cup that David says he will receive is nothing other than the death of the saints, 263.

### To grasp

In spiritual matters, “to grasp” is “to see”; and “to see” is nothing other than “to understand,” while “to understand” is nothing other than “to know,” 256.

### Charity

Charity itself is love, 183. Charity is the fountain and source of all good things, 558. Praises of charity, 42. God is charity, and charity is from God, 190, 341, 465. Among spiritual gifts, the first fruit is charity, 182. Love of God and neighbor is the fullness of the law and the end of the commandment, 185. Charity brought Christ down from heaven to earth, 556. The excellence of charity is that whoever possesses it in the heart can never explain it adequately in words, 182. Charity increases to the extent that desire is diminished, 565. Comparison of the two, ibid. Whoever has not begun to possess love or charity does not love it, 183. If someone admires charity, it is of no benefit unless he loves it, 182–183. Once charity begins to dwell somewhere, it does not permit sin to rule, 196. The gift of prophecy can be loved without being possessed; charity is not loved unless it is possessed, 183. Charity is an outstanding protection, 558. Charity is the way that leads to heaven, ibid. Charity lifted Stephen from earth to heaven, 555. Charity earned for Stephen and Paul the possession of the kingdom of heaven, 557. Armed with charity, Stephen overcame the fury of the Jews, 558. The grace of Christ, which displayed in his mother the miracle of perpetual virginity, demonstrated in the martyr Stephen the sign of unconquerable charity, 556. Whoever is good ought to imitate Stephen’s perseverance in charity, 557. Holy and tireless charity desired to obtain through prayer those whom it could not convert by admonition, 556. Whoever does not possess the beginning of charity does not love its increase, 183. Unless we receive God, we cannot love him, 465. A benevolent person is the dwelling-place of charity, 183. Every irrational animal, just as it lacks reason, so also lacks charity, 185. A multitude of coins can be loved without possessing a coin; the increase of charity cannot exist without charity, 183. Whoever loves his brother according to charity, which is God, loves charity itself in him as much as possible, 184. Charity does not permit the will in which it exists to become evil, 183. The gains and benefits of charity, 563. Whoever brings destruction upon his soul by living badly does not preserve the proper order of charity and mercy, 388. What the charity of neighbor consists in, 373. In charity one person is to be preferred to another, yet no one is to be excluded, 564. Thus we ought to grow in charity by loving one another while we live, just as we are commanded always to render it, [Col. 0980] 563. A person loves his neighbor when he takes as much care as he can that his neighbor may reach God through right faith and good conduct, 373. It is characteristic of charity that it increases in the one who gives it, but departs from the one who wishes only to possess it for himself, 184. The burden of charity is not heavy, 42. All spiritual gifts, when possessed without charity, burden rather than honor, 183, 620. The true wisdom and understanding of a rational creature is love of the Creator, 15. Charity is commanded to be rightly ordered so that sin may be avoided, 16. Charity must continually adhere to right faith, which by the zeal and effectiveness of good works covers a multitude of sins, 286. The love of God is greater when love of oneself is lesser, 15. The principal fitting and ordered reason is love, 185. Whoever receives the mystery of unity but does not preserve the bond of charity does not receive the mystery for himself, but testimony against himself, 227. What madness is it to call charity separable, when it habitually joins separated minds in inseparable love? 344. The effect of charity is remission of sins, 563. Those who despair of the remission of sins reject charity, 190. Christ wished to free from the slavery of sin those who had once been free in an evil way, so that he might teach us to serve one another in free charity, 163. To whom charity is owed, 564. No believer demands that charity be rendered to him in such a way that he himself does not owe it to the one to whom he is indebted, 164. The debt of charity is the only debt from which it is not permitted to be released in this life, 563. When charity is rendered, more is owed, 564. And it is acquired all the more when it is rendered because it is owed, ibid. It must also be extended to enemies, 564–565. Compelled by Christ’s charity, we exhort the good to remain in the good, and compel the wicked to depart from evil, 557. The holy Trinity, making its dwelling in a person, multiplies love in him, 411. There is no simplicity of heart in divided love, ibid. God is sometimes offended by a harsh refusal and a prolonged delay in giving a response, 163. Christian charity should display the parts of its work in both directions, so that it may humbly acknowledge God’s sufficiency and patiently forgive the servant’s need, 165. Charity is God’s gift; desire is the devil’s snare, 565. Charity is the principal gift of the Holy Spirit, 34. A clean heart is the dwelling-place of charity, according to the Apostle, 563. Not all who admire and praise charity immediately love it, 182. No one is willing in any way to repay the holy debt unless the merciful God grants that he may be willing, 165. While demons appear to have faith because they believe, it benefits them nothing because they do not have charity, 35. Without charity one may produce a sound, but one cannot possess life, 34. God exalts us to the extent that he raises our souls toward himself and instills the truth of his knowledge and love, 254. Charity neither begins nor grows in us from our own will, but is poured out by God into our hearts, 456. Charity must be preserved very closely among Christians, 164, 570. Whoever does not have charity for himself does not bestow it on another, 183. A rational creature loses salvation by losing the order of love, 16. A malevolent person does not bestow charity on another because he does not have it for himself, 184. Charity and the unity of faith must be religiously preserved, 379. Those truly love God who obey his commandments, 395. The body can be handed over without charity; the soul cannot, 130. Christ did not say, “What people have done to you,” but, “What you want people to do for you.” Why, 373. A person loves himself when, devotedly and humbly, he places the love of God before himself, 373. We grow in charity when, through the gift of spiritual grace, we receive an increase of charity, 34.

### Flesh

Flesh by itself neither lives nor perceives, neither grieves nor desires, 128. In Scripture “flesh” is used for “human being,” 83, 294. Mary’s flesh was the flesh of sin, 292. He gave birth to the Son of God in the likeness of sinful flesh, ibid. The flesh of all human beings is conceived under the law of sin, 437. Meat and wine are not abstained from by God’s servants because of any evil in their nature, but for the chastisement of the body, 530. What it means to follow the deeds of the flesh, 381. The resurrection of the flesh is common to the good and the wicked, but the recompense is different, 528. Why the flesh is to be punished together with the soul, 6.

### Cherubim

“Cherubim” means fullness of knowledge, 250. What it means to ascend above the Cherubim, 250.

### Christian

A Christian receives his name from Christ, 200. No one can in any way be a Christian who does not say that Christ himself is his Lord and God, ibid. The duty of a Christian, 373. Christians are trees in the Lord’s field, 548. Not all who share in Christ can also defend what they believe by giving an answer, 198. Jews and Gentiles were made one and received the single name “Christian,” 558.

### Christ

The one person in Christ is demonstrated by the form of baptism, 298. Whoever admits two persons in Christ is not a worshiper of the Trinity but of a Quaternity, 298–299. Why Christ’s deity could not receive the Spirit, 252. How Christ is the author and perfecter of our faith, 309. Christ’s first birth was from God, his second from a human being; but our first is from a human being and our second from God, 293. Why God had to be born from a virgin, [Col. 0981] 436. Christ is the firstborn of all creation according to the mystery of the incarnation, 56. He is the firstborn of restored creation, not of created creation, 55. He was made the beginning of creation not in order to create a new one, but to renew the one lost through old age, 54. In what sense Christ is the beginning of creation, ibid. Christ is the firstborn from the dead—that is, the first human being from sinful human beings, Christ exalted into the Son of God, 56. Christ is the bread of angels and human beings, 553. Christ is the farmer and cultivator, 548. Although Christ is the bread of angels, he did not assume an angelic nature, 553. What it means that Christ “was not,” “is,” and “is not,” 118. What Christ will be like at the second coming, 393. Christ’s first coming was a day of abasement, 152. Christ, sent by the Father, came once for the fall and resurrection, 410. Christ comes continually with the Father for the resurrection of many, 410. Christ deigns to come with the Father as his equal, ibid. Christ’s poverty is human mortality, 351. How all things were created in Christ and all things are reconciled in him, 322. Christ, remaining God, for whom we offer sacrifices, was made a priest through whom we can offer a living sacrifice; yet no sacrifice could have been offered by us if Christ had not been made a sacrifice for us, 258. Through him we offer a sacrifice of praise and prayer, because through his death we have been reconciled, 258. Why the conclusion of a prayer says “Through Jesus Christ,” and not “through the Holy Spirit”: because there is one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, 258. Through him, who deigned to become a sacrifice for us, our sacrifice can be found acceptable in God’s sight, 258. The conclusion of a prayer sometimes says, “Through your eternal Priest, your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ,” so that the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation may be displayed, 258. From both conclusions of the prayer there are many points by which heretics may be convicted, 259–260. We are participants in Christ, and how, 253. To sanctify Christ is to think of what is holy about him; likewise, to exalt him is to think of what is most exalted about him, 104. From Saint Augustine: the passage “For he does not give the Spirit by measure,” etc., is understood of Christ alone, 251. Christ received the Spirit not by measure, 250 and following. Christ gives and receives the Spirit, and how both are true, 251. God pours out from his Spirit upon us, but upon Christ the Spirit descends and remains, ibid. The issuing forth of power from Christ is the effect of divine healing, 105. In Christ there were true but voluntary weaknesses, 130–131 and following. Christ took upon himself our sufferings in order to free us from sufferings, 126. Christ became weak in order to conquer weakness, 131. The inseparable unity of the person, in which God and a human being were born, makes it possible to say that Christ was truly born from God and truly suffered, 117. Whatever Christ suffered, he endured wholly according to the unity of his person; according to the natural property, however, these truths belong to the flesh alone, 357. Certain seeds of our virtues are contained in Christ’s sufferings, 134. God felt suffering in the flesh, but did not feel it with the flesh, 124. According to the testimony of Scripture, it is one thing to say that God suffered in the flesh, another to say that he suffered together with the flesh, ibid. Christ’s deity did not suffer together with the flesh or the soul, ibid. What Peter means when he says that Christ suffered in the flesh, 118. Christ rose according to the flesh, 553. Christ suffered with us in that in which we ourselves suffer, 136. The weakness of the one and the same Christ, human, endured suffering; the omnipotence of divine power performed miracles of beneficence, 122. In true suffering Christ remained impassible, ibid. Although only the human being was handed over in Christ, because of the unity of the person the whole Christ is said to have been handed over, 132. As Christ was about to die for human sins, he displayed in himself the feeling of human weakness; and, wishing to remove despair from weaker members, the very power that wished to be our head did not disdain, out of divine love, to say what his members would later say out of human fear, 262–263. The humanity of the Son of God was neither wholly in the tomb nor wholly in hell, but the deity was wholly everywhere, 140. God did not suffer together with the suffering Christ, 118.
