The soul abandoned the dying flesh of Christ, but not the deity, 122. Christ’s death destroyed both kinds of death in us; Christ’s resurrection bestowed the grace of both resurrections, 294. How Christ tasted death without God, 126. Christ died through the weakness of his humanity, but lives through the power of his deity, 132. Christ did not come to conquer kings by fighting, but to subdue them wondrously by dying, 559. Christ was made to die by his own goodness, not by another’s wickedness, 561. Christ’s soul did not die together with the flesh, 124. Through death Christ freed us from the fear and slavery of death, 466. Christ’s flesh could not decay in the tomb, because it was always without sin, 137. Christ’s body did not undergo corruption, not because of incorruptibility, but because of the swiftness of the resurrection, 326. Christ’s body was in the corruption of death, but not in the corruption of putrefaction, 326. Christ’s flesh did not undergo corruption in the tomb, nor did his soul undergo punishment in hell, 135. What Christ’s body was like before the resurrection and what it is like now, according to Augustine, 326. Christ’s soul did not feel pain in hell, 137. Christ brought the work of grace, begun when he was conceived in the womb, to completion when he was raised from the tomb, 554. Why God the human being was born without sin, ibid. Christ’s self-emptying was his reception of the form of a servant, 288. Christ’s conception from the Virgin, 290. Christ’s descent is not local, 90. God the Only-begotten did not have the assumption of the form of a servant in common with the Father, because he received the truth and fullness of the form of a servant not in unity of nature but in unity of person, 246. In Christ, the properties of the natures do not divide the person, nor can the unity of the person confuse the properties of either nature, 297. Why Christ was born from the Virgin without sin, 507–508. Christ fled not from human fear but by divine dispensation, 560. True faith, just as according to the flesh it knows and declares the crucified one to be God’s power and wisdom, so it does not doubt that the deity was crucified according to the flesh, 240. Christ received corruption not voluntarily but as a penalty, and not that which is accompanied by sin but that which is without sin, 305. Christ possessed the weaknesses of our souls without corruption—true indeed, but voluntary; why both, 327. Christ’s handing over was voluntary, 132. Christ became poor so that we might become rich through his poverty, 351. Christ’s deity did not descend into hell, 87. Not only Jesus’ body, but Jesus himself was also in the tomb, because the deity never abandoned the body, 131. Christ tasted death while the immortality of his deity remained intact, 296. Christ died because he was human; he raised himself because he was God, 297. Christ showed that he possessed a soul when he declared that he had power to lay it down, 128. What distinguishes Christ’s soul from angels or holy human beings, 250. In Christ, what belongs to the flesh and the soul must not be attributed to the deity, 124. Peter would not have named the laying down of his soul on Christ’s behalf if Christ had not possessed a soul, 129. Christ would not provide help for our soul if he did not have a soul in which he was tempted, 80. The soul of the Church could not be saved if Christ lacked a soul, 78. Christ’s soul cannot possess less than the fullness of truth, since it is the soul of Truth itself, 254. Christ’s soul possesses the full knowledge of the whole deity, 251. Christ is not known according to his deity by his own soul in the same way that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit know one another; for although his soul possesses full knowledge of the Trinity, it does not nevertheless possess one nature with the Trinity, 254. Christ’s soul is not of the same nature as God because it knows his entire deity, since God himself is not of the same nature as the thing that he made and certainly knows fully, 255. Nor will we ourselves, because we shall see God, be consubstantial with God himself, 255–256. What is said, “in whom are all the treasures,” etc., pertains not only to Christ’s deity but also to his soul, 252. It is contrary to the soundness of faith to hold that Christ’s soul did not possess full knowledge of his deity, with which it is believed naturally to have one person, 250. Christ’s soul knew its deity as much as the deity knows it, but not as the deity knows itself: for the deity knows itself in such a way that it naturally discovers itself to be what it knows, whereas the soul knows its entire deity in such a way that it is nevertheless not itself the deity, 254. The two natures in the one person of Christ are not confused but united, 115. Christ’s two births, 281. One Christ is the Son of God and of a human being, 115. Christ has participants according to his humanity, not according to his deity, 127. Christ is said to be from Nazareth and anointed because of his human nature, 120. Christ is the only-begotten Son of God by nature, not by grace, 113. Christ’s body was earthly, not heavenly, because he took hold not of angels but of the seed of Abraham, 140. Christ is heavenly from heaven not because of the substance of his body, but because of his freedom from desire, 436. Without the Word, Christ’s flesh was neither Christ nor ever conceived, 295. The excellence of Christ’s flesh is due to its union with the Word, 507. Christ’s flesh was of the same nature as that of other human beings, but without sin, ibid. In Christ’s body there was corruptibility; in his soul, perfect incorruptibility, 326. Christ is the power and wisdom of the Father, 90. God is not in Christ in the same way as in the patriarchs or prophets, 291–292. God was made Christ, not Christ made God, 280–281. Christ is mediator of human beings because of the union of the natures, 82. Christ is proclaimed by the holy Fathers as composed through the joining of deity and humanity, 279. In what sense Christ is called the beginning and the end, 93. He does not have a beginning because he is called “the beginning,” nor does he have an end because he is named “the end,” 92–93. Christ is rightly a priest because he is surrounded by weakness, namely, human nature, 136. Christ is priest and victim, 80, 136. Priest, sacrifice, and temple according to the form of a servant, 510. Christ is high priest because he is a human being, 80. Christ prays because he is a priest, 586. Christ is the one who offers the gift and the gift itself. Why, 80. Christ is life and power, 132. Christ is eternal life, 93. Christ is also the paraclete, or comforter, 579–580. Christ is teacher and giver of eternal salvation, 298. Christ is king of justice and king of peace, 94. [Col. 0983] Christ is rightly shepherd, sheep, and lamb, bridegroom and bride, 79–80. Christ will be our nourishment on the way and our reward in the homeland, 547. Christ is our Samaritan, 193. Christ provides us help in that in which he was tempted, 80. Christ made his body both temple and sacrifice, 641. Christ is, according to both deity and humanity, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, 633. Whoever does not invoke the name of Christ possesses neither grace nor peace, 662. We are saved through the name of Christ alone, 658 and following. Christ is true God just as he is true human being, 205. Christ is the Son of God, and we also are sons: he by nature, we redeemed; he born, we made; he true, we adopted, 261. David agrees with John and Paul in proclaiming one person in Christ and two unconfused natures, 82. “The Word became flesh” is said because of the unity of the person in Christ, 85. “He dwelt among us” is said because the two substances are unconfused, 85. In the one Christ there are not two persons, 86. In Christ there is one person and two natures, 112, 206. Just as the distinction of persons in God does not multiply substances, so the distinction of natures in Christ does not multiply persons, 117. In Christ, a child is one thing and God another substantially, but not personally, 86. In the one person of Christ there is complete God and perfect human being, ibid. Christ must be treated carefully because of the two natures in one person, 112. Whoever fully recognizes in Christ the unity of the divine and human nature will attain everlasting salvation, 51. In the personal unity, both substances have been undivided and unconfused from the beginning of the conception, 122. The truth of the divine and human nature in Christ is established from prophetic and apostolic testimonies, 75. Because of the union of the two natures in Christ, the human being is called Son of God and God Son of Man, 85. Christ has always possessed in himself the properties of humanity and deity, 117. Christ remained full of grace and truth in the form of a servant, 113. Christ assumed all human weaknesses except sin, 122. Christ had true flesh and a true soul with true understanding, 86. Christ could in no way be mediator if he did not possess either, with the Father, the nature of deity, or, with human beings, the common substance of flesh and soul, 206. Because the whole nature had been taken captive, the whole nature had to be assumed, 81. Christ and Jesus Christ are the same, 594. Christ is the eternal day, God from God the Father, 553. Christ’s deity did not need anointing or sanctification, 121. Christ is truly God and truly human, and displayed in himself, without confusion, the properties of God and of a human being, 505 and following. Christ’s names demonstrate the impassibility of his deity, 134. Christ’s deity is impassible and present everywhere, 137. He did not abandon either the flesh in the tomb or the soul in hell, 129. Christ is naturally eternal, boundless, and most high God, 90. Christ, who is not divided in his gifts, must not be divided in his persons, 562. Although humanity was exalted, the deity in Christ was not diminished, 87. The two natures in Christ exist without confusion, 278. Christ would have been neither priest nor victim if he had possessed anything less of human nature, 80. The one who suffered was none other than he who remained impassible in the true suffering of the flesh and immortal in death, 112. Christ’s assumption of a soul is demonstrated, 81. In Christ the soul is especially the seat of the Word, 85. Christ possessed true flesh and soul, according to the testimony of Peter and David, 136. Soul and flesh were assumed by God so that he might save both in us, 51. What is said, “no deceit was found in Christ’s mouth,” cannot be referred to the deity, 79. There is one Christ: without a beginning as generated from the Father, and with a beginning as born from the Virgin, 295. Christ’s statement, “I have power to lay down my soul,” must be believed to belong to the whole human being, 128. Human flesh would not have been assumed by Christ if it were not to be saved, 76. For the full effect of our redemption, a human being without sin, assumed by God, had to descend into hell and the tomb, 135. In Christ there is the fullness of grace and truth, 255. Christ’s flesh did not receive the form of God; God received the form of a servant, 295. Christ was both human and made from human beings, 413. Christ advanced in wisdom according to his soul, not according to his deity, 124. Christ’s wound belongs to the flesh, his weakness to the soul, 128. Christ assumed immaculate flesh in order to remove the stain of flesh, 73. Christ is God in such a way that he is his own deity; he is strong in such a way that he is his own power, 241. Christ advanced in wisdom and grace according to his soul, and in age according to his flesh, 75–76. The human Christ had power to lay down his soul because of the unity of the divine person, 129. Christ displayed both natures in himself, 352. Christ received his body from the earth; he did not bring it down from heaven, 121. Just as Christ received in his own body the body of all the faithful, so in his own soul he received the souls of all the faithful through unity of nature and the grace of justification, 78. According to his deity, Christ is the only-begotten Son without brothers; according to his humanity, he became the firstborn among many brothers, 56. The human being could not have been saved if something of either the divine or human nature had been lacking in the mediator, 75. Christ always has the same true flesh that he assumed from his mother, 526. According to the form of a servant, he received possession of the ends of the earth, not according to the form of God, [Col. 0984] 56–57. Christ is without a mother as God and without a father as a human being, 94. There are two natures, substances, or forms in Christ, 335. Both natures in Christ are unconfused, 333. The property of each nature in Christ must be observed, so that he may be understood without error as created, founded, and begotten, 57. Christ is coeternal with the Father and later than his mother, 295. The two natures in Christ must be distinguished, and what belongs to each must be seen, 54. Christ ascended into heaven according to his entire humanity, 358. The deity is inseparable from the humanity as the Son is from the Father, 117. Christ is most high according to both natures, and how, 253. Christ saved in us what he assumed for us, 77. Each nature in Christ is inseparable, 236. What was done in Christ is not referred to his divine nature but to his person, 358. Christ lay in the tomb according to the flesh, descended into hell according to the soul, and remained boundless according to the deity, 357–358. There are two natures and one person in Christ, 124, 246, 287, 584. Both natures in Christ are inseparable, although neither is eternal, simple, and boundless; therefore the three persons are much more inseparable, since their unity, eternity, simplicity, and boundlessness are natural, 237. Christ’s humanity is impeccable because of the union of the deity, 134. Christ is fully human because he is full of grace, 116. Christ, as a human being possessing nothing of his own, bore the sins of others, 134. By accepting circumcision and saying, “What is born from flesh is flesh,” Christ showed that he possessed true flesh, 86. In Christ there is a divine and human nature, 347. To the latter belong hunger, thirst, and so forth, 325. True faith is to believe Christ to be true God and true human being, 297. Christ is not spatial, since he made space, nor temporal, since he made all time, 96. Christ is called the only-begotten Son of God not only in deity but also truly in the flesh, 408. Just as a true human being is believed to have been produced from the Virgin’s womb, so a true God is believed to have been produced from God’s womb, lest the human nature be considered superior to the divine, 65. Christ is less than the Father according to his humanity, 515. Christ has one person of his deity and flesh, 525. The child Christ is the Word, the power, and the wisdom of God, 560. In Christ’s response, “Destroy this temple,” etc., the truth of the divine and human nature is displayed, 122. There were those who said that Christ was God in name, not in substance, and who, unwilling to acknowledge a human soul in him, attributed his sufferings to the deity, 74. The Apostle says that Christ died, not merely that Christ’s body died, so that the unity of the person of God and human being might be preserved, 131–132. Christ’s deity could not be called his soul, 128. What is said, “no deceit was found in Christ’s mouth,” cannot be referred to the flesh alone, 78–79. There would be no great praise in Christ that he was without sin if he had lacked a human soul, 78. Christ was displayed in the flesh to some so that they might believe and to others so that they might crucify him, 410. Christ had to assume the whole of human nature, since the whole had gone astray, 77. Why Christ is full of grace and truth, 116, 509. What is said of Christ, that he was made a little lower than the angels, must be referred to his human substance, 126. From the passage “I have power to lay down my soul and to take it up again,” the divine and human substance in Christ is demonstrated, 129.

### Food

Excess of food and delicacies often provoked God’s anger, 170. Through the pleasure of foods the alms of the poor are diminished, and through fullness the body is made warlike, 170. When we take food, we provide for the flesh, certainly, not the soul; nevertheless, in the very taking of food the soul works together with the flesh, 247.

Circumcision was divinely granted to our fathers as a sign of the righteousness of faith, 439. The sacrament of circumcision was commended to Abraham not without threatening the little child, 303.

### Thought

Thought is found in the human soul alone and in no way in the body, 45. Thought is where there is discrimination between good and evil, 45. Thought is the inner word and inward speech, 553. To think is the same as to speak within oneself, ibid. We love what we think about, 549. Holy thought, speech, and action are from God, 165. The origin of good thoughts and their assent are from God, 283. Without grace, human things are thought about and desired, not divine things, 282. Although the souls of the righteous are freed by the gift of grace from the contagion of evil works, they are nevertheless held captive by the variety of their thoughts, 175. Each person errs in that by which he defiles himself through assent to an evil thought, 77. A perverse thought is dashed against the rock when, overcome by the swift recollection and aid of Christ, it is trampled down, 180–181. The thoughts of mortals are fearful—those through which they serve sin, 467. When the cause of worldly thought ceases, worldly thought ought to cease, 156.

### Dove

The dove in whose form the Holy Spirit came upon baptized Christ was made to signify something and immediately dissolved, 413. In the dove the simplicity of the heart was signified, 413. Through the dove and the fiery tongues under which he appeared, the Holy Spirit showed that charity was to be given to us through his gift, 412. [Col. 0985]

### Contrition

Contrition of heart arouses the feeling of prayer, 177. Contrition of heart looks upon its own wounds, ibid. Since God is frequently offended by us, it is necessary that he be appeased by frequent prayer and continual contrition of heart, ibid.

### Council

The Council of Antioch against Paul of Samosata, 279. The four general councils, 281. The letter of the African councils to Pope Zosimus, 284.

### Desire

Desire is not from God, 16. Desire exists even in the saints, 427. Desire existed in the evil angels, 14. The desire to sin is the torment of the sinner, ibid. In the loins with which the Lord commands one to be girded, the restraint of carnal desire is commanded, 550.

### Confession

Saul’s confession arose from fear of punishment, not from horror of sin, 398. Not everyone who confesses sin receives forgiveness, ibid. and 368. Confession is beneficial when the person who has confessed no longer does what he did wrongly and strives by good works to surpass the merits of his former crimes, 399. Confession of the mouth is commanded by divine precept, 70. It is necessary for salvation, because the word of God is not bound, ibid. When the subject is God, it is no slight guilt to keep silent about what pertains to salvation, ibid. Whoever is ashamed of Christ and his words destroys himself and harms himself, ibid. Whoever remains silent and does not affirm the truth strengthens error, ibid. In the person of Isaiah, confession of the mouth is commanded to all preachers of the word of God, ibid.

### Confidence

Confidence has a great reward, 162. One must not therefore distrust divine power, because nothing should be attributed to one’s own power, ibid.

### Marriage

Marriage is among the gifts of God, though not among the chief ones, 155. The marriages of Christians are holy, 153. Marriage derives from God’s institution, not from the filth of sin, 154. Having a spouse or taking wine and meat is not evil, 520. Christ does not condemn marriage, 156. Marriage does not make vessels for dishonor, 479. Conjugal modesty and widowly continence are both gifts of God, 154. Conjugal chastity is owed more to Christ than to a husband, ibid. Conjugal dignity does not lack its own honor, conferred by God, 145. The legitimate power of the woman over the man’s body and of the man over the woman’s body is from God, ibid. The conjugal obligation is called an obligation because it is legitimately rendered, ibid. The use of conjugal authority, if there is no excess, is blameless, ibid. In legitimate conjugal excess there is venial fault, 526. The proper use of marriage is when it is for offspring, not for lust, 145. When spouses modestly render the debt of the flesh to each other, they keep Christ’s commandments, 154. In carnal intercourse the future renewal of offspring is to be kept in view, 146. Carnal intercourse between spouses is not counted as sin if lust is not served in it, ibid. To have intercourse with one’s spouse for the sake of offspring, not lust, is worthy of much praise, but scarcely possible, 146. Holy marriages do not love lust but tolerate it, 439. Married people must avoid those deeds that divine severity both forbids to be done and condemns when done, 149. Modesty must be preserved in the marital act, ibid. Every fornication is damnable, especially within marriage, 146–147. Conjugal propriety abhors adulterous intercourse, 154. Every intercourse outside one’s wife is mortal sin for married persons; excess with one’s wife is venial, 146. Marriage provides for weakness, 154. The Apostle commands that the conjugal debt be rendered in order to provide for the weakness of certain people, 145. The union of spouses is for consolation on the journey, not for blessedness in the homeland, 154. If married and widowed women remain faithful to Christ in this life, in the future they will not be deprived of virginity lost in marriage, 171. Paul said that married people are concerned with the things of the world, but virgins with the things of God, because the thought of holy virgins turns more toward spiritual matters, whereas that of holy married women turns more toward marital matters.
serves necessity, 168. The Apostle did not prescribe holiness of body and spirit to virgins in such a way as to deny it either to married women or to widows, 166. The Apostle Peter does not hesitate to call faithful married women holy, 168. Marriage may rightly be despised, 156. Faithful married persons ought to obtain from God, by asking in prayers and almsgiving, a higher degree of continence, 150. The disadvantages of marriage with regard to bodily offspring, 169. How useful it is for holy living to abstain from marriage, meat, and wine, 520. In carnal marriage, unless bodily integrity is lost, one does not attain fertility; in spiritual marriage, the more bodily integrity flourishes, the more abundantly immortal fertility prevails, 169. The dress of married women ought to be modest, 157. Legitimate and marital conception is not free from the guilt of iniquity, 418. Consolation is not given without exhortation, 579. Continence is to be desired from God by all, 149, 150. Whoever cannot abstain from the flesh should abstain from iniquity, ibid. The death of a spouse is an opportunity for continence, 151. After a profession of continence, even the desire to marry is condemnable, 148.

True conversion consists in right faith toward God and sincere love toward one’s neighbor, 373. Conversion is true in a person when impiety and iniquity are driven from the heart, 372. Conversion from impiety and iniquity is commanded, 369. Paul would not have mourned for the many who had sinned and had not done penance [Col. 0986], if he had believed that forgiveness was granted without conversion of heart, 369. No one who is unwilling to be converted will go unpunished, 381. Through conversion of heart we are reconciled to God, 368. God is always pleased by our conversion, 194. Isaiah promises that all sins are forgiven those who are converted, 291. No one fails to see how impious and sacrilegious it is to believe that any sin cannot be forgiven a person converted through penance, 191. Such is God’s goodness in omnipotence and omnipotence in goodness that there is nothing he does not wish, or cannot, forgive for one who is converted, 192. It is unjust if we think that one who was once just but has turned away can be condemned, while one who has turned back cannot be saved, 193. By saying, “When you have turned back and groaned, you will be saved,” God testifies that he is always able to grant salvation to one who has turned back, 193. The wicked, once converted, will attain the kingdom of God, because God is merciful, 371. Because God is just and merciful, he receives those who have turned back and punishes those who have become hardened, 367. The promise of salvation depends entirely upon the condition of conversion, 368. Saving conversion consists in two things: neither should hope abandon the penitent, nor repentance the one who hopes, 192. Conversion removes every guilt, 364. Every moment of the present life is most suitable for conversion, 193. To whom is it said, “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” 195, 196. Whoever is evil ought to follow Paul’s example of conversion, 557. Forgiveness of sins is granted only to those who have truly converted, who are established in the bosom of the Church and still live in this age, 364. Forgiveness of sins takes effect only in conversion of heart, 369. It is said, “When you have turned back and groaned, you will be saved,” so that we might recognize conversion and groaning as necessary for attaining the effect of salvation, 368. Every heretic converted to the Church, if he perseveres, will be wheat, not chaff, 374. The gracious warning of divine Scripture ought not to be disregarded: it salutarily commands us to convert quickly and commends the future wrath of divine vengeance against those who delay, 400. Neither conversion nor renewal is to be attributed to our own free choice, 462. David attributes the conversion which we are commanded to effect to a work from above, 461. It belongs to the Lord to effect the conversion that he commands and to open the mouth which he promises to fill, 462. Those wish to be saved in whom the Lord works the will to be saved, 462. In those who do not wish to be saved, human hardness persists in making them unwilling, 492. The confession of sins and groaning over them, if they occur without conversion, irritate God rather than please him, 368. In everyone who exercises his own will, forgiveness of sins begins through conversion of heart, 370. The effect of forgiveness consists in conversion of heart, 371. In the Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews, not only is conversion in the present time indicated as necessary, but perseverance to be maintained until the end is also commanded, 391. Whoever has not been changed through conversion in this age will not be changed into incorruption, 393. True conversion can exist only where there is true faith and a good life, 383. David effectively obtained mercy from God because, having turned back, he groaned with his whole heart, 369. In the similarity between Saul’s and David’s confessions there was a dissimilarity of will, 398. In David and Saul, God considered not the words of the mouth but the intention of the heart, ibid. Groaning without conversion is a wound without medicine, ibid. The conversion of the powerful of this age greatly advances Christ’s acquisitions, 186. To swear falsely or commit homicide is a much lesser sin than to kill Christ; yet the latter is forgiven to one who is converted, whereas the former is not forgiven to one who is not converted—why? 400. That evangelical work is nothing other than true conversion of heart, 401. Woe to the one who, before the time of the final winnowing, has not taken care to become wheat rather than chaff, 400. God is understood to have assigned every moment of the present life to our conversion, 194. We must neither despair of God’s mercy nor remain in sins under the hope of mercy, 404.

**Creation.**

Creatures were not created out of God, but by God, 188, 512. The substance of created spirits is not divine—why? 512. Every creature that is inferior to the nature of God the Father is without doubt a created nature, 201. No creature is of the same nature as God, 516. Every created nature is capable of failing, because it has been brought forth from nothing, ibid. Every created nature is good, because it is from God, ibid. The whole Trinity made every creature, 345. Whoever asserts that some creature was not made by God or could not be healed is rebellious against God, 81. These words, “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made,” subject everything to God’s creation, 119. Each thing is what it has received by the Creator’s ordering, 311. The Father made all things through the Son, 91. If the Son were a creature, the authority of the Holy Scriptures would not command that he be served, but would rather forbid it, 200. Created things are unequal among themselves in perfection, 511. God made nothing disordered, 16. All God’s works are good, 14. The rational creature was made better than the others, ibid. Reason could not exist in a creature unless the love of the Creator could also exist in it, 15. Among creatures, only angels and human beings were granted the faculty of understanding, 526. The lowest creatures are not therefore evil, 14. God is praiseworthy in the elephant and in the little worm, 432. God prepared scourges for the human being who would sin when he created harmful animals, ibid. God created harmful animals before the human being’s sin, ibid. The creator of flies, scorpions, and fleas is the same as the creator of angels and of all visible and invisible things, 420. God did not create harmful animals so that human beings would feel their power before sin, 432. The fly was created so that the proud human being might be humbled, 430. In all created things there are God’s goodness and omnipotence, 511. Why creatures can advance and fail, ibid. We are in God not through natural unity but through the power of the Creator or the mercy of the Redeemer, 50. Evil angels do not create the things they are permitted to produce, 429. God alone is the creator of angels and little worms, ibid. God exalted the rational creature through the privilege of reason and eternity so that it might recognize the essence of its Creator as without beginning and wholly incomprehensible, while recognizing that, although it was not made without beginning, it would nevertheless not cease to exist, and that it is comprehensible to the Creator alone, not to itself, 89. The term “creation” is to be understood as applying to the Son only in this sense: that, for the redemption of human beings, he became human from human beings, 64. What is begotten is not the same as what is created, 55. After the fall, the rational creature cannot turn to God by its own powers, 515.

**Belief.** What is to be believed, 282. See **Faith**.

The cross is the small key by which the passage of heaven was unlocked, 567. Three crosses and three causes on Mount Calvary, 68. The cross of Christ was in the middle of the tribunal, ibid. Through the word “cross,” those perish who subject the divinity of the Son of God to the Passion, 112. Guilt is frequently contracted even in things that are lawful, 520. The cultivation of God is the infusion of spiritual grace, 548.

**Worship.**

There are two forms of worship, *latria* and *douleusis*: one is offered to God alone, the other also to human beings, 593. Worship of *latria* is offered to God chiefly through sacrifices, ibid. In the first commandment of the Decalogue, just as the worship and service of the one God are most clearly commanded, so the worship and service of every creature are most emphatically forbidden to the faithful, 200. The Scriptures proclaim that the Son is to be adored just as the Father is, ibid.

**Desire.**

The struggle with desires is greater and more difficult because it is interior, 180. If visible desire is conquered in the body, the invisible hostile power does not rule in the heart, 170. A mind devoted to carnal desire makes for itself a god whatever it loves above all else, 220.

**CYPRIAN.**

Praise of Saint Cyprian, 566. Saint Cyprian’s steadfastness, 567. Saint Cyprian’s pastoral care for all orders, 566, 567. Cyprian’s book *On the Simplicity of Prelates*, according to the old copies, *On the Unity of the Catholic Church*, 375.

# D

**DAMNATION** is from God, 15. It is justly repaid, 440. The wicked will be condemned for the iniquity which God does not commit, 11. The condemned are not consumed by the eternity of punishment, 116. The death of the wicked cannot itself die, 396. The wicked will be corrupted but not consumed; they will die but not be extinguished, ibid. Evil pleasure will be for the condemned an addition to their punishment, 389. In eternal damnation, the cause of the adults is worse than that of little children, 49. Those who are condemned cannot either love or desire justice, 517.

**DANIEL** and the three youths were accustomed to pour forth prayers, 68.

**DATIANUS**, bishop, 269, 277.

**DAVID**, when converted, immediately rejected the desire to sin; Saul did not, 398. Why he obtained mercy, 369. When David said, “I said in my prosperity, ‘I shall never be moved,’” he had been abandoned by the help of divine grace, 174.

**Denarius.** What is meant by the denarii, 39. Who are to receive the denarius, 10.

**Desire.** Holy desire is greatly to be praised, 163.

**Despair.** Judas’s despair was repentance without hope, 192.

## GOD

The name “God” is not the name of a person but of a nature, 590. Why God placed in human beings the testimony of his recognition, 600. It is absurd for someone disputing about God to derive his arguments only from denser bodies, 43. There is one essence, or nature, of the Godhead, 503. Testimonies concerning the one God, 536, 537. Heretics assigned to the Father alone the testimonies by which it is proved that the one God is the Holy Trinity, 199. Authority demonstrates that the God of the Old and New Testaments is one, ibid. God is one in essence and three in persons, 521. Scripture shows that there is both a Trinity in persons and unity in nature, 605. The true God is he who is God by nature; God by nature is he who possessed deity from the eternity of his birth, not from the grace of a gift, 59. Unbelief is either believing something false about the true God or worshiping a false god under the name of the true God, 221.

One must not think of God as of created things, because he himself does not think as we think, 345. The name of God is found in Scripture in four ways, 219, 220. The deity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit from Scripture, 331, 332. The Father is our God just as the Son is, and is one God with the Son, 589.

[Col. 0988] God is immutable, 345. Nothing temporal happens to God, 487. God, being immutable, neither progresses toward what is better nor changes toward what is worse, 187. Mutability and locality are contrary to God, 72. It is impious to believe that something which was not always in God has newly occurred in him, 59. God is said to walk in us—not because he moves locally in our heart, but because our heart is enlarged in God, 109. According to his divinity, God does not pass from place to place, 410. When God is said to have rested, it is shown that we too shall rest after good works, 101. By the immutable counsel of God all things are changed, 187. In God alone there is perfect fullness, security, and glory, 187. God is what he has, and he has what he is, 242. In God, because he is not subject to quality, all absolute things are identical with his essence, 241. No one would suspect that hunger, thirst, and the like could fall upon the Godhead, 133. Sadness, grief, weariness, and fear cannot fall upon the Godhead, 125.

God is incorporeal, 12. We find in God various names for bodily members, so that through the activity of these things the character of his incorporeal substance may be understood, 64. God is invisible in himself, although he appeared visibly, 119. God is not seen by bodily eyes, 254. Nor is he seen by Christ’s own eyes, because eyes see only bodily things and things distant from themselves, 254, 255. With what eyes God is seen, 255. He is invisible in a different way from an angel or a soul, 653.

**GOD.** He is immeasurable, from whom nothing is locally separate, 343. God is in all creatures, ibid. He can be enclosed by no place, 87. God is wholly everywhere, 409. God’s immeasurability is proved by the fact that he commanded us to pray in secret places, 106. God’s immensity is diffused through every place without quantity, 512. God’s immensity is not to be evaluated by the qualities of creatures, 71. God is immense in power, not in bulk, 343, 345, 523. Whatever is naturally everlasting must necessarily be declared naturally immense, 96. God is everywhere by nature, although he is not in all things by grace, 31, 345, 409. God is everywhere by power, but not everywhere by grace, 97. God is naturally near the good and near them by grace; in the wicked, however, there is only his natural immensity, 231. God is not contained by place but perceived by affection, and therefore is not seen by one in whom he does not dwell, 255. The Son and the Spirit are immense, as is the Father, 588. The immensity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, ibid. How God dwells and walks in us, 109. What “descending” and “ascending” mean in God, 101. God comes and departs in an ineffable and incomprehensible manner, yet does not move locally, 100. Supreme and true divinity cannot pass from place to place, 417.

**God’s eternity.** In God’s substance there is nothing that was not; nothing that was can cease to be, 88. God established all things not from a need arising from poverty but from the abundance of his goodness, 572. God is light, because we are children of light, 61.

**God’s knowledge.** God’s wonderful wisdom provides remedies for healing from the very source from which destruction proceeds, 422. For God, seeing is the same as being, 98. Whatever God sees, he does not see outside himself, because he fills all the things he sees, 97. God’s substance is as great as his vision, 98. In one sense God sees everything, and in another sense he does not see certain things, 97. By his power God sees all things; by grace, he is said to see what he himself bestows, ibid. It is impiously said that God’s knowledge depends on human wills and actions, 487. How certain ways are said to be unknown to God, 23. The true God is recognized as the one found to be the knower of hidden things, 231. In the eternity of his unchangeable will, the Creator is said already to have done what he arranged should be done suitably in mutable creation; thus, what he has rightly ordained, he brings about, 10. That one truth is naturally the one true Godhead, 201. God gives that with which he is always full, 164, 165.

**God’s mercy and justice.** God is always merciful and just, 449. Divine Scripture principally proclaims the Holy Trinity, one God, to be as merciful as he is just, 364. God’s justice is to be feared, 8, 365. God’s mercy and piety are proclaimed everywhere in Scripture, 17. Things that are neither good nor just are unworthy of the good and just God, 12. Things from which human beings are liberated by God are perversely attributed to God, 134. God is our skilled and good physician; therefore there is no illness he cannot heal, 191. God is to be feared and honored far more than a temporal king, 71. Whoever fears God little greatly despises him, ibid. God is light and truth, 15. No one can declare God adequately, nor may anyone remain ignorant of him without penalty, 53. Ignorance of God is slavery to demons, ibid. A human being cannot speak about God as is fitting, 552.

God’s foreknowledge is true and immutable, 441, 529. What God foreknows as future is immutably future, 442. In God there is foreknowledge only of things that will truly be future, not of things that will not be future, 441, 442. Nothing is thought more wrongly about God than to deny his immutable plan concerning future action, 487. How future things are said already to have been done with God, 482. Where he does not see certain things in order to bestow, he sees them in order to repay, 97. God foreknew all human sins, 23. Saint Augustine sufficiently and clearly showed that God saw, by foreknowledge, the human sins concerning which he pronounced the sentence of predestination, 23, 24. What things pertain to God’s predestination, 484.

Whatever does not pertain to the nature of the Lord God alone is not to be worshiped by us as God, 65. An angel or a holy human being is called “god” in such a way that he is in no respect called the God of angels or human beings, 250.

God’s power is no less than his will, 488. The Godhead alone possesses full power, 129. It is not improper to say that God does not will something which he could do; but it is impious if anyone says that the omnipotent God cannot do something he wills, 322. In God, to will is nothing other than to be able, 11. God can as much as he wills, ibid. Of God alone it is fittingly said that he has done all things whatsoever he willed, ibid. There is no weakness in God, 133. Power is naturally full where there can be no weakness from suffering, 129. In God the power of will is as great as the will of power, 11. The effect of God’s will is never lacking, because it is itself nothing other than power, ibid. Full power is rightly believed to be in the one for whom the ability to do as much as he wills and the will to do as much as he can are naturally joined, 129.

God’s will is not subject to mutability, because it has no beginning of existence, 10. His will cannot be new in a new work, 7. God always does inseparably whatever he wills, 384. Nothing opposing God prevents him from doing what he has promised either less fully or more slowly than he wills, 11. God’s will is always fulfilled, because his power is in no way overcome, 275. Just as God’s will cannot be changed in its determination, so his power cannot be prohibited or hindered in its operation, 384.

God’s will concerning the salvation of human beings, 488, 489, 490. God saves those whom he wills, 317. God’s will concerning the salvation of all is not equal, 317 and following. The Apostle’s statement, “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills,” is to be understood as the statement of one who confirms, 273. Those who think that God has an equal will concerning the redemption and condemnation of all have no answer when asked why all are not saved, 318. Who are all those whom God wills to be saved, 274. Who those “all” are is understood from the words of blessed Peter, 320. It is shown in another passage of Saint Paul, 321. Why they are called “all,” ibid. Scripture does not always understand “all” to mean the entire human race without exception, ibid.

“Those whom God wills to be saved” must be understood in such a way that we neither think anyone can be saved except by God’s will, nor that his will fails to be fulfilled or is hindered in any way, 319, 320. All the human beings whom God wills to be saved are called “all” because they are chosen from every group, 491. The word “all” denotes not each individual of every kind, but the kinds of individuals, 320. This is a familiar usage in sacred Scripture, ibid.

“Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” is not a question but the conclusion of the statement—why? 474. The argument of those who ask why God does not make everyone believe is answered: there is no partiality with him, and it is written that he wills all human beings to be saved, 282, 283. Christ did not will to save those to whom he revealed neither the Father nor himself, 488. Christ spoke to certain people in the Gospel in such a way that he willed his words to be heard but did not will them to be understood, ibid. God denies salvation to those to whom he denies recognition of himself, 489.

The devil is called prince of flies, not because he creates flies but because he reigns in the wicked, 430. Anyone who believes either that the devil was not created by Christ or that he will someday be restored to reconciliation with Christ is guilty of a single impiety, 322. The devil did not have the origin of sin from his creation, 172. Demons believe but do not love, 310. The devil’s endeavor is to drag human beings, even unwillingly, into fellowship in punishment, 363. Fornicators, idolaters, adulterers, and others openly serve the devil, 172. The devil’s spiritual snares are more hidden, ibid. The devil makes pride sprout up in works of mercy, 171.

**DIOSCORUS**, the heretic, is anathematized, 281.

Discerning good or evil spirits is counted among spiritual gifts, 463.

Who is the evangelical steward, 547.

**To divide.** To divide means that each person should know, according to the suitability of the time, what he ought to omit and what he ought to retain, 265.

**Riches.** Temporal goods may be possessed and despised well or badly, 155. The goods of this life do not make a person happier, ibid. Job was happier in poverty than in wealth, ibid. Lazarus was happier in poverty than the rich banqueter in his wealth, ibid. The rich man was poor amid his riches and hungry amid abundance, ibid. The rich man burns in unquenchable flames for no other reason than that, possessed of deadly iniquity, he never wished to give even crumbs from his banquet to poor Lazarus, who suffered continual hunger, 307.

Who are those who trust in power and glory in the abundance of riches, 188. Nature does not give human beings the ability to despise riches and not become proud of what they have despised; grace does, ibid. He despises his possessions in vain who keeps in his heart riches that are harmful because of boastfulness, [Col. 0990] 160. In those who despise riches, God considers not the amount of their means but the quality of their will, ibid. The desire to acquire riches is blameworthy in those who will leave children of the flesh behind, but much more blameworthy in those who will leave none behind, ibid. A son is cared for more by doing good than by gathering riches, 150. The Lord’s rebuke of the foolish rich man is greatly to be feared, 160. Christ’s prohibition against storing up riches applies to all the faithful, ibid. How much the rich ought to assist the poor, 576. Whoever lives holily in true faith is rich, 47.

A gift is not called a gift if it is not given freely, 13. How giving and repaying differ, 434. Some gifts of God will cease, others will endure, 154, 155.

**Doubt.** What disposition one ought to have in doubtful matters, 496.

# E

**SACRED DRUNKENNESS:** what it is, 264.

The Church is one, 374. The Church is one, yet several churches are named within it, 233. In the house of Rahab the harlot, the Catholic Church from the Gentiles was prefigured, 376. In Noah’s ark and in the house of Rahab the harlot, one and the same Church was prefigured, 375. The Catholic Church is not found named as such in the Scriptures, 63.

The Church is the bride of Christ, 166. It is the body of Christ, 641. The household over which the master appointed a servant is the Church, 547. In that virgin who was made from the rib of a man, the future Church was already then prefigured, 165. The Church is a virgin because she remains undefiled in Christ, 166. The Church is a mother because she is made fruitful by Christ, ibid. Isaiah foretold the name of the Church by which she is called both mother and virgin, ibid. The Church is called both virgin and man by the Apostle, ibid. Unless the Church were always a virgin, she could not be a mother, ibid. The Church’s virginity is not corrupted by fruitfulness, nor is her fruitfulness hindered by virginity, ibid. The dwelling of the young man with the virgin, mentioned by Isaiah, signifies the union of Christ and the Church, ibid.

The Church is called a dove because of charity and simplicity, 143. The Church alone possesses true charity, ibid. The Church alone possesses true simplicity, ibid. The Church’s growth is promised throughout all Scripture, 539. The value of the unity of ecclesiastical fellowship, 526. Outside the Lord’s ark, which is the Church, nothing can remain except chaff, 374. In the Catholic Church alone forgiveness of sins is given and received, 374. The merit of baptism does not save if fellowship in ecclesiastical faith and charity is absent, 375. Whoever preserved the unity of charity within the Church until death is saved by the sacrament of baptism, 375. Because of the unity of the Church’s communion, another person’s confession is beneficial, 223.

Christ granted the power of binding and loosing to the Church alone, saying, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth…” and so forth, 379. God granted the Catholic Church, in the person of blessed Peter, the power of binding and loosing, 517. Every person whom the Church does not loose is bound, 379. Outside the Church, the sacraments do not benefit people unto life but bring death, 377. In the Catholic Church alone charity covers a multitude of sins, 380. No one will receive a reward in the future unless he works in this life and within the Catholic Church, 402. Not all who are baptized within the Catholic Church will receive eternal life, 530. The name “Catholic” is not sufficient for salvation, 380.

In the gift of tongues granted to the first believers, it was signified that the Church would speak in all languages, 569. Whatever is given and received according to the Church’s constitutions is given and received with firm truth, 224. How the Church divides, 265. There are different ranks in the Church, and in each rank different merits, 338. Within the Catholic Church in the present age, the just and the wicked are held mingled by communion in the sacraments, not in morals, 374. Within the Church there are both wicked and just; outside the Church there is no just person, 374. The threshing floor of God is the Catholic Church, within which good and evil are mingled through sacramental communion until the end of the age, 530, 531. Jews, heretics, and schismatics, if they die outside the Church, will go into eternal fire, 530.

The Church is a city set upon a mountain, 45. The Catholic Church is the lawful mother of all the baptized, even of heretics, 378. Just as no one was saved outside Rahab’s house, so no heretic, schismatic, or pagan is saved outside the Church, 377. The Church can be attacked but cannot be conquered, 534. However much heretics strive with every force to shake the Church of God, they will not be able to overthrow it, 45. The Church is neither deceived by seduction nor overcome by violence because she is supported by the integrity of inward virginity, 166. All heresies have gone out from the Catholic Church like useless branches cut off from the vine, 534.

Why the elect are irreproachable, 457. Almsgiving benefits nothing those who therefore believe they may sin with impunity, 338. Riches are to be sent ahead to Christ, 160. What is spent on display should be withdrawn and expended on the needy, ibid. The giver must not consider himself superior to the one to whom he gives, ibid. If not everyone can fulfill what the Lord said, “Sell what you possess,” nevertheless what he added—“Give alms”—is possible for everyone and ought to be common to all, if good will is present, 549. Not everyone possesses the ability to sell his property in order to give alms, 548.

**ELISHA** asked for a double spirit compared with what had been in Elijah, 251. Elisha, making himself equal to the child’s body, raised him, 209.

What is demonstrated by the name **EMMANUEL**, 75.

**Epiphany** is interpreted as “manifestation,” 558. We have received from the Fathers the tradition that on the very day on which Epiphany is celebrated Christ was worshiped by the Magi, ibid. The day of the Magi’s worship is reverently called Epiphany by the mouths of all the faithful, ibid.

The office of a bishop, 477. A bishop ought not to dominate but to be an example of piety to all, ibid. In the Church no one is more important than a pontiff or bishop, ibid. A bishop is also God’s steward, 547. The Lord gave certain special commands to the stewards of the Church, 546. The office of holy preaching is specially enjoined upon the stewards of the Church, ibid. The stewards of the Church are those servants whom the Lord appointed over his household, ibid. Refuting heretics is part of episcopal service, 43.

The letters of blessed Leo, 281.

The error of the sheep must not be attributed to the body alone, 76.

**ISAIAH** was a preacher of Christ’s incarnation and passion, 135.

Esau and Jacob are figures of the Jewish people and the Gentile people, 271. Esau is a figure not only of those who deny the faith but also of those who persevere in evil works until the end of life, 272. Esau is a vessel of wrath, Jacob a vessel of mercy, ibid. In Esau and Jacob, gratuitous goodness and just severity are to be recognized, 271. Carnal circumcision did not benefit Esau; why, 439. What God hated in Esau, ibid. Though circumcised in the flesh, Esau was not taken out of the mass of perdition, ibid. After receiving the sacrament of circumcision, Esau was free from the guilt of original sin, but through the wickedness of his heart he remained in the oldness of the earthly person, 272.

“Essence” is called in Latin *essentia* and in Greek οὐσία (*ousia*), 503.

**Eucharist.** Why the Eucharist is made in bread, 227. Each person becomes a participant in the Lord’s body and blood even if he departs from this world before eating that bread and drinking the cup, 227.

Eutyches preached one nature in Christ, 236, 562. Eutyches the heretic is anathematized, 281. The madness of Eutyches, who refused to confess both natures in Christ as true, is refuted by the offering of the Magi, 562.

The harmonization of the Gospels concerning Mary Magdalene’s touching Christ’s body, 101 and following.

The examples of the powerful of this world have great force, 186, 187.

**Explorers.** What it means to place the “explorers” of Jesus among those above or below, 376, 377.

# F

**CRIME:** what it is, 425.

The management of a household, 150.

Fastidiosus attacked the Catholics under the name of the Homousians and the Donatists in a single discourse, 209. The passages adduced by Fastidiosus do not take away from the Son the unity of the Father’s substance, but demonstrate the incarnation, 347. Fastidiosus was a heretic from being a monk and presbyter, 340. He was led from bodily fornication into spiritual fornication, 358. Fulgentius mourns Fastidiosus’s fall, ibid. In the profane discourse he delivered, whatever Fastidiosus said against the Donatists he appropriated from the letters of Saint Fulgentius and of the other bishops exiled in Sardinia to Stephania, 349.

Weariness in resisting desires, 180.

Faustus, bishop of Gaul, advanced from the monastery of Lérins, 284. His writings against predestination, ibid. and 276. He joins grace to human labor, ibid. How he was refuted by Fulgentius, ibid. Fulgentius’s seven books against Faustus of Riez, ibid.

**FELIX**, bishop, 286.

**FERRANDUS**, deacon of the Church of Carthage, 216. Ferrandus read Augustine very frequently, 238.

What the Catholic faith is, 328. Faith excludes doubt, 151. Faith is right belief; everything not from it is sin, and without it it is impossible to please God, 402. There is one faith, which is true and not feigned, 218. It must not be called faith where it is not true, ibid. Faith is a virtue—not the kind found in demons, but the kind God gives to his saints whom he justifies from ungodliness, 310.

A human being can naturally believe, because God grants him the ability to believe, 311. The foundation of all things is to believe in the Lord of glory who was crucified, 282. Faith is given by God, 9, 282, 305. Christ liberates a person not by finding faith but by giving it, 305. Faith is not given to everyone, 455. Faith is not given equally to those to whom it is given, ibid. and 452. The fact that God does not make everyone believe belongs to his more hidden judgments, 317. Just as faith without works is dead, so everything that is not from faith is sin, 383. Faith is the life of the just, 197.

Faith is formed in us in the same way as Christ was formed in the virgin, [Col. 0992] 308. Christ is formed in us through faith, ibid. A person is sought so that he may seek, while he is illuminated so that he may believe, 311. Each person grows in faith to the extent that he learns what is true and conducive to salvation, 197. Whoever holds the beginning without doubt will advance in faith, ibid. The Catholic faith has never grown except through tribulations and persecutions, 536. Why the Apostles asked that their faith be increased in them, 452.

How necessary faith is, 500. How knowledge of God through faith differs from knowledge without faith, 314. Without the faith by which we believe in God, it is impossible to please God, 453. Faith in the one mediator alone frees from wrath, 527. There will be no true salvation where there is no true faith, 406. There is no good conscience where there is no unfeigned faith, 375. A good life is not truly so called if it is not joined to right faith, 383. Right belief of the heart alone does not free from eternal damnation one whom deadly fellowship with heretics condemns to the end of life, 363. Faith and merciful action are necessary in this life; they will not be necessary in the next, 155.

A believer’s mind must not grow sluggish in seeking if he sees something ambiguous in the sacrament of faith, 406. Conversion without faith is vain and null, 500. Without faith no one, from the beginning of the world to its end, could be absolved from the guilt of either original or actual sin, 529. The beginning of good will consists in faith, 451. Those who do not hold the truth of faith in heart and mouth do not receive salvation in baptism, 218. Purity of heart cannot exist where faith is absent, 21. The beginning of a holy life is from faith, 308. Right faith in this life is true salvation, 286. The Apostle calls feigned faith “faith” not according to the truth of the matter but according to opinion, 219. Good faith is insufficient without good works, 383. Faith is perfected through works, 309.

True faith does not fail to know what it believes, even though it cannot yet see what it hopes for and believes, 58. The saints now believe what they will someday see, 10. Those who believe in God with a pure heart will see God, 296. Paul had the same Spirit of faith as Moses and David, 47. Among Christians, it is almost the same to refuse to confess the faith as to deny it, 69. Faith and baptism are necessary for salvation, 528. Jesus is the author and perfecter of our faith, 309.

The Apostle’s declaration, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth…,” applies to every ecclesiastical preacher not only through a certain fellowship in faith but also in service, 70. At blessed Peter’s command to give an account of our faith and hope to everyone who asks, every exception based on rank or person completely ceases, ibid. A free response on behalf of the faith must not be branded as obstinacy or insult, ibid. Part of victory is that, as long as one cannot defend the truth in speech, one nevertheless avoids error with a faithful heart, 198.

A defect in assertion is recognized when someone tries to destroy another’s rule of faith in such a way that he is unwilling to state firmly what he himself believes, 57. No one denies the faith unwillingly; therefore all who deny it are without excuse, 354. Many things that were not formerly said are found inserted into the profession of faith according to the opportunities presented by times and circumstances, 63. How those who think differently in matters of faith are to be treated, 275.

**Figures.** Holy Church distinguishes figures from truth and shadows from the body, 266.

## THE SON OF GOD

That the Son is God equal to the Father, highest as the Father is, life as the Father is, and does the same things as the Father, 577 and following. The Son is equal to the Father because he was begotten from the immutable and eternal Father, 60. The Son is equal to the Father as radiance is to light, 98. The Father is light, and the Son is the radiance of the Father, ibid. The Son is called true God in such a way that the Father is not called a truer God, 202. The saying “I am who I am” applies to the Son, 118. The Son is from the Father, day from day, and one day, one God, 553. What it means for the Son of God to exist in the form of God, 287.

The Son is not less than the Father but equal to the Father, 202. “I and the Father are one” must be referred not to concord of will but to substantial unity, 62. The words “Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise” demonstrate the Son’s equality with the Father, 199. The Son is equal to the Father because of divinity and less than the Father because of humanity, 202. Right faith concerning the divinity of the Son of God, 112. Testimonies concerning the Son’s deity, 538, 539, 540. The Son of God testifies that the Father is in him and he in the Father, 49. The Son is with the Father not as a guest is with a host, but as a word is in the mind and a plan in the heart, 56.

In the form of the true God, he could be nothing other than true God, 203. The Son is to be honored equally with the Father because, begotten from the Father’s essence, he is one God with the Father, 59. The angels worship the Son of God in heaven, 65. Indeed, they are commanded to worship him placed in the form of a servant, ibid. The Son is the Son of the Father alone from eternity, 523. The Son is from the Father’s nature and coeternal with the Father, 602, 637. The Son does not imitate the Father or do similar things with him, but the same things, 599.

In the statement “one,” it is recognized that the Son is not other than what the Father is; in the statement “we are,” it is recognized that the Son himself is not the Father, 63. What personal properties the Son of God has and what he shares with the Father and the Spirit, 509. The Son or Spirit is not different from the Father because of the unity of essence, but is another because of the distinction of person, 503.

[Col. 0993] The Son does the same things as the Father not by imitation but through the natural unity of power and operation, 599. The equality of the Father and Son is demonstrated by this: whatever is derogatory or honorific is common to both alike, 60. When the Son is distinguished from the Father’s equality, the Father is disparaged more than the Son, ibid. Injury is done to the Father by those who assert that the Son is lesser, 64. Indeed, it is an insult to the divine nature if the Father, begetting the Son, could not be in the Son as great as he remains in himself, ibid. An insult to the Son of God redounds upon the Father, 45.

The words “I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them in the Lord their God” prove the Son’s divinity, 199. The Arians affirm that God the Father is Lord of all in such a way that they strive to subject the Son’s divinity to him as that of a lesser god, 199. The Son was born from the Father’s substance, not from his will, neither from nothing nor from anything else, 58.

He is God who swears by himself, saves his people, judges justly, to whom every knee is bent, and from whom each person receives the repayment of his deeds: this, however, is the Son, 67. Those oppose the Son of God who deny that the Father is in him and he in the Father through natural unity, 91. The Son’s generation did not show separation but excluded the error of confusion, 91. It has been granted to recognize the Son’s true birth, although it has not been granted to explain how he was born, 53.

Whenever the Son’s divine birth is demonstrated, the time of his birth is not stated; rather, “before” is always placed first, so that whatever a human being wishes to conceive of infinity and eternity, the Son’s birth may always be conceived as preceding everything conceived by thought, 55. We do not understand the Son as God in such a way that we separate the Father and the Holy Spirit from him, 67. The name “begotten” refers not to divinity in the Son but to birth in God, 113. Whoever does not know the Father in his entirety cannot know the Son in his entirety, 250.

The Son is coeternal with the Father, the Father’s power and hand, 91. Nor did his birth precede the Son, 608. In the beginning of the Gospel according to John, the Son’s eternity, immensity, and nature are shown where it says, “In the beginning,” and so forth, 92. The Son is another from the Father in person, not another in nature, 552. The eternity of the Father did not in any way precede the Son’s first birth, 203. What is said of the only-begotten God is also proclaimed of his divinity, 245. In the fact that God the Father made all things through the Word, it is shown that he himself begot this Word, not made him, 552.

The Son is piously called less than the Father if human nature is considered, but impiously if divine nature is meant, 347. The Son is immutable as the Father is, 118. To assign local movement to the divinity of the Son of God is not possible without loss of eternal salvation, 72. The Son of God is said to have died and risen because of the unity of the person of God and man, 138. The Son of God is everywhere always through power and divinity; according to grace he came into the world when he came to the aid of the perishing world, 105.

The Son, born essentially from the Father, was essentially conceived and born from the Virgin, 524. The Son became human without diminution of divinity, 509. The Son is said to have come into the world in that respect in which he is known to have assumed the form of a servant, 410. The Son did not assume the person of a human being but a nature, 412. The Son alone put on flesh, 416. The Son was born perfect man from his mother, just as he is perfect God from the Father, 524. The Son alone was incarnate and died for us, 414. In the Son of God both divinity and humanity are perfect, 15. The Son alone assumed the form of a servant for us and remained inseparable from the Father and the Spirit, 417. The Son of God alone assumed flesh, 414.

There was no prior place for the Son of God in which he might be born, 96. God made all things through the Son, 119, 524. He himself, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, also gave the law, 524. We were reconciled through the Son alone, but not to the Son alone, 510. The Son alone lived among human beings and was handed over, 415. The Son of God became human so that we might be sons of God, 293, 412. The Son of God had to become a participant in our nature, 413. Because the Son of God alone was born from the Father, he alone could be born from the Virgin, 413. The Son handed himself over and was handed over, 414. According to human nature, the Son of God was humbled and exalted, 412.

In Fulgentius’s time there were people who asserted that the divinity had suffered; their impiety was greater than that of the soldiers who pierced Christ’s side, 111, 112. The Son reveals the Father in such a way as to make him loved, 456. Both the Father raised the Son and the Son raised himself, 138. The Son alone is seen by the wicked according to the flesh; by the just, the whole Trinity will be seen and known according to divinity, 256.

**Sons of God.** Many are sons of God by grace; one is so by nature, 114. The distinction between being a son of God by grace and being the Son of God by nature is necessary, 50.

**Education of children.** Eli was rejected because he did not correct his sons with appropriate severity, 150. Children are to be raised in the discipline and correction of the Lord, ibid. Parents’ negligence toward their children is to be judged with the utmost severity, ibid. Children must not be permitted a luxurious or immodest life; rather, a rule of chaste living must be imposed upon them, ibid.

**SHAMEFUL DEED:** what it is, 425.

The weeping of the humble is the destruction of carnal desire, 179. One must weep in this life, ibid.

[Col. 0994] **Fountain.** Why the coming of the Holy Spirit is requested in the blessing of the font, 286.

**FORTUNATUS**, bishop, 269, 277.

Christ’s flight into Egypt, 560.

**FULGENTIUS** endured various occupations unwillingly, 3. Monimus demanded a reply from Fulgentius in frequent letters, ibid. Fulgentius’s humility and moderation in teaching, 5. Fulgentius’s love for those eager for the truth, 3. Fulgentius’s books *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, 275, 276. What the scarlet cord hung in Rahab’s window signifies, 377. Who possess the scarlet cord suspended from the window of their house, ibid.

The future cannot have a name that is not at some time judged by the designation of the present, 442.

## G

**Nobility of Gaul**, 160. The hen was created so that the weak human being might be restored, 430. The objections of the Gauls to St. Augustine’s work *On the Predestination of the Saints*, 26. Prosper’s response, ibid. The teaching of Pope Gelasius concerning the two natures of Christ, 243, 244. **To groan.** How the Holy Spirit is said to groan or petition, 584. Christ prays for us, but does not groan, 586. The generation of the Son of God is ineffable, though not unknowable, 53. We know the divine generation worthily when we both call it a true generation and proclaim it ineffable, 53. Generation properly belongs to the Father alone, 245. “Begotten” does not mean the same as “created,” 55. The sharp, two-edged sword proceeding from Jesus’ mouth is the Holy Spirit, 523. “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit” in hymns and psalms, 642. One glory is given to the Trinity, ibid. and following. In the Apocalypse, by the angels and elders, 645 and following. The glory of this life is the hope of future glory, 13. Glory is not to be sought in riches, 138. The glorification of the saints is the most perfect of gifts, 13. The perfect gift is to be given to all in glorification, ibid. To glorify is to make glorious, ibid. No one has true righteousness unless justified, nor true glory unless glorified, ibid. The repayment of glory is called mercy in Scripture, 9. The repayment of glory incomparably exceeds every merit of good will and action given by God, ibid. In the glorification of the saints God foresaw the works of his grace, 10. The gift of glory is from God, 13. Why glorification is the work of grace, 9. How God brings people to glory, 7. What grace is, 9. In Scripture it is called mercy, ibid. An example of grace in soul and flesh, 312. The prayer of St. Basil, bishop of Caesarea, in commendation of grace, 283. Grace is God’s freely given gift, 450. Grace is freely given to the unworthy in such a way that it itself produces both the beginning and the progress of good will, 287. The gift of grace is not like someone giving money after receiving a pledge, 273. We did not receive grace because we willed it; rather, grace was given to us while we did not yet will, 452. In treating grace, whoever desires to become a participant in eternal life should adhere to the opinions of the holy Fathers who have spoken about it, 472. What the Roman Church thinks about grace may be read in Augustine, 275. Grace is given freely only to the humble, 175. Just as grace is given only to the humble, so a person cannot be humble unless grace is given, ibid. Just as we ought humbly to praise God when he gives grace, so no one can justly accuse him when he withholds it, 446. The purpose of God’s will, by which he grants gratuitous mercy to the wretched or repays due justice to the unjust, is not unjust but hidden, 7. It must be held firmly that no capacity for good will or action can exist unless God has bestowed it through the gratuitous gift of his mercy, 161. We cannot possess from ourselves everything that we are able to possess, 312. No one would love Christ unless Christ’s grace had first come to him, 176. Before grace is chosen, it first chooses, 450. The necessity of prevenient grace, 307, 308. It does not await the beginning of the human will, 275. Scripture promises that the will is to be prepared and given, 7. It does not await the human will in order to make it good, 318. The example of Paul, ibid. This is proved from the psalm, “And I said, Now I have begun,” etc., ibid. Anyone to whom grace is not given must necessarily oppose him in word or deed, 270. Every work that is done by us in God is done by God in us, 8. The help of divine grace, even when already possessed, must humbly be sought without ceasing, 174. The reception and desire of grace are themselves the work of grace, 450. That manifestation by which they came to know God, although they did not love the God whom they knew, did not possess the grace by which God is known in such a way that he is loved, 457. All the wisdom of the human mind is powerless for understanding divine preaching unless God, who teaches outwardly through the speaking human being, illuminates and assists the hearer by teaching inwardly through himself, 456. The divine word sounds uselessly in outward ears unless God opens the hearing of the inner person by a spiritual gift, [Col. 0995] 323. The Gentiles who naturally do what belongs to the law are Christians assisted by grace, not unbelievers, 313, 317. No one can escape the devil’s snares by his own powers unless God has deemed him worthy to free him through his grace by Jesus Christ, 179. Just as we receive all good things only because God gives them, so we preserve all that we receive only because God guards it, 472. A person never guards his heart with appropriate vigilance unless that heart has itself been preserved by God’s guarding it, 471. Grace is in no way acknowledged unless it is given, 270. Good speech and good action come from the grace of God, ibid. Grace is acknowledged by those to whom it is given; by those to whom it is not given, it is unknown, ibid. The opinions of the Fathers concerning the beginning, progress, and completion of the grace that works in us, 472. That we should desire the help of grace is itself also the work of grace, 188. No human being, whether for thinking or for doing any good whatsoever, can be capable unless assisted by the gratuitous gift of divine help, 178. God is to be praised in both respects: when he rouses us from sleep to seek him, and when he grants us to find him while we seek him, 4. He is never found unless he himself awakens us to seek him, ibid. No one can ask for grace unless he wills to do so; but unless God works that very will in him, he cannot will it at all, 188. God alone can preserve in the recipient what he has given, 178. An example and assistance are necessary for the knowledge of God, 89. That he gives so that we may observe and do his judgments belongs to the effect of good action, 7, 8. The perseverance of creatures in the good and the increase of grace are the work of grace, 188. In the damned, the grace of the Savior did not erase the bond by which the malice of the deceiver had subjected them to himself, 449. When God’s assistance ceases, we cannot will or do anything good, 161. The course by which we run toward God cannot be attributed to our own powers; why, 189. Unless he who descended from heaven and gave himself to satisfy the hungry grants hunger, we cannot hunger for the heavenly bread, 4. No one is released from condemnation except by the grace of the Redeemer, 282. Concerning what was said, “I will cause you to do,” 12. It is impossible for anyone to receive grace without performing the works of grace, with grace itself working in him, 485. Those who knew God did not give thanks because they had not received grace, 457. Everything, even what we call our own, must be attributed to God, 12. Grace is poured out more abundantly when it is given to those who ask, 188. Grace is not given to everyone, 272. Nor is it given equally to all to whom it is given, ibid. The holy Fathers knew, and left in books and letters for knowledge, that God’s grace is not given generally to all human beings, 450. Grace is revealed to infants and hidden from the wise; it is not given to everyone, 456. It belongs to God to bestow grace upon undeserving human beings, to whom he wills and in whatever measure he wills, 459. Grace is not given to all, and to those to whom it is given, it is not given equally, 451, 452. The grace by which we are saved is not given on account of a preceding good merit, nor is it withheld except on account of a bad merit, 437. It is not the case that everyone is born by grace as by nature, 409. The wicked complain unjustly about grace justly withheld, 474, 475. Greater and more powerful grace is given to the saints than was given to Adam, 494. The grace in each person who receives it is as great as God pours into the heart of the recipient through gratuitous mercy, 450. The first human being had grace by which he could persevere in uprightness or depart from it if he wished, 492. Paul had in his mind the strength of grace and in his flesh the weakness of free choice, ibid. The grace that God freely gives to the vessels of mercy begins with the illumination of the heart, 450. The operation of grace, 498. The grace of God acts so as to make good people out of bad people, 455. The effects of prevenient and subsequent grace, 468, 469. In this life God, by freely justifying through mercy, goes before those whom in the next life he intends to glorify through justice, 516. First he begins a good will in a person, 7. He assists what has been begun so that it may be good and may overcome evil desire, ibid. Finally, he makes it so that the person cannot possess evil desire, ibid. The beginning of grace consists solely in the illumination of the heart, 454. Grace is wrongly placed after the will, 305. The grace of God precedes and follows free choice, 466. Grace precedes the ungodly person so that he may become just; it precedes the fallen so that he may rise; it follows the just lest he become ungodly; it follows the one who has been raised lest he fall, 9. God precedes not only with the love by which he loves, but also with the love that he freely pours in so that he may be loved, 176. The same grace works in the salvation of adults, who possess a will, the beginnings of good will that it works in infants without a will, producing the effect of salvation, 319. God does not await the good will of a human being, but himself grants it, 348. This is proved by the example of infants who are saved, ibid. Grace is given for no other reason than that it may first work good will in a human being, 450. Grace both precedes and follows the will, 451. Through gratuitous grace not only original and actual guilt are erased, but also the capacity for holy thought, lost in the first human being, is restored, 299. Grace does not find a person’s good will; it makes it, 450. Grace does not find good will but works it in a person, 320. That God gives a new heart so that we may walk in it belongs to the beginning of good will, 7. [Col. 0996] God works in us both to will and to do, 451. That grace is received by a human being is the work of grace itself, 450.
