It is by grace not only that the good life given to the justified exists, but also that eternal life given to the glorified exists, 8. The death of sin is its wage, but eternal life is grace—why, ibid. and 9. In the repayment of the eternal reward, God gives grace to the worthy, 7. The operation of grace is the same operation that both initiates the good merit of a person toward righteousness and brings it to completion toward glory, ibid. That the heavenly kingdom was prepared for the elect from the beginning of the world is the work of grace, 8. When grace precedes and when it follows, 468. How God’s grace has freed human beings from servitude, 467. It is the benefit of grace that the human mind should always consider itself anticipated and aided by divine power, 171. Calling, justification, and glorification are from the one God, 13. The wills both of infants and of rational human beings are converted solely by God’s mercy, 474. Why the repayment of glory is called grace, 9. The one whom the Lord has deemed worthy to guard cannot fall away, 161. The grace of the present life remains grace in the recompense of the age to come, 9. Why the Apostle calls eternal life the grace of God, 485. Through the grace of God it comes about that many human beings are called by one name, 233. The Virgin’s obedient will and the conception of the Savior are from grace, 308. The helps of grace must not be abused for idleness; rather, one must work for salvation, 469. Through concern for the salvation of a brother, grace is displayed and increased in us, 269. While grace or free choice is defended, the distinction must be preserved in such a way that the defense of one does not abolish the other, 459. How free choice and the command accord with the grace of God, 273, 274. The grace of God does not remove free choice but liberates it, 283. Both must rightly be held: that a human being is saved solely by God’s mercy, and yet cannot be saved unless he has labored, provided the proper order of divine mercy and human will is preserved, so that the former precedes and the latter follows, 273. How the Apostle joins both together: commands are given to a human being so that he may will and act, while God works both in the human being, ibid. God commands a human being to will, but also works willing; he commands him to act, but God works acting in him, ibid. Through grace human free choice is not removed but healed, 309. Concerning those who say, “It is mine to believe rightly, but it belongs to God’s grace to assist,” 305. Each person ought to attribute his labor to grace, not to himself, 470. No one should attribute to his own powers the effort of asking, seeking, and knocking, by which he finds while seeking, receives while asking, and so forth, 471. In Paul grace worked so that he was neither sluggish through failure nor ungrateful to grace itself through pride, ibid. That Paul labored was the work of grace working in him, 470. Thanks must always be given to God, 181. How we give thanks to the Father and the Son, and to the Father through the Son, 642. We find both practices in the sacred utterances, 642, 643. We must give thanks just as certainly as we have received grace, 643, 644. The delights of the appetite are fuel for lust, 171. Those who serve their appetite make their belly their god, 220.

## H

**The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit dwell in us**, 108, 109. This dwelling is not local, ibid. The Holy Spirit is the pledge of our inheritance, 35. Heretics ought not to be called believers, 221. Deprived of the light of truth, they think that they will overcome the truth by those propositions by which they themselves are overcome, 27. It is characteristic of heretics to be named after their founder, 535. Heretics are carnal and animal, 355. Therefore they are incapable of spiritual things, ibid. They are blinded by their own wickedness, 28. Among heretics there is no grace of the Holy Spirit, nor are their sacrifices pleasing to God while they remain such, 38. They worship a false god under the name of the true God, 221. The Arians [and other] heretics are to be lamented for this: they read the Scriptures but do not understand them, 352. Among heretics there is no truth but a pretended faith; therefore there is no love from a pure heart either, 218. Heretics are said to have gone out from us, yet not to have belonged to us, 329. They are not blessed in the seed of Abraham, ibid. They have become sons of the devil, not sons of God, ibid. They attempt to tear Christ’s seamless tunic, which is the Church, ibid. Those who pursue good works in heresy work outside the vineyard, 402. The various sects of heretics, 535.

**Jerome.** The translation of St. Jerome according to the Hebrew truth, 165.

**Murder.** Whoever loves iniquity is more a murderer than one who hates his brother, 389.

**The human being** is a rational mortal animal, 230. From himself he has unbelief, not faith, 452. No creature on earth more worthy of God than the human being can be found, 573. The human being was made in the image not of one divine person alone but of the whole Trinity, 604. A human father precedes a human son in time, because he too began to exist temporally, 246. In the human being there is a separation of nature without a separation of person, but not the reverse, 230. What the human being was like before sin, 435. [Col. 0997] The condition of the human being before the fall, 513. The condition of the human being after the fall, 314. The only-begotten God loved human nature so greatly that he not only freed it from the power of the evil angel but also placed it in himself, above all good angels, at the Father’s right hand, 554. What is meant by “The second man is from heaven, heavenly”? 121. Through the guilt of the first human being the devil began to rule over humanity; through the grace of the second human being he began to be overcome by humanity, 554. Why the human being rules over great four-footed animals but is disturbed by the most insignificant fleas, 421. The human being ought to seek in himself his accusation, defense, and judgment, 573. The old human being includes not only those who are ignorant of God, but also those of whom the Apostle says, “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him,” 273.

**Ὁμούσιον.** What the Greek term sounds like in Latin according to St. Fulgentius, 535. It is not found in the Scriptures, yet it is used against Sabellius, 63. It is said on account of those who tried to separate the only-begotten Son from the substance of the begetter, ibid. In this name we must consider not the sound of the word but its meaning; we must not attend to the novelty of the expression but understand the power of the sacrament, ibid. In this term some attend to the sound, ibid. The three hundred and eighteen Nicene Fathers established *Ὁμούσιον* in accordance with evangelical truth, 535. The Arians called the Catholics “Homousians,” 209, 340.

**The hour.** Christ’s hour was not the hour of a compelled death but of a voluntary passion, 263. In those hours in which the laborers were called, the ages of this world are understood, during which God called to good work those whom he converted to himself through gratuitous justification, 401. In this diversity of hours we may not improperly understand the ages of each human being, 194.

**Hormisdas**, Supreme Pontiff. His testimony concerning Augustine’s books, 274.

Humility and gentleness are possessed only when received from God, 465. God gives by grace that the recipient may become humble, 15. The increase of humility is the increase of grace, 189. In giving grace God does not find the humble but makes them, 15. The weeping of the humble is the great destruction of carnal desire, 179. Christ came to cast fire upon the earth so that he might burn up every shoot of pride, 177. A rational creature becomes humble through exaltation and exalted through humility, 15. Humility of heart causes us to attribute to God what his kindness gives us, and to attribute to ourselves those things in which our weakness provokes him, 177. The dead, whose life is hidden with Christ in God, are humble and poor in spirit in this age, 187. Those who love the world are not humble, nor are those who attribute to their own powers the fact that they despise it, 187, 188. While established in this body, we do not render perfect humility to God’s commands, 181. True, perfect, and exalted humility will then be in us when no evil desire remains either in our flesh or in our mind, 181. Following the Apostle’s example, a person ought to compare himself not with others but with himself, 174. Since the rational creature has nothing above itself, it cannot investigate itself wholly, so that, the more it marvels at the greatness of the supreme infinity, it might look back and advance toward knowledge of the Most High by the ascent of humility alone—from whom it once deserved to be separated by the fall of proud thought, 89. In the sight of the merciful and just Judge, proud boasting of good works is not accepted, but humble confession of sins is, 173. Hypocrites are proud in mind, 172. Hypocrites cunningly practice iniquity so that righteousness may deceptively be displayed to human eyes, 172.

## I

**Ignorance.** As ignorance of sin decreases, so the sinner’s guilt increases, 304. Sins are committed through ignorance, but are not forgiven without conversion of heart, 370. Paul’s ignorance when he sinned teaches that no one should flatter himself with ignorance while committing sins, 370.

**Illusions.** The soul is filled with illusions when it is shaken by frequent temptation from carnal desires, 179.

What the image of God in the human being is, 61 and following. Imitation is found only among things that are unlike or unequal, 599. The emperor is a vessel for glory if he lives in upright faith and subjects the height of royal dignity to holy religion, 477. No one in the world is higher than a Christian emperor, ibid.

What impiety is, 372. Every impious person is unjust, but not every unjust person is impious, 373.

**Incarnation.** How Christ’s incarnation was appropriate for restoring human salvation, 301. Human nature could in no way become sufficient and capable of taking away the sin of the world unless it passed into union with the Word of God, 291. The human being could not restore the human being, since he himself needed another’s help, 89. Nor could an angel restore the human being, whose nature was constrained by the instability of falling, ibid. The Virgin conceived and bore God the Word according to the flesh, 291. The Word was made flesh not only in the Virgin but also from the [Col. 0998] Virgin, 289. This is proved by scriptural testimony, ibid. Christ’s flesh was not conceived without divinity, 525. Neither a human being without God nor God without a human being was conceived, 292. He who had created for himself the mother from whom and in whom he would be created was created in and from the Virgin, 289. There was no interval between the beginning of the flesh’s conception and the advent of the majesty to be conceived, 290. From the Virgin’s flesh he received not the filth of sin but the complete truth of nature, 292. The Word did not take a previously conceived flesh, 289. Heretics believed that the indwelling of the Son of God was the incarnation, and that “inoperation” was the unity and composition, 279. The Blessed Virgin deserved to conceive and bear God not through human merits but through God’s favor, 292, 293. Because all human beings born from the intercourse of male and female have the beginning of their conception polluted by the contagion of original sin, Christ therefore graciously united human nature to himself precisely where the devil had been accustomed to claim it for his own party and dominion, 290. The Word took flesh in such a way that it became flesh, 291. Christ became what he made, ibid. God became human without any change in himself, 116, 118. When Christ was conceived temporally, he did not lose the state of his divinity any more than when he died, 291. Before the Word became flesh, he was not Christ, 295. Through his self-emptying, Christ is not to be believed to have lost or diminished the equality of his paternal divinity, 288. From a slave woman was born the servant who was generated from the Father as Lord, 55. Christ’s birth in the flesh is the cause of our spiritual birth, 293. Why Christ was born from the Virgin alone, 508. Mary gave birth in time to him whom the Father begot from eternity, ibid. Both births properly belong to the only-begotten God alone, 408. The true faith concerning the eternal and temporal birth of the Son, 504, 505. Both births are indicated at the beginning of the Creed, 634. It was not the whole Trinity that assumed flesh, but the person of the Son alone, because two natures remained in him, 350. Neither nature was confused, nor was either consumed by the other, 350, 351. Where the truth of the incarnation is shown, 347, 348. The Son alone put on flesh, 415. Not the Father, 408, 413, 415. The Trinity did not assume flesh, 409. The assumption of human nature is not common to the Son with the Father and the Holy Spirit, because the person is not common, 355. It was fitting that the Son alone should be born from the Virgin, ibid. Christ’s humanity was not assumed by the whole Trinity in the same way that it was made by the whole Trinity, 352, 633. It was not the Trinity, nor the Father or the Spirit, but the Son alone who was incarnate, 296. He also suffered, ibid. He rose and ascended into heaven, ibid. The Father alone begot the Son, but did not make him alone, 247, 347. Just as in the mind alone a thought receives bodily speech, so in the Trinity the Word alone received human nature, 354. Those who say that there is one incarnate nature do not escape the significance of two, 144. God the Word assumed the nature of a human being, not a person, 525. The whole Trinity could not assume flesh, 413. The Word assumed human nature, not a person, 291. The Son of God assumed flesh into the unity of his person, not into the unity of nature, 350. The self-emptying of the Son of God is the assumption of humanity, 115. There was one conception of the Word and the flesh—not so that both natures should become one, but so that from both there should be constituted the one person of Jesus Christ, which had always existed, 633. The same Christ, God and human being, underwent death in his humanity and destroyed death in his divinity, 97. Through the mystery of the incarnation, righteousness, life, salvation, and freedom were given to human beings, 406. When one incarnate nature of God the Word is spoken of, two united natures are signified, 278. After the incarnation there was no quaternity in the Trinity, 280. In the sacrament of the incarnation the lines of right understanding are found, 417. The authority of the canonical volumes together with the teaching and instruction of the Fathers’ sayings, for confirming the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, 287. Christ became human so that whatever he had created whole in the human being, he might restore wholly in himself after assuming it, 292. One and the same Son of God, born temporally and eternal, bounded by place and immeasurable, absent from heaven and leaving the earth, yet neither abandoning heaven nor leaving the earth, 107. Communion in the assumption of human passion or death is not therefore to be attributed to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because although the nature of the three is one, the person is not one, 245. Christ incarnate is a stone of stumbling, 72. The incarnation of the Son of God is an occasion of blindness and illumination, 73. Not believing or believing wrongly in the incarnation is the origin of many heresies, 72.

The punishment of infants who die without baptism, 302, 319. God is not cruel in condemning infants to whom he does not grant the benefit of baptism, just as he is not unjust toward adults to whom he does not give good will, 319. [Col. 0999]

What weakness is, 125. Weakness is spoken of in two ways, 324. Weakness is the punishment of sin, 125. The soul’s weakness is twofold, 324. Why Christ subjected himself to human weaknesses, 128. They were real in Christ but voluntary, 130, 131. Why the saints are not to be freed from human weaknesses before death, 493.

**Enemy.** The reward of those who love their enemies is to be sons of the heavenly Father, 565. Whoever lives badly and does not change his life before it ends is his own most destructive enemy, 389.

What iniquity is, 372, 564. Just as iniquity is not in God, so neither is it from God, 16. Iniquity is evil desire, ibid. It arises from disordered love of the world, ibid. God can punish iniquity but cannot make it, ibid. Iniquity alone separates from God, 343. Why the short life of the wicked will be followed by the eternity of torments, 404. The unjust do not perish in the way they wish, 16. What God will punish in the unjust, 21. Who should be called unjust, 373. The death of the wicked is twofold, 23.

The innocent became martyrs of Christ, 560. The innocents would have died in vain unless they were saved by Christ’s blood, 561. Herod raged against the innocents to good effect, 560. Christ permitted and ordered Herod’s fury for the glory of the innocents, ibid. An unmarried woman ought not to think carnal thoughts in her heart, ibid. The condition of the unmarried woman is better than that of the married woman, 154.

**Intellect.** The eye of the rational creature is the intellect, 610. For angels to look upon is to understand, ibid. What understanding is, 553.

**To invoke.** To invoke the name of the Lord is the same as to invoke in the name of the Lord, 29, 630. An invincible argument from Abraham’s sacrifice and faith, 29. The patriarchs and martyrs also invoked the Son, 639, 640.

In Scripture, wrath is used for condemnation, 11. Sometimes it is called destruction, ibid. The wrath of God exists only where human iniquity has preceded it—why, 21.

## J

**Jacob** is a figure of the seed of Abraham, 271. Jacob and Esau are figures of the elect and the reprobate, 404. In Jacob and Esau there were no merits of works that would cause one to be chosen and the other rejected, 458. Human works were not chosen in Jacob, but divine gifts, 271. In Jacob God is merciful; in Esau, just, 438. The grace of justification was prepared for Jacob before the ages, 439. Jacob was saved not by foreknowledge of future works but by God’s mercy, 435. Jacob was chosen according to the purpose of God who predestines, not according to the merit of a past or future work, 437.

**Januarius**, bishop, 269, 277, 286.

Voluntary fasting should relieve the hunger of those who fast, 160. Moderation must be applied to fasts so that neither fullness excites our body nor excessive hunger weakens it, 170. One must devote oneself to fasts and prayers, 160.

**Jesus** is interpreted as “savior,” 415. Jesus Christ is not the name of a human being alone, and is sometimes understood according to both natures, 634, 635. Jesus Christ is not the Son of the Trinity, although according to the flesh he is the work of the whole Trinity, 633. Jesus is the author and perfecter of our faith, 452.

**John**, presbyter and archimandrite, 269, 434. **John**, deacon and bearer of the Letter to the African bishops from Fulgentius and the others, 286. **John**, lector, 277, 285. **John**, monk, 277, 285, 478.

**Job** was blessed in riches, more blessed in poverty, 155.

**Joseph**, Mary’s husband, was not for intercourse and corruption of the flesh, but for the testimony and guardianship of sacred virginity and most chaste fecundity, 289.

Judas did penance for his sin, 192. The Jews believe neither in Christ’s divinity nor in Mary’s incorrupt fecundity, 73. Isaiah foretold that the Jews would hear of the incarnation with the ear but would not understand it, ibid. The Jews were the wall brought near, because they worshiped God, 558. Jews and Gentiles were far different from one another because they believed different things, ibid. Paul unquestionably indicates the Gentiles by the name of the foreskin and the Jews by the name of circumcision, ibid.

**Judge.** The office of a judge, 449. What judgment is, 573. What it means to execute judgment, ibid. The day of greatness is the day of the final judgment, 152. The future judgment is affirmed, 527. Why Paul, before calling God’s judgments incomprehensible, first mentioned the height of his wisdom and knowledge, 449. The common repayment of soul and flesh that will occur in judgment, 495, 496. What things are to be judged in us, 574. The time of judgment is deferred until the number of the saints is complete, 387.

**Judith** knew that Christ would be born in the flesh, whom Anna recognized after he had been born, 159. Although Judith and Anna lived at different times, they served the mystery of one faith, ibid.

The just sin, 424. How different are the sins of the just and of the wicked, 427. God does not depart from the fallen just person, because the just person does not consent to desire, 427. The just person is heaven, 186. In the just and unjust, three things must be considered: the beginning of the will, the progress of the work, and the end of the recompense, 12. The just are distinguished from the unjust not by bodily quality but by faith and life, 420. The affections of the just, 433. Through good conduct the just are also the temple of God, 386. Through good conduct the just present their bodies as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God, 386.

**Justification.** The cause of justification is God’s good will, not human merits, 20, 483. The grace of justification erases every evil merit in those who are justified, 9. The grace of justification belongs to the present life; the grace of glorification to the future, 10. God provides assistance to those who are justified and supplies growth through his gifts, 468. To do righteousness means not to do to another what you do not wish to be done to you, 574, 575. Righteousness from the law is from the human being; righteousness from faith is from God, 316. With the former righteousness Paul was ungodly and an enemy of God, ibid. The justice of God is such that he condemns those who turn away and saves those who turn back, 194. The person who does not subject his proud neck to God’s righteousness is deficient in his own injustice, 173.

**Tears** should be poured forth more from the heart than from the body, 80. The seeds of good works ought to be watered with a stream of tears, 179.

**Thief.** The faith of the thief crucified with Christ, 568.

**Praise.** The desire for human praise is to be feared in all good works, 161. God is praised in works if praise from human beings is not sought by those performing them, ibid. Let the hand work in such a way that the soul is not deprived of its reward through the intention of human praise, ibid. In pursuing good works and despising human praise, one must beware lest we wish to attribute the good we do not to God’s grace but to our own virtue, ibid. Paul avoided human praise, yet, when recalling his conversion, he joyfully remembers God glorified by the churches at the report of it, ibid. Reading ought always to be joined with good works, and good works with devotion to reading, 189. Through divine reading the inner, not the outer, person is nourished; and often, while the flesh fasts, the soul is more richly fed, 247.

**Leontius**, a monk, 277, 285.

The law of faith and the law of works, 315. The law of faith is the law that God writes in human hearts, not through the condition of nature but through the generosity of grace, 316. It is not on stone but in the heart, ibid. The law of works in the heart of the Gentiles and of unbelieving Jews does not justify, 315. The same law was in Paul’s heart when he was an unbeliever, 316. The law was given first so that human beings might recognize their weakness, 460. The law demonstrates sin, which grace alone heals, 454. The difference between the commanding letter and the life-giving Spirit is this: the law convicts, but grace converts the human will, 463. The law of sin also presses upon holy people in this life, 492. To serve the law of God is not to consent to carnal desire, 180. To serve the law of sin is to experience in oneself a perverse desire, ibid. In this life the faithful are partly subject to God and partly not subject, ibid. We are not yet wholly subject to God in this life, because from us arises what resists the divine command, ibid. From the law of sin that is in our members, no virtue of any strong person and no skill of the wise can liberate us; only the grace of the Savior can do so, 175.

**Book.** It is not necessary that what is understood in multiple ways be inserted in multiple ways in every writing, 40. It is useful for many books to be produced by many people in different styles, though not in different faith, even concerning the same questions, so that the matter itself may reach the greatest number—one way to some, another way to others, 41.

Freedom, true and false, 282. True freedom is obtained through Christ’s blood, 498. What freedom was lost through Adam’s sin, 497. The Jews thought themselves truly free, although they served human occupations with the most vain intention, 282. Christ freed those whom he found free from sin, 163. There is free choice in human beings, 460. After sin, free choice is indeed free, but not good, 307, 231. Free in a servile manner, 307. The sinner has free choice for evil, but for good only when liberated, 336. Free choice remains in human beings, though in the wicked it is not liberated, 231. In human beings there is free choice—not sound, but weakened, 459. Free choice exists in the good and in the ungodly: in the good it is rightly directed, in the wicked it is wholly turned away from God, 460. Free choice was sound before sin; now it is weak and supported by greater grace, 275. Before the generosity of grace there is free choice in human beings, but it is not good, 270. It is like an eye without light, ibid. The condition of free choice in the first parents, 527. It was created upright, 492. Adam possessed greater freedom before sin than we possess after sin, 493. The weakness of free choice acquired through Adam’s sin must always be kept in mind, 495. One must know and confess both the needy poverty of human choice and the unfailing generosity of divine grace, 270. Free choice without grace cannot perform anything good, 465. The beginning of liberation arises from a good will, and through the fruits of sanctification it attains its effect, 307. Free choice is in no way made capable of fulfilling the commandments unless it is helped by God, 273. The apostle and the prophet testify that free choice is insufficient for those things that are holy—not only to do them but even to think them, 462. To the extent that human choice is corrected, to that extent it is liberated, 492. We are not sufficient of ourselves—that is, from the free choice of the will, 463. Our free choice is made capable of loving God and neighbor insofar as divine charity is given to it, 465. The commandments of the apostles and prophets summon free choice so that we may serve God voluntarily, 462.

Desire is not a creature of God but the punishment of sin, 439. Desire is also found in lawful marriages, 43. Desire also defiles those lawfully conceived, 439.

The tongue signifies the confession of faith and the exhortation to holy charity, 413. How it can be said that everyone who has received the Holy Spirit speaks in all languages, 569.

**Speech.** The eternal generation of the Son is itself the Father’s eternal speech, 417.

What the burning lamps signify, 550. By commanding that our lamps be burning, Christ urges us to love and do good and to shine with the light of true faith, ibid.

**Lucifer.** A name for the star, 64.

**Loins.** What the Lord said—“Let your loins be girded and your lamps,” etc.—is to be understood spiritually, 549. What it means to have one’s loins girded, 550.

The healthy are helped by light, while the weak are restored by darkness, 424. Whoever does not possess the name “light” substantially cannot possess the designation “Deity” substantially, 60. The Father of lights is light, 61. “Light” and “splendor” are neither confused in name, nor separated in kind, nor different in quantity, 98.

## M

**Macedonians** said that the Holy Spirit was less than the Father and the Son, 205.

Why the Magi’s gifts were different, and what they signify, 640. The Magi are the firstfruits of the nations that would believe, 144, 640. The one and the same Christ is honored by these gifts so that he may be recognized as one and the same God and human being, 562. Through the three kinds of gifts offered by the Magi, the divine majesty, royal power, and human mortality of the one and the same Christ are indicated, 561. The Apostle calls Pharaoh’s magicians Jannes and Jambres, 428.

A person is properly called malevolent who harbors the will to harm, whether what he desires is good or evil, 184.

**Wicked.** God sometimes declares good things through the wicked, 534. In the Church, the good ought to be separated from the wicked only by the dissimilarity of their works, 531. On the day of judgment the good will also be separated bodily from the wicked, ibid. Which wicked people are to be tolerated in the Church for the sake of the good, ibid. The obstinate wicked will be punished because God is just, 371. The wicked are warned not to remain in slavery to sin, and why, 365. How God will destroy the wicked, 15. Their own iniquity destroys the wicked before God’s judgment does, 16. God is good even in abandoning the wicked, 21. God works through the wicked what pleases him, 22. Why, therefore, the wicked must be punished, ibid.

**Evil.** What evil properly is, 574. To possess and to receive the evils of the present life—in what they differ, 195. Every evil arises from a defect of voluntary thought, not from God’s action, 372. Since God is the author of good, he cannot be the author of evil, 17. Evil is not to be repaid with evil, 575. For a Christian it is not enough not to inflict evil unless he also learns not to return it, 574. God brings good out of an evil deed, 120. What evil must not be done to one’s neighbor, 574.

**Commandment.** In God’s commandments both milk and solid food are found, 546. Obedience to the commandments is enjoined generally upon all human beings, ibid.

The Manichaeans denied the reality of Christ’s flesh, 205, 206, 347. The Manichaeans introduce a God of light and a God of darkness, 423. The Manichaean error concerning the substance of the soul, 497. The Manichaeans call those natures evil by which the senses are offended, 425. They call those natures good by whose love they are pleased, 423. The Manichaeans trace the defect of human flesh to nature, not to human fault, 73. The error of the Manichaeans was extinguished in the Book of Wisdom before it was born, ibid. It is refuted from the Epistle of John, ibid. In the offering of myrrh the Manichaean is confounded, since he does not believe that Christ truly died for our salvation, 562. In the gold both the Arian and the Manichaean are confounded, ibid.

**Dwelling.** The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have a dwelling in a human being—not external but internal, 46.

The Son of God is the Father’s hand, 105.

**Mary**, Mother of God, 508. The mother of Christ alone was a virgin before conception and childbirth, and after childbirth, 436.

How Mary Magdalene is forbidden to touch Christ, 102, 103.

## [Col. 1002]

**Martyr.** In martyrs the Holy Spirit speaks, 571. In the steadfastness of martyrs God is to be praised, for he gave them strength, 570.

**Mediator.** In the Mediator neither any element of humanity should be lacking, nor should humanity be absorbed by divinity, 116. Unless he were the God-man, complete in each substance, he could not reconcile humanity to God, 82. God alone is the physician of the wounded, 78.

**Melchizedek.** Melchizedek is a figure of Christ as God and human being, and of his two births, 94. Yet Melchizedek was not without a beginning, which belongs to God alone, nor without father and mother, which belongs only to the first human being, 94.

What memory is, 553. The human mind is a mirror of the Trinity, 600, 601. The mind in a human being is the image of God, 352.

The measure of wheat is the measure of faith, 547. To give a measure of wheat is to discuss, having been enlightened by the gift of grace, according to the rule of true faith, 547. The faithful receive the measure of wheat from the Lord’s dispensers when each day they hear the word of truth through God’s servants, ibid.

The reward of God’s children is from grace, though it differs according to the diversity of their labors, 114.

**Merit.** All human merits are preceded by God, 283. Every good merit of any human being is from God, 165. God’s holy gift is always gratuitous, because no demand for human merits ever precedes it, 165. A person cannot have good merit unless it has been given by God, nor possess it perseveringly unless it is preserved by God himself, 165.

Who the prophet Micah was in relation to God, 572.

“Ministry” refers to human activity, whereas “supply” and “administration” pertain to divine grace, 583.

**Miseries.** The just and the wicked shun the miseries of life, but in different ways, 428. God’s mercy is to be loved and his justice feared, 365, 518. Prophetic speech does not cease to commend God’s mercy and justice, 367. A human being is saved by God’s mercy alone, 466. No one who adds sins to sins ought to flatter himself with divine mercy, 380. No one ought to remain in his iniquities on the mere hope of God’s mercy, and why, 517. Mercy must be practiced, 575. It is necessary for all Christians, especially married people, 146. Mercy is bestowed in two ways, 575. The first work of mercy is to offer oneself to God, 338. The order of mercy requires that the mercy a person is commanded to extend to another be first shown to oneself, ibid. What it means to love mercy, 575.

**Mission.** The term “mission” is used in more than one way, 626. Not every mission involves an appearance, 627. By the name “mission” we must understand an act of granted manifestation, 32. What the missions of the Son and the Holy Spirit are, 32, 499, 12, 624 and following. How the missions of the Holy Spirit differ from the mission of the Son, 334. Just as the Holy Spirit is read to have been sent by the Father and the Son, so the Son is found to have been sent by the Father and the Spirit, 32. The Father sends the Holy Spirit through the origin of majesty, not by the authority of a command, 62, 74. The mission of the Holy Spirit is the granting of an invisible gift, not a personal appearance, ibid.

Monks and poor clerics who live holy lives are to be preferred to wealthy laymen endowed with whatever dignity, 478.

**Monimus.** The first book addressed to Monimus is said by Fulgentius to concern the diversity of predestination, 27.

**Mountain.** The powerful of the world are called mountains, 187.

**Death.** The word “death” is used in two ways, 324. The twofold death that God justly repays in judgment, 6. By what death those are dead of whom it is said, “Let the dead bury their dead,” etc., and “She who lives in pleasure is dead,” etc., 23. The death of the spirit is abandonment by God; the death of the body is abandonment by the soul, 356. The death of the wicked is always premature, but not that of the good, 152, 153. The death of soul and body in the wicked will not itself die, 396. The second death is everlasting punishment, 395. The second death is the lake of sulfur and fire, 22. The second death is the punishment of the first, 23. The death with which the Apostle threatens those who live according to the flesh is eternal condemnation, 381. The death of the good is never bitter or premature, 153. Unless the death of the soul in sin had preceded it, the death of the body would never follow in punishment, 300. God does not desire the death by which a person dies in sins, 23. Through an evil will—that is, through sin—the soul dies, 49. Whatever kind of faith and work the end of this life finds in each human being, such will be the person’s recompense, and it will have no end, 404.

**Moses** was afflicted by God because of the people’s sin, 426.

Love of the world is not evil except insofar as it turns one away from love of God, 16. The world presses upon the saints but does not crush them, 551. By “world” are signified people who love the world, 16. The person who tramples upon the world truly triumphs, 186.

**Fly.** In flies the marvelous omnipotence of God appears, 432. Flies and worms sometimes even originate from human bodies themselves, 431.

## N

**Nativity.** How Christ’s temporal birth leads to knowledge of the eternal one, 95. The function of the second birth consists in faith and confession, while its effect consists in regeneration, 221. How being born from someone and being adopted by someone differ, 59. In Christ’s one person there is a twofold birth, 94. The temporal birth of the mother preceded the second birth of the Son of God, 203. The day of Christ’s birth is the day of visitation, 554. On the day of the Lord’s birth, the day of the resurrection was solemnly proclaimed, 554. A comparison of carnal birth with spiritual birth, 498.

**Nature.** Every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good, 222. All natures are good because they were made by God, 424. The two natures—soul and flesh—constitute one human nature and one person, 418. That the lowest animals harm human beings is an incompatibility among natures, not wickedness in the nature of animals, 421. God fittingly uses the incompatibilities of natures to punish human sins, ibid. The nature that polluted the world with sin in the first human being cleansed the world from sin in the second human being, 554.

**Nestorius.** A disciple of Theodore of Mopsuestia, 281. Peter the deacon and others anathematize his writings, ibid. Nestorius, asserting two persons in Christ, is confounded by the gifts of the Magi, which were offered to one and the same person, 562. A profession of the Catholic faith against the Nestorians: in Christ there are two inseparable natures and one person, 584.

The nobility of the spirit is to be pursued through perfect humility of heart, 160. Nobility of the flesh is fuel for pride and therefore must be rejected, ibid.

Marriage is good and instituted by God, 439, 530. Marital honor restrains desire, 146. Marriage is not sin but God’s work and gift, 168. Second and third marriages are permitted, 520. Second and third marriages too were instituted by God, 530. A married woman who belongs to the world is permitted to think about worldly matters, 153. It is damnable for those who have vowed continence to desire marriage, 530. Marriage and widowhood’s continence are gifts of God, but are far inferior to virginity, 67. To abstain from marriage is better than to marry, 530.

## O

**Hardening.** Who live in a hardened state, 518. They sin more obstinately against the Holy Spirit unto the end, ibid. God hardens not because he drives anyone toward iniquity, but when he does not rescue a person from iniquity, 273.

What is worthy to be offered to the Lord is shown by Micah, 573. Whoever wishes to offer something worthy should offer nothing but himself, ibid. In faith we ought to offer Christ what the Magi offered as gifts, 562. In the law, to offer or to be offered was fitting only for those who were perfect and whole, 80.

The Holy Spirit is signified by the name “oil,” 121. The richness of oil is the strength of spiritual grace, 264. The head anointed with oil is the mind strengthened by the gift of the Holy Spirit, ibid. The oil of gladness with which Christ was anointed is the Holy Spirit, 253.

“Omnipotence” is said of the power by which God made all things, 552.

**All.** In Scripture the word “all” does not always signify complete universality, 490, 491.

Good works are God’s gift, 286, 287. When Christ forbids us to perform our righteousness before human beings, etc., and commands that our light shine before human beings, he commands good works to be done in such a way that we wish not ourselves but God to be praised in our action, 161. The beginning of a good will, the effect of good action, and the gift of perseverance must be sought from God, 161. Good works are then done well and profitably when they proceed from a good will, 575. Works performed without faith and charity do not benefit salvation, 314, 315. Why, concerning works and faith, although they are ours, we are forbidden to claim anything for ourselves, 12. We ought to be praised for good works, not await human praise, 161. God is not to be regarded as the author of a good work in such a way that, once his assistance ceases, human nature by itself could wish or do any good whatsoever, 177. The barrenness of good works is to be punished with eternal punishment, 397. It is necessary for everyone that no one be sluggish or barren in good works and that no one despise the future for the sake of present pleasures, 549. The harvest of the good works he has sown will be enjoyed only by the one who has sown good works to the end, 391. A good work without humility does not please God, 165. How greatly to be feared is Christ’s saying, “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire,” 548. The wage of evil works is death, 352. They are not from God, 485. Through the fault of subsequent iniquity, all the good labor of the righteous person who came before is rendered fruitless, 391.

The laborers called at different hours signify the different ages at which sinners are called, 19. Who the laborers of the master of the household are, 10. From the parable of the Gospel laborers we understand that only the time of the present age has been granted for human conversion, 401.

**Optatus of Milevis** testifies that Paul performed an act of supererogation concerning virgins, 39.

Wealth is poverty, or poverty is wealthy, when the speech of the mouth cannot match the affection of the heart, 182.

## [Col. 1004]

**Prayer.** The disposition to pray is a gift of God, 177, 188, 466. No one can pray worthily or keep watch unless the Holy Spirit has poured himself into that person, 33. Not even the disposition to pray itself can be possessed unless it has been divinely granted, 188. Nor can perseverance in prayer, 177. The service of prayer must be ascribed to the one who brings about what is requested, 631. Prayer to God washes away the sins of the righteous, 427. Prayer asks for the remedy of health, 177. Humble prayer obtains divine assistance, ibid. Public prayers must not be loudly thrust forward but modestly commended to God, because God is the hearer of the heart, 105.

We ask that, by the same grace through which it came about that the Church became Christ’s body, all the members may also persevere in the unity of the body, 37. Spiritual edification is never sought more appropriately than when, by the very body of Christ—which is the Church—in the sacrament of the bread and cup, Christ’s body and blood themselves are offered, ibid. God should be asked to turn our eyes away so that they do not see vanity, to show us the way, and to direct our steps and the works of our hands, 161.

Every good work is prayer in the sight of God, 157. We return mutual charity when we pray for those by whom we are instructed, 164. The faithful are helped by the prayers of the faithful, ibid. Prayer is a debt owed and to be demanded from everyone, ibid. One service of prayer is owed to the holy Trinity, 630. Why prayer is concluded with “Through our Lord Jesus Christ,” 630, 631. This conclusion may be called an adjuration, but it is better understood as showing through whom the Father accomplishes what is requested, 630. Why prayers are directed to the Father and brought to completion through the Son and the Holy Spirit, 626. When we ask the Father, the whole Trinity is asked at once, because whatever is beneficial to us is granted by the whole Trinity through its inseparable power and goodness, 628. The Lord’s Prayer is directed to the person of the Father, 629. In the invocation of one person the whole Trinity is invoked, 629, 620, 631.

Daily prayer is sufficient for the forgiveness of minor offenses for those who have kept the white garment, 338. In prayers the unity of nature is maintained and the distinction of persons preserved, so that the impiety of Arius and Sabellius may be defeated, 632, 633. Christ prays for us and is prayed to by us—how both are true, 628. God does not allow a holy petition to be deprived of the result of discovery, since he kindles the person who seeks to inquire spiritually, 3.

**Order.** In the disordered sinner the reason of the divine order does not perish, 14. God does not abandon his order when he abandons an evil will, 277.

**Orontius**, bishop, 269, 277, 286.

The wandering sheep signifies human nature, 76. The parable of the wandering sheep carried back on the shepherd’s shoulders proves that Christ assumed human nature, ibid.

## P
**BREAD** and wine harm the sick but benefit the healthy, 422. Excess of bread and wine is harmful, ibid. The Paraclete is also the Father, 579, 580. *Paraclete* in Latin means advocate and consoler, 579.

**Wall.** Jews and Gentiles are the two walls that came together in the unity of faith into Christ, the cornerstone, 558. The Gentiles are the wall from afar because they served idols, 558.

**Little ones.** In little children reason lies sluggish, sunk in sleep, 440. Little children are born in the death of the soul, 6. They bear another’s iniquity, 370. Little children who are baptized are saved by God’s gratuitous goodness; but those who die without baptism are condemned on account of original sin, 272. What should be believed concerning little children who die without baptism, 441. What each person ought to believe concerning the question debated about little children, 435. Why God condemns one of two little children, both guilty of the same sin, and liberates the other, 448. The fact that little children depart without baptism is to be attributed not to foreknowledge of future works but to the depth of God’s counsels, 441, 442. Little children are not baptized on the merit of future works, 434. God prepares opportunities, supplies dispositions, assigns persons, and grants places for the little child whom he wills to reach baptism, 443, 444, 445. Little children are saved not by their own will but by the right belief of the faithful who confess on their behalf, 370. Little children ought to be absolved through the ministry of another’s confession, ibid. The pious concern of devout parents for their offspring, 445. How criminal is the negligence of Christian parents concerning the baptism of their children, 446. God brings about a holy concern for their children even in wicked parents, ibid. God’s judgment is profound and just when the pious concern of parents hastening to baptism sometimes does not benefit a little child, ibid. and 447. The negligence or care of parents or any other people, whether wicked or good, concerning the baptism of little children belongs to the hidden depth of God’s judgments, 443, 444. Little children who die without baptism will burn in everlasting fires, 449. God is not unjust in the death of little children who die without baptism, 319. Those who deny that human wills are preceded by God’s grace are nevertheless compelled to confess this, ibid.

**Passover.** *Pascha* is interpreted as “Passage,” 567. Christ ate the Passover by which he was signified as about to suffer, before he voluntarily suffered, 264. At the same supper Christ ate the Jewish Passover and instituted our Passover, ibid.

**Father.** The Father did not exist before the generation of the Son, because he generated without beginning, 607, 694. God the Father is the God of the Son according to his humanity, not according to his divinity, 589. God the Father is not the source of the Trinity but of the Son and the Holy Spirit, 651, 652. Thus the Father is in the Son just as the Son is in the Father, 91. The same person is both Father and Son in relation to different things, 52. The Father and the Son are neither two unbegotten beings nor two begotten beings, 59. The Father was not born according to the flesh, nor ought he to have been born, 504. The Father did not appear to Moses in his own substance but in an assumed creature, 118. The different names of the Father and the Son signify not different natures but distinct persons, 51. The Fathers called the Father and the Son of one substance, 65. The Father is begotten from no one; the Son from the Father, 606. The word “unbegotten” is not read of the Father in Scripture, 63.

A householder ought to preserve a balance of severity and clemency, 150.

**Fathers.** Concerning matters that are found set forth in different ways by the holy Fathers, whatever we set forth is so established as to accord with the truth, without denying assent to other statements of the Fathers that likewise accord with the truth, 41. In individual statements where we are uncertain because of some obscurity, we must adhere to the definitions of the holy Fathers, 450.

**Patience.** The fact that Christ, when cursed, did not curse in return pertains to patience of soul, 79.

**PAUL.** The more Paul was enlightened concerning the secret counsels of God, the more he was terrified, 317. Paul desired something contrary to himself and was not malicious, 184. Paul, when asking that the thorn be removed from him, wished the health of his body more for the benefit of preaching than for his own sake, 184. The love of Christ urged Paul, both when he asked that the thorn be removed from him and when, although desiring something else, he wished to remain in the flesh, ibid.

Paul of Samosata said that wisdom dwelt in Christ as we dwell in houses, 279. He was condemned by the Council of Antioch because he denied composition in Christ, ibid.

A sinner has no evil will except by departing from God, 14. If a sinner is not moved by the pleasure of the promise, he ought to be moved by fear of punishment, 368.

**Sin.** No human being is born without being bound by the chain of original sin, except Jesus Christ, who was born by a new manner of generation in order to break this chain of sin, 281. Original sin is proved by the death of infants, 301, 302. The transmission of original sin, 300, 301, 327. The punishments of original sin are the shortness of life, sin, and death, 301. The stain of original sin is in the conception of little children, not in the lawful intercourse of marriage, 438. Sin is transmitted to little children not by propagation but by lust, 507. There is one common participation in original sin for all, 449. Holy David, born from a lawful union, was not without the stain of original sin, 439. The obligation of original sin added everlasting torments, 515. One punishment of sin is simultaneously sin itself; another is punishment only for sin, 321, 325. Human conception cannot be without sin, because it is not without lust, 507. Through sin humanity lost the capacity for good thought and good will, 300. Not death alone but also sin passed from the first human being into the human race, 282, 301. Why neither nature’s capacity nor the law frees from original sin, but only faith in the Redeemer, 304, 305. The flesh of sin is human flesh, 302. How the likeness of the flesh of sin is to be understood in Christ, 351. Christ was made sin—that is, a sacrifice for sins, 301. The man Christ Jesus alone was born free from slavery to sin, 436. God will punish the wicked for both original and actual sin, 485. One who died without the grace of justification is not to be called rescued from future ungodliness; he is counted among the ungodly, 272. Sin is not from God’s predestination, 22. Why sin is called the sting of death, 301. A sinner ought to be angry with himself because he sins, not with God because he does not grant grace, 475. The unjust person destroys himself when he falls away from the highest good to the lowest, 16. By the pronouncement of God’s sentence, the punishment prepared for the sinner is to be understood, 24. Paul was first among all sinners, not in the course of time but in excess of iniquity, 370. Of whom it is said, “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises,” 190. The beginning of sin is nothing other than the rational creature’s disordered love of ordered things, 16. Every sin takes its beginning from the heart, 77. A person does not sin except by departing from God, 9. Both Scripture, human laws, and conscience distinguish crimes from lesser sins, 328. Some sins are grave and others light, 426. The sins of the saints are not like those of the wicked, 425 and following. The faults of the saints are called sins, not crimes, 427. The sins of the wicked are either sacrileges, shameful deeds, or crimes, 425. The sins of the wicked occur in three ways, ibid. Of those who sin lightly it is said, “The righteous falls seven times and rises again,” [Col. 1006] 427. Just as sin is not in God, so it is not from God, 6. Death and sin are not God’s work, ibid. Why sin must be punished by God, 16. Except for little children newly baptized, not even the saints can live here without sin, 530. Delight in sins is an accumulation of perdition, 396. To kill sins is not to obey sins, 574. The absurd consequences of the opinion of those who deny sin in infants, 302. In sins neither mercy nor justice is found, 27. God’s justice in the permission of sins, 11. God is the avenger of that of which he is not the author, 16. No human sins can be hidden from God, 381. No human being sins justly, 11. Evil cannot be repaid by God as punishment for sin, 18. The one who abandons God is justly abandoned by God, 11. The repayment of eternal punishment begins when the wicked person receives within himself the reward of his error that he deserved, 396. Certain conditions harmful to human beings exist because of guilt, 424. To save from sins means nothing other than to forgive sins, 4.

**Perfection.** The perfection common and undivided among the saints before Christ and after Christ, 13. In this life there is no perfect perfection, ibid. How Paul was both perfect and imperfect, ibid. It is a great blessedness to live in the present age in such a way that every faithful person devotes himself to spiritual progress, yet never arrogantly attributes it to his own powers, 178.

**Person.** The distinction of persons in divine matters, 116, 522. How it is known, 503. Apart from the name “person,” no name in God is used in the plural, 233. The Trinity is distinguished in persons, but its nature must not thereby be divided or separated, 355. Every name by which any person is called either applies to all three or shows that it refers to one of the persons, 232, 235. In proper terms there is no separation of nature but a certain personal recognition, 245. Because the three persons in God cannot be separated, they are not called three gods, three eternal beings, three omnipotent beings, or three immeasurable beings, but one God, and so forth; but because three persons among angels are separate, they cannot be called one angel but three angels, 232, 233. What personal property is and what it accomplishes, 247. The individual divine persons possess their own properties, appropriate to each, 587. The person of the Father is distinct from that of the Son within one nature, 113. In the persons there is one Father, another Son, and another Holy Spirit, 416. The three persons cannot be called three gods. Why, 198. In the three persons, without diversity of nature, personal property remains unconfused, 198. The substantial equality of the divine persons in one nature, ibid. God does not show partiality between persons when he causes those whom he wills to believe, 309, 310. A response to those who call God a respecter of persons because he does not cause everyone to believe, 310.

**PETER.** Peter left less for Christ than Zacchaeus spent; nevertheless, so that the rich might not derive any boastfulness from despised riches, Christ placed Peter before Zacchaeus, 160. Blessed Peter confessed Christ as the Son of God when Christ himself had called himself the Son of Man, 297. Peter’s response was praised by Christ’s mouth, 122. In Peter, a confession of love preceded the capacity to lay down his life for Christ, 130. Peter followed Christ along the straight path of love and suffered for Christ, ibid. Christ granted blessed Peter—that is, his Church—the power of binding and loosing on earth, 403. Christ gave the Church the power of binding and loosing in the person of blessed Peter, 374. Peter the deacon and others were sent to Rome concerning the matter of the faith, 277.

Pharaoh is an example of God’s power with respect to the wills of human beings endowed with reason, 474.

**PHOTINUS**, or **FONTIUS**, bishop, 269, 286. Photinus asserted that the Son of God did not exist before Mary, 74. The Photinians took divinity away from Christ, 206. Photinus’s error is refuted from the beginning of John’s Gospel, 74.

God’s rain is the word of holy preaching, 548.

**Repentance.** Repentance is a change of will in a human being, 305. Repentance is supremely necessary for those who have fallen after baptism, 528. Repentance is a gift of God, 305. No one can practice repentance in this life unless God has converted and enlightened that person, 528. Repentance is also necessary for the just in this life, 530. For every person living in this life, at whatever age, repentance is useful, 517. With God repentance is never too late, 193. Repentance is fruitful only in this life, 516. By killing himself, Judas took away from himself the time for conversion, 399. Judas sinned more seriously by repenting because he despaired of the forgiveness of sins, ibid. Judas lost salvation because he did not hope for pardon, 192. Repentance without a suitable time is sterile, 384. Why the Apostle mourns those who do not repent, 194. Scripture does this one thing: it warns the wicked, through fear of God’s justice, to bring evil deeds swiftly to an end, and the good to remain carefully and humbly in good works, 367. Repentance is useless if pardon is despaired of, 192. The impenitent are to be condemned; the penitent are to be saved, 381. In the future there will be repentance among the wicked, [Col. 1007] but it will be fruitless, 389. Who will have fruitless repentance on the day of judgment, 385. The hope of those who truly repent and turn with their whole heart will not be in vain, 386. The chief benefit of the call to repentance is the gratuitous forgiveness of sins, 362. What true repentance is, 5[.....]7. What the repentance of the damned is like, ibid. The repentance of the damned arises from the torment of punishment, not from the generosity of God, 398. The repentance of the damned increases punishments rather than remitting sins, 404. Repentance in the future will be such that it cannot earn pardon, 397.

**Commandment.** Every commandment given by God benefits the person who performs it willingly and humbly, 465. When we are commanded to will, it is shown what we ought to possess and from whom we ought to receive it, 461. God works in us what he commands, 434. For living well, knowledge of the commandment is never sufficient for anyone unless love guards the command, 464.

The possibility of believing as something present in human nature, 310 and following.

**Predestination.** What predestination is, 21, 481. Whoever denies the predestination of Christ and the saints attacks the apostolic faith, 274. If anyone refuses to acknowledge the truth of predestination until death, he does not belong to the number of the predestined, 323. One ought to pray for such people, ibid. Saint Augustine, in the book he wrote *On the Predestination of the Saints*, shows more clearly that God’s foreknowledge can exist without predestination, but predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge, 25. The recognition of predestination is established from Scripture, 7. God’s predestination is the preparation of his works that, in his eternal disposition, he foresaw himself going to perform either mercifully or justly, 27. God carries out a work no differently from how he has established it in his eternal and unchangeable will, 323. Predestination is the eternal preparation of future works, 16. Predestination is preparation both of grace and of glory, 519. What the faithful ought suitably to believe concerning God’s predestination, 19. Predestination is preparation for a gratuitous gift, 529. Foreknowledge extends more broadly than predestination, 19. God’s eternal and unchangeable disposition concerning things that occur mutably in time, 487. Just as the blessed Apostle preached predestination with confidence and truth, so he commanded us to preach it with confidence and truth, 486. Whoever denies predestination must first erase it from the apostolic writings, 486. Why predestination is usefully known and preached, 483. Blessed Paul did not wish to keep silent what he wished to be written, 486. Paul knew that God had predestined everything that he had foreseen himself mercifully and justly going to do in his saints, 486. It is useless to fear that the assertion of predestination introduces fate, genesis, or astrology, 487. By the term predestination no coercive necessity of the human will is expressed; rather, the eternal, merciful, and just disposition of a future divine work is proclaimed, 7. It is impious to attack the assertion of predestination, 486. The evangelical and apostolic commandments are not abolished by predestination, ibid. The Church sings of mercy and judgment to God, 7. Because of the promise of a longer life, Hezekiah did not neglect to take food; likewise the predestined do not neglect to pray and keep watch, 485. Calling, justification, and glorification are effects of divine predestination, 482. God by grace acts as he has always held in predestination, 7. The grace of predestination is given so that we may pray and keep watch, 485. What God does in the predestined and what in the reprobate, 11. The elect are predestined to glory, faith, and good merits, 481, 482. How badly it is said, “If there is predestination, prayer or action should be neglected,” 485, 486. The predestined are designated by the multitude of the stars, 484. In the predestined, the work of grace is begun by gratuitous mercy and completed by just recompense, ibid. God predestined to punishment those whom he foresaw would end this life in iniquity, 19. Why God always held in predestination the beginnings of our calling, the growth of justification, and the rewards of glorification, 10. God predestined to the grace of a good life and to the grace of eternal life, 484. In predestination God has already accomplished whatever he determined should be done at the appropriate time, 10. God foresaw all human works but predestined only the good, 19. The Trinity predestined the beginning of good will, 12. God did not choose us because we were going to be holy and blameless, but so that we might be holy and blameless, 483. Why God is said to have predestined us in love, ibid. In his unchangeable will he determined the future effect of the human being’s renewal, 7. When Paul says, “Those whom God justified, he also glorified,” he does not assign either matter to the present life, 10. Those who are disturbed by this question can easily be instructed by the testimonies of the divine books, by the books of Saint Augustine, and by the responses of Prosper, ibid. Just as the will by which we will what is good has been prepared by the Lord through predestination, so God also prepared good works for us to walk in, 8. Whom God predestined to the kingdom and whom to punishment, 19. Those whom he predestined to glory he predestined to righteousness, [Col. 1008] 11. The predestined are known by God from eternity, 483. God will grant perseverance in prayer and in performing what is good to those whom he predestined to life, 472. God determined what he would repay to both the good and the wicked, 482. God grants what he prepared from eternity, 12. The cause of divine predestination in the saints is the preparation of unmerited justification, 17. God prepared by an unchangeable disposition not only what he would give but also what he would repay, 472. When promising Abraham a multitude of children, God promised the predestined, 482. God confirms that he himself does what he grants the faithful to do, 12. God made and makes those whom he predestined conform to the image of his Son, 482. From the condemned mass no one is distinguished by foreknowledge of future works, 437. God’s will is the cause of election; election is not the cause of his will, 438. After the first human being’s sin, God predestined those whom he willed and left those whom he willed in the mass of perdition, 314, 315. The sole cause of the predestination of the elect is found in God’s merciful love, 17, 483. In the predestination of the saints everything must be ascribed to God’s goodness. Why, ibid. Why the human will is not the cause of predestination, 17. Predestination is eternal and unchangeable, 481, 483. The predestination of the saints is eternal, 483. None of the predestined can perish, 529. The certainty of predestination is indicated, 275. The number of the predestined is certain and unchangeable before God, 484. The firmness and firm eternity of predestination apply both to the disposition of works and to the number of persons, 483, 484. The certainty of predestination has God’s power and wisdom as its foundation, 482. All those are predestined of whose number God wills no one to perish, 384. All those are predestined whom God wills to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, 384. Why all the predestined are called “all,” and in what manner, 488. All those whom God wills to be saved are predestined, and why they are called “all,” 27. God prepared in the eunuch, Cornelius, and Paul everything by which they would be baptized, 443, 444. Whether God predestines the works of the wicked by which they are condemned just as he predestines the works of the saints by which they are saved, 12. Calling and justification are effects of predestination, 481. God did not predestine the wicked to iniquity. Why, 21. Why he predestined them to destruction, and in what manner, ibid. God could not have predestined the first human being to sin. Why, 18. Those whom he predestined to punishment he did not predestine to guilt, 11. His punishment would be unjust if God had predestined someone to sin, 18. Why no cause of evil can be found in predestination, 36. God did not predestine what he was not going to do, 11. Predestination to destruction is not predestination to doing evil but to deserved punishment, 5 and following. Why God did not predestine human beings to an evil will, 15. What predestination to punishment is, 21. Augustine’s statement on predestination to destruction—not to sin, but to punishment—is explained, 5 and following. Why predestination to punishment is just, 24. He could predestine some to glory and others to punishment, 11. Why, just as the good are predestined to good, the wicked are not predestined to evil, 18. There is no predestination to the destruction of the love of God and of salvation, 16. God foresaw those who would sin; he did not predestine them to sin, 19. If God predestined to evil, he would perform a work in which neither mercy nor justice could be found. Why, 17. Sin is not in God’s predestination, because it cannot be in his work, 7. If predestination made unjust people, God’s justice would not be just, 18. The predestination of evil works is not like that of good works, 19. God did not prepare evil works for the wicked, 440. God did not predestine them to commit sins but to undergo punishments, 485. There can be no reason by which God is believed to predestine anyone to sins, 17. Predestination is not to the sin that the reprobate unjustly commit, but to the torment that their own iniquity wickedly produces for them, 5 and 6. The predestined are not predestined to the evil they unjustly perform, but to the suffering they justly undergo, 7. Predestination is to the second death, not to the first, 22. Before Fulgentius’s time, certain Gauls began, on the basis of the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, to bring against Augustine the charge that, in asserting divine predestination, he said that sinners were predestined not only to judgment but also to sin, 25. From Saint Augustine it is readily understood that God predestines not to sin but to punishment, 23. It is impious and contrary to the Christian faith to establish the cause of iniquity in God’s predestination, 24, 25. Predestination to sin is rashly asserted, 18. Prediction concerning good and evil, 18. How “to predict” and “to promise” differ, 19, 20.

**Principle.** What is essentially eternal is truly a principle, 92. That is called the true principle which is preceded by no principle of existence, 418. Angels and human beings who are rulers are called “princes” in Scripture, 430. The religious princes of this world submitted themselves truly and laudably, under the pretext of the Christian religion, not only to bishops but also to monks who despised the world, 478.

**PROBA**, humble among titles of honor, 159. The foremost example of virginity in the city of Rome, ibid. She had vowed the virginity of heart and body to the Lord, 159. She used cheap food and clothing so that she would have more to distribute to the poor, ibid.

Why the term “procession” is not granted to creatures, 312, 613. The procession of the divine persons, 504.

A promise concerns good things only, ibid. Among the most honorable customs, whatever is promised by postponing is generally counted as a lie, 208. There is no falsehood in God’s promises, because for the omnipotent there is no difficulty in carrying them out, 20.

The prophets possessed the grace of Christ who was to come and who remains in them, 410.

**PROSPER**, a most learned man, 27. Those who are disturbed by the question of the difference between the predestination of the just and that of the wicked can be instructed by his responses, ibid. Prosper, a learned and holy man, rightly defended the sayings of blessed Augustine in faithful and copious discourse, 25. Fulgentius refers to passages from two responses of the holy Prosper to the Gauls, 25, 26.

**Providence.** Providence exercised over uncertain things is itself uncertain, 467.

# Q

**QUODVULTDEUS**, bishop, 269, 286.

# R

**RAHAB.** Rahab hid Jesus’ spies in the upper part of the house. Why, 376. In the two spies whom Rahab received are signified either the chaste knowledge of both Testaments or love of God and neighbor, 376. The scarlet cord hung in Rahab’s window prefigured the mystery of Christ’s blood, 377.

**Redemption.** The order of divine redemption, 460. The Redeemer ought to declare the assumption of humanity, while the redeemed human being ought to proclaim his divinity, 122.

**Religion.** True religion consists in the service of the one true God, 201. Kings reign with Christ when they believe in him, 560. The power of kings comes from God’s generosity, 71.

**Kingdom.** An earthly kingdom comes from God’s generosity, 143. Nothing will reign in the members except what preceded in the head, Christ, into heaven, 78.

The relational force of the personal term prevents the persons from being separated: although it does not name them together, it insinuates them together, 234. A relative name is one that we refer to in order to acknowledge another, 52. Relative names do not separate nature but signify one nature, 52. “Father” and “Son” are names of relation; “God” is the one name of substance, 53.

The greatness of the benefit of the forgiveness of sins, 362. Everyone—or nearly everyone—who is called by the Christian name in any way desires to find forgiveness of sins, 363. To obtain forgiveness means nothing other than to be freed from the condemnation of sin, 371. God’s justice and mercy are the foundation of the forgiveness of sins, 363. The devil causes people to imagine God’s mercy without justice or justice without mercy in order to take away the forgiveness of sins, 363. God alone can grant pardon, 78. Three things—faith, good works, and time—are so necessary for the forgiveness of sins that salvation cannot be obtained if any one of them is lacking, 363. Forgiveness of sins is granted only to those who persevere to the end, 392. When the Apostle Peter says that God patiently endures, not wishing anyone to perish but all to turn to repentance . . . we must understand “all” here as those to whom God grants repentance in such a way that he also grants perseverance, 385. The sin of betrayal could be forgiven Judas, but not the sin of his own killing, 399. The Son of God became incarnate for the forgiveness of sins, 9. Forgiveness of sins is given freely, 362. Forgiveness of sins occurs only in this life, 363, 387, 403, 404. In the future life, sins that have not been forgiven in this life will be demanded, 403. God’s severity condemns in the future those whom God’s goodness does not free from the dominion of sin in the present age, 365. When Christ says that a word against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven in the future, he does not imply that there are sins to be forgiven in the future age that were not forgiven in this age; rather, he shows that only those sins will be forgiven in the future age that were forgiven in this age to each person within the one true Catholic Church, 379. No one who lives wickedly and has not been converted in this age ought to promise himself any hope of forgiveness, 386. The cleansing of sins, recognition of the truth, and love of God and neighbor begin in this life and will be completed in the next, 155. Scripture would not command us to pray for sins if there were any sins that would not be forgiven those who pray, 197. Whoever does not believe that all sins can be forgiven within the Catholic Church denies forgiveness of sins to himself if, persisting in the same impenitent hardness of heart, he departs from this world alienated from the Church’s fellowship, 378. Forgiveness is promised not only to those who sin before baptism but also to those who sin after baptism, 191. When Christ says, “Seek and you will find,” and so forth, he shows that forgiveness of sins committed after baptism can be found, ibid. When John says that if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, this must be understood of those who sin after baptism, ibid. The effect of the forgiveness of sins must frequently be investigated, 361. Through the forgiveness of sins, a distinction is made between the wicked and the good, 362. At times the devil takes away hope from a repentant person, or removes repentance from one who hopes for it, 192.

The reprobate are without excuse, 457. None of the reprobate can be saved, 529.

The necessity of answering imposes the duty of a free response, 70. Suspicion of pride must be avoided in the duty of a free response, ibid.

**Resurrection of bodies**, 515. The resurrection of the dead will be of each person in his or her own sex, 339. The male or female sex will remain in the resurrection as it was in creation, 516. In the resurrection the just will be changed, but not the wicked, 516. There will be different degrees of glory in the bodies of those who rise, 338, 339. That someone receives the crown of labors is the work of subsequent grace, 472. What the recompense of the just and the wicked will be in the resurrection, 527. The flesh and soul of the just will be changed, but will remain the same, 395. The just will be equal to the angels in recompense, 125. The day of Christ’s resurrection is the day of redemption, 554. The first resurrection consists in the conversion of the heart, 395. Why the body is said to become spiritual in the resurrection, 528. Why Paul leaves no ambiguity concerning those who will be changed in the resurrection, 393. Why Paul, when saying, “We shall all rise,” added, “but we shall not all be changed,” ibid. Flesh will rise together with the soul, 495. In this life resurrection occurs when there is a conversion from evil to good, 395.

The Roman Church is the summit of the world, 298. It has been enlightened by the words of Peter and Paul and adorned by their bodies, ibid.

By the name “wheel,” the world is sometimes signified, 581. Why the path of a wheel is called an orbit, that is, the path of the world, ibid. What is meant by “the voice of your thunder in the wheel,” ibid.

# S
## S

**Sabellius** introduced unity of person because of the unity of nature in the three persons, 74, 287, 408. He impiously proclaimed that the Trinity had assumed flesh, 408. Sabellius confused the Father and the Son, not by communion of substance but by personal singularity, 63. The heresies of Sabellius and Arius are refuted from the Scriptures, 331. The Sabellians, who were likewise Patripassians, believed that the whole Trinity had become incarnate and had been crucified, 350. They were compelled to this because they said that the Trinity was one person, ibid. Why the followers of Sabellius are called Patripassians, 408. The Sabellians acknowledged one person in God, 205. The Sabellians rightly believe concerning the nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but not likewise concerning the persons, 205. The impiety of the Sabellian and Arian heresies, 408.

**Priest and victim:** the names and functions of human nature, 136. The true person of a priest cannot be found where there is not true humanity, 586.

**Sacraments** are so called because in them one thing is seen and another understood, 227. In the New Testament there is not a division of sacraments but of gifts, 66. From the side of Christ hanging on the cross flowed the sacrament of the font and the chalice, 299.

**Sacrifice.** Monimus’s second question concerning the sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood, 27. The question of sacrifice is determined from the faith of the patriarchs, ibid. The sacrifices of the patriarchs correspond to ours because they were offered to the whole Trinity, 30. Sacrifice is offered to the whole Trinity, 638. The Arians suppose that sacrifice is offered to the Father alone, 27. The striking question of the heretics, ibid. The sacrifices of the ancient law were offered to the Holy Trinity, 510. The sacrifices of the ancient law prefigured the sacrifice by which Christ offered himself to the Father, ibid. Sacrifice is offered to the whole Trinity even when the name of the Father alone is expressed, 510. God takes pleasure in sacrifices belonging to the Church alone, 38. The prophet’s testimony concerning the sacrifice now performed in the Church, 31. Throughout the whole world the holy Church continually offers to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit the sacrifice of bread and wine, 525. In the sacrifice of Christ’s body we begin with thanksgiving, so that we may show Christ to be given to us in truth, not merely to be about to be given, 265. What should be requested at the time of sacrifice, 618, 619. Why the coming of the Holy Spirit is requested at the time of sacrifice, 617, 168.
